en: The Saṃyukta Āgama, Scroll One.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra during the Song Dynasty.
1 (1) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At the Jeta Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should contemplate that form is impermanent."
One who observes in this manner is observing correctly.
One who observes correctly gives rise to weary detachment;
one who is weary and detached exhausts delight and craving.
The exhaustion of delight and greed is called the liberation of the mind.
To contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness as impermanent in this way is right contemplation.
One who possesses right contemplation gives rise to disenchantment;
one who is disenchanted brings an end to delight and greed;
when delight and greed are exhausted, it is said that the mind is liberated.
"In this way, bhikkhus, one whose mind is liberated, if they wish to realize it for themselves, can realize:
'Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence.'"
"Just as one contemplates impermanence, so too should one contemplate suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
2. (ii) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should correctly contemplate form and know form as it truly is:
impermanent. Why is this so? O Bhikṣus!
When one correctly contemplates form and observes form as impermanent, knowing it as it truly is, craving and lust for form are abandoned;
when craving and lust are abandoned, this is called liberation of the mind.
"In the same way, one should correctly contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, observing consciousness as impermanent and knowing it as it truly is. Why is this?
By correctly contemplating consciousness and observing consciousness as impermanent, desire and greed for consciousness are abandoned."
When sensual desire is abandoned, it is said that the mind is liberated.
One whose mind is thus liberated, if they wish to realize this for themselves, is able to realize:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence."
"Thus one should correctly contemplate impermanence; suffering, emptiness, and non-self are likewise.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
3. (Three) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one does not know, does not understand, does not abandon, and does not become free from desire for form, then one cannot bring an end to suffering.

Likewise, if one does not know, does not understand, does not abandon, and does not become free from desire for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, then one cannot bring an end to suffering."
“Monks! If one knows form, understands it, abandons it, and becomes free from desire for it, then one can sever suffering.
Likewise, if one knows feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, understands them, abandons them, and becomes free from desire for them, then one is able to sever suffering.”
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
4 (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If one does not know form, is not clear about it, does not sever it, is not free from desire for it, and the mind is not liberated from it, then one cannot transcend the terrors of birth, old age, sickness, and death."

In the same way, if one does not know, does not understand, does not abandon, and does not become free from sensual desire for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and if the mind is not liberated, then one cannot transcend the terrors of birth, aging, sickness, and death.
“Monks! If one knows, understands, abandons, and becomes dispassionate toward form, then one can transcend the fear of birth, old age, sickness, and death.”
"O bhikṣus!
Those who have knowledge, clarity, and liberation of mind through the fading away of desire and lust, are able to transcend the fears of birth, old age, sickness, and death."

In the same way, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—if one knows them, understands them, abandons them, becomes free from desire and greed for them, and attains liberation of mind—then one can transcend the fears of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
5 (V) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Those who delight in and take pleasure in form delight in suffering;
those who delight in and take pleasure in suffering do not attain liberation from suffering, lack clarity, and are not free from desire."

In this way, one who feels craving and delight for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness craves and delights in suffering; and one who craves and delights in suffering cannot attain liberation from suffering.
“Monks! One who does not find delight in form does not take pleasure in suffering;
one who does not take pleasure in suffering attains liberation from suffering.”
In this way, one who does not delight in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness does not delight in suffering;
one who does not delight in suffering attains liberation from suffering.

“Monks! If one does not know form, is not clarified regarding it, has not abandoned desire and lust for it, and the mind is not liberated—when the mind of lust is not liberated, one cannot sever suffering.

Likewise, if one does not know feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; is not clarified regarding them; has not abandoned desire and lust for them; and the mind is not liberated, one cannot sever suffering.”
"If one knows form, understands it, and becomes free from desire and lust for it, so that the mind attains liberation, then one can sever suffering.

Likewise, if one knows feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, understands them, and becomes free from desire and lust for them, so that the mind attains liberation, then one can sever suffering."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(6) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If one does not know form, is not clear about it, has not abandoned desire and greed for it, and the mind is not liberated from it, then one cannot transcend the fear of birth, old age, sickness, and death.

It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness: if one does not know them, is not clear about them, has not abandoned desire and greed for them, and the mind is not liberated from them, then one cannot transcend the fear of birth, old age, sickness, and death."

“Monks! If, regarding form, one knows it, understands it, becomes free from desire and greed for it, and the mind is liberated, then one is able to transcend the fear of birth, aging, sickness, and death.

Likewise, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, if one knows them, understands them, becomes free from desire and greed for them, and the mind is liberated, then one is able to transcend the fear of birth, aging, sickness, and death.”
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Those who love and delight in form love and delight in suffering;
those who love and delight in suffering shall not attain liberation from suffering."

In this way, one who feels craving and delight for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness craves and delights in suffering; and one who craves and delights in suffering cannot be liberated from suffering.
“Monks! One who does not delight in form does not delight in suffering;
one who does not delight in suffering attains liberation from suffering.”
In this way, when one does not find delight in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, one does not take pleasure in suffering;
when one does not take pleasure in suffering, one attains liberation from suffering.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Impermanence and suffering, emptiness, Non-self, right reflection, ignorance,
and the four kinds [of craving], As well as delight and pleasure in form.
8. (Eight) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Past and future form are impermanent; how much more so present form!

Noble disciple, one who contemplates in this way does not look back to past form, does not desire future form, and regarding present form, becomes weary of it, becomes detached from it, and is rightly directed toward its cessation.”
In this way, past, future, and present feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent; how much more so is present consciousness!

Noble disciple, one who contemplates in this manner does not look back to past consciousness, does not delight in future consciousness, and regarding present consciousness, becomes weary of it, detaches from desire for it, and proceeds rightly toward its cessation.
"As it is with impermanence, so it is with suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Form is impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering; that which is suffering is not-self; and that which is not-self is also not mine.
To observe in this way is called true and correct contemplation.”

In this way, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering; that which is suffering is not-self; and that which is not-self is also not mine.
One who contemplates in this way is said to practice true contemplation.
"Noble disciple!

One who contemplates in this way becomes weary of form; one becomes weary of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Through weariness, one does not delight in them; through lack of delight, one attains liberation."
In one who is liberated, true knowledge arises:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 10 (10) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Form is impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering; that which is suffering is not-self; and that which is not-self is not mine."
One who contemplates in this manner is said to practice the contemplation of reality.

In this way, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering; that which is suffering is not-self; and that which is not-self is not "mine."
One who contemplates in this way is said to practice the contemplation of reality.
"Noble disciple!
One who contemplates in this way is liberated from form, and liberated from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
"I declare that these individuals are liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
11 (11) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Form is impermanent; whatever causes or conditions give rise to form, they too are impermanent.
How could form, which is produced by impermanent causes and impermanent conditions, be permanent?”
In this way, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent. Whatever causes or conditions give rise to these various forms of consciousness, they too are impermanent.
How could the various forms of consciousness produced by impermanent causes and impermanent conditions be permanent?
Thus it is, monks! Form is impermanent;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.
That which is impermanent is suffering; that which is suffering is not-self; and that which is not-self is not mine.
“Noble disciple!
One who contemplates in this way becomes weary of form; one becomes weary of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Being weary, one does not delight in them; not delighting, one is liberated; being liberated, one possesses the knowledge and vision of liberation:”
"My births have been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had spoken, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
12 (12). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Form is impermanent; whatever causes or conditions give rise to forms, they too are impermanent.
How could the various forms produced by impermanent causes and impermanent conditions be permanent?"
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent; those causes and conditions that give rise to consciousness are also impermanent.
Thus, the various forms of consciousness are produced by impermanent causes and impermanent conditions.
"How can there be permanence?
'In this way, bhikṣu, form is impermanent;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent. That which is impermanent is suffering; that which is suffering is not-self; that which is not-self is not mine.'"
One who contemplates in this way is said to practice the contemplation of reality.
Noble disciple!
One who contemplates in this way is liberated from form, and liberated from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"I declare that these individuals are liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
13 (13) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“If sentient beings did not relish form, they would not be stained by form;
because sentient beings relish form, they become attached to it.
Likewise, if sentient beings did not relish feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, those sentient beings would not be stained by consciousness.”
Because sentient beings experience feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as objects of attachment, those sentient beings become defiled by and attached to consciousness.

“Monks, if form were not a source of affliction for sentient beings, those sentient beings would not feel weary of form; because form is a source of affliction for sentient beings, those sentient beings feel weary of form.”
If feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness were not a source of affliction for sentient beings, those beings would not feel weary of consciousness;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are a source of affliction for sentient beings, those beings consequently feel weary of consciousness.
“Monks! If form were not subject to transcendence for sentient beings, those sentient beings would not be able to transcend form;
because form is subject to transcendence for sentient beings, those sentient beings transcend form.”
In this way, if feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness did not bring about liberation for sentient beings, those sentient beings would not be liberated from consciousness.
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do bring about liberation for sentient beings, those sentient beings are liberated from consciousness.

“Monks! If I had not, regarding these five aggregates of clinging, known as they truly are their gratification as gratification, their danger as danger, and the escape from them as escape, I would not have been liberated, emerged, or detached from the assembly of devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gods, and humans; I would have remained forever in perversion, and I could not have personally realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

“Monks! Because I have known these five aggregates of clinging as they truly are—knowing their gratification as gratification, their danger as danger, and the escape from them as escape—I have, among the assembly of devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gods, and humans, realized for myself liberation, attainment, release, and deliverance from the fetters; I dwell forever free from perversion, and I have also personally realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
14 (14) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, I sought and practiced for the flavor of form; when I awakened to the flavor of form in accordance with reality, I then saw the flavor of form as it truly is through wisdom."

In this way, there is seeking and striving for the gratification in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; if one is awakened to the gratification in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness in accordance with reality, then one sees the gratification in consciousness as it truly is through wisdom.

“Monks! Regarding the peril of form, I have practiced the pursuit of its understanding; if one understands the peril of form in accordance with reality, then one sees the peril of form as it truly is with wisdom.

Likewise, regarding the peril of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, I have practiced the pursuit of their understanding; if one understands the peril of consciousness in accordance with reality, then one sees the peril of consciousness as it truly is with wisdom.”

“Monks! Regarding form, I have practiced seeking freedom from it and cultivated the path toward it; if one understands freedom from form in accordance with reality, then one sees freedom from form with wisdom as it truly is.

Likewise, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, I have practiced seeking freedom from them and cultivated the path toward them; if one understands freedom from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness in accordance with reality, then one sees freedom from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness with wisdom as they truly are.”

“O bhikṣus! If I had not known, as they truly are, the gratification in the five aggregates of clinging as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape, I would not have been liberated, separated, or emerged from the assembly of devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gods, and humans; I would have remained forever in perversion, unable to realize for myself unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

“Monks! Because I have, through direct knowledge, understood the gratification as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape regarding these five aggregates of clinging, I—among the assembly of devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, among this generation of devas and humans—having been liberated, having escaped, and having emerged, never again dwell in perversion; I was able to realize for myself unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The fourfold discourse on the past, The two kinds of discourse on disenchantment and liberation,
And likewise the two kinds regarding the gratification of causes and conditions.
15 (Fifteen) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
Now please briefly explain the essential points of the Dharma for me; having heard the Dharma, I shall dwell alone in a quiet place and practice with diligence.”
Having cultivated heedfulness, one should further reflect:

"The reason a son of good family goes forth, shaving off hair and beard, donning the dharma robes, and with faith leaving the home life for the homeless, is for the sake of the ultimate, unsurpassed holy life, realizing it in this very life:
'Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence.'"
At that time, the World-Honored One said to those bhikṣus:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"It would be well for the bhikṣu to speak these words, saying:

'Please teach me the essentials of the Dharma in brief; having heard the Dharma, I shall dwell alone in a quiet place, practicing with diligence, until I know for myself that there will be no further existence.'"
“Is it spoken thus?
The bhikṣu replied to the Buddha,
“It is so, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!”
Reflect upon this well; I shall speak for you. Monks!
If one follows the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), one dies following those underlying tendencies.
If one follows along with death, one is bound by grasping.
Monks! If one does not follow along with the underlying tendencies, then one does not die following along with those underlying tendencies.
"One who does not die following the underlying tendencies is liberated from grasping.
The bhikṣu said to the Buddha,
"I understand, World-Honored One!"
“Having understood it, O Sugata!
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu:
“How have you extensively explained the meaning within my brief teaching?”
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Form is driven by latent tendencies; form dies accompanied by latent tendencies.”
Those who are driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and die driven by the underlying tendencies are bound by grasping (*upādāna*).
In the same way, feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are driven by the underlying tendencies and die driven by the underlying tendencies;
those who are driven by the underlying tendencies and die driven by the underlying tendencies are bound by grasping.
“World-Honored One!
If form is not driven by latent tendencies and does not die through latent tendencies;
if it is not driven by latent tendencies and does not die through latent tendencies, then it is liberated from grasping.”
In this way, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not driven by underlying tendencies, nor do they die following those tendencies;
being neither driven by underlying tendencies nor dying following them, one is liberated from grasping.
"So it is, World-Honored One!
You have spoken the Dharma in brief, and I have explained its meaning in detail.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
“Excellent! Excellent, bhikṣu!”
Within this brief teaching of mine, you should extensively explain its meaning.
Why is this? Form is driven by the underlying tendencies and dies driven by the underlying tendencies.
Those who are driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and die driven by the underlying tendencies are bound by grasping (*upādāna*).
In the same way, feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are driven by the underlying tendencies and die driven by the underlying tendencies;
those who are driven by the underlying tendencies and die driven by the underlying tendencies are bound by grasping.
“Monks! Form is not driven by underlying tendencies, nor does it die following those tendencies;
that which is not driven by underlying tendencies and does not die following them is liberated from grasping.”
In this way, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not driven by underlying tendencies, nor do they die following those tendencies;
being neither driven by underlying tendencies nor dying following them, one is liberated from grasping.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that bhikṣu was filled with great joy; he prostrated to the Buddha and withdrew.
Remaining alone in a quiet place, he practiced with diligent application, dwelling in heedfulness.
Having practiced with diligence and dwelt in heedfulness, he reflects:

"This is why a son of good family goes forth from home, shaves off his hair and beard, dons the dharma robes, and out of faith leaves the household life for the homeless state, until he knows for himself that there will be no further existence."
At that time, that bhikṣu immediately became an arhat, and his mind attained liberation.
16 (16) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, another bhikṣu came to where the Buddha was.
His questions were as above, with this difference:
"Those who are driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and die driven by the underlying tendencies increase the various reckonings; [but those who are not so driven do not]."
"If one is not driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and does not die driven by them, then one does not increase the various reckonings.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"How is it that you have extensively understood the meaning within my brief teaching?"
At that time, the bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If form is driven by latent tendencies and dies driven by latent tendencies;
Those who are driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and die driven by the underlying tendencies increase the various reckonings.

In the same way, feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are driven by the underlying tendencies and one dies driven by the underlying tendencies;
those who are driven by the underlying tendencies and die driven by the underlying tendencies increase the various reckonings.
“World-Honored One!
If form is not driven by underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and does not die driven by underlying tendencies;
if it is not driven by underlying tendencies and does not die driven by underlying tendencies, then it does not increase the various reckonings.”
In this way, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not driven by underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), nor do they die following those tendencies;
for one who is not driven by underlying tendencies and does not die following them, the various enumerations do not increase.
"So it is, World-Honored One!
I have extensively explained the meaning within this brief teaching.
Thus, he proceeded until he attained arhatship and his mind was liberated.
17 (17) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
A certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent,
World-Honored One!
Please briefly expound for me the essential points of the Dharma.”
Having heard the Dharma, I shall dwell alone in a quiet place, applying myself with diligence to reflection and abiding in heedfulness:

"For what reason has this son of good family gone forth, shaved his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of faith left the home life for homelessness to study the Path? It is for the sake of the ultimate, unsurpassed holy life, to realize for himself in this very life:
'Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence.'"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those bhikṣus:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
You made this statement:

"Bhagavān, please teach me the essentials of the Dharma in brief; within that brief teaching, I shall extensively understand its meaning, and dwelling alone in a quiet place, with focused and diligent reflection, remaining heedful, I shall proceed until I know for myself that there will be no further existence."
“Do you speak thus?
The bhikṣu replied to the Buddha,
“It is so, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!”
Reflect upon this well; I shall speak for you. Bhikṣus!
Those things which are not the Dharma appropriate for you should be swiftly abandoned.
"By abandoning those phenomena, one will be enriched by their meaning and find peace and happiness for a long night.
Then, that bhikṣu said to the Buddha,
"I understand."
"World-Honored One!
We understand. Sugata!"
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu,
“How do you extensively understand the meaning within my brief teaching?
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Form is not what belongs to me; it should be swiftly abandoned.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not what belong to me; they should be swiftly abandoned.”
This will benefit them through its meaning and bring them peace and happiness for a long night.
Therefore, World-Honored One,
I have extensively explained the meaning within the brief teaching spoken by the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Monk! You have extensively explained the meaning within my brief teaching. Why is that? Because..."
Form is not yours; it should be swiftly abandoned.
Likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not yours; they should be swiftly abandoned.
"Having severed [these defilements], you shall benefit others through the Dharma and enjoy peace and happiness for a long night.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that bhikṣu was filled with great joy; he prostrated before the Buddha and withdrew.
Dwelling alone in a quiet place, he practices with diligence and abides in heedfulness.
Having practiced with diligence and abided in heedfulness, he reflects:

"This is why a son of good family goes forth from the home life, shaving off hair and beard, donning the dharma robes, and out of right faith leaving the household for homelessness, until he knows for himself that there will be no further existence."
At that time, that bhikṣu became an arhat, and his mind attained liberation.
18 (18) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, paid homage to the Buddha, and standing to one side, addressed the Buddha, saying:

He replied, "No, Śūḷuna! "Śūḷuna! [the Buddha said.]
"In this way, are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent?
He replied, "Impermanent."
He asked again:
"If it is impermanent, is it suffering?
He replied:
"This is suffering.
He asked again:

"If it is impermanent and suffering, and subject to change, would a noble disciple therein regard consciousness as 'this is my self,' or 'the self possesses consciousness,' or 'consciousness exists within the self'?"
He replied, “No. “Śūḷuna!

One should know that regarding form—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; beautiful or ugly; distant or near—all such forms are not the self, are not distinct from the self, and do not exist within one another. This is called knowing it as it truly is.

Śūṇa! When a noble disciple gives rise to revulsion toward form, becomes dispassionate toward it, and attains liberation, he is liberated from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.

“In this same way, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; superior or inferior; far or near—all such consciousness is not the self, is not distinct from the self, and does not exist within the self, nor does the self exist within it. This is called knowing it as it truly is.”

Śroṇa! The noble disciple develops revulsion toward consciousness, becomes dispassionate toward it, and attains liberation; through this liberation, he is freed from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.
At that time, Śroṇa, having heard what Śāriputra had said, was filled with joy and exultation; he paid his respects and departed.
32 (32) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa, the Bamboo Grove.

"If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa knows, as they truly are, the form, the origin of form, the cessation of form, the gratification of form, the danger of form, and the escape from form, then that śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa is capable of transcending form."

If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa knows, as they truly are, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—the origin of consciousness, the cessation of consciousness, the gratification of consciousness, the danger in consciousness, and the escape from consciousness—then that śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa is capable of transcending consciousness.
“Śroṇa! What do you think?

"Śroṇa! [the Buddha said.]

“Śroṇa! What do you think?
Are such feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent?”
He replied, “It is impermanent.

He replied, “It is suffering. “Śroṇa!

"If something is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, would a noble disciple regard it as 'this is my self,' 'this is distinct from my self,' or 'this and my self exist within one another'? He replied, "No."

“Śroṇa! You should know that regarding form—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; beautiful or ugly; far or near—in all such forms, there is no ‘self,’ nor is it distinct from a self, nor do they exist within one another. “Śūṇa! Regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; excellent or inferior; far or near—in all cases of consciousness, one knows them as they truly are: ‘This is not my self, this is not distinct from my self, nor does it exist within my self, nor do I exist within it. “Śroṇa! A noble disciple correctly contemplates these five aggregates of clinging as not-self and not belonging to self.
Contemplating in this way, one is not grasped by anything in the world.”
One who is without grasping has no attachment;
one who has no attachment attains nirvāṇa for themselves:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence."
At that time, the householder’s son Śūḍodana, having heard what Śāriputra had said, was filled with joy and exultation; he paid his respects and departed.

"Monks! What do you think?

The monks replied to the Buddha:

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
"Monks! A well-taught noble disciple sees these five aggregates of clinging as not-self and not belonging to self."

Observing in this way, one grasps at nothing whatsoever in all the worlds; because there is no grasping, there is no attachment; because there is no attachment, one personally realizes Nirvana, knowing:

35 (Thirty-five). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Cetiya.
At that time, there were three noble sons who had recently gone forth as monastics: namely, the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimbila.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in his mind, gave this instruction: "Bhikṣu!

“Bhikkhus!
Could there be such a thing as form that is permanent, unchanging, and eternally abiding?
The bhikkhus replied to the Buddha:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!
Form is impermanent, a phenomenon subject to change; it is to be weary of, to be detached from, to be extinguished, to be stilled, and to be submerged.
Thus, from its very origin, form is entirely impermanent, suffering, and a phenomenon subject to change.

Having understood this, one completely cuts off all taints, harms, burning fevers, and distresses that arise conditioned by those forms. Once they are cut off, there is no attachment; once there is no attachment, one dwells in peace and happiness.
Dwelling in peace and happiness, one attains parinirvāṇa.
"Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

36 (36) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Campaka Āmra Grove on the banks of the Bahudā River in the kingdom of Mathurā.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Abide with yourself as an island, abide with yourself as a refuge;
abide with the Dharma as an island, abide with the Dharma as a refuge."

"Monks, you should correctly observe that one should dwell with oneself as an island and oneself as a refuge, with the Dharma as an island and the Dharma as a refuge— not another island, not another refuge."
For what cause do sorrow, lamentation, vexation, and suffering arise?
How do they exist?
By reason of what?
"To what is one bound and attached?
How does one examine for oneself how unarisen sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair arise, and how arisen sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair grow, increase, and expand?
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha:
“The Blessed One is the root of the Dharma, the eye of the Dharma, and the refuge of the Dharma; we pray that you will speak for us!
Having heard it, the bhikṣus shall practice in accordance with your instructions.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you. Bhikkhus!

There is form, there is the cause of form, and there is attachment to form. By observing this for oneself, unarisen sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress arise, and those already arisen increase and expand."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Monks, is there any form that is permanent, constant, unchanging, and remains eternally?
He replied, “No,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu:

Form is impermanent.

If a son of good family knows that form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—knowing it as the departure from desire, cessation, tranquility, and disappearance—and having understood from the very beginning that all forms are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, then the sorrow, lamentation, vexation, and pain born of the conditions of form are severed. Once these are severed, there is no attachment; because of non-attachment, one dwells in peace and happiness. Having dwelt in peace and happiness, this is called Nirvana.
"Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

37 (37) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I do not dispute with the world; it is the world that disputes with me.
Why is this? O bhikṣus!
If one speaks in accordance with the Dharma, one does not dispute with the world. Regarding what the wise of the world say exists, I also say it exists.
What is it that the wise of the world say exists, and which I likewise say exists?
"Monks! Form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change; that which the wise of the world say exists, I too say exists.

Regarding that which the wise of the world say does not exist, I also say does not exist;
namely, that form is permanent, constant, unchanging, and eternally abiding—regarding this, the wise of the world say it does not exist, and I also say it does not exist.

Regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as permanent, eternal, unchanging, and abiding in stability: what the wise of the world say does not exist, I also say does not exist; this is called "what the wise of the world say does not exist, and I also say does not exist."

"Monks! There are the world and the phenomena of the world, which I myself have known and realized, and which I analyze, expound, and reveal for others; that those who are blind and sightless in the world do not know or see them is not my fault."

"Monks! Form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change; this is called the world and the worldly phenomena.
Likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent and suffering; these are the world and the worldly phenomena."

"Monks! This is the world and its worldly phenomena; I have known them myself and awakened to them myself, and I have analyzed, expounded, and revealed them for others. Yet those who are blind and sightless do not know them and do not see them."
"As for those who are blind, sightless, ignorant, and without vision—what can be done for them?
