38 (Thirty-eight). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"It is known to the world that people perform base occupations and seek wealth by various means to sustain their lives, thereby attaining great riches;
as it is known by the world, so do I speak."
Why is this? Let me not be different from the people of the world. "O bhikṣus!

For example, in a single vessel, there are people from different regions who call it a *kaṃsa*, some call it a *pātra*, some call it a *śarāva*, some call it a *cullī*, some call it a *viṣṭi*, some call it a *vyañjana*, and some call it a *sāra*.
As it is known by them, so do I likewise speak. Why is this?
So that I may not differ from the people of the world.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!

There are worldly dharmas that I have known for myself and awakened to for myself; I analyze, expound, and reveal them for others, speaking from my knowledge and vision. Yet those who are blind and sightless in the world do not know or see them;
since those who are blind and sightless in the world do not know or see them, what can I do for them?
“Bhikkhus! What is the world and the phenomena of the world that I have known for myself and realized for myself, yet [others] do not know or see?
Form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change; this is the world and the phenomena of the world.”
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change; these are the worldly and mundane phenomena. Monks!
These are called the worldly and mundane phenomena. I know them myself and see them myself, yet as for those who are blind and sightless, they neither know nor see—what can be done for them?
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
39 (39) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are five kinds of seeds. What are the five?
These are root-seeds, stem-seeds, joint-seeds, spontaneously falling seeds, and fruit-seeds.

If these five kinds of seeds are not cut, not destroyed, not rotted, and not affected by wind, yet are fresh, mature, firm, and solid, and possess the earth element but lack the water element, those seeds will not grow, increase, or expand.

If that seed is newly ripened, firm, and solid, and is not cut, not damaged, and not affected by wind, yet possesses the water element but lacks the earth element, that seed will likewise not grow, develop, or expand.

If that seed is fresh, ripe, firm, and solid, and is not cut, not destroyed, not rotten, and not struck by wind, and if the elements of earth and water are present, that seed will grow, develop, and expand.
“Bhikṣus! Those five kinds of seeds are a metaphor for consciousness together with grasping (upādāna);
the earth element is a metaphor for the four stations of consciousness (vijñānasthiti).”
The water element is an analogy for consciousness abiding by clinging to the four types of grasping through craving and delight. What are these four?
Consciousness abides within form, clinging to form; moistened by the moisture of craving and delight, it grows, develops, and expands.

Within feeling, perception, and formations, consciousness dwells; it takes feeling, perception, and formations as its object, and through the moisture of craving and delight, it grows, increases, and expands. Monks!
"Consciousness, within this [body], comes, goes, stays, disappears, or grows, develops, and expands. Monks!

If consciousness were to come, go, stay, or arise apart from form, feeling, perception, and formations, that would be a mere empty expression; having been questioned, one would not know it, and it would only increase delusion, for it is not within the sphere of experience."
Having become free from craving for the realm of form, once craving is abandoned, the mental bond that arises from attachment to form is severed.
When the mental bond arising from attachment to form is severed, the objective support is severed.
When the objective support is severed, consciousness has no place to dwell and no longer grows, develops, or expands.
When the realm of feeling, perception, and formations is free from craving, and once it is free from craving, the mind-contact that arises through attachment to formations is severed;

when the mind-contact arising through attachment to formations is severed, the objective support is severed; when the objective support is severed, that consciousness has no place to abide and no longer grows, develops, or expands.
Because there is no further growth, one does not perform volitional formations;
having ceased performing volitional formations, one abides; abiding, one is content; being content, one is liberated;
being liberated, one has nothing whatsoever to grasp or to cling to in all the worlds.
Having nothing to grasp and nothing to cling to, he realized nirvana for himself:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence."

I say that this consciousness does not go to the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, or below; it has no destination whatsoever. It perceives only phenomena, desiring to enter nirvāṇa—quiescence, coolness, purity, and reality.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
40 (40) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Those who are obstructed by attachment are not liberated; those who are not obstructed by attachment are liberated.
What is meant by being obstructed by attachment and thus not being liberated?"
"Monks! Consciousness dwells supported by the four aggregates of clinging.
What are the four?"

Form obstructs and stagnates the dwelling of consciousness; feeling, perception, and formations obstruct and stagnate the dwelling of consciousness. Because it is not their proper domain, this is called "obstruction and stagnation," and therefore one is not liberated.
What is meant by "not being obstructed or stagnant is liberation"?

To be free from craving for the realm of form, to be free from craving for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and so on until one reaches purity and reality—this is what is meant by "not being obstructed or stagnant is liberation."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
41 (41) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are five aggregates of clinging—the aggregate of form, and the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."

Regarding these five aggregates of clinging, I know them as they truly are in five ways: I know form as it truly is; I know the arising of form, the gratification of form, the danger of form, and the escape from form as they truly are.

In this way, one knows feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they truly are; one knows the origin of consciousness, the gratification of consciousness, the danger of consciousness, and the escape from consciousness as they truly are.
"How does one know form as it truly is?"
Whatever form exists—all the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements—is called "form"; such form one knows as it truly is.
How does one know the arising of form as it truly is?
Craving and delight for form is called the origin of form; thus one knows the origin of form as it truly is.
How does one know the gratification of form as it truly is?
That pleasure and joy arise conditioned by form is called the gratification of form; thus one knows the gratification of form as it truly is.
What is the knowledge of the peril of form as it truly is?
If form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, this is called the peril of form; such is the knowledge of the peril of form as it truly is.
What is the knowledge of the fading away of form as it truly is?

If, regarding form, one subdues desire and greed, abandons desire and greed, and transcends desire and greed, this is called the fading away of form; such is the knowledge of the fading away of form as it truly is.
"How does one know feeling as it really is?

There are six classes of feeling—the feeling born of eye-contact, and those born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact. These are called feelings; in this way, one knows feelings as they really are."
How does one know the arising of feeling as it really is?
The arising of contact is the arising of feeling; in this way, one knows the arising of feeling as it really is.
How does one know the gratification of feeling as it really is?
The arising of joy and pleasure conditioned by the six types of feeling is called the gratification of feeling; such is the gratification of feeling as it truly is.
What is the danger of feeling as it truly is?
That feeling is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is called the danger of feeling; such is the danger of feeling as it truly is.
What is the knowledge of the departure from feeling as it really is?

To subdue desire and lust for feeling, to abandon desire and lust, and to transcend desire and lust—this is called the departure from feeling; such is the knowledge of the departure from feeling as it really is.
"How does one know perception as it really is?
It refers to the six groups of perception. What are the six? "
That is to say: the perception born of eye-contact, and the perceptions born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact—these are called "perception. One knows such perception as it truly is.
How does one know the arising of perception as it really is?
It is said that the arising of contact is the arising of perception; thus one knows the arising of perception as it really is.
How does one know the gratification of perception as it really is?
The arising of joy and pleasure conditioned by perception is called the gratification of perception; one knows this gratification of perception as it truly is.
What is knowing the danger of perception as it truly is?
That perception is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is called the danger of perception; one knows this danger of perception as it truly is.
What is the knowledge of the departure from perception as it truly is?

If one subdues sensual desire for perception, abandons sensual desire for perception, and transcends sensual desire for perception, this is called the departure from perception; such is the knowledge of the departure from perception as it truly is.
"What is the knowledge of formations as they really are?

It refers to the six groups of volition: volition born of eye-contact, and volition born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact. These are called formations; such is the knowledge of formations as they really are."
How does one know the origin of volitional formations as they really are?
The origin of contact is the origin of volitional formations; in this way, one knows the origin of volitional formations as it really is.
How does one know the gratification of volitional formations as it really is?
That which is the pleasure arising from conditioned formations is called the gratification of formations; such is the gratification of formations as it truly is.
What is the danger of formations as it truly is?
That formations are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is called the danger of formations; such is the danger of formations as it truly is.
What is the knowledge of the departure from formations as it really is?

If one subdues sensual desire, abandons sensual desire, and transcends sensual desire regarding formations, this is called the departure from formations; such is the knowledge of the departure from formations as it really is.
"How does one know consciousness as it truly is?

It refers to the six groups of consciousness—the group of eye-consciousness, and the groups of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness. These are called the groups of consciousness; in this way, one knows the groups of consciousness as they truly are."
How does one know the arising of consciousness as it really is?
It is said that the arising of name-and-form is the arising of consciousness; in this way, one knows the arising of consciousness as it really is.
How does one know the gratification of consciousness as it really is?
The joy and pleasure that arise with consciousness as their condition are called the gratification of consciousness; thus one knows the gratification of consciousness as it really is.
What is knowing the danger of consciousness as it really is?
If consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, this is called the danger of consciousness; thus one knows the danger of consciousness as it really is.
What is the knowledge of the dissociation from consciousness as it truly is?

It means that regarding consciousness, one subdues sensual desire, abandons sensual desire, and transcends sensual desire; this is called dissociation from consciousness. Thus one knows the dissociation from consciousness as it truly is.
“Monks! If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa understands form in this way and sees it in this way;
having understood it thus and seen it thus, they turn away from desire—this is called right direction.”
If one is rightly directed, I say that they have entered [the path].
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa knows form as it truly is and sees it as it truly is, they become weary of form, become detached from it, and by not giving rise to the outflows (āsrava), their mind attains liberation.
If the mind attains liberation, it becomes pure and unified;
when it is pure and unified, the holy life (brahmacarya) is established;
when the holy life is established, one is independent of others and self-mastered—this is called the end of suffering.
"Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
42. [Sutra 42] Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are seven points of proficiency and three types of contemplation.

By exhausting these teachings, one attains the destruction of the taints, becomes free from taints, and achieves liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. In this very life, one realizes for oneself and dwells in the fulfillment of direct realization, knowing:
‘Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I myself know that there will be no further existence.’”
"What is a bhikkhu skilled in the seven points?

Bhikkhus, it is when one knows as they really are: form, the arising of form, the cessation of form, the path leading to the cessation of form, the gratification of form, the danger in form, and the escape from form."

In this same way, one knows as it truly is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the arising of consciousness, the cessation of consciousness, the path leading to the cessation of consciousness, the gratification of consciousness, the danger of consciousness, and the escape from consciousness.
“How does one know form as it truly is?
Whatever forms there are—all the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements—this is called ‘form. In this way, one knows form as it truly is.”
How does one know the arising of form as it really is?
Craving and delight are called the arising of form; in this way, one knows the arising of form as it really is.
How does one know the cessation of form as it really is?
The cessation of craving and delight is called the cessation of form; thus one knows the cessation of form as it truly is.
How does one know the path leading to the cessation of form as it truly is?

It is the Noble Eightfold Path—right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This is called the path leading to the cessation of form; thus one knows the path leading to the cessation of form as it truly is.
How does one know the gratification of form as it truly is?
It is said that the joy and pleasure arising from the conditions of form is called the gratification of form; in this way, one knows the gratification of form as it truly is.
How does one know the danger of form as it truly is?
If form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, this is called the peril of form; such is the peril of form as it truly is.
What is the escape from form as it truly is?

That is to say, regarding form, one subdues desire and greed, abandons desire and greed, and transcends desire and greed; this is called detachment from form. Thus one knows detachment from form as it truly is.
"How does one know feeling as it truly is?"

That is to say, there are six feelings: feeling born of eye-contact, and feeling born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact. These are called feeling; such feeling one knows as it truly is.
How does one know the arising of feeling as it really is?
The arising of contact is the arising of feeling; in this way, one knows the arising of feeling as it really is.
How does one know the cessation of feeling as it really is?
With the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; thus one knows the cessation of feeling as it truly is.
How does one know the path leading to the cessation of feeling as it truly is?

It is the Noble Eightfold Path—right view up to right concentration. This is called the path leading to the cessation of feeling; thus one knows the path leading to the cessation of feeling as it truly is.
How does one know the gratification of feeling as it really is?
The joy and pleasure born of the conditions of feeling is called the gratification of feeling; in this way, one knows the gratification of feeling as it really is.
How does one know the danger of feeling as it really is?
If something is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, this is called the danger of feeling; such is the danger of feeling as it truly is.
What is knowing the escape from feeling as it truly is?

If, regarding feeling, one subdues desire and greed, abandons desire and greed, and transcends desire and greed, this is called "separation from feeling"; such separation from feeling is known as it truly is.
"How does one know perception as it truly is?"

That is to say, there are six types of perception: perception born of eye-contact, and perception born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact. These are called perception; one should know such perception as it truly is.
How does one know the arising of perception as it really is?
The arising of contact is the arising of perception; thus one knows the arising of perception as it really is.
How does one know the cessation of perception as it really is?
The cessation of contact is the cessation of perception; thus one knows the cessation of perception as it truly is.
How does one know the path leading to the cessation of perception as it truly is?

It is the Noble Eightfold Path—from right view up to right concentration—this is called the path leading to the cessation of perception; thus one knows the path leading to the cessation of perception as it truly is.
What is knowing the gratification of perception as it really is?
The joy and pleasure born of the conditions of perception is called the gratification of perception; this is how one knows the gratification of perception as it really is.
What is knowing the danger of perception as it really is?
If one perceives perceptions as impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, this is called the danger of perception; such is the danger of perception known as it truly is.
What is the knowledge of the departure from perception as it truly is?

If one subdues sensual desire for perceptions, abandons sensual desire for perceptions, and transcends sensual desire for perceptions, this is called "separation from perceptions. One knows this separation from perceptions as it truly is.
What is knowing formations as they truly are?

That is to say, the six groups of volition: volition born of eye-contact, and volition born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact. These are called formations (*saṃskāra*); such formations he knows as they truly are.
What is the knowledge of the arising of volitional formations as it really is?
The arising of contact is the arising of volitional formations; thus one knows the arising of volitional formations as it really is.
What is the knowledge of the cessation of volitional formations as it really is?
With the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of volitional formations; thus one knows the cessation of volitional formations as it truly is.
How does one know the path leading to the cessation of volitional formations as it truly is?

It is the Noble Eightfold Path—right view up to right concentration; this is called the path leading to the cessation of volitional formations, and thus one knows the path leading to the cessation of volitional formations as it truly is.
What is knowing the gratification of formations as it really is?
The joy and pleasure born of the causal conditions of formations is called the gratification of formations; this is how one knows the gratification of formations as it really is.
What is knowing the danger of formations as it really is?

If one practices that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, this is called the danger of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-ādīnava*). Thus, one knows the danger of conditioned phenomena as it truly is.
What is knowing the departure from conditioned phenomena as it truly is?

If one has subdued desire and greed for formations, severed desire and greed, and transcended desire and greed, this is called "separation from formations. Thus one knows separation from formations as it truly is.
"How does one know consciousness as it truly is?"

That is to say, the six groups of consciousness—the visual consciousness, and the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness groups—these are called consciousness; such consciousness is known as it truly is.
How does one know the arising of consciousness as it really is?
The arising of name-and-form is the arising of consciousness; thus one knows the arising of consciousness as it really is.
How does one know the cessation of consciousness as it really is?
The cessation of name-and-form is the cessation of consciousness; thus one knows the cessation of consciousness as it truly is.
What is knowing the path leading to the cessation of consciousness as it truly is?

It is the Noble Eightfold Path—right view up to right concentration—which is called the path leading to the cessation of consciousness; thus one knows the path leading to the cessation of consciousness as it truly is.
How does one know the gratification of consciousness as it truly is?
The joy and pleasure born of the conditions of consciousness is called the gratification of consciousness; in this way, one knows the gratification of consciousness as it truly is.
How does one know the danger of consciousness as it truly is?
If consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, this is called the peril of consciousness; such is the peril of consciousness as it truly is.
What is the escape from consciousness as it truly is?
If one tames craving for consciousness, abandons craving for consciousness, and transcends craving for consciousness, this is called knowing "consciousness is disjoined" as it truly is.
Bhikkhus, this is called being skilled in the seven bases.
“What are the three kinds of contemplation of meaning? Bhikkhus!

If, in a secluded place, at the foot of a tree, or in the open air, one contemplates the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, and correctly applies effort to contemplate their meaning—this is called the bhikkhu’s three kinds of contemplation of meaning.”
This is called the bhikṣu’s skill in the seven points and the threefold contemplation of meaning.

By exhausting these dharmas, one attains the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya), attains the state of being without outflows (anāsrava), and achieves liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. In this very life, one knows for oneself and realizes, dwelling in its fulfillment:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
43 (43) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Grasping gives rise to attachment; not grasping, there is no attachment.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for your sake."
The bhikṣu replied to the Buddha:
“Indeed, we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"How does grasping lead to attachment?
An ignorant, unlearned worldling regards form as 'this is me,' 'it is different from me,' or 'it exists within me'; they regard form as 'me' or 'mine' and grasp it.
Having grasped it, if that form changes or alters, the mind also undergoes a corresponding transformation."
Once the mind has followed after [objects], it further gives rise to a state of attachment and grasping;
because the mind dwells in grasping, fear, hindrances, and mental distraction arise, due to that attachment.

Ignorant, unlearned worldlings, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, perceive them as the self, as distinct from the self, or as existing within the self; they perceive consciousness as "I" or "mine" and grasp at it.
Having grasped it, if that consciousness changes or alters, their mind follows along with it.
Because the mind follows along with it, there arises a state of mind characterized by attachment, clinging, and appropriation.
Once one has so abided, fear, hindrances, and mental distraction arise because of grasping and attachment; this is called "grasping and attachment.
What is meant by "not grasping and not attaching"?
The well-versed noble disciple does not perceive form as self, as distinct from self, or as existing within self; nor does he perceive form as "mine" and thereby grasp it.
Not perceiving it as "I" or "mine," he does not grasp form. If that form changes or alters, his mind does not follow after it.
Because his mind does not follow after it, no state of mind arises that is characterized by grasping, attachment, or appropriation.
Because they do not grasp at or dwell upon [these aggregates], no fear, obstruction, or mental distraction arises, for they do not cling to them.

Thus, regarding feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, they do not perceive a self, nor something other than a self, nor the two existing together; they do not perceive a self or what belongs to a self, and thus do not grasp.
If that consciousness undergoes transformation or alteration, the mind does not follow along with it;
because the mind does not follow along, it does not grasp, cling to, or settle upon it;
because the mind does not settle upon it, the mind is not terrified, obstructed, or distracted, for it does not grasp or cling—this is called non-clinging.
"This is called grasping and non-grasping.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
44 (44) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“If there is arising, there is bondage and attachment; if there is no arising, there is no bondage and attachment.”
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you.
"How is it that one is bound by attachment when there is birth?

Because an ignorant, unlearned worldling does not know, as they truly are, the arising of form, the cessation of form, the gratification of form, the danger of form, and the escape from form, he feels craving, delight, praise, and grasping toward form; he grasps at form as 'I' and 'mine'."
Having grasped it, if that form changes or alters, the mind changes accordingly;

because the mind changes accordingly, one becomes attached to the abiding of the mind; because of this attachment to the abiding of the mind, fear, hindrance, and longing arise, due to the production of clinging.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
This is called being bound by attachment.
What is non-arising and non-attachment?
The learned noble disciple knows, as they truly are, the arising of form, the cessation of form, the gratification of form, the danger of form, and the escape from form.
Because he knows them as they truly are, he does not feel craving for them, does not praise them, does not cling to them, and does not grasp at them with the notions of "I" or "mine.
Because he does not grasp them, when that form changes or alters, his mind does not undergo change along with it.
Because the mind does not undergo transformation, it dwells in a state of non-attachment and non-appropriation;
because it dwells in a state of non-appropriation, the mind is free from fear, obstruction, and retrospective longing, for it neither arises nor clings.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
This is called "non-arising and non-attachment.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
45. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are five aggregates of clinging. What are the five?
They are the aggregate of clinging to form, and the aggregates of clinging to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”
If any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas perceive a self, they all perceive it within these five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādānaskandha).
Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who perceive form as the self, or the self as possessing form, or form as being in the self, or the self as being in form;

or who perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as the self, or the self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as being in the self, or the self as being in consciousness.
Due to ignorance, foolish and unlearned worldlings perceive form as the self, as distinct from the self, or as existing within the self; they claim, "The self is real," and do not relinquish it.
Because they do not relinquish it, the sense faculties increase;
once the sense faculties have increased, various contacts increase.
Because they are contacted by the six bases of contact (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), the ignorant, unlearned worldling gives rise to perceptions of pleasure and pain arising from those bases of contact.
What are these six?
That is to say: the sense-base of eye-contact, and the sense-bases of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.
"In this way, bhikṣu!

There is the element of mind, the element of phenomena, and the element of ignorance. Because of contact with ignorance, the foolish, unlearned worldling—due to that contact with ignorance—gives rise to the thought 'I have,' the thought 'I do not have,' the thought 'I both have and do not have,' the thought 'I am superior,' the thought 'I am equal,' the thought 'I am inferior,' and the thought 'I know and I see.'"
Such knowledge, such seeing, and such awakening all arise because of the six bases of contact (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).

A well-taught noble disciple, regarding these six bases of contact, abandons ignorance and gives rise to clarity; they do not give rise to the thought "there is perception," nor "there is no perception," nor "there both is and is not perception," nor "there is superior perception," nor "there is equal perception," nor "there is inferior perception," nor the thought "I know" or "I see."
"Having known thus and seen thus, the previously arisen contact of ignorance ceases, and the subsequently arising awareness of the contact of clarity emerges.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
46. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are five aggregates of clinging.
What are the five?

They are the aggregate of clinging to form, the aggregate of clinging to feeling, the aggregate of clinging to perception, the aggregate of clinging to formations, and the aggregate of clinging to consciousness.”

If śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, by means of the knowledge of past lives, recognize their various past existences—whether already recognized, yet to be recognized, or currently being recognized—they all [recognize them] as these five aggregates of clinging;
whether already recognized, yet to be recognized, or currently being recognized, they think: "This is what I have experienced in the past."
Such is form, such is feeling, such is perception, such are formations, such is consciousness.
That which is obstructive and divisible is called the aggregate of form-feeling (*rūpa-vedanā-skandha*).

That which is obstructed by a finger, or by the hand, a stone, a staff, a sword, cold, heat, thirst, hunger, mosquitoes, gadflies, various venomous insects, wind, or rain—this is called obstruction by contact. Therefore, this obstruction constitutes the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).
Furthermore, this aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.
The characteristic of sensation (saṃjñā) is the aggregate of feeling; what is it that is sensed?
One senses pain, one senses pleasure, and one senses that which is neither painful nor pleasant; therefore, the characteristic of sensation is called the aggregate of feeling.
Furthermore, one regards this feeling as the aggregate of feeling, which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.
All perceptions are the aggregate of perception; what is perceived?

Whether it be few perceptions, many perceptions, immeasurable perceptions, or the perception of nothingness regarding that which is entirely non-existent—therefore, it is called the aggregate of perception.
Furthermore, one contemplates that this aggregate of feeling and perception is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.
That which acts as a conditioning mark is the aggregate of formations. What does it act upon?
It acts upon form; it acts upon feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. Therefore, that which acts as a conditioning mark is the aggregate of formations.
Furthermore, by means of this practice, one understands that the aggregate of feeling is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.
One discerns its specific characteristics as the aggregate of perception;
what does it perceive? It perceives forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena. Therefore, it is called the aggregate of perception.
Furthermore, one regards this consciousness-aggregate of feeling as impermanent, suffering,
and subject to change. "Monks,
a learned noble disciple trains himself in regard to this aggregate of form-feeling in this way:"
"I am now being consumed by present form; in past lives as well, I was already consumed by that form, just as I am now.
He further reflects:
"I am now being consumed by present form; if I were again to delight in and cling to future form, I would likewise be consumed by that form, just as I am now."

Having understood this, one does not look back at past forms, does not take delight in or cling to future forms, and regarding present forms, gives rise to disenchantment, detachment from desire, the destruction of affliction, and proceeds toward their cessation.
The learned noble disciple trains in this aggregate of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness:
"I am now being consumed by present consciousness; as I am now, so too was I consumed by consciousness in the past."

I have now already been consumed by the present consciousness; if I were again to delight in and cling to future consciousness, I would likewise be consumed by that consciousness, just as I am now by the present one.

Having understood this, he disregards past consciousness, does not delight in future consciousness, and regarding present consciousness, he gives rise to disenchantment, becomes free from desire, eliminates affliction, and inclines toward its cessation; it ceases without increasing, recedes without advancing, is extinguished without arising, and is relinquished without being grasped.
"In what does it cease without increasing?
Form ceases without increasing; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cease without increasing.
In what does it recede without advancing?"
Form recedes and does not advance; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness recede and do not advance.
In what do they cease so as not to arise?
Form ceases and does not arise; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cease and do not arise.
What is it that one relinquishes and does not grasp?
One relinquishes and does not grasp form; one relinquishes and does not grasp feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
"Ceasing without increasing, one abides in tranquility."
Retreating without advancing, one dwells in tranquil withdrawal;
ceasing without arising, one dwells in tranquil extinction;
relinquishing without grasping, one does not give rise to attachment.
Being unattached, he realized for himself his parinirvāṇa:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, many bhikṣus were freed from outflows and their minds attained liberation.
After the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Self, lowliness, seed; stagnation, five turnings, seventy-two fetters, attachments, and perceptions;
the aggregates of the three times and the nutriment of the world.
(47) [47] Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“A son of good family with faith should reflect in this way:”

"I should conform to the Dharma; I shall dwell frequently cultivating disenchantment toward form, and I shall dwell frequently cultivating disenchantment toward feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
A son of good family with faith dwells frequently cultivating revulsion toward form;

he dwells frequently cultivating revulsion toward feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Therefore, he becomes weary of form, and he becomes weary of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Having become weary [of them], he becomes dispassionate, attains liberation, and possesses the knowledge and vision of liberation:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I myself know that there will be no further existence."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
48 (48) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"A son of good family with faith, having gone forth from the home life out of right faith, reflects to himself:

'I should conform to the Dharma; I should cultivate dwelling in revulsion toward form extensively, and I should cultivate dwelling in revulsion toward feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness extensively.'"

A son of good family with faith, having gone forth from the home life out of right conviction, dwells frequently in the cultivation of revulsion toward form; having dwelt frequently in the cultivation of revulsion toward feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, he attains detachment from form and attains detachment from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"I declare that these individuals are all completely free from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
49 (Forty-nine). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"If a faithful householder or the son of a householder were to come and ask you,
'In what phenomena do you recognize arising and ceasing? how would you answer?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
If there should be elders or sons of elders who come to question me, I shall answer them thus:”
“‘One knows that form is a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing; one knows that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing.
World-Honored One, if a householder or a householder’s son were to ask such a question, I would answer them in this way.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
One should answer in this way. Why is that?
Form is a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing.
To know that form is a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing is called "knowing form";
to know that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing is called "knowing consciousness."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
50 (50) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"If various non-Buddhist renunciants should come and ask you, saying: 'Ānanda!'"
“World-Honored One, for what reason do you teach people to cultivate the various holy life (brahmacarya)?
If one asks this, how should one answer?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
If a renunciant of other paths were to come and ask me, saying: ‘Ānanda!’”
To the one who asks, "For what reason, Blessed One, do you teach people to cultivate the various holy life (brahmacarya)? I shall answer:
"It is for the sake of cultivating revulsion toward form, detachment from desire, its cessation, liberation, and non-arising that the Blessed One teaches people to cultivate the various holy life."

For the sake of cultivating weariness toward feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, as well as detachment, cessation, liberation, and non-arising, he teaches people to practice the various holy life (brahmacarya).
"World-Honored One!
If there are non-Buddhist renunciants who ask such questions, I shall answer them in this way.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Excellent! Excellent!
You should answer in this way.”
Why is that? It is because I truly teach people to practice the holy life for the sake of cultivating weariness toward form, detachment from desire, cessation, liberation, and non-arising;

and for the sake of cultivating weariness toward feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, detachment from desire, cessation, liberation, and non-arising, I teach people to practice the holy life.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
51 (51) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now explain to you the phenomena of disintegration and non-disintegration.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for your sake.”
"O bhikṣus!
Form is a phenomenon subject to destruction; the nirvāṇa that is the cessation of that form is a phenomenon not subject to destruction.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are phenomena subject to destruction; the nirvāṇa that is the cessation of that consciousness is a phenomenon not subject to destruction."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
52 (52) The Udayi Sūtra is as explained in the "Four Dharmas" section of the Ekottarika Āgama.
53. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the human realm in the kingdom of Kosala and stayed in the Siṃsapā Forest north of the village of Sālā.

At that time, the village head, a brahmin of great lineage, heard that a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākya clan, had shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of right faith had gone forth from home into homelessness to study the Path, having attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. He was now wandering among the people in the kingdom of Kosala and had arrived at the village of Bhaṇḍagāma, where he was staying in the Siṃsapā Grove to the north of the village.

Furthermore, that śramaṇa Gautama possesses such a physical appearance and reputation, and his true merits are praised by devas and humans, heard throughout the eight directions. He is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. Because one does not delight in them and does not dwell upon them, craving for form ceases; with the cessation of craving, grasping ceases; with the cessation of grasping, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; and with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering cease.

The Buddha told the brahmins, “Know that now is the time!
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the brahmins, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and delighted in it; they prostrated at his feet and departed.
54 (54). Thus have I heard:

55 (Fifty-five). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park, the Abode of the Sages.

It is the same for all feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousnesses that exist.

What is the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*)?

If form (*rūpa*) is with outflows (*sāsrava*) and subject to grasping (*upādāna*), and if that form—whether past, future, or present—gives rise to desire, hatred, delusion, and various other secondary afflictions of the mental factors;
and if feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are likewise so—it is called the aggregate of sensation.

56 (56) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now speak of dharmas with outflows and dharmas without outflows.

In this way, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are with outflows and are objects of clinging; that consciousness can give rise to craving and aversion—these are called phenomena with outflows.
What are the untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*)?
Whatever form (*rūpa*) exists that is untainted and not grasped (*anupātta*), whether that form is past, future, or present, it does not give rise to craving or aversion.

Likewise, whatever feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) exist that are untainted and not grasped, whether that consciousness is past, future, or present, it does not give rise to greed or aversion; these are called untainted phenomena.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

57 (Fifty-seven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

"Why is this? Because today the World-Honored One wishes to dwell in tranquility and eliminate minor matters.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, together with a great number of bhikṣus, set aside their robes and bowls, washed their feet, and approached the World-Honored One; having prostrated at his feet with their heads, they sat down to one side.

At that moment, a certain bhikṣu in the assembly had this thought:

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those bhikṣus, addressed the bhikṣus:

'By what way of knowing and by what way of seeing can one swiftly attain the destruction of the outflows?'"
As for that, I have already taught the Dharma, saying:

"One should skillfully observe the aggregates, namely: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path."
"I have already taught such a Dharma for the observation of the aggregates.

Yet, there are still sons of good family who do not apply themselves with diligence, who do not apply themselves with joy, who do not apply themselves with mindfulness, and who do not apply themselves with faith; being thus self-conceited and indolent, they are unable to progress toward the exhaustion of all outflows."

Furthermore, if a son of good family, regarding the Dharma taught by me, observes the aggregates with diligent desire, diligent joy, diligent mindfulness, and diligent faith, he will be able to swiftly attain the exhaustion of all outflows.
Ignorant, unlearned worldlings perceive form as "this is the self. To perceive it thus is called a formation (*saṃskāra*).
What is the cause of that formation?
What is its origin?
What arises?
What evolves?
Craving arises from contact conditioned by ignorance; conditioned by craving, those volitional formations arise.
What is the cause of that craving?
What is its origin?
From what does it arise?
What turns?
That craving is the cause of feeling, the origin of feeling, the arising of feeling, and the turning of feeling.
What is the cause of that feeling?
By what are they accumulated?
By what are they produced?
By what do they evolve?
That feeling has contact as its cause, contact as its origin, contact as its birth, and contact as its transformation.
What is the cause of that contact?
What is its origin?
What is its arising?
What is its turning?
It is said that contact has the six sense bases as its cause, the six sense bases as its origin, the six sense bases as its arising, and the six sense bases as its turning.
Those six sense bases are impermanent, conditioned, and phenomena arisen through mental conditions;
contact, feeling, craving, and formations are likewise impermanent, conditioned, and phenomena arisen through mental conditions...
One who observes in this way does not see form as self... nor does one see form as self.
One views form as belonging to me... or does not view form as belonging to me; one views form as being within me... or does not view form as being within me;
one views myself as being within form... or does not view myself as being within form;
one views feeling as the self... or does not view feeling as the self; one views feeling as belonging to the self.
...not seeing feeling as "mine," yet seeing feeling as being in me; not seeing feeling as being in me, yet seeing me as being in feeling;
not seeing me as being in feeling, yet seeing perception as "I";
not seeing perception as "I," yet seeing perception as "mine"; not seeing perception as...
One perceives "mine" while seeing the perception as being in me... one does not perceive "mine" while seeing me as being in the perception...
one does not perceive me as being in the perception while seeing formations as being self...
one does not perceive formations as being self while seeing formations as being mine... one does not perceive formations as being mine while seeing formations [as they are].
In me... one does not see "action" as being in me, but sees "me" as being in action... one does not see "me" as being in action, but sees "consciousness" as being me...
one does not see "consciousness" as being me, but sees "consciousness" as belonging to me...
one does not see "consciousness" as belonging to me, but sees "consciousness" as being in me... one does not see... [end].

One perceives the self in consciousness and sees the self in consciousness... Not seeing the self in consciousness, one further forms the view of annihilationism or the view of the destruction of existence.
Without forming the view of annihilationism or the view of the destruction of existence, yet one does not abandon the conceit "I am."
One who is not free from the conceit of "I" yet perceives a self—this perception of a self is itself volitional formation (*saṃskāra*).
What is the cause of that formation?
What is its origin?
What arises?
What evolves?
As previously stated, up to and including the conceit "I am."
"One who knows thus and sees thus will swiftly attain the destruction of the outflows.

When a learned noble disciple contemplates in this manner, they cultivate disenchantment; being disenchanted, they become dispassionate; being dispassionate, they are liberated; and through liberation, they possess the knowledge and vision of liberation.

What is the cessation of form?

In the same way, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness: if one does not delight in consciousness, does not praise consciousness, does not grasp at consciousness, and does not cling to consciousness, then by not delighting in consciousness, the mind attains liberation. In this way, not delighting in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, the mind attains liberation; it neither ceases nor arises, abiding in equanimity with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.
“When that bhikṣu knows thus and sees thus, he perceives the past together with its entirety, exhausting it without remainder;
having perceived the past together with its entirety and exhausted it without remainder,
he also perceives the future together with its entirety, exhausting it without remainder.”
Having seen both the future limit and the past limit as completely exhausted without remainder;
having seen both the past and future limits as completely exhausted without remainder, one is free from attachment.
Being free from attachment means that, regarding all worlds, there is nothing whatsoever to be grasped.
One who has nothing to grasp also has nothing to seek;
one who has nothing to seek realizes nirvana for themselves:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and I know for myself that there will be no further existence."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
61 (61) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandhāḥ*).
What are the five? [They are as follows:]”
That is to say: the aggregate of form, and the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"What is the aggregate of form?
Whatever is form, all that consists of the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements; this is called the aggregate of form."
Furthermore, that form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.

If that aggregate of feeling associated with form is severed without remainder, completely relinquished, extinguished, detached from desire, stilled, and vanished, such that no further aggregate of feeling associated with form continues, arises, or emerges—this is called the sublime, this is called tranquility, and this is called the exhaustion of all remaining craving, dispassion, cessation, and nirvana.
"What is the aggregate of feeling?
It refers to the six groups of feeling. What are the six? "
That is to say: feeling born of eye-contact, and feelings born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact; these are called the aggregate of feeling.
Furthermore, that aggregate of feeling is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change; it culminates in cessation and nirvana.
"What is the aggregate of perception?

It refers to the six classes of perception. What are the six? [They are: perception of forms, perception of sounds, perception of odors, perception of tastes, perception of tangibles, and perception of mental phenomena."
That is to say, the perception born of eye-contact, up to and including the perception born of mind-contact—this is called the aggregate of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedanā-skandha*).
Furthermore, that aggregate of perception and feeling is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change; it culminates in cessation and nirvāṇa.
"What is the aggregate of feeling as it functions?
It refers to the six groups of volition. What are the six?
This refers to volition born of eye-contact, up to and including volition born of mind-contact; this is called the aggregate of feeling consisting of formations (*saṃskāra-vedanā-skandha*).
Furthermore, that aggregate of feeling consisting of formations is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change; it culminates in cessation and nirvāṇa.
"What is the aggregate of feeling associated with consciousness?
It refers to the six groups of consciousness. What are the six?
That is to say, the collection of visual consciousness up to the collection of mental consciousness; this is called the aggregate of feeling associated with consciousness.
Furthermore, that aggregate of feeling associated with consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, up to its cessation and nirvana.
“Monks! If one contemplates, examines, discerns, and accepts these teachings with wisdom, this is called ‘one who follows by faith.

Having transcended and emerged from the state of ordinary beings, though not yet having attained the fruit of stream-entry, such a person will certainly attain the fruit of stream-entry without dying in the interim.”
“Monks! If one contemplates, examines, and accepts these teachings with superior wisdom, this is called ‘Practice in Accordance with the Dharma’ (Dharmānusārī).

“Monks! When one views this Dharma with suchness and right wisdom, one knows through direct knowledge the exhaustion and abandonment of the three fetters, namely: the view of a self-identity, attachment to precepts and rituals, and doubt. Monks!”

This is called the fruit of srotāpanna; one does not fall into the evil realms, but is certain to proceed directly toward perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), being reborn seven times among gods and humans before finally reaching the ultimate end of suffering.

“Monks! If one views these phenomena with suchness and right wisdom as they really are, and no mental outflows arise, he is called an Arhat—one whose taints are exhausted, who has done what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, attained his own benefit, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and whose mind is liberated through right knowledge.”
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
62 (62) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

"There are five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādānaskandhāḥ), namely: the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha), the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha), the aggregate of mental formations (saṃskāra-skandha), and the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha)."

Ignorant, unlearned worldlings, lacking wisdom and shrouded in nescience, give rise to the view of a self toward the five aggregates of clinging and become bound by attachment; thus their minds become fixated, giving rise to craving.

"Monks! A learned noble disciple possesses wisdom and clarity; regarding these five aggregates of clinging, he does not view them as a self with attachment, nor does he allow his mind to become fettered and give rise to craving."

"How is it that foolish, unlearned worldlings, lacking wisdom and shrouded in ignorance, perceive a self within the five aggregates of clinging, becoming bound and fettered by them, and thus give rise to craving?"
"Monks! The foolish, unlearned worldling, lacking wisdom and obscured by ignorance, regards form as 'I,' or 'distinct from I,' or 'in me';
and likewise regards feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as 'I,' or 'distinct from I,' or 'in me.'"

In this way, foolish and unlearned ordinary people, lacking wisdom and obscured by ignorance, speak of a self regarding the five aggregates of clinging; thus they become bound and fettered in mind, giving rise to craving.
“Monks! How is it that a noble disciple possesses wisdom and clarity, such that he does not speak of himself as being bound by attachment, nor allow fetters to bind his mind and give rise to craving?
A noble disciple does not view form as ‘I,’ nor as ‘other than I,’ nor as ‘existing within me.’”
In this same way, one does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as self, as distinct from the self, or as existing within the self.

Thus, the learned noble disciple possesses wisdom and clarity; regarding the five aggregates of clinging, he does not perceive them as "I" or become bound by attachment, nor do they cause fetters to bind his mind and give rise to craving. Whether it be form—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; beautiful or ugly; far or near—he correctly contemplates all of it as entirely impermanent.

In this same way, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; beautiful or ugly; far or near—all of these, when correctly contemplated, are entirely impermanent.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
63 (63) Thus have I heard:

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Monks! If any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas conceive of a self, they all conceive of a self in relation to these five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādānaskandhāḥ).
What are the five?"
Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas regard form as the self, as distinct from the self, or as existing within the self;
likewise, they regard feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as the self, as distinct from the self, or as existing within the self.
In this way, ignorant and unlearned ordinary people conceive of a self and, through ignorance and discrimination, perceive things in such a manner that they do not depart from "mine-ness.
Not departing from "mine-ness," they enter into the sense faculties;
having entered into the sense faculties, contact arises.
Contacted by the six bases of contact, the foolish, unlearned worldling gives rise to suffering and pleasure; from this arise these and other states.
These are called the six groups of contact. What are the six?
That is to say: the sphere of eye-contact, and the spheres of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.
Monks! There is the element of mind, the element of phenomena, and the element of ignorance; one is touched by contact associated with ignorance.

Ignorant, unlearned worldlings speak of existence, they speak of non-existence, they speak of both existence and non-existence, they speak of neither existence nor non-existence; they say, "I am superior," or "I am equal," or "I know," or "I see."
"Furthermore, bhikṣus!
A learned noble disciple dwells within the six bases of contact and is able to become weary of and detached from ignorance, thereby giving rise to clear knowledge."

Through the fading away of ignorance, he gives rise to clear knowledge; it is neither existent nor non-existent, neither both existent and non-existent, nor neither existent nor non-existent; it is not that I am superior, nor that I am inferior, nor that I am equal; "I know" and "I see."
Having thus known and thus seen, the previously arisen contact of ignorance ceases, and the subsequently arising contact of clarity is produced.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
64 (Sūtra 64). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Eastern Park, in the Lecture Hall of Migāramātā.
Then, in the late afternoon, the World-Honored One arose from meditation, left the lecture hall, and sat down on a seat prepared before the great assembly in the shade of the hall.

“The bhikṣu who is liberated from this severs the lower fetters.

The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "The ignorant,
unlearned worldling conceives of form as 'this is me,' or 'it is other than me,' or 'it exists within me.'"
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—these are the self, or distinct from the self, or existing within one another.

A well-learned noble disciple does not view form as the self, as distinct from the self, or as existing within one another; nor do they view feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as the self, as distinct from the self, or as existing within one another;
nor are they a knower, nor are they a seer.
This form is impermanent; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.
Form is suffering; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are suffering.
Form is non-self; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-self.
This form will not exist in the future; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness will not exist in the future.
This form is subject to destruction; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are subject to destruction.
Therefore, they are not self, nor do they belong to a self; self and what belongs to a self will not exist in the future.
"One who is liberated in this way severs the five lower fetters.
At that time, the bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"

Having severed the five lower fetters, how does one attain the exhaustion of taints, with the mind liberated from taints and liberated by wisdom, knowing and realizing for oneself in this very life and dwelling in its fulfillment:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence"?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Ignorant worldlings and unlearned sentient beings give rise to fear where there is no cause for fear."
There is no self and nothing belonging to a self; both are not to be produced, yet they serve as the objective supports for the four stations of consciousness. What are these four?
That is to say: consciousness dwells in form; it takes form as its object, delights in form, and increases, expands, and grows therein.
It likewise dwells in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; it takes them as its objects, delights in them, and increases, expands, and grows therein.
Monks! In this regard, consciousness—whether coming, going, staying, arising, or ceasing—increases, expands, and grows.
If one were to say:
"There is yet another distinct phenomenon such that consciousness comes, goes, abides, arises, ceases, or increases, expands, and grows."
"Those who say this have only words; having been questioned, they do not know, and their delusion increases further, because it is not within their sphere of experience.
Why is that? O Bhikṣus!"

Having become free from craving for the realm of form, the mental fetters regarding form are also severed; once the mental fetters regarding form are severed, the cognitive objectification of consciousness is also severed.

Consciousness no longer dwells there, nor does it further increase, expand, or grow. Having become free from craving for the realms of feeling, perception, and formations, the mental fetters regarding feeling, perception, and formations are also severed.

Once the mental fetters of feeling, perception, and formations have been severed, their objective referents are also severed; consciousness has no place to abide and can no longer further increase, expand, or grow.

Because consciousness has no abiding place, it does not increase; because it does not increase, there is nothing to be done; because there is nothing to be done, one abides; because one abides, one is content; because one is content, one is liberated; because one is liberated, one grasps at nothing whatsoever in all the worlds; because one grasps at nothing, one is without attachment; because one is without attachment, one personally realizes nirvana, knowing:
"Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and I myself know that there will be no further existence."

"Monks! I say that consciousness does not abide in the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, or below—except for the vision of the Dharma, which is nirvāṇa, cessation, tranquility, and coolness."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The arising and ceasing through lack of delight, And the observation of the three kinds of conceptualization,
attachment, and so forth— This is called the Udāna.
65 (Sixty-fifth). Thus have I heard:

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

How does one observe according to reality?
"This is form; this is the origin of form; this is the cessation of form.

An ignorant, unlearned worldling does not contemplate painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings as they truly are.

With clinging as condition, there is becoming; with becoming as condition, birth; and with birth as condition, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, despair, and suffering."

In this way, this entire great mass of suffering arises from its accumulation; this is called the accumulation of form, and this is called the accumulation of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"What is the cessation of form, and the cessation of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?"

The learned noble disciple experiences feelings of pain, pleasure, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure; he observes them as they truly are. Because he observes the arising of feeling, the cessation of feeling, the gratification of feeling, the danger of feeling, and the escape from feeling as they truly are, his attachment to feeling ceases. Through the cessation of attachment, clinging ceases; through the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; through the cessation of existence, birth ceases; and through the cessation of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, despair, and suffering cease. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering is utterly extinguished. This is called the cessation of form, and the cessation of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"Therefore, bhikṣus!
You should always cultivate skillful means and meditative reflection, bringing the mind to inner stillness.
Bhikṣus!"
“Abiding in meditative reflection, internally quieting the mind, and applying diligent skillful means, one observes things as they truly are.

68 (68) Thus have I heard:

In the same manner, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are explained at length; this, bhikṣus, is called the path leading to the origination of the body.

What is the path leading to the cessation of the existence-body?
