As it was taught regarding "existence" (bhava), so too should it be understood and explained for "that which is to be known" (ājñeya).
70. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now explain the limit of suffering regarding the body of existence, the limit of the origin of the body of existence, and the limit of the cessation of the body of existence.
Listen attentively and reflect well upon it; I shall speak for you."
What is the limit of suffering regarding the body?
It refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandhāḥ*). What are the five?
The aggregate of form and the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—these are called the limit of suffering regarding the existence-body (*sakkāya*).
What is the limit of the origin of the existence-body?
It refers to the craving for future existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding pleasure and attachment in this and that; this is called the limit of the origin of the existence-body.
What is the limit of the cessation of the existence-body (*bhavānta*)?

It is the craving for future existence that accompanies this very feeling, joined with lust and delight, and the attachment to this and that; the remainderless cutting off, vomiting out, exhaustion, fading away, cessation, stilling, and disappearance of these—this is called the limit of the cessation of the existence-body.
"Therefore, I shall speak of the limit of suffering regarding the body, the limit of the origin of the body, and the limit of the cessation of the body.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As it was taught regarding "existence" (*bhava*) and "that which should be known," so too should it be explained. 71 (71). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now speak of the body of existence, the origin of the body of existence, the cessation of the body of existence, and the path leading to the cessation of the body of existence."
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall explain it for you.
What is the "existence with a body"?
It refers to the five aggregates of clinging.
What are the five?
They are the aggregate of form, and the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; these are called the "body of existence" (sakkāya).
What is the origin of the body of existence?
Craving for future existence, accompanied by lust and delight, which leads to attachment here and there—this is called the origin of the personal existence (*sakkāya*).
What is the cessation of the personal existence?

The complete abandonment, relinquishing, exhaustion, fading away, and cessation of craving for future existence, accompanied by lust and delight, and the non-attachment to it without remainder—this is called the cessation of the personal existence.
"What is the path leading to the cessation of the existence-body?

It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This is called the path leading to the cessation of the existence-body."

"This is what is called: 'the existence of the body, the origin of the existence of the body, the cessation of the existence of the body, and the path leading to the cessation of the existence of the body.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The rest is as previously stated.
The distinction is as follows:

"One should know the existence-body; one should know the abandonment of the accumulation of the existence-body; one should know the realization of the cessation of the existence-body; and one should know the cultivation of the path leading to the abandonment of the existence-body."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As it was taught regarding "existence" (bhava), so too should it be understood regarding "that which is to be known" (ājñeya); it is to be explained in the same manner.
Furthermore, as for the distinctions:

"A bhikṣu knows the existence-body (satkāya), abandons the accumulation of the existence-body, realizes the cessation of the existence-body, and cultivates the path that abandons the existence-body. This is called a bhikṣu who has severed the bonds of craving and desire, the fetters, and other such dharmas; he has cultivated clear realization (abhisamaya) and reached the ultimate end of suffering."
Furthermore, as for the distinctions:
"This is called a bhikṣu who has reached the ultimate limit, who is ultimately free from defilement, who has perfected the holy life, and who is a pure and supreme person."
Furthermore, as for the distinction:

"This is called a bhikṣu who is an arhat, one who has exhausted all taints (āsrava), accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, attained his own benefit, completely destroyed the fetters of existence, and whose mind is liberated through right knowledge."
Furthermore, as for the distinctions:
"This is called a bhikṣu who has severed the barriers, crossed the moat, transcended the boundaries, escaped from all sentries, and raised the banner of the Noble Dharma."
Furthermore, as for the distinctions:
"What is the severing of the barrier?
It refers to the severing of the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni*)."
What is meant by "crossing the moat"?
It means crossing the deep moat of ignorance.
What is meant by "transcending the realm"?
This refers to the ultimate end of beginningless birth and death.
How does one escape all sentries?
It is through the exhaustion of craving.
"How does one raise the banner of the noble Dharma?
It means the exhaustion of the conceit 'I am'.
Furthermore, there is another distinction:

"This is called a bhikṣu who has severed the five branches, perfected the six branches, guarded one, relied upon the fourfold, abandoned all truths, detached from all seeking, purified his thoughts, stilled bodily activity, and is well-liberated in mind and well-liberated through wisdom; he stands alone in the pure conduct of the Brahma-faring, an unsurpassed being."
There are three kinds of paths, And likewise three kinds of true awakening;
The body is said to be of four kinds, And the Arhat is of six kinds. (72) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now speak of the dharmas to be known, of knowledge, and of the knower.”
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall explain it for you.
What are the phenomena that are to be known?
They are the five aggregates of clinging.
What are the five?
They are the aggregate of form, and the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
these are called the phenomena to be known. What is wisdom?
To subdue desire, sever desire, and transcend desire—this is called wisdom.
"Who is the wise one? It is the Arhat."

An Arhat does not exist after death in another world, nor is it that he does not exist after death in another world, nor is it that he both exists and does not exist after death in another world, nor is it that he neither exists nor does not exist after death in another world; this is explained at length as being immeasurable, for all conceptual reckonings have been eternally extinguished.
"This is called the teaching on the objects of knowledge, the wisdom, and the knower.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
73 (Seventy-three). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now explain the heavy burden, the taking up of the burden, the laying down of the burden, and the bearer of the burden.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you.
What is the heavy burden?"
They are the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandhāḥ*). What are the five?

They are the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), and the aggregates of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), and consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
“What is the taking up of the burden?
It is craving for future existence, accompanied by lust and delight, finding pleasure and attachment in this and that.
What is the laying down of the burden?”

If there is craving for the future, accompanied by lust and delight, which leads to attachment to this and that—when this has been abandoned without remainder, ceased, vomited out, exhausted, detached from desire, extinguished, and vanished.
“What is the bearer? It is the person.
A person is one who has such a name, such a birth, such a clan, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, such longevity, such a duration of stay, and such a limit to their lifespan.”
"These are called the heavy burden, the taking up of the burden, the laying down of the burden, and the bearer of the burden.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The heavy burden has been laid down; One should not take it up again."
The burden of responsibility is great suffering; relinquishing that burden is great bliss.
One should sever all craving, thereby exhausting all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
Having clearly understood the realm of remainder, one shall no longer return to rebirth.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
74 (74) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are five aggregates of clinging. What are the five?
The form-aggregate of clinging, and the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness-aggregates of clinging.
An ignorant, unlearned worldling does not know, as it truly is, form, the origin of form, the cessation of form, the gratification of form, the danger of form, and the escape from form.

Because they do not know things as they truly are, they dwell delighting in, praising, and becoming attached to form; bound by the fetters of form and bound by internal fetters, they do not know its root, they do not know its limit, and they do not know the way out—these are called foolish, unlearned worldlings.
Bound by fetters, one is born; bound by fetters, one dies; bound by fetters, one passes from this world to another world.
There too, again, one is born bound by fetters and dies bound by fetters; such is called an ignorant, unlearned worldling.
They follow the sovereignty of Māra, entering into Māra’s net; they follow what is transformed by Māra, bound by Māra’s fetters, and led astray by Māra.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise thus.
“The learned noble disciple knows form as it really is, the arising of form, the cessation of form, the gratification of form, the danger of form, and the escape from form.

Because he knows them as they really are, he does not crave or delight in form; he does not praise it, nor does he dwell attached to it. He is not bound by the fetter of form, nor is he bound by internal fetters. He knows the root, he knows the crossing over, and he knows the transcendence; such a one is called a learned noble disciple.”

He is not born bound, nor does he die bound; he does not go from this world to another world bound. He is not subject to the sovereignty of Māra, does not fall into the hands of Māra, does not follow what is done by Māra, is not bound by Māra, is liberated from the bonds of Māra, and is free from being led away by Māra.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
75 (75) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandhāḥ*).
What are the five? [They are as follows:]"

That is to say, regarding the aggregate of form and feeling, a bhikṣu becomes weary of form, detaches from desire for it, brings it to cessation, does not give rise to it, and attains liberation; this is called a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Likewise, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, he becomes weary of them, detaches from desire for them, brings them to cessation, does not give rise to them, and attains liberation; this is called a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha.
When a bhikṣu also becomes weary of form, detached from desire for it, and brings about its cessation, he is called an arhat liberated by wisdom;

likewise, when he becomes weary of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, detached from desire for them, and brings about their cessation, he is called an arhat liberated by wisdom.
“Bhikkhus!
What is the difference between a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, and one who is an Arhat liberated by wisdom?
The bhikkhu addressed the Buddha:

“The Tathāgata is the root of the Dharma, the eye of the Dharma, and the refuge of the Dharma. We pray that the World-Honored One will explain this matter in detail for the sake of the bhikṣus; having heard it, the bhikṣus shall receive and practice it accordingly.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you.

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—having realized the Dharma through his own awakening without having heard it from others, and having attained unsurpassed Bodhi—will, in future ages, awaken the śrāvakas and preach the Dharma to them, namely: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path.”

"Monks! This is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who has attained what was not yet attained, realized what was not yet realized; who knows the path, discerns the path, teaches the path, and masters the path; and who is further able to accomplish the instruction and admonition for all śrāvakas.
Thus he speaks correctly and in accordance with the Dharma, delighting in wholesome qualities. This is called the distinction between the Tathāgata and the arhats."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
76 (76) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are five aggregates of clinging. What are the five?
The aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
You, monks, should contemplate form; having contemplated form, do you see it as the self, as distinct from the self, or as existing within the self?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha,
“No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Excellent! Excellent!
Form is non-self; that which is non-self is impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering.”
If it is suffering, one should contemplate that all of it is not self, is not distinct from the self, and does not exist within the self;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
The learned noble disciple contemplates these five aggregates of clinging as not-self and not belonging to self.
Having contemplated them thus, he grasps at nothing in the world;
and by grasping at nothing, he is not attached.
One who is free from attachment realizes nirvana for oneself:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I myself know that there will be no further existence."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
77 (77) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should sever craving and lust for form; once craving and lust for form are severed, then form is severed;
once form is severed, one attains the knowledge of its cessation."
Once this knowledge of abandonment is attained, the root is severed.
Just as when the head of a *tāla* tree is cut off, it will never grow again in the future;
so too, when desire and greed for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are abandoned, they will never arise again in future lives.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
78 (78) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“If form arises, abides, and ceases, then suffering arises therein, illness abides therein, and old age and death cease therein;
the same is said for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”
"Monks! If form ceases, subsides, and vanishes, then suffering ceases therein, illness subsides therein, and old age and death vanish therein;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
79 (79) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Past and future form are still impermanent, how much more so present form!

Having observed this, the learned noble disciple does not look back to past form, does not delight in future form, and regarding present form, feels weary of it, becomes free from desire for it, and attains its cessation and tranquility."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
"Monks, if past form did not exist, the well-taught noble disciple would not be free from concern regarding past form; [but because it does exist, he is so]."
Because past form exists, the learned noble disciple does not look back upon past form.
If future form did not exist, the learned noble disciple would not fail to delight in future form;
because future form exists, the learned noble disciple does not delight in future form.
If present form did not exist, the learned noble disciple would not give rise to disenchantment toward present form, nor would they proceed toward detachment from it and its cessation;
because present form does exist, the learned noble disciple gives rise to disenchantment toward present form and proceeds toward detachment from it and its cessation.
"Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also to be explained in this same way.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As with the discourse on impermanence, so too are the three discourses on suffering, emptiness, and non-self spoken in this same manner. 80 (80). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now speak of the Seal of the Noble Dharma and the Purification of Vision.
Listen attentively and reflect well upon it."
If there is a bhikṣu who makes this statement:
"I have not yet attained anything regarding the samādhi of emptiness, yet I have given rise to the knowledge and vision of signlessness, nothingness, and freedom from conceit."
Do not speak thus. Why is this?
If one who has not yet attained emptiness were to claim, "I have attained the signless, the non-existent, and the knowledge and vision free from conceit," such a thing is impossible!
If there is a bhikṣu who speaks thus:
"I have attained emptiness, and am able to give rise to the signless, the nothingness,
and the knowledge and vision free from conceit," this is well-spoken.
Why is this? If, having attained emptiness, one is able to give rise to the signless, the non-existent, and the knowledge and vision that is free from conceit—this is indeed possible!
"What is meant by 'the noble disciple and the purification of vision'?
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"The Buddha is the root of the Dharma, the eye of the Dharma, and the refuge of the Dharma; we only pray that you will explain this for us!"
Having heard the teaching on the Dharma, the bhikṣus practiced in accordance with what was taught.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place or at the foot of a tree, he should skillfully contemplate that form is impermanent, subject to decay, and a phenomenon characterized by the fading away of desire."
In this way, one contemplates feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as impermanent, subject to decay, and phenomena characterized by dispassion.
Contemplating those aggregates as impermanent, subject to decay, unstable, and subject to change, with a mind that is joyful, pure, and liberated—this is called emptiness.
One who contemplates in this manner is still unable to abandon conceit, even though their knowledge and vision are pure.

Furthermore, there is the samādhi of right reflection, which contemplates the cessation of the characteristics of form, and the cessation of the characteristics of sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena; this is called the signless (animitta).
One who contemplates in this manner has not yet abandoned conceit, nor is their knowledge and vision completely purified.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of right reflection, which observes the severance of the marks of greed and the severance of the marks of hatred and delusion; this is called "nothingness."
One who contemplates in this manner has not yet abandoned conceit, nor is their knowledge and vision completely purified.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of right reflection, in which one observes: "From what does my 'self' arise?"
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of right reflection, which observes that the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self" arise from what is seen, heard, smelled, tasted, touched, or cognized.
Again, he observes thus:
"If consciousness arises by means of causes and conditions, are those causes and conditions of that consciousness permanent or impermanent?"
"Furthermore, he reflects thus:
'If consciousness arises by means of causes and conditions, then those causes and those conditions are all impermanent.
Moreover, since those causes and those conditions are all impermanent, how could the consciousness produced by them be permanent?"

"That which is impermanent is conditioned, volitional, and dependently arisen; it is subject to affliction, subject to cessation, subject to dispassion, and subject to abandonment through knowledge. This is called the Noble Seal of Dharma, the purification of knowledge and vision;
this is what is called the monk’s teaching on the Noble Seal of Dharma, the purification of knowledge and vision... Thus it is explained in detail.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
81 (81) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, in the Gabled Lecture Hall beside the Monkey Pond.
At that time, there was a Licchavi named Mahānāman who used to travel about daily to visit the Buddha.
On one occasion, that Licchavi had this thought:

"If I go to the World-Honored One's dwelling early, both the World-Honored One and the bhikṣus who are my acquaintances will all be absorbed in meditation; I shall now go instead to the place where the heterodox teacher Acelaka Kāśyapa resides at the Seven Mango Trees."
He then went to the dwelling place of Pūraṇa Kāśyapa.

At that time, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa—the leader of a group of non-Buddhist outsiders—was surrounded by five hundred non-Buddhists before and behind him, laughing loudly and playing, while discussing worldly matters.
At that time, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa saw Mahānāma the Licchavi approaching from afar and told his followers to remain silent:
"Be quiet! Be silent!"

"This Licchavi Mahānāma is a disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama; he is a lay disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama who is the foremost among those in Vaiśālī. He always delights in tranquility and praises tranquility; wherever he goes, he approaches a community of tranquility. Therefore, you all should be tranquil."
Then Mahānāma went to where Pūraṇa Kāśyapa was, exchanged greetings with him, and after exchanging polite inquiries and expressions of courtesy, sat down to one side.
At that time, Mahānāma said to Pūraṇa:
"I have heard, Pūraṇa, that you preach the Dharma to your disciples thus:
'Without cause and without condition, sentient beings become defiled; without cause and without condition, sentient beings become pure.'"
"There is such a discourse in the world; do you truly have this yourself, or is it merely the disparaging speech of outsiders?

Is what has been composed by worldly people in accordance with the Dharma or contrary to the Dharma? Have there been any instances where worldly people have collectively debated, questioned, or censured it?"
Pūraṇa Kāśyapa said:
"This doctrine is indeed real; it is not a mere worldly rumor.

I have established this doctrine as a teaching in accordance with the Dharma. All these teachings I proclaim are consistent with the Dharma, and there is no one among the people of the world who comes to challenge, question, or censure them."
Why is that? Mahānāma!
I see it thus and speak thus:
“‘Without cause and without condition, sentient beings become defiled; without cause and without condition, sentient beings become pure.

At that time, Mahānāma, having heard what Pūraṇa had said, was not pleased in his heart. After rebuking him, he rose from his seat and went to where the Blessed One was. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and related to the Buddha in detail the matter he had previously discussed with Pūraṇa.
The Buddha told Mahānāman the Licchavi:
"That Pūraṇa speaks out of his own whims; it is not worth recording.
Thus, Pūraṇa is foolish, lacking discernment, unskilled, and speaking thus without cause."
"It is without cause and without condition that sentient beings become defiled; it is without cause and without condition that sentient beings become pure. Why is this?
It is with cause and with condition that sentient beings become defiled; it is with cause and with condition that sentient beings become pure.
“Mahānāma! For what cause and for what condition are sentient beings defiled? For what cause and for what condition are sentient beings purified? Mahānāma!”

If form were exclusively suffering—neither pleasure, nor accompanied by pleasure, nor nourished by pleasure, nor separated from pleasure—sentient beings would not, on account of it, give rise to attachment.

Mahānāma! Because form is not exclusively suffering, but is pleasure, accompanied by pleasure, nourished by pleasure, and inseparable from pleasure, sentient beings become stained by and attached to form;
because of attachment they are bound, and because of being bound they experience affliction.

Mahānāma! If feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness were exclusively suffering—neither pleasure, nor accompanied by pleasure, nor nourished by pleasure, nor separated from pleasure—sentient beings would not, on account of them, give rise to attachment with delight.
Mahānāma! Because consciousness is not exclusively suffering, but is pleasure, is nurtured by pleasure, is inseparable from pleasure, sentient beings become stained and attached to consciousness;
through attachment they are bound, and through being bound they give rise to affliction.
Mahānāma! This is called having causes and conditions for the defilement of sentient beings. Mahānāma!
For what cause and for what reason are sentient beings purified? Mahānāma!

If form were exclusively pleasure—neither suffering, nor accompanied by suffering, nor nourished by sorrowful suffering, and free from suffering—sentient beings would not, on account of form, give rise to disenchantment.

Mahānāma! Because form is not exclusively pleasant, but is suffering, accompanied by suffering, nourished by sorrow and pain, and inseparable from suffering, sentient beings feel weary of and detached from form;
through weariness they do not delight in it, and through lack of delight they attain liberation.

Mahānāma! If feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness were exclusively pleasant—neither painful, nor accompanied by pain, nor nourished by grief and suffering, and were free from suffering—sentient beings would not experience weariness and detachment toward consciousness.

Mahānāma! Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not exclusively pleasant, but are suffering, accompanied by suffering, nourished by sorrow and suffering, and inseparable from suffering, sentient beings feel weary of and detached from consciousness;
through weariness they do not delight in it, and through lack of delight they are liberated.
"Mahānāma! This is called the purification of sentient beings through causes and conditions.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Mahānāma rejoiced and approved with gladness; he paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew.
Knowing the Dharma and the heavy burden; approaching, observing, the arising of sensual desire, and the brief summary;
the Dharma-seal and Pūraṇa. (82) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Cetiya.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“In what regard does a learned noble disciple perceive impermanence and suffering?”
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The World-Honored One is the root of the Dharma, the eye of the Dharma, and the refuge of the Dharma; we pray that you will explain it for us!
Having heard it, the bhikṣus shall practice in accordance with your instructions.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you.
A learned noble disciple perceives form as impermanent and suffering; he perceives feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as impermanent and suffering.”
“Bhikṣus!
Is form permanent or impermanent?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha:
“Impermanent, Blessed One. “Monks!”
“Is that which is impermanent suffering?

What is "perfection of protection"?

It refers to when a son of good family possesses money and grain acquired through skillful means, produced by his own hand, and obtained in accordance with the Dharma; he is able to protect them thoroughly so that kings, thieves, water, or fire do not plunder, carry off, flood, or destroy them. "What is meant by being endowed with right livelihood?

one will attain peace in this very life and dwell in happiness in this very life.
"In future lives, you shall dwell in joy and happiness.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Ujjaya, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and approved with gladness; he paid homage and departed.
92 (Ninety-two). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of Kosala and arrived at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there lived in the kingdom of Śrāvastī a haughty brāhmaṇa whose parents and lineage were both pure and without blemish, a man capable of eloquent exposition. For seven generations his ancestry had been entirely pure;

he served as a teacher to other brāhmaṇas, was proficient in discourse, and fully mastered all treatises and scriptures. He understood the relative merits of various doctrines and clearly distinguished them; he was skilled in explaining every word and phrase, and his appearance was handsome.

Or they may be born with pride regarding their lineage, pride regarding their clan, pride regarding their physical appearance, pride regarding their intelligence, or pride regarding their wealth, such that they do not respect their parents, elders, or teachers.
Having heard that the śramaṇa Gautama was wandering among the people of Kosala and had arrived at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, he thought to himself:
"I shall go to where that śramaṇa Gautama is; whatever he may have to say, I shall debate with him."
"Since there is nothing to be said, I shall return in silence.

At that time, the arrogant brāhmaṇa, riding in a white horse chariot and escorted before and behind by young brāhmaṇas, carrying a golden-handled parasol and holding a golden pitcher in his hand, went to see the World-Honored One.
Upon reaching the garden gate, he descended from his carriage and proceeded on foot.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the great assembly as he preached the Dharma, and he occasionally turned his attention toward the arrogant Brahmin.
At that time, the arrogant brahmin thought to himself, "The śramaṇa Gautama pays no heed to me; I shall now depart.
Then, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the mind of the arrogant brahmin, spoke these verses:
“Since you, Māna, have come here, your unwholesome pride increases further.
Because you came for the sake of the Dharma, you should instead increase your practice of that Dharma.
At that time, the brahmin Māna thought to himself:
“The śramaṇa Gautama already knows my mind,” [he thought],
and wished to pay his respects.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the arrogant brāhmaṇa:
"Stop! Stop! There is no need to prostrate; the purity of your mind is sufficient."
At that time, the entire great assembly cried out in unison with loud voices:
"How marvelous!
World-Honored One!"
"Venerable and of great power!

This arrogant Brahmin now relies on the arrogance of his birth, the arrogance of his lineage, the arrogance of his physical appearance, the arrogance of his intelligence, and the arrogance of his wealth; he does not respect his parents, elders, or teachers, yet now before the śramaṇa Gautama he humbles himself most deeply, desiring to prostrate at his feet."
Then, the arrogant brahmin called for silence before the great assembly and spoke these verses:
"How does one not give rise to pride?
How does one give rise to reverence?"
"What is skillful consolation?
What is skillful making of offerings?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"Parents, elder brothers, preceptors, various teachers and elders,
and all those who are worthy of respect— one should never give rise to arrogance toward them.
One should instead show sincere reverence, remain humble, and offer salutations."
Serving with all one's heart, providing every kind of offering;
free from the minds of greed, hatred, and delusion, an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted,
perfectly liberated through right wisdom, and having subdued all prideful thoughts.
"To these noble ones and sages, I join my palms and pay homage with my head bowed.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached various teachings for the arrogant brahmin, instructing, exhorting, illuminating, and gladdening him.

Just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, teaches the Dharma in successive stages—expounding upon the merits of giving, ethical discipline, and rebirth in heaven; the gratification, the danger, and the defilement of sensual desires; and the purification, the renunciation, the seclusion, and all factors conducive to purity... thus he taught extensively. It is like a pure white cloth, free from all black stains, which quickly takes on the color of the dye.
At that very seat, the arrogant brāhmaṇa realized the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—and attained immediate and perfect realization (*abhisamaya*).

At that time, the arrogant brāhmaṇa saw the Dharma, attained the Dharma, knew the Dharma, and entered the Dharma; he crossed beyond all doubt and uncertainty, and without depending on others for his deliverance, he attained fearlessness within the True Dharma.
He immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, prostrated before the Buddha, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha:
"May I now go forth in the True Dharma and receive full ordination?"
The Buddha told the arrogant brāhmaṇa:
"You may now go forth in this True Dharma and receive full ordination.
He immediately went forth and, reflecting correctly and alone, [attained realization].
"Therefore, noble son, having shaved off hair and beard, donned the saṃghāṭī robe, and with right faith gone forth from home into homelessness to study the Path...
[he] attained arhatship, with a mind well-liberated."
93 (Ninisan): Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of Kosala and arrived at Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a tall-bodied brahmin who organized such a heterodox grand assembly: seven hundred bulls were tied in rows to pillars; bulls, cows, water buffaloes, various sheep and lambs, and all kinds of small insects were likewise bound. He prepared various foods and drinks and practiced extensive almsgiving, while followers of various non-Buddhist paths from every country gathered at the site of this heterodox grand assembly.
At that time, the brahmin Dīrgha heard that the śramaṇa Gautama had been wandering among the people of Kosala and had arrived at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
He thought to himself:
"I am now preparing a grand and magnificent assembly; for this reason, seven hundred bulls have been lined up and tied to posts, and even the smallest insects have all been bound."
"Because of this great festival of heterodox practices (*pāṣaṇḍa-mahāmaha*), various followers of different paths have come from all the kingdoms to the site of the assembly.

I shall now go to the place where the śramaṇa Gautama is to inquire about the methods of these heterodox festivals, so that my great festival of heterodox practices will not suffer any deficiency in its constituent elements."

Having formed this thought, he mounted a white horse chariot, accompanied by young Brahmins leading and following him in front and behind; holding a golden-handled parasol and grasping a golden water-pitcher, he departed from Śrāvastī and went to where the World-Honored One was, to pay his respects and serve him.

Upon reaching the gate of the vihāra, he alighted from his carriage and proceeded on foot. Arriving before the Buddha, he exchanged greetings and inquiries of courtesy with the Buddha face-to-face; having done so, he withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Gautama!..."
I now wish to perform a grand sacrificial assembly of heresy; seven hundred bulls have been tied in rows to pillars, and even the smallest of insects have all been bound.
Because of the great festival of the heretics, people from various different paths have all come from their respective countries to the site of the heretics' festival.
Furthermore, it has been heard that Gautama is traveling through the human realm of Kosala and has arrived at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, in the city of Śrāvastī.

I have now come specifically to inquire of Gautama regarding the quantities of the various items for the Great Assembly of the Heretics, so that there may be no deficiency among the various components of the Great Assembly of the Heretics that I am to organize.
The Buddha told the brahmin:

"There may be a master of a great heretical assembly who, while practicing giving and performing meritorious deeds, generates demerit; he is carved and cut by the three swords and obtains an unwholesome karmic retribution."
What are the three?
They are the sword of body, the sword of speech, and the sword of mind.
What is the sword of mind that gives rise to various retributive sufferings?
Suppose a festival organizer prepares for a great assembly and thinks to himself:
"In order to hold this grand and magnificent festival, I shall slaughter so many young bulls, so many water-buffaloes and buffalocows, so many lambs and calves, as well as various kinds of insects."
"This is called the sword of the mind giving rise to various retributions of suffering.
Thus, although such a donor intends to perform various acts of giving and various offerings, they actually produce sin!"
"What is meant by the sword of the mouth giving rise to various retributions of suffering?
There was once a leader of a great assembly who organized a massive gathering and gave this instruction:
'I am now holding a grand, heterodox assembly; you must slaughter such-and-such numbers of young bulls, and even kill such-and-such numbers of minute insects.'"
"This is called the sword of the mouth producing various retributions of suffering; although the master of the great assembly performs such giving and offerings, it actually produces sin!
What is meant by the sword of the body producing various retributions of suffering?"

This refers to a case where a master of a great assembly organizes such a gathering and, with his own hands, slaughters a certain number of bulls, even down to killing various kinds of minute insects; this is called the retribution of suffering arising from the sword of the body.
Although that master of the great assembly thinks thus, performing various kinds of giving and various kinds of offerings, he actually generates demerit!
"However, O Brahmin, you should diligently make offerings to the three fires, honoring them at the proper times, prostrating and serving them, and bestowing peace and happiness upon them."
What are the three?
First is the root, second is the household, and third is the field of merit.
What is the fire of the root?
To serve, attend to, and make offerings with respect at all times, bestowing peace and happiness upon them— namely, when a son, through skillful means,

acquires wealth through the diligent toil of his own hands and feet, and having obtained it in accordance with the Dharma, makes offerings to his parents and enables them to attain peace and happiness— this is called the "Root Fire."
Why is it called the "root"?
If a son of good family is born from them—namely, his father and mother—they are therefore called the root.
Because the son of good family honors the root, he at all times shows reverence, serves and makes offerings to them, bestowing peace and happiness upon them.
“What is the fire of the household?
Noble son, it is that which nurtures and provides comfort and happiness at the proper times.

That is to say, noble son, one acquires wealth through skillful means, with diligent toil of hand and foot, obtained in accordance with the Dharma; one provides for one’s wife, children, kinsmen, retinue, servants, and laborers, giving them at the proper times and bestowing respect and comfort—this is called the fire of the household.”
Why is it called a "house"?

Because when that son of good family dwells in the household, he shares in joy when there is joy and shares in suffering when there is suffering; in all his actions, they follow one another in harmony, and for this reason it is called a house.
Therefore, son of good family, provide for them according to the season and bestow peace and happiness upon them.
What is called the "field of fire"?
Son of good family, how does one show respect, honor, and make offerings according to the season, bestowing peace and happiness?

It refers to a son of good family who acquires wealth through skillful means and diligent labor of hand and foot, obtained in accordance with the Dharma, and offers it as service and support to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who are well able to subdue greed, hatred, and delusion. To establish such śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas as fields of merit, to revere and advance toward them, and to delight in sharing the fruits of that merit so as to be reborn in heaven in the future—this is called the "fire of the field."
Why is it called a "field"?
Because it serves as a field of merit for the world, meaning it is worthy of offerings; therefore, it is called a "field.
These sons of good family, according to the occasion, show respect, serve, and make offerings to it, bestowing peace and happiness upon it.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The root and the household, the fire of the field of merit worthy of offerings—
this fire increases through offerings, providing sufficiency, peace, and happiness."
The wise, who find joy in a world free from fault, are reborn there;
like wealth acquired through Dharma, they reunite with those worthy of support.
Because they honor those who should be honored, they are born in heaven and attain renown.
“However, brahmin!
Now, the three fires that a son of good family previously made offerings to should be abandoned and extinguished.
What are these three?
These are the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion.

Why is this so? If the fire of lust is neither severed nor extinguished, it harms oneself, harms others, and harms both self and others; one incurs fault in the present life, incurs fault in future lives, and incurs fault in both the present and future lives. Based on that, mental states of sorrow and suffering arise. The fires of hatred and delusion are likewise.
"O Brahmin!
If a son of good family tends a fire of piled wood, undergoing hardship at all times—kindling it at times and extinguishing it at times—he suffers due to these causal conditions."
At that time, the brahmin Dīrgha remained silent.
Then, there was a son of a brahmin named Uttara, who was seated among the assembly.
The tall-bodied brahmin remained silent for a moment;

having reflected, he said to Uttara, "Are you able to go to the site of the sacrificial assembly and release that bull tied to the pillar, as well as all those living beings who are bound, setting them all free?"
And he spoke to him, saying:
"The tall-bodied Brahmin said to you:
'Act as you please; in the mountains, marshes, and vast wilderness, eat the uncut grass and drink the pure flowing water, enjoying all manner of pleasures amidst the winds from the four directions.'"
Uttara replied, "I shall follow the Great Master’s instruction!
He then went to that site of the heterodox festival, released all the sentient beings, and addressed them, saying:
The tall-bodied brahmin said to you:
"Go wherever you please; in the mountains, marshes, or wilderness, drink water, eat grass, and find comfort in the four winds."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing Uttara, and having known him,
preached the Dharma to the brahmin Dīrgha in various ways, instructing, exhorting, illuminating, and gladdening him.

In accordance with the Vinaya, the Blessed One taught the Dharma in its proper sequence: he spoke of the precepts, of giving, and of the merit of rebirth in heaven; he revealed and made manifest the gratification and the peril of sensual desires, as well as the escape from them, purification, and the purification of the afflictions.
Just as fresh, clean white cotton cloth easily takes dye, so it was with the long-bodied brāhmaṇa.
Right there on his seat, he perceived the Four Noble Truths and attained immediate realization.

At that time, the brahmin Dīrgha saw the Dharma, attained the Dharma, knew the Dharma, and entered the Dharma; he crossed beyond all doubts and perplexities, no longer relying on others for guidance, and attained fearlessness within the True Dharma.
He immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
"I have crossed over, World-Honored One!
From this day forth for as long as my life lasts, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus; may you accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka) and bear witness to this."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly, will accept my meal.
At that time, the World-Honored One silently granted his consent.
Then, the brahmin Dīrgha, knowing that the Buddha had accepted his invitation, paid homage to the Buddha, circumambulated him three times to the right, and departed.
The tall-bodied brahmin returned to his residence and prepared all manner of pure and exquisite offerings. He arranged the seats and sent a messenger to invite the Buddha, saying:
"The time has come; may the Holy One know it is time."
At that time, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and, surrounded by a great assembly, went to the meeting place of the brahmin Dīrgha and sat down before the multitude.
Then, when the brahmin Dīrgha knew that the World-Honored One was seated, he personally served various kinds of food and drink.

When the meal was finished, and the washing of hands, rinsing, and cleaning of the bowl were complete, he spread out a low seat separately and sat upright at the head of the great assembly to listen to the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having taught, instructed, illuminated, and gladdened the brahmin Dīrgha with various dharmas, rose from his seat and departed.
94 (Ninety-four). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a young brahmin named Saṃkāra who came to where the Buddha was. After exchanging greetings and polite inquiries with the World-Honored One, he withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Gautama! How can one recognize an unwholesome man?
The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa:
"It is like the moon.
The Brahmin asked again:
"Virtuous man, how can this be known?"
The Buddha told the brahmin,
"It is like the moon.
The brahmin addressed the Buddha:
“How is it that an unwholesome man is like the moon?
The Buddha told the brahmin:
“Just as during the dark fortnight of the moon, its radiance is lost, its color is lost, its connection [to the sky] is lost, and it wanes day by night until it no longer appears.”

In this way, there are those who, in the presence of the Tathāgata, attain a mind of faith and devotion, uphold the pure precepts, cultivate learning through diligent study, practice selfless generosity, and maintain right view regarding reality.

Having cultivated pure faith, ethical discipline, generosity, extensive learning, and upright right view toward the Tathāgata, they subsequently fall away; they completely forget and lose their ethical discipline, learning, generosity, and right view, wasting away day and night until, in even a mere moment, everything is entirely lost.
"Furthermore, brahmin!

If a son of good family does not associate with virtuous friends, does not frequently hear the Dharma, and does not engage in correct reflection; he practices evil conduct of body, evil conduct of speech, and evil conduct of mind."
Due to the causes and conditions of having committed evil, at the breaking up of the body after death, he falls into the miserable destinies, into hell.
Thus it is, brahmin;
an unwholesome man is like the moon.
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying,
"In what way is this son of good family like the moon?
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"Just as the light of the bright phase of the full moon increases in radiance and color day and night until it reaches its fullness, becoming perfectly pure and complete;

so too, noble son, one who gains pure faith in the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata sees their right view become truly pure and increasingly radiant. Their virtue increases, their generosity increases, their learning increases, and their wisdom increases, growing day and night.

Furthermore, at another time, by associating with spiritual friends, hearing the teaching of the True Dharma, reflecting correctly within, and practicing wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind—for these causes and conditions, when the body breaks up and life ends, they are reborn spontaneously in the heavens."
"O Brahmin! Therefore, a son of good family is like the moon.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Just as the stainless moon, traversing the void,
possesses the most brilliant radiance among all the minor stars;
so too is pure faith, which, through precepts, learning, and the relinquishing of stinginess in giving,"
"In a world full of stinginess, his generosity stands out with particular clarity.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the brahmin Saṃkāśya, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and delighted in it; he rose from his seat and departed.
95 (95) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a certain Brahmin named Janaka came to where the Buddha was. After exchanging greetings and polite inquiries with the World-Honored One, he withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Gautama! I have heard you, Gautama, say:
'One should give only to me; one should not give to others.'"
Giving to me yields great fruit; giving to others does not yield great fruit.
One should give to my disciples and not to the disciples of others;
by giving to my disciples one obtains a great reward, whereas by giving to the disciples of others one does not obtain a great reward.
"How so? Gautama! Is one who speaks thus speaking the truth?"
"Is this not an act of slandering the Gautama?
Is it spoken according to what was said, and spoken according to the Dharma?
Is it an exposition of the Dharma following the Dharma, such that others who come with the same Dharma would not censure you?"
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"One who speaks in such a manner slanders me!

It is not speaking according to what is, nor speaking according to the Dharma, nor speaking the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma; it does not lead others to come and reprove one with the same Dharma."
Why is that? I do not speak thus: "One should give to me, but one should not give to others;..."
Giving to me yields great fruit and retribution; giving to others does not yield great fruit and retribution.
One should give to my disciples; giving to my disciples yields great fruit and retribution; giving to other disciples does not yield great fruit and retribution.
"However, O Brahmin!
When I speak in this manner, I create two kinds of obstacles:
I obstruct the giver from giving and I obstruct the recipient from receiving their benefit."

"O Brahmin, even if a man were to place the leftovers from a washed vessel upon clean ground, causing the sentient beings in that place to immediately obtain benefit and happiness—I say that such acts also enter the gateway of merit;
how much more so, then, when one gives them to others?"
“O Brahmin! Nevertheless, I further declare that the fruit and retribution obtained by giving to one who observes the precepts is not the same as that obtained from one who violates them.
The Brahmin Janavasabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So it is, Gautama! I also say this:
giving to one who upholds the precepts yields great fruit and reward, whereas giving to one who violates the precepts does not.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
Whether black or white, red or of various colors, brindled or golden,
pure yellow or the color of a pigeon— such cows as these,
when they give birth to calves of beautiful appearance, [are worthy of being offered].
When one is young and strong, fully endowed with vigor, well-trained, skillful, and swift of action,
provided they are capable of bearing heavy burdens, it matters not what their original appearance was;
so too it is with human beings, each according to their respective birth.
Whether Kṣatriya, Brāhmaṇa, Vaiśya, Śūdra,
or a low-born Caṇḍāla, their births are all different; yet if one maintains the pure precepts,
they shall cast off the heavy burden of afflictions.
To one who practices the holy life with single-minded purity, an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted,
a Sugata in this world— giving to such a person yields great fruit.
But the fool lacks wisdom and has never heard the True Dharma.
Giving to them yields no great fruit, for one does not draw near to virtuous friends;
yet if one associates with good spiritual mentors— the Tathāgatas and their Śrāvakas—
and develops pure faith in the Sugata, the roots of virtue will grow with firm strength.
"Those who dwell in the happy realms, And are born into noble families, Will ultimately attain parinirvāṇa; Thus has the Great Sage spoken.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the brahmin Jātiśroṇa, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and approved with gladness, paid his respects, and departed.
96 (Ninety-six). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then, in the early morning, the World-Honored One dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms.
At that time, there was a certain brahmin, aged and with mature faculties, who carried a staff and held an alms bowl, begging for food from house to house.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the brahmin:
"Why is it that you, now aged and with mature faculties, carry a staff and hold an alms bowl, begging for food from house to house?"
The brahmin said to the Buddha, “Gautama!

I have entrusted all the wealth and property in my home to my son and provided him with a wife; only then did I leave the household life. For this reason, I carry a staff and hold an alms bowl, begging for food from house to house.”
The Buddha said to the brahmin,
“Are you able to receive and recite a single verse from me, and then return to the assembly to speak it for your son?
The brahmin replied to the Buddha:
"I can receive it, Gautama.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"His son rejoiced at his birth; for his son he gathered wealth and also took a wife for him, yet the father himself abandoned them to go forth into homelessness.
This boy from a remote village has betrayed and gone against his own father."
With the hearts of man-eating rākṣasas, they abandon their elders;
like old horses no longer of use, they seize even their parched grain.
When the children are young and the father is old, every household goes out to beg for food.
The curved staff is most excellent; it is not you who provide such affection.
It protects me from wild oxen, frees me from perilous places, and grants me safety.
It can ward off fierce dogs and support me as I walk through the darkness.
"Avoiding deep pits and empty wells, And forests of grass, trees, and thorns,
By relying on the power of the staff, One stands firm and does not fall. Then,
having received these verses from the World-Honored One, the brahmin returned to the assembly of brahmins and recited them for his son.
First, he addressed the great assembly:
"Listen to what I shall say.
Then he recited the verses... as explained at length above.

The son, filled with shame and fear, immediately embraced his father and brought him back into the house; he rubbed his body and bathed him, covered him with a green robe, and established him as the head of the household.
At that time, the brahmin had this thought:
"I have now obtained a superior lineage; this is due to the grace of the śramaṇa Gautama.
As it is said in my own scriptures:"
"One who acts as a teacher should be honored as a teacher; one who acts as an upādhyāya should be honored as an upādhyāya.
All that I have now obtained is through the power of the śramaṇa Gautama; he is indeed my teacher. I shall now offer him the most excellent and fine robes.

At that time, the brahmin took a superior, exquisite robe and went to where the World-Honored One was. After greeting and comforting him face-to-face, he withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Gautama!
"The success I have now in my household is due to the power of Gautama.
As it is recorded in our scriptures:
'One who has been a teacher should be honored as a teacher; one who has been an upādhyāya should be honored as an upādhyāya.'"
"Today, Gautama, you are my teacher; I pray that you will accept this robe out of compassion!
The World-Honored One then accepted it out of compassion.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught various dharmas to the brahmin, instructing, exhorting, illuminating, and gladdening him.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the brahmin rejoiced and delighted in it; he paid homage and departed.
97 (Ninety-seven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then, in the early morning, the World-Honored One dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
At that time, there was a certain brahmin, aged and with mature faculties, who carried a staff and held an alms bowl, begging for food from house to house.
Seeing the World-Honored One from afar, that brahmin thought to himself:

"The śramaṇa Gautama carries a staff and holds an alms bowl, begging for food from house to house; I too carry a staff and hold an alms bowl, begging for food from house to house. I and Gautama are both bhikṣus."
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"One who is called a bhikṣu is not so merely by begging for food;
if one upholds the ways of a householder, how can such a person be named a bhikṣu?"
"One who is free from both merit and fault, who practices correct conduct,
and whose mind is without fear— he is called a bhikṣu.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, that brahmin, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and approved with gladness, paid homage, and departed.
98 (Ninety-eight). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of Kosala and arrived at a village called Nāla, where he stayed in the Nāla Forest.
At that time, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the village of Dhānañjāni to beg for food, thinking to himself:
"It is still very early today; I shall first pass by the meal-preparation site of the brahmin Kāravaṇa, who is tilling the field."
At that time, the brahmin Kārāyaṇa was plowing with five hundred plows to prepare a meal.
Seeing the Blessed One from afar, the brahmin Kārāyaṇa addressed him, saying: "Gautama!"
"I now plow the fields and sow seeds to provide for my food and drink; the śramaṇa Gautama should likewise plow the fields and sow seeds to provide for his food and drink.
The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa:
"I too plow the fields and sow seeds to provide for my food and drink."
The brahmin said to the Buddha,
“I do not see any plow, yoke, collar, tether, plowshare, or whip belonging to the śramaṇa Gautama; yet now Gautama says,
‘I too plow the fields and sow seeds to provide for my food and drink.’”
At that time, the brahmin Krṣīvala Bharadvāja spoke these verses:
"You call yourself a plowman, yet I do not see your plowing.
Explain to me the art of plowing, so that I may understand the method of cultivation."
At that time, the World-Honored One answered with a verse:
"Faith is the seed; ascetic practice is the seasonal rain;
wisdom is the yoke; and a sense of shame and remorse is the shaft."
Guarding oneself with right mindfulness is the mark of a skilled driver;
Containing the actions of body and speech within, knowing the place of food and its internal storage,
Taking reality as the true vehicle, and dwelling in joy as one's rest.
With diligence one clears away the wasteland, proceeding with ease and speed;
going straight ahead without turning back, one reaches the state beyond sorrow.
Such a cultivator of the field attains the fruit of the Deathless.
"Such a plowman shall not return to undergo further existence.
Then, the Brahmin Brahmadatta, the Plowman, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent plowman!"
"Gautama! You have truly plowed the field well! Gautama!"

Thereupon, when the brahmin Kārṣaka Parāśarya heard the verses spoken by the Blessed One, his faith increased all the more; he then offered a bowl filled with fragrant and delicious food to the Blessed One.
The World-Honored One did not accept it, because he had received it as a result of his reciting verses.
He then spoke these verses:
"Not for the sake of preaching the Dharma, Do I accept and eat that food."
Thus it was explained in detail, as previously explained at length to the brahmin Agni.
Then, the brahmin Kārṣaka Bharadvāja said to the Buddha: “Gautama!
"Now, upon what shall this food be set so that it may rest securely?
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"I see no one among the devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, celestial deities, or worldly people who is capable of eating this food and thereby sustaining their bodies."
"Brahmin! Take this food and place it in water free of insects, or upon a patch of grass where little has grown.
At that time, the brahmin immediately took the food and placed it in water free of insects; instantly, smoke rose from the water, which began to boil and overflow, making a sizzling sound.
Just as when a hot ball is thrown into cold water, it makes a sizzling sound;
so too, when that food is thrown into the insect-free water, smoke rises and it boils over, making a sizzling sound.
At that time, the brahmin thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama is truly extraordinary!
Possessing such great virtue and great power, he can manifest such a miraculous transformation of food and drink."
At that time, seeing this auspicious omen regarding the food, the brahmin’s faith increased even further, and he said to the Buddha:
“Gautama! May I now go forth in the True Dharma and receive full ordination?”
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"You may now go forth within this True Dharma, receive full ordination, and attain the status of a bhikṣu.
Having thus gone forth, he reflected in solitary stillness:
"Therefore, sons of good family shave off their hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and with right faith leave the home life for homelessness to study the Way...
until they attain arhatship, with minds well-liberated."
99. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a venerable one named Śuddhadeva, who was wandering through the human realm among the people of Videha and arrived at the Āmra Garden in the city of Mithilā.
Then, in the early morning, the Venerable Suddhavāsa dressed himself, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Mithilā for alms.
Proceeding from house to house in regular order, he arrived at his own home.

At that time, the mother of Śuddhadeva was old; she was in the central hall offering food to the fire in hopes of being reborn in the Brahma Heaven, unaware that the Venerable Śuddhadeva was standing outside the gate.
At that time, King Vaiśravaṇa conceived profound faith and reverence for the Venerable Śuddhavāsas.
Then, King Vaiśravaṇa, accompanied by a retinue of yakṣas, traveled through the air and saw the Venerable Śuddhavāsas standing outside the gate.
Furthermore, he saw his mother holding food and drink in her hands, making offerings and performing a fire sacrifice in the central hall, yet not seeing her son standing at the outer gate.
Having seen this, he descended from the sky and, arriving before the Pure Mother of Heaven, spoke these verses:
“This Brahmin woman, though Brahmā is most remote, is here performing rites; how could she know of me?”
"Seeking to give birth to that [child], you offer oblations here into the fire.
This is not the path of the Brahmas; why do you perform these offerings in vain?
You, O Brāhmaṇī, dwell outside the gate of the Pure Heaven."
With defilements forever and entirely gone, he is the God among Gods;
serene and possessing nothing, solitary and independent,
he enters a house for alms— he who is worthy of all offerings.
The Pure Heaven has well cultivated its body; it is a noble field of merit for humans and devas.
Having distanced itself from all evil, it is not defiled by taints.
Its virtue is equal to that of Brahmā, yet its form dwells among humanity.
Not clinging to any phenomena, like a fully matured dragon,
the bhikṣu dwells in right mindfulness; with his mind well-liberated,
he should be honored as the First Buddha— he is indeed the supreme field of merit.
With a mind of right faith, you should give promptly;
you ought to establish an island in advance, so that there may be peace and happiness in the future.
Behold this Sage, who has already crossed the flowing current of the ocean of suffering.
Therefore, one should have faith and give promptly;
one should establish an island in advance to ensure peace and happiness in the future.
Thus did the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa exhort him to practice renunciation.
Then, the Venerable Śuddhāvāsa immediately preached the Dharma to his mother in various ways; having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened her, he departed by the same path.
100. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain brāhmaṇa approached the Buddha; having exchanged greetings and pleasantries with him face-to-face, he withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Gautama! Regarding what is called a 'Buddha,' how does one become a Buddha?
Is it a name bestowed by one's parents?"
"Is this a name established by the Brahmins?
At that time, the Brahmin spoke in verse:
"Buddha is the supreme name for one who has transcended and crossed over the world."
"Is it because of this parental decree that he is named 'Buddha'?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"The Buddha perceives the past; likewise, he perceives the future."
He also perceives the present world, wherein all conditioned phenomena arise and cease.
This is what the one of clear wisdom fully understands:
that which was to be cultivated has been cultivated, and that which was to be abandoned has been entirely abandoned; for this reason, he is called a Buddha.
Seeking through kalpas, one selects [the path], yet there is only pure suffering with no momentary joy;

all that is born must perish. By distancing oneself from and stilling the dust and defilements, and by uprooting the thorns of the latent proclivities (*anuśaya*), one attains equal awakening; therefore, one is called a Buddha.
When the Buddha had spoken these verses, that brahmin, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and delighted in it;
he rose from his seat and departed. 101 (101) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of Kosala when he sat beneath a tree between the two villages of Kātiya and Dvāruka and entered into meditative absorption for the day.

At that time, there was a brahmin of the Māṭhara clan traveling along that same path who followed behind the Buddha; he saw the footprints of the Buddha, marked with the sign of the thousand-spoked wheel, its lines clearly manifest, with even spokes and a perfect rim, complete with all auspicious characteristics.

Having seen this, he thought to himself: "I have never before seen such footprints as these among humans; I shall now follow the tracks to seek out the person. He immediately followed the footprints until he reached the place where the Buddha was.

Upon arriving, he saw the World-Honored One sitting beneath a tree, having entered the meditative absorption of the day (*divāvihāra*). His majestic countenance surpassed that of the world; his sense faculties were serene and still, his mind was tranquil and settled, and he was supremely self-subdued. Having perfected right contemplation, his radiant marks were magnificent, like a mountain of gold.
Having seen him, he said,
"Is this a deva?
The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa:
“I am not a deva. “Am I a nāga, yakṣa, gandharva, asura, garuḍa, kiṃnara, mahoraga, human, or non-human?”
The Buddha told the brahmin,
“I am not a nāga, nor anything up to a human, nor a non-human.
The brahmin addressed the Buddha:
“If it is said that he is neither a deva nor a nāga, and so on, up to neither a human nor a non-human, what kind of being is he?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered with a verse:
“Devas, nāgas, gandharvas, kinnaras, and yakṣas,”
The asuras who lack virtue, the mahoragas, humans,
and non-humans alike— all arise from afflictions.
Such outflows of affliction as these, I have entirely abandoned.
Already shattered and utterly extinguished, like the birth of a puṇḍarīka lotus,
though it grows within the water, it is never defiled by the water;
so too, though I am born into the world, I am not defiled by the world.
Throughout kalpas you have constantly discerned that there is only pure suffering and not a moment’s joy;
because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely subject to arising and ceasing,
you have become free from defilement and remain unshakable, having already extracted all the swords and thorns.
"Having ultimately brought an end to birth and death, he is therefore named Buddha.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Brahmin of the Dramiḍa clan, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and delighted in it, and departed from the road.
102 (One Hundred and Two). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
Then, in the early morning, the World-Honored One dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms.
Proceeding on his almsround by successive houses, he arrived at the residence of the brahmin Bharadvāja.
At that time, the brahmin was standing by the gate holding a wooden ladle filled with various foods and drinks as offerings for the sacrificial fire; from afar, he saw the Buddha approaching.
Having seen this, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "Stop! Stop!"
"You outcaste!
Be careful not to approach my gate!
The Buddha said to the brahmin:
"Do you know what it is to be a caṇḍāla, and the dharma of a caṇḍāla?
The brāhmaṇa replied, "I do not know what it is to be a caṇḍāla, nor do I know the dharma of a caṇḍāla. Does the śramaṇa Gautama know what it is to be a caṇḍāla, and the dharma of a caṇḍāla?"
The Buddha said,
"I thoroughly understand these outcasts as well as the ways of outcasts.
At that moment, the brahmin immediately set aside his fire-offering implements, quickly prepared a seat, invited the Buddha to sit, and addressed him, saying:
"Gautama! Please explain to me the *kaṇṭaka* and the dharma of the *kaṇṭaka*.
The Buddha then took his seat and spoke these verses for him:
"One who harbors malice and resentment, conceals various faults and evils,
violates the precepts and gives rise to wrong views, and is hypocritical and insincere—
such a person, you should know, is a *kaṇṭha* (a contemptible wretch)."
Fierce and violent, greedy and stingy, with evil desires, parsimony, flattery, and deceit,
lacking a sense of shame or dread of blame— one should know such a person to be a beast among men.
Whether born once or born twice, they slaughter them all.
One who lacks a heart of compassion is a beast among men (pudgala).
If one kills, binds, or beats others, whether in villages or cities,
and treats them with harshness without the Way, know that such a person is a beast among men.
Whether dwelling at home or traveling on the road, acting as a leader for the multitude,
one who oppresses subordinates with harshness, intimidating them with fear,
and seizing their gains for one's own use— know such a person to be a bull among men (a leader).
Whether in a village or an open space, whether things have an owner or no owner,
one who seizes and guards them for oneself should be known as a beast among men (*piṇḍola*).
One who abandons his own wife and yet does not enter a house of prostitution— [he too is such a one].
One who assails those dear to others should be known as a beast among men;
one who plunders the possessions of internal and external kinsmen,
or of spiritual friends who share the same heart, should be known as a beast among men.
One who speaks falsehoods to deceive others, Fraudulently takes wealth for which there is no proof,
And does not return what another demands— Know that such a person is a *piṇḍaka* (outcaste).
Whether for oneself or for another, One who raises debts and hands over wealth [only to evade them],...
Or again, one may comply with the words of others and speak falsehood as a witness for them;
such a liar should be known as a caṇḍāla.
Though they perform evil and unwholesome deeds, there is no one who knows it.
One who conceals and hides their evil deeds should be known as a caṇḍāla. If,
when asked about the meaning of the Dharma, one answers with what is not the meaning,
thereby deluding and deceiving others, they should be known as a caṇḍāla.
Reality is empty and devoid of anything;
yet those who disparage the wise out of folly for the sake of gain should be known as mere outcasts.
Arrogant and self-exalting, they bring ruin upon others.
One who is utterly base and arrogant should be known as a caṇḍāla;
one who creates various faults and evils for oneself, yet shifts the blame and falsely accuses others,
speaking lies to slander the pure— such a person should be known as a caṇḍāla.
Having previously accepted the offerings of others, yet when those others come to one’s own door,
one lacks a heart of respect and reciprocity— one should know such a person to be a mere beast among men.
When śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas come according to the Dharma to beg for alms, [one should respond with honor].
If one rebukes [one's parents] and does not provide for them, know that such a person is a caṇḍāla.
If one’s parents have grown old and their youthful vigor has faded,
yet one does not diligently provide for them with care, know that such a person is a caṇḍāla.
Parents, elders, brothers, and kinsmen—
those who are not truly Arhats yet manifest the virtues of an Arhat for themselves are great thieves in the world; know them to be outcasts.
At first born into a noble lineage, he studied the Brahmanical scriptures;
yet in the interim, he practiced various evil deeds.
Because of his superior birth, he was shielded from the reproach of the evil realms.
In this present life one receives reproach, and in future lives one falls into the evil realms;
one is born into the family of a caṇḍāla.
Though the world calls him Sūḍāyī and his fame pervades the whole earth, these things are not found among the caṇḍālas.
Whether a brahmin or a kṣatriya, honored by those of great lineage,
one mounts the path of the pure devas; abiding in equanimity and uprightness,
one is not hindered by the circumstances of birth, ensuring that one will be born in the Brahma Heaven.
Good reputation in this present life, and birth in a happy realm in the next—
know these two births, as I have revealed them,
to be what constitutes a true *gaṇaputra*, not merely by virtue of one's biological birth.
"One is not called a brāhmaṇa by virtue of birth;
karma makes one a caṇḍāla, and karma makes one a brāhmaṇa.
The brāhmaṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
