“Such is this great diligence; such is this Great Muni.
It is not because of birth that one is called a *kaṇṭha* (leader of the herd);
it is not because of birth that one is called a *brāhmaṇa*.”
"By karma one becomes a caṇḍāla; by karma one becomes a brāhmaṇa.
At that time, the fire-worshipping brāhmaṇa Bharadvāja conceived faith and offered a bowl full of excellent food to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One did not accept it, because he had already received it through the recitation of verses, as described above.
At that time, the fire-worshipping Brahmin Bharadvāja, having witnessed this auspicious response regarding the food, his faith increased, and he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"May I now go forth in this true Dharma and Vinaya, receive the full ordination?
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"You may now go forth in this true Dharma and Vinaya and receive the full ordination."
He immediately went forth as a monk. Meditating alone in solitude, as previously described, he attained arhatship with a mind well-liberated.
At that time, the brahmin Brahmadatta, having attained arhatship with a mind well-liberated and experiencing joy within himself, spoke this verse:
"Seeking purity through what is not the Path, Making offerings and sacrificing to the fire,"
Not knowing the path of purity, he was like one born blind;
now having attained peace and happiness, having gone forth and received full ordination,
and having reached the three knowledges, he has accomplished what the Buddha taught.
"Formerly a Brahmin who raised objections, now for the sake of the Brahmins, I bathe to leave behind dust and defilement, and ferry all devas to the other shore.
In the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, Volume Four, the textual meaning of this sūtra is entirely identical in both the Guo and Song editions; both contain nineteen sūtras, totaling twenty-five pages.
The Dan edition contains fifteen scriptures; if transcribed according to the format of the Songzang, they would amount to twenty-seven sheets.
Furthermore, its textual meaning differs entirely from the Guo and Song editions, so it is uncertain which should be adopted or rejected.
Now, upon examining the Koryo and Song editions of the canon, this [text] is actually the forty-second fascicle within the lower section of the collection.
It was an error for the Song Canon to reprint that fascicle here as the first four fascicles; the Koryo edition likewise followed this mistake!
Therefore, I have discarded that [version] and adopted this Sutra from the *Dān-běn* (the "Cinnabar" edition).
*Saṃyukta Āgama*, Fascicle Five,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
5. 103 (103) Thus have I heard: At one time, a great number of elder bhikṣus were staying at the Gośṛṅga Park in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the bhikṣu Kṣema was staying at the Bhadrayāṇī Park in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī when he fell gravely ill.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Dhosa who served as his attendant for the sick.
At that time, the bhikṣu Dāsa approached the elder bhikṣus, prostrated at the feet of the elder bhikṣus, and stood to one side.
The elder bhikṣus addressed the bhikṣu Dāsa, saying:
"Go to the place of the bhikṣu Kṣema and say to him:"
"The elder monks ask you: Is your body feeling somewhat better and at ease? Has your suffering not increased or become more severe?
Then, the bhikṣu Dāsa, having received the instructions of the elder bhikṣus, went to where the bhikṣu Kṣema was and said to him:
"The elder bhikṣus inquire after you: Is your suffering gradually subsiding?"
"Have your many sufferings not increased?
The bhikṣu Kṣema addressed the bhikṣu Dāsa, saying:
"My illness does not subside; my body is not at ease, and my various sufferings increase further without any relief."

It is as if a man of great strength were to seize a weak and inferior person, bind his head with a rope, and twist it tightly with both hands, causing extreme agony; my present suffering exceeds even that.
It is like a butcher who, with a sharp knife, makes a living incision in a cow's belly to extract its internal organs; how could that cow’s abdominal pain possibly be endured!
My abdominal pain now is even more severe than that of the cow.
"It is as if two strong men were to seize a weak man and suspend him over a fire, burning both his feet; the heat in my two feet now is even greater than that.
Then, the bhikṣu Dāsaka returned to where the senior monks were and reported in detail to them the symptoms of the illness as described by the bhikṣu Kṣema.
Then, the senior monks sent the bhikṣu Dāsa back to the bhikṣu Kṣema, saying to him:
"The World-Honored One has taught that there are five aggregates of clinging."
What are these five?

They are the aggregate of form, and the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Khemā, are you able to observe even slightly that these five aggregates of clinging are not self and do not belong to a self?
Then, having received the instruction from the elder bhikṣus, the bhikṣu Dāsa went to the bhikṣu Khemaka and said to him: “The elders have spoken to you:
‘The World-Honored One has taught the five aggregates of clinging; are you able, even slightly, to contemplate them as not-self and not belonging to self?’”
The bhikṣu Kṣema said to the bhikṣu Dāsa:
"I am able to contemplate those five aggregates of clinging as neither self nor belonging to a self.
The bhikṣu Dāsa returned and reported this to the elders.
The bhikṣu Kṣema said,
"I am able to contemplate the five aggregates of clinging as neither self nor belonging to a self.
The elder bhikṣus again sent the bhikṣu Dāsa to speak to the bhikṣu Kṣema, saying:
“Are you able to contemplate the five aggregates of clinging as neither self nor belonging to self, just like an Arhat whose taints are exhausted?
Then, having received the instruction of the senior bhikṣus, the bhikṣu Dāsa went to where the bhikṣu Kṣemaka was and said to him:
“Is a bhikṣu who contemplates the five aggregates of clinging in this way like an Arhat whose taints are exhausted?”
The bhikṣu Kṣema said to the bhikṣu Dāsa:
"I contemplate the five aggregates of clinging as neither self nor belonging to a self; I am not an arhat whose outflows are exhausted."
Then, the bhikṣu Dāsa returned to where the elder monks were and addressed them, saying:
"The bhikṣu Khaṇḍa said:
'I contemplate the five aggregates of clinging as not-self and not belonging to self, yet I am not an arhat whose outflows are exhausted.'"
Then the senior elders said to the bhikṣu Dāsa:
"Go back again and say to the bhikṣu Kṣema:
'You said:'"
"I observe the five aggregates of clinging as neither self nor belonging to self, yet I am not an Arhat whose taints are exhausted.
This is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows.
Having received these instructions from the senior bhikṣus, the bhikṣu Dāsa went to speak to the bhikṣu Khemaka:
"You have said:
'I observe the five aggregates of clinging as neither self nor belonging to self, yet I am not an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted.
This is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows."
The bhikṣu Kṣema addressed the bhikṣu Dāsa, saying:

"Although I contemplate the five aggregates of clinging as neither self nor belonging to self, yet I am not an arhat; for regarding the conceit 'I am,' the desire 'I am,' and the underlying tendency 'I am,' I have not yet abandoned them, I have not yet known them fully, I have not yet detached from them, and I have not yet vomited them out."
The bhikṣu Dāsa returned to where the elder monks were and addressed them, saying:
"The bhikṣu Khaṇḍa said:

'While I observe the five aggregates of clinging as neither self nor belonging to self, I am not yet an Arhat whose taints are exhausted; regarding the five aggregates of clinging, my conceit of "I," my desire for "I," and my underlying tendencies toward "I" have not been abandoned, fully understood, relinquished, or cast out.'"
The elders again sent the bhikṣu Dāsa to speak to the bhikṣu Kṣema, saying:
"You say there is a self; in what does this self exist?"
Is form the self? Is the self distinct from form?
Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness the self?
"Is it that the self is distinct from consciousness?
The bhikṣu Kṣema addressed the bhikṣu Dāsa, saying:
"I do not say that form is the self, nor that the self is distinct from form."
"Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the self; the self is distinct from consciousness.

Yet, regarding these five aggregates of clinging, the conceit "I am," the desire for "I," and the underlying tendencies of "I" have not been abandoned, not yet fully understood, not yet relinquished, and not yet vomited out.
The bhikṣu Kṣema said to the bhikṣu Dāsa:
"Why trouble you by having you go back and forth so much?
You take a staff; I shall support myself with it as we go to those elders, and I pray they will grant me a staff."
The bhikṣu Kṣema then supported himself with a staff and approached the senior elders.

Seeing the bhikṣu Kṣema approaching from afar while leaning on his staff, the senior elders prepared seats for him themselves, set out a footstool, went forward to welcome him, took his robe and bowl, invited him to take his seat, and exchanged greetings with one another.
Having comforted him, he said to the bhikṣu Kṣema:
"You speak of 'I' and 'mine'; what do you perceive as the self?
Is form the self?"
Am I different from form?
Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness me?
Am I different from consciousness?
The bhikṣu Kṣema addressed him, saying:
"Form is not the self, nor is the self distinct from form;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not the self, nor is the self distinct from consciousness."

If one has not yet abandoned, has not yet known, has not yet detached from, and has not yet vomited out the conceit of "I," the desire for "I," and the underlying tendencies of "I" regarding the five aggregates of clinging—
just as, for example, the fragrance of an *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, or *puṇḍarīka* lotus, is that fragrance identical to the fragrance of the roots?
Is the fragrance distinct from the root?
Is it the fragrance of the stem, leaves, stamens, or the subtle and coarse parts?
Or is the fragrance distinct from the subtle and coarse parts?
"Did you explain it equally?
The elders replied, "No, Bhikṣu Kṣema."

It is not that the roots of the *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, or *puṇḍarīka* are themselves the fragrance; nor is the fragrance something other than the root. Furthermore, it is not that the stem, leaves, filaments, or their coarse and subtle qualities are the fragrance; nor is the fragrance something other than these coarse and subtle qualities.
The bhikṣu Kṣema asked again:
"What kind of incense is that?
The Elder replied:
"This is flower fragrance.
The bhikṣu Kṣema replied again,
"I am also like this."
Form is not the self, nor am I separate from form;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not the self, nor am I separate from consciousness.

Yet, regarding these five aggregates of clinging, although I see them as neither self nor belonging to a self, I have not yet abandoned, fully understood, detached from, or cast out the conceit "I am," the desire for "I," and the underlying tendencies toward "I."
Venerable elders, listen as I speak a parable, for those who are wise gain understanding through analogies.

It is like the garment of a wet nurse that has been entrusted to a washerman; though the dust and grime have been washed away with various alkaline solutions, a residual odor remains, which can only be eliminated by perfuming it with various blended fragrances.

In this way, the learned noble disciple, being detached from the five aggregates of clinging, correctly contemplates them as not-self and not belonging to self. While he has not yet abandoned, fully understood, relinquished, or vomited out the conceit "I am," the desire for "I," and the underlying tendencies toward "I" regarding these five aggregates of clinging, he subsequently applies himself further to the contemplation of the five aggregates, observing their arising and passing away: "This is form, this is the origin of form, this is the cessation of form; this is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; this is the origin of consciousness, this is the cessation of consciousness."

Having thus contemplated the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates of clinging, all conceit of "I," desire for "I," and latent tendencies toward "I" are entirely eliminated; this is called true and correct contemplation.
When the bhikṣu Kṣema spoke this Dharma, those elders became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
The bhikṣu Kṣema, not giving rise to any outflows, attained liberation of mind; through the benefit of the joy of the Dharma, his physical illness was entirely cured.
Then, the elder bhikṣus said to the bhikṣu Kṣema:
"We have already understood and rejoiced in what you first said; how much more so upon hearing it again!"

The reason I ask is that I wish to elicit your subtle and wondrous eloquence; it is not to trouble you, but so that you may be able to expound extensively upon the Dharma of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, having heard what the bhikṣu Khemaka had said, the elder monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 104 (104) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Yamaka who gave rise to a wicked and heterodox view, speaking thus:
"As I understand the Dharma taught by the Buddha, for an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted, once the body is destroyed and life has ended, nothing further exists."
At that time, many bhikṣus, having heard what he had said, went to where he was and addressed the bhikṣu Yamaka, saying:
"Is it true that you have made this statement:
'As I understand the Dharma taught by the Buddha, when an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted passes away with the breaking up of the body, nothing further exists'?"
He replied, "It is indeed so,
Venerable Sirs."
Then the bhikṣus said to Yamaka:
"Do not slander the Blessed One!
It is unwholesome to slander the Blessed One; the Blessed One does not speak such words. You should completely abandon this evil and false view."
When the bhikṣus spoke these words, the bhikṣu Yamaka still clung to his evil and false views and said:
"Venerable sirs!
Only this is true; anything else is false."
Thus he spoke three times.
At that time, the bhikṣus were unable to subdue the bhikṣu Yamaka; they immediately departed and went to the Venerable Śāriputra, saying to him:
"Venerable One!..."
You should know that the bhikṣu Yamaka gave rise to such a wicked and false view, saying:
"I understand the Dharma taught by the Buddha: for an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, nothing further exists."
Having heard what he said, we went to question the bhikṣu Yamaka:
"Is it true that you hold such a view and understanding?
He replied to us, saying:
"O Venerable Ones!
It is indeed so; otherwise, it would be the speech of a fool.
I then spoke these words:
"Do not slander the Blessed One!
The Blessed One does not speak such words; you should abandon this evil and false view.

Although I admonished him thus a second and a third time, he still did not abandon his evil and false view. Therefore, I have now come to the Venerable One’s presence; I only pray that the Venerable One will cause the bhikṣu Yamaka to cease from his evil and false view, out of compassion for him!
Śāriputra said, "So be it;
I shall cause him to cease his evil and false views.
Then, having heard Śāriputra’s words, the many bhikṣus rejoiced and expressed their approval, and returned to their respective abodes.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, having dressed in the morning and taken up his bowl, entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms.
Having finished his meal, he left the city and returned to the monastery; after putting away his robe and bowl, he went to where the bhikṣu Yamaka was.

At that time, when the bhikṣu Yamaka saw the Venerable Śāriputra approaching from afar, he immediately prepared a seat, washed his feet, set out a footstool to receive him, took up his robes and bowl, and invited him to take his place.
After the Venerable Śāriputra had taken his seat and washed his feet, he said to the bhikṣu Yamaka:
"Is it true that you spoke these words:
'I understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One such that for an Arhat whose taints are exhausted, upon the breaking up of the body at the end of life, nothing remains'?"
The bhikṣu Yamaka said to Śāriputra,
“It is indeed so, Venerable Śāriputra! Śāriputra said:
"I now ask you; answer me as you see fit.
What do you think, Yamaka?
Is form permanent?"
"Is it impermanent?
He replied,
"Venerable Śāriputra!..."
"It is impermanent.
He asked again:
"If it is impermanent, is it suffering?"
He replied, "It is suffering.
He asked again:
“If something is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, would a well-taught noble disciple regard it as ‘this is my self,’ or ‘this is distinct from my self,’ or ‘my self exists within it’?”
He replied, “No,
Venerable Śāriputra! Feeling, perception,
mental formations, and consciousness are likewise thus.”
He asked again:
"What do you think, Yamaka!
Is form the Tathāgata?"
He replied, “No,
Venerable Śāriputra! Is feeling, perception,
volitional formations, or consciousness the Tathāgata?”
He replied, “No, Venerable Śāriputra!
He asked again:
"What do you think, Yamaka?
Is there a Tathāgata apart from form?
Is there a Tathāgata apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?"
He replied, "No, Venerable Śāriputra!
He asked again:
"Is there a Tathāgata within form?
Is there a Tathāgata within feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?
He replied:
"No, Venerable Śāriputra.
He asked again:
"Is there form within the Tathāgata?"
"Are there feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness within the Tathāgata?
He replied, "No, Venerable Śāriputra!"
He asked again:
"Is there a Tathāgata who is not form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?
He replied:
"No, Venerable Śāriputra! It is so, Yamaka!
The Tathāgata perceives phenomena as they truly are, as they abide; there is nothing to be apprehended and nothing to be designated. How then can you say: [that he sees a self]?"
"I understand what the Blessed One has taught: that for an Arhat whose taints are exhausted, upon the breakup of the body and the end of life, there is nothing remaining.
Is this what you have said at the proper time? He replied:
"No, Venerable Śāriputra!
He asked again: "Yamaka!
Previously you said:
"I understand what the World-Honored One has taught: that for an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, there is nothing remaining.
Why do you now say it is not so?
The bhikṣu Yamaka said: "Venerable Śāriputra!

Previously, because I did not understand and was ignorant, I made such evil and false views. Having heard what the Venerable Śāriputra has said, my lack of understanding and ignorance have been entirely severed."
He asked again:
"Yamaka! If one were to ask further: [what would you say?]"
“Bhikṣu! Regarding what was previously stated by your evil and heterodox views, how have you now come to know and see so as to be entirely free from them?
How would you answer?”
Yamaka replied: "Venerable Śāriputra!
If anyone were to come and ask me, I would answer them in this way:"
"For an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted, form is impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering; that which is suffering is tranquil, cool, and forever extinguished.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise."
"If anyone comes to ask, answer them in this way.
Śāriputra said, "Excellent!"
Excellent, Bhikṣu Yamaka!
You should answer in this way.

Why is this? For an Arhat whose taints are exhausted, form is impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering; and that which is impermanent and suffering is a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing.
"Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
When the Venerable Śāriputra had spoken this Dharma, the bhikṣu Yamaka became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
The Venerable Śāriputra said to the bhikṣu Yamaka:
"I shall now provide an analogy, for the wise attain understanding through analogies.
It is like the son of a householder; this son of a householder was very wealthy and possessed much property, and he sought out many servants to properly guard his wealth."

At that time, there was a hostile and wicked person who feigned intimacy, acting as a servant and constantly watching for an opportunity. Sleeping late and rising early, he attended to him at his side, performing his duties with diligence and using humble speech to please his master’s mind. The master regarded him as a close friend or even a son, placing absolute trust in him without suspicion and failing to maintain any self-protection. Only then did the man take a sharp blade in hand and take his life.
"Yamaka Bhikṣu! What do you think?

That wicked enemy, though acting as a friend to the householder, does not employ this as his initial stratagem; rather, with a mind intent on harm, he constantly watches for an opportunity until the very end?"
Yet that householder was unable to perceive this, and until now he has suffered harm.
He replied, “It is indeed so.”
"Venerable one!
Śāriputra said to the bhikṣu Yamaka:
"What do you think?"
“Did that householder, knowing from the outset that the man was feigning friendship while intending to harm him, protect himself well so as not to suffer injury?
He replied, “It is so, Venerable Śāriputra!”

“In this way, Yāmaka, a foolish, unlearned worldling conceives notions of permanence, security, health, self, and ‘mine’ regarding the five aggregates of clinging; he cherishes and guards these five aggregates of clinging, only to be ultimately harmed by these very five aggregates as his enemies.”
Just as that householder was harmed by a deceitful enemy without realizing it, so too, Yamaka!

A learned noble disciple contemplates these five aggregates of clinging as being like a disease, like an abscess, like a thorn, like a murderer; as impermanent, suffering, empty, non-self, and not belonging to self. Toward these five aggregates of clinging, he does not cling and does not grasp; because he does not grasp, he does not cling; and because he does not cling, he personally realizes Nirvana: [“Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.”]
“Birth has been exhausted for me; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence.

When the Venerable Śāriputra spoke this Dharma, the bhikṣu Yamaka’s outflows were extinguished and his mind attained liberation. Having taught, instructed, illuminated, and gladdened the bhikṣu Yamaka with this Dharma, the Venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat and departed.
105 (One Hundred and Five). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa, the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, a renunciant of another sect named Seniya came to where the Buddha was, paid his respects with greetings, and sat down to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
On the day before yesterday, whether they were śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, carakas, or renunciants, they had gathered in the Hall of Rare Occurrences.”
Regarding this reputation, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa was the leader of a great assembly, surrounded by five hundred disciples before and behind him.
Among them were those of extreme intelligence as well as those of dull faculties; yet when they passed away, he did not record or declare the places where they had been reborn.
Furthermore, there was Makkhali Gosāla, who served as the leader of a great assembly and was surrounded by five hundred disciples, both before and behind him.
Among those disciples were some of sharp intelligence and others of dull faculties; yet when he passed away, he did not record or declare where they had been reborn.

In this manner, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Sañjaya Vairaṭīputra, Ajita Keśakambalin, Kakuda Kātyāyana, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra each had five hundred disciples surrounding them in front and behind, just as described before.
At that time, the śramaṇa Gautama was also present in that discussion, saying:
"The śramaṇa Gautama is the leader of a great assembly; among his disciples, there are those who have passed away."
He then declared:
"So-and-so was born in that place; so-and-so was born in this place.
At that, I first gave rise to doubt:
"How has the śramaṇa Gautama attained such a dharma?
The Buddha told Śreṇika:
"Do not give rise to doubt."
Because they possess delusion, they give rise to doubt.
Śāṇakavāsin!
You should know that there are three kinds of teachers.
What are the three?

There is one teacher who perceives the self as truly existing in the present life and speaks according to what he knows; yet he is unable to know what occurs after the end of life. This is called the first teacher appearing in the world.
Furthermore, Śoṇa!
There is a teacher who perceives that the true self exists in the present world, and he also perceives it to exist after the end of life, speaking according to what he knows.
Furthermore, Śreṇika!
There is a teacher who does not perceive a true self in the present life, nor does he perceive a true self after the end of life.
"Śāṇi! That first teacher who perceives the present world as truly being 'I' and speaks according to what he knows is called one with the view of annihilationism (uccheda-dṛṣṭi).
That second teacher who perceives both this world and the future world as truly being 'I' and speaks according to what he knows is one with the view of eternalism (śāśvata-dṛṣṭi)."

That third teacher does not perceive a true self in the present life, nor does he perceive a self after the end of life; this, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha declares, is the cessation of craving for the present existence, the fading away of desire, its extinction, and Nirvāṇa.
Sreṇika addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Having heard what the World-Honored One has said, my doubts have only increased all the more.”
The Buddha told Seniya:
"It is only natural that your doubt should increase. Why is this so?"

This profound realm is difficult to see and difficult to know; it must be illuminated with profound insight and reached through subtle discernment. It is understood by those who are wise and intelligent, whereas ordinary sentient beings are unable to distinguish or comprehend it.
"Why is this? Because sentient beings have, throughout the long night, held different views, different tolerances, different pursuits, and different desires.
Sreṇika addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

My mind has attained pure faith in the World-Honored One; I only pray that the World-Honored One will preach the Dharma for me, so that my eye of wisdom may become pure while I remain in this very seat.”
The Buddha told Seniya:
"I shall now speak for you according to what you desire.
The Buddha told Seniya:
"Is form permanent, or is it impermanent?
He replied:
"It is impermanent," [he replied].
The Blessed One asked again:
"Saññika!..."
"If it is impermanent, is it suffering?
He replied, "It is suffering."
The Blessed One again asked Seniya:
"If something is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, would a well-taught noble disciple regard it as 'this is my self,' or 'my self is in this,' or 'this is in my self'?"
He replied, “No,
World-Honored One! Feeling, perception,
mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.”
He asked again:
"What do you think, Sāṇa?"
"Is form the Tathāgata?
He replied, "No,
World-Honored One!"
“Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness the Tathāgata?
He replied, “No,
World-Honored One!”
He asked again:
"Saññika! Is there a Tathāgata apart from form?"
"Is there a Tathāgata apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
He replied, "No,
World-Honored One!"
He asked again:
"Saññika! Is there a Tathāgata within form?"
"Is there a Tathāgata within feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?
He replied, "No,
World-Honored One!"
He asked again:
“Sañjī, is there form within the Tathāgata?”
“Is there feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness within the Tathāgata?
He replied, “No,
World-Honored One!”
He asked again: "Sañjīva!
Is it that there is a Tathāgata who is neither form, nor feeling, perception, mental formations, nor consciousness?"
He replied, “No,
World-Honored One.
The Buddha said to Seniya:
"My disciples, having heard what I have taught, do not fully understand its meaning and thus give rise to conceit and a lack of clear realization (*aviparīta-saṃbodha*).
Because they lack clear realization, conceit is not severed;
because conceit is not severed, after casting off these aggregates (*skandha*), they arise again in continuity with further aggregates."
Therefore, Sāṇa! I declare that these disciples, upon the dissolution of the body after death, are reborn in such and such places. Why is this?
Because they still possess residual conceit. "Sañjaya!

Among my disciples, those who are able to understand the meaning of what I have taught attain direct realization regarding all forms of conceit. Because they have attained direct realization, their conceits are severed; because their conceits are severed, when the body breaks up at the end of life, they do not continue in further existence."
"Śāṇavāsin!
Regarding such disciples, I do not say that after they have abandoned these aggregates, they are born in this or that place. Why is that?"
Because there is no causal basis upon which to provide a declaration.
If you wish me to provide a declaration, you should declare:
"He has severed all craving and desire, is forever free from the fetters of existence, is liberated through right mindfulness, and has reached the ultimate end of suffering."

"From the past until the present, I have always spoken of the fault of conceit, the accumulation of conceit, the arising of conceit, and the emergence of conceit; if one contemplates conceit with immediate and thorough insight, no suffering will arise."
When the Buddha taught this Dharma, the renunciant Seniya became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.

At that time, the renunciant Seniya saw the Dharma and realized the Dharma; he severed all doubts and hesitations, no longer relying on others for knowledge and no longer relying on others for deliverance, gaining fearlessness of mind within the True Dharma.
Rising from his seat, he joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
May I go forth within the True Dharma to cultivate the holy life?"
The Buddha said to Seniya,
“You have gone forth in this True Dharma, received full ordination, and attained the status of a bhikṣu.
At that time, having gone forth, Seniya practiced with diligence in solitary seclusion and dwelt in such reflection:

"Therefore, noble son, one shaves off hair and beard, out of right faith leaves the home life for homelessness to study the Path, practices the holy life, and perceives the Dharma, knowing for oneself that one has attained realization:
'Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence.'"
Having attained arhatship,
they heard what the Buddha had said and, filled with joy,
practiced accordingly. 106 (106) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Aṇurādha who was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain.
At that time, a great number of non-Buddhist renunciants went to where Anurādha was, and they exchanged greetings with one another.
Having finished their greetings, they stood to one side and said to Anurādha:
"We wish to ask a question; would you have the leisure to explain it for us?"
Anuruddha said to the non-Buddhists, "Ask whatever you wish; those who know shall answer.
The non-Buddhists asked again:
"How is it, Venerable One?
Does the Tathāgata exist after death?"
Anurādha said, “As the Blessed One has taught, this is undeclared.
He asked again:
"Does the Tathāgata exist after death? Anurādha replied,
"As the World-Honored One has taught, this too is undeclared."
He asked again:
"Does the Tathāgata exist after death? Does he not exist? Does he both exist and not exist?
Or does he neither exist nor not exist?"
Anurādha said, "As the Blessed One has taught, this too is undeclared.
He then asked Anurādha again:
"How is it, Venerable One?
Does the Tathāgata exist after death?"
It is declared to be indeterminate.
Is there no [self] after death?
It is declared to be indeterminate.
"Does one exist after death? Does one not exist?
Does one both exist and not exist? Or does one neither exist nor not exist?
To these, he replied that they are "undetermined."
"How is this,
Venerable One?
Does the śramaṇa Gautama neither know nor see?"
Anurādha said, "The World-Honored One is not without knowledge; he is not without vision.
At that time, the various non-Buddhists were not pleased with what Anurādha had said; having reviled him, they rose from their seats and departed.

At that time, Āniruddha, knowing that the various non-Buddhist practitioners had departed, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and recounted to the Buddha in detail all that the non-Buddhist practitioners had asked, saying to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!”
When he asked thus, I answered thus: "Is this in accordance with the teaching of all dharmas?
Does it not constitute slandering the World-Honored One?
Is it in accord with the Dharma?"
"Is this contrary to the Dharma?
Is there no one else who might come to challenge you and cause you to fall into a position of reproach?
The Buddha said to Anuruddha:
"I now ask you; answer as you see fit. Anurādha!
Is form permanent?"
"Is it impermanent?
He replied, "It is impermanent."
“Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent?
He replied, “Impermanent.”
“World-Honored One!
As extensively explained in the Yamaka Sūtra, up until: “Is consciousness the Tathāgata?
He replied:
"No," the Buddha told Anurādha.
"One who speaks in this manner accords with all the prophecies, does not slander the Tathāgata, and does not overstep the proper order."
As the Tathāgata has taught, regarding these successive teachings, there is no one who can come to challenge, interrogate, or reproach them. Why is this?
Because I have known form as it truly is, and I have known the arising of form, the cessation of form, and the path leading to the cessation of form as they truly are.
"Āniruddha! If one were to abandon what has been done by the Tathāgata and speak without knowledge or vision, this would not be an impartial teaching.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Āniruddha, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
107 (One Hundred and Seven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Deer Park in the dense forest of Ṛṣipatana on Mount Saptaparṇa in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.

At that time, there was an elder named Nakula, one hundred and twenty years of age; advanced in years and with mature faculties, he was frail, weak, and afflicted by illness. Desiring to pay his respects to the World-Honored One and to the bhikṣus who were his long-standing honored teachers and friends, he approached the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

"I am advanced in years, frail and afflicted by suffering and illness; yet with all my strength and perseverance, I have come to behold the World-Honored One and the bhikṣus who were formerly my honored teachers and friends. I only pray that the World-Honored One will preach the Dharma for me, so that I may find peace and happiness throughout the long night."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the householder Nakula:
“Excellent, householder! Excellent!”

"You are indeed advanced in years and your faculties are mature; you are frail, weak, and afflicted by suffering. Yet, through your own effort, you have been able to come before the Tathāgata and other venerable bhikṣus who are esteemed by the community.
Householder, you should know that while this body is subject to suffering, you must constantly train yourself toward a body free from suffering."
At that time, the World-Honored One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the householder Nakula, and then remained silent.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the householder Nakula rejoiced and delighted in it; he paid homage to the Buddha and departed.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was seated under a tree not far from the World-Honored One.
The householder Nakula approached the Venerable Śāriputra, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked the householder:
"Your faculties are now harmonious and joyful, and your complexion is bright; have you heard the profound Dharma from the World-Honored One?"
The householder Nakula said to Śāriputra:

"Today the World-Honored One has taught me the Dharma, instructing, exhorting, illuminating, and gladdening me. With the nectar-like Dharma, he has sprinkled my body and mind; therefore, my faculties are now harmonious and joyful, and my countenance is bright and clear."
The Venerable Śāriputra asked the householder:
"What Dharma has the World-Honored One taught for you, which instructs, teaches, illuminates, and gladdens, moistening you with the nectar of immortality?"
The householder Nakula said to Śāriputra:
"I recently went to where the World-Honored One was and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
'I am advanced in years, frail and afflicted by suffering; yet with my own strength I have come to behold the World-Honored One and the bhikṣus who are my revered teachers and friends.'"
The Buddha said to me:
"Excellent, householder!"
"You are indeed aged, frail, and afflicted by suffering, yet you have been able to come to me of your own accord and see the bhikṣus whom I formerly revered.
Now, within this body afflicted by suffering, you should constantly practice and train toward a body free from suffering."
“The World-Honored One has taught me the Dharma in this way—showing, instructing, illuminating, and gladdening me, moistening me with the nectar of immortality.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra asked the householder:
“Why did you not just now ask the World-Honored One again:”
"What is it to have both body and mind afflicted by suffering?
What is it to have the body afflicted by suffering while the mind is not?
The householder replied:
"For this reason, I have come to visit the Venerable One; I only wish that you would briefly expound for me the essentials of the Dharma.
The Venerable Śāriputra said to the householder, "Excellent!"
"Householder!
Listen now attentively;
I shall speak for you."
Ignorant and unlearned worldlings do not know, as it truly is, the arising of form, the cessation of form, the danger in form, the gratification in form, and the escape from form.
Because they do not know this as it truly is, they delight in form, saying, "Form is my self" or "Form belongs to my self," and thus they grasp at and cling to it.
If that form is destroyed or altered, consciousness follows along, and affliction and suffering arise;
once affliction and suffering have arisen, there is fear, obstruction, longing, sorrowful distress, and attachment.
It is the same with feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
This is called the suffering and affliction of body and mind.
What is meant by "suffering and affliction of the body, but no suffering and affliction of the mind"?
The well-learned noble disciple knows, as they truly are, the arising of form, the cessation of form, the gratification of form, the danger of form, and the escape from form.

Having known them as they truly are, he does not give rise to craving or delight; nor does he see form as "I" or "mine. If that form changes or alters, his mind does not follow after it, and thus affliction and suffering do not arise.
Since affliction and suffering do not arise, he does not experience fear, obstruction, longing, or attachment.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
This is called bodily suffering and affliction, but not mental suffering and affliction.
When the Venerable Śāriputra spoke this Dharma, the householder Nakula attained the pure Dharma-eye.

At that time, the householder Nakula saw the Dharma, attained the Dharma, knew the Dharma, and entered the Dharma; having crossed beyond all doubts, he was no longer dependent on others and attained fearlessness of heart regarding the True Dharma.
Rising from his seat, adjusting his robes, and joining his palms in reverence, he addressed the Venerable Śāriputra:

"I have transcended and crossed over. I now take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; may you bear witness that I am a lay follower (*upāsaka*). From this day forth, for as long as life shall last, I take refuge in the Three Jewels."
At that time, the householder Nakula, having heard what the Venerable Śāriputra had said, rejoiced and approved with gladness;
he paid homage and departed. 108 (108) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Devadaha, a village of the Śākyas.

At that time, a great number of bhikṣus from the western regions, wishing to return to the west for the rainy season retreat, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for them, instructing, exhorting, illuminating, and gladdening them.
Having thus instructed, exhorted, illuminated, and gladdened them in various ways, many bhikṣus from the west rose from their seats, joined their palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"We, the many bhikṣus from the West, wish to return to the West for the rains retreat; we now request leave to depart.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus from the West:
"Have you taken your leave of Śāriputra yet?"
He replied,
"I have not yet taken my leave.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus of the western direction:
“Śāriputra has purely cultivated the holy life; you should bid him farewell, for he will be able to benefit you with the Dharma and bring you peace and happiness for a long night.
At that time, the bhikṣus from the western regions took their leave and were about to depart.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was sitting under a sturdy tree not far from the Buddha. Monks from the western regions approached the Venerable Śāriputra, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"We wish to return to the western regions for the rains retreat; therefore, we have come to take our leave."
Śāriputra said,
"Have you all taken leave of the World-Honored One?
They replied:
"I have already taken my leave," Śāriputra said.
"When you return to the western lands, among the various nations and diverse assemblies, they will surely question you."

"Now that you have heard the well-spoken Dharma from the World-Honored One, should you not receive it well, uphold it well, contemplate it well, and enter into it well, so as to be fully capable of proclaiming it for others without disparaging the Buddha?"
“Will you not allow that assembly to be subjected to difficult questioning, censure, or defeat?
Those bhikṣus said to Śāriputra:
“We have come to visit the Venerable One for the sake of hearing the Dharma; we only pray that the Venerable One will explain it fully for us out of compassion!”
The Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus:
"The people of Jambudvīpa are intelligent and of sharp faculties; whether they be kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, householders, or śramaṇas, they will surely ask you:
'How does your great teacher preach the Dharma?'"
"With what teaching do you instruct them?
You should answer:
"The Great Teacher teaches only the subduing of sensual desire; he instructs with this teaching."
"Furthermore, you should be asked:
'In regard to which phenomena do you subdue desire and greed?
To this, you should answer:"

"The Great Teacher has taught only this: to subdue sensual desire for the aggregate of form, and to subdue sensual desire for the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; such is the Dharma taught by our Great Teacher."
"He will further ask:
'What fault or disadvantage does sensual desire have, such that the Great Teacher taught the subduing of sensual desire for form,
and the subduing of sensual desire for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?'"
"You should further answer:

'If one does not abandon desire for form, does not abandon greed, does not abandon craving, does not abandon mindfulness, and does not abandon thirst for it, then if that form changes or alters, sorrow, lamentation, vexation, and suffering will arise.'"
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Seeing that sensual desire has such faults, one subdues sensual desire for form, and subdues sensual desire for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
He should further ask:

"What benefit does one see in the abandonment of sensual desire that the Great Teacher taught the subduing of sensual desire for form, and the subduing of sensual desire for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?"
One should further answer:

"If, regarding form, one has abandoned desire, abandoned lust, abandoned mindfulness, abandoned craving, and abandoned thirst, then even if that form changes or alters, no sorrow, lamentation, vexation, or suffering will arise."
"Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
"Venerable sirs!

If, by reason of practicing unwholesome dharmas, one were now to attain a pleasant dwelling in the present life—without suffering, without obstruction, without affliction, and without fever—and upon the breakup of the body after death were to be reborn in a happy destination, the Blessed One would certainly not have said: [that such a person is bound for a state of misery]."
"One should abandon all unwholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, one should not fail to instruct others to practice the various holy conducts within the Buddha-dharma so as to reach the end of suffering.

Because of the causes and conditions of experiencing these unwholesome dharmas, one dwells in suffering in the present life, facing obstacles and burning afflictions; and at the breaking up of the body after death, one falls into the evil realms."
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
"One should abandon unwholesome dharmas and cultivate the various holy practices within the Buddha-dharma, so as to equally exhaust suffering and reach the ultimate end of suffering."

“If the undertaking of various wholesome dharmas results in dwelling in suffering in the present life, being obstructed and tormented, and falling into the evil destinies at the breaking up of the body after death, then the Blessed One would never say that one should undertake and uphold wholesome dharmas, practice the holy life within the Buddha’s teaching, and equally bring an end to suffering to reach its ultimate limit.”

By upholding wholesome dharmas, one dwells in happiness in the present life—without suffering, without obstruction, without affliction, and without fever—and at the breaking up of the body after death, one is reborn in a good destination. For this reason, the Blessed One praises and instructs people to receive all wholesome dharmas, to cultivate the holy life within the Buddha’s Dharma, and to equally bring an end to suffering and reach the ultimate limit of suffering.
When the Venerable Śāriputra had spoken this Dharma, the bhikṣus from the western regions were freed from their outflows, and their minds attained liberation.
When the Venerable Śāriputra had spoken this Dharma, the bhikṣus rejoiced and approved, paid their respects, and departed.
109 (One Hundred and Nine). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Suppose there were a pool of water fifty yojanas square and fifty yojanas deep, filled to the brim.
Then a man were to take a hair, or a blade of grass, or even his fingernail, and draw from that water a single drop.”
"Monks, what do you think? Which is more:
the drops of water from that man, or the water in the pond?"
The bhikṣu said to the Buddha:
“The water droplets that man has taken up with a hair, a blade of grass, or even his fingernails are so few as to be beyond description;
the water in the pond is vast, exceeding them by hundreds of thousands of millions of times, such that no comparison can be made.”
“Thus it is, monks!
The manifold sufferings severed by one who has seen the truths are like that pool water; in future lives, they shall never arise again.”
At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished preaching this Dharma, he entered his room to sit in meditation.
Then, while the Venerable Śāriputra was seated among the assembly, after the World-Honored One had entered his room and departed, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This is something I have never heard before!"
World-Honored One, today you have excellently expounded the parable of the pond. Why is this?

Because a noble disciple who is fully endowed with the vision of the Truths has attained the fruit of immediate realization; whereas for ordinary people there exist wrong views, the root of the view of a self-identity, the accumulation of the view of a self-identity, the arising of the view of a self-identity, and the manifestation of the view of a self-identity.

That is to say: sorrowful concealment, celebrating auspiciousness, cherishing and guarding, speaking of a self, speaking of sentient beings, and speaking of oneself as extraordinary or superior—all such various evils are completely extinguished;
their roots are severed so that they are like a cut-down tāla tree, never to arise again in future lives.
“Monks! What is it that a noble disciple who has seen the Truth abandons regarding the higher group of wrong views, such that they never arise again in future lives?
An ignorant, unlearned worldling regards form as self, or self as distinct from form, or form as being within self, or self as being within form.”
One views feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as "this is me," "I am distinct from consciousness," "I exist within consciousness," or "consciousness exists within me.
How does one view form as "this is me"?
Having attained the meditative absorption of the earth-totality (pṛthivī-kṛtsnāyatana), he contemplates it and forms this thought:
"The earth is myself; I am the earth. Myself and the earth are one and non-dual, neither different nor distinct."
Having thus meditated upon the totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) of water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, and white, he reflects:
"Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are indeed the self; the self is indeed volitional formations. They are one and not two, neither different nor distinct."
"In this way, regarding each of the sense bases (*āyatana*), one reckons 'I' in each one; this is called 'form itself is the self.
How does one see form as distinct from the self?

If one sees feeling (*vedanā*) as the self, having seen feeling as the self, one then sees form as 'mine'; or one sees perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*) as the self, and sees form as 'mine.'"
"What is meant by seeing form within the self?
It means seeing feeling as the self, with form being within that self;
or seeing perception, mental formations, and consciousness as the self, with form being within them."
What is the view of a self within form?
It is the view that feeling itself is the self, which dwells within form, enters into form, and pervades its four limbs;
or the view that perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the self, which dwells within form and pervades its four limbs. This is called the self within form.
“What is the view that feeling itself is the self?
It refers to the six bodies of feeling: feeling born of eye-contact, and feelings born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.”
Regarding these six bodies of feeling (*ṣaḍ-vedanā-kāya*), one by one views each as "I" and "I am the feeling"; this is called "feeling itself is the self.
How does one view feeling as distinct from the self?
It means viewing form (*rūpa*) as the self and feeling as belonging to the self (*mama*).
That is to say: "Perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the self; feeling is mine. This is called "feeling as distinct from the self.
What is the view of "feeling within the self"?
It is to say: "Form is the self, and feeling is within it; perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the self, and feeling is within them."
What is the view of a self within feeling?
It is to regard form as the self, which dwells within feeling and pervades its four limbs;
or to regard perception, mental formations, and consciousness as the self, which dwells within feeling and pervades its four limbs. This is called the self within feeling.
"What is the perception of 'perception itself is the self'?
It refers to the six groups of perception: perception born of eye-contact, and perceptions born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact."
If one regards each of these six groups of perception (*ṣaḍ-saṃjñā-kāya*) as the self, this is called "perception is the self.
What is meant by regarding perception as distinct from the self?

It refers to regarding form (*rūpa*) as the self and perception as belonging to the self; or regarding consciousness (*vijñāna*) as the self and perception as belonging to the self. This is called "perception is distinct from the self."
"What is the perception of a self within [the aggregates]?
It is to regard form as the self, with perception dwelling within it; or to regard feeling, formations, or consciousness as the self, with perception dwelling within them."
What is the view that the self exists within perception (*saṃjñā*)?
It is the view that "form (*rūpa*) is the self, which dwells within perception and pervades its four limbs"; this is called the self within perception.
What is the view that formations (*saṃskāra*) are the self?
That is to say, the six groups of volition: volition born of eye-contact, and volition born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.
To view each of these six groups of volition as "this is the self" is called the view that "formations themselves are the self."
What is the view that formations are distinct from the self?
It means: "Form is the self; formations are mine.
Feeling, perception, and consciousness are the self; formations are mine. This is called the view that formations are distinct from the self.
"What is the view of the self abiding within the formations?
It is to say: 'Form is the self, and the formations abide within it. Or:
'Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the self, and the formations abide within them. This is called the view of the self abiding within the formations."
What is the view of a self within formations (*saṃskāra*)?

It is to regard form (*rūpa*) as the self, abiding within formations and pervading its four limbs; or to regard feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) as the self, abiding within formations and pervading its four limbs. This is called the self within formations.
"How does one view consciousness as the self?
It refers to the six groups of consciousness—the group of eye-consciousness, and the groups of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness."
To view each of these six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-kāya*) as "this is the self" is called "consciousness itself is the self.
How does one view consciousness as distinct from the self?

To view form (*rūpa*) as the self and consciousness as belonging to the self; or to view feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*) as the self and consciousness as belonging to the self—this is called "consciousness is distinct from the self."
"What is meant by 'consciousness within the self'?
It refers to the view that form is the self and consciousness dwells within it;
or that feeling, perception, and formations are the self and consciousness dwells within them. This is called 'consciousness within the self.'"
What is the self within consciousness?
It is the view that form is the self, which dwells within consciousness and pervades its fourfold body;
or that feeling, perception, and formations are the self, which dwells within consciousness and pervades its fourfold body. This is called the self within consciousness.
"In this way, the noble disciple who perceives the Four Noble Truths attains the fruit of direct realization; having severed all false views, they shall never again arise in the future."
Regarding all forms—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; beautiful or ugly; far or near—one should contemplate them collectively as follows:
"All are impermanent, all are suffering, all are empty, and all are non-self. They should not be cherished, grasped, or maintained."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this; one should not delight in them, nor grasp or maintain them.
Observing in this way, one dwells with the mind well-restrained and is not deluded regarding phenomena.

Furthermore, he contemplates diligence, abandoning all sloth; his mind attains joy and happiness, and both body and mind become supple and at rest. Abiding in tranquil equanimity, he is endowed with all the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas); his practice is fulfilled, and he is forever free from all evils. It is not that he does not undergo refinement, nor is it that he does not attain cessation.
Ceased and not arising, diminished and not increasing, severed and not being born, neither grasping nor clinging, he personally realized nirvana:
"Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence."
When Śāriputra had spoken this Dharma, sixty bhikṣus were freed from outflows, and their minds attained liberation.
After the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
110. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying by the side of the Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī.
In the kingdom of Vaiśālī there was a Nirgrantha who was wise and sagacious, well-versed in all treatises, yet possessed the pride of his own intelligence.

Having extensively collected various treatises and attained profound subtlety through his wondrous wisdom, he expounded the Dharma for the multitude, surpassing all other masters of discourse. He frequently thought to himself:
"Among the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, there is no one who can rival me; even the Tathāgata could engage in debate with me."
When the various masters of treatises hear my name, their foreheads perspire, sweat breaks out from their armpits, and water flows from their pores;

my wind of debate can lay low the grass and break the trees, shatter metal and stone, and subdue dragons and elephants—how much more so the masters of treatises among men! Who could possibly withstand me?

At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Aśvajit who, having dressed in his robes and taken up his alms bowl at dawn, entered the city for alms with dignified and orderly deportment, looking straight ahead and walking steadily.

At that time, Satyaka Nirgranthīputra had some minor business and was traveling through various villages. As he was leaving the city gate, he saw from afar the bhikṣu Aśvajit; he immediately approached him and asked:
"How does the śramaṇa Gautama teach the Dharma to his disciples?"
"By what Dharma do you instruct your disciples, leading them to practice it?
Aśvajit replied: "Householder Agniveśya!..."
The World-Honored One thus taught the Dharma to his disciples, instructing them to practice and train accordingly,
saying: "O Bhikṣus!
One should contemplate form as non-self; one should contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as non-self.
One should diligently and skillfully contemplate these five aggregates of clinging as a disease, as an abscess, as a thorn, as a murderer, and as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
When Saccaka Nigaṇṭhaputra heard these words, his heart was not pleased, and he spoke thus:
"Aśvajit! You must have misheard;
the śramaṇa Gautama would never speak in such a way."
"If the śramaṇa Gautama makes such a statement, it is a false view; I shall go to him, challenge him, and cause him to desist.
At that time, Satyaka Nirgranthīputra went to the village where the Licchavis were assembled and said to them:

"Today I saw the foremost disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama, named Aśvajit, and debated with him briefly. If he remains as he has spoken, I shall go to that śramaṇa Gautama and debate with him, advancing, retreating, and turning back, until he must surely follow my will."
"Just as a man might cut down a clump of grass, grasp it by its stalk, and shake it in the air to remove all the tangled filth;
so too do I, when debating and cross-examining the śramaṇa Gautama, seize him by his vital points, advancing, retreating, and turning about as I wish, to strip away his erroneous doctrines."
"Just as a wine-seller grasps his wine-sack, presses out the clear and pure essence, and discards the dregs;
so too do I, approaching the śramaṇa Gautama for debate and cross-examination, advancing, retreating, and turning back, in order to extract the pure truth and discard all erroneous doctrines."
"Just as a mat-weaver, having filled his mats with various filthy things, washes them with water to remove the stench and filth when he wishes to sell them in the market;
so too do I go to the presence of the śramaṇa Gautama, engage in debate with him, advancing, retreating, and turning back, grasping the essential principles to remove all foul doctrines."

"It is just as when a royal elephant trainer leads a large, intoxicated elephant into deep water to wash its body, its four limbs, its ears, and its trunk, bathing it thoroughly to remove all coarseness and filth;

I shall do the same, approaching the śramaṇa Gautama to debate and challenge him, advancing, retreating, and turning about with complete mastery as I please, seizing his vital points to remove his defiled doctrines."
"You Licchavis, you should also go together to observe his strengths and weaknesses.
Among them, a certain Licchavi spoke thus:
"It is impossible that Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putra could engage in debate with the Śramaṇa Gautama."
Furthermore, it was said:
"Satyaka Nirgranthaputra is wise and of sharp faculties; he is capable of engaging in debate.
At that time, five hundred Licchavis went together with Satyaka Nirgranthaputra to the place where the Buddha was, for the purpose of debate.
At that time, the World-Honored One was sitting beneath a tree in the great forest, dwelling in the celestial abodes (*divyavihāra*).

Then, a large number of bhikṣus were walking for exercise outside their quarters in the forest when they saw from afar Saccaka Nigaṇṭhaputta approaching. He gradually made his way to where the bhikṣus were and asked them:
"Where does the śramaṇa Gautama reside?"
The bhikṣu replied, “I am staying in the Great Forest,
dwelling beneath a tree, abiding in the celestial abodes.
Satyaka Nirgranthīputra then went to where the Buddha was, paid his respects with greetings, and sat down to one side.
The Licchavi elders also went to where the Buddha was; some paid him homage, while others joined their palms in greeting. Having offered their greetings, they stood to one side.
Then, Satyaka Nirgranthīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I have heard that Gautama teaches the Dharma in this way and instructs his disciples in this manner—he teaches his disciples to contemplate form as non-self, and to contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as non-self; he teaches them to diligently and skillfully contemplate these five aggregates of clinging as being like a disease, like an abscess, like a thorn, like a murderer, and as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self."
"Is it that Gautama has given such a teaching, or is it that the transmitters have defamed Gautama?
Is it as he said, or is it not as he said?"
"Was it spoken in accordance with the Dharma?
Was it spoken as the Dharma follows from the Dharma?
Is there no dissenting view that comes forward to challenge you and cause you to fall into a position of defeat?"
The Buddha said to Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha:

"As you have heard, he speaks according to what was taught, speaks according to the Dharma, and speaks the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma; this is not slanderous, nor does it provide grounds for censure or defeat through cross-examination."

Why is this? It is because I have indeed taught the Dharma to my disciples in this way; I have indeed constantly instructed my disciples to follow the teachings of the Dharma and to contemplate that form is non-self.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-self; one contemplates these five aggregates of clinging as a disease, as an abscess, as a thorn, as a killer, as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, and as non-self.
Saccaka Nigaṇṭhaputta said to the Buddha: “Gautama!
I shall now speak a simile.”
The Buddha said to Saccaka Nigaṇṭhaputra,
“You should know that now is the time.
“It is, for example, as all things produced in the world depend upon the earth.”
In this way, form is the self and the person, from which good and evil arise;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the self and the person, from which good and evil arise.
Furthermore, it is like the human realm, the divine realm, medicinal herbs, and trees, all of which grow and flourish by depending upon the earth.
"In this way, form is my self, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are my self.
The Buddha said to the householder Aggivessana:
"Do you say that form is your self, and that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are your self?"
He replied: "It is so, Gautama!
Form is my self; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are my self."
"All these people have spoken thus.
The Buddha said to the householder Agniveśya:
"Set forth the basis of your own doctrine; what need is there to cite the opinions of others?"
Saccaka Nigaṇṭhaputta said to the Buddha,
“Form is truly the self.
The Buddha then addressed the householder Aggivessana:
"I now ask you; answer me as you see fit.
Suppose there were a king who, regarding those with offenses within his own realm, might execute them, bind them, exile them, flog them, or sever their hands and feet;
yet regarding those with merit, he might bestow upon them elephants, horses, chariots, cities, and treasures—would he be able to do all this?"
He replied,
“I am able to do so, Gautama!”
The Buddha said to the householder Agniveśyāyanaputra,
"Does every master possess complete autonomy?
He replied:
"So it is, Gautama! The Buddha said to the householder Agniveśyāyana:

"Do you say that form is the self, and that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the self, such that you can exercise mastery over them at will, making them thus or not thus?"
At that time, Satyaka Nirgranthīputra remained silent.
The Buddha said to the householder Agniveśyāyaniputra,
"Speak quickly!"
"Speak quickly!
Why do you remain silent?
Thus he asked a second and a third time, yet Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha remained silent as before.
At that time, a yakṣa named Vajrabala, wielding a vajra-pestle from which fierce flames blazed, stood in the air directly above the head of Saccaka Nigaṇṭhaputta and spoke these words:
"The World-Honored One has questioned you twice and even thrice; why do you not answer?"
"I shall shatter your head with my vajra-pestle and reduce it to seven pieces!
By the Buddha's supernatural power, only Saccaka the Nirgrantha saw the Vajra deity; the rest of the assembly did not see him.
Saccaka Nigaṇṭhaputta was seized with great terror and said to the Buddha:
"It is not so, Gautama!"
The Buddha said to Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha:
“Reflect slowly, and then explain.
Previously, in the midst of the assembly, you said that form is the self, and that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the self; do you now say otherwise?”
This is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows.
You previously stated repeatedly:
"Form is the self; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the self."
"Aggivessana! I now ask you: Is form permanent, or is it impermanent?"
He replied, "It is impermanent, Gautama!"
He asked again:
"Is that which is impermanent suffering?
He replied:
"It is suffering, Gautama.
He asked again:

"That which is impermanent and suffering is subject to change; would a well-taught noble disciple regard it as 'this is my self,' or 'this is other than my self,' or 'this and my self exist together'?"
He replied, “No, Gautama.
The same was said regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
The Buddha said to the householder Agniveśyāyanaputra,
"Reflect well before you speak.
He then questioned the householder Agniveśyāyanaputra again:

"If one has not yet become free from greed for form, not yet free from desire for it, not yet free from mindfulness of it, not yet free from craving for it, and not yet free from thirst for it—would sorrow, lamentation, vexation, and suffering arise if that form were to change or alter?"
He replied, “It is so, Gautama!
He spoke in the same way regarding feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.
He asked again:
"Householder Aggivessana!

When one is free from greed for form, free from desire for form, free from thoughts of form, free from craving for form, and free from thirst for form—if that form should change or alter, would sorrow, lamentation, vexation, and suffering not arise?"
He replied: "It is so, Gautama."
"It is exactly as it is, without difference.
The same is said for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"Householder Agniveśya!"

The Buddha told Rādha:

I shall explain it for you.

That which is called ‘with-outflows’ (sāsrava) refers to the fact that foolish, unlearned worldlings do not know, as they truly are, the arising of form, the cessation of form, the gratification of form, the danger of form, and the escape from form.”
Because they do not know things as they truly are, they find delight in form, praise it, grasp at it, and become stained by attachment to it.

With delight in form as condition, grasping arises; with grasping as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises; and with birth as condition, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, vexation, and suffering increase.
In this way, this entire great mass of suffering arises.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
This is called the flow of existence (*bhava-srotas*).
“The learned noble disciple understands, as they truly are, the arising of form, the cessation of form, the gratification of form, the danger in form, and the escape from form.
Because he understands them as they truly are, he does not give rise to craving, delight, praise, grasping, or attachment toward that form.

Because he does not crave, delight in, praise, grasp, or become attached to it, craving for form ceases; with the cessation of craving, grasping ceases; with the cessation of grasping, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; and with the cessation of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair cease. Thus, this entire great mass of suffering ceases.”
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
This is called what the Tathāgata has taught regarding the outflows and the cessation of the outflows.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣu Rādha, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
