188 (188). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should correctly observe that the eye is impermanent.
To observe in this way is called right view."

Through right contemplation, disenchantment arises; through disenchantment, one becomes detached from joy and detached from lust. Because of this detachment from joy and lust, I say that the mind is rightly liberated.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind: they become detached from joy and detached from lust; because of this detachment from joy and lust, [the mind is rightly liberated].
"Monks! I say that the mind is rightly liberated. One whose mind is rightly liberated can declare of themselves:
'Birth has been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been done; I myself know that there will be no further existence.'"
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As it was said regarding impermanence, so it was likewise spoken regarding suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
189 (189). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should correctly contemplate and observe the eye as impermanent.

Why is that? Because by correctly contemplating and observing the eye as impermanent, desire and greed for the eye are abandoned; because desire and greed are abandoned, I say that the mind is rightly liberated."
Through right reflection and contemplation of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, sensual desire is abandoned; when sensual desire is abandoned, I say that the mind is rightly liberated.
In this way, bhikkhus, one whose mind is rightly liberated can declare of himself:
"Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I myself know that there will be no further existence."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
190 (190) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one does not recognize the eye, does not understand it, does not abandon it, and is not free from desire for it, one is incapable of bringing an end to suffering."
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue,
body, and mind. Monks,
one who has recognized, understood, abandoned, and become free from desire regarding the eye is capable of bringing an end to suffering.
Regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, one who discerns them, understands them, abandons them, and becomes free from desire for them is capable of rightly bringing an end to suffering.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
191 (191) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one does not recognize, does not know, does not abandon, and does not become free from desire for the eye, one is incapable of transcending the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death."

If one does not recognize, does not know, does not abandon, and does not become free from desire for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, one is incapable of transcending the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
"O bhikṣus!

If one has recognized, understood, abandoned, and become free from desire for the eye—whether it be its consciousness or its cognition—one is capable of transcending the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death."

Regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind: if one cognizes, knows, abandons, and becomes free from desire for them, one is capable of transcending the suffering of birth, aging, illness, and death.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
192 (192) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one is not free from desire for the eye and the mind is not liberated, one is incapable of rightly bringing an end to suffering."
"Bhikṣus! One who is not free from desire for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and whose mind is not liberated, is incapable of rightly bringing an end to suffering."
If one becomes free from desire for the eye and forms, and the mind is liberated, that person is capable of rightly bringing an end to suffering.
If one becomes free from desire for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and the mind is liberated, that person is capable of rightly bringing an end to suffering.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
193 (193) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one is not free from desire for the eye and forms, and the mind is not liberated, one is incapable of transcending the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death."

If one does not depart from desire regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and the heart is not liberated, one is incapable of transcending the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
"Monks! If one becomes detached from the eye and forms, and the mind is liberated, one is capable of transcending the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
If one becomes detached from the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and the mind is liberated, one is capable of transcending the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
194 (194) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one gives rise to delight toward the eye, one gives rise to delight toward suffering; if one gives rise to delight toward suffering, I say that such a person is not liberated from suffering."
One who finds delight in the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind finds delight in suffering; and one who finds delight in suffering, I say, is not liberated from suffering.

“Monks, if one does not give rise to delight toward the eye, then one does not give rise to delight toward suffering. If one does not give rise to delight toward suffering, I say that such a person is liberated from suffering.”

One who does not give rise to delight regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind does not give rise to delight regarding suffering; one who does not give rise to delight regarding suffering, I declare, is liberated from suffering.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
195 (195) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"All things are impermanent.
In what way are all things impermanent?"

That is to say, the eye is impermanent; and likewise, visible forms, eye-consciousness, and eye-contact, as well as the feeling produced through the causal condition of eye-contact—whether it be a painful feeling, a pleasant feeling, or a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—are also impermanent.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

When a learned noble disciple observes in this way, they become weary of the eye; they also become weary of forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feelings—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arise conditioned by eye-contact. They become weary of these.

The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena; mind-consciousness, mind-contact, and the feeling born of mind-contact as a condition—whether it be a painful feeling, a pleasant feeling, or a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—one becomes weary of these as well. Through weariness, one does not delight in them; through lack of delight, one is liberated. Being liberated, one possesses the knowledge and vision:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As it was said in the *Anitya-sūtra*, so too were the *Duḥkha*, *Śūnya*, and *Anātman* sūtras spoken in the same manner.
196 (One Hundred and Ninety-Six). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"All is impermanent. What is all?

It refers to the eye as impermanent; likewise, forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feeling born of eye-contact as a condition—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—are also impermanent."

In the same way, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; as well as mental phenomena, the mind-consciousness, mind-contact, and the feeling born of mind-contact as a condition—whether it be painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—all these are also impermanent.

For a well-heard noble disciple who contemplates in this way, there is liberation regarding the eye; likewise, they are liberated from forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.

In the same way, regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and mental objects—the mental consciousness, mental contact, and the feeling born of the condition of mental contact, whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one is liberated from them as well. I declare that such a person is liberated from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, despair, and suffering.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

As it was said that "all is impermanent," so too it has been extensively explained in the two preceding sūtras that all is suffering, all is empty, all is non-self, all is a phenomenon of vain activity, all is a phenomenon of disintegration, all is a phenomenon of birth, all is a phenomenon of aging, all is a phenomenon of illness, all is a phenomenon of death, all is a phenomenon of sorrow and lamentation, all is a phenomenon of affliction, all is a phenomenon of origination, all is a phenomenon of cessation, all is a phenomenon of knowledge, all is a phenomenon of consciousness, all is a phenomenon of abandonment, all is a phenomenon of awakening, all is to be realized, all is Māra, all is the power of Māra, all is the weapon of Māra, all is burning, all is ablaze, and all is consumed by fire.
197. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Caitya of Kāśaśirīṣa together with a thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were formerly brahmins who wore their hair in matted locks.
At that time, the World-Honored One performed three kinds of demonstrations to instruct the thousand bhikṣus.
What are these three?
The demonstration of supernormal transformations, the demonstration of knowing the minds of others, and the demonstration of exhortation.

Regarding the manifestation of the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*), the World-Honored One, according to what is appropriate, manifests entering meditative absorption (*dhyāna-samādhi*). He ascends into the void and proceeds toward the east, displaying the four dignified postures (*īryāpatha*)—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining. He enters the fire-trance (*tejo-dhātu-samādhi*) and emits various kinds of fire-light: blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and crystal-colored. Water and fire appear simultaneously; sometimes fire issues from the lower part of his body while water issues from the upper part, or water issues from the lower part while fire issues from the upper part. This is likewise done throughout the four directions.
At that time, having performed various miraculous transformations, the World-Honored One sat among the assembly; this is called the manifestation of supernormal power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).

As for the manifestation of the knowledge of others' minds (*ādeśanā-prātihārya*): according to their hearts, according to their intentions, and according to their consciousnesses—thinking "they should form such a thought, they should not form such a thought," or "they should practice such equanimity, they should dwell in such bodily realization"—this is called the manifestation of the knowledge of others' minds.
Regarding the manifestation of instruction, as the Blessed One said:
"O bhikṣus! Everything is ablaze."
What is meant by "everything is ablaze"?

It means that the eye is ablaze; likewise, forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feeling born of eye-contact as a condition—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—are also ablaze.

In this way, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are ablaze; and whatever phenomena, mental consciousness, mind-contact, and the feeling born of mind-contact as a condition—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—those too are ablaze. By what are they ablaze? They are ablaze with the fire of greed, ablaze with the fire of hatred, and ablaze with the fire of delusion; they are ablaze with the fires of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, despair, and suffering.

At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the thousand bhikṣus were freed from all outflows, and their minds attained liberation. When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
198 (One Hundred and Ninety-Eight). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, the Venerable Rāhula went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How should I know and how should I see my internal consciousness-body and all external phenomena, so that the fetters of attachment arising from ‘I,’ ‘mine,’ and the underlying tendency of the conceit ‘I am’ do not arise?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Rāhula:
"Excellent, Rāhula! Excellent!"
"You are able to inquire about the profound meaning of the Tathāgata.

The Buddha told Rāhula: "Whether the eye is past, future, or present; whether internal or external; whether coarse or subtle; whether beautiful or ugly; whether distant or near—all of these, one should know as they truly are: they are not self, they are not distinct from the self, and they do not exist within one another."
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are also like this. "Rāhula!
By knowing and seeing my consciousness-body and all external phenomena in this way, you shall cause the arising of 'I,' 'mine,' and the underlying tendency of the conceit 'I am' to cease."
Rāhula! In this way, the underlying tendencies of "I," "mine," and the conceit "I am" do not arise. Rāhula!
"This is called severing the turbidity of craving and views, attaining right clear comprehension, and reaching the ultimate end of suffering.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Rāhula, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

As with the internal sense bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), so it is with the external sense bases (*bāhyāyatana*)—namely, forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects; eye-consciousness, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness; eye-contact, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact; feelings born of eye-contact, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact; perceptions born of eye-contact, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact; volitions born of eye-contact, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact; and cravings born of eye-contact, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact—all are to be understood as explained above.
199. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa, the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Rāhula:

"How does one know, how does one see, so that regarding this consciousness-body and all external phenomena, there is no 'I,' no 'mine,' and no fettering attachment to the underlying tendency of the conceit 'I am'?"
Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The World-Honored One is the root of the Dharma, the eye of the Dharma, and the refuge of the Dharma.
Excellent!”
“World-Honored One!
You should explain this meaning in detail for the bhikṣus; having heard it, the bhikṣus will receive and practice it accordingly.
The Buddha told Rāhula:
“Excellent! Listen attentively, and I shall explain it for you.

Whatever eyes there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; beautiful or ugly; far or near—all of them are not-self, not distinct from the self, and do not exist within one another. One should view them thus with right and correct contemplation according to reality.”
Rāhula! The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are also like this. Rāhula!
Knowing thus and seeing thus, regarding this consciousness-body and all external phenomena, no conceit of "I," "mine," or the underlying tendency of self-conceit arises.
Rāhula! In this way, a bhikṣu transcends duality, is free from all signs, and is liberated through cessation. Rāhula!
"In this way, a bhikṣu severs all craving and desire, casts off all fetters, and reaches the ultimate end of suffering.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Rāhula, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As it is with the internal sense bases, so it is with the external sense bases; this is to be explained in detail up to the feeling born of the condition of mental contact.
(200) [Discourse 200] Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Rāhula went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent!
"Bhagavān, teach me the Dharma. Having heard the Dharma, I shall dwell alone in a quiet place, reflecting with focused diligence and remaining heedful;
having dwelt alone in a quiet place, reflecting with focused diligence and remaining heedful, I shall reflect as follows:"

"It is for this reason, noble son, that one shaves off hair and beard, out of right faith leaves the home life for homelessness, trains in the path, and practices the holy life (brahmacarya), so as to see the Dharma, know it for oneself, and realize it:
'Birth for me has been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been done; I myself know that there will be no further existence.'"
At that time, the World-Honored One observed Rāhula’s mind and saw that his wisdom regarding liberation was not yet matured and that he was not yet capable of receiving the higher Dharma.
He asked Rāhula:
“Have you already taught the five aggregates of clinging to others?”
Rāhula addressed the Buddha:
“Not yet, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Rāhula, "You should expound the five aggregates of clinging for others.

At that time, having received the Buddha’s instruction, Rāhula at another time expounded the five aggregates of clinging for others. Having finished speaking, he returned to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I have already explained the five aggregates of clinging to others; I only pray that the World-Honored One will teach me the Dharma. Having heard the Dharma, I shall dwell alone in a quiet place, applying myself with focused reflection and living without negligence, until I know for myself that there will be no further existence.”
At that time, the World-Honored One again observed Rāhula’s mind and saw that his wisdom regarding liberation was not yet matured and that he was not yet capable of receiving the superior Dharma.
He asked Rāhula:
“Have you explained the six sense bases to others?”
Rāhula addressed the Buddha:
“Not yet, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Rāhula:
"You should expound the six sense bases for others.

At another time, after Rāhula had expounded the six sense bases for others, he went to where the Buddha was, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet in salutation, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I have already expounded the six sense bases for others; I only pray that the World-Honored One will teach me the Dharma. Having heard the Dharma, I shall dwell alone in a quiet place, applying myself with diligence and reflection, abiding without negligence, until I personally know that there will be no further existence.”
At that time, the World-Honored One observed Rāhula’s mind and saw that his wisdom regarding liberation was not yet matured and he was not yet capable of receiving the higher teaching (*abhidharma*).
He asked Rāhula:
"Have you already explained the *nidāna* dharma to others?"
Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Not yet, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Rāhula:
"You should expound the *nidāna* dharma for others.

At that time, after Rāhula had extensively expounded the *nidāna* dharma for others on another occasion, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Please teach me the Dharma. Having heard the Dharma, I shall dwell alone in a quiet place, applying myself with diligent reflection and remaining heedful, until I know for myself that there will be no further existence.”
At that time, the World-Honored One again observed Rāhula’s mind and saw that his wisdom regarding liberation was not yet mature... [as explained at length] ...and addressed Rāhula, saying:
"Regarding all the dharmas just described, you should dwell alone in a quiet place, contemplate them with focused diligence, and investigate their meaning."
At that time, Rāhula, having received the Buddha’s instruction, reflected upon and weighed the Dharma as he had heard it and as it was taught; examining its meaning, he thought to himself:
“All these dharmas tend toward nirvāṇa, flow toward nirvāṇa, and ultimately abide in nirvāṇa.”
At that time, Rāhula went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Having alone in a quiet place reflected upon, weighed, and examined the meaning of the Dharma as I have heard it and as it has been taught, I know that all these dharmas lead toward Nirvāṇa, flow toward Nirvāṇa, and ultimately abide in Nirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One observed Rāhula’s mind and saw that his wisdom for liberation had matured and he was capable of receiving the superior Dharma.
He addressed Rāhula, saying: “Rāhula!
"All things are impermanent.
What dharmas are impermanent?
It refers to the eye as impermanent, as well as forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact... and so forth, with the full exposition on impermanence as above.
At that time, Rāhula, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and approved with gladness; he paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew.
Then, having received the Buddha’s instruction, Rāhula dwelt alone in a quiet place, meditating with focused diligence and remaining free from negligence, [reflecting]:

"For this reason, sons of noble family shave off their hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and out of right faith go forth from home into homelessness to study the Path, purely practicing the holy life, even unto the point of seeing the Dharma for themselves and realizing it through personal knowledge:"
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence.
Thus he became an arhat, his mind well-liberated.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Rāhula, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(201) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what knowledge and by what vision does one swiftly attain the exhaustion of the outflows in successive stages?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those bhikṣus:
"You should correctly contemplate impermanence.
Which phenomena are impermanent?"

That is to say: the eye is impermanent; likewise, visible forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feeling—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arising with eye-contact as its condition, should be contemplated as impermanent.
One should contemplate the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as impermanent.

Whether it be mental phenomena, the mental consciousness, mental contact, or the feeling born of the condition of mental contact—be it painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent.
"Monks! Knowing thus and seeing thus, one gradually exhausts all out-flows (*āsrava*).
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that monk rejoiced, paid homage, and departed.
Thus, monks, is the discourse spoken.
If there is a distinction:

"How knowing and how seeing does one, in succession, exhaust all fetters (*saṃyojana*), sever all bonds (*bandhana*), sever all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), sever all higher afflictions (*upakleśa*), sever all ties (*saṃyojana*), sever all floods (*ogha*), sever all yokes (*yoga*), sever all graspings (*upādāna*), sever all contacts (*sparśa*), sever all hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), sever all envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), sever all stains (*mala*), sever all cravings (*tṛṣṇā*), sever all mental intentions (*manasikāra*), abandon wrong view and give rise to right view, and abandon ignorance and give rise to knowledge?"
“Monks! Thus one contemplates the eye as impermanent; even so, through such knowledge and such vision, ignorance is gradually abandoned and clear knowledge arises.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, those monks rejoiced; having rejoiced, they paid homage and departed.
202 (Two Hundred and Two). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
How does one know, and how does one see, such that the view of self is gradually abandoned and the view of non-self arises?
The Buddha told that bhikṣu:

"One correctly contemplates the eye as impermanent; likewise, one correctly contemplates forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feeling—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by eye-contact as being without self."
In this way, even up to the feeling born of the condition of mental contact—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—a bhikkhu also correctly contemplates it as being without self.
Bhikkhus!
"Knowing thus and seeing thus, my view of self was gradually severed, and the vision of non-self arose.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that bhikṣu rejoiced; having rejoiced, he paid homage and departed.
203 (Two Hundred and Three). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī in Jīvaka-kumāra-bhṛtya’s Mango Grove.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
“If there is a bhikṣu who is able to abandon a single dharma, he will attain right knowledge and be able to declare of himself:
‘Birth for me has been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that I shall not undergo further existence.’”
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One, you are the root of the Dharma, the eye of the Dharma, and the refuge of the Dharma.
We pray that you will expound it; having heard it, we, the bhikṣus, shall receive and practice it accordingly.”
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you. Bhikṣus!"
What is this one dharma whose abandonment leads, ultimately, to no further existence?
It is ignorance. Through the fading away of desire, clear knowledge arises; one attains right wisdom and is able to declare of oneself:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence."

At that time, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, prostrated before the Buddha, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“How does one know, how does one see, so that ignorance is abandoned and clear knowledge arises?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“One should correctly contemplate the eye as impermanent; likewise, one should correctly contemplate forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feeling—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by eye-contact, as being impermanent.”
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. Bhikṣus!
When one knows and sees ignorance in this way, desire for it ceases and clear knowledge arises.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
204 (Two hundred four) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī in Jīvaka-kumārabhṛta’s Mālava-ārāma medicinal mango grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:

"One should know the eye as it truly is and see it as it truly is; likewise, one should know and see as they truly are the forms, the eye-consciousness, the eye-contact, and the feeling—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by eye-contact."
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

Having known this as it truly is and seen it as it truly is, he develops disenchantment toward the eye; he also develops disenchantment toward forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feeling—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by eye-contact.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Having become weary of them, one no longer finds delight in them; having no further delight, one attains liberation. With the knowledge and vision of liberation, one knows:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and I myself know that there will be no further existence."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
205 (Two Hundred and Five) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī in Jīvaka-kumārabhṛta’s Mālava-ārāma.
At that time, having spoken all the udāna verses, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:

“The eye is impermanent, suffering, subject to change, and of a nature to undergo transformation. Likewise, visible forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feeling born of eye-contact as its condition—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—are also impermanent, suffering, subject to change, and of a nature to undergo transformation.”
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

For a well-heard noble disciple who contemplates in this way, there is liberation from the eye; likewise, they are liberated from forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feeling arisen with eye-contact as its condition.

The ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, mental phenomena, mind-consciousness, mind-contact, and the feeling born of mind-contact as a condition—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one is liberated from these. I say that such a person is liberated from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, vexation, and suffering.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
206 (Two Hundred and Six) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī in Jīvaka-kumārabhṛtya’s Mālava Mango Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should diligently apply skillful means and practice meditative reflection, bringing the mind to inner stillness. Why is this so?"
"Monks! Through skillful means and meditative reflection, one quiets the mind within; in this way, one knows things as they truly are, and they become manifest.
What is it that one knows as it truly is, such that it becomes manifest?"

He knows and clearly perceives the eye as it truly is; he also knows and clearly perceives as they truly are forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feeling—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by eye-contact.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
These phenomena are impermanent and conditioned; they are likewise clearly known and manifested as they truly are.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 207 (207) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī in Jīvaka Kumārabhṛtya’s Mālava Mango Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“You should cultivate immeasurable samādhi, applying yourselves with diligence and maintaining mindfulness. Why is this?
Having cultivated immeasurable samādhis and applied diligent mindfulness, they manifest as they truly are.
In what do they manifest as they truly are?
They manifest as they truly are in the eye... [and so on,] as explained at length, up to: "These phenomena are impermanent and conditioned; this manifests as it truly is."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 208 (208) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī in Jīvaka-kumārabhṛta’s medicinal mango grove.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
“The eye of the past and the future is impermanent; how much more so the eye of the present!

A learned noble disciple who contemplates in this way does not look back to the eye of the past, does not delight in the eye of the future, and regarding the eye of the present, feels weary of it, finds no pleasure in it, becomes free from desire for it, and turns toward disenchantment.”
"The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As it was said regarding impermanence, so it should be spoken regarding suffering, emptiness, and non-self.

Just as with the four discourses on the internal sense bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), so too should the four discourses on external sense bases—form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental objects—and the four discourses on both internal and external sense bases be spoken in the same manner.
209. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī in Jīvaka-kumāra-bhṛtya’s Mānava-ārāma.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are six bases of contact. What are the six?
The sphere of eye-contact, and the spheres of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.

Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who do not know these six spheres of contact as they really are—in their arising, their cessation, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them—should be known as being far from my Dharma and Vinaya, as distant as the sky is from the earth.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, paid homage to the Buddha, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I fully and truly know the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these six bases of contact.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
“I shall now question you; answer me according to my questions. Bhikṣu!”
"Do you see the sense-sphere of eye-contact as being the self, as distinct from the self, or as existing within the self?
He replied, "No,
World-Honored One!"
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
“Excellent! Excellent!”

Regarding this sphere of eye-contact, when one knows and sees it as it truly is—not as self, not as distinct from self, and not as existing within one another—one does not give rise to the outflows (*āsrava*), the mind is not stained by attachment, and the mind attains liberation. This is called the first sphere of contact being abandoned and fully known; its root is severed like the head of a *tāla* tree cut off, so that in the future, those phenomena will never arise again—namely, eye-consciousness and forms.
"Do you see the spheres of sensory contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as being the self, as distinct from the self, or as existing within the self?
He replied, "No, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Excellent! Excellent!”

Regarding the spheres of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental contact, one who knows and sees them as they truly are—neither as self, nor as distinct from self, nor as existing within one another—does not give rise to the outflows (*āsrava*), the mind is not defiled by attachment, and thus attains liberation. This is called a bhikṣu for whom the six spheres of contact have been abandoned and fully understood; their root has been severed like the head of a *tāla* tree, so that in future lives desire shall not arise again—namely, consciousness and mental objects (*dharma*).
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 210 (210) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī in Jīvaka-kumārabhṛta’s Mālava-āmra-vana (the Mango Grove of the Physician Kumārabhṛta).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Neither delight in pleasure, nor dwell in suffering. Why is this so?

There are six bases of contact that constitute hells. When sentient beings are born into those hells, they see unpleasant forms with their eyes and do not see pleasant forms; they see forms that are not worth reflecting upon and do not see forms worth reflecting upon; they see unwholesome forms and do not see wholesome forms. For these reasons, they experience nothing but sorrow and suffering.

Regarding sounds heard by the ear, odors smelled by the nose, flavors tasted by the tongue, tangibles felt by the body, and mental phenomena cognized by the consciousness: one perceives what is unlovely and does not perceive what is lovely; one perceives what is unworthy of mindfulness and does not perceive what is worthy of mindfulness; one perceives unwholesome dharmas and does not perceive wholesome dharmas. For these reasons, one long endures sorrow and suffering.
"Monks! There are six bases of contact.

When beings are born in that place, their eyes see what is lovely and do not see what is unlovely; they see forms that are agreeable and not disagreeable, they see beautiful forms and not ugly forms. By reason of these conditions, they experience exclusively and continuously joy and happiness."

Sounds heard by the ear, odors smelled by the nose, flavors tasted by the tongue, tangibles felt by the body, and mental objects cognized by the mind—these are lovely and not unlovely, memorable and not unmemorable, and seen as wholesome and not unwholesome.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
211 (211) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī in Jīvaka-kumārabhṛta’s Mālava-ārāma medicinal mango grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, before I had attained perfect enlightenment, while dwelling alone in a quiet place, I practiced meditation and reflected:
'To what does my own mind most often tend when it observes? "
"My own mind frequently pursues the objects of the five sensual pleasures of the past, less frequently pursues those of the present, and even more rarely pursues those of future lives;

having observed that my mind frequently pursues the objects of the five sensual pleasures of the past, I shall exert every possible means and apply diligent effort to protect myself, so that it no longer follows after the objects of the five sensual pleasures of the past."
“Because I have protected myself through such diligent effort, I gradually draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

You bhikṣus likewise pursue past objects of the five desires to a great extent, while those of the present and future are but slight. Now, because you too pursue past objects of the five desires with your minds to a great extent, you should increase your self-protection; before long, you shall attain the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*), and achieve the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom that are free from outflows.

In this very life, you shall know and realize for yourselves: ‘Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and I know for myself that there will be no further existence.’”
"Why is this so? Because conditioned by the eye and forms, there arises an internal feeling—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Conditioned by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind and mental objects (*dharma*), there likewise arises an internal feeling—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant."
Therefore, bhikṣus!
You should be aware of those sense bases: when the eye ceases, the perception of forms departs;
when the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind cease, the perception of phenomena departs.
The Buddha said,
"One should be mindful of the six sense bases.
Having spoken these words, he entered his room to sit in meditation.
At that time, after the Blessed One had departed, a great number of bhikṣus engaged in this discussion:
"The Blessed One has briefly taught us the essentials of the Dharma without detailed analysis, and then entered his room to sit in meditation."
The World-Honored One said:
"One should awaken to the six sense bases. When the eye ceases, the perception of forms is detached;
when the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind cease, the perception of phenomena is detached."

"Even now, we do not yet fully understand the brief teaching given by the World-Honored One today. Within this assembly, who possesses the power of wisdom to explain for us in detail the meaning of the World-Honored One’s brief teaching?"
Again, he thought:
"Only the Venerable Ānanda constantly attends upon the World-Honored One; he is always praised by the Great Teacher as one who is wise and pure in conduct."

"Only the Venerable Ānanda is capable of expounding the meaning for us within the brief teaching given by the Blessed One. Let us all go together today to the Venerable Ānanda’s dwelling, inquire about its essential meaning, and we shall all uphold it exactly as Ānanda explains it."
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus went to where the Venerable Ānanda was, and after exchanging greetings with him, they sat to one side.
They addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
“Venerable One!...”

"You should know that the World-Honored One has briefly taught us the essential Dharma as described above; you should now question Ānanda fully so that he may explain its meaning in detail for our sake."
The Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikṣus:

"Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall explain to you in detail the meaning of that which was spoken in brief by the Blessed One. That which was spoken in brief by the Blessed One is the teaching on the cessation of the six sense bases with remainder. Therefore it is said:
'When the eye-base ceases, perception of forms is detached.'"
"When the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind cease, the perception of phenomena is abandoned.
Having briefly taught this Dharma, the World-Honored One entered his room to sit in meditation; I have now analyzed and explained its meaning for you all.
When the Venerable Ānanda had spoken this meaning, the bhikṣus, having heard what he said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 212 (212) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I do not teach the practice of heedfulness for all bhikṣus, nor do I fail to teach the practice of heedfulness for all bhikṣus."
"To what kind of bhikṣu should one not speak of heedfulness?

It is to a bhikṣu who has attained arhatship, exhausted all outflows, laid down the heavy burden, achieved his own benefit, completely ended the fetters of existence, and whose mind is rightly liberated."
For monks of such a kind, I do not preach the practice of heedfulness. Why is this?

Because those monks have already practiced heedfulness; they are no longer capable of committing acts of negligence. Since I now see that these venerable ones have attained the fruit of heedfulness, I do not preach the practice of heedfulness to them.
"For what kind of bhikṣus do I teach the practice of heedfulness?

For those bhikṣus who are still in the stage of training (śaikṣa), who have not yet attained the supreme peace of mind, and who dwell directed toward nirvāṇa—for such bhikṣus as these, I teach the practice of heedfulness."

Why is this? Because that bhikṣu trains in the faculties, his mind delights in following the requisites for life, and he draws near to virtuous friends; before long, he shall attain the exhaustion of all outflows (āsrava), achieving the liberation of mind through the absence of outflows and the liberation by wisdom, realizing for himself in this very life:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence."

Why is this? Regarding those forms that are lovely, delightful, and objects of attachment for eye-consciousness, when that bhikṣu has seen them, he does not rejoice in them, does not praise them, is not stained by them, and does not dwell in attachment to them.

Because he does not rejoice, does not praise, is not stained, and does not dwell in attachment, he applies himself with diligence and excels; his body and mind are stilled, his mind dwells in supreme peace and mindfulness, he is constantly concentrated in a single state of mind, and with immeasurable joy in the Dharma, he attains only the foremost samādhi and right reception, never regressing or being led astray by eye-objects.
"It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness regarding mental phenomena.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
213 (213). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now expound two dharmas for you.
Listen attentively and reflect well upon them.
What are these two?
The eye and forms constitute a duality.
The ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena constitute dualities;
these are called the two dharmas. "If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who speak thus:"
"Regarding these two—'is' and 'is not'—these are the two dharmas spoken of by the śramaṇa Gautama; yet these do not constitute duality.

As for those who, according to their own views, speak of these two dharmas, they possess nothing but mere words; having heard them, they do not understand and their doubts increase, because this is not within their sphere of experience.

"Why is this? Conditioned by the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; through the coming together of these three factors, conditioned by contact, feeling arises—whether it be painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant."

If one does not know, as they truly are, the arising of feeling, the cessation of feeling, the gratification of feeling, the danger of feeling, and the escape from feeling, then one plants the bodily contact of lustful desire, the bodily contact of ill will, the bodily contact of clinging to precepts and observances, and the bodily contact of the view of self; thus one plants and increases various evil and unwholesome states.

"In this way, this entire great mass of suffering arises from its origin. Likewise, with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as conditions for mental objects, mental consciousness arises; the meeting of these three factors is contact... as explained in detail above.

"Furthermore, with the eye as condition and forms as object, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three factors is contact; with contact as condition, feeling arises—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant. One thus knows the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these various feelings."

Having understood this, one does not cultivate bodily contact associated with sensual desire, nor bodily contact associated with ill will, nor bodily contact associated with attachment to precepts and rituals, nor bodily contact associated with the view of self, nor does one cultivate various evil and unwholesome dharmas.
In this way, with the cessation of these various evil and unwholesome states, this entire great mass of suffering ceases.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind with respect to mental phenomena.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
214 (214) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are two conditions for the arising of consciousness. What are these two?"

That is to say: the eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, the mind and mental phenomena... [and so on, as extensively explained], up to: "because they are not within its domain."

Why is this so? Eye-consciousness arises conditioned by the eye and visible forms; it is impermanent, conditioned, and mind-originated. Visible forms, as well as the eye and consciousness, are impermanent, conditioned, and mind-originated. The conjunction of these three factors is contact (*sparśa*); having contacted, there is feeling (*vedanā*); having felt, there is volition (*cetanā*); having willed, there is perception (*saṃjñā*). All these phenomena—namely contact, perception, and volition—are impermanent, conditioned, and mind-originated.
"The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
215 (Two hundred fifteen). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The Blessed One teaches the present life; he teaches the extinguishing of the burning fires; he teaches that which does not depend on time; he teaches the direct path; he teaches what is to be seen right here; he teaches that which is to be personally realized.”
“World-Honored One!
What is the ‘present dharma,’ and so forth, up to ‘realized through personal awakening’?
The Buddha told Pūrṇa:
"Excellent, Pūrṇa! You are able to ask such a question."
Pūrṇa! Listen attentively and reflect well;
I shall speak for you. Pūrṇa!

When a bhikkhu has seen a form with the eye, he discerns the form and discerns the lust for the form; he knows as it truly is: "There is this lust for forms within me, cognized by the eye-consciousness."

Pūrṇa! If, after the eye has seen a form, one perceives the form and perceives the craving for the form, and knows as it truly is: "I have this internal eye-consciousness and craving for forms," this is called a dharma that is directly perceived.
"How does one extinguish the blazing?
How does one not wait for time?
How does one proceed correctly?"
What is this very seeing?
How does it take self-awakening as its object? Pūrṇa!

When a bhikkhu has seen a form with the eye, he perceives the form and does not give rise to a perception of lust for the form; he knows as it truly is: "I have no internal lust for forms cognized by the eye," and thus he does not give rise to a perception of lust for forms.

If, Pūrṇa! a bhikṣu, having seen a form with the eye and having cognized it, does not give rise to a thought of craving for forms, and knows the form as it truly is; knowing as it truly is that he does not give rise to a thought of craving for forms—this is called the extinguishing of the burning, independent of time, rightly directed, to be seen here and now, and realized through one's own direct knowledge.
"The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣu Pūrṇa, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
216 (Two hundred and sixteen). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"To speak of a 'great ocean' is the talk of fools, not the talk of the noble ones; it is merely a matter of great and small amounts of water.
What, then, is the ocean spoken of by the noble ones?
It is this: having perceived forms with the eye, one conceives longing and deep attachment, and craves the pleasures of bodily, verbal, and mental actions—this is called the ocean."

All the asura hosts of the world, up to and including devas and humans, all greedily delight in and sink into this [existence], like a dog’s belly or a heap of tangled grass; likewise, they are constricted, bound, and fettered in this world and the next.

The ear-consciousness of sounds, the nose-consciousness of odors, the tongue-consciousness of tastes, and the body-consciousness of tangibles—these fetters, entanglements, and shackles regarding this world and the next are likewise thus.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As it was said regarding the actions of body, speech, and mind, so it was likewise said regarding greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as old age, sickness, and death.
As it was said regarding the three sūtras on the five faculties, so too were the three sūtras on the six faculties spoken.
217 (217) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"What is called 'the ocean' is spoken of by the foolish people of the world, not by the noble ones.
The ocean is merely water of varying depths; the eye is the great ocean of man, and visible forms are its waves."
If one can withstand the waves of form, one will cross the great ocean of the eye, having reached the end of its surging billows, eddies, various waters, predatory creatures, and rākṣasī demons.

The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind constitute this person’s great ocean; sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are its waves. If one can endure those waves of phenomena, one attains crossing over the ocean of the mind, having reached the end of the waves, whirlpools, predatory creatures, and rākṣasī-demons.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The great ocean with its massive waves, Terrifying with evil creatures and rākṣasas— That which is difficult to cross, he has crossed;
Having gathered [the assembly], they are forever free from remainder."
"Able to sever all suffering, one shall no longer undergo further existence;
attaining eternal parinirvāṇa, one shall never again fall back into negligence.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
218. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now explain to you the path leading to the origin of suffering and the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for your sake.
What is the path leading to the origin of suffering?

Conditioned by the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three factors is contact. Conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving; conditioned by craving is clinging; conditioned by clinging is existence; conditioned by existence is birth; conditioned by birth, there arises this entire mass of suffering—namely, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and pain. Thus it is.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
This is called the path leading to the origination of suffering.
"What is the path leading to the cessation of suffering?"

Conditioned by the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three factors is contact. With the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, despair, and suffering cease. Thus, this entire great mass of suffering ceases.
The same is said for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; this is called the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
219 (Two hundred nineteen). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now explain the path leading to Nirvāṇa.
What is the path leading to Nirvāṇa?

It is the contemplation that the eye is impermanent; and that whatever feeling—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises through the causal condition of form, eye-consciousness, and eye-contact, that too is impermanent."
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; this is called the path leading to Nirvana.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
220 (Two Hundred and Twenty). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There is that which resembles the path leading toward Nirvana.
What is this resemblance to the path leading toward Nirvana?

One contemplates the eye as non-self; likewise, one contemplates as impermanent the forms, the eye-consciousness, and the feeling—whether internal, whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by eye-contact.”
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; this is called the path that resembles the track leading to Nirvana.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
221 (Two Hundred Twenty-One). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There is a path that leads to all forms of grasping.
What is this path that leads to all forms of grasping?

Dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three factors is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving; conditioned by craving is grasping, because of what is grasped through grasping.”
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Because of grasping at what is grasped, this is called the path leading to all grasping.
What is the path leading to the abandonment of all grasping?

Conditioned by the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three factors is contact. With the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases;
with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases. The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
222 (222) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should know all dharmas that are known and all dharmas that are cognized.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you."
"What are the phenomena that are known and the phenomena that are cognized?

Monks, the eye is a phenomenon that is known and a phenomenon that is cognized. So too are forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feeling—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by eye-contact; all these are phenomena that are known and phenomena that are cognized."
"It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
223 (Two Hundred and Twenty-three). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I do not say that one can reach the ultimate end of suffering without knowing and without recognizing even a single dharma.
Why do I not say that one can reach the ultimate end of suffering without knowing and without recognizing even a single dharma?"

That is to say, it is not said that one attains the ultimate end of suffering by being unaware of or unrecognizing the eye; nor is it said that one attains the ultimate end of suffering by being unaware of or unseen as to whether forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, or the feeling born of eye-contact as its condition—be it internal feeling of pain, pleasure, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—are known or seen.
"The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
224 (Two Hundred Twenty-Four). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"All phenomena of desire should be abandoned.
How should all phenomena of desire be abandoned?

It means that the eye is a phenomenon of desire that should be abandoned; likewise, forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feeling—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by eye-contact, which is internally experienced—all these phenomena of desire should be abandoned."
"The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
225 (225). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I do not say that one can reach the ultimate end of suffering without knowing and abandoning even a single dharma.
Why do I not say that one can reach the ultimate end of suffering without knowing and abandoning even a single dharma?"

That is to say, one does not declare that the eye is unknowable or that it cannot be abandoned while reaching the ultimate end of suffering; nor does one declare that forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feeling arisen through the condition of eye-contact—whether internally experienced as painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—are all unknowable or cannot be abandoned while reaching the ultimate end of suffering.
"The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
226 (Two hundred and twenty-six). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now explain the severance of all conceptual reckonings.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you.
How is it that one does not reckon?"

That is to say: one does not conceive of a self that sees forms; one does not conceive of the eye as "mine"; one does not conceive of them as being interconnected. Whether it be form, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, or the feeling born of the condition of eye-contact—whether internally experienced as painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one likewise does not conceive of that pleasure as "I" or "mine," nor does one conceive of it as being interconnected.
This is also the case for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

"One who does not calculate in this way never grasps at anything in the world. Because there is no grasping, there is no attachment; because there is no attachment, one realizes nirvana for oneself, knowing:
'Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and I myself know that there will be no further existence.'"
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As stated above, one does not calculate the eye and so forth; likewise, one does not calculate any phenomena whatsoever.
227 (227). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“Conceptualization is a disease, conceptualization is an abscess, conceptualization is a thorn; because the Tathāgata dwells without conceptualizing, he is free from disease, free from abscesses, and free from thorns.”

"Therefore, bhikkhus, one who desires to seek non-identification with a dwelling, being free from disease, free from abscesses, and free from thorns, should not identify the eye as 'I' or 'mine,' nor should they identify it as belonging to the self; nor should they identify forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, or the feeling arisen in dependence on eye-contact—whether internal feeling be painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—as 'I,' 'mine,' or 'this is my self.'"
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are also like this.
"Monks! One who does not calculate in this way has nothing to grasp; because there is nothing to grasp, there is no attachment; because there is no attachment, one personally realizes Nirvana."
“Birth has been exhausted for me; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As it has been explained regarding the eye and so forth, the same applies to each and every other thing. 228 (228). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now speak of the dharma of increase and the dharma of cessation.
What is the dharma of increase?"

That is to say: conditioned by the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three factors is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling... [as explained at length] up until: "Thus is the arising of this entire great mass of suffering. This is called the dharma of increase.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; these are called the factors of increase. "What are the factors of cessation?

Conditioned by the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three is contact. With the cessation of contact, feeling ceases... and so on, as explained at length, until: "...the entire great mass of suffering ceases."
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; these are called the phenomena of diminution.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As with increase and decrease, so too regarding phenomena that arise, phenomena that undergo transformation, phenomena that accumulate, and phenomena that cease, it is as explained above.
229 (229) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now speak of the dharmas with outflows (sāsrava) and the dharmas without outflows (anāsrava).
What are the dharmas with outflows?

That is to say: the eye and forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feeling born of the causal condition of eye-contact—whether it be internally experienced as painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.

The ear, nose, tongue, body, mind-objects, mental consciousness, mind-contact, and the feeling produced with mind-contact as its condition—whether internally experienced as painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—which is worldly: these are called tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
"What are the untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*)?

They are the supramundane mind, or any phenomenon, or mental consciousness, or mental contact, or the feeling produced with mental contact as its condition—whether internal sensation be painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that is supramundane; these are called untainted phenomena."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

9.230 (230). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Samiddhi who went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"What is called 'the world'—what is meant by the term 'world'?
The Buddha told Samiddhi:

"It refers to the eye, forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feeling born of the condition of eye-contact, which is internally experienced as painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant."

The ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, mental objects, mind-consciousness, mind-contact, and the feeling born of mind-contact as a condition—whether internally experienced as painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—this is called the world.
Why is that? With the arising of the six sense bases, there is the arising of contact; and so on, until the arising of this entire mass of suffering. "Samiddhi!..."

If there were no eye, no forms, no eye-consciousness, no eye-contact, and no feeling born of eye-contact as its condition—whether internal feeling be painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant;

and if there were no ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, mental objects, mind-consciousness, mind-contact, and no feeling born of mind-contact as its condition—whether internal feeling be painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—then there would be no world, nor would the world be designated.
"Why is this so? Because with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; and in this way, up to the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As it is with the world, so it is with sentient beings and so it is with Māra; thus it is said. 231 (231). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Samiddhi who went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"What is meant by 'the world' (loka)? Why is it called the world?
The Buddha told Samiddhi:
"That which is precarious, fragile, and subject to decay—this is called the world."
What is meant by "perishable, fragile, and subject to decay"? Samiddhi!

The eye is a phenomenon that is perishable, fragile, and subject to decay; so too are visible forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and whatever feeling—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by eye-contact, which is internally experienced. All of these, as well, are perishable, fragile, and subject to decay.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
These are called the world, being phenomena that are precarious, fragile, and subject to decay.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣu Samiddhi, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
232 (Dvātriṃśaduttaradviśatatama). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Samiddhi who went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what is called ‘the emptiness of the world,’ why is it named the emptiness of the world?
The Buddha told Samiddhi:
“The eye is empty; it is empty of a permanent, eternal, and unchanging dharma, and empty of ‘mine. Why is this?
Because its nature is such by itself.

Whether it be form, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, or the feeling born of the condition of eye-contact—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is empty; it is empty of a permanent, eternal, and unchanging dharma, and empty of ‘mine.’”
Why is this so? Because this nature is inherently such.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; this is called the "empty world."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣu Samiddhi, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
233 (233) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now teach you about the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the path leading to the cessation of the world.”
Listen attentively and reflect well. What is the world?
It refers to the six internal sense bases.
What are the six?
They are the internal sense-base of the eye, and the internal sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
What is the origination of the world?
It refers to craving for future existence, accompanied by delight and greed, finding attachment here and there.
What is the cessation of the world?

It is the remainderless abandonment, relinquishing, vomiting out, exhausting, fading away from desire, ceasing, stopping, and vanishing of that craving for future existence, accompanied by delight and greed, which finds attachment here and there.
"What is the path leading to the cessation of the world?
It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
234 (234) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I do not say that there is anyone who travels to the edge of the world; nor do I say that one can reach the ultimate end of suffering without traveling to the edge of the world."
Having spoken thus, he entered his room to sit in meditation.
Thereupon, after the Blessed One had departed, a great number of bhikṣus gathered together and discussed it, saying:
"The Blessed One has just now briefly spoken these words of Dharma:"
"I do not say that there is anyone who reaches the end of the world; nor do I say that one can reach the ultimate end of suffering without reaching the end of the world."
Having spoken thus, he entered his room to sit in meditation.

"We have not yet understood the meaning of the brief teaching given by the World-Honored One. Among you venerable ones here, who is capable of explaining the meaning of the World-Honored One’s brief teaching in detail for our sake?"
They further said:

"Only the Venerable Ānanda is wise and possesses the power of retention (*dhāraṇī*); he constantly attends upon the World-Honored One at his side. The World-Honored One has praised him for his vast learning and holy life (*brahmacarya*), and he is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of the Dharma that the World-Honored One has spoken in brief for us. We should now go to the Venerable Ānanda’s dwelling and request him to speak."
Then, a great number of bhikṣus went to where the Venerable Ānanda was, and after exchanging greetings with him, they sat down to one side.
They questioned Ānanda extensively regarding all the aforementioned matters.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall now speak for you.
Whatever is worldly, the name of the worldly, worldly perception, worldly terminology, and worldly discourse—all these are included within the category of the worldly.”
Venerable sirs!

That which is called the eye is the world, a name for the world, a perception of the world, a designation for the world, and a verbal expression for the world; all such things are included within the reckoning of the world.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
