When a learned noble disciple knows, as they truly are, the arising, cessation, gratification, danger, and escape regarding these six sense bases, this is called a noble disciple who has reached the end of the world, who understands the world, who is esteemed by the world, and who has transcended the world.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda spoke again in verse:
"One who does not travel the path cannot reach the end of the world;
without reaching the end of the world, one cannot escape manifold sufferings."
Therefore, the Honored Muni is called the Knower of the World;
he has reached the world’s limit and established all holy practices.
At the world’s limit there is only right wisdom that can discern with truth.
"Because awakened wisdom penetrates the world, it is called 'crossing to the other shore.
Thus, venerable ones,
after the Blessed One had briefly taught the Dharma earlier and entered his room to sit in meditation, I shall now analyze and explain it to you in detail."
When the Venerable Ānanda had spoken this Dharma, the many bhikṣus, having heard what he said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
235 (235) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"When there is a teacher and an attendant disciple, one dwells alone in suffering; when there is no teacher and no attendant disciple, one dwells alone in happiness."
"What is it for a teacher to have a resident disciple yet dwell in suffering alone?

When, conditioned by the eye and forms, an evil and unwholesome thought arises accompanied by greed, hatred, and delusion—if a bhikkhu practices this dharma, he is called 'one who has a teacher'; if one dwells at this extreme, he is called 'a resident disciple.'"
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Thus, there is a teacher and a resident disciple who constantly suffer while dwelling alone.
"What is meant by 'having no teacher and no resident disciple, always delighting in dwelling alone'?
When, conditioned by the eye and forms, unwholesome and evil thoughts arise accompanied by greed, hatred, and delusion, and that bhikṣu does not engage in them, this is called 'having no teacher.'"
Not dwelling in dependence upon them is called being without a resident disciple.
This is called being without a teacher and without a resident disciple, always delighting in dwelling alone.
If that bhikṣu is without a teacher and without a resident disciple, I say that he attains the merit of the holy life (brahmacarya).
Why is that? Because there is no teacher and no resident disciple;
it is the bhikṣu who establishes the holy life under me, capable of rightly exhausting suffering and bringing an end to the accumulation of suffering.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
236 (236) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, having dressed in the morning and taken up his bowl, entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms.

Having finished his alms-round, he returned to the monastery, put away his robe and bowl, and after washing his feet, took his sitting mat and entered the forest to practice meditation during the day.
At that time, Śāriputra arose from meditation and went to where the World-Honored One was; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
Then the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
“From where have you come?”
Śāriputra replied,
“World-Honored One,
I have come from sitting in meditation in the forest during the day.”
The Buddha asked Śāriputra,
"In what kind of dhyāna are you currently dwelling?
Śāriputra replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
I am now dwelling in the forest, abiding in the meditative concentration of the emptiness samādhi.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Excellent! Excellent!
Śāriputra, you have now entered the meditation of the Elder and are sitting in dhyāna."
If any bhikṣus wish to enter the meditation of the elders, they should train themselves in this way:
"When entering a city, when walking for alms, or when leaving a city, I should reflect thus:
'As I now see forms with my eyes, do desire, affection, or attachment arise within me?'"

“Śāriputra, when a bhikṣu contemplates in this manner, if his visual consciousness harbors craving, affection, or attachment toward forms, that bhikṣu, for the sake of abandoning evil and unwholesome states, should apply himself with diligence and skillful means, being capable of fixing his mindfulness and practicing with study.”
For example, suppose there were a person whose head or clothing were on fire; in order to extinguish it completely, they would apply superior effort and exert themselves diligently to put it out.
That bhikṣu should likewise apply superior diligence, desire, and skillful means, binding his mindfulness as he practices and trains.

“If, when a bhikṣu observes, whether on the road, while walking for alms in a village, or having left the village, his visual consciousness encounters forms during that interval without affection, longing, or attachment, that bhikṣu—wishing to dedicate these roots of merit born of joy and delight to diligent practice day and night with focused mindfulness—is said to have purified his alms-gathering while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. For this reason, this sutra is titled ‘Abiding in Pure Alms-Gathering.’”
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Śāriputra, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 237 (237) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, by the side of the Monkey Pond, in the Multi-storied Lecture Hall.
At that time, there was an elder named Ugga who went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"For what reason does one bhikṣu attain parinirvāṇa in this very life?
For what reason does another bhikṣu not attain parinirvāṇa in this very life?
The Buddha told the householder:
"If there is a bhikṣu who, regarding forms with eye-consciousness, feels affectionate attachment; because of this affectionate attachment, he constantly relies upon that consciousness;
being bound by it and grasping at it, he cannot see the Dharma and attain parinirvāṇa."
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness regarding mental phenomena.

"If a bhikṣu, when perceiving forms with the eye-consciousness, does not delight in them nor become stained by attachment; because he does not delight in them nor become stained by attachment, he does not rely upon that consciousness. Because he does not touch it, does not adhere to it, and does not grasp it, these bhikṣus attain parinirvāṇa in this very life."
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness regarding mental phenomena.
"Therefore, householder,
there are bhikṣus who attain parinirvāṇa in this very life, and there are those who do not attain parinirvāṇa in this very life."

As it was with the *Sūtra on the Questions of the Householder*, so too it was with the *Sūtra on the Questions of Ānanda* and the sūtras spoken by the Buddha himself for the bhikṣus, all of which are as described above.
238. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, in the Multi-storied Lecture Hall by the side of the Monkey Pond.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what cause and by what condition does visual consciousness arise?”
“By what cause and by what condition do the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness arise?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“With the eye as condition and forms as condition, eye-consciousness arises.”
Why is this so? If visual consciousness arises, it is due to the causal conditions of the eye and visible forms. Auditory consciousness arises due to the causal conditions of the ear and sounds;

olfactory consciousness arises due to the causal conditions of the nose and odors; gustatory consciousness arises due to the causal conditions of the tongue and flavors; and mental consciousness arises due to the causal conditions of the mind and mental phenomena.
Why is this so? Because all instances of mental consciousness arise with the mind and mental objects as their conditions.
This is called, monks, the arising of visual consciousness through conditions, and so on, up to the arising of mental consciousness through conditions.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that bhikṣu rejoiced and approved with gladness;
he paid homage and departed. 239 (239). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, by the side of the Monkey Pond, in the Multi-storied Lecture Hall.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now explain the phenomena bound by the fetters (saṃyojana) and the phenomena that are the fetters themselves.
What are the phenomena bound by the fetters?"

The eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena—these are called the phenomena bound by fetters (*saṃyojana*).
What are the phenomena that are fetters?
"It refers to sensual desire; this is called the phenomenon of fetter.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
240 (240) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Gabled Hall beside the Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now speak of the objects of grasping and the act of grasping."
What are the phenomena that are grasped?
They are the eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental objects; these are called the phenomena that are grasped.
"What is the phenomenon of clinging?
It is sensual desire; this is called the phenomenon of clinging.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
241 (Two Hundred Forty-One). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, in the Multi-storied Lecture Hall beside the Monkey Pond.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Bhikṣus, it would be better for an ignorant,

unlearned worldling to have his eyes burned and set ablaze with glowing, heated copper rods than to grasp at the signs of forms or grasp at their secondary characteristics with the eye-consciousness.”
Why is this? Because by grasping at the signs of form (*rūpa-nimitta*) and grasping at its secondary details (*anuvyañjana*), one falls into the evil destinies like a sinking iron ball.
"A foolish, unlearned worldling would rather burn an iron awl and bore it into their ear than, with the ear-consciousness, grasp at the signs of sound or grasp at its secondary details."

Why is this? Because when the ear-consciousness grasps the characteristics of sound and grasps what is agreeable to the sound, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one falls into the evil destinies like a sinking iron ball.

“Foolish, unlearned worldlings would rather have their noses severed with a sharp blade than take up the signs of fragrance or grasp at the pleasant qualities of fragrance through nose-consciousness.”

Why is this? Because by grasping at the signs of fragrance and grasping at the secondary qualities of fragrance, when the body breaks up and life ends, one falls into the evil destinies like a sinking iron ball.

"It would be better for a foolish, unlearned worldling to have his tongue cut off with a sharp blade than to grasp at the signs of taste or grasp at the secondary qualities of taste with the tongue-consciousness."

Why is this? Because by grasping at the signs of flavor and following after the gratification of flavor, when the body breaks up and life ends, one falls into the evil destinies like a sinking iron ball.

"A foolish, unlearned worldling would rather have a sharp spear of tempered iron pierce their body than, with the body-consciousness, grasp at the signs of tangibles and follow after the gratification of tangibles."

Why is this? Because they grasp at the characteristics of contact and pursue the pleasant aspects of contact, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, they fall into the evil destinies like a sinking iron ball. "Monks!
Sleep is the livelihood of a fool, it is the life of delusion; it brings neither benefit nor merit. Nevertheless, monks, it would be better to sleep than to give rise to perceptions of those forms;

for if such perceptions arise, they will inevitably produce entanglements and disputes, causing many people to engage in what is unrighteous, and failing to bring benefit, peace, or happiness to gods and humans.
That learned noble disciple trains himself thus:
"I would rather have a blazing iron spear pierce my eyes than, through eye-consciousness, apprehend the signs of forms and thereby fall into the three evil destinies to suffer for a long night."
From this day forward, I shall correctly reflect:

"I contemplate the eye as impermanent, conditioned, and a phenomenon produced by mental conditions; likewise, visible forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feeling—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by eye-contact are also impermanent, conditioned, and phenomena produced by mental conditions."
“In the same way, one should train regarding the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, and body:

‘It would be better for an iron spear to pierce my body than for me, on account of the body-consciousness grasping at the signs of tangibles or following after the pleasure of tangibles, to fall into the three evil destinies.’”
From this day forward, I shall correctly reflect thus:

"The body is observed to be impermanent, conditioned, and a phenomenon produced by mental conditions; likewise, contact, body-consciousness, body-contact, and the feeling produced with body-contact as its condition—whether internally experienced as painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—are also impermanent, conditioned, and phenomena produced by mental conditions."
“The learned noble disciple trains himself thus:

‘Sleeping is a life of folly, a life of delusion; it is without fruit, without benefit, and without merit. I shall not sleep, nor shall I give rise to the thought of waking; for the arising of such a thought gives birth to fetters and disputes, which bring harm and disadvantage to many people and prevent them from attaining peace and happiness.’”

“When a learned noble disciple observes in this way, he becomes weary of the eye; he also becomes weary of forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feeling—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by eye-contact, experienced internally. Through weariness, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. Being liberated, he knows and sees:
‘Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and I myself know that there will be no further existence.’”
“The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
242 (Two Hundred Forty-Two). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, in the Multi-storied Lecture Hall beside the Monkey Pond.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“If one does not know, does not recognize, does not sever, and does not become free from desire for the eye, one is incapable of rightly exhausting suffering.
If one knows, recognizes, severs, and becomes free from desire for the eye, one is capable of rightly exhausting suffering.”
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As with the four sūtras concerning the eye, so it is for each of the [other] senses up to the mind, as twenty-four sūtras described above.
243 (Two Hundred Forty-Three). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Gabled Hall beside the Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If any bhikṣus find gratification in the eye, you should know that these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas have not attained mastery to escape the hand of Māra; they are bound by the fetters of Māra and have entered into the bonds of Māra."
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa does not relish the eye, it should be known that this śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa does not follow Māra, is liberated from Māra’s hand, and does not enter the bonds of Māra.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
As it was with "taste," so it should be spoken regarding "joy," "praise," "attachment," "firm abiding," "delight," and "hostility."
As it was said in the seven discourses on the internal sense bases, so too were the seven discourses on the external sense bases spoken.
244 (244) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vesālī, by the side of the Monkey Pond, in the Gabled Hall.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are six hooks of Māra. What are the six?

To relish and become attached to forms with the eye is the hook of Māra; to relish and become attached to sounds with the ear is the hook of Māra; to relish and become attached to odors with the nose is the hook of Māra; to relish and become attached to flavors with the tongue is the hook of Māra; to relish and become attached to tangibles with the body is the hook of Māra; to relish and become attached to mental objects with the mind is the hook of Māra.

If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa relishes and becomes attached to forms with the eye, you should know that the hook of Māra has caught their throat; such a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa does not possess mastery over Māra.
"Speaking of the impure as pure," and so forth, as explained in detail above.
245 (245) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the village of Kuruṇḍa, where tamed and wild oxen were gathered.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

"I shall now teach you the Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; it is excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing, purely complete and pure, the holy life of total clarity—namely, the Sūtra on the Fourfold Dharma."
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall explain it for you.
What are the four categories of the Dharma-discourse?

There are forms cognizable by the eye that are lovely, agreeable, delightful, and enticing. When a bhikṣu sees them, he rejoices, praises them, delights in them, and remains firmly attached to them. There are also forms cognizable by the eye that are unlovely, disagreeable, not delightful, and loathsome.
Having seen this, the bhikṣu becomes angry and feels contemptuous.
Thus, that bhikṣu does not attain mastery over Māra, nor does he attain liberation from the bonds of Māra.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

When there is a form cognized by the eye that is lovely, desirable, pleasant, and enticing, a bhikṣu, having seen it, recognizes it with joy but does not praise it, nor does he delight in or cling to it as substantial. When there is a form cognized by the eye that is unlovely, undesirable, unpleasant, and unenticing, a bhikṣu, having seen it, does not become angry or feel aversion toward it.
In this way, the bhikṣu does not follow Māra; he attains mastery and even liberation from the bonds of Māra.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
"This is called the Discourse on the Fourfold Dharma of a Bhikṣu. (246) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having dressed in the morning and taken up his bowl, entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food.
At that moment, the Māra Pāpīyān thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama, having dressed in the morning and taken up his bowl, has entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food; I shall now go to disturb his resolve."

At that time, Māra Pāpīyas transformed himself into the likeness of a cowherd: he carried a staff, sought out cattle, wore tattered clothes, had disheveled hair, and his hands and feet were cracked and split; holding a cow-herding stick in his hand, he approached the World-Honored One and asked:
"Gautama!..."
“Did you see my ox?
The World-Honored One thought to himself:
“This is Māra, the Evil One, who wishes to come and disturb me.”
He then addressed Māra, saying: "Evil Māra!
Where is there a cow?"
"What use have I for an ox?
The Māra thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama knows that I am Māra."
He then addressed the Buddha, saying: "Gautama!
The sphere of visual contact is that which I ride upon."
"The spheres of contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are what I ride upon.
He asked again:
"Gautama!..."
"Where do you wish to go?
The Buddha said to Māra:
"You have the sphere of eye-contact, as well as the spheres of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact."
If there were no sphere of eye-contact, no spheres of ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact, and you could not reach it, yet I could go there—[would that place exist?]
At that time, the Māra Pāpīyān spoke these verses:
"If there were always a self, then all those things would be mine;
everything would belong to me— where, Gautama, would you go?"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"If one says there is a self, That which they speak of as 'self' is not [the true self].
Therefore, know that Pāpīyas Has fallen into a position of defeat."
Māra spoke again in verse:
"If you say you have known the Way and are proceeding peacefully toward Nirvāṇa, then go alone on your own;
why trouble yourself to teach others?"
The World-Honored One again answered with a verse, saying:
"If there be one who has left Māra behind, And asks for the path to cross to the other shore,
For that person I shall speak with impartiality, Of the truth, forever without remainder."
"By practicing heedfulness at all times, one will forever be free from the power of Māra.
Māra spoke again in verse:
"There is a stone that resembles a piece of meat; a hungry crow comes wishing to eat it."
He conceived the thought that it was soft and delicious, wishing to satisfy his hunger;
yet he failed to obtain its flavor and flew off with broken beak into the void.
I am now like that crow, while Gautama is like a stone-born plant.
Not entering [the city], he departed with shame;
like a bird soaring through the void, his inner heart harbored sorrow and bitterness, and thereupon he vanished from that place, no longer appearing. (247) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas become habitually attached to forms with their eyes, they will fall under the sway of Māra, and so on, until they fail to attain liberation from the bonds of Māra."
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
"If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa does not habitually associate with forms through the eye, does not follow Māra, and remains self-mastery, he will even attain liberation from the bonds of Māra."
"The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

As with frequenting [them], so too is attachment, so too is relishing, so too is proximity. If one should take them up and become attached, seeking and desiring them with intense and persistent longing, it is also as described above.
248. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Pāṭaliputra in the Kalandaka Garden.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda went to where the Venerable Mahācunda was, and after exchanging greetings with him, sat down to one side.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Venerable Cunda:
"I wish to ask a question; would you have the leisure to grant me an answer?
The Venerable Cunda said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Whatever you wish to ask, O Venerable One, the Knower shall answer.
The Venerable Ānanda asked the Venerable Cunda:

"Just as the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, knows and sees, he has taught that the four great elements and the form derived from them are designated and manifested; and just as these forms of the four great elements are not-self according to what the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha knows and sees, does he likewise teach that consciousness is not-self?"
The Venerable Cunda said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Virtuous one, you are preeminent in your great learning. I have come from afar to visit you for the purpose of inquiring about this Dharma. Today, O Venerable One!"
"I only wish that you would explain this meaning for me.
Venerable Ānanda said to Cunda:
"I shall now question the Venerable One; please answer according to your own understanding."
"Venerable Cunda!
Are there eyes, are there forms, and is there eye-consciousness?
He replied:
“Yes, Venerable Ānanda. He asked again:
“Does eye-consciousness arise conditioned by the eye and forms?”
He replied, "It is so.
Venerable Ānanda asked again:
“If the eye and forms give rise to eye-consciousness, are those causes and conditions permanent or impermanent?
He replied: “Impermanent.”
The Venerable Ānanda asked again:
"When those causes and those conditions that give rise to visual consciousness are impermanent and subject to change, does that consciousness abide?"
He replied, “No,
Venerable Ānanda. Venerable Ānanda asked again:
"What do you think?
If those phenomena were known to arise or cease, would a learned noble disciple perceive therein: 'This is me,' or 'This is different from me,' or 'This and that exist within one another'?"
He replied: “No, Venerable Ānanda!
As for the ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and mental objects—what do you think?”
"Is there intention, is there phenomena, and is there mental consciousness?
He replied, "There is."
"Venerable Ānanda!
He asked again:
"Does mental consciousness arise conditioned by the mind and mental phenomena?"
He replied, “So it is, Venerable Ānanda!
He asked again:
"If the mind takes dharmas as its object and gives rise to mental consciousness, are those causes and conditions permanent or impermanent?
He replied, "They are impermanent."
"Venerable Ānanda!
He asked again:
"If consciousness arises due to a certain cause and condition, when that cause and that condition are impermanent and subject to change, does that consciousness remain?"
He replied, "No, Venerable Ānanda!
He asked again:
"What do you think?
If those phenomena were known to arise or to cease, would a learned noble disciple see therein a self, or something distinct from a self, or the two existing in mutual dependence?"
He replied, "No,
Venerable Ānanda! Then the Venerable Ānanda spoke to Cunda:
"Therefore, Venerable One!
That which is known and seen by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, he declares consciousness to be impermanent as well.

It is, for example, like a man who enters a mountain with an axe and sees a plantain tree; thinking it might be fit for timber, he cuts its roots, chops off its stalks and leaves, and strips away its bark, seeking its solid core. He strips it until it is exhausted, yet there is no place of solidity at all."
In this way, the well-versed noble disciple correctly contemplates eye-consciousness, as well as ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness.

While correctly contemplating them, there is nothing at all to be grasped. Because there is nothing to be grasped, there is no attachment. Because there is no attachment, he personally realizes Nirvana, knowing:
"Birth for me has been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been done; I myself know that there will be no further existence."
"When those two noble men had spoken this Dharma, they expressed mutual appreciation for one another and each returned to his own place.
(249) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Venerable Śāriputra and said to him, "I wish to ask a question;
would you have the leisure to explain it for me?"
Śāriputra said,
"I shall answer according to whatever you ask, O worthy one.
Then the Venerable Ānanda questioned the Venerable Śāriputra:
"Once the six bases of contact have been exhausted, having become detached from desire, ceased, stilled, and vanished—does anything further remain?
Venerable Sāriputta said to Ānanda:
"Do not ask such a question."
"Once the six bases of contact have been exhausted, and having become detached from them, ceased, stilled, and vanished, is there anything remaining?
Ānanda again asked the Venerable Śāriputra:
"Once the six bases of contact have been exhausted, and having become detached from them, ceased, stilled, and vanished, is there nothing remaining?"
Venerable Śāriputra replied to Ānanda:
"Furthermore, one should not ask such a question as:
'When the six bases of contact have been exhausted, and through the fading away of desire, their cessation, their subsiding, and their disappearance, is there nothing remaining?'"
Ānanda again asked the Venerable Śāriputra:
"When the six bases of contact have been exhausted, and there is detachment, cessation, stilling, and disappearance, is there a remainder, or no remainder, or neither a remainder nor no remainder?"
The Venerable Śāriputra replied to Ānanda:
"This, too, should not be asked in such a manner:
'When the six bases of contact have been exhausted, detached from desire, ceased, stilled, and vanished, is there a remainder, or no remainder, or neither a remainder nor no remainder?'"
The Venerable Ānanda again asked Śāriputra:
“As the Venerable has said:

‘When the six bases of contact have been exhausted, having become detached from desire, ceased, stilled, and vanished, one should not say it exists, nor should one say it does not exist, nor should one say it both exists and does not exist, nor should one say it neither exists nor does not exist.’”
"What is the meaning of these words?
Venerable Śāriputra said to Venerable Ānanda:
"When the six bases of contact have been exhausted, and there is detachment, cessation, stilling, and disappearance, does anything remain?"
This is but empty talk.
Is there nothing more?
This is but empty talk.
Is there a remainder, or is there no remainder?
Such [a claim] is empty talk.
Is it neither with remainder nor without remainder?
This is merely empty talk.

If one says that when the six bases of contact have been exhausted, and one has become free from desire, ceased, stilled, and vanished, thereby departing from all falsehood and attaining parinirvāṇa—this is the teaching of the Buddha.
Then, the two noble beings expressed mutual appreciation for one another and each returned to their own abode.
250 (250). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra and the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila were both at Vulture Peak Mountain.

In the late afternoon, the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila arose from meditation and went to where the Venerable Śāriputra was. After they had exchanged greetings and polite inquiries, he withdrew to sit at one side and said to Śāriputra:
"I wish to ask a question; would you have the leisure to grant me an answer?"
The Venerable Śāriputra said to Mahākauṣṭhila:
"Answer whatever you wish to ask, and I shall respond as I know.
The Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila then asked the Venerable Śāriputra:
"How is it, Venerable Śāriputra? Is the eye bound to forms,
or are forms bound to the eye?"
“Regarding the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and flavors, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental objects—
does the mind fetter the mental objects, or do the mental objects fetter the mind?
Venerable Śāriputra replied to Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila:

“Form is not bound by the eye, nor is the eye bound by form; and so on, up to: phenomena are not bound by the mind, nor is the mind bound by phenomena. Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila, whatever desire and lust there is therein—that is the bond.”
Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila!
It is like two oxen, one black and one white, bound together by a single yoke and harness. Someone asks:
"Is it the black ox that binds the white ox, or is it the white ox that binds the black ox?"
"Was that not a question asked with equanimity? He replied,
"No, Venerable Śāriputra."
It is not that the black ox binds the white ox, nor is it that the white ox binds the black ox; rather, it is the yoke or the thong between them that constitutes the binding.
“Thus it is, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila! It is not that the eye is bound to forms, nor that forms are bound to the eye;
and so on, up to: it is not that the mind is bound to mental phenomena, nor that mental phenomena are bound to the mind. The desire and greed for them in between is what constitutes the bondage.”
“Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila!

If the eye were bound to forms, or forms were bound to the eye, and so on until if the mind were bound to mental phenomena, or mental phenomena were bound to the mind, the Blessed One would not instruct people to establish the holy life in order to reach the end of suffering. Because the eye is not bound to forms, nor are forms bound to the eye, and so on until the mind is not bound to mental phenomena, nor are mental phenomena bound to the mind, the Blessed One instructs people to establish the holy life in order to reach the end of suffering.”
"Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila!

When the Blessed One sees forms with his eye, whether beautiful or ugly, he does not give rise to sensual desire; yet other beings, when they see forms with their eye, whether beautiful or ugly, do give rise to sensual desire. Therefore, the Blessed One has said that one should abandon sensual desire so that the mind is liberated. This applies likewise to the mind and mental objects."
Then, the two noble beings expressed mutual appreciation for one another and each returned to their respective abodes. 251 (251) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra and the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila were both staying on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.

In the late afternoon, the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila arose from meditation and went to where the Venerable Śāriputra was. After they had exchanged greetings, he withdrew to sit at one side and said to the Venerable Śāriputra:
"I wish to ask a question; would you have the leisure to grant me an answer?"
Śāriputra said: "I shall answer according to what you, Venerable One, have asked.
Then the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila questioned the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"Regarding what is called 'ignorance' (avidyā):
what constitutes ignorance?
Venerable Śāriputra said:
"What is called 'ignorance'—this ignorance is what constitutes 'nescience' (avidyā).
What is this ignorance?

It means not knowing, as it truly is, that the eye is impermanent; this is called ignorance. Not knowing, as it truly is, that the eye is a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing; this is called ignorance."
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. Thus, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila,
not knowing these six bases of contact as they truly are,
not seeing them, not attaining clear comprehension regarding them, but being deluded, obscured by darkness, and possessed of great ignorance— this is called ignorance.
The Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila again asked the Venerable Sāriputta:
"Regarding what is called 'clear knowledge' (vidyā),
what constitutes clear knowledge?"
Śāriputra said:
"What is called 'knowing'—knowing is clarity. What is it that is known?
It is knowing as it truly is that the eye is impermanent; knowing as it truly is that the eye is a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing."
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are also like this.
Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila!
To know, see, clarify, awaken to, realize, understand, and penetrate these six bases of contact as they truly are—this is called clear knowledge (*vidyā*).
At that time, the two noble beings, having each heard what was said, rejoiced in turn and returned to their respective abodes.
252 (Two Hundred Fifty-Two). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Upasena, who dwelt at the Serpent’s Head Rock in the Śītavana cemetery near Rājagṛha, in the place frequented by the Kalinga people.
At that time, the Venerable Upasena was sitting in solitary meditation within.
Then, a venomous snake about a foot long fell from between the stones above onto Upasena’s body. Upasena called out to Śāriputra:
“Tell the bhikṣus that a venomous snake has fallen upon my body and I am poisoned. Come quickly to support my body and carry it outside, lest it perish and disintegrate within like a heap of chaff.”
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was staying under a tree nearby. Hearing Upasena’s words, he immediately went to where Upasena was and said to him:

“I observe your physical appearance and your faculties; they do not differ from their usual state. Yet you say you have been poisoned and must carry my body out so that it does not scatter and rot like a heap of chaff—what exactly is the matter?”
Upasena said to Śāriputra: "If one were to say:
'My eye is my self, it belongs to me.'"
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are "I" or "mine.
Form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental objects; form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental objects are "I" or "mine."
The earth element: "The earth element is my self, it is mine.
The water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements: "The water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are my self, they are mine."
If one were to think, "The aggregate of form is my self or what belongs to my self;

the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are my self or what belongs to my self," then there would necessarily be a transformation in the facial features and the sense faculties.
I am not like that now; the eye is neither self nor belonging to a self;
and so on, up to the aggregate of consciousness, which is neither self nor belonging to a self. Therefore, my facial complexion and the various sense faculties undergo no change.
Śāriputra said: "It is so, Upasena!

If you have for a long night been free from the latent tendencies of 'I' and 'mine,' and from the fetters of ego-conceit, having severed their root like the head of a tāla tree so that they shall never arise again in future lives—how could there be any change in your facial complexion or your faculties?"
Then Śāriputra immediately supported Upasena’s body on all sides and carried him out of the cave; Upasena’s body was shattered by the poison, like a heap of chaff and dregs.
At that time, Śāriputra spoke these verses:
"Having long cultivated the various pure practices (*brahmacarya*) And well cultivated the Noble Eightfold Path,
He joyfully relinquished his life-span, Just as one would cast away a bowl of poison."
Having long cultivated the various holy practices (*brahmacarya*) and well cultivated the Noble Eightfold Path,
he joyfully relinquished his life-span, like a person whose grave illness has been cured.
Having long cultivated the various holy practices and well cultivated the Noble Eightfold Path...
Like one who has escaped from a burning house, facing death without sorrow or regret;
having long cultivated the various holy practices and well-trained in the Eightfold Noble Path,
one views the world with wisdom as if it were foul grass and wood.
"No further seeking remains, nor does anything else continue.
Then, having made offerings to the body of Upasena, the Venerable Śāriputra went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The Venerable Upasena had a small, venomous snake, about the size of an eye-stick, which fell upon his body; his body was immediately destroyed, like a heap of chaff and dregs.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If Upasena had recited this verse, he would not have been poisoned, nor would his body have been destroyed like a heap of chaff."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what verses are being recited?”
"What are these words and phrases?
The Buddha then spoke this verse for Śāriputra:
"Always maintain thoughts of loving-kindness toward him, The steadfast Rāṣṭrapāla."
Compassionate Elāpattra, Śivabhadra,
and the supreme horse Cimbala; likewise compassionate Kakuda,
as well as that Kṛṣṇa Gautama, Nanda and Upananda.
He extends compassion to those without feet, And to those with two feet;
To those with four feet and those with many feet, He likewise gives rise to compassion for all.
He extends compassion to all the nāgas, And to those who dwell upon water and land.
Be compassionate toward all sentient beings, both those who are finite and those who are infinite;
bring peace and happiness to all, and likewise remain free from the arising of afflictions.
May all who are virtuous desire that no one at all give rise to evil.
Dwelling constantly at Sappasīsa Rock, no evils gather there;
the fierce and venomous snakes that can harm the lives of beings—
these words of truth were spoken by the Unsurpassed Great Teacher.
I now recite and practice these true words of the Great Teacher;
no evil poisons whatsoever can harm my body.
Greed, hatred, and delusion—these three poisons of the world—[cannot harm me].
Thus, these three poisons are evil; their eternal removal is called the Buddha Jewel.
The Dharma Jewel extinguishes all poisons, and the Sangha Jewel likewise leaves none remaining.
It destroys malignant and wicked poisons, while gathering in and protecting virtuous people.
“The Buddha has destroyed all poisons; your snake venom is now destroyed.
Thus he spoke these words of the incantation, namely:
“Uḍaṃbare | daṃbare | ṇaḷu-pava-daṃlu | nade | su-nade | kībadade | vana-ye | sama-ye | dante | nilakīśe | bala-kubey-uḷe | u-yuḷe | svāhā. Śāriputra!
"Upasena, son of good family, at that time, one who speaks these verses and recites these phrases will not be struck by snake venom, nor will their body be destroyed, remaining like a heap of chaff."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Upasena has never heard this verse, nor has he ever heard these mantric phrases. World-Honored One, you have spoken this today specifically for the sake of future generations.”
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Śāriputra rejoiced, paid his respects, and departed.
253 (Two Hundred Fifty-Three) Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Venerable Udāyin was traveling through the human settlements of Kosala and arrived at the village of Kūṭadanta, where he stayed in the Āmra garden belonging to the Brahmin lady Viṇḍuka-cāyanī.

At that time, there were several young disciples of the brahmin woman Viṇṭhā-Kaccāyanī who, while wandering about gathering firewood, arrived at the Āmra grove. There they saw the Venerable Udāyin sitting beneath a tree; his appearance was upright and handsome, his faculties were tranquil, his mind was serene and composed, and he had achieved the highest degree of self-mastery.
Having seen him, he approached his location; after exchanging greetings with one another, he withdrew to sit at one side.

At that time, Udāyin taught the various young men the Dharma in many ways and, having exhorted them, remained silent. Having heard what the Venerable Udāyin had said, those young men rejoiced and approved, rose from their seats, and departed.

At that time, the young men, carrying bundles of firewood, returned to the place of the brahmin lady Viṇḍuka-cāyanī. They set their bundles of wood on the ground and approached the brahmin lady Viṇḍuka-cāyanī, saying:
"Our preceptor lady, you should know that in the Āmra Garden there is a śramaṇa named Udāyin, of the Gautama clan, who dwells there and is exceedingly skilled in preaching the Dharma."
The brahmin woman Viṇḍuka-cāyanī said to the young men:
"You should go and invite the śramaṇa Udāyin Gautama to take his meal here tomorrow."
Then, having received the instructions of the brahmin woman Viṣṇu-kanyā, the young disciples went to the Venerable Udāyin and said to him:
"Venerable sir, you should know that our preceptor, the brahmin woman Viṣṇu-kanyā, invites the Venerable Udāyin for a meal tomorrow morning."
Then Udāyin accepted the invitation in silence.
When those young men knew that Udāyin had accepted the invitation, they returned to their preceptor, the Brahmin lady Viṇḍuka-kañcana, and said to her:
"Preceptor, we have invited the Venerable Udāyin on behalf of you, and the Venerable Udāyin has accepted the invitation in silence; Preceptor, you yourself know the proper time."
Then, when the night had passed and at the break of dawn, the Venerable Udāyin dressed himself, took his bowl, and went to the dwelling of the brahmin lady Viṇḍuka-cāyanī.

At that time, the brahmin woman Viṇṭhaka-caṇḍāyanī saw from afar that the Venerable Udāyin was approaching; she quickly prepared a seat and invited him to sit down. She set out various kinds of food and drink, personally serving them to him with abundance and excellence until he was fully satisfied.
Having finished eating, and having completed his rinsing and washing of the bowl, he returned to his original seat.

At that time, the Brahmin woman Venukātyāyanī, knowing that the meal was over, put on fine leather sandals, covered her head with her robe, and sat upon a specially prepared high couch; manifesting an air of levity, she sat there with haughty pride and said to Udāyin:
"I wish to ask something; would you have the leisure to grant me an answer?"
Udāyin replied, “Sisters,
now is not the right time.”
Having spoken these words, she rose from her seat and departed.
It was thus.

On the following day, the disciples again went to the Āmra Grove to gather firewood and listen to the Dharma; upon their return, they again informed the Preceptor Nun. The Preceptor Nun again sent them to invite [the monks] for a meal. As before, this occurred three times, even up to the invitation for the Dharma, to which she replied:
"It is not the proper time," she said,
and did not preach the Dharma for them.
The young disciples then spoke again to the preceptress, saying, "The śramaṇa Udāyin in the Āmra Garden is extremely skilled at preaching the Dharma."
The Upādhyāyī replied:

"I too know that she is an excellent speaker of the Dharma; though I invited her repeatedly to come, provide food, and inquire about the Dharma, she always said it was not the proper time and would not speak before departing."
The disciples said to their preceptor nun:
"Wearing fine leather sandals, covering her head with her robe, and sitting without showing respect—how could she possibly teach?"
"Why is that? Because that venerable Udāyin, out of reverence for the Dharma, did not speak and departed.
The preceptor nun replied:
“If it is so, please request him on my behalf once more.
The disciples received these instructions and again requested the offering as before.
At that time, the preceptor nun, knowing the meal was finished, removed her leather sandals, adjusted her robes, sat upon a low seat, and spoke with reverence:
"I wish to ask a question; would you have the leisure to grant me an answer?
Udāyin replied, "You may ask now, and I shall explain it for you."

He then asked: "There are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who say that suffering and pleasure are created by oneself; others say they are created by another; others say they are created by both oneself and another; and still others say they are created by neither oneself nor another."
"Venerable sir!
What else? Venerable Udāyin replied:
"Sister! The Arhat speaks of suffering and pleasure as distinct from the ordinary person; he does not speak in such a manner.
The Brahmin woman asked again:
"What is the meaning of this?
Udāyin replied: "The Arhat said:"
"From those causes and conditions, all forms of suffering and pleasure arise.
Udāyin spoke again to the Brahmin woman, saying:
"I shall now question you; answer me as you please."
"What do you think?
Does the eye exist?
He replied:
"There is. "Is there form? He replied:
“Yes. “Is there eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and feeling born of eye-contact as its condition—whether it be internal feeling that is painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant?”
He replied, "So it is,
Venerable Udāyin! Udāyin asked again:
“Are there ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; and are there feelings born of the condition of mental contact—whether internal sensations be painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant?”
He replied, "So it is, Venerable Udāyin! Udāyin said:
"This is what the Arhat has said:
'From causes and conditions, suffering and pleasure arise.
The Brahmin woman said:
"Venerable Udāyin!
Does an Arhat thus say that suffering and pleasure arise from their causes and conditions? Udāyin replied:
"So it is, Brahmin lady! The Brahmin lady asked again:
"Ascetic!..."
“How does an Arhat explain the arising of suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure through causes and conditions, and their cessation?
Udāyin replied, “I shall now question you; answer me as you see fit.”
"Brahmin lady!

When all eyes have been extinguished without remainder at all times, could there still be feeling born of the causal condition of eye-contact, experienced internally as either painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant?"

He replied, “No, śramaṇa! Likewise, when the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind have all at all times ceased, being forever exhausted without remainder, could there still be feeling born from the condition of mental contact— an internal sensation that is either painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant?”
He replied, "No, śramaṇa. "So it is, brāhmaṇī!"
"This is what the Arhat has taught:
'The cessation of suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure arises through causes and conditions.
When the Venerable Udāyin spoke this Dharma, the Brahmin lady Viṇṭukacānī became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.

At that time, the Brahmin woman Viṇṭhaka-cāndanī saw the Dharma, attained the Dharma, knew the Dharma, and entered the Dharma; she crossed beyond doubt and uncertainty, and having entered the Buddha’s teaching through no other means, she attained fearlessness regarding the Dharma.
Rising from his seat, he adjusted his robes, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Venerable Udāyin:

"Today I have entered the state of certainty. From this day forth, I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, and I take refuge in the Saṅgha; from this day forth, for as long as life lasts, I take refuge in the Triple Gem."
At that time, Udāyin taught the Dharma to the brahmin woman, instructing, exhorting, illuminating, and gladdening her;
having done so, he rose from his seat and departed. 254 (254) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra (Viśākha) was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain, constantly and diligently cultivating the factors of enlightenment.
Then, while the Venerable Śāriputra was meditating in solitary stillness, this thought occurred to him:

"Among the diligent śrāvakas who are disciples of the Blessed One, I am numbered among them; yet today I have not exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*). I am from a noble family and possessed of abundant wealth and treasures; I should now rather return to the enjoyment of the five sensual pleasures and extensively practice giving to create merit."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing what was in the mind of Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, addressed a certain bhikṣu: "Go now to where Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa is and say to him:
'The World-Honored One calls for you.'"
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, that bhikṣu went to where Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa was and said to him,
“The World-Honored One calls for you.
Upon hearing that bhikṣu deliver the Master’s summons, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa immediately went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa: "Is it true that while you were meditating in solitary stillness, this thought occurred to you:
'Among those who diligently train under the World-Honored One as śrāvakas, I am numbered among them, yet even now I have not attained liberation through the exhaustion of outflows'?"
"I am of a noble lineage and possess great wealth; would it not be better for me to return to lay life, enjoy the pleasures of the five senses, and extensively practice giving to create merit?
At that time, Śāriputra thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One already knows my mind."
Startled and terrified, his hair standing on end, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, "I shall now question you; answer me as you see fit.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, when you were in the secular world, were you skilled at playing the lute?"
He replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One! The Buddha asked again:
"What do you think?
When you play the lute, if you tighten its strings too much, can it produce a subtle, harmonious, and elegant sound?
He replied:
"No, World-Honored One.
He asked again: "How so?"
“If its strings were loosened, would it produce a subtle, exquisite, and harmonious sound?
He replied, “No,
World-Honored One.”
He asked again:
"How does one properly tune the strings of a lute, neither too loose nor too tight, so that it then produces a wondrous, harmonious, and elegant sound?
He replied:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa:

"Excessive haste in diligence increases restlessness and regret; excessive laxity in diligence leads to indolence. Therefore, you should practice with equanimity and maintain self-mastery; do not be attached, do not be negligent, and do not grasp at signs."
Then, having heard what the Blessed One had said, the Venerable Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa rejoiced and approved, paid homage, and departed.
Thereafter, the Venerable Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa constantly kept in mind the simile of the lute spoken by the Blessed One, dwelling alone in quiet seclusion in meditative reflection.
As previously described, up until the exhaustion of the outflows, his mind attained liberation and he became an arhat.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, having attained arhatship and experiencing the joy and bliss of internal liberated awareness, thought to himself:
"I should now go to pay my respects to the Blessed One."
At that time, the Venerable Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Having attained arhatship within the Dharma of the Blessed One, with all taints exhausted, having done what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, attained one's own goal, and with the destruction of the fetters of existence, being liberated in mind through right knowledge—at that very moment, one is liberated from the six sense bases.
What are the six?

Liberation through the fading away of desire, liberation through the fading away of ill will, liberation through seclusion, liberation through the exhaustion of craving, liberation from all clinging, and liberation through mindfulness of the mind.
“World-Honored One!
If one relies on a small measure of faith and claims to have attained liberation through the departure from desire, this is not appropriate;
the total exhaustion of greed, hatred, and delusion is what is called true liberation through the departure from desire.”
"Furthermore, if there is someone who, based on a small degree of observed precepts, claims, 'I have attained liberation from ill-will,' this too is not appropriate;
only when greed, ill-will, and delusion are exhausted is it called true liberation from ill-will."
"Furthermore, if there is a person who, based on the cultivation of detachment from gain and offerings, claims to have attained detachment and liberation, this too is not appropriate;
the complete exhaustion of greed, hatred, and delusion is true detachment and liberation."
“The total exhaustion of greed, hatred, and delusion is also called freedom from craving, freedom from clinging, and liberation through the absence of forgetfulness.
Thus it is, World-Honored One!”
If bhikṣus have not yet attained arhatship and have not exhausted all outflows (āsravas), they shall not attain liberation within these six bases.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu is on the stage of training (śaikṣa) and has not yet attained superior bliss, but dwells with a mind inclined toward the practice of nirvāṇa, at that time he accomplishes the precepts of training and accomplishes the faculties of training; later, he shall attain the exhaustion of outflows and the untainted liberation of mind, until he personally knows that there will be no further existence.
At that time, one attains the precepts of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) and attains the faculties of one beyond training.

It is like an infant, small and foolish, lying on its back; at that time it possesses the faculties of an infant, but later, as it gradually grows and matures, it comes to possess the faculties of a youth, and at that time, it comes to possess the faculties of an adult.

It is the same for those on the stage of training (*śaikṣa*): as long as they have not yet attained superior bliss, up until the accomplishment of the precepts of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and the faculties of one beyond training.

"If the eye constantly perceives forms, it can never obstruct liberation of mind (*ceto-vimukti*) or liberation by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*), because the mind is firmly established; thus, within, one cultivates immeasurable wholesome liberation, observing arising and passing away, up to impermanence."

Ear-consciousness of sounds, nose-consciousness of odors, tongue-consciousness of flavors, body-consciousness of tangibles, and mind-consciousness of mental phenomena cannot obstruct the liberation of the mind or the liberation by wisdom; because the mind is firmly established, one internally cultivates immeasurable wholesome liberation and contemplates arising and ceasing.

For example, suppose there were a village or town near a great mountain of rock that was unbroken, indestructible, and unpierced, being consistently thick and dense; even if winds blew from the four directions, they could not shake it nor pierce through it.

It is the same for that one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*): although the eye constantly perceives forms, and so on up to the mind constantly perceiving phenomena (*dharma*), it cannot obstruct the liberation of the mind (*ceto-vimukti*) or the liberation by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*). Because the mind is firmly established, he internally cultivates immeasurable wholesome liberation and observes arising and ceasing.
At that time, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa spoke again in verse:
“With a mind liberated from desire, and likewise liberated from ill will;
with a mind liberated through detachment, craving is forever without remainder.”
When the mind is liberated from all grasping, and the intellect is free from forgetfulness, one understands the arising of the sense bases; therein the mind is liberated.
For one whose mind is thus liberated, the bhikṣu’s mind comes to rest.
Having done what was to be done, one no longer performs further action.
Like a great mountain of rock, it cannot be moved by the four winds.
Whether it be forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects—whether pleasant or unpleasant—[they do not disturb the mind].
"Though the six sense bases are constantly present before him, they cannot move his mind.
His mind dwells ever in steadfastness, clearly observing the arising and passing away of phenomena.

When the Venerable Śāriputra (Viṃśatikoṭīkarṇa) spoke this Dharma, the Great Teacher’s heart was gladdened; and many learned fellow-practitioners who heard what the Venerable Śāriputra had said were all greatly rejoiced.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra (Viṃśatikoṭīkarṇa), having heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, rejoiced and approved with gladness;
he paid homage and departed. Not long after Śāriputra had left, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"One whose mind is liberated through goodness should provide an exposition in this manner, just as Śāriputra has expounded it through wisdom—neither exalting himself nor disparaging others, but correctly explaining its meaning."
"It is not like those of overweening pride who, failing to grasp the true meaning, boast that they have attained superhuman states, thereby bringing about their own ruin. (255) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana was staying in the country of Aparāntaka, at the Monkey’s Cave hermitage on the banks of the Śiprā River.
There was a brahmin named Rukṣa who attended upon him with reverence, as one would toward an arhat.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, having dressed in the morning and taken up his bowl, entered the village of Markaṭahradaka. He went on his alms round in succession, and having returned from begging for food, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, and sat in meditation in his cell.

At that time, there were several young disciples of the brahmin Rucīra who, while wandering about gathering firewood, arrived at the vicinity of the Venerable Mahākātyāyana’s cave. They spoke to one another with mocking laughter, saying:
"A shramana with a shaved head dwells here; he is a man of darkness, not a superior person in this world, yet the brahmin Rucīra honors and makes offerings to him as if he were an arhat."
At that time, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana said to the young men:
"Young men! Young men!"
"Do not make a sound.
When the youths had finished speaking, they did not dare speak again.
Even after this was repeated three times, their speech still did not cease.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana went out of the room and said to the young men:
"Young men! Young men!"
"Do not speak.
I shall now preach the Dharma for you; listen attentively.
The youths replied:
“Very well, I pray that you will teach the Dharma; I shall listen and receive it.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke these verses:
“In ancient times, the brahmins Cultivated the most excellent and sublime precepts.”
Having attained the knowledge of past lives, he delights in the dhyāna of the True Dharma;
ever abiding in loving-kindness and compassion,
he closes the gates of the sense faculties and subdues verbal transgressions— such was his conduct in ages past.
Abandoning the practice of fundamental truth, they persist in hollow and deceptive affairs;
guarding their lineage with negligence, they follow the six sense objects.
They starve themselves while dwelling among burial mounds, bathing three times a day and reciting the three Vedas.
Failing to guard the doors of the senses, like one who finds treasure only in a dream;
with matted hair and garments of hide or coarse wool, stealing the precepts while smearing their bodies with ash;
clothing their forms in rough rags, they carry staves and hold water jars.
Assuming the form of a brāhmaṇa in order to seek gain and offerings,
yet well-restraining and protecting his body, pure and free from defilement,
not causing affliction to sentient beings— this is the path of a brāhmaṇa.
At that time, the young brahmins were filled with anger and displeasure, and they said to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana:
"You slander our scriptures, destroy what has been taught, and insult the brahmins."
Carrying the bundle of firewood, he returned to where the brahmin Rohiṣa was and said to him,
"Does the Upādhyāya know?"
"That Mahā-Kātyāyana slanders the scriptures, reviles his speech, and insults the brahmins.
The brahmin Rūḍhika said to the young men: "Young men!..."
Do not speak such words.
Why is this? Mahākātyāyana has long held the precepts and virtues in high esteem; he ought not to slander the scriptures, disparage their teachings, or revile the brāhmaṇas.
The youths said, "If our preceptor does not believe our words, he should go and see for himself.
At that time, the brahmin Rohitaka did not believe the words of the youths and went to Mahākātyāyana. After they had exchanged greetings and expressions of courtesy, he withdrew to sit at one side.
He said to Mahākātyāyana,
"Have my young disciples come here?
He replied:
"Have you arrived there?
"Did you engage in any conversation with him?
He replied:
"Speak with me. The brahmin Rāṣṭrapāla said, "You have conversed with these youths; you may now relate all of that to me."
Mahākātyāyana then explained it to him in detail.
At that time, the brahmin Rohitaka also became enraged; his mind was displeased, and he said to Mahākātyāyana:
"I did not previously believe the words of those youths, but now Mahākātyāyana truly slanders the scriptures, speaks with contempt, and insults the brahmins."
Having spoken these words, he remained silent for a short while.
After a moment, he spoke again to Mahākātyāyana:
"Venerable sir, regarding what you have said concerning 'the gate'..."
"What is meant by 'gate'?
Mahākātyāyana replied, "Excellent!"
Excellent, O Brahmin!
Your question is in accordance with the Dharma; I shall now explain to you the "gate."
"Brāhmaṇa! The eye is a gate, because it sees forms.
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are gates, because they cognize phenomena."
The brahmin said:
"How marvelous! Mahākātyāyana!"
When I asked him about the doors, he explained those very doors, just as Mahākātyāyana spoke regarding the non-guarding of the doors.
What is meant by "non-guarding of the doors"?
Mahākātyāyana said: "Excellent! Excellent!"
"Brahmin! To ask about the non-guarding of the doors is a question in accordance with the Dharma; I shall now explain the non-guarding of the doors for you. Brahmin!"
When a foolish, unlearned worldling sees a form with the eye, they give rise to attachment toward an agreeable form and give rise to aversion toward a disagreeable form.
Because they do not abide in the foundation of mindfulness of the body, they lack knowledge as it truly is regarding liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.
Various evil and unwholesome states arise therein, which cannot be extinguished without remainder; they obstruct the liberation of mind and the liberation by wisdom, preventing their fulfillment.

Because the liberation of mind and the liberation by wisdom are not fulfilled, one’s body is filled with misconduct and finds no rest; the mind is not tranquil. Because it is not tranquil, the sense-faculties are not tamed, not guarded, and not cultivated.
"As it is with the eye and forms, so it is likewise with the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and flavors, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena.
The brahmin Rūcika said:
"How marvelous!"
How wonderful!
Mahākaccāyana, when I asked about the non-guarding of the sense-doors, you have explained to me the non-guarding of the sense-doors. Mahākaccāyana!
"What, then, is meant by 'skillfully guarding the gates'?
Mahākātyāyana said to the brahmin:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!
You are able to ask me about the meaning of the well-guarded gate.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall explain for you the meaning of guarding the gates.
“When a well-learned noble disciple has seen forms with the eye, he does not give rise to attachment toward agreeable forms, nor does he give rise to aversion toward disagreeable forms;

he constantly restrains his mind and dwells in the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*). He knows as it truly is the liberation of mind (*cetovimukti*) and liberation by wisdom (*prajñāvimukti*) that are immeasurable. Whatever evil and unwholesome states have arisen therein are extinguished without remainder, and he attains fulfillment in the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.

Having attained fulfillment in liberation, all bodily contact with misconduct comes to rest, and the mind attains right mindfulness. This is called the first gateway for skillful taming, guarding, and cultivation.”
"Just as it is with the eye and visible forms, so it is with the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena.
The brahmin Rucīra said:
"How marvelous!"
Mahākātyāyana! I asked about guarding and the meaning of guarding, and you have explained to me the meaning of the gateway of guarding.

It is as if a man seeking poisonous herbs instead obtained ambrosia; even so am I now, having come to this seat in a state of anger, yet Mahākātyāyana has showered the rain of the Great Dharma upon my person, like the raining down of ambrosia.
“Mahākātyāyana!
There are many affairs at home; we now invite you to return home.
Mahākātyāyana said:
“Brahmin! You should know that the time has come.
Then, having heard what Mahākātyāyana had said, the brahmin Rohitaka rejoiced and approved, rose from his seat, and departed.
Saṃyukta Āgama, Volume Nine;
Saṃyukta Āgama, Volume Ten.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
10.256 (256) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra and the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila were on Vulture Peak Mountain.

At that time, in the late afternoon, the Venerable Kauṣṭhila arose from meditation and went to where the Venerable Śāriputra was. After they had exchanged greetings and conversed with one another in various ways to their mutual delight, he withdrew and sat to one side.
Then, the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila said to Śāriputra:
"I wish to ask a question; would you have the leisure to explain it to me?"
Śāriputra said, "I shall speak according to what you ask, O worthy one, for I know.
Mahākauṣṭhila then asked Śāriputra:
"What is called ignorance? What is this ignorance?
Who possesses this ignorance?"
Śāriputra replied:
“Ignorance (avidyā) means not knowing; that which does not know is ignorance.
[The Buddha asked: “What is it that is not known?”

"It means that form is impermanent, yet one does not know form as it truly is—impermanent; form is subject to disintegration, yet one does not know form as it truly is—subject to disintegration; form is subject to arising and ceasing, yet one does not know form as it truly is—subject to arising and ceasing."

Regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness: one does not know as it truly is that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent; one does not know as it truly is that consciousness is subject to the law of disintegration; one does not know as it truly is that consciousness is subject to the law of arising and ceasing.

Mahākoṭṭhila! Not knowing these five aggregates of clinging as they truly are, not seeing them, lacking clear comprehension, being deluded, obscured, and ignorant—this is called ignorance. One who possesses this is said to have ignorance.
He asked again:
"Śāriputra, as for what is called 'clarity' (vidyā), what constitutes clarity?"
"Who possesses this clarity?
Śāriputra said, "Mahākauṣṭhila!"
"What is called 'clarity' (vidyā) is knowing; that which knows is termed clarity.
He asked again:
"What is it that is known?"
"It means knowing that form is impermanent, knowing form as impermanent as it truly is;
knowing that form is subject to decay, knowing form as subject to decay as it truly is;
knowing that form is subject to arising and ceasing, knowing form as subject to arising and ceasing as it truly is."

Regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness: one knows as it truly is that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent; one knows as it truly is that consciousness is subject to the law of disintegration; one knows as it truly is that consciousness is subject to the law of arising and ceasing.
Kauṣṭhila!
To know, see, understand, awaken to, discern, and realize these five aggregates of clinging as they truly are—this is called "clarity.
One who has accomplished this dharma is said to possess clarity.
Thus these two noble beings, having each heard what was spoken, rejoiced in one another’s words, rose from their seats, and returned to their respective abodes. 257 (257) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra and the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila were on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.

Then, in the late afternoon, Mahākauṣṭhila arose from meditation and went to where the Venerable Śāriputra was. They exchanged greetings and various pleasantries with one another, and having done so, sat down to one side.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila said to Śāriputra:
"I wish to ask a question; would you have a little leisure to explain it to me?"
Śāriputra said: "Virtuous one, ask first; the knower shall explain.
Mahākauṣṭhila then asked Śāriputra:
"What is called 'ignorance' (avidyā)—furthermore, what constitutes ignorance?
Who possesses this ignorance?
Śāriputra replied:
“Ignorance means not knowing; that which does not know is ignorance.
“What is it that is not known?
“It is not knowing form as it truly is, nor knowing the arising of form, the cessation of form, and the path leading to the cessation of form as they truly are.”

Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are not known as they truly are; the arising of consciousness, the cessation of consciousness, and the path leading to the cessation of consciousness are not known as they truly are.
Mahākoṭṭhila!

To lack knowledge of these five aggregates of clinging as they truly are, to not know them, to not see them, to lack clear comprehension of them, and to be deluded, obscured, and ignorant regarding them—this is called ignorance (*avidyā*). One who possesses this is said to have ignorance.
He asked Śāriputra again:
“What is illumination?
Who possesses this illumination?”
Śāriputra said: "That which is called 'clarity' (vidyā) is knowledge; that which is knowledge is clarity.
He asked again:
"What is it that he knows? Śāriputra replied:
"He knows form as it truly is; he knows the arising of form, the cessation of form, and the path leading to the cessation of form as they truly are."

One knows feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as they truly are; one knows the arising of consciousness, the cessation of consciousness, and the path leading to the cessation of consciousness as they truly are. Kūṭadanta!

Regarding these five aggregates of clinging, such knowing, seeing, clarity, awakening, wisdom, and perfect realization is called "knowledge" (vidyā). One who has accomplished this dharma is said to be "possessed of knowledge."
When these two noble ones had each heard what was said, they rejoiced in one another’s words, rose from their seats, and returned to their respective abodes.
258 (258) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra and the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila were on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Then, in the late afternoon, Mahākauṣṭhila arose from meditation and went to where Śāriputra was. After they had exchanged greetings and pleasantries, he sat down to one side.
Then Mahākauṣṭhila said to Śāriputra:
"I wish to ask a question; would you, O Venerable One, have the leisure to grant me an answer?
Śāriputra replied:
