At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī had departed, asked the Venerable Ānanda:
"Who is next in turn to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs?"
The Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The elder monks have taken turns in succession to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, and now it is Nanda’s turn; yet Nanda does not wish to instruct them.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Nanda, saying:
"You should instruct the bhikṣuṇīs and preach the Dharma for them. Why is this so?"
"I myself instruct the bhikṣuṇīs; you should do likewise.
I expound the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs; you should do likewise.
At that time, Nanda silently accepted the instruction.
Then, when the night had passed and it was morning, Nanda put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
Having finished his meal, he returned to the vihāra, put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and entered his room to sit in meditation.

Emerging from meditative absorption, he put on his saṃghāṭī robe and, taking a bhikṣu with him, went to the King’s Garden. Seeing Venerable Nanda approaching from afar, the bhikṣuṇīs quickly spread out mats and seats, inviting him to take his place. Once Venerable Nanda was seated, the bhikṣuṇīs prostrated themselves in respectful salutation and withdrew to sit at one side.
The Venerable Nanda said to the bhikṣuṇīs: "Sisters!
You should question me; I shall now preach the Dharma for you."
Those of you who understand should say that you understand;
those who do not understand should say that you do not understand.
Regarding the meaning of what I have taught, if you do understand it, you should receive and uphold it well.
"If you do not understand, you should ask further, and I shall explain it for you.
The bhikṣuṇīs said to the Venerable Nanda:
"Today we heard the Venerable’s instruction, which told us to ask, and he addressed us, saying:"
"If among you there are those who do not yet understand, you should now all ask;
those who have already understood should say they have understood, and those who have not yet understood should say they do not understand.
Regarding the meaning of what I have taught, those who have understood should uphold it, and those who have not yet understood should ask further."
“Having heard this, our hearts are filled with great joy; those of us who do not yet understand its meaning shall now ask about it.
At that time, the Venerable Nanda addressed the bhikṣuṇīs:
“What do you say?”
"Sisters!
When you examine the internal sense base of the eye, do you regard it as 'this is me,' 'it is different from me,' or 'it exists within me'?
They replied: [No.]
"No, Venerable Nanda!
When one observes the internal sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, does one regard them as 'this is I,' 'this is other than I,' or 'this is the self within me'?"
He replied:
"No, Venerable Nanda! Why is that? Because..."
Venerable Nanda!
We have already known and seen this Dharma as it truly is; we have observed the six internal sense bases as being without self, and we have already formed this understanding:
"The six internal sense bases are without self."
The Venerable Nanda said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Sisters! You should understand it thus:
"One observes the six internal sense bases as being without self."
"O bhikṣuṇīs! Is the external sense-base of form 'I', or 'different from me', or 'contained within me'?
They replied:
"No, Venerable Nanda!
Are the external sense bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena the self, distinct from the self, or contained within the self?"
He replied:
"No, Venerable Nanda! Why is that? Because..."
Venerable Nanda!
I have already observed the six external sense bases as they truly are, as being without self; I constantly maintain this understanding that the six external sense bases are truly without self.
The Venerable Nanda praised the bhikṣuṇīs:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
You should contemplate this matter in this way:
"The six external sense bases are non-self.
If, conditioned by the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises, is that eye-consciousness the self, is it distinct from the self, or does it exist within the self?
He replied: "No, Venerable Nanda!

When ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness arises conditioned by mental phenomena (dharma), is that mind-consciousness the self, is it distinct from the self, or does it exist within the self?"
He replied, “No, Venerable Nanda! Why is that? Because...”
I have already observed these six groups of consciousness as they truly are, without self; I also constantly maintain this understanding that the six groups of consciousness are truly without self.
The Venerable Nanda said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Sisters! You should observe this matter in this way:
"The six groups of consciousness are, in reality, without self."
“Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three factors gives rise to contact. Is that contact self, other than self, or contained within [self]?
He replied, “No, Venerable Nanda.”

“With the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as conditions, and mental phenomena as objects, mental consciousness arises; the meeting of these three things gives rise to contact. Is that contact the self, is it other than the self, or does it exist within the self?”
He replied: "No, Venerable Nanda! Why is that?"
"I have already observed these six contacts as truly being without self; I also constantly resolve with my mind that the six contacts are truly without self.
The Venerable Nanda told the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!
One should observe according to reality:
"In the six groups of contact, there is truly no self."

"Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three things is contact. Contact conditions feeling. Is that contact-conditioned feeling my self, other than my self, or does it exist within me?"
He replied, "No, Venerable Nanda!

When ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind take mental phenomena as conditions, consciousness arises; the meeting of these three things is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling. Is that feeling 'I', or different from 'I', or does it exist within 'I'?"
He replied:
"No, Venerable Nanda! Why is that? Because..."
"We have previously observed these six bases of feeling as they truly are, without self; I also constantly maintain this understanding that the six bases of feeling are truly without self."
The Venerable Nanda said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
You should examine this matter in this way:
"These six bodies of feeling are, in reality, without self.

Conditioned by the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the conjunction of these three factors gives rise to contact; conditioned by contact, there arises perception. Is that perception the self, is it distinct from the self, or does it exist within the self?
He replied: "No, Venerable Nanda!

When ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind take mental phenomena as conditions, consciousness arises; the meeting of these three factors gives rise to contact; conditioned by contact, there arises perception. Is that perception 'I', or 'different from me', or 'contained within me'?"
He replied:
"No, Venerable Nanda! Why is that? Because..."
I have observed these six classes of perception as they truly are, as being selfless; I also constantly maintain this understanding that the six classes of perception are truly selfless.
The Venerable Nanda said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"O Bhikṣuṇī! You should observe this matter in this way:
'These six groups of perception are, in reality, without self.'"

"Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three is contact. With contact as condition, volition arises. Is that volition the self, different from the self, or does it exist within the self?"
He replied, "No, Venerable Nanda!

When ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind take mental phenomena as conditions, consciousness arises; the meeting of these three factors is contact; conditioned by contact is volition. Is that volition the self, other than the self, or does it exist within the self?"
He replied:
"No, Venerable Nanda! Why is that? Because..."
I have previously observed these six groups of volition as they truly are, without self; I have constantly maintained this understanding:
"These six groups of volition are truly without self."
The Venerable Nanda said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"O Bhikṣuṇī! You should observe this matter in this way:
'These six groups of volition are, in reality, without self.'"

"Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three is contact. With contact as condition, there is craving. Is that craving self, other than self, or does it exist within [self]?"
He replied: "No, Venerable Nanda!

When ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind take mental phenomena as conditions, consciousness arises; the meeting of these three things is contact; conditioned by contact is craving. Is that craving self, other than self, or does it exist within me?"
He replied:
"No, Venerable Nanda! Why is that? Because..."
I have observed these six bases of craving as they truly are, as being without self; I have constantly maintained this understanding:
"These six bases of craving are truly without self."
The Venerable Nanda told the bhikṣuṇīs:
"In this matter, you should observe it thus:
'These six bases of craving are, in reality, without self.'"
"Sisters! It is just as a lamp’s light is able to burn because of oil and a wick;
yet that oil is impermanent, the wick is also impermanent, the flame is impermanent, and the vessel is also impermanent."
If someone were to say:
"There is no oil, no wick, no fire, and no vessel, yet the lamp-light that arises dependent upon them is permanent, eternal, abiding, and unchanging."
“Is one who speaks in this way speaking correctly?
He replied, “No, Venerable Nanda!”
Why is this so? Because a lamp is lit by depending upon oil, a wick, and a vessel; yet that oil, wick, and vessel are all impermanent.
If there is no oil, no wick, and no vessel, the light of the lamp—which depends upon them—likewise ceases, subsides, vanishes, becomes cooled, and attains reality.
“Thus it is, sisters!
These six internal sense bases are impermanent.
If anyone should say:”
"Is it not a correct statement to say: 'The pleasure and joy born of these six internal sense bases are permanent, constant, enduring, unchanging, and secure'?"
He replied:
"No, Venerable Nanda! Why is that? Because..."
We have observed according to reality that from this or that condition, this or that phenomenon arises;
when this or that conditioned phenomenon ceases, this or that arisen phenomenon likewise follows in cessation, subsides, vanishes, becomes cooled, and attains truth.
The Venerable Nanda said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
“Bhikṣuṇī! You should observe this matter in this way:

‘When such-and-such phenomena arise conditioned by such-and-such phenomena, and when those conditions cease, those arisen phenomena likewise follow in ceasing, subsiding, vanishing, becoming tranquil, cooling, and reaching the ultimate reality.’”
"O sisters! It is just as with a great tree:
its roots, trunk, branches, and leaves—the roots are impermanent, and the trunk, branches, and leaves are all likewise impermanent."
If someone were to say:
"There is no root, trunk, branch, or leaf of that tree; there is only its shadow, which is permanent, eternal, abiding, unchanging, and secure," would they be speaking correctly?
He replied: "No, Venerable Nanda! Why is that? Because..."

Just as with that great tree—its roots, trunk, branches, and leaves—the roots are impermanent, and the trunk, branches, and leaves are likewise impermanent. When there are no roots, no trunk, no branches, and no leaves, the shadow supported by the tree is entirely non-existent.

“Sisters! If the six external sense bases are impermanent, would it be correct to say that because they arise through conditions, the joy and pleasure produced by them are permanent, stable, unchanging, and secure?”
He replied: "No, Venerable Nanda! Why is that?"
I have observed this matter as it truly is: conditioned by this or that phenomenon, this or that phenomenon arises; when this or that phenomenon ceases, this or that phenomenon ceases.
Furthermore, those phenomena that arise likewise subside, come to rest, vanish, become tranquil, grow cool, and reach the state of reality.
The Venerable Nanda addressed the bhikṣuṇīs:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Sisters! You should examine this meaning as it truly is:

"With this or that phenomenon as condition, this or that phenomenon arises; with the cessation of this or that phenomenon as condition, those arisen phenomena likewise cease, subside, vanish, become extinguished, grow cool, and reach reality."
"O sisters! Listen as I speak a parable, for the wise gain understanding through parables.

Suppose there were a skilled butcher or a butcher’s apprentice who, holding a sharp knife in his hand, dissects and skins a cow. He peels it away along the natural seams, neither wounding the inner flesh nor damaging the outer hide; he separates the joints, the sinews, and the bones, and then covers it again with the hide."
If someone were to say,
"This ox-hide and its flesh are whole and not separated," would that be a correct statement?
He replied: "No, Venerable Nanda! Why is that?"

Suppose a skilled butcher or his apprentice, holding a sharp knife, skins a cow by following its natural joints, without damaging the hide or the flesh, severing all the branches, joints, tendons, and bones, and then covering it back with the hide; though the hide and flesh are separated, they are not truly detached from one another.
“Sisters! I have spoken the parable; now I shall explain its meaning.
‘The ox’ is a metaphor for the coarse physical form of the human body... [as explained at length in the *Khadgaviṣāṇa-sūtra*].”

"Meat" refers to the six internal bases; "outer skin" refers to the six external bases; "the butcher" refers to one who has attained the vision of the path; "the sinews and bones between the skin and flesh" refers to craving accompanied by delight; and "the sharp knife" refers to keen wisdom.
The learned noble disciple, with the sharp sword of wisdom, severs all fetters, bonds, underlying tendencies, afflictions, secondary afflictions, and envelopments. Therefore, sisters!
One should train in this way:
"Regarding phenomena that are agreeable, the mind should not become attached, for the sake of abandoning greed;
regarding phenomena that provoke aversion, one should not give rise to anger, for the sake of abandoning hatred."
Regarding those phenomena that can give rise to delusion, one should not produce delusion, for the purpose of severing delusion.
One should contemplate the arising and passing away of the five aggregates of clinging;
one should contemplate the accumulation and cessation of the six bases of sensory contact.
Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, one should skillfully bind the mind.
Abiding in the seven factors of enlightenment and having cultivated them, the mind does not cling to the outflow of sensual desire and thus attains liberation;
the mind does not cling to the outflow of existence and thus attains liberation.
"Regarding the outflow of ignorance, the mind does not cling to it, and the mind attains liberation.
"Sisters, you should train yourselves in this way."
At that time, the Venerable Nanda taught the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them;
having thus instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them, he rose from his seat and departed.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, surrounded by a retinue of five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side; she did so until, having paid homage to the Buddha, she departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī had departed, addressed the bhikṣus:
"Suppose it were the fourteenth night of the month, when a great multitude gazes at the moon; would they consider it to be full?"
Is it not yet full?
You should know that the moon has not yet reached its ultimate fullness.

In the same way, son of good family, although Nanda provides correct instruction and preaches the Dharma correctly for five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, he has not yet reached the ultimate consummation of their liberation.
"However, at the time of these bhikṣuṇīs' passing away, not a single fetter was seen to remain unsevered that could cause them to be reborn again in this world.
At that time, the World-Honored One further addressed Nanda:
"Preach the Dharma once more for the sake of the bhikṣuṇīs."

At that time, the Venerable Nanda silently accepted the instruction. When the night had passed and morning dawned, he took his bowl and entered the city for alms. Having finished eating, he proceeded to the Royal Garden, where he sat down on his seat and taught the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them, he rose from his seat and departed.

On another occasion, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, surrounded by five hundred bhikṣuṇīs before and behind her, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and after performing these salutations, departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī had departed, addressed the bhikṣus:
"Suppose it were the night of the fifteenth day of the bright moon; no one would doubt whether the moon was full or not, for that moon is ultimately and perfectly full."
In this way, the noble son Nanda gave such correct instruction to the bhikṣuṇīs that they attained ultimate liberation;
when their lives ended, there was no one who could describe the path by which they departed—this should be known as the end of suffering.
"In this way, the World-Honored One conferred upon the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs the prediction of their attainment of the first fruit.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly."
277 (277). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There is non-restraint and restraint.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall explain them to you.
What is non-restraint?”
The eye faculty is not protected by restraint;
when visual consciousness becomes attached to forms, because of that attachment as its object, it gives rise to painful feeling;
because of painful feeling, the mind is not unified.
Because they are not single-minded, they do not attain knowledge and vision according to reality;
because they do not attain knowledge and vision according to reality, they do not depart from doubt and confusion;
because they do not depart from doubt and confusion, they are led astray by others and constantly dwell in suffering.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
This is called non-restraint. What is restraint?
Guarded by the restraint of the eye-faculty,
when the eye-consciousness cognizes forms, the mind does not become stained or attached;
once the mind is unstained and unattached, it constantly delights in remaining further therein.
Once the mind dwells in joy, it remains constantly one-pointed;
once the mind is one-pointed, one knows and sees according to reality;
once one knows and sees according to reality, one is free from all doubt and confusion.
Having abandoned all doubts and delusions, one dwells in constant peace and happiness without being led astray by others.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
"This is called restraint.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
278 (278) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are states of decline and non-decline, and the six bases of sensory contact.”
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you.
What is the "dharma of decline"?

It is when, upon seeing a form with the eye-consciousness, a sensual thought arises, and that bhikṣu rejoices in it, praises it, grasps at it, becomes attached to it, and turns in accordance with that dharma. You should know that such a bhikṣu declines from all wholesome dharmas; this, as spoken by the World-Honored One, is called the dharma of decline.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
What is called the "dharma of non-retrogression"?

When visual consciousness conditions a form and gives rise to the fetter of sensual desire, that bhikṣu does not delight in it, does not praise it, does not grasp at it, and does not become attached to it; he does not follow after or revolve within those phenomena. It should be known that this bhikṣu does not regress from wholesome dharmas; the World-Honored One calls this the dharma of non-retrogression.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
What are the six superior bases?
When the eye perceives forms, if no sensual thoughts, fetters, or attachments arise, one should know that this bhikṣu has mastered those bases.
"Victory over these bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana) is what the Blessed One has taught.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
If a bhikkhu has achieved victory over these six bases of mastery, his fetter of sensual desire is severed, and his fetters of ill will and ignorance are severed."
"Just as a king who crushes his enemies and overcomes his foes is called a 'Victorious King' (Jina-rāja),
so too one who has severed all fetters is called a 'Victorious Brahmin' (Jina-brāhmaṇa).
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
279 (279). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one does not subdue, close, guard, maintain, and cultivate these six sense faculties, one will inevitably experience bitter retribution in future lives."
“What are the six faculties?
If the faculty of the eye is not subdued, not closed, not guarded, not cultivated, and not mastered, one will inevitably experience bitter retribution in future lives;
the same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.”

When an ignorant, unlearned worldling sees forms with the eye faculty, they grasp at their general characteristics and grasp at their secondary details; following the inclinations of that eye faculty, they grasp at non-restraint, abide in worldly greed, craving, and evil unwholesome states, and thereby allow their minds to leak. Such persons are unable to maintain restraint or guard the eye faculty.
The same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Thus, if one does not subdue, close, guard, maintain, or cultivate these six faculties, one will inevitably experience bitter retribution in future lives.
"How are the six sense faculties well-tamed, well-shut, well-guarded, well-maintained, and well-cultivated, so that one will certainly receive pleasant retribution in future lives?"

The learned noble disciple, when seeing forms with the eye, does not grasp at their signs nor grasp at their secondary details. He remains constantly restrained according to the inclination of his faculty of sight; worldly greed, craving, and unwholesome states do not leak into his mind, and he is able to give rise to restraint and well-guard the faculty of sight.
The faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are also like this.
When these six faculties are well-tamed, well-restrained, well-guarded, well-maintained, and well-cultivated, one will certainly receive pleasant retribution in future lives.
Then he spoke these verses:
"Those bhikṣus who dwell in non-restraint Regarding the six bases of contact,
They shall undergo great suffering Throughout the long night."
Regarding these points of discipline, one should always practice them with diligence;
with right faith and non-dual mind, no outflows shall leak into the heart.
When the eye sees forms, whether they be pleasing or unpleasing, [one remains undisturbed].
Toward the agreeable, desire does not arise; toward the disagreeable, one does not feel aversion.
Hearing those various sounds with the ear, there are both the agreeable and the disagreeable;
regarding the agreeable, one does not delight in attachment, and regarding the disagreeable, one does not give rise to ill will.
Regarding the objects smelled by the olfactory faculty— whether fragrant or foul—
one maintains equanimity toward both fragrance and stench, having neither desire nor aversion.
As for the various flavors consumed, they likewise possess both the beautiful and the base.
One does not give rise to craving for delicious flavors, nor does one reject unpleasant ones.
When touched by pleasant sensations, one does not become negligent;
when touched by painful sensations, one does not conceive thoughts of malice.
Equanimously abandoning both suffering and pleasure, one brings to cessation that which has not yet ceased;
through the mental observation of various signs and their respective characteristics,
false conceptualization arises, and sensual desire increases and expands.
Awakening from those evils, one dwells securely in a mind free from desire.
Skillfully restraining these six sense faculties, one remains unmoved by contact with the six objects.
Having crushed and subdued the hosts of Māra’s enemies, one crosses to the further shore of birth and death.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 280 (280) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the World-Honored One was wandering among the people of Kośala and arrived at the Śiṃśapā Grove north of the city of Piṇḍada.
At that time, the brahmins and householders in the city of Piṇḍada heard that the World-Honored One, while wandering among the people of the Kosalans, was staying in the Siṃsapā Forest at Piṇḍada.
Having heard this, they all went out of the city together to the Śiṃśapā Grove, approached the Blessed One, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the brahmin householders of the city of Piṇḍada:
"If someone were to ask you: [text continues]"
"What kind of śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas should not be honored, revered, respected, served, and supported?
You should answer:

"If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, upon seeing forms with the eye, has not abandoned greed, has not abandoned desire, has not abandoned craving, has not abandoned thirst, and has not abandoned mental preoccupation; if his inner mind is not tranquil, his conduct is unrighteous, and his conduct is harsh and obstructive."
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind with respect to mental objects (*dharma*).
Monks of such a kind should not be revered, honored, served, or supported.
"Having spoken thus, one should further ask:
'For what reason should such types of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas not be honored, revered, worshipped, and supported?'"
"You should answer:
'When we see forms with our eyes, we are not free from desire, not free from craving, not free from thirst, and not free from longing; thus, the internal mind is not tranquil.'"
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind regarding mental phenomena.

When those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas see forms with the eye, they are not free from greed, not free from desire, not free from affection, not free from thirst, and not free from fixation; their inner minds are not tranquil, and they practice what is unrighteous and practice harsh conduct.
It is likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-objects.
When I sought the distinctions among these, I did not perceive any distinct characteristics.
"Therefore, I should not revere, respect, honor, or make offerings to such types of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
If it is further asked:
"What kind of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas should be revered, respected, honored, and provided with offerings?"
"You should answer:

'If, when seeing forms with the eye, one is free from greed, free from desire, free from craving, free from thirst, and free from longing; if the inner mind is tranquil, and one does not engage in unrighteous conduct, but engages in balanced conduct and conduct that is not harsh.'"
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind with respect to mental objects (*dharmas*).
Such individuals as these—śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas—are worthy of being honored, revered, saluted, and supported with offerings.
"Furthermore, if it should be asked:
'For what reason do you revere, respect, honor, and make offerings to these types of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas?'"
"You should answer:

'When we see forms with our eyes, we do not depart from greed, we do not depart from desire, we do not depart from craving, we do not depart from thirst, and we do not depart from mindfulness; our inner minds are not tranquil, and we practice unrighteous conduct and harsh conduct.'"
"It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind with respect to mental phenomena.

Such śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas as these are free from greed, free from desire, free from thirst, and free from longing; their inner minds are tranquil, they practice in accordance with the Dharma, and they do not engage in harsh or abrasive conduct.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind with respect to mental phenomena (*dharma*).
We seek their distinctions therein, and because we perceive such distinctions, we should pay homage to, revere, honor, and make offerings to those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess such qualities.
“Having spoken thus, if one were further to ask:
‘What is the conduct of those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas?
What is their appearance?’”
What are their characteristics?

Do you know those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who are free from greed and are oriented toward the subduing of greed; who are free from hatred and are oriented toward the subduing of hatred; and who are free from delusion and are oriented toward the subduing of delusion?

"You should answer: 'I see those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess such characteristics: dwelling in secluded places, in groves, beneath trees, on low beds or straw mats, practicing seclusion, staying away from women, associating with those who delight in solitude and share their meditative reflections;

and in those places, there are no forms visible to the eye that could give rise to attachment to pleasure, nor sounds for the ear, odors for the nose, flavors for the tongue, or tangibles for the body that could give rise to attachment to pleasure. If those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas have such conduct, such appearance, and such marks, they cause us to know that these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are free from greed and are tending toward the subduing of greed; free from hatred and are tending toward the subduing of hatred; free from delusion and are tending toward the subduing of delusion.'"
At that time, the śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and elders addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How marvelous!
World-Honored One!”

Without praising oneself or disparaging others, he correctly explains their meaning; for each of the sense bases (*āyatana*), he distinguishes between defilement and purification, and extensively expounds dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) just as the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has taught it.
Just as a man who can rescue those drowning, open for those who are locked out, show the way to those who are lost, and light a lamp in the darkness—
the World-Honored One is likewise so.
“Do not praise yourself, do not disparage others; speak of the meaning correctly, even as it was taught by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, the brahmin elders of the city of Piṇḍada, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced, paid their respects, and departed.
281 (281). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the renunciant Jaṭila Maudgalyāyana came to where the Buddha was, exchanged greetings with him, and after the greetings were concluded, withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked Jaṭāmakuṭa Maudgalyāyana,
"From where have you come?
Jaṭāmakuṭa Maudgalyāyana replied to the Buddha:
"I have come from that forest after having gone to the assembly hall where many various ascetics and brahmins of different sects, including the Carakas, have gathered to hear the Dharma."
The Buddha said to Jaṭila Maudgalyāyana:
"By what power of merit did you go to hear the Dharma being preached by those many various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of different paths, including the Carakas who have gone forth?"
The matted-hair Maudgalyāyana said:
"I shall listen to the benefit of their competing discourse on the principles of debate, and to the benefit of their mutually opposing arguments."
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:

"Throughout the long night of vast antiquity, various heterodox śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and cāraṇas who have gone forth have vied with one another in debate, engaging in contradictory arguments regarding merit and welfare, and mutually destroying one another."
The matted-hair ascetic Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying: “Gautama!

What kind of Dharma does the Blessed One teach to his disciples for their benefit, such that they may in turn explain it to others without slandering the Tathāgata, neither adding to nor subtracting from it, but speaking truthfully, speaking the Dharma, and speaking the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, so that no other person can come to compare, challenge, or censure it?”
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:

"One who explains to others the fruits and benefits of clear knowledge and liberation does not slander the Tathāgata, does not deviate from the principle, and speaks in accordance with the Dharma following the Dharma; no one can come to compare, challenge, or reproach such a person."
The matted-hair ascetic Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha,
“Gautama! Is there a dharma among your disciples which, through cultivation and repeated practice, brings about the fulfillment of the benefits of clarity and liberation?”
The Buddha told Jaṭila Maudgalyāyana:
"There are seven factors of enlightenment; by cultivating and frequently practicing them, the benefits of clear knowledge and liberation will be fully realized."
The matted-hair ascetic Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is there a dharma, through the cultivation of which, one can bring the seven factors of enlightenment to fulfillment?
The Buddha told the matted-hair ascetic Maudgalyāyana:
“There are four foundations of mindfulness; by practicing and cultivating them extensively, one can bring the seven factors of enlightenment to fulfillment.
The matted-hair Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha:
“Is there another dharma which, through practice and extensive cultivation, brings the four foundations of mindfulness to fulfillment?”
The Buddha told Jaṭila Maudgalyāyana:
“There are three types of sublime conduct; when practiced and cultivated repeatedly, they can bring the four foundations of mindfulness to fulfillment.
Jaṭila Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Furthermore, is there a dharma which, through cultivation and repeated cultivation, brings the three types of wholesome conduct to fulfillment?
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
“There are the six bases of contact and their restraint; through cultivation and repeated cultivation, these bring the three types of wholesome conduct to fulfillment.”
The matted-hair ascetic Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How is it that the restraint of the six bases of contact, through cultivation and repeated practice, brings the three types of sublime conduct to fulfillment?”
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:

"If a bhikṣu sees with his eye a form that is pleasing, lovely, capable of nourishing desire, and causing attachment—having seen it, he does not rejoice in it, does not praise it, does not dwell upon it, does not become attached to it, and does not abide in it.
If he sees with his eye a form that is displeasing, not lovely, conducive to painful feeling—he, having seen it, does not fear it, does not loathe it, does not despise it, and does not become angry."
Having seen with the eye forms that are beautiful, one never again becomes attached to them;
having seen with the eye forms that are unattractive, one never again becomes attached to them.
With the inner mind dwelling in immovability, one skillfully cultivates liberation, and the mind remains free from indolence.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness regarding phenomena.
Thus, by practicing and cultivating these six bases of contact extensively, one fulfills the three types of sublime conduct.
"How does one cultivate the three types of sublime conduct so as to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness?
A well-taught noble disciple, in a secluded place, in a forest, or at the foot of a tree, trains thus and reflects thus:
'These bodily misdeeds will certainly result in retribution, both in the present life and in future lives.'"

If I were to engage in bodily misconduct, I would surely feel self-reproach and remorse; others would also look upon me with disdain; the Great Master would rebuke me; and my fellow practitioners of the holy life would likewise censure me according to the Dharma.
My ill repute would spread in all directions, and at the dissolution of the body after death, I would fall into hell.

Regarding bodily misconduct, one perceives such fruits and retributions in both the present life and future lives; for this reason, one abandons bodily misconduct and cultivates sublime conduct of the body, and the same applies to verbal and mental misconduct.
"This is called having cultivated the three types of sublime conduct, one attains the purity and fulfillment of the four foundations of mindfulness.
How does one cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness so as to attain the fulfillment of the seven factors of enlightenment?"
"Maugandalyāyana!
A bhikṣu dwells thus observing the body as the body. When he dwells observing the body as the body, he collects his mindfulness, abides securely, and does not forget.

At that time, he skillfully cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Having skillfully cultivated the awakening factor of mindfulness, he attains its fulfillment. He then discriminates phenomena within that mental mindfulness, awakening to them, perceiving them, and reflecting upon them."

At that time, one skillfully cultivates the factor of enlightenment of discrimination of phenomena; having skillfully cultivated the factor of enlightenment of discrimination of phenomena, one attains the fulfillment of the factor of enlightenment of discrimination of phenomena, thereby discerning those phenomena through awareness, perception, and reflection.

One skillfully cultivates the awakening factor of energy; having skillfully cultivated the awakening factor of energy, one attains the fulfillment of the awakening factor of energy, and having exerted diligent effort, a mind of joy arises.

At that time, he cultivates the factor of awakening of joy through skillful means; having cultivated the factor of awakening of joy, he attains the fulfillment of the factor of awakening of joy; once his mind is joyful, body and mind come to rest.

At that time, one cultivates the awakening factor of tranquility; having cultivated the awakening factor of tranquility, one attains its fulfillment. Once body and mind have become tranquil, one attains samādhi.

At that time, he cultivates the awakening factor of concentration; having cultivated the awakening factor of concentration, the awakening factor of concentration becomes fulfilled—namely, by unifying the mind, extinguishing greed and sorrow, and maintaining equanimity regarding bodily formations. He skillfully cultivates the awakening factor of equanimity; having skillfully cultivated the awakening factor of equanimity, he attains the purity and fulfillment of the awakening factor of equanimity.
The applications of mindfulness regarding feelings, the mind, and phenomena are also explained in this same way.
Thus, by practicing the four applications of mindfulness, the seven factors of enlightenment are fulfilled.
"How does one practice the seven factors of enlightenment?"
"Clear knowledge and liberation fulfilled?
Maudgalyāyana!

If a bhikṣu cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and culminating in relinquishment; as he practices the cultivation of the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, he attains and fulfills the purity of clear knowledge and liberation."

The cultivation of the enlightenment factor of equanimity is also described in the same manner; this is called having cultivated the seven factors of enlightenment, whereby clear knowledge and liberation are purified and fulfilled.
"Thus it is, Maudgalyāyana!
The Dharma is regulated by the mutual relationship of phenomena; from this shore one reaches the further shore.
When this Dharma was spoken, the matted-hair Maudgalyāyana was distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.

At that time, Jaṭila Maudgalyāyana saw the Dharma, attained the Dharma, knew the Dharma, and entered the Dharma; he crossed beyond all doubt and uncertainty, and, no longer dependent on others, he attained fearlessness regarding all dharmas and the Vinaya.
Rising from his seat, he adjusted his robes, paid homage to the Buddha, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"May I now go forth into homelessness within this True Dharma and Discipline, and receive full ordination as a bhikṣu?"
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:

“You have now attained ordination in the True Dharma and Vinaya, fully obtaining the status of a bhikṣu. Having gone forth, you should apply yourself with focused contemplation, dwelling in heedfulness, until you achieve arhatship.”
282. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Kāpiśī-karanda-vinataka forest.

At that time, there was a youth named Uttara, a disciple of Praśnaka, who came to where the Buddha was staying; after paying his respects and inquiring after His well-being, he withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Uttara:
"Did your teacher Pārasaṇa teach you how to cultivate the sense faculties?
Uttara replied:
“Having spoken thus, Gautama,” [he replied].
The Buddha said to Uttara:
“How does your teacher Pārasambara teach the cultivation of the sense faculties?”
Uttara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"My teacher Pārasaṇa says that when the eye does not see forms and the ear does not hear sounds, this is called the cultivation of the sense faculties."
The Buddha told Uttara:
"If it is as you, Pārasaṇa, have said, is one who is blind a practitioner of the sense-faculties? Why is that?"
"It is just as one who is blind does not see forms with their eyes.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was behind the Blessed One, fanning him with a fan. The Venerable Ānanda said to Uttara:
"Is it as Pāṭikāputra has said—that a deaf person is one who has cultivated his faculties?"
"Why is this? It is because, just as one who is merely deaf does not hear sounds with their ears.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Distinct from the Dharma and Vinaya of the noble ones, there is the unsurpassed cultivation of the faculties.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I pray that the World-Honored One will explain to the bhikṣus the unsurpassed cultivation of the faculties according to the Dharma and Vinaya of the noble ones; having heard it, the bhikṣus shall receive and practice it accordingly.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you.

Dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. When one sees a pleasing form and wishes to cultivate the Tathāgata’s right mindfulness and right clear comprehension of disenchantment, [one should do so]."

When eye and forms as conditions give rise to eye-consciousness that is disagreeable, one wishes to cultivate the Tathāgata’s right mindfulness and right clear comprehension regarding non-aversion; when eye and forms as conditions give rise to eye-consciousness that is agreeable or disagreeable, one wishes to cultivate the Tathāgata’s right mindfulness and right clear comprehension regarding aversion and non-aversion.

Eye and forms are conditions for the arising of eye-consciousness, whether it be unpleasant or pleasant; one should cultivate, regarding the Tathāgata, mindfulness and clear comprehension that are neither weary nor detached.

With the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises—whether agreeable, disagreeable, or both agreeable and disagreeable—one should cultivate a mind of equanimity that is free from both aversion and non-aversion, abiding in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension regarding the Tathāgata.
"In this way, Ānanda!

If one has well-tamed, well-shut, well-guarded, well-restrained, and well-cultivated the mind regarding these five points, then one has cultivated the faculty of the eye with respect to forms in an unsurpassed manner."
The same is said for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind with respect to mental objects (*dharma*). Ānanda,
this is called the unsurpassed cultivation of the faculties according to the Dharma and Vinaya of the noble ones.
The Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does the Dharma and Vinaya of the noble ones constitute the noble cultivation of the faculties?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"With the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises; it gives rise to what is agreeable, what is disagreeable, and what is both agreeable and disagreeable."
That noble disciple knows thus according to reality:

"Dependent upon my eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; there arises what is agreeable, what is disagreeable, and what is both agreeable and disagreeable. This is their cessation; this is their excellence, namely, equanimity toward both.
Having attained that equanimity, one is free from aversion and non-aversion."

Just as in the blink of an eye, so too, conditioned by the eye and forms, visual consciousness arises—arising as agreeable, arising as disagreeable, or arising as both agreeable and disagreeable—and in an instant it ceases entirely; one attains detachment from the agreeable and the disagreeable, and dwells in equanimity.
“In the same way, ear-consciousness arises conditioned by the ear and sounds; it arises as agreeable, arises as disagreeable, and arises as both agreeable and disagreeable.
A noble disciple knows this as it truly is:

‘My ear-consciousness hears sounds and gives rise to what is agreeable, disagreeable, and both agreeable and disagreeable; yet this is subject to cessation and is surpassed by the sublime, which is called equanimity.’”
Having attained equanimity (*upekṣā*), one is free from both aversion and non-aversion.
It is like a strong man snapping his fingers: as soon as the sound is produced, it immediately ceases.

In the same way, when ear-consciousness arises conditioned by the ear and sounds—whether it be pleasant, unpleasant, or neither pleasant nor unpleasant—it ceases as soon as it has arisen. This is what is meant by equanimity; having attained that equanimity, one is free from both aversion and non-aversion.
"Through the nose and odors as conditions, nose-consciousness arises; it gives rise to what is agreeable, what is disagreeable, and what is both agreeable and disagreeable.
A noble disciple knows this as it truly is:

'Through the nose and odors as conditions, nose-consciousness arises; it gives rise to what is agreeable, what is disagreeable, and what is both agreeable and disagreeable. This is its cessation, this is its excellence, namely, equanimity.'"
Having attained that equanimity, one is free from both aversion and non-aversion.

Just as a lotus leaf is unstained by water, so too, when nose-consciousness arises conditioned by the nose and odors—whether it arises as agreeable, disagreeable, or both agreeable and disagreeable—it ceases completely once it has arisen; this is what is called equanimity.
"Having attained that equanimity, one is free from both aversion and non-aversion.
"In dependence upon the tongue and flavors, tongue-consciousness arises; there arises what is agreeable, what is disagreeable, and what is both agreeable and disagreeable."
That noble disciple knows thus according to reality:

"Dependent upon the tongue and flavors, tongue-consciousness arises; there arise what is agreeable, what is disagreeable, and what is both agreeable and disagreeable. Once arisen, they are completely extinguished, stilled, and sublime—this is called equanimity.
Having attained that equanimity, one is free from aversion and non-aversion."

Just as a strong man spits the saliva from the tip of his tongue until it is completely exhausted and ceases, so too, conditioned by the tongue and flavors, tongue-consciousness arises—arising as agreeable, arising as disagreeable, and arising as both agreeable and disagreeable—and having arisen, it is entirely extinguished. This is called equanimity (*upekṣā*). Having attained that equanimity, one is free from both aversion and non-aversion.

"Body and contact are conditions for the arising of body-consciousness; it arises as agreeable, arises as disagreeable, and arises as both agreeable and disagreeable; having arisen, it utterly ceases."
The noble disciple knows this as it truly is:

"Body-consciousness arises conditioned by the body and contact; it arises as agreeable, arises as disagreeable, and arises as both agreeable and disagreeable. Once arisen, it is exhausted, ceased, stilled, and sublime—this is called equanimity.
Having attained that equanimity, one is free from aversion and non-aversion."
For example, when an iron ball has been heated until it is extremely hot, even a small drop of water sprinkled upon it is immediately extinguished.

In the same way, body-consciousness arises conditioned by the body and contact; whether it arises as agreeable, disagreeable, or both agreeable and disagreeable, once it has arisen, it is completely extinguished. This is what is called equanimity (*upekṣā*). Having attained that equanimity, one is free from both aversion and non-aversion.

"Mind and mental phenomena as conditions give rise to mind-consciousness; it arises as agreeable, it arises as disagreeable, and it arises as both agreeable and disagreeable. Having arisen, it quickly ceases."
The noble disciple knows this as it truly is:

"With the mind and mental phenomena as conditions, mind-consciousness arises; there arises what is agreeable, there arises what is disagreeable, and there arises what is both agreeable and disagreeable. Once arisen, they are completely extinguished; this is tranquility, this is sublime, namely, equanimity.
Having attained that equanimity, one is free from both aversion and non-aversion."

Just as a strong man might cut off the crown of a *tāla* tree, so too, when the mind and mental objects serve as conditions for the arising of consciousness, there arises what is agreeable, what is disagreeable, and what is both agreeable and disagreeable; once arisen, they are utterly extinguished. This is called equanimity (*upekṣā*). Having attained that equanimity, one is free from both aversion and non-aversion.
"Ānanda! This is the Dharma and Vinaya of the noble ones; it is for the noble disciple to cultivate the faculties.
"What is the Dharma and Vinaya of the noble ones that leads to the realization of the tracks?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Visual consciousness arises conditioned by the eye and forms; it gives rise to what is agreeable, what is disagreeable, and what is both agreeable and disagreeable. Toward these, the noble disciple feels shame, abashment, and revulsion."

When ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind take mental phenomena as their object, consciousness arises; it arises as agreeable, it arises as disagreeable, and it arises as both agreeable and disagreeable. Toward these, the noble disciple feels shame, embarrassment, and revulsion.
Ānanda! This is called the noble and holy Dharma and Vinaya, the realization of the tracks of awakening. Ānanda!
This is called the unsurpassed cultivation of the faculties according to the Dharma and Vinaya of the noble ones.
Thus have I explained the noble cultivation of the faculties; thus have I explained the realization and vision of the tracks. Ānanda!
"What I had to do for the sake of the śrāvakas has been done; you yourselves must now do what is to be done... as explained at length in the *Khadgaviṣāṇa-sūtra* (The Sūtra of the Snake in the Box).
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*Saṃyukta Āgama*, Scroll 11. *Saṃyukta Āgama*, Scroll 12.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
1.2.283 (283). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If, regarding the phenomena bound by the fetters, one gives rise to attachment to their flavor, cherishes them with longing, and becomes mentally bound by them, then craving arises.

With craving as condition, grasping arises; with grasping as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises; and with birth as condition, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering arise."

In this way, in this manner, this entire mass of suffering arises. It is like a person planting a tree: at first it is small and tender; they protect it so that it remains secure, mound it with soil and manure, water it at the proper times, and regulate the temperature of the water suitably. Through these causes and conditions, that tree subsequently grows large.

In this way, monks, when one is bound by the fetters of the dharmas that are tasted and cherished, craving arises; conditioned by craving is grasping; conditioned by grasping is existence; conditioned by existence is birth; and conditioned by birth arise old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering.
"In this way, this entire great mass of suffering arises.

If, regarding those phenomena bound by fetters, one contemplates them in accordance with impermanence, abides in the contemplation of arising and ceasing, the contemplation of dispassion, the contemplation of cessation, and the contemplation of relinquishment; if one does not give rise to longing or attachment, and the mind is not bound or clung to, then craving ceases.

With the cessation of craving, grasping ceases; with the cessation of grasping, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, despair, and suffering cease. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering ceases."

It is like planting a tree that is initially small and tender; if it is not protected, not kept secure, not nourished with manure and soil, not watered at the proper times, and not provided with a suitable balance of heat and cold, it will fail to grow.

Furthermore, if its roots are severed, its branches cut, if it is hacked into pieces and dissected limb by limb, exposed to the wind and scorched by the sun, or burned with fire until it becomes ash—whether blown away by a swift wind or cast into a flowing stream.
"Monks! What do you think?
Would that tree, having its roots cut off and even being burned until it is utterly extinguished, become a phenomenon that will not arise again in future lives?"
He replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One! “So it is, bhikṣu!”

Regarding those phenomena bound by the fetters, one contemplates them in accordance with impermanence, abides in the contemplation of arising and ceasing, and practices the contemplations of dispassion, cessation, and relinquishment. Without giving rise to longing or attachment, the mind is not bound or clung to; thus craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, grasping ceases; with the cessation of grasping, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, vexation, and suffering cease. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering ceases.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
284 (284) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

“If, regarding the phenomena that are grasped, one gives rise to attachment through relishing them, turns back to them with longing, and binds the mind to them, the mind will be driven about, pursuing name-and-form (nāmarūpa). With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact (sparśa); with contact as condition, feeling (vedanā); with feeling as condition, craving (tṛṣṇā); with craving as condition, grasping (upādāna); with grasping as condition, existence (bhava); with existence as condition, birth (jāti); and with birth as condition, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering arise.”

In this way, this entire great mass of suffering arises, just as a great tree—with its roots, trunk, branches, twigs, leaves, flowers, and fruit—has deep and firm roots that are nourished with manure and water; that tree remains solid and does not decay for all eternity.
In this way, bhikṣus!

Regarding the phenomena that are grasped, through the arising of attachment to their flavor, longing for them, and the mind being bound to them, the mind races about, pursuing name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact (*sparśa*) arises; with contact as condition, feeling (*vedanā*) arises; with feeling as condition, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arises; with craving as condition, grasping (*upādāna*) arises; with grasping as condition, existence (*bhava*) arises; with existence as condition, birth (*jāti*) arises; and with birth as condition, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering arise.
"Thus, in this way, this entire great mass of suffering arises.

If one contemplates the phenomena that are grasped as impermanent, and dwells in contemplation of arising and passing away, contemplation of dispassion, contemplation of cessation, and contemplation of disenchantment; if the mind does not dwell upon them with longing and is free from bondage and attachment, then consciousness does not rush toward or pursue name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). When name-and-form ceases, the six sense bases cease; when the six sense bases cease, contact ceases; when contact ceases, feeling ceases; when feeling ceases, craving ceases; when craving ceases, clinging ceases; when clinging ceases, existence ceases; when existence ceases, birth ceases; and when birth ceases, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, despair, and suffering cease."

In this way, and in this manner, this entire mass of suffering ceases. It is like planting a tree: if one does not protect it according to the season to ensure its well-being, does not nourish it with soil and manure, does not water it at the proper times, and provides it with unsuitable heat or cold, it will not grow.

Furthermore, if one cuts its roots, lops off its branches, hacks it into pieces, dissects it bit by bit, lets it be scattered by the wind or scorched by the sun, burns it with fire until it becomes ash, or blows it away with a swift wind or casts it into flowing water.
"Monks! What do you think?
Would that tree, having its roots cut off and even being burned until it is utterly extinguished, become a thing that will not arise again in future lives?"
He replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One! “So it is, bhikṣu!”

Regarding the phenomena that are grasped, one contemplates them in accordance with impermanence, abiding in the contemplation of arising and ceasing, the contemplation of dispassion, the contemplation of cessation, and the contemplation of relinquishment. Without giving rise to longing or attachment, the mind is not bound or fettered; consciousness does not race or pursue name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Thus, name-and-form ceases. With the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease. With the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases. With the cessation of contact, feeling ceases. With the cessation of feeling, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, clinging ceases. With the cessation of clinging, existence ceases. With the cessation of existence, birth ceases. With the cessation of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, despair, and suffering cease. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering ceases.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
285 (285) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I recall that in a past life, before I had attained perfect enlightenment, while dwelling alone in a quiet place and concentrating my mind in meditative reflection, this thought arose in me:

'The world is difficult to enter—namely, birth, aging, illness, death, transition, and rebirth—and yet sentient beings do not know, as it truly is, these states of birth, aging, and death, nor their underlying basis.'"
I then thought: "Due to the existence of what phenomenon does 'existence' arise?
With what phenomenon as its condition does 'existence' arise?"
He then applied right reflection and gave rise to direct knowledge (*abhisamaya*): "Because existence exists, birth exists; because existence is the condition, birth exists.
He further reflected:
"Because what exists does existence exist?"
"By what condition does existence (bhava) come to be?

He then applied right reflection and, through immediate and accurate realization, knew as it truly is: "Because of grasping (upādāna), there is existence; with grasping as condition, there is existence."
Furthermore, he reflects thus:
"With what as condition does grasping arise? Because of what dharma being present does grasping exist?
With what dharma as its condition does grasping exist?"

He then applied right reflection and, through immediate and thorough knowledge as it truly is, understood: "The attachment to the flavor of phenomena, the longing for them, and the binding of the mind lead to the increase of craving.

Because that craving exists, grasping exists; conditioned by craving, there is grasping; conditioned by grasping, there is existence; conditioned by existence, there is birth; and conditioned by birth, there arise old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering."
"In this way, in this way, this entire great mass of suffering arises. Bhikṣus,
what do you think?"
“Suppose, for example, that a lamp’s light is able to burn by depending on oil and a wick; if one repeatedly increases the oil and the wick, would that lamp’s light be able to endure for a long time?
He replied, “It would, World-Honored One.”
“In this way, monks!

One takes delight in form, becomes attached to it, dwells upon it, and is bound by craving; because of this, craving increases as a condition for grasping (*upādāna*). With grasping as condition, there is becoming (*bhava*); with becoming as condition, there is birth (*jāti*); and with birth as condition, there arise old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering.”
"Thus, in this way, this entire great mass of suffering arises.
At that time, I further thought:
"In the absence of what dharma do old age, sickness, and death not exist?"
"By the cessation of what phenomena do aging, sickness, and death cease?

He then engaged in right reflection and gave rise to suchness and non-interruption: "In the absence of birth, there is no aging, sickness, or death; through the cessation of birth, aging, sickness, and death cease."
Again, he thought:
"In the absence of what dharma is there no arising?
Through the cessation of what dharma does arising cease?"
He then applied right reflection and gave rise to the realization of reality as it is: "Because existence is absent, birth is absent; because existence ceases, birth ceases.
He further reflected:
"In the absence of what dharma is existence absent?"
"By the cessation of what dharma does existence cease?

He then engaged in right reflection and gave rise to the immediate realization of things as they truly are: "Because grasping is absent, existence is absent; because grasping ceases, existence ceases."
Furthermore, he reflects thus:
"In the absence of what dharma is grasping absent?
Through the cessation of what dharma does grasping cease?"

He then applied right reflection and gave rise to the realization of reality through immediate insight (*yathābhūta-anuprekṣā*): that the grasped phenomena are impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing, free from desire, subject to cessation, and to be relinquished. His mind no longer dwells upon them, his mind is not bound or attached to them; thus craving ceases. Because craving ceases, grasping ceases; because grasping ceases, existence ceases; because existence ceases, birth ceases; because birth ceases, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering cease. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering ceases.
“Monks, what do you think? Suppose, for example, an oil lamp is burning with oil and a wick;
if one does not replenish the oil or trim the wick, would it not be the case that the light of that lamp will not arise in the future, but will instead be exhausted and extinguished?”
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
“So it is, World-Honored One! “So it is, bhikṣus!”

Regarding the phenomena that are grasped, one contemplates their impermanence, arising and ceasing, dispassion, cessation, and relinquishment; the mind does not dwell upon them and is not bound by attachment. Thus craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, grasping ceases, and so on, until this entire great mass of suffering ceases.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
286 (286) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“I recall that in a former life, before I had attained perfect enlightenment, I dwelt alone in a quiet place, single-mindedly and diligently engaged in meditative reflection... as explained at length above.
As for the distinction:

"Suppose, for example, ten bundles, twenty bundles, thirty bundles, forty bundles, fifty bundles, a hundred bundles, a thousand bundles, or a hundred thousand bundles of firewood were piled up and set ablaze, forming a great mass of fire. Then, O monks, suppose someone were to add more dry grass and firewood to it."
"What do you think?
Would this continuity of fire burn fiercely throughout the long night?
The bhikṣu replied to the Buddha:
"So it is, World-Honored One!

So it is, monks! When one relishes, longs for, and becomes mentally bound by the dharmas that are grasped, craving increases with grasping as its condition; with grasping as condition, there is existence, and so on, until this entire great mass of suffering arises."
"Monks! If that mass of fire were blazing but no more wood or grass were added, monks!"
"What do you think?
Would that fire be extinguished?
He replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, monks!

By observing the phenomena of grasping as impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing, free from desire, subject to cessation, and to be relinquished, the mind does not dwell upon them with attachment; thus craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, grasping ceases... [and so on] in detail, until: 'there is the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.'"
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
287 (287) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I recall that in a past life, before I had attained perfect enlightenment, while dwelling alone in a quiet place and practicing meditation with focused diligence, I had this thought:
'Due to the existence of what phenomenon do old age and death exist?'"
"By what condition does aging and death exist?

He then applied correct reflection, and there arose in him a direct realization of reality as it is: "Because birth exists, aging and death exist; because birth is the condition, aging and death exist."
Thus there are existence, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, and name-and-form.
By the existence of what dharma does name-and-form exist?
By what dharma as condition does name-and-form exist?

I then engaged in right reflection, and thus there arose a realization of reality as it is: because consciousness exists, name-and-form exist; because consciousness is the condition, name-and-form exist.

While I was reflecting in this way, I reached as far as consciousness and could not go beyond it—namely, that conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form arise; conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense bases arise; conditioned by the six sense bases, contact arises; conditioned by contact, feeling arises; conditioned by feeling, craving arises; conditioned by craving, clinging arises; conditioned by clinging, existence arises; conditioned by existence, birth arises; and conditioned by birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, despair, and suffering arise.
"Thus, in this way, this entire great mass of suffering arises.
At that time, I had this thought:
"In the absence of what phenomenon do aging and death not exist?"
“By the cessation of what dharma do aging and death cease?

He then applied right reflection and attained the reality of things as they truly are: “In the absence of birth, there is no aging and death; through the cessation of birth, aging and death cease. Thus he spoke extensively regarding birth, becoming, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, and volitional formations.
I further reflected thus:
"In the absence of what dharma do volitional formations not exist?
Through the cessation of what dharma do volitional formations cease?"

He then applied right reflection and attained clear realization as it truly is: because ignorance does not exist, volitional formations do not exist; because ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease; because volitional formations cease, consciousness ceases; because consciousness ceases, name-and-form cease; because name-and-form cease, the six sense bases cease; because the six sense bases cease, contact ceases; because contact ceases, feeling ceases; because feeling ceases, craving ceases; because craving ceases, clinging ceases; because clinging ceases, existence ceases; because existence ceases, birth ceases; because birth ceases, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, despair, and suffering cease. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering ceases.
"At that time, I had this thought:
'I have attained the path of the ancient seers, the trail of the ancient seers, the track of the ancient seers; the ancient seers departed by this track, and I now follow it.'"

"It is, for example, like a person wandering through a vast wilderness who, clearing away the undergrowth in search of a path, suddenly encounters an ancient track where people of old have traveled. He follows it and gradually moves forward, seeing an ancient city, an ancient royal palace, gardens, pavilions, bathing pools, and pure groves of trees."
He thought to himself:
"I should now go and inform the king.
He immediately went and informed the king:
"Great King, you should know this: while wandering through the wilderness, stripping away the brush to seek a path, I suddenly saw an ancient road where people of old had traveled. I followed it;
having followed it, I saw an ancient city, an ancient royal palace, gardens, pavilions, bathing pools, groves, and streams—all pure and serene. Great King, you may go and dwell within them."
The king immediately went there, took up residence within it, and it became prosperous, peaceful, and secure, with its population flourishing.

"Now I am likewise; I have attained the path of the ancient seers, the track of the ancient seers, the trail of the ancient seers, the destination of the ancient seers—the Eightfold Noble Path that I have followed: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration."

Following that path, I saw aging, sickness, and death; the origin of aging, sickness, and death; the cessation of aging, sickness, and death; and the path leading to the cessation of aging, sickness, and death. I saw birth, existence, clinging, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, and volitional formations; the origin of volitional formations; the cessation of volitional formations; and the path leading to the cessation of volitional formations.

Having personally known and personally realized this Dharma and attained supreme perfect enlightenment, I have revealed and expounded it for the sake of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as other outsiders—śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, householders, and renunciants. Those fourfold assemblies, having heard the Dharma, have turned toward it correctly with faith and joy; they have understood the Dharma well, their holy life has increased and expanded, and they have received great benefit.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
288 (288) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra and the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila were on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.

Then, in the late afternoon, the Venerable Śāriputra arose from meditation and went to the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila. After they had exchanged greetings and expressions of mutual courtesy and comfort, he sat down to one side.
He addressed the Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila:
"I wish to ask a question; would you have the leisure to grant me an answer?
The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila said to the Venerable Śāriputra:
“Let the benevolent one ask, and the wise one shall answer.
Venerable Śāriputra asked Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila: “How is it so?”
"Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila, do you have old age?
He replied, "I do."
The Venerable Śāriputra asked again:
"Is there death? He replied:
“There is. He asked again,
“In what way?”
Is old age and death created by oneself?
Is it created by another?
Or is it created by both oneself and another?
"Is it created by neither self nor another, nor without cause?
He replied, "Venerable Śāriputra!"
Old age and death are not self-made, not made by another, not made by both self and another, nor are they produced without cause; rather, old age and death exist because of the condition of birth.

“Are birth, existence, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, and name-and-form created by oneself, created by another, created by both oneself and another, or created neither by oneself nor by another, being without cause?”
He replied: "Venerable Śāriputra!
Name-and-form is not self-made, not made by another, not made by both self and another, nor is it made without cause; rather, that name-and-form arises conditioned by consciousness."
He asked again:
"Is that consciousness created by itself, created by another, created by both itself and another, or is it created neither by itself nor by another, being without cause?
He replied:
"Venerable Śāriputra!
That consciousness is not self-made, not made by another, not made by both self and another, nor is it made without cause; rather, that consciousness arises conditioned by name-and-form."
The Venerable Śāriputra asked again:
"Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila!

Previously you stated that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is not self-made, not made by another, not made by both self and another, nor produced without cause; yet you said that name-and-form arises conditioned by consciousness (vijñāna). Now, however, you say again that name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness—what is the meaning of this?"
The Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila replied:
“I shall now provide an analogy, for the wise gain understanding through analogies.

Suppose three bundles of reeds were standing in an open space, leaning against one another so as to remain upright; if one were removed, the other two would no longer stand, and if two were removed, the remaining one would also not stand. They remain upright only by leaning against one another. Consciousness conditioned by name-and-form is just like this.”
"By depending upon one another in succession, they are able to grow.
Venerable Śāriputra said,
"Excellent!"
Excellent, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila!

Among the World-Honored One’s śrāvakas, you are one whose wisdom is clear and penetrating, who is well-disciplined and fearless, who has seen the Dharma of ambrosia, and who has fully realized the body through the Dharma of ambrosia. It is indeed you, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila, who possess such profound eloquence regarding the meaning; that you are able to answer all manner of difficult questions, like a priceless jewel held upon the crown of the world—so too do I now hold the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila upon my crown.
I have now gained great benefit from you; likewise, those who practice the holy life and frequently visit you will also gain great benefit, for that venerable one preaches the Dharma well.
“Because of this Dharma taught by the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila, I shall now praise, extol, and rejoice in it with thirty kinds of verses.
The Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila said:
“To feel weary of old age and death, to be free from desire for them, and to bring them to cessation—this is called a Dharma teacher.”

One who teaches the weariness with, the fading of desire for, and the cessation of birth, becoming, clinging, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, and consciousness is called a Dharma teacher;
if a bhikṣu is directed toward the weariness with, the fading of desire for, and the cessation of aging and death, he is called a Dharma teacher;
