and so on, up to being directed toward the weariness with, the fading of desire for, and the cessation of consciousness, he is called a Dharma teacher.

If a bhikṣu, through weariness with old age and death, through dispassion toward them, and through their cessation, gives rise to no outflows and his mind is well-liberated, he is called a Dharma teacher;

and so on, up to: through weariness with consciousness, through dispassion toward it, and through its cessation, giving rise to no outflows and his mind being well-liberated, he is called a Dharma teacher.
The Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila said to the Venerable Śāriputra:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

Among the Blessed One’s disciples, there is one who is brilliant in wisdom, well-disciplined and fearless, who has seen the Dharma of the Deathless and has fully realized it through his own body with the Dharma of the Deathless—this is the Venerable Śāriputra. He is able to pose such various questions of profound right knowledge, just as a priceless jewel in the world is borne upon the heads of all; even so do you now stand, universally borne upon the heads of all fellow practitioners of the holy life, and revered, honored, and served by them.
"Today I have gained a great and wholesome benefit, having been able to discuss the sublime meaning with the Venerable One.
Then, the two noble men rejoiced in one another's words and each returned to their respective abodes.
289 (Two Hundred Eighty-Nine). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Foolish, unlearned worldlings feel revulsion for, become detached from, and relinquish the body composed of the four great elements, yet they do not do so regarding consciousness. Why is this?

Because they see the body of the four great elements as subject to increase and decrease, to grasping and abandoning; however, regarding the mind, the intellect, and consciousness, foolish, unlearned worldlings are unable to give rise to revulsion, detachment, and liberation.”
Why is this? Because for a long night they have cherished and bound themselves to this, whether by acquisition or by grasping, saying:
"This is me; this is mine; it exists within me."
Therefore, ignorant and unlearned worldlings are unable to develop revulsion toward it, detachment from it, or renunciation of it.

An ignorant and unlearned worldling would rather bind this self and what belongs to the self to the body composed of the four great elements than bind this self and what belongs to the self to consciousness.

Why is this? The material body composed of the four great elements may be seen to remain for ten years, twenty, thirty, or even a hundred years; if one carefully attends to it, it may even exceed that slightly.
That mind, mentation, and consciousness undergo transformation day and night, from moment to moment; they arise as one thing and cease as another.
It is just like a monkey roaming among the trees in a forest, which from moment to moment moves from place to place, grasping at branches, letting go of one and seizing another.
That mind, thought, and consciousness are likewise thus: they arise differently and cease differently.

A well-versed noble disciple skillfully contemplates and examines dependent origination, namely: conditioned by a pleasant contact, a pleasant feeling arises; when one experiences that pleasant feeling, one knows as it truly is, "I experience a pleasant feeling.
With the cessation of that pleasant contact, the feeling born of the causal condition of that pleasant contact also ceases, subsides, becomes cooled, comes to rest, and vanishes.

Just as with pleasant feeling, when a neutral feeling arises conditioned by a contact of equanimity—whether painful, joyful, or sorrowful—at the time one experiences that neutral feeling, one knows the experience of the neutral feeling as it truly is.
When that contact of equanimity ceases, the neutral feeling arisen through the condition of that contact also ceases, subsides, becomes cooled, comes to rest, and vanishes.
He reflects thus:

"This feeling arises from contact, is pleasant through contact, and is bound by contact; because of this or that pleasant contact, there is this or that pleasant feeling. With the cessation of this or that pleasant contact, this or that pleasant feeling also ceases, stops, becomes cooled, subsides, and disappears."

"In this way, the learned noble disciple gives rise to disenchantment with form; he gives rise to disenchantment with feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Through disenchantment, he does not delight in them; through lack of delight, he is liberated. Being liberated, he knows and sees:
'Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and I myself know that there will be no further existence.'"
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
290 (290) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"The ignorant, unlearned worldling gives rise to revulsion for, becomes detached from, and turns away from the physical body composed of the four great elements, yet he does not do so regarding consciousness."

Why is this? Because the material body composed of the four great elements is subject to increase and decrease, and involves grasping and relinquishing; yet the foolish, unlearned worldling is unable to develop disenchantment toward consciousness, to become free from desire for it, and to practice equanimity toward it. For a long night they cherish and cling to it as "I," and whether they acquire it or grasp at it, they declare:
"This is me, this is mine, this is my self."
Therefore, the foolish, unlearned worldling is unable to develop disenchantment toward it, detachment from it, or the practice of equanimity.

"The foolish, unlearned worldling would rather bind the self and what belongs to the self to this material body composed of the four great elements than bind the self and what belongs to the self to consciousness."

Why is this? The physical body composed of the four great elements may be seen to remain for ten years, twenty, thirty, or even a hundred years; if well-maintained through proper care, it may even exceed that.

That mind, thought, and consciousness do not rest for even a moment throughout the days and nights, hours and instants; they undergo various transformations, arising differently and ceasing differently.
It is like a monkey roaming among the trees in a forest, from moment to moment moving from place to place, grasping at branches, letting go of one and seizing another.
That mind, mentation, and consciousness are likewise thus: they undergo various transformations, arising differently and ceasing differently.

A learned noble disciple contemplates and examines dependent origination as follows: "Conditioned by pleasant contact, pleasant feeling arises; when one experiences pleasant feeling, one knows as it really is: 'I experience pleasant feeling.
When that pleasant contact ceases, the pleasant feeling born of the condition of pleasant contact also ceases, subsides, cools, stills, and vanishes."

Just as with pleasant feeling, when a neutral feeling arises conditioned by a contact of equanimity—whether painful, joyful, or sorrowful—at the time one experiences that neutral feeling, one knows the experience of neutral feeling as it truly is.
When that contact of equanimity ceases, the neutral feeling arisen from the condition of that contact also ceases, stops, becomes cooled, subsides, and vanishes.
For example, when two pieces of wood are rubbed together, fire is produced through their conjunction;
if the two pieces of wood are separated, the fire is likewise extinguished.

In the same way, these various feelings arise conditioned by the accumulation of contact; contact arises and accumulates, and because of the accumulation of this or that contact, this or that feeling also accumulates.
With the arising and cessation of this and that contact, this and that feeling also arises and ceases; it is stilled, cooled, pacified, and subsides.

For the learned noble disciple who contemplates in this way, there is liberation from form, liberation from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; there is liberation from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, vexation, and suffering. I declare that such a person has attained liberation from suffering.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
291 (291) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa, the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I speak of the internal dharma of contact; do you accept it?
Then, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms, and said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
The internal dharma of contact that you have taught, I have already grasped.
At that time, that bhikṣu thus declared his realization in the presence of the Buddha.
"In this way, in this way, the Blessed One was displeased.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the Buddha fanning him with a fan. The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"The internal touch of the Dharma within the Noble Dharma and Vinaya is different from what this bhikṣu has spoken."
Ānanda said to the Buddha:

“Now is precisely the right time; may the World-Honored One, for the sake of the bhikṣus, expound the Dharma and Vinaya of the noble ones—the internal contact of the Dharma. Having heard it, the bhikṣus shall receive and practice it accordingly.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Excellent! Listen attentively, and I shall explain it for you."
These bhikṣus, taking up the internal phenomena of contact, should reflect in this way:
"When various kinds of suffering arise for sentient beings, what is the cause of this suffering? What is its origin? From what does it arise? By what is it conditioned?"
When one grasps in this manner, it should be known that this suffering has *opapatti* as its cause, *opapatti* as its origin, *opapatti* as its arising, and *opapatti* as its manifestation.
"Furthermore, when a bhikṣu internally contacts mental phenomena, he should further know: what is the cause of *nāmakāya*, what is its origination, what gives it birth, and what is its contact?
At the time of grasping, he should know that *nāmakāya* has craving as its cause, craving as its origination, craving as its birth, and craving as its contact."
"Furthermore, when a bhikṣu takes up internal objects of contact, he should further know: what is the cause of craving, what is its origin, from what is it born, and by what is it contacted?
When taking them up in this way, he should know that the true and correct forms contemplated in the world give rise to craving therein; they arise and are bound, they abide and remain fixed."

"If any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas perceive the forms that are considered true and real in the world as being permanent, eternal, secure, free from illness, a self, or belonging to a self, then craving for those forms increases.
When craving increases, *upādāna* (clinging) increases; when *upādāna* increases, suffering increases.
When suffering increases, they are not liberated from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and pain; I say that such persons are not liberated from suffering."

It is like a pool of cool water by the side of a road, replete with fragrance and flavor; yet someone places poison within it. During the months of spring, when travelers on the road are oppressed by wind, heat, and thirst, they vied with one another to come and drink.
Someone says to them:
"O men! This is refreshing, endowed with perfect color, fragrance, and flavor; however, there is poison within it, so do not drink."
If one were to drink it, it would either cause death or bring about suffering near death.
Yet that thirsty person, not believing this, drinks it; though he obtains a delicious flavor, in a moment he may die or encounter suffering near death.

"In this way, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who perceive the beautiful and attractive forms of the world conceive them as permanent, eternal, secure, and free from illness; they conceive of them as 'I' and 'mine,' and consequently fail to attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering."

“If any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas contemplate the beautiful forms in the world that are worthy of recollection as being like a disease, like an ulcer, like a thorn, like a murderer, as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, their craving will be abandoned. Because craving is abandoned, upādāna is abandoned; because upādāna is abandoned, suffering is abandoned; because suffering is abandoned, there is the abandonment of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, vexation, and pain.”

It is like a pool of cool water by the side of a road, replete with fragrance and flavor. Someone places poison within it. In the month of spring, travelers on the road, oppressed by wind, heat, and thirst, come vying to drink from it. Another person says to them:
"This water is poisonous!"
"Do not drink this; if you should drink it, it may cause your death or bring you near the suffering of death.
Then he thought: "This water is poisonous;
if I should drink it, it may cause my death or bring me near the suffering of death. I shall rather endure thirst and eat dry parched grain, and not take water to drink."

"In this way, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas contemplate the forms in the world that are objects of thought as being like a disease, like an ulcer, like a thorn, like a murderer, impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, until they are liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, affliction, and suffering."
Therefore, Ānanda!
Regard this Dharma thus, hear it thus, perceive it thus, and know it thus; for the past and the future, it is likewise through this path.
"Observe in this manner.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
292 (292) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"How does one contemplate and examine so as to rightly bring an end to suffering and reach the ultimate limit of suffering?"

At that time, he reflected upon all the various sufferings of sentient beings and their manifold distinctions, considering: what is the cause of these sufferings? What is their origin? What gives rise to them? What is their condition?
One contemplates the cause of clinging, the origin of clinging, the arising of clinging, and the contact of clinging.

When that clinging ceases without remainder, all suffering ceases; one knows, as it truly is, the path leading to the cessation of suffering upon which one relies, and practices the successive dharmas directed toward it. This is called a bhikṣu who is progressing toward the complete extinction of suffering and reaching the ultimate end of suffering, namely, the cessation of clinging.
"Furthermore, when a bhikkhu reflects and examines how to rightly bring about the end of suffering and reach the ultimate limit of suffering, he then reflects:
'What is the cause of that clinging? What is its origin? What is its birth? What is its condition?'"
He reflects upon that grasping as the cause of craving, the origin of craving, the arising of craving, and the contact of craving.

When that craving is extinguished without remainder, grasping also ceases accordingly. He knows, as it truly is, the path leading to the cessation of that grasping upon which he rides; he cultivates the successive dharmas directed toward that end. This is called a bhikṣu who is proceeding toward the complete extinction of suffering and reaching the ultimate limit of suffering, namely, the extinction of craving.
"Furthermore, when a bhikkhu reflects and examines how to rightly bring about the end of suffering and reach the ultimate limit of suffering, he then reflects:
'What is the cause of that craving? What is its origin? From what does it arise? By what is it conditioned?'"
He understands that craving is the cause of feeling, the origin of feeling, the arising of feeling, and the contact [conditioned by] feeling.

When that feeling is extinguished without remainder, then craving ceases; he understands, as it truly is, the path leading to the cessation of that craving upon which he relies, and he cultivates the successive dharmas directed toward that end. This is called a bhikṣu who is proceeding toward the complete extinction of suffering and reaching the ultimate limit of suffering, namely, the cessation of feeling.
"Furthermore, when a bhikkhu reflects and examines how to rightly bring an end to suffering and reach the ultimate limit of suffering, he then reflects:
'What is the cause of that feeling? What is its origin? From what is it born? By what is it conditioned?'"
He understands that feeling has contact as its cause, contact as its origin, contact as its birth, and contact as its condition.

When that contact is extinguished without remainder, then feeling ceases; he understands, as it truly is, the path leading to the cessation of that contact upon which it depends, and he cultivates the successive states of dharma directed toward that end. This is called a bhikṣu who is heading toward the complete extinction of suffering and reaching the ultimate limit of suffering.
"Furthermore, when a bhikkhu reflects and examines how to rightly bring an end to suffering and reach the ultimate limit of suffering, he then reflects:
'What is the cause of that contact? What is its origin? From what is it born? By what is it conditioned?'"
One should know that contact has the six sense bases as its cause, the six sense bases as its origin, the six sense bases as its arising, and the six sense bases as its condition for contact.

When desire for those six sense bases ceases without remainder, then contact ceases; one knows, as it truly is, the path leading to the cessation of those six sense bases upon which contact depends, and cultivates the successive states directed toward that end. This is called a bhikṣu who is progressing toward the complete destruction of suffering and reaching the ultimate limit of suffering.
"Furthermore, when a bhikkhu reflects and examines how to rightly bring an end to suffering and reach the ultimate limit of suffering, he then reflects:
'What is the cause, what is the origin, what is the birth, and what is the condition for these six sense bases?'"
He understands that those six sense bases have name-and-form as their cause, name-and-form as their origin, name-and-form as their arising, and name-and-form as their condition for contact.

He knows, as it truly is, the path leading to the complete cessation of name-and-form—the cessation of those very six sense bases upon which they depend—and he cultivates the successive states leading toward that. This is called a bhikṣu who is proceeding toward the right exhaustion of suffering and reaching the ultimate end of suffering, namely, the cessation of name-and-form.
"Furthermore, when a bhikkhu reflects upon the complete destruction of suffering and the ultimate end of suffering, he reflects:

'What is the cause of name-and-form? What is its origination? What is its arising? What is its condition? He knows that name-and-form has consciousness as its cause, consciousness as its origination, consciousness as its arising, and consciousness as its condition."

When that consciousness ceases without remainder, then name-and-form cease; he knows, as it truly is, the path leading to the cessation of that consciousness upon which he rides, and he cultivates the successive states leading toward it. This is called a bhikkhu who is heading toward the complete destruction of suffering and the ultimate end of suffering, namely, the cessation of consciousness.
"Furthermore, when a bhikkhu reflects and examines how to rightly exhaust suffering and reach the ultimate end of suffering, he then reflects:
'What is the cause of this consciousness? What is its origination? What gives rise to it? What is its condition?'"

One knows the cause of that consciousness’s activity, its accumulation, its arising, and its contact: when one performs meritorious activities, a wholesome consciousness arises; when one performs non-meritorious and unwholesome activities, an unwholesome consciousness arises;
when one performs activities of nothingness, a consciousness of nothingness arises—this is the cause of that consciousness’s activity, its accumulation, its arising, and its contact.

When that volitional formation is extinguished without remainder, consciousness ceases; he knows, as it truly is, the path leading to the cessation of that formation upon which it depends, and he cultivates the successive states leading toward it. This is called a bhikkhu who is proceeding toward the complete extinction of suffering and reaching the ultimate end of suffering, namely, the cessation of formations.
"Furthermore, when a bhikkhu reflects and examines how suffering is rightly exhausted and how the ultimate end of suffering is reached, he then reflects:
'What is the cause of those formations? What is their origin? What is their arising? What is their condition?'"
He knows that those formations have ignorance as their cause, ignorance as their origin, ignorance as their birth, and ignorance as their contact.

Those meritorious formations have ignorance as their condition; non-meritorious formations also have ignorance as their condition; and formations that are neither meritorious nor non-meritorious also have ignorance as their condition.
"Therefore, you should know this: those volitional formations have ignorance as their cause, ignorance as their origin, ignorance as their birth, and contact with ignorance as their condition.

When that ignorance is extinguished without remainder, then volitional formations cease. One who knows, as it truly is, the path leading to the cessation of that ignorance which they have mounted upon, and cultivates the successive states leading toward it—this is called a bhikṣu who is heading toward the complete extinction of suffering and reaching the ultimate end of suffering, namely, the cessation of ignorance."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"What do you think?
If one does not delight in ignorance but gives rise to clarity, would one still, conditioned by that ignorance, perform meritorious actions, non-meritorious actions, or imperturbable actions?"
The bhikṣu said to the Buddha:
“No, World-Honored One! Why is this so?”

The learned noble disciple does not delight in ignorance but gives rise to clear knowledge; with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; and so on, until birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, despair, and suffering cease. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering comes to cease.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Monks! I too speak in this way, and you also know this:
regarding various phenomena, various phenomena arise; various phenomena are produced; various phenomena cease, come to an end, become cooled, subside, and vanish."
If a learned noble disciple, through the fading away of ignorance, gives rise to clear knowledge, he knows as it truly is when he experiences a feeling limited to the body;
he knows as it truly is when he experiences a feeling limited to the span of his life.
When the body breaks up and life comes to its end, all these feelings that were being experienced cease and pass away without remainder.
It is just as when a strong man takes a newly fired earthen vessel, places it on the ground while it is still hot, and it soon crumbles and breaks apart, its heat completely extinguished.

In the same way, bhikṣu, when one becomes free from desire for ignorance and gives rise to clear knowledge, one knows as it truly is the sensations experienced within the limits of the body; one knows as it truly is the sensations experienced within the limits of the lifespan. When the body breaks up and life ends, all sensations and perceptions are extinguished without remainder.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
293 (293) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed a certain bhikṣu:
"I have already crossed over doubt, departed from hesitation, and pulled out the thorn of false views; I shall no longer regress."
Because the mind is without attachment, where could there be a self for whom I might preach the Dharma?
For those bhikṣus, I preach the Dharma that accords with the noble supramundane emptiness and dependent origination—namely, "because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises."

That is to say: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arise; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises; and with birth as condition, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, despair, and suffering arise.
"In this way, this entire great mass of suffering arises; and in this way, this entire great mass of suffering ceases.

Although he was taught the Dharma in this manner, that bhikṣu still remained in doubt and hesitation; previously not having attained, he conceived the notion that he had attained; not having acquired, he conceived the notion that he had acquired; not having realized, he conceived the notion that he had realized. Now, having heard the Dharma, his mind gave rise to distress, regret, despondency, and obstruction.

Why is this? This profound point, namely dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), is even more profound and difficult to see—namely, the relinquishing of all grasping, the exhaustion of craving, dispassion, cessation, and nirvāṇa.

Regarding these two phenomena—the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*): the conditioned is characterized by arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing; the unconditioned does not arise, does not abide, does not change, and does not cease. This is called the nirvāṇa that is the cessation of suffering for all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), O bhikṣus.

With the arising of causes, suffering arises; with the cessation of causes, suffering ceases. By cutting off all paths and extinguishing the continuity, and by the extinction of that continuity, this is called the end of suffering.
"Monks! What is it that ceases?
It is the remainder of suffering; when that ceases, stops, becomes cooled, subsides, and vanishes—namely, the cessation of all clinging, the exhaustion of craving, dispassion, peace, and Nirvana."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
294 (294) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"The ignorant, unlearned worldling—shrouded by ignorance and bound by the conditions of craving—obtains this body of consciousness."
Within there is this body of consciousness, and without there are name-and-form; through these two conditions, contact arises.
When these six bases of contact are contacted, the ignorant, unlearned worldling experiences feelings of pleasure and pain, which give rise to various [mental proliferations].
What are the six?
They are the sense bases of eye-contact, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact.
If one who is wise is shrouded by ignorance and bound by the condition of craving, they obtain this consciousness-body.

Thus, with an internal body of consciousness and external name-and-form, these two conditions give rise to the six bases of contact. Because they are touched by the six contacts, the wise experience feelings of pleasure and pain, from which various [mental states] arise.
What are the six?
They are the sense-bases of eye-contact, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact.
Between the foolish and the wise, what difference is there among those who practice the holy life under me?
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, you are the root of the Dharma, the eye of the Dharma, and the refuge of the Dharma.
Excellent!”
“World-Honored One!
We only pray that you will expound it; having heard it, the bhikṣus shall receive and practice it accordingly.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you.

Monks, that foolish, unlearned worldling, shrouded by ignorance and bound by the conditions of craving, acquires this body of consciousness. Because he does not sever ignorance and does not exhaust the conditions of craving, when his body breaks up at the end of life, he again receives a new body."
Because they again receive a body, they cannot attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering. Why is this so?

Because these foolish worldlings have not originally cultivated the holy life for the sake of rightly ending suffering and reaching the ultimate limit of suffering, their bodies break up and their lives end, and they receive a body once again;
because they receive a body again, they do not attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, vexation, and suffering.

"If a wise person, though covered by ignorance and bound by the conditions of craving, has obtained this body of consciousness, yet that ignorance is severed and the conditions of craving are exhausted;
because ignorance is severed and the conditions of craving are exhausted, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, they will not receive another existence.
Because they do not receive another existence, they attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, vexation, and suffering."

Why is this so? Because he previously practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*) correctly directed toward the exhaustion of suffering and the ultimate end of suffering; therefore, upon the breakup of the body after death, he does not undergo further existence.

Because he does not undergo further existence, he attains liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, vexation, and suffering. This is called the distinction between the ordinary person and the wise one regarding the various holy lives practiced under me.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
295 (295) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This body does not belong to you, nor does it belong to anyone else.
It is called the six bases of contact; through the original practice of vows, one receives and obtains this body."
What are the six?
They are the sense-sphere of eye-contact, and the sense-spheres of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.
A learned noble disciple correctly contemplates and examines these through dependent origination:
"There are these six groups of consciousness, six groups of contact, six groups of feeling, six groups of perception, and six groups of volition.

Because these exist, there come to be future birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering; in this way and no other, this entire great mass of suffering arises. This is called the arising of the world with cause and condition."

Because this does not exist, the six groups of consciousness do not exist; because these do not exist, the six groups of contact, the six groups of feeling, the six groups of perception, and the six groups of volition do not exist. Because these do not exist, there is no future birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, or suffering; and in this way, this entire great mass of suffering ceases.

"If a learned noble disciple possesses right knowledge as it truly is regarding the arising of the world and the cessation of the world, and has seen it well, awakened to it well, and entered into it well—this is called a noble disciple who summons these wholesome qualities, attains these wholesome qualities, knows these wholesome qualities, and enters into these wholesome qualities; one who perceives and sees the arising and passing away of the world, and who accomplishes the noble transcendence, true peace, the complete extinction of suffering, and the ultimate end of suffering."
"Why is this? It is because the learned noble disciple knows, as they truly are, the arising and cessation of the world; he has seen it well, awakened to it well, and entered into it well.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
296 (Two hundred and ninety-six). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now explain the law of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and dependently arisen phenomena (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*). What is the law of dependent origination?

It is: 'When this exists, that exists. That is to say: conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*), there are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); conditioned by volitional formations, there is consciousness (*vijñāna*); and so on, until: 'In such a way, this entire great mass of suffering arises.'"
"What are dependently arisen phenomena?
They are ignorance and volitional formations.

Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, this dharma remains constant; it is the stability of the dharma and the realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*). That Self-Arisen One, having realized it for himself, attained equal and perfect enlightenment, and taught, revealed, disclosed, and clarified it for others: namely, conditioned by ignorance there are volitional formations, and so on, up to conditioned by birth there are old age and death."

Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, this Dharma remains constant; it abides in the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu). That Tathāgata, having awakened to it through his own realization and attained equal and perfect enlightenment, proclaims, reveals, elucidates, and makes manifest for others that because of dependent origination, there are old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering.

These dharmas abide as such, are empty as such, are suchness as such, and are so by nature; they do not depart from suchness, nor do they differ from suchness; they are profound, true, and non-erroneous.
Thus, that which accords with dependent origination is called "dependently arisen phenomena.

That is to say: ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering—these are called dependently arisen phenomena.
“The well-taught noble disciple, possessing right knowledge and clear vision regarding this dependent origination and dependently arisen phenomena, does not seek after the past, saying:
‘Did I exist in the past, or did I not exist?’”
"What was my nature in past lives?
How was I in past lives?"—
one does not seek after the future limit:
"Will I exist in future lives, or will I not?
Of what kind will I be?
What will I be like?"
Internally, he was not hesitant: "What is this?
How can this exist as a precursor?"
Who will ultimately go where?
From where do these sentient beings come?
Having passed away here, where will they go?

If śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas give rise to views bound by the mundane—namely, views bound by the notion of a self, views bound by the notion of a sentient being, views bound by the notion of a life-span, or views bound by superstitious taboos regarding auspiciousness—at that time, he completely severs and fully understands them; he cuts off their root, like the head of a tāla tree, so that in future lives they become dharmas that do not arise.

This is called the learned noble disciple’s correct knowledge of the dharma of causes and conditions and the dharma of dependent origination as it truly is—seeing it well, awakening to it well, cultivating it well, and entering into it well.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
297 (Two hundred and ninety-seven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the village of Go-yoke in the Kuru country.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“I shall preach the Dharma for you—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing; purely singular, pure, and the stainless holy life—which is called the Mahāśūnyatā Sūtra.”
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall explain it to you.
What is the Mahāsuññata Sutta? It is this:

"Because this exists, that exists; with the arising of this, that arises. That is to say: conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations; conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness, and so on, until the entire mass of suffering arises.
Regarding "old age and death conditioned by birth," if someone were to ask:
"Who is it that ages and dies?
To whom does old age and death belong?"
He then replied:
"I am indeed old age and death; now old age and death belong to me; old age and death are my self.
As it is said:
"Life is identical to the body," or else they say:
"Life is one thing and the body is another."
"This is a single meaning, yet it is explained in various ways.
For instance, one might say:
'The life-principle is identical to the body.'"
"Such [views] do not exist among those who lead the holy life.
Furthermore, if one sees and says:
'The life-principle is different from the body.'"
"Such things do not exist for those who practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Regarding these two extremes, the mind does not follow them, but proceeds directly toward the Middle Way.
This is the noble, supramundane, reality-conforming, non-perverted right view, which is to say: conditioned by birth, there is old age and death."

In this way, birth, becoming, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, and volitional formations exist; volitional formations exist conditioned by ignorance.
"If it should further be asked:
'Who is the one who acts?
To whom do these formations belong? "
He then replied:
"Volition is my self; volition is mine.
He spoke thus:
"Life is identical to the body," or some say:
"Life is different from the body."
For those who view the life-principle as identical to the body, the holy life does not exist;
nor does the holy life exist for those who say that the life-principle is one thing and the body another.
Free from these two extremes, one correctly proceeds toward the Middle Way.

This is what is known by the noble ones who have transcended the world through right view—free from inversion and in accordance with reality—which is to say: conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise.
“Monks! If, through the fading away of ignorance, clear knowledge arises, who is it that ages and dies?
To whom does aging and death belong?”
When old age and death are severed, one knows that their root has been cut; like the head of a *tāla* tree being cut off, they become subject to the law of non-arising in future lives.
If a bhikṣu, through detachment from ignorance, gives rise to clear knowledge (*vidyā*), who is it that is born?
To whom does birth belong?
And so on, up to: who is the one for whom there is volitional formation (*saṃskāra*), and to whom does volitional formation belong?

When formations are ceased, one knows that their root has been severed; like cutting off the head of a *tāla* tree, they become subject to the law of non-arising in future lives. If a bhikṣu, through detachment from ignorance, gives rise to clear knowledge, then with the cessation of that ignorance, formations cease, and so on until the entire great mass of suffering ceases. This is called the Mahāsuññatā Sutta.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 298 (298) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the village of Go-yoke near Kuru.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now speak on the Dharma of dependent origination—both its literal exposition and its exposition of its meaning.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you."
"What is the Dharma-exposition on dependent origination?

It is: 'When this exists, that exists; with the arising of this, that arises. That is to say: conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations, and so forth, until the entire great mass of suffering arises. This is called the Dharma-exposition on dependent origination."
"What is the meaning of this teaching?
It refers to the formations conditioned by ignorance.
What, then, is ignorance?"

If one does not know the past, does not know the future, and does not know both the past and the future; if one does not know the internal, does not know the external, and does not know both the internal and external; if one does not know karma, does not know its retribution, and does not know both karma and its retribution; if one does not know the Buddha, does not know the Dharma, and does not know the Saṅgha; if one does not know suffering, does not know its origin, does not know its cessation, and does not know the path; if one does not know causes, does not know the phenomena arising from causes, and does not know what is wholesome or unwholesome, blameworthy or blameless, to be cultivated or not to be cultivated, inferior or superior, defiled or pure—then one knows nothing at all regarding the analysis of dependent origination.

Regarding the six bases of contact, not knowing things as they truly are—being ignorant, not seeing, lacking clear comprehension, being shrouded in delusion and darkness, and possessing ignorance regarding this or that—is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
"With ignorance as condition, there are volitional formations:
what are volitional formations? There are three kinds of volitional formations—bodily formations, verbal formations, and mental formations.
With volitional formations as condition, there is consciousness: what is consciousness?"

That is to say, the six groups of consciousness: the group of eye-consciousness, the group of ear-consciousness, the group of nose-consciousness, the group of tongue-consciousness, the group of body-consciousness, and the group of mind-consciousness.
Regarding "conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form [arises]": what is "name"?
It refers to the four formless aggregates—the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
What is "form"?
That is to say, the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements—this is called "form.
This form, together with the "name" previously described, constitutes "name-and-form.
Regarding the statement that the six sense bases are conditioned by name-and-form: what are the six sense bases?
That is to say, the six internal sense bases: the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, and the mind base.
Regarding "contact conditioned by the six sense bases," what is contact?
It refers to the six classes of contact: visual contact, auditory contact, olfactory contact, gustatory contact, tactile contact, and mental contact.
Regarding "conditioned by contact is feeling," what is feeling?
It refers to the three types of feeling: painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Regarding "conditioned by feeling is craving," what is that craving?
This refers to the three types of craving: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for form, and craving for the formless.
Regarding "clinging conditioned by craving," what constitutes clinging?
There are four types of clinging: clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to precepts and observances, and clinging to a self-theory.
Regarding "conditioned by grasping, there is becoming": what is becoming?
It is the threefold becoming—sensual becoming, form becoming, and formless becoming.
Regarding "conditioned by becoming, there is birth": what is birth?

When various sentient beings, through various types of bodies, undergo a single birth, emerging from the conjunction [of conditions], and obtain the aggregates (skandhas), the elements (dhātus), the sense bases (āyatanas), and the life-faculty (jīvitendriya)—this is called birth.
Regarding "conditioned by birth, there is aging and death," what is meant by aging? It refers to the state where the hair has turned white and the crown is bald;

the skin becomes slack and the faculties mature; the limbs grow weak and the back becomes hunched; the head droops and one groans; breath is short and one leans forward; one walks supported by a staff; the body turns dark and sallow, and the four limbs become mottled; one is dull-witted and near the end of life; and one’s movements are difficult, frail, and debilitated. This is called aging.
What is death?

When various sentient beings, belonging to various classes, pass away, transmigrate, undergo the breaking up of the body, the exhaustion of the life-span, the separation from heat, the cessation of vitality, and the time for the casting off of the aggregates arrives—this is called death.
"This death, together with the aging previously described, is called 'aging and death.
This is the explanation of the meaning of dependent origination.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
299 (Two hundred and ninety-nine). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the village of Go-yoke in Kuru.
Then, a certain bhikṣu approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is this Dharma of dependent origination created by the World-Honored One, or was it created by others?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"This Dharma of dependent origination was not made by me, nor was it made by anyone else.

Rather, whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) remains eternally present. That Tathāgata, having personally awakened to this Dharma, attained equal and perfect enlightenment, and for the sake of all sentient beings, analyzed, expounded, revealed, and manifested it."

That is to say: because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises. That is, conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations, and so on, until the entire great mass of suffering arises. Because ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease, and so on, until the entire great mass of suffering ceases.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣu, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
300 (Three Hundred): Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the village of Go-yokan (Cow-herd) in Kuru.

At that time, a certain brahmin approached the place where the World-Honored One was, exchanged greetings with the World-Honored One, and after the greetings were concluded, withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying: "How is it?"
"Gautama!
Is it that one creates oneself and awakens oneself?
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"I declare this to be indeterminate; that one acts for oneself and experiences for oneself—this is indeterminate.
"In what way, Gautama?"
"Is it that another acts and another experiences the result?
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"That another acts and another experiences the result—this is indeterminate."
The brahmin said to the Buddha:
"How is it that when I ask about what one does oneself and what one realizes oneself, you declare it to be undeclared?"
"If one says that another acts and another perceives, yet declares this to be indeterminate (avyākṛta), what is the meaning of this?
The Buddha told the brahmin:

"If one holds that one acts and one perceives, one falls into the view of eternalism (śāśvatadṛṣṭi); if one holds that another acts and another perceives, one falls into the view of annihilationism (ucchedadṛṣṭi)."

He teaches according to the meaning and teaches according to the Dharma; departing from these two extremes, he dwells in the Middle Way and teaches the Dharma: namely, "Because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises. Conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations, and so on, until the entire great mass of suffering arises. With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease, and so on, until the entire great mass of suffering ceases.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, that brahmin rejoiced and approved, rose from his seat, and departed.
301 (301) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Nāli village, in the guest-house within the deep forest.
At that time, the Venerable Revata Kaccāyana approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Blessed One has spoken of right view:
what is right view?
How does the Blessed One designate right view?
The Buddha told Revata Kātyāyana:
“In the world there are two kinds of reliance: either existence or non-existence, both of which are touched by grasping;
because they are touched by grasping, one relies either on existence or on non-existence.”

If there were no such grasping, the mind and its objects would not be bound by attachment; one would not grasp, would not dwell, and would not conceive of a self. Thus, suffering arises and ceases as it occurs. One would have no doubt or confusion regarding this, knowing it for oneself without depending on another. This is called right view; this is called the right view established by the Tathāgata.

Why is this? To know and see the arising of the world as it truly is: that which does not exist in the world is not present; and to know and see the cessation of the world as it truly is: that which exists in the world ceases to be. This is called speaking of the Middle Way, free from the two extremes: namely, "because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises"—that is, conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations, and so on, until the entire great mass of suffering arises. "Because ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease," and so on, until the entire great mass of suffering ceases.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Revata Kaṇṭhaka, having heard what the Buddha taught, was liberated from all outflows; his mind attained liberation, and he became an Arhat.
302. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak near the city of Rājagṛha.
Then, in the early morning, the World-Honored One dressed himself, took his bowl, and descended from Vulture Peak to enter the city of Rājagṛha for alms.
At that time, Ajita Kesakambalin, having gone out from Rājagṛha on some minor business, was heading toward Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain when he saw the World-Honored One from afar.
Having seen him, he approached the Buddha and addressed him, saying: “Gautama!
"I wish to ask a question; would you have the leisure to grant me an answer?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "Now is not the time for discussion. I am now entering the city to beg for food; when I have returned, that will be the time. I shall explain it for you then."
The second time he spoke likewise, and the third time he asked again:
“Gautama, why do you create obstacles for me?”
"Gautama! In what way is there a difference?
I now wish to ask a question; please explain it for me."
The Buddha said to Ajita Kesakambalin,
“Ask whatever you wish.
Ajita Kesakambalin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it, Gautama? Is suffering created by oneself?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"That suffering is self-created—this is indeterminate.
Kāśyapa asked again:
"How is it, Gautama? Is suffering created by another?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"If suffering is created by another, this too is indeterminate.
Kāśyapa asked again:
“Is suffering created by oneself or by another?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“That suffering is created by oneself or by another is also undeclared.”
Kāśyapa asked again:
"How is this so, Gautama?"
"Is suffering neither self-made nor made by another, but produced without cause?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"That suffering is neither self-made nor made by another—this too is undeclared."
Kāśyapa asked again:
"What is meant by 'acting without a cause,' Gautama?"
"Is it asked whether suffering is self-created?
He replied: "It is undeclared."
“Is it created by another?
Is it created by both self and another?
Or is it created neither by self nor by another, being produced without cause?”
He replied, “It is indeterminate.
[The other asked,] “Is there no such suffering now?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"It is not that there is no such suffering; rather, there is this suffering.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, Gautama!
You have declared that this suffering exists; please teach me the Dharma so that I may know suffering and see suffering."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"If that which experiences were the very same as that which undergoes the experience, I would say that suffering is self-made. If that which experiences were different from that which undergoes the experience, then it would be made by another. If the one who experiences were both the self-experiencer and the other-experiencer, and yet again gave rise to suffering..."
I do not say that suffering is created by both self and other; nor do I say that suffering arises without cause, being produced neither from self nor from other.

Departing from these extremes, he taught the Middle Way: "When this exists, that exists; with the arising of this, that arises. That is to say, conditioned by ignorance, there are volitional formations, and so on, until the entire great mass of suffering arises. With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease, and so on, until the entire great mass of suffering ceases.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Acela Kāśyapa was distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.

At that time, Acela Kāśyapa saw the Dharma, attained the Dharma, knew the Dharma, and entered the Dharma; he crossed beyond all doubt, no longer relying on others for knowledge nor depending on others for deliverance. His mind attained fearlessness regarding the True Dharma and Discipline, and with palms joined, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

I have now crossed over; from this day forward, I take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha. For as long as life lasts, I shall be an upāsaka; may you bear witness to me.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, Ajita Kesakambalin rejoiced and approved, paid homage, and departed.

Not long after Ajita Kesakambalin had left the World-Honored One, he was gored to death by a cow protecting her calf; at the moment of his death, his faculties were pure and his complexion was bright and clear.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the city to beg for food.
At that moment, a great number of bhikṣus also entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food, and they heard this report:

"Ajita Keśakambalin, having heard the Dharma from the World-Honored One, departed not long ago; he was gored to death by an ox. At the moment of his death, his faculties were pure and his complexion was bright and clear."

When the bhikṣus had finished their almsround, they returned, put away their robes and bowls, washed their feet, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

"This morning, as many bhikṣus and I entered the city for alms, we heard that Aciravata Kāśyapa, having heard the Dharma and Vinaya from the World-Honored One, had departed not long ago when he was gored to death by a cow protecting its calf; at the moment of his death, his faculties were pure and his complexion was bright and clear."
"Bhagavān!
To which realm of existence was he born?
In what place did he take birth?"
"What has he attained?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"He has seen the Dharma, known the Dharma, followed the Dharma, and has not clung to the Dharma; he has already entered parinirvāṇa. You should go and make offerings to his body."
At that time, the World-Honored One bestowed the first prediction upon Acela Kāśyapa.
303 (Three Hundred and Three). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl, entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms. On the road, he saw the renunciant outsider Tiṣya, who was traveling toward Vulture Peak with some minor business. Seeing the World-Honored One from afar, Tiṣya went to where he was, and after exchanging greetings and mutual expressions of courtesy, he stood to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying: “Gautama!
"I wish to ask something; would you have the leisure to explain it for me?
The Buddha told the renunciant outsider Dāmali:
"Now is not the time for discussion; we must enter the city to beg for food. When we have returned, I shall explain it for you."
The second time he spoke was also like this.
A third time he requested:
“Śramaṇa Gautama!
"Will you not create obstacles for me?
I wish to ask something; please explain it to me.
The Buddha addressed the renunciant of the Tīrthika sect, Dhanika:
"Ask whatever you wish, and I shall explain it for you.
The renunciant heretic Dāmali then asked:
"Śramaṇa Gautama!..."
“Are suffering and pleasure created by oneself?
The Buddha told the renunciant outsider Tiṣya:
“To say that suffering and pleasure are created by oneself is an indeterminate matter.”
He asked again:
"Śramaṇa Gautama!
Are suffering and pleasure created by another?"
The Buddha told the renunciant outsider Tiṣya:
"To say that suffering and pleasure are created by another is an indeterminate matter.
He asked again:
"Gautama! Are suffering and pleasure created by oneself or by another?
The Buddha addressed the renunciant outsider Tiṣya:
"To say that suffering and pleasure are created by oneself, by another, or by both—this is indeterminate.
He asked again: "Gautama!"
“Are suffering and pleasure neither self-made nor made by another, but produced without cause?
The Buddha told the renunciant heretic Dantamūla:

“To say that suffering and pleasure are neither self-made nor made by another, but produced without cause—this is an undeclared matter (*avyākṛta*)…” [The discourse continues] as extensively explained in the *Acelakāśyapa Sūtra*, until the World-Honored One granted the first formal prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) to the renunciant heretic Dantamūla.
Saṃyukta Āgama, Scroll 12; Saṃyukta Āgama, Scroll 13.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
1.304 (304) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the village of Go-yokan in the Kuru country.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"I shall now preach the Dharma for you—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing; purely unified, complete, and pure; the holy life that is stainless."
Listen attentively and reflect well; there are six sets of six dharmas.
What are these six sets of six dharmas?
They are the six internal sense bases, the six external sense bases, the six groups of consciousness, the six groups of contact, the six groups of feeling, and the six groups of craving.
"What are the six internal sense bases?
They are the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, and the mind base."

What are the six external sense bases? They are the sense base of forms, the sense base of sounds, the sense base of odors, the sense base of tastes, the sense base of tangibles, and the sense base of mental phenomena.
What are the six groups of consciousness?

They are the group of eye-consciousness, the group of ear-consciousness, the group of nose-consciousness, the group of tongue-consciousness, the group of body-consciousness, and the group of mind-consciousness.
What are the six classes of contact?
They are eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact.
What are the six classes of feeling?
That is to say: feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact, feeling born of body-contact, and feeling born of mind-contact.
What are the six groups of craving?
They are: craving born of eye-contact, craving born of ear-contact, craving born of nose-contact, craving born of tongue-contact, craving born of body-contact, and craving born of mind-contact.
"If anyone should say that the eye is the self, this is not so. Why is this?
Because the eye arises and perishes;
if the eye were the self, the self would undergo birth and death. Therefore, to say that the eye is the self is not so."
In this way, if form, or eye-consciousness, or eye-contact, or the feeling born of eye-contact were the self, that would not be so. Why is that?

The feeling born of eye-contact is a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing. If the feeling born of eye-contact were the self, then the self would further undergo birth and death. Therefore, it is said that if one holds the feeling born of eye-contact to be the self, that is not so; thus, the feeling born of eye-contact is not the self.
In this same way, the feelings born of contact with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are not self.

Why is this? Feelings born of contact with the mind are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing; if they were the self, the self would further undergo birth and death. Therefore, that feelings born of contact with the mind are the self is not so; thus, feelings born of contact with the mind are not self.
“In this way, bhikṣus!
You should know, as it truly is, what is done by the eye, what is done by wisdom, and what is done by tranquility; thus you shall develop supernormal powers and proceed directly toward Nirvāṇa.”
How does one know and see, as it truly is, the function of the eye, up to its leading directly toward Nirvāṇa?
It is thus, bhikṣus!

The eye is not self; likewise, forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feeling born of eye-contact as a condition—whether it be experienced internally as painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one should also contemplate these as not self.

The same is said for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. This is called knowing and seeing the function of the eye as it truly is, up to and including being rightly directed toward Nirvana; this is known as the Sutra on the Six Sets of Six.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
305 (Three Hundred and Five) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the village of Go-yoke in the Kuru country.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

“I shall now teach you the Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing; purely unified, complete, and pure—a holy life that is stainless. It is called the Sūtra on the Sixfold Analysis of the Six Bases.”
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall explain it for you.
What is the Discourse on the Sixfold Analysis of the Six Bases?

It refers to one who does not know and see as they truly are the eye-base, nor knows and sees as they truly are forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feeling born of eye-contact as a condition—whether that internal sensation is painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.

Because they do not know and see things as they truly are, they become stained by attachment to the eye; likewise, they become stained by attachment to forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feeling—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by eye-contact, all of which are internal sensations.

In the same way, regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind: if one does not know and see as they truly are the mental phenomena, the mental consciousness, the mental contact, and the feeling born of the condition of mental contact—whether it be internal feeling that is painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—then because of not knowing and seeing them as they truly are, defiled attachment arises.

Thus, through association with defilement and attachment, through delusion and darkness, through longing and fettering of the mind, one nourishes the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*). Furthermore, future existence, clinging, greed, and delight all increase; body and mind become weary and corrupt, body and mind are broken and consumed by fire, body and mind are ablaze, body and mind are deranged, and painful sensations arise in the body.

Because painful sensations arise in that body, birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering all increase in future lives. This is called the accumulation of this entire mass of pure suffering.

“Monks! If one knows and sees the eye as it truly is; if one knows and sees as they truly are the forms, the eye-consciousness, the eye-contact, and the feeling—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by eye-contact, which is experienced internally;

and having seen this, one is not stained by attachment to the eye, nor is one stained by attachment to the forms, the eye-consciousness, the eye-contact, and the feeling—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by eye-contact and is experienced internally.”

In this way, one knows and sees the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as they truly are. Regarding mental phenomena, consciousness, mind-contact, and the feeling born of the condition of mind-contact—whether it be internally felt as painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one knows and sees them as they truly are.
Because one knows and sees them as they truly are, one is not stained by or attached to the mind.

If one is not defiled by any phenomenon, by mental consciousness, by mind-contact, or by the feeling born of mind-contact as a condition—whether that internal sensation be painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—and because of this lack of defilement, one is not entangled, not deluded, does not dwell on it with longing, and is not bound;

then the five aggregates of clinging are diminished, and craving for future existence, greed, delight, and all forms of attachment to various things are completely extinguished. Thus the body is not exhausted by suffering and the mind is not exhausted by suffering; the body is not scorched and the mind is not scorched; the body is not inflamed and the mind is not inflamed; the body experiences happiness and the mind experiences happiness.

Because one experiences pleasure with body and mind, birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering will all be extinguished in future lives; thus, this entire mass of suffering, this aggregate of suffering, is brought to cessation.

"One who knows thus and sees thus is said to have fulfilled the cultivation of right view; likewise for right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. As previously stated, one has fulfilled the pure cultivation of right speech, right action, and right livelihood. This is called the fulfillment of the pure cultivation of the Noble Eightfold Path."

Having brought the cultivation of the Eightfold Noble Path to fulfillment, one brings the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness to fulfillment, as well as the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, and the seven factors of enlightenment to fulfillment.
"Regarding those phenomena that should be known and fully understood, he has known them all and fully understood them.
Regarding those phenomena that should be known and abandoned, he has known them all and abandoned them."
Whatever dharmas should be known and realized, all have been realized;
whatever dharmas should be known and cultivated, all have been cultivated.
What dharmas should be known and fully understood?
They are name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
What dharmas should be known and abandoned?
What are called ignorance and craving for existence—what dharmas should be known and realized?
They are namely: clear knowledge and liberation.
What dharmas should be known and cultivated?
They are namely *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).
If a bhikṣu should know and comprehend these dharmas, he knows them all and comprehends them all.
If there are phenomena that should be known and abandoned, he knows them all and abandons them all.
If there are phenomena that should be known and realized, he knows them all and realizes them all.

If there are dharmas that should be known and should be cultivated, he knows them all and cultivates them all; this is called a bhikṣu who has severed the fetters of craving, attained right and immediate realization, and reached the ultimate end of suffering.
“Monks! This is called the Discourse on the Sixfold Analysis of the Six Bases.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the monks, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
306 (Three Hundred and Six) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu, dwelling alone in a quiet place, applied himself with diligence to reflection and had this thought:
“How does a bhikkhu know and how does he see so as to attain the vision of the Dhamma?
Having reflected thus, he rose from meditation, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
While dwelling alone in seclusion, I applied myself with focused reflection and had this thought:
"How does a bhikkhu know, how does he see, so as to realize the Dharma?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you.
There are two dharmas."
"What are the two? The eye and forms are two... Thus it is explained in detail, up to:
"...because they are not its domain. Why is that?"

With the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three factors is contact. Along with contact arise feeling, perception, and volition. These four formless aggregates, together with the eye and forms—these phenomena are called a "person. Regarding these very phenomena, one forms the conceptualization of a person, a sentient being (*sattva*), a man (*nara*), a human (*manuja*), a youth (*māṇava*), a spirit (*puruṣa*), a soul (*pudgala*), a life-principle (*jīva*), or a creature (*jantu*).
Furthermore, it is said thus:
"I see forms with my eye; I hear sounds with my ear; I smell odors with my nose; I taste flavors with my tongue; I feel tangibles with my body; I cognize mental phenomena with my mind."
That person who makes such designations further speaks thus:
"This venerable one has such a name, such a birth, such a clan, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, such longevity, such a duration of stay, and such a limit to his lifespan."
"Monks! These are perceptions, these are mental signs, these are verbal expressions; all these phenomena are impermanent, conditioned, and produced through volitional formations and conditions.
Whatever is impermanent, conditioned, and produced through volitional formations and conditions—that is suffering."
Furthermore, that suffering arises as suffering, abides as suffering, and ceases as suffering; it arises repeatedly as nothing but suffering.

If, moreover, that suffering is abandoned without remainder, vomited out, exhausted, detached from desire, ceased, stilled, and vanished, such that no further suffering continues or arises—this is tranquility, this is sublime excellence.
That which is called the relinquishing of all existence, the exhaustion of all craving, dispassion, cessation, and *nirvāṇa*.

When the ear, nose, tongue, and body are conditioned by contact, body-consciousness arises; the conjunction of these three factors is contact; and with contact as its condition, feeling, perception, and volition arise. These four are the formless aggregates (*arūpaskandha*), while the body-faculty is the form aggregate (*rūpaskandha*). This is what is called a "person"... [as stated above], up to "...cessation, *nirvāṇa*."

“Conditioned by the mind, mental phenomena arise as mental consciousness; the conjunction of these three factors is contact (*sparśa*). Born together with contact are feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*). These four formless aggregates (*skandha*) and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are the basis for the person (*pudgala*); these phenomena are called ‘the person. As explained at length above, up until: “...cessation, nirvāṇa.”
If, regarding these phenomena, one’s mind enters into them and abides in liberation without falling back, there is no "I" in that which gives rise to attachment therein. Monks!
"To know thus and to see thus is to see the Dharma.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
307 (Three Hundred and Seven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu, dwelling alone in a quiet place, applied himself with focused diligence and reflection, and this thought arose in him:
"How does one know, how does one see, so as to be said to 'see the Dharma'?
Having reflected thus, he rose from his meditation, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"Alone in a quiet place, I applied myself with focused reflection and had this thought:
'How does a bhikkhu know and how does he see so that he is said to have "seen the Dharma"?'"
"I now ask the World-Honored One; I only pray that you will explain this.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for your sake."
“There are two factors: the eye and forms; conditioned by these, eye-consciousness arises... as explained at length above.
“Venerable Sir!
As it is said in the verse:”
With the two conditions of eye and form, there arise the mind and mental factors—consciousness, contact, and those co-arising with them, such as feeling and perception. These have causes;
they are neither "I" nor "mine," nor are they a *pudgala*.
Nor is it a mānuṣa, nor is it a mānava;
this is but arising and ceasing, the dharma of the transformation of the aggregates of suffering.
Forming conceptions regarding these, one designates them as "sentient beings."
Naramaṇuṣya and likewise mānava,
as well as many other perceptions— all arise from the aggregates of suffering.
Through karma, craving, and ignorance, one accumulates the aggregates of future lives.
Other recluses of different paths, who propound dualistic doctrines, possess nothing but mere words;
having heard them, one's delusion and confusion increase.
When craving has ceased without remainder, ignorance is submerged and forever extinguished.
"When craving is exhausted, all suffering ceases; thus has the unsurpassed Buddha-eye taught.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
308 (Three Hundred and Eight). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Devas and worldlings dwell attached to, enamored of, and delighting in forms; when those forms are impermanent, subject to change, and perish, those devas and humans experience great suffering.

They dwell attached to, enamored of, and delighting in sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena; when those phenomena are subject to change, impermanent, and perish, those devas and humans dwell in great suffering.”

“The Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the form, the origin of form, the cessation of form, the gratification of form, the danger in form, and the escape from form. Having known them as they truly are, he no longer dwells with attachment, craving, or delight in form; when that form changes, becomes impermanent, and ceases, he experiences a dwelling in happiness.

He knows, as they truly are, the sound, odor, taste, tactile object, and mental phenomena—their origin, cessation, gratification, danger, and escape. Having known them as they truly are, he no longer dwells with attachment, craving, or delight in them; when those phenomena change, become impermanent, and cease, he experiences a dwelling in happiness.”

Why is this so? Eye and visible forms condition the arising of eye-consciousness; the conjunction of these three factors is contact. Contact conditions feeling—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant. When one knows as it truly is the arising of these three feelings, the cessation of these feelings, the danger in these feelings, and the escape from these feelings, then regarding those visible forms that arise through causes and conditions as obstacles, once those obstacles are exhausted, it is called unsurpassed peace and security: Nirvana.

When the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind take mental phenomena as conditions, consciousness arises; the conjunction of these three factors is contact. With contact as condition, there is feeling—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant. One knows, as it truly is, the arising of that feeling, its cessation, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it.
