Having known this as it truly is, those phenomena arise through causes and conditions; when those obstructions are exhausted, it is called unsurpassed peace and security, Nirvana.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Regarding the six objects of the senses— form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena—
one gives rise to constant joy and delight, becoming deeply attached through craving and defilement."
The gods and the people of the world find joy only in this;
when it changes and perishes, they experience great suffering.
Only the noble sages perceive its cessation as true happiness.
That which the world delights in, when examined, is seen entirely as an enemy.
What the noble ones perceive as suffering, the world regards as pleasure;
what the world regards as suffering, to the noble ones it is pleasure.
The Dharma is profoundly deep and difficult to understand; the world gives rise to doubt and confusion.
Enshrouded by great darkness, they are blinded and see nothing.
Only those possessed of wisdom can dispel the gloom and open up the great radiance.
"Such profound words—who other than the Noble Ones could know them?
Only those who no longer undergo rebirth have deeply penetrated the Truths with clarity.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
309 (Three Hundred and Nine) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the side of the Gaggarā Pond in the kingdom of Campā.
At that time, the Venerable Migajāla approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the World-Honored One has said, there is a second dwelling and there are individual dwellings.
What is that second dwelling?”
"How does each one abide?
The Buddha told Mṛgaśiras:
"Excellent!"
Excellent, Mṛgadhara!
You are able to ask the Tathāgata about such a matter.
The Buddha told Mṛgalaiputra:
"If a bhikṣu sees with his eye a form that is lovely, pleasant, delightful, agreeable, and nourishes desire;

having seen it, he dwells in delighting in it, praising it, and being bound by attachment to it. Having dwelt in delighting in, praising, and being bound by attachment to it, his mind becomes further gladdened. Being gladdened, he experiences deep pleasure. Experiencing deep pleasure, he develops craving. Having developed craving, he becomes obstructed."
That which is characterized by joy, deep delight, craving, and obstruction is called the second dwelling.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Mṛga-nanda!
Even if a bhikṣu of such a kind dwells alone in a secluded place, he is still said to be one who abides in the second stage. Why is this?
Because craving and delight are neither severed nor extinguished, and because sensual desire is not severed and remains unrecognized, the Buddhas and Tathāgatas describe this as the second dwelling.
"If there is a bhikṣu who, regarding what is lovely, pleasant, cherished, and agreeable, nourishes desire for form;

yet that bhikṣu, having seen it, does not take delight in it, does not praise it, and does not dwell in attachment to it—having not taken delight in it, not praised it, and not dwelt in attachment to it—he does not rejoice. Because he does not rejoice, he does not deeply delight in it; because he does not deeply delight in it, he does not crave it; because he does not crave it, he is not obstructed."
That which is not joyful, deeply delighted, craved after, or obstructed is called "dwelling one by one.
The same is said for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Mṛga-nābhi!
Monks of such a kind, even if they dwell in high towers or multi-storied pavilions, are still those who abide in solitude. Why is this?

"Because craving has been exhausted and fully understood, those for whom craving has been exhausted and fully understood are called by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, 'those who abide in each [of the fruits].
" At that time, the Venerable Mṛgalaṇḍika, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and approved with gladness; he paid homage and departed.
310. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Campā on the banks of the Gaggarā Pond.
Then, the Venerable Migajāla approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!

Please teach me the Dharma. Having heard the Dharma, I shall dwell alone in a quiet place, applying myself with diligent reflection and abiding without negligence, until I know for myself that there will be no further existence.”
The Buddha said to Mṛgaśiras:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Mṛgadhvaja!
You are able to ask the Tathāgata about such a matter.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall explain it for you.
The Buddha told Mṛgalaṇḍika:
"If one sees with the eye forms that are lovely, pleasant, agreeable, and delightful—forms that nourish desire—and having seen them, one praises, becomes attached to, and rejoices in them;
having praised and become attached, then joy accumulates; and when joy has accumulated, suffering accumulates."
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. Lakuṇḍaka!
If there is a bhikṣu who, with the eye, sees forms that are lovely, pleasant, delightful, agreeable, and which nourish desire;

Having seen it, one does not rejoice, does not praise, and does not become attached. Because one does not rejoice, does not praise, and does not become attached, there is no accumulation of delight; because there is no accumulation of delight, suffering ceases.
"The same should be said for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind with respect to mental objects.
At that time, the Venerable Mṛgalaṇḍaka, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and approved, paid homage, and departed.

At that time, having heard the Buddha’s teaching and instruction, the Venerable Mṛgalaṇḍaka dwelt alone in a quiet place, reflecting with focused diligence and living without negligence, until he attained arhatship and his mind was well-liberated.
311 (311). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇa approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!

Teach me the Dharma so that, dwelling alone in a quiet place, I may apply myself with diligence and reflection, abiding without negligence, until I know for myself that there will be no further existence.”
The Buddha said to Pūrṇa:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"You have been able to ask the Tathāgata about such a matter.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall explain it for you.
Suppose there is a bhikṣu!"
One sees with the eye forms that are lovely, delightful, memorable, and agreeable, which nourish desire;

having seen them, one rejoices, praises, and becomes attached to them; having rejoiced, praised, and become attached, one experiences gladness; having experienced gladness, one becomes infatuated; having become infatuated, one feels craving; and having felt craving, one is obstructed.
Because of delighting in, attachment to, craving for, and being obstructed by [these things], one is far removed from nirvāṇa.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

“Pūrṇa! If a bhikṣu sees with the eye forms that are lovely, pleasant, memorable, and agreeable—forms that nourish desire—and having seen them, does not rejoice, does not praise, and does not become attached;

because he does not rejoice, praise, or become attached, he does not experience delight; because he does not experience delight, he does not feel deep pleasure; because he does not feel deep pleasure, he does not give rise to craving; and because he does not give rise to craving, he is not obstructed.
Because one does not feel delight, does not deeply rejoice, does not crave, and is not obstructed, one gradually approaches Nirvāṇa.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
The Buddha told Pūrṇa:
"I have already briefly explained the teachings of the Dharma; where do you wish to abide?
Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Having received from the World-Honored One this brief instruction, I wish to travel among the people of Śūrasena in the western region.
The Buddha said to Pūrṇa:
“The people of Aparāntaka in the west are fierce, flighty, cruel, and fond of reviling. Pūrṇa!
If you hear that they are fierce, flighty, cruel, fond of reviling, and prone to insulting others, what will you do?”
Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If there are people from the land of Śūrasena in the western direction who, right before one's face, are fierce, abusive, and insulting."
I had this thought:

"Those people of Śroṇāparāntaka in the west are virtuous and wise; although they were fierce, cruel, abusive, and insulting toward me in my presence, they did not even strike or pelt me with their hands or stones."
The Buddha told Pūrṇa:

"If those people of Śroṇāparāntaka were merely fierce, impulsive, cruel, and abusive, you might still be able to escape them; but what would you do if they were to strike and pelt you with their hands and stones?"
Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the people of Śroṇāparāntaka were to strike me with their hands or stones, I would think to myself:”
“The people of Śroṇāparāntaka are virtuous and wise; although they strike me with their hands or stones, they do not use swords or staves.
The Buddha said to Pūrṇa:
“If those people were to strike you with swords or staves instead, what would you do then?”
Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If that person were to actually strike me with sword or staff, I would think thus:”
"Those people of Śroṇāparāntaka are virtuous and wise; even though they have used swords and staves against me, they did not kill me.
The Buddha said to Pūrṇa:
"Suppose those people were to kill you by chance—what would you do then?"
Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If the people of Śūrpāraka were to kill me, I would think thus:"

"There are disciples of the World-Honored One who, out of revulsion for their bodies, commit suicide by means of a blade, or by taking poison, or by hanging themselves with a rope, or by throwing themselves into deep pits;
yet those people of Sūlū in the West, being virtuous and wise, have attained liberation from this decaying body through a minor application of skillful means."
The Buddha said: “Excellent, Pūrṇa!”

"You have well trained in patience; you are now capable of dwelling among the people of Śroṇāparāntaka. You should now go to deliver those not yet delivered, to settle those not yet settled, and to lead those who have not attained nirvāṇa to attain nirvāṇa."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, Pūrṇa rejoiced and approved with gladness; he prostrated and departed.

Then, when the night had passed and morning dawned, the Venerable Pūrṇa put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms. Having finished his meal, he returned and, after entrusting his bedding to others, took his robes and bowl and departed, traveling through the human settlements of Aparāntaka in the western region.

Having arrived, he entered the summer retreat and preached the Dharma for five hundred upāsakas; he established five hundred monasteries, fully providing them with all necessary requisites such as rope beds, bedding, and various articles of worship.
After three months had passed, having perfected the three knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*), he entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* right there.
312 (Three hundred twelve). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Mālukyaputra came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent!
World-Honored One!

Please teach me the Dharma; having heard the Dharma, I shall dwell alone in a quiet place, contemplating with focused diligence and abiding without negligence, until I no longer undergo further existence.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed Mālukyaputta, saying:

“When young men of intelligence and keen faculties have not long gone forth into homelessness in my Dharma and Vinaya, they are already free from indolence regarding my Dharma and Vinaya; how much more so, then, you who today are advanced in years and mature in faculties, yet desire to hear my brief instruction?”
Mālakyaputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Although I am advanced in years and my faculties have matured, I still wish to hear the World-Honored One briefly deliver an instruction."

I only pray that the World-Honored One will briefly explain the instruction for me; having heard the Dharma, I shall dwell alone in a quiet place, applying myself with diligence to reflection, until I know for myself that there will be no further existence.
A second and a third time he made this same request.
The Buddha said to Mālukyaputta:
"Stop now! Do not speak further."
Thus he asked a second and a third time, yet [Mālukyaputta] still did not explain it.
Then the Blessed One addressed Mālukyaputta:
“I shall now question you; answer me as you see fit.”
The Buddha said to Mālukyaputta:
"If you have never before seen a form that you now wish to see, would you give rise to desire, affection, longing, or defiled attachment toward that form?"
He replied, “No, World-Honored One! “The same applies to the ear and sounds,
the nose and odors, the tongue and flavors, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena.”
The Buddha said to Mālukyaputta:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"O Mālukyaputta!

One should take what is seen as the measure of what is seen; one should take what is heard as the measure of what is heard; one should take what is sensed as the measure of what is sensed; one should take what is cognized as the measure of what is cognized.
And he spoke this verse:
“If you are not there, and that is not here, nor is it in between the two— this is the end of suffering.
Mālukyaputta said to the Buddha:
"I have understood,
Blessed One!
I have understood!"
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha said to Mālukyaputta:
“How is it that you have extensively understood the meaning within my brief teaching?”
At that time, Mālukyaputta spoke in verse to the Buddha,
saying: "If, having already seen a form with the eye, One loses right mindfulness,
Then regarding that seen form, One grasps at the signs of craving and attachment."
One who grasps at the signs of delight has a mind that is constantly bound and attached;
various kinds of craving arise, and an immeasurable mass of forms is produced.
Sensual desire, ill will, and harmful thoughts cause the mind to decline and diminish.
They nurture manifold sufferings and remain forever alienated from nirvana.
When seeing forms, they do not grasp at their characteristics; their minds follow right mindfulness, unstained by the love of an evil mind, nor do they give rise to attachment.
Not giving rise to various cravings, though immeasurable forms arise,
The perceptions of greed, ill-will, and harm cannot disturb their minds.
Gradually nurturing the end of all suffering, they draw ever closer to Nirvana.
As taught by the Honored One of Solar Lineage, one attains parinirvāṇa through the relinquishing of craving.
Yet, if upon hearing various sounds, the mind loses right mindfulness and grasps at the characteristics of those sounds, clinging to them and refusing to let go.
With the nose smelling scents, the tongue tasting flavors, the body touching tangibles, and the mind attending to mental objects, one loses right mindfulness; grasping at signs is likewise so.
The mind gives rise to craving and delight, becoming bound and firmly attached.
Giving rise to various kinds of craving, The immeasurable collection of phenomena is born.
Thoughts of greed, malice, and harm Cause the mind to decline, perish, and be destroyed;
They nourish the mass of all suffering And lead one forever away from Nirvana.
Unstained by any phenomena, established in right wisdom and right mindfulness,
his mind is neither defiled nor does it find delight in attachment.
Without giving rise to any cravings, immeasurable qualities arise within him.
When thoughts of greed, ill will, and cruelty do not diminish his mind, all sufferings follow in being destroyed; one gradually approaches parinirvāṇa.
"The extinction of craving is parinirvāṇa"—this is what the World-Honored One has taught.
"This is called the Blessed One’s brief teaching of the Dharma with its detailed explanation of the meaning.
The Buddha said to Mālukyaputta:
"You have indeed, within my brief teaching of the Dharma, detailed its meaning."
Why is this so? It is as stated in the verse you recited:
"If the eye sees various forms, One loses right mindfulness."
"Then, regarding the forms seen, one grasps at the signs of affection and longing.
As previously explained in detail.
At that time, the Venerable Mālukyaputta, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and welcomed it with gladness; he paid homage and departed.

At that time, the Venerable Mālukyaputta, having extensively understood the meaning within the brief teaching given by the Blessed One, dwelt alone in a secluded place, applying himself with diligence and remaining heedful; he proceeded until he attained arhatship and his mind was liberated.
313 (313). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“There is a teaching that the bhikṣus revere, yet regarding this teaching they have different faiths, different aspirations, different learning, different reflections on practice, and different views through which they reach certitude and acceptance; yet with right knowledge they declare:
‘Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and I myself know that there will be no further existence.’”
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“The World-Honored One is the root of the Dharma, the eye of the Dharma, and the refuge of the Dharma.
Excellent!”
“World-Honored One!
We only pray that you will explain this in detail; having heard it, the bhikṣus shall receive and practice it accordingly.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you. Bhikkhus!

When the eye has seen a form, one perceives the form but does not perceive craving for the form. One knows as it truly is: 'Previously my eye-consciousness had craving for forms, but now my eye-consciousness has no craving for forms.'"

If, monks, a bhikṣu, having seen a form with the eye, perceives the form and does not give rise to craving for the form, and perceives, "Previously my eye-consciousness had craving, but now my eye-consciousness has no craving for the form," and knows this as it truly is—monks! [this is called right knowledge.]
"What do you think?
Does he possess faith, aspiration, learning, reflective contemplation, and discerning acceptance regarding this?
He replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
Having taken refuge in this Dharma, do you know and see with correct knowledge as it truly is?
He replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
"The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind with mental objects are also to be explained in this same way.
'O bhikṣus!'"

This is called a discourse on the Dharma; regarding this discourse on the Dharma, a bhikkhu inclines toward it with a distinct faith, a distinct desire, a distinct hearing, a distinct reflection on practice, and a distinct view characterized by careful discernment and acceptance, and he declares with clear knowledge:
"Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and I myself know that there will be no further existence."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
314 (314). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"One should abandon desire. Having abandoned desire for the eye, the eye is then severed and fully understood; its root is cut off like the head of a tāla tree, so that it shall never again arise in future lives."
"The same is said for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
315 (315). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If the eye arises, abides, and emerges, then suffering arises, illness abides, and old age and death emerge.
The same is said for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind."
If the eye ceases, subsides, and disappears, then suffering that arises ceases, illness subsides, and death disappears.
The same is said for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
316 (316) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"The eye is impermanent. If the eye were permanent, it would not be subject to oppression and suffering, and one could also say regarding the eye: 'Let it be thus; let it not be thus.'"
Because the eye is impermanent, the eye experiences oppression and suffering arises; therefore, one cannot command the eye, "Let it be thus," or "Let it not be thus."
"The same is said for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
317. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“The eye is suffering; if the eye were pleasure, it would not be subject to the suffering of oppression, and one would be able to wish regarding the eye, ‘Let it be thus,’ or ‘Let it not be thus. Because the eye is suffering, it is subject to the suffering of oppression, and one cannot wish regarding the eye, ‘Let it be thus,’ or ‘Let it not be thus.’”
“The same is to be said for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
318 (318). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"The eye is not self. If the eye were self, it would not be subject to affliction and suffering; one could exercise one's will over the eye, saying, 'Let it be thus,' or 'Let it not be thus. Because the eye is not self, it is subject to affliction and suffering, and one cannot exercise one's will over the eye, saying, 'Let it be thus,' or 'Let it not be thus.'"
"The same is said for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As it was said regarding the three discourses on the six internal sense bases, so too were the three discourses on the six external sense bases spoken.
319 (319) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the brahmin Jātiśroṇa went to where the Buddha was staying. After exchanging greetings with him, he withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying: “Gautama!
"What is meant by 'all'? What is called 'all'?
The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa:
"'All' refers to the twelve bases (āyatana): eye and forms, ear and sounds, nose and odors, tongue and tastes, body and tangibles, mind and mental phenomena. This is called 'all'."

If, however, one were to say: "This is not the 'all' spoken of by the śramaṇa Gautama; I now reject that 'all' and establish another 'all' of my own," such a person would merely be engaging in empty talk; having been questioned, they would remain ignorant and only increase their doubt.
"Why is this? Because it is not within their domain.
At that time, the brahmin Jātiśroṇa, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced, approved, and practiced accordingly.
320. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a brahmin named Janaka who went to where the Buddha was staying. After exchanging greetings with him face-to-face, he withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Gautama! Regarding what is called ‘all that exists,’ what is meant by ‘all that exists’?
The Buddha told the brahmin Jātiśroṇa:
"I now ask you; answer me as you see fit.
Brahmin, what do you think?"
"Is the eye existent?
He replied,
"It is existent, Śramaṇa Gautama!"
“Is form existent? He replied,
“It is existent, Śramaṇa Gautama!”

“Brahmin! Is there form, is there eye-consciousness, is there eye-contact, and is there feeling born of the causal condition of eye-contact—whether it be painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant?”
He replied: "There is, Śramaṇa Gautama!
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind."
Thus it was explained in detail, up until: "Because it is not within their domain.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the brahmin Jātiśroṇa, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and approved, rose from his seat, and departed.
321 (Three-Hundred-and-Twenty-One). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain Brahmin named Jātiśroṇa went to where the Buddha was staying. After exchanging greetings with him, he withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Śramaṇa Gautama!
Regarding what you call ‘all phenomena,’ what constitutes all phenomena?
The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa:
"The eye and forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feeling born of eye-contact as a condition—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant;

likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—the mental objects, mind-consciousness, mind-contact, and the feeling born of mind-contact as a condition—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant: these are called 'all phenomena' (sarvadharma)."

Furthermore, if there should be one who says, "This is not 'all dharmas' as spoken by the śramaṇa Gautama; I now renounce that and establish my own 'all dharmas'," this is merely a matter of words. Having been questioned, they do not know the answer, thereby increasing their delusion and confusion.
"Why is this? Because it is not within their domain.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the brahmin Janavasabha, having heard the Buddha's words, rejoiced and expressed his approval; he then rose from his seat and departed.

Just as with the three sūtras asked by the brahmin Jātiśroṇa, so too are the three sūtras asked by certain bhikṣus, the three sūtras asked by the Venerable Ānanda, and the three sūtras concerning the Dharma-eye, the root of the Dharma, and the reliance on the Dharma spoken by the Blessed One; these are also as explained above.
322 (Three Hundred and Twenty-Two). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the World-Honored One has said, the eye is an internal sense base (*ādhyātmikam āyatanaṃ*); yet the World-Honored One has spoken briefly without detailed analysis.
In what way is the eye an internal sense base?”
The Buddha told that bhikṣu:
"The eye is an internal sense base (āyatana), consisting of translucent matter derived from the four great elements; it is invisible and possesses resistance.
The same applies to the internal sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, and body."
He addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One!
As the World-Honored One has taught, the mind is an internal sense base (āyatana), yet you have not analyzed it in detail."
"What is the internal sense-base of the mind?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"As for the internal sense-base of the mind, that which is mind, thought, and consciousness—non-material, invisible, and non-resistant—is called the internal sense-base of the mind."
He asked again:
"As the Blessed One has said regarding the external sense-base of form, the Blessed One has spoken briefly without detailed analysis. What is it?"
“World-Honored One!
The external sense-base of form.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"Visible form as an external sense base (*bāhyāyatana*)—if it is form produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), visible, and resistant—this is called 'form' as an external sense base.
He then addressed the Buddha again:
"The World-Honored One has spoken of sound as an external sense base, but has not analyzed it in detail."
"What is sound as an external sense base?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"If sound is composed of the four great elements, is invisible, and possesses resistance—just as with sound, so it is with odor and taste."
He asked again:
"The Blessed One has spoken of the external sense-base of tangibles, but has not analyzed it in detail.
What is the external sense-base of tangibles?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"The external sense base of tangibles refers to the four great elements and the derivative matter produced from the four great elements; it is invisible and possesses resistance. This is called the external sense base of tangibles."
He asked again:
"The World-Honored One has taught the external sense bases, but has not analyzed them in detail.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
“The sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) is that which is not included within the eleven spheres; it is invisible and non-obstructive. This is called the sphere of mental objects.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are six internal sense bases:
namely, the internal sense base of the eye, and the internal sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
325 (325) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

"There are six groups of consciousness. What are the six?

326 (326) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

"There are six groups of contact.
What are the six groups of contact?"

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are six bodies of feeling.
What are the six? They are as follows:"
“Feeling born of eye-contact, and feeling born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact—these are called the six groups of feeling.

“There are six classes of perception. What are the six?

329 (329) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are six groups of volition. What are the six?
"This refers to volition born of eye-contact, and volition born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact; these are called the six groups of volition.

330 (Three Hundred and Thirty) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are six groups of craving.

331 (331) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

332 (Three Hundred and Thirty-Two). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

"These are called the six obscurations.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 333 (333) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“The eye of the past and the future is impermanent; how much more so the eye of the present! A learned noble disciple who contemplates in this way does not look back to the eye of the past, does not delight in the eye of the future, and regarding the eye of the present, gives rise to disenchantment, detachment, and the tendency toward its cessation.”
"The same is said for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
As it was with impermanence,
so it is also said regarding suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
As it was said in the four sūtras on the internal sense bases and likewise in the four sūtras on the external sense bases, so it was also spoken here. 334 (334) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the village of Kuruṇḍa, the Taming of Bulls.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"I shall now teach you the Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing; purely unified, complete, and pure—a holy life that is stainless."
Listen attentively and reflect well upon this Discourse on Phenomena with Causes, Conditions, and Bonds.
"What is the Discourse on Phenomena with Causes, Conditions, and Bonds?
It means that the eye has a cause, has a condition, and has a bondage.
What are the cause, the condition, and the bondage of the eye?
It means that the eye has karma as its cause, karma as its condition, and karma as its bondage; and karma itself has a cause, has a condition, and has a bondage.
What are the cause of karma, the condition of karma, and the bondage of karma? They are:
karma has craving as its cause, craving as its condition, and craving as its bondage; craving has existence as its cause, existence as its condition, and existence as its bondage.
What are the cause, condition, and bond of craving?
It is that craving has ignorance as its cause, ignorance as its condition, and ignorance as its bond; and ignorance likewise has a cause, a condition, and a bond.
What is the cause of ignorance, the condition for ignorance, and the bondage of ignorance?

It is said that improper attention is the cause of ignorance, improper attention is its condition, and improper attention is its bondage; improper attention likewise has a cause, has a condition, and has a bondage.

What is the cause of improper mental attention, the condition for improper mental attention, and the bondage of improper mental attention? It refers to the arising of improper mental attention and the arising of delusion based upon the eye and forms.

“Conditioned by the eye and forms, improper mental attention arises; from this, delusion arises. That delusion is ignorance (*avidyā*). The seeking of desire born of delusion is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*). What is produced by craving is called karma.”
In this way, bhikṣus!
Through improper reflection, ignorance becomes the cause of craving; ignorance causes craving, craving causes karma, and karma causes the eye.
The same is said for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; this is called the Discourse on Phenomena with Causes and Conditions and Subject to Bondage.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
335. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the village of Go-yokanḍaka (The Cow-Herd’s Settlement).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"I shall now preach the Dharma for you—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing; entirely complete, pure, and pristine—a holy life that is immaculate. It is called the Discourse on the Emptiness of the Ultimate Truth."
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall explain it for you.
"What is the Sūtra on Emptiness in the Ultimate Sense? Monks!..."
When the eye arises, it has no place from which it comes; when it ceases, it has no place to which it goes.

Thus, the eye arises without reality; having arisen, it is exhausted and ceases. There is karmic retribution, but no agent. Once this aggregate has ceased, another aggregate continues in succession, except for conventional designations.
The same is said for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, with the exception of conventional designations (*saṃketa-dharma*).

Conventional designations refer to: "Because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises. As it is said: "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises... and so on, in detail, up until: "Thus there is the arising of this entire great mass of suffering."

Furthermore: "Because this does not exist, that does not exist; because this ceases, that ceases. With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases... Thus it is explained at length, up until: "...the entire great mass of suffering ceases."
"Monks! This is called the Discourse on the Dharma of Emptiness in the Ultimate Sense.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the monks, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
336 (Three Hundred and Thirty-Six). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are six modes of joy.
What are the six?
They are as follows.”
"Monks! If one feels joy upon seeing a form with the eye, one dwells in relation to that form.

If one feels joy upon hearing a sound with the ear, smelling an odor with the nose, tasting a flavor with the tongue, touching a tangible object with the body, or cognizing a mental phenomenon with the mind, one dwells in relation to those phenomena."
"Monks! These are called the six modes of joyful conduct.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the monks, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
337 (Three Hundred and Thirty-Seven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are six modes of sorrowful conduct.
What are the six? Monks!
If one feels sorrow upon seeing forms with the eye, one dwells in relation to those forms.

If one feels sorrow regarding sounds with the ear, odors with the nose, tastes with the tongue, tangibles with the body, or mental phenomena with the mind-consciousness, one dwells in relation to those phenomena.
“Monks! These are called the six modes of sorrowful conduct.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the monks, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
338 (Three Hundred Thirty-Eight). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are six modes of equanimity.
What are the six? Monks!
That is to say: when the eye sees forms, there is equanimity, and one dwells with regard to those forms;

when the ear hears sounds, the nose smells odors, the tongue tastes flavors, the body feels tangibles, and the mind cognizes mental phenomena, there is equanimity, and one dwells with regard to those mental phenomena. This is called a bhikṣu’s six modes of dwelling in equanimity.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 339 (339) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are six constant practices. What are the six?
If a bhikṣu sees forms with the eye, he dwells with equanimity, mindful and clearly aware, neither experiencing pain nor pleasure."

When the ear hears sounds, the nose smells odors, the tongue tastes flavors, the body feels tangibles, and the mind cognizes mental phenomena—neither experiencing pain nor pleasure, but abiding in equanimity with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension—this is called the bhikṣu’s six constant practices.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 340 (340) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are six constant practices. What are the six?
If a bhikṣu, seeing forms with the eye, dwells with equanimity, free from both suffering and pleasure, established in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension;

and likewise, hearing sounds with the ear, smelling odors with the nose, tasting flavors with the tongue, touching tangibles with the body, or cognizing mental phenomena with the mind, dwells with equanimity, free from both suffering and pleasure, established in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension—if a bhikṣu accomplishes these six constant practices, he is rare to find in the world.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 341 (341) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are six constant practices. What are the six?
If a bhikṣu sees forms with the eye, he dwells with equanimity, free from both suffering and pleasure, possessing right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.

With respect to sounds heard by the ear, odors smelled by the nose, flavors tasted by the tongue, tangibles felt by the body, and mental phenomena cognized by the mind, he dwells with equanimity, free from both suffering and pleasure, possessing right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.

If a bhikṣu accomplishes these six constant practices, he is rare to find in the world; he is one who should be served, revered, and supported, and thus becomes the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 342 (342). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are six constant practices. What are the six?
If a bhikṣu sees forms with the eye, he dwells with equanimity, free from both suffering and pleasure, possessing right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.

With regard to sounds heard by the ear, odors smelled by the nose, flavors tasted by the tongue, tangibles felt by the body, and mental phenomena cognized by the mind, he dwells with equanimity, free from both suffering and pleasure, possessing right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.
If a bhikṣu accomplishes these six constant practices, you should know that he is one such as Śāriputra.
When the bhikṣu Śāriputra has seen forms with his eyes, he is neither pained nor pleased; he dwells in equanimity, established in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.

Regarding sounds heard by the ear, odors smelled by the nose, flavors tasted by the tongue, tangibles felt by the body, and mental phenomena cognized by the mind—being neither painful nor pleasant—one dwells with equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension.

Because the bhikṣu Śāriputra has accomplished these six constant practices, he is difficult to find in the world; he is one who should be served, revered, and made offerings to, and thus he is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*Saṃyukta Āgama*, Volume Thirteen;
*Saṃyukta Āgama*, Volume Fourteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
1.4.343 (343). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Bhikṣu Pūrṇa was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain.

Then, a great number of non-Buddhist renunciants approached the Venerable Pūrṇa; they exchanged greetings and expressions of courtesy with him, and having finished their greetings and expressions of courtesy, they sat down to one side and said to the Venerable Pūrṇa:
"We wish to ask a question; would you have the leisure to grant us an answer?"
The Venerable Bhumī said to the various non-Buddhist renunciants,
“Ask whatever you wish, and I shall explain it to you.
Then, the various non-Buddhist renunciants questioned the Venerable Bhumī:
“Is suffering and pleasure created by oneself?
The Venerable Bhūmī replied:
“Regarding those who say that suffering and pleasure are created by oneself, the World-Honored One has said:”
"This is indeterminate.
He asked again:
"Are suffering and pleasure created by another?"
He replied:
"Regarding the view that suffering and pleasure are created by another, the World-Honored One has declared:
'This is indeterminate.'"
Again he asked:
"Are suffering and pleasure created by oneself or by another?
He replied:
"Regarding the claim that suffering and pleasure are created by oneself or by another, the Blessed One has declared:
'This is indeterminate (avyākṛta).
He asked again:"
"Are suffering and pleasure neither created by oneself nor by another, but produced without cause?
He replied:
"Regarding suffering and pleasure being neither created by oneself nor by another, but produced without cause, the Blessed One has said:"
"This is indeterminate.
The renunciant non-Buddhists asked again:
"In what way?"
"Venerable Pūma, do you say that suffering and pleasure are self-made?
You replied that this is undeclared (avyākṛta).
Do you say that suffering and pleasure are made by another?"
It is declared to be indeterminate.
Is suffering and pleasure created by oneself or by another?
It is declared to be indeterminate.
"Are suffering and pleasure neither self-made nor other-made, but produced without cause?
You have declared them to be indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Now, how does the śramaṇa Gautama say that suffering and pleasure arise?"
The Venerable Bhūmī replied:
“O renunciants of other sects!
The Blessed One has taught that suffering and pleasure arise from conditions.”
At that time, when the various non-Buddhist renunciants heard what the Venerable Bhūmī had said, they were not pleased in their hearts; they rebuked him and departed.
At that moment, the Venerable Śāriputra was sitting under a tree not far from the Venerable Bhūmī.

At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇa, knowing that the various non-Buddhist renunciants had departed, went to where the Venerable Śāriputra was; having arrived, he exchanged greetings with Śāriputra in person.
Having offered his congratulations and condolences, he reported in full to the Venerable Śāriputra the matters concerning which those various non-Buddhist renunciants had questioned him:
"In giving this answer, have I not slandered or misrepresented the Blessed One?"

If one speaks as they have been taught, yet speaks contrary to the Dharma and does not act in accordance with the practice of the Dharma, will those who come to challenge, interrogate, and reproach them—not being proponents of the causal discourse on the unconditioned—do so?
The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Venerable Pūrṇa! What you have said is truly as the Buddha has taught;

it does not misrepresent the Tathāgata. You have spoken according to what was taught, spoken according to the Dharma, and spoken as a practitioner of the Dharma speaks the Dharma; it cannot be challenged, refuted, or censured by those who come to debate for other reasons."
Why is that? Because the Blessed One has taught that suffering and pleasure arise from conditions.
Venerable Pūrṇa!
Regarding those ascetics and brahmins who claim that suffering and pleasure are self-created, their view also arises from causes;
it is impossible for them to say that they do not arise from conditions.

Those who assert that suffering and pleasure are created by another, created by both self and another, or created neither by self nor by another but without cause—these [assertions] likewise arise from conditions;
it is impossible for them not to arise from conditions.
Venerable Bhūmī!
That which those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas describe as pleasure and pain created by oneself also arises conditioned by contact;
it is impossible that they do not arise from contact.

Whether suffering and pleasure are created by another, created by both self and another, or created neither by self nor by another but without cause—these too arise conditioned by contact; it is impossible that they could arise without being conditioned by contact.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was sitting under a tree not far from Śāriputra, and he heard the discourse between the Venerable Śāriputra and the Venerable Bhumija.
Having heard this, he rose from his seat, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
He then reported to the World-Honored One, in full detail, every point of the discussion that had taken place between the Venerable Bhūmī and the Venerable Śāriputra.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Ānanda! When those who come to question Venerable Śāriputra, he is able to answer them according to the occasion.
Excellent!"
Śāriputra! Because there is wisdom that accords with the occasion, when someone comes to question me, I am able to answer according to the time.
If my śrāvakas have questions that accord with the occasion, they should answer according to the time, just as Śāriputra has spoken.

“Ānanda! In the past, when I was staying at the abode of seers in the mountains near Rājagṛha, there were certain non-Buddhist renunciants who came to question me with such meanings, such phrases, and such expressions, as those spoken by the Venerable Śāriputra. For their sake, I explained and taught them with such meanings, such phrases, and such expressions.”
“Ānanda! If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who maintain that suffering and pleasure are created by oneself, I would go to them and ask:
‘Do you truly say that suffering and pleasure are created by oneself?’”
He replied to me, saying: "It is so. I then asked him:
"If you can firmly uphold this doctrine, declaring it to be the truth while others are fools, I do not approve of it.
Why is that? For I teach that the arising of suffering and pleasure is different from this."
If he were to ask me:
"In what way, Gautama, do you say that the origins of suffering and pleasure are different?
I would answer him thus:
"Suffering and pleasure arise from their conditions.

Thus, regarding those who claim that suffering is created by another, created by both self and another, or created neither by self nor another and is without cause, I have likewise gone to them and spoken as above."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"As for the meaning spoken by the World-Honored One, I have already understood it: because there is birth, there is old age and death, and not due to any other condition;
because there is birth, there is old age and death, and so on, up to: because there is ignorance, there are volitional formations, and not due to any other condition."

Because there is ignorance, there are volitional formations; with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease, and so on until: with the cessation of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering cease; thus this entire great mass of suffering ceases.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and delighted in it, paid his respects, and departed.
344 (344) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra and the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila were staying on Vulture Peak Mountain.

Then, in the late afternoon, the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila arose from meditative concentration and went to where the Venerable Śāriputra was. They exchanged greetings and pleasantries; having finished their greetings, he withdrew to sit at one side and said to the Venerable Śāriputra:
"I wish to ask a question. Would you have the leisure to grant me an answer?"
The Venerable Śāriputra said to the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila:
"Virtuous one, ask whatever you wish; I shall answer what I know.
The Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila then spoke to the Venerable Śāriputra:

"What dharma does a learned noble disciple accomplish within this Dhamma and Vinaya such that he is said to be 'endowed with vision,' to have 'accomplished right view,' to have 'accomplished unwavering confidence in the Buddha,' to have entered the true Dhamma, attained this true Dhamma, and awakened to this true Dhamma?"
The Venerable Śāriputra said to the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila:

“The learned noble disciple knows unwholesome phenomena as they truly are; he knows the roots of the unwholesome as they truly are; he knows wholesome phenomena as they truly are; and he knows the roots of the wholesome as they truly are.”
"What is the knowledge of unwholesome phenomena as they truly are?
Unwholesome bodily action, verbal action, and mental action—these are called unwholesome phenomena; in this way, one knows unwholesome phenomena as they truly are."
How does one know the unwholesome roots as they truly are?

There are three unwholesome roots—the unwholesome root of greed, the unwholesome root of hatred, and the unwholesome root of delusion. These are called the unwholesome roots; in this way, one knows the unwholesome roots as they truly are.
"What is the knowledge of wholesome phenomena as they truly are?
Wholesome bodily action, verbal action, and mental action—these are called wholesome phenomena; thus one knows wholesome phenomena as they truly are."
How does one know the roots of goodness as they truly are?
It refers to the three roots of goodness—non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion—which are called the three roots of goodness; in this way, one knows the roots of goodness as they truly are.
“Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila!

Thus, a well-versed noble disciple knows unwholesome states as they truly are, knows the roots of the unwholesome as they truly are, knows wholesome states as they truly are, and knows the roots of the wholesome as they truly are. Therefore, in this Dhamma and Vinaya, he is endowed with right view, possesses direct vision, and achieves unwavering confidence in the Buddha; he enters this True Dharma, attains this True Dharma, and awakens to this True Dharma.”
The Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila said to the Venerable Śāriputra: "Is it only these, or are there others?
The Venerable Śāriputra replied:
“There is. If a learned noble disciple understands food as it really is, understands the origin of food, the cessation of food, and the path leading to the cessation of food as they really are.
How does one understand food as it really is?”
It refers to the four nutriments (*āhāra*).

What are the four? First, gross edible food; second, subtle contact-nutriment; third, mental volition-nutriment; fourth, consciousness-nutriment. These are called "nutriments"; such nutriment is to be known as it truly is.
What is knowing the origin of nutriment as it really is?

It is the craving for future existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding pleasure and attachment here and there; this is called the origin of nutriment. In this way, one knows the origin of nutriment as it really is.
What is knowing the cessation of nutriment as it really is?

If there is craving for future existence, accompanied by delight and greed, which finds pleasure and attachment in this and that, and which is abandoned without remainder, relinquished, vomited out, exhausted, free from desire, ceased, stilled, and vanished—this is called the cessation of nutriment. Thus one knows the cessation of nutriment as it really is.
What is the path leading to the cessation of nutriment, known as it really is?

It is the Noble Eightfold Path—namely, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This is called the path leading to the cessation of nutriment; in this way, one knows the path leading to the cessation of nutriment as it really is.

“If a learned noble disciple understands this nutriment as it really is, understands the origin of nutriment as it really is, understands the cessation of nutriment as it really is, and understands the path leading to the cessation of nutriment as it really is, then that learned noble disciple is endowed with right view and possesses a straight vision regarding this true Dharma and Discipline; he achieves unshakable confidence in the Buddha, enters into the true Dharma, attains this true Dharma, and realizes this true Dharma.”
The Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila asked the Venerable Śāriputra again: "Is it only these, or are there others?
The Venerable Śāriputra replied:
"Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila!

Furthermore, there is another way in which a well-taught noble disciple understands illness as it really is, understands the origin of illness as it really is, understands the cessation of illness as it really is, and understands the path leading to the cessation of illness as it really is."
"What is the knowledge of illness as it really is?
It refers to the three illnesses—the illness of desire, the illness of existence, and the illness of ignorance—which are called 'illness. In this way, one knows illness as it really is."
What is knowing the origin of illness as it really is?
The origin of ignorance is the origin of illness; this is called knowing the origin of illness as it really is.
What is knowing the cessation of illness as it really is?
The cessation of ignorance is the cessation of this disease; thus one knows the cessation of the disease as it truly is.
What is knowing the path leading to the cessation of the disease as it truly is?
It is the Eightfold Noble Path, as previously described; thus one knows the path leading to the cessation of the disease as it truly is.

“If a learned noble disciple understands illness as it really is, understands the origin of illness as it really is, understands the cessation of illness as it really is, and understands the path leading to the cessation of illness as it really is, then that learned noble disciple is endowed with right view regarding this Dharma and Vinaya, and even attains realization of this True Dharma.”
The Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita asked the Venerable Sāriputta: "Is it only these, or are there others?
The Venerable Sāriputta said to the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita:

"Furthermore, there is another thing: the learned noble disciple knows suffering as it really is, knows the origin of suffering as it really is, knows the cessation of suffering as it really is, and knows the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is."
"What is the knowledge of suffering as it truly is?

It is the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from what is loved, the suffering of encountering what is hated, and the suffering of not obtaining what one desires; in brief, these five aggregates of clinging are suffering. This is called suffering, and thus one knows suffering as it truly is."
What is the knowledge of the origin of suffering as it really is?

It is the craving for future existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there; this is called the origin of suffering. In this way, one knows the origin of suffering as it really is.
What is the knowledge of the cessation of suffering as it truly is?

When whatever craving for future existence—accompanied by delight and greed, finding delight here and there—is abandoned without remainder, even unto its subsiding and disappearance, this is called the cessation of suffering; such is the knowledge of the cessation of suffering as it truly is.
What is the knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is?

It is the Noble Eightfold Path, as described above; this is called the path leading to the cessation of suffering, and such is the knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is.

“The well-heard noble disciple thus knows suffering as it really is; he knows the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering as they really are.

Thus, this noble disciple is endowed with right view and possesses direct vision regarding my Dharma and Vinaya; he is endowed with unshakable confidence in the Buddha, has entered the true path, has attained this True Dharma, and has awakened to this True Dharma.”
He asked Venerable Śāriputra again:
"Is this the only teaching, or are there others?
Venerable Śāriputra replied:

“There is more yet: namely, the learned noble disciple knows aging-and-death as it really is, knows the origin of aging-and-death as it really is, knows the cessation of aging-and-death as it really is, and knows the path leading to the cessation of aging-and-death as it really is, as explained in detail in the *Vibhaṅga-sutta*.”
How does one know, as it really is, the origination of aging and death?

The origination of birth is the origination of aging and death; the cessation of birth is the cessation of aging and death; and the path leading to the cessation of aging and death is the Noble Eightfold Path, as previously described. A learned noble disciple knows this aging and death as it really is, up to knowing, as it really is, the path leading to the cessation of aging and death.

In this way, the noble disciple is endowed with right view regarding my Dharma and Vinaya; he achieves straightforward vision and accomplishes indestructible confidence in the Buddha; he enters into the True Dharma, attains this True Dharma, and awakens to this True Dharma.

In this way, regarding birth, becoming, clinging, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, and volitional formations—the noble disciple knows volitional formations as they truly are; he knows the arising of volitional formations, the cessation of volitional formations, and the path leading to the cessation of volitional formations as they truly are.
"What is the knowledge of formations as they truly are?
There are three kinds of formations—bodily formations, verbal formations, and mental formations; such are the formations known as they truly are."
How does one know the origination of volitional formations as they really are?
The origination of ignorance is the origination of volitional formations; thus one knows the origination of volitional formations as it really is.
How does one know the cessation of volitional formations as it really is?
With the cessation of ignorance, formations cease; thus one knows the cessation of formations as it truly is.
How does one know the path leading to the cessation of formations as it truly is?
It is the Noble Eightfold Path, as previously described.
Mahākoṭṭhila! This is called the noble disciple’s knowledge of things as they truly are:

knowledge of the practice, the origin of the practice, the cessation of the practice, and the path leading to the cessation of the practice, as they truly are. He is endowed with right view regarding my Dharma and Vinaya; he is accomplished in straight vision and accomplished in unshakable confidence in the Buddha. He has entered this True Dharma, attained this True Dharma, and awakened to this True Dharma.
Mahākoṭṭhila asked the Venerable Śāriputra again:
"Is this the only teaching, or are there others?
Śāriputra replied:
“Mahākoṭṭhila! Why do you pursue this?
You will never be able to reach the ultimate conclusion or the final limit of all these doctrines.
If a noble disciple has severed ignorance and produced clear knowledge, what further need is there to seek?”
At that time, having finished their discussion on the meaning of the Dharma, the two noble men each returned to their respective abodes. 345 (345) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra:
"As I have taught, regarding what Pārāyaṇa Ajita asked:
'If one attains the enumeration of all dharmas, and if one further trains in various ways...'"
“Please explain to me in detail what constitutes proper deportment and conduct. “Śāriputra,
what is meant by training?”
"What is the enumeration of dharmas?
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra remained silent and did not answer; for a second and a third time, he likewise remained silent.
The Buddha said:
"It is true,
Śāriputra. Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is so, World-Honored One! It is so,
World-Honored One!"
A bhikkhu who is a true practitioner proceeds toward disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation.
Since the arising of food leads to birth, that bhikkhu, on account of food, gives rise to disenchantment, dispassion, and proceeds toward its cessation.
When that nutriment ceases, it is truly ceased; having realized this, that bhikṣu becomes disenchanted with it, detaches from desire for it, and proceeds toward its cessation—this is called training.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, it is true!
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"It is true."
"World-Honored One!
World-Honored One!
If a bhikṣu is one who is true, he becomes weary of [suffering], detached from desire, and brings about its cessation; he does not give rise to any outflows, and his mind is well-liberated."

That arises from the accumulation of nutriment; if it is truly so, it is subject to cessation. Having realized this, a bhikkhu becomes weary of cessation, becomes dispassionate toward it, and brings about its extinction. He does not give rise to the taints, and his mind is well-liberated—this is the reckoning of the Dhamma.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"So it is, so it is; it is as you have said.
When a bhikṣu gives rise to revulsion toward reality, becomes free from desire for it, and brings about its cessation, this is called a dharma-category."
When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One rose and entered his room to sit in meditation.
Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"I was unable to respond to the Blessed One’s initial question; therefore, I remained silent and composed in mind.

After a short while, the Blessed One again posed a question intended to inspire joy, whereupon I immediately understood such a meaning as this. Even if the Blessed One were to question me on this same meaning for one day and night, or even for seven nights, using different phrasing and different nuances, I would likewise be able to explain it throughout those seven nights with different phrasing and different nuances."
At that time, a certain bhikṣu went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Venerable Śāriputra made a marvelous and unprecedented statement, and amidst the great assembly, he uttered a lion’s roar with single-minded resolve:
"When the World-Honored One first questioned me, I was entirely unable to respond; even when questioned a second and a third time, I remained silent without an answer."

The World-Honored One then proceeded to pose questions intended to inspire joy; I immediately understood them. Even if the World-Honored One were to question me on this meaning for one day and night, or even for seven nights, using different phrasing and different nuances each time, I would likewise be able to explain it all, providing explanations with different phrasing and different nuances for up to seven nights.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“That bhikṣu Śāriputra is truly able, within a single day and night, and even throughout seven nights, to provide explanations for the meanings asked about—using different phrasing and different nuances throughout those seven nights.”
"Why is this? Because the bhikṣu Śāriputra has skillfully entered the dharma-realm.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, that bhikṣu, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
346. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are three things that the world does not love, does not cherish, and finds disagreeable.
What are these three?
They are aging, illness, and death.”

If these three things—unlovely, unrecalled, and disagreeable—did not exist in the world, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha would not appear in the world; nor would the world know that there is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha who possesses knowledge and vision, and who teaches the True Dharma and Vinaya.

Because the three phenomena of old age, sickness, and death exist in the world—phenomena that are unlovely, unworthy of recollection, and disagreeable—the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has appeared in the world. The world knows that there is a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, who possesses knowledge and vision, and who proclaims the True Dharma and Discipline.
“Because three things are not abandoned, one is unable to escape old age, sickness, and death.
What are these three?
They are greed, hatred, and delusion. Furthermore, because three other things are not abandoned, one is unable to escape greed, hatred, and delusion.”
What are the three?

They are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*). Furthermore, because these three factors have not been abandoned, one is unable to relinquish the view of a self-identity, adherence to precepts and rituals, and doubt.
What are these three?

They are improper reflection, associating with wrong paths, and a lazy mind. Furthermore, because these three factors are not abandoned, one is unable to free oneself from improper reflection, associating with wrong paths, and a lazy mind.
What are these three?

They are loss of mindfulness, lack of clear comprehension, and a distracted mind. Furthermore, because three other factors are not abandoned, one is unable to free oneself from loss of mindfulness, lack of clear comprehension, and a distracted mind.
What are these three?

They are restlessness, lack of discipline, and failure to train in the precepts. Furthermore, because these three factors are not abandoned, one is unable to free oneself from restlessness, lack of discipline, and failure to train in the precepts.
What are these three?

They are lack of faith, being difficult to instruct, and indolence. Furthermore, because three other factors are not severed, one is unable to abandon lack of faith, being difficult to instruct, and laziness.
What are these three? They are:

not wishing to see the noble ones, not wishing to hear the Dharma, and constantly seeking out the faults of others. Furthermore, because one does not abandon another three factors, one is unable to free oneself from not wishing to see the noble ones, not wishing to hear the Dharma, and constantly seeking out the faults of others.
What are these three? They are:

lack of respect, harsh speech, and associating with evil friends. Furthermore, because one does not abandon three other factors, one is unable to free oneself from lack of respect, harsh speech, and associating with evil friends.
What are these three?
They are lack of shame, lack of remorse, and negligence. Because these three factors are not abandoned, one is unable to avoid disrespect, harsh speech, and associating with evil companions.
"Why is this so?

Because of a lack of shame and a lack of dread, there is heedlessness; because of heedlessness, there is a lack of reverence; because of a lack of reverence, one associates with evil friends; because of associating with evil friends, one does not wish to see the noble ones, does not wish to hear the Dharma, and constantly seeks out the faults of others; because of seeking out the faults of others, there is lack of faith, difficulty in being taught, harsh speech, and laziness; because of laziness, there is restlessness, lack of moral discipline, and failure to train in the precepts; because of failing to train in the precepts, there is loss of mindfulness, lack of clear comprehension, and a distracted mind; because of a distracted mind, there is improper reflection, following false paths, and a lazy mind; because of a lazy mind, there arise the view of a self-identity, attachment to rules and rituals, and doubt; because of doubt, one does not abandon greed, hatred, and delusion; and because one does not abandon greed, hatred, and delusion, one is unable to escape old age, sickness, and death.
“By abandoning three things, one is capable of being free from old age, sickness, and death.
What are these three?

They are greed, hatred, and delusion. Once these three things have been abandoned, one is capable of being free from old age, sickness, and death. Furthermore, by abandoning another three things, one is capable of being free from greed, hatred, and delusion.”
What are the three?

They are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*). Because these three factors are abandoned, one is capable of being free from greed, hatred, and delusion; furthermore, because [these] three factors are abandoned, one is capable of being free from the view of a self-identity, clinging to precepts and rituals, and doubt.
What are the three?

They are improper reflection, associating with wrong paths, and giving rise to a lazy mind. Because these three factors are abandoned, one is able to leave behind the view of a self-identity, attachment to precepts and rituals, and doubt. Furthermore, because another three factors are abandoned, one is able to leave behind improper reflection, associating with wrong paths, and a lazy mind.
What are the three?

They are loss of mindfulness, lack of clear comprehension, and a distracted mind. Because these three factors are abandoned, one is able to abandon improper reflection, the pursuit of wrong paths, and mental indolence. Furthermore, because another three factors are abandoned, one is able to abandon loss of mindfulness, lack of clear comprehension, and a distracted mind.
What are these three?

They are restlessness, lack of discipline, and transgression of the precepts. Because these three factors are abandoned, one is capable of being free from forgetfulness, lack of clear comprehension, and a distracted mind. Furthermore, because another three factors are abandoned, one is capable of being free from restlessness, lack of discipline, and transgression of the precepts.
What are the three?

They are lack of faith, being difficult to instruct, and indolence. Because these three factors are abandoned, one is capable of abandoning restlessness, non-restraint, and transgression of the precepts. Furthermore, because there are another three factors that are abandoned, one is capable of abandoning lack of faith, being difficult to instruct, and indolence.
What are these three? They are:

not wishing to see the noble ones, not delighting in hearing the Dharma, and taking pleasure in seeking out the faults of others. Because these three factors are abandoned, one is capable of being free from lack of faith, being difficult to instruct, and laziness. Furthermore, because another three factors are abandoned, one is capable of being free from not wishing to see the noble ones, not wishing to hear the Dharma, and taking pleasure in seeking out the faults of others.
What are these three? They are:

lack of respect, harsh speech, and associating with evil friends. Because these three factors are abandoned, one is freed from the desire not to see the Noble Ones, the desire not to hear the Dharma, and the habit of seeking out the faults of others. Furthermore, because another three factors are abandoned, one is able to remain free from lack of respect, harsh speech, and associating with evil friends.
What are the three?
They are lack of shame, lack of remorse, and heedlessness. Why is that?

Because of a sense of shame and dread of blame, one is not negligent; because of non-negligence, one respects and accords with wholesome speech and takes virtuous friends as companions. Because of having virtuous friends, one delights in seeing the noble ones, delights in hearing the true Dharma, and does not seek out the faults of others. Because of not seeking out the faults of others, faith, accordant speech, and diligence arise. Because of diligence, one is not restless, abides in restraint, and trains in the precepts. Because of training in the precepts, one does not lose mindfulness, possesses clear comprehension, and dwells in an undisturbed mind. Because of an undisturbed mind, one engages in right reflection, draws near to the True Path, and the mind does not become indolent. Because the mind is not indolent, one does not cling to the view of a self-identity, does not cling to attachment to rules and rituals, and crosses beyond doubt. Because of being free from doubt, one does not give rise to greed, hatred, or delusion. Being free from greed, hatred, and delusion, one is capable of severing old age, sickness, and death.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 347 (347) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.

If kings, ministers, brahmins, householders, laypeople, and other members of the world all together revere, respect, and make offerings to the Buddha and the assembly of his śrāvakas, providing them with great gains of robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites;
yet they do not at all revere, respect, or make offerings to the various heterodox paths, nor provide them with robes, food and drink, bedding, or medicinal requisites.
At that time, a great assembly of followers of various heterodox paths gathered in the Unprecedented Lecture Hall and held this discussion:
