"In the past, we have always been served, honored, and provided with robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites by kings, ministers, elders, householders, and all others; yet now all such offerings have ceased, and instead, only the śramaṇa Gautama and his assembly of disciples are honored and provided with robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites."

“Who among this assembly possesses wisdom and great strength, capable of going secretly into the midst of that śramaṇa Gautama’s followers to leave the household life, and having heard his Dharma, returning to proclaim it extensively? We shall then use that heard Dharma to transform the various kings, ministers, elders, and householders, causing them to have faith and joy, so that we may once again receive offerings as before.”
At that time, someone said:

"There is a young man named Susīma, who is clever and wise; he is capable of going secretly among the assembly of the śramaṇa Gautama to leave the household life, and having heard his Dharma, returning to proclaim it."
At that time, the various non-Buddhist practitioners went to where Susīma was and spoke as follows:
"Today, our great assembly gathered in the lecture hall and held this discussion:

'In the past, we were honored, served, and supported by kings, ministers, elders, householders, and the people of the world, who provided us with clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites; now all such support has been cut off, for kings, ministers, elders, householders, and the entire world are collectively serving the śramaṇa Gautama and his assembly of disciples.'"

"In this assembly of mine, who is clever and wise enough to go secretly among the followers of the śramaṇa Gautama to leave the household life and study the Path? Having heard his Dharma, they may return and proclaim it, converting kings, ministers, elders, and householders so that this assembly of mine may once again receive honor, respect, and offerings."
Among them, some said:

"Only one who is profoundly deep, intelligent, and wise would be capable of going secretly into the Dharma of Gautama to leave the household life and study the Path; having heard his teaching, being able to receive and uphold it all, and returning to proclaim it."
"Therefore, we have come specifically to invite you; O worthy one, you should go.
At that time, Susīma accepted the invitation in silence and proceeded to the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus were walking up and down on the open ground outside their lodgings.
Then, Susīma approached those many bhikṣus and spoke these words:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"May I now go forth in the True Dharma and receive full ordination, practicing the holy life?
Then, a great many bhikṣus led Susīma to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Now this outsider, Sudeva, desires deeply to go forth from home and receive full ordination within the True Dharma to practice the holy life.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the mind of the outsider Sudeva, addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should deliver that outsider Sudeva and enable him to go forth."
At that time, the bhikṣus wished to ordain Susīma.
After he had been ordained for half a month, one bhikṣu said to Susīma:
"Susīma, you should know: our saṃsāra is exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been done, and we know for ourselves that there will be no further existence."
Then, that bhikṣu Suśīla said:
"Venerable sir!
How is this so?"

By training to be detached from sensual desires and unwholesome, evil states, with directed thought and evaluation, born of seclusion, joyful and blissful, and fully attaining the first dhyāna, has he not given rise to any outflows, and is his mind well-liberated?
The bhikṣu replied, “No, Sūṣma!
He asked again:

"How is it? Having transcended applied thought and sustained thought, with internal purity and one-pointedness of mind, free from applied and sustained thought, possessing the joy and happiness born of concentration, and being fully endowed with the second dhyāna, does one not give rise to any outflows and achieve the complete liberation of the mind?"
The bhikṣu replied, “No, Susīma!
He asked again:

"How is it, Venerable One? Having been detached from joy, do you dwell with equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, experiencing happiness with the body—of which the Noble Ones say, 'One who dwells with equanimity and is mindful'—and thus, possessing the third dhyāna, are your mind well-liberated without giving rise to any outflows?"
He replied, “No, Susīma.
He asked again:

"How is it, Venerable One? Having abandoned both suffering and pleasure, and with the prior cessation of grief and joy, abiding in equanimity, pure mindfulness, and one-pointedness of mind, do you fulfill the fourth dhyāna and, with the non-arising of all outflows, possess a mind well-liberated?"
He replied, “No, Susīma.
He asked again:

“Furthermore, if one gives rise to form or the formless within peaceful liberation, realizes it with one’s own body, and dwells in its fulfillment, are the outflows not produced, and is the mind well-liberated?”
He replied, “No, Susīma. Susīma asked again:
"How is this? What the Venerable One has said is inconsistent; the earlier and the later contradict one another.
How can you bestow a prediction [of enlightenment] without having attained meditative concentration?"
The bhikṣu replied,
“I am one liberated through wisdom.
Having said this, many bhikṣus rose from their seats and departed.
At that time, having seen that the many bhikṣus had departed, Sūśruta reflected thus:

"The assertions of these venerable ones are inconsistent; they contradict one another from beginning to end. They claim not to have attained right concentration, yet they further declare that they know and testify to it for themselves."
Having reflected thus, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Those many bhikṣus declared in my presence: "Birth for us has been exhausted;
the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been done; we ourselves know that there will be no further existence."
I then asked that venerable one:
"Have you attained freedom from sensual desires and unwholesome states, up to and including realizing it with your own body, such that no taints arise and your mind is well-liberated?"
He replied to me, saying:
"No, Susīma! I then asked him:

"Your statements are inconsistent and your earlier and later words contradict one another; you say that you have not entered into meditative absorption (samāpatti), yet you further declare that you have personally realized and witnessed [the truth] for yourself.
He replied to me, "I have attained liberation through wisdom (prajñā-vimukti)."
Having spoken thus, they each rose from their seats and departed.
I now ask the World-Honored One:

"How is it that what they have said is inconsistent, with the earlier and the later contradicting one another, such that they do not attain right concentration, yet they further claim: [that they have attained it]?"
"Having known it for oneself, one realizes it.
The Buddha told Susīma:
"He first understands the persistence of phenomena, and subsequently understands Nirvana.

Those sons of good family, dwelling alone in a quiet place, contemplate with focused diligence; through the practice of heedfulness, they abandon the view of self and do not give rise to the outflows, their minds being well-liberated."
Susīma addressed the Buddha:
“I do not know how it was that they first knew the persistence of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhiti*) and subsequently knew nirvana.

Those sons of good family, dwelling alone in seclusion, with focused and diligent reflection, practiced the dharma of heedfulness; they were free from the view of self, did not give rise to the outflows (*āsrava*), and their minds were well-liberated.”
The Buddha told Susīma:
"Whether you know it or not is of no concern; rather, first understand the persistence of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhiti*), and afterwards understand *nirvāṇa*.

Those sons of good family, dwelling alone in a quiet place, with focused and diligent contemplation, abiding without negligence, and having abandoned the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*), have their minds well-liberated."
Susīma addressed the Buddha:

"I only pray that the World-Honored One will teach me the Dharma, so that I may come to know the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa) and attain the vision of the knowledge of the stability of phenomena."
The Buddha said to Susīma:
“I shall now question you; answer me as you see fit. Susīma!”
"What do you think?
Is it because there is birth that there is aging and death; is it not the case that aging and death are inseparable from birth? Suśīma replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
Because there is birth, there is aging and death; aging and death do not exist apart from birth.

Likewise, because there is becoming, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, volitional formations, and ignorance—because there is ignorance, there are volitional formations; do volitional formations not exist apart from ignorance?"
Susīma addressed the Buddha:
“So it is, World-Honored One!
Because of ignorance there are volitional formations; volitional formations do not exist apart from ignorance.”
The Buddha told Susīma:
"Because there is no birth, there is no aging and death; is it not by not being apart from the cessation of birth that aging and death cease?
Susīma addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
Because there is no birth, there is no aging and death; aging and death do not cease apart from the cessation of birth.
"So it is... down to: because there is no ignorance, there is no volitional formations; do volitional formations not cease apart from the cessation of ignorance?"
Susīma addressed the Buddha:
“So it is, World-Honored One!
Because there is no ignorance, there is no volitional formations; it is not apart from the cessation of ignorance that volitional formations cease.”
The Buddha told Susīma:

"For one who knows thus and sees thus, is there the state of being free from sensual desires and unwholesome, evil states, up to and including realizing it for oneself with the body and dwelling in its fulfillment?"
Susīma replied to the Buddha,
“No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Susīma:
"This is called first knowing the persistence of phenomena (*dharmasthiti*) and subsequently knowing nirvāṇa.

Those sons of good family, dwelling alone in a quiet place, with focused and diligent reflection, abiding in heedfulness, free from the view of self, and not giving rise to the outflows (*āsrava*), have their minds well-liberated."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Susīma was distanced from dust and free from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.

At that time, Susīma saw the Dharma, attained the Dharma, realized the Dharma, and transcended doubt; no longer relying on the faith of others and no longer relying on the deliverance of others, he attained fearlessness in his heart regarding the True Dharma. Bowing his head at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I now repent my transgression; I secretly joined the monastic order within the True Dharma by means of deception, and for this reason I repent.
The Buddha told Susīma:
"In what way did you secretly join the monastic order within the True Dharma?"
Susīma addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Many non-Buddhist practitioners have come to my place and said to me:"

"Suśīma, you should know this: formerly we were honored and provided for by kings, ministers, elders, householders, and other people of the world; now that has all ceased, and they instead collectively provide offerings to the śramaṇa Gautama and his assembly of śrāvakas."

"You should now go secretly among the śramaṇa Gautama and his assembly of disciples to leave the household life and receive the Dharma. Once you have obtained that Dharma, return and proclaim it to us; we shall then use that heard Dharma to transform the world, causing them to respect and make offerings to us as they did before."
"Therefore, World-Honored One!

I have gone forth as a secret thief within the True Dharma and Discipline. Today I repent my transgression; I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion, will grant me forgiveness for this repentance."
The Buddha told Susīma: “I accept your confession of transgression. You should speak fully thus:

‘In the past, I was foolish, unwholesome, and lacking wisdom; I secretly stole ordination into the True Dharma and Discipline. Today I confess my transgression; I recognize my fault and acknowledge my crime. In future lives, may I achieve restraint, increase in merit, and never again fall away.’”

Why is this so? If an ordinary person has committed an offense and, seeing and knowing it for themselves, repents their transgression, they will achieve restraint in future lives, their merit will increase, and they will never again fall away or diminish.
The Buddha told Susīma:
"I shall now speak a parable, for those with wisdom attain understanding through parables.
Suppose there were a king who had a patrolman who captured a thief, bound him, and brought him before the king, saying:"
"Great King!
This man has committed robbery; we pray that Your Majesty will punish him.
The King said:

"Take the sinner away, bind his two hands behind his back, and proclaim his wickedness with a harsh voice throughout the entire kingdom; then lead him out beyond the city walls to the place of execution and pierce his entire body and four limbs with a hundred spears."

The executioners, having received the king’s command, bound the hands of that criminal behind his back and, proclaiming his wicked deeds with a harsh voice, led him through the entire city to the place of execution outside the walls; there, they pierced his entire body and four limbs with a hundred spears.
At midday, the King asked,
"Is the criminal alive?
The minister replied:
"Revive! The king again commanded his ministers:
"Pierce him once more with a hundred spears."
"When the time of the afternoon meal arrived, he was again stabbed with a hundred spears, yet he still did not die.
The Buddha told Susīma:
"When that king punished the criminal by stabbing him with three hundred spears, would there have been any part of that man's body left intact, even as large as the palm of a hand?"
Susīma replied to the Buddha,
“No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha asked Susīma again:
“Would that sinner, by reason of being pierced with three hundred spears, experience suffering that is extreme and most intense?
Susīma replied to the Buddha,
“It would be extremely painful.”
“World-Honored One!
If one were struck by a single spear, the pain would be unbearable; how much more so for three hundred spears—could it possibly be endured?
The Buddha told Susīma:

"This may still be tolerable, but if one secretly leaves the home life by stealing from the True Dharma and Discipline, or steals the teachings to uphold them and proclaim them to others, they shall suffer pain many times greater than that."

When the Buddha had spoken this Dharma, the outsider Suśīma attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind. After the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Suśīma, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
348. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“The Tathāgata has accomplished the ten powers, attained the four fearlessnesses, knows the dwelling places of former Buddhas, and is able to turn the Brahma-wheel, uttering the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, saying:

‘Because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises—namely, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise…’” This is explained at length until: “Thus there is the arising of this entire great mass of suffering; thus there is the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.”
"O bhikṣus! This is the manifestation of the true teaching that cuts off the stream of birth and death, until that person has fully manifested it.

Such a manifestation of the true teaching that cuts off the stream of birth and death is sufficient to cause a son of good family to leave the household life with right faith, to practice skillful means, to dwell without negligence, and to apply himself with diligent asceticism to the True Dharma and Vinaya, until his skin, sinews, and bones remain standing while his flesh and blood are withered away."
If one has not yet attained what ought to be attained, one does not abandon diligent and energetic effort, but remains firm and capable through skillful means. Why is this?

Because dwelling in indolence is a state of suffering that gives rise to various evil and unwholesome dharmas; it causes the fetters of future existence to blaze and increase, leading to birth, old age, sickness, and death in future lives, thereby causing one to fall away from the Great Purpose.

One who exerts diligence and delights in dwelling alone does not give rise to various evil and unwholesome states, nor to the fetters of future existence or the blazing retribution of suffering. Such a person does not increase birth, aging, sickness, and death in future lives; their great purpose is fulfilled, and they attain the field of the foremost teaching.

That is to say, in the presence of the Great Teacher, one has personally received his teaching on the extinction of nirvana, the direct path to enlightenment, the Well-Gone One, and the Perfectly Awakened One.
Therefore, O bhikṣus!

One should contemplate one's own benefit, the benefit of others, and the benefit of both self and others, and apply oneself with diligence to training. Having now gone forth from the household life, I am neither deluded nor confused; there is fruit and there is happiness. All those who provide offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites shall all obtain great fruit, great merit, and great benefit. One should train in this manner.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 349 (349). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: “Welcome, bhikṣus!

You have left the home life well; you have well attained your own benefit. At long intervals throughout the ages, one is born in a noble place, with all faculties complete, neither dull nor deluded, not requiring hand gestures, and capable of understanding the meaning of both good and bad speech.”

I am now a Buddha in this world—a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān—teaching the Dharma of cessation, nirvāṇa, and the right path toward bodhi, the state of the Sugata and the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

That is to say: because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises. Namely, conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations; conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness, and so on, until the entire great mass of suffering arises. When ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease; and so on, until the entire great mass of suffering ceases.

“O bhikṣus! That which is difficult to obtain has been obtained; you have been born in a noble place with all faculties complete, [and thus] the entire mass of great suffering has arisen, and the entire mass of great suffering will cease.”
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should train yourselves thus: for your own benefit, for the benefit of others, and for the benefit of both self and others.

Thus departing from the household life, one is neither deluded nor foolish; there is fruit and happiness, and the karmic retribution of happiness. Those who provide offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites shall all obtain great fruit, great merit, and great benefit.
"Therefore, bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves in this way.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
350. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“A well-heard noble disciple does not think:
‘Because of what existing does this exist?
Because of what arising does this arise?’”
"Because what does not exist is this not?
Because what ceases is this ceased?

However, that learned noble disciple knows: "Because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises"—namely, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be, and so on, until there is the arising of this entire great mass of suffering. "Because ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease," and so on, until there is the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 351 (351) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Venerable Nara, the Venerable Mausrila, the Venerable Viśeṣa, and the Venerable Ānanda were staying at Śrāvastī beside the Elephant-Ear Pond.
At that time, the Venerable Nāla said to the Venerable Mūsila:

"There are differences in faith, differences in aspiration, differences in learning, differences in conduct, perceptions, and views, and differences in the certainty of conviction; yet there arises such a right self-awakened knowledge and vision, namely: 'Because of birth there is aging and death; is it not the case that apart from birth there is aging and death?'"
The Venerable Māṭhara said:

"There are distinct faiths, distinct desires, distinct learning, distinct perceptions and conceptions of practice, and distinct views of definitive certainty; there arises such a right self-awakened knowledge and vision, namely: 'Because birth exists, aging and death exist; apart from birth, there is no aging and death.'"
"Thus you say that 'it exists. Venerable Mūsila!

Is there another kind of faith, and so on, up to another kind of tolerance, through which the realization, knowledge, and vision arises that there is the cessation of existence, its stilling, and nirvāṇa?"
The Venerable Maudgalyāyana replied:
“There is a distinct faith, and so on, up to a distinct resolve, by which one attains self-realization and vision regarding what is called the cessation of existence, its stilling, and nirvāṇa.”
He asked again:
"Venerable Mūsila!
Since there is cessation, which is quiescence and nirvāṇa, are you now, as you say, an arhat whose outflows are exhausted?"
The Venerable Maudgalyāyana remained silent and did not answer; though asked a second and a third time, he likewise remained silent and did not answer.
Then, the Venerable Viśeṣagāmin said to the Venerable Maudgalyāyana:
"Cease for a moment; I shall answer the Venerable Nārada on your behalf."
The Venerable Maudgalyāyana said:
"I shall now desist; you answer for me.
At that time, the Venerable Viśeṣagāmin addressed the Venerable Nārada:

“There is a distinct faith, and so on, up to a distinct acceptance, through which the arising of self-realized knowledge and vision occurs—namely, that with the cessation of existence comes peace and *nirvāṇa*.
Then, the Venerable Nara asked the Venerable Viśeṣagāmin:

“Regarding this distinct faith, and so on, up to a distinct acceptance, through which the arising of self-realized knowledge and vision occurs—namely, that with the cessation of existence comes peace and *nirvāṇa*—are you now an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted?”
The Venerable Viśeṣa said:
"I say that the cessation of existence is quiescence and nirvāṇa, but it is not the arhatship of one whose outflows are exhausted.
The Venerable Nara said:

“Your explanations are inconsistent and your earlier and later statements contradict one another. According to what you have said, the cessation of existence is itself nirvāṇa; yet you further say that it is not the state of an Arhat who has exhausted all outflows?”
The Venerable Viśeṣagāmin addressed the Venerable Nara, saying:

"I shall now provide a simile, for the wise attain understanding through similes. Suppose there were a well by the side of a road in a vast wilderness, yet it had neither rope nor bucket, so that its water could not be drawn."

At that time, there was a traveler, oppressed by heat and thirst, who wandered around the well searching for water; finding neither rope nor bucket, he gazed intently at the well-water and perceived it as it truly is, yet it did not touch his body.
"In this way, I say that where there is cessation, there is peace and *nirvāṇa*, yet I myself have not attained the state of an Arhat with outflows exhausted.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Venerable Nara:
"Regarding what the Venerable Viśeṣa has said, what do you say?"
The Venerable Nara said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Venerable One, you have excellently spoken the truth; what more need be said?
Then, having each spoken thus, those noble ones rose from their seats and departed.
352. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

“If any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas do not know phenomena as they really are, and do not know the arising of phenomena, the cessation of phenomena, and the path leading to the cessation of phenomena as they really are, they are not śramaṇas nor counted among the śramaṇas; they are not brāhmaṇas nor counted among the brāhmaṇas; and they do not possess the goal of a śramaṇa or the goal of a brāhmaṇa, whereby one sees the Dharma for oneself and realizes:
‘Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and I myself know that there will be no further existence.’”
"What is the dharma that one does not know as it really is?
What is the origin of the dharma that one does not know as it really is?
What is the cessation of the dharma that one does not know as it really is?"
What is the failure to know, as it truly is, the path leading to the cessation of phenomena?

It refers to not knowing, as it truly is, the phenomenon of aging and death; not knowing, as it truly is, the origin of aging and death, the cessation of aging and death, and the path leading to the cessation of aging and death.

In this way, one does not know as they really are birth, existence, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, and the six sense bases; nor does one know as they really are the arising of the six sense bases, the cessation of the six sense bases, and the path leading to the cessation of the six sense bases.
Thus, these phenomena are not known as they truly are; the arising of phenomena, the cessation of phenomena, and the path leading to the cessation of phenomena are not known as they truly are.

"If any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas know phenomena as they truly are, and know the arising of phenomena, the cessation of phenomena, and the path leading to the cessation of phenomena as they truly are, you should know that those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are reckoned among the ranks of true śramaṇas and true brāhmaṇas."
By means of the meaning of a śramaṇa and the meaning of a brāhmaṇa, he has seen the Dharma and known it for himself, realizing:
"Birth for me has been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence."
“What phenomena are to be known as they really are?
What phenomena are to be known as they really are in their arising, their cessation, and the path leading to their cessation?

It is said that one knows old age and death as they really are; one knows the arising of old age and death, the cessation of old age and death, and the path leading to the cessation of old age and death as they really are.”

In this way, one knows birth, existence, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, and the six sense bases as they truly are; one knows the arising of the six sense bases, the cessation of the six sense bases, and the path leading to the cessation of the six sense bases as they truly are.
"In this way, one knows these phenomena as they truly are; one knows the arising of phenomena, the cessation of phenomena, and the path leading to the cessation of phenomena as they truly are.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
353. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas do not know the Dharma as it truly is, nor know the origination of the Dharma, the cessation of the Dharma, and the path leading to the cessation of the Dharma as they truly are, you should know that these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas do not belong to the number of those who are śramaṇas among śramaṇas, nor to the number of those who are brāhmaṇas among brāhmaṇas; they possess neither the meaning of a śramaṇa nor the meaning of a brāhmaṇa. [Only those] see the Dharma and know for themselves, realizing:
'Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and I myself know that there will be no further existence.'"
“What phenomena are not known as they really are?
What is the arising of phenomena, their cessation, and the path leading to their cessation that is not known as it really is?

It is this: to claim that one does not know the six sense bases as they really are, nor the arising of the six sense bases, their cessation, and the path leading to their cessation, yet claims to know contact as it really is—this is impossible. To claim that one knows contact as it really is, yet does not know the arising of contact, its cessation, and the path leading to its cessation—this is impossible.”
"It is impossible that one who perceives feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age and death as they truly are would not [attain liberation].

However, it is possible for a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who knows the six sense bases as they truly are, who knows the arising of the six sense bases, the cessation of the six sense bases, and the path leading to the cessation of the six sense bases as they truly are, to know contact as it truly is."
"It is possible for one who knows feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death as they truly are.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
354 (Three Hundred and Fifty-Four). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus... as explained above.
As for the distinction:

"If any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas do not know the six sense bases as they truly are, yet wish to transcend contact, that is impossible; it is impossible to transcend the arising of contact, the cessation of contact, and the path leading to the cessation of contact."

It is impossible for one to transcend feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age and death; it is impossible for one to transcend the origin of old age and death, the cessation of old age and death, and the path leading to the cessation of old age and death.

If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa knows the six sense bases as they truly are, knows the arising of the six sense bases, the cessation of the six sense bases, and the path leading to the cessation of the six sense bases as they truly are, and thereby transcends contact—this is possible.
It is possible for one to thus transcend feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age and death; it is even possible to transcend the path leading to the cessation of old age and death.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As with the discourse on old age and death, so it was for the three discourses up to the six sense bases.
In this same way, the three sūtras concerning old age and death, up to those concerning volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), are also spoken thus. 355 (355) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

“One should clearly understand aging and death; one should clearly understand the origin of aging and death, the cessation of aging and death, and the path leading to the cessation of aging and death.”

In this way, one should come to fully understand volitional formations, the arising of volitional formations, the cessation of volitional formations, and the path leading to the cessation of volitional formations.
"How should one come to fully understand aging and death?"
One understands that because of dependent origination there is aging and death; thus one understands aging and death.
What is the arising of aging and death?
The arising of birth is the arising of aging and death; thus one understands the arising of aging and death.
What is the knowledge of the cessation of aging and death?
It is that the cessation of birth is the cessation of aging and death; such is the knowledge of the cessation of aging and death.
What is the knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of aging and death?

It is said that the Noble Eightfold Path is the track leading to the cessation of aging and death; thus one awakens to the track leading to the cessation of aging and death. ... [down to] ... how does one awaken to practice?
It is by means of the three types of formations: bodily formations, verbal formations, and mental formations; thus one awakens to practice.
What is the awakening to the origination of volitional formations?
It is that the origination of ignorance is the origination of volitional formations; such is the awakening to the origination of volitional formations.
What is the awakening to the cessation of volitional formations?
With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations; thus one understands the cessation of volitional formations.
What is the understanding of the path leading to the cessation of volitional formations?
It is the Noble Eightfold Path that is the path leading to the cessation of volitional formations; thus one understands the path leading to the cessation of volitional formations.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
356 (356) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are forty-four kinds of knowledge.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall explain them for you."
What are the forty-four kinds of knowledge? They are:
knowledge of aging and death, knowledge of the origin of aging and death, knowledge of the cessation of aging and death, and knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of aging and death.

In this way, there is knowledge of birth, becoming, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, and volitional formations; knowledge of the origination of volitional formations, knowledge of the cessation of volitional formations, and knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of volitional formations—these are called the forty-four kinds of knowledge.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 357 (357) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are seventy-seven kinds of knowledge.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall explain them for you."
What are the seventy-seven kinds of knowledge? They are: the knowledge of birth as the condition for aging-and-death, and not the knowledge of anything else as the condition for aging-and-death;
the knowledge of past birth as the condition for aging-and-death, and not the knowledge of anything else in the past as the condition for aging-and-death;
the knowledge of future birth as the condition for aging-and-death, and not the knowledge of anything else in the future as the condition for aging-and-death.

And the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*), which is the knowledge of the abandonment [of defilements] regarding impermanence, conditioned states, that which is produced by the mind as its object, the nature of exhaustion, the nature of change, the nature of dispassion, and the nature of cessation.

Thus, there is knowledge of birth, becoming, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, volitional formations, and the conditionality of volitional formations through ignorance; it is not knowledge of anything other than the conditionality of volitional formations through ignorance.
There is knowledge of past volitional formations conditioned by past ignorance; it is not knowledge of anything other than past volitional formations conditioned by past ignorance.
There is knowledge of future volitional formations conditioned by future ignorance; it is not knowledge of anything other than future volitional formations conditioned by future ignorance.

And the knowledge of the persistence of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*), which is the knowledge of cessation regarding impermanence, conditioned states, that which arises from the mind as its object, that which is subject to exhaustion, that which is subject to change, that which is subject to dispassion, and that which is subject to cessation—these are called the seventy-seven kinds of knowledge.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 358 (358). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are dharmas that increase and dharmas that decrease.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you."
What are the phenomena of increase?

That is to say: because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises. Namely, conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations; conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness, and so on, until the entire great mass of suffering arises. These are called the phenomena of increase.
What is the dharma of diminution?

It means that because this does not exist, that does not exist; because this ceases, that ceases. That is to say: with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease, and so on, until the entire great mass of suffering ceases. This is called the dharma of diminution.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As with the teachings on the increase and decrease of phenomena,
so it was with the teachings on arising phenomena, changing phenomena, originating phenomena, and ceasing phenomena, as explained above.
As with the three sūtras to be explained hereafter, there are three other sūtras that should be understood as being as previously described. 359 (359). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If discursive thought or false conceptualization arises, the underlying tendencies take that as an object and consciousness dwells therein;
because consciousness dwells by taking an object, there is birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering in future lives."
In this way, this entire great mass of suffering arises.
If one does not reflect upon it and does not conceptualize it, there is no causal condition for consciousness to dwell, nor an object of clinging for consciousness to dwell upon.

Because consciousness has no object of clinging to dwell upon, birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, vexation, and suffering will cease in future lives; in this way, this entire great mass of suffering ceases.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 360 (360) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“If there is deliberation or conceptualization, then there is the proclivity for consciousness to find a basis and dwell;
because consciousness finds a basis and dwells, one enters into name-and-form.”
Because of entry into name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), there are birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering in future lives.

Thus occurs this entire great mass of suffering. If one does not engage in deliberation and is without conceptual proliferation (*papañca*), there will be no underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and no object of attachment for consciousness to dwell upon.

Because consciousness does not dwell upon an object, it does not enter into name-and-form. Because it does not enter into name-and-form, birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering cease; thus, this entire great mass of suffering ceases.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
361 (361) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If there is deliberation and there is conceptualization, then there is the latent tendency for consciousness to dwell by way of an object.
Because consciousness dwells by way of an object, one enters into name-and-form."
Because of entry into name-and-form, there is coming and going;
because of coming and going, there is birth and death;
because of birth and death, there is future existence, along with birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering.

In this way, this entire great mass of suffering arises. If one does not engage in deliberation or conceptual proliferation, there will be no underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and no consciousness abiding through grasping (*ālambana*).
Because consciousness does not abide through grasping, it does not enter into name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Because it does not enter into name-and-form, there is no coming and going.
Because there is no coming and going, there is no birth and death;

because there is no birth and death, birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering are extinguished in future lives, and thus this entire great mass of suffering is extinguished.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
362 (362) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There is the learned bhikṣu.
In what way does the Tathāgata designate one as a learned bhikṣu?"
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“The World-Honored One is the root of the Dharma, the eye of the Dharma, and the refuge of the Dharma.
We pray that you will explain what it means to be a ‘bhikṣu of much learning’; having heard it, the bhikṣus shall receive and practice it accordingly.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you.
O bhikṣus!”
If there is a bhikṣu who, upon hearing of old age, sickness, and death, gives rise to revulsion, detachment from desire, and the realization of their cessation, he is called a learned bhikṣu.

Likewise, if he gives rise to revulsion, detachment from desire, and the realization of the cessation of birth, existence, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, and volitional formations, he is called a learned bhikṣu; this is what the Tathāgata designates as a learned bhikṣu.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
363 (363) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Regarding what is called a 'bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma,' how is one a bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma?
How does the Tathāgata designate a bhikṣu as a preacher of the Dharma?"
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One, you are the root of the Dharma, the eye of the Dharma, and the refuge of the Dharma.
We pray that you will explain what it means to be a ‘bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma’; having heard it, the bhikṣus shall receive and practice it accordingly.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"If there is a bhikṣu who speaks of old age, sickness, and death, and teaches the Dharma for the sake of engendering revulsion, detachment from desire, and cessation, he is called a bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma."

Thus, one who teaches that birth, becoming, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, and volitional formations are subject to disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation—such a person is called a monk who teaches the Dharma.
“Monks! This is what is called a monk who speaks the Dharma as established by the Tathāgata.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the monks, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
364. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"It refers to 'progressing in accordance with the Dharma. Monks!
What is meant by 'progressing in accordance with the Dharma'?"

“The World-Honored One is the root of the Dharma, the eye of the Dharma, and the refuge of the Dharma.
Excellent!”
“World-Honored One!
We only pray that you will explain this for us; having heard it, the bhikṣus shall receive and practice it accordingly.

“Monks! This is called the Dharma established by the Tathāgata that leads in accordance with the Dharma.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the monks, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

15.365 (365) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"It is said that one attains parinirvāṇa by seeing the Dharma in this very life.
How does the Tathāgata describe one who attains parinirvāṇa by seeing the Dharma in this very life?"
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha:
“The World-Honored One is the root of the Dharma, the eye of the Dharma, and the refuge of the Dharma.
Excellent!”
“World-Honored One!
We only pray that you will explain for us the parinirvāṇa in this very life, so that upon hearing it, the bhikṣus may receive and practice it accordingly.
How does a bhikṣu attain parinirvāṇa in this very life?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you.

If there is a bhikṣu who, regarding old age, sickness, and death, feels weary of them, becomes free from desire for them, and brings about their cessation, such that no taints arise and his mind is well-liberated—this is called a bhikṣu who has attained parinirvāṇa in this very life.”
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
366 (366) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"When Vipaśyin Buddha had not yet attained perfect enlightenment, he dwelt alone in a quiet place, applying himself with diligence to meditative reflection, and formed this thought:

'All in the world enter into birth and death; they are born by themselves and matured by themselves, and they perish and sink by themselves. Yet those sentient beings do not know, as it truly is, the supramundane path that leads beyond old age and death.'"
He then observed for himself:
"By what condition does this aging and death exist?
Through such correct reflection and observation, he attained knowledge of reality as it is, arising without interval:
"Because there is birth, there is this old age and death; conditioned by birth, there is old age and death.
He then reflected correctly:
"Conditioned by what is there this birth?"
He then further applied correct reflection and, through immediate and thorough realization, knew:
"Conditioned by existence (bhava), there is birth (jāti).
He then further applied correct reflection:
"For what reason is there existence?
He then further engaged in correct contemplation and, through immediate and thorough knowledge as it truly is, realized:

“What is the cause of these four nutriments? What is their origin? What gives rise to them? What is their condition?

What is the cause of this craving? What is its origin? What is its arising?
What is its condition? It is said: craving has feeling as its cause, feeling as its origin, feeling as its arising, and feeling as its condition.
What is the cause of this feeling? What is its origin? What is its arising? What is its condition?

That is to say, feeling has contact as its cause, contact as its origin, contact as its arising, and contact as its condition. Of this contact, what is the cause, what is the origin, what is the arising, and what is the condition?
That is to say, contact has the six sense bases as its cause, the six sense bases as its origin, the six sense bases as its arising, and the six sense bases as its condition.

In this way, there is the arising of this entire great mass of suffering.

"In this way, with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, sustenance ceases. Once the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya had understood the Dharma, the Earth Deity raised her voice and proclaimed:
"O noble ones!

In the country of Vārāṇasī, at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Sages, the Blessed One has turned the Wheel of Dharma with its three revolutions and twelve aspects—a wheel that has never before been turned by any śramaṇa, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā. It brings great benefit, brings great peace and happiness, out of compassion for the world; it benefits through the truth, bringing profit, peace, and security to gods and humans, increasing the hosts of devas and diminishing the hosts of asuras."

After the earth deity had proclaimed this, the proclamation was heard by the deities of the space realm, the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, who passed it on in succession until, in a mere moment, it reached the body of Brahmā.
Brahmā, mounting his voice, proclaimed:

"O worthy ones, the World-Honored One, at the Abode of the Sages in the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī, has turned the Wheel of Dharma with its three revolutions and twelve aspects—a wheel that no śramaṇa, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā, nor anyone else in the world, has ever turned before hearing this Dharma. It brings great benefit and great peace; it benefits all devas and humans through its meaning, increasing the hosts of devas and diminishing the hosts of asuras."
The World-Honored One turned the Wheel of Dharma at the Deer Park, the Abode of Sages, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī; therefore, this sutra is titled the "Sutra on Turning the Wheel of Dharma."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

387 (387). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four noble truths. What are the four?

That is to say: the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

If a bhikṣu has already known and understood the noble truth of suffering; has already known and abandoned the noble truth of the origin of suffering; has already known and realized the noble truth of the cessation of suffering; and has already known and cultivated the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, monks, being without bolts or bars, having leveled the moats and crossed over all steep difficulties, they are called noble sages who have raised the banner of the holy ones. Monks!
What is meant by "there being no bolt"?
It refers to the five lower fetters having been abandoned and fully understood; this is called "being free from the bolt.
What is meant by "leveling the moat of the city"? Ignorance is called the deep moat; when that is abandoned and fully understood, it is called "leveling the moat of the city."
What is meant by "crossing over all perils and difficulties"?
It refers to reaching the ultimate end of suffering within the boundless cycle of birth and death; this is called crossing over all perils and difficulties.
What is meant by "liberation from fetters and bonds"?
It means that craving has been abandoned and fully understood.
How is the noble banner established?
It means that the conceit "I am" has been abandoned and fully understood; this is called establishing the noble banner.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
388 (388). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.

389 (389) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four qualities which, when perfected, constitute one who is called a Great King of Physicians; these are the requisites of a king and the attributes of a king."
What are the four?

First, skillfully knowing the illness; second, skillfully knowing the origin of the illness; third, skillfully knowing the remedy for the illness; and fourth, skillfully knowing how, once the illness has been treated, it shall not recur or arise again in the future.
What is meant by a skilled physician who thoroughly understands diseases?
It means that a skilled physician thoroughly understands such and such various kinds of diseases; this is called a skilled physician who thoroughly understands diseases.
What is meant by a skilled physician who well understands the origins of disease?

It means that a skilled physician well understands that this disease arises from wind, arises from phlegm-humor, arises from saliva, arises from various cold-natures, arises from present circumstances, or arises from the seasons; this is called a skilled physician who well understands the origins of disease.
What is meant by a skilled physician who well understands the remedies for diseases?

It means that a skilled physician well understands various diseases and knows when one should apply medicinal ointments, induce vomiting, administer purgatives, apply nasal drops, perform fumigation, or induce perspiration.
Such various remedies as these are called the physician’s skillful knowledge of counteractive measures.
How does the physician, having skillfully treated the disease, ensure that it never recurs in future lives?

This means that a skilled physician effectively treats various illnesses, ensuring they are eradicated completely so that they never arise again in the future; this is called a skilled physician who thoroughly understands the treatment of diseases such that they are never provoked or reactivated.
“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is the Great King of Physicians; his accomplishment of the four virtues in healing the illnesses of sentient beings is likewise so.
What are these four?

That is to say, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, that "this is the noble truth of suffering"; he knows, as it truly is, that "this is the noble truth of the origin of suffering"; he knows, as it truly is, that "this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering"; and he knows, as it truly is, that "this is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering."

"Monks! Those physicians of the world do not know, as it truly is, the remedy for the root of birth; they do not know, as it truly is, the remedy for the roots of old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering. The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is the Great King of Physicians; he knows, as it truly is, the remedy for the root of birth, and he knows, as it truly is, the remedy for the roots of old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering. For this reason, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is called the Great King of Physicians."

The same applies to the *anupādāya-parinirvāṇa* (attaining nirvana without clinging), which is also spoken of in this way. 395 (395) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“If the sun and moon did not appear in the world, none of the various stars would appear in the world either. The world would be perpetually shrouded in darkness, lacking any luminous illumination; there would be only a long night, and the great suffering of total obscurity would prevail in the world.”

If a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha does not appear in the world, then the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering are not proclaimed and do not appear in the world; the world remains blind and dark, devoid of illumination.
Thus, for a long night, there appeared in the world only great darkness.

When the sun and moon emerged in the world, the various stars also appeared; day and night, the half-months, the months, the seasons, the years, the *kṣaṇas*, and the *muhūrtas* all appeared in the world, and the long night was illuminated as they emerged into the world.

In this way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world; he proclaims the Noble Truth of Suffering to the world, and the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering appear in the world. No longer shrouded in darkness, there is illumination throughout the long night, as pure wisdom appears in the world.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 396 (396) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park, the Abode of the Sages.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"It is like the rising of the sun, which travels throughout the sky, destroying all darkness and illuminating everything with its brilliant light."

In this way, when all phenomena subject to arising have been extinguished for the noble disciple, they become free from all dust and defilement; the Dharma-eye arises, they attain clear realization, and the three fetters are simultaneously severed.

That which is called the view of a self, attachment to precepts and rituals, and doubt—when these three fetters are exhausted, one is named a *srotāpanna*. Such a person is no longer subject to rebirth in the miserable realms, is destined for perfect awakening, and will undergo seven more births among gods and humans before making an end to suffering.

Even though that noble disciple may experience mental distress and physical pain in the interim, one should listen as that noble disciple—free from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, and filled with the joy and happiness born of seclusion—abides fully established in the first dhyāna.

It is not seen that there is even a single dharma which that noble disciple has not abandoned yet is capable of causing rebirth in this world; this is the great significance of the noble disciple’s attainment of the Dharma-eye.
Therefore, monks, those who have not yet attained the direct realization of these Four Noble Truths should apply themselves with skillful means, arouse a superior desire, and train with diligence.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
397 (397) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Abode of the Sages in the Deer Park near Bārāṇasī.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus: "One should speak thus:

'I have not yet attained immediate and perfect realization regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering; I have not yet attained immediate and perfect realization regarding the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering and the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.'"
To say, "I shall attain the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering through immediate realization," is an improper statement. Why?
Because such a thing is impossible.

"If one has not attained direct realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, and the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, yet desires to attain direct realization regarding the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering—that is impossible."
For example, suppose someone were to say, "I wish to take *khadira* leaves, assemble them to make a vessel, fill it with water, and carry it while traveling"—this is impossible. Why is that?
Because such a thing is impossible:

it is impossible that one who has not attained direct realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, and the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, should desire to attain direct realization of the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Such a thing cannot exist.

"If, moreover, there should be one who says: 'I have already attained the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, and the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and I shall further attain the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering,' this would indeed be well-spoken."
Why is this? Because such a case exists.

"If, having attained direct realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, and the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, one then desires to attain direct realization regarding the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering—that is indeed possible."
For example, if someone were to say, "I shall collect pure *tāla* leaves and *māluka* leaves, fill them with water, and carry them along," this would be a well-spoken statement. Why is that?
Because such a possibility exists,

it is rightly said that if one has attained direct realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, yet desires to attain direct realization regarding the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering, this is a correct statement.
Why is this? Because such a possibility exists:

it is possible that after one has attained direct realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, and the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, one then seeks to attain direct realization regarding the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Such a thing is indeed possible.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 398 (398) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Suppose a small ball of cotton or a small ball of *karpāsa* flower were placed at a crossroads; when the winds from the four directions blow upon it, it would be carried by the wind toward one direction."

In this way, if a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa does not know the noble truth of suffering as it truly is, and does not know the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering as they truly are, it should be known that such a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa constantly observes the faces of others and constantly follows what others say. Because they do not know things as they truly are, when they hear what is said, they accept it merely by following the speaker; it should be known that this person has not previously cultivated wisdom.
"Just as an Indra-pillar made of copper or iron, when firmly driven into the earth, cannot be moved by the fierce winds from the four directions;

even so, those recluses and brahmins who know the noble truth of suffering as it really is, and who know the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering as they really are—know that these recluses and brahmins do not look to the faces of others, nor do they follow the words of others."
These śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas possess firm wisdom; because they have followed their original training, they do not follow the words of others.
Therefore, bhikṣus!
You should apply yourselves diligently to skillful means regarding the Four Noble Truths, giving rise to superior desire and practicing with vigor.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 399 (399) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Suppose there were a stone pillar sixteen cubits long, with eight cubits buried in the ground; even if winds blow from the four directions, they could not cause it to move."

In this way, those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who know the noble truth of suffering as it really is, and who know the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering as they really are—such śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas cannot be defeated when they arrive at any place of debate.
One whose mind is liberated and whose wisdom is liberated can cause other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas to give rise to sorrow and suffering.
To know and see this as it truly is—that all such things are due to habitual tendencies from previous lives—is what renders one’s wisdom unshakable.
"Therefore, monks,
you should apply yourselves with diligent skillful means to the Four Noble Truths, giving rise to superior desire and training with vigor.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the monks, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
400. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Suppose there were a person whose head or clothing were on fire; they should arouse an exceptional desire and strive with urgency to extinguish it."
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"Do not speak thus!
You should set aside your head-cloth and, regarding the Four Noble Truths, give rise to superior desire, apply yourself diligently with skillful means, and cultivate uninterrupted realization."
What are the four?

They are the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Regarding these which have not yet been fully realized through immediate insight (*abhisamaya*), one should diligently apply skillful means to cultivate such immediate insight.
Why is that? Bhikṣus!
For a long night, hell, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts have been ablaze.

"O monks! As long as one has not yet attained immediate and perfect realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering—seeing them as the ultimate suffering—one should endure physical pain, pleasure, grief, and lamentation. One should apply oneself with diligence to these Four Noble Truths and train in the skillful means of practicing until immediate and perfect realization is attained."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
401 (401) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Suppose there were a man one hundred years of age, and someone were to say to him:

'If you, O man, wish to hear the Dharma, you must undergo suffering three times each day; at dawn you shall endure the pain of a hundred spears, and at midday and in the late afternoon, it shall be the same.'"
"One undergoes the suffering of three hundred spears in a single day.
If this continues day after day for a hundred years, and only then hears the Dharma and attains the realization of the Path of No-Interval (anupadhiśeṣa), would you be able to endure it?"
“At that time, that man was fully capable of enduring it for the sake of hearing the Dharma. Why is this?
A person born into this world suffers through the long night;

at times in hell, at times as an animal, and at times as a hungry ghost, one undergoes manifold sufferings in the three evil realms without ever hearing the Dharma. Therefore, for the sake of attaining immediate realization (*abhisamaya*), I do not consider enduring three hundred spears throughout my life to be a great suffering.”
Therefore, bhikṣus!

Those who have not yet attained direct realization (abhisamaya) regarding the Four Noble Truths should apply themselves with diligent skillful means, arouse superior desire, and train in direct realization.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
402 (402) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Abode of the Sages in the Deer Park near Bārāṇasī.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"One who has attained equal and perfect enlightenment regarding the Four Noble Truths is called a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha."
What are these four?

They are the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
One who has attained perfect and equal enlightenment regarding these four noble truths is called a Tathāgata, an Arhat, and a Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Therefore, monks, those who have not yet attained uninterrupted realization regarding the Four Noble Truths should apply themselves with diligent means, arouse superior desire, and train in uninterrupted equanimity.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
403 (Four Hundred and Three) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of Magadha, between Rājagṛha and Pāṭaliputra, at the village of Veṇugrāmaka, where the king had built a house of merit.
At that time, the World-Honored One stayed for the night among the great assembly.
Then, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If you and I were ignorant of the Four Noble Truths, lacked vision of them, lacked compliant awakening to them, and lacked compliant acceptance of them, we would have been driven through birth and death for a long night."
What are these four?

They are the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

Because both you and I have correctly understood and correctly entered into this Noble Truth of Suffering, we have severed all taints of existence, brought an end to all birth and death, and shall not undergo further existence.

He correctly understood and correctly entered into the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering; he severed all taints of existence, brought an end to all birth and death, and would not undergo further existence.
