Those who have not yet attained the immediate realization of the Four Noble Truths should apply themselves with diligent skillful means, arouse superior desire, and cultivate immediate realization.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"I have always been with you all, Wandering through birth and death for a long night;
Because you have not seen the Noble Truths, Great suffering increases day by day."
"If one perceives the Four Noble Truths, One cuts off the great flood and ocean of existence;
Birth and death are forever eliminated, And one shall no longer undergo future rebirth.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
404 (Four Hundred and Four). Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of Magadha. Between Rājagṛha and Pāṭaliputra, there was a village called Veṇugrāmaka, where the Great King had built a hall for the accumulation of merit.
At that time, the World-Honored One stayed overnight there with the great assembly.
Then, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should set out together and go to the Śiṃśapā Grove."
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly, arrived at the Śiṃśapā Grove and sat beneath a tree.
Then, the World-Honored One took some leaves in his hand and addressed the bhikṣus:
"Are these leaves in my hand more numerous, or [the leaves on the trees]?"
"Which is more numerous: the leaves on the great forest trees?
The bhikṣu replied to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"

The leaves in my hand are very few, whereas the leaves in that great forest are immeasurable—hundreds of thousands of millions of times more, such that even calculation or analogy cannot compare them.
“In this way, monks!
The Dharma that I have realized through my own perfect enlightenment and which I have definitively taught to others is like the leaves on a tree in my hand.”

Why is that? Because those teachings are beneficial in meaning, beneficial in the Dharma, and beneficial for the holy life; they lead to clarity, wisdom, and perfect awakening, and are directed toward Nirvana.
It is like the leaves of a great forest tree: that which I have not spoken of, even though I have attained perfect enlightenment and personally realized the True Dharma, is likewise so. Why is this?

That teaching does not provide benefit in terms of the Dharma, nor benefit in terms of the non-Dharma, nor benefit in terms of the holy life, nor in terms of clear knowledge, wisdom, perfect enlightenment, or the direct path to Nirvana.

Therefore, monks, those who have not yet attained the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Four Noble Truths should apply themselves with diligent skillful means, arouse superior desire, and train in direct realization.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
405 (405) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, by the side of the Monkey Pond, in the Multi-storied Lecture Hall.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl, entered the city of Vaiśālī to beg for alms.

At that moment, a great number of Licchavi youths were leaving the city in the morning and arrived at the gate of the vihāra; carrying bows and arrows, they vied with one another to shoot through the keyhole of the gate, and every arrow passed straight through.
Having seen this, the Venerable Ānanda marveled at how extraordinary it was that those Licchavi youths were capable of such a difficult feat.

Having entered the city for alms and returned with his robe and bowl, he washed his feet, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! [They have performed this marvel.]”

This morning, having dressed and taken my bowl, I entered the city of Vaiśālī to beg for food. I saw a great many Licchavi youths coming out from within the city toward the gate of the vihāra, competing to shoot through the keyhole; every arrow they fired entered it.
I thought to myself:
"This is most extraordinary!
These Licchavi youths are capable of performing difficult deeds."
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"What do you think?
Is it difficult for the Licchavi youth to shoot arrows through the keyhole, with every arrow entering?"
"If one were to split a single hair into a hundred parts and shoot at each of those hundred parts, hitting every single one with an arrow— would this be difficult?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha,
"To split a single hair into a hundred parts and hit each of those hundred hair-parts with an arrow, hitting them all, would indeed be difficult."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"It is even more difficult than that to give rise to knowledge in accordance with reality regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering.

Likewise, it is even more difficult to know and see in accordance with reality the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"To divide a single hair into a hundred parts, and to strike one of those parts with an arrow is extremely difficult;
yet to contemplate each individual aggregate of suffering as being 'not-self' is likewise no less difficult."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
406 (Four Hundred and Six) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Gabled Lecture Hall beside the Monkey Pond.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Suppose the entire great earth were to become a vast ocean. There was a blind turtle with a lifespan of immeasurable kalpas who would raise its head once every hundred years. In the sea there was a floating piece of wood with only a single hole, drifting upon the ocean waves, tossed to and fro by the winds from east to west."
"If a blind turtle emerges from the water once every hundred years, would it be able to encounter this hole?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha, "It could not."
World-Honored One! Why is this so?

If this blind turtle were to reach the eastern side of the ocean while the floating wood drifts with the wind toward the western, southern, northern, or any of the four intermediate directions, it would likewise be surrounded by them; thus, they would not necessarily meet.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Though the blind turtle and the floating log may miss each other time and again, they might still encounter one another.
For a foolish ordinary person to drift through the five realms of existence and briefly regain a human body is far more difficult than that."

Why is this so? Because those sentient beings do not practice its meaning, do not practice the Dharma, do not practice goodness, and do not practice truth; they kill and harm one another in succession, the strong oppress the weak, and thus commit immeasurable evils.

Therefore, monks, those who have not yet attained the uninterrupted realization of the Four Noble Truths should apply themselves with diligent skillful means, arouse a superior desire, and train in that uninterrupted realization.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Because this does not lead to benefit in meaning, does not lead to benefit in Dharma, does not lead to benefit in the holy life, is not wisdom, is not right awakening, and does not tend toward Nirvana.
"O bhikṣus, you should discuss together:

'This is the noble truth of suffering, this is the noble truth of the origin of suffering, this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and this is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.'"
Why is this so? Because this meaning is beneficial, the Dharma is beneficial, the holy life is beneficial; it leads to right knowledge, right awakening, and is directed toward Nirvana.
Therefore, bhikṣus!
Those who have not yet attained the immediate realization of the Four Noble Truths should apply themselves with diligent skillful means, arouse superior desire, and train in immediate realization.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
415 (415) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus gathered in the dining hall and engaged in this discussion:
"A certain donor has prepared coarse food; having eaten it, we have no flavor and lack strength. It would be better for us to abandon that coarse food and go out to beg for alms."

Why is this? When a bhikṣu goes on almsround, he obtains fine food; he also sees beautiful forms and hears pleasant sounds; he is well-known to many people, and he also receives robes, bedding, and medicines.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was in meditative concentration, he heard with his divine ear the voices of the bhikṣus as they were discussing [the matter]. He immediately proceeded to the refectory... [as described at length] ...up until: "They are rightly directed toward Nirvāṇa."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
416 (416). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you all uphold the Four Noble Truths as I have taught them?
Then, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, prostrated before the Buddha, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha:
"Yes, indeed, World-Honored One; I have fully received and upheld the Four Noble Truths as you have taught them.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu:
"In what manner have you received and upheld the Four Noble Truths?"
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The World-Honored One has declared:

‘This is the Noble Truth of Suffering; I have received and upheld it. This is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, this is the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and this is the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.’”
"In this way, the World-Honored One taught the Four Noble Truths, and I immediately received and upheld them.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!
You have truly accepted and upheld what I have taught as the Noble Truth of Suffering;

you have truly accepted and upheld what I have taught as the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
417 (417) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you all uphold the Four Noble Truths as I have taught them?
Then, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, prostrated before the Buddha, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha:
"Yes, indeed, World-Honored One; I have fully received and upheld the Four Noble Truths as you have taught them.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu:
"In what way do you uphold the Four Noble Truths as I have taught them?"
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Blessed One has taught the Noble Truth of Suffering; I have received and upheld it all.

That which is suchness (tathatā), not departing from suchness, not differing from suchness—true, real, authentic, non-perverted, and the truth realized by the noble ones—is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.”

The Blessed One has taught the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering—just as they are, not departing from suchness, not differing from suchness, true, real, authentic, non-erroneous, and the truths realized by the noble ones. These are the Four Noble Truths taught by the Blessed One, which I have fully received and uphold.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Excellent! Excellent!”

If you truly uphold the Four Noble Truths as taught by me—just as they are, not departing from suchness, not differing from suchness, true, real, authentic, and non-perverted—then you are called a bhikṣu who truly upholds my Four Noble Truths.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
418 (418) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Do you uphold the Four Noble Truths as I have taught them?
Then, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, paid homage to the Buddha, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One; I have fully retained all that you have taught regarding the Four Noble Truths.
What are the four truths?

The World-Honored One has taught the Noble Truth of Suffering, which I have fully retained; the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering—I have fully retained them all.”
The Buddha said to that bhikṣu:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Monks, you must all uphold the Four Noble Truths as I have taught them.

If any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas should say, 'The Noble Truth of Suffering as taught by the śramaṇa Gautama—I shall abandon it and establish my own Noble Truth of Suffering,' they are merely engaging in empty words; when questioned, they will not know the answer, and their doubts will increase, for this is not within their domain."

"If one were to say, 'I shall now abandon the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering, and instead establish four other noble truths,' that would be a mere verbal assertion; having been questioned, one would not know the answer and would only increase their doubt, because it is not within their domain."
Therefore, bhikṣus!
Those who have not yet attained the direct realization of the Four Noble Truths should apply themselves with diligent skillful means, arouse superior desire, and train in direct realization.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
419 (419) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If a bhikṣu has doubt regarding the Buddha, he will have doubt regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering, and will likewise have doubt and uncertainty regarding the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.

If he has doubt regarding the Dharma or the Saṅgha, he will have doubt regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering, and will likewise have doubt and uncertainty regarding the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering."

If one has no doubt regarding the Buddha, then one has no doubt regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering, and no doubt regarding the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.

If one has no doubt regarding the Dharma and the Saṅgha, then one has no doubt regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering, and no doubt regarding the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 420 (420) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas have doubts regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering, they have doubts regarding the Buddha, and they have doubts regarding the Dharma and the Saṅgha;
if they have doubts regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, they have doubts regarding the Buddha, and they have doubts regarding the Dharma and the Saṅgha."
If one has no doubt regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering, then one has no doubt regarding the Buddha, nor regarding the Dharma or the Saṅgha;
if one has no doubt regarding the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path, then one has no doubt regarding the Buddha, nor regarding the Dharma or the Saṅgha.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
421 (421) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Come, all of you, let us go together to the deep and precipitous crags.
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!

At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly, went to a deep and precipitous cliff. Having spread his seat and sat down, he surveyed the deep and precipitous cliff all around and addressed the bhikṣus:
“This cliff is exceedingly vast, deep, and precipitous.”
At that time, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, paid homage to the Buddha, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"This is extremely deep and perilous; however, is there not something even more extremely deep and perilous than this, which is truly terrifying?
The Buddha, knowing his intention, immediately told him:
"It is so, bhikṣu!"

This is extremely perilous; yet there is another peril even more profound and dangerous than this, which is truly terrifying: namely, when certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas do not know the noble truth of suffering as it really is, nor do they know the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, or the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering as they really are. They take delight in those formations that are the root of birth, and they take delight in those formations that are the root of old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, despair, and suffering, and thus they engage in such practices.
Because these practices of old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, despair, and suffering increase further and further, they fall into the perilous state of birth;
they fall into the perilous state of old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, despair, and suffering.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!
This is a great abyss; more perilous than this is that which follows.
Therefore, bhikṣus!

"Those who have not yet attained the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Four Noble Truths should apply themselves with diligent skillful means, arouse superior desire, and train in direct realization.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
422. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There is a Great Heating Hell; if sentient beings are born therein, they are continuously subjected to blazing heat.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, paid homage to the Buddha, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“According to what the World-Honored One has said, this is indeed the Great Heating Hell.”
“World-Honored One!
Is this Great Heat the only one, or is there another Great Heat even more intense than this—one that is utterly terrifying and beyond compare? “It is so, bhikṣu!”
This is indeed a great heat, yet there is another heat even greater than this, which is most terrifying and unsurpassed.
What is this other heat, more terrifying and greater than this?

That is to say, certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas do not know this noble truth of suffering as it really is; they do not know the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering as they really are.

In this way, even up to birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering—this great fever burns intensely; this is called a bhikṣu being scorched by a great fever, which is most terrifying and beyond compare.
Therefore, bhikkhus,

those who have not yet attained the direct realization of the Four Noble Truths should apply themselves with diligence and skillful means, arouse a superior desire, and train for the sake of direct realization.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
423 (IV, 23) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There is a Great Darkness Hell; those sentient beings born therein cannot even see their own bodies."
At that time, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, paid homage to the Buddha, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"This is indeed a great darkness; yet, there is another great darkness even more terrifying than this.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "It is so.

There is indeed another great darkness, even more terrifying than this: namely, when śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas do not know the Four Noble Truths as they truly are, and consequently fall into the great darkness of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering."

Therefore, monks, those who have not yet attained the direct realization of the Four Noble Truths should apply themselves with diligent means, arouse superior desire, and train for the sake of direct realization.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
424 (424) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“Just as the sun travels, illuminating all worlds—even a thousand suns and a thousand moons illuminating a thousand worlds, a thousand Sumeru mountains, a thousand Pūrvavidehas, a thousand Jambudvīpas, a thousand Aparagoyānīs, a thousand Uttarakurus, a thousand Cāturmahārājikas, a thousand Trāyastriṃśas, a thousand Yāmas, a thousand Tuṣitas, a thousand Nirmāṇaratis, a thousand Paranirmita-vaśavartins, and a thousand Brahmās—this is called a small chiliocosm.”

In this thousandfold world system, there are regions of profound darkness between the worlds where the light of the sun and moon cannot reach; despite their great power and majesty, they do not illuminate them. Any sentient beings born within those regions cannot even see their own limbs.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, paid homage to the Buddha, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“As the World-Honored One has said, this is a great darkness; is there yet another great darkness that exceeds this?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:

“There is a great darkness that exceeds this: namely, when śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas do not know the Noble Truth of Suffering as it truly is, and so forth, they fall into the great darkness of birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, affliction, and suffering. This, bhikṣu, is called the great darkness that exceeds the darkness between worlds.”

Therefore, monks, those who have not yet attained the immediate realization of the Four Noble Truths should apply themselves with diligent skillful means, arouse a superior desire, and train for the sake of immediate realization.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
425 (425) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"When one counts from a small thousand-world system up to a full thousand of them, this is called a medium thousand-world system.

Within this medium thousand-world system, there are regions of darkness as previously described; furthermore, for those who have not yet attained the uninterrupted realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Four Noble Truths, they should diligently apply skillful means, arouse superior desire, and train in uninterrupted realization."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
426 (426) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"When one counts from a medium chiliocosm up to a thousand, it is called a trichiliocosm."

In the midst of the world, in places of profound darkness where the sun and moon travel and illuminate the world everywhere, they do not see; thus, they fall into the great darkness of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering.

Therefore, monks, those who have not yet attained the immediate and complete realization of the Four Noble Truths should apply themselves with diligent skillful means, arouse superior desire, and train in that immediate and complete realization.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
427 (427) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now speak of the Four Noble Truths.
Listen attentively!"
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well.
What are the four?

"They are the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering; these are called the four noble truths.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As it shall be explained, so it exists; thus it should be known, as was also stated above. 428 (428). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should diligently practice meditative reflection, arouse right effort, and bring the mind to inner stillness. Why is this so?"
When a bhikṣu has practiced meditative reflection and achieved internal tranquility of mind, things manifest as they truly are.
How do they manifest as they truly are?

It means that this noble truth of suffering manifests as it truly is; this noble truth of the origin of suffering, this noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and this noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering manifest as they truly are.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
429 (429) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should cultivate immeasurable samādhi with single-mindedness and right mindfulness. Why is this so?"
Having cultivated immeasurable samādhis with single-minded right mindfulness,
they manifest in accordance with reality.
How do they manifest in accordance with reality?

That is to say: this noble truth of suffering is manifested as it truly is; the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering are manifested as they truly are.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
430 (430) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa, the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"It is like a person throwing a staff into the air; it immediately falls back down, either with its base touching the ground, or its middle touching the ground, or its tip touching the ground."

In this way, if śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas do not know this noble truth of suffering as it really is, and do not know the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering as they really are, you should know that such śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas will fall into hell, or fall among the animals, or fall among the hungry ghosts.

"Therefore, monks, those who have not yet attained the immediate realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the Four Noble Truths should apply themselves with diligent skillful means and train for that immediate realization.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the monks, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
431 (Four Hundred and Thirty-One). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Just as when a person hurls a staff into the air, it must inevitably fall back down— either onto pure ground or onto impure ground— in the same way,

śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who do not know the noble truth of suffering as it really is, and who do not know the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering as they really are;
because they do not know them as they really are, they are born either in a happy destination or in an unhappy destination."

Therefore, monks, those who have not yet attained the immediate realization of the Four Noble Truths should apply themselves with diligent skillful means, arouse superior desire, and train in immediate realization.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
432 (432) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Suppose there were a five-jointed wheel connected in succession, which a powerful man causes to spin rapidly.

In this same way, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who do not know this Noble Truth of Suffering as it really is, and who do not know this Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering as they really are, revolve through the five destinies, spinning rapidly; they fall into hell, or into the animal realm, or into the realm of hungry ghosts, or among humans, or among devas, returning to the evil paths and revolving for a long night.”
Therefore, bhikṣus!

Those who have not yet attained the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Four Noble Truths should apply themselves with diligent skillful means, arouse a superior desire, and train in direct realization.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
433 (433) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, teaches with emphasis the Four Noble Truths; he reveals, establishes, founds, analyzes, expounds, manifests, and discloses them."
What are these four?

They are the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
Therefore, bhikṣus!

"Those who have not yet attained the immediate realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the Four Noble Truths should diligently apply skillful means, arouse superior desire, and train in immediate realization.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
434. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"What constitutes wisdom?

Is it the knowing of this noble truth of suffering as it truly is; the knowing of this noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering as they truly are—or is it not knowing them?"
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha:
“As we understand what the World-Honored One has taught, one who knows the Four Noble Truths as they truly are is wise.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
“Excellent! Excellent!”

One who knows, as they truly are, the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering, is one of wisdom.

Therefore, monks, those who have not yet attained the immediate realization of the Four Noble Truths should apply themselves with diligent skillful means, arouse a superior desire, and train for that immediate realization.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
435 (435) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the householder Sudatta went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Are these Four Noble Truths to be realized through gradual and successive direct comprehension,
or are they to be realized all at once?
The Buddha told the householder:
"These Four Noble Truths are realized gradually and without interval, not instantaneously and without interval.
The Buddha told the householder:

"If someone were to say that while they have not yet attained immediate realization regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering, they have nonetheless attained immediate realization regarding the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering, such a statement would be incorrect."

Why is this? If one has not attained direct realization regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering, it is impossible that one could attain direct realization regarding the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, or the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.
"It is impossible, for example, that a person might take two small leaves, join them together to form a vessel, fill it with water, and carry it along; such a thing cannot happen.

Likewise, it is impossible that one who has not yet attained direct realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering should desire to attain direct realization regarding the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, or the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering; such a thing cannot happen."
“Suppose, for example, there were a person who took lotus leaves and joined them together to form a vessel, filled it with water, and traveled about; such a thing is possible.
In the same way, householder!”

Once one has attained direct realization regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering, it is possible that one will then seek to attain direct realization regarding the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.
Therefore, householder,

those who have not yet attained the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Four Noble Truths should apply themselves with diligent means, arouse superior desire, and train in that direct realization.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
436 (436) Just as it was asked by the householder Sudatta, so too was it asked by another bhikṣu, and it was explained in the same way, with only a difference in the analogy:

"Suppose there were a staircase of four steps leading up to a hall. If someone were to say that without ascending the first step, one could ascend the second, third, or fourth step and reach the hall, such a thing is impossible."
Why is this? It is because one must first ascend the first step; only then can one subsequently ascend the second, third, and fourth steps to reach the hall.
Thus it is, bhikṣu!

If one has not yet attained direct realization regarding the noble truth of suffering, it is impossible that one could attain direct realization regarding the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, or the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
“Monks, it is just as if someone were to say: ‘One ascends a palace by means of four stairways;
one must first take the first step, and only then successively ascend the second, third, and fourth steps to reach the palace. It should be explained in this way.
Why is this? It is because one must first rely on the initial step; only then can one subsequently ascend the second, third, and fourth steps to enter the hall. Such is the principle.
"In this way, bhikṣu!

If one says that after having attained direct realization (abhisamaya) regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering, one subsequently and in sequence attains direct realization regarding the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering, it should be stated thus."

Why is that? Because it is possible for one who has attained direct realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering to subsequently, in due order, attain direct realization regarding the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
437 (IV.337) As was asked by another bhikṣu, so too was it asked by Ānanda; it was explained in the same manner, with only the difference in the parable.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Suppose there is a four-rung ladder for ascending to a palace hall.
If someone were to say that one could reach the second, third, or fourth rung and ascend to the hall without passing through the first rung, such a thing is impossible."
In this way, Ānanda,

if one has not yet attained the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering, yet wishes to attain the direct realization regarding the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering, this is not possible.

Why is that? It is impossible for one who has not yet attained clear comprehension (*abhisamaya*) regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering to attain clear comprehension regarding the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, or the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.
“Ānanda, it is just as if one were to ascend to a palace by means of a four-staged staircase.
If someone were to say that one must first take the first step, and only then successively ascend the second, third, and fourth steps to reach the palace— this is what ought to be said.”
Why is this? Because it is possible for one who has first ascended the first step, and subsequently climbed the second, third, and fourth steps, to ascend to the hall.
Thus it is, Ānanda!

Having attained direct realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering, it is possible that one subsequently attains direct realization regarding the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
438 (438) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

The bhikṣu said to the Buddha:
"I cannot, World-Honored One!"
"Why is this? Because the various creatures in the great ocean are of diverse forms and types; some are so minute they cannot be pierced, while others are so immense they cannot be pierced.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"So it is, so it is. The realm of sentient beings is incalculable and immeasurable.
Therefore, bhikṣus!"
“Those who have not yet attained clear realization regarding the Four Noble Truths should apply themselves diligently to skillful means, arouse superior aspiration, and train in clear realization.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
439 (Four Hundred Thirty-Nine). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One took up some soil and dust in his hand and asked the bhikṣus:
"What do you think?
Which is more: the earth and stones in this hand, or the earth and stones of that Great Snowy Mountain?"
The bhikṣu said to the Buddha:

“World-Honored One, the soil and stones in Your hand are but very few; the soil and stones of the Snowy Mountains are exceedingly many and immeasurable—hundreds of thousands of millions—that no calculation or analogy can compare with.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Those sentient beings who know the Noble Truth of Suffering as it truly is, and who know the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering as they truly are, are like the clods of earth and stones held in my hand.

Those sentient beings who do not know the Noble Truth of Suffering as it truly is, and who do not know the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering as they truly are, are like the earth and stones of the Snowy Mountains, their number being immeasurable."
Therefore, bhikṣus!

Those who have not yet attained the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Four Noble Truths should apply themselves with diligent skillful means, arouse a superior desire, and train in direct realization.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
440 (440) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Suppose there were a lake, fifty yojanas deep and wide, its waters overflowing to the brim.

"What do you think, bhikṣu?
Is the amount of water droplets dropped by that man great?"
“Is there more water in the lake?
The bhikṣu replied to the Buddha:

“The water droplets dropped by that man with his hair, fingers, and fingertips two or three times are extremely few; the water in that great lake is immeasurable, such that even calculation or analogy cannot compare to it.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“It is like a great lake of water, vast and immeasurable.

In this same way, a learned noble disciple who has fulfilled the vision of the truths, attained the fruit of the noble path, and severed the root of all suffering—just as one would cut off the head of a tāla tree—is established in the state of non-arising for future lives. Therefore, bhikṣus!

Those who have not yet attained the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Four Noble Truths should apply themselves with diligent skillful means, arouse a superior desire, and train in direct realization.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Just as with the analogy of the great lake, so too are the analogies for the Saradvatīkā—namely the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarayū, Airāvatī, and Mahī—as well as the four great oceans, as explained above.
441 (Four Hundred and Forty-One). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, the ball of earth in Your hand is but a tiny amount; that King of Mountains, the Snowy Range, possesses an immense quantity of earth and stone—hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas—that no calculation or analogy can compare with.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Just as the lump of clay I have grasped,

so too it is with those sentient beings who know the Noble Truth of Suffering as it really is, and who likewise know the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering as they really are.”
Just as with the earth and stones of the Great Snowy Mountain King,

so too it is with sentient beings who do not know the Noble Truth of Suffering as it truly is, and who likewise do not know the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering as they truly are.
Therefore, bhikṣus!

Those who have not yet attained the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Four Noble Truths should apply themselves with diligent skillful means, arouse superior desire, and train in direct realization.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

As it was with the King of Mountains, the Snowy Range, so too it was with Mount Nimindhara, Mount Vinataka, Mount Aśvakarṇa, Mount Sudarśana, Mount Khadiraka, Mount Īṣādhara, Mount Yugandhara, Mount Sumeru the King of Mountains, and the earth, stones, and soil.
As with the pear fruit, so it is with the āmalaka fruit, the bhallātaka fruit, the karaka fruit, the bean fruit, and even the analogy of the garlic seed; it is likewise.
442 (Four Hundred Forty-Two). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One took up some soil with his fingernail and addressed the bhikṣus:
"What do you think?
Is the amount of soil on my fingernails greater,
or is the amount of soil in this great earth greater?"
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One, the soil upon the fingernail is extremely small; the soil of this great earth is vast and immeasurable, such that even calculation or analogy cannot compare with it.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Those who are like the dust on a fingernail—if all sentient beings were visible in form, they would be just like that.
Those whose forms are so subtle as to be invisible are like the dust of the great earth."
"Therefore, bhikṣus!
Those who have not yet attained the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Four Noble Truths should apply themselves with diligent skillful means and train in that direct realization.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As it is with dry land, so it is with the realm of water.
As is the dust upon a fingernail, so too are sentient beings who belong to the human path.
As is the soil of the great earth, so too are those who are not human beings.
As is the soil upon a fingernail, so too are those born in the central lands.
As is the soil of the great earth, so too are those born in the borderlands.
As the dust upon a fingernail, so too are those who have accomplished the noble eye of wisdom;
as the soil of the great earth, so too are those who have not accomplished the noble eye of wisdom.
Just as the soil on a fingernail, so too are those sentient beings who know this Dharma and Vinaya;
just as the soil of the great earth, so too are those sentient beings who do not know the Dharma and Vinaya.
As with "knowing," so it is with "knowing thus," "knowing universally," right reflection, right awakening, right understanding, and the direct realization of the Dharma (*dharmābhisamaya*).
As the soil upon a fingernail, so too is the number of sentient beings who know they have parents.
Just as the soil of the great earth, so too are those sentient beings who do not know that they have parents.

Just as the soil upon a fingernail, so too are those who recognize the elders of the families of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, perform what ought to be done, cultivate merit, fear the commission of transgressions in this world and the next, practice giving, observe the fasts, and maintain the precepts.

Just as the soil of the great earth does not know of the elders of the families of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who perform what ought to be done, cultivate merit, practice giving out of fear of wrongdoing in this world and the next, observe the fasts, and maintain the precepts—it is said that it is the same for them.

Just as the soil upon a fingernail, so too are those sentient beings who do not kill, do not steal, do not engage in sexual misconduct, do not speak falsely, do not speak divisively, do not speak harshly, and do not speak frivolously.
Just as with the soil of the great earth, so it is with sentient beings who do not uphold the precepts.
The same is said for those who are free from greed, hatred, and wrong views, as well as those who are not free from greed, hatred, and wrong views.
The number of those who do not kill, do not steal, do not engage in sexual misconduct, do not speak falsely, and do not drink intoxicants is like the soil on a fingernail;
the number of those who do not observe these five precepts is like the soil of the great earth.
As the soil on a fingernail, so too are those sentient beings who observe the eight precepts;
as the soil of the great earth, so too are those sentient beings who do not observe the eight precepts.
As the soil upon a fingernail, so too are those sentient beings who uphold the ten wholesome paths of action;
as the soil of the great earth, so too are those sentient beings who do not uphold the ten wholesome paths of action.
As the soil on a fingernail, so too are those sentient beings who, having passed away from hell, are reborn among human beings.
As the soil of the great earth, so too are those sentient beings who, having passed away from hell, return to be born in hell.
As it is with those in hell, so it is with animals and hungry ghosts.
As the soil upon a fingernail, so too are those sentient beings who, having passed away from hell, are reborn in the heavens.
Just as the soil of the great earth is vast, so too are those sentient beings who, having passed away from hell, are reborn again in hell.
As it is with hell, so it is with the animal realm and the realm of hungry ghosts.
As is the soil on a fingernail, so too are those sentient beings who, having passed away from the human realm, are reborn again within the human realm.
As is the soil of the great earth, so too are those sentient beings who, having passed away from the human realm, are reborn in the hells.
As it is with those in hell, so it is with animals and hungry ghosts.
Just as the dust upon one's fingernail, so too are those sentient beings who, having passed away from the heavens, are reborn again in the heavens.
Just as the soil of the great earth is vast, so too are those sentient beings who pass away from the heavens and are reborn in the hells.
As it is with the hells, so it is with the animal realm and the realm of hungry ghosts.
443 (Four Hundred Forty-Three). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Before I had heard the Dharma, I attained right reflection regarding this Noble Truth of Suffering, and right view arose;
regarding this Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, this Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and this Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering, right view arose.”
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As it was with those who have already been born, so it is with those being born now and those yet to be born.
As it is with "arising," so it is with "origination," "cultivation," "frequent practice," "contact," and "realization.
(444) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Suppose there were an eye-salve pill, one yojana deep and wide. If a man were to take this pill and place it in every world-system, he could exhaust it quickly, yet he would not reach its limit within those world-systems."
One should know that the elements (*dhātu*) are immeasurable in number.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should train well in the elements;
you should train yourselves thus, becoming skilled in the various elements.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 445 (445) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Sentient beings are always accompanied by the elements (dhātu) and are conjoined with the elements.
In what way are sentient beings always accompanied by the elements?"
That is to say, when sentient beings engage in unwholesome thoughts, they are associated with the unwholesome realm;

when they engage in wholesome thoughts, they are associated with the wholesome realm; when they engage in superior thoughts, they are associated with the superior realm; and when they engage in inferior thoughts, they are associated with the inferior realm.
"Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
'We shall be skilled in the various elements.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the monks, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
446 (Four Hundred and Forty-Six). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus... [as explained in detail above].
Regarding the distinction, a verse is spoken:
"Because they constantly meet, they are constantly born; If separated, birth is severed.
It is like a person grasping a small piece of wood And entering into the vast ocean."
Just as a person and a tree both sink [when submerged], so it is with those who are indolent.
One should abandon indolence and inferior diligence;
the noble ones do not indulge in indolence, but dwell securely in seclusion.
Through diligent and ardent meditation, one transcends the stream of birth and death;
as glue and lacquer find their natural affinity, and fire blazes when met with wind;
as conch and milk share the same color, so do sentient beings and the realms coexist.
“Similar things come together in harmony, and their growth is likewise so. 447 (447) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Sentient beings are always accompanied by the elements (dhātu) and are in union with the elements.
In what way are they accompanied by the elements?”

That is to say, when sentient beings possess an unwholesome mind, they are conjoined with the unwholesome realm; when they possess a wholesome mind, they are conjoined with the wholesome realm; when they possess a base mind, they are conjoined with the base realm; and when they possess a superior mind, they are conjoined with the superior realm.

At that time, the Venerable Kauṇḍinya was walking up and down nearby with a large number of bhikṣus; all of them were senior elders of great learning and virtue, who had long since gone forth and fully cultivated the holy life.

“Venerable Śāriputra was walking for exercise nearby with a large company of bhikṣus, all of whom possessed great wisdom and eloquence.
At that time, Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was walking for exercise nearby with a large company of bhikṣus, all of whom possessed great supernormal powers and strength.”
"At that time, Anuruddha was walking in meditation in the vicinity with a large number of bhikṣus, all of whom possessed clear and penetrating divine vision.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was walking in meditation in the vicinity with a large number of bhikṣus, all of whom were courageous and diligent, devoted to earnest practice."
At that time, the Venerable Dabba was walking for exercise near them with a large number of bhikṣus, all of whom were capable of preparing offerings for the great assembly.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli was walking in meditation nearby with a large number of bhikṣus, all of whom were thoroughly proficient in the practice of the Vinaya.
At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇa was walking in meditation nearby with a large number of bhikṣus, all of whom were eloquent and skilled in preaching the Dharma.

At that time, the Venerable Kaccāyana was walking in meditation together with a large number of bhikkhus in a nearby area; they were all capable of analyzing various sūtras and were skilled in explaining the characteristics of dharmas.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was walking in meditation with a large number of bhikṣus nearby; all of them were learned and possessed of total retention (*dhāraṇī*).
At that time, the Venerable Rāhula was walking in meditation with a large number of bhikṣus nearby; all of them were well-versed in the practice of the Vinaya.

"At that time, Devadatta was walking up and down nearby with a large number of bhikṣus, all of whom were habituated to various evil practices. This is what is called a bhikṣu who constantly dwells together with the elements and is in harmony with the elements. Therefore, O bhikṣus!"
"One should skillfully discern the various elements.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra,
the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
448 (Four Hundred Forty-Eight). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove... [as extensively described above], he then spoke these verses:
"Through constant association, there is constant birth; When separated from it, birth is severed."
Like a person grasping a small piece of wood while entering the great ocean, both the person and the wood sink together;
so it is with those who possess indolence. One should abandon indolence and inferior diligence.
The noble and wise are never indolent; they dwell securely in seclusion.
With earnest diligence in meditation, they cross over the stream of birth and death.
As glue and lacquer find their proper substrate, and as fire blazes when it meets the wind.
Just as conch shells and milk share the same color, so too do sentient beings and their realms;
they are similar and harmoniously united, and their growth is likewise so. (449) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“Sentient beings are always accompanied by elements (*dhātu*) and are in harmony with elements... Thus it was explained in detail, up to: “When a superior mind arises, it is accompanied by a superior element; when a base mind arises, it is accompanied by a base element; when there is a mind of killing, it is accompanied by the element of killing; when there is a mind of stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, or drinking alcohol, it is accompanied by the element of drinking alcohol.”

When one refrains from killing, one is conjoined with the realm of non-killing; when one refrains from stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants, one is conjoined with the realm of not drinking intoxicants.
"Therefore, monks, you should skillfully discern the various elements.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the monks, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
450. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Sentient beings are always accompanied by elements and are in union with elements. When they lack faith, they are accompanied by the element of lack of faith;

when they violate the precepts, they are accompanied by the element of violating the precepts; when they are without shame or remorse, they are accompanied by the element of shamelessness and lack of remorse.

When they have faith, they are accompanied by the element of faith; when they uphold the precepts, they are accompanied by the element of upholding the precepts; when they possess a sense of shame and remorse, they are accompanied by the element of shame and remorse.”
"Therefore, monks, you should skillfully discern the various kinds of elements.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the monks, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

As with faith and lack of faith, so it is with diligence and lack of diligence, loss of mindfulness and non-loss of mindfulness, right concentration and wrong concentration, much learning and little learning, the miserly and the generous, evil wisdom and wholesome wisdom, being difficult to support and easy to support, being difficult to satisfy and easy to satisfy, having many desires and few desires, contentment and lack of contentment, and grasping and non-grasping; these are all associated with the elements (*dhātu*), as described in the aforementioned sūtra.
Thus it was extensively explained. (451) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now speak of the various elements (dhātu).
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall explain them for you."

What are the various elements (*dhātu*)? They are the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element; the nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element; the body element, the tangible object element, and the body-consciousness element; and the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element. These are called the various elements.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 452 (452) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Conditioned by various elements (dhātu), various contacts (sparśa) arise; conditioned by various contacts, various sensations (vedanā) arise; conditioned by various sensations, various cravings (tṛṣṇā) arise."
What are the various elements (dhātus)?

They refer to the eighteen elements: the eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element, and so forth, up to the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element. These are called the various elements.
"How do various kinds of contact arise conditioned by various kinds of elements, and so on, up to how do various kinds of craving arise conditioned by various kinds of feeling?

It is said: conditioned by the eye-element, eye-contact arises; conditioned by eye-contact, feeling born of eye-contact arises; and conditioned by feeling born of eye-contact, craving born of eye-contact arises."

Conditioned by the ear-element, nose-element, tongue-element, body-element, and mind-element, there arises mind-contact; conditioned by mind-contact, there arises feeling born of mind-contact; conditioned by feeling born of mind-contact, there arises craving born of mind-contact.

“Monks! It is not by depending on various cravings that various feelings arise; it is not by depending on various feelings that various contacts arise; it is not by depending on various contacts that various elements arise. Rather, it is by depending on various elements that various contacts arise; by depending on various contacts that various feelings arise; and by depending on various feelings that various cravings arise. This, monks, is called: depending on various elements, various contacts arise; depending on various contacts, various feelings arise; and depending on various feelings, various cravings arise.”
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 453 (453) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Conditioned by various elements (dhātu), various contacts (sparśa) arise; conditioned by various contacts, various feelings (vedanā) arise; conditioned by various feelings, various cravings (tṛṣṇā) arise."
What are the various elements?

They are the eighteen elements: the eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element, and so on, up to the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element. These are called the various elements.
"How is it that, conditioned by various elements (*dhātu*), various contacts (*sparśa*) arise;
conditioned by various contacts, various feelings (*vedanā*) arise;
and conditioned by various feelings, various cravings (*tṛṣṇā*) arise?"

That is to say: visual consciousness arises conditioned by the eye-element, not the eye-element arising conditioned by visual consciousness; rather, visual consciousness arises only conditioned by the eye-element.

Visual sensation arises conditioned by visual consciousness, not visual consciousness arising conditioned by visual sensation; rather, visual sensation arises only conditioned by visual consciousness.
Visual craving arises conditioned by visual sensation, not visual sensation arising conditioned by visual craving; rather, visual craving arises only conditioned by visual sensation.

In this way, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind element condition the arising of mind-contact; it is not that mind-contact conditions the arising of the mind element, but rather that the mind element conditions the arising of mind-contact.
Mind-contact conditions the arising of mind-feeling; it is not that mind-feeling conditions the arising of mind-contact, but rather that mind-contact conditions the arising of mind-feeling.
Mind-feeling conditions the arising of mind-craving; it is not that mind-craving conditions the arising of mind-feeling, but rather that mind-feeling conditions the arising of mind-craving.

"Therefore, bhikṣus! It is not that various feelings arise conditioned by various cravings; it is not that various contacts arise conditioned by various feelings; it is not that various elements arise conditioned by various contacts.

Rather, various contacts arise conditioned by various elements; various feelings arise conditioned by various contacts; various cravings arise conditioned by various feelings. This, bhikṣus, is called skillfully discerning the various elements."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
454 (No. 454) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus: "Conditioned by various elements arise various contacts;

conditioned by various contacts arise various feelings; conditioned by various feelings arise various perceptions; conditioned by various perceptions arise various desires; conditioned by various desires arise various thoughts; conditioned by various thoughts arise various fevers; conditioned by various fevers arise various seekings."
"What are the various elements?
They are the eighteen elements, from the eye element up to the mental-object element.
How do various contacts arise conditioned by various elements?"
...up to: conditioned by various heats, various seekings arise?

That is to say: conditioned by the eye-element, eye-contact arises; conditioned by eye-contact, eye-feeling arises; conditioned by eye-feeling, eye-perception arises; conditioned by eye-perception, eye-desire arises; conditioned by eye-desire, eye-apperception arises; conditioned by eye-apperception, eye-heating arises; conditioned by eye-heating, eye-seeking arises.

In the same way, conditioned by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-element, mental contact arises; conditioned by mental contact, mental feeling arises; conditioned by mental feeling, mental perception arises; conditioned by mental perception, mental volition arises; conditioned by mental volition, mental fever arises; conditioned by mental fever, mental seeking arises. This is called, monks, how various contacts arise conditioned by various elements, and so on, until various seekings arise conditioned by various fevers.

“Monks! It is not by depending on various kinds of seeking that various kinds of fever arise; it is not by depending on various kinds of fever that various kinds of perception arise; it is not by depending on various kinds of perception that various kinds of ideation arise; it is not by depending on various kinds of ideation that various kinds of feeling arise; it is not by depending on various kinds of feeling that various kinds of contact arise; it is not by depending on various kinds of contact that various kinds of elements arise. Rather, it is by depending on various kinds of elements that various kinds of contact arise, and so on, up to: by depending on various kinds of fever that various kinds of seeking arise.”
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.

(456) [Sūtra Number 456] Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“There is the realm of light, the realm of purity, the realm of the base of infinite space, the realm of the base of infinite consciousness, the realm of the base of nothingness, the realm of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and there is the realm of cessation.”
At that time, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The element of light, the element of purity, the element of the base of infinite space, the element of the base of infinite consciousness, the element of the base of nothingness, the element of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and the element of cessation.
"By what causes and conditions can these various elements (dhātus) be known? The Buddha told the bhikṣu: "That element of light is known by reason of darkness;

the pure element is known by reason of the impure; the element of the sphere of infinite space is known by reason of form; the element of the sphere of infinite consciousness is known by reason of the internal; the element of the sphere of nothingness is known by reason of 'something'; the element of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is known by reason of the first existence; and the element of cessation is known by reason of the body."
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what meditative attainment (samāpatti) are that realm of light, up to and including the realm of cessation, obtained?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“That light-element, the purity-element, the element of the base of infinite space, the element of the base of infinite consciousness, and the element of the base of nothingness—these elements are attained through the meditative attainments (samāpatti) of their respective practices. The element of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is attained through the meditative attainment of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra). As for the element of cessation (nirodha-dhātu), it is attained through the meditative attainment of the cessation of the basis of existence (sakkāya-nirodha).”
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
457 (457) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Eastern Garden, in the Mṛgāramātṛpūrvārāma Lecture Hall.

At that time, the World-Honored One arose from meditation in the late afternoon and, having spread his seat in the shade of the lecture hall, sat before the great assembly and spoke these *udāna* verses, addressing the bhikṣus:

"It is conditioned by the elements (*dhātu*) that speech arises, not without the elements; it is conditioned by the elements that views arise, not without the elements; it is conditioned by the elements that perceptions (*saṃjñā*) arise, not without the elements."

Conditioned by the lower realm, I say there is birth in the lower, lower views, lower perceptions, lower volitions, lower desires, lower aspirations, lower persons, lower actions, lower designations, lower establishments, lower divisions, lower manifestations, and lower rebirths.

In this way, regarding such a superior realm and conditioned by that superior realm, I say that there arise for them superior speech, superior views, superior perceptions, superior volitions, superior aspirations, superior persons, superior actions, superior designations, superior establishments, superior divisions, superior manifestations, and superior rebirths.
At that time, the bhikṣu Vakkali was standing behind the Buddha fanning him with a fan. He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, if one conceives the view that a Samyaksaṃbuddha is not a Samyaksaṃbuddha, does that view also arise conditioned by the elements (dhātu)?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“To give rise to the view that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One is not the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is likewise dependent upon the elements (dhātu) and does not arise apart from them.”

Why is this so? The realm of ordinary persons is the realm of ignorance. As I have previously stated, conditioned by an inferior realm, there arise inferior speech, inferior views, and even the arising of inferior sensations; conditioned by a middling or superior realm, there arise superior speech, superior views, and even the arising of superior sensations.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 458 (458) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

"There is a cause for the arising of thoughts of desire; it does not arise without a cause. There is a cause for the arising of thoughts of ill will and thoughts of harm; they do not arise without a cause."
"What is it that gives rise to thoughts of desire?
It is by taking the realm of desire as an object.
Because one takes the realm of desire as an object, there arise thoughts of desire, longing for desire, perceptions of desire, fever of desire, and seeking after desire."
When foolish worldlings give rise to the pursuit of desire, these sentient beings give rise to perversity in three areas, namely: body, speech, and mind.

Due to such perverse causes and conditions, they dwell in suffering in the present life—possessing pain, obstruction, affliction, and fever—and at the dissolution of the body after death, they are reborn in the evil destinies. This is called the arising of the perception of desire through causes and conditions.
"How do anger and harmful thoughts arise through causes and conditions?
It is due to the element of harm (*vihimsā-dhātu*).

Conditioned by the element of harm, there arise harmful thoughts, harmful desires, harmful perceptions, harmful fevers, and harmful pursuits. Once a foolish worldling has given rise to these harmful pursuits, this sentient being gives rise to perversity in three spheres: namely, body, speech, and mind."

Having given rise to these three types of wrong conditions, one dwells in suffering in the present life—possessing pain, obstruction, affliction, and fever—and at the breaking up of the body after death, one is reborn in an evil destination; this is called the arising of the perception of harm through conditions.

“Monks! If those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas thus abide in birth, perceiving it as perilous, yet do not seek its relinquishment, do not awaken to it, and do not vomit it out, they will dwell in suffering in this very life—possessing pain, obstruction, affliction, and fever—and at the breaking up of the body after death, they will be reborn in the woeful states.”

For example, suppose there is a wilderness not far from a city or village where a great fire suddenly breaks out, and there is no one with the power to extinguish it; you should know that all the sentient beings within that wilderness will be harmed by the fire.

"In this way, those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, though dwelling securely in life, conceive a sense of peril regarding life; when their bodies break up and their lives end, they are reborn in the evil destinies. Monks!"

The desire for renunciation arises from causes; it does not arise without cause. What are the causes from which the desire for renunciation arises? They are the realm of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa-dhātu*).

Taking the realm of renunciation as an object, there arises the desire for renunciation, the will for renunciation, the thought of renunciation, the fever for renunciation, and the seeking of renunciation. When that wise person seeks renunciation, three bases of right action arise in sentient beings: namely, body, speech, and mind.
