Having thus produced these right causes and conditions, they dwell in happiness in the present life—free from suffering, free from obstruction, free from affliction, and free from fever—and at the dissolution of the body after death, they are reborn in a happy destination. This is called the arising of the desire for renunciation through causes and conditions.
"What is the causal condition for the arising of thoughts of non-ill will and non-harming?

It is the element of non-harming (*avihiṃsā-dhātu*). Through the causal condition of the element of non-harming, there arise thoughts of non-harming, the desire for non-harming, perceptions of non-harming, fevers of non-harming, and quests for non-harming. When that wise person pursues non-harming, their three bases are rectified: namely, body, speech, and mind."

Having arisen from those very causes and conditions, one dwells in happiness in the present life—without suffering, without obstruction, without affliction, and without fever—and at the breaking up of the body after death, one is reborn in a happy destination; this is called the perception of non-harming arising from causes and conditions.

“If any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas are established in birth and conceive the notion of non-harming toward birth, and do not relinquish it, do not awaken to its cessation, and do not vomit it out, they dwell in happiness in the present life—without suffering, without obstruction, without affliction, and without fever—and at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in a happy destination.”

For example, suppose there were a wilderness on the outskirts of a city or village where a great fire suddenly broke out; if there were someone capable of extinguishing that fire with their hands and feet, you should know that all those sentient beings relying upon the grasses and trees would not be harmed.

In this way, those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who are established in birth, who give rise to right perception, and who do not abandon, do not awaken to, and do not reject it, dwell in happiness in the present life; they are without suffering, without obstruction, without affliction, and without fever. At the breaking up of the body, after the end of life, they are reborn in a happy destination.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 459 (459) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a brahmin approached the Buddha; after exchanging greetings with the World-Honored One, he stood to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Are sentient beings not created by themselves, nor created by another?"
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"One who speaks such doctrines as these, I do not meet with; yet you have come here yourself and say, 'I did not create it myself, nor did another create it'?"
The brahmin said: "How is it so, Gautama?"
"Are sentient beings created by themselves, or are they created by another?
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"I shall now question you; answer me as you see fit."
"Brahmin! What do you think?
Is there a realm of skillful means among sentient beings that enables all sentient beings to know how to apply skillful means?"
The brahmin said: “Gautama!
There is a realm of skillful means for sentient beings, which enables all sentient beings to know how to apply skillful means.”
The Buddha told the brahmin:

"If there were a realm of skillful means that caused all sentient beings to know that skillful means exist, then it would be that sentient beings act for themselves, and it would be that another acts for them."
"Brahmin! What do you think?

Are there sentient beings who, dwelling in the realm of existence, the realm of solidity, the realm of emergence, and the realm of conditioned activity, cause those sentient beings to know that there is such conditioned activity?"
The brahmin said to the Buddha:
“There are sentient beings who abide in the realm, the firm realm, the emerging realm, and the realm of activity, causing all sentient beings to know that there is activity.”
The Buddha told the brahmin:

"If that realm of stability, realm of solidity, realm of emergence, and realm of formation were to cause all sentient beings to know that there is an agent of formation, then it would be that sentient beings act themselves, and it would be that another acts."
The brahmin said to the Buddha:
“There are beings who act for themselves and those who act for others, Gautama!
The world has many affairs; I must now take my leave.”
The Buddha told the brahmin, "The world has many affairs; you should know that this is the time.
Then, having heard what the Buddha had said, that brahmin rejoiced and approved with gladness, rose from his seat, and departed.
460. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kosambī in the Ghosira Park.
At that time, the householder Ghosita approached the Venerable Ānanda, prostrated at the Venerable Ānanda’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Regarding the various elements that have been taught, what are these ‘various elements’?
Venerable Ānanda replied to the householder Ghoṣila:

"The eye-element is distinct, the form-element is distinct, and the sphere of joy is distinct; from these two conditions, consciousness arises. From the conjunction of these three factors, contact arises. Furthermore, with contact as a condition, pleasant feeling arises."
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as mental objects (*dharma*); it is explained in the same way.

Furthermore, householder, there is a distinct eye-element and a distinct form-element that are objects of sorrow; through these two conditions, consciousness arises. From the conjunction of these three factors, painful contact (*duḥkha-sparśa*) arises, and with that painful contact as condition, a painful feeling (*duḥkhā-vedanā*) arises.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as mental objects (*dharma*); it is explained in the same way.
"Furthermore, householder!

There is a distinct eye-element and a distinct form-element; when these two conditions give rise to consciousness, and through the conjunction of these three factors, there arises a contact that is neither painful nor pleasant. With this contact that is neither painful nor pleasant as a condition, there arises a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant."
"In the same way, the ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and mental objects are also to be explained thus.
At that time, the householder Ghoṣita, having heard what the Venerable Ānanda had said, rejoiced and approved, prostrated at his feet, and departed.
461 (Four Hundred and Sixty-One). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kosambī in the Ghosira Park.
At that time, the householder Ghosita went to where the Venerable Ānanda was, prostrated at his feet, and sat down to one side.
He addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Regarding the various elements you have spoken of— what are these 'various elements'?"
The Venerable Ānanda said to the householder Ghoṣita:
"There are three realms.
What are the three?"
"Namely, the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda spoke these verses:
"Thoroughly understanding the desire realm, The form realm is likewise so."
Having relinquished all that remains, one attains the nirvana without remainder.
Regarding the elements combined in this body, one realizes their eternal exhaustion without residue;
this is the teaching of the Tathāgata, the word of sorrowless and stainless liberation.
When the Venerable Ānanda had spoken this sutra, the householder Ghoṣila rejoiced and delighted in it;
he paid his respects and departed. 462 (462) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Ghoṣila Park in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the householder Ghoṣila approached the Venerable Ānanda, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Regarding the various elements (*dhātu*) you have spoken of."
"What is meant by 'various realms'?
Venerable Ānanda replied to the householder Ghoṣila:
"There are three realms: the realm of form, the formless realm, and the realm of cessation; these are called the three realms."
Then he spoke in verse:
"If beings of the form realm, And those dwelling in the formless realm,
Do not recognize the realm of cessation, They will return once more to undergo various states of existence."
"If one has severed attachment to the realm of form, does not dwell in the formless realm,
and attains liberation of mind through the element of cessation, one is forever freed from birth and death.
When the Venerable Ānanda had spoken this sutra, the householder Ghoṣila rejoiced and approved, paid his respects, and departed.
463 (Four Hundred and Sixty-Three). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kosambī in the Ghosira Park.
At that time, the householder Ghosita went to where the Venerable Ānanda was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Regarding the various elements that have been taught, what are these 'various elements'?
Venerable Ānanda replied to the householder Ghoṣila:
"It refers to the three spheres of transcendence (*niḥsaraṇadhātu*).
What are the three? They are:

transcending the desire realm to reach the form realm; transcending the form realm to reach the formless realm; and the sphere of the cessation of all conditioned formations and all ideations. These are called the three spheres of transcendence."
He then spoke in verse:
"Knowing how to emerge from the desire realm, Transcending the form realm, All conditioned phenomena are stilled;
One diligently cultivates the correct means."
"Having severed all craving, with all formations extinguished, knowing that existence has been fully understood, one shall no longer undergo rebirth.
When the Venerable Ānanda had spoken this sutra, the householder Ghoṣila rejoiced and delighted in it; he paid his respects and departed.
464. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kosambī in the Ghosita Park.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda went to where the foremost elder named Soṇa was; having approached him, he paid his respects with greetings, and after the greetings were concluded, he withdrew to sit at one side and asked the foremost elder Soṇa:
“If a bhikṣu dwells in an empty place, at the foot of a tree, or in a quiet chamber for contemplation, with what dharma should he practice focused and diligent reflection?
The Elder replied, “Venerable Ānanda!

"One who contemplates in an empty place, at the foot of a tree, or in a quiet room should contemplate with single-minded diligence by means of two dharmas, namely: serenity (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
The Venerable Ānanda again asked the Elder:
"When one cultivates serenity and has cultivated it extensively, what is accomplished? When one cultivates insight and has cultivated it extensively, what is accomplished?"
The Elder replied:
"Venerable Ānanda!
One who cultivates tranquility (śamatha) ultimately achieves insight (vipaśyanā); having cultivated insight, one likewise achieves tranquility."
"It means that a noble disciple cultivates both tranquility and insight together, thereby attaining the various spheres of liberation.
Ānanda again asked the Elder,
"What are the various spheres of liberation?"
The Elder replied:
"Venerable Ānanda!
The realm of abandonment, the realm of dispassion, and the realm of cessation—these are called the realms of liberation."
The Venerable Ānanda again asked the Elder:
"What is the realm of abandonment? ...
up to ... the realm of cessation?"
The Elder replied:
“Venerable Ānanda!
The cessation of all formations is called the realm of cessation.”
“The severance of craving is the realm of the desireless; the cessation of all formations is called the realm of cessation.

Then, having heard what the Elder had said, the Venerable Ānanda rejoiced and approved, went to where the five hundred bhikṣus were, paid his respects with greetings, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the five hundred bhikṣus:
“When a bhikṣu is reflecting in a secluded place, at the foot of a tree, or in a quiet chamber, with what dharma should he single-mindedly and diligently reflect?”
Then, the five hundred bhikṣus replied to the Venerable Ānanda:
“We shall apply ourselves with diligence to two dharmas for contemplation, up to the realm of cessation, just as the Elder has taught.”

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the five hundred bhikṣus had said, rejoiced and expressed his approval. He went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“If a bhikṣu is meditating in an empty place, at the foot of a tree, or in a quiet room, with what dharmas should he single-mindedly and diligently practice meditation?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“If a bhikṣu is meditating in an empty place, at the foot of a tree, or in a quiet room, he should single-mindedly and diligently practice meditation by means of two dharmas, up to the realm of cessation, just as the five hundred bhikṣus have explained.”
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How marvelous,
World-Honored One!”

The Great Teacher and all his disciples are entirely identical in their Dharma, identical in their phrases, identical in their meanings, and identical in their flavor. When I recently approached the elder named Sthavira and asked about this matter, he answered me with these same meanings, these same phrases, and this same flavor, just as the World-Honored One has taught. Furthermore, when I approached five hundred bhikṣus and asked about this matter with these same meanings, these same phrases, and this same flavor, those five hundred bhikṣus also answered me with these same meanings, these same phrases, and this same flavor, just as the World-Honored One has taught.
"Therefore, you should know that the teacher and the disciple are identical in all things: identical in the Dharma, identical in the meaning, identical in the phrases, and identical in the flavor.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do you know what kind of bhikṣu that elder is?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
“I do not know,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This Elder is an Arhat; his taints are exhausted, he has laid down the heavy burden, and through right knowledge his mind is well-liberated. Those five hundred bhikṣus are also all like this."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
465 (465) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Rāhula approached the World-Honored One, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

How does one know, and how does one see this consciousness-body of mine and all marks of external objects, so that one attains freedom from the views of "I" and "mine," and from the latent tendencies of pride and attachment?
The Buddha said to Rāhula:
"Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you, Rāhula."

If a bhikṣu, regarding the entire earth element—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; beautiful or ugly; far or near—knows it all as it truly is: "This is not mine, this is not I, this does not exist within me. It is the same for the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.

“Rāhula! When a bhikṣu knows thus and sees thus, regarding this consciousness-body of mine and all signs of external objects, he has no view of ‘I’ or ‘mine,’ nor any underlying tendency of conceit, attachment, or fetter.”

Rāhula! If a bhikṣu, regarding this consciousness-body and all signs in external objects, is free from the views of "I" and "mine," and free from the underlying tendencies of the conceit "I am," he is said to have severed the bonds of craving and the fetters, to have cut off all cravings, to have attained the right destruction of pride, and to have reached the ultimate end of suffering.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Rāhula, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
466 (466) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Rāhula went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How does one know and how does one see this consciousness-body of mine and all phenomena in external objects, so as to attain freedom from the views of "I" and "mine," and from the underlying tendencies of pride and attachment?
The Buddha told Rāhula:
"There are three feelings—painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
What is the cause of these three feelings? What is their origin? What gives rise to them? What conditions their manifestation?"
That is to say, these three feelings have contact as their cause, contact as their origin, contact as their birth, and contact as their transformation;
from this or that contact as cause, this or that feeling arises. If this or that contact ceases, this or that feeling also ceases, stops, becomes cooled, and vanishes.

Knowing thus and seeing thus these consciousnesses of mine and all marks of external objects, one attains freedom from the views of "I" and "mine," and from the underlying tendencies of pride and attachment.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Rāhula, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
467 (No. 467) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Rāhula went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

How does one know, and how does one see this consciousness-body of mine and all phenomena of external objects, so as to attain freedom from the views of "I" and "mine," and from the underlying tendencies of pride and attachment?
The Buddha told Rāhula:
"There are three types of feeling: painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
One should contemplate pleasant feeling as suffering; contemplate painful feeling as being like the piercing of a sword; and contemplate neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as impermanent."

If that bhikṣu contemplates pleasant feeling with the perception of suffering, contemplates painful feeling with the perception of being pierced by a sword, and contemplates neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling with the perception of impermanence and cessation, this is called right view.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Contemplate pleasure as suffering; Regard painful sensations as being like the thrust of a sword;
Regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensations, Cultivate the perception of impermanence and cessation."
This one is truly a bhikṣu:
abiding in the path of tranquil extinction and peace, dwelling at the ultimate limit,
forever free from all afflictions, and having vanquished the armies of Māra.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Rāhula, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
468 (468) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Rāhula went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How does one know, and how does one see this consciousness-body of mine and all phenomena of external objects, so that one attains freedom from the views of "I" and "mine," as well as the underlying tendencies of pride and attachment?
The Buddha told Rāhula:
"There are three feelings—painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
One practices the holy life under me by contemplating pleasant feeling for the purpose of abandoning the underlying tendency of craving for pleasant feeling."
Because they have severed the underlying tendency toward aversion regarding painful feelings, they practice the holy life under me;
because they have severed the underlying tendency toward delusion regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings, they practice the holy life under me.

“Rāhula! If a bhikṣu has abandoned and fully understood the underlying tendency of craving toward pleasant feelings; has abandoned and fully understood the underlying tendency of aversion toward painful feelings; and has abandoned and fully understood the underlying tendency of delusion toward neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings—this is called a bhikṣu who has severed the bonds of craving, removed all fetters, attained the destruction of pride, and reached the ultimate end of suffering.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"When experiencing a pleasant feeling, one does not recognize it as a pleasant feeling;
driven by the latent tendency of craving, one does not perceive the path to liberation."
When experiencing a painful sensation, one does not recognize it as a painful sensation;
driven by the underlying tendency of aversion, one does not see the path leading to deliverance.
The sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant is what the Perfectly Awakened One has taught.
Those who do not examine with skillfulness will never cross to the further shore.
A bhikṣu who is diligent and energetic, possessing right knowledge and remaining unshakable—
such a wise person is able to fully comprehend all these sensations.
One who clearly understands all sensations exhausts all taints in this very life;
when such a wise person passes away, they do not fall among the ranks of beings.
Once the ranks of beings have been severed, they dwell forever in parinirvāṇa.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Rāhula, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
469 (469) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"That which is called 'deep and perilous' by the foolish people of this world refers to the great ocean; it is not what is called 'deep and perilous' in the Dharma and Vinaya of the noble ones."

What is spoken of in the world is merely a designation for a vast accumulation of water; however, when various sensations arise from the body, and one is oppressed by manifold sufferings—whether through affliction or death—this is called the ocean’s most profoundly deep and perilous place.

Ignorant and unlearned worldlings experience various sensations within this body; oppressed by painful suffering, they become distressed or die, lamenting with grief and sorrow, wailing and crying out, their minds deranged and driven to madness, sinking deep into despair without any place of rest.

When a learned noble disciple experiences various sensations within the body—whether painful and oppressive, or distressing, or even unto death—he does not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, weeping, wailing, or mental derangement; he does not sink into the cycle of birth and death, but attains a state of cessation.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Various painful sensations arise within the body, Oppressing it until death;
Grief and lamentation do not cease, One wails and cries out in madness.”
The mind itself gives rise to obstacles, Summoning and increasing all manner of suffering;
Forever submerged in the ocean of birth and death, One knows no place of rest.
If one can relinquish the various sensations of the body, And the afflictions born of the body,
Even when faced with urgency up to death, one does not give rise to thoughts of sorrow or grief;
without weeping or wailing, one is able to endure all sufferings within oneself,
so that the mind produces no obstructions that would cause a gathering and increase of manifold pains.
"Without sinking into the cycle of birth and death, one shall forever attain a place of peace and security.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
470 (Four Hundred and Seventy): Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa, the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“Foolish, unlearned worldlings give rise to painful feelings, pleasant feelings, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings; the learned noble disciple likewise gives rise to painful feelings, pleasant feelings, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings.”
“Monks! What is the distinction between an ordinary person and a noble one?
The monks addressed the Buddha:
“The Blessed One is the root of the Dharma, the eye of the Dharma, and the refuge of the Dharma.
Excellent,
Blessed One!
"I only pray that you will explain this extensively; having heard it, the bhikṣus shall receive and practice it accordingly.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"When an ignorant, unlearned worldling experiences various sensations through bodily contact, they are oppressed by painful suffering, even unto the loss of life; they become sorrowful and weep, uttering complaints and crying out in lamentation."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you. Bhikṣus!”

When an ignorant, unlearned worldling experiences various sensations through bodily contact, their suffering increases, even unto the loss of life; they become despondent, voice grievances, weep and wail, and their minds fall into derangement. At that time, two types of sensation increase: either bodily sensation or mental sensation.
"Just as a man whose body has been pierced by two poisoned arrows experiences extreme pain, so too is the ignorant, unlearned worldling:
he increases two types of feeling—bodily feeling and mental feeling—and experiences extreme pain."

Why is this? Because those foolish, unlearned worldlings do not understand, they experience pleasant sensations upon contact with the five objects of desire and enjoy these sensual pleasures. Because they enjoy these sensual pleasures, they are driven by the underlying tendency of greed (*rāgānuśaya*).
When they experience painful sensations upon contact, they give rise to aversion; because they give rise to aversion, they are driven by the underlying tendency of hatred (*pratighānuśaya*).
Regarding these two feelings, if one does not know them as they truly are— whether in their arising, their cessation, their gratification, their peril, or their escape—
one gives rise to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling because of this lack of true knowledge, and is thereby driven by the underlying tendency of delusion.

One is bound by pleasant feeling and never separated from it; one is bound by painful feeling and never separated from it; one is bound by neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling and never separated from it.
How are they bound?
That is to say, they are bound by greed, hatred, and delusion; they are bound by birth, aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, vexation, and suffering.

When a learned noble disciple experiences a painful bodily sensation that is intensely oppressive—even unto the taking of life—he does not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, resentment, weeping, wailing, or mental derangement. At that time, he gives rise to only one kind of sensation, namely, a bodily sensation, and no mental sensation.

"Suppose, for example, a man were struck by one poisoned arrow but not by a second poisoned arrow; at that time, he would experience only a single sensation, namely a bodily sensation, and no mental sensation would arise."
When experiencing pleasant contact, one is not defiled by sensual desire; because one is not defiled by sensual desire, the underlying tendency of greed does not underlie that pleasant feeling.
When experiencing painful contact, one does not give rise to aversion; because one does not give rise to aversion, the underlying tendency of hatred does not underlie it.

Regarding those two underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), one knows their origin, cessation, gratification, danger, and escape as they truly are. Because of knowing them as they truly are, the underlying tendency of delusion does not underlie the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. One is liberated and unbound from that pleasant feeling, and liberated and unbound from painful and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings.
To what is one unbound?
It means being unbound by greed, hatred, and delusion; being unbound by birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"One who is well-versed in learning regarding suffering and pleasure is not one who lacks perception and awareness;
compared to ordinary people, such a person is truly one of great learning."
In pleasant feeling, one is not heedless; in painful contact, one does not increase sorrow.
Regarding both pain and pleasure, one maintains equanimity—neither following nor opposing them.
With diligent application of effort, the bhikṣu remains unshakable through right wisdom.
Regarding all these feelings, the wise one is able to understand them thoroughly.
Because of this thorough understanding of all feelings, he exhausts all taints in the present life;
after the death of the body, he does not fall into further reckoning, but dwells forever in parinirvāṇa.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
471 (471) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“Suppose a violent wind suddenly arises in the sky, blowing from the four directions—winds with dust and winds without dust, Viśvabhū winds, Vairambha winds, thin winds, and thick winds, even up to the winds arising from the wind-circles.”

The sensations of wind within the body are likewise thus: various sensations arise—pleasant sensation, painful sensation, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation; pleasant bodily sensation, painful bodily sensation, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant bodily sensation; pleasant mental sensation, painful mental sensation, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant mental sensation; pleasant sensation regarding food, painful sensation regarding food, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation regarding food; pleasant sensation regarding non-food, painful sensation regarding non-food, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation regarding non-food; pleasant sensation of craving, painful sensation of craving, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation of craving; and pleasant sensation of renunciation, painful sensation of renunciation, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation of renunciation.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Just as within the void of space, Various violent winds arise—
Winds from the east, west, south, and north, And likewise from the four intermediate directions."
Whether there is dust or no dust, even until the wind-circles arise—
so too, within this body, the various sensations arise in the same way:
whether they be pleasant sensations, painful sensations, or those that are neither painful nor pleasant.
There is food and there is non-food; attachment and non-attachment.
A bhikkhu who is diligent in his application, possessing right knowledge and remaining unshakable, can with wisdom clearly understand all these sensations.
"By thoroughly understanding all feelings, one exhausts all outflows in this very life;
after death, one does not fall into further reckoning, but dwells forever in parinirvāṇa.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
472 (Four Hundred and Seventy-Two). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

"It is like a guest house where all kinds of people reside: whether Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, elders, householders, commoners, or hunters; those who observe the precepts or violate them; whether laypeople or renunciants—they all dwell within it."

This body is also like this, undergoing various kinds of feelings: painful feelings, pleasant feelings, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings; pleasant bodily feelings, painful bodily feelings, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant bodily feelings; pleasant mental feelings, painful mental feelings, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant mental feelings; pleasant feelings regarding food, painful feelings regarding food, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings regarding food; pleasant feelings regarding non-food, painful feelings regarding non-food, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings regarding non-food; pleasant feelings of attachment, painful feelings of attachment, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings of attachment; and pleasant feelings of renunciation, painful feelings of renunciation, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings of renunciation.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Just as in a guest house, Various people reside—
Kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, Householders, and lay devotees."
Whether a caṇḍāla or a wild man, one who observes the precepts or violates them,
a householder or a renunciant— of all such various kinds,
this body is likewise.
Whether it be pleasant or painful feeling, or that which is neither painful nor pleasant;
whether accompanied by nutriment or without nutriment, or characterized by craving and non-craving—
the bhikṣu who exerts himself with skillful means, possessing right wisdom, remains unshakable.
Regarding all these feelings, the wise one is able to understand them;
because he understands all feelings, he exhausts all taints in this very life.
At the death of the body, he does not fall into further reckoning, but dwells forever in parinirvāṇa.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
473 (473) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu who, dwelling alone in a quiet place, engaged in meditative reflection and thought to himself:

"The World-Honored One has spoken of three feelings—pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; yet he has also said that all feelings whatsoever are suffering. What is the meaning of this?"
Having had this thought, that bhikṣu arose from his meditation, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
While I was meditating in a secluded place, this thought arose:

"The World-Honored One has spoken of three feelings—pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—and yet he has also said that all feelings whatsoever are suffering. What is the meaning of this?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Because all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, and because all conditioned phenomena are subject to change, I declare that whatever is felt is entirely suffering.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Knowing that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, And that they are all subject to change,
Therefore it is said that sensation is entirely suffering— This is what the Perfectly Awakened One knows."
The bhikṣu who is diligent in his application of effort, whose right wisdom is unshakable,
and who possesses keen intelligence, is able to fully comprehend all sensations.
Having thoroughly understood all sensations, he exhausts all outflows within this very life.
"When the body dies, one does not fall into the realms of rebirth, but dwells forever in parinirvāṇa.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
474 (Four Hundred and Seventy-Four). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was meditating alone in a quiet place, and this thought occurred to him:

“The Blessed One has spoken of three feelings—the pleasant feeling, the painful feeling, and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—and yet he has also said that all feelings whatsoever are suffering. What is the meaning of this?”
Having formed this thought, he arose from meditation, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
While I was meditating alone in a quiet place, this thought arose:

"The World-Honored One has spoken of three types of feeling—pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; yet he has also said that all feelings are entirely suffering. What is the meaning of this?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Because all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, and because all conditioned phenomena are subject to change, I declare that whatever is felt is entirely suffering."
Furthermore, Ānanda!
I teach that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are suffering because they gradually subside, and I teach it because they gradually cease; thus, all sensations (*vedanā*) are entirely suffering.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “How is this so,
World-Honored One?”
"Why is it said that 'all sensations gradually become tranquil'?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"When one is in the meditative attainment of the first dhyāna, speech is tranquil; when one is in the meditative attainment of the second dhyāna, applied and sustained thought are tranquil; when one is in the meditative attainment of the third dhyāna, the mind of joy is tranquil; and when one is in the meditative attainment of the fourth dhyāna, inhalation and exhalation are tranquil."

When one enters the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite space, the perception of form is stilled; when one enters the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the perception of the sphere of infinite space is stilled; when one enters the meditative attainment of the sphere of nothingness, the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness is stilled; when one enters the meditative attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the perception of the sphere of nothingness is stilled; and when one enters the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, perception and feeling are stilled. This is called the gradual stilling of all conditioned phenomena.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How do all conditioned phenomena gradually cease?”

The Buddha told Ānanda: “When one is in the meditative attainment of the first dhyāna, speech ceases; when in the meditative attainment of the second dhyāna, applied and sustained thought cease; when in the meditative attainment of the third dhyāna, joy ceases; when in the meditative attainment of the fourth dhyāna, inhalation and exhalation cease;

when in the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite space, the perception of form ceases; when in the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the perception of the sphere of infinite space ceases; when in the meditative attainment of the sphere of nothingness, the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness ceases; when in the meditative attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the perception of the sphere of nothingness ceases; and when in the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, perception and feeling cease. This is called the gradual cessation of all conditioned formations.”
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
This is called the gradual cessation of all conditioned formations.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Furthermore, there is a superior cessation, a marvelous cessation, a supreme cessation, and an unsurpassed cessation.
Such a cessation is beyond all other cessations."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“What is that supreme cessation, extraordinary cessation, superior cessation, and unsurpassed cessation, such that no other cessation surpasses it?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"To find no delight in a mind of sensual desire and to be liberated from it; to find no delight in a mind of ill will or delusion and to be liberated from them—this is called the superior cessation, the extraordinary cessation, the supreme cessation, the unsurpassed cessation; among all other cessations, none surpasses this."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
475 (475) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"When Vipaśyin Tathāgata had not yet attained Buddhahood, he dwelt alone in a quiet place, practicing dhyāna and contemplation, and made this observation, examining all sensations."
What is feeling? What is the origination of feeling?
What is the cessation of feeling?
What is the path leading to the origination of feeling?
What is the path leading to the cessation of feeling?
What is the gratification of feeling?
What is the danger in feeling?
What is the escape from feeling?
Contemplating in this way, one finds there are three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The arising of contact is the arising of feeling; the cessation of contact is the cessation of feeling.
If one delights in, praises, becomes attached to, and remains firmly established in feeling, this is called the path leading to the arising of feeling.
If one finds delight in feeling, praises it, becomes attached to it, and remains firmly established in it, this is called the path leading to the cessation of feeling.
If pleasure and joy arise with feeling as their condition, this is called the gratification of feeling. If feeling is subject to impermanence and change, this is called the danger of feeling.
"If one cuts off desire and lust for feeling, and transcends desire and lust for feeling, this is called 'separation from feeling.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Just as with Vipaśyin Buddha, so it was with Śikhin Buddha, Viśvabhū Buddha, Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, Kāśyapa Buddha, and myself, Śākyamuni Buddha; when we had not yet attained Buddhahood, our contemplation and observation of all sensations were likewise.
476 (Four Hundred Seventy-Six). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu was meditating alone in a quiet place.
Thus one observes all feelings.
What is feeling?
What is the arising of feeling?
What is the cessation of feeling?
What is the path leading to the origination of feeling?
What is the path leading to the cessation of feeling?
What is the gratification of feeling?
What is the danger of feeling?
What is the escape from feeling?
Then, that bhikṣu, having arisen from meditation, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
While dwelling alone in seclusion, I practiced meditation and contemplated the various feelings (vedanā). What are feelings?
How do feelings arise?
What is the cessation of feeling?
What is the path leading to the origination of feeling?
What is the path leading to the cessation of feeling?
What is the gratification of feeling?
What is the danger of feeling?
What is the escape from feeling?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are three feelings—pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The arising of contact is the arising of feeling; the cessation of contact is the cessation of feeling."
If one delights in feeling, praises it, becomes stained by attachment to it, and remains firmly established in it, this is called the path leading to the origination of feeling.
If one does not delight in feeling, does not praise it, is not stained by attachment to it, and does not remain firmly established in it, this is called the path leading to the cessation of feeling.
If pleasure and joy arise conditioned by feeling, this is called the gratification of feeling. If feeling is a phenomenon subject to impermanence and change, this is called the danger of feeling.
To sever desire and lust for feeling and to transcend desire and lust for feeling—this is called the escape from feeling.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
477 (477) As it was with the sutra asked by another bhikṣu, so too was the sutra asked by the Venerable Ānanda.
478 (Four Hundred and Seventy-Eight). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"What is feeling? What is the arising of feeling?
What is the cessation of feeling?"
"What is the path leading to the origination of feeling?
What is the path leading to the cessation of feeling?
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Blessed One is the root of the Dharma, the eye of the Dharma, and the refuge of the Dharma.
Excellent,
Blessed One!”
“I only wish that you would explain this in detail; having heard it, the bhikṣus will receive and practice it accordingly.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for your sake.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are three feelings—pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The arising of contact is the arising of feeling; the cessation of contact is the cessation of feeling."
If one finds delight in feeling, praises it, becomes stained by attachment to it, and remains firmly established in it, this is called the path leading to the origination of feeling;

if one does not find delight in feeling, does not praise it, is not stained by attachment to it, and does not remain firmly established in it, this is called the path leading to the cessation of feeling.
If pleasure and joy arise conditioned by feeling, this is called the gratification of feeling;
if feeling is impermanent and subject to change, this is called the danger of feeling;
if one abandons desire and lust for feeling and transcends that desire and lust, this is called the escape from feeling.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
479 (479) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If I had not known feelings as they truly are—feeling, the origin of feeling, the cessation of feeling, the path leading to the cessation of feeling, the gratification of feeling, the danger of feeling, and the escape from feeling as they truly are—I would not have attained liberation, transcendence, and freedom from all perversions within the world of devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the assembly of gods and humans; nor would I have attained unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment."

Because I have known, as they truly are, all feelings, the origin of feelings, the cessation of feelings, the path leading to the origin of feelings, the path leading to the cessation of feelings, the gratification of feelings, the danger of feelings, and the escape from feelings, I have, among the assembly of devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gods, and humans, attained liberation, transcendence, and freedom from all perversions, and have realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 480 (480) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa, the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa does not know feelings as they really are—does not know the arising of feelings, the cessation of feelings, the path leading to the arising of feelings, the path leading to the cessation of feelings, the gratification of feelings, the danger of feelings, and the escape from feelings as they really are;

then he is not a śramaṇa, not a brāhmaṇa, one who does not conform to a śramaṇa, one who does not conform to a brāhmaṇa, and he possesses neither the meaning of a śramaṇa nor the meaning of a brāhmaṇa, [yet claims] to have realized for himself through direct knowledge in this very life:"
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence.

If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa knows feelings as they truly are—knows the arising of feelings, the cessation of feelings, the path leading to the arising of feelings, and the path leading to the cessation of feelings; knows the gratification of feelings, the danger of feelings, and the escape from feelings as they truly are—then he is a śramaṇa among śramaṇas and a brāhmaṇa among brāhmaṇas; he is a true śramaṇa and a true brāhmaṇa, possessing the qualities of a śramaṇa and the qualities of a brāhmaṇa, who realizes and witnesses for himself in this very life:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As it is with those who are śramaṇas and those who are not śramaṇas, so it is likewise with those counted among the śramaṇas and those counted among those who are not śramaṇas.
481 (Four Hundred and Eighty-One). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Iṣiganagara, in the Iṣiganagara Forest.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I wish to sit in meditation here for half a month. Bhikṣus!"
Do not wander about again, except for the sake of alms and the uposatha; instead, sit in meditation and do not wander about again, except for the sake of alms and the uposatha.
At that time, when half a month had passed, the World-Honored One spread out his sitting mat, sat before the assembly, and addressed the bhikṣus:

"Regarding the slight portion of the dhyāna-factors from the meditative dharmas I contemplated at the time of my initial enlightenment, during this past half-month I have contemplated them and formed this thought:
'All sentient beings who experience birth do so because of causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions.'"
"What are the conditions?
Desire is a condition, perception is a condition, and contact is a condition. "O bhikṣus!"

When desire is not stilled, awareness is not stilled, and contact is not stilled, by reason of those conditions, feelings arise in sentient beings; because of the condition of their being unstilled, feelings arise in sentient beings.

His desire is tranquil, but his perception is not tranquil and his contact is not tranquil; by reason of those causes and conditions, sentient beings experience feelings. Because of these non-tranquil causes and conditions, sentient beings experience feelings.

His desire is stilled and his perception is stilled, yet his contact is not stilled; by reason of those causes and conditions, sentient beings experience feeling. Because of the condition of that which is not stilled, sentient beings experience feeling.

He desires cessation, awakens to cessation, and touches cessation; by reason of those causes and conditions, sentient beings experience feelings, and by reason of that cessation, sentient beings experience feelings.
Due to the causal conditions of wrong view, sentient beings give rise to feeling; due to the causal condition of the non-cessation of wrong view, sentient beings give rise to feeling.

Due to the causal conditions of wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, wrong liberation, and wrong knowledge, sentient beings give rise to feeling; due to the causal condition of the non-cessation of wrong knowledge, sentient beings give rise to feeling.
Due to the causal condition of right view, sentient beings experience feeling; due to the causal condition of the cessation of right view, sentient beings experience feeling.

Due to the causal conditions of right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, right liberation, and right knowledge, sentient beings experience feeling; due to the causal condition of the cessation of right knowledge, sentient beings experience feeling.

If there arises for them the birth of a feeling through the cause and condition of obtaining what was desired but not obtained, acquiring what was not acquired, or realizing what was not realized; and if there arises for them the birth of a feeling through the cause and condition of the cessation of those very things.
This is called the cause and condition for non-cessation, whereby sentient beings give rise to feeling; this is the cause and condition for cessation, whereby sentient beings give rise to feeling.

"If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa does not know, as they truly are, the conditions for conditions, the arising of conditions for conditions, the cessation of conditions for conditions, the path leading to the arising of conditions for conditions, and the path leading to the cessation of conditions for conditions, then he is not a śramaṇa among śramaṇas, nor a brāhmaṇa among brāhmaṇas; he is no different from a non-śramaṇa or a non-brāhmaṇa. He does not possess the meaning of a śramaṇa or the meaning of a brāhmaṇa, and he does not, by his own knowledge, realize and witness for himself in the present life:
'Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and I myself know that there will be no further existence.'"

“If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa understands, as they truly are, this object-condition, the origination of the object-condition, the cessation of the object-condition, the path leading to the origination of the object-condition, and the path leading to the cessation of the object-condition, you should know that he is a true śramaṇa among śramaṇas and a true brāhmaṇa among brāhmaṇas; he is equal to a śramaṇa and equal to a brāhmaṇa. By means of the qualities of a śramaṇa and the qualities of a brāhmaṇa, he realizes for himself and attains realization in this very life:
‘Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I myself know that there will be no further existence.’”
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
482 (482) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

During the summer retreat, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada came to where the Buddha was staying, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side. The Buddha taught him the Dharma, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him, and spoke on various aspects of the Dharma.
Having thus instructed, exhorted, illuminated, and gladdened them, he rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, paid homage to the Buddha, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly, will accept my invitation for three months to receive robes, food and drink, and medicinal decoctions as needed."
At that time, the World-Honored One granted his consent by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted the invitation through his silence, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada rose from his seat and departed. He returned to his own home, and after three months had passed, he came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha said to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
"Excellent, householder! Excellent!"
For three months, you have provided robes, food and drink, and medicinal decoctions according to their needs.

You have adorned and purified the supreme path; in future lives, you shall obtain the fruit of peace and happiness. Yet, do not remain silent and merely enjoy this Dharma; you must apply yourself with diligence, training from time to time to realize through bodily experience the joy of seclusion.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada rejoiced and approved, rose from his seat, and departed.
Then, while the Venerable Śāriputra was seated among the assembly, he knew that the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had left and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How marvelous! How marvelous!"
"Bhagavān!
You have well expounded the Dharma for the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and have well exhorted the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, saying:
'During these three months, you have fully made offerings to the Tathāgata and his great assembly; having purified the supreme path, you shall receive the retribution of happiness in future lives.'"
"Do not remain silent and attached to this merit; you should from time to time train in the full realization through the body of the joy and pleasure of seclusion.
"World-Honored One!
If a noble disciple trains in the full realization through the body of the joy and pleasure of seclusion, he attains the seclusion from five things and cultivates the fulfillment of five things."
What is meant by "distancing oneself from five things"?

It refers to: abandoning joy nurtured by desire, abandoning grief nurtured by desire, abandoning equanimity nurtured by desire; and abandoning joy nurtured by unwholesome states, abandoning grief nurtured by unwholesome states. These are called the five things to be distanced from.
"What are the five dharmas to be cultivated to fulfillment?
They are: sympathetic joy, gladness, tranquility, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"It is so, it is so. If a noble disciple trains in the cultivation of seclusion from joy and bliss, fully realizing it with the body, he abandons five qualities and fulfills five qualities."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 483 (483) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are those who have the mindfulness of nutriment, those who have the mindfulness of non-nutriment, and those who have the mindfulness of neither-nutriment-nor-non-nutriment;
there are those who have the pleasure of nutriment, those who have the pleasure of non-nutriment, and those who have the pleasure of neither-nutriment-nor-non-nutriment."
There are those who abandon through nutriment, those who abandon without nutriment, and those who abandon without nutriment and without non-nutriment;
there are those who are liberated through nutriment, those who are liberated without nutriment, and those who are liberated without nutriment and without non-nutriment.
"What is 'nourished mindfulness' (āhāraka-smṛti)?
It refers to mindfulness arising with the five objects of desire as its causal condition.
What is 'non-nourished mindfulness' (anāhāraka-smṛti)?"

It refers to a bhikṣu who, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by directed thought and evaluation, and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion; this is called mindfulness without nutriment.
What is the nutrimentless mindfulness of nutrimentlessness?

It refers to a bhikṣu who, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, becomes inwardly pure and one-pointed, free from applied and sustained thought, and attains and abides in the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss; this is called the nutrimentless mindfulness of nutrimentlessness.
"What is pleasure with nutriment?
It refers to the pleasure and joy born from the causes and conditions of the five sensual desires; this is called pleasure with nutriment.
What is pleasure without nutriment?"

That is to say: when the breath is accompanied by directed thought and sustained evaluation, with internal clarity and one-pointedness of mind, free from directed thought and sustained evaluation, and characterized by the joy and happiness born of concentration—this is called the nutrimentless joy.
What is the nutrimentless joy of the nutrimentless?

That is to say, a bhikṣu, detached from joy and craving, dwells with equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension; he abides in that bliss of which the Noble Ones declare, "Equanimous and mindful, one dwells in bliss"—this is called the nutrimentless, nutrimentless bliss.
"What is 'equanimity with nutriment'?
It refers to equanimity arising from the causes and conditions of the five sensual desires; this is called equanimity with nutriment.
What is 'equanimity without nutriment'?"

That is to say, that bhikṣu, detached from joy and craving, dwells with equanimity, mindful and clearly aware; he dwells in bliss, experiencing that "noble equanimity" spoken of by the Sage, and fully attains the third dhyāna. This is called the nourishment-free equanimity.
What is the equanimity that is without nutriment?

It refers to a bhikṣu who, having abandoned suffering and stilled pleasure, and having already transcended sorrow and joy, dwells in the fourth dhyāna—neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by pure mindfulness and one-pointedness of mind; this is called the equanimity that is without nutriment.
"What is liberation with nutriment?
It is that which proceeds together with form.
What is liberation without nutriment?"
This refers to that which is accompanied by the formless.
What is the liberation through non-nutriment?
It is when that bhikṣu is untainted and liberated from desire, and his mind is untainted and liberated from hatred and delusion; this is called liberation through non-nutriment.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
484 (484) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Bhaddāli Bhikkhu and the Venerable Ānanda were both staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
Then, the Venerable Ānanda went to where the Venerable Bhaddāli was, and after exchanging greetings and pleasantries with him, he stood to one side.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Venerable Bhaddāli Bhikṣu:
"What is meant by 'seeing foremost'?
What is meant by 'hearing foremost'?"
What is the foremost among pleasures?
What is the foremost among perceptions?
What is the foremost among states of existence?
The Venerable Bhaddāla said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"There is a Brahmā who is sovereign, creative, and able to manifest things at will; he is the father of the world. To see that Brahmā is called 'seeing the foremost.'"

“Ānanda! There are sentient beings who possess the joy and happiness born of seclusion; they are moistened everywhere, suffused with delight everywhere, and their entire bodies are filled, with no part left unsatisfied.”
Regarding what is called "joy and happiness born of seclusion," he arose from samādhi and raised his voice to proclaim to the great assembly:
"The utterly tranquil is joy and happiness born of seclusion; the supremely blissful is joy and happiness born of seclusion."
“Those who hear that sound are said to have the foremost hearing.

Furthermore, Ānanda, there are sentient beings whose bodies are moistened by the joy of seclusion from rapture; they are moistened everywhere, suffused with delight and fullness, their entire bodies filled such that no part remains unsatisfied. This so-called joy of seclusion from rapture is called the foremost bliss.”
“What is the foremost perception? Ānanda!

There are sentient beings who, having transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, dwell fully possessing the sphere of nothingness. If they give rise to that perception, it is called the foremost perception.”
"What is the first existence?

Furthermore, Ānanda, there are beings who, having transcended the sphere of nothingness, dwell fully possessed of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; if such an existence arises, this is called the first existence."
The Venerable Ānanda said to the Venerable Bhaddāla Bhikṣu:
"Many people hold such a view and speak thus; you are the same as they—what difference is there?"
I shall employ a skillful means to question you; listen attentively, for I shall explain it to you.
According to what is observed, one gradually exhausts all outflows (*āsrava*); this is called the first vision.
To exhaust all outflows (āsrava) in successive order according to what one has heard is called the foremost in hearing.
To exhaust all outflows in successive order through the joy that has arisen is called the foremost in joy.
To exhaust all outflows through successive stages according to one's conceptualization is called the foremost among conceptions.
To exhaust all outflows through successive stages by means of observing reality as it is is called the foremost among existents.
Then, having finished their discussion together, the two noble men rose from their seats and departed.
485 (485) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, King Bimbisāra went to where the Venerable Udāyin was, prostrated himself in salutation, and withdrew to sit at one side.
Then, King Bimbisāra addressed the Venerable Udāyin, saying:
"In what way does the Blessed One describe the various feelings?"
Udāyin said: "Great King!
The Blessed One has taught three types of feeling: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."
King Bimbisāra said to the Venerable Udāyin:
"Do not speak thus:
'The World-Honored One has taught three types of feeling—pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.'"
"There should properly be two kinds of feeling—pleasant feeling and painful feeling.
If there were neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, that would be cessation.

Thus he spoke three times, yet Udāyin could not establish three feelings for the king, nor could the king establish two feelings. Together they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Then, the Venerable Udāyin, based on what he had previously said, addressed the Blessed One in detail:

"I am unable to establish three types of feeling, and the King is also unable to establish two types of feeling; therefore, we have come together to inquire fully of the Blessed One regarding this matter: how many types of feeling are there, definitively?"
The Buddha told Udāyin:

“I sometimes speak of one feeling; at other times, I speak of two feelings; or I speak of three, four, five, six, eighteen, thirty-six, or even one hundred and eight feelings; and at other times, I speak of immeasurable feelings.”
"What do I mean by 'one feeling'?
As it is said: 'Whatever feeling there is, all of it is suffering'—this is what I mean by 'one feeling.
What do I mean by 'two feelings'?"
To speak of bodily feeling and mental feeling is called the two types of feeling.
What are the three types of feeling?
They are pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
What are the four types of feeling?
They are: feeling bound to the desire realm, feeling bound to the form realm, feeling bound to the formless realm, and unbound feeling.
Why are five types of feeling taught?
That is to say: the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of joy, the faculty of pain, the faculty of grief, and the faculty of equanimity; these are called the teaching on the five feelings.
What is the teaching on the six feelings?
It refers to the feeling born of eye-contact.
There are feelings born of contact with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
How are the eighteen feelings explained?
They are the feelings that follow the six types of joy, the six types of grief, and the six types of equanimity; these are called the eighteen feelings.

What are the thirty-six feelings? They are: those based on the six kinds of attachment to joy, those based on the six kinds of detachment from joy; those based on the six kinds of attachment to sorrow, those based on the six kinds of detachment from sorrow; and those based on the six kinds of attachment to equanimity, those based on the six kinds of detachment from equanimity. These are called the thirty-six feelings.
What is meant by the teaching of the one hundred and eight feelings?
It refers to thirty-six feelings of the past, thirty-six of the future, and thirty-six of the present; this is called the teaching of the one hundred and eight feelings.
What is meant by "teaching immeasurable feelings"?
It refers to teaching them as "this feeling" or "that feeling," and so forth; just as they are taught through such immeasurable names, this is called "teaching immeasurable feelings."

“Udāyin! Although I have thus explained the meaning of feeling in its various aspects according to reality, the world does not understand it; therefore, they engage in disputes and contradictions with one another, ultimately failing to attain the true meaning within my Dharma and Vinaya for the sake of their own cessation.”

Udāyin! If one understands, as it truly is, the meaning of these various kinds of feelings taught by me, one will not give rise to disputes or mutual opposition; and regarding disputes already arisen or those yet to arise, one will be able to bring them to rest through the Dharma and the Vinaya.
"However, Udāyin! There are two kinds of feeling:
the feeling of sensual desire and the feeling of freedom from sensual desire.
What is the feeling of sensual desire? Feeling that arises conditioned by the five strands of sensual pleasure is called the feeling of sensual desire."
What is the feeling of detachment from desire?

It refers to a bhikṣu who, detached from desires and unwholesome, evil states, possessing applied and sustained thought, and experiencing the joy and happiness born of detachment, dwells having fully attained the first dhyāna; this is called the feeling of detachment from desire.
"If anyone were to say that sentient beings rely on this first dhyāna and that it alone constitutes bliss, and nothing else, this would not be so. Why is that? "
Furthermore, there is a superior bliss that surpasses this; what is it?

It refers to a bhikṣu who, having transcended applied and sustained thought, with internal purity, attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss; this is called superior bliss.
In this manner, it is explained with increasing excellence up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
"If someone were to say:
'Only this place exists, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which is the ultimate bliss and nothing else.'"
"Nor is it so. Why is this? Because there is a superior bliss that exceeds this. What is it?"

That is to say, a bhikṣu transcends the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, attains the cessation of perception and feeling, realizes it with his own body, and dwells in its full possession; this is called a superior happiness that surpasses the former.
"If there are followers of other schools who have gone forth and say:
'The Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim that only the cessation of perception and feeling is called the ultimate bliss,' this is not appropriate."
Why is that? One should say:
"This is not the enumeration of pleasant feelings taught by the Blessed One; as for the enumeration of pleasant feelings taught by the Blessed One, it is as he has explained."
“Udāyin! There are four kinds of happiness. What are the four?
"Namely, the joy of detachment from desire, the joy of seclusion, the joy of tranquility, and the joy of awakening.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Udāyin and King Bimbisāra, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
486. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If one develops right disenchantment toward, lack of delight in, and turning away from even a single dharma, one attains the exhaustion of all taints; that is to say, the fact that all sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment."
Furthermore, there are two things: name and form (*nāma-rūpa*).
Furthermore, there are three things, namely the three feelings (*vedanā*).
Furthermore, there are four things, namely the four nutriments (*āhāra*).
Furthermore, there are five dharmas, namely the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
Furthermore, there are six dharmas, namely the six internal and external sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
Furthermore, there are seven dharmas, namely the seven stations of consciousness (*sapta-vijñāna-sthiti*).
Furthermore, there are eight things, namely the eight worldly dharmas.
Furthermore, there are nine things, namely the nine abodes of sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are ten things, namely the ten paths of karmic action.
"Regarding these ten dharmas, by giving rise to revulsion, dispassion, and renunciation, one attains the exhaustion of all outflows.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
487 (Four Hundred and Eighty-Seven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If one develops right weary detachment, lack of delight, and turning away from even a single dharma, one reaches the ultimate end of suffering and is liberated from suffering—namely, that all sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment."
Furthermore, there are two dharmas: name and form.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas, namely the three feelings.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four nutriments.
Furthermore, there are five dharmas, namely the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
Furthermore, there are six dharmas, namely the six internal and external sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
Furthermore, there are seven dharmas, namely the seven stations of consciousness (*sapta-vijñāna-sthiti*).
Furthermore, there are eight things, namely the eight worldly dharmas.
Furthermore, there are nine things, namely the nine abodes of sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are ten things, namely the ten paths of karmic action.
"Regarding these ten phenomena, one should develop right disenchantment, lack of delight, and renunciation; thus reaching the ultimate end of suffering, one is liberated from suffering.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
488. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If one observes a single dharma as impermanent, observes it as subject to change, observes it as free from desire, observes it as cessation, and observes it as relinquishment, one attains the exhaustion of all taints; that is to say, all sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment."
Furthermore, there are two dharmas: name and form.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas, namely the three feelings.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four nutriments.
Furthermore, there are five dharmas, namely the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
Furthermore, there are six dharmas, namely the six internal and external sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
Furthermore, there are seven dharmas, namely the seven stations of consciousness (*sapta-vijñāna-sthiti*).
Furthermore, there are eight things, namely the eight worldly dharmas.
Furthermore, there are nine things, namely the nine abodes of sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are ten things, namely the ten paths of karmic action.

Regarding these ten phenomena, by correctly contemplating their impermanence, observing their changeability, observing dispassion toward them, observing their cessation, and observing their relinquishment, one attains the exhaustion of all taints.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 489 (489) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If one contemplates a single dharma as impermanent, as subject to change, as characterized by dispassion, as subject to cessation, and as something to be relinquished, one will reach the ultimate end of suffering and be liberated from suffering—namely, that all sentient beings exist by means of nutriment."
Furthermore, there are two phenomena: name and form.
Furthermore, there are three phenomena, namely the three feelings.
