When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Saṃyukta Āgama, Volume 17, Sūtra 455 (455). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

“Due to various elements, various contacts arise; due to various contacts, various perceptions arise; due to various perceptions, various desires arise; due to various desires, various thoughts arise; due to various thoughts, various fevers arise; due to various fevers, various seekings arise.”
"What are the various elements?
They are the eighteen elements: the eye element, up to and including the mental-object element.
How do various contacts arise conditioned by these various elements?"
How so? Up to: conditioned by various heats, various seekings arise.
That is to say, conditioned by the eye-element, eye-contact arises; it is not that eye-contact conditions the eye-element, but rather that eye-contact arises only conditioned by the eye-element.
Visual perception arises conditioned by visual contact; visual contact does not arise conditioned by visual perception—visual perception arises solely conditioned by visual contact.
Visual desire arises conditioned by visual perception; visual perception does not arise conditioned by visual desire—visual desire arises solely conditioned by visual perception.
Visual cognition arises conditioned by visual desire; visual desire does not arise conditioned by visual cognition—visual cognition arises solely conditioned by visual desire.

Conditioned by the eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsparśa*) arises; it is not that conditioned by eye-contact, eye-consciousness arises, but rather that conditioned by eye-consciousness, eye-contact arises.
Conditioned by eye-contact, eye-thirst (*cakṣutr̥ṣṇā*) arises; it is not that conditioned by eye-thirst, eye-contact arises, but rather that conditioned by eye-contact, eye-thirst arises.

In the same way, it should be explained in detail that mental contact arises conditioned by the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-element, up to and including how mental seeking arises conditioned by mental fever.

This is called a bhikṣu for whom various contacts arise conditioned by various elements, and so on, up to various seeking arising conditioned by various fevers; it is not that various fevers arise conditioned by various seeking, nor even that various elements arise conditioned by various contacts, but rather that various contacts arise conditioned by various elements, and so on, up to various seeking arising conditioned by various fevers.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As it was said regarding the six internal bases, so too should it be spoken regarding the six external bases.
Saṃyukta Āgama, Volume XVIII,
translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Song Dynasty;

18.490 (490) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Nāla Village in the kingdom of Magadha.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was also in Nāla Village in the kingdom of Magadha.

At that time, there was a renunciant of the non-Buddhist path named Jambukhādaka, who was an old friend of Śāriputra. He approached Śāriputra, and after exchanging greetings and mutual expressions of courtesy, he withdrew to sit at one side and asked Śāriputra:
"In the Dharma and Vinaya of the Noble Ones, what is difficult?"
Śāriputra said to Yaśas:
"Only renunciation is difficult.
"In what way is renunciation difficult?"
He replied, “It is difficult to find those who delight [in this].
“In what way is it difficult to find those who delight?”
He replied,
"It is difficult to delight in constantly cultivating wholesome dharmas.
He asked again:
“Śāriputra! Is there a path, is there a way, which, through cultivation and repeated cultivation, leads to the constant practice of wholesome dharmas and their increase?
He replied:
"There is. It is the Eightfold Noble Path, namely:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration."
Yaśas said: "Śāriputra! This is indeed the good path;
this is indeed the good direction. By practicing it and practicing it repeatedly, one constantly cultivates and increases all wholesome dharmas."
"Śāriputra!
Those who have left the household life and constantly cultivate this path will, before long, swiftly attain the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).
At that time, having finished their discussion, the two noble men rose from their seats and departed.
Thus ends the introductory section of forty sūtras concerning the questions asked by Yaśas.
Yaśas asked Śāriputra:
"What is meant by one who is called a 'well-expounder of the Dharma'?"
"He is the one who leads the world toward the right direction.
Why is he called the Sugata of the world?
Śāriputra said:
"If one preaches the Dharma for the purpose of subduing sensual desire, subduing ill will, and subduing delusion, such a person is called a worldly preacher of the Dharma.
If one is directed toward subduing sensual desire, directed toward subduing ill will, and directed toward subduing delusion, this is called being rightly directed."
"If greed has been exhausted and is known to be abandoned without remainder; if hatred and delusion have been exhausted and are known to be abandoned without remainder—this is called 'well-severed.
He asked again: "Śāriputra!"
“Is there a path and a direction, through the cultivation and repeated practice of which one can give rise to wholesome abandonment?
Śāriputra replied, “There is.”
That is to say, the Eightfold Noble Path—right view, and so forth, up to right concentration.
Then, having finished their discussion together, the two noble men rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśoda asked Śāriputra,
"Regarding what is called 'nirvāṇa,' what is nirvāṇa?
Śāriputra replied:
“Nirvana is the eternal exhaustion of greed, the eternal exhaustion of hatred, the eternal exhaustion of delusion, and the eternal exhaustion of all afflictions; this is called nirvana.”
He asked again:
"Śāriputra! Is there a path, is there a way, which, through cultivation and repeated practice, leads to the attainment of nirvāṇa?"
Śāriputra said: "There is.
It refers to the Eightfold Noble Path—right view, and so forth, up to right concentration."
Then, after the two noble men had finished their discussion, they each rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśas asked Śāriputra:
"For what reason have you gone forth under the śramaṇa Gautama to practice the holy life?"
Śāriputra said:
"It is for the sake of severing greed, for the sake of severing hatred, and for the sake of severing delusion that one goes forth under the Śramaṇa Gautama to practice the holy life."
He asked again:
"Śāriputra! Is there a path, is there a way, which, through cultivation and repeated practice, leads to the abandonment of greed, hatred, and delusion?"
Śāriputra said: “There is.
It refers to the Eightfold Noble Path—from right view up to right concentration.”
Then, after the two noble men had finished their discussion, they each rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśas asked Śāriputra:
"What is meant by the exhaustion of the outflows?"
"What is meant by 'the exhaustion of outflows'?
Śāriputra replied, "As for 'outflows,' there are three outflows: namely, the outflow of desire, the outflow of existence, and the outflow of ignorance."
"When these three outflows are exhausted without remainder, it is called the exhaustion of the outflows.
He asked again: "Śāriputra!"
“Is there a path and a direction which, through cultivation and repeated practice, lead to the destruction of the outflows?
Śāriputra replied, “There is.”
That is to say, the Eightfold Noble Path—right view, and so forth, up to right concentration.
Then, having finished their discussion, the two noble men rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśas asked Śāriputra,
"Regarding what is called an 'arhat,' why is one named an arhat?
Śāriputra replied:
"Having abandoned greed without remainder, and having abandoned hatred and delusion without remainder—this is called an Arhat.
He asked again: "Śāriputra!"
“Is there a path and a direction, through the cultivation and repeated practice of which one attains arhatship?
Śāriputra replied, “There is.”
That is to say, the Eightfold Noble Path—right view up to right concentration.
At that time, having finished their discussion, the two noble men rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśoda asked Śāriputra:
"Regarding what is called an 'arhat,' why is one named an arhat?
Śāriputra replied:
"One for whom greed is forever exhausted without remainder, and hatred and delusion are forever exhausted without remainder—this is called an Arhat.
He asked again:
"Is there a path, is there a way, which, through cultivation and repeated practice, leads to the attainment of Arhatship?"
Śāriputra said: “There is.
It refers to the Eightfold Noble Path—from right view up to right concentration.”
Then, after the two noble men had finished their discussion, they each rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśas asked Śāriputra:
"Regarding what is called ignorance, what constitutes ignorance?"
Śāriputra said:
"That which is called ignorance is lack of knowledge regarding the past, lack of knowledge regarding the future, and lack of knowledge regarding the past, future, and middle [present];
it is lack of knowledge regarding the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; and it is lack of knowledge regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path."

Ignorance regarding what is wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; ignorance regarding the internal and ignorance regarding the external; whatever lack of knowledge, darkness, or obscuration there may be with respect to various matters—this is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Yaśas said to Śāriputra,
“This is a mass of great darkness.
He asked again:
“Śāriputra! Is there a path, is there a way, which, through cultivation and repeated practice, brings about the abandonment of ignorance?
Śāriputra replied:
“There is. It is the Eightfold Noble Path—right view, up to and including right concentration.
Then, having finished their discussion, the two noble men rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśas further asked the Venerable Śāriputra:
"Regarding what is called 'with outflows' (sāsrava), what constitutes being with outflows?
[The answer was] as previously stated.
Yaśoda asked Śāriputra, "What is meant by 'existence'? What constitutes existence?
Śāriputra replied:
"There are those who say there are three realms of existence—the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.
He asked again: "Śāriputra!"
“Is there a path and a direction, through the cultivation and repeated practice of which this existence can be abandoned?
Śāriputra replied, “There is.”
That is to say, the Eightfold Noble Path—from right view up to right concentration.
Then, having finished their discussion, the two noble men rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśoda asked Śāriputra, "What is meant by 'the existence of a body' (satkāya)? How is there a body?
Śāriputra replied:
"One who possesses a body" refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandhāḥ*).
What are the five aggregates of clinging?

They are the aggregate of clinging to form (*rūpa-upādānaskandhaḥ*), and the aggregates of clinging to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
He asked again:
"Śāriputra! Is there a path, is there a way, that brings an end to this personal existence?"
Śāriputra said: “There is.
It refers to the Eightfold Noble Path—from right view up to right concentration.”
Then, after the two noble men had finished their discussion, they each rose from their seats and departed.
Yaṃvuka asked Śāriputra:
"What is that which is called 'suffering'?"
"What is suffering? Śāriputra replied,

"Suffering refers to the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from what one loves, the suffering of encountering what one hates, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks."
"In brief, the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging is called 'suffering.
He asked again: "Śāriputra!"
Is there a path and a direction that can sever this suffering?
Śāriputra replied, “There is.”
That is to say, the Eightfold Noble Path—right view, and so forth, up to right concentration.
At that time, having finished their discussion together, the two noble men rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśoda asked Śāriputra,
"Regarding what is called 'the floods' (oghāḥ),
what are these floods? Śāriputra replied:
"The floods refer to the flood of desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance.
He asked again: "Śāriputra!"
"Is there a path and a direction, through cultivation and repeated practice of which, this stream may be severed?
Śāriputra replied, "There is."
That is to say, the Eightfold Noble Path—right view, and so forth, up to right concentration.
Then, having finished their discussion, the two noble men rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśas asked Śāriputra:
"Regarding what is called 'the yoke' (yoga),
what constitutes a yoke?"
He spoke thus as he had been instructed.
Yaśas asked Śāriputra:
"Regarding what is called 'clinging' (upādāna), what constitutes clinging?"
Śāriputra said:
"As for 'grasping,' there are four graspings: namely, grasping at sense-pleasures, grasping at self, grasping at views, and grasping at precepts and rituals.
He asked again:
“Śāriputra! Is there a path, is there a way, which, if cultivated and practiced extensively, will sever this grasping?
Śāriputra replied:
“There is. It is the Eightfold Noble Path—right view, and so forth, up to right concentration.
Then, having finished their discussion, the two noble men rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśoda asked Śāriputra:
"Regarding what is called 'bondage,' what constitutes bondage?"
Śāriputra said:
"As for 'bondage,' there are four bonds, namely: the bond of sensual desire, the bond of ill will, the bond of attachment to precepts and rituals, and the bond of the view of self."
He asked again:
“Śāriputra, is there a path,
is there a way, which, when cultivated and practiced extensively, brings about the severance of these fetters?”
Śāriputra said: "There is.
It is called the Eightfold Noble Path."
"Right view, up to and including right concentration.
Then, having finished their discussion, the two noble men rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśas asked Śāriputra:
"What is meant by 'fetters'?
What constitutes a fetter?
Śāriputra asked.

“Fetters” refers to the nine fetters, namely: the fetter of craving, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of ignorance, the fetter of views, the fetter of adherence to precepts and observances, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of envy, and the fetter of avarice.
He asked again:
"Śāriputra, is there a path,
is there a way, which, when cultivated and practiced repeatedly, brings about the abandonment of these fetters?"
Śāriputra said: "There is.
It refers to the Eightfold Noble Path—right view, up to and including right concentration."
Then, after the two noble men had finished their discussion, they each rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśas asked Śāriputra: "Regarding what you called a 'messenger'..."
"What are the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)?
Śāriputra replied: "The underlying tendencies are seven:

namely, the underlying tendency of sensual desire, the underlying tendency of ill will, the underlying tendency of craving for existence, the underlying tendency of pride, the underlying tendency of ignorance, the underlying tendency of views, and the underlying tendency of doubt."
He asked again:
"Śāriputra! Is there a path, is there a way, which, if practiced and cultivated repeatedly, will sever these underlying tendencies?"
Śāriputra said: "There is.
It refers to the Eightfold Noble Path—right view, and so forth, up to right concentration."
Then, after the two noble men had finished their discussion, they each rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśas asked Śāriputra:
"As for what is called 'desire'—"
"What is desire? Śāriputra replied,
"Desire refers to forms cognized by the eye that are lovely, pleasant, and cherished, and to being stained by and attached to those forms."

Yajñavalkya! Sounds heard by the ear, odors smelled by the nose, flavors tasted by the tongue, and tangibles cognized by the body that are lovely, pleasant, and delightful—these are contacts of attachment.
Yajñavalkya! These qualities are not desire; they are merely perceptions, conceptions, and mental constructions.
At that time, Śāriputra spoke these verses:
"It is not the driving force of sensual desire, nor the various forms of the world;
it is only the conceptualization of perception—this is the desire of the person."
"Those various forms that constantly exist in the world—
those who subdue the mind of craving for them are indeed the wise.
He asked again:
"Śāriputra! Is there a path, is there a way, by practicing and cultivating it extensively, through which this desire can be abandoned?
Śāriputra replied:
“There is. It is the Eightfold Noble Path—right view, and so on, up to right concentration.
Then, having finished their discussion, the two noble men rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśoda asked Śāriputra,
"Regarding what is called 'nurturing,' what constitutes nurturing?
Śāriputra replied:

“There are five kinds of nourishment: namely, the nourishment of sensual desire, the nourishment of ill-will, the nourishment of sloth and torpor, the nourishment of restlessness and remorse, and the nourishment of doubt.
He asked again: “Śāriputra!”
"Is there a path and a method, through cultivation and repeated practice of which, these five modes of sustenance can be abandoned?
Śāriputra replied, "There is."
That is to say, the Eightfold Noble Path—right view, and so forth, up to right concentration.
Then, having finished their discussion, the two noble men rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśodeva asked Śāriputra:
"Regarding what is called 'resting,' what constitutes resting?"
Śāriputra said,
"To find rest means to sever the three fetters.
He asked again:
“Śāriputra! Is there a path, is there a way, which, through cultivation and repeated practice, brings about the abandonment of the three fetters?
Śāriputra replied:
“There is. It is the Eightfold Noble Path—right view, and so forth, up to right concentration.
Then, having finished their discussion, the two noble men rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśoda asked Śāriputra:
"Regarding those who have attained relief—
what is it to have attained relief?"
Śāriputra said:
"To have attained relief means that the three fetters have been exhausted and fully understood.
He asked again:
“Is there a path and a method by which these fetters can be severed?
Śāriputra replied, “There is.”
That is to say, the Eightfold Noble Path—from right view up to right concentration.
At that time, having finished their discussion, the two noble men rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśoda asked Śāriputra:
"It is said that one has attained supreme relief.
What is meant by attaining supreme relief?"
Śāriputra said:
"To have attained supreme relief means that greed has been forever exhausted, and hatred and delusion have been forever exhausted; this is called having attained supreme relief."
He asked again:
"Śāriputra! Is there a path, is there a way, which, through cultivation and repeated practice, leads to attaining supreme relief?"
Śāriputra replied: "There is.
It refers to the Eightfold Noble Path—right view, and so forth, up to right concentration."
At that time, after the two noble men had finished their discussion, they each rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśas asked Śāriputra:
"What is meant by 'attaining the state of supreme relief'?"
"What is meant by 'attaining the place of supreme relief'?

Śāriputra replied, "To have attained the place of supreme relief means that sensual desire has been abandoned and fully understood, exhausted without remainder; that ill will and delusion have been abandoned and fully understood, exhausted without remainder—this is what is meant by attaining the place of supreme relief."
He asked again:
"Śāriputra, is there a path,
is there a way, by practicing and cultivating it repeatedly, that one may attain the state of supreme rest?"
Śāriputra replied: “There is.
It refers to the Eightfold Noble Path—right view up to right concentration.”
At that time, after the two noble men had finished their discussion, they each rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśas asked Śāriputra:
"What is meant by 'the cool'?"
"What is meant by 'coolness'? Śāriputra replied:
"Coolness refers to the exhaustion of the five lower fetters, namely: the view of a self, adherence to precepts and rituals, doubt, sensual desire, and ill will."
He asked again:
"Is there a path, is there a way, by practicing and cultivating which one may sever these five lower fetters and attain coolness?
Śāriputra replied:
“There is. It is the Eightfold Noble Path—from right view up to right concentration.
Then, having finished their discussion, the two noble men rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśoda asked Śāriputra:
"It is said that one attains coolness.
What is meant by 'attaining coolness'?"
Śāriputra said:
"When the five lower fetters have been completely exhausted and fully known, this is called attaining coolness.
He asked again:
“Śāriputra! Is there a path, is there a way, which, through cultivation and repeated practice, leads to the attainment of coolness?
Śāriputra replied:
“There is. It is the Eightfold Noble Path—right view, and so on, up to right concentration.
Then, having finished their discussion, the two noble men rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśoda asked Śāriputra:
"Regarding what is called 'supreme coolness,' what constitutes supreme coolness?"
Śāriputra said:

"That which is called 'supreme coolness' refers to the eternal exhaustion of sensual desire without remainder, the eternal exhaustion of hatred and delusion without remainder, and the eternal exhaustion of all afflictions without remainder; this is termed supreme coolness."
He asked again:
"Is there a path, is there a way, by which one may attain this supreme coolness?
Śāriputra replied:
“There is. It is the Eightfold Noble Path—from right view up to right concentration.
Then, having finished their discussion, the two noble men rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśoda asked Śāriputra:
"It is said that one attains supreme coolness.
What is meant by 'attaining supreme coolness'?"
Śāriputra said:

"One who has attained supreme coolness is one for whom sensual desire has been forever exhausted without remainder, having been abandoned and fully understood; and for whom ill will and delusion have been forever exhausted without remainder, having been abandoned and fully understood—this is called having attained supreme coolness."
He asked again:
"Śāriputra! Is there a path, is there a way, by which one attains this supreme coolness?"
Śāriputra said: "There is.
It refers to the Eightfold Noble Path—right view, and so forth, up to right concentration."
Then, after the two noble men had finished their discussion, they each rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśas asked Śāriputra:
"What is that which is called 'craving'?"
"What is craving? Śāriputra replied, "There are three kinds of craving:
namely, craving for the realm of desire, craving for the realm of form, and craving for the formless realm."
He asked again:
"Is there a path and a way that severs these three kinds of craving?
Śāriputra replied:
“There is. It is the Eightfold Noble Path—from right view up to right concentration.
Then, having finished their discussion, the two noble men rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśas asked Śāriputra:
"Regarding what you call 'the tracks of karma'—
what are these tracks of karma?"
Śāriputra said:

"As for 'tracks of karma,' they are the ten unwholesome tracks of karma, namely: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view."
He asked again:
“Śāriputra! Is there a path, is there a way, that cuts off these ten tracks of action?”
Śāriputra said: “There is.
It refers to the Eightfold Noble Path—from right view up to right concentration.”
Then, having finished their discussion together, the two noble men rose from their seats and departed.
Yaśas asked Śāriputra, "Regarding that which is called 'defilement'..."
"What is defilement? Śāriputra replied, "Defilement refers to the three defilements:
the defilement of sensual desire, the defilement of hatred, and the defilement of delusion."
He asked again:
"Śāriputra! Is there a path, is there a way, that cuts off these three defilements?"
Śāriputra said: “There is.
It refers to the Eightfold Noble Path—from right view up to right concentration.”
Then, having finished their discussion together, the two noble beings rose from their seats and departed.
As it is with impurity, so it is with defilement, grease, thorns, attachment, and bondage.
491 (491) As in the *Yamavati-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, so too is it regarding the questions asked by the renunciant śramaṇa.
492 (492) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was also staying there.
Then, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus:

"If a bhikṣu attains the immeasurable samādhi, realizes it through bodily witness, and dwells in its fulfillment, yet his mind does not delight in or cling to nirvāṇa as the extinction of the body, but rather looks back with concern upon the body."
It is like a man whose hand is smeared with glue; when he grasps a tree branch, his hand adheres to the tree and he cannot free himself.
Why is this? Because his hand is smeared with glue.

"Monks! Having personally realized the immeasurable samādhi with the body, if the mind does not delight in the nirvāṇa that is the extinction of the body, but instead looks back with attachment toward the body, one will ultimately fail to be liberated. One will not attain the Dharma in accordance with the teachings in this present life, and even at the end of life, nothing will be gained; one will return again to be born in this realm, and in the end, will never be able to shatter the darkness of ignorance."

It is, for example, like a muddy pool beside a village where the mud is so deep that one sinks into it; after a long drought with no rain, the water in the pool has dried up and vanished, and the ground has cracked open.
In this same way, bhikṣus!

One will not be able to see the Dharma or follow the teachings of the Dharma; even until the end of one's life, nothing will be attained, and in a future birth, one shall again fall back into this realm.

"If there is a bhikṣu who attains immeasurable samādhis, realizes them through bodily witness, and dwells fully therein, he gives rise to faith and delight in the nirvāṇa that is the extinction of the body, and does not dwell upon the existence of the body."
It is, for example, like a man who grasps a tree branch with clean hands;
his hands do not adhere to the tree.
Why is this? Because the hands are pure.

In this way, bhikṣu, having attained immeasurable samādhi, dwelling fully in personal realization, one gives rise to faith and joy in the nirvāṇa that is the cessation of consciousness. Not dwelling on the existence of a body, one accords with the Dharma teachings in the present life; until the end of life, one will no longer return to be born in this realm.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should apply yourselves diligently to skillful means in order to destroy ignorance.

It is like a muddy pond beside a village where water flows in from the four directions and falls frequently from the heavens; though water constantly enters the pond until it overflows, the filth and impurities flow out, leaving the pond pure and clear.
In this way, they all attain the teachings that accord with the Dharma in the present life, and until the end of their lives,
they will no longer be reborn in this realm. Therefore, bhikṣus,
you should diligently apply skillful means to destroy ignorance.
When the Venerable Śāriputra had spoken this discourse, the bhikṣus, having heard what he said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
493 (493) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a forest-dwelling bhikṣu is in an open space, in a grove, or at the foot of a tree, he should train himself thus, observing within and reflecting:
'Do I personally perceive any thought of desire within my mind?'"
"If one is not mindful, then regarding sensory objects or pure signs, if sensual desire arises, it will contradict seclusion.
It is like a man who exerts effort to board a boat and rows upstream; if his body becomes slightly weary, the boat will turn back and drift downstream with the current."
Thus it is, bhikṣus!
When one contemplates the perception of purity, love and desire arise again, which is contrary to seclusion.

While training, this bhikṣu practices inferior means and fails to attain pure clarity; therefore, he is once more swept away by love and desire, does not obtain the power of the Dharma, his mind is not tranquil, and his mind is not unified. Regarding those signs of purity, love and desire arise accordingly, flowing and surging forth, contrary to seclusion.
It should be known that such a bhikṣu does not dare to declare for himself that he is liberated through detachment from the qualities of the five desires.
"If a bhikṣu, whether in an open space, in a forest, or at the foot of a tree, reflects thus:
'Is my inner mind free from desire or not?'"
That bhikṣu, within his objective sphere, may grasp at signs of purity; yet if he perceives that his mind is detached from them, it will flow away and recede.
It is like the feathers of a bird which, when entering fire, curl up and cannot be stretched out again.
In this way, bhikkhus, one may take up a mark of purity (*śubhanimitta*), whereby one proceeds toward seclusion, flowing and streaming forward.
Bhikkhus, you should know this:

when practicing with skillful means, with a mind free from indolence, one attains the stillness of the Dharma—tranquility, cessation, and bliss—and achieves a pure, unified mind. Thinking, "I have reflected thus," and having proceeded toward seclusion by means of the mark of purity, following the path of cultivation, one is then able to declare of oneself that one has become detached from the objects of the five sensual pleasures and is liberated.
When the Venerable Śāriputra had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what he said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
494 (494) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
The Venerable Śāriputra was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain.

At that time, in the early morning, the Venerable Śāriputra dressed himself, took his bowl, and left Vulture Peak Mountain to enter the city of Rājagṛha for alms. Along the road, he saw a large, withered tree; he immediately spread out his sitting mat beneath it, straightened his body, sat upright, and addressed the bhikṣus:

"If there is a bhikṣu who cultivates meditative concentration and attains the power of supernormal faculties, such that his mind has attained mastery, and he wishes to cause this withered tree to become earth, it shall immediately become earth."
Why is this so? It is because within this withered tree there exists the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*).
Therefore, when a bhikṣu who has attained the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*) forms the mental resolve that it is earth, it immediately becomes earth, no different from the original.

"If there is a bhikṣu who has attained the power of supernatural faculties (abhijñā) and possesses mastery according to his will, and desires to cause this tree to become water, fire, wind, gold, silver, or other such things, he shall accomplish them all exactly as intended, without any difference."
Why is this? It is because this withered tree possesses the water element.
Therefore, bhikṣus!

Through meditative concentration, he attained supernormal powers with sovereign mastery; wishing to transform a withered tree into gold, it immediately became gold without distinction, and all other various kinds of things likewise became so without distinction.
Why is this? Because that withered tree possesses various elements (*dhātu*).
Therefore, O bhikṣus!

Through meditative concentration, one attains supernormal powers (ṛddhi) that are sovereign and as one desires; one can manifest various objects such that they are all accomplished without distinction. Monks, you should know that the realm of a monk’s supernormal powers attained through meditative concentration is inconceivable.
"Therefore, bhikṣus,
you should diligently practice meditative concentration and train in the various supernormal powers.
When Śāriputra had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what he said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
495 (Four Hundred and Ninety-Five). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was on Vulture Peak Mountain.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus:
"Those who violate the precepts, because of their broken discipline, find that their basis for practice declines and their minds no longer dwell in joy.

Once they no longer dwell in joy, they lose joy, tranquility, bliss, meditative concentration (*samādhi*), knowledge and vision according to reality, disenchantment, dispassion, and liberation; consequently, they can never attain *nirvāṇa* without remainder."
Just as when the roots of a tree are destroyed, its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits will not flourish, so it is with a bhikṣu who violates the precepts.

His merits decline, his mind finds no delight in dwelling [in the Dharma], and having lost faith and joy, he loses rapture (*prīti*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), bliss (*sukha*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), knowledge and vision according to reality (*yathābhūta-jñānadarśana*), disenchantment (*nirveda*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and liberation (*vimukti*). Having lost liberation, he can never attain *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
“A bhikṣu who maintains the precepts is fully endowed with the root and fully endowed with the basis; his mind attains faith and joy.

Having attained faith and joy, his mind attains rapture, tranquility, bliss, meditative concentration (*samādhi*), knowledge and vision according to reality, disenchantment, dispassion, and liberation.
Having attained liberation, he is able to swiftly attain *nirvāṇa* without remainder.”
Just as when the roots of a tree are not destroyed, its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits all reach fulfillment, so it is with a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts.

With the root fully complete and his support established, his mind attains faith and joy; having attained faith and joy, he swiftly attains rapture, tranquility, bliss, the samādhi of stillness, knowledge and vision in accordance with reality, disenchantment, dispassion, and liberation, and finally, nirvāṇa without remainder.
When the Venerable Śāriputra had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what he said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 496 (496) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a dispute arises among the bhikṣus involving mutual accusations, there will be both the bhikṣu who has committed an offense and the bhikṣu who accuses him of that offense."

If he does not rely on right reflection to examine himself, you should know that this bhikkhu will remain obstinate for a long time; his disputes will increase, he will continue to act in opposition, his resentment will deepen further, and regarding the offenses he has committed, he will be unable to bring them to rest through the True Dharma and the Discipline.

If a bhikṣu has such a dispute already arisen—whether it be the bhikṣu who committed the offense or the bhikṣu who raised the charge—if both rely upon right reflection to examine and reproach themselves, you should know that those bhikṣus will not remain obstinate or antagonistic for a long night, nor will their resentment increase; regarding the offense that arose, they will be able to bring it to rest through the Dharma and the Vinaya.
“How does a bhikṣu engage in right reflection and examine himself?
A bhikṣu should reflect thus:
‘I am not one who commits offenses that would cause others to see me; I am not of such a kind, nor should I act in such a way.’”
If I had not committed this offense, he would not have seen it; because he saw my offense, he was displeased, censured me, and brought it up.

Other monks who hear of it will likewise censure me. Thus, for a long night, disputes and litigation will increase, and as they argue with one another, they will be unable to use the True Dharma and the Vinaya to bring these offenses to rest. I now recognize this for myself, as if I were paying a tax.
This is called a bhikṣu who is able to examine himself regarding the offense he has committed.
How does a bhikṣu who reproves another examine himself?
A bhikṣu who reproves another should reflect in this way:
"That elder bhikṣu has committed an improper offense, which has caused me to see it; had he not committed this improper offense, I would not have seen it."

Because I see his offense, I raise it up out of displeasure; when other bhikṣus see it, they too will raise it out of displeasure. Thus, disputes and litigation will increase and continue without ceasing through the long night, and one will be unable to use the True Dharma and the Vinaya to stop the offenses that have arisen and bring them to rest.
"From this day forward, I shall personally relinquish it, just as one pays a tax.
In this way, the bhikṣu who has been accused of an offense is well able to rely on right reflection and examine himself within.

"Therefore, monks, those who have committed an offense and those who have charged another with an offense should rely on right reflection to examine themselves, so that their arrogance does not increase throughout the long night."
"O monks! One should attain non-contention; whatever contention has arisen, one should be able to bring it to rest through the Dharma and the Vinaya.
When the Venerable Śāriputra had spoken this sutra, the monks, having heard it, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
497 (Four Hundred and Ninety-Seven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bhikṣu who intends to charge another with an offense wishes to cause that person’s mind to abide in peace, by how many qualities may he charge them with an offense?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“If a bhikṣu causes his mind to abide securely, he may charge another with an offense by means of five qualities. What are these five?
[The charge must be] true and not untrue; timely and not untimely; beneficial and not non-beneficial; gentle and not harsh; and motivated by a mind of loving-kindness and not by anger.”
“Śāriputra, a bhikṣu who reproves another for their offense must possess these five qualities in order to reprove that person’s offense.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By how many dharmas does a bhikṣu who has been subject to formal suspension pacify his own mind?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"A bhikkhu who has been subject to formal suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma) should settle his mind by means of five things, reflecting:

'Where did he obtain this? Let it be true and not untrue; let it be timely and not untimely; let it be for the benefit of the Dhamma and not for the detriment of the Dhamma; let it be gentle and not harsh; let it be with a heart of loving-kindness and not with a heart of ill-will.'"
“Śāriputra! A bhikṣu who has been subject to formal censure should employ these five dharmas to settle his own mind.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I have observed those who point out the faults of others do so with what is untrue rather than true, at an improper time rather than the proper time, without benefit to the meaning rather than for the benefit of the meaning, with harshness rather than gentleness, and out of malice rather than with a compassionate heart.”
“World-Honored One!
By how many methods should one benefit a bhikṣu who falsely accuses another of an offense, so that he may repent and reform?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"A bhikṣu who raises a charge that is untrue should be benefited by five methods to cause him to repent and reform; one should say to him:
'Venerable sir!
The charge you have now raised is untrue and not true; you should repent and reform.'"
It is untimely, not the proper time; it is not beneficial, not conducive to welfare; it is coarse and harsh, not gentle; it is born of anger, not of a compassionate mind—you must repent and reform.

"Śāriputra! A bhikṣu who falsely accuses another of an offense should benefit that person by means of these five methods to cause them to repent and reform, and so that bhikṣus in future ages will not falsely accuse others of offenses."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By how many further methods can a bhikṣu who has been falsely accused of an offense be prevented from failing to repent?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“A bhikṣu who has been falsely accused of an offense should not change his mind or feel regret;
he should reflect as follows:”

"That bhikṣu has raised a charge that is untrue rather than true, untimely rather than timely, not conducive to benefit rather than conducive to benefit, harsh rather than gentle, and motivated by malice rather than a mind of loving-kindness; I am indeed firm and do not regret it."
"A bhikṣu who has been falsely accused of an offense should use these five methods to settle his own mind and not feel regret or change his course.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If there is a bhikṣu who accuses another of an offense that is true and not false, timely and not untimely, beneficial in meaning and not non-beneficial, gentle and not harsh, and done with a mind of loving-kindness and not with anger—how many qualities must this bhikṣu who truly accuses possess so as to benefit the accused and prevent him from changing his mind?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"A bhikṣu who has truly charged another with an offense should benefit them through five methods so that they do not waver or regret; he should speak thus:
'Venerable sir!'"

What you have truly brought forth as a charge is not untrue; it was at the proper time, not an improper time; it is meaningful and beneficial, not meaningless; it is gentle, not harsh; and it is spoken with a mind of loving-kindness, not with malice.

“Śāriputra! When a bhikṣu who has truly censured another should act, he ought to benefit them through these five principles so that they do not become regretful; furthermore, he should ensure that in future generations, those bhikṣus who truly censure others likewise do not become regretful.”
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by how many dharmas should a bhikṣu who has been legitimately accused be benefited so that he does not change his mind or regret?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"A bhikṣu who has been subjected to the formal act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma) should be benefited by five things so that he does not change his mind or regret [his confession], and one should say to him:
'That bhikṣu’s accusation was true and not untrue; you must not change your mind or regret it.'"
It is timely, not untimely; it is beneficial in meaning, not non-beneficial in meaning; it is gentle, not harsh; it is with a mind of loving-kindness, not with malice—do not later feel regret.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have seen bhikṣus who, when being formally accused of an offense, become angry.”
“World-Honored One!
By how many dharmas should a bhikṣu who has become angry after being reproved for a factual offense bring himself to awakening regarding that resentment?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"A bhikkhu who is angry when his fault has been pointed out by one who speaks truthfully should be awakened by five methods;
you should say to him: 'Venerable sir!
That bhikkhu pointed out your fault truthfully, not falsely; do not harbor anger toward him... [and so on] ...with a mind of loving-kindness, not with anger; do not harbor anger.'"
"Śāriputra! A bhikṣu who has been accused of a true offense and who feels anger should, by means of these five dharmas, bring about the awakening from that resentment.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there are those who accuse me of faults, whether their words be true or false, I shall maintain peace of mind toward both of them.
If they are true, I shall acknowledge it myself; if they are not true, I shall explain and resolve the matter for myself, saying:”
"This is not true; I now know for myself that such a thing does not exist.
World-Honored One!
I shall be thus, as the World-Honored One has taught the śramaṇas in the *Dāru-khaṇḍa-upama-sūtra*:
“If bandits should come and seize you to saw apart your bodies, if you were to give rise to evil thoughts or speak evil words toward those bandits, you would create obstacles for yourselves.
Therefore, O bhikṣus!
If your body were to be dismembered with a saw, you should not give rise to thoughts of malice, agitation, or harsh speech toward them, nor create obstacles for yourselves.

Toward that person, you should generate a mind of loving-kindness, free from enmity and resentment, and you should train yourselves to dwell fully established in the meditative attainment of loving-kindness throughout the four quarters of the world.
"Therefore, World-Honored One!
I shall act in this way: as the World-Honored One has taught, I shall understand the suffering of the body and endure it myself; how much more so should I endure minor suffering and minor slander?"
A śramaṇa’s benefit and a śramaṇa’s desire consist in wishing to abandon unwholesome states and wishing to cultivate wholesome states;

regarding these unwholesome states that should be abandoned and wholesome states that should be cultivated, one should train oneself with diligent application, guarding oneself well, maintaining mindfulness and reflection, and practicing without negligence.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One!

If I were to bring up the offense of another bhikṣu, it would be true and not false; timely and not untimely; beneficial in meaning and not non-beneficial; gentle and not harsh; and done with a compassionate heart and without anger. Yet, that bhikṣu whose offense has been brought up might harbor resentment."
The Buddha asked Śāriputra,
“What kind of bhikṣu, upon hearing his own faults being exposed, gives rise to anger?
Śāriputra replied to the Buddha:

“World-Honored One! If those bhikṣus are crooked, deceitful, hypocritical, and fraudulent; if they are deceptive and lack faith; if they have no sense of shame or dread of blame; if they are indolent, have lost mindfulness, are undisciplined, and possess evil wisdom; if they are arrogant and lax; if they oppose seclusion; if they do not respect the precepts, disregard their status as śramaṇas, fail to apply themselves diligently to training, do not engage in self-examination, have left the home life for the sake of livelihood, and do not seek nirvāṇa—[then they are not true followers].”
"Such persons as these, upon hearing me raise their faults, will give rise to anger.
The Buddha asked Śāriputra, "What kind of bhikṣus, when you raise their faults, do not become resentful?"
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there is a bhikṣu who is not crooked, not deceitful, and not fraudulent; who possesses faith, a sense of shame and dread of blame, diligence, right mindfulness, right concentration, and wisdom; who is neither lax nor negligent, does not abandon seclusion, deeply reveres the precepts, regards the conduct of a śramaṇa, honors nirvāṇa, and has gone forth for the sake of the Dharma rather than for the sake of life or limb.”
When a bhikṣu hears me thus proclaim his transgression, he receives it with joy and reverence, as if drinking ambrosia.
It is like a woman of the kṣatriya or brāhmaṇa castes who, having bathed until she is pure, obtains a beautiful and exquisite flower; she cherishes it and wears it upon her head as a crown.

In this way, a bhikṣu is without flattery or crookedness, without deceit or hypocrisy, and without deception; he possesses right faith, a sense of shame and dread of blame, diligence, right mindfulness, and right concentration and wisdom; he is not lax or indolent, his mind dwells in seclusion, he deeply reveres the precepts, he regards the conduct of a śramaṇa, he diligently practices self-examination, he has left the home life for the sake of the Dharma, and he aspires to seek nirvāṇa.
"In this way, when a bhikṣu hears me charge him with an offense, he receives it with joy and reverence, as if drinking nectar.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"If that bhikṣu is crooked, deceitful, hypocritical, fraudulent, faithless, shameless and without remorse, lazy, forgetful, undisciplined, and of evil wisdom; if he is arrogant and lax, contrary to seclusion, disrespectful toward the precepts, heedless of the conduct of a śramaṇa, does not seek nirvāṇa, and has left the home life merely for the sake of his livelihood—"
In this way, a bhikṣu should neither instruct nor converse with them. Why is that?
Because these bhikṣus have violated the holy life (brahmacarya).

If that bhikṣu is not sycophantic, not deceitful, and not fraudulent; if he possesses faith, a sense of shame and dread of blame, diligence, right mindfulness, right concentration, and wisdom; if he is not lax or indolent, but keeps his mind detached, deeply reveres the precepts, attends to the conduct of a śramaṇa, aspires to the exaltation of nirvāṇa, and has gone forth for the sake of the Dharma.
In this way, a bhikṣu should provide instruction. Why is that?
Because in this way, a bhikṣu is able to cultivate the holy life and is able to establish himself.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Śāriputra, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 498 (498) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Nalakanda in the mango grove of the cloth-seller.
At that time, Śāriputra approached the World-Honored One, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I have deep faith that among all the wisdom possessed by śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the past, future, and present, there is none equal to the Bodhi of the World-Honored One, much less superior to it."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Excellent! Excellent!”

“Śāriputra, excellent is what you have said; it is the foremost teaching. You have been able to let out a lion’s roar amidst this assembly, declaring that you have deep faith in the World-Honored One, saying that the wisdom possessed by any śramaṇas or brahmins—whether of the past, future, or present—is none equal to the Buddha’s bodhi, much less superior to it.”
The Buddha asked Śāriputra:
"Are you able to know with certainty all the superior precepts (adhiśīla) possessed by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past?
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I do not know.
The World-Honored One asked again: “Śāriputra!
"Do you know such a Dharma, such wisdom, such illumination, such liberation, and such an abiding?
Śāriputra replied to the Buddha,
"I do not know."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Do you also know the superior precepts possessed by all those who will become Samyaksaṃbuddhas in the future?”
"Is it thus with his Dharma, thus with his wisdom, thus with his clarity, thus with his liberation, and thus does he abide?
Śāriputra replied to the Buddha,
"I do not know."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Furthermore, are you able to know all the superior precepts possessed by the Buddhas of the present?”
"Is it thus with his Dharma, thus with his wisdom, thus with his clarity, thus with his liberation, and thus does he abide?
Śāriputra replied to the Buddha,
"I do not know."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“If you do not know all the dharmas within the minds of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present.”
How is it that he praises in this way?
In the midst of the great assembly, he utters a lion’s roar, saying:
"I have deep faith that among all the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the past and the future, there is no wisdom equal to the awakening of the World-Honored One, much less any that surpasses it."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I am unable to know the extent of the minds of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, the future, and the present; however, I am able to know the extent of the Dharma of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.”

I have heard the Dharma taught by the Blessed One; it becomes increasingly deep, increasingly superior, increasingly exalted, and increasingly sublime. Having heard the Dharma taught by the Blessed One, I understand that by knowing one thing, one thing is abandoned; by knowing one thing, one thing is realized; and by knowing one thing, one thing is cultivated. Having reached the ultimate in the Dharma, I have attained pure faith in the Great Teacher, and my mind has become purified.
“The Blessed One is the Truly Self-Awakened One.
World-Honored One!

It is as if a king had a frontier city, its perimeter square and straight, firm and solid, with only a single gate and no second gate. A gatekeeper was stationed there, and all the people entering or exiting did so through this gate alone. Whether entering or exiting, although the gatekeeper might not know the exact number of people, he certainly knew that the people passed only through this gate and nowhere else.”

In this way, I know that all past Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas completely severed the five hindrances—which afflict the mind, weaken the power of wisdom, belong to the category of obstructions, and do not lead toward Nirvāṇa—and by abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness and cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment, they attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

The Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of those future ages will likewise sever the five hindrances—which afflict the mind, weaken the power of wisdom, belong to the category of obstacles, and do not lead toward Nirvana—and by abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness and cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment, they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

The Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the present time also sever the five hindrances—which afflict the mind, weaken the power of wisdom, belong to the category of obstacles, and do not lead toward Nirvāṇa—and by abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness and cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment, they attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: “So it is, so it is, Śāriputra!”

The Buddhas of the past, future, and present have all severed the five hindrances—which afflict the mind, weaken the power of wisdom, belong to the category of obstacles, and do not lead toward Nirvana—and by abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness and cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment, they have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Śāriputra, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
499 (499) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.

Then, there was a bhikṣu named Candraprabha, a disciple of Devadatta, who approached the Venerable Śāriputra; after they had exchanged greetings and expressions of courtesy, he withdrew and stood to one side.
Having stepped back to one side, the Venerable Śāriputra asked the bhikṣu Moon-child:
"Did the bhikṣu Devadatta preach the Dharma to the bhikṣus?"
The bhikṣu Candropama replied,
“I am preaching the Dharma.
The Venerable Śāriputra asked the bhikṣu Candropama:
“How does Devadatta teach the Dharma?
The bhikṣu Candraprabha said to the Venerable Śāriputra:
“That Devadatta teaches the Dharma in this way, saying:”
"A bhikṣu who cultivates the mind through mental phenomena is able to declare of himself:
'I have abandoned desire and am liberated from the qualities of the five sensual pleasures.
Śāriputra then spoke to the bhikṣu Candana:
“Devadatta, why do you not teach the Dharma by saying:

‘A bhikkhu who has well-cultivated the mental states, whose mind is free from desire, free from ill will, and free from delusion, who has attained the state of non-greed, non-ill will, and non-delusion, and who does not turn back toward existence in the realm of desire, existence in the realm of form, or existence in the formless realm—that bhikkhu is able to declare of himself:
“Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence.”’”
"Is that so? The monk Moon-Child replied, "He cannot."
"Venerable Śāriputra!
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra said to the bhikṣu Moon-son:

"If there is a bhikṣu who has well-cultivated the mind through mental phenomena, and is able to abandon the mind of greed, the mind of hatred, and the mind of delusion, attaining the state of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion, that bhikṣu is able to declare of himself: [I am an arahant]."
“Birth for me has been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence.

It is like a village or town near a great mountain of rock—unbroken, indestructible, unpierced, thick and dense—which, even if a wind were to come from the east, could not cause it to move, nor could it pass through to the west.
In this way, when winds come from the south, west, north, or the four intermediate directions, they cannot shake it, nor can they pass over it.

Likewise, bhikkhus, one who has well-cultivated the mind regarding mental phenomena abandons the mind of sensual desire, abandons the mind of ill will, and abandons the mind of delusion; having attained the state of non-greed, the state of non-ill will, and the state of non-delusion, that bhikkhu is able to declare of himself:
"Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I myself know that there will be no further existence."

“It is, for example, like Indra’s copper-iron pillar, which is driven deep into the earth and compacted until it is firm and dense; even when the winds blow from the four directions, they cannot shake it.”

In this way, bhikkhus, when one has well cultivated the mind with respect to mental phenomena, the mind becomes free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion; having attained the state of non-lust, the state of non-hatred, and the state of non-delusion, that bhikkhu is able to declare of himself:
"Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I myself know that there will be no further existence."
“Suppose, for example, there were a stone pillar sixteen cubits long, eight of which were buried in the ground; it could not be shaken or moved by winds blowing from the four directions.

In the same way, bhikkhu, when one has well cultivated the mind through mental phenomena, having completely abandoned the mind of lust, the mind of ill will, and the mind of delusion, and having attained the state of non-lust, non-ill will, and non-delusion, one is able to declare of oneself:
‘Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence.’”
"Just as fire burns what has not yet been burned, but once it has burned it does not burn again;

so too, bhikkhu, when the mind has cultivated the mental qualities, having become free from a mind of lust, free from a mind of ill will, and free from a mind of delusion, one attains the state of non-lust, the state of non-ill will, and the state of non-delusion, and is able to declare of oneself:
'Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence.'"
When Śāriputra had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what he said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
500 (Five Hundred). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was also staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.
Then, the Venerable Śāriputra, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl, entered Rājagṛha for alms. Having finished his almsround, he ate beneath a tree.

At that time, a female ascetic of the Nirgrantha sect named Śuddhavāsinī was leaving Rājagṛha on some minor business when she saw the Venerable Śāriputra sitting under a tree eating. Having seen him, she asked:
"Are you eating, śramaṇa?"
The Venerable Śāriputra replied,
"I have eaten.
He asked again:
“How is it? Does the śramaṇa eat with his face turned downward?
He replied:
"No, sister! She asked again,
"Do you subsist by 'looking up' for food?"
She replied, "No, sisters!
They asked again:
"How so? Do you eat with your mouth square?
He replied:
"No, sisters! She asked again,
"Does he eat from all four sides?"
She replied, “No, sisters!
They asked again:
"I asked the śramaṇa, 'Do you eat?
and he replied to me,
'I eat.'"
I asked, "Is it by 'looking upward' (āyukha)?
He replied to me, "No."
"Did you eat from the lower end of the bowl?
He replied to me, "No."
“Do you eat with your mouth square?
He answered me, “No.”
"Does he eat with his mouth from the four intermediate directions?
He replied to me, "No."
"What is the meaning of what has been said thus?
The Venerable Śāriputra replied: "Sister!"
Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas are skilled in worldly affairs, skilled in perverse doctrines, and seek food through wrong livelihood—such śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas subsist by "mouth-downward" eating.
If any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas gaze upward at the stars and constellations, seeking food through such wrong livelihood, these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are said to subsist on "upward-facing food."
If any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas act as messengers for others and seek food through such wrong livelihood,
these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are those who eat with their mouths turned toward the four quarters.

If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who treat various illnesses through medical arts and seek food by such wrong livelihoods, such śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are those who subsist on the food of the four quarters.
Sisters! I do not seek food by falling into these four kinds of wrong livelihood.
However, sisters!
"I live my life by seeking food solely for the sake of the Dharma; therefore, I say that I do not subsist on the four kinds of nutriment.
At that time, the female wanderer of the Net-mouth sect, having heard what the Venerable Śāriputra had said, rejoiced and approved, and then departed.
At that time, the female wanderer Śuddhavādinī praised [the Buddha] in the streets, lanes, and crossroads of the city of Rājagṛha, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, live by a pure livelihood; they live by an utterly pure livelihood!
All those who wish to give alms should give to the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas."
"If you wish to perform meritorious deeds, you should perform them toward the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas.

At that time, there were certain non-Buddhist renunciants who, upon hearing the voice of the female renunciant Prakīrti praising the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, were moved by jealousy and killed her. After her life ended, she was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven because she had conceived faith in the Venerable Śāriputra.
501 (Five Hundred and One). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was staying on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the bhikṣus:
"Once, the Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove."
While I was dwelling here on Vulture Peak Mountain, staying alone in a secluded place, I had this thought:
"What is noble silence?
Then I further thought:

"If there is a bhikṣu who, with the subsiding of applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra), attains internal purity and one-pointedness of mind, and dwells having fully realized the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss without applied or sustained thought—this is called noble silence."
Again, he thought:

"I should now likewise abide in noble silence; having stilled directed thought and evaluation, with internal purity and one-pointedness of mind, free from directed thought and evaluation, I shall dwell fully and frequently in the rapture and happiness born of concentration;
and having dwelt thus frequently, a mind with directed thought and evaluation will arise."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing my thoughts, vanished from the Bamboo Grove Monastery and appeared before me on Vulture Peak Mountain, saying to me:
"Maudgalyāyana!
"You should maintain noble silence; do not give rise to negligence.

Having heard what the World-Honored One said, I immediately transcended both directed thought and sustained evaluation; with internal purity and a unified mind, free from directed thought and sustained evaluation, I attained the joy and bliss born of samādhi and dwelt fully in the second dhyāna.
Thus he spoke a second and a third time, and the Buddha likewise instructed me a second and a third time:
"You should remain in noble silence; do not be negligent.

I then again stilled directed thought and evaluation; with internal purity and one-pointed mind, free from directed thought and evaluation, I entered and dwelt in the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss.

“If one were to speak correctly of those sons of the Buddha who are born from the Buddha’s mouth, transformed by the Dharma, and have obtained a portion of the Buddha-Dharma, it is I myself who am such a person. Why is this so?

I am a son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s mouth, transformed by the Dharma, and having obtained a portion of the Buddha-Dharma; through slight means, I have attained dhyāna, liberation, samādhi, and right concentration.

For example, the eldest son of a wheel-turning sage king, although not yet consecrated, has already acquired the royal dharma; without exerting effort or employing expedient means, he is able to obtain the merits of the five desires.

I am likewise thus: as a son of the Buddha, though I did not exert myself in skillful means, I attained dhyāna, liberation, samādhi, and right concentration. Within a single day, the World-Honored One came to my place three times by means of his supernormal powers and instructed me three times, establishing me in the station of a Great Man.
When the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what he said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
502 (502). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the bhikṣus:
"Once, when the World-Honored One was staying in the city of Rājagṛha, I was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain."
While dwelling alone in a secluded place, I had this thought:
"What is called the noble abiding?
Then I further thought:
"If there is a bhikṣu who does not attend to any signs, but dwells having fully realized through bodily witness the signless mental attainment, this is called the noble dwelling.
I thought to myself:
"In this noble dwelling, I shall dwell without attending to any signs, in the signless mental attainment."
"Having fully realized it through bodily witness and dwelling therein extensively, once I had dwelt there extensively, a mind characterized by grasping at signs arose.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing my thoughts, vanished from the Bamboo Grove Monastery and appeared before me on Vulture Peak Mountain in the time it takes a strong man to flex or extend his arm. By means of his supernormal power, he spoke to me, saying:
"Maudgalyāyana!..."
"You should abide in the noble abiding; do not give rise to negligence.
Having heard the World-Honored One's instruction, I immediately departed from all signs and dwelt fully, having realized with my own body the signless mental attainment.
Thus it was repeated three times, and the World-Honored One likewise came to instruct me three times:
"You should abide in the noble dwelling; do not give rise to negligence.
Having heard this instruction, I detached from all signs and attained the signless mental absorption, realizing it through my own body and abiding fully therein.
"Venerable sirs!
If one speaks correctly of those who are sons of the Buddha, then my own person is born from the mouth of the Buddha, transformed by the Dharma, and has obtained a portion of the Buddha-Dharma."

Why is this? I am a son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s mouth, transformed by the Dharma, and having obtained a portion of the Buddha-Dharma, I have attained dhyāna, liberation, samādhi, and samāpatti through slight means.

For example, it is like the crown prince of a wheel-turning sage king: although he has not yet received the consecration, he has already attained the royal dharma and, without exerting effort or employing expedient means, is able to obtain the merits of the five desires.
I am likewise so.

As a son of the Buddha, though I did not exert myself in skillful means, I attained dhyāna, liberation, samādhi, and right concentration. Within a single day, the World-Honored One came to my place three times by means of his supernormal powers and instructed me three times, establishing me in the station of a Great Man.
When the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what he said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 503 (503) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and the Venerable Ānanda were staying together in a single room at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.
Then, during the latter part of the night, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Venerable Maudgalyāyana:
“How marvelous!
Venerable Maudgalyāyana!”
"Tonight, you should abide in the meditative attainment of cessation.
Having heard the words of the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana said to him:
"I do not hear the sound of your breathing at all."
The Venerable Maudgalyāyana said:
"This is not the meditative absorption of cessation; it is merely abiding in a coarse meditative absorption, Venerable Śāriputra."
"Tonight, I shall converse with the World-Honored One.
Venerable Śāriputra said, "Maudgalyāyana!"
"The World-Honored One resides at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Jeta’s Grove at Śrāvastī, which is extremely far from here.
How can we converse with him?
You are now at the Bamboo Grove; how can we converse with you?"
"Did you come to the presence of the Blessed One by means of your supernormal power,
or did the Blessed One come to your presence by means of his supernormal power?
Venerable Maudgalyāyana said to Venerable Śāriputra:

"I did not go to the Blessed One's presence by means of supernormal power, nor did the Blessed One come to my presence by means of supernormal power; rather, I heard it in the cities of Śrāvastī and Rājagṛha that both the Blessed One and I have attained the divine eye and the divine ear."
I am able to ask the World-Honored One:
"Regarding what is called 'earnest diligence,' what is meant by 'earnest diligence'?"
The World-Honored One replied to me, saying:
"Maudgalyāyana!
If this bhikṣu, whether walking or sitting during the day, purifies his own mind by means of the unobstructed dharmas."
During the first watch of the night, whether sitting or walking, he purifies his mind by means of unobstructive dharmas.

During the middle watch of the night, he goes outside the cell to wash his feet, returns to the cell, and lies down on his right side with one foot upon the other, fixing his mindfulness on the sign of light, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, maintaining the thought of rising.
In the latter part of the night, he slowly awakens and slowly rises; whether sitting or walking in meditation, he purifies his own mind through unobstructive dharmas, Maudgalyāyana!
"This is what is called a bhikṣu who is diligent and energetic.
The Venerable Śāriputra said to the Venerable Maudgalyāyana:
"Great Maudgalyāyana, you truly possess the power of great supernormal faculties and the power of great merit; you sit so serenely. I too possess great power, and I am able to be with you."
"Maugalyāyana!

It is as if there were a great mountain, and someone were to take a small stone and throw it upon it; the color and flavor of the small stone would become entirely the same as those of the great mountain. In the same way, I have attained the ability to sit on the same seat as you, O Venerable One of great power and great virtue."
Just as people in the world all carry upon their heads objects that are fresh, pure, and excellent,
so too should all fellow practitioners of the holy life carry upon their heads the Venerable Mahā-Moggallāna, who possesses great virtue and great power.

All those who have had the opportunity to associate with the Venerable Maudgalyāyana, coming and going with him, and who have honored and made offerings to him, have gained great and wholesome benefit; now I too have associated with the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, coming and going with him, and have likewise gained wholesome benefit.
Then, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said to the Venerable Śāriputra:

"That I am now able to sit on the same seat as the Venerable Śāriputra, who possesses great wisdom and great virtue, is like throwing a small stone into a great mountain so that it takes on the same color; I too am thus, having obtained the privilege of sitting on the same seat as the Venerable Śāriputra of great wisdom as my second companion."
At that time, having finished their discussion together, the two noble beings rose from their seats and departed.
*Saṃyukta Āgama*, Scroll 18; *Saṃyukta Āgama*, Scroll 19.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
19. 504 (504). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, who possessed a magnificent upper hall, came at night to the place where the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra’s radiance shone everywhere upon Vulture Peak Mountain, illuminating it all around with great brilliance.
Then, having taken his seat, Śakra Devānām Indra spoke these verses:
“Those who can subdue the stain of stinginess, And practice giving at the proper time with great virtue—”
"This is called the noble among those who give; in future lives, one shall behold the sublime.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana asked Śakra, saying: "Kauśika!"
How is it that one overcomes the stain of stinginess and perceives excellence? You have said:
"One who can overcome the stain of stinginess, A virtuous person who gives at the proper time— Such a one is noble among givers, And shall see excellence in future lives."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!"

Because they prostrate and pay homage to the most eminent great clans of brahmins, the most eminent great clans of kṣatriyas, the most eminent great clans of householders, the most eminent gods of the Four Great Kings, and the most eminent gods of the Thirty-three.
Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!

I have paid homage with reverence to the most eminent brahmin clans, the most eminent kṣatriya clans, the most eminent householder clans, and the most eminent gods of the Four Great Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; seeing this fruit of retribution, I have spoken this verse.
"Furthermore, Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!

As far as the sun travels, illuminating all directions—reaching a thousand worlds, a thousand moons, a thousand suns, a thousand Sumeru Kings, a thousand Pūrvavidehas, a thousand Uttarakurus, a thousand Aparagoyānīs, a thousand Jambudvīpas, a thousand Cāturmahārājikas, a thousand Trāyastriṃśas, Yāmas, Tuṣitas, Nirmāṇaratis, Paranirmita-vaśavartins, and a thousand Brahmās—this is called a small chiliocosm."

In this small chiliocosm, there is no hall or pavilion equal to the Vaijayanta Hall. The Vaijayanta has one hundred and one towers and pavilions; each pavilion has seven tiers, each tier has seven chambers, each chamber has seven celestial queens, and each queen has seven handmaidens.
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!

Within a small thousand-world system, there is no hall or pavilion as magnificent and dignified as the Vaijayanta. I have seen that because of taming stinginess, such a sublime fruit arises; therefore, I spoke this verse."
Mahāmaudgalyāyana said to Śakra:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Kauśika! Since you were able to see this sublime and wondrous karmic fruition, you have spoken these verses.
At that time, having heard what the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had said, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, rejoiced and expressed his approval, then suddenly vanished.
505 (505). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was meditating alone in a quiet place and had this thought:

"In the past, Śakra Devānām-indra asked the Blessed One about the meaning of liberation through the exhaustion of craving while they were in a stone cave on Mount Khaṇḍa.
