The Blessed One explained it for him, and having heard it, he rejoiced; yet it seems he wishes to ask further regarding its meaning. I shall now go and inquire about the cause of his joy."

Having formed this thought, in the time it takes a strong man to bend or extend his arm, he vanished from Vulture Peak Mountain and arrived in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, staying not far from Lake Pundarika.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, was sporting with five hundred celestial maidens in a bathing pool; there were various goddesses whose voices were exquisite and beautiful.
Then, Śakra saw from afar the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and said to the celestial maidens:
"Do not sing."
"Do not sing.

At that time, the celestial maidens immediately became silent. Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, went to where the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna asked Śakra:
"Previously, in the Gijjhakūṭa mountain range, you questioned the Blessed One regarding the meaning of liberation through the exhaustion of craving; having heard it, you rejoiced. What do you think?"
"Is it because you have heard this teaching that you rejoice,
or do you rejoice because you wish to ask further questions? Śakra,
Lord of the Devas, said to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
“In the Heaven of the Thirty-three, we are often indulgent in the pleasures of negligence; at times we recall past events, and at other times we do not.

The Blessed One is now at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha. Venerable sir, if you wish to know about the matters I previously asked concerning the mountain range of Sīhagiri, you should go now and ask the Blessed One; as the Blessed One explains them, you should accept and uphold them.”
"However, I have here a fine hall and pavilion, newly completed and not long since finished; you may enter and view it.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana silently accepted the invitation and immediately entered the hall together with Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
When those celestial maidens saw Śakra approaching from afar, they all played heavenly music, some singing and others dancing.

Adorned with necklaces and various ornaments, the host of celestial maidens produced exquisite sounds that blended with the five musical instruments; their voices were no different from those of a master musician performing a concert.
When the celestial maidens saw the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, they were all filled with shame and modesty, and withdrew into their rooms to hide themselves.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Behold how beautiful, level, and even is the ground of this hall; its walls, pillars, beams, multi-storied galleries, windows, lattices, and curtains are all exquisitely adorned."
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said to Śakra:
“Kauśika! It is through the causal conditions of merit from having previously cultivated wholesome dharmas that this wondrous fruit has been accomplished.”
In this manner, Śakra praised himself three times and questioned the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana likewise answered him three times.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"Now this Śakra is exceedingly self-indulgent; attached to his dwelling among the deities of the realm, he praises this palace hall. I shall cause him to give rise to a sense of weary detachment."
He immediately entered samādhi and, by means of his supernormal powers, struck the hall with a single toe, causing it all to tremble.
At that moment, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana vanished from sight.
When the host of celestial maidens saw this hall and pavilion trembling, shaking, and reeling, they became distressed and terrified, fleeing hither and thither, and said to Śakra:
"Is this the Great Teacher Kauśika who possesses such great power of merit?"
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to the celestial maidens:
"This is not my teacher; he is Mahāmaudgalyāyana, a disciple of the Great Teacher, whose holy life is pure, and who possesses great virtue and great power."
The goddesses said: "Excellent, Kauśika!"
"If there are fellow practitioners of the holy life (brahmacarya) with such great virtue and great power as these, what must the virtue and power of the Great Teacher himself be like?
506 (Five Hundred and Six). Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling on a soft, pale-white stone slab in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, not far from the Pāriyātra and Kovidāra fragrant trees, observing the summer retreat and preaching the Dharma for his mother and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was observing the rains retreat at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Jeta’s Grove near Śrāvastī.
Then, the fourfold assembly went to where the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and said to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
“Do you know where the World-honored One is spending the summer retreat?”
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied:

"I have heard that the Blessed One is currently observing the summer rains retreat upon the pale-colored, soft stone slab in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, not far from the Pāriyātra and Kovidāra fragrant trees, where he is teaching the Dharma to his mother and the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three."
At that time, having heard what the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had said, the fourfold assembly rejoiced and approved; they each rose from their seats, paid their respects, and departed.
At that time, after the three-month summer retreat had concluded, the fourfold assembly went again to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana preached various teachings to the fourfold assembly, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them;
having thus instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them, he remained silent.
Then, the fourfold assembly rose from their seats, prostrated in homage, and addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!..."
"You should know that it has been a long time since we last saw the Blessed One; the assembly is deeply parched with longing to see him.
Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
If you do not find it too much trouble, we pray that you will go to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven on our behalf and inquire after the Blessed One’s welfare for us all."
"Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you light and agile in your daily activities, and do you dwell in peace and happiness?
He further addressed the World-Honored One:

"The fourfold assembly of Jambudvīpa wishes to see the World-Honored One; yet, lacking the supernormal power to ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to pay homage to the World-Honored One, while those in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven possess the supernormal power to descend to the human realm, we pray only that the World-Honored One would return to Jambudvīpa out of compassion."
Then, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana consented in silence.
When the fourfold assembly knew that the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had consented by remaining silent, they each rose from their seats, paid their respects, and departed.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, knowing that the fourfold assembly had departed, immediately entered into meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Just as a strong man might bend or extend his arm, he vanished from Śrāvastī and appeared upon a pale, soft stone in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, not far from the Pāriyātra and Kokubidūra fragrant trees.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by an immeasurable assembly of followers from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven as he preached the Dharma.
Then, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana saw the World-Honored One from afar; leaping for joy, he thought to himself:
"Today the World-Honored One is preaching the Dharma surrounded by a great multitude of devas, no different from the assemblies in Jambudvīpa."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the mind of the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana!

It is not by my own power; when I wish to preach the Dharma to the devas, they immediately assemble, and when I wish for them to depart, they immediately leave. They come according to my mind and go according to my mind.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Blessed One:

“A great multitude of various devas has gathered like clouds. Among those deva hosts, are there any who, having heard the Dharma taught by the Blessed One, attained indestructible faith, and upon the dissolution of the body after death, were reborn here?”
The Buddha told the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "It is so, it is so.

Among those various devas who have gathered here like clouds, there are some who, having heard the Dharma in a previous life, attained unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and were perfected in the noble precepts; at the breaking up of the body after death, they were reborn here."

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having seen the World-Honored One and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana conversing and praising one another, and having finished speaking with the assembly of devas, addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: “So it is, so it is.”
Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!

All these various assemblies here have been so in previous lives; they have heard the true Dharma in the past, attained unshakable confidence in the Buddha, unshakable confidence in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and were accomplished in the noble precepts. When their bodies dissolved at the end of their lives, they were reborn here.

At that time, a certain bhikṣu, having seen the World-honored One and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana engage in excellent mutual discourse with Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "So it is, so it is!"
Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!

Those various devas who have come to this assembly have all, in previous lives, heard the True Dharma; they attained indestructible confidence in the Buddha, indestructible confidence in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and were accomplished in the noble precepts. When their bodies perished and their lives ended, they were reborn here.
Then, a certain devaputra rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
I too have attained indestructible confidence in the Buddha; therefore, I have been reborn here.”
Again, another devaputra said:
"I have attained indestructible clarity regarding the Dharma.
Another said: "I have attained indestructible clarity regarding the Saṃgha. Another said: "Because I have accomplished the noble precepts, I have come to be born here."

In this manner, immeasurable thousands of devas, each individually declaring before the World-Honored One that they had attained the dharma of srotāpanna, all vanished from before the Buddha and became invisible.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, knowing that the assembly of devas had departed, rose from his seat before long, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The fourfold assembly of Jambudvīpa bowed their heads in respectful salutation at the feet of the World-Honored One and inquired after his well-being, saying:
"Are you free from illness and affliction? Are your daily activities light and easy? Do you dwell in peace and happiness?"
The fourfold assembly yearned for him and wished to see the World-Honored One.
They further addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"Among us humans, there is no one with the supernormal power to ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to pay homage and visit the World-Honored One. However, those devas possess great merit and power and are all able to descend here to Jambudvīpa. We only pray that the World-Honored One will return to Jambudvīpa out of compassion for the fourfold assembly."
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
“You may return there and say to the people of Jambudvīpa:
‘Seven days from now, the World-Honored One shall return from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to the city of Saṃkāśya in Jambudvīpa, beneath an Udumbara tree outside the outer gate.’”
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having received the instruction of the Blessed One, immediately entered into samādhi.
In the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he vanished from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and arrived in Jambudvīpa. He addressed the fourfold assembly:

"All you people, you should know that seven days from now, the Blessed One will return from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Jambudvīpa, to the city of Saṃkāśya, beneath an Udumbara tree outside the outer gate."

When the seven days had passed as scheduled, the World-Honored One descended from the Heaven of the Thirty-three to Jambudvīpa, beneath an Udumbara tree in the city of Saṃkāśya. The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and even those up to the Brahmā heavens all descended together with him; at that very moment, this assembly was named "The Place Where [the Buddha] Descended."

Then, forty devaputras stood before the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, each individually declaring that they had attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*, and immediately vanished from sight.
As it was with the forty devaputras,

At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and the Venerable Bhikṣu Lekhaṇa were together on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
In the early morning, the Venerable Lekhaṇa went to where the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was and said to him,

Then, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana silently gave his consent. They immediately departed together from Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food.
As they proceeded, they came to a certain place where the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having a thought arise in his mind, smiled joyfully.
Having seen the Venerable Lekhana smile, he immediately asked the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"When the Buddha or his disciples smile with joy, it is never without cause or condition. For what reason and for what cause has the Venerable one smiled today?"
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said:

"The question you have asked is ill-timed. First enter the city of Rājagṛha to beg for alms; once you have returned before the Blessed One, you may ask about this matter. That will be a timely question, and he shall explain it to you."

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and the Venerable Lekhaṇa, having entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms and returned, washed their feet, put away their robes and bowls, and together approached the Buddha. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit at one side.
The Venerable Lekhaṇa asked the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:

"This morning, I went out from Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain with you to beg for alms. At one spot, you smiled joyfully; I immediately asked you the reason for your smile, and you replied that the time for such a question was not yet right. Now, once again, I ask you: by what cause and by what condition did you smile so joyfully?"
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said to the Venerable Lekhana:
"On my way, I saw a sentient being whose body was like a multi-storied pavilion, weeping and wailing, filled with grief and suffering, traveling through the air."
Having seen this, I reflected:
"Such sentient beings, having received such bodies, yet undergo such great suffering of grief and lamentation.
For this reason, I smiled.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Excellent! Excellent!”

Among my śrāvakas, those who abide in true vision, true wisdom, true meaning, and true Dharma, and who have attained definitive penetration, see these sentient beings; I too see these sentient beings, yet I do not speak of them, fearing that people would not believe it.
"Why is this? Those who do not believe what the Tathāgata has spoken are foolish people who shall suffer for a long night.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"In a past life, that being of great body was a butcher of oxen here in this city of Rājagṛha. Due to the karmic conditions of slaughtering oxen, he fell into hell for hundreds of thousands of years. Having emerged from hell, there remained residual karma from the slaughter of oxen, whereby he obtained such a body and constantly undergoes such sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering."
"In this way, monks!
Just as the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana has seen it, so should you receive and uphold it.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the monks, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

535. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha was staying at the Pine Forest Monastery.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was staying at the Śīśumāragiri mountain in the dense forest of Bheraṇḍaka in the Vṛji country, a place frequented by wild beasts.
At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha was alone in a quiet place, practicing meditation and reflection, and he thought to himself:

"There is a single vehicle path that purifies sentient beings, removes sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering, and leads to the attainment of the Dharma of suchness; that is, the four foundations of mindfulness."
What are the four?
They are the foundation of mindfulness of the body as body, and the foundations of mindfulness of feelings, mind, and phenomena as phenomena.
If one is distant from these four foundations of mindfulness, one is distant from the dharmas of the noble ones.
One who distances themselves from the dharmas of the noble ones distances themselves from the Noble Path;
one who distances themselves from the Noble Path distances themselves from the Dharma of the Deathless;
and one who distances themselves from the Dharma of the Deathless cannot escape birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering.
If one has faith and delight in the four foundations of mindfulness, one has faith and delight in the noble Dharma;
if one has faith and delight in the noble Dharma, one has faith and delight in the noble path;
if one has faith and delight in the noble path, one has faith and delight in the Dharma of the Deathless.
"Those who have faith and delight in the Dharma of the Deathless shall be liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, knowing the thoughts in the mind of the Venerable Aniruddha, vanished from the Śiṃśapā Forest on Mount Isigili in the Vajjian territory—a place of dense forest and wild beasts—by means of his supernormal power, as swiftly as a strong man might extend or contract his arm. He appeared before the Venerable Aniruddha at the Sāla Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī and said to him:
"While you were alone in a quiet place, practicing meditation and reflection, you had this thought:"

"There is a single vehicle path that purifies sentient beings, causing them to leave behind birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, affliction, and suffering, and to attain the Dharma of Suchness; this is what is called the four foundations of mindfulness."
What are the four?
They are the foundation of mindfulness regarding the body as body, and the foundations of mindfulness regarding feelings, the mind, and phenomena as phenomena.
If one does not delight in these four foundations of mindfulness, one does not delight in the Dharma of the noble ones.
One who does not delight in the noble Dharma does not delight in the noble path;
one who does not delight in the noble path also does not delight in the Dharma of the Deathless;
and one who does not delight in the Dharma of the Deathless is unable to be liberated from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering.
If one has faith and delight in the four foundations of mindfulness, one delights in the dharmas of the noble ones;
if one delights in the dharmas of the noble ones, one delights in the noble path;
if one delights in the noble path, one attains the dharma of the deathless.
"Those who have attained the Dharma of the Deathless (amṛta) have attained liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering.
Did he not say this? The Venerable Anuruddha said to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"So it is, so it is, Venerable One! Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said to Venerable Aniruddha.
"What is meant by 'delighting in the four foundations of mindfulness'?
Venerable Mahā-Moggallāna replied:
"If a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body as body, with the mind taking the body as its object, established in right mindfulness, tamed, stilled, and tranquil, his single-mindedness increases."

In this way, Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, regarding the foundations of mindfulness of feelings, mind, and phenomena—abiding in right mindfulness, taming, calming, and pacifying them, with the mind progressing toward unification—this is called a bhikṣu who delights in the four foundations of mindfulness.

Then, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately entered a state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) according to his mental image, and from the gate of the Sāla Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī, he returned to the dense forest of beasts and birds on Mount Isigili at the village of the Vrjis.
536 (Five Hundred and Thirty-Six). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. ...
[as before] ... until the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana questioned the Venerable Aniruddha:
"What is meant by 'the cultivation and repeated cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness'?
Venerable Anuruddha said to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:

"If a bhikkhu gives rise to the perception of disenchantment toward the internal body, gives rise to the perception of non-disenchantment toward the internal body, and gives rise to the perception of equanimity toward both disenchantment and non-disenchantment, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension."

As with the internal body, so it is with the external body and the internal-external body; with internal feeling, external feeling, and internal-external feeling; with the internal mind, external mind, and internal-external mind; and with internal phenomena, external phenomena, and internal-external phenomena—one cultivates the perception of disenchantment, the perception of non-disenchantment, and the perception of equanimity toward both disenchantment and non-disenchantment, abiding in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.
"Thus it is, Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
This is called the cultivation and repeated cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately entered into samādhi. From the Sāla Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī, by means of the power of his samādhi and supernormal faculties, he returned to the village of the Vṛjis at Mount Isigili, in the Gabled Forest, the dwelling place of birds and beasts, in the space of time it takes a strong man to bend or extend his arm.

20537 (537) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and the Venerable Aniruddha were staying near the Hand-made Bathing Pond in Śrāvastī.
The Venerable Śāriputra went to where the Venerable Aniruddha was, and after they had exchanged greetings and pleasantries, he sat down to one side.
The Venerable Śāriputra said to the Venerable Aniruddha:
"How marvelous, Aniruddha!"
"By cultivating and repeatedly practicing what kind of merit can one attain such great power and majesty?
Venerable Aniruddha said to Venerable Śāriputra,
"By cultivating and repeatedly practicing the four foundations of mindfulness, one accomplishes this great power and majesty."
What are the four foundations of mindfulness?

They are: the foundation of mindfulness of the body as a body internally, practicing with diligence and skillful means, with right mindfulness and clear comprehension, to subdue worldly greed and sorrow.

In this way, one dwells contemplating the body as a body—both externally and both internally and externally; feelings as feelings—both externally and both internally and externally; the mind as mind—both externally and both internally and externally; and phenomena as phenomena—both externally and both internally and externally. With diligence and skillful means, with right mindfulness and clear comprehension, one thus subdues worldly greed and sorrow.
"Venerable Śāriputra!
This is called the cultivation and repeated cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness, by which one achieves such great virtue and supernormal power.
Venerable Śāriputra!"

Because I have well cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness, I am able to observe the small thousandfold world system with little effort, just as a man with clear vision standing atop a multi-storied pavilion observes various objects on the ground below; my observation of the small thousandfold world system with little effort is likewise so.
"In this way, by practicing and cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness extensively, I have achieved this great virtue and supernormal power.
When the two noble men had finished their discussion, they each rose from their seats and departed.
538 (Five Hundred and Thirty-Eight). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Ānanda, and the Venerable Aniruddha were also staying at Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana went to where the Venerable Aniruddha was; after they had exchanged greetings and inquiries of courtesy, he sat down to one side.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana asked the Venerable Aniruddha:
"By practicing and cultivating what qualities has one accomplished such great and virtuous supernormal power?"
The Venerable Anuruddha said to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
“It is through the cultivation and repeated practice of the four foundations of mindfulness that I have accomplished this great and virtuous supernormal power.”

What are the four? One dwells with the mind bound in contemplation of the body internally, diligent in application, with right mindfulness and clear comprehension, removing worldly greed and sorrow; likewise for the body externally, the body both internally and externally; for feelings internally, externally, and both internally and externally; for the mind internally, externally, and both internally and externally; and for phenomena internally, externally, and both internally and externally—one dwells with the mind bound in contemplation, diligent in application, removing worldly greed and sorrow. This is called the cultivation and repeated cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness.

Having accomplished such great virtue and supernormal power, one is able to observe all within a thousand Sumeru mountains through slight means, just as a man with clear vision standing on the summit of a high mountain looks down upon a forest of a thousand tāla trees below.

In this way, through the repeated cultivation and intensive practice of the four foundations of mindfulness, I have achieved this great virtue and supernormal power, by which, with little effort, I can see a thousand Mount Sumerus.
"It is so, Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
It is by practicing and cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness that I have accomplished this great virtue and supernormal power.
When the two noble ones had finished their discussion, they each rose from their seats and departed.
539 (Five Hundred and Thirty-nine). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Ānanda, and the Venerable Aniruddha were staying by the side of the Hand-made Bathing Pond in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda went to where the Venerable Anuruddha was, and after exchanging greetings and expressions of courtesy, he sat down to one side.
The Venerable Ānanda asked the Venerable Anuruddha:
"By cultivating and practicing what qualities have you achieved such great virtue, great power, and great supernormal powers?"
The Venerable Anuruddha said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"By practicing and cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness extensively, I have achieved this great virtue and great power."
What are the four?

One dwells with the mind bound to the contemplation of the body as a body internally, applying diligent effort, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, removing worldly greed and sorrow.

In this way, he fixes his mind upon the contemplation of the external body, the internal and external body; the internal feelings, the external feelings, and the internal and external feelings; the internal mind, the external mind, and the internal and external mind; and the internal phenomena, the external phenomena, and the internal and external phenomena. With diligent application of skillful means, he removes worldly greed and sorrow.
Thus it is, Venerable Ānanda!

Having cultivated and practiced these four foundations of mindfulness, even with little effort, I see with the purified divine eye, which surpasses the eyes of gods and humans, all sentient beings at the time of death and at the time of birth—those of beautiful color and those of ugly color, those of superior form and those of inferior form, those in good destinations and those in bad destinations—all according to their karma as they undergo rebirth; I see all this exactly as it is.

These sentient beings, due to their misconduct of body, speech, and mind, their slandering of the noble ones, and the causal conditions of their wrong views, at the dissolution of the body after death, are reborn in the hells.

Such beings, having practiced wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind, not reviling the noble ones, and being endowed with right view—by reason of these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they attain rebirth in the heavens.

"Just as a man with clear vision standing at a crossroads sees people coming, going, sitting, or lying down, so too do I, having practiced and cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness, having accomplished these great virtues, great powers, and supernormal knowledges, see all sentient beings at the time of death and at the time of birth, in good destinations and in evil destinations."

In this way, sentient beings who engage in misconduct of body, speech, and mind, who revile the noble ones, and who possess wrong views, as a result of these causes and conditions, are born in the hells.

Likewise, sentient beings who engage in good conduct of body, speech, and mind, who do not revile the noble ones, and who possess right views, as a result of these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, attain birth in the heavens.
"In this way, Venerable Ānanda,
through the cultivation and repeated practice of the four foundations of mindfulness, I have accomplished these great virtues, great powers, and supernormal knowledges. Then,
having finished their discussion, the two noble men rose from their seats and departed.
540. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha was staying at the Pine Forest Monastery in Śrāvastī, afflicted by physical illness.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus approached the Venerable Aniruddha; having exchanged greetings and words of comfort, they stood to one side and addressed the Venerable Aniruddha, saying:
"Venerable Aniruddha!"
"Is the ailment you suffer from stable, neither increasing nor diminishing?
Is the force of the illness gradually subsiding rather than continuing to grow?
Venerable Aniruddha replied:
"I am ill and uneasy; it is difficult for me to endure. The various pains in my body are increasing and do not diminish.
He then spoke three similes, as described above in the *Camma-vatthu Sutta* (The Leather).
"However, since my body has already encountered this suffering, I shall endure it with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.
The bhikṣus asked the Venerable Aniruddha:
"In what does the mind abide that you are able to endure such great suffering with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension?"
The Venerable Anuruddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness, I am able to endure with equanimity all the bodily pains that arise within me, maintaining right mindfulness and clear comprehension."
What are the four foundations of mindfulness?

They are the foundation of mindfulness consisting of the contemplation of the body as body, and so on, up to the contemplation of feelings, mind, and phenomena as feelings, mind, and phenomena. This is called abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness; therein one is able to endure all physical pains with self-composure, possessing right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.
At that time, having finished their discussion together, those noble beings rejoiced and approved with gladness;
each rose from his seat and departed. 541 (541). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha was staying at the Sāla Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī, having recently recovered from an illness.
Then, a great number of bhikṣus went to where Anuruddha was, and after exchanging greetings and words of comfort, they sat to one side and asked the Venerable Anuruddha:
"Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?"
Ānanda said, “I am dwelling in peace and happiness; the various pains in my body have gradually subsided.
The bhikṣus then asked the Venerable Ānanda:
“Abiding in what does one find peace amidst the various pains of the body?
Venerable Anuruddha replied,
“By abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness, one gradually finds peace amidst the various pains of the body.”
What are the four?
They are the application of mindfulness to the body as body, and so on, up to the application of mindfulness to phenomena as phenomena; these are called the four applications of mindfulness.
By abiding in these four applications of mindfulness, all physical pains gradually come to rest.
When the various noble ones had finished their discussion, they rejoiced and approved, rose from their seats, and departed.
542 (542) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha was staying at the Sāla Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī.
Then, a great number of bhikṣus approached the Venerable Anuruddha; after exchanging greetings and polite inquiries, they sat to one side and asked the Venerable Anuruddha:

"If a bhikṣu is on the stage of training (śaikṣa-bhūmi) and seeks to dwell in the supreme peace of nirvāṇa, how should the noble disciple practice and cultivate extensively so that, within this Dharma and Vinaya, he may exhaust all outflows (āsrava), attain the outflow-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and realize for himself in this very life, attesting to it: [I have attained it]?"
"Birth has been exhausted for me; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence.
Thus spoke the Venerable Anuruddha to the bhikṣus.
“If a bhikkhu is on the stage of training and dwells with a mind seeking the security of nibbāna, how does that noble disciple practice and cultivate much?

By means of this Dhamma and Vinaya, he attains the destruction of all taints, and through the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, he realizes for himself in this very life, attaining direct knowledge:
‘Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I myself know that there will be no further existence.’”
...should abide in the four foundations of mindfulness.
What are these four?
That is to say: the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body as body, up to the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of phenomena as phenomena.

By practicing and frequently cultivating these four foundations of mindfulness, one attains the exhaustion of all taints within this Dharma and Vinaya; with the mind liberated from taints and liberated through wisdom, one realizes for oneself in the present life:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence."
At that time, having heard what the Venerable Ānanda had said, the bhikṣus rejoiced and approved, rose from their seats, and departed.
(543) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha was staying at the Sāla Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī.
Then, a great number of bhikṣus approached the Venerable Anuruddha; after exchanging greetings and polite inquiries with him, they sat down to one side.
He addressed the Venerable Anuruddha, saying:

"If an Arhat bhikṣu has exhausted all outflows, accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, detached from the fetters of existence, and is well-liberated in mind through right knowledge, does he also cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness?"
The Venerable Anuruddha said to the bhikṣus:

"If a bhikṣu has exhausted all outflows, accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, detached from the fetters of existence, and whose mind is well-liberated through right knowledge, he too cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness."
Why is this? It is because one attains what was not yet attained and realizes what was not yet realized, for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life. Why is this?
I too am free from all taints and have attained arhatship; what was to be done has been done, and my mind is well-liberated, likewise through the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness.
That which was not attained, I have attained; that which was not reached, I have reached; that which was not realized, I have realized, even unto dwelling in peace and happiness in this very life.
At that time, having finished their discussion together, those noble beings rejoiced and expressed their approval;
each rose from his seat and departed. 544 (544). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha was staying at the Sāla Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī.
Then, a large number of non-Buddhist renunciants approached the Venerable Anuruddha; after exchanging greetings and pleasantries with one another, they sat down to one side.
He said to the Venerable Anuruddha,
"Venerable sir, for what reason have you gone forth in the Dharma of the ascetic Gautama?
The Venerable Anuruddha replied:
"It is for the sake of cultivation.
He asked again:
"What is it that is cultivated?"
He replied:

"It refers to the cultivation of the faculties, the cultivation of the powers, the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment, and the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness. Which kind of cultivation do you wish to hear about?"
He asked again:
"I do not even know the names of the faculties, powers, and factors of awakening, much less their meanings; however, I wish to hear about the foundations of mindfulness."
The Venerable Anuruddha said:
"Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you.
If a bhikṣu dwells in the application of mindfulness to the body internally, and so on, up to the application of mindfulness to phenomena as phenomena."
At that time, having heard what the Venerable Ānanda had said, the many non-Buddhist renunciants rejoiced and approved, each rising from their seats and departing.
545 (545). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha was staying in the Śiṃśapā Grove Monastery at Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Suppose there is a great tree that grows leaning downward; as it sinks deeper and further inclines, if one were to cut its root, the tree would surely fall down in the direction it was leaning."
In this way, a bhikkhu cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness; for a long night he proceeds toward, flows toward, and inclines toward seclusion;
he proceeds toward, flows toward, and inclines toward the essential outlet; he proceeds toward, flows toward, and inclines toward Nirvana.
When the Venerable Anuruddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what he said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 546 (546). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākaccāna was staying near the Uṇṇābha Lake in the village of Bhaṇḍagāma.
Then, a brahmin carrying a water-pot and a staff approached Mahākaccāna; after they had exchanged greetings and pleasantries, he sat to one side and asked Mahākaccāna:
"By what cause and by what condition do kings quarrel with kings, and brahmins and householders quarrel with brahmins and householders?"
Mahākātyāyana replied to the brahmin:
"It is due to the causes and conditions of attachment to craving that kings quarrel with kings, and brahmins and householders quarrel with brahmins and householders."
The brahmin asked again:
"For what cause and by what condition do you go forth, and having gone forth, why do you still quarrel with one another?
Mahākātyāyana replied:
“Because they see themselves as bound by desire, though they have gone forth, having gone forth they again engage in disputes.
The brahmin asked again:
“Mahā-Kaccāyana!...”
"Is there anyone capable of being free from the fetters and attachments of sensual desire, as well as being free from the fetters and attachments of this view?
The Venerable Mahākaccāyana replied, "Brahmin!"

There is my Great Teacher—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān—who is able to be free from this bondage and attachment of sensual desire as well as the bondage and attachment of views.
The brahmin asked again:
"Where is the Buddha, the World-Honored One, now?
He replied:
“The Buddha, the World-Honored One, is currently among the people of the Vajjis, at Śrāvastī in the kingdom of Kosala, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the brahmin rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined toward the place where the Buddha was staying, offered praise.

“Homage, homage to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is able to leave behind all attachments of desire and greed, who is fully able to distance himself from the bonds of craving and all desires for views, and whose root is pure.”
Then, having heard what the Venerable Mahākātyāyana had said, the brahmin who carried a water-pot and a staff rejoiced and expressed his approval; he rose from his seat and departed.
547 (547). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Venerable Mahākātyāyana was at the side of the Bhaṇḍagāva Pond, gathered with a large number of bhikṣus in the refectory for the purpose of distributing robes.
At that time, there was an elderly brahmin named Daṇḍapāṇi, whose faculties were fully matured; he approached the refectory and stood leaning on his staff to one side.
After remaining silent for a moment, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Venerable elders!..."
"Why is it that you do not speak with or inquire after this elderly venerable man, nor show him respect by inviting him to sit?
At that time, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana was also sitting among the assembly.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana said to the brahmin:
"In my Dharma, whenever elder men come, we always converse with them, exchange greetings, pay them respectful homage, and invite them to be seated."
The brahmin said:
"In this assembly, I see no one who is older than myself; yet you do not show me respect or prostrate, nor do you bid me sit. Why then do you say:
'In my Dharma, I recognize those who are senior and treat them with respect and prostration, bidding them to sit'?"
Mahākātyāyana said: "O Brahmin!"
If there is one who is eighty or ninety years old, with white hair and fallen teeth, yet who possesses the qualities of a youth, this person is not an elder;
whereas even if one is young, twenty-five years of age, with fair complexion and black hair, in the full vigor of youth, if they possess the qualities of an elder, they are reckoned among the elders.
The brahmin asked:

"How is it that one who is eighty or ninety years old, with white hair and fallen teeth, can yet possess the qualities of youth, being twenty-five years of age, with fair skin and black hair, in the full bloom of vigor and beauty, and be counted among the elders?"
The Venerable Mahākaccāyana said to the brahmin:
"There are five strands of sensual pleasure:

namely, the love for, delight in, and mindfulness of forms cognized by the eye; sounds cognized by the ear; odors cognized by the nose; tastes cognized by the tongue; and tangibles cognized by the body."
Regarding these five strands of sensual pleasure, one is not free from greed, not free from desire, not free from craving, not free from longing, and not free from turbidity.
Brahmin, if it is thus, then even if one is eighty or ninety years old, with hair white and teeth fallen out, this is called being accomplished in the qualities of youth.

Even if one is twenty-five years of age, with fair skin and black hair, in the full vigor of youth and beauty, yet if they are free from greed, free from desire, free from craving, free from obsession, and free from turbidity regarding the qualities of the five senses—if such a person is thus, then despite being young at twenty-five with fair skin and black hair, in the full vigor of youth and beauty, they have attained the dharma of an elder and are counted among the ranks of the aged.
At that time, the brahmin said to the Venerable Mahākaccāyana:

"According to the meaning of what you have said, though I am old, I am young in spirit; though you are young, you have attained the qualities of the aged. Since there are many affairs in the world, please accept my invitation to return."
The Venerable Mahākaccāyana said:
"Brahmin, you yourself know the proper time."
At that time, having heard what the Venerable Mahākātyāyana had said, the brahmin rejoiced and approved, then returned to his own abode. 548 (548) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Venerable Mahākaccāna was dwelling in the Gahapati Grove.
At that time, the King of Mathurā, a prince from the western regions, approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and asked the Venerable Mahākaccāna:
"The Brahmins say of themselves:"
"I am supreme; others are base and inferior. I am white; others are black. The Brahmins are pure; those who are not Brahmins are not so.
These Brahmins are sons born from my mouth; they were created by me and belong to me."
"Venerable Mahākaccāyana! What is the meaning of this?
The Venerable Mahākaccāyana spoke to King Mathura, saying:
“Great King!
This is merely worldly convention.
Worldly convention says:”
"The Brahmins are foremost; other people are base and inferior. The Brahmins are white; other people are black. The Brahmins are pure; those who are not Brahmins are not so."
"Brahmins are born from Brahmins; they are born from the mouth [of Brahmā], created by the Brahmin, and belong to the Brahmin.
Great King, you should know that karma is real, for it is that upon which karma depends.
The King said to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana:
"This has been explained in brief; I do not understand it. I pray that you will explain it further.
The Venerable Mahākātyāyana replied:
"I shall now question you; answer me according to my questions.
He then asked: "Great King!

When you were a Brahmin king, did you summon all four classes of people from your own realm—the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, householders, and elders—and by means of wealth and power, cause them to attend upon you, rising before you and retiring after you, and carrying out all your commands according to your will?
He replied, "As you wish.
He asked again:
"Great King!

Whether it be a Kṣatriya king, a householder king, or a merchant king, when you summon all four castes within your own realm and employ them with wealth and power to serve as your guard—rising before you and retiring after you, and carrying out all your commands—is everything according to your wishes?"
He replied, “As you wish.
He asked again:
“Great King!
Thus, these four castes are all equal; what difference is there?
You should know, Great King!
"The four castes are all entirely equal; there is no distinction of superiority or inferiority.
King Mathura said to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana:
"It is truly so, Venerable Sir!"
"The four castes are all equal; there are no various distinctions of superiority or inferiority.
Therefore, Great King, you should know that the four castes are merely distinguished by worldly convention; even in relation to karma, in reality, there is no distinction."
"Furthermore, Great King!
In this kingdom there are brahmins and there are those who commit theft; what should be done with them?
The king addressed the Venerable Mahākātyāyana:

"Among the brahmins, there are those who commit theft; they may be whipped, or bound, or driven out of the country, or fined gold, or have their hands, feet, ears, and noses cut off, and if the crime is grave, they are executed—punishing the thief accordingly."
"However, O Brahmin, you are called a thief.
He asked again:
"Great King!"
“If there are among the kṣatriyas, householders, or elders those who commit theft, what should be done with them?
The king said to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana:
“They shall be whipped, bound, driven out of the country, fined gold, or have their hands, feet, ears, and noses cut off; if the crime is grave, they shall be executed.”
“In this way, Great King!
Are not the four castes entirely equal?
Is there any distinction or difference between them?”
The king said to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana,
"Regarding such matters as these, in truth there are no various distinctions of superiority or inferiority.
The Venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke again to the king, saying:
"Know this, Great King!
Regarding the four castes, worldly convention says:
'The Brahmins are foremost, while all others are inferior; the Brahmins are white, while other people are all black; the Brahmins are pure, whereas those who are not Brahmins are not.'"
"Should one rely on the reality of karma, or rely on karma itself?
He asked again:
"Great King!..."

If a brahmin commits the ten unwholesome courses of action—killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, harsh speech, divisive speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view—and having performed these ten unwholesome karmic paths, will he be reborn in the evil destinies?
"Have you been reborn in a happy realm? What have you heard from the Arhat?
The King addressed the Venerable Mahākaccāyana: [as follows:]
"It has been heard by the Arhats that if a brahmin commits the ten courses of unwholesome action, he shall fall into the evil destinies.
The same is said for kṣatriyas, householders, and elders."
He asked again:
"Great King!
If a brahmin practices the ten paths of wholesome action—abstaining from taking life up to right view—where will he be reborn?"
Is it a happy rebirth or an evil rebirth?
What has been heard from the Arhat?
The King said to the Venerable Mahākaccāyana:

"If a brahmin practices the ten paths of wholesome action, he will be reborn in a happy destination, in the presence of an Arhat. Thus it has been said, and thus it has been heard; the same applies to kṣatriyas, householders, and elders."
He asked again: "How so,
Great King?"
"Are these four castes equal,
or are there various distinctions of superiority and inferiority among them?
The king addressed the Venerable Mahākātyāyana:
"Such a principle is one of equality, without any distinctions of superiority or inferiority among various types.
Therefore, Great King, you should know that the four castes are entirely equal; there are no distinctions of superiority or inferiority among them."
According to worldly convention, it is said:
"The Brahmins are foremost; the Brahmins are white, while all others are black; the Brahmins are pure, and those who are not Brahmins are not so;
the Brahmins are born, born from the mouth; the Brahmins are the makers, the Brahmins are the transformers, and everything belongs to the Brahmins."
"You should know that karma is real and karma is the basis.
The King said to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana:
"It is truly as you have said; all these are merely worldly conventions, and thus they exist:"
"The Brahmins are superior and all others are base; the Brahmins are white and all others are black; the Brahmins are pure, while those who are not Brahmins are not so;
the Brahmins are born from birth, born from the mouth; the Brahmins are transformed, and everything belongs to the Brahmins."
"All this is truly karma; it depends upon karma.
At that time, King Mathurā, having heard what the Venerable Mahākātyāyana had said, rejoiced and approved, paid his respects, and departed.
549 (549). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana was staying in the Kuralaṭa Monastery in the country of Avanti.

In the early morning, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana dressed in his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the Kullūpattaka Monastery to beg for alms in sequence until he reached the house of the laywoman Kālikā.

At that time, the upāsikā saw the Venerable Mahākātyāyana; she immediately prepared a seat and invited him to sit. She approached and prostrated at the feet of the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, then withdrew to stand to one side and addressed the Venerable Mahākātyāyana:
"As the Blessed One spoke in response to the questions asked by the young girl Saṃghadattā, so the Blessed One spoke these verses regarding the questions asked by the young girl Saṃghadattā:
'The true meaning resides in the mind, Tranquil and undisturbed. "
Having subdued all the fierce and powerful, possessing a lovely and upright countenance,
contemplating alone with a single mind and partaking of the wondrous bliss of dhyāna—
this is true seclusion.
"The factions of the world, all the various factions of the world— none of them associate with me,
Venerable Mahākaccāyana!"
“World-Honored One, what is the meaning of this verse?
The Venerable Mahākātyāyana said to the upāsikā: “Sister!”
There are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who say:
"The meditative attainment of the sphere of totality of earth is supreme; it is for the sake of seeking this fruit. Sisters!

If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa attains the meditative absorption of the totality of earth (pṛthivī-kṛtsnāyatana), which is pure and bright, they will see its origin, see its danger, see its cessation, and see the path leading to its cessation.
Because they see its origin, see its danger, see its cessation, and see the path leading to its cessation, they attain the true meaning that dwells in the mind, becoming tranquil and undisturbed.
Sisters!

These ten totalities—the totality of water, the totality of fire, the totality of wind, the totality of blue, the totality of yellow, the totality of red, the totality of white, the totality of space, and the totality of consciousness—are supreme; it is for the sake of seeking this fruit that they are practiced.

"Sisters! If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, even regarding the sphere of consciousness among all the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana), have attained meditative absorption that is pure and bright; and who see the origin, see the danger, see the cessation, and see the path leading to the cessation [of that sphere];

because they see the origin, see the danger, see the cessation, and see the path leading to cessation, then the true meaning dwells in their minds, which are tranquil and undisturbed, well-seeing and well-entered."
Therefore, the World-Honored One answered the questions posed by the maiden Saṃghadattā with these verses:
"The true meaning abides in the mind, Tranquil and undisturbed;
Having subdued all that is fierce and powerful, One possesses a lovely and upright countenance."
With single-minded focus, I contemplate in solitary stillness, partaking in the wondrous bliss of dhyāna;
this is my seclusion from the factions of the world—
for among all the factions of the world, none shall associate with me.
"In this way, sisters!
It is because I understand the World-Honored One’s meaning in this manner that I have spoken these verses.
The upāsikā said:
“Excellent! Venerable sir, you have spoken the true meaning. I pray only that the Venerable sir will accept my invitation for a meal.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākaccāna accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

Then, the female lay disciple Kālikā, knowing that the Venerable Mahākātyāyana had accepted her invitation, immediately prepared various kinds of pure and delicious food; with reverence and respect, she personally served the meal to him.

Then, the upāsikā, knowing that the Venerable Mahākātyāyana had finished eating, washed his bowl and rinsed his mouth; she then prepared a low seat and sat before the Venerable Mahākātyāyana to listen to the Dharma with reverence.
The Venerable Mahākaccāyana taught the Dhamma to the female lay follower Kāliṅgā in various ways, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening her;
having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened her, he rose from his seat and departed.
550. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana was also staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Venerable Mahākātyāyana addressed the bhikṣus:

“That which is known and seen by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—he has taught six dharmas for emerging from the state of suffering and ascending to the superior state; he has taught the Single Vehicle path for purifying all sentient beings, freeing them from all afflictions and sufferings, extinguishing grief and lamentation entirely, and attaining the dharma of suchness.”
What are the six?

They are that the noble disciple recollects the purity of the qualities practiced by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha: the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, the Sugata, the Lokavid, the Anuttara, the Puruṣadamyasārathi, the Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, the Buddha, the Bhagavān.
Because the noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata and the Dharma that he has practiced, he abandons thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of cruelty.
In this way, the noble disciple emerges from a mind of defiled attachment.
What is the mind of attachment?

It refers to the qualities of the five sensual pleasures. To be free from greed, hatred, and delusion regarding these five sensual pleasures, to abide in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, to ride upon the straight path, to cultivate the recollection of the Buddha, and to head directly toward Nirvana—this is what the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha knows and sees. He declares this to be the foremost way of emerging from suffering and ascending to the supreme state; it is the One Vehicle path that purifies sentient beings, freeing them from affliction and distress, extinguishing sorrow and lamentation, and enabling them to attain the Dharma as it truly is.

"Furthermore, the noble disciple recollects the True Dharma; he recollects the Dharma and Vinaya of the World-Honored One as being free from all feverish afflictions, timely, and penetrative, such that it is realized through one's own personal awakening right here in the present life."
At that time, when the noble disciple contemplates this True Dharma, thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, and harmfulness do not arise.
In this way, the noble disciple emerges from a mind of defiled attachment.
What is the mind of attachment? It refers to the objects of the five sensual pleasures (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).

To be free from greed, hatred, and delusion regarding these five objects of sensual pleasure, to abide in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, to ride upon the straight path, to cultivate the recollection of the Dharma, and to be rightly directed toward *nirvāṇa*—this is what is known and seen by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. He has proclaimed this as the second way out of suffering, leading to the higher state; it is the One Vehicle path that purifies sentient beings, freeing them from suffering and affliction, extinguishing sorrow and lamentation, and attaining the Dharma as it truly is.

"Furthermore, the noble disciple recollects the Dharma of the Saṅgha: those who are well-directed, rightly directed, straightforwardly directed, and equally directed; those who practice in accordance with the path—namely, those who are stream-enterers, those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry; those who are once-returners, those who have attained the fruit of once-returning; those who are non-returners, those who have attained the fruit of non-returning; and those who are arhats, those who have attained the fruit of arhatship."

These four pairs and eight types of noble persons are called the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples, who are endowed with virtue, endowed with concentration, endowed with wisdom, endowed with liberation, and endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation; they are worthy of offerings, respect, and prostration, and are the unsurpassed field of merit in the world.
When a noble disciple recollects the Saṅgha in this way, at that time the noble disciple does not give rise to thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, or cruelty.
In this manner, the noble disciple emerges from a mind of defiled attachment.
What is the mind of attachment? It refers to the objects of the five sensual pleasures.

To be free from greed, hatred, and delusion regarding these five objects of sensual pleasure; to abide in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension; to mount the straight path and cultivate mindfulness of the Saṅgha; to be directed toward Nirvāṇa—this is what is known and seen by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. He has proclaimed this as the third way of emerging from suffering and ascending to a superior state, the single vehicle path that purifies sentient beings, freeing them from suffering and distress, extinguishing grief and lamentation, and attaining the Dharma as it truly is.

"Furthermore, the noble disciple recollects the virtue of his precepts: he recollects the precepts that are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unfaulted, liberating, well-undertaken, praised by the wise, and not misappropriated; precepts that are conducive to the holy life and free from aversion."
When a noble disciple recollects this precept, reflecting upon the precepts accomplished within his own person, at that time he does not give rise to thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, or cruelty.
In this way, the noble disciple emerges from a mind of attachment.
What is the mind of attachment?
It refers to the objects of the five sensual pleasures.

Regarding these five strands of sensual pleasure, one becomes free from greed, hatred, and delusion, abiding in right mindfulness and clear comprehension, riding upon the straight path, cultivating mindfulness of virtue, and proceeding directly toward Nirvāṇa. This is what is known and seen by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; he proclaims this as the fourth way of emerging from suffering, ascending to a superior state—the single vehicle path that purifies sentient beings, freeing them from suffering and distress, extinguishing grief and lamentation, and attaining the Dharma as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the noble disciple reflects upon the practice of giving and rejoices within his own mind:

'I am now free from the defilement of stinginess and greed; though dwelling in a household, my mind is liberated in giving—giving constantly, giving with relinquishment, giving with joy, giving fully, and giving with equanimity.'"
When a noble disciple recollects the Dharma that he himself has practiced, no sensual thoughts, thoughts of ill will, or thoughts of cruelty arise.
In this way, the noble disciple emerges from a mind of defiled attachment.
In what is one stained and attached?
It is said: in the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇāḥ*).

By becoming free from greed, hatred, and delusion regarding these five strands of sensual pleasure, and by abiding in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, one mounts the straight path, cultivates the mindfulness of giving, and proceeds directly toward *nirvāṇa*. This is what is known and seen by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; he declares it the fifth way of emerging from suffering and ascending to a superior state—the single vehicle path that purifies sentient beings, frees them from suffering and distress, extinguishes sorrow and lamentation, and leads to the attainment of the Dharma as it truly is.

"Furthermore, the noble disciple recollects the virtues of the devas; he recollects the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven—how they, with pure faith, passed away from this life and were reborn among those various devas."
I am also like this: through faith, virtue, generosity, learning, and wisdom, having passed away from this life, I was reborn in that heavenly realm.
Thus, when a noble disciple recollects the merits of the devas, thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, or harmfulness do not arise.
In this way, the noble disciple emerges from a mind of attachment.
To what is he attached?
Namely, to the qualities of the five sensual pleasures.

Regarding these five strands of sensual pleasure, one becomes free from greed, hatred, and delusion; abiding in right mindfulness and clear comprehension, one mounts the straight path, cultivates the recollection of the devas, and proceeds directly toward Nirvāṇa. This is what is known and seen by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, whom he proclaims as the sixth way of emerging from suffering and ascending to a superior state—the single vehicle path that purifies sentient beings, frees them from suffering and distress, extinguishes grief and lamentation, and leads to the attainment of the Dharma as it truly is.
When the Venerable Mahākaccāyana had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what he said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
551 (551) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Mahā-Kaccāyana was staying at the monastery in the Śākya village of Hāliddavasana.
Then, the householder of Hāliddavasana approached the Venerable Mahā-Kaccāyana, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Venerable Mahā-Kaccāyana:
"Regarding the verse from the *Arthavargīya* in which the World-Honored One answered the question posed by Makkhali: [The verse follows]"
“Having severed all outflows and also blocked their source,
the Sage does not praise the close association found in villages.
Regarding the five desires as empty space, he never again returns to fill them.”
"Regarding worldly disputes and litigation, one ultimately never engages in them again.
"Venerable Mahākātyāyana,
what is the meaning of this verse?"
The Venerable Mahākātyāyana replied to the householder:
"Regarding the 'outflows of the eye': when visual consciousness gives rise to craving, it flows forth from the realm of the eye due to that desire; therefore, they are called outflows."

Regarding the "streams" of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind: this refers to the arising of craving through the mental consciousness; because the consciousness of craving flows forth based upon the mind-element (*manodhātu*), they are called "streams."
The householder again asked the Venerable Mahākātyāyana,
"What is meant by 'not flowing'?
The Venerable Kātyāyana said to the householder:

"It refers to eye-consciousness and the forms cognized by eye-consciousness; when craving, delight, and attachment toward them are exhausted, rendered desireless, ceased, stilled, and vanished, this is called 'non-outflow'."

The ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, mental consciousness, and the phenomena cognized by mental consciousness give rise to lustful desire; when these are exhausted, without desire, ceased, stilled, and vanished, this is called "non-flowing."
He asked again,
"How so? Venerable Mahākātyāyana replied:

"It means that conditioned by the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the conjunction of these three factors gives rise to contact; conditioned by contact, feeling arises—namely, pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—and based on this, one flows with defiled attachment."

The ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, mental consciousness, and mental phenomena—through the coming together of these three things, contact arises; conditioned by contact, feeling arises: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Based on this feeling, craving, delight, and the flow arise; this is called the source of the flow.
What is meant by "also blocking the source of the stream"?

It refers to the fetters (*saṃyojana*) that arise from attachment to the objects of mental phenomena (*dharmaviṣaya*) through the eye-faculty (*cakṣurdhātu*). When these are exhausted, rendered desireless, ceased, stilled, and vanished, this is called "blocking the source of the stream."

When the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind take up mental objects as their domain and become bound by and driven by them, if these are exhausted, rendered desireless, ceased, stilled, and vanished, this is called "blocking the source of the stream."
He asked again:
“What is meant by ‘associating with and praising one another’?
The Venerable Mahākātyāyana replied:

"When householders and renunciants associate with one another, sharing in joy and sorrow, pleasure and pain, and whatever they do, they all do it together; this is called 'praising through association.'"
He asked again: "What is meant by 'not praising one another'? [The Buddha replied:

"Laypeople and monastics do not associate with one another; they do not share in joy, do not share in sorrow, do not share in suffering, and do not share in pleasure. Whatever they do, they do not find mutual approval in it. This is called 'not praising one another.'"
“What is non-empty desire?
It refers to the qualities of the five desires: the eye-consciousness perceiving forms, which are cherished, delighted in, and nourished by mindfulness; it is a deep, defiled attachment to craving.”

The ear’s delight in sounds, the nose’s in fragrances, the tongue’s in flavors, and the body’s in tactile sensations—these are nurtured by longing and memory; one is deeply stained by craving and attachment, not being free from greed, not free from love, not free from longing, and not free from thirst for these five desires. This is called "not empty of desire."
"What is meant by 'emptiness of desire'?
It refers to being free from greed, free from desire, free from craving, free from longing, and free from thirst regarding these five strands of sensual pleasure; this is called emptiness of desire."
I have taught that the fetters, attachments, and underlying tendencies are what cause the mental factors to become full again.
For those Arhat bhikṣus whose outflows are exhausted, the roots have been severed; like the head of a tāla tree cut off, they shall not arise again in future lives.
How could one possibly engage in further disputes with others? For this reason, the World-Honored One spoke the verse from the *Arthavargīya* in response to the question of Māgandiya:
"If all streams are cut off, And their source is also blocked, The Sage does not praise Dwelling in close proximity to a village."
"Regarding all desires, space has forever ceased to be filled;
it no longer engages with the world in speech or dispute.
This is the analytical explanation of the meaning of the verse spoken by the Tathāgata."
At that time, the elder of the village of Haliddavasana, having heard what the Venerable Mahākaccāyana had said, rejoiced and approved, paid his respects, and departed.
552 (Five Hundred and Fifty-Two). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana was residing in a monastery in the village of Haliddavasana, belonging to the Śākyas.

At that time, the householder headman of the village of Haliddavasana went to the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Venerable Mahākaccāyana:
"As the Blessed One spoke while at the cave of Sakka, King of Devas, on Mount Vediyaka: 'Kosiya!'"

If śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas have attained liberation through the exhaustion of supreme craving, their minds are rightly and well-liberated; they have reached the ultimate limit, are ultimately stainless, have perfected the holy life, and are ultimately pure.
"What is the ultimate limit of this Dharma and Vinaya, its ultimate stainlessness, its ultimate holy life, and its ultimate purity?
The Venerable Mahākaccāna said to the householder:

"It is that which arises dependent upon the eye, eye-consciousness, and the forms cognizable by eye-consciousness, giving rise to delight. When these are exhausted, devoid of desire, ceased, stilled, and vanished—this is the ultimate limit of this Dharma and Vinaya, its ultimate stainlessness, its ultimate holy life, and its ultimate purity."

The ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, mental consciousness, and the phenomena cognized by mental consciousness—dependent upon these, joy arises. When these are exhausted, ceased, stilled, and vanished, the bhikṣu is, in this Dharma and Vinaya, ultimately stainless, having reached the ultimate holy life, and is finally pure.
At that time, the householder, the head of the village of Haliddavasana, having heard what the Venerable Mahākaccāyana had said, rejoiced and approved, paid his respects, and departed.
553 (Five Hundred and Fifty-three). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana was in the Śākya village of Halidra.
The village headman and elder approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and asked the Venerable Mahākaccāna:
"As the Blessed One said while staying in the mountain cave of Sīlavantaguhā for the sake of Sakka, the Lord of Devas: 'Kosiya!'"

If śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas have attained liberation through the exhaustion of supreme craving, their minds are well-liberated; they have reached the ultimate limit, are ultimately stainless, have perfected the holy life, and are ultimately pure.
"How does one reach the ultimate limit, the ultimate stainlessness, the ultimate holy life, and the ultimate purity within this Dharma and Vinaya?
Venerable Kaccāyana said to the householder:

"If a bhikkhu’s grasping at the sphere of the eye, and the underlying tendencies that bind him to the objects of mental phenomena, are exhausted, devoid of desire, stilled, and ceased—then he has reached the ultimate limit, the ultimate stainlessness, the ultimate holy life, and the ultimate purity within this Dharma and Vinaya."

The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—the grasping of the mind-element, the fetters, attachments, and underlying tendencies toward mental objects—if these are exhausted, detached from, ceased, stilled, and vanished, then within this Dharma and Vinaya, one has reached the ultimate limit, the ultimate stainlessness, the ultimate holy life, and the ultimate purity.
Then, having heard what the Venerable Mahākātyāyana had said, the householder, the head of the village of Haliddavasana, rejoiced and approved, paid his respects, and departed.
554 (Five Hundred and Fifty-Four). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana was residing in the Śākya village of Haliddavasana.
At that time, the householder who was the head of the village of Haliddavasana was afflicted by the suffering of illness.

Having heard that the householder, the head of the village of Haliddavasana, was afflicted by the suffering of illness, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana dressed in the morning, took his bowl, and entered the village of Haliddavasana for alms; proceeding in order, he entered the residence of the householder, the head of the village of Haliddavasana.
The householder, the head of the village of Pāṭaligāma, saw Venerable Mahākaccāyana from afar and rose from his seat.
Seeing that the householder was about to rise, Venerable Mahākaccāyana said to him:
"Householder, do not rise!
"Fortunately there are spare seats; I shall sit on one of them.
He then said to the householder, "What do you think?"
"Householder!
Is your illness bearable?
Are your various physical pains gradually subsiding?"
"Has there been no increase?
The householder replied,
"Venerable Sir!"
"My illness is difficult to endure; the various pains in my body continue to increase and do not diminish.
He then spoke three similes, as previously explained in the *Camma-bhikkhu Sutta*.
The Venerable Mahākaccāyana said to the householder:

"Therefore, you should cultivate unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dharma, and unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha, and achieve accomplishment in the noble precepts; you should train yourself in this way."
The householder replied:

“Regarding the four kinds of unshakable confidence spoken of by the Buddha, I have fully accomplished them all; I have now accomplished unshakable confidence in the Buddha, unshakable confidence in the Dharma, unshakable confidence in the Sangha, and the accomplishment of the noble precepts.”
The Venerable Mahākaccāyana said to the householder:
"Householder, you should cultivate the six recollections based upon these four bases of unwavering confidence.
Householder!
