One should recollect the merits of the Buddha: this Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

One recollects the merit of the Dharma: the Blessed One’s true Dharma and Discipline is visible in this very life, free from feverish affliction, timeless in its penetration, based on personal realization. One recollects the merit of the Saṅgha: those who are well-directed, rightly directed, straightforwardly directed, and equally directed; those who practice in accordance with the path—namely, those who are stream-enterers, those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry; those who are once-returners, those who have attained the fruit of once-returning; those who are non-returners, those who have attained the fruit of non-returning; and those who are arahants, those who have attained the fruit of arhatship.

These four pairs and eight types of individuals are called the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples; they are endowed with virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; they are worthy of offerings, reverence, and respect, and are fit to be the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.

Reflecting on the merit of the precepts, one upholds the right precepts oneself—precepts that are unimpaired and unblemished, uninterrupted and indestructible, precepts not acquired by theft, ultimate precepts, praiseworthy precepts, precepts of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), and precepts free from malice.

Reflecting on the merit of giving, one contemplates one's own acts of generosity; the mind rejoices within itself, abandoning stinginess and greed. Although remaining in the household life, one practices liberation through the mind in giving—giving constantly, giving joyfully, giving fully, and giving with equanimity.

One should reflect upon the merit of the devas, reflecting on the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; through pure faith and precepts, one will, at the end of this life, be reborn among those devas.
I, too, having likewise cultivated pure faith, ethical discipline, generosity, learning, and wisdom, was born among those devas.
Householder!
Thus, awakening based upon the four kinds of indestructible purity increases the six foundations of mindfulness.
The householder said to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana:

“The World-Honored One has taught that based upon the four kinds of indestructible confidence (*aveccappasāda*), one increases the six foundations of mindfulness (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*). I have fully accomplished them all; I shall now cultivate the recollection of the Buddha’s qualities, and the recollection of the Dharma, the Sangha, the precepts, generosity, and the devas.”
The Venerable Mahākātyāyana said to the householder,
“Excellent, householder!”
"He was able to declare for himself that he had attained the stage of Anāgāmin.
At that time, the householder addressed the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, saying, "I pray that you will accept a meal here."
The Venerable Mahākātyāyana accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Venerable Mahākātyāyana had accepted, the householder, the head of the village of Hālī, prepared various kinds of pure and delicious foods and personally offered them with his own hands.
When the meal was finished, and he had washed his bowl and rinsed his mouth, he preached various teachings to the elder, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him;
having thus instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him, he rose from his seat and departed.
555 (Five Hundred and Fifty-Five). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana was residing in the Śākya village of Hāliddavasana.
At that time, there was an elder of Aṭṭhakanāgara named Taṇḍula who was afflicted by the suffering of illness.

When the Venerable Mahākaccāna heard that the elder Taṇḍula was suffering from such affliction, he dressed in the morning, took his bowl, and entered Aṭṭhakanāgara for alms. He eventually arrived at the house of the elder Taṇḍula, as described in detail in the *Kāliṅga-putta Sutta*.
556 (Five Hundred and Fifty-Six). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Anjana Grove at the city of Sāketa.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣuṇīs approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma in various ways to a great multitude of bhikṣuṇīs, instructing, exhorting, illuminating, and gladdening them;
having instructed, exhorted, illuminated, and gladdened them, he remained silent.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!

Regarding this signless mental concentration (animitta-cittasamādhi), which neither surges nor sinks, wherein liberation has already been established and one abides in liberation—what fruit and what merit does the World-Honored One declare for this signless mental concentration?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣuṇīs:

"If, in the signless mind-samādhi, one neither surges nor sinks, but having attained liberation abides, and having abided attains liberation—this signless mind-samādhi is the fruit of knowledge and the merit of knowledge."
At that time, having heard what the World-Honored One had said, the bhikṣuṇīs rejoiced and were filled with joy; they paid their respects and departed.
Then, a great number of bhikṣuṇīs went to where the Venerable Ānanda was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Venerable Ānanda:

"Regarding this samādhi of the signless mind—which neither surges nor sinks, wherein liberation has already been established and one abides, and wherein one abides and is liberated—what is the fruit and what is the merit of this teaching on samādhi?"
The Venerable Ānanda said to the bhikṣuṇīs: "Sisters!

If the signless mind-concentration neither surges nor sinks, but having attained liberation remains steady, and having remained steady is liberated—the Blessed One has declared this to be the fruit of wisdom and the merit of wisdom."
The bhikṣuṇīs said:
"How marvelous!
Venerable Ānanda!"
The Great Teacher and his disciples share the same words, the same flavor, and the same meaning—namely, the foremost words and meanings.

Now these bhikṣuṇīs have approached the World-Honored One and questioned him with such words, such flavor, and such meaning; the World-Honored One has likewise explained it to us with such words, such flavor, and such meaning, no different from what the Venerable Ānanda has said. Therefore, it is extraordinary that the Great Teacher and his disciples share the same words, the same flavor, and the same meaning.
At that time, having heard what the Venerable Ānanda had said, the bhikṣuṇīs rejoiced and delighted in it;
they paid him homage and departed. 557 (557) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Gośīrṣa Park in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was also staying there.
Then, the bhikṣuṇī Śāṭhā approached the Venerable Ānanda, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and asked the Venerable Ānanda:
"If the signless mind-samādhi neither surges nor sinks, but is liberated and remains steady, and having remained steady, it is liberated; [how is this so?]"
"Venerable Ānanda!
What is the fruit and what is the merit of this that the Blessed One has spoken?
Venerable Ānanda said to the bhikṣuṇī Śāṭhacarā:

“If the signless mind-samādhi neither surges nor sinks, but having attained liberation remains steady, and having remained steady is liberated—the Blessed One says this is the fruit of wisdom and the merit of wisdom.”
The bhikṣuṇī Śāṭhī said:
"How marvelous!
Venerable Ānanda!"
The Great Master and his disciples share the same words, the same flavor, and the same meaning.
Venerable Ānanda!
Once, in the past, the Buddha was staying at the Anupiya Mango Grove near the city of Sāketa.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣuṇīs went to where the Buddha was and inquired about this matter.

Then, the World-Honored One explained it to the bhikṣuṇīs with such phrases, such flavor, and such meaning. Therefore, you should know that it is extraordinary that what is spoken by the disciples of the Great Teacher is identical in phrase, identical in flavor, and identical in meaning—namely, the foremost meaning of the phrases.
Then, having heard what the Venerable Ānanda had said, the bhikṣuṇī Śāṭhikara rejoiced and approved, paid her respects, and departed.
As it was with the bhikṣuṇī Śāṭhikara, so it was with the bhikṣuṇī Kālī.
558 (Five Hundred and Fifty-Eight). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kosambī in the Ghosita Park.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was also staying at Kosambī in the Ghosita Park.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu who had attained the signless mind-samādhi and thought to himself:
"If I were to go to the Venerable Ānanda and ask him:
'If a bhikṣu attains the signless mind-samādhi, neither surging nor sinking, liberated and abiding, abiding and liberated—what is the fruit of this signless mind-samādhi?'"
"What merit does the Blessed One say lies in this?
If the Venerable Ānanda were to ask me:
"Bhikkhu!..."
"Have you attained this signless mind-samādhi?
"I have never had it. He answered differently from what was truly asked.
"I shall follow the Venerable Ānanda so that, should anyone else ask about this matter, I may hear it.
That bhikṣu then followed the Venerable Ānanda for six years, during which time no one else asked about this matter. He then asked the Venerable Ānanda himself:

"If a bhikṣu asks about the signless concentration of mind (*animitta-cittasamādhi*)—which neither surges nor sinks, being liberated and abiding, and abiding and liberated—what does the World-Honored One say is its fruit and what its merit?"
The Venerable Ānanda asked that bhikṣu: "Bhikṣu,
have you attained this samādhi?"
That bhikṣu remained silent. The Venerable Ānanda said to that bhikṣu:

“If a bhikṣu attains the signless mind-samādhi, neither surging nor sinking, abiding in liberation and liberated through abiding—the World-Honored One has declared this to be the fruit of wisdom and the merit of wisdom.”
When the Venerable Ānanda had spoken this Dharma, the other bhikṣus, having heard what he said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*Saṃyukta Āgama*, Scroll 20; *Saṃyukta Āgama*, Scroll 21.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
21.559 (559). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the country of Pāṭaliputra;
the Venerable Ānanda and the Venerable Kama were also at the Kāliṅga Monastery in Pāṭaliputra.
Then, the Venerable Kama approached the Venerable Ānanda; after they had exchanged greetings and expressions of courtesy, he sat down to one side and said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"How marvelous!..."
Venerable Ānanda!

There is the eye and visible forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena; yet there is a bhikṣu who, despite possessing these dharmas, is unable to perceive them.
"How so? Venerable Ānanda!
Is that bhikṣu unaware because he possesses perception, or is he unaware because he lacks perception?"
The Venerable Ānanda said to the bhikṣu Kāma:
"Even one who possesses perception does not perceive; how much more so one who lacks perception.
He then asked the Venerable Ānanda again:
“What is it to have perception regarding existence yet not be fully aware of it?
Venerable Ānanda said to the bhikṣu Kāma:
“If a bhikṣu, detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, dwells having attained the first dhyāna.”
In this way, a bhikṣu possessing perception has a dharma that he does not discern.
Likewise, he dwells having fully attained the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, as well as the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness.
In this way, a bhikṣu who possesses perception does not cognize existing phenomena.
How is it that one who lacks perception does not cognize existing phenomena?

In this way, a bhikṣu does not bring any perceptions to mind; he realizes for himself with his own body the concentration of mind that is signless (*animitta-citta-samādhi*) and dwells therein in its full perfection. This is called a bhikṣu who, being signless, does not cognize existing phenomena.
The Venerable Kāmabhū again asked the Venerable Ānanda:

"If a bhikkhu, through the concentration of the mind of non-perception, neither surges nor sinks, but dwells liberated and remains liberated, what fruit and what merit does the Blessed One say this entails?"
The Venerable Ānanda said to the bhikṣu Kāma:

"If a bhikṣu, through the samādhi of the signless mind, neither surges nor sinks, but dwells in liberation and is liberated while dwelling—this, the Blessed One has declared, is the fruit of wisdom and the merit of wisdom."
At that time, after the two noble men had finished their discussion, they rejoiced and expressed their approval, then each rose from his seat and departed.
560 (560) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Ghoṣitārāma in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was also staying there.
Then, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikṣus:
"Bhikṣus! If a bhikṣu..."
When a bhikṣuṇī confesses her own transgression before me, I shall praise her with words of "well done," comfort her, and inquire after her welfare, or I shall seek to lead her toward the four paths.
What are these four?

If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, while seated, dwells with a mind thus established, well-established, restricted, tamed, unified in śamatha and vipaśyanā, and equanimous; and having analyzed, measured, cultivated, and repeatedly practiced the Dharma, they attain the severance of all latent tendencies (anuśaya).
If there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who declare their realization in my presence, I then comfort them with words such as "Excellent! or inquire further; this is called the first stage of the path.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī sits upright and reflects, discerning phenomena, dwelling with a mind that is well-stabilized, firmly established, concentrated, tamed, unified through calm abiding and insight, and equanimous."

If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, dwelling thus correctly and frequently, attains freedom from the underlying tendencies (anuśaya), and they declare this before me, I shall comfort them with the words "Excellent! or grant them what they seek; this is called the second way of teaching.

"Furthermore, monks and nuns who are possessed by restlessness sit with a mind to be tamed; they sit upright, dwelling the mind, dwelling it well, dwelling it with focused attention, taming it, and through concentration on both tranquility and insight, they receive transformation with one-pointedness of mind."

When one has thus correctly directed oneself and dwelt therein extensively, one then severs all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). If there is a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī who declares this before me, I then console them with the words "Excellent! or grant them what they seek; this is called the third teaching of the path.

"Furthermore, when a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī practices tranquility and insight in union and together, and thus correctly applies themselves and dwells therein frequently, they will sever all underlying tendencies."

If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī makes a self-declaration in my presence, I then comfort, exhort, and instruct them with words such as "Excellent! or inquire further; this is called the fourth way of teaching the path.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Venerable Ānanda had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 561 (561) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kauśāmbī in the Ghosira Park, and the Venerable Ānanda was also staying there.
At that time, a certain brahmin approached the Venerable Ānanda; after they had exchanged greetings and pleasantries, he sat to one side and asked the Venerable Ānanda:
"For what reason do you practice the holy life under the ascetic Gautama?"
The Venerable Ānanda said to the brahmin,
“For the sake of severing [craving].
He asked again:
"What has the Venerable One abandoned?
He replied, "I have abandoned craving."
He asked again:
"Venerable Ānanda,
by depending on what is craving abandoned?"
He replied:
"Brahmin, one abandons craving by relying on desire."
He asked again:
"Venerable Ānanda!
Is it not indeed boundless?"
He replied:
"Brahmin, it is not without limit."
"In this way, there is a limit; it is not without limit.
He asked again:
"Venerable Ānanda!
"What is it that has a limit, rather than being limitless? He replied, "Brahmin!"
I now ask you; answer me as you see fit.
Brahmin, what do you think?
"Did you previously intend to come to this monastery?
The brahmin replied, "It was so, Ānanda!"
“In this way, brahmin!
Having come to the monastery, do you wish to rest?
He replied:
"So it is, Venerable Ānanda!
Having applied diligence, skillful means, and deliberation, he has come to the monastery.
He asked again:
“Once you have arrived at the monastery, have your diligence, skillful means, and deliberation ceased?
He replied, “It is so, Venerable Ānanda.”
He spoke again to the brahmin: "It is so, brahmin!

That which is known and seen by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, he proclaims as the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), by which path of the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*) he purifies sentient beings, extinguishes suffering and affliction, and cuts off sorrow and lamentation."
What are the four?

They are the basis of psychic power consisting in the concentration of desire and the accomplishment of the formations of abandonment; the basis of psychic power consisting in the concentration of energy; the basis of psychic power consisting in the concentration of mind; and the basis of psychic power consisting in the concentration of investigation and the accomplishment of the formations of abandonment.

In this way, the noble disciple cultivates the basis for psychic power consisting of concentration through desire and the exercise of volition; relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on relinquishment, relying on cessation, and tending toward abandonment, he proceeds until craving is severed. Once craving is severed, that desire also subsides.

One cultivates the concentration of energy, the concentration of mind, and the concentration of investigation, accomplishing the formations of abandonment; relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on relinquishment, and relying on cessation, one proceeds toward equanimity, until craving is exhausted. Once craving is exhausted, conceptualization ceases.
"Brahmin! What do you think?
Is this not the ultimate limit?"
The brahmin said:
"Venerable Ānanda!
This is the limit; it is not without a limit."
At that time, having heard what the Venerable Ānanda had said, the brahmin rejoiced and approved, rose from his seat, and departed.
562 (562). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kosambī in the Ghosita Park; the Venerable Ānanda was also staying there.
At that time, the householder Ghoṣila approached the Venerable Ānanda, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"What is meant by one who is called a teacher of the Dharma in the world?"
"What is meant by 'the world’s good direction,' and what is meant by 'the world’s good arrival'?
Venerable Ānanda said to the householder Ghoṣita:
"I now ask you; answer me as you see fit.
Householder, what do you think?"
"If there were one who preached the Dharma to subdue greed, to subdue hatred, and to subdue delusion, would he be called a teacher of the Dharma in the world?
The householder replied,
"Venerable Ānanda!"
"If there is a teaching of the Dharma that can subdue greed, hatred, and delusion, this is what is called 'teaching the Dharma in the world.
He asked again:
"Householder!"
What do you think?
If people in the world are tending toward the subduing of greed, the subduing of hatred, and the subduing of delusion, is this called "tending rightly" in the world?
And if people in the world have already subdued greed, hatred, and delusion, is this called "having arrived rightly"?
"Is it not so? The householder replied,
"Venerable Ānanda!"
"If one has tamed greed so that it is severed without remainder, and has severed anger and delusion so that they are severed without remainder, this is called 'having reached excellence.
Venerable Ānanda replied,
"Householder!"
"I shall question you; you should answer me truthfully. Since the meaning is such as this, you should uphold it.
Having heard what the Venerable Ānanda had said, the householder Ghoṣila rejoiced and delighted in it, paid his respects, and departed.
563 (Five Hundred and Sixty-Three). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Gabled Hall beside the Markaṭahrada Pond in Vaiśālī; the Venerable Ānanda was also staying there.

At that time, the Licchavi Abhaya, a disciple of the Nirgranthas, and the young Licchavi Citta, a disciple of the Ājīvikas, both went together to where the Venerable Ānanda was. After exchanging greetings and salutations with one another, they sat down to one side.
Then, the Licchavi Abhaya said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"My teacher, the Nirgrantha, teaches a dharma that is extinguished, blazing, pure, and transcendent; he speaks thus to his disciples regarding the path:
'The karma of past lives can all be cast off by practicing asceticism.'"
By not performing bodily actions, one severs the bridge; thus, in future lives there will be no further outflows, and all karma will be forever exhausted.
Because karma is forever exhausted, all suffering is forever exhausted;
because suffering is forever exhausted, one reaches the ultimate end of suffering.
"Venerable Ānanda!
What is the meaning of this?
Venerable Ānanda spoke to the Licchavi, saying:

"What the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha knows and sees, he proclaims as the threefold path that is free from burning, pure, and transcendent: by means of this single vehicle path, he purifies sentient beings, frees them from sorrow and lamentation, overcomes suffering and affliction, and causes them to attain the Dharma of True Suchness."
What are the three?

In this way, the noble disciple abides in pure ethical discipline, having received the *prātimokṣa* vows, is complete in dignified conduct, and, with faith regarding all transgressions, gives rise to a sense of dread.

By upholding such complete and pure precepts, one gradually expels past karma, attains freedom from the fever of the present life, and—without depending on the passage of time—is able to attain the True Dharma, achieve penetrating insight and direct observation, and realize awakening through wisdom.
"O Licchavi elder!

This is what the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha calls the teaching of that which is known and seen, free from burning, pure, and transcendent; by means of the single vehicle path, it purifies sentient beings, extinguishes suffering and affliction, overcomes sorrow and lamentation, and attains the Dharma of suchness."
"Furthermore, Licchavi!

Thus, being fully endowed with pure ethical discipline, one dwells having transcended sensual desires and unwholesome states, up to and including full attainment of the fourth dhyāna; this is what the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha calls 'being free from burning fever,' up to and including the attainment of the Dharma as it truly is."

Furthermore, there is a samādhi-samāpatti wherein one knows this noble truth of suffering as it truly is, and knows this noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering as they truly are.

Possessing such a mind of wisdom, one no longer creates karma; past karma is gradually severed, and one attains the true Dharma in the present. Free from all burning afflictions, one does not depend on time or season, but penetrates direct perception and gives rise to self-awakened knowledge.
Licchavi!

This is called the third state of being free from burning, as known and seen by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, which is pure and transcendent; it is the One Vehicle path that purifies sentient beings, frees them from suffering and affliction, extinguishes grief and lamentation, and leads to the attainment of the Dharma as it truly is.
At that time, the Licchavi Abhaya, disciple of the Nirgranthas, remained silent.
Then the Licchavi Cunda, disciple of the Ājīvikas, spoke again to the Licchavi Abhaya:
"How strange! How marvelous!"
Abhayā! Why do you remain silent?
Having heard the well-expounded Dharma as taught, known, and seen by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, do you not rejoice in it?
The Licchavi Abhaya replied,
“I remained silent because I was reflecting on its meaning. Who,
having heard the Dharma taught by the Blessed One, the Śramaṇa Gautama, would not rejoice in it?”

If there are those who hear the Dharma taught by the śramaṇa Gautama and do not rejoice in it, they are but fools; for a long night they shall experience suffering that is meaningless and unbeneficial.

Then, the Licchavi Vīra, disciple of the Nirgranthas, and the intelligent Cūḷapanthaka, disciple of the Ājīvakas, having heard the Dharma taught by the Buddha and the words spoken by the Venerable Ānanda, rejoiced and approved, rose from their seats, and departed.
564 (564). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Venerable Ānanda was also staying there.
At that time, a certain bhikṣuṇī conceived a lustful attachment toward the Venerable Ānanda and sent a messenger to inform him:
"I am suffering from illness; I only pray that the Venerable One will take pity on me and come to see me."
In the early morning, the Venerable Ānanda dressed himself, took up his bowl, and went to where that bhikṣuṇī was.
Seeing the Venerable Ānanda approaching from afar, the bhikṣuṇī lay upon her bed with her body exposed.
When the Venerable Ānanda saw the body of that bhikṣuṇī from afar, he immediately restrained his sense faculties and turned his body away to stand with his back toward her.

When that bhikṣuṇī saw the Venerable Ānanda restrain his sense faculties and turn his body away to stand with his back toward her, she felt shame and remorse; she rose, put on her robes, spread out a sitting mat, went out to meet the Venerable Ānanda, invited him to take a seat, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda spoke these words of Dharma: "Sisters!
This body is nourished by impure food, nourished by pride, nourished by craving, and nourished by sensual desire."
Sisters! Relying on impure food, you should abandon impure food; relying on pride, you should abandon arrogance; relying on craving, you should abandon sensual desire.
Sisters! What is meant by "relying on impure food, one should abandon impure food"?

It means that a noble disciple eats while reflecting with careful consideration: without the notion of pleasure, without the notion of pride, without the notion of grooming, and without the notion of adornment; solely for the sake of maintaining the body, for the sake of sustaining life, for the sake of curing the ailments of hunger and thirst, and for the sake of supporting the holy life (*brahmacarya*). He intends to extinguish old sensations and prevent new sensations from arising, and he practices moderation so as to maintain strength, ease, and well-being. Thus should he abide.

It is, for example, like a merchant who greases his cart with oil and ghee, yet has no thought of attachment, no thought of pride, no thought of polishing, and no thought of adornment; it is solely for the purpose of transport. It is like one with a festering wound who applies oil and ghee, yet has no thought of pleasure in the sensation, no thought of pride, no thought of polishing, and no thought of adornment; it is solely for the purpose of healing the wound.

In this way, the noble disciple eats with deliberate awareness, without thoughts of attachment, without thoughts of pride, without thoughts of grooming, and without thoughts of adornment; rather, it is for the sake of sustaining life, for the sake of alleviating hunger and thirst, and for the sake of supporting the holy life (brahmacarya), so that old feelings may pass away and new feelings may not arise, and he may dwell in comfort, touched by strength, ease, and blamelessness.
Sisters! This is called abandoning food by relying on food.
As for "abandoning conceit by relying on conceit":
How does one rely on conceit to abandon conceit?

It is when a disciple hears that a certain venerable one, or a disciple of a certain venerable one, has exhausted all taints (*āsrava*) and attained the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, realizing for himself in this very life:
"Birth is exhausted, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) is established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence."
Having heard this, he thought:
"That noble disciple has exhausted all taints, up to and including knowing for himself that he will not undergo further existence.
Why is it that I have not yet exhausted all taints, and why is it that I do not yet know for myself that I will not undergo further existence?"
At that time, one is able to sever all taints (*āsrava*), up to and including knowing for oneself that there will be no further existence.
Sisters, this is called "relying on pride to sever pride."
"Sisters! How does one rely on craving to abandon craving?

It is when a noble disciple hears that a certain venerable one or a disciple of a certain venerable one has exhausted all taints, and so forth, until he knows for himself that there will be no further existence."
"Why do we not exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*) and even come to know for ourselves that we shall not undergo further existence?
At that time, they were able to sever all outflows and even came to know for themselves that they would not undergo further existence.
Sisters! This is called abandoning craving by relying on craving. Sisters!
"One who acts without attachment severs the bridge of sensual desire.

When the Venerable Ānanda had spoken this Dharma, that bhikṣuṇī was distanced from dust and free from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye. Having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, realized the Dharma, and entered the Dharma, she crossed beyond doubt; no longer dependent on others, her mind attained fearlessness regarding the True Dharma and Vinaya.
He prostrated at the feet of the Venerable Ānanda and said to him:
"I now confess and repent my transgression;
out of folly and unwholesomeness, I have committed such an unworthy act as this."
"Now, in the presence of the Venerable Ānanda, I recognize my own faults and acknowledge my own transgressions; I confess and repent out of compassion!
The Venerable Ānanda said to the bhikṣuṇī:

"You have now truly recognized your fault and acknowledged your transgression. Though you were foolish and unwholesome, you yourself knew that you committed an improper offense. Since you now know and see it for yourself and repent, you shall attain full ordination in a future life."
I now accept your confession out of compassion, so that your wholesome qualities may increase and never decline.

Why is this? If one perceives their own faults, recognizes their own faults, and is able to repent, they will attain the full precepts in future lives; their wholesome qualities will increase and never decline.
The Venerable Ānanda, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened that bhikṣuṇī with various teachings on the Dharma, rose from his seat and departed.
565 (565) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of the Kośala country together with the Venerable Ānanda, and arrived at the Śiṃśapā Grove north of the village of Bhadrapāla.
At that time, the youths of the village of Bhaddiya heard that the Venerable Ānanda was wandering through the human realm and was staying in the Simsapā Grove to the north of the village of Bhaddiya.
Having heard this, they called out to one another and gathered together, went to where the Venerable Ānanda was, prostrated at the feet of the Venerable Ānanda, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the youths:
"O sons of the Ikṣvāku clan!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has taught four kinds of purity: purity of ethical discipline, purity of mind, purity of view, and purity of liberation."
"What is purity of virtue?

It means that a noble disciple dwells in virtue, in the *prātimokṣa*, with virtue increasing, fully endowed with dignified conduct, feeling dread regarding even minor offenses, and undertaking the training rules."
Regarding the body of precepts (*śīlaskandha*): for those who have not yet fulfilled it, one causes them to fulfill it;

for those who have already fulfilled it, one maintains it with compliance, desiring to transcend through diligence and skillful means. With tireless vigor and courage, one is capable regarding all mental and physical phenomena, constantly able to sustain them; this is called the abandonment of purity of precepts.
“O Seed of Suffering!
What is called the purification of the mind through abandonment?
It refers to the noble disciple who, having detached from sensual desires and unwholesome, evil states, dwells having fully attained up to the fourth dhyāna.”

To cause the body of meditative concentration that is not yet complete to become complete, and for that which is already complete to be maintained in accordance with its nature—desiring diligence and so forth until it is constantly maintained—is called the abandonment through mental purity.
“O you who sow the seeds of suffering!
What is called ‘purification through vision and abandonment’?
It refers to when a noble disciple hears the Master teach the Dharma.”
When the Dharma is taught in such and such a way, one enters into the correct contemplation of reality accordingly;
thus one attains joy, attains sympathetic rejoicing, and attains compliance with the Buddha.

"Furthermore, when a noble disciple does not hear the Teacher expounding the Dharma, but hears it from another wise and venerable fellow-practitioner of the holy life, and hears that venerable fellow-practitioner speak in such and such a way, he then enters into such and such a manner of observing reality as it is."
Observing in this way and that, one attains joy and sympathetic joy toward those teachings and gains faith in the True Dharma.

Furthermore, a noble disciple may not hear the Teacher expound the Dharma, nor hear it from wise and venerable fellow practitioners of the holy life; rather, they repeatedly recite and practice what was previously heard and upheld, having thus repeatedly recited it according to what was previously heard and upheld.
"In this way and that way, one gains entry into that Dharma, even unto faith in the True Dharma.

Furthermore, a noble disciple does not hear the Master teaching the Dharma, nor does he hear wise and venerable fellow-practitioners of the holy life teach it; nor is he able to recite and rehearse what he has previously received and mastered. Nevertheless, he extensively explains to others the Dharma he has previously heard, extensively explaining to others the Dharma he has previously heard in such and such a manner."
In this way and that, one enters into the Dharma, examines it with right wisdom, and even gains faith in the True Dharma.

Furthermore, a noble disciple may not hear the Teacher expound the Dharma, nor hear wise and venerable fellow practitioners of the holy life speak it; nor can he recite and rehearse what he has previously received and upheld, nor extensively explain to others the Dharma he has previously heard. Nevertheless, in a solitary and quiet place, he reflects upon and examines the Dharma he has previously heard.
Reflecting and examining in this way, one enters the True Dharma accordingly and even comes to have faith in the True Dharma.
Thus, hearing from others and reflecting correctly within, this is called causing right view that has not yet arisen to arise, and causing right view that has already arisen to increase and expand;

it is called causing the aggregate of morality (*śīlaskandha*) that is not yet fulfilled to be fulfilled, and for that which is already fulfilled, to follow after and embrace it with the application of diligence and effort, up to its constant embrace—this is called the abandonment of purification of view (*diṭṭhipariyodāpana*).
“O you who sow the seeds of suffering!
What is the pure abandonment that constitutes liberation?
It means that the noble disciple attains liberation through the mind’s freedom from desire for greed, and liberation through the mind’s freedom from desire for hatred and delusion.”

Regarding such liberation, causing that which is incomplete to become complete, and for that which is already complete, following it and embracing it with desire and diligence, even up to constant embracing—this is called the purification of abandonment through liberation.

"O Kaccāna! When the Venerable Ānanda had spoken this Dharma, the young boys of the village of Bhaṇḍagāma, having heard what the Venerable Ānanda had said, rejoiced and delighted in it; they paid their respects and departed."
566 (566). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the village of Āmra, in the Āmra Grove, together with a community of senior bhikṣus.
At that time, the householder Citta approached the elder bhikṣus, prostrated at their feet, and withdrew to sit at one side.
Then, the elder bhikṣus taught the Dharma to the householder Citta in various ways, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him;
having taught the Dharma in various ways, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him, they remained silent.

Then, the householder Citta prostrated at the feet of the senior bhikṣus, went to the dwelling of the bhikṣu Nāgadatta, prostrated at the feet of the bhikṣu Nāgadatta, and withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, the bhikṣu Nāgadatta questioned the householder Citta as follows:
"With branches green and covered by white, A single-spoked wheel rolls on;
Observing the arrival of one free from fetters, The stream is severed and no longer bound."
"Householder!
What is the meaning of this verse?
Citta the householder replied:
"Venerable Nāgadatta!
Did the Blessed One speak this verse?
He replied:
"So it is," the householder Citta said to the Venerable Nāgadatta:
"Venerable sir!..."
He remained silent for a moment, saying, "I shall contemplate this meaning.
Having reflected in silence for a moment, he addressed the Venerable Nāgadatta:

"The blue refers to the precepts; the white covering refers to liberation; the single spoke refers to mindfulness of the body; 'turning' refers to turning out; the chariot refers to serenity and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*); and as for 'being free from fetters,' there are three kinds of fetters, namely: greed, hatred, and delusion."

That Arhat has exhausted all outflows; they have been extinguished, known, and their roots severed. Like the head of a tāla tree cut off, they will not grow again; they are destined for extinction in future lives and shall not arise.
“The observer” refers to seeing; “the one who comes” refers to a person; “the severing of the stream” refers to the stream of craving that flows through birth and death.

That Arhat bhikṣu has exhausted all outflows and attained full knowledge; he has severed their root so that they will not grow again, just as when the head of a *tāla* tree is cut off, it can never sprout again, and in future lives he has become one subject to the law of non-arising.

“‘Not bound’ refers to the three bonds: the bond of sensual desire, the bond of ill will, and the bond of delusion. For that Arhat bhikṣu, all outflows have been exhausted, severed, and fully known; their root has been cut off, like the head of a tāla tree, so that they shall not grow again, having become one for whom non-arising is the law in future lives.”
Therefore, Venerable Nagadasa,
the Blessed One spoke this verse:
"With green branches covered by white, a single-spoked wheel rolls on."
"Having come free from the fetters, observing, one severs the currents and is no longer bound.
"This verse spoken by the Blessed One has been analyzed by me," said the Venerable Nāgadatta to the householder Citta.
The Venerable Nāgadatta then asked the householder Citta:
"Did you hear this meaning previously? He replied, "I did not."
The Venerable Nāgadatta said:
"Householder!
You have gained a great benefit, for you have entered this profound Buddha-dharma through the noble eye of wisdom."
At that time, the householder Citta, having heard what the Venerable Nāgadatta had said, rejoiced and approved, paid his respects, and departed. 567 (567) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the village of Āmra at the Āmrapālī Grove Monastery, together with a great assembly of senior bhikṣus.
At that time, the householder Citta approached the senior bhikṣus, prostrated at their feet, and withdrew to sit at one side.
Then, the senior bhikṣus taught the Dharma to the householder Citta in various ways—showing, instructing, illuminating, and gladdening him;
having shown, instructed, illuminated, and gladdened him, they remained silent.
At that time, the householder Citta approached the venerable bhikṣu Nāgadatta, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit at one side.
The venerable Nāgadatta addressed the householder Citta:
"There is the concentration of immeasurable mind, the concentration of signless mind, the concentration of nothingness mind, and the concentration of empty mind."
"How is it, householder?
Are these dharmas given various names for the sake of their various meanings?"
"Are there various names for a single meaning?
The householder Citta asked the Venerable Nāgadatta:
"Were these various samādhis taught by the Blessed One?"
"Is this spoken from your own intention, Venerable One?
The Venerable Nagasena replied:
"This was spoken by the Blessed One."
The householder Citta said to the Venerable Nāgadatta:
"Listen, and allow me to reflect briefly on this matter before I answer.
After reflecting for a moment, he spoke to the Venerable Nāgadatta:
“There are teachings with various meanings, various phrases, and various flavors; there are also teachings with a single meaning and various flavors.
He then asked the householder again:
“In what way are there teachings with various meanings, various phrases, and various flavors?”
The householder replied:

"The immeasurable samādhi refers to when a noble disciple’s mind is imbued with loving-kindness—free from enmity, free from malice, and free from ill will—and having cultivated it extensively, with a vast, exalted, and profound heart, pervasively directed toward all objects, filling one quarter."

In this way, toward the second direction, the third, the fourth, and above and below—in all directions of the world—one’s mind is imbued with loving-kindness (*maitrī*); free from enmity, free from malice, and free from ill will, it is vast, exalted, profound, and immeasurably cultivated, filling all directions. Abiding with universal focus upon the entire world, this is called the "Immeasurable Samādhi" (*apramāṇa-samādhi*).
What is the signless concentration?
It refers to when a noble disciple does not attend to any signs, personally realizes the signless mental concentration with the body; this is called the signless mental concentration.
What is the concentration of the mind of nothingness?

It refers to the noble disciple who, having transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, dwells with a mind of nothingness in the sphere of nothingness; this is called the concentration of the mind of nothingness.
What is the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*)?

It refers to when a noble disciple contemplates the world as empty, as it truly is: "The world is empty; it is permanent, unchanging, neither self nor belonging to a self. This is called the concentration on the mind of emptiness. This is what is meant by the various meanings, various phrases, and various flavors of the Dharma.
He asked the householder again:
"In what way is it that a single dharma has various flavors?
He replied:
"Venerable sir!
Greed is limited; the absence of contention is the foremost immeasurable. Greed has a sign, hatred has a sign, and delusion has a sign; the absence of contention is signless."
That which belongs to greed is "possessed," and that which belongs to hatred and delusion is "possessed"; that which is without contention is "without possession.

Furthermore, that which is without contention is empty: it is empty of greed, empty of hatred and delusion, and it is the eternally abiding, unchanging emptiness, neither self nor belonging to a self. This is called the single meaning of phenomena having various expressions.
The Venerable Nagadasa asked: "How so,
householder?"
"Did you hear this meaning previously?
He replied,
"Venerable sir!"
"I have not heard it.
He further addressed the elder:
"You have attained a great benefit; regarding the most profound Buddha-dharma, you have now entered by means of the noble and holy eye of wisdom."
Having heard what the Venerable Nāgadatta had said, the householder Citta rejoiced and approved, paid his respects, and departed. 568 (568) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Āmra Grove at the village of Āmrapālī together with a number of senior bhikṣus.

At that time, the householder Citta approached the senior bhikṣus; having paid homage to the senior bhikṣus, he went to the venerable Bhikṣu Kāma, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the venerable Bhikṣu Kāma:
"Regarding what is called 'one who practices' (*yogin*), what is meant by 'practice' (*yoga*)?"
The bhikṣu Gāma said:
"As for 'formations,' it refers to the three formations: bodily formation, verbal formation, and mental formation.
He asked again:
"What are bodily formations?
What are verbal formations?
What are mental formations?"
He replied: "Householder!
Exhalation and inhalation are called bodily formations (kāyasaṃskāra)."
"Initial application (vitarka) and sustained application (vicāra) are called verbal formations;
perception (saṃjñā) and volition (cetanā) are called mental formations.
He asked again:
"Why are exhalation and inhalation called bodily formations (*kāyasaṃskāra*)?
Why are directed thought and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) called verbal formations (*vāksaṃskāra*)?
And why are perception and volition (*saṃjñā-cetanā*) called mental formations (*manaḥsaṃskāra*)?"
He replied:
"Householder!

Exhalation and inhalation are bodily phenomena; they depend upon the body, belong to the body, and proceed in reliance upon the body. Therefore, exhalation and inhalation are called bodily formations."

Because there is initial application (*vitarka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*), there is verbal expression; therefore, initial application and sustained application are verbal formations (*vāk-saṃskāra*).

Perception (*saṃjñā*) and volition (*cetanā*) are mental formations (*manas-saṃskāra*); they depend upon the mind, belong to the mind, and revolve around the mind; therefore, perception and volition are mental formations.
He asked again:
"Venerable sir!
After initial application (vitakka) and sustained application (vicāra), one utters speech; these initial application and sustained application are called verbal formations (vacī-saṅkhāra)."
"Perception and volition are mental factors; they depend upon the mind and operate in association with the mind. Therefore, perception and volition are called 'mental formations' (*manosaṃskāra*).
He asked again:
"Venerable sir!"
How many dharmas are there?
"When a person abandons the body, that corpse lies upon the ground,
cast away among the hills and tombs, heartless as wood or stone."
He replied: "O Householder!
'Vitality, warmth, and consciousness—these are all abandoned together when one leaves the body.'"
"That body has been cast away among the tombs, / Heartless as wood or stone.
He asked again:
"Venerable One!..."
"If there is a distinction between one who has died and one who has entered the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti)?
He replied:
"The abandonment of life-span and warmth, the total destruction of the sense faculties, and the separation of body and life—this is called death."

Regarding the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*): the activities of body, speech, and mind cease; yet life-force is not abandoned, warmth is not departed from, and the faculties do not perish. Body and life remain interconnected; this is the distinguishing characteristic between the end of life and the entry into the meditative attainment of cessation.
He asked again:
"Venerable sir,
how does one enter the meditative attainment of cessation?"
He replied: "O Householder!
One who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation does not speak."
"I shall enter the meditative attainment of cessation; I am about to enter the meditative attainment of cessation.
Yet, he first employs such gradual methods of calming, and through those preliminary methods, he proceeds toward entering the attainment.
He asked again:
"Venerable sir!
When entering the meditative attainment of cessation, which dharma ceases first?"
"Is it bodily conduct, verbal conduct, or mental conduct?
He replied, "Householder!"
"One who enters the meditative attainment of cessation first ceases verbal formations, next bodily formations, and finally mental formations.
He asked again:
"Venerable sir!"
"What is the 'emergence from the meditative attainment of cessation'?
He replied, "Householder!"
One who emerges from the meditative attainment of cessation does not think,
"I am now emerging from this attainment," nor "I shall emerge from this attainment.
Rather, having previously formed the preparatory intention, they arise in accordance with that prior intention.
He asked again:

“Venerable sir, regarding the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saññā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*), which phenomenon arises first: bodily activity, verbal activity, or mental activity?”
He replied: "Householder!
For one who has arisen from the meditative attainment of cessation, mental activity arises first, followed by bodily activity, and finally verbal activity."
He asked again:
"Venerable sir!
One who has entered the meditative attainment of cessation."
"What is meant by 'conforming and proceeding,' 'flowing and pouring forth,' and 'gushing and conveying'?
He replied, "Householder!"

One who enters the meditative attainment of cessation proceeds toward detachment, flows toward detachment, and is carried away toward detachment; proceeds toward emergence, flows toward emergence, and is carried away toward emergence; proceeds toward nirvana, flows toward nirvana, and is carried away toward nirvana.
He asked again:
"Venerable sir!
When abiding in the meditative attainment of cessation, how many contacts does one experience?"
He replied: "Householder!
Contact is immovable; contact is signless; contact is non-existent."
He asked again:
"Venerable One!
When entering the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), how many factors are activated?"
He replied: "Householder!
This should have been asked earlier; why do you ask now? Nevertheless, I shall explain it to you."
"When a bhikkhu enters the meditative attainment of cessation, he performs two things: serenity and insight.
Then, having heard what the Venerable Kāmabhū had said, the householder Citta rejoiced and approved, paid his respects, and departed.
569 (569). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Āmra Grove at the village of Āmrapālī, together with a great assembly of senior bhikṣus.
At that time, the householder Citta went to where the senior bhikṣus were, prostrated at their feet, and sat down to one side.
The senior bhikṣus taught the Dharma to the householder Citta in various ways—showing, instructing, illuminating, and gladdening him;
having shown, instructed, illuminated, and gladdened him, they remained silent.
Then, the householder Citta rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the senior elders, saying:
"I pray that the Venerable Ones will accept my humble meal."
At that time, the elders accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
When the householder knew that the elders had accepted by their silence, he prostrated at their feet and departed.
Returning to his own home, he prepared various kinds of food and drink, arranged seats, and early in the morning sent a messenger to announce:
"The time has come.

Then, the elders put on their robes, took up their bowls, and went to the house of the elder, where they sat down in their assigned places. The elder prostrated at the feet of the elders and sat to one side.
He addressed the elders:
"Regarding what is called 'the various elements' (nānādhātu), what constitutes these various elements?
At that time, the elders remained silent.
This was repeated a second and a third time.
At that moment, the Venerable Rāhula, who was seated at the lowest rank among the assembly, addressed the elder bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"I wish to answer the question posed by that householder.
The elders replied, "You may do so."
The householder Citta then asked:
"Venerable sir!
Regarding what is called 'the various elements' (nānādhātu), what are these various elements?"
Ratthapāla replied: "Householder!
The eye-element is distinct, the form-element is distinct, and the eye-consciousness-element is distinct."
The ear element is distinct, the sound element is distinct, and the ear-consciousness element is distinct;
the nose element is distinct, the odor element is distinct, and the nose-consciousness element is distinct;
the tongue element is distinct, the taste element is distinct, and the tongue-consciousness element is distinct.
The body element is distinct, the tangible object element is distinct, and the body-consciousness element is distinct;
the mind element is distinct, the mental object element is distinct, and the mind-consciousness element is distinct.
Thus it is, householder!
"This is called the various elements.
At that time, the householder Citta provided various kinds of pure and delicious food and drink as an offering.
After the community of monks had finished eating, rinsed their mouths, and washed their bowls, the householder Citta spread out a low seat and sat before the elders to listen to the Dharma.
At that time, the Elder taught the householder the Dharma in various ways—showing, instructing, illuminating, and gladdening him—and having done so, rose from his seat and departed.
On the way, the Elders said to Riṣidatta:
"Excellent!"
Excellent, Bhikṣu Liśidatta! You are truly eloquent and swift;
you speak with knowledge of the matter. At other times as well, you should always act in this manner.
At that time, the elder monks, having heard what Riṣidatta had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
570 (Five Hundred and Seventy): Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the village of Āmra, in the Āmra Grove, together with a great assembly of elder bhikṣus.
At that time, the householder Citta went to where the senior monks were, prostrated at their feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the senior monks, saying:

"Regarding what is seen by those in the world, some say there is a self, some say there are sentient beings, some say there is a life-span, and some speak of the auspiciousness or misfortune of the world."
"How so, Venerable One?
What is the root of these various wrong views, what is their origin, what is their arising, and what is their development?"
At that time, the senior monks remained silent and did not answer.
When he asked this three times, they likewise remained silent on all three occasions.
Then, a junior monk named Revata addressed the senior monks, saying:
"I wish to answer the question posed by that householder.
The elders said, "Let him who is well able to answer respond."
Then the householder asked Revata:
"Venerable One!
Regarding all that is seen in the world, what is its root, what is its origin, what is its arising, and what is its transformation?"
The Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla replied:
"Householder!

Whatever views are seen in the world—whether they speak of a self, or speak of a sentient being, or speak of a life-span, or speak of the auspiciousness and misfortune of the world—all such views have the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as their root; they arise from the view of a self, are produced by the view of a self, and evolve from the view of a self."
He asked again:
"Venerable sir,
what is the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi)?"
He replied: "Householder!

An ignorant, unlearned worldling regards form as self, or form as distinct from self, or self as being within form, or form as being within self; they regard feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as self, or consciousness as distinct from self, or self as being within consciousness, or consciousness as being within self."
"Householder!
This is called the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
He asked again:
"Venerable One!
How does one come to be free from this view of a self-existent body?
He replied:
“Householder!
It means that the learned noble disciple does not see form as self, nor sees form as distinct from self, nor sees self within form or form within self;

he does not see feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as self, nor sees consciousness as distinct from self, nor sees self within consciousness or consciousness within self. This is called attaining the absence of the view of a self-existent body (sakkāyadṛṣṭi).”
He asked again:
"Venerable sir!
What was his father's name?"
"In what place were you born?
He replied, "Householder!"
"I was born later into the family of a householder.
The householder Citta said to the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla,
"The two of us, father and son, were originally good friends."
Liṣidatta replied, "So be it,
householder! Then the householder Citta said to Liṣidatta:

“Venerable sir, if you would dwell in this Āmra grove, I shall provide you with robes, food and drink, and medicinal requisites for illness for as long as I live. The Venerable Rishidatta accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

At that time, because the Venerable Rāhula had accepted the invitation of the householder Citta and was occupied with providing the offerings, he did not go to the presence of the Blessed One for a long time.
Then, the elder bhikṣus expounded the Dharma to the householder Citta in various ways, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him, the householder Citta rejoiced and was filled with joy; he paid homage and departed.
571 (571). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the village of Āmra, in the Āmra Grove, together with a great assembly of senior bhikṣus.
At that time, the householder Citta went to where the senior monks were, prostrated at their feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the senior bhikṣus, saying:
"I pray that the Venerable Ones will accept my invitation for a meal at the cattle-pasture."
Then the elders accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Knowing that the elders had accepted by their silence, the householder Citta returned home.
Throughout the night, various kinds of food and drink were prepared; at dawn, seats were arranged, and a messenger was sent to inform the senior elders:
"The time has come.
The senior elders put on their robes, took up their bowls, and went to the house of the elder Citta in the cattle-pasture, where they took their seats.
Then, the householder Citta personally served various kinds of food and drink.
When the meal was finished, and the bowls had been washed and the rinsing completed, the householder Citta spread out a low seat and sat before the Elder to listen to the Dharma.
Then the elders taught the householder various dharmas, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him;
having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him, they rose from their seats and departed, and the householder Citta followed after them.
The elders had eaten their fill of ghee, curd, and honey; during the heat of the late spring months, they were utterly exhausted while traveling on the road.
At that time, a junior bhikṣu named Mahākā addressed the elders, saying:
"It is very hot today; I wish to raise clouds, rain, and a gentle breeze—would this be acceptable?"
The elders replied, "If you can do so,
it is excellent. Thereupon, Mahākāśyapa entered into samādhi,
remaining in that state of meditative absorption as he had intended.

At that moment, clouds arose and a fine rain fell lightly; a cool breeze blew steadily from the four directions until it reached the gate of the vihāra. Then, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the elders, saying:
"May you cease what you are doing?"
He replied, "You may stop. Thereupon,
the Venerable Mahākāśyapa immediately withdrew his supernormal power and returned to his own cell.
At that time, the householder Citta thought to himself:
"If even this most junior bhikṣu possesses such great supernormal power, how much more so must those of middle rank and senior rank!"
He then prostrated at the feet of the elder bhikṣus and followed the bhikṣu Mahākāla to his dwelling. Having prostrated at the feet of the Venerable Mahākāla, he withdrew to sit at one side and said:
"Venerable One!
"I wish to see the Venerable One’s superhuman state, his supernormal powers, and his miraculous transformations.
The Venerable Mahākātyāyana said:
"Householder!"
"Do not be afraid.
Thus he requested three times, yet three times the Venerable One did not grant his wish.
The householder then requested once more, wishing to see the Venerable One’s supernormal transformations.
The Venerable Mahaka said to the householder,
"Go outside for a moment, gather dry grass and wood, and pile them up, then cover them with a single piece of fine cotton cloth."
The householder Citta followed these instructions; he went outside, gathered firewood, and stacked it into a pyre. He then returned and informed the Venerable Mahākātyāyana:
"The pyre is prepared, and it has been covered with cotton cloth."

Then, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa immediately entered the fire-light samādhi; from the hole of the door-bolt, he emitted flames that completely consumed the stacked firewood, yet the white cotton cloth remained unburnt.
He said to the householder, "Do you see this now?"
He replied, “I have seen them,
Venerable Sir.”
"It is truly extraordinary.
The Venerable Mahākātyāyana said to the householder:

"You should know that all these things have heedfulness as their root; they are accumulated by heedfulness, produced by heedfulness, and proceed from heedfulness. It is through heedfulness that one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Therefore, householder!

These and all other merits have heedfulness as their root; they are accumulated through heedfulness, born from heedfulness, and proceed by means of heedfulness. It is because of heedfulness that one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, as well as the other factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
The householder Citta addressed the Venerable Mahaka:
"I pray that you will remain constantly in this grove; for as long as I live, I shall provide you with robes, bedding, food and drink, and medicinal decoctions for illnesses."
Because the Venerable Mahākātyāyana had prior commitments, he did not accept his invitation.
Having heard the Dharma teaching, the householder Citta rejoiced and expressed his approval; he then rose from his seat, paid homage, and departed.
Venerable Mahākāla, fearing that the merit of the offerings would be obstructed by his own offense, rose from his seat and departed, never to return. 572 (572).
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Āmra Grove together with a great number of senior bhikṣus.
At that time, a great number of senior bhikṣus gathered in the dining hall and held this discussion:
"Venerable sirs,
what do you think?"
That is to say: is the eye bound to visible forms, or are visible forms bound to the eye?
Likewise for the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles; and as for the mind and mental phenomena—does the mind bind the phenomena?
"Is the mind bound by phenomena?

At that time, the householder Citta was on his way to attend to some business when he passed by the monastery. Seeing the elder bhikṣus gathered in the dining hall, he approached and prostrated at the feet of the elders.
Having prostrated, he asked, "Venerable ones, for what teaching have you gathered in the dining hall? What dharma are you discussing?"
The elders replied: "Householder!
Today we gathered here in this dining hall and held such a discussion:"
"Is it that the eye is bound to forms,
or are forms bound to the eye?
Likewise, regarding the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena— is it that the mind is bound to mental phenomena?"
"Is it because the mind is bound by the Dharma?
The householder asked,
"How do the Venerable Ones explain this matter?"
The elders asked,
"What do you think, householder?
The householder replied to the elders:

"In my view, it is not that the eye is bound to forms, nor that forms are bound to the eye, and so on up to: it is not that the mind is bound to phenomena, nor that phenomena are bound to the mind; rather, there is desire and lust in the interval, and by means of that, one is bound."
It is like two oxen, one black and one white, yoked together by a collar and harness.
Someone asks:
"Is the black ox tied to the white ox?"
"Is it a white ox tied to a black ox?
Is this not a question of equality?
He replied:
“Householder!
This is not an appropriate question. Why is that?
"It is not the black ox that binds the white ox, nor is it the white ox that binds the black ox; rather, it is the yoke and the thong that bind them.
"So it is, Venerable Sir!"

It is not that form is bound to the eye, nor that the eye is bound to form; and so on, up to: it is not that mental phenomena are bound to the mind, nor that the mind is bound to mental phenomena. Rather, between these, sensual desire and greed constitute the bondage.
Then, having heard what the elders had said, the householder Citta rejoiced and approved, paid his respects, and departed.
573 (573) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Āmra Grove.

At that time, there was a non-Buddhist Ājīvika who had been a close relative of the elder Citta in former times; he came to where the elder Citta was, and after exchanging greetings and words of comfort with him, stood to one side.
The householder Citta asked the non-Buddhist Ājīvika,
"How long has it been since you went forth?
He replied:
“Householder!
It has been more than twenty years since I went forth.
Citta the householder asked:
"You have been a renunciant for more than twenty years; have you attained the state beyond the human, the ultimate knowledge and vision, and do you dwell in peace?
He replied, "Householder!"

Although he has been a renunciant for more than twenty years, he has not attained any superhuman states, ultimate knowledge and vision, or a dwelling in peace and happiness; he does nothing but go naked, pluck out his hair, beg for food, wander through the human world, and sleep upon the bare earth.
The householder Citta said:

"This is not the Dharma or the Vinaya as it is known; this is a false understanding, not the path to liberation, not the teaching of the Fully Awakened One, not a point for praise, and it is not to be relied upon."

"It is said that those who have been ordained for over twenty years in the Táng [tradition] go about naked, pluck out their hair, beg for food, wander through the human world, and lie upon ashes and dust.
Then Aṅgīrasa asked the householder Citta:
"How long has it been since you became a disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama?"
The householder Citta replied,
"I have been a disciple of the Blessed One for more than twenty years.
He then asked the householder Citta again:
“After you have been a disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama for more than twenty years, have you attained any superhuman state (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), or any superior, ultimate knowledge and vision?
The householder Citta replied: “You should know this:

the householder Citta shall no longer be born from a womb; he shall no longer increase the number of graves; he shall no longer give rise to further vital breath. Regarding the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni*) as spoken by the Blessed One, I do not see even a single fetter that remains unsevered; if even one fetter were not severed, I would have to return again to this world.”
When this was said, Aggivessana sighed with grief and wept; wiping his face with his robe, he said to the householder Citta:
"What plan should I now make?"
The householder Citta replied,
"If you can go forth into homelessness within this True Dharma and Discipline, I shall provide you with robes, a bowl, and all the requisites for your sustenance."
After reflecting for a moment, Aggivessana said to the householder Citta:
"I now rejoice; show me what I must do."
Then, the householder Citta took those Ajivikas and went to where the senior monks were; he prostrated at the feet of the senior monks and sat down to one side.
He addressed the senior bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable sirs!

This Aṅgīrasa was a close relative of my ancestors; he now seeks to go forth and become a bhikṣu. I pray that the senior sirs will ordain him and let him go forth, and I shall provide him with robes, alms bowls, and all necessary requisites."
The elders immediately caused him to go forth, shaving off his hair and beard and donning the saṃghāṭī robe.
Having gone forth, he reflected:
"For what reason do sons of good family shave off their hair and beard, don the saṃghāṭī robe, go forth to advance in the study of the Path, and purely cultivate the holy life..."
He attained arhatship.
574 (Five Hundred and Seventy-Four) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the village of Āmra, in the Āmra Grove, together with the elder bhikṣus.
At that time, the Nirgrantha Jñātiputra, accompanied by five hundred followers, went to the Āmra Grove, desiring to entice the householder Citta to become his disciple.

When the householder Citta heard that the Nirgrantha Jñātiputra was coming with five hundred followers to the Āmra Grove, intending to entice him to become his disciple, he went at once to where the Nirgrantha was. After they had exchanged greetings and pleasantries, they each sat down to one side.
At that time, the Nirgrantha Jñātiputra said to the householder Citta:
"Do you believe that the śramaṇa Gautama has attained the samādhi without vitarka and vicāra?"
The householder Citta replied,
"I have not come out of faith. Ajīva said:
“Householder!
You are without guile, without deceit, upright, and born of uprightness.
Householder!”

If one can still the state of both directed thought and evaluation, one can likewise bind the wind with a rope; if one can still the state of both directed thought and evaluation, one can also cut the flow of the Ganges with a handful of earth; thus, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, my knowledge and vision are constantly present.
The householder Citta asked the Nirgrantha Jñātiputra:
"Does faith come first,
or does wisdom come first?"
"Between faith and wisdom, which comes first?
Which is superior? Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta replied:
"Faith should come first, and only then does wisdom arise; when faith and wisdom are compared, wisdom is superior.
The householder Citta said to the Nirgrantha Jñātiputra:

"I have already attained the second dhyāna—abiding fully in the joy and bliss born of samādhi, which is without directed thought or sustained evaluation, with internal clarity and a unified mind, having stilled directed thought and sustained evaluation."

"I dwell in this samādhi by day, I dwell in this samādhi by night, and throughout the entire night I constantly abide in this samādhi; since I possess such wisdom, what need is there to rely on the faith of the World-Honored One?"
The Nirgrantha Jñātiputra said:
"You are crooked, deceitful, dishonest, and born of dishonesty.
The householder Citta replied:

"You previously stated that I am without flattery or crookedness, free from illusion, upright, and born of uprightness; why do you now say that I am flatterous and crooked, illusory and deceitful, not upright, and born of lack of uprightness?"
If what you previously said was true, then what you said later is false; if what you said later is true, then what you said before is false.
You previously stated:
"In walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, my knowledge and vision are constantly present."
"You were ignorant of even minor matters before and after [that event].
How then could you claim to know or see any state beyond that of ordinary humans, or any matter concerning dwelling in peace and happiness?"
The householder again asked Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:
"Do you possess the capacity for one question, one statement, and one categorical response; or even for ten questions, ten statements, and ten categorical responses?"
"If there were not even one question, one teaching, or one formal exposition— up to ten questions, ten teachings, or ten formal expositions—
how could you have enticed me to come here to this Āmra grove, desiring to seduce and deceive me?"
Thereupon, the Nirgrantha Jñātiputra clenched his teeth, shook his head, and departed with his hands folded behind his back, never looking back again.
575 (Five Hundred and Seventy-Five) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Āmra Grove at the village of Āmrapālī, together with a great assembly of senior bhikṣus.
At that time, the householder Citta was suffering from illness, surrounded by his kinsmen; many devas came to where the householder was and said to him:
"Householder!
"You should make a vow to become a wheel-turning monarch.
The householder Citta said to the devas,
"Even if one becomes a wheel-turning monarch, that too is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self."
Then the kinsmen said to the householder:
"You must maintain mindfulness!
You must maintain mindfulness!"
The householder Citta said to his kinsmen,
"Why do you all instruct me to 'fix my attention, fix my attention'?
His kinsmen replied:
"You have said:
'It is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
For this reason, I teach you to bind your mindfulness, to bind your mindfulness."
The elder said to his kinsmen:
"Devas and humans came to my place and spoke to me, saying:
'You should make a vow to become a Wheel-Turning Sage King; according to your vow, you shall obtain the fruit.'"
I then replied:
"That universal monarch is likewise impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
Those kinsmen then spoke to the householder Citta:
“What does a wheel-turning monarch possess that the devas have taught you to aspire for?

The householder replied, “A wheel-turning monarch rules and transforms the world through the True Dharma; therefore, because the devas see such merit and benefit, they have come to teach me to make this aspiration.”
The relatives said,
"Now that you have applied your mind to this,
what should be done? The elder replied:

"O kinsmen! I now resolve that I shall never again be born from a womb; I shall no longer increase the number of graves, nor shall I receive further blood and breath. As the World-Honored One has said, I do not see any of the five lower fetters within myself; I do not perceive even a single fetter that is not severed. Were any fetter not severed, I would return to birth in this world."
Thereupon, the elder rose from his seat, sat down cross-legged, established right mindfulness before him, and spoke these verses:
"Having consumed what was accumulated through long accumulation, I have extensively crossed over many hardships.
By giving to the supreme field of merit, I plant these five kinds of power."
By this intended meaning, though worldly people dwell in the household,
I have fully attained these benefits and am already freed from all hardships.
Whatever is heard and practiced in the world, I have distanced myself from all such troublesome matters.
It is somewhat difficult for one born into this world to know how to follow the Perfectly Awakened One; yet,
by making offerings to those who uphold the precepts, who have well-cultivated the various holy conducts,
and who are Arhats with out-flows exhausted, as well as the Śrāvaka Munis, [one attains this].
Thus transcending views, one who constantly practices the giving of a man toward these superior and sublime states will surely obtain great fruit at the end.
By habitually practicing manifold acts of giving and bestowing upon excellent fields of merit, one attains the highest reward.
Having ended their lives in this world, they are born by transformation in the heavens.
Fully endowed with the five desires and possessing immeasurable mental joy,
they obtain this wondrous karmic fruit because they were free from stinginess.
"Wherever he takes birth, he is never without joy.
After the householder Citta had spoken this verse, he immediately passed away and was reborn in the Avṛha Heaven.
At that time, the devaputra Citta had this thought:
"I should not remain here; I must go to Jambudvīpa to pay homage to the elder bhikṣus."

In the time it takes a strong man to flex and extend his arm, by the power of a deva, he arrived at the Āmra grove and emitted a celestial radiance from his body that illuminated the entire Āmra grove.

At that time, a certain bhikṣu rose from his bed at night and went out of his cell to walk in meditation upon the open ground. There he saw a magnificent light shining everywhere throughout the forest.
He then spoke this verse:
"Whose is this wondrous celestial form, Dwelling in the midst of the void?"
"Just like a mountain of pure gold, with the radiant light of Jāmbūnada.
The devaputra Citta replied in verse:
"I am the king of gods and humans, the son of the one renowned as Gautama."
In this Āmra grove, the householder Citta,
endowed with pure precepts, maintains mindfulness and dwells in self-serenity;
he is fully perfected in the body of liberation, and likewise so is his body of wisdom.
"I have come because I know the Dharma; you, O virtuous one, should know this.
One shall attain nirvāṇa therein; such is the nature of this Dharma.
Having spoken this verse, the devaputra Citta vanished and was no longer seen.

One should sever the fire of craving And seek seclusion through right mindfulness."
