At that time, the World-Honored One answered with these verses:
"Just as a sharp sword causes harm, Or as a fire burning upon one's head,
So should one sever the future body And seek seclusion through right mindfulness."
Then, that deva spoke again in verse:
"I have long beheld the Brahmin, Who has attained parinirvāṇa;
All fears have been transcended, Forever surpassing worldly affection."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that devaputra rejoiced and approved with gladness; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.
587 (Five Hundred and Eighty-Seven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a certain devaputra of exquisite and peerless countenance came to the Buddha’s dwelling during the late night; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and the radiance from his body illuminated the entire Jeta Grove and Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then that devaputra spoke in verse:
"Surrounded by a host of celestial maidens, like a swarm of bumblebees,
how can one emerge from this thicket of delusion?"
At that time, the World-Honored One answered with a verse:
“The straight and impartial path, The method for departing from fear;
Mounting the chariot of silence, With the perception of Dharma as its secret canopy.”
Shame and remorse serve as the long tether; right mindfulness is the halter and bridle.
Wisdom is the skilled charioteer, and right view is the guide.
Such is this wondrous vehicle, mounted by both men and women.
"Having emerged from the thicket of birth and death, he has attained the state of peace and happiness.
Then, that deva spoke again in verse:
"I have long beheld this Brahmin; he has attained parinirvāṇa."
"Having transcended all fears, you have forever surpassed worldly affection.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that devaputra rejoiced and expressed his approval; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.
588. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

Then a certain devaputra of exquisite and peerless countenance approached the Buddha during the late hours of the night. He prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and the radiance from his body illuminated the entire Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then that deva-son spoke a verse to ask the Buddha:
"With four turnings and nine gates, Filled with the dwelling of craving and desire,
Deeply submerged in the mire— How does the great elephant emerge?"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse, saying:
"Sever the long tether of craving and delight, And abandon all evils such as greed and desire.
Uproot the very root of sensual longing, And proceed directly toward that state."
Then, that deva spoke again in verse:
“I have long beheld the Brahmin, Who has attained parinirvāṇa;
All fears have been transcended, And he has forever surpassed worldly affection.”
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that devaputra rejoiced and expressed his approval; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.
589 (589) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain devaputra of exquisite countenance came to the Buddha’s dwelling during the late night, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The various radiances from his body illuminated the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain devaputra addressed the Buddha in verse:
“In the kingdom of Rājagṛha, there were many merchant travelers.”
Amidst great abundance of wealth and treasures, each vies to seek further riches;
through skillful means they desire profit and gain, like a blazing, raging fire.
With such a mind intent on victory, the craving for sensual desires constantly gallops forth.
"How should one sever craving and bring to rest the worldly pursuit?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"Abandoning the secular life to go forth from home, leaving behind wife, children, and wealth,"
"Free from greed, hatred, and delusion, the Arhat has exhausted all outflows;
with right wisdom his mind is liberated, and with the extinction of craving, he rests in the cessation of conditioned means.
Then, that devaputra spoke again in verse:
“I have long beheld this brahmin, who has attained parinirvāṇa;
he has transcended all fears and forever surpassed worldly affection.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that devaputra rejoiced and approved with gladness; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.
590. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In a past age, there were merchants in the kingdom of Kosala who, with five hundred wagons, were traveling together for trade when they reached a wilderness."
In the wilderness, there were five hundred bands of robbers following behind, watching for an opportunity to commit robbery.
At that time, a deva resided by the side of the road in that wilderness.
At that time, the deva thought to himself:
"I shall go to where the merchants of the Kosalas are and inquire about the principles of their doctrine.
If those merchants are pleased with my inquiry and explain it to me, I shall employ skillful means to ensure they remain safe and are delivered from the peril of the bandits."
"If you do not approve of my questions, you should let them go, just like the other devas.
Then, having formed this thought, that deva immediately emitted light from his body, which illuminated the entire caravan camp of merchants, and spoke these verses:
"Who is awake while others sleep? And who is asleep while others are awake?"
"Who understands this meaning? Who can explain it for me?

At that time, among the merchants there was one upāsaka who had faith in the Buddha, faith in the Dharma, and faith in the Saṅgha of bhikṣus; he directed his whole heart toward the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, taking refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha. He was free from doubt regarding the Buddha, free from doubt regarding the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and free from doubt regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Having seen the Four Noble Truths, he had attained the fruit of the first stage of clear realization (ānantarya-phala), and he was traveling as a companion among the merchants.

Later in the night, that upāsaka sat upright in meditation, binding his mindfulness before him, and observed the twelve links of dependent origination both in reverse and in direct order, namely: "Because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises."

That is to say: conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise; conditioned by volitional formations, consciousness arises; conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form arise; conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense bases arise; conditioned by the six sense bases, contact arises; conditioned by contact, feeling arises; conditioned by feeling, craving arises; conditioned by craving, clinging arises; conditioned by clinging, existence arises; conditioned by existence, birth arises; and conditioned by birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, despair, and suffering arise.

In this way, there is the arising of this entire great mass of suffering; in this way, with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, despair, and suffering cease. In this way, there is the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
At that time, having reflected thus, that upāsaka spoke these verses:
“I am awake while others sleep; I sleep while others are awake.
I understand this meaning, And am able to explain it to others.”
Then, that deva asked the upāsaka:
"How does one awaken from sleep?
How does one sleep while awake?"
"How can one understand it?
How can one explain it?
At that time, the upāsaka replied with a verse:
“‘Having abandoned greed and hatred, and having become free from delusion,
the Arhat with taints exhausted, whose mind is liberated through right knowledge—
he is truly awakened, while I am merely sleeping.’”
Not knowing that suffering arises from causes, nor the accumulation of the conditions for suffering,
one fails to attain the complete extinction of all this suffering;
furthermore, not knowing the Noble Path that leads equally to the state where suffering ceases.
These people are in constant sleep, while I am awake among them;
thus I am awake within their sleep, and they are asleep while I am awake.
Thus I well understand the meaning, and thus I am able to explain it.
Then, that deva spoke again in verse:
“Excellent is awakening from sleep; Excellent is being awake within sleep.
Excellent is understanding the meaning; Excellent is being able to explain it.”
After a long time, we have finally seen you today; all our brothers have come because of the power of your kindness.
By your grace, the multitude of merchants has been spared from bandits and shall proceed along the road in peace and happiness.
"Thus it was, monks! Those merchants in the Kosalaka marshes all attained safety and emerged from the wilderness.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the monks, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
591 (Five Hundred and Ninety-one). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In a past age, an upāsaka on a sea-island went to the house of another upāsaka for a gathering. There, he severely disparaged sensual desires, saying:
'These sensual desires are false and unreal; they are deceptive phenomena, like magical illusions that delude infants.'"
"Returning to his own home, he indulges in the five desires. Now, a deva dwells in this upāsaka’s house.
At that time, the deva thinks to himself:
'This upāsaka is neither superior nor peerless; in the midst of the assembly gathered at the houses of other upāsakas, he utterly reviles desire, saying:'"
“Such desires are hollow, unreal, and deceptive by nature, like a trick played upon an infant.
Having returned to my own home, I indulged in the five sensual pleasures; I now think it best to rouse myself to awakening.
And he spoke in verse:
“In the midst of a great assembly, he reviled desire as impermanent;
yet he himself was submerged in craving, like an ox mired in deep mud.”
I observe those in that assembly— The various upāsakas who are learned and clearly understand the Dharma, And who uphold the pure precepts.
Seeing that they delight in the Dharma, You speak of desire as impermanent.
"How can you indulge in self-will, not severing your craving and attachment?
For what reason do you delight in the world, maintaining a wife, children, and kin?
Thus did that deva awaken that upāsaka in various ways.

In this way, having thus awakened, that upāsaka shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saṃghāṭī robe, and with right faith left the home life for homelessness to study the Path. Through diligent cultivation, he exhausted all outflows and attained arhatship.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 592 (592) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, in the Śītavana cemetery among the burial mounds.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had some minor business that led him to the city of Rājagṛha, where he stayed overnight at the house of another householder.
During the night, he saw the householder addressing his wife, children, servants, and laborers, saying:
"All of you, rise! Split wood and kindle a fire; cook rice and prepare various delicacies; and adorn the hall."
When the householder Anāthapiṇḍika saw this, he thought to himself:
"What is this householder doing now? Is he preparing to give away his daughter in marriage or to take a wife?"
"Are you inviting guests, a king, or a minister?
Having thought this, he immediately asked the elder, "What are you doing?"
"Is it for giving away a daughter in marriage or taking a wife?
Or is it for inviting guests, the king, or high ministers?
At that time, the elder replied to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
"I am not marrying off a daughter nor taking a wife, nor am I inviting the king or his ministers; I merely wish to invite the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus to provide them with offerings."

At that time, having heard the name of the Buddha—something he had never heard before—the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was filled with great joy; all the pores of his body were thrilled with delight, and he asked the other householder:
"Who is called the Buddha?"
The householder replied:

"There is a śramaṇa named Gautama, a son of the Śākyas, who among the Śākyas shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of right faith left the home life to study the Path. He has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; he is called a Buddha."
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada asked,
"What is meant by 'the Saṅgha'?
The other householder replied:
"If there are those of the Brahmin caste who shave off their hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and out of faith leave the home life for homelessness to follow the Buddha and go forth;

or if there are sons of good family from the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes who shave off their hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and with right faith leave the home life for homelessness to follow that Buddha and go forth—these are called the Saṃgha."
"Today I have invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha present here to provide various offerings.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada asked that householder,
"May I now go to see the World-Honored One?"
The householder replied, "Stay here for a while;
I shall invite the World-Honored One to my home, where you will be able to see him.
Then, that very night, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada meditated on the Buddha with a focused mind and consequently fell asleep.

The sky was not yet bright when he suddenly saw the signs of dawn and thought that day had already broken. Desiring to leave his house, he set out toward the city gate. Upon reaching the foot of the gate, it was only the second watch of the night; the gate was not yet open. It was the customary law of the royal household to wait for the arrival and departure of envoys from afar: the gates were closed at the end of the first watch and opened again once the middle watch had passed, so as to allow travelers to come and go early.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada saw the city gate open and thought to himself:
"Surely the night has passed and dawn has broken, so the gate is open.
He mounted his carriage and set out through the city gate; but once he had passed through the gate, the light vanished and it immediately returned to darkness.

The householder Anāthapiṇḍada was immediately seized with terror; the hair on his body stood on end as he wondered, "Could it be that a human, a non-human, or some crafty rogue intends to terrify me?"
Even as he was about to return,
at that time there was a deva dwelling beside the city gate.
Then, that deva emitted a bodily radiance, which shone everywhere from the city gate to the charnel ground in the cold forest, and addressed the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, saying:
“Advance for now; you shall attain victory. Be careful not to retreat.
Then, that deva spoke this verse:
“A hundred fine horses, A hundred pounds of gold—”
Mule-carts and horse-drawn carriages, each numbering a hundred;
various kinds of rare and wondrous things, with precious treasures laden upon them—
having planted roots of goodness in past lives, one obtains such meritorious retribution as this.
"If a person with a mind of profound devotion takes even a single step toward the Buddha,
it surpasses the aforementioned merit by a factor of sixteen. Therefore, householder!"
"You must press forward; be careful not to retreat!
He then spoke another verse:
"The great dragon-elephant of the Snowy Mountains, Adorned entirely with pure gold,"
"A large-bodied elephant with great tusks—
giving such an elephant to others does not equal even one-sixteenth of the merit gained by directing [one's mind] toward the Buddha. Therefore, householder!"
"You should advance swiftly to obtain great benefit; it is not the time to retreat.
He further spoke in verse:
"The maidens of the kingdom of Kāmpilya, Their number being one hundred,"
Various kinds of exquisite jewels, Adorned with necklaces and ornaments—
Even giving these as a gift does not equal One-sixteenth part of the merit Of taking a single step toward the Buddha.
"Therefore, householder!
You should advance quickly; you will obtain victory, not retreat.
Then, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada asked the deva:
“Wise one! Who are you? The deva replied:

"I am the great māṇava named Matuṣkaṇḍa; I was formerly a spiritual friend to this elder. Having conceived a heart of faith and reverence toward the Venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, by virtue of this merit, I have now been reborn in heaven and am appointed to guard this city gate. For this reason, I tell the elder:
'You should simply proceed forward; be careful not to retreat. Advancing brings profit, whereas retreating does not.'"
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada thought to himself:
"The arising of a Buddha in the world is no small matter;
to hear the True Dharma is likewise no small matter."
"Therefore, a deva has exhorted me to proceed and see the World-Honored One.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada followed the light and went straight to the Śītavana cemetery.

At that time, the World-Honored One emerged from his chamber and was walking in meditation on the open ground. Having seen the Buddha from afar, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went before him and, according to the customary etiquette of a layperson, respectfully inquired after his well-being: "How are you?"
“World-Honored One!
Are you lying down in peace?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered with a verse:
“The Brahmin who has attained *nirvāṇa* is eternally at peace;
unstained by sensual desires, he is liberated without remainder.
Having severed all longing and tamed the blazing fire of the mind,”
"The mind attains tranquility; with tranquility, one sleeps in peace.
At that time, the World-Honored One took the householder Anāthapiṇḍika into the room, sat down upon a seat, and sat with his body upright and his mindfulness focused.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma for him, instructing, exhorting, illuminating, and gladdening him. Having done so, the World-Honored One said:

"All phenomena are impermanent; one should perform the meritorious deeds of giving, the meritorious deeds of observing the precepts, and the meritorious deeds of being reborn in heaven. One should [reflect upon] the gratification of sensual desires, the peril of sensual desires, and the escape from sensual desires—the merit of renouncing them."

Having heard the Dharma, seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, entered the Dharma, and understood the Dharma, Anāthapiṇḍika the householder crossed beyond all doubt and uncertainty; no longer relying on another for faith, nor relying on another for deliverance, he entered the True Dharma and Vinaya, and his mind attained fearlessness. He then rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, prostrated before the Buddha, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have been delivered."
"Bhagavān,
they have already crossed over! Sugata!"
"From this day forth, for as long as life lasts, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus; may you bear witness that I am an upāsaka.
Then the World-Honored One asked the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, "What is your name?"
The householder said to the Buddha,
“My name is Sudatta.
Because I constantly provide for the solitary, the poor, and the distressed, people of the time call me ‘Givaka’ (the Provider for the Solitary).”
The World-Honored One asked again:
"Where do you reside?
The elder addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

In the human realm of Kosala, there is a city named Śrāvastī. We pray that the World-Honored One will come to the kingdom of Śrāvastī; I shall provide for my entire life offerings of robes, food and drink, dwellings, bedding and seats, and medicinal decoctions for illnesses.”
The Buddha asked the householder,
"Is there a vihāra in Śrāvastī?
The householder replied to the Buddha:
“There is not, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told the householder:
“You may establish a vihāra there, so that the bhikṣus may come and go and stay overnight.”
The householder addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If only the World-Honored One would come to Śrāvastī, I shall construct monasteries and vihāras so that the bhikṣus may come and go and dwell therein."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had accepted the invitation through his silence, the householder rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and departed.
593. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada passed away from his illness and was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven as a son of the Tuṣita devas. He then had this thought:
"I should not remain here for long; I must go to see the World-Honored One.

Having formed this thought, in the time it takes a strong man to bend or extend his arm, he vanished from the Tuṣita Heaven and appeared before the Buddha. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew, and sat to one side.
At that time, the devaputra Anāthapiṇḍada emitted a radiance from his body that illuminated the entire Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then, the devaputra Anāthapiṇḍada spoke these verses:
“In this Jeta Grove forest, where the community of seers dwells,
The various kings also dwell here, increasing my heart’s joy;
with deep faith in the karma of pure precepts, they take wisdom as their supreme life-span,
purifying sentient beings thereby— not by means of lineage or wealth.
"Śāriputra of great wisdom, / Always silent in right mindfulness,
/ Dwelling in seclusion and practicing detachment, / You are my true friend in establishing this initial work.
Having spoken these verses, he immediately vanished and was no longer seen.
At that time, when the night had passed, the World-Honored One entered the assembly of monks, spread out his sitting mat (niṣīdana), and sat before the multitude, addressing the bhikṣus:
"During this very night, a son of heaven of exquisite and peerless countenance came to where I was, prostrated at my feet, and withdrew to sit to one side."
And he spoke these verses:
“In this Jeta Grove, where sages and monks dwell,
and where kings also reside, my heart is filled with joy.”
Deep faith, pure precepts, and karma, with wisdom as the supreme life—
by these one purifies sentient beings, not by lineage or wealth.
Śāriputra of great wisdom, with right mindfulness, is ever serene and silent.
"Dwelling in seclusion and practicing detachment is a true friend when first establishing one's spiritual work.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

"As I understand what the Blessed One has said, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika has been reborn in that heavenly realm and has come to see the Blessed One; yet, that householder Anāthapiṇḍika holds the Venerable Śāriputra in the utmost reverence."
The Buddha told Ānanda: "So it is, so it is, Ānanda!"
"The householder Anāthapiṇḍika has been reborn in that heavenly realm and has come to see me.
At that time, for the sake of the Venerable Śāriputra, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"In all the worlds, there is no wisdom Except for that of the Tathāgata."
Compared to the wisdom of Śāriputra, [the wisdom of all others] does not equal even one-sixteenth.
If the wisdom of Śāriputra were equal to that of all devas and humans,
compared to the wisdom of the Tathāgata, it would still not equal even one-sixteenth.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
594 (594) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Nivāpa Monastery.
At that time, the householder Āṭavika passed away from his illness and was reborn in the Avṛha Heaven.
Having been born in that heaven, he immediately thought to himself:
"I should not remain here for long without seeing the Blessed One."
Having formed this thought, in the time it takes a strong man to flex or extend his arm, he vanished from the Avīci Heaven and appeared before the Buddha.
At that moment, the celestial son’s divine body collapsed to the ground, unable to support itself, just as clarified butter or oil falls to the ground and cannot stand on its own.
Thus it was that the body of that deva-son was so delicate and soft that he could not support himself standing.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed that deva-son:
"You should manifest a transformation into this coarse body and stand upon the ground."
Then, that devaputra immediately transformed his own form, assuming this coarse body, and stood upon the ground.
Thereupon, the devaputra went forward, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the devaputra Hasta:
"Hasta, when you were formerly a human being in this world, did you not still remember the sūtras and dharmas you received, without having completely forgotten them?"
The Devaputra Hasta addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
That which was originally received and upheld, I have not now forgotten at all.”
"Regarding the Dharma I heard while I was among humans, that which I did not fully grasp, I now recall just as the World-Honored One has well explained it.
The World-Honored One said:
'If a person dwells in a state of peace and happiness, they can remember and uphold the Dharma; this is not a place of suffering.'"
"This is said to be true.

Just as when the World-Honored One was in Jambudvīpa, surrounded by the fourfold assembly of various kinds, he preached the Dharma for them; and those fourfold assemblies, having heard what the Buddha taught, all wholeheartedly practiced it."
"I am also like this; in the Heaven Free from Heat (Anatappā), I preach the Dharma for a great assembly of devas and humans, and that multitude of devas all receive it and practice accordingly.
The Buddha said to the Devaputra Hastin:
"During your time in this human world, because you were never satiated with how many dharmas did you attain rebirth in that Heaven Free from Heat?"
The deva Hasta addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Because I was never satiated with three things, at the dissolution of my body after death, I was reborn in the Heaven Free from Heat.”
What are the three dharmas?
Because I never grew weary of seeing the Buddha, at the dissolution of the body after death, I was reborn in the Heaven Free from Heat;
because I never felt satiated with the Buddha’s Dharma, I was reborn in the Heaven Free from Heat.
"Because he made offerings to the Saṃgha without weariness, when his body perished at the end of his life, he was reborn in the Heaven Free from Heat.
Then, the hand-deva spoke this verse:
"Beholding the Buddha, one never tires; Hearing the Dharma, one likewise never tires."
Making offerings to the Saṅgha, they were never satisfied;
upholding the Dharma of the noble ones, they subdued the defilements of stinginess and attachment.
Because they were insatiable regarding these three dharmas, they were born in the Avṛha Heaven.
At that time, the devaputra Hasta, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and expressed his approval, and immediately vanished from sight.
595 (595) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a devaputra from the Heaven Free from Affliction (Avṛha), whose countenance was exquisitely beautiful. He approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The radiance of his body shone everywhere throughout the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then that deva spoke in verse:
"Born in that Heaven Free from Affliction, The seven bhikṣus are liberated;
Greed and hatred are exhausted, They have transcended the world and crossed over craving."
"Who has crossed over the various floods? Who has overcome the army of the Death-Māra that is so difficult to conquer?
Who has severed the fetters of the Death-Māra and forever transcended the yoke of afflictions?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
“The Venerable Upaka, as well as Pāṭikāputra, Vakula, Bhaṭṭika, Gaṇḍa, Revata, Nandika, and Bhadraka.”
All such as these have completely crossed over all floods,
severed the fetters of the Lord of Death, and delivered those who were difficult to deliver;
having cut all the fetters of the Lord of Death, they have transcended the yoke of the devas.
"You preach the profound and wondrous Dharma, awakening those for whom it is difficult to know.
You skillfully inquire about the deep meaning; who are you now?
At that time, the deva-son spoke a verse to the Buddha:
"I am an Anāgāmin, born in that Heaven Free from Affliction;
therefore I am able to know these things. These seven bhikṣus have attained liberation, exhausted all greed and hatred, and forever transcended worldly attachment."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, And the sixth, the sphere of mind—
If name and form Attain total extinction without remainder."
"Being able to know these phenomena, the seven bhikṣus have attained liberation;
craving for existence is entirely exhausted, and they have forever transcended worldly affection.
At that time, the devaputra spoke again in verse:
"In the village of Veṭhadīpa, I dwelt there;
my name was Nandipāla. As a disciple of Kāśyapa Buddha, I fashioned various earthenware vessels and maintained the dharma of an upāsaka."
Having made offerings to their parents and practiced the pure life free from desire,
they have been my friends in birth after birth, and I too have been their kinsmen;
such great beings as these were in harmony with me throughout their past lives.
"Having well cultivated body and mind, you maintain this final body.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Thus it is, O worthy one, just as you have said."
In the village of Veṭhadīpa, there was one named Nandipāla,
a disciple of Kāśyapa Buddha who had received the upāsaka precepts.
He supported his parents, remained free from desire, and practiced the holy life.
In the past you were their kinsman, and they too were your good friends;
such upright men have been united in harmony throughout their past lives.
Having well cultivated their bodies and minds, they now bear this final body.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the devaputra, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and expressed his approval, and immediately vanished from sight.
596 (596) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain devaputra of exquisite countenance came to the Buddha’s dwelling during the late night, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The various radiances from his body illuminated the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the devaputra addressed the Buddha in verse:
“This world is full of terrors; Sentient beings are constantly afflicted and disturbed.”
"What has already arisen is suffering; what has not yet arisen will also be suffering.
Is there perhaps a place free from fear? I pray that you, with your eye of wisdom, will explain.
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
“There is no asceticism other than this; there is no subduing of the senses other than this;
there is no renunciation of all else other than this, by which one attains the vision of liberation.
Then, that deva spoke again in verse:
“I have long beheld this brahmin, who has attained parinirvāṇa;
he has transcended all fears and forever surpassed worldly affection.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that devaputra rejoiced and followed with approval, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and immediately vanished from sight.
597 (Five Hundred and Ninety-Seven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain devaputra of exquisite and peerless complexion came to the place where the Buddha was during the late night, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The radiance from his body illuminated the entire Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain devaputra addressed the Buddha in verse:
“How do sentient beings receive a body and obtain such wondrous beauty?”
How does one cultivate skillful means to attain the path that leads out [of saṃsāra]?
In what dharma do sentient beings abide? For the sake of what do they practice?
What kind of sentient beings are those who are honored by the devas?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse, saying:
“Maintaining the precepts and possessing clear wisdom, Cultivating meditative absorption for oneself,
With an upright mind focused in mindfulness, The blazing fires of sorrow are all extinguished.”
Having attained impartial wisdom and with minds well-liberated,
by virtue of these causes and conditions, they receive bodies of wondrous form,
accomplish the path that leads out [of suffering], and dwell within the training with their minds.
"One who is thus endowed with such virtues is honored by all the devas.
At that time, that devaputra spoke again in verse:
"I have long observed this brahmin; he has attained parinirvāṇa."
"Having transcended all fears, you have forever surpassed worldly affection.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, that devaputra rejoiced and expressed his approval; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.
598 (Five Hundred and Ninety-Eight). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then a certain devaputra of exquisite complexion came to the Buddha’s dwelling during the late night, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit at one side.
The various radiances from his body illuminated the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
At that time, the devaputra spoke these verses:
"Sunk in sleep, yawning and lacking joy,"
"Eating to satiety, the mind is confused and agitated;
indolence and a lack of diligent effort—these ten obscurations shroud sentient beings, so that the Noble Path does not manifest.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse, answering:
"The mind sinks into sleep, yawns without joy, and becomes turbid after a full meal;
through indolence one fails to be diligent,
yet for those who practice with diligence, they are able to develop the Noble Path."
Then, that devaputra spoke again in verse:
"I have long beheld the Brahmin, Who has attained parinirvāṇa;
All fears have been transcended, And he has forever surpassed worldly affection."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that devaputra rejoiced and approved with gladness; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.
599 (599) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain devaputra of exquisite countenance came to the Buddha’s dwelling during the late night, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The various radiances from his body illuminated the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the devaputra spoke these verses:
"External fetters are not true fetters; Internal fetters bind sentient beings."
"Now I ask you, Gautama: who is it that is bound by fetters and who is free from them?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"The wise person establishes precepts and cultivates wisdom within the inner mind."
“The bhikṣu who practices with diligence can untie the fetters.
Then that deva spoke again in verse:
“I have long beheld the brāhmaṇa who has attained parinirvāṇa.”
"Having transcended all fears, he has forever surpassed worldly affection.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that devaputra rejoiced and expressed his approval; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.
600. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain devaputra of exquisite and peerless countenance approached the Buddha during the late night, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The various radiances from his body illuminated the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the devaputra spoke these verses:
"Difficult to cross and difficult to endure, Because the śramaṇa lacks knowledge."
Many hardships arise; heavy, dull, and submerged one sinks again and again.
The mind follows perceptions with ease, sinking repeatedly.
How should a śramaṇa act? How should he skillfully restrain and protect his mind?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"Just as a tortoise, through skillful means, Withdraws its six limbs into its own shell,
So too should a bhikṣu practicing dhyāna and reflection Skillfully restrain all perceptions and thoughts."
"His mind has no basis, and others cannot terrify him;
this is his own concealment, such that none can revile him.
Then, that devaputra spoke again in verse:
“I have long beheld this brahmin, who has attained parinirvāṇa;
he has transcended all fears and forever surpassed worldly affection.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the devaputra rejoiced and approved with gladness; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.
601 (Six Hundred and One). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a son of the gods of exquisite and peerless beauty approached the Buddha during the late night. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and the radiance from his body illuminated the entire Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then, that devaputra addressed the Buddha in verse:
“When the waters of the Sarayū flow in a small stream, where must they turn back?
On what path of birth and death does one no longer turn?”
"By what means can all the sufferings and pleasures of the world be extinguished without remainder?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and the sense-base of the mind—"
"When name-and-form (nāmarūpa) ceases without remainder, the stream of existence flows back to its source;
the path of birth and death no longer turns, and suffering and pleasure cease without remainder.
At that time, the devaputra spoke again in verse:
"I have long beheld this brahmin, who has attained parinirvāṇa;
he has transcended all fears and forever surpassed worldly affection.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the devaputra rejoiced and expressed his approval; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.
602 (Six Hundred Two). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a son of the gods of exquisite and peerless countenance approached the Buddha during the late hours of the night. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and the radiance from his body illuminated the entire Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then that deva addressed the Buddha in verse:
“The deer of the Eṇeya breed, The most honored among sages,
Eating little and disliking flavors, Delighting in meditation within the mountain forests.”
I now respectfully prostrate and ask Gautama:
How does one transcend suffering?
How is one liberated from suffering?
"I now ask concerning liberation: in what is it extinguished?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"The virtues of the five worldly desires, and the mental phenomena as the sixth,"
Having no desire for that which is desired, one is liberated from all suffering;
thus one emerges from suffering, and thus is one liberated from suffering.
That liberation of which you asked is extinguished therein.
Then that devaputra spoke again in verse:
"I have long beheld the Brahmin, Who has attained parinirvāṇa;
All fears he has transcended, Forever surpassing worldly affection."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that devaputra rejoiced and approved with gladness; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.
603 (Six Hundred and Three). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a son of the gods of exquisite and peerless beauty who, during the late hours of the night, came to where the Buddha was staying. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
The radiance from his body illuminated the entire Jeta Grove and Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then that devaputra spoke a verse to question the Buddha:
"How does one cross over the various floods?
How does one cross over the great ocean?"
"How can one abandon suffering?
How can one attain purity?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Faith can cross over all floods; heedfulness crosses the ocean;
diligence can eliminate suffering; and wisdom attains purity.
Then, that devaputra spoke again in verse:
“I have long beheld this brahmin, who has attained parinirvāṇa;
he has transcended all fears and forever surpassed worldly affection.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that devaputra rejoiced and expressed his approval; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.
Saṃyukta Āgama, Volume Twenty-two;
Saṃyukta Āgama, Volume Twenty-three.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Song Dynasty.
2.3 604 (604) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
Then, in the morning, the World-Honored One dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the city for alms together with the community of bhikṣus, as it is said in the verse:
“The color of his body is like a mountain of gold, Exceedingly subtle and majestic;
his gait is like that of a king of geese, And his face is like the pure, full moon—
The World-Honored One is here together with the assembly.”
Then, the World-Honored One stepped upon the threshold of the city gate with his foot, causing the earth to quake in six ways,
as described in the verse: “The great ocean and the vast earth, The cities, towers, and all the mountains—
Touched by the feet of the Muni, They tremble like a boat upon the waves.”
The Buddha manifested such supernatural powers.
At that time, the people raised their voices and cried out:
"How extraordinary! A dharma never before seen!"
He manifested supernatural powers just like the Buddha, the World-Honored One, entering the city and displaying such various unprecedented phenomena.
As it is said in the verse:
"The ground beneath becomes level, and the high ground is turned into low."
By the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, thorns, brambles, and all rubble were no longer to be seen;
those who were deaf, blind, or mute immediately regained their sight, hearing, and speech;
and the various musical instruments throughout the city and its walls—
“Without being struck, wondrous sounds emerge.
At that time, the radiance of that World-Honored One shone everywhere, like the blaze of a thousand suns. As it is said in a verse:
“The light of the World-Honored One’s body Shines universally throughout the city.”
"The people are bathed in the Buddha’s light; it is as cool as being anointed with sandalwood.
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the village.
There were two boys there, one of noble birth and the other of lesser birth, playing together in the sand.

One was named Jayasena and the other was named Vijayasena. Seeing from afar the World-Honored One approaching, his body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the youth Jayasena thought to himself:
"I shall offer him parched barley flour."
He then took a pinch of fine sand in his hand and placed it into the World-Honored One’s bowl.
At that time, Viśākha joined his palms in sympathetic joy, as expressed in this verse:
“Beholding the World-Honored One of Great Compassion, Whose entire body radiates light one fathom in height,”
When Vīra beheld the World-Honored One, a heart of great reverence and faith arose within him;
he took up some sand and immediately offered it as a gift, thereby attaining liberation from the bounds of birth and old age.
At that time, the youth made this vow:

"By the merit of the roots of goodness from this act of giving, may he become a universal monarch (cakravartin) with a single parasol over the entire world, and in this very life, may he obtain the opportunity to make offerings to all Buddhas.
As it is said in verse:
"The Muni knows his mind, And the aspirations of his heart."
"Because he has received the fruit [of his merit], increased his roots of goodness, and by the power of the field of merit,
he shall, with a heart of great compassion, receive the sand offered to him. At that time, because Jayā,
through these roots of goodness, was destined to become a king and rule over Jambudvīpa, and would eventually attain unexcelled perfect enlightenment, the World-Honored One smiled.
At that time, Ānanda, seeing the World-Honored One emit a smile, immediately joined his palms toward the Buddha and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, do not manifest a smile without cause or condition. By what cause and condition has the Buddha, the World-Honored One, now manifested a smile?"
As stated in the verse:
"The World-Honored One is free from frivolous laughter; he is the Unsurpassed Honored One among the worlds.
His teeth are as white as jade and crystal; why does the Most Victorious One now smile?"
Valiant and diligent in his exertion, self-awakened without a teacher,
his wondrous words are a joy to hear; with a supreme and gentle voice,
and a Brahma-sound clear and far-reaching, he bestowed a prophecy upon that youth.
“The Unsurpassed Honored One among Two-legged Beings has prophesied the fruit of that gift of sand.
Then the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
“So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said.”
The Buddhas do not smile without cause or condition; that I now smile has its own cause and condition.

Ānanda, you should know that one hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, this boy shall rule over a region in the city of Pāṭaliputra as a Cakravartin king, of the Maurya clan and named Aśoka. He shall govern according to the True Dharma and further widely distribute my relics, constructing eighty-four thousand stūpas for the Dharma King to bring peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings.
As it is said in the verse:
"After my parinirvāṇa, this person shall become a king;
his name shall be Śuka, of the Kauśika clan, just like King Mūrdhaja."
"In this Jambudvīpa, you alone shall be the king, honored by the world. Ānanda!
Take the sand offered into this bowl and place it at the place where the Tathāgata walks; you should go to that spot."
Ānanda, having received these instructions, immediately took the bowl and sand and left the place of walking meditation.
“Ānanda, you should know that in the city of Pāṭaliputra there is a king named Candraprabha.”
That king shall have a son named Bimbisāra, who shall rule that kingdom.
He, in turn, shall have a son named Udayibhadra.

At that time, there was a Brahmin girl in the kingdom of Campā who was exceedingly beautiful, pleasing to behold, and highly esteemed by the nation. When the various physiognomists saw her marks, they immediately prophesied concerning her:
"You shall become the queen of a king and give birth to two sons; one shall rule over a realm, while the other shall leave the household life to study the Way and achieve the traces of holiness."

At that time, having heard what the physiognomist had said, the brahmin was filled with immeasurable joy. He immediately took his daughter, adorned her body with various ornaments, and went to Pāṭaliputra, intending to give her in marriage to Prince Udayibhadra.
The physiognomist said, "She should be married to King Bimbisāra; she shall give birth to a son of merit and virtue, and that son shall succeed to the royal throne.
The brāhmaṇa then married his daughter to this king.
When the king saw that his daughter was upright and possessed of virtue, he immediately made her his consort.
When the former consort and the various court ladies saw this new consort approaching, they thought to themselves:
"This woman is exceedingly beautiful and is a treasure of the kingdom; if the king enjoys himself with her, he will abandon us, not even casting a glance our way."
"Then those women were made to train in the craft of barbers.
Once they had completed their training, they attended to the king's hair and beard.
While he was being groomed, the king was greatly delighted and immediately asked those women:"
"What do you seek? the woman replied to the king,
"I only pray that Your Majesty’s heart will hold me in affection!"
Thus he made this request three times. Then the king said:
"I am a Kṣatriya consecrated king, and you are a barber; how could I possibly love and cherish you?"
The girl said to the king:
"I am not born of a low caste; I am the daughter of a high-ranking Brahmin family.
A physiognomist said to my father:"
"This girl ought to be married to the king;
that is why she has come here!
The king said:
"If this is so, who caused you to practice such a base craft?
The woman replied to the king,
"It was the former consort and the court ladies who made me learn this."
The king immediately issued a command, saying:
"From this day forward, do not again engage in such lowly occupations.
The king then established her as his first consort.

The king constantly enjoyed himself with her, and she subsequently conceived. When the months were complete, she gave birth to a son; at the time of his birth, all was peaceful and secure, and the mother felt no distress or anxiety.
After seven days had passed, they established his name as Aśoka (Free from Sorrow).
Furthermore, another son was born named Vigataśoka.
As for Aśoka, his body was coarse and rough; the King, his father, did not fondle him much and held no affection for him.
Furthermore, the king, wishing to test his two sons, summoned Piṅgala and said to the brahmin:
"Preceptor, observe my sons; after my passing, which one shall become king?"
The Brahmin said, "Take these children out of the city to the palace gardens; there you shall observe their marks.
They then went out to those gardens.
At that time, King Aśoka’s mother said to Aśoka:
"I have heard that Your Majesty has gone out to the Golden Palace Garden to observe the various princes to see who shall become king after my passing."
"Why do you not leave now? Aśoka replied,
"Since Your Majesty no longer regards me, nor does he take pleasure in seeing me."
The mother spoke again:
"Just go to that place.
Aśoka replied once more:
"The mother again commanded him to go, saying, 'I shall go now; I pray that you, mother, will provide me with food and drink.
The mother replied, 'So be it.'"
"I shall go out of the city.
At that time, as he was leaving the gate, he encountered a high minister named Anurādha.
This minister asked Aśoka:
"Where has the Prince gone now? Aśoka replied,
"I have heard that Your Majesty has gone out to the Golden Palace Garden to observe the princes and see who shall become king after my passing."
"I shall now go to him.
The king first commanded his great minister:
"If Aśoka comes, you must have him arrive riding an old, sluggish elephant, and let an old man serve as his attendant."
Then, King Aśoka, riding that old elephant, arrived at the pleasure grove and sat upon the ground among the princes.
At that time, each of the princes provided food and drink for themselves, while Aśoka’s mother filled a clay vessel with curd-rice and sent it to him.
As each of these princes ate his meal,
the father-king asked the teacher,
"Among these, who possesses the marks of a king and shall succeed to my throne?"
At that time, the physiognomist examined the princes and saw that Aśoka possessed the marks of a king and was destined to succeed to the throne.
He further thought to himself:
"This Aśoka is unsuitable for the king; if I were to say that he should become king, the monarch would surely become sorrowful and unhappy."
He immediately said,
"I shall now record them all.
The king replied:
"As the teacher has instructed.
The teacher said:
"If there is anyone among these who rides upon a fine vehicle, that person shall become a king."
At that time, having heard what he said, each of the princes thought to themselves,
"I am riding on a fine vehicle. Then, Aśoka said:
"I rode upon an old, aged elephant; thus I attained the status of king.
At that time, the king spoke again to the master, saying:
"I pray that you will observe me once more and grant me a prophecy."
The master replied again,
"Whosoever among you occupies the foremost seat shall become king.
The princes then spoke to one another:
"I am sitting on the foremost seat," said Aśoka.
"I am now sitting upon the earth; this is my superior seat, and I shall become king."
He spoke again to his teacher, saying,
"Please observe once more.
The teacher replied:
"In this matter, one who has superior vessels and superior food shall become king.
Even so, Aśoka thought to himself:
"I possess superior vehicles, superior seats, and superior food."
At that time, after the king had finished examining his son’s marks, he immediately returned to the palace.
Then, Aśoka’s mother asked Aśoka,
"Who shall become the king?"
"Whom did the brāhmaṇa further prophesy? Aśoka replied:
"The one of superior vehicle, the elder, the superior vessel, and the recipient of superior food—these shall become princes; as for myself, I see that I shall become king."
"An old elephant shall be his vehicle, the earth his seat, and plain vessels shall hold his food—rice mixed with curd.
At that time, the Brahmin, knowing that Aśoka was destined to become king, frequently paid homage to his mother.
His mother also made a generous offering to the brahmin and immediately asked him,
"After the Great King passes away, who shall become king?
The teacher replied:
"This cannot be said.
Thus he was asked three times.
The teacher replied:
"I shall tell you: be careful not to let anyone know. This son born to you is named Aśoka; he is that very person. The lady replied, "Upon hearing these words, I am filled with joy and exultation.
However, if the King were to hear this, he would no longer feel reverence and faith toward the Teacher. Therefore, may the Teacher now return to his original dwelling place."
“If my son becomes king, you, Master, shall receive all prosperity and good fortune; I shall provide for you with offerings for as long as I live.
At that time, Takṣaśilā, a border state of King Bimbisāra, rose in rebellion.
At that time, the king said to Aśoka,
"Lead the fourfold army and go to subdue that kingdom.
When the prince departed, the king provided him with no armor or weapons at all.
At that time, an attendant said to the prince:
"If we go now to attack that country, we will have no weapons.
How can we achieve peace?"
Aśoka said, "If I am to become king as a result of the ripening of my roots of goodness, let the weapons and armor appear spontaneously.
As soon as these words were spoken, the earth split open at the sound, and the weapons and armor emerged from the ground. He then took the fourfold army and went to wage war against that kingdom.

At that time, when the people of those various kingdoms heard that Aśoka was coming, they immediately leveled the roads and adorned the city walls. Carrying auspicious jars of water and various offerings, they went out to welcome the prince, saying:
"We have not rebelled against the Great King or Prince Aśoka; rather, it is because our ministers acted against our interests that we have turned away from your holy transformation."
He immediately provided various offerings to the prince and invited him into the city.
Having pacified this kingdom, he sent him again to invade the kingdom of Kāśi.
At that time, those two great strongmen leveled the roads for the king, pushing aside mountain rocks.
Furthermore, the devas proclaimed throughout this kingdom:
"Aśoka shall rule over this world; you must not harbor rebellious intentions.
Thereupon, the kings of those lands immediately submitted.
In this manner, he eventually brought the whole world under his control, reaching as far as the shores of the ocean.
At that time, Prince Susīma went out for recreation and encountered a high minister; the minister failed to observe the proper etiquette, so the prince immediately had men beat him.
The minister thought to himself:
"This prince, not yet having attained the throne, acts with such a nature;
were he to become king, it would be unbearable."
Furthermore, we have heard that Aśoka has gained control of the world and has eliminated five hundred ministers; therefore, let us join together in establishing Aśoka as king to rule over this world.
"Furthermore, when the kingdom of Takṣaśilā rebelled, the ministers deliberated together, saying:
'Let Prince Surasama go. The King also agreed, and he immediately departed for that country, yet he was unable to subdue it."
"At that time, the father-king again fell gravely ill. The king said to his ministers:
'I now wish to appoint Śuśīma as king and have Aśoka go to that country.'"
At that time, the ministers wished to have Aśoka made king; they smeared yellow substances upon Aśoka’s body, face, hands, and feet, and then addressed the king, saying:
"Prince Aśoka has now fallen gravely ill."
The ministers immediately adorned Aśoka and led him to the king's presence, saying:
"Let us first establish this son as king; we shall later gradually install Śuśrūṣa as king."
When the king heard these words, he was deeply displeased; filled with sorrow and distress, he remained silent and gave no reply.
At that time, Aśoka thought to himself and spoke aloud:
"If I am truly destined to obtain the royal throne, the devas shall naturally come and pour water upon my head, binding a white silk cloth around my crown."
Hearing this sound, the various devas immediately poured water over Aśoka’s head and bound his head with white silk.
At that moment, the king, seeing this sight, was overcome with extreme grief and distress, and he passed away.
"After King Aśoka had performed the funeral rites for his father according to the prescribed dharma, he appointed Anuruddha as his chief minister.

At that time, Prince Susīma, hearing that his father had passed away and that Aśoka was now established as king, felt unbearable resentment; he immediately assembled his troops and came to wage war against Aśoka."
Among the four gates of King Aśoka’s palace, two *malla* warriors were stationed at two gates, a high minister was stationed at the third gate, and the king himself guarded the eastern gate.

At that time, the minister Anuruddha constructed a mechanical wooden elephant and further fashioned an image of King Aśoka; the image was then mounted upon the elephant and stationed outside the eastern gate.
Furthermore, he constructed a pit of smokeless fire and covered it with objects.
When Prince Śuśima arrived, the minister Anuruddha said to him, "If you wish to become king, Aśoka is at the eastern gate;
you may go there to attack him. If you can capture this prince, you will naturally obtain the kingship."
At that time, the prince immediately went toward the eastern gate and fell into a pit of fire, whereupon he died.

At that moment, there was a great strongman named Bhadrayudha who, hearing that Śūṣma had passed away, grew weary of the world. He took countless followers and left the household life to study the Path within the Buddha-dharma; through diligent and energetic exertion, he attained the exhaustion of outflows and realized the state of an Arhat.

"When King Aśoka ruled according to the True Dharma, we ministers, because we had collectively established Aśoka as king, treated him with contempt and failed to observe the rites due between sovereign and subject; the king, too, was aware that the ministers were treating him with disdain."
At that time, the king said to his ministers,
"You may cut down the trees bearing flowers and fruit, and plant thorny brambles instead.
The ministers replied:
"I have never seen or heard of anyone removing flowers and fruits to plant thorny trees, yet I see people cutting down thorny trees to plant fruit-bearing ones.
Thus he spoke, and even when the king commanded him three times to cut them down, he still did not comply.
"At that time, the king was enraged with his ministers; he immediately took up a sharp sword and slew five hundred of them.
On another occasion, the king, accompanied by his retinue of court ladies, went out to a park for recreation and saw an *aśoka* tree in full, magnificent bloom."
Having seen this, the king thought, "This flower tree bears the same name as I," and his heart was filled with joy.

However, the king’s physical form was ugly and his skin was coarse and rough; consequently, the court ladies did not love the king and, out of hatred for him, used their hands to break and snap the branches of the *aśoka* tree.
The king woke from his sleep and saw the flowers of the *aśoka* tree strewn in disarray upon the ground; filled with rage, he bound the female attendants and burned them to death with fire.
Because the king practiced tyranny and cruelty, he was called the Tyrant Aśoka.
At that time, the minister Anuruddha addressed the king, saying:
"Your Majesty should not practice such a dharma."
"How can one kill people with one's own hands, such as ministers and court ladies?
Your Majesty should now appoint executioners; those who are to be executed should be handed over to them."
The king immediately issued a proclamation to establish an executioner.
There was a mountain named Giri, and upon it lived the house of a weaver. The weaver had a son, also named Giri, who was cruel and violent;

he beat, struck, and bound young boys and girls, and even captured living beings from both water and land, going so far as to defy and rebel against his own parents. For this reason, the people of the world called him the "Cruel Son of Giri."
At that time, the king’s messengers said to him:
"Are you able to execute these wicked men for the king? He replied:
"I am able to purify and remove the transgressions of all those with guilt throughout Jambudvīpa; how much more so for this one region alone?
At that time, the messengers returned and reported to the king:
"That man has already captured the criminal."
The king said,
"Search for him and bring him here!
The messengers called out to him, and he replied:
"Xiaoren, first take your leave of your parents.
He related the aforementioned matter in detail, and his parents said,
"My son, you ought not to do such a thing."
Thus he commanded three times; having conceived a heart of unkindness, he immediately killed his parents, and only then did he arrive.
The messengers asked, "Why have you not come quickly for so long?"
Then, that wicked man related the aforementioned matter in full.
The messengers reported these events to the king in detail.
The king immediately commanded him:
"Know this, my man: the offense for which you stand condemned should result in death.
He replied to the king, "Please build a dwelling for me."

The king even had a dwelling constructed for him, which was exceedingly magnificent and adorned with a single gate that was likewise most exquisite. Within it, he arranged various methods of punishment in a manner resembling a hell; that prison was most splendid and well-crafted.
Then that wicked man addressed the king, saying:
"I now beg a boon from Your Majesty: if anyone enters within this place, they shall never again be able to leave.
The king replied:
"I shall grant you whatever boon you have requested.
Then, that butcher went to the monastery and listened as the bhikṣus spoke of the matters concerning the hells.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu preaching the Sūtra on the Hells:
"There are beings born in the hells; once they are there, the hell-wardens seize those sinners, pry open their mouths with hot iron tongs, and place glowing iron balls within their mouths."

Next, molten copper is poured into their mouths; next, iron axes repeatedly hack and sever their bodies; next, cangues, shackles, and neck-irons bind and fetter them; next, they encounter the fire chariots and glowing coals; next, the iron cauldrons; next, the River of Ashes; and finally, the Mountains of Blades and the Forests of Swords.
It is exactly as described in the *Devadūta Sūtra*.

When the butcher heard the bhikṣu explain these matters, he opened his residence and applied the methods for punishing offenders as they had been taught; he punished the criminals according to this law.
"Furthermore, at another time, a merchant leader took his wife into the great ocean. While they were on the sea, his wife gave birth to a son whom they named Sāgara.

Thus he remained at sea for more than ten years, gathering various precious treasures. Upon returning to his native land, he encountered five hundred bandits on the way who killed the merchant leader and seized his treasures."

At that time, the son of the merchant leader, having seen his father wounded and dead and having lost his precious treasures, became weary of the sufferings of the world; he therefore left the household life to study the Path within the Dharma of the Tathāgata. Returning to his native land, he traveled through various kingdoms until he eventually arrived at the city of Pāṭaliputra.
When that night had passed, the bhikṣu dressed in the morning, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food in due order. By mistake, he entered a slaughterhouse.

At that time, seeing from afar within the house sentient beings being tortured with iron chariots, furnaces, glowing coals, and the like—just as in the hells—the bhikṣu was immediately seized with terror; his hair stood on end, and he sought to leave through the door.
Then, the fierce and evil ones immediately went there and seized that bhikṣu, saying:
"No one who enters within this can emerge; you shall die here now."
When the bhikṣu heard what was said, a feeling of bitter grief arose in his heart and tears filled his eyes.
The cruel master asked,
"Why are you crying like a small child?"
At that time, the bhikṣu replied in verse:
"I am not afraid of death; my aspiration is to seek liberation.
Because the goal I seek has not yet been achieved, for this reason I weep."
“A human body is extremely difficult to obtain, and so too is renunciation.
Having encountered the Lion-King of the Śākyas, from this day forth we shall not behold him again.
At that time, the fierce leader spoke to the bhikṣu, saying:
"You shall surely die now; why do you harbor such grief and distress?
The bhikṣu replied again with words of lamentation:
"Grant me a brief extension of life, for as long as one month."
The ruffian would not listen.
In this manner, the number of days gradually decreased until it reached seven; at that point, he finally gave his consent.
Then, knowing that his death would soon be imminent, this bhikṣu applied himself with courageous diligence, sitting in meditation to still his mind, yet in the end he was unable to attain the Path.
When the seven days had passed, there was a woman in the royal palace who committed a crime punishable by death; she was handed over to a cruel executioner to be punished for her offense.
The executioner placed the woman inside a mortar and pounded her with a pestle until she was reduced to fine powder.
At that time, the bhikṣu, seeing this matter, felt extreme revulsion toward this body, exclaiming: "Alas!
What suffering!"
"I, too, shall soon be like this.
And he spoke in verse:
"Alas, O Great Compassionate Teacher, You have expounded the true and wondrous Dharma!"
This body is like a mass of foam; in its true nature, it possesses no reality.
That beauty of the fair woman from before—where has she gone now?
Birth and death are utterly fit to be abandoned, yet the foolish remain greedily attached to them.
Fixing the mind upon that object, one shall now be released from the shackles of wood;
may they cross the ocean of the three realms of existence, never to be born again.
Thus, through diligent means, apply yourself with single-minded devotion to the cultivation of the Buddha-dharma.
"Having severed all fetters, he has attained arhatship.
Then that wicked man said to the bhikṣu:
"The time limit has expired."
The bhikṣu asked,
“I do not understand what you have said.
The ruffian replied:
"Seven days were previously appointed, and now they have already passed.
The bhikṣu replied with a verse:
"My mind has attained liberation; The great darkness of ignorance [is dispelled]."
Having severed the veils of existence and slain the thieves of affliction, the sun of wisdom has now arisen.
Examining the mind, intellect, and consciousness, he clearly perceives birth and death; now is the time to have compassion for humanity.
"Following and practicing the noble Dharma, I now leave this body and its remains to whatever you may do; I have no further regret or attachment.

At that time, the cruel leader seized the bhikṣu and placed him in an iron cauldron filled with oil. He added fuel and lit a fire, but the flames would not ignite at all; even if they had ignited, the oil did not grow hot.
When the executioner saw that the fire would not ignite despite his beating the messenger, the fire spontaneously burst forth with fierce intensity.

After a long time, he lifted the lid of the iron cauldron and saw that bhikṣu sitting upon a lotus flower within the cauldron. Struck with wonder, he immediately informed the king. The king then prepared his carriage and, leading a vast multitude, went to see the bhikṣu.

"At that time, when the bhikṣu’s moment for subduing [the opponent] had arrived, he immediately ascended into the air like a king of geese and displayed various transformations, as described in the verse."
When the king saw this bhikṣu, his body ascending into the void, he felt great joy in his heart;
with palms joined, he gazed upon that noble one and said:
"I now have something to report, which my mind cannot comprehend."
Your physical form is no different from that of humans, yet your supernormal powers are unprecedented.
For my sake, explain in detail: what dharmas should be practiced so that you may attain purity? Expound upon this for me extensively.
"May you cause me to attain the supreme and wondrous Dharma;
having realized the characteristics of phenomena, I shall become your disciple, never to have any regret.
At that time, that bhikṣu thought to himself:

"I have now subdued this king; having been guided by him in many ways and having upheld the Buddha-dharma, I shall widely distribute the relics of the Tathāgata to bring peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, and cause all throughout this Jambudvīpa to place their faith in the Triple Gem."
For these reasons, he manifested his own virtue and spoke this verse to the king:
"I am a disciple of the Buddha, Who has attained the exhaustion of all outflows."
Furthermore, these sons of the Buddha do not cling to any form of existence;
having now been disciplined by me, the Unsurpassed Honored One among two-legged beings,
their minds have attained tranquility and peace from the great terrors of birth and death.
"Now I have attained complete liberation; having severed the bonds of the three realms of existence, I have obtained such benefits within the noble Dharma of the Tathāgata.
When King Aśoka heard what that bhikṣu had said, he conceived great reverence and faith toward the Buddha, and further addressed the bhikṣu, saying:
"What did the Buddha record and proclaim before his parinirvāṇa?
The bhikṣu replied:
"The Buddha recorded for the Great King:"

"After my parinirvāṇa, when more than a hundred years have passed, there will be thirty million households in the city of Pāṭaliputra. In that land there will be a king named Aśoka, who shall rule over this Jambudvīpa as a Cakravartin King, governing by means of the True Dharma;
furthermore, he shall widely distribute my relics and establish eighty-four thousand stūpas throughout Jambudvīpa."
The Buddha thus gave this prophecy to the Great King.

However, Your Majesty, you have now created this great hell by slaughtering immeasurable people; therefore, Your Majesty should now conceive compassion for all sentient beings, grant them fearlessness, and cause them to attain peace and security. As for the prophecy the Buddha has given regarding the Great King, the King should practice accordingly in accordance with the Dharma.
And he spoke in verse:
"One should practice a heart of compassion, Do not afflict any living beings;
One should cultivate the Buddha-dharma And widely disseminate the Buddha’s relics."
At that time, King Aśoka conceived the utmost reverence and faith toward the Buddha; with palms joined, he prostrated before the bhikṣu and said:
"I have committed a great transgression. I now repent before this bhikṣu. What I have done was most improper; I pray that as a son of the Buddha, you will accept my repentance."
"Forgive me and do not reproach me further; I, a fool, now once again take refuge in you.
He then spoke in verse:
"I now take refuge in the Buddha And the unsurpassed, supreme, and wondrous Dharma."
“O Bhikṣus, honored by all the multitudes, I now take refuge for the rest of my life.
From this day forth, I shall be courageous and respectfully receive the World-Honored One’s command:
throughout this Jambudvīpa, I shall universally establish stupas for all the Buddhas.”
"Various kinds of offerings, including suspended silk streamers, banners, and pennants,
have adorned the stūpa of the World-Honored One, so exquisite and beautiful as to be rare in the world.
At that time, having guided King Aśoka across, that bhikṣu ascended into the air and vanished.
At that time, the king emerged from the hell, and the cruel master said to him:
"The King shall not go forth again.
The king said:
"Do you now wish to kill me?
He replied, "It is so."
The king asked,
"Who entered this place first?
He replied:
"I am. The king said, "If that is so,
you should have died first."

The king immediately commanded his men to take this wicked leader to a lacquer house and burn him with fire; he further ordered that this hell be demolished, bestowing fearlessness upon all sentient beings.

At that time, the king, wishing to construct a stūpa for the relics, led his fourfold army to Rājagṛha, took the relics from King Ajātaśatru’s stūpa, and returned to restore this stūpa so that it was no different from its original state.
Having thus taken the śarīra relics from the stūpas of the seven Buddhas, he arrived at the village of Rāma.

At that time, the nāga kings led the king into their nāga palace; the king requested the śarīra relics from the nāgas for the purpose of making offerings, and the nāgas immediately granted them to him.
The King departed from there, as it is said in the verse:
"In the village of Rāma-rā, All the stūpas of the Buddhas,
Which were served by the Nāga Kings, Were guarded and venerated."
"The King requested a portion from the dragons; the dragons opened their hearts and gave it to him.
He then took these relics and gradually proceeded toward other regions.
At that time, the King fashioned eighty-four thousand caskets of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal to enshrine the Buddha’s relics.

Furthermore, he fashioned eighty-four thousand vases made of the four precious substances to contain this casket, and he also created immeasurable hundreds of thousands of banners, standards, and parasols. He commanded the various spirits and deities to each take up the implements for the worship of the śarīra, saying to them:
"From Jambudvīpa to the edge of the ocean, in every city, town, and village containing ten million households, erect a stūpa for the śarīra of the World-Honored One."
“At that time, there was a country named Takṣaśilā with thirty-six hundred million households. The people of that country said to the spirits and deities:
‘Give us thirty-six caskets of relics so that we may erect a stūpa for the Buddha.’”

The king devised a skillful means: he had those among the people of the kingdom who were few in number divided and assigned to others so that the household quota was filled, and thus the stupas were established.
At that time, there was a senior elder (sthavira) in the city of Pāṭaliputra named Yaśas. The king went to his location and said to the elder:
"I wish to establish eighty-four thousand Buddha-stupas in a single day throughout this Jambudvīpa; such is my aspiration."
As it is praised in verse:
"The Great King named Aśoka, from among the eight previous stupas,
took a portion of relics from each, and here in Jambudvīpa..."
"Establish stupas for all the Buddhas, numbering eighty-four thousand,
vast, exquisite, and magnificent, completing them all in a single day.
Then, that Elder addressed the King, saying:
"Excellent, Great King!
Fifteen days from now, at the time of a lunar eclipse, cause these stūpas for the Buddhas to be erected throughout Jambudvīpa."
In this manner, within a single day, eighty-four thousand stupas were erected; the people of the world rejoiced immeasurably and collectively named him King Dharma-Aśoka.
As it is said in a verse of praise:
“The King, a noble scion of the Peacock lineage, Brings peace and happiness to the people of the world;
In this Jambudvīpa, He has established a supreme and wondrous stūpa.”
"Originally known as an evil king, now having performed sublime and wondrous deeds, he is collectively hailed as a Dharma King, a title passed down to posterity.
Having thus erected eighty-four thousand stūpas, the king was filled with joy and exultation; accompanied by his ministers, he went to the Kukkuṭārāma monastery and addressed the Elder Yaśas, saying:
