“Are there other bhikṣus who have been prophesied by the Buddha to perform the work of a Buddha?
I shall go to where they are to make offerings and pay them respect.
The Elder replied:
"When the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he subdued the Naga King Apalāla, the potter, and the Caṇḍāla Kūvalaya.
He then proceeded to the kingdom of Mathurā and addressed Ānanda, saying:

'One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there shall be an elder named Ghoṭamukha; his son shall be named Upagupta. He shall leave the household life to study the Way, and in teaching people as a Buddha without marks, he shall be foremost; he shall perform the work of a Buddha.'"
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you see that mountain in the distance?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“I see it, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This mountain is named Urumanda; this is the hermitage named Nata-pada, which accords with tranquility.
And it is praised in verse:
'Upagupta the bhikṣu, The foremost in instruction.'"
His fame shall resound throughout the four quarters; as prophesied by the Most Victorious One,
after my parinirvāṇa, he shall perform the work of a Buddha,
delivering all classes of sentient beings in numbers beyond measure.
Then the king asked the Elder,
“Has the Venerable Upagupta now appeared in the world?
The Elder replied:

"Having transcended the world, he left the household life to study the Way and subdued all afflictions; he is an Arhat who dwells in a forest hermitage on Mount Urumanda with a retinue of eighteen thousand immeasurable bhikṣus. Out of compassion for sentient beings, he preaches the pure and wondrous Dharma as taught by the Buddha, delivering immeasurable devas and humans and causing them to enter the City of Ambrosia."

Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he immediately commanded his ministers to quickly prepare the ceremonial carriage and, accompanied by an immeasurable retinue, went to that place to pay homage and make offerings to Upagupta.
At that time, the minister addressed the king, saying:
"Since that Sage is already within your kingdom, you ought to dispatch messengers to welcome him; he will surely come of his own accord.
The king replied to the minister:
"It is not appropriate to send a messenger to that place; you should go there yourself, for it is not fitting for him to come here.
Then he spoke in verse:
"You have obtained a vajra-tongue; how could you not sever and destroy [the enemy]?"
"Admonish me not to go there, to associate with those who dwell in the fields and villages.
The king immediately sent a messenger to the Venerable One, saying:
"I shall come to your presence on such-and-such a day."
At that time, the Venerable One reflected:
"If the king comes, he will have immeasurable followers and will undergo great suffering, as he will forcibly kill and harm tiny insects and the people of the villages."
Having formed this thought, he replied to the messenger, "I shall go to the king's presence myself.

At that time, when the king heard that the Venerable One was coming of his own accord, he leaped for joy. From Mathurā to Pāṭaliputra, he prepared boats and ships along the way, and hung various banners and canopies upon them.
At that time, out of compassion for the king, the Venerable Upagupta led a community of eighteen thousand arhats and proceeded directly to the kingdom by way of water.
At that time, a person from among the citizens addressed the king, saying, "The Venerable Upagupta has arrived, leading a community of eighteen thousand bhikṣus.
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with great joy and leaped for gladness; he immediately removed a necklace worth ten million pieces of gold and presented it to him.

The king, together with his ministers and retinue, immediately went out to the Venerable’s dwelling. He served him food, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground in homage toward him, knelt for a long time with palms joined, and spoke these words:
"I now preside over this Jambudvīpa and hold the royal throne, yet I do not consider this a cause for joy.
Now that I behold the Venerable One, my exultation is immeasurable. That a disciple of the Tathāgata can be thus is like beholding the Buddha himself."
And he spoke these verses:
"Having attained quiescence and transcended the world, you now perform the work of a Buddha;
the folly of the world is extinguished, like the sun illuminating the world of Buddhas."
“He acts as a guide for the world, supreme among those who preach the Dharma;
a refuge for all sentient beings—now I am filled with great joy.
At that time, the king commanded his messengers to proclaim throughout the realm:
"The Venerable Upagupta Bhikṣu has now arrived in this country.
Thus he proclaimed:
"Those who desire wealth and honor, and wish to distance themselves from the suffering of poverty,"
Those who always dwell in the bliss of the heavens, those who have attained liberation and nirvāṇa,
shall encounter Upagupta; by practicing reverence and making offerings now,
even those who have not seen the various Buddhas shall now behold Upagupta.
At that time, the king adorned the realm, leveled the roads, hung silk banners and canopies, burned incense, scattered flowers, and provided various musical performances.
The people of the entire kingdom all came out to welcome the Venerable Upagupta, making offerings to him with reverence.
At that time, the Venerable Upagupta addressed the king, saying:
"Great King!..."

One should govern and transform others through the True Dharma, out of compassion for sentient beings; for the Triple Gem is difficult to encounter, one should always make offerings and show reverence to the Triple Gem, cultivate mindfulness and offer praise, and widely explain it to others.
Why is this? The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who knows people and perceives people, has always declared:
"My True Dharma is entrusted to the kings and to my community of bhikṣus."
And he spoke in verse:
"The Hero of the World, the Honored One among men, Entrusts this most excellent and sublime Great Dharma To the Great King,
As well as to me and the community of bhikṣus."
Then the king said to Upagupta,
"I have established the True Dharma," and he spoke this verse:
“I have already constructed various stūpas, adorning all the realms;
I have offered diverse kinds of worship with banners, pennants, and various jewels,
and have widely distributed the Buddha’s relics throughout Jambudvīpa.”
I have generated such merit, and my wishes are now entirely fulfilled;
myself, my wife and children, these treasures, and this very earth—
I have now renounced them all as offerings to the stūpas of the Worthy and Holy Ones.
Then, the Venerable Upagupta praised the king, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Great King, you should practice such a Dharma.
Then he spoke in verse:
"Relinquishing body, wealth, and life, One has no cause for anxiety in every lifetime."
"The merit one receives shall be inexhaustible, and one will surely attain unsurpassed awakening.

At that time, the king invited the Venerable Upagupta into the city, prepared various seats, and requested the Venerable to take his place; he then directed the assembly of monks to proceed to the Kukkuṭārāma Monastery.
He said to the Venerable One:
"The Venerable One’s countenance is upright and handsome, and your body is supple; whereas my own form is ugly and my skin is coarse and rough."
The Venerable One spoke in verse:
"When I practiced giving, with a pure mind and excellent wealth,
it was not like the King’s practice of giving, who offered sand to the Buddha."
Then the King replied with a verse:
"When I was a child, I gave a gift of sand;
Now I have obtained such a fruit as this— How much more so for other sublime gifts!"
The Venerable One further praised him with a verse:
"How wonderful, O Great King! By bestowing these grains of sand, Within this unsurpassed field of merit, You have planted fruits that shall never end."
At that time, King Aśoka said to his ministers:
"I gave a mere grain of sand as an offering to the Buddha and obtained such a karmic fruit as this.
How could I not cultivate reverence for the World-Honored One?"
The King spoke again to Upagupta:
"Venerable One!

Show me the places where the Buddha preached the Dharma and traveled; I shall go there to make offerings and pay homage, so as to gather roots of goodness for the sake of sentient beings in future generations."
Then he spoke in verse:
"Show me where the Buddha taught the Dharma, The various lands and his dwelling places;
I shall offer worship and cultivate reverence there, For the sake of future sentient beings."
The Venerable One said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
“Great King, since you have been able to make such a sublime vow, I shall show you the location for the sake of future sentient beings.
At that time, the king, leading his fourfold army and carrying various offerings of incense, flowers, banners, and streamers, as well as musical instruments, set out with the Venerable One.
The Venerable Luṇovana said: "This is the birthplace of the Tathāgata. He then spoke this verse:
"At the place where the Tathāgata was first born, Upon being born, he took seven steps.
He gazed toward the four quarters And raised his hand toward the heavens."
"This is my final birth; I shall attain the Unsurpassed Way.
Among gods and humans alike, I shall be the Unsurpassed Honored One.
At that time, the king prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, made offerings and paid homage, and immediately erected a stūpa for the Buddha.
The Venerable One addressed the King, saying:
"Great King, do you wish to see the place where the various devas beheld the Buddha at birth as he took seven steps?
The King replied:
"I wish to see her.
Then, the Venerable One raised his hand, pointed to the branch of the tree that Queen Māyā had grasped, and addressed the tree deity, saying:
"O Tree Deity!
"I shall now manifest myself so that the King may see me and give rise to great joy.
Upon hearing these words, he was immediately seen standing beside the Venerable One, who spoke thus:
"What are your instructions?"
"I shall respectfully practice it.
The Venerable One said to the king:
"This deity witnessed the Buddha at the time of his birth."
The King questioned the deity with a verse:
“You saw his adorned body, who at birth was like a blue lotus;
who took seven steps as he walked, and spoke words from his mouth.”
The deity replied in verse:
"I beheld his body of marks and signs, When he was born, the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings;
He took seven steps as he walked, And spoke these words from his mouth:"
"Among all devas and humans, I am the unsurpassed Honored One.
At that time, the king asked the deity:
"What auspicious signs accompanied the Buddha’s birth?"
The deity replied:
"I cannot fully proclaim all these sublime matters; now I shall briefly state a small portion:
'His radiance can penetrate and illuminate everything, and his body is endowed with the primary and secondary marks.'"
"Delightful for all to behold, it moves both heaven and earth.
At that time, the king, hearing what the deity had said, was filled with joy and departed after bestowing one hundred thousand taels of precious jewels.
Furthermore, they led the king into the city and said to him:
"In this place, the Bodhisattva has manifested the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, adorning his body with a lustrous purple-gold hue."
At that time, the king prostrated toward this place and made various kinds of offerings.
He then led the king into the celestial temple and said to him:
"When the prince was born, he was made to pay homage to that deity."
At that time, all the deities paid homage to the Bodhisattva.
Then, the people gave the Bodhisattva a name, saying, "Now he is the God among Gods.
At that time, the King again made various kinds of offerings.
He then led [the king] to that place and said to him:
"In this place, the father-king showed the Bodhisattva to the various brahmins so they might examine his marks and virtues.
The king, in turn, made various kinds of offerings.
Furthermore, he showed them:
"This is the Bodhisattva’s school; here one learns to ride elephants, and here one learns to ride horses, drive chariots, and use bows and crossbows."

Thus he trained in all arts and crafts: in this place the Bodhisattva attended to his physical needs; in this place the Bodhisattva’s sixty thousand ladies-in-waiting engaged in recreation; and in this place the Bodhisattva beheld the old, the sick, and the dead.

At this place, the Bodhisattva sat beneath a Jambū tree; while practicing dhyāna, he attained freedom from desire, and the shadow of the tree never left his body, so that his father, the King, prostrated himself before him.
At this place, the Bodhisattva, accompanied by hundreds of thousands of devas, departed from the city.
At this place, the Bodhisattva removed his jeweled necklaces and sent Chandaka back to the kingdom with the horse.
And he spoke in verse:
"At this place, the Bodhisattva removed his jeweled necklace and crown,
gave them to Chandaka, and sent the horse back to the kingdom."
"Traveling alone without a companion, he entered the Mountain of Learning the Way.
Furthermore, at this place, the Bodhisattva exchanged his garments with a hunter; having donned these robes, he went forth into homelessness.

This is the place where the rishis made their entreaty; this is the place where King Bimbisāra offered half his kingdom to the Bodhisattva; this is the place where he questioned the rishi Uruvilvā; and this is the place where the Bodhisattva practiced austerities for six years.
As stated in the verse:
"Having practiced asceticism for six years and endured the utmost suffering and affliction,
he realized that this was not the true path and abandoned the practices he had cultivated."
"In this place, the two women offered the Bodhisattva the milk-rice, as it is said in the verse:
'The Great Sage, within this very spot, Received the milk-rice from the two women;
From here he arose and departed, Proceeding toward the Bodhi tree. "
"In this place, the Naga Kali praised the Bodhisattvas, as it is said in verse:
'In this place, the Naga Kali Praised all the Bodhisattvas:
"You shall follow the ancient path And realize the unsurpassed, wondrous fruit."'"
Then the king addressed the Venerable One in verse:
"I now wish to see the dragon; that dragon who has seen the Buddha will proceed from here toward Bodhi and realize the supreme, wondrous fruit."
Then, the Venerable One pointed toward the dragon palace with his finger and said,
“Kāli Nāgarāja! Since you have seen the Buddha, you should now manifest your form.”
At that moment, the Dragon King emerged at the sound of his voice and stood before the Venerable One. Joining his palms, he said:
"What are your instructions?
Then the Venerable One spoke to the King:
"This Dragon King has seen the Buddha and praised the Tathāgata.
At that time, the king joined his palms toward the dragon and spoke in verse:
"You have seen the Vajra-body, my peerless Teacher."
"With a face like the pure full moon, tell me of his virtues—
of the merits of the One Possessing Ten Powers— at the time he went to the site of enlightenment.
Then the Dragon King replied in verse:
"I shall now proclaim: when his feet tread upon the earth, the great earth shook in six ways;
its radiance was twice that of the sun, illuminating the entire trichiliocosm as he proceeded toward the Bodhi tree."
“At that time, the king made various kinds of offerings in these and other places, and erected stupas and shrines.
Then, the Venerable One led the king to the foot of the Bodhi tree and said to him:
‘Under this tree, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, by the power of the Samādhi of Compassion, defeated the hosts of Māra and attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.’”
And he spoke these verses:
“The Muni, the Bull-King among men, beneath this Bodhi tree,
Subdued the armies of the evil Māra And attained the fruit of supreme enlightenment.”
"Among gods and humans, he is uniquely honored; none can equal him.
At that time, the king relinquished immeasurable treasures and various offerings, and erected a great stūpa and temple.
"At this place, the Four Great Kings each held a bowl and offered them to the Buddha, who joined them into a single bowl.
At this place, he received various offerings of food from the merchant brothers."
This is the place where the Tathāgata went to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī; there, the non-Buddhist Āśīva questioned the Buddha.
This is the Deer Park in the Garden of the Sages, where the Tathāgata, for the sake of the five bhikṣus, turned the Wheel of Dharma with its three revolutions and twelve aspects.
And he spoke in verse:
"In this place, the Deer Park, the Tathāgata turned the Wheel of Dharma;
With three turnings and twelve aspects, the five men attained the tracks of the Path."
At that time, the King established various kinds of offerings at this site and erected a stupa and temple.
"In this place, the Tathāgata brought the seers Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and his followers across to the Way."
In this place, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for King Bimbisāra; the king attained the vision of the Truths (*satyadarśana*), as did immeasurable commoners and devas who attained the Path.
In this place, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for Śakra, Lord of Devas; Śakra and eighty thousand devas attained the Path.
In this place, the Tathāgata manifested great supernormal powers and various transformations.
In this place, the Tathāgata ascended to the heavens to preach the Dharma for his mother, and then, leading immeasurable hosts of devas, descended back to the human realm.
The king again made various kinds of offerings and erected stupas and shrines.
At that time, the Venerable One spoke to King Aśoka as they arrived at the kingdom of Kuśinagara, saying:
"In this place, the Tathāgata fully completed his Buddha-work and entered parinirvāṇa in the nirvana without remainder."
And he spoke in verse:
“Having delivered all devas and humans, Asuras, nāgas, and yakṣas, I have established the inexhaustible Dharma; The Buddha’s work is now complete.”
"Having attained tranquility within existence, he enters nirvana out of great compassion;
like a fire extinguished when the wood is exhausted, he has finally attained eternal abiding.
When the king heard these words, he was overcome with grief and confusion, and fell prostrate upon the ground.
At that time, the ministers washed his heart and face with water; after a long while, he regained consciousness and wept, shedding tears profusely.
In this manner, they even offered various kinds of worship and erected a great stupa and temple.
At that time, the king spoke again to the Venerable One, saying:
"It is my wish to see those great disciples of the Buddha whom the Buddha himself has certified; I desire to make offerings to their relics, and I pray that you will show them to me."
Then, the Venerable One said to the King:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Great King, you have been able to give rise to such a sublime mind.
At that time, the Venerable One led the king to Śrāvastī and entered the Jetavana Monastery. Pointing to a stūpa with his finger, he said:
"This is the stūpa of the Venerable Śāriputra; Your Majesty should make offerings to it."
The King asked,
"What meritorious qualities does he possess?
The Venerable One replied:
"This is the second Dharma King, who turns the wheel of Dharma in accordance [with the Buddha]," he said,
and spoke this verse:
"The wisdom of all sentient beings, Compared to that of Śāriputra,..."
A single sixteenth part [of it] is used to set aside the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
as for the turning of the wheel of Dharma by the Tathāgata, one is able to turn in accordance with it—
yet who could possibly proclaim his immeasurable virtues?
At that time, the king was filled with great joy; he offered one hundred thousand *tolas* of precious jewels to the stupa and spoke this verse:
"I pay homage to Śāriputra, Who has liberated himself from all terrors;
His fame pervades the world, And his wisdom is without equal."
"Next, he again pointed out the stupa of Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:
'The King should make offerings to this stupa.
The King asked again:"
"What meritorious qualities does he possess?
The Venerable One replied:

"He is foremost in supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). With his toe he treads upon the earth, and the earth immediately quakes; he reaches the celestial palaces and subdues the dragon kings Nanda and Upananda."
And he spoke in verse:
"Moving the earth with a toe As far as the palace of Śakra,
With supernormal powers beyond compare— Who could fully describe them?"
"The two dragon kings were fierce and violent; none who saw them were not terrified.
Yet, through the power of his supernormal faculties, he subdued them and caused their anger to cease.
At that time, the king relinquished one hundred thousand measures of precious jewels to make offerings to this stupa, praising it with these verses:
"Foremost among those with supernormal powers, Free from old age, sickness, and death,
Possessing such merit as this— I now pay homage to Maudgalyāyana."
"Next, he again showed the stupa of Mahākāśyapa and said to the king:
'This is the stupa of Mahākāśyapa; it should be venerated.'"
The King asked,
"What merits does he possess?
He replied:

"He possesses few desires and is content; he is foremost among those who practice the dhūta austerities. The Tathāgata offered him half of his seat and his saṃghāṭī robe, out of compassion for sentient beings, so that he might establish the True Dharma."
Then he spoke in verse:
“The foremost field of merit, who takes pity on the poor and destitute;
wearing the saṃghāṭī robe of the Buddha, he is able to establish the True Dharma.”
"Who could fully proclaim the virtues he possesses?
Then, the king offered one hundred thousand measures of precious jewels as an offering to this stūpa and praised it with these verses:
"He always delights in tranquility, Taking refuge among the forest thickets."
"Rich in fewness of desires and contentment, I now pay homage to Mahākāśyapa.
Next, he again pointed out the stūpa of the Venerable Bakula:
"This is the stūpa of Bakula; it should be honored with offerings."
The King asked,
"What merits does he possess?
The Venerable One replied:
"He is foremost among those free from illness; he has not spoken even a single word of Dharma for others, remaining silent and without speech.
The King said, "I shall offer him one coin as an act of devotion."
The ministers said to the king,
"Since their merits are equal, why do you offer but a single coin to this one?
The king told them:
"Listen to what I say:
'Though one has eliminated ignorance and delusion, and though wisdom is able to discern clearly,
if one merely bears the name "Bakula," what benefit is there for the world?'"
Then, that single coin returned to the place where the king was.
At that time, the ministers, witnessing this rare occurrence, praised him with one voice:
"O! How marvelous!"
"Venerable One!
You have few desires and are content; you do not require even a single coin.
He then showed Ānanda’s stūpa to the king and said to him:
"This is the stūpa of Ānanda; it should be venerated.
The King asked, "What meritorious qualities did he possess?"
He replied:
"This person is an attendant of the Buddha, foremost in extensive learning, and the compiler of the Buddha’s scriptures.
Then he spoke this verse:
“Holding the Sage’s almsbowl, his mindfulness is capable of decisive resolution;
an ocean of vast learning, with eloquence and a gentle voice, he delights the multitudes of devas and humans;
well-knowing the minds of the three Buddhas...”
All things are fully understood; he is a precious casket of merit.
Praised by the Most Victorious One, he has subdued afflictions and strife.
Such virtues as these—one should cultivate offerings to him.
The king immediately relinquished ten billion taels of precious jewels to make offerings to that stupa.
At that time, the ministers said to the king,
"For what reason are these acts of giving and offering all superior to those previously performed?"
The King said:
"Listen to what I have to say regarding the reason within my heart:
'The body of the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body, whose nature is pure.'"
He is able to uphold them all; therefore, his offering is supreme.
The lamp of Dharma remains forever in the world, extinguishing the darkness of this ignorance;
since all this proceeds from him, his offering is supreme.
Just as the waters of the great ocean cannot be contained within a cow’s footprint,
so too the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom cannot be sustained by others.
Only the venerable Ānanda, upon hearing it but once, receives and upholds it all in its entirety.
"Never shall there be a time of forgetfulness; therefore, this offering is supreme.
At that time, the king, having made such various offerings, joined his palms toward the Venerable One and spoke these words:
"Now that I have received this form, I shall no longer be a burden to this body."
Having cultivated immeasurable merit, you are now the sovereign among men;
I now take hold of the essential core and erect various stūpas and temples,
adorning the world like stars adorning the moon.
The Dharma of the disciples who revere the Buddha requires that one observe all ritual proprieties;
these I have now fully performed. I bow my head at the feet of the Venerable One;
through the power of the Venerable One’s grace, I have now witnessed this most excellent and wondrous thing.
"Swiftly you shall obtain great and wholesome benefit; from this, distinguish the Dharma.
At that time, the King made various kinds of offerings and constantly went specifically to the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment.
Beneath this tree, the Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; it was with rare and precious offerings that he made worship to the Bodhi tree.
At that time, the king’s consort was named Tiṣyarakṣitā. The consort thought to herself:
"The king holds me in extreme affection, and I too hold him in affection; yet now the king abandons me and departs for the vicinity of the Bodhi tree, taking all his precious jewels with him."

I shall now employ a skillful means to kill this Bodhi tree; once the tree has withered and died, its leaves will fall away, and the King will no longer go there, so that I may constantly enjoy myself with him.
He immediately summoned a mantra-master and said to him:
"Are you able to kill the Bodhi tree? He replied:
"I can, provided you give me a thousand taels of gold.
At that time, the lady immediately gave him the thousand taels of gold.
The incantation master went to the Bodhi tree, cast spells upon the tree, and bound it with thread.
At that time, the tree gradually withered and its leaves began to fall; even before it was completely dead, its foliage was already decaying.
He said to the lady:
"Furthermore, you must pour hot milk upon the tree in order to cause it to wither."
The lady said to the king,
"I now wish to offer my milk as an offering to the Bodhi tree.
The king replied:
"Is it according to your wish?
Thus it continued until he poured hot milk over it, and the tree immediately withered.
At that time, the ladies said to the king:
"The Bodhi tree has suddenly withered, and its leaves have fallen one by one.
Then he spoke in verse:
"The tree upon which the Tathāgata relies, Known by the name of Bodhi,"
Having thus attained perfect enlightenment and become fully endowed with all-knowledge,
Great King, you should now know that this tree has now withered and died,
and the color of its leaves has also changed; we do not know for what reason.
When the king heard these words, he immediately fainted and fell to the ground. His attendants sprinkled water on his heart and face; after a long while, he revived and spoke with tears:
"When I saw the Bodhi tree, I saw the Tathāgata.
Now that I hear that tree has died, I too shall perish along with it."
At that time, seeing the king sorrowful and unhappy, the lady addressed him, saying:
"Lord, do not be distressed; I shall gladden your heart."
The king said:
"If that tree did not exist, my life would also not exist.
Since it was under that tree that the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, if that tree were gone, what use would I have for living?"
When the queen heard the king’s firm resolve, she returned once more and poured cold milk upon the Bodhi tree; the tree immediately sprouted again.
Hearing that the tree had been restored to life by being irrigated with milk, the king sent a thousand jars of milk every day to water its roots, and the tree was restored to its former state.
The ladies-in-waiting said to the king, "The Bodhi tree is now just as it was before; there is no difference at all.
When the king heard this, he immediately felt great joy and went beneath the Bodhi tree. Gazing upon the Bodhi tree, his eyes did not waver for a moment, and he spoke these verses:
"That which no kings have previously performed, King Bimbisāra, the protector of the land, now offers as an act of worship; I shall now bathe the Bodhi tree."
“With various milks and scented waters, Flowers, incense, and unguents, I shall further make offerings to the Sangha, The noble assembly of the five divisions.

At that time, the king prepared four jars for each of the precious substances—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—filled with various fragrant milks and scented decoctions. He brought diverse foods and drinks, a thousand kinds of banners, pennants, and jeweled parasols, as well as various flowers, perfumes, and musical instruments. Having observed the eightfold fast (upoṣadha), dressed in pure white garments, and holding incense burners, he stood upon the palace terrace, paid homage toward the four directions, and spoke these words with his mind:
"The noble disciples of the Tathāgata who dwell in various directions, out of compassion for me, accept my offerings.
He then spoke this verse:
"The noble sons of the Tathāgata, Rightly following and pacifying their faculties,"
Having transcended all desires of the three realms, you gods worthy of offerings, now gather here in full; receive this humble gift of my heart.
Out of compassion, respond to my intent and cause the seeds of the Dharma to flourish.
Always delighting in tranquil stillness, liberated from all attachments,
true sons of the Tathāgata, born through transformation from the Dharma,
and honored by the devas— out of compassion for me, [they have come].
Now you shall all assemble here to fulfill my humble wish.
You holy ones who dwell in various places— in Kaśmīra, Tāpasa, Mahāvana,
and Lumbinī, and by the side of the great lake Anavatapta— [come now].
From rivers, mountains, and marshes— indeed, from all such places—
may all those who dwell among the noble ones now gather together;
out of compassion for me, may they fulfill my humble wish.
Furthermore, those who dwell in the heavens, in the Śīrṣa palace,
and within the stone chambers of Mount Gandhamādana— those endowed with supernormal powers—
should now all assemble here out of compassion for me.
When the king had spoken thus, three hundred thousand bhikṣus all assembled.
Among that great multitude, one hundred thousand were arhats, and two hundred thousand were learners (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary bhikṣus; yet, no one sat upon the seat of the Elder.
At that time, the king asked the bhikṣus, "Why is there no one sitting upon the seat of the Elder?
Then, among that great assembly, there was a bhikṣu named Yaśas, who was a great arhat endowed with the six supernormal powers; he addressed the king, saying:
"This seat is the seat of the senior elder; how could anyone else dare to sit upon it?
The king asked again, "Is there yet another elder more senior than the Venerable One?"
The Venerable replied,
"There is another elder, Great King!
One spoken of by the Buddha named Piṇḍola— this is the elder who should sit in this place."
The king was greatly delighted and said:
"Is there any bhikṣu among you who has seen the Buddha?
The Venerable One replied:
“There is, Great King!
Piṇḍola still remains in this world.
The king spoke again, saying:
"Is it possible to see that bhikṣu?
The Venerable One replied,
"Great King!"
"Before long you shall see him; he will arrive shortly.
At that time, the king was filled with great joy and spoke these verses:
"I have now gained a swift benefit, For you have accepted me."
"May I see with my own eyes the Venerable Piṇḍola.
At that time, the Venerable Piṇḍola was followed in succession by immeasurable arhats.
It was as if a king of geese had come through the air and sat upon the seat of the presiding elder.
The assembly of bhikṣus each performed their salutations and took their seats in order.

At that time, seeing that the Venerable Piṇḍola had hair as white as snow and possessed the physical form of a pratyekabuddha, the king prostrated with his head at his feet, knelt for a long time with palms joined, and beholding the Venerable’s countenance, spoke this verse:
“This royal throne of mine, Ruling over Jambudvīpa, Brings me no joy;
Now that I have been able to see the Venerable.”
"Now that I behold the Venerable One, it is as if I behold a living Buddha;
my heart leaps with great joy, surpassing even the sight of royal sovereignty.
He then addressed the Venerable One again, saying:
"Venerable sir, have you seen the World-Honored One,
who is venerated by all within the three realms?
At that time, Venerable Piṇḍola raised his eyebrows with his hand, looked at the king, and said:
"I behold the Tathāgata, who has no peer in the world;
his body is the color of gold, adorned with the thirty-two marks of excellence.
His face is like the pure, full moon, and his Brahma-voice is soft and melodious."
"Having subdued the strife of all afflictions, he always dwells in quiescence.
The King asked again,
"In what place did the Venerable One see the Buddha?"
The Venerable said:
"The Tathāgata, together with five hundred arhats, was first entering the rains retreat at Rājagṛha; at that time, I was also among them."
And he spoke these verses:
“The Great Muni, the World-Honored One, Surrounded by those free from desire,
Is staying in the city of Rājagṛha, Observing the three-month summer retreat.”
"At that time, I was among that assembly, constantly dwelling by the side of the Tathāgata.
Great King, you should now know that I saw the True Buddha with my own eyes.

"Furthermore, when the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, the Tathāgata manifested great supernormal powers and various transformations, assuming the forms of all Buddhas that filled every direction up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven. At that time, I was also there, witnessing the various signs of the Tathāgata’s transformative supernatural powers."
And he spoke in verse:
“By the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, All non-Buddhists have been subdued.
As the Buddha travels through the ten directions, I have personally witnessed those signs.”
"Furthermore, when the Tathāgata was preaching the Dharma to his mother while in the heavens, I was also there among them;
having finished preaching the Dharma to his mother, he led the host of devas from the heavens down to the kingdom of Saṃkāśya."
At that time, I witnessed these two things:

gods and humans receiving blessings and joy, and the bhikṣuṇī Utpalā transforming herself into a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin), leading immeasurable retinues and traveling through the air to the place where the World-Honored One was; this too I witnessed.
And he spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata was in the heavens, observing the rains retreat there;
I too was among them, a member of the Muni’s retinue.”
"Furthermore, when the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī together with five hundred arhats,
it so happened that the daughter of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was residing in the country of Pūrṇabhadra."
At that time, she invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
Then, while the various bhikṣus each traveled there by means of the air, I at that moment used my supernatural power to join together a great mountain and went there to accept the invitation.
At that time, the World-Honored One rebuked me:
"How could you manifest such supernormal powers?
I now punish you: you shall remain forever in this world and not attain nirvana, so that you may protect and uphold my True Dharma and prevent it from perishing."
And he spoke in verse:
“The World-Honored One accepted his invitation, accompanied by five hundred bhikṣus;
at that time, by means of my supernormal power, I uprooted a great mountain and departed.”
"The World-Honored One has reprimanded me: 'While remaining in the world and not yet entering parinirvāṇa, you must protect and uphold my True Dharma, lest it perish and be extinguished.
"Furthermore, the Tathāgata, together with the community of bhikṣus, entered the city to beg for alms."
At that time, while the king was playing with two youths in the dust, he encountered the Buddha approaching; he took up the dust and sand and offered it to the Buddha.
Then the World-Honored One prophesied concerning those youths:
"A hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, this youth shall receive the royal throne in the city of Pāṭaliputra, rule over Jambudvīpa, and be named Aśoka."
"You shall widely distribute my relics, and within a single day, you shall construct eighty-four thousand stūpas.
This present king is that very person.
At that time, I was also among them.
And he spoke in verse:
"When the King was a young boy, He offered sand to the Buddha;
When the Buddha gave his prediction to the King, I was also personally present therein."
Then the king said to the Venerable One:
"Venerable One, where do you currently reside?
The Venerable One replied to the king:
"He is on the northern mountain, named Gandhamādana, together with a community of fellow practitioners of the holy life.
The king asked again,
"How many attendants does he have?"
The Venerable replied:
"Sixty thousand bhikṣus who are arhats.
The Venerable said:
“O King, why ask so many questions?
We shall now provide offerings to the Sangha;
when the meal is finished, we will cause the King to rejoice.”
The king said, "So be it, Venerable One! However,
I shall first make offerings to the Bodhi tree awakened by the Buddha's mindfulness, and only thereafter provide fragrant and delicious food for the Saṃgha."
He commanded his ministers to proclaim throughout the realm:

"The King now bestows one hundred thousand taels of gold as alms upon the assembly of monks; he has poured ten thousand jars of fragrant water over the Bodhi tree and has gathered the fivefold assembly."
At that time, the prince named Kunāla was on the king’s right side; he raised two fingers without speaking, intending to provide double the offerings.
When the great assembly saw this, they all burst into laughter; the king also laughed and said:
"Alas! Prince!"
"Therefore, there shall be an offering to increase merit.
The King spoke again:
"I shall further offer three hundred thousand taels of gold to the assembly of monks, and additionally provide a thousand jars of fragrant water to bathe the Bodhi tree."
At that time, the prince again raised four fingers, intending them to mean four times as much.
Then the king, filled with anger, said to his ministers:
"Who instructed the prince to do this and provoke a contest with me?"
The minister addressed the king, saying:
"Who would dare to compete with Your Majesty?
However, it is because the prince is wise, of sharp faculties, and increases his merit that he has performed this deed!"
Then the king looked back toward his son and said to the Elder:

"With the exception of the items in my treasury, I give all other things—my Jambudvīpa queens, court ladies, ministers, retinue, and even my son Kuṇāla—to the assembly of noble monks. Let a proclamation be made throughout the realm to assemble the fivefold community."
And he spoke in verse:
"Except for the treasures of the royal treasury, The queen, the court ladies,
and all the subjects— I give these as alms to the assembly of noble and holy monks."
"My own body and my princes, I shall likewise give them all away.
At that time, the King, the Elder, and the community of bhikṣus bathed the Bodhi tree with jars of fragrant water.
At that time, the Bodhi tree became even more magnificent and grew increasingly lush and flourishing. It was described in verse:
"The King bathes the Bodhi tree, The site of supreme awakening.
The tree increases its lushness and vigor; Its branches, twigs, and leaves are soft and supple."
At that time, the king and his ministers were filled with great joy.
Then, having bathed the Bodhi tree, the king proceeded to make offerings to the assembly of monks.
Then, the Elder Yaśas said to the king:
"Great King!
A great assembly of bhikṣus has gathered; you should give rise to pure faith and make offerings."
At that time, the king, from top to bottom, personally made offerings with his own hands.
Then there were two śrāmaṇeras who, having received their food, each took a ball of parched grain and a *modaka* and threw them at one another.
Upon seeing this, the king laughed and said,
"This śrāmaṇera is playing children's games.
Having finished making his offerings, the king returned to stand before the presiding elder.
The Elder said to the king,
"May Your Majesty not give rise to a mind of lack of faith or disrespect.
The king replied to the Elder:
"It was not that they lacked faith or respect; rather, they saw two śrāmaṇeras playing childish games, just like worldly children who toss lumps of earth back and forth at one another."
"In this way, those two śrāmaṇeras took balls of flour and *modaka* sweets, and threw them at one another.
The Elder addressed the King, saying,
"Those two śrāmaṇeras are Arhats liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta), who were offering food to each other."
Having heard this, the king’s faith increased, and he thought:
"Since these two śrāmaṇeras are able to give to one another in succession, I too shall now bestow silk and cotton cloth upon all the monks."
At that time, the two śrāmaṇeras, knowing what was in the king’s mind, said to one another:
“Let us cause the king’s reverence and faith to increase all the more.
One śrāmaṇera took a cauldron and presented it to the king; the other śrāmaṇera presented him with dyeing plants.
The king asked those two śrāmaṇeras,
"What were you using it for?
The two śrāmaṇeras replied to the king:
"Because of me, the King has bestowed silk and cotton cloth upon the community of monks; I wish to have the Great King dye these into color so that they may be given to the community of monks."
At that time, the king thought to himself:
"Although I had this thought in my mind but had not yet spoken it aloud,
these two realized ones possess the knowledge of others' minds and thus know my heart."
The king then bowed his head in reverent salutation to the assembly of monks and spoke this verse:
"Of the lineage of the peacock, All internal and external kinsmen and relatives,
By virtue of this act of giving, Shall all obtain great benefit."
"Having encountered this excellent field of merit, one should give with joy at the proper time.
At that time, the king said to the śrāmaṇeras:

"Because of you, I have given robes to the Saṃgha; having already given the robes to the Saṃgha, I further offer these three robes along with four hundred million taels of precious jewels as a donation to the five divisions of the assembly."
Having completed the offering of alms, he further used four hundred billion taels of precious jewels to redeem the palace ladies, court beauties, the crown prince, and the ministers of Jambudvīpa.
"Such are the immeasurable merits performed by King Aśoka.
*Saṃyukta Āgama*, Scroll Twenty-three;
*Saṃyukta Āgama*, Scroll Twenty-four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
The Fifth Recitation, Chapter One:
The Path (Mārgavarga). 24605 (605). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are four foundations of mindfulness.”
“What are the four? They are:
the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating the body as body, and the foundations of mindfulness by contemplating feelings, the mind, and phenomena as phenomena.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
606 (Six Hundred and Six). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are four foundations of mindfulness.
What are the four? They are:
the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplating the body as body, and the foundations of mindfulness consisting in contemplating feelings, the mind, and phenomena as phenomena.”
In this way, bhikṣus!
You should train yourselves in the cultivation and fulfillment of these four foundations of mindfulness, with diligent application, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
607 (Six hundred and seven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"There is a single vehicle path that purifies all sentient beings, enabling them to transcend sorrow and lamentation, to extinguish affliction and suffering, and to attain the Dharma as it truly is; this is known as the four foundations of mindfulness."
"What are the four?
They are the application of mindfulness by contemplating the body as body, and the applications of mindfulness by contemplating feelings, the mind, and phenomena as phenomena.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
608. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu is separated from the four foundations of mindfulness, he is separated from the noble dharmas that accord with reality;
being separated from the noble dharmas that accord with reality, he is separated from the noble path;
being separated from the noble path, he is separated from the dharma of the deathless."

Those who depart from the Dharma of the Deathless cannot escape birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering; I say that they do not attain liberation from suffering.
"If a bhikṣu does not depart from the four foundations of mindfulness, he will not depart from the noble, true Dharma;
if he does not depart from the noble, true Dharma, he will not depart from the noble path;
if he does not depart from the noble path, he will not depart from the Dharma of the Deathless."

One who does not depart from the nectar-like Dharma attains liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering; I declare that such a person is liberated from all suffering.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
609 (Six hundred and nine). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now speak of the arising and the passing away of the four foundations of mindfulness.
Listen attentively and reflect well upon this."
What are the arising and the passing away of the four foundations of mindfulness?
With the arising of nutriment comes the arising of the body; with the cessation of nutriment comes the passing away of the body.

Thus, one dwells contemplating the arising of the body, one dwells contemplating the passing away of the body, and one dwells contemplating both the arising and the passing away of the body. Then, being without dependence or dwelling, one never grasps at anything in the world.
"In this way, with the arising of contact, feeling arises; with the cessation of contact, feeling subsides.

Thus, one dwells contemplating feeling according to its principle of arising, dwells contemplating feeling according to its principle of cessation, and dwells contemplating feeling according to its principles of both arising and cessation. Then, being without any basis for dwelling, one grasps at nothing whatsoever in all the worlds."
"With the arising of name-and-form, the mind arises; with the cessation of name-and-form, the mind subsides.

When one dwells contemplating the mind according to the principle of its arising, dwells contemplating the mind according to the principle of its cessation, and dwells contemplating the mind according to the principle of both its arising and cessation, then one has no basis for dependence and grasps at nothing within the world."
“When mindfulness arises, phenomena arise; when mindfulness ceases, phenomena vanish.

One dwells contemplating phenomena according to their arising; one dwells contemplating phenomena according to their cessation; one dwells contemplating phenomena according to both their arising and cessation. Thus, there is no basis for dwelling, and one grasps at nothing within all the worlds.”
"This is called the arising of the four foundations of mindfulness and the disappearance of the four foundations of mindfulness.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
610. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall speak on the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness.
Listen attentively and reflect well.
How does one cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness?"

That is to say: he dwells contemplating the body as a body internally, diligent, resolute, with right knowledge and right mindfulness, subduing worldly sorrow and lamentation; he dwells contemplating the body externally and both internally and externally, diligent, resolute, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, subduing worldly sorrow and lamentation.

In this way, one dwells contemplating feelings, mind, and phenomena—internal phenomena, external phenomena, and both internal and external phenomena—with diligence and skillful means, with right mindfulness and clear comprehension, subduing worldly sorrow and lamentation; this is called a bhikṣu practicing the four foundations of mindfulness.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The same is said regarding the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness in the past and the future.
611 (611). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There is a collection of wholesome dharmas and a collection of unwholesome dharmas.
What is the collection of wholesome dharmas?
It is said that the four foundations of mindfulness constitute it; this is the correct teaching.”
Why is this? That which is a mass of pure, singular, and complete purity is what is called the four foundations of mindfulness. What are the four?
That is to say: the application of mindfulness to the body as body, and the applications of mindfulness to feelings, mind, and phenomena as phenomena.
What is the mass of the unwholesome?
The mass of the unwholesome refers to the five hindrances; this is the correct explanation.
Why is this so? Because a pure, uniform, and complete mass of unwholesome states consists of what are called the five hindrances.
What are these five?
"They are the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
612. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Just as a person holding four powerful bows, using great strength and skill, shoots at the shadow of a *tāla* tree, passing it by with such speed that there is no obstruction;

so too are the four kinds of śrāvakas of the Tathāgata. With superior application, sharp faculties, and wisdom, throughout a hundred-year lifespan, they receive the Tathāgata’s teachings and instructions for a hundred years—excepting only the time for eating, resting, relieving themselves, and sleeping—they constantly speak and constantly listen.
Their wisdom is clear and sharp; regarding what the Tathāgata has spoken, they grasp it thoroughly and completely without any hindrance, and they do not need to ask the Tathāgata again."

The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma has no end; one may listen to the Dharma for the duration of one's life, yet even at the end of a hundred years, the Tathāgata’s teaching would still not be exhausted.

One should know that what the Tathāgata speaks is immeasurable and boundless; the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables are likewise immeasurable and have no end—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness.
"What are the four?
They are the foundation of mindfulness of the body, and the foundations of mindfulness of feelings, the mind, and phenomena.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
All sūtras on the four foundations of mindfulness employ this summary statement:

"Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves in the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness, giving rise to superior desire, applying diligent effort, and maintaining right mindfulness and right clear comprehension."
613 (613). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There is a mass of unwholesomeness and a mass of wholesomeness.
What is the mass of unwholesomeness?
It refers to the three roots of unwholesomeness; this is called the correct teaching.”
Why is this so? That which is a pure accumulation of unwholesomeness refers to the three unwholesome roots.
What are these three?
They are the unwholesome root of greed, the unwholesome root of hatred, and the unwholesome root of delusion.
What is the aggregate of the wholesome?
It refers to the four foundations of mindfulness.
Why is this? That which is fully perfected by pure goodness refers to the four foundations of mindfulness; this is called the well-spoken teaching.
What are these four?
"Namely, the foundation of mindfulness of the body, and the foundations of mindfulness of feeling, mind, and phenomena.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Just as with the three unwholesome roots, so it is with the three types of misconduct—misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind; the three perceptions—the perception of sensual desire, the perception of ill will, and the perception of cruelty; the three thoughts—the thought of sensual desire, the thought of ill will, and the thought of cruelty; and the three realms—the realm of sensual desire, the realm of ill will, and the realm of cruelty.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
614 (614) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what has been called ‘a Great Man’ (mahāpuruṣa):”
"What is meant by a 'great man' and one who is not a great man?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!
Bhikṣu, you are able to ask the Tathāgata about the meaning of a mahāpuruṣa (great man).
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall explain it for you.

If a bhikṣu dwells contemplating the body as body, yet while dwelling thus in the contemplation of the body as body, his mind does not become free from desire and he does not attain liberation by exhausting all taints, I do not call him a great man.
Why is that? Because the mind is not liberated.

If a bhikṣu dwells contemplating feelings, the mind, and mental phenomena as phenomena, yet his mind is not free from desire and does not attain liberation, nor does he exhaust all taints, I do not call him a great man.
Why is this? Because the mind has not attained liberation.
"If a bhikṣu dwells contemplating the body as body, and his mind attains detachment from desire and his mind attains liberation, exhausting all outflows (āsravas), I call him a Great Man."
Why is this? Because of the liberation of the mind.

If one dwells in the contemplation of feelings, the mind, and mental phenomena as they truly are, and having so dwelled, the mind becomes detached from craving and attains liberation, exhausting all taints—of such a person I say, "He is a great man."
Why is this? Because the mind is liberated.
This, monks, is called...
“Great beings and those who are not great beings.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and were filled with gladness; they prostrated at his feet and departed.
615. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then, in the early morning, the Venerable Ānanda dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms. While on the road, he reflected:
"I shall go first to the bhikṣuṇī monastery.
He then proceeded to the bhikṣuṇī monastery.
Seeing Venerable Ānanda approaching from afar, the bhikṣuṇīs quickly prepared a seat and invited him to take his place.
Then, the bhikṣuṇīs prostrated at the feet of the Venerable Ānanda, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"We bhikṣuṇīs practice the four foundations of mindfulness, dwelling with the mind bound [to them], and we ourselves know our own progress and decline."
The Venerable Ānanda said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

Sisters! You should train yourselves as you have said. For anyone who practices the four foundations of mindfulness and dwells with the mind well-restrained, they should understand the progression and regression in this manner.
Then, the Venerable Ānanda taught the various bhikṣuṇīs the Dharma in many ways; having finished teaching the Dharma in many ways, he rose from his seat and departed.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda returned from begging for alms within the city of Śrāvastī; having put away his robes and bowl and washed his feet, he went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit at one side.
He reported in full what the bhikṣuṇī had said to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Excellent!”
Excellent!
You should train in this way: dwelling with the mind well-anchored through the four foundations of mindfulness, knowing its prior and subsequent rises and falls. Why is that?
When the mind seeks outwardly, he subsequently restrains it and causes it to seek the mind itself; he knows the distracted mind and the lack of liberation as they truly are.

If a bhikṣu dwells in the contemplation of the body as body, and while dwelling thus in the contemplation of the body as body, his body becomes drowsy and his mental states become indolent, that bhikṣu should arouse pure faith and grasp a pure sign.
Having aroused pure faith and recollected the pure sign, his mind then becomes gladdened; being gladdened, joy arises.
When his mind is joyful, the body becomes tranquil;
when the body is tranquil, he experiences physical bliss;
having experienced physical bliss, his mind becomes concentrated.
One whose mind is concentrated, a noble disciple, should train himself thus:

"Regarding this matter, I shall withdraw my outwardly scattered mind and cause it to rest; free from applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), I shall dwell in equanimity, mindfulness, and happiness;
having dwelt in happiness, I shall know it as it truly is."
"The same is to be said regarding the mindfulness of feeling, mind, and phenomena.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
616. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
“One should grasp the signs within one’s own mind and not allow them to scatter outwardly. Why is this?
If that bhikṣu is foolish, undiscerning, and unskilled, and instead of grasping the signs within his own mind grasps external signs, he will subsequently decline and create obstacles for himself.”

It is like a cook who is foolish and undiscerning, lacking skillful means in blending various flavors to serve his lord; whether the food is sour, salty, bitter, or bland, it does not suit his master's taste.
He was unable to skillfully discern what his master relished—the balance of sour, salty, bitter, and bland flavors among the various tastes.

He could not personally attend to his master’s side to manage his needs, listen to his desires, or skillfully grasp his mind; instead, he used his own judgment to blend the various flavors to present to his master.

If one does not act in accordance with their wishes, the sovereign will be displeased; being displeased, one will receive no rank or reward, nor will they hold one in affection. It is the same for the foolish bhikṣu:

being undiscerning and unskilled, he dwells in the contemplation of the body as body, yet cannot sever the higher afflictions, cannot master his mind, and likewise fails to attain inner tranquility. He does not attain sublime right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, nor does he attain the four types of higher mental states, the dwelling in happiness in this very life, or the peace of Nirvāṇa previously unattained. This is called a bhikṣu who is foolish, undiscerning, and unskilled; unable to properly master the signs of the internal mind, he grasps at external signs and thus creates obstacles for himself.

"If there is a bhikṣu who is wise and eloquent, skillful in means, and having first grasped the internal mind, subsequently grasps external signs, he will never later fall away or diminish, nor will he create obstacles for himself."

For example, suppose there is a cook who is clever, wise, and eloquent, possessing skillful means to serve his lord; he can prepare a variety of flavors—sour, salty, pungent, and bland—and is adept at discerning the signs of what his lord enjoys. He blends the various flavors to suit the lord’s mind, listening to the tastes his lord desires and repeatedly serving them. Once the lord is pleased, the cook will certainly receive rank and emolument, and the lord’s affection and regard for him will redouble.
Just as a wise cook skillfully captures the heart of his master, so too is it with a bhikṣu.

Abiding in the contemplation of the body as body, he severs the higher defilements, skillfully gathers his mind, and attains inner tranquility. With right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, he attains the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), dwells in happiness in this very life, and attains the previously unattained peace of *nirvāṇa*. This is called the bhikṣu’s wise eloquence and skillful means: he grasps the internal signs and maintains the external signs, never falling away or creating obstacles for himself. The same applies to the contemplations of feeling, mind, and phenomena.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 617 (617) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In a past age, there was a bird named Rāva who was seized by a hawk. As it soared through the void, it cried out in the sky, saying:
'I did not realize it myself, yet suddenly I have encountered this calamity. It is because I abandoned the domain of my parents to wander in other places that I have met with this disaster.'"
"How is it that today you are beset by others and lack autonomy?
The hawk said to Lopa,
"In what place could you possibly have your own domain where you might attain autonomy?"
Rāva replied, "Within the furrows of my plowed field, I have my own domain that is sufficient to avoid all calamities; this is the domain of my parents' home."
The hawk, conceiving arrogance toward Rāva, said:
"I release you to go; once you have returned to the furrow of the plow, will you be able to escape?

Thereupon, Rāva escaped the hawk's talons and returned to the base of a large clod of earth in the furrow, settling there in his place of rest; only then did he intend to fight the hawk atop the clod.

The hawk became violently enraged, thinking, "That is but a small bird, yet dares to fight me! His fury reaching its peak, he flew swiftly and struck directly at him. Thereupon, Rāva entered beneath a clod of earth; the force of the hawk’s flight caused his breast to collide with the hard clod, shattering his body and killing him instantly.
At that time, the raven was crouching deeply beneath a clod of earth; looking up, he spoke this verse:
“The hawk has come with great effort; The raven relies upon his own domain.
Yet, driven by the fierce power of his rage, He brings about disaster and shatters his own body.”
I am fully possessed of thorough penetration;
relying upon my own domain, I subdue enmity and rejoice accordingly, observing myself and delighting in that power.
Even if you were to possess the fierce and foolish strength of hundreds of thousands of nāga-elephants, [it would avail you nothing].
"It does not equal even a sixteenth part of my wisdom.
Behold the excellence of my insight, which utterly destroys the blue hawk.
Thus it was, O bhikṣus!
Just as that hawk, out of folly, abandoned its own kin, its parents, and its natural domain to wander elsewhere, thereby bringing upon itself this calamity;

so too should you, O bhikṣus, likewise act: you should skillfully maintain yourselves within your own domain and sphere of activity, and you should train yourselves to remain aloof from the domains of others.

“Bhikkhus! ‘Another place, another realm’ refers to the realm of the five sensual desires: seeing with the eye forms that are agreeable, desirable, and pleasing to the mind, one becomes stained by attachment through desire;

likewise, with the ear one cognizes sounds, with the nose scents, with the tongue flavors, and with the body tangibles that are agreeable, desirable, and pleasing to the mind, one becomes stained by attachment through desire.”
This is called the bhikṣu’s other place and other domain. Bhikṣus!
One’s own place and the domain of one’s parents refers to the four foundations of mindfulness.
What are the four?
They are the application of mindfulness to the body as body, and the applications of mindfulness to feelings, the mind, and phenomena as phenomena.
Therefore, bhikṣus!
"One should train oneself thus: 'I shall wander within my own domain and the domain of my parents, remaining far removed from other places and the domains of others.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
618. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"By frequently practicing the four foundations of mindfulness, one shall attain the four fruits and four kinds of benefits.
What are these four?
They are the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 619 (619) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of Kośala, staying in the Śiṃśapā Grove north of the village of Sāketa.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, there was a master of the banner-entertainment (yaṣṭi-kāraka). He erected a banner upon his shoulder and said to his disciples:

'You all must protect me from above and below on this banner, and I shall likewise protect you; thus, by mutually supporting one another, we shall travel about, perform our entertainments, and obtain much wealth and profit.'"
Then, the apprentice said to the master: "It is not as you say;
we should simply each take care of ourselves, travel about, and enjoy our play, so that we may acquire much wealth and profit, and descend safely in peace and security."
The master of the arts replied:

"As you have said, each must protect themselves; however, this principle is also as I have explained: when one protects oneself, one protects others, and when others protect themselves, they also protect oneself.
When the mind draws near to itself, cultivating, guarding, and realizing [this state], this is called protecting oneself and protecting others."

What is protecting others while protecting oneself? It is not terrifying others, not opposing others, and not harming others; with a mind of loving-kindness and compassion for them—this is called protecting others while protecting oneself.
"Therefore, bhikṣus, you should train yourselves thus:
those who protect themselves cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness; those who protect others also cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 620 (620) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the Great Snow Mountains, even in places of cold ice and perilous terrain, there are not even monkeys, much less human beings."
Furthermore, there are mountains inhabited by monkeys but devoid of humans;

and there are other mountains where humans and animals dwell together. In such places frequented by monkeys, hunters smear sticky resin upon the grass. A clever monkey avoids it from afar and departs, but a foolish monkey, unable to avoid it, touches it with his hand and immediately has his hand stuck.
Seeking to free himself, he tries to pull both hands away, and thus both hands become stuck.
Seeking release with his feet, he again had his feet stuck;
chewing on grass with his mouth, he immediately had his mouth stuck as well.
With all five limbs stuck together, he lay on the ground, curled up and entangled.
When the hunter arrived, he immediately impaled it with his staff and carried it away on his shoulder.
"Bhikṣus, you should know that this foolish monkey abandoned its own domain and the dwelling place of its parents to roam in another's territory, thereby bringing upon itself such suffering."

In this way, bhikṣus, foolish worldlings dwell in dependence upon a village. In the morning, they put on their robes and take up their bowls to enter the village for alms. They do not skillfully guard their bodies nor restrain the gates of their sense faculties. Having seen forms with the eye, they give rise to defiled attachment;
having heard sounds with the ear, smelled odors with the nose, tasted flavors with the tongue, or felt tangibles with the body, they likewise give rise to defiled attachment.
When a foolish bhikṣu’s internal faculties and external objects are bound by the five fetters, he follows whatever the Māra desires.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should train yourselves in this way:
dwell relying upon the sphere of your own parents as your domain of practice; do not follow the conduct of other places or other spheres.
What is the domain of one's own practice and the sphere of one's parents for a bhikṣu?
It refers to the four foundations of mindfulness: dwelling in the contemplation of the body as body, and dwelling in the contemplation of feelings, mind, and phenomena as phenomena.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
621 (621) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, together with a great number of bhikṣus, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet in salutation, and withdrew to sit at one side.
The Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"How should these young bhikṣus be instructed?
How should the Dharma be taught to them?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“O young bhikṣus, you should instruct these [monks] to practice the four foundations of mindfulness.
What are the four? They are:

dwelling in the contemplation of the body as body, with diligent application, heedfulness, right knowledge, and right mindfulness, with the mind settled in tranquility, even unto the full understanding of the body;”

He dwells contemplating feelings as feelings, the mind as mind, and mental phenomena as mental phenomena, with diligence and skillful means, practicing heedfulness, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, calming the mind, and even coming to know mental phenomena.

Why is this so? If a bhikṣu abides on the stage of training and has not yet attained further progress, when he aspires for the peace of nirvāṇa, he dwells contemplating the body as body, applying himself with diligence and skillful means, practicing without negligence, with right mindfulness and clear comprehension, and bringing tranquility to the mind;

he dwells contemplating feelings, the mind, and phenomena as phenomena, applying himself with diligence and skillful means, practicing without negligence, with right mindfulness and clear comprehension, and bringing tranquility to the mind, even unto detachment from phenomena.

If an Arhat, whose taints are exhausted, who has done what was to be done, who has laid down the heavy burden, who has destroyed the fetters of existence, and who is rightly liberated through perfect knowledge, even at that time continues to dwell in the contemplation of the body as the body, applying himself with diligence and skillful means, practicing heedfulness, with right mindfulness and clear comprehension, his mind being tranquil;
he likewise dwells in the contemplation of feelings, the mind, and mental phenomena as phenomena, until he attains seclusion regarding those phenomena.
Then the Venerable Ānanda rejoiced and approved, paid homage, and departed.
622 (622) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of the Vṛji country and arrived at the Āmra Park in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, where he stayed.

At that time, having heard that the World-Honored One was traveling through the Vṛji country and had arrived to stay in the Āmra Park, the lady Āmrapālī adorned herself, mounted her carriage, and departed from the city of Vaiśālī to go to where the World-Honored One was, in order to pay him respectful homage and offerings.
She went to the gate of Āmrapālī’s grove, alighted from her carriage, and proceeded on foot. From afar, she saw the World-Honored One surrounded by a great assembly as he preached the Dharma.
Seeing Āmrapālī approaching from a distance, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Bhikṣus, you must diligently restrain your minds and abide in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension."
Now that the woman Āmrapālī has arrived, I therefore admonish you:
How does a bhikṣu dwell with a mind diligently restrained?
If a bhikṣu perceives that unwholesome and evil states have arisen, he should generate the desire and apply the means to abandon them, exerting himself to restrain his mind.

Not allowing unarisen evil and unwholesome states to arise; causing unarisen wholesome states to arise; and ensuring that arisen wholesome states remain, are not forgotten, and are cultivated to fulfillment—generating desire, applying means, and exerting effort to restrain the mind: this is called a bhikṣu dwelling with diligent restraint of the mind.
"What is meant by a bhikṣu possessing right mindfulness?

If a bhikṣu, in all his movements and postures—whether going or coming, looking back or looking ahead, bending or stretching, bowing or rising, holding his robes and bowl, walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, speaking, or remaining silent—always dwells in accordance with right mindfulness, this is called right mindfulness."
"What is right mindfulness?
It is when a bhikṣu dwells contemplating the body as the body internally, ardent, with clear comprehension and right mindfulness, having subdued worldly greed and sorrow."

In this way, one dwells contemplating feelings, the mind, and mental phenomena as phenomena; with diligence and skillful means, with right knowledge and right mindfulness, one subdues worldly greed and sorrow—this is called a bhikṣu’s right mindfulness.
"Therefore, you all must diligently restrain your minds with right wisdom and right mindfulness; since Āmrapālī is now approaching, I have warned you.
At that time, Āmrapālī went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.

having thus instructed, exhorted, illuminated, and gladdened her, he remained silent.
At that time, Āmrapālī adjusted her robes, paid homage to the Buddha, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha:

At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

Knowing that the World-Honored One had accepted by his silence, Āmrapālī bowed her head at his feet, returned to her own home, prepared various kinds of food, arranged the seats, and sent a messenger in the early morning to inform the Buddha:

Then, the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly, went to the house of Āmrapālī and sat down upon the prepared seats.
