the lady Āmrapālī took a small seat and sat before the Buddha to listen to his teaching of the Dharma. At that time,
the World-Honored One spoke these verses of rejoicing for the lady Āmrapālī:
"The giver is loved and cherished by others, followed by a great multitude;
his fame increases day by day, heard by all far and near.
Amidst the assembly he is always harmonious and refined, free from stinginess and without fear."
Therefore, through the gift of wisdom, one cuts off stinginess forever without remainder.
Reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, one enjoys happiness throughout the long night;
practicing virtue constantly for the duration of one's life, one delights in the Nandana Grove.
With a hundred kinds of celestial music, their hearts are gladdened by the five desires.
Yet, in this human realm, having heard the Dharma taught by the Buddha,
they become disciples of the Sugata and delight in that state of transformation through birth.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to the woman Āmrapālī in various ways, instructing, exhorting, illuminating, and gladdening her;

Guarding one's own mind, one has never reached a place where it is exceedingly difficult to transcend;

One should unify the mind and maintain it with focused diligence;

When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Thereupon, having heard the words of the novice Cunda, the Venerable Ānanda went to where the Buddha was and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
My entire body now feels as if it were being torn apart; my four limbs have lost their strength, and my eloquence is stifled. The novice Cunda came and spoke these words to me:"
“‘The Upādhyāya Śāriputra has already entered parinirvāṇa; he has brought these remaining relics, as well as his robes and bowl.
The Buddha said, “How is this so?”
Ānanda! Did that Śāriputra enter parinirvāṇa by means of the aggregate of morality he had received?
Or did he enter parinirvāṇa by means of the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, or the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha,
“No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"Are those dharmas which I have known for myself and proclaimed upon attaining perfect enlightenment—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold path—the same as nirvāṇa?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha: “No, World-Honored One!

Although one may enter parinirvāṇa without maintaining the aggregate of precepts received, up to the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma), nevertheless, the Venerable Śāriputra maintains the precepts and is widely learned; he has few desires and is content, constantly practices seclusion, is diligent in skillful means, and dwells with collected mindfulness. He possesses swift wisdom, sharp and penetrating wisdom, transcendent wisdom, analytical wisdom, great wisdom, vast wisdom, profound wisdom, and unequaled wisdom. Having accomplished this jewel of wisdom, he is able to demonstrate, instruct, illuminate, and gladden; he is skilled at praising [the Dharma] and preaching the Dharma for the sake of the multitude.”
"Therefore, World-Honored One,
for the sake of the Dharma and for the sake of those who receive the Dharma, I am grieved, distressed,
and afflicted. The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do not grieve, lament, or be distressed. Why is this?

Whether sitting, standing, or acting, all conditioned things are subject to decay and destruction; how could they not perish? It is impossible for them not to perish. As I have previously said, all cherished objects and pleasing matters are by nature subject to separation and cannot be preserved forever."

It is like a great tree with flourishing roots, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit; first its great branches break off, just as from a great mountain of jewels, first its great crags collapse.

In this way, among the great assembly of the Tathāgata’s retinue, if those great śrāvakas have already entered parinirvāṇa, yet Śāriputra remains in that region, then I have no concern regarding that region; however, that region is not empty for me because Śāriputra is there, as I have already stated previously.
"Now, Ānanda!
As I have said before, all things that are cherished and pleasing to the mind are subject to separation; therefore, do not now be overcome by great grief and anguish."
Ānanda! You should know that the Tathāgata will also pass away before long. Therefore, Ānanda!
"You should make yourself an island and rely upon yourself; you should make the Dharma an island and rely upon the Dharma; you should make the non-different an island and rely upon the non-different.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
What is it to have oneself as an island and to rely upon oneself?
What is it to have the Dharma as an island and to rely upon the Dharma?
What is it to have nothing else as an island and nothing else as a reliance?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If a bhikṣu dwells contemplating the body as body, with diligence and skillful means, with right knowledge and right mindfulness, he subdues worldly greed and sorrow."
In this same way, the applications of mindfulness regarding the external body, the internal-external body, feelings, the mind, and mental phenomena are also explained thus.

Ānanda! This is called taking oneself as an island and relying upon oneself, taking the Dharma as an island and relying upon the Dharma, and not taking anything else as an island and not relying upon anything else.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 639 (639) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying on the bank of the Bhadrā River in the kingdom of Mathurā, in the Campaka-āmra grove, not long after the parinirvāṇa of the Venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.
At that time, on the fifteenth day of the month during the *poṣadha* ceremony, the World-Honored One arranged his seat and sat before the great assembly.
Having surveyed the gathered multitude, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I observe this great assembly and see it as empty, for Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana have entered parinirvāṇa."
"Among my śrāvakas, only these two are well able to preach the Dharma, provide exhortation and instruction, and possess perfect eloquence.

There are two kinds of wealth: material wealth and the wealth of the Dharma. Material wealth is sought from worldly people; the wealth of the Dharma is sought from Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana. The Tathāgata has already relinquished both material wealth and the wealth of the Dharma."
“Do not grieve, suffer, or be distressed because of the parinirvāṇa of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.

It is like a great tree with flourishing roots, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit, whose large branches have first broken off; it is also like a mountain of jewels, whose great cliffs have first collapsed.”
Thus, within the great assembly of the Tathāgata, the two great śrāvakas, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, have already entered parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, bhikṣus!
Do not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, or distress; for how could any phenomenon that is born, arisen, conditioned, and subject to volitional formation—not be subject to destruction?
To wish that this should not perish is impossible; as I have already said, all beloved things inevitably lead to separation and dispersal, and I too shall soon pass away.

Therefore, you should know this: take yourself as your island and rely on yourself; take the Dharma as your island and rely on the Dharma; do not have another as your island or another as your reliance. This means abiding in the contemplation of the body within the body, applying diligent effort, with right wisdom and right mindfulness, to subdue worldly greed and sorrow.

In this way, one dwells contemplating the body as body externally, the body internally and externally, and likewise with regard to feelings, the mind, and phenomena; with diligence and skillful means, with right knowledge and right mindfulness, one subdues worldly greed and sorrow. This is called making oneself an island and relying on oneself, making the Dharma an island and relying on the Dharma, having no other island and no other reliance.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*Saṃyukta Āgama*, Scroll Twenty-four.
*Saṃyukta Āgama*, Scroll Twenty-five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
25.640 (640). At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:

"In this country of Mathurā, in a future age, there shall be a son of a merchant named Gopadatta. Gopadatta shall have a son named Upagupta, who, one hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, shall perform the work of a Buddha and be the foremost among teachers."
"Ānanda! Do you see from afar that blue forest?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
"Yes, indeed, I have seen them,
World-Honored One! " "Ānanda!"

This place is named Mount Urumanda; one hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, there shall be a forest hermitage (āraṇyaka) called Nāthabhaṭika on this mountain, and this location will be foremost in its conformity with silent seclusion.
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:
"If I were to entrust the teaching to human beings, I fear my teaching would not endure for long;
if I were to entrust it to devas, I fear my teaching would likewise not endure for long, and there would be no one among the people of the world to receive the Dharma."
I shall now entrust the True Dharma to humans and devas; as long as gods and people of the world together uphold the Dharma, my teaching shall remain unshakable for a thousand years.
At that time, the World-Honored One gave rise to a mundane thought.

Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the Four Great Heavenly Kings, knowing the Buddha’s mental intention, approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the Four Great Heavenly Kings:
“The Tathāgata will before long enter parinirvāṇa in the nirvana without remainder. After my parinirvāṇa, you all shall protect and uphold the True Dharma.”
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Heavenly King of the East:
"You should protect and uphold the True Dharma in the eastern direction.
He then addressed the Heavenly Kings of the South, the West, and the North.
“You shall protect and uphold the True Dharma in the northern region.
After a thousand years have passed, when my teaching is about to perish, unrighteousness will emerge in the world and the ten wholesome paths will all be destroyed.”

Within Jambudvīpa, violent winds arose and rain fell out of season; the world suffered much from famine, and when it did rain, there were calamitous hailstorms. Rivers and streams dried up, flowers and fruits failed to ripen, and people lost their luster. The villages of insects and the villages of ghosts were all utterly destroyed; food and drink lost their flavor, precious gems sank away, and the people subsisted on coarse and bitter herbs and wood.
"At that time, there were King Śākya, King Jayanana, King Prabhāsa, and King Tuṣāra, along with their numerous retinues.
The Tathāgata’s cranial bone, his tooth, and his alms bowl were enshrined in the eastern direction."
In the west there is a king named Prabhāva, with hundreds of thousands of attendants, who destroys stūpas and monasteries and slaughters bhikṣus.
In the north there is a king named Jayana, with hundreds of thousands of attendants, who destroys stūpas and monasteries and slaughters bhikṣus.
In the south there is a king named Śākya, with hundreds of thousands of attendants, who destroys stūpas and monasteries and slaughters bhikṣus.
In the east there is a king named Tuṣāra, with hundreds of thousands of attendants, who destroys stūpas and monasteries and slaughters bhikṣus.
The four quarters were in total turmoil, and the bhikṣus came together in the Middle Kingdom.

At that time, there was a king in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī named Mahendrasena; he had a son whose hands resembled blood-stained palms and whose body resembled armor, and who possessed great heroic strength.
On the day he was born, five hundred ministers each gave birth to five hundred sons, all resembling the prince, with blood-stained hands and bodies clad in armor.
At that time, it rained blood for one day in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
When the King of Kauśāmbī saw these evil omens, he was seized with great terror and questioned his diviners.
The diviners said to the king:
"The son born to you today shall rule over Jambudvīpa and will kill many people. Seven days after his birth, he shall be named Duryodhana (Difficult to Withstand), and as he gradually grows older..."
"At that time, four wicked kings will come from the four directions to slaughter the people, and when King Mahendrasena hears of this, he will be terrified.
Then, a celestial deity addressed him, saying:
"Great King, establish Durdharsa as king; he is fully capable of subduing those four wicked kings."

Then, King Māhendrasena, having received the instruction of the celestial deity, immediately abdicated his throne in favor of his son; he placed the bright pearl from his topknot upon the crown of his son’s head, assembled all the great ministers, and performed the consecration with scented water.
He summoned five hundred ministers who were born on the same day as himself; clad in armor, they followed the king on an expedition to wage war against the four wicked kings and their great hosts.
Having been victorious, he slaughtered them all and ruled over Jambudvīpa, with his capital in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Four Great Heavenly Kings:
"In the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, there shall be a brahmin named Agnidatta who is thoroughly versed in the Vedas and their commentaries; that brahmin shall take a wife."
At that time, a being in the intermediate state (antarābhava) was destined to become his son. When he entered the mother’s womb, she felt a desire to engage in debate with others.
That brahmin immediately questioned the physiognomists, and the physiognomists replied:
"The being within this womb will master all treatises; therefore, it has caused the mother to give rise to such a desire for debate, wishing to argue with others."

When the months and days were thus fulfilled, he was born from his mother’s womb and became a youth. He thoroughly mastered all the sūtras and śāstras, and constantly taught the five hundred sons of brahmins the sūtras and śāstras; he taught other persons various other treatises, and he taught medical practitioners the art of medicine. In this way, he had a great many disciples.
Because he has many disciples, he is called "Disciple.

Subsequently, he shall seek to leave the household life and study the Path under his parents; eventually, when his parents grant him permission to renounce the world, he will immediately go forth within my Dharma to study the Path. He will master the Tripitaka, become skilled in preaching the Dharma, possess subtle eloquence, and through his speech and discourse, gather a great multitude of followers.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One addressed the Four Great Heavenly Kings:
"In this city of Pāṭaliputra, there shall be a great caravan leader named Sudhana, into whose mother’s womb a being from the intermediate state (antarābhava) will enter."
When that sentient being entered his mother’s womb, he caused the mother to become upright and gentle, free from all perverse thoughts, and with her faculties in a state of tranquility.
At that time, the merchant leader questioned the physiognomist, who replied:
"The being within the womb is exceedingly virtuous; therefore, he causes the mother to be thus, even to the point of her faculties being tranquil."
When the months were fulfilled, a boy was born, named Śūradatta.
As he gradually grew older, he eventually addressed his parents, requesting to leave the household life to study the Path.

His parents immediately granted permission; he left the household life within my Dharma to study the Path, practicing with diligent effort and cultivating the tasks of the Way, whereby he attained the exhaustion of outflows and realized the fruit of Arhatship.
However, he was one of few learning, with few desires, contented, and of little knowledge; he formerly dwelt among the mountains, thickets, and forests on a mountain named Gandhamādana.
At that time, that holy man would constantly come to preach the Dharma for King Dhananjaya.

When his father, the king, was about to pass away, on the day of that passing, finding it difficult to bear seeing his father depart this world, he embraced his father’s corpse with both hands, wailing and weeping in grief, his heart pierced by sorrow and distress.

At that time, the Tripitaka Master, accompanied by a large retinue, came to the king’s presence and preached the Dharma for him. Having heard the Dharma, the king’s distress and anxiety immediately ceased; he conceived great reverence and faith in the Buddha’s teachings and cried out:
"From this day forward, I grant all bhikṣus freedom from fear, allowing them to dwell in comfort and joy."
He then asked the bhikṣus:
"For how many years have these four previous wicked kings destroyed the Buddha-dharma?
The bhikṣus replied:
"Having completed twelve years," the King thought in his heart and spoke these words, making a lion’s roar:
"For twelve years, I shall provide offerings to the fivefold assembly, even providing all manner of requisites."
"Immediately perform acts of giving; on the day you give, the heavens shall send down a fragrant and moist rain throughout Jambudvīpa, so that all actual seeds may grow and flourish."
People from all directions, bringing offerings, came to the kingdom of Kauśāmbī to make offerings to the community of monks.
At that time, the bhikṣus received great offerings.
These monks, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, do not recite or study the scriptures, nor do they engage in formal instruction for others.

They pass their days in frivolous chatter and spend the entire night in sleep. Greedily attached to gain and offerings, they delight in self-adornment, wearing exquisite robes, and thereby distance themselves from the essential path, from tranquility, from the life of renunciation, and from the bliss of *sambodhi*.

These individuals who merely bear the outward form of bhikṣus have abandoned the merits of a śramaṇa; they are great thieves within the Dharma. They assist in the destruction of the banner of the True Dharma during the final age, erecting the banner of Māra instead. They extinguish the torch of the True Dharma, kindling the fires of affliction; they destroy the drum of the True Dharma and ruin the wheel of the True Dharma; they cause the ocean of the True Dharma to evaporate and the mountain of the True Dharma to crumble; they break down the city of the True Dharma and uproot the tree of the True Dharma; they demolish meditative concentration and wisdom, sever the jeweled necklace of precepts, and defile the Right Path.

At that time, those devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others conceived malicious intentions toward the bhikṣus; they reviled the bhikṣus, detested and shunned them, and no longer associated with them, saying with one voice: "Alas!..."
"Such evil bhikṣus should not be within the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Then he spoke this verse:
"Practicing what is inauspicious and performing evil deeds, They practice various dharmas of false views."
These ignorant people strike down the mountain of the True Dharma;
they practice various evil precepts and abandon all conduct in accordance with the Dharma.
They cast aside the supreme and wondrous teachings and uproot the Buddha-Dharma of the present age.
Lacking faith and unsubdued, they delight in practicing various evil deeds;
deceitful and hypocritical, they deceive the world.
They shatter the Dharma of the Muni, ruin their appearance while habituating themselves to all manner of evils, including violence and a thousandfold transgressions.
Deceiving the world by relying on the Dharma, harboring resentment and self-conceit,
greedily clinging to the pursuit of fame and profit— they fail to avoid any kind of evil karma.
As the Buddha has taught, when the Dharma perishes, these are its characteristics.
Now all have been seen, those things despised by the wise;
now that this dharma has emerged, the ocean of the Muni’s true Dharma shall soon dry up; the true Dharma now remains but little.
"Evil men shall come again to extinguish it, destroying my True Dharma.
At that time, those devas, nāgas, and spirits all gave rise to a heart of displeasure; they would no longer protect the bhikṣus, and with one voice they cried out:
"The Buddha-Dharma will be utterly extinguished seven days from now!"
Wailing and weeping with grief, they said to one another:
"When the day comes for the bhikṣus to recite the precepts, if they quarrel and dispute among themselves, the True Dharma of the Tathāgata will perish therein."
Thus the devas wept in grief and distress.

At that time, there were five hundred upāsakas in the city of Kauśāmbī who, having heard the words of the devas, went together to the assembly of bhikṣus to admonish the bhikṣus for their quarreling, and spoke this verse:
“Alas! What bitter suffering! We take pity on the multitude of living beings.”
That Dharma now perishes; the Dharma of the Lion-King Śākyamuni is destroyed by the wheel of evil.
Even such adamantine things may not be immediately destroyed, yet the time of peace and security has already passed away.
The perilous dharma has arisen; the wise have already passed away.
Seeing such signs as these now, one should know that it will not be long before the Dharma of the Muni is extinguished and the world is left without illumination.
The mouth of stainless quiescence, the Sun of the Muni, has now set;
the people of the world have lost their hidden treasure.
With no distinction between good and evil, and once good and evil are no longer distinguished, who will be able to attain perfect awakening?
The Lamp of Dharma now dwells in this world; practice all manner of virtues while there is still time.
Among the immeasurable fields of merit, this Dharma is now about to perish.
Therefore, we recognize that wealth is not firm or lasting.
"Seize the opportunity while it is firm and solid.

When the time for the recitation of the precepts on the fifteenth day arrived, the Dharma was about to perish; on this very day, five hundred upāsakas constructed five hundred Buddha-stūpas within a single day.
At that time, the lay devotees (upāsakas) each had other affairs and no longer frequented the assembly of the Sangha.
At that moment, the Arhat Śūradatta, dwelling on Mount Gandhamādana, surveyed Jambudvīpa and thought:
"Where today is there a community of monks reciting the precepts?"
Seeing that the disciples of the Tathāgata in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī were performing the *poṣadha* by reciting the precepts, he immediately went to Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the monastic community there numbered hundreds of thousands, among whom there was only a single arhat named Surādha.
Furthermore, there was another Tripitaka master named Śiṣya; this was the final great assembly of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Karmadāna distributed the śalākā voting sticks and addressed the Tripitaka Elder, saying:
"The Saṃgha has assembled, numbering hundreds of thousands; now please recite the Prātimokṣa for them."
At that time, the Elder replied:
"The disciples of the Tathāgata from Jambudvīpa have all gathered here, numbering in the hundreds of thousands.
Among such a multitude, I am the foremost; yet even I, who have mastered the Tripitaka, do not study the Vinaya, much less do others have anything to learn."
"Now for whom shall I preach the Vinaya?
He then spoke in verse:
"Today is the fifteenth day; The night is tranquil and the moon is clear and bright."
Thus, O bhikṣus, you have now gathered to hear the precepts.
This is the final assembly of the Saṅgha throughout all of Jambudvīpa;
I am the foremost among this multitude. If one does not study the laws of the Vinaya, [what benefit shall there be?]
How much less could other members of the monastic community have anything to learn?
How could they possibly [master] the Dharma of the Muni, the Lion-King Śākyamuni?
Who among them could uphold those precepts? Only such a person as this can truly speak [of them].
At that time, the Arhat Śrutasoma stood before the Elder, joined his palms, and addressed the Elder, saying: "Elder!
Simply recite the Prātimokṣa. Just as when the Buddha was in the world, the great assembly of bhikṣus such as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana studied the Dharma, I have now fully mastered it."
"Although the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, more than a thousand years have passed since then; yet the disciplinary rules he established, I have fully mastered.
Then he spoke in verse:
"Listen, O Elder, to my words: My name is Śūlata."
The Arhat whose outflows are exhausted, the lion’s roar among the Saṅgha—
the true disciple of the Muni— was heard by the various devas and spirits who have faith in the Buddha;
hearing what that Sage had spoken, they wept with sorrow, their tears flowing down.
Bowing my head, I contemplate the extinction of the Dharma;
from this day forward, there shall be no one to preach the Dharma, nor the Vinaya and the Prātimokṣa.
No longer remaining in the world, the Bridge of the Dharma has now collapsed.
The water of the Dharma no longer flows; the ocean of the Dharma has already run dry.
The mountain of the Dharma has collapsed; from now on, the assemblies of the Dharma are severed.
The banner of the Dharma will not be seen again; the feet of the Dharma will no longer walk.
The precepts of discipline have forever vanished;
the lamp of Dharma no longer shines, and the wheel of Dharma no longer turns. The gate to the Deathless is closed.
With the Dharma Master no longer in the world, the virtuous ones cease to proclaim the wondrous Path.
"Sentient beings do not recognize what is wholesome; they are no different from wild beasts.
At that time, the Buddha’s mother, Lady Mahāmāyā, descended from the heavens and went to where the assembly of monks was, wailing and weeping: "Alas!"

Alas! This son of mine, having passed through incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), practiced various asceticisms without regard for his own body, accumulated merit to become a Buddha, and now suddenly perishes.
And he spoke in verse:
"I am the Buddha’s own mother; my son has accumulated ascetic practices throughout countless kalpas, until he finally perfected the True Way."
Weeping, we could not restrain ourselves; now the Dharma has suddenly vanished.
Alas, O man of wisdom, where are you now?
You who upheld the Dharma and abandoned contention, born from the very mouth of the Buddha.
The supreme among all kings, true disciples of the Buddha,
practicing the wondrous conduct of dhūta while dwelling in forests and thickets—
where now are such true sons of the Buddha?
Now, in this world, there is no one possessing such majestic virtue;
even in the vast wildernesses and mountain forests, the various deities remain silent.
Through generosity and precepts, they take pity on all living beings; adorned with faith and the precepts, they themselves are perfected.
"Patience, self-restraint, and upright conduct— observing all that is good and evil—
such supreme dharmas as these have now suddenly come to an end.
At that time, the senior disciple thought to himself:
"That bhikṣu, Śūra, declared of himself:
'I fully observe all the precepts established by the Tathāgata.
At that time, an elder had a disciple named Aṅgada, who gave rise to an intolerant mind and became extremely resentful."
Rising from his seat, he reviled that noble one, saying:
"You are a junior bhikṣu, foolish and ignorant, yet you have insulted my upādhyāya.
He then took a sharp knife and killed that noble person, speaking this verse:
"I am named Aṅgada, the disciple of Śiśapā;
with a sharp sword I shall slay your body, for I consider myself virtuous."
At that time, there was a ghost named Mahātimukha who thought to himself:
"In this world, there is only this one Arhat, and he has been slain by the disciples of an evil bhikṣu."
Grasping a sharp vajra-pestle with flames blazing from its tip, he shattered his head with it, whereupon he immediately passed away. Then he spoke this verse:
"I am an evil spirit, Named Mahātimukha;
With this vajra-pestle, I have shattered your head into seven pieces."

“At that time, the disciple of the Arhat, seeing that his own disciple had murdered his teacher, was overcome with indignation and resentment; unable to endure it, he immediately killed the Tripitaka master.
Then, the devas and the people of the world wept in sorrow, crying out: ‘Alas!’”
"Alas! The True Dharma of the Tathāgata has now come to its complete end.
Immediately, this great earth shook in six ways, and immeasurable sentient beings wailed and wept, overcome with extreme grief and distress.
"Alas! Today the True Dharma no longer appears in the world.
Having spoken these words, they each dispersed.
At that time, five hundred upāsakas of the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, having heard this, went to the monastery, beat their heads with their hands, and wailed aloud: "Alas!..."
The Tathāgata takes pity on the world and seeks to deliver all living beings, regardless of whether they are great or small. Who then shall expound the meaning of the Dharma for me?

Now, liberation for humans and devas can no longer be attained; sentient beings today still dwell in the darkness of ignorance, lacking any guide. They habitually practice various evils and take pleasure in them, like wild beasts.
Failing to hear the sublime Dharma of the Muni, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they will fall into the three miserable realms.
"It is like a falling star; from this day forward, the people of the world will no longer possess mindfulness, wisdom, tranquility, samādhi, or the sublime Dharma of the Ten Powers.

At that time, when King Kauśāmbī heard that the bhikṣus had killed a true person, an arhat, as well as a Tripiṭaka master, his heart was filled with grief and distress, and he sat there in lamentation.

"At that time, those of wrong views will contend with one another to destroy stūpas and temples, and they will harm bhikṣus; from this point on, the Buddha-dharma will suddenly perish, becoming utterly desolate.
Then the World-Honored One said to Śakra-devānām-indra:
"The Four Great Heavenly Kings, the various devas, and the people of the world—after my parinirvāṇa, the signs of the exhaustion of the Dharma shall be as described above."
"Therefore, you all must now apply diligent effort to your spiritual exertion, so as to protect and uphold the True Dharma, causing it to remain long in the world.

At that time, the devas and the people of the world, having heard what the Buddha had said, each with a sorrowful countenance, wiped away their tears with their hands, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and then withdrew.
641 (641). The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of King Aśoka’s Gift of Half an Āmalaka Fruit. King Aśoka attained great reverence and faith within the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the king asked the bhikṣus,
"Who has practiced great giving within the Dharma of the Tathāgata?
The bhikṣus replied to the king:
“Anāthapiṇḍika the householder practices the greatest generosity.
The king asked again,
“How much wealth does he give away?”
The bhikṣu replied,
“For one hundred million gold pieces.
When the king heard this, he [acted].
He reflected thus:
"If that householder was able to give away a thousand million gold pieces, for what reason should I, being now a king, not likewise give a thousand million gold pieces as a gift?"
"One should give one hundred thousand *koṭis* of gold.

At that time, the king erected eighty-four thousand Buddha-stūpas, and within those stūpas he further gave one hundred thousand *koṭis* of gold. He then convened a great quinquennial assembly (*pañcavārṣika*), at which three hundred thousand bhikṣus were present; he used three billion pieces of gold to make offerings to that community of monks.
The first portion consists of Arhats, the second portion consists of those in training (śaikṣas), and the third portion consists of true ordinary worldlings.

With the exception of his private treasury, he gave all the ladies, court beauties, princes, and ministers of this Jambudvīpa to the noble Saṃgha; he then redeemed them by means of forty billion pieces of gold.
While they were thus engaged in these calculations, ninety-six billion gold pieces were expended. Eventually, when the king fell gravely ill, he knew for himself that his life was drawing to a close.
At that time, there was a great minister named Rādhagupta.
At that time, the king was a young boy who had been his companion when he made offerings to the Buddha in a previous life.
Then, the minister Raudhaka, seeing that the king was gravely ill and his life was about to end, prostrated himself and questioned the king with a verse:
"Your countenance is ever fresh and radiant, Surrounded by hundreds of thousands of court ladies."
"Just as when bees gather around various lotus flowers,
now that we behold the countenance of the Holy King, they possess no fresh luster at all.
The King then replied with a verse:
"I have no cause for grief now over the loss of wealth or my royal throne,
nor for this body or other kinsmen, nor for all manner of various treasures.
That which I now lament is that I shall no longer behold the Noble Ones."
I have provided these four things as offerings; now I think only of this, for my complexion has changed and my mind finds no peace.

Furthermore, it was my constant wish to fulfill a vow by making merit with one hundred billion gold pieces; yet now that wish remains unfulfilled, and when I calculate the gold, silver, and precious jewels bestowed before and after, I am short by four hundred million and have not reached the full amount.
The king immediately prepared various precious treasures and sent them to the Kukkuṭārāma monastery.
The son of Dharmavardhana, named Tripaṭi, addressed the crown prince and his ministers, saying: "The Great King will not live much longer;

he is now sending these precious treasures to the monastery. Our treasury is already exhausted, yet the law of kings holds material wealth to be paramount. Your Highness should now put a stop to this, lest the Great King exhaust his resources."
At that time, the Crown Prince immediately commanded the treasurer not to provide any more items for the Great King’s use.
When the Great King realized for himself that he could no longer obtain the various objects he sought, he sent his eating utensils made of gold to the monastery.
At that time, the Crown Prince ordered that gold vessels be discontinued and silver vessels provided; after the King had finished eating, he sent these back to the monastery.
Again, silver vessels were discontinued and copper vessels provided; the King likewise sent these as well to the monastery.
Furthermore, he had the bronze vessels broken and replaced them with earthenware.
At that time, the Great King held half an *āmalaka* fruit in his hand and, with tears of sorrow, addressed his ministers:
"Who now is the lord of the earth?"
Then, the ministers addressed the Great King,
saying, "The King is the lord of the earth. Thereupon, the King replied with a verse:
“Do you protect my heart; why resort to false speech?
Now that I sit upon the royal throne, I no longer possess autonomy.
This half-fruit of the *āmra* tree now rests in my hand.”
"This is indeed my property; herein I have attained freedom.
Alas, noble wealth and status—how wearying, how fit to be abandoned!
Having previously ruled over Jambudvīpa, today in a single day I have fallen into poverty."
"Just as the swift current of the Ganges flows on once and never returns, so too it is with wealth and honor; that which has passed away shall not return.
Furthermore, as stated in a verse by the Buddha:
"Where there is prosperity, there must be decline;
that decline is the ultimate end—so the Tathāgata has spoken with his divine mouth, which is true and without deviation.
The instructions previously given are swift and unimpeded."
Now that you have something to seek, you no longer follow my teaching;
like wind obstructed by a mountain, or water obstructed by a bank,
the instructions I now give have been forever severed for you.
Surrounded by immeasurable hosts, beating drums and blowing conchs and horns,
constantly performing various musical entertainments, they enjoy the pleasures of the five senses;
with hundreds of maidens, they amuse themselves day and night.
Now all is forever exhausted, like a tree without flowers or fruit;
my countenance grows ever withered, and my physical strength is likewise so.
Like a flower that has faded and withered, I am now just the same.
At that time, King Aśoka called to his attendant, saying: "Do you now remember my care and support?

Take this half-āmala fruit and send it to the Kukkuṭārāma monastery. Convey my intent: prostrate at the feet of the assembly of bhikṣus and say, 'King Aśoka inquires after the health of the Great Holy Ones.

I am King Aśoka; I once ruled over this Jambudvīpa, and Jambudvīpa was my possession. Now it is entirely exhausted; I have no wealth or jewels to bestow upon the Sangha, and I have lost all mastery over any possessions.'"

"Now I have attained freedom through this single half-āmala fruit; this is my final gift, my perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā). Out of compassion for me, please accept this offering so that I may obtain the merit of making an offering to the Saṃgha."
And he spoke in verse:
"This half-amarā fruit is my possession;
over it I have mastery. Now I relinquish it to the great assembly."
With a mind focused on the Noble Ones, there is no other who can save me;
out of compassion for me, please accept this *āmalaka* fruit.
By eating this offering for my sake, may immeasurable merit arise from it.
"From life to life they shall enjoy sublime bliss, And its use shall never be exhausted.

At that time, having received the king’s command, the messenger took this half-āmala fruit and went to the Kukkuṭārāma monastery. Arriving before the Elder, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, knelt for a long time with palms joined, and addressed the Elder in verse, saying:
"Ruling over Jambudvīpa, With a single parasol and a single drum,"
Wandering without obstruction, like the sun illuminating the world, the retribution for one's karmic actions has already arrived; not long shall he remain in this world.
Devoid of royal majesty and power, he is like the sun obscured by clouds.
Known as King Aśoka, he bowed his head in reverence at the feet of the Saṅgha and offered this gift of alms— a single half-āmala fruit—
seeking merit for future lives. Out of compassion for that king, [the Buddha accepted it].
"Out of compassion for him, the Noble Assembly has accepted this offering of half a fruit.
At that time, the Elder addressed the great assembly:
"Who, having heard these words, would not grow weary of the world?"
Upon hearing these matters, we cannot but feel weary and detached, as taught in the Buddha’s sutras.

Seeing the decline and misfortune of others, one should give rise to weariness and detachment; if there are sentient beings possessing consciousness, how could they not renounce the world upon hearing such things?
And he spoke in verse:
"The King of Men is supreme in the world; Aśoka, of the Maurya clan, is the sovereign of Jambudvīpa, ruling over the Āmalaka fruit."
The Crown Prince and his ministers together took back the King’s gift;
by sending back half of an āmalaka fruit, they subdued those who were arrogant regarding their wealth, causing them to give rise to a sense of revulsion.
The foolish do not recognize the true nature of giving.
"Through the fruit of cause and effect, one receives sublime joy; thus he showed and offered half of an āmalaka fruit.
At that time, the Elder thought to himself:
"How can this half-āmalaka fruit be made so that all the members of the Saṃgha may receive their share of it?"
He immediately instructed that it be ground and added to the pomegranate soup; once it was served, the entire assembly of monks received their full share.
Then the king asked his attendants:
"Who is the King of Jambudvīpa?"
The minister addressed the king, saying:
"It is the Great King.

Then, the king rose from his reclining position and sat up; looking toward the four quarters, he joined his palms in reverence, contemplated the virtues of the Buddhas, and spoke these words with his mind:
"I now further offer this Jambudvīpa to the Triple Gem; may it be used as you please.
Then he spoke in verse:
"This Jambudvīpa today Is adorned with many rare treasures."
By bestowing gifts upon a fertile field of merit, the fruit of retribution is naturally obtained;
through the merit of such giving, one seeks neither the status of Śakra, Lord of Devas,
nor that of Brahmā or a sovereign of men, nor any of the exquisite pleasures of the world.
Such fruits of retribution as these, I do not wish to receive at all;
by virtue of this merit from giving, may I swiftly attain the Way of the Buddha,
be revered and looked up to by the world, and achieve all-encompassing wisdom.
"In this world, he acts as a virtuous friend; he is the foremost of guides.
At that time, the king wrote these words in full upon a sheet of paper, sealed it, and impressed his tooth-mark upon the seal.
When these rites were completed, [the body] was immediately consumed by fire.

At that time, the prince, the ministers, the palace attendants, the court ladies, and the people of the realm offered various kinds of offerings for the funeral procession and performed the cremation according to the royal custom.
At that time, the ministers wished to establish the crown prince to succeed to the royal throne. Among them was a great minister named Anurādha, who said to the other ministers:
"The crown prince must not be established as king."

Why is this? When King Aśoka was alive, his original vow was to fulfill one hundred thousand koṭis of gold by performing various meritorious deeds; however, he fell short by four koṭis and did not reach the full hundred thousand. For this reason, he now relinquishes Jambudvīpa as an offering to the Triple Gem, desiring to bring that vow to completion.
"Now that this great earth belongs to the Triple Gem, how can you establish yourself as king?
When the ministers heard this, they immediately sent four hundred million pieces of gold to the monastery and then installed the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra as king, naming him Tripradyota.
Next, there was a prince named Vīrakabhadra; to succeed to the royal throne, the prince Vīrakabhadra had a son named Vīrakṣiṇa, who next succeeded to the royal throne.
The Prince Virahasiṇa, named Puṣyasūma, succeeded to the royal throne.
The Prince Puṣyasūma, named Puṣyamitra, succeeded to the royal throne.
At that time, Viśākhāmātṛ asked his ministers,
"What deeds should I perform so that my name and virtue may endure long in the world? Then,
the virtuous ministers who placed their faith and joy in the Triple Gem addressed the king, saying:

"King Aśoka was of the same royal lineage as this king. While that king was alive in the world, he erected eighty-four thousand stūpas for the Tathāgata and revived various forms of offerings; his fame and virtue have been passed down to the present day."
“If the King wishes to attain this name, he should construct eighty-four thousand stūpas and perform various offerings.
The King said, “King Aśoka possesses great majesty and virtue and is capable of accomplishing this; I cannot do it, so let us consider another matter.”
Among them was a wicked minister who did not have faith; he addressed the king, saying:
"There are two kinds of dharmas in the world that are transmitted through generations without ceasing: first, the performance of good deeds, and second, the performance of evil deeds."
"Great King Aśoka performed all manner of virtuous deeds, yet you, O King, now practice evil by destroying eighty-four thousand stūpas.
At that time, the king, following the words of his sycophantic ministers, immediately mobilized the fourfold army and went to the monasteries to destroy the various stūpas and temples.
The king first went to the Kukkuta-vihāra (Chicken and Sparrow Monastery). In front of the monastery gate stood stone lions, which immediately let out lion’s roars.
Hearing this, the king was struck with great terror; thinking that these were not born of the animal realm yet were capable of such roaring, he returned to the city.
Thus he repeated this twice more, wishing to destroy that monastery.
Then the king summoned the bhikṣus and asked them:
"Is it virtuous for me to destroy the stūpa?"
"Is it virtuous to destroy a monastic dwelling?
The bhikṣu replied,
"Neither of these two should be done."
"O King, if you must destroy anything, it would be better to destroy monastic dwellings than to destroy a Buddha-stūpa.
At that time, the king killed bhikṣus and destroyed stūpas and monasteries.
In this manner, he gradually proceeded to the kingdom of Bāgara and again issued a proclamation:
"If anyone can bring me the head of a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākya, I shall reward them with a thousand pieces of gold."

At that time, there was an Arhat in that country who manifested the heads of many bhikṣus and gave them to the common people, ordering them to deliver these to the king’s palace so that the king’s treasury and storehouses of wealth and jewels would be completely exhausted.
At that time, when the king heard that the Arhat had performed such deeds, his anger redoubled and he desired to kill that Arhat.
Then, as the Arhat entered the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the king employed countless means to slay the noble one, yet in the end he was unable to do so.
By the power of having entered the samādhi of cessation, his body was not harmed.
Thus he gradually advanced to the gate of the Buddha’s stūpa.
Within that stūpa there lived a spirit who resided therein to protect the stūpa; his name was Dantī (Tooth).
That spirit thought to himself:
"I am a disciple of the Buddha; I uphold the prohibitive precepts and do not harm living beings. I cannot now kill the king."
Again, she thought to herself:
"There is a deity named Bug (Kīṭa) who commits various evil deeds and is fierce, violent, and powerful; he sought my daughter, but I did not give her to him.
Now, for the sake of protecting the True Dharma, I shall marry her to him so that he may guard the Buddha-dharma."
He then called out to that deity, saying:

"I now give my daughter in marriage to you; however, we must establish a covenant and oath: you must surely subdue this king and prevent him from inciting various evil deeds or destroying the True Dharma."
At that time, the king had a great spirit named Uccha, who was endowed with full majesty and power; therefore, that deity could do nothing against the king.
Then, the Tooth-Spirit devised a stratagem: "Today, the king’s sovereign power naturally derives from this spirit; I shall now entice him and deceive him into becoming our close confidant."
Having thus become acquainted with that deity and established a close friendship, he led the deity to the great southern ocean.
At that time, the deity of the insects pushed aside a great mountain and pressed it down upon the king and his fourfold army, so that not one died without being crushed to death.
The multitude cried out:
"How wonderful!
How wonderful!"
This is what is traditionally recounted among the people of the world, known as "How Joyful!
When that king passed away, the lineage of the Peacock King came to an end forever; therefore, worldly wealth and pleasure are not worth coveting.

King Aśoka was a man of wisdom who realized that the world is impermanent and that life and body are difficult to preserve; he understood that wealth belonging to the five families is like a magical illusion.

Having awakened to these truths, he practiced with diligent vigor and performed various meritorious deeds. Even as his end approached, he focused his mind on the Triple Gem without interruption from moment to moment; free from all stinginess, he made only this vow: "May I fully attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

2.642 (642) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are three faculties—the faculty of ‘I shall come to know the unknown,’ the faculty of ‘knowing,’ and the faculty of ‘one who has known.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"When one realizes the stage of training, proceeding along the straight path in accordance with it,
exerting oneself with diligent application, and skillfully guarding one's own mind—
just as when one knows for oneself that birth has been exhausted, and the unobstructed path is already known."
Having known liberation, one finally attains the state beyond knowledge;
with unshakable liberation of mind, one is able to exhaust all existence.
With all faculties fully perfected, one delights in the tranquility of the senses.
"Maintaining this in his final body, he shall subdue all demonic adversaries.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
643 (Six Hundred Forty-Three). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
644 (644) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are five faculties. What are the five?
These are the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.

If a bhikṣu correctly and thoroughly examines these five faculties, and having correctly and thoroughly examined them, realizes the abandonment of the three fetters—namely, the view of a self-identity, attachment to precepts and rituals, and doubt—he is called a *srotāpanna*. He is no longer subject to rebirth in the woeful states; he is destined for full awakening, will be reborn among gods and humans for seven more existences, and will reach the ultimate end of suffering.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 645 (645) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"One who observes these five faculties as they truly are does not give rise to outflows; the mind attains liberation through detachment from desire. Such a person is called an arhat—one whose outflows are exhausted, who has done what was to be done, who has laid down the heavy burden, who has attained his own benefit, who has destroyed the fetters of existence, and whose mind is well-liberated through right knowledge."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
646 (646) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are five faculties. What are the five?
These are the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
It should be understood that the faculty of faith consists of the four kinds of unshakable confidence;
the faculty of energy consists of the four right efforts.
The faculty of mindfulness should be understood as the four foundations of mindfulness;
the faculty of concentration should be understood as the four dhyānas;
and the faculty of wisdom should be understood as the four noble truths.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
647 (647) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are five faculties. What are the five?
They are the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. What is the faculty of faith?

If a bhikṣu gives rise to pure faith toward the Tathāgata, with a root that is firm and solid, such that no other śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or anyone else in the world can obstruct or destroy his mind—this is called the faculty of faith.
“What is the faculty of energy?
It is the arising of desire, the application of means, the gathering of the mind, and the exertion to abandon evil, unwholesome states that have already arisen;
it is the arising of desire, the application of means, the gathering of the mind, and the exertion so that evil, unwholesome states not yet arisen do not arise.”
To cause unarisen wholesome dharmas to arise, one generates desire, applies effort, exerts the mind, and progresses;

to maintain already arisen wholesome dharmas so they are not forgotten, and to cultivate, increase, and expand them, one generates desire, applies effort, exerts the mind, and progresses—this is called the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*).
"What is the faculty of mindfulness?
If a bhikṣu dwells contemplating the body as body internally, with diligent application, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension, subduing worldly greed and sorrow;
and if he likewise dwells contemplating the body externally, the body both internally and externally, feelings, the mind, and phenomena as phenomena—this is called the faculty of mindfulness."
"What is the faculty of concentration?

If a bhikṣu, detached from desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, experiencing the joy and happiness born of seclusion, dwells having fully attained up to the fourth dhyāna—this is called the faculty of concentration."
“What is the faculty of wisdom?

If a bhikṣu knows the noble truth of suffering as it really is, and knows the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering as they really are, this is called the faculty of wisdom.”
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 648 (648). Thus have I heard:

What are these three?

This is called a Srotāpanna; one does not fall into the evil destinies, but is certain to head directly toward perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), being reborn seven times among gods and humans before reaching the ultimate end of suffering.

649 (649) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

All taints have been exhausted; what was to be done has been accomplished; the heavy burden has been laid down; his own welfare has been attained; the fetters of existence have been destroyed; through right knowledge, his mind has been liberated.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 650 (650) Thus have I heard:

If I had not known, as they truly are, this faculty of faith, the origin of the faculty of faith, the cessation of the faculty of faith, and the path leading to the cessation of the faculty of faith, I would never have emerged from or transcended among gods, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas; my mind would not have been freed from perversion, nor would I have attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
As it was with the faculty of faith, so it was for the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. "O bhikṣus!

"As with the faculty of faith, so too should the faculties of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom be explained.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
651 (Six Hundred and Fifty-one). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus... as described above.

The same applies to the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.

"Monks, because I have known, as they truly are, the faculty of faith, the origin of the faculty of faith, the cessation of the faculty of faith, the gratification of the faculty of faith, the danger in the faculty of faith, and the escape from the faculty of faith, among the assembly of devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, I am liberated, I have emerged, and I have departed; with a mind free from inversion, I have attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

652 (Six Hundred Fifty-Two). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus... as stated above.

if weak or inferior, one attains the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin;
if weak or inferior, one attains the stage of Srotāpanna.

Those who fulfill these [faculties] accomplish what is to be accomplished; those who do not fulfill them accomplish what is not to be accomplished. Regarding these five faculties, they are not empty and are not without fruit. If one lacks all of these five faculties, I declare that person to be among the ranks of the heterodox and the worldlings.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 653 (653) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus... as stated above.
The difference is this:
"If a bhikṣu has attained excellence, sharpness, and fulfillment regarding those five faculties, he attains the analytical liberation of an arhat."
If they are weak or inferior, one attains bodily realization (*kāyasākṣin*).
If they are weak or inferior therein, one attains the stage of seeing (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).

If those are weak or inferior, one attains the practice of Dharma (dharmānusārin).

rather, if one relies upon wisdom, one abandons unwholesome dharmas and cultivates all wholesome dharmas.

He is able to proclaim the true Dharma in future ages to awaken the śrāvakas, namely: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path. "Furthermore, there are the five powers of training and the ten powers of a Tathāgata.

They are the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom."

the Tathāgata knows, in accordance with reality, what is possible and what is impossible; this is called the first power of the Tathāgata.

One who has accomplished this power—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—attains the knowledge of the supreme state of former Buddhas, turns the Brahma-wheel, and utters the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly.

If a bhikṣu comes to me as a śrāvaka, being without flattery or deceit and with a straightforward mind, I then instruct, exhort, and teach him the Dharma."
If he provides instruction and teaching by preaching the Dharma to them in the early morning, they attain a state of superior progress by midday;
if he provides instruction and teaching by preaching the Dharma to them in the evening, they attain a state of superior progress by the following morning.

Having been thus instructed, he gives rise to an upright mind; he knows what is real as real and what is unreal as unreal, and he knows what is superior as superior and what is unsurpassed as unsurpassed. That he will fully comprehend all that ought to be known, seen, attained, and realized—this is indeed possible.
"They are the five powers of training and the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
What are the five powers of training?
They are the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom."
The ten powers of the Tathāgata.
What are the ten? They are:
knowing as it truly is what is possible and what is impossible... [as extensively explained above for the ten powers].

"If anyone comes to ask about the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible, I shall explain it to them exactly as it is known, seen, and realized by the Tathāgata through his perfectly awakened knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible; and so on, up to the power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of the outflows, I shall likewise explain."
"O Bhikṣus!

Regarding the power of knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible, I say it is certain and not uncertain; up to the power of knowledge of the destruction of the outflows, I say it is certain and not uncertain. That which is certain is the right path; that which is not certain is the wrong path."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 704 (704) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

the hindrances of ill-will (*vyāpāda*), sloth-and-torpor (*styāna-middha*), restlessness-and-regret (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) that have not yet arisen will arise, and those that have already arisen will be reborn and further increased."
The awakening factor of mindfulness that has not yet arisen does not arise; that which has already arisen declines.

The awakening factor of mindfulness that has not yet arisen arises; that which has already arisen is further developed and expanded.

The awakening factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity that have not yet arisen arise; those which have already arisen are further developed and expanded.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 705 (705) Thus have I heard:

"There are five factors of decline. What are the five?

What are the seven?

They are the awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, the awakening factor of energy, the awakening factor of tranquility, the awakening factor of rapture, the awakening factor of concentration, and the awakening factor of equanimity; these are called the dharmas of non-retrogression.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 706 (706) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"There are five things that can produce darkness, can cause blindness, can result in a lack of wisdom, can weaken wisdom, and are neither clarity nor equal enlightenment; they do not lead toward Nirvana."
What are these five?
They are sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.
These five factors act as darkness, act as blindness, and act as lack of wisdom; they are neither clarity nor right awakening, and they prevent one from proceeding toward Nirvana.
"If there are the seven factors of enlightenment, they can produce great illumination and serve as eyes; they increase wisdom, acting as light and as right awakening, leading one toward Nirvana."

"It serves as illumination and as eyes; it increases wisdom, serves as light and as perfect awakening, and leads toward Nirvana.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
707 (Seven Hundred and Seven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“There are five hindrances and five coverings that afflict the mind, weaken wisdom, and constitute obstacles; they are neither clarity nor perfect awakening, and prevent one from proceeding toward Nirvāṇa.”
What are the five?
They are the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt.

These five hindrances act as a covering and a veil that afflict the mind, causing wisdom to become feeble; they constitute an obstacle, being neither clarity nor perfect awakening, and prevent one from proceeding toward Nirvana.
"If these seven factors of enlightenment are neither obscuring nor veiling, do not afflict the mind, increase wisdom, serve as illumination and right awakening, and lead toward Nirvana."
"What are the seven?
They are the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, and so forth... as explained above, up to the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.
"These seven factors of enlightenment are neither cataracts nor veils; they do not afflict the mind, but increase wisdom, serving as illumination and right awakening, leading toward Nirvana."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
The hindrance of sensual desire and ill will, Sleep, restlessness-and-regret, and doubt—
These five kinds of hindrances Cause all afflictions to increase.
These five obscurations shroud the world; deeply attached, they are difficult to cross over.
They veil sentient beings, preventing them from seeing the Noble Path.
If one attains the seven factors of enlightenment, then one can provide illumination.
These alone are the words of ultimate truth, spoken by the Fully Awakened One:
mindfulness as the factor of awakening, the investigation of phenomena with right reflection,
energy, tranquility, joy, concentration, and equanimity as the factors of awakening.
"These seven factors of enlightenment are the true path of the Muni;
by following the Great Sage, one is liberated from the fear of birth and death.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
708. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If a son of noble family abandons all worldly affairs, leaves the home life to study the Path, shaves off his hair and beard, dons the saffron robe, and with right faith goes forth from the household to study the Path."

Thus, among those who have gone forth, there may be a foolish man who relies on villages and towns; rising early in the morning, he puts on his robes and takes up his bowl to enter the village for alms. Failing to guard his body, failing to restrain the gates of his senses, and failing to collect his mindfulness, he observes women in their youth and beauty and gives rise to defiled attachment. With improper reflection, his mind races to seize upon signs, pursuing thoughts of sensual desire. As his lustful mind becomes intense, it burns his heart and his body, causing him to return to secular life and abandon his precepts, thus falling back and sinking away.

Having grown weary of worldly affairs, they left the home life to study the Way, yet instead became defiled by attachment; their various karmic offenses increased, leading to their own ruin, as they sank and were submerged in obscurity.

"There are five kinds of great trees whose seeds are extremely minute, yet once the trees grow, they become immense. They are able to overshadow and obstruct all other miscellaneous small trees, causing them to wither and fade so that they cannot grow."
What are the five?
They are the *kaccayā* tree, the *kapittha* tree, the *aśvattha* tree, the *udumbara* tree, and the *nyagrodha* tree.

These five kinds of heartwood trees have seeds that are exceedingly minute, yet they gradually grow large, spreading their shade over the joints and causing those joints to be covered and fall prostrate.
What are these five?

They are the hindrance of sensual desire, which gradually increases; the hindrances of sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-remorse, and doubt, which gradually increase. Because they increase, they cause the wholesome mind to be shrouded and fallen into a state of lying down.
"If one cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment and, having cultivated them extensively, becomes irreversible— what are these seven?

They are the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, the enlightenment factor of energy, the enlightenment factor of rapture, the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the enlightenment factor of concentration, and the enlightenment factor of equanimity."
"When these seven factors of awakening have been cultivated and practiced extensively, they become irreversible.
After the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
709 (Seven Hundred and Nine). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
“If a bhikṣu concentrates his mind and listens attentively to the True Dharma, he will be able to abandon five things, cultivate seven things, and cause them to progress toward fulfillment.”
What are the five things to be abandoned?

They are the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt; these are called the five things to be abandoned.
What are the seven factors to be cultivated?

They are the awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, the awakening factor of energy, the awakening factor of tranquility, the awakening factor of rapture, the awakening factor of concentration, and the awakening factor of equanimity. By cultivating these seven factors, one progresses further toward their fulfillment.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
710 (710). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"A noble disciple who possesses pure faith and listens to the Dharma with single-minded diligence is able to sever five dharmas, cultivate seven dharmas, and bring them to fulfillment."
What are the five?
They are the hindrance of sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt; these hindrances are then severed.
What are the seven factors?
That is to say, the awakening factor of mindfulness, and the awakening factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, tranquility, rapture, concentration, and equanimity.
When these seven factors have been cultivated to fulfillment, "pure faith" refers to liberation of mind;
"wisdom" refers to liberation by wisdom.
One whose mind is defiled by greed cannot attain happiness;
one whose mind is defiled by ignorance lacks pure wisdom.
Therefore, O bhikṣus!
One who is free from sensual desire attains liberation of mind; one who is free from ignorance attains liberation by wisdom.

If that bhikṣu, being free from sensual desire, attains liberation of mind and realizes it through bodily witness, and being free from ignorance, attains liberation by wisdom—this is called a bhikṣu who has severed the fetters of craving, attained the destruction of conceit, and reached the ultimate end of suffering.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly. 711 (711) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, there was a prince named Abhaya, who, walking about daily for recreation, came to where the Buddha was staying. After exchanging greetings and pleasantries with the World-Honored One, he withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
There are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
"The afflictions of sentient beings are without cause and without condition; the purification of sentient beings is without cause and without condition."
“What did the World-Honored One further say?
The Buddha told Abhaya:

“Certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas speak without reflection; they speak out of folly, without discernment, and without skill. Lacking wisdom and reflection, and ignorant of measure, they speak in this manner:”
"There is no cause and no condition for the afflictions of sentient beings; there is no cause and no condition for the purification of sentient beings. Why is this?
It is because there is indeed a cause and a condition for the afflictions of sentient beings, and there is indeed a cause and a condition for the purification of sentient beings.
For what cause and for what condition do sentient beings become afflicted?
For what cause and for what condition do sentient beings become purified?
It is said that when desire for sensual pleasure increases in sentient beings, they give rise to covetous speech regarding the wealth and possessions of others, saying:
"Thinking, 'This thing belongs to me;

it is pleasant, not to be parted from, and cherished,' one gives rise toward other sentient beings to resentment, ferocity, calculation, the desire to strike, the desire to bind, the desire to subdue, and inflicts various unrighteous acts."

They create many difficulties, do not abandon anger, are drowsy in body, indolent in mind, and agitated in mind; they lack inner tranquility, their minds are constantly full of doubt, and they harbor doubts regarding the past, the future, and the present.
Fearlessness.
Such are the causes and such are the conditions for the afflictions of sentient beings;
such are the causes and such are the conditions for the purification of sentient beings.
Abhaya said to the Buddha:
“Gautama! A single portion of the hindrances is sufficient to afflict the mind; how much more so, then, when they are all present?”
Abhaya said to the Buddha:
“Gautama! For what cause and for what reason are sentient beings purified?”
The Buddha told Abhaya:

"If a brahmin possesses one superior mindfulness that is decisively accomplished, such that he is able to recollect with clarity what was done long ago and what was spoken long ago, at that time he is practicing the awakening factor of mindfulness."

Having cultivated the awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of mindfulness becomes fulfilled; once the awakening factor of mindfulness is fulfilled, one then engages in discernment, analysis, and reflection, at which time the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena is cultivated.

Having cultivated the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena, the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena becomes fulfilled; having thus selected, analyzed, and deliberated upon phenomena, one then applies diligence as a skillful means.

One cultivates the awakening factor of energy; having cultivated the awakening factor of energy, the awakening factor of energy becomes fulfilled. Once that application of energy has been perfected, joy arises, and one is free from all perceptions of nutriment.

One cultivates the factor of enlightenment of joy; having cultivated the factor of enlightenment of joy, the factor of enlightenment of joy becomes fulfilled. When the factor of enlightenment of joy is fulfilled, body and mind become tranquil and at rest, whereby one cultivates the factor of enlightenment of tranquility.

Having cultivated the awakening factor of tranquility, the awakening factor of tranquility becomes fulfilled; once the body is at ease, one experiences joy; having experienced joy, the mind becomes concentrated, whereby one cultivates the awakening factor of concentration.

Having cultivated the awakening factor of concentration, the awakening factor of concentration becomes fulfilled; once the awakening factor of concentration is fulfilled, greed and sorrow are extinguished, and a mind of equanimity arises, whereby one cultivates the awakening factor of equanimity.
Having cultivated the factor of awakening of equanimity, the factor of awakening of equanimity is fulfilled.
Thus, O Fearless One, through these causes and conditions, sentient beings are purified.
Abhaya said to Gautama,
"If even a single part being fulfilled can bring sentient beings to purity, how much more so when it is complete?
Abhaya addressed the Buddha:
"Gautama! What should this sutra be named?
How should it be upheld?"
The Buddha told Prince Abhaya:
"This should be named the 'Sūtra on the Factors of Enlightenment' (Bodhyanga-sūtra).
Abhaya addressed the Buddha:
"Gautama! This is the most excellent factor of enlightenment. Gautama!"

"I am a prince, and though I always seek peace and happiness, I long for the freedom of coming and going. Having come up this mountain today, my four limbs were utterly exhausted; yet upon hearing the Gautama preach the *Bodhyaṅga Sūtra*, all my fatigue has vanished."

When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, Prince Abhaya, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and approved with gladness. He rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and departed.
Saṃyukta Āgama, Scroll Twenty-Six;
Saṃyukta Āgama, Scroll Twenty-Seven.

"There are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:

'There is no cause and no condition by which sentient beings lack wisdom and insight; there is no cause and no condition by which sentient beings possess wisdom and insight'... Thus it is explained in detail, until the Prince Abhaya, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and approved, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and departed.
713. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then, a great number of bhikṣus, having dressed in the morning and taken their bowls, entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
At that time, many bhikṣus had this thought:
"It is too early today; the time for almsround has not yet arrived. Let us first visit the monasteries of the various non-Buddhist practitioners."
