The many bhikṣus then entered the hermitage of the non-Buddhists and exchanged greetings and pleasantries with them. Having finished their greetings and pleasantries, they sat to one side. The non-Buddhists then asked the bhikṣus:

"The śramaṇa Gautama teaches the Dharma to his disciples, instructing them to abandon the five hindrances—which shroud the mind, weaken the power of wisdom, constitute obstacles, and prevent progress toward Nirvāṇa—and to abide in the four foundations of mindfulness while cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment."

We, likewise, for the sake of our disciples, teach the severing of the five hindrances—which shroud the mind and weaken the power of wisdom—and the skillful abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness and the cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment.
"What difference is there between us and that śramaṇa Gautama?
We are both able to preach the Dharma.
When the many bhikṣus heard what the non-Buddhists said, their hearts were not pleased; instead, they reviled them and rose from their seats to depart.

Having entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food, he returned to the vihāra, put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit at one side.
He reported in full to the Blessed One everything that had been said by those non-Buddhists.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the many bhikṣus:
"When those non-Buddhists speak these words, you should question them back, saying: "
"O you heterodox practitioners!
As for the five hindrances, there should be ten categories.
As for the seven factors of enlightenment, there should be fourteen categories."
"What are the ten factors of the five hindrances and the fourteen factors of the seven factors of awakening?

When asked thus, those non-Buddhists become startled and scattered; as they expound their own non-Buddhist doctrines, thoughts of anger, arrogance, disparagement, resentment, and intolerance arise within them. Some remain silent with heads bowed, losing their eloquence and withdrawing into deep reflection.

Why is this? Because among the hosts of devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gods, and humans, I see none who, upon hearing what I have spoken, would rejoice and comply with it, except for the Tathāgata and his assembly of śrāvakas who hear it here.
“Monks! What are the ten aspects of the five hindrances? They are:
there is internal sensual desire, and there is external sensual desire.”
Internal sensual desire is itself an obscuration; it is not wisdom, not full awakening, and does not lead toward Nirvāṇa.
External sensual desire is itself an obscuration; it is not wisdom, not full awakening, and does not lead toward Nirvāṇa.

That is to say, ill will has the characteristic of ill will; if there is ill will and the characteristic of ill will, that is itself an obscuration. It is neither wisdom nor equal enlightenment, and it does not lead toward Nirvana.
There is drowsiness and sleep; that drowsiness and that sleep are themselves hindrances, not wisdom, not equal enlightenment, and do not lead toward Nirvana.
There is restlessness and remorse; that restlessness and that remorse are themselves hindrances, not wisdom, not equal enlightenment, and do not lead toward Nirvana.

There is doubt regarding wholesome phenomena and doubt regarding unwholesome phenomena; that doubt concerning wholesome phenomena and doubt concerning unwholesome phenomena is itself an obscuration—it is neither wisdom nor equal enlightenment, and it does not lead toward Nirvana.
These are called the five hindrances spoken of as ten.
What are the seven factors of enlightenment spoken of as fourteen?
There is the foundation of mindfulness on internal mental phenomena, and there is the foundation of mindfulness on external mental phenomena.

That mindfulness of internal phenomena (*adhyātma-dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*) is itself the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*); it is wisdom, it is perfect awakening, and it is capable of turning toward and proceeding to *nirvāṇa*.

That mindfulness of external phenomena (*bahirdhā-dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*) is itself the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness; it is wisdom, it is perfect awakening, and it is capable of turning toward and proceeding to *nirvāṇa*.
“There is the discernment of wholesome phenomena and the discernment of unwholesome phenomena.
That discernment of wholesome phenomena is precisely the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena; it is wisdom, it is full awakening, and it leads toward Nirvana.”

The discernment of those unwholesome dharmas is itself the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of dharmas; it is wisdom, it is perfect awakening, and it is capable of turning one toward Nirvana.
There is diligence that abandons unwholesome dharmas, and there is diligence that cultivates wholesome dharmas.
His diligence in abandoning unwholesome states is itself the factor of enlightenment that is diligence;
it is wisdom, it is perfect awakening, and it can lead one toward Nirvāṇa.
His diligence in cultivating wholesome states is itself the factor of enlightenment that is diligence; it is wisdom, it is perfect awakening, and it can lead one toward Nirvāṇa.
“There is joy, there is the basis for joy.
That joy is itself the factor of enlightenment called joy; it is wisdom, it is perfect awakening, and it leads toward Nirvana.
That basis for joy is also the factor of enlightenment called joy; it is wisdom, it is perfect awakening, and it leads toward Nirvana.”
“There is the tranquility of the body and the tranquility of the mind.
That tranquility of the body is itself the factor of enlightenment that is tranquility; it is wisdom, it is perfect awakening, and it leads toward Nirvāṇa.”
That mind being tranquil and at rest is precisely the factor of enlightenment of tranquility; it is wisdom, it is perfect awakening, and it is capable of turning toward and proceeding to nirvāṇa.
"There is concentration; there is the characteristic of concentration."
That concentration is itself the factor of enlightenment of concentration; it is wisdom, it is perfect awakening, and it can lead one toward Nirvana.
That characteristic of concentration is itself the factor of enlightenment of concentration; it is wisdom, it is perfect awakening, and it can lead one toward Nirvana.
“There is the relinquishing of wholesome dharmas and the relinquishing of unwholesome dharmas.
That relinquishing of wholesome dharmas is precisely the factor of enlightenment called equanimity; it is wisdom, it is perfect awakening, and it is capable of leading one toward Nirvāṇa.”

The relinquishing of those unwholesome dharmas is itself the factor of enlightenment called equanimity; it is wisdom, it is perfect awakening, and it is able to lead toward Nirvana. These are called the seven factors of enlightenment, which are explained as fourteen.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the many bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
714 (714). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there were many bhikṣus... [as described above].
The difference is as follows:
"If there are those among the renunciant followers of other paths who speak in such a manner, one should further question them, saying:"
"If the mind is weak or hesitant, what factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) should one cultivate at that time?
What is the improper time for cultivation?
Furthermore, if the mind is agitated or if the agitated mind is hesitant, what factors of enlightenment should one cultivate then?"
"What constitutes 'the improper time'?

When asked thus, those non-Buddhists become startled and distracted; they speak of various heterodox doctrines, their minds filled with anger, arrogance, disparagement, resentment, and intolerance, or they remain silent with heads bowed, losing their eloquence and retreating into deep thought.

Why is this? Among the hosts of devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gods, and humans, I see none who, upon hearing what I have spoken, would rejoice and approve with gladness, except for the Tathāgata and his assembly of śrāvakas who hear it here.

“Monks! If at that time the mind is feeble or the mind is hesitant, one should not cultivate the awakening factor of tranquility, the awakening factor of concentration, or the awakening factor of equanimity.
Why is this? Because a feeble mind arises and feeble hesitation occurs, for these various dharmas increase that feebleness.
It is like a small fire that one wishes to kindle, yet one adds charred embers to it.
"How so? Bhikṣu! Would adding more charcoal not cause the fire to be extinguished?"
The bhikṣu said to the Buddha,
“So it is, World-Honored One! “So it is, bhikṣu!”

If one who is weak and hesitant cultivates the awakening factor of tranquility, the awakening factor of concentration, or the awakening factor of equanimity, this is not the proper time, as it increases indolence.

If a restless mind arises, or if the restless mind wavers in hesitation, at that time one should not cultivate the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, the awakening factor of energy, or the awakening factor of joy.
Why is this? Because an agitated mind arises and an agitated mind wavers, and these various phenomena cause that agitation to increase.
It is like a blazing fire: if one wishes to extinguish it but supplies it with dry fuel, what do you think will happen?
"Would this not cause the fire to blaze up even more fiercely?
The bhikṣu replied to the Buddha,
"It would, World-Honored One."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"In this way, when the mind is restless and the mind is wavering, to cultivate the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, the awakening factor of energy, and the awakening factor of joy increases that restlessness of the mind."
"O bhikṣus!

If a feeble mind arises or if there is feeble hesitation, at that time one should cultivate the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena, the awakening factor of energy, and the awakening factor of joy."
Why is this? Because when a feeble mind arises and feeble hesitation occurs, these dharmas are used to demonstrate, instruct, illuminate, and gladden them.
It is like a small fire that one wishes to cause to blaze up by providing it with sufficient dry fuel.
"What do you think, bhikṣu?
Would this fire burn fiercely?"
The bhikṣu replied to the Buddha,
“So it is, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu:

"When such inferior thoughts arise and such inferior hesitations occur, at that time one should cultivate the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena, the awakening factor of energy, and the awakening factor of joy, demonstrating, instructing, illuminating, and gladdening them."

If a restless mind arises or if the restless mind wavers, one cultivates the awakening factor of tranquility, the awakening factor of concentration, and the awakening factor of equanimity. Why is this?
Because when a restless mind arises or when the restless mind wavers, these dharmas are able to cause the mind to abide within and be gathered in one-pointedness.
It is just as when one wishes to extinguish a fire: by adding more burning charcoal, that fire is extinguished.

In the same way, bhikkhu, when the mind is restless and wavering, it is the wrong time to cultivate the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, energy, and rapture; it is the right time to cultivate the awakening factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, whereby these various qualities cause the mind to dwell inwardly in one-pointedness and remain collected.
"The factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness assists all [the others].
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
715 (715). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are the five hindrances and the seven factors of awakening; there are their nutriment and their lack of nutriment, which I shall now explain.
Listen closely and reflect well; I will speak for you.”
Just as the body stands by depending on food and not without food,
so too the five hindrances stand by depending on their nutriment and not without nutriment.
What is the nutriment for the hindrance of sensual desire?

It refers to the characteristic of contact; through improper mental attention toward it, it causes unarisen sensual desire to arise and causes arisen sensual desire to increase and expand. This is called the nutriment for the hindrance of sensual desire.
"What is the nutriment of the hindrance of ill will?

It is the perception of obstruction; by engaging in improper mental attention toward it, one causes the hindrance of ill will that has not yet arisen to arise, and causes that which has already arisen to increase and expand. This is called the nutriment of the hindrance of ill will."
“What are the foods for the hindrance of sloth and torpor?
There are five factors. What are the five?”

Lassitude, lack of joy, yawning, overeating, and indolence—these constitute improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) which causes the hindrance of sleep (*middhanīvaraṇa*) to arise where it has not yet arisen, and causes it to increase and expand where it has already arisen; this is called the nutriment of the hindrance of sleep.
“What are the fuels for the hindrance of restlessness and remorse?
There are four factors. What are the four?”
This refers to thoughts of relatives, thoughts of assemblies of people, thoughts of devas, and thoughts of past enjoyments.

Whether arising from one's own recollections or being prompted by others to remember, one engages in improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) toward these; thus, agitation and regret (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*) that have not yet arisen are caused to arise, and those already arisen are allowed to increase and expand. This is called the nutriment for the hindrance of agitation and regret.
"What is the nutriment of the hindrance of doubt?
There are three times.
What are the three?"
This refers to the past, future, and present worlds. To have doubt regarding the past, doubt regarding the future, and doubt regarding the present;

to give rise to improper mental attention toward them; to cause the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*) that has not yet arisen to arise, and to cause the hindrance of doubt that has already arisen to increase and expand—this is called the nutriment of the hindrance of doubt.

"Just as the body depends on food for its growth and sustenance, and cannot exist without food, so too these seven factors of enlightenment depend on nourishment for their abiding and depend on nourishment for their growth; they do not exist without nourishment."
"What is the non-nutriment for the awakening factor of mindfulness?

It refers to not reflecting upon the four foundations of mindfulness; thus, the awakening factor of mindfulness that has not yet arisen does not arise, and that which has already arisen causes to decline. This is called the non-nutriment for the awakening factor of mindfulness."
"What is the non-nutriment for the factor of enlightenment of discrimination of phenomena?

It is the discrimination of wholesome phenomena and the discrimination of unwholesome phenomena; it is not reflecting upon them, causing the factor of enlightenment of discrimination of phenomena that has not yet arisen not to arise, and causing the factor of enlightenment of discrimination of phenomena that has already arisen to decline. This is called the non-nutriment for the factor of enlightenment of discrimination of phenomena."
"What is the non-nutriment for the awakening factor of energy?

It refers to the four right endeavors: not reflecting upon them, causing the unarisen awakening factor of energy not to arise, and causing the already arisen awakening factor of energy to decline—this is called the non-nutriment for the awakening factor of energy."
"What is the non-nutriment for the factor of enlightenment that is joy?

There is joy, and there are phenomena that are objects of joy; if one does not attend to them, the factor of enlightenment that is joy which has not yet arisen will not arise, and that which has already arisen will decline. This is called the non-nutriment for the factor of enlightenment that is joy."
"What is the non-nutriment for the factor of enlightenment of tranquility?

There is tranquility of body and tranquility of mind; if one does not attend to them, the unarisen factor of enlightenment of tranquility will not arise, and the arisen factor of enlightenment of tranquility will decline. This is called the non-nutriment for the factor of enlightenment of tranquility."
"What is the non-nutriment for the factor of enlightenment that is concentration?

There are the four dhyānas; if one does not direct one's attention toward them, the factor of enlightenment that is concentration which has not yet arisen will not arise, and that which has already arisen will decline. This is called the non-nutriment for the factor of enlightenment that is concentration."
"What is the non-nutriments for the factor of enlightenment of equanimity?

There are three realms, namely: the realm of abandonment (*prahāṇadhātu*), the realm of dispassion (*virāgadhātu*), and the realm of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*). If one does not direct one's attention toward them, the factor of enlightenment of equanimity that has not yet arisen will not arise, and that which has already arisen will decline; this is called the non-nutriments for the factor of enlightenment of equanimity."
"What is the non-nutriment for the hindrance of sensual desire?

It is the contemplation of impurity; by reflecting upon it, the hindrance of sensual desire that has not yet arisen does not arise, and that which has already arisen is brought to cessation. This is called the non-nutriment for the hindrance of sensual desire."
"What is the non-nutriment for the hindrance of ill will?

It is the cultivation of a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*): by this, the hindrance of ill will that has not yet arisen does not arise, and the hindrance of ill will that has already arisen is brought to cessation. This is called the non-nutriment for the hindrance of ill will."
"What is the non-nutriment for the hindrance of sloth and torpor?

It is the cultivation of clear illumination; through this, the unarisen hindrance of sloth and torpor does not arise, and the arisen hindrance of sloth and torpor is brought to cessation. This is called the non-nutriment for the hindrance of sloth and torpor."
"What is the non-nutriment for the hindrance of restlessness and remorse?

It is the cultivation of tranquility through reflection: it prevents the unarisen hindrance of restlessness and remorse from arising, and causes the arisen hindrance of restlessness and remorse to be extinguished. This is called the non-nutriment for the hindrance of restlessness and remorse."
"What is the non-nutriment for the hindrance of doubt?

It is the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); by this, the hindrance of doubt that has not yet arisen does not arise, and the hindrance of doubt that has already arisen is brought to cessation. This is called the non-nutriment for the hindrance of doubt."
"Just as the body dwells by depending on food and stands by depending on food,
so too do the seven factors of enlightenment dwell by depending on food and stand by depending on food.
What is the food for the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness?

That is to say, having contemplated the four foundations of mindfulness, one causes the awakening factor of mindfulness that has not yet arisen to arise, and causes the awakening factor of mindfulness that has already arisen to further develop and increase; this is called the nutriment for the awakening factor of mindfulness.
"What is the nutriment for the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena?

There is the investigation of wholesome phenomena and the investigation of unwholesome phenomena; having reflected upon them, one causes the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena which has not yet arisen to arise, and causes the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena which has already arisen to be renewed and further increased. This is called the nutriment for the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena."
"What is the nutriment for the awakening factor of energy?

It is the contemplation of the four right endeavors: causing the awakening factor of energy that has not yet arisen to arise, and causing the awakening factor of energy that has already arisen to be renewed, increased, and expanded. This is called the nutriment for the awakening factor of energy."
"What is the nutriment for the factor of enlightenment that is joy?

There is joy, there are objects of joy; one contemplates them, whereby the factor of enlightenment that is joy which has not yet arisen is caused to arise, and that which has already arisen is caused to recur, increase, and expand. This is called the nutriment for the factor of enlightenment that is joy."

"What is the nutriment for the awakening factor of tranquility? It is the contemplation of the subsiding of bodily formations and the subsiding of mental formations; this causes the unarisen awakening factor of tranquility to arise, and causes the arisen awakening factor of tranquility to recur, increase, and expand. This is called the nutriment for the awakening factor of tranquility."
"What is the nutriment for the awakening factor of concentration?

It refers to the four dhyānas of contemplation: they cause the awakening factor of concentration that has not yet arisen to arise, and they cause the awakening factor of concentration that has already arisen to be further developed and expanded. This is called the nutriment for the awakening factor of concentration."
"What is the nutriment for the factor of enlightenment of equanimity?
There are three realms.
What are the three?"
That is to say: the realm of relinquishment (*prahāṇadhātu*), the realm of dispassion (*virāgadhātu*), and the realm of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*).

When one contemplates these, the awakening-factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*) that has not yet arisen is caused to arise, and that which has already arisen is caused to recur, increase, and expand; this is called the nutriment (*āhāra*) of the awakening-factor of equanimity.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 716 (716) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Among internal phenomena, I do not see a single phenomenon that causes unarisen evil and unwholesome states to arise, or causes already arisen evil and unwholesome states to recur and increase; nor does it cause unarisen wholesome states not to arise, or causes already arisen wholesome states to decline. That is to say: improper attention."

"Monks! Improper attention causes the unarisen hindrance of sensual desire to arise, and causes that which has already arisen to recur and increase. It causes the unarisen hindrances of ill will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-regret, and doubt to arise, and causes those which have already arisen to recur and increase."

The unarisen factor of enlightenment of mindfulness does not arise, and that which has already arisen is allowed to decline; the unarisen factors of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity do not arise, and those which have already arisen are allowed to decline.

"I do not see a single dharma that can cause unarisen evil and unwholesome states not to arise, cause those already arisen to be abandoned, cause unarisen wholesome states to arise, and cause those already arisen to be further developed and expanded—namely, right reflection."

"Monks! For one who practices right reflection, the unarisen hindrance of sensual desire does not arise, and that which has already arisen is abandoned; the unarisen hindrances of ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt do not arise, and those which have already arisen are abandoned."

He causes the unarisen factor of enlightenment of mindfulness to arise; he causes those already arisen to arise again and to increase and expand. He causes the unarisen factors of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity to arise; he causes those already arisen to arise again and to increase and expand.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 717 (717) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Among external phenomena, I do not see a single phenomenon that causes unarisen evil and unwholesome states to arise, or causes those already arisen to recur and increase; nor one that prevents unarisen wholesome states from arising, or causes those already arisen to decline—such as an evil friend or an evil companion."

Those who are evil associates and evil companions cause the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*) that has not yet arisen to arise, and cause that which has already arisen to recur and increase.

They cause the hindrances of ill will (*vyāpāda*), sloth-and-torpor (*styāna-middha*), restlessness-and-regret (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) that have not yet arisen to arise, and cause those that have already arisen to recur and increase.

He causes the unarisen factor of awakening of mindfulness not to arise, and causes those already arisen to decline; he causes the unarisen factors of awakening of investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity not to arise, and causes those already arisen to decline.

“Monks! I do not see a single thing that, when not yet arisen, prevents unwholesome and unskillful states from arising, and when already arisen, causes them to be abandoned; nor that, when not yet arisen, causes wholesome states to arise, and when already arisen, causes them to recur and increase—namely, a good friend, a good companion, and a good associate. For if one has a good friend, a good companion, and a good associate, the hindrance of sensual desire, when not yet arisen, will not arise, and when already arisen, will be abandoned; the hindrances of ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt, when not yet arisen, will not arise, and when already arisen, will be abandoned.”

He causes the unarisen factor of enlightenment of mindfulness to arise; he causes those already arisen to arise again and to increase and expand. He causes the unarisen factors of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity to arise; he causes those already arisen to arise again and to increase and expand.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 718 (718) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are seven factors of enlightenment. What are the seven?

That is to say: the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, the enlightenment factor of energy, the enlightenment factor of joy, the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the enlightenment factor of concentration, and the enlightenment factor of equanimity.
These seven factors of enlightenment are attained with certainty and attained without effort; I enter the meditative absorption of the factors of enlightenment according to my desire.
Whether at dawn, at midday, or in the evening, whenever I wish to enter meditative absorption, I enter it frequently according to my desire.

It is like a king’s high minister who possesses various garments kept in chests and trunks; as needed—whether required during the day or at dusk—he may use them according to his will with complete freedom.
Thus, bhikṣus!
These seven factors of enlightenment are attained with certainty, attained without exertion, and experienced as one wishes.

This factor of mindfulness of mine is pure and stainless; when it arises, I know its arising; when it ceases, I know its cessation; when it subsides, I know its subsiding; when it has arisen, I know it has arisen; when it has ceased, I know it has ceased. The same is said for the factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.
When the Venerable Śāriputra had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what he said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
719 (719) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Pāṭaliputra.
At that time, the Venerable Upama and the Venerable Aṭimuttaka were staying at the Kalandakanivāpa Monastery in Pāṭaliputra.

Then, in the late afternoon, the Venerable Aṭimuttaka arose from meditation and went to where the Venerable Upama was. After they had exchanged greetings and expressions of courtesy, he withdrew to sit at one side and asked the Venerable Upama:
"Venerable sir!..."
"One who is able to know the skillful means of the seven factors of enlightenment—how does such a one dwell in pleasant meditative attainment?
How does such a one dwell in painful meditative attainment? Upama replied, "Venerable Aṭimuktaka!"
“A bhikṣu who skillfully knows the means cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment; thus he dwells in pleasant meditative attainment, and thus he dwells in painful meditative attainment.
He asked again:
“In what way does a bhikṣu skillfully know the means to cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment?”
Upama replied: “When a bhikṣu practices the awakening factor of mindfulness through skillful means, he knows that he is thinking:

‘That mind is not well-liberated; it is not free from sleepiness, nor is it well-subdued regarding restlessness and regret; it is not free from sleepiness. Although I contemplate the factors for the station of mindfulness and apply myself with diligence and skillful means, I do not attain equanimity.’”
The same applies to the awakening factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity; they are also explained in this way.
When a bhikkhu is applying the means for the awakening factor of mindfulness, he first reflects:

"The mind is well-liberated, it rightly overcomes sloth and torpor, and it subdues restlessness and remorse; having reflected upon these phenomena pertaining to the awakening factor of mindfulness, I shall attain equanimity without needing to exert further effort."
"So it is, Atimuktaka!

A bhikṣu who knows the skillful means cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment; thus he dwells with delight in meditative absorption, and thus he does not dwell with delight in meditative absorption."
At that time, after the two noble men had finished their discussion on the Dharma, they each rose from their seats and departed. 720 (720). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha was also staying at the Sāla Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī.

Then, a great number of bhikṣus went to where Anuruddha was, exchanged greetings and expressions of courtesy with him, and after having so done, sat down to one side and said to the Venerable Anuruddha:
"Venerable sir, do you know a skillful means for dwelling in happiness when cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment?"
The Venerable Anuruddha said to the bhikṣus:
"I know the skillful means by which a bhikṣu, when cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment, gives rise to a pleasant dwelling.
The bhikṣus then asked the Venerable Anuruddha:
“How does a bhikkhu, through skillful means, experience a pleasant dwelling while cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment?
Venerable Anuruddha addressed the bhikkhus:

“A bhikkhu, through skillful means, cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness; he understands well his reflections, his mind is well-liberated, he has effectively overcome sloth and torpor, and he has effectively subdued restlessness and remorse.”

Having thus reflected upon the factors of enlightenment in their respective domains, he applies himself with diligent skill, his mind free from indolence; his body is at ease and undisturbed, his mind is bound so as to remain settled, free from discursive thoughts, and he enters one-pointed meditative absorption.

The same applies to the awakening factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity; this is called knowing the bhikṣu’s skillful means for dwelling in happiness when cultivating the seven awakening factors.
Then, having heard what the Venerable Ānanda had said, the many bhikṣus rejoiced and approved, rose from their seats, and departed.
721 (721). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"When a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, seven treasures manifest in the world: the gold wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the divine jewel treasure, the precious queen treasure, the minister-treasure of the treasury, and the minister-treasure of the military."

In this same way, when a Tathāgata appears in the world, the jewels of the seven factors of enlightenment also manifest. While staying atop a pavilion for the observance of the fast, surrounded by his ministers, a precious golden wheel appeared from the east. The wheel had a thousand spokes, with hubs and rims perfectly aligned; its characteristics were complete. Seeing such an auspicious omen, [the king thought]: "This must surely be a Wheel-turning Sage King; I am now certainly destined to be a Wheel-turning King."
He then received the precious golden wheel with both hands, placed it in his left hand, and rotated it with his right hand, saying these words:
"If you are indeed the precious golden wheel of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, you should proceed along the ancient path of the Wheel-Turning Sage Kings."

Thereupon, the Wheel-Treasure set forth, and the king followed behind it as it ascended into the void toward the east, traveling through the eastern direction along the path of the upright way of the ancient sage-kings.
The king follows the wheel-treasure, and the fourfold army follows him as well; to whatever region the wheel-treasure halts, the king halts there, and the fourfold army also halts.
The minor kings throughout the various kingdoms of the eastern regions, upon seeing the Holy King’s arrival, all submitted and came under his rule.

“When a Tathāgata appears in the world, seven factors of enlightenment manifest in the world; namely: the factor of mindfulness, the factor of investigation of phenomena, the factor of energy, the factor of joy, the factor of tranquility, the factor of concentration, and the factor of equanimity.”
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
722 (722) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"When a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, seven treasures manifest in the world.
How is it that when a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, the precious golden wheel manifests?

At that time, the Kṣatriya consecrated holy king, on the fifteenth day of the month, having bathed for purification and undertaken the observance of the fast, sat upon a multi-storied pavilion surrounded by his ministers.

The precious golden wheel-treasure appeared from the east; its wheel had a thousand spokes, with hubs and rims perfectly aligned, complete in all the characteristics of a wheel, made of natural, genuine gold.
According to ancient tradition, when a consecrated Kṣatriya great king observes the poṣadha on the fifteenth day of the month, he bathes for purity and undertakes the observance of merit and virtue.

"Welcome, Great King! This is your kingdom; this land is peaceful and secure, and its people are prosperous and happy. We pray that you will dwell here and teach the people of the nation, and we shall follow you."
The Holy King replied: "O heads of villages!

You should now simply transform the people of your lands well. Should there be those who do not comply, you must come and inform me; I shall then transform them according to the Dharma. Do not practice what is contrary to the Dharma, nor cause the people of your lands to practice what is contrary to the Dharma. If you act in this manner, then you follow my transformation."
Thereupon, the Holy King crossed from the eastern sea, following the path of the ancient holy kings, and arrived at the southern sea;
having reached the southern sea, he crossed it and went to the western sea;
following the path of the ancient holy kings, he crossed the western sea and arrived at the northern sea.
The minor kings of the south, west, and north welcomed him and made their requests, just as was extensively described regarding the east.

Thereupon, the precious golden wheel followed the noble king as he crossed the northern sea and returned to his palace; it came to rest in mid-air above the Hall of Righteous Governance. This is how a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, and how the precious golden wheel manifests in the world.
"What is it for a Wheel-Turning Sage King to appear in the world that the white elephant treasure manifests in the world?

If there is a pure-colored elephant belonging to a consecrated Great King of the Kṣatriya caste, its color being bright and beautiful, with its seven limbs touching the ground—when the Sage King sees it, his heart is filled with joy, thinking: 'Now this precious elephant has appeared in response to me. He then commands the skilled elephant trainer: 'Quickly train this precious elephant; once trained, bring it here.'"

Upon receiving his command, the elephant trainer subdued the elephant in less than a single day; it was fully endowed with all the marks of a well-trained animal, just like other elephants that have been trained for years. Thus, this jewel of an elephant was likewise subdued in a single day.
Once tamed, it was sent to the king’s presence, where the attendant addressed the Great King:
"This elephant is now fully trained; the King himself may determine the proper time.

At that moment, the Holy King observed that the signs of the elephant's training were complete, and he immediately mounted the precious elephant. In the early morning, he traveled across the four seas, returning to the royal palace at midday. This is called the appearance of a Wheel-Turning Holy King in the world, and thus the treasure of the elephant manifests in the world.
"What is it that constitutes the appearance of a Wheel-Turning Sage King in the world and the manifestation of the horse-treasure in the world?

The horse-treasure possessed by the Wheel-Turning Sage King is purely blue in color, with a black head and a glossy tail. When the Sage King sees this horse, his heart is filled with joy, thinking: 'Now this divine horse has appeared in response to me. He then entrusts it to a master of horse-training, commanding him to train it quickly and bring it back once it is trained."

Following these instructions, the horse trainer tamed the horse in less than a single day; it was as if it had been trained for years like other horses. The taming of the Horse-Treasure was likewise so.
Knowing that the horse was now tamed, he returned it to the king and said:
"Great King!
This horse is now tamed."

At that time, the Holy King, having observed that the precious horse was fully prepared with the marks of a well-trained steed, mounted it at dawn and traveled across the four seas, returning to the royal palace by midday. This is called the appearance of a Wheel-Turning Holy King in the world, and the manifestation of the Horse Treasure in the world.
"What is it that when a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, the maṇi jewel manifests in the world?

If the precious jewel possessed by a Wheel-Turning Sage King is eight-faceted in shape, radiant and luminous, and free from all internal flaws, it constantly serves as a lamp within the royal palace."

The Wheel-Turning Sage King examines the precious jewel on a night of dark rain; leading his fourfold army into the gardens, he holds the jewel before him as it radiates light for one yojana in every direction. This is how the Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, and the maṇi jewel manifests in the world.
"What is it that when a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, the precious jade-like woman manifests in the world? Regarding all the women possessed by the Wheel-Turning Sage King:

she is neither black nor white, neither tall nor short, neither coarse nor delicate, neither fat nor thin; her limbs are upright and graceful. In cold weather her body is warm, and in hot weather her body is cool. Her body is as soft as *kāliṅga* cloth. From all the pores of her body, the fragrance of sandalwood issues forth, and the breath from her mouth and nose produces the scent of the *utpala* lotus."

She sleeps after him and rises before him; observing the king’s facial expression and demeanor, she serves him appropriately with gentle words and affectionate speech. With an upright mind and right mindfulness, she gives rise to the aspiration for the Way of Kings, her heart never transgressing his will—how much less so her body or speech. This is the Precious Woman of a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
"What is the manifestation of the Wheel-Turning King’s Treasure of the Minister of the Treasury in the world?

It is because the Wheel-Turning King’s minister of the treasury practiced giving in his previous lives that he was born with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). He is able to see hidden treasures—whether they have an owner or not, whether they are in water or on land, and whether they are far or near—and he can perceive them all. Whenever the Wheel-Turning King requires precious jewels, he issues a command; whatever the King requires, [the minister] immediately presents to him."
Thereupon, the Sage-King once tested that great minister to observe his capabilities; he boarded a ship to travel upon the sea and said to the minister, "I require precious objects."
The minister addressed the king, saying:
"Please wait by the riverbank; I shall present it to you.
The king said to that minister:
“I have no need for treasures from the shore; give me all that you have.

Thereupon, the minister brought forth four golden jars from the water, filled with gold and jewels, and presented them to the Holy King. The King took what he required and used it; once he had taken enough, the remainder returned to the water.
When a holy wheel-turning monarch appears in the world, there likewise appears in the world such a minister who oversees the treasury.
"How is it that when a holy wheel-turning monarch arises in the world, there appears in the world a minister who oversees the military?"
It refers to a minister in charge of the military who is intelligent and possesses eloquence;

like one in the world who has achieved excellence through careful deliberation, he follows all that is appropriate for the noble king—whether it be what should be departed from, what should be stayed with, what should be gone out, or what should be entered.

As the Holy King marches with his fourfold army, wherever he halts along the way, they do not allow him to become weary; knowing all that the Holy King ought to perform regarding matters of merit pertaining to both the present life and future lives, they report these to the Holy King.
When a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, there is such a minister of the military.
In the same way, when a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world, the seven factors of awakening appear in the world.
What are the seven?

They are the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment of energy, the factor of enlightenment of joy, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 723 (722) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Excellent, bhikṣus! Excellent!”
When the monks hear the Dharma, the junior bhikṣus serve and honor the venerable elders. Why is this?

Because when junior bhikṣus serve and honor the elder bhikṣus, they are able from time to time to hear the profound and sublime Dharma; having heard the profound Dharma, they achieve two forms of rectitude: rectitude of body and rectitude of mind.
At that time, one cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness; having cultivated the awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of mindfulness becomes fulfilled.
Once the awakening factor of mindfulness is fulfilled, one discriminates among phenomena, analyzes phenomena, and reflects upon phenomena.
At that time, one practices the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena through skillful means, and so on, until the awakening factor of equanimity is cultivated to fulfillment.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
724 (Seven Hundred and Twenty-Four). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu maintains the precepts, cultivates virtue, possesses a sense of shame and dread of blame, and has perfected the true Dharma, those who see such a person will obtain great rewards.

Furthermore, those who hear of him, or who follow and recollect him, or who follow him into the homeless life, will obtain great merit; how much more so for those who draw near to him, revere him, and serve him."
Why is this so? Because those who draw near to and serve such persons as these will, from time to time, hear the profound and sublime Dharma;
having heard the profound Dharma, they achieve the two kinds of rectitude—rectitude of body and rectitude of mind—and through skillful means, they cultivate the awakening factor of concentration.
Having practiced them, he brought their practice to fulfillment, even up to the fulfillment of the practice of the awakening factor of equanimity.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
725 (Seven Hundred and Twenty-Five). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"To speak of an accumulation of the unwholesome refers to the five hindrances; this is the correct teaching.
Why is that? Because the pure and singular accumulation of the unwholesome consists of the five hindrances."
What are the five?
They are the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt.
When it is said that "the accumulation of the wholesome" refers to the seven factors of enlightenment, this is the correct teaching.
Why is this? Because that which is purely one, full, and pure consists of the seven factors of enlightenment.
What are these seven?

That is to say: the awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, the awakening factor of energy, the awakening factor of rapture, the awakening factor of tranquility, the awakening factor of concentration, and the awakening factor of equanimity.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
726 (726). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Nivāpa in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was also staying there.
Then, while the Venerable Ānanda was meditating and reflecting in solitude, this thought arose in him:
"Half of the holy life consists of having good friends, good companions, and good associates, rather than evil friends, evil companions, and evil associates."
Then, the Venerable Ānanda arose from his meditation, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
While I was dwelling alone in seclusion, reflecting and contemplating, this thought arose:
"Half of the holy life consists of having virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates, rather than evil friends, evil companions, and evil associates."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do not speak these words:
'Half of the holy life consists of having good friends, good companions, and good associates, rather than evil friends, evil companions, and evil associates.'"

Why is this? Because it is pure, unified, tranquil, and a holy life that is stainless—namely, having virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates, rather than evil friends, evil companions, or evil associates.

For the sake of being a good friend, there are sentient beings who, in my presence, take up the factors of enlightenment, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and tending toward relinquishment.

In this way, the factors of enlightenment—discrimination of phenomena, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity—rely upon seclusion, rely upon dispassion, rely upon cessation, and lead toward relinquishment.
Therefore, Ānanda, you should know this:
that which is purely one, full, and tranquil, a pure and holy life, consists in having good friends, good companions, and good associates, and not evil friends, evil companions, or evil associates.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 727 (727) Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people in the village of Malla and stayed between the city of Kuśinagara and the Hiraṇyavatī River. From the side of that village, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Fold the Blessed One’s upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) into four layers and spread it out; I have a back ailment and wish to lie down for a short rest.
Venerable Ānanda, having received this instruction, folded the upper robe into four layers and spread it out, then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“Having folded the *uttarāsaṅga* fourfold and spread it out, let the World-Honored One know that it is time.

At that moment, the World-Honored One folded his *saṃghāṭī* thickly to serve as a pillow and lay down on his right side, with one foot upon the other, fixing his mindfulness on the light, possessing right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, and maintaining the perception of rising. He then addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Recite the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).”
Then, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Regarding what is called the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the World-Honored One, having personally realized full and perfect enlightenment, has taught it as relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and tending toward relinquishment. Regarding the factors of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, the World-Honored One, having personally realized full and perfect enlightenment, has taught them as relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and tending toward relinquishment.”
The Buddha asked Ānanda,
“Are you speaking of diligence?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
"I speak of diligence,
World-Honored One!
I speak of diligence."
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Only through diligence, cultivated and practiced repeatedly, does one attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
Having spoken these words, he sat upright with his body straight and his mindfulness fixed.
At that time, another bhikṣu spoke this verse:
“Delighting in hearing the exquisite Dharma, He endured his illness to tell it to others.”
The bhikṣu then preached the Dharma, turning the wheel of the seven factors of enlightenment.
"Excellent, Venerable Ānanda! Your exposition is clear, insightful, and skillful;
it possesses the supreme, pure dharmas and is a subtle teaching free from defilement."
Mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity—
these are the seven factors of enlightenment, a subtle and excellent teaching.
Having heard the teaching on the seven factors of enlightenment, he deeply realized the flavor of true awakening.
Though his body was afflicted by great suffering and illness, he sat upright and listened;
regarding [the Buddha] as the King of the True Dharma, he constantly expounded it for the sake of others.
If even he delights in hearing what is spoken, how much more so others who have not yet heard it?
He who possesses the supreme great wisdom and is honored by those with the ten powers—
he too should quickly come to hear the True Dharma.
Those who have heard much and attained mastery, who are well-versed in the Sūtras and Abhidharma,
and who are skilled in the Vinaya— such persons should listen, let alone others;
hearing the teaching of the Dharma as it truly is, they should listen with single-minded attention and discerning wisdom.
Regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddha, one attains the joy of detachment;
with joy, the body becomes tranquil, and the mind likewise finds its own ease.
With a joyful mind, one attains meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and through right contemplation, one engages in the practice of the objective reality.
One who loathes the three realms of existence attains liberation through a mind free from desire;
loathing all states of becoming, they do not accumulate karma for rebirth among humans or gods.
Like a lamp extinguished, they enter final parinirvāṇa without remainder.
"Hearing the Dharma brings great benefit; this is what the Most Victorious One has taught.
Therefore, you should contemplate it with single-minded focus and listen to what the Great Teacher has spoken.
Having spoken these verses, the other bhikṣu rose from his seat and departed.
728 (Seven Hundred and Twenty-Eight). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are seven factors of enlightenment. What are the seven?
They are the factor of mindfulness-enlightenment, up to and including the factor of equanimity-enlightenment.”
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 729 (729) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“You should cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment.
What is the cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment?”

That is to say, the factors of enlightenment beginning with mindfulness and ending with equanimity; if a bhikṣu cultivates the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, he does so by relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and tending toward relinquishment.

In this way, one cultivates the awakening factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, which rely on seclusion, rely on dispassion, rely on cessation, and lead toward relinquishment.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 730 (730) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus... as stated above.
The difference is this: "Bhikṣus!..."
"In the past, they cultivated the seven factors of awakening in this way; in the future, they shall likewise cultivate the seven factors of awakening in this way.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
731 (Seven Hundred and Thirty-One). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If a bhikṣu’s factor of awakening of mindfulness is pure and bright, without branches or joints, free from all afflictions, and neither arisen nor about to arise—except for the training and instruction of the Buddha’s discipline—the same applies up to the factor of awakening of equanimity."
"O Bhikṣus!

The factor of awakening that is mindfulness is pure, bright, and white; it has no limbs or joints, is free from all afflictions, and arises where it had not yet arisen. It is that which is tamed and taught by the Buddha, and nothing else. This applies likewise up to the factor of awakening that is equanimity."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
732 (Seven Hundred and Thirty-Two) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus... as stated above.
The difference is this:

"That which has not arisen does not arise—except through the training and instruction of the Sugata; that which has not arisen does arise—this is the training and instruction of the Sugata, and none other."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 733 (733) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, you have spoken of the factors of enlightenment."
“World-Honored One!
What are the factors of awakening?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"What is called the factors of enlightenment refers to the seven limbs of the path.
Now, monks, these seven factors of enlightenment arise in succession and, through cultivation, reach fulfillment."
Another bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
How do the factors of awakening arise in succession, and how are they cultivated to fulfillment?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu dwells contemplating the body as body internally, when he so dwells, he collects his mind and binds his mindfulness so that it is not lost."

At that time, he applies himself to the cultivation of the awakening factor of mindfulness through skillful means; having cultivated the awakening factor of mindfulness through skillful means, he brings its cultivation to fulfillment.
Having fulfilled the awakening factor of mindfulness, he discriminates, analyzes, and reflects upon phenomena.

At that time, one practices the skillful means of the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena; having practiced these skillful means, they reach fulfillment. In this manner, one proceeds until the awakening factor of equanimity is practiced to fulfillment.

Just as one dwells contemplating the body as a body internally, so too does one dwell contemplating the body externally, both internally and externally, and likewise contemplating feelings, the mind, and phenomena as phenomena. At that time, one should focus the mind with mindfulness, not forgetting; this is also said to apply to the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.
"For one who abides in this way, the factors of enlightenment arise gradually; having arisen gradually, they are cultivated to fulfillment.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
734 (Seven Hundred and Thirty-Four). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those bhikṣus as above.
As for the distinction:

"If a bhikṣu has thus cultivated the seven factors of enlightenment, he shall attain two kinds of fruits: either the exhaustion of outflows and nirvāṇa without remainder in this very life, or the fruit of non-returning."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 735 (735) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park... as described above.
As for the distinction:
"When a bhikṣu has thus cultivated the seven factors of enlightenment and practiced them extensively, he attains four kinds of fruits and four kinds of benefits."
"What are the four?
They are the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala), the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmi-phala), the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmi-phala), and the fruit of arhatship (arhat-phala).
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the other bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
736 (Seven Hundred Thirty-Six). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park... as described above.
As for the distinction:
"If a bhikṣu cultivates the seven factors of awakening and, having cultivated them extensively, shall obtain seven kinds of fruits and seven kinds of benefits."
What are the seven? They are:
a bhikṣu attains the realization of the knowledge of the present life and experiences bliss;
or, at the time of death, he does not attain the realization of the knowledge of the present life and experience bliss.
At the time of death, they attain the exhaustion of the five lower fetters and enter parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state;
if they do not attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, they attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth;
if they do not attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, they attain parinirvāṇa without exertion.
If one does not attain parinirvāṇa through non-exertion (asaṃskāra-parinirvāṇa), one attains parinirvāṇa through exertion (sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāṇa);
if one does not attain parinirvāṇa through exertion, one attains parinirvāṇa by ascending to the upper realms (ūrdhvasrotas-parinirvāṇa).
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the other bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 737 (737) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"What is called the factor of enlightenment?
What are the factors of enlightenment?"
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha:
“The World-Honored One is the root of the Dharma, the eye of the Dharma, and the refuge of the Dharma; we pray that you will explain it for us.
Having heard it, the bhikṣus shall receive and practice it accordingly.”
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs:
"The seven factors of enlightenment refer to the seven dharmas of the path.
O bhikṣus!"
"These seven factors of awakening arise in succession; having arisen in succession, they are cultivated to fulfillment.
The bhikṣus asked the Buddha, "In what way do the seven factors of awakening arise in succession, and having arisen in succession, how are they cultivated to fulfillment?"
"If a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body as body, having so dwelt, he fixes his mind with focused mindfulness without forgetfulness;

at that time, he skillfully cultivates the enlightenment factor of mindfulness. Having skillfully cultivated the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, he brings its cultivation to fulfillment. That is to say, having cultivated the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, he discriminates phenomena; at that time, he skillfully cultivates the enlightenment factor of discrimination of phenomena. Having skillfully cultivated the enlightenment factor of discrimination of phenomena, he brings its cultivation to fulfillment."
The same applies to the awakening factors of energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.

Just as with the internal body, so too with the external body, the internal-external body, and with feelings, the mind, and mental phenomena—dwelling in the contemplation of these phenomena, focusing the mind with mindfulness without forgetting—at that time, one skillfully cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness. Having skillfully cultivated the awakening factor of mindfulness, its cultivation reaches fulfillment.

The same should be said up to the factor of enlightenment of equanimity; this is called the gradual arising of a bhikṣu’s seven factors of enlightenment, and having arisen gradually, their cultivation is brought to fulfillment.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 738 (738) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus... as described above.
The difference is this:

"If these seven factors of enlightenment are cultivated and practiced extensively, one shall attain two fruits: the attainment of nirvāṇa with remainder through knowledge in the present life, and the fruit of anāgāmin."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
739 (Seven Hundred Thirty-Nine). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus... as stated above.
The difference is this:
"If a bhikṣu cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment and practices them extensively, he shall attain the four fruits."
"What are the four?
They are the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala), the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmi-phala), the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmi-phala), and the fruit of arhatship (arhat-phala).
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
740. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park… as described above.
As for the distinctions:
"If a bhikṣu cultivates these seven factors of enlightenment and practices them extensively, he shall attain seven fruits.
What are the seven?"

That is to say, there is parinirvāṇa with remainder in the present life, as well as at the time of death; otherwise, having exhausted the five lower fetters, one attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
If not so, one attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadya-parinirvāyī).
If not so, one attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyī).
If not so, one attains parinirvāṇa with exertion (sābhisamskāra-parinirvāyī).
"If it were not so, one would attain parinirvāṇa as an 'up-streamer' (ūrdhvasrotas).
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
741 (Seven Hundred Forty-One). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should cultivate the meditation on impurity; having cultivated it extensively, one will obtain great fruit and great benefit.
How does one cultivate the meditation on impurity so that, having cultivated it extensively, one obtains great fruit and great benefit?

This bhikṣu cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness accompanied by the contemplation of impurity, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and tends toward relinquishment;

he cultivates the awakening factors of discrimination of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, which are based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and tend toward relinquishment.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
742 (742) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu cultivates the mindfulness of death and, having cultivated it extensively, attains great fruit and great benefit."
How does a bhikṣu cultivate the mindfulness of death?
Having cultivated it extensively, he attains great fruit and great benefit.

This bhikṣu cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness accompanied by the mindfulness of death; it is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and leads toward relinquishment. This is also said for each of the awakening factors up to the awakening factor of equanimity.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
743 (743) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Śākya village of Koṭigāma.
At that time, a large number of bhikṣus, having dressed in the morning and taken up their bowls, entered the village of Yellow Pillows to beg for food.
Then, these many bhikṣus had this thought:
"It is still too early today; the time for begging has not yet arrived. We might go to the heretics' monastery."

At that time, a great number of bhikṣus entered the hermitage of the non-Buddhists; after exchanging greetings and expressions of courtesy with the non-Buddhist renunciants, they sat down to one side.
The various non-Buddhist renunciants said:
"Does the śramaṇa Gautama not teach his disciples such a Dharma as this:

'Abandon the five hindrances—which afflict the mind, weaken the power of wisdom, constitute factors of obstruction, and do not lead toward Nirvāṇa—and having fully gathered the mind, abide in the four foundations of mindfulness'?"

With a mind imbued with loving-kindness, free from enmity and jealousy, and without ill will—vast, immeasurable, well-cultivated, and pervasive—one dwells pervading the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, throughout the entire world.
With a mind imbued with loving-kindness, free from enmity and jealousy, and without ill will—vast, immeasurable, well-practiced, and pervasive—one dwells thus, cultivating it in this manner.
"The same is said regarding the states of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
We also speak thus to our disciples; what difference, then, is there between us and that śramaṇa Gautama?"
"This is what is meant by being able to preach the Dharma together.

At that time, when the many bhikṣus heard what the various non-Buddhist renunciants had said, their hearts were not pleased; they remained silent and did not rebuke them, but rose from their seats and departed.

Having entered the village of Huangzhen to beg for food, he returned to the vihāra, put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, paid homage, and withdrew to sit at one side.
He reported in detail to the Blessed One what that renunciant of another sect had said.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Regarding what that renunciant of another sect has said, you should question him thus:"
"When asked, 'What is the excellence of cultivating a mind of loving-kindness?
What is the excellence of cultivating a mind of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity?

those non-Buddhist renunciants become startled and distracted; some speak of irrelevant matters, while others respond with anger, pride, derision, hostility, or intolerance; or they remain silent and dejected, lowering their heads, losing their eloquence, and dwelling in thought."

Why is this? Among the hosts of devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gods, and humans, I see none who, upon hearing what I have spoken, would find it agreeable with their pleasure, except for the Tathāgata and his assembly of śrāvakas.
"Monks! When the mind is cultivated extensively in conjunction with loving-kindness, it is most excellent for purification;
when compassion is cultivated extensively, it is most excellent for the sphere of infinite space."
Through the cultivation and frequent practice of a mind of joy, the sphere of consciousness is most excellent;
through the cultivation and frequent practice of a mind of equanimity, the sphere of nothingness is most excellent.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
744 (744) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu cultivates a mind of loving-kindness and, having cultivated it extensively, attains great fruit and great benefit."
How does a bhikṣu cultivate a mind of loving-kindness and thereby attain great fruit and great benefit?

This bhikṣu, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness; it is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
He continues in this way until he cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity; it is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 745 (745) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu cultivates the sphere of infinite space and practices it extensively, he will attain great fruit and great benefit."
How does a bhikṣu cultivate the sphere of infinite space, and having cultivated it extensively, attain great fruit and great benefit?

This bhikṣu, with his mind associated with the sphere of infinite space, cultivates the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness; it is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and leads toward relinquishment.
This continues up to the cultivation of the factor of enlightenment of equanimity; it is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and leads toward relinquishment.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

As it was with the discourse on the sphere of infinite space, so too were the three discourses on the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, as explained above.
746 (Seven Hundred Forty-Six). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“If a bhikkhu cultivates mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati) and, having cultivated it extensively, attains great fruit and great benefit.
How does he cultivate mindfulness of breathing so that, having cultivated it extensively, he attains great fruit and great benefit?”

This bhikṣu’s mind is conjoined with mindfulness of breathing; he cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness, which relies on seclusion, relies on dispassion, relies on cessation, and leads toward relinquishment;
and so on, until he cultivates the awakening factor of equanimity, which relies on seclusion, relies on dispassion, relies on cessation, and leads toward relinquishment.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
747 (747) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu cultivates the perception of impermanence and practices it extensively, he will attain great fruit and great benefit."
How does a bhikṣu cultivate the perception of impermanence such that, having cultivated it extensively, he attains great fruit and great benefit?

This bhikṣu, with his mind and speech conjoined with the perception of impermanence, cultivates the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness; it relies on seclusion, relies on dispassion, relies on cessation, and leads toward relinquishment.
This continues until he attains the factor of enlightenment of equanimity, which relies on seclusion, relies on dispassion, relies on cessation, and leads toward relinquishment.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.

As with the perception of impermanence (*anicca-saññā*), so too were the perception of impermanence and suffering (*anicca-dukkha-saññā*), the perception of non-self in suffering (*dukkha-anatta-saññā*), the perception of reflecting on food (*āhāre paṭikūla-saññā*), the perception that all worlds are not to be delighted in (*sabbaloke anabhirata-saññā*), the perception of exhaustion (*khaya-saññā*), the perception of abandonment (*pahāna-saññā*), the perception of dispassion (*virāga-saññā*), the perception of cessation (*nirodha-saññā*), the perception of danger (*ādīnava-saññā*), the perception of impurity (*asubha-saññā*), the perception of a livid corpse (*vinīlaka-saññā*), the perception of a festering corpse (*vipubbaka-saññā*), the perception of a bloated corpse (*uddhumātaka-saññā*), the perception of a decomposed corpse (*vicchiddaka-saññā*), the perception of a corpse half-eaten by scavengers (*vikkhāyitaka-saññā*), the perception of blood (*lohitaka-saññā*), the perception of a scattered corpse (*aṭṭhika-saññā*), the perception of bones (*aṭṭhi-saññā*), and the perception of emptiness (*suññata-saññā*)—each sutra was spoken as above.
Saṃyukta Āgama, Volume Twenty-seven and Volume Twenty-eight,
translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Song Dynasty.
28.748 (748) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Just as the precursor to the rising of the sun is the first light of dawn,
