so too, O bhikṣus, the precursor to the complete exhaustion of suffering and the ultimate end of suffering is right view.”
That person of right view is able to give rise to right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Because they have given rise to concentration and its meditative attainments, the noble disciple’s mind is rightly liberated from greed, hatred, and delusion; thus their mind is well-liberated.
The noble disciple attains right knowledge and vision:
"Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
749 (749) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If ignorance serves as the precursor, then various evil and unwholesome dharmas arise.
At that time, shamelessness and lack of dread accordingly arise."
Once shamelessness and lack of dread have arisen, they give rise to wrong view;
once wrong view has arisen, it can give rise to wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration.
If clarity arises as a precursor, giving birth to all wholesome dharmas, then at that time, shame and remorse arise accordingly.

Once shame and remorse have arisen, they are able to give rise to right view. Once right view has arisen, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration arise in succession.
Having emerged from right concentration, the noble disciple attains right liberation from sensual desire, ill will, and delusion.
Having thus attained right liberation, the noble disciple gains right knowledge and vision:
"Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I myself know that there will be no further existence."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
750 (Seven Hundred and Fifty): Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: “Bhikṣus!
As for all evil and unwholesome dharmas, bhikṣus, they all have ignorance as their root; they arise from the accumulation of ignorance, are produced by ignorance, and originate from ignorance.”
Why is this so? Ignorance (*avidyā*) is a lack of knowledge;

it is the failure to know, as they truly are, wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, those that are blameworthy and blameless, inferior and superior phenomena, defiled and undefiled, the differentiated and the undifferentiated, and dependent origination and non-dependent origination.

Because one does not know them as they truly are, wrong view arises. Having given rise to wrong view, one is able to give rise to wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration.
"If all wholesome dharmas arise, they all have clarity as their root; they are the accumulation of clarity, the birth of clarity, and the emergence of clarity.

One who clearly knows wholesome and unwholesome dharmas as they truly are—knowing as they truly are what is blameworthy and blameless, what is to be approached and not approached, inferior dharmas and superior dharmas, defiled and pure dharmas, conditioned and unconditioned, and dependent origination and non-dependent origination—one who knows them as they truly are possesses right view."
One with right view is able to give rise to right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

Once right concentration has arisen, the noble disciple attains right liberation from greed, hatred, and delusion. Having been liberated from greed, hatred, and delusion, this noble disciple attains right knowledge and vision:
"Birth for me has been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been done; I myself know that there will be no further existence."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
751 (751) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Whether one is a householder or one who has left the home life, if they give rise to unwholesome actions, I do not speak of them. Why is this so?
If those who are householders or those who have left the home life engage in unwholesome practices, they will not delight in the True Dharma.
What are these unwholesome practices?
They are wrong view, and so on, up to wrong concentration. If householders or those who have left the home life engage in wholesome practices, I praise them.
Why is this? One who undertakes right practice delights in the true Dharma and excels in the true Dharma.
What constitutes right practice?
That is to say: right view, up to and including right concentration.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Whether layperson or renunciant, those who give rise to wrong actions...”
They will never find joy in the unsurpassed True Dharma,
whether as householders or those who have gone forth, if they do not engage in right practice.
Those who always find joy in their hearts in the unsurpassed True Dharma [shall attain it].
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 752 (752). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣu Kāma approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
regarding what is called ‘desire’...”
"What is desire? The Buddha told Kāma:
"Desire refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure."
What are these five? They are:
visual consciousness perceiving forms that are lovely, agreeable, and pleasing, which nourish sensual desire.
Likewise, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses perceive objects that are lovely, agreeable, and pleasing, which nourish sensual desire; this is called desire.
"However, that is not desire; rather, the attachment to it is what is called desire.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The various five colors in the world Are not themselves the craving for desire; It is the mind that becomes attached to them That is truly called desire."
"One who perceives thoughts of sensual desire is a man of lust;
though various forms remain ever-present in the world, the practitioner severs the desire of the mind.
The bhikṣu Kāma addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is there a path, is there a track, by which this craving and desire can be severed?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:

“There is the Eightfold Noble Path that can sever craving and desire; namely, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.”
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣu Kāma, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
753 (753) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Ariṣṭa who went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"As for what is called 'ambrosia' (amṛta), why is it named ambrosia?
The Buddha told Ariṣṭa:
“‘Amṛta’ (the Deathless) is a designation for the *dhātu* (element), yet I have spoken this name specifically for one who has exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*).
The bhikṣu Ariṣṭa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“Is there a path and a practice which, through cultivation and repeated cultivation, leads to the attainment of the Dharma of the Deathless?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu: “There is;
it is the so-called eightfold noble path—namely, right view up to right concentration.”
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 754 (754) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
Regarding what are called the requisites for the root of the samādhis of the noble ones:
"What are the requisites for the root of the samādhis of the noble ones?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"It refers to the seven factors of the Noble Eightfold Path as the foundation and the requisite equipment for the samādhis of the noble ones and so forth.
What are the seven?
They are right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right mindfulness."
Śāriputra! Having established these seven paths as the foundation, one attains a single-mindedness; this is called the fundamental equipment for the samādhi of the noble ones.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
755–7 (755–7) As in the three preceding sutras.
The Buddha questioned the bhikṣus in this manner; the three sūtras are likewise explained in this way. 758 (758). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There is no fear for mother and son; there is fear for mother and son.
This is what the foolish, unlearned worldlings say, yet they do not understand that there is no fear for mother and son, nor that there is fear for mother and son."
“Monks, there are three kinds of fear regarding the absence of mother and son, which are spoken of by foolish,
unlearned worldlings. What are the three?
"O bhikṣus!

There may be times when violent military conflict breaks out and ravages the land, causing people to scatter with the current like drifting foam; sons lose their mothers, and mothers lose their sons. This is called the first fear of being separated from mother and son, as described by foolish, unlearned worldlings."
"Furthermore, bhikṣus!

There may come a time when a great fire suddenly breaks out, burning down cities, towns, and villages. People flee in all directions, mothers and sons losing one another. This is called the second fear of being without mother or son, as described by foolish, unlearned worldlings."
"Furthermore, bhikṣus!

There may be a time when it rains heavily in the mountains and floods flow out, sweeping away villages and submerging them. People flee in haste, and mothers and children lose one another. This is called the third fear of being without mother or child, as described by foolish, unlearned worldlings."
"However, these fears are fears of being with one's mother and child; the foolish, unlearned worldling calls them 'fears of being without mother and child.

Suppose there arises a time of military conflict and chaos that ravages the land, and people are driven along by the surging waves of flight until mother and child lose each other. Yet, at some point, they may see one another again. This is called the first 'fear of being with mother and child,' which the foolish, unlearned worldling calls the 'fear of being without mother and child.'"

"Furthermore, suppose a great fire suddenly breaks out, burning down cities, towns, and villages; people flee in all directions, mothers and children losing one another, or perhaps finding one another again. This is called the second fear regarding mother and child, which the foolish, unlearned worldlings call the absence of fear regarding mother and child."

"Furthermore, when heavy rains fall upon the mountains and floodwaters surge forth, submerging villages, people flee in haste; mothers and children lose one another, yet sometimes they find each other again. This is called the third fear regarding mother and child, which ignorant, unlearned worldlings call the 'fear of being without mother and child.'"
“Monks! There are three kinds of fear regarding the loss of mother and son, which I have personally realized upon attaining full enlightenment and have proclaimed.
What are these three?
If, monks, when a son has grown old, there is no mother who can say to him: "Son!..."
"Do not grow old; I shall take your place.
When his mother grew old, she likewise had no son who would say to her:
"Mother!..."
"May you not grow old; let me take your place and grow old.
This is called the first fearlessness regarding mother and son, which was proclaimed by me upon my own realization of *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Furthermore, bhikṣu!
There may be a time when a son is ill and his mother is unable to say: 'Son!'"
“Do not fall ill; I shall take your place.
When the mother was ill, the son was likewise unable to say: “Mother!”
"Do not be distressed; I shall take the mother's place.
This is called the second fearlessness, "the absence of a mother," which was proclaimed by me upon my own realization of *sambodhi*.
"Furthermore, my son, when you die, there is no mother who can say: 'Son!
Do not die; I shall now take your place.'"
When the mother is on the verge of death, there is no son who can say:
"Mother! Do not die; I shall take your place."
"This is called the third fear of being without mother or son, as proclaimed by me upon my own awakening to *sambodhi*.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha:

"Is there a path, is there a way, through the cultivation and repeated practice of which one may sever the three previous fears of being without mother or son, and sever the three subsequent fears of being without mother or son?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“There is a path, there is a track, for severing those three fears.
What is that path?”

What is the path that, through cultivation and repeated practice, abandons the first three kinds of fear regarding mother and son, and abandons the latter three kinds of fear regarding mother and son?
It is the eightfold noble path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 759 (759) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are three feelings—impermanent, conditioned, and arisen from mental objects.
What are the three?"
"They are pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Is there a path, is there a track, by the cultivation and repeated practice of which these three feelings are abandoned?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“There is a path, there is a track, by the cultivation and repeated practice of which these three feelings are abandoned.”
“What is the path, what is the track, by the cultivation and repeated practice of which these three feelings are abandoned?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.”
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
760 (Seven Hundred and Sixty): Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are three things in the world that are not pleasing, not lovable, and not worth dwelling upon.
What are these three?"
That is to say: old age, sickness, and death—these three phenomena are not delightful, not lovable, and not to be longed for.

If these three phenomena—which are not delightful, not lovable, and not to be longed for—did not exist in the world, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha would not appear in the world; nor would the world know that the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, provides instruction, and offers guidance.

Because these three things exist in the world—which are unpleasant, unlovely, and unworthy of recollection—the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world; thus the world knows that there is a Tathāgata who teaches the Dharma, provides instruction, and offers guidance.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“Is there a path, is there a way, by which these three things—which are not delightful, not lovely, and not worth dwelling upon—can be abandoned?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There is a path, there is a way, by practicing and cultivating it extensively, to abandon these three things that are unpleasant, unlovely, and unworthy of mindfulness."
What is the path? What is the track?
By practicing and cultivating it extensively, how are these three things—which are unpleasant, unlovely, and unworthy of mindfulness—abandoned?
That is to say, the Eightfold Noble Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 761 (761) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall speak of those in training and those beyond training.
Listen attentively and reflect upon it well."
What is training?

It refers to training in the accomplishment of right view, and training in the accomplishment of right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; this is called training.
What is the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa)?

It refers to the accomplishment of the right view of one beyond training, and the accomplishment of right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; this is called the state of one beyond training.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As it was for those in training and those beyond training, so it was for the *saddharmasatva* (true persons) and the *mahāsattva* (great beings), who were also addressed in the same way.
762 (Seven Hundred and Sixty-Two). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall speak of the noble exhaustion of the outflows (ārya-āsravakṣaya).
What is the noble exhaustion of the outflows?

It refers to the accomplishment of the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), up to and including the accomplishment of the right concentration of one beyond training; this is called the noble exhaustion of the outflows."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
763 (Seven Hundred and Sixty-Three). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now speak of the eight factors of the noble path.
What are these eight?"
"Namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
764 (Seven Hundred and Sixty-Four). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now explain the cultivation of the Noble Eightfold Path.
Listen attentively and reflect well.
What is the cultivation of the Noble Eightfold Path?"

This bhikṣu cultivates right view, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and leads toward relinquishment; he cultivates right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration, each based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and leading toward relinquishment. This is called the cultivation of the Noble Eightfold Path.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 765 (765) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now speak of the eightfold noble path already cultivated by bhikṣus in the past, and the eightfold noble path to be cultivated in the future."
...and so forth. Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
766 (766) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“If a bhikṣu possesses right view that is pure, bright, and white, free from all faults and afflictions, neither arising nor having arisen—except for that which has been tamed by the Buddha—and so on up to right concentration, it is also to be explained in the same way.”
If right view is pure, bright, and white, free from all faults and afflictions, and has not yet arisen but is capable of arising—this is likewise said for everything up to right concentration.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As it was said regarding what the Buddha spoke, so it was also said regarding what the Sugata spoke, as described above.
767 (Seven Hundred and Sixty-Seven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"To speak of the collection of the unwholesome refers to the five hindrances; this is the correct teaching.
Why is that? Because the collection of purely unwholesome states is precisely what is called the five hindrances."
What are these five?
They are the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt.
That which is called the collection of wholesome dharmas is the so-called Eightfold Noble Path; this is termed "correct teaching."
Why is this so? That which is a "pure, singular, full, and perfect mass of goodness" refers to the Noble Eightfold Path.
What are the eight?
"Namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
768 (Seven Hundred and Sixty-Eight). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kūṭāgāraśālā in the valley of Rājagṛha.
Then, the Venerable Ānanda, while alone in a quiet place, had this thought:
"Half of the holy life consists of good friends, good companions, and good associates," and so forth.
The Buddha then told Ānanda:
"One who is purely and perfectly pure, possessing the holy life, is called a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Why is this?

Because for the sake of being a spiritual friend, I cause all sentient beings to cultivate right view—relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and leading toward relinquishment—and even to cultivate right concentration, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and leading toward relinquishment."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 769 (769). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl, entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms.

At that moment, a Brahmin named Jātiśroṇa was riding in a white horse-drawn chariot, accompanied by a large retinue of young attendants. His horses were white, his chariot was white, his reins were white, and his whip was white; he wore a white cap and a white parasol, held a white fly-whisk in his hand, and was dressed in white garments and white necklaces. His body was anointed with white perfumes, and all his attendants were likewise white. As he left the city of Śrāvastī intending to go to the grove to instruct others in recitation, the people who saw him all said, "What a magnificent carriage!"
"Excellent vehicle!
It is the vehicle of the brahmins.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda saw that the brahmin’s retinue and all their belongings were entirely white; having seen this, he entered the city to beg for alms.

Returning to the vihāra, he took up his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

This morning, having dressed and taken up my alms bowl, I entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms and saw the Brahmin Jātivāda riding in a white horse-drawn chariot; his retinue and all his equipment were entirely white, and the people cried out, "A magnificent carriage!"
"Excellent vehicle!
It is the vehicle of the brahmins.
What do you think?
"Bhagavān!
Within the True Dharma and Vinaya, is this the vehicle of the worldlings,
or is it the vehicle of the brahmins?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“This is the vehicle of worldly people; it is not the vehicle of the Brahmins according to my Dharma and Vinaya, Ānanda!”

Listen attentively and reflect well upon this; I shall explain for you my True Dharma and Discipline—the vehicle of the devas, the vehicle of the brahmins, and the Great Vehicle—which is capable of subduing the army of the afflictions.
Ānanda! What are the vehicle of the True Dharma and Discipline, the vehicle of the devas, the vehicle of the brahmins, and the Great Vehicle, which are able to subdue the army of afflictions?
That is to say, the Eightfold Noble Path—from right view up to right concentration. Ānanda!
This is called the vehicle of the True Dharma and Discipline, the vehicle of the devas, the vehicle of Brahmā, and the Great Vehicle; it is that which can subdue the army of afflictions.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Faith and precepts are the yoke of the Dharma; Shame and remorse are the long tether.
With right mindfulness as a skillful guardian, One becomes a capable charioteer."
Equanimity is the pole, wisdom and diligence are the wheels;
The armor of non-attachment and patience, Practicing the Dharma with peace and stability,
Advancing straight on without turning back, One goes forever to the place beyond sorrow.
"The wise man mounts the battle chariot To crush and subdue the enemy of ignorance.
(770) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should abandon wrong view and one should sever wrong view. If wrong view were impossible to sever, I would never say that one should abandon or sever it."
Because wrong view can be abandoned, I say that a bhikṣu should abandon wrong view.
If one does not abandon wrong view, wrong view will result in what is non-beneficial, harmful, and suffering; therefore, I say that one should abandon wrong view.
In this same way, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration are also explained. "Monks!..."
Having abandoned wrong view, one should cultivate right view; if one cannot cultivate right view, I would never say that one is practicing right view.
Because one has attained the cultivation of right view, I say that a bhikṣu should cultivate right view.

If one does not cultivate right view, it will result in what is unwholesome, non-beneficial, and suffering; because failing to cultivate right view results in what is unwholesome, non-beneficial, and suffering, I therefore say that one should cultivate right view, for it is wholesome and beneficial, and one shall always attain peace and happiness.
Therefore, bhikṣus,
you should cultivate right view.
The same applies to right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 771 (771) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇī approached the place where the Buddha was, exchanged greetings and pleasantries with the World-Honored One, and having finished his greetings and pleasantries, withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying: “Gautama!
That is to say, neither the non-far shore nor the far shore. Gautama,
what is the non-far shore?
"What, then, is the 'other shore'?
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"Those with wrong views are not the other shore."
Right view is the further shore;
wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration are not the further shore.
Right view is the further shore; right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration are the further shore.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"How rare are those people Who can cross to the further shore!
All beings in every world Wander and roam upon this shore."
"Those who are able to properly conform to this true Dharma and Vinaya, they shall be able to cross over that shore of birth and death which is so difficult to traverse.
At that time, the brahmin Jātiśroṇa, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and expressed his approval; he rose from his seat and departed.

772–4 (772–4): In this same manner, there are three sūtras concerning a different bhikṣu who questioned the Venerable Ānanda, the Buddha, and the bhikṣus respectively; these are also as explained above.
775 (Seven Hundred Seventy-Five). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Among internal phenomena, I do not see a single phenomenon that can cause unarisen evil and unwholesome states to arise, or cause those already arisen to recur, increase, and expand, such as what is called 'incorrect attention.'"
"O monks! Improper reflection causes unarisen wrong views to arise, and causes those already arisen to recur and increase.
It is the same for wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration."

“Monks! Among internal phenomena, I do not see a single factor that prevents unarisen evil and unwholesome states from arising and causes arisen evil and unwholesome states to cease as effectively as right reflection.”

"Monks! For one who practices right reflection, unarisen wrong view is prevented from arising, and that which has already arisen is brought to cessation. As it is with wrong view, so it is for wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration; thus it should be spoken of."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
776 (Seven Hundred Seventy-Six). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

“Among internal phenomena, I do not see a single phenomenon that causes unarisen wholesome qualities not to arise, or causes already arisen wholesome qualities to decline, as does what is called ‘incorrect attention.’”
"O monks! Improper reflection causes right view that has not yet arisen not to arise, and causes right view that has already arisen to decline.

Likewise, it causes right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration that have not yet arisen not to arise, and causes those that have already arisen to decline."

“Monks! Among internal phenomena, I do not see a single factor that causes unarisen wholesome states to arise and causes arisen wholesome states to recur, increase, and expand as much as right reflection.”
"O monks! Right reflection causes right view that has not yet arisen to arise, and causes right view that has already arisen to recur and increase.

In this same way, it causes right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration that have not yet arisen to arise, and causes those that have already arisen to recur and increase."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 777 (777) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Among internal phenomena, I do not see a single factor that causes unarisen evil and unwholesome states to arise, causes already arisen evil and unwholesome states to recur and increase, prevents unarisen wholesome states from arising, or causes already arisen wholesome states to decline—namely, improper attention."
"O bhikṣus!

They cause unarisen right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration not to arise; and they cause those already arisen to decline.

“Monks! Within my own teachings, I do not see a single dharma that—like right reflection—causes unarisen evil and unwholesome states not to arise, causes arisen evil and unwholesome states to cease, causes unarisen wholesome states to arise, and causes arisen wholesome states to recur, increase, and expand.”

"O monks! Right reflection causes unarisen wrong views not to arise, and causes arisen wrong views to be extinguished; it causes unarisen right views to arise, and causes arisen right views to be renewed and further increased."

In this way, he causes unarisen wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration not to arise; he causes those already arisen to be abandoned. He causes unarisen right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration to arise; he causes those already arisen to be further developed and expanded.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 778 (778) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Among external phenomena, I do not see a single factor that causes unarisen evil and unwholesome states to arise, or causes already arisen evil and unwholesome states to recur and increase, such as what is called evil friends, evil companions, and evil associates."
"Monks! Evil friends, evil companions, and evil associates can cause unarisen wrong views to arise, and they can cause already arisen wrong views to recur and increase."

In this way, they cause unarisen wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration to arise; and those that have already arisen, they cause to recur and increase further.

“Monks! Among external phenomena, I do not see a single thing that prevents unarisen evil and unwholesome states from arising and causes arisen evil and unwholesome states to cease, as does a virtuous friend, a virtuous companion, and a virtuous associate.”
"Monks! A virtuous friend, a virtuous companion, and a virtuous follower can cause unarisen wrong views not to arise, and cause those already arisen to be extinguished;

they can cause unarisen wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration not to arise, and cause those already arisen to be extinguished."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 779 (779) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

“Among external phenomena, I do not see a single phenomenon capable of causing unarisen wholesome qualities to arise, or causing arisen wholesome qualities to recur and increase, as is the case with what is called a virtuous friend, a virtuous companion, and a virtuous follower.”

"Monks! A virtuous friend, a virtuous companion, and a virtuous follower can cause right view that has not yet arisen to arise, and can cause right view that has already arisen to be renewed and further increased."

In this way, he causes the unarisen right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration to arise; and those already arisen, he causes to recur, furthering and expanding them.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 780 (780) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“Among external phenomena, I do not see a single thing that can cause unarisen evil and unwholesome states to arise, or cause already arisen evil and unwholesome states to recur and increase, or prevent unarisen wholesome states from arising, or cause already arisen wholesome states to perish—such as what is called an evil friend, an evil companion, or an evil follower.”
"Monks! Evil friends, evil companions, and evil associates can cause unarisen wrong views to arise, and cause those wrong views that have already arisen to recur and increase."
It causes unarisen right view not to arise, and causes arisen right view to decline.

It causes right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration that have not yet arisen not to arise, and it causes those that have already arisen to decline.

“Monks! Among external phenomena, I do not see a single phenomenon that can cause unarisen evil and unwholesome states to arise, cause arisen evil and unwholesome states to cease, cause unarisen wholesome states to arise, or cause arisen wholesome states to recur, increase, and expand, as much as a virtuous friend, a virtuous companion, and a virtuous associate.”
"O bhikṣus!

A virtuous friend, a virtuous companion, and a virtuous follower can cause unarisen wrong views not to arise, cause arisen wrong views to be extinguished, cause unarisen right views to arise, and cause arisen right views to be renewed and further increased."

In this way, he causes unarisen wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration not to arise; he causes those that have already arisen to be abandoned. He causes unarisen right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration to arise; he causes those that have already arisen to be further developed and expanded.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 781 (781) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

“Among internal phenomena, I do not see a single phenomenon that can cause unarisen evil and unwholesome states to arise, or cause those already arisen to recur and increase, or prevent unarisen wholesome states from arising, or cause those already arisen to decline—such as what is called improper attention.”
"O bhikṣus!

Improper attention can cause unarisen wrong views to arise, and cause arisen wrong views to recur and increase; it prevents unarisen right views from arising, and causes arisen right views to decline."

“Monks! Among internal phenomena, I do not see a single phenomenon that is capable of preventing unarisen evil and unwholesome states from arising, causing arisen evil and unwholesome states to cease, causing unarisen wholesome states to arise, and causing arisen wholesome states to recur, increase, and expand, as is the case with right reflection.”
"O bhikṣus!

Right reflection can cause unarisen wrong views not to arise and cause those already arisen to be extinguished; it can cause unarisen right views to arise and cause those already arisen to be renewed and further increased."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Just as it was taught regarding wrong view and right view, so too were seven sutras taught as above concerning wrong intention and right intention; wrong speech and right speech; wrong action and right action; wrong livelihood and right livelihood; wrong effort and right effort; wrong mindfulness and right mindfulness; and wrong concentration and right concentration.

As with the eight discourses on internal phenomena (*adhyātma-dharma*), so too should the eight discourses on external phenomena (*bāhya-dharma*) be recited in the same manner. 782 (782) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There is what is not the Dharma and what is the Dharma.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you.”
What constitutes the unrighteous (adharma) and the righteous (dharma)?
That is to say: wrong view is unrighteous; right view is righteous. This continues up to: wrong concentration is unrighteous; right concentration is righteous.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

As with "what is not the Dharma" and "what is the Dharma," so too for "what is not the Vinaya" and "the correct Vinaya," "what is non-noble" and "what is noble," "unwholesome dharmas" and "wholesome dharmas," "dharmas not to be cultivated" and "dharmas to be cultivated," "dharmas that are not excellent" and "excellent dharmas," "dark dharmas" and "bright dharmas," "what is not the meaning" and "the correct meaning," "inferior dharmas" and "superior dharmas," "dharmas with fault" and "dharmas without fault," and "dharmas to be abandoned" and "dharmas not to be abandoned"—each sutra is to be recited as explained above.
783. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kosambī in the Ghosira Park.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was also residing there.

A certain brahmin approached the Venerable Ānanda and exchanged greetings and pleasantries with him. Having finished the exchange of greetings and pleasantries, he sat down to one side and said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"I wish to ask a question; would you have the leisure to explain it to me?"
Ānanda replied, “I shall answer whatever you ask, provided that I know.
The brāhmaṇa asked:
"Venerable Ānanda!
For what reason have you gone forth under the ascetic Gautama to practice the holy life?
Ānanda replied:
“Brahmin! It is for the sake of severing [them].
He asked again:
"What is it that is severed?
He replied, "Greed is severed; hatred and delusion are severed."
He asked again:
"Ānanda! Is there a path, is there a track, that can sever greed, hatred, and delusion?"
Ānanda replied:
"There is, namely, the Eightfold Noble Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration."
The brahmin said: “Ānanda!
How excellent is this Way!”
"Wondrous indeed is this practice!
Through cultivation and repeated cultivation, one can sever such greed, hatred, and delusion.
When the Venerable Ānanda had spoken these words, that brahmin, having heard what was said, rejoiced and expressed his approval; he then rose from his seat and departed.
Just as with the abandoning of greed, hatred, and delusion, so too regarding the subduing of greed, hatred, and delusion;

the attainment of *nirvāṇa*; the state of wearying revulsion; the non-attainment of *nirvāṇa*; the meaning of a *śramaṇa*; the meaning of a *brāhmaṇa*; liberation; the abandonment of suffering; the ultimate end of suffering; and the complete extinction of suffering—each of these sūtras is to be recited exactly as stated above.
784. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There is the wrong and there is the right.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall explain it to you.
What is the wrong?
This refers to wrong view, up to and including wrong concentration.
What is right? It refers to right view, up to and including right concentration.

What is right view? It is the teaching that there is giving, there is sacrifice, there is almsgiving; that there is wholesome conduct and unwholesome conduct; that there is the fruit and retribution of wholesome and unwholesome conduct; that there is this world and the other world; that there are parents and the rebirth of beings; that there are arhats who have well-attained and well-proceeded, who have realized for themselves through direct knowledge and dwell in its fulfillment, [knowing]:
"Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and I myself know that there will be no further existence."
What is right intention?
It is the intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill will, and the intention of non-harming.
What is right speech?
That is to say: abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, and abstaining from frivolous speech.
What is right action?
It refers to abstaining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
What is right livelihood?
It means seeking clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites in accordance with the Dharma, and not in a manner contrary to the Dharma.
What is right effort?
This refers to desire, diligence, skillful means, renunciation, exertion, capability, and constant practice without regression.
What is right mindfulness?
It is mindfulness that is compliant, mindfulness that is neither delusive nor false.
"What is right concentration?
It is the dwelling of the mind in non-distraction, steadfastness, sustained application, tranquility, samādhi, and one-pointedness.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
785 (Seven Hundred and Eighty-Five). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus... as described above.
As for the distinctions:
"What is right view? There are two kinds of right view:

there is right view that is worldly, conventional, with outflows, and with clinging, which leads toward a favorable rebirth; [and there is right view that is noble, supramundane, without outflows, and without clinging, which leads to the complete destruction of suffering]."
There is right view that is noble, supramundane, untainted, and without grasping, which leads to the complete exhaustion of suffering and turns one toward the end of suffering.
What is right view that is tainted, with grasping, and leads to a favorable rebirth?

If one perceives that there is giving and there is teaching, up to the point of knowing that there are arhats in the world who do not undergo further existence—this is called mundane right view; it is worldly, conventional, with outflows, and with grasping, leading toward a fortunate rebirth.
What is right view that is noble, supramundane, taintless, and non-clinging, which leads to the complete destruction of suffering and turns one toward the end of suffering?

It is when a noble disciple contemplates suffering as suffering, and contemplates its origin, its cessation, and the path leading to its cessation; it is associated with taintless contemplation, consisting of the discernment of phenomena, investigation, searching, awakening, wisdom, enlightenment, and examination. This is called right view that is noble, supramundane, taintless, and non-clinging, which leads to the complete destruction of suffering and turns one toward the end of suffering.
What is right intention?
Right intention is of two kinds:

there is right intention that is worldly, conventional, with outflows, and with clinging, which leads toward the happy realms; [and there is right intention that is noble, supramundane, without outflows, and without clinging].
There is right intention that is noble and supramundane, untainted, not grasping, which leads to the complete destruction of suffering and turns toward the end of suffering.
What is right intention that is worldly and conventional, tainted, grasping, and leading toward a happy destination?

That is to say, right intention consisting of the awakening of renunciation, the awakening of non-ill will, and the awakening of non-harming; this is called right intention that is worldly, conventional, with taints, with acquisitions, and leading toward a happy destination.
What is right intention that is noble, supramundane, untainted, and non-clinging, which rightly brings an end to suffering and leads toward the end of suffering?

It refers to the mental factors associated with untainted contemplation when a noble disciple contemplates suffering as suffering, and contemplates its origin, its cessation, and the path leading to its cessation; it is the discernment, self-determination, resolution, calculation, and establishment of the mind. This is called right intention that is noble, supramundane, untainted, and non-clinging, which rightly brings an end to suffering and leads toward the end of suffering.
"What is right speech? Right speech is of two kinds.

There is right speech that is worldly, conventional, with outflows, and with clinging, which leads toward the happy realms; [and there is right speech that is transcendent, supramundane, without outflows, and without clinging, which leads to the cessation of suffering]."
There is right speech that is noble, supramundane, outflow-free, and non-clinging; it leads to the complete destruction of suffering and turns toward the end of suffering.
What is right speech that is worldly, conventional, with outflows, and with clinging, which leads to a favorable rebirth?

That is to say, right speech consists of abstaining from false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech; this is called mundane, worldly, with outflows, and with clinging, leading toward a favorable rebirth.
What is right speech that is noble, supramundane, untainted, non-clinging, which rightly brings an end to suffering and leads toward the end of suffering?

It is when a noble disciple contemplates suffering as suffering, and contemplates its origin, its cessation, and the path leading to its cessation; having abandoned wrong livelihood, he reflects upon the four types of verbal misconduct and all other verbal misdeeds, and from them he abstains—untainted, detached, unattached, firmly guarding, restrained, and not transgressing; not overstepping the proper time, nor violating the boundaries of restraint. This is called right speech that is noble, supramundane, untainted, non-clinging, which rightly brings an end to suffering and leads toward the end of suffering.
"What is right action? Right action is of two kinds.

There is right action that is worldly, conventional, with outflows, and with clinging, which leads toward the happy realms; [and there is right action that is transcendent, supramundane, without outflows, and without clinging, which leads to the cessation of suffering]."
There is right action that is noble, supramundane, untainted, and non-clinging; it leads to the complete exhaustion of suffering and turns one toward the end of suffering.
What is right action that is worldly, conventional, tainted, and clinging, which leads toward a favorable rebirth?
That is to say, abstaining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct is called right action that is worldly, mundane, with outflows, and with clinging, which leads toward a favorable rebirth.
What is right action that is noble, supramundane, without outflows, and without clinging, which rightly brings an end to suffering and leads to the end of suffering?

That is to say, when a noble disciple contemplates suffering as suffering, and contemplates its origin, its cessation, and the path leading to its cessation; when, setting aside wrong livelihood, he reflects upon the three types of bodily misconduct and all other instances of bodily misconduct, remaining untainted and without mental attachment; when he firmly guards, maintains, and does not transgress them, neither failing to observe the proper timing nor overstepping the boundaries of restraint—this is called right action that is noble, supramundane, untainted, and non-clinging; it rightly brings about the exhaustion of suffering and leads toward the end of suffering.
"What is right livelihood?
There are two kinds of right livelihood.

There is right livelihood that is worldly, conventional, with outflows, and subject to clinging, which leads toward a favorable rebirth; [and there is right livelihood that is transcendent, supramundane, without outflows, and free from clinging, which leads to the destruction of suffering]."
There is right livelihood that is noble, supramundane, untainted, and non-clinging; it rightly brings an end to suffering and leads toward the final limit of suffering.
What is right livelihood that is worldly, conventional, tainted, and clinging, which leads toward a favorable rebirth?

This refers to seeking clothing, food, bedding, and medicinal decoctions for illness in accordance with the Dharma, and not in a manner contrary to the Dharma; this is called right livelihood that is worldly, with outflows, and with clinging, which leads toward the happy realms of rebirth.
What is right livelihood that is noble, supramundane, untainted, and non-clinging, which rightly brings an end to suffering and leads toward the limit of suffering?

It is when a noble disciple contemplates suffering as suffering, and contemplates its origin, its cessation, and the path leading to its cessation; regarding all forms of wrong livelihood, they are untainted and do not delight in or cling to them, but firmly maintain and uphold [right livelihood] without transgression, not overstepping the proper time, and not exceeding the bounds of restraint. This is called right livelihood that is noble, supramundane, untainted, and non-clinging, which rightly brings an end to suffering and leads toward the limit of suffering.
"What is right effort? There are two kinds of right effort.

There is right effort that is worldly, conventional, subject to outflows, and subject to clinging, which leads toward a favorable rebirth; [and there is right effort that is noble, supramundane, without outflows, and without clinging, which leads to the complete destruction of suffering]."
There is right effort that is noble, supramundane, untainted, and non-clinging, which leads to the complete destruction of suffering and turns one toward the end of suffering.
What is right effort that is worldly, conventional, tainted, and clinging, which leads toward a favorable rebirth?

That is to say: desire, diligence, skillful transcendence, and firm establishment; the capacity for the performance of diligence, the mental factor of sustained application, constancy, and non-cessation—this is called right effort that is worldly, mundane, with outflows, and with clinging, which leads toward a favorable rebirth.
What is right effort that is noble, supramundane, untainted, non-clinging, leading to the exhaustion of suffering, and turning one toward the end of suffering?

It refers to the noble disciple’s contemplation of suffering as suffering, and contemplation of its origin, its cessation, and the path to its cessation; the mental factors associated with untainted mindfulness; desire, diligence, application, exertion, transcendence, steadfast establishment, and the capacity for the performance of vigor; and the mental factors of sustained engagement and constant, unceasing practice. This is called right effort that is noble, supramundane, untainted, non-clinging, which rightly exhausts suffering and turns one toward the end of suffering.
"What is right mindfulness?
Right mindfulness is of two kinds:

that which is worldly, mundane, with outflows, and with grasping, which leads toward a favorable rebirth; [and that which is transcendent, supramundane, without outflows, and without grasping, which leads to the cessation of suffering]."
There is right mindfulness that is noble, supramundane, untainted, and non-clinging; it leads to the complete destruction of suffering and turns toward the end of suffering.
What is right mindfulness that is worldly, conventional, tainted, and clinging, which leads toward a favorable rebirth?

If one recollects, follows in recollection, repeatedly recollects, and remembers with no falsehood and no delusion, this is called right mindfulness that is worldly, mundane, subject to outflows, and accompanied by grasping, yet directed toward a fortunate rebirth.
What is right mindfulness that is noble, supramundane, taintless, non-clinging, and leads to the end of suffering?

It refers to when a noble disciple contemplates suffering as suffering, and contemplates its origin, its cessation, and the path leading to its cessation; it is associated with taintless contemplation, and consists of mindfulness, recollection, repeated mindfulness, and remembrance that is neither delusive nor false. This is called right mindfulness that is noble, supramundane, taintless, non-clinging, and leads to the end of suffering.
"What is right concentration?
Right concentration is of two kinds.
There is right concentration that is mundane, conventional, with outflows, and with clinging, which leads toward a favorable rebirth;..."
There is right concentration that is noble, supramundane, untainted, and non-clinging; it leads to the complete destruction of suffering and turns toward the end of suffering.
What is right concentration that is mundane, worldly, tainted, and clinging, which leads toward a favorable rebirth?

If the mind abides undistracted, immovable, collected, stilled, concentrated, and one-pointed, this is called right concentration that is worldly and conventional, with outflows and clinging, which leads toward a favorable rebirth.
What is right concentration that is noble, supramundane, untainted, non-clinging, which rightly brings an end to suffering and leads to the cessation of suffering?

It refers to the dwelling of a noble disciple’s mental factors in association with untainted contemplation—contemplating suffering as suffering, and contemplating its origin, its cessation, and the path—as being undistracted, unscattered, collected, stilled, concentrated, and one-pointed. This is called right concentration that is noble, supramundane, untainted, non-clinging, which rightly brings an end to suffering and leads to the cessation of suffering.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 786 (786). Thus have I heard:

It refers to wrong view, up to and including wrong concentration.

That is to say: right view, up to and including right concentration.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 787 (787) Thus have I heard:

Why is this? It is because of seeing correctly;
that is to say, right view.

One with right view is able to give rise to right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; this is called one who is oriented toward the right, delighting in the Dharma and not deviating from the Dharma.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 788 (788) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

One who holds wrong view gives rise to wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration.

Such people with wrong views act according to what they see in their bodily karma, speak according to what they see in their verbal karma; whether in thought, desire, aspiration, or action, they all conform to it, and thus they obtain every result that is unloved, unremembered, and disagreeable.
Why is this so? "Evil views" refers to wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

If a person of right view acts with the body in accordance with what they have seen, and acts with speech in accordance with what they have seen—if their thoughts, desires, and deeds all follow accordingly—then all of these will result in fruits that are lovely, praiseworthy, and agreeable."

One who possesses right view is able to give rise to right intention, and so on, up to right concentration.

Why is this so? "Good vision" refers to right view.

One with right view is able to give rise to right intention, and so on, up to right concentration; this is called one who is directed toward what is right, delighting in the Dharma and not deviating from the Dharma.

The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa:

There is right view that is worldly, vulgar, with outflows, and subject to grasping, which leads toward a favorable rebirth;

It is right view that there is giving, there is sacrifice, and there is almsgiving, up to and including knowing for oneself that there will be no further existence.
"Brahmin! This is called right view that is worldly, mundane, subject to outflows, and accompanied by grasping, which leads toward a favorable rebirth. Brahmin!"

This is called right view that is noble, supramundane, taintless, and non-clinging, which rightly brings about the exhaustion of suffering and leads toward the end of suffering.

803 (Eight Hundred and Three). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Cultivate mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti).

If a bhikṣu cultivates mindfulness of breathing and practices it extensively, he attains the stilling of body and mind; with directed thought and sustained thought, he becomes tranquil and unified, and fulfills the cultivation of the perception belonging to the factor of clarity.”

What is the cultivation of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) such that, through its frequent practice, the body and mind come to rest, and with directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), one cultivates to fulfillment the perception of tranquility, singleness, and the factors of clarity?

If that bhikṣu dwells in dependence upon a village or town, he puts on his robes and takes up his bowl in the morning and enters the village to beg for food, well-guarding his body, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, and dwelling with his mind well-restrained.

Having finished his almsround, he returns to his dwelling, puts away his robe and bowl, washes his feet, and then—whether entering a forest, a quiet room, or beneath a tree, or staying in an open, unsheltered space—he sits upright with body straight, fixing his mindfulness before him. He cuts off worldly craving and attachment, becoming pure through the departure from desire; he abandons ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-regret, and doubt; he crosses over all perplexity and attains certainty of mind regarding wholesome states.
He remains far removed from the five hindrances that afflict the mind, which weaken the power of wisdom, constitute obstacles, and prevent one from proceeding toward Nirvana.
He attends to inward breathing, training himself well by fixing his mindfulness; he attends to outward breathing, training himself well by fixing his mindfulness.

Whether the breath is long or short, one is aware of the entire body while inhaling and trains well in the inhalation throughout the entire body; one is aware of the entire body while exhaling and trains well in the exhalation throughout the entire body.

He is aware of the entire body while breathing in as he calms it, training himself well in calming the entire body while breathing in; he is aware of the entire body while breathing out as he calms it, training himself well in calming the entire body while breathing out.

He discerns joy, he discerns pleasure, he discerns mental formations; he discerns the calming of mental formations while inhaling, training himself well in discerning the calming of mental formations while inhaling;
he discerns the calming of mental formations while exhaling, training himself well in discerning the calming of mental formations while exhaling.

He trains himself well in breathing in while clearly knowing the mind; he trains himself well in breathing in while clearly knowing the gladdening of the mind; he trains himself well in breathing in while clearly knowing the concentration of the mind; he trains himself well in breathing in while clearly knowing the liberation of the mind. He trains himself well in breathing out while clearly knowing the mind; he trains himself well in breathing out while clearly knowing the liberation of the mind. He observes impermanence, observes cessation, observes dispassion, and observes extinction as he breathes in, training himself well in observing extinction as he breathes in.

He observes extinction as he breathes out, training himself well in observing extinction as he breathes out. This is called the cultivation of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati), wherein the body is stilled and the mind is stilled; accompanied by directed thought and evaluation, it is tranquil and unified, and the perception belonging to the factor of clarity is fully cultivated.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 804 (804). Thus have I heard:
