Then, in the early morning, the World-Honored One dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.

Having finished his meal, he returned to the vihāra, put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and taking his sitting mat (niṣīdana), entered the Andhavana forest, where he sat beneath a tree to practice dhyāna during the day.
At that time, the Venerable Kāśyapa also rose early in the morning, donned his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms.

Having returned, he set aside his robe and bowl, washed his feet, and taking his sitting mat (niṣadana), entered the Andhavana forest. Sitting beneath a tree not far from the Buddha, he sat in meditation with his body upright and motionless, his mind and body rectified, engaged in sublime contemplation.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus arose from meditation in the late afternoon and went to where the Buddha was. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Do you see the Venerable Kasmīraputra?"
"Not far from me, he sits upright with his body straight, unmoving in body and mind, abiding in a sublime state.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"We have frequently seen that venerable one sitting with body upright and端正, well-restraining his body so that it does not lean or move, his mind focused on the sublime.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"If a bhikṣu cultivates samādhi, dwelling peacefully in body and mind, neither leaning nor moving, abiding in a sublime dwelling, then this bhikṣu, having attained this samādhi, will obtain it at will without needing to exert effort in skillful means."
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“What is this samādhi, by attaining which a bhikṣu remains with body and mind unmoving, dwelling in a sublime and wondrous state?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"If a bhikṣu who relies on a village puts on his robes and takes up his bowl in the morning, enters the village for alms, and having returned to the monastery, sets aside his robe and bowl, washes his feet, and enters the forest, or stays in a quiet room or sits in the open air, contemplating with focused mindfulness, and even trains well in the observation of the cessation of the breaths—this is called samādhi. If a bhikṣu sits upright in contemplation, with body and mind unmoving, he dwells in a sublime and wondrous abode."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly. 807 (807). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Ekanālā forest.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I wish to practice seated meditation for two months; let no bhikṣus come or go, except for those who bring food and during the time of the uposatha."

At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these words, he sat in meditation for two months; not a single bhikṣu dared to come or go, except for those bringing food and during the time of the poṣadha ceremony.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had completed two months of sitting in meditation, he arose from dhyāna and sat before the community of bhikṣus, addressing the bhikṣus:
"If various non-Buddhist renunciants come and ask you:
'In what manner did the śramaṇa Gautama sit in meditation during these two months?'"
"You should answer:
'The Tathāgata dwelt in meditation for two months, contemplating through the mindfulness of ānāpāna. Why is this so?"

During these two months, I practiced mindfulness of *ānāpāna* (breathing), dwelling frequently in contemplation: when inhaling, I was mindful of inhaling and knew it as it truly is; when exhaling, I was mindful of exhaling and knew it as it truly is.
Whether long or short, he knows as it truly is the mindfulness of inhaling while experiencing the whole body; he knows as it truly is the mindfulness of exhaling while experiencing the whole body.
He knows as it truly is the mindfulness of inhaling while calming the bodily formations; he knows as it truly is the mindfulness of exhaling until their cessation.
Having fully understood this, I then had this thought:
"This is a coarse dwelling of reflection; having now brought this reflection to rest, I shall further cultivate and dwell in another, more subtle dwelling of cultivation."
"At that time, having stilled coarse reflection, I entered into subtle reflection and remained there dwelling for a long while.
Then, three sons of the gods, possessing most exquisite and sublime forms, came to me at the end of the night."
One deva said,
"The time has come for the śramaṇa Gautama.
Another deva then said:
"This is not the arrival of time; this is the approach of time.
The third devaputra said:
"It is neither the arrival of time nor the approach of time; this is abiding in cultivation, which is simply the nirvana of an Arhat!"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"If there is a correct teaching regarding the noble dwelling, the celestial dwelling, the Brahma dwelling, the dwelling of those in training, the dwelling of those beyond training, and the dwelling of the Tathāgata—wherein that which has not yet been attained by one in training shall be attained, that which has not yet been reached shall be reached, and that which has not yet been realized shall be realized; and wherein one beyond training dwells in happiness in the present life—it is this, namely, mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti), that is the correct teaching."
Why is this so? Mindfulness of breathing is the noble abode, the celestial abode, and the Brahma abode, up to and including the dwelling in happiness in the present life of one beyond training.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 808 (808). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Grove.

At that time, Mahānāma the Śākya went to the place where the Venerable Kama Bhikṣu was, prostrated at the feet of the Venerable Kama Bhikṣu, withdrew to sit at one side, and said to the Venerable Kama Bhikṣu: "How is it?"
Venerable Kāma!
Is the dwelling of one in training the same as the dwelling of a Tathāgata?
Or is the dwelling of one in training different from the dwelling of a Tathāgata?
The bhikṣu Kāma replied: “Mahānāman!
There is a difference in the training, and there is a difference in the Tathāgata.”
Mahānāma! One who dwells in training dwells frequently having abandoned the five hindrances.

One who dwells as a Tathāgata has already abandoned and fully understood the five hindrances, cutting them off at the root so that they are like the head of a tāla tree severed, never to grow again, becoming a state of non-arising in future lives.
"At one time, the Blessed One was staying in the Sāṇa Forest.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

'I wish to dwell in meditation for two months in this Sāṇa Forest; you, bhikṣus, must not come and go, except for the bhikṣu who brings food and during the time of the Poṣadha ceremony... [The full explanation is as before], up until: 'the state of dwelling in happiness in the present life for those beyond training.'"
"Therefore, Mahānāman, you should know that the training is one thing and the Tathāgata’s dwelling is another.
Having heard what the bhikṣu Kama had said, the Śākya Mahānāman rejoiced, rose from his seat, and departed.
809. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Sāla-forest on the banks of the Bhagīrathī River near the village of Vajjiputta.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught the contemplation of impurity to the bhikṣus, praising the contemplation of impurity by saying:
"Bhikṣus, those who cultivate the contemplation of impurity and practice it extensively will attain great fruits and great benefits."

At that time, after the bhikṣus had practiced the meditation on impurity, they became so utterly weary of their bodies that some took their own lives with knives, some ingested poison, some hanged themselves with ropes or threw themselves from cliffs, and some ordered other bhikṣus to kill them.
There was a certain bhikṣu who felt such intense revulsion toward the impurity of the foul body that he went to the brahmin son Mṛgadāyin and said to him:
"O worthy one!
"If you can kill me, my robes and bowl shall belong to you.

Then, the brahmin youth Mṛgadāsa killed that bhikṣu and went with his sword to the banks of the Bhagīrathī River. While he was washing the sword, a māra-deva stationed in the air praised the brahmin youth Mṛgadāsa, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!
O Worthy One!

You have attained immeasurable merit, for you are able to cause these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, to uphold the precepts and possess virtue; you enable those who have not crossed over to cross over, those who have not been liberated to be liberated, those who have not found rest to find rest, and those who have not attained nirvāṇa to attain nirvāṇa. All long-term benefits, robes, bowls, and miscellaneous items shall belong entirely to you.
At that time, having heard this praise, Māgandiya the son of a brahmin from Deer Park increased his malicious wrong views and thought to himself:

"I have now truly performed great meritorious deeds; let those śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas who possess the merit of observing the precepts—those not yet crossed over, those not yet liberated, those not yet refreshed, and those not yet attained to nirvāṇa—be caused to cross over, be liberated, find refreshment, and attain nirvāṇa, so that their robes, bowls, and miscellaneous belongings shall all belong to me."
Thereupon, grasping a sharp sword in his hand, he went through the various dwellings, the walking paths, the private rooms, and the meditation cells. Seeing the bhikṣus there, he spoke these words:

"Which śramaṇa possesses the precepts and virtue such that I may cause those who have not crossed over to cross over, those who have not been liberated to be liberated, those who have not found rest to find rest, and those who have not attained nirvāṇa to attain nirvāṇa?"
At that time, there were certain bhikṣus who were weary of the body; they all left their lodgings and said to the brahmin youth Mṛgadāyin:
"We have not yet attained liberation; you should deliver us.
We have not yet attained release; you should release us."
"I have not yet found rest; you must cause me to find rest.
I have not yet attained nirvāṇa; you must cause me to attain nirvāṇa.
At that time, the brahmin youth Mṛgadāya immediately killed that bhikṣu with a sharp knife, and in succession, he went on to kill sixty men.
At that time, on the fifteenth day at the hour for reciting the precepts, the World-Honored One sat before the assembly of monks and addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"For what cause and by what condition have the bhikṣus become increasingly few, increasingly diminished, and increasingly exhausted?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One, for the sake of the bhikṣus you have taught the cultivation of the contemplation of impurity and praised the contemplation of impurity.

After the bhikṣus had cultivated the contemplation of impurity, they became utterly weary of and disgusted with their own bodies... [The passage continues] at length until: “...they killed sixty bhikṣus.”
World-Honored One!
Because of these causes and conditions, the bhikṣus are becoming fewer, diminishing, and nearly extinct.

We only pray that the World-Honored One will further expound other teachings, so that once the bhikṣus have heard them, they will diligently cultivate wisdom, joyfully receive the True Dharma, and joyfully abide in the True Dharma.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Therefore, I shall now explain in sequence: by abiding in subtle dwelling and conforming to awakening, one causes arisen and unarisen evil and unwholesome states to quickly cease, just as a great rain from heaven causes dust that has arisen and dust that has not yet arisen to settle."
"In this way, bhikkhus, one cultivates subtle abiding, whereby arisen and unarisen evil, unwholesome states are brought to rest.
Ānanda, what is this subtle abiding that, when practiced extensively, conduces to awakening and causes arisen and unarisen evil, unwholesome states to come to rest?"
"It is the mindfulness-establishment of ānāpānasmṛti (mindfulness of breathing).
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:

"How does one cultivate the mindfulness-establishment of ānāpānasmṛti so as to accord with awakening, such that evil and unwholesome states—whether already arisen or not yet arisen—are brought to rest?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If a bhikṣu relies on a village... [as extensively explained before] ...up to: 'He trains as in the mindfulness of the cessation of the out-breath.'"
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
810 (810) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying on the bank of the river Vajravālukā in the Sālālī grove.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was alone in a quiet place, reflecting and meditating, and he had this thought:
"Is there perhaps one dharma which, through cultivation and repeated cultivation, brings four dharmas to fulfillment;
and when these four dharmas are fulfilled, seven dharmas are fulfilled?"
“When seven factors are fulfilled, what two factors are fulfilled?
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having arisen from meditation, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
While dwelling alone in seclusion, reflecting and meditating, this thought arose in me:
"Is there perhaps one dharma which, when cultivated and frequently practiced, brings four dharmas to fulfillment, even unto two dharmas?"
"I now ask the World-Honored One: Is there perhaps one dharma which, through much cultivation, can cause even two dharmas to reach fulfillment?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"There is one dharma which, through much cultivation, can cause even two dharmas to reach fulfillment."
What is this one dharma?
It is mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti).
Having cultivated it extensively, it can cause the four foundations of mindfulness to be fulfilled.
When the four foundations of mindfulness are fulfilled, the seven factors of enlightenment are fulfilled;
when the seven factors of enlightenment are fulfilled, clear knowledge and liberation are fulfilled.
How does one cultivate mindfulness of breathing so that the four foundations of mindfulness are fulfilled?
This bhikṣu, depending on a village, trains even up to the mindfulness of the cessation of exhalation. Ānanda!
Thus, when a noble disciple is mindful of inhalation, he trains in mindfulness of inhalation; when mindful of exhalation, he trains in mindfulness of exhalation.
Whether long or short, he is aware of all bodily activities: when practicing mindfulness of inhalation, he trains himself thus; when practicing mindfulness of exhalation, he trains himself thus;
when breathing in with the cessation of bodily activities, he trains himself thus;
when breathing out with the cessation of bodily activities, he trains himself thus.
At that time, the noble disciple dwells contemplating the body as body; regarding that which is distinct from the body, he likewise reflects upon it in accordance with the body.

"When at times the noble disciple perceives rapture, perceives pleasure, perceives mental formations, and perceives the stilling of mental formations, when he is mindful of the in-breath, he trains himself thus: 'I shall breathe in mindful of the stilling of mental formations'; when he is mindful of the out-breath, he trains himself thus: 'I shall breathe out mindful of the stilling of mental formations.'"
At that time, this noble disciple dwells contemplating feelings as feelings; furthermore, regarding any other feelings, he also contemplates them by way of analogy with the body.

At times, the noble disciple becomes aware of the mind—becoming aware of the mind’s joy, the mind’s concentration, and the mind’s liberation. When mindful of the inhalation, he trains himself in mindfulness of inhalation as the mind is liberated; when mindful of the exhalation, he trains himself in mindfulness of exhalation as the mind is liberated. At that time, this noble disciple dwells contemplating the mind as mind; regarding any other states of mind, he also contemplates them by way of analogy with the mind.

"If a noble disciple at times contemplates impermanence, cessation, dispassion, and extinction, and dwells in training while contemplating according to impermanence, cessation, dispassion, and extinction—if at that time this noble disciple dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena (dhammānupassī) regarding a phenomenon distinct from [the breath], and also reflects by way of inference upon that phenomenon, this is called the cultivation of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati), which fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“In this way, by practicing mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti), one brings the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni) to fulfillment.
How does one practice the four foundations of mindfulness so as to bring the seven factors of awakening (saptabodhyaṅgāni) to fulfillment?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If a bhikṣu dwells contemplating the body as the body, having established mindfulness, he binds his attention to that dwelling so that it is not forgotten.
At that time, he skillfully cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness; having cultivated the awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of mindfulness becomes fulfilled."
Once the awakening factor of mindfulness is fulfilled, one discriminates, contemplates, and reflects upon phenomena.

At that time, one skillfully cultivates the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena; having cultivated the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena, it becomes fulfilled. Having discriminated, analyzed, and reflected upon phenomena, one attains the skillful means of diligent effort.

At that time, one practices the awakening factor of vigor through skillful means; having cultivated the awakening factor of vigor, the awakening factor of vigor becomes fulfilled. Having applied skillful means through vigor, the mind then becomes joyful.

At that time, one practices the awakening factor of joy through skillful means; having practiced the awakening factor of joy, the awakening factor of joy becomes fulfilled. Once there is joy, the body and mind become tranquil and at rest.

At that time, one cultivates the awakening factor of tranquility through skillful means; having cultivated the awakening factor of tranquility, the awakening factor of tranquility becomes fulfilled; once physical and mental bliss are attained, one achieves samādhi.

At that time, one cultivates the awakening factor of concentration; having cultivated the awakening factor of concentration, the awakening factor of concentration becomes fulfilled. Once the awakening factor of concentration is fulfilled, greed and sorrow are extinguished, and one attains equanimity.

At that time, one practices the awakening factor of equanimity through skillful means; having practiced the awakening factor of equanimity, the awakening factor of equanimity becomes fulfilled. The same is said for the foundations of mindfulness regarding feelings, mind, and phenomena. This is called practicing the four foundations of mindfulness and fulfilling the seven factors of awakening.
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
“This is called cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness to fulfill the seven factors of awakening.
How does one cultivate the seven factors of awakening to fulfill clear knowledge and liberation?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“If a bhikṣu cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and tending toward relinquishment;
having cultivated the awakening factor of mindfulness, he fulfills clear knowledge and liberation.”

...up to the cultivation of the awakening factor of equanimity, which relies on seclusion, relies on dispassion, relies on cessation, and leads toward relinquishment. Having thus cultivated the awakening factor of equanimity, clear knowledge and liberation are fulfilled.
Ānanda! This is called the mutual correspondence of phenomena and the mutual moistening of phenomena.
Thus, regarding these thirteen phenomena, with one phenomenon as the predominant factor and another as the gateway, they progress in succession until their cultivation is perfected.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
811–812 (811–812). Thus was it asked by another bhikṣu; the Buddha’s questioning of the bhikṣus was also as described above.
813 (813). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the village of Kimpila, in the Kimpila Forest.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Kimpila:
"I shall now speak on the diligent cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for your sake.
At that time, the Venerable Kimbila remained silent; this was repeated a second and a third time.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Venerable Kumbhīra:
"The Great Teacher has spoken to you!
He spoke thus three times.
The Venerable Kimbila said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"I have understood,
Venerable Ānanda!"
"I have already understood,
Venerable Gautama! Then,
the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
At that time,
World-Honored One!”
At this time, O Sugata!
We pray that you will explain to the bhikṣus how to diligently cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness; having heard it, the bhikṣus shall receive and practice it accordingly.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall explain it for you.

If a bhikṣu, when mindful of the inhalation, trains himself in accordance with the inhalation, and so on until, when mindful of the exhalation, he trains himself in accordance with the exhalation;..."

At that time, when the noble disciple is mindful while inhaling, he trains himself thus: "I am mindful while inhaling"; and so on, until, when the bodily formations have ceased and he exhales, he trains himself thus: "I am mindful while exhaling as the bodily formations have ceased. At that time, the noble disciple dwells contemplating the body as the body.
"At that time, when the noble disciple dwells contemplating the body as the body, he knows thus and reflects skillfully within.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Suppose there were a person riding in a carriage who came tumbling from the east; at that moment, would he not trample over the mounds and hillocks of the earth?"
Ānanda replied to the Buddha,
“So it is, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"In this way, when the noble disciple is mindful of the in-breath, he trains himself in mindfulness of the in-breath; and so on, until he is well-reflecting within.
If at that time the noble disciple perceives rapture, and so on, up to perceiving the stilling of mental formations, the noble disciple dwells contemplating feelings as feelings."
When a noble disciple has practiced the mindfulness of feelings, he understands them well through internal reflection.
It is, for example, like a person traveling in a carriage who comes tumbling from the south; what do you think?
"Ānanda! Should one tread upon mounds and hillocks?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In this way, the noble disciple dwells contemplating feelings as feelings, knowing them well through internal reflection."

When a noble disciple perceives the mind as liberated, the gladdened mind, and the concentrated mind, he trains himself thus: "I shall breathe in with a liberated mind," and he trains himself thus: "I shall breathe out with a liberated mind. At that time, the noble disciple dwells with mindfulness established by attending to the mind as a mental object.
In this way, when the noble disciple dwells with mindfulness established by contemplating the mind as mind, he knows his own internal reflection.
It is, for example, like a person riding in a carriage coming from the west; would he not tread upon mounds and hillocks of earth?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha,
“So it is, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"In this way, the noble disciple understands the mind, and even as he exhales with a liberated mind, he trains himself: 'I shall exhale with a liberated mind.
Thus, at that time, the noble disciple dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, knowing his internal reflection well."
Being skilled regarding the body, feelings, and the mind, when greed and sorrow have ceased and there is equanimity, at that time the noble disciple dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena.
Having thus dwelt contemplating phenomena as phenomena, the noble disciple knows his own internal reflection well.
Ānanda! Suppose there were a mound of earth at a crossroads, and a person traveling in a carriage came from the north in a state of distress; would they not trample over that mound of earth?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha,
“So it is, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"In this way, the noble disciple dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena and knows his own internal reflection well.
Ānanda, this is called a bhikkhu who, through diligent application of skillful means, cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
814 (814). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should cultivate mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti).

Having cultivated and frequently practiced mindfulness of breathing, the body will not become weary, the eyes will not suffer affliction, one will dwell in joyful compliance with contemplation, joyfully cognizing, and without being stained by or attached to pleasure."

How does one cultivate mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) such that the body does not grow weary, the eyes do not suffer, one dwells in the joy of contemplation, experiences joy through clear comprehension, and remains unattached to that joy?

This bhikṣu, depending on a village for his residence, practices the mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) up to the point of observing the exhalation as it ceases, training himself thus: "I shall breathe out as it ceases. This is called the cultivation of mindfulness of breathing; his body does not grow weary, nor do his eyes suffer affliction. He dwells delighting in contemplative observation, delighting in clear comprehension, and without becoming attached to the pleasure [of meditation].
For one who practices mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) in this way, there is great fruit and great benefit.

When that bhikṣu seeks to become free from sensual desires and unwholesome states, and dwells having attained the first dhyāna—accompanied by applied and sustained thought, born of seclusion, and filled with joy and happiness—he should practice mindfulness of breathing.
Cultivating mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) in this manner, one attains great fruit and great benefit.

If that bhikṣu seeks the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, or the [immeasurables of] loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, or the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he will—having fulfilled these—exhaust the three fetters and attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*);
or, having exhausted the three fetters and attenuated greed, hatred, and delusion, he will attain the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*).

Having exhausted the five lower fetters, they attain the fruit of *anāgāmin* and acquire immeasurable kinds of supernormal powers: the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, knowledge of past lives, knowledge of the death and rebirth of beings, and knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows.
"In this way, monks, you should cultivate mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
Through such mindfulness of breathing, one attains great fruit and great benefit.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the monks, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
815 (815). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, during the summer retreat.
At that time, many senior śrāvakas were observing the rains retreat under trees and in caves near the World-Honored One.
Then, a great number of junior bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to the young bhikṣus in various ways, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them;
having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them, he remained silent.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the young bhikṣus rejoiced and approved, rose from their seats, paid homage, and departed.
The young bhikṣus then went to where the elder bhikṣus were, prostrated at the feet of the elders, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the elder bhikṣus had this thought:
"We should take these young bhikṣus under our care; perhaps one person shall take charge of one, or one person shall take charge of two, three, or many."
Having formed this thought, he immediately accepted them—whether accepting one person at a time, or two, three, or many people, or even as many as sixty people, including the elders.
At that time, on the fifteenth day of the fortnight during the uposatha ceremony, the World-Honored One prepared a seat before the great assembly and sat down.
Having surveyed the bhikṣus, the World-Honored One addressed them:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!
I am now glad that the bhikṣus perform all manner of righteous deeds. Therefore, bhikṣus!
"You should apply yourselves with diligent effort.

Now, in this city of Śrāvastī, during the full month of Kārttika, the bhikṣus in various human settlements heard that the World-Honored One was observing the rains retreat at Śrāvastī. When the full month of Kārttika had ended and he had finished making his robes, he took up his robe and bowl and traveled through the human settlements around Śrāvastī.

Gradually arriving at Śrāvastī, he took up his robe and bowl, washed his feet, and approached the World-Honored One. Having prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet in salutation, he withdrew to sit at one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One taught the bhikṣus of the human realm with various discourses on the Dharma, instructing, exhorting, illuminating, and gladdening them. Having done so, he remained silent.
Then, having heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, the bhikṣus of the human realm rejoiced and expressed their approval; they rose from their seats, paid homage, and departed.
He went to where the senior bhikṣus were, prostrated at their feet, and withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, the senior bhikṣus thought to themselves:

Those elder bhikṣus, having accepted the bhikṣus from among the people, instructed and exhorted them, being well-versed in the proper sequence of what comes first and what follows.

At that time, on the fifteenth day of the month during the uposatha, the World-Honored One arranged his seat before the great assembly and sat down. Surveying the community of bhikṣus, he addressed them:
"Excellent!
Excellent, monks!
I rejoice in the righteous conduct you practice; I delight in the righteous conduct you practice.
"O bhikṣus!

The assemblies of bhikṣus of all past buddhas also performed their proper practices just as this assembly does now; the assemblies of all future buddhas shall likewise perform their proper practices just as this assembly does now."

Why is this so? Because among the elder bhikṣus in this assembly, there are those who have attained the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna; and who dwell fully established in loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; and in the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

There is a bhikṣu who has exhausted the three fetters and attained the stage of *srotāpanna*; he is no longer subject to rebirth in the evil realms, is destined for full awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and after seven more births among gods and humans, will reach the ultimate end of suffering.
There is a bhikṣu who, having exhausted the three fetters and attenuated greed, hatred, and delusion, attains the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*.
There is a bhikṣu who, having exhausted the five lower fetters, attains the stage of *anāgāmin*, attaining parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), and no longer returning to this world.

There was a bhikṣu who attained immeasurable spheres of supernormal power: the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, knowledge of past lives, knowledge of birth and death, and knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows.

There is a bhikṣu who cultivates the contemplation of impurity to sever sensual desire; cultivates a mind of loving-kindness to sever ill-will; cultivates the perception of impermanence to sever the conceit "I am"; and cultivates mindfulness of breathing to sever discursive thoughts.
How is it, bhikṣu, that one cultivates mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti) to eliminate perceptions of sensory objects?

When that bhikṣu, depending on a village settlement, practices the contemplation of the ceasing of the out-breath as the contemplation of the ceasing of the out-breath, this is called the cultivation of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti) for the purpose of abandoning discursive thoughts.

As for the distinction:
"What is the training in higher virtue?

Regarding those various subtle precepts, one should repent immediately upon transgressing them. Why is this?
It is not that I say they are incapable;

rather, if those precepts accord with the holy life (*brahmacarya*), benefit the holy life, and lead to the long endurance of the holy life, then such a bhikṣu should maintain and train in them with firm precepts, with a constant preceptor, and with precepts that constantly arise in accordance with him.
Knowing thus and seeing thus, one abandons the three fetters—namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).

Having abandoned these three fetters, one attains the stage of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*); one is no longer subject to rebirth in the miserable realms, is destined for perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and will be reborn seven times at most among gods and humans before reaching the ultimate end of suffering. This is called the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*).
"What is the training in higher mind?

[he practices] those various subtle precepts, even down to the undertaking and training in the precepts."
Knowing thus and seeing thus, one severs the five lower fetters, namely: the view of a self, attachment to precepts and rituals, doubt, sensual desire, and ill will.
Having severed these five lower fetters, one attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth; such a person is a non-returner who does not return to this world. This is called the training in higher mind.
What is the training in higher wisdom?
This bhikṣu values the precepts and is preeminent in the precepts; he values concentration and is preeminent in concentration; he values wisdom and is preeminent in wisdom.

Knowing thus and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire, his mind is liberated from the outflow of existence, and his mind is liberated from the outflow of ignorance. He possesses the knowledge and vision of liberation:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence."
“This is called the training in higher wisdom.

Those who have not yet fully awakened to that stage are called *sakṛdāgāmin*; those who have not yet fully awakened to that stage are called *kulaṃkula*; those who have not yet fully awakened to that stage are called *saptakṛdbhava*; those who have not yet fully awakened to that stage are called *dharmānusārin*; those who have not yet fully awakened to that stage are called *śraddhānusārin*. "O bhikṣus! Yet, after that householder has plowed his field, irrigated it, and sown the seed, he does not form this thought:

He does not form this thought:
"By means of natural spiritual power, may I today, or tomorrow, or the day after, give rise to no outflows and achieve the excellent liberation of mind."

Having thus cultivated the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom according to the appropriate time, he attained, at that very moment, the non-arising of all taints and the complete liberation of his mind.

829 (829). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the village of Vaṅgī, with the Venerable Vaṅgīputra attending upon him to his left and right.
At that time, the Venerable Vāgīśa approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Buddha has spoken two hundred and fifty precepts, commanding sons of good family to recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra in turn every half-month, so that all sons of good family may study them according to their inclination.
"But now, World-Honored One!
I am not capable of learning by following [the teachings].
The Buddha told Bāhīputra:
“Are you able to train in the three trainings at all times?
Vatsagotra replied to the Buddha,
“I am able, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Vatsagotra:
“You should, from time to time, train in the higher training of virtue, the higher training of mind, and the higher training of wisdom.

Having diligently applied yourself from time to time to the higher training of virtue, the higher training of mind, and the higher training of wisdom, before long you shall attain the destruction of all taints and realize for yourselves in this very life, through direct knowledge, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.”
“Birth has been exhausted for me; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence.
At that time, the Venerable Vaṅgīśa, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and approved, paid homage, and departed.

At that time, having received the Buddha’s instruction and exhortation, the Venerable Vāgīśa dwelt alone in a quiet place, applying himself with focused reflection... as described above, until "his mind was well-liberated, and he attained arhatship."

30.830 (830) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Pāṭali-gaṇa in the Pāṭali-gaṇa forest.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma associated with the precepts to the bhikṣus, praising the method of establishing the disciplinary rules.

At that time, the Venerable Kāśyapa was staying in the village of Bhṛgu. Having heard the World-Honored One’s teaching on the Dharma associated with the precepts, and hearing him praise those precepts, he felt such extreme intolerance and displeasure in his heart that he said:
"This śramaṇa excessively praises these precepts and excessively restricts them."

At that time, the World-Honored One, having stayed as long as he pleased in the village of Bhṛgu, set out for Śrāvastī; traveling by stages, he arrived at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Jeta’s Grove in Śrāvastī.
At that time, not long after the World-Honored One had departed, the Venerable Kāśyapa felt regret in his heart, thinking:

"I have now suffered a loss; I have met with great misfortune. When the World-Honored One was expounding the Dharma corresponding to the precepts and praising the establishment of the rules, my mind toward the World-Honored One was neither patient nor joyful, nor did it feel glad, as I spoke these words:
'The śramaṇa has established these precepts too strictly; he praises these precepts too highly.'"
Then, when the night had passed and at the break of dawn, the Venerable Kāśyapa put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the village of Bhaṅga to beg for food.

Having finished eating, he returned to the monastery, entrusted his bedding to others, and taking his robes and bowl himself, set out toward Śrāvastī. Traveling by stages, he arrived at the kingdom of Śrāvastī; there, having set down his robes and bowl and washed his feet, he approached the World-Honored One, prostrated at his feet, and said to the Buddha:
“I repent my transgression.”
World-Honored One!
We repent. Sugata!
"I was foolish and deluded; I was neither skillful nor discerning.

When I heard the World-Honored One teaching the Dharma corresponding to the precepts for the bhikṣus and praising the establishment of the Vinaya, I could not endure it before the World-Honored One, nor did I rejoice; my heart found no delight, and I spoke these words:
'This śramaṇa has established these precepts excessively; he praises these precepts.'"
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"When did you, in my presence, feel such lack of forbearance and lack of joy, failing to give rise to delight, as to speak these words:
'This śramaṇa excessively enforces these precepts and praises these precepts'?"
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: “At that time,
the World-Honored One was in the village of Bhoganagara, in the Bhoganigama forest, where he taught the Dharma corresponding to the precepts to the bhikṣus and praised these precepts.”
At that time, in the presence of the World-Honored One, my mind felt resentment and lack of joy; it was not delighted, and I spoke these words:
"This śramaṇa has established this precept with extreme severity and praises this precept."
"O World-Honored One!

Today I recognize my transgression for myself and repent of it; I see my transgression for myself and repent of it. I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept my confession of fault out of compassion!"
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:

"You yourself should recognize your regret, your folly, your lack of virtue, and your lack of discernment. Having heard me preach the Dharma corresponding to the precepts for the bhikṣus and praising the establishment of the rules, you felt neither patience nor joy toward me; your mind was not delighted, and you spoke these words:
'This śramaṇa excessively establishes these precepts and excessively praises these precepts.'"
“Now, Kāśyapa, since you have recognized your remorse and seen your remorse for yourself, I grant you the arising of the morality of restraint in future lives out of compassion.”
Kāśyapa! For one who repents in this manner, wholesome dharmas increase and never decline. Why is this?

If there are those who recognize their own transgressions, perceive their own faults, and repent them, then in future lives, the precepts of restraint will arise, wholesome dharmas will increase, and they will not fall back or diminish.

"Even if Kāśyapa were the senior elder, if he did not wish to train in the precepts, did not hold the precepts in high regard, and did not praise the establishment of the rules of training, such a bhikṣu I would not commend."
Why is this so? If those whom the Great Master praises are then associated with, honored, and held in high esteem by others;
and if others associate with, honor, and hold them in high esteem, they will come to share the same views and engage in the same actions as those others.
Those who act in such a manner shall experience disadvantageous suffering throughout the long night.
For this reason, I did not initially praise that elder, because from the very beginning he took no pleasure in training in the precepts.
As it is with the elders, so it is with those of middle age and the young.

"If an elder senior monk, at the outset, values the training in the precepts and praises the establishment of the rules of discipline, such an elder I praise, because he initially delights in the training in the precepts."
Those whom the Great Master praises, others should also associate with, hold in high regard, and align their views with his;
because they share his views, in future ages they shall be long-term beneficiaries through the benefit of the Dharma.
Therefore, one should always praise those elder bhikṣus because they initially delighted in training in the precepts;
the same applies to those of middle age and the young.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 831 (831) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If there are elder bhikṣus who, from the very beginning, do not delight in training in the precepts and do not revere the precepts, and when they see other bhikṣus who initially delight in training in the precepts, revere the precepts, and praise the established rules of training, they likewise do not praise them in accordance with the occasion—I, too, do not praise such bhikṣus, because they did not initially delight in training in the precepts."
Why is this? If the Great Teacher praises them, others will in turn associate with, revere, and adopt their views;
because they adopt those views, they will undergo disadvantageous suffering for a long night.
"Therefore, I am likewise toward those elders, those of middle age, and those who are young.
One who delights in training in the precepts is as previously described.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
832 (832). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are three trainings.
What are the three?
They are the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.”
What is the training in higher virtue?

If a bhikṣu dwells in the precepts of the Prātimokṣa, is complete in his deportment and conduct, perceives fear even in the slightest transgression, and undertakes and trains in the precepts—this is called the training in higher virtue.
What is the training in higher mind?

If a bhikṣu, having departed from all evil and unwholesome states, possessing directed thought and evaluation, with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, dwells having fully attained the first dhyāna, and so on up to dwelling having fully attained the fourth dhyāna—this is called the training in higher mind.
What is the training in higher wisdom?

If a bhikṣu knows this noble truth of suffering as it really is, and knows this noble truth of the origin of suffering, this noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and this noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering as they really are, this is called the training in higher wisdom.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The remaining sūtras on the three trainings are as previously explained in the section on the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
As it is with the dhyānas, so it is with the immeasurables and the formless attainments.

As it is with the Four Noble Truths, so it should be spoken of regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the four paths, the four dharma-phrases, and the cultivation of serenity and insight.
833 (833). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, by the side of the Monkey Pond, in the Multi-storied Lecture Hall.
At that time, there was a Licchavi elephant trainer named Nanda who approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Licchavi Nanda, saying:

"If a noble disciple accomplishes the four kinds of indestructible purity, should he seek long life, he shall obtain long life; should he seek beauty, strength, happiness, eloquence, or mastery, he shall obtain them."
What are the four?
They are the accomplishment of unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dharma and the Sangha, and the accomplishment of noble ethical discipline.
I see that when such a noble disciple passes away from this life, they are reborn in the heavens, where they attain ten qualities in those celestial realms.
What are these ten?
They are celestial life-span, celestial form, celestial renown, celestial happiness, and celestial sovereignty, as well as celestial form, sound, fragrance, flavor, and touch.
If a noble disciple passes away from the heavenly realm and is reborn among human beings, I see that they are endowed with ten things.
What are these ten? They are:
human lifespan, human beauty, reputation, happiness, sovereignty, visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.

I say that this learned noble disciple does not rely on faith in others, does not rely on the desires of others, does not follow what he hears from others, does not adopt the opinions of others, and does not depend on the reflections of others; I say that he possesses such knowledge and vision through right wisdom as it truly is.
At that time, Nanda had an attendant who said to him, "The time for bathing has arrived; you may go now! Nanda replied:
"I have no need now for bathing in the human world; I shall now bathe myself with this sublime and wondrous Dharma—namely, the pure faith and joy I have attained toward the World-Honored One."
At that time, the Licchavi elephant trainer Nanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and approved with gladness; he rose from his seat, paid homage, and departed.
834. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Gabled Hall beside the Monkey Pond in the kingdom of Vaiśālī.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If a noble disciple accomplishes the four kinds of indestructible purity, he does not live a life of poverty among humans; he does not suffer from cold or beg for alms, but is naturally wealthy and sufficient."
What are the four?
They are the accomplishment of unwavering confidence in the Buddha, and the accomplishment of unwavering confidence in the Dharma, the Sangha, and the noble precepts.
Therefore, bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves thus:
'I shall achieve unshakable confidence in the Buddha, unshakable confidence in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and the achievement of the noble precepts.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
835. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“The Wheel-Turning King, fully endowed with the seven treasures and having accomplished the four kinds of supernormal powers among humans, rules over the four continents; when his body perishes and his life ends, he is reborn in the heavens.”

Although a Wheel-Turning Sage King may be fully endowed with the seven treasures, achieve human supernormal powers, and rule over the four continents, yet upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, even if he is reborn in the heavens, he has still not severed the sufferings of the evil realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.
Why is this? Because a wheel-turning monarch does not attain unshakable confidence in the Buddha, unshakable confidence in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, nor does he achieve the noble precepts.
“The learned noble disciple wears rag-robes, begs for alms from house to house, and uses bedding made of grass;
yet that learned noble disciple is liberated from the suffering of the miserable realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.”
Why is that? Because that learned noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dharma and the Sangha, and is endowed with the noble precepts.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "To possess unwavering confidence in the Buddha,
unwavering confidence in the Dharma and the Sangha, and to be accomplished in the noble precepts."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 836 (836). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should give rise to a heart of compassion and a heart of loving-kindness.
If there are those who wish to hear and receive what you have to say, you should explain to them the four kinds of unbreakable confidence, causing them to enter and abide therein."
What are the four? They are:
unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dharma, unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha, and the accomplishment of noble ethical discipline. Why is that?
If the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—undergo change, increase, or decrease, these four unshakable purities never undergo increase, decrease, or alteration.

Regarding that which is without increase, decrease, or transformation: it is impossible for a learned noble disciple who has achieved unwavering confidence in the Buddha to fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts. Such a thing cannot occur.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:

"I shall achieve unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dharma, and unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha; I shall achieve the noble precepts, and I shall also establish others so that they may achieve them."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 837 (837) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one trusts a person, five kinds of faults and afflictions arise; at times that person may violate the precepts or contravene the Vinaya, and thus be abandoned by the assembly."
One who respects such a person should think:
"This is my teacher, whom I hold in high esteem; since the Sangha has rejected and slighted him, for what reason should I now enter his stupa or monastery?"
Having failed to enter the monasteries and temples, they do not show respect to the Saṅgha;
having failed to show respect to the Saṅgha, they do not hear the Dharma;
having failed to hear the Dharma, they fall away from wholesome qualities and are unable to abide long within the True Dharma.
This is called the first fault of a person who possesses faith and reverence.

"Furthermore, regarding a person who is reverent and faithful: if the person they revere violates the precepts and transgresses the discipline, the Sangha shall perform the formal act of 'reproving for not seeing [the offense]' against them."
Those who revere and have faith in that person should form this thought:

"This is my teacher, whom I hold in high esteem; yet now the community of monks has performed a formal act of suspension against him for refusal to see an offense. For what reason, then, should I enter a monastery or temple again?"
Having failed to enter the monasteries and temples, they do not show respect to the Sangha;
having failed to show respect to the Sangha, they do not hear the Dharma;
having failed to hear the Dharma, they fall away from wholesome qualities and are unable to abide long within the True Dharma.
This is called the second fault arising from having faith in that person.
Furthermore, if that person takes up his robes and bowl and travels to another region,
those who revere him will think:
"The person I revere has put on his robes and taken up his bowl to wander among the people; for what reason should I now enter that monastery?
Having failed to enter the monastery, he could not pay respect to the Sangha;
having failed to respect the Sangha, he could not hear the Dharma.
Having failed to hear the Dharma, one falls away from wholesome qualities and is unable to abide long within the True Dharma.
This is called the third fault arising because of one who respects and has faith in others.
"Furthermore, suppose the person whom one trusts and reveres abandons the precepts and returns to lay life.
Those who revere and trust that person will think:
'That person was my teacher and one I held in high esteem; since he has abandoned the precepts and returned to lay life, I should no longer enter his monastery or temple.'"
Having failed to enter the monastery, they do not show respect to the Saṃgha;
having failed to show respect to the Saṃgha, they do not hear the Dharma;
having failed to hear the Dharma, they fall away from wholesome qualities and are unable to abide long within the True Dharma.
This is called the fourth fault arising from having faith in such a person.
Furthermore, when that person whom he has come to revere and trust dies and his body perishes,
those who have faith in him think to themselves:
"He was my teacher and one whom I revered; now that he has passed away, for what reason should I enter his stupa-temple?
Because he did not enter the temple, he could not revere the Sangha;
because he did not revere the Sangha, he could not hear the Dharma.
Because they do not hear the Dharma, they fall away from wholesome qualities and are unable to abide long within the True Dharma.
This is called the fifth fault arising from having respect and faith for such people.
"Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
'We shall achieve unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dharma and the Sangha, and we shall achieve the noble precepts.'"
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 838 (838) Thus have I heard:

They are the food of bolus, the food of contact, the food of volition, and the food of consciousness.
In this way, merit is moistening and serves as the food of peace and happiness.
What are these four?
That is to say: unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dharma and the Sangha, and the accomplishment of noble ethical discipline.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"I shall achieve unshakable confidence in the Buddha, unshakable confidence in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and the accomplishment of the noble precepts.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
839 (Eight Hundred Thirty-Nine). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus... as described above.
As for the distinctions:
"One who has accomplished unshakable confidence in the Buddha is mindful of the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and is accomplished in the noble precepts.

840. The subsequent sutra is also as explained above.
The difference is as follows:

"If one achieves unshakable confidence in the Buddha, and likewise in the Dharma and the Sangha; if, among sentient beings entangled by the defilement of stinginess, one dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, liberated, with a mind inclined toward giving, constantly practicing the joy of giving, always delighting in renunciation, practicing impartial giving, and achieving noble ethical discipline."
