841 (841) The subsequent sutra is also explained as above.
Regarding the distinction:

"In this way, the noble disciple possesses four kinds of moisture of merit, moisture of wholesome qualities, and the accumulation of measurable and immeasurable virtues. While one cannot measure such a mass of resultant merit, such a result, or such a collection of fruits of merit, he nevertheless attains manifold benefits and blessings; this is reckoned as a great mass of merit."

For example, when five rivers flow together—the Ganges, Yamunā, Sarayū, Airāvatī, and Mahī—it is impossible to measure their waters by hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands of millions of jars; nevertheless, those waters are vast and constitute what is reckoned as a great mass of water.

Thus, when a noble disciple is endowed with these four qualities of moisture, no one is able to measure the extent of their merit; yet that great merit constitutes a vast accumulation of sublime virtue.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "I shall accomplish unshakable confidence in the Buddha,
unshakable confidence in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and the accomplishment of the noble precepts."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The great ocean of all auspiciousness, Pure by nature, it can purify others;
Vast and flowing level, It is truly the sovereign of all rivers."
All rivers and streams, upon which all living beings depend, ultimately flow back to the great ocean; this body is likewise so:
it is where the hundred blessings of giving, precepts, and cultivated merit converge.
842. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
“The Brahmins preach a path of falsehood, which is foolish, evil, and heterodox; it is not a correct orientation, nor does it lead toward wisdom, perfect enlightenment, or Nirvana.”
He thus transformed his disciples in this way:

on the fifteenth day, they were to bathe their bodies with powdered sesame and powdered *āmramālaka*, put on new cotton garments, hang long strands of thread from their heads, smear cow dung upon the ground, and lie down upon it, saying:
"O noble sons!..."

Rising early at dawn, one should strip off one's clothes and pile them in one place, then run toward the east with the body bare. Even if one encounters fierce elephants, vicious horses, mad oxen, rabid dogs, thorns, thickets, pits, ravines, or deep waters along the way, one must press straight ahead without avoiding them. If one meets death there, one will certainly be reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
"This is called the foolish and false view of the non-Buddhists; it is not the wisdom of equal enlightenment that leads toward Nirvana.

For my disciples, I have taught the level and upright path—not that of folly, but that which leads toward wisdom and equal enlightenment, and toward Nirvana—namely, the Eightfold Noble Path, from Right View through to Right Concentration."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 843 (843) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra:
"Regarding what is called 'flood' (ogha): what are the floods?"
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
“The ‘stream’ spoken of by the World-Honored One refers to the Eightfold Noble Path.
The Buddha then asked Śāriputra again:
"It refers to the factors conducive to stream-entry.
What are these factors conducive to stream-entry?
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
There are four factors conducive to stream-entry. What are these four?”
That is to say: associating with virtuous friends, hearing the true Dharma, correct internal reflection, and practicing the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma.
He then asked Śāriputra:
“How many dharmas does one who has entered the stream accomplish?”
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“There are four factors that constitute one who has entered the stream. What are these four?”
That is to say: unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dharma, unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha, and the accomplishment of noble ethical discipline.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Regarding what you have said, ‘the stream’ refers to the Noble Eightfold Path.”
There are four factors conducive to stream-entry: namely, associating with virtuous persons, hearing the true Dharma, correct internal reflection, and practicing in accordance with the Dharma.

One who has entered the stream accomplishes four qualities: namely, indestructible confidence in the Buddha, indestructible confidence in the Dharma, indestructible confidence in the Sangha, and the accomplishment of noble ethical discipline.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Śāriputra, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
844 (844) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra went to where the Venerable Ānanda was, and after exchanging greetings and words of comfort, he withdrew to stand to one side.
The Venerable Śāriputra said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"I wish to ask a question; would you have the leisure to explain it for me?"
The Venerable Ānanda said to Śāriputra:
"Ask whatever you wish; I shall answer what I know.
Śāriputra then questioned the Venerable Ānanda:

"By the abandonment of how many factors does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—knowing and seeing them—declare that a person has attained the stage of Srotāpanna, is no longer subject to rebirth in the woeful states, is destined for full enlightenment, and will undergo seven more births among gods and humans before reaching the ultimate end of suffering?"
Venerable Ānanda said to Venerable Sāriputta:

"By abandoning four things and accomplishing four things, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has declared that such a person has attained the stage of stream-entry (srotāpanna), is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, is destined for full enlightenment (samyakbodhi), and will undergo seven more births among gods and humans before reaching the ultimate end of suffering."
What are the four? They are as follows:
when a noble disciple has abandoned and fully understood lack of faith in the Buddha, they achieve unshakable confidence in the Buddha;

when they have abandoned and fully understood lack of faith in the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and immoral conduct, they achieve unshakable confidence in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, as well as the achievement of noble ethical discipline.

When these four factors are abandoned and these four factors are accomplished, as known and seen by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, he declares that such a person has attained the stage of Srotāpanna; they are no longer subject to rebirth in the woeful states, are certain to be directed toward full enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), and after wandering through seven more existences among gods and humans, they will reach the ultimate end of suffering.
Venerable Ānanda said to Venerable Śāriputra: “So it is! So it is!”

Through the abandonment of four things and the accomplishment of four things—known and seen by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—it is declared that such a person has attained the stage of Srotāpanna, is fixed and headed toward perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), will undergo seven more births among gods and humans, and will ultimately reach the end of suffering.
At that time, after the two noble men had finished their discussion, they expressed mutual appreciation for one another’s views, rose from their seats, and departed.
845 (845) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“If a bhikṣu has brought rest to the five fearsome adversaries and enemies, is certain in three matters, gives rise to no doubt, and knows and sees the noble, right path as it truly is, that noble disciple can declare of himself:

‘The evil destinies of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts are exhausted; I have attained the stage of Srotāpanna; I am no longer subject to falling into the evil destinies; I am fixed and heading toward perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi); after seven more births among gods and humans, I shall reach the ultimate end of suffering.’”
“What are the five ways in which the fear of hostile adversaries is stilled?

If, due to the causes and conditions of killing living beings, the fear of the hostility of karmic retribution arises, then for one who abstains from killing, that fear arising from the causes and conditions of the hostility of karmic retribution for killing is stilled.”
If one experiences fear due to the causes and conditions of the enmity of the offenses of stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants;

if that person abstains from the enmity of the offenses of stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants, then the fear arising from those causes and conditions ceases. This is called the cessation of the five fears arising from the causes and conditions of the enmity of offenses.
"What are the three matters of certainty that give rise to no doubt? They are:
being certain regarding the Buddha and free from doubt; being certain regarding the Dharma and the Saṅgha and free from doubt. These are called the three dharmas of certainty and freedom from doubt."
"What is called the noble path of knowing and seeing things as they truly are?

It is the knowing of this noble truth of suffering as it truly is; the knowing of this noble truth of the origin of suffering, this noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and this noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering as they truly are. This is called the noble path of knowing and seeing things as they truly are."

"If one has brought to rest these five terrors, enemies, and adversaries; if one is certain regarding the three dharmas and free from doubt; and if one knows and sees the noble intention as it truly is—then this noble disciple can declare of himself:

'Hell is exhausted for me; the animal realm and the realm of hungry ghosts, the evil destinies, are exhausted. I have attained the stage of Srotāpanna; I am no longer subject to falling into the evil destinies. I am fixed in the right course toward full enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), with seven more births remaining among gods and humans before reaching the ultimate end of suffering.'"
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 846 (846). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus... as stated above.
The difference is as follows:
"What is the noble path known and seen as it truly is?"
That is to say, the Eightfold Noble Path—from right view up to right concentration.
The subsequent sutra also speaks in this same way.
The difference is as follows:
"What is the noble path of knowing and seeing things as they truly are?
It is the knowing and seeing of the twelvefold dependent origination as it truly is.
As it has been said:"
"Because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises. That is to say: conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations; conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness;

conditioned by consciousness is name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving; conditioned by craving is clinging; conditioned by clinging is existence; conditioned by existence is birth; conditioned by birth arise aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair."
"This is called the noble disciple’s knowledge and vision according to reality.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
847. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are four heavenly paths that purify sentient beings who are not yet purified and further purify those who are already purified.
What are these four? They are:

the noble disciple’s unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dharma, unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha, and the accomplishment of noble ethical discipline. These are called the four heavenly paths that purify sentient beings who are not yet purified and further purify those who are already purified.”
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 848 (848). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are four kinds of heavenly paths for the devas.
What are these four?
It means that the noble disciple recollects the qualities of the Tathāgata as follows:

the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the One Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.

Regarding these deeds of the Tathāgata, one gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy; having given rise to sympathetic joy, the mind becomes gladdened; with a gladdened mind, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one experiences happiness; experiencing happiness, one enters meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
having entered meditative concentration, the noble disciple trains as follows: "What is the path of the devas?"
Again, he thought:
"I have heard that non-anger is the supreme path of the devas.
Having formed this thought:

"From this day forward, whether in fear or in security within the world, I shall not give rise to ill will; I shall instead experience for myself the purely singular, complete, and pure heavenly path."
"This is called the first heavenly path of the devas: it purifies sentient beings who are not yet pure, and further purifies those already purified.
Furthermore, bhikṣu!"

The noble disciple recollects the Dharma, namely that the Tathāgata has taught the True Dharma and Discipline, which is a Dharma for the present life, free from all burning fevers, not dependent on time, leading to the penetration of Nirvana, to be observed by one's own body, and to be personally realized through direct knowledge.
Having thus understood the nature of phenomena, joy arises in the mind;

having rejoiced, the body becomes tranquil; with the body tranquil, one experiences happiness; experiencing happiness, one attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*); having attained meditative concentration, the noble disciple trains himself in this way:
"What is the path of the devas?"
He further thought:

"I have heard that non-anger is the supreme path of the devas. From this day forward, whether in fear or in security within this world, I shall not give rise to anger; I shall uphold the purely singular, full, and pure path of the devas."
This is called the second heavenly path.
"Furthermore, bhikṣu!

If one gives rise to right mindfulness regarding the affairs of the Saṃgha—namely, that the Saṃgha of the World-Honored One’s disciples is upright, impartial, and directed toward the truth; that it is worthy of reverence, respect, and offerings; and that it is the unsurpassed field of merit."
Having thus correctly recollected the affairs of the Sangha, his mind gives rise to sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*);

with a mind full of sympathetic joy, he attains gladness; being glad, his body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, he experiences happiness; experiencing happiness, he enters meditative concentration (*samādhi*); having entered meditative concentration, that noble disciple trains himself thus:
"What are the paths to the various heavens?"
Again, he thought:

"I have heard that for the devas, freedom from anger is the supreme heavenly path. From this day forward, whether in fear or in security within the world, I shall not give rise to ill will; I shall instead uphold the purely singular, full, and pure heavenly path."
This is called the third heavenly path of the devas.
"Furthermore, bhikṣu!
It means that a noble disciple reflects upon his own observance of the precepts, recollecting them as follows:"
"I possess these precepts that are unimpaired, unstained, untainted, praised by the wise, and not despised by the wise.
Having correctly recollected such matters regarding the precepts, joy arises in his heart;
having rejoiced, he becomes glad; having become glad, [he experiences rapture].

When the body is at ease, having the body at ease, one experiences happiness; experiencing happiness, one attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*); having attained meditative concentration, the noble disciple reflects thus:
"What is the path of the devas?"
Again, he forms this thought:

"I have heard that among the devas, the absence of ill will is supreme. From this day forward, whether in fear or in security within all worlds, I shall not give rise to anger; I shall uphold the purely singular, complete, and pure path of the devas."
"This is called the fourth heavenly path of the devas:
it purifies sentient beings who are not yet pure, and further purifies those who are already pure.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
849 (849). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are four celestial paths of the devas that purify sentient beings who have not yet been purified and increase the purity of those already purified.
What are these four?
It means that the noble disciple recollects the qualities of the Tathāgata as follows:

the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the One Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Having thus reflected upon the deeds of the Tathāgata, he abandons evil craving and severs the mental faults of unwholesome states.
Because he recollects the Tathāgata, a mind of sympathetic joy arises;
once the mind is filled with sympathetic joy, he becomes gladdened.
Having attained joy, the body becomes tranquil;
with the body tranquil, one experiences happiness;
experiencing happiness, one enters meditative concentration.
Having attained concentration through samādhi, the noble disciple trains himself thus:
"What is the path to the devas?
He further reflects:
"I have heard that non-ill will is the supreme heavenly path among the devas.

From this day forth, whether in fear or in security within all worlds, I shall not give rise to anger; I shall instead uphold and practice this pure, singular, full, and clean heavenly path of the devas."
"In the same way, the accomplishment of the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the noble precepts is also to be explained thus.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
850. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are four celestial paths of the devas that cause unpurified sentient beings to become purified and increase the purity of those already purified.
What are these four?
They are when a noble disciple recollects the qualities of the Tathāgata as follows:”
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
When that noble disciple has recollected the qualities of the Tathāgata, his mind becomes free from the entanglements of sensual desire, ill will, and delusion, and his mind becomes upright.

By recollecting the qualities of the Tathāgata, this noble disciple attains the stream of Dharma, attains the stream of meaning, and attains the sympathetic joy of benefiting through the recollection of the Tathāgata;
having felt sympathetic joy, he gives rise to gladness.
Having attained joy, the body becomes tranquil;
with the body tranquil, one experiences happiness;
experiencing happiness, one enters meditative concentration.
Having attained concentration in samādhi, this noble disciple trains himself thus:
"What is the path of the devas?
He further reflects:

"I have heard that non-ill will is the supreme heavenly path of the devas. From this day forth, I shall not give rise to anger toward any in the world; I shall maintain the heavenly path of the devas, which is purely one, full, and pure."
"In the same way, the accomplishment of the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the noble precepts is also to be explained thus.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
851 (851). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now teach the *Dhammādāsa Sutta* (The Mirror of the Dhamma). Listen closely and attend well; I shall speak for you.
What is the *Dhammādāsa Sutta*?

It refers to a noble disciple possessing unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dhamma and the Saṅgha, and being accomplished in the noble precepts—this is called the *Dhammādāsa Sutta*.”
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 852 (852) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus, having dressed themselves and taken their bowls, entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
While begging, they heard that the bhikṣu Durdharṣa had passed away, the bhikṣuṇī Nandā had passed away, the upāsaka Susīma had passed away, and the upāsikā Susīma had passed away.

Having finished his almsround, he returned to the vihāra, put away his robe and bowl, and after washing his feet, went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This morning, as I entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms, I heard that the bhikṣu Durdurūka, the bhikṣuṇī Nandā, the upāsaka Sujāta, and the upāsikā Sujātā have passed away.
“World-Honored One!
Where will those four persons be reborn after their lives have ended?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Those bhikṣus, Dhanika and Nanda, have exhausted all taints; they possess the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized and witnessed for themselves in this very life:
‘Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; we know for ourselves that there will be no further existence.’”

The lay follower Sujāta and the lay follower Sujātā, having exhausted the five lower fetters, attained the stage of non-returner (anāgāmin); they were reborn in the heavenly realms and there attained parinirvāṇa, never again to return to this world.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

"I shall now teach you the Dhammādāsa Sutta (The Mirror of the Dhamma). From unwavering confidence in the Buddha, up to the accomplishment of noble ethical discipline—this is called the Dhammādāsa Sutta."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 853 (853) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park... [as extensively described above].
As for the distinctions:
“There is another bhikṣu, another bhikṣuṇī, another upāsaka, and another upāsikā who pass away…” as was also explained above.
854 (854). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Paṅgikā Vihāra in the village of Naḷakalāpa.
At that time, many people in the village of Naḷakalāpa had passed away.

At that time, a large number of bhikṣus, having dressed themselves and taken their bowls, entered the village of Naḷakalāpa to beg for food. There they heard that the upāsaka Kṛkī of the village of Naḷakalāpa had passed away, and that Nikata, Khara-karāla, Katamoraka-tiṣya, Sala, Upasala, Likhita, Arilikhita, Bhadra, Subhadra, Yasa-yajñadatta, and Yasa-uttara had all likewise passed away.

Having heard this, he returned to the vihāra, took up his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"O World-Honored One! This morning, we many bhikṣus entered the village of Nālika for alms and heard that the upāsaka Kevaddha and others had passed away."
“Where will they be reborn when their lives come to an end?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“Kaśyapa and the others have severed the five lower fetters and attained the stage of non-returner (anāgāmin); they shall attain parinirvāṇa in the heavenly realms and will no longer return to be born in this world.”
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!

Furthermore, more than two hundred and fifty upāsakas have passed away; additionally, five hundred upāsakas have passed away here in the village of Naḷika. Have they all, with the five lower fetters exhausted, attained the state of an anāgāmin, and having entered parinirvāṇa in that heavenly realm, will no longer return to be born in this world?"

Furthermore, more than two hundred and fifty upāsakas have passed away; all had exhausted the three fetters, with greed, hatred, and delusion attenuated, attaining the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*, destined for only one more birth before reaching the ultimate end of suffering?

Furthermore, there were five hundred upāsakas in this village of Nālika who passed away here; having exhausted the three fetters, they attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, are no longer subject to rebirth in the evil destinies, are destined for full awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and after wandering through seven more existences among gods and humans, will reach the ultimate end of suffering. Is this so?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"For you to inquire about his passing away and what happens after death is merely a waste of effort;
it is not a matter that the Tathāgata delights in answering."
Now, that which is born must die; how can this be considered extraordinary?
Whether the Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) remains eternally constant.
That Tathāgata, having personally realized the attainment of perfect enlightenment, manifests it, proclaims it, analyzes it, and reveals it.

That is to say: because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises. Conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations, and so on, up to: conditioned by birth are old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering.
In this way, this aggregate of suffering arises;

with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease, and so on, until with the cessation of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, despair, and suffering cease—thus does this aggregate of suffering cease.
I shall now teach you the *Dhammādāsa Sutta* (The Mirror of the Dhamma). Listen closely and attend well; I shall speak for you.
What is the *Dhammādāsa Sutta*?
It refers to a noble disciple possessing unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dhamma and the Saṅgha, and being accomplished in the noble precepts.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 855 (855) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the upāsaka Nanda came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"If a noble disciple were at all times not endowed with these five faculties,
would he be negligent or non-negligent?
The Buddha told Nandiya:
"If one does not possess all five of these faculties at all times, I declare such persons to be among the ranks of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
If a noble disciple (*ārya-śrāvaka*) does not possess them, it is due to negligence; if they do possess them, it is due to non-negligence."

"Nanda! If a noble disciple has achieved unshakable confidence in the Buddha, yet does not seek higher attainment, nor sits in a secluded grove or in the open air to practice dhyāna day and night with diligent application toward the sublime and transcendent deliverance that brings great benefit;

if, failing to rejoice in that [deliverance], joy does not arise in him; if, joy not arising, his body does not become tranquil; and if, his body not being tranquil, painful feelings arise; and if, painful feelings having arisen, his mind does not attain concentration—then such a noble disciple is said to be negligent."
The same is said regarding the unshakable confidence in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, as well as the accomplishment of noble ethical discipline. Thus, Nandiya!
If a noble disciple accomplishes unshakable confidence in the Buddha, his mind does not give rise to the notion of being satisfied.

In a secluded forest, at the foot of a tree, or in the open air, he meditates day and night with diligent application of skillful means, able to give rise to sublime and wondrous sympathetic joy regarding renunciation.

Having given rise to sympathetic joy, he experiences gladness; having experienced gladness, his body becomes tranquil; his body being tranquil, he experiences happiness; experiencing happiness, his mind becomes concentrated.

"If a noble disciple’s mind is concentrated, this is called heedfulness; the same is said for the indestructible clarity regarding the Dharma and the Sangha, as well as the accomplishment of noble ethical discipline.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the lay follower Nandi, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and delighted in it. He rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and departed.
856 (856). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Nandiya of the Śākya clan came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a noble disciple does not at all times possess the four kinds of indestructible confidence, is that noble disciple considered negligent?”
"What constitutes non-negligence?
The Buddha told Nandiya of the Śākyas:
"If one does not achieve the four kinds of unshakable confidence at all times, I declare such persons to be reckoned among the ranks of external worldlings."
“Nanda of the Śākya clan!
Whether a noble disciple is negligent or diligent, I shall now explain this... [The discourse continues] as extensively set forth above.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Nanda of the Śākya clan, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and delighted in it; he rose from his seat, paid homage, and departed.
857. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
When the three-month summer retreat had concluded, a great number of bhikṣus gathered in the dining hall to sew robes for the Buddha.
Before long, the Tathāgata will have finished making his robes; he will then put on his robe, take up his bowl, and depart from the monastery to wander among the people.

At that time, Nandiya the Śākyan heard that many bhikṣus had gathered at the dining hall to sew robes for the Buddha, saying that before long the Tathāgata would have finished making his robes and would then put on his robe, take up his bowl, and wander among the people.
Having heard this, Nandiya of the Śākya clan went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

My four limbs are now as if they were being torn apart and my sense of direction is confused; the Dharma I previously heard, I have now entirely lost and forgotten. I heard that many bhikṣus had gathered at the refectory and were sewing robes for the World-Honored One, saying:
"The Tathāgata will not long remain before his robes are finished; having donned them and taken up his bowl, he will wander among the human realms."
"Therefore, great suffering now arises in my heart: when shall I again behold the World-Honored One and the bhikṣus who are my spiritual friends?
The Buddha told Nandiya of the Śākya clan:
"Whether you see the Buddha or do not see the Buddha, whether you see the bhikṣus who are your spiritual friends or do not see them, you should at all times cultivate the five bases of joy."
What are these five?
You should, from time to time, bring to mind the matters concerning the Tathāgata:

that he is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, the Sugata, the Lokavid, the Anuttara, the Puruṣadamyasārathi, the Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, the Buddha, the Bhagavān. Furthermore, you should bring to mind the matters concerning the Dharma, the matters concerning the Saṅgha, the matters concerning your own observance of the precepts, and the matters concerning your own practice of the holy life.
At all times, he reflects:

"I have attained my own benefit; among beings who are defiled by stinginess, I shall extensively cultivate dwelling free from the stain of stinginess, practicing the gift of liberation, the gift of relinquishment, the gift that is ever-blazing, delighting in renunciation, bestowing gifts with equanimity, and constantly maintaining a mind of generosity."
"Thus it is, Śākyan Nandi!
Whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down—even when accompanied by wife and children—one should always bind the mind to this mindfulness of samādhi."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Śākya Nandi, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and delighted in it;
he paid homage and departed. 858 (858) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, observing the three-month summer rains retreat.

At that time, there was a Śākya named Nandi who heard that the Buddha was observing the three-month summer retreat at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī. Having heard this, he thought to himself:
"I shall go there and, furthermore, perform various acts of offering and provide for the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus."
He went there immediately. When the three months had concluded, a great number of bhikṣus gathered in the dining hall to sew robes for the World-Honored One, saying:
"The Tathāgata will not long remain before his robes are finished; having donned them and taken up his bowl, he will travel through the human world."
At that time, Nandiya of the Śākya clan heard that many bhikṣus had gathered in the dining hall and said:
"The Tathāgata will soon finish making his robes; having put them on and taken up his bowl, he will travel through the human world."
Having heard this, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
My four limbs now feel as if they are being torn apart; my sense of direction has shifted, and all the teachings I previously received have now become confused and forgotten.”
"I have heard that the World-Honored One is wandering among human beings; when shall I see the World-Honored One again, as well as my venerable kinsmen, the bhikṣus?
The Buddha told Nandiya of the Śākyas:
"Whether you see the Tathāgata or not, whether you see your venerable kinsmen, the bhikṣus, or not, you should at all times cultivate the six recollections."

"What is abandonment through cultivation?
If a bhikṣu cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth, this is called abandonment through cultivation.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“The abandonment through the exertion of abandoning, the abandonment through the cultivation of guarding—
these four right efforts were taught by the Perfectly Awakened One;
a bhikṣu who applies himself with diligent effort shall bring all outflows to an end.”
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Just as it was for the four foundations of mindfulness, so it was for the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, the eightfold path, the four paths, the four dharma-phrases, and the cultivation of right contemplation—all were explained in the same manner.
880. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Just as when someone establishes things in the world, they all depend upon the earth;

so too, when a bhikṣu practices the dharma of meditation, it all depends upon heedfulness as its root. It is gathered through heedfulness, born from heedfulness, and proceeds by means of heedfulness. A bhikṣu who is heedful is able to cultivate the four dhyānas."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 881 (881) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus... as described above.
The difference is this:
"In this way, a bhikṣu is able to sever greed, hatred, and delusion."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Just as with the severing of greed, hatred, and delusion, so too is there the subduing of greed, hatred, and delusion;
and regarding the ultimate exhaustion of greed, the ultimate exhaustion of hatred and delusion, the way out, seclusion, and nirvana, it was likewise spoken.
882. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Just as all grasses, medicinal herbs, and trees grow by depending upon the earth, so too do these various wholesome dharmas all depend upon heedfulness (*apramāda*) as their foundation... " as stated above, up to and including *nirvāṇa*.
"Just as black aloeswood incense is the foremost among all fragrances, so too, among all these various wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is the most supreme.
Just as among solid fragrances, red sandalwood is the first,
so too, for all wholesome dharmas, every one has heedfulness as its root."
Thus it continues, even unto Nirvana.
"For example, among all flowers growing in water and on land, the Utpala lotus is the foremost;
likewise, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is the root, even unto Nirvana."
"Just as among flowers growing on land, the *mālatī* flower is the foremost;
so too, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness (*apramāda*) is their root, even unto *nirvāṇa*."
“Just as, bhikkhus, among all the tracks of animals, the elephant’s track is supreme;
even so, among all wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*), heedfulness (*appamāda*) is the foremost... [as stated above], up to and including Nirvāṇa.”
"Just as among all animals, the lion is the foremost—being the lord of animals—in the same way, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is their root... as stated above, up to and including nirvāṇa.
"Just as among all houses, halls, and pavilions, the ridgepole is foremost;
so too, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is their root."
"Just as among all the fruits of Jambudvīpa, only those that bear the name 'Jambu' are considered the foremost;
so too, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is their root."
"Just as among all *kovidāra* trees, the *sarvayaṣṭi-kovidāra* tree is the foremost;
so too, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness (*apramāda*) is the root... as stated above, up to and including *nirvāṇa*.
"Just as among all mountains, Sumeru, the king of mountains, is the foremost;
so too, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is their root... as explained above, up to and including nirvāṇa.
"Just as among all golds, that of Jambudvīpa is the foremost;
so too, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is their root... as stated above, up to and including *nirvāṇa*.
"Just as, among all garments, the fine cotton cloth of Kāśī is the foremost;
so too, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is their root... as explained above, up to and including *nirvāṇa*.
"Just as, among all forms, white is considered the foremost;
so too, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is their root... as stated above, up to and including *nirvāṇa*.
"Just as among all birds, the golden-winged bird is the foremost;
so too, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is their root... as stated above, up to and including nirvāṇa.
"Just as among all kings, the Wheel-Turning Sage King is the foremost;
so too, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is their root... as explained above, up to and including nirvāṇa.
"Just as among all the celestial kings, the Four Great Kings are foremost;
so too, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is their root... as explained above, up to and including *nirvāṇa*.
"Just as among all the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens, Śakra is the foremost;
so too, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is their root... as stated above, up to and including nirvāṇa.
"Just as among the Yāma gods, the former King of the Yāmas is foremost;
so too, for all wholesome dharmas, non-heedlessness is their root... as explained above, up to and including nirvāṇa.
"Just as among the Tuṣita devas, the King of the Tuṣitas is foremost;
so too, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is their root... as stated above, up to and including nirvāṇa.
"Just as among the gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati), the King of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations is foremost;
so too, for all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is their root... as stated above, up to and including nirvāṇa.
"Just as among the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), the Son of Goodness who Makes Use of Others' Emanations is foremost;
so too, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness (*apramāda*) is their root... as explained above, up to and including *nirvāṇa*.
"Just as among the Brahmā deities, the Great Brahmā King is foremost;
so too, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is their root... as stated above, up to and including *nirvāṇa*.
"Just as all the streams of Jambudvīpa flow toward the great ocean, and that great ocean is the foremost because it receives them;
so too do all wholesome dharmas flow toward heedfulness... [as stated above], up to nirvāṇa."
"Just as all drops of rain flow toward the great ocean, so too do all wholesome dharmas flow toward and enter the ocean of heedfulness... as stated above, up to and including nirvāṇa.
"Just as, among all lakes, the Anavatapta Great Lake is the foremost;
so too, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is the foremost... as stated above, up to and including nirvāṇa.

"Just as among all the rivers of Jambudvīpa, the four great rivers are foremost—namely the Gaṅgā, the Sindhu, the Vakṣu, and the Sītā—so too, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is foremost... as stated above, up to and including nirvāṇa.
"Just as among all the luminaries of the stars, the moon is foremost;
so too, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is foremost... as explained above, up to and including nirvāṇa.
"Just as among all large-bodied beings, Rāhula the Asura is the foremost;
so too, among all wholesome dharmas, non-heedlessness is their root... as explained above, up to and including Nirvāṇa.
"Just as, among all those who enjoy the five sensory pleasures, King Mūrdhaja is the foremost;
so too, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is their root... as stated above, up to and including nirvāṇa.
"Just as among all the supernatural powers in the desire realm, the celestial Māra Pāpīyān is foremost;
so too, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is their root... as explained above, up to and including nirvāṇa.

"Just as among all sentient beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed; whether with form or formless; with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—the Tathāgata is the foremost;
so too, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is their root... as explained above, up to and including nirvāṇa.
"Just as among all phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, freedom from desire is supreme;
so too, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is their root... as stated above, up to the point of nirvāṇa.
"Just as, among all assemblies of dharmas, the assembly of Tathāgatas is foremost;
so too, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is their root... as stated above, up to and including nirvāṇa.
"Just as among all realms and ascetic practices, the Brahma-realm and the noble realm are foremost;
so too, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is their root... as stated above, up to and including nirvana.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 883 (883) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four kinds of dhyāna: there is dhyāna that is skilled in samādhi but not skilled in samāpatti;
there is dhyāna that is skilled in samāpatti but not skilled in samādhi;"

There are meditative absorptions (dhyāna) that are wholesome through concentration (samādhi) and also wholesome through meditative attainment (samāpatti); there are meditative absorptions that are not wholesome through concentration and not wholesome through meditative attainment.
Furthermore, regarding the four kinds of meditative absorptions, there are those that abide in concentration but do not abide in meditative attainment.
There is dhyāna that is skilled in abiding in samāpatti but not skilled in abiding in samādhi;
there is dhyāna that is skilled in abiding in samādhi and also skilled in abiding in samāpatti;
and there is dhyāna that is neither skilled in abiding in samādhi nor skilled in abiding in samāpatti.
"Furthermore, regarding the four kinds of dhyāna: there is dhyāna that gives rise to excellence through samādhi, but not through meditative attainment (samāpatti);
there is dhyāna that gives rise to excellence through meditative attainment, but not through samādhi;
and there is dhyāna that gives rise to excellence both through samādhi and through meditative attainment."
There are meditations that are wholesome when emerging from samādhi, but not wholesome when entering meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).
Furthermore, regarding the four kinds of meditation: there are meditations that are wholesome at the time of samādhi, but not wholesome at the time of meditative absorption;
and there are meditations that are wholesome at the time of meditative absorption, but not wholesome at the time of samādhi.
There is dhyāna that is wholesome at the time of samādhi and also wholesome at the time of right attainment (*samāpatti*);
there is dhyāna that is not wholesome at the time of samādhi and also not wholesome at the time of right attainment.
Furthermore, regarding the four kinds of dhyāna, there is dhyāna that is wholesome in the sphere of samādhi but not wholesome in the sphere of right attainment; [and so forth].
There is dhyāna that is skillful in the state of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) but not skillful in the state of samādhi;
there is dhyāna that is skillful both in the state of samādhi and in the state of meditative attainment;
and there is dhyāna that is neither skillful in the state of samādhi nor skillful in the state of meditative attainment.
"Furthermore, regarding the four kinds of dhyāna: there is dhyāna where one is welcomed by samādhi but not welcomed by samāpatti;
there is dhyāna where one is welcomed by samāpatti but not welcomed by samādhi;
and there is dhyāna where one is welcomed both by samādhi and by samāpatti."
There are meditations that are neither accompanied by the excellence of samādhi nor accompanied by the excellence of right reception (*samāpatti*).
Furthermore, regarding the four kinds of meditation, there are meditations where one is mindful of the excellence of samādhi but not mindful of the excellence of right reception;
and there are meditations where one is mindful of the excellence of right reception but not mindful of the excellence of samādhi.
There are meditations that are samādhi and involve mindfulness of the wholesome, as well as those that are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and involve mindfulness of the wholesome;
there are meditations that are neither samādhi nor meditative attainments and do not involve mindfulness of the wholesome.

Furthermore, regarding the four kinds of dhyāna: there are meditations that are samādhi and involve neither mindfulness of the wholesome nor mindfulness of the unwholesome, and are not meditative attainments involving neither mindfulness of the wholesome nor mindfulness of the unwholesome.
There is dhyāna that is meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) but not concentration (*samādhi*), being good whether attended to or unattended to;
there is dhyāna that is concentration but not meditative attainment, being good whether attended to or unattended to;
and there is dhyāna that is neither concentration nor meditative attainment, being good whether attended to or unattended to.
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of dhyāna: there is dhyāna that is excellent by way of samādhi, but not excellent by way of samāpatti;
there is dhyāna that is excellent by way of samāpatti, but not excellent by way of samādhi;
and there is dhyāna that is excellent both by way of samādhi and by way of samāpatti."
There are meditations that are not well-established through the arrival of samādhi, nor are they well-established through the arrival of right reception (*samāpatti*).
Furthermore, regarding the four kinds of meditation, there are meditations that are ill-established through the arrival of samādhi but well-established through the arrival of right reception;
and there are meditations that are well-established through the arrival of right reception but ill-established through the arrival of samādhi.
There are dhyānas that are both samādhi and skillful in the unwholesome and wholesome, and also skillful in meditative attainment (samāpatti) regarding the unwholesome and wholesome;
there are dhyānas that are neither samādhi nor skillful in the unwholesome and wholesome, and also not skillful in meditative attainment regarding the unwholesome and wholesome.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of dhyāna: there are dhyānas that are skillful in the means (upāya) of samādhi, but not skillful in the means of meditative attainment; [and so forth].
There are those who possess skill in the means of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samāpatti*) but not in the means of meditative absorption (*samādhi*);
there are those who possess skill in the means of both meditative concentration and meditative absorption;
and there are those who possess neither skill in the means of meditative concentration nor skill in the means of meditative absorption.
"Furthermore, regarding the four kinds of dhyāna: there is dhyāna that is excellent in the stillness of samādhi, but not excellent in the stillness of meditative attainment (samāpatti);
there is dhyāna that is excellent in the stillness of meditative attainment, but not excellent in the stillness of samādhi;
and there is dhyāna that is excellent both in the stillness of samādhi and in the stillness of meditative attainment."
There are meditations that are skillful in the stillness of samādhi, yet not skillful in the stillness of right attainment (*samāpatti*).
Furthermore, regarding the four kinds of meditation, there is a meditation that is skillful in the uplifting of samādhi, but not skillful in the uplifting of right attainment;
and there is a meditation that is skillful in the uplifting of right attainment, but not skillful in the uplifting of samādhi.
There is dhyāna that is samādhi and characterized by the excellence of uplifting, yet not characterized by the excellence of meditative attainment;
there is dhyāna that is neither samādhi nor characterized by the excellence of uplifting, yet is characterized by the excellence of meditative attainment.
Furthermore, regarding the four kinds of dhyāna, there is dhyāna that is samādhi and characterized by the excellence of equanimity, yet not characterized by the excellence of meditative attainment.

There is dhyāna that is the relinquishment of wholesome states through meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), but not the relinquishment of wholesome states through meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
there is dhyāna that is both the relinquishment of wholesome states through meditative concentration and the relinquishment of wholesome states through meditative attainment;
and there is dhyāna that is neither the relinquishment of wholesome states through meditative concentration nor the relinquishment of wholesome states through meditative attainment.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 884 (884) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are the three types of clear-knowledge of one beyond training.
What are these three?"

"The supernormal knowledge of the realization of the recollection of past lives of one beyond training; the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the death and rebirth of beings of one beyond training; and the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the exhaustion of outflows of one beyond training.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Observing and knowing past lives, Seeing births in heavenly realms and evil destinies,"
The exhaustion of all outflows regarding birth and death—this is the clarity of the Muni.
His mind has attained liberation; having fully penetrated all cravings throughout three nights, he is therefore said to possess the Threefold Knowledge.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 885 (885) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are three types of clear-knowledge (vidyā) of one beyond training (aśaikṣa). What are the three?

That is to say: the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the recollection of past lives of one beyond training, the supernormal knowledge of the realization of death and rebirth of one beyond training, and the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the destruction of the outflows of one beyond training.
What is the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the recollection of past lives of one beyond training?

It refers to the noble disciple’s knowledge of various past lives, from one birth through hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions of births, even up to the kalpas of cosmic formation and destruction. He knows fully that he and other sentient beings have undergone such names, such births, such natures, such food, such experiences of suffering and pleasure, such longevity, such durations of stay, and such limits of experience;

and that he and other sentient beings died here and were born elsewhere, or died elsewhere and were born here, possessing such conduct, such causes, and such inclinations. To know all these various matters of past lives is called the realization of the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
"What is the clear knowledge and realization of birth and death?

It means that a noble disciple possesses the purified divine eye, surpassing that of humans, by which they see beings at the time of their death and at the time of their birth—those of beautiful form and those of ugly form, those of superior appearance and those of inferior appearance—and they know according to reality how they proceed toward the woeful states, being born there in accordance with their karma;

and how such beings, having accomplished evil conduct of body, evil conduct of speech, and evil conduct of mind, having reviled the noble ones and held wrong views, through the causal conditions of receiving false teachings, at the breaking up of the body after death, are reborn in the woeful states, in the hells."

These sentient beings, having practiced wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind, not reviling the noble ones, and being endowed with right view, at the breaking up of the body after death, are reborn in a happy destination among gods or humans; this is called the direct knowledge of the realization of the destruction of birth and death.
"What is the knowledge and vision of the destruction of the taints?

It is when a noble disciple knows as it really is: 'This is suffering'; knows as it really is: 'This is the origin of suffering'; knows as it really is: 'This is the cessation of suffering'; and knows as it really is: 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

Knowing thus and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, his mind is liberated from the taint of existence, and his mind is liberated from the taint of ignorance. This is the knowledge and vision of liberation:"
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence.
This is called the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Observing and knowing past lives, Seeing births in heavens and in evil realms,
The exhaustion of all outflows of birth and death— This is the illumination of the Muni."
"Knowing that the mind has attained liberation, and having fully mastered all cravings in the three spheres,
one is therefore said to possess the three clear knowledges (*vidyā*).
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
886. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain brahmin approached the place where the Buddha was; having exchanged greetings with the World-Honored One and concluded his salutations, he withdrew to sit at one side.
And he spoke thus:
"This is the threefold knowledge of a brāhmaṇa; this is the threefold knowledge of a brāhmaṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the brāhmaṇa, saying:
“What is meant by a ‘Brahmin of the Three Vedas’?
The Brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying,
“Gautama!...”

The Brahmin’s parents were endowed with the [auspicious] marks and free from all blemishes. For seven generations their lineage had been passed down without any reproach; for generations they had served as teachers and elders, possessing perfect eloquence. They were thoroughly proficient in these five types of records:

the recitation of various scriptures, the names of things and categories, the classifications of all phenomena, the combinations of characters and syllables, and the origins and developments of successive ages. Furthermore, his countenance was upright and handsome.
"This, Gautama, is called the threefold knowledge of a brahmin.
The Buddha said to the brahmin:

“I do not consider verbal expressions using names to be the three knowledges (*vidyā*). Within the Dharma of the noble ones, the essential and true three knowledges are spoken of; that is to say, the noble ones’ knowledge and vision, the noble ones’ Dharma and Vinaya, and the true three knowledges.”
The brahmin addressed the Buddha,
saying: "How is it so, Gautama?"
"What is the noble ones' knowledge and vision, and the threefold clear knowledge (tevijjā) as taught in the Dhamma and Vinaya of the noble ones?
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"There are three kinds of clear knowledge of one beyond training (asekha)."
"What are the three?

They are the realization of the knowledge of past lives of one beyond training, the realization of the knowledge of death and rebirth of one beyond training, and the realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows of one beyond training... as explained at length in the sutra above.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"All phenomena are impermanent; Through upholding the precepts, tranquility, and meditation, One knows all past lives, And the births in heavens and evil realms."
Having attained the cessation of birth and the exhaustion of outflows—this is the supernormal knowledge of the Muni.
Fully knowing the liberation of the mind from all greed, hatred, and delusion—I declare these to be the three knowledges; they cannot be fully expressed by words.
“Brahmin! These are what are called the three knowledges (vidyā) as taught in the Noble Dharma and Vinaya.
The Brahmin addressed the Buddha:
“Gautama! This is the true threefold knowledge.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the brahmin rejoiced and expressed his approval; he rose from his seat and departed.
887 (887). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain brahmin came to where the Buddha was, exchanged greetings with the World-Honored One, and having finished his greetings, sat down to one side and addressed the Buddha:
“Gautama! My name is Śraddhā.
The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa:
"What is called faith is faith in superior morality, giving, learning, renunciation, and wisdom; this is what constitutes faith, not merely the name 'faith'."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the brahmin rejoiced and approved, rose from his seat, and departed.
888 (888) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain brahmin approached the Buddha, exchanged greetings with him, and having concluded his salutations, sat down to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Gautama!
“My name is Vardhana.
The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa:
“What is called ‘Vardhana’ refers to the increase of faith, the increase of ethical discipline, learning, relinquishment, and wisdom; this is what constitutes ‘Vardhana,’ not merely the name.”
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the brahmin rejoiced and approved, rose from his seat, and departed.
889 (889) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain brahmin approached the Buddha, exchanged greetings regarding his well-being, and having finished his greetings, withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
“My name is ‘Origin’ (samudaya).
The Buddha told the brahmin:
“As for what is called ‘origin,’ it refers to the arising of faith, the arising of ethical discipline, learning, relinquishment, and wisdom; this is what constitutes an origin, not a mere name.”
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the brahmin rejoiced and delighted in it; rising from his seat, he departed. 890 (890). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now explain for you the unconditioned dharma and the path leading to the unconditioned.
Listen attentively and reflect well upon it."
What are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)?
They are the eternal exhaustion of greed, the eternal exhaustion of hatred and delusion, and the eternal exhaustion of all afflictions; these are unconditioned phenomena.
What is the track to the unconditioned?
It refers to the eight factors of the noble path:
right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; these are called the track to the unconditioned.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

As it was said regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), so it was likewise said regarding that which is difficult to see, immovable, unbending, deathless, outflow-free (*anāsrava*), shelter, island, crossing, refuge, protection, non-transmigration, free from blazing, free from burning, circulating, cool, sublime, peaceful, healthy, nothingness, and nirvāṇa.
891. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Suppose there were a lake, fifty yojanas wide and long, and likewise deep.
If a man were to take a single drop from that lake with the tip of a single hair, [what do you think?]”
"What do you think, bhikṣu?
Is that lake water more abundant?"
"Which is more: the water on the tip of a hair of a man, or [the water in] the great ocean?
The bhikṣu said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"
"The hair-tips on a man are but a tiny fraction; the water of the lake is countless thousands, tens of thousands, and millions of times greater, such that it cannot be compared to them.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"One who fully perceives the True Reality possesses right view in its entirety."

When a disciple of the Blessed One perceives the fruit of the vision of the Truths and attains right immediate realization (*samyag-anantarya-samāpatti*), at that time they have already abandoned and fully known [the defilements], cutting them off at the root so that they are like the head of a *tāla* tree severed, never to grow again. The suffering thus abandoned is vast and immeasurable, like a great lake; the remaining suffering is like a drop of water on the tip of a hair.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As it was with drops of water from the tip of a hair, so too were the drops of water from the tips of the grass counting-sticks.
Just as with the waters of a lake or pond, so too it is said for the Sarassatī, the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Aciravatī, the Mahī, the Vitastā, the Irāvatī, the Mahī, and the great ocean.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 892 (892) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are six internal sense bases. What are the six?
That is to say, the internal sense-base of the eye, and the internal sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

One who observes and endures these six phenomena is called a "faith-follower" (śraddhānusārin). Having transcended and departed from the state of birth, having left the stage of ordinary worldlings, and though not yet having attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala), they will certainly attain the fruit of stream-entry before their life comes to an end.

If one possesses this superior contemplation and patience regarding these dharmas, it is called "Dharma-practice" (dharmacārin). Having transcended and emerged from the state of birth-and-death, and having left behind the stage of ordinary worldlings, although one has not yet attained the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), one will certainly attain the fruit of a stream-enterer before the end of one's life.

If one observes these phenomena with suchness and right knowledge, the three fetters—namely, the view of a self-identity, adherence to precepts and rituals, and doubt—are exhausted and fully understood; this is called a *srotāpanna*.
One does not fall into the fixed evil realms, but is certain to proceed toward full enlightenment; after seven more births among gods and humans, one reaches the ultimate end of suffering.
When these phenomena are observed with right wisdom, no taints arise; through the abandonment of desire and liberation, one is called an Arhat.

All taints have been exhausted; what was to be done has been accomplished; the heavy burden has been laid down; his own goal has been attained; the fetters of existence are ended; through right knowledge, his mind is well-liberated.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.

As with the six internal sense bases (*āyatana*), so it is with the six external sense bases, the six groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*), the six groups of contact (*sparśakāya*), the six groups of feeling (*vedanākāya*), the six groups of perception (*saṃjñākāya*), the six groups of volition (*cetanākāya*), the six groups of craving (*tṛṣṇākāya*), the six groups of elements (*dhātukāya*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*), all as explained above.
893. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are five kinds of seeds that grow. What are the five?
They are: root-seeds, stem-seeds, joint-seeds, broken-seeds, and seed-seeds.”

If these seeds are not cut off, not destroyed, not rotten, not damaged, and not pierced through, yet they encounter the earth element but do not obtain the water element, those seeds will not grow, increase, or expand;
if they obtain the water element but do not obtain the earth element, those seeds will not grow, increase, or expand;
only when they obtain both the earth element and the water element will those seeds grow, increase, and expand.
In this way, karma arises from afflictions, existence, craving, views, conceit, and ignorance;
if there were karma but no afflictions, craving, views, or ignorance, then karma would cease.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

As it was said regarding volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), so it was also said regarding consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), clinging (*upādāna*), existence (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
894. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"In this world, as long as I did not understand the world and the origin of the world in such a way, I could never, among the devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the entire world, be liberated, transcend, or escape from them; I was not free from inverted perceptions, nor was it called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. "

Because I have known the world and the origin of the world as they truly are, I have attained liberation, emergence, and detachment from all devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and other sentient beings; with a mind free from inversion, I dwell in full possession [of this state] and have realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Thus: the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world; the origin of the world, the emergence from the world; the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, the gratification of the world, the danger of the world, the escape from the world; the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, the path leading to the emergence from the world; the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, the path leading to the origin of the world, the path leading to the cessation of the world; the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, the gratification of the world, the danger of the world, the escape from the world; the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, the path leading to the origin of the world, the path leading to the cessation of the world, the gratification of the world, the danger of the world, and the escape from the world.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 895 (885). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are three kinds of craving. What are the three?
That is to say: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for form, and craving for the formless.
To sever these three cravings, one should seek out a Great Teacher.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Just as one seeks a great teacher, so too does one seek a secondary teacher,
an instructor, a guide, a deliverer, a broad deliverer, an expounder, a broad expounder, a follower-expounder, an ācārya, a companion,
a true friend who is a spiritual friend, one who feels compassion, one who possesses loving-kindness, one who desires one's welfare, and one who desires one's peace.
One who desires joy, one who desires contact, one who desires penetration, one who desires, one who exerts effort,
one who employs skillful means, one who emerges, one who is steadfast, one who is courageous, one who is capable, one who gathers,
one who is constant, one who trains, one who is heedful, one who practices, one who reflects, and one who is mindful.
The same applies to the one who perceives, the one who cogitates, the one who practices the holy life, the one with supernormal powers, the wise one, the one with consciousness,
the one with insight, the one who discriminates, the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment,
the path, serenity and insight, the mindfulness of the body, and the pursuit of right reflection. It is explained in this same way for all of them.
896. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are three outflows (*āsrava*). What are the three?
They are the outflow of sensual desire, the outflow of existence, and the outflow of ignorance. To sever these three outflows, one should seek a Great Teacher.”
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Just as it was said regarding the seeking of a great teacher, so too should it be understood for everything up to the seeking of right reflection; it is explained in the same way.
897. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
Then the Venerable Rāhula approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should one know, and how should one see, so that I may not recollect any signs—neither this conscious body nor external objects—and therein exhaust all outflows?”
The Buddha told Rāhula:
"There are six internal sense bases (*ṣaḍ-ādhyātmikāyatana*). What are the six?

That is to say: the sense-base of the eye, and the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. When these phenomena are observed with right wisdom, all taints (*āsrava*) are exhausted; through right wisdom, the mind is well-liberated. This is called an Arhat—one who has exhausted all taints, completed what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, attained his own benefit, and through the exhaustion of all fetters of existence, whose mind is liberated by right wisdom.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As it was with the six internal bases, so it was also spoken regarding the six external bases and even the five aggregates.
898. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If a bhikṣu has abandoned desire and lust for the eye, and having abandoned desire and lust, he is said to have 'already severed' and 'already known' the eye; he has cut off its root, like the head of a tāla tree, such that it becomes a dharma of non-arising in future lives."
"As with the eye, so it is with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; they are also explained in this same way.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As it was said regarding the six internal sense bases, so too should it be spoken regarding the six external sense bases and even the five aggregates.
899 (889). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If the eye arises, persists, and is manifested in its full accomplishment, then suffering arises, illness persists, and old age and death are manifested;
the same applies, up to and including the mind."
"If the eye ceases, subsides, and vanishes, then suffering ceases, illness subsides, and old age and death vanish;
this applies likewise to the mind.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As it was with the six internal sense bases, so it should be spoken of for the six external sense bases and even up to the five aggregates. 900 (900). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If a bhikṣu relishes the eye, then higher afflictions arise. For one in whom higher afflictions have arisen, they cannot become free from desire for defiled states of mind, nor can those obstacles be severed. This is likewise taught regarding the sphere of the mind."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
