As it was taught regarding the six internal sense bases (*āyatana*), so it was likewise taught for the six external sense bases and even up to the five aggregates (*skandha*).
901 (Ninety-One). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Just as all things created in the world are established by depending upon the earth, so too are all wholesome dharmas established by depending upon the six internal sense bases."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As it was said regarding the six internal sense bases, so too should it be spoken regarding the six external sense bases and even the five aggregates.
902. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“If there are sentient beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed; whether with form or formless; with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—they are all surpassed by the Tathāgata as the most supreme, and this applies even to the noble precepts.”
903. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Whatever actions are performed by sentient beings in the world, all of them are established in dependence upon the earth;

likewise, among all phenomena—whether conditioned or unconditioned—the phenomenon of detachment from desire is the foremost... Thus it is explained in detail, up until: "The noble precepts are also described in this same way."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 904 (904) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Just as all sentient beings in the world rely upon the earth for their establishment, so too among all such assemblies, the assembly of the Tathāgata’s śrāvakas is the foremost... Thus it was explained in detail, up to: "...the noble precepts."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*Saṃyukta Āgama*, Scroll 31; *Saṃyukta Āgama*, Scroll 32.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
32.905 (905). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa and the Venerable Śāriputra were dwelling on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.

Then, a large number of non-Buddhist renunciants approached the Venerable Śāriputra; after exchanging greetings and polite inquiries with the Venerable, they withdrew to sit at one side and said to the Venerable Śāriputra: "How is it?"
“Śāriputra, does the Tathāgata have future birth and death?
Śāriputra replied:
"O followers of other paths!
The World-Honored One has declared that this is an indeterminate matter.
They asked again:
"What do you think, Śāriputra?
Does the Tathāgata have no further birth and death?"
Śāriputra replied:
"O followers of other paths!
The World-Honored One has declared that this is an indeterminate matter."
He asked again:
"Śāriputra, does the Tathāgata have a future birth and death, or does he not have a future birth and death?"
Śāriputra replied,
“The World-Honored One has stated that this is an undeclared matter (avyākṛta).
He asked Śāriputra again:
"Does the Tathāgata neither exist after death nor not exist after death?
Śāriputra replied:
"O followers of external paths!"
The World-Honored One has declared, "This is indeterminate.
The wandering ascetics again asked the Venerable Śāriputra:

"Regarding the questions as to whether the Tathāgata exists after death, does not exist after death, both exists and does not exist after death, or neither exists nor does not exist after death—why did he answer all of them thus?"
“The World-Honored One has declared that this is indeterminate.
Why is it, Venerable Elder, that you are so foolish and deluded, so unskilled and lacking in discernment, like an infant devoid of innate wisdom?
Having spoken these words, he rose from his seat and departed.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa and the Venerable Śāriputra were not far apart, each sitting beneath a tree, meditating in contemplation during the day.

When the Venerable Śāriputra knew that the various non-Buddhist renunciants had departed, he went to where the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was, exchanged greetings and words of comfort with him, and then withdrew to sit at one side.
He reported in full to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa the matter concerning what had been discussed with the various non-Buddhist renunciants, saying:
"Venerable Mahākāśyapa!..."

For what cause and for what reason does the Blessed One not declare whether there is a future existence after death, or no future existence after death, or both a future existence and no future existence after death, or neither a future existence nor no future existence after death?
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa said to Śāriputra:
"If one says that the Tathāgata has birth and death hereafter, this is form;
if one says that the Tathāgata has no birth and death hereafter, this is also form."
If one says that the Tathāgata has a future birth and death, or that he has no future birth and death, this is form;
if one says that the Tathāgata neither has nor does not have a future birth and death, this is form.
The Tathāgata is one whose form has been exhausted and whose mind is well-liberated.
To say that there is a future birth and death is not so;
to say there is no future birth and death, or both, or neither, is also not so.
"The Tathāgata is one whose form has been exhausted and whose mind is well-liberated; he is profoundly deep and vast, immeasurable and innumerable, abiding in the quiescence of nirvāṇa. Śāriputra!"

If one were to say that the Tathāgata has a future birth and death, this would be sensation, perception, mental formations, consciousness, movement, deliberation, falsehood, conditioned existence, and craving; even the statement that there is neither existence nor non-existence regarding future existence is to be explained in the same way.

The Tathāgata has exhausted all craving and his mind is well-liberated; therefore, it is not the case that there is a future existence, nor that there is no future existence, nor that there is both a future existence and no future existence, nor that there is neither a future existence nor no future existence. The Tathāgata, having exhausted all craving and being well-liberated in mind, is profoundly deep, vast, immeasurable, incalculable, and abides in the stillness of nirvāṇa.
Śāriputra! For such causes and such conditions, there was one who asked the World-Honored One:
"Does the Tathāgata exist after death, or does he not exist, or does he both exist and not exist, or does he neither exist nor not exist?"
"It cannot be explained.
At that time, after the two noble men had finished their discussion, each returned to his own place.
906 (906). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was staying at the Eastern Garden, the Mṛgāramātṛ-pariveṇa in Śrāvastī. In the late afternoon, having arisen from meditation, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
For what cause and for what reason, when the World-Honored One first established few precepts for the śrāvakas, many bhikṣus took delight in practicing and studying them;
yet now, although many precepts have been established for the śrāvakas, the bhikṣus take little delight in practicing and studying them?
The Buddha said, “It is so, Kāśyapa!

Because the impurity of lifespan, the impurity of afflictions, the impurity of the eon, the impurity of sentient beings, and the impurity of views have arisen, and because the wholesome dharmas of sentient beings have declined, the Great Teacher has established many prohibitions and precepts for his śrāvakas; yet they take little pleasure in practicing and studying them, Kāśyapa.”
For example, when a kalpa is about to end, before the true jewels have perished, various counterfeit jewels resembling them appear in the world;
once these counterfeit jewels have appeared, the true jewels then vanish.
In this way, Kāśyapa,
when the True Dharma of the Tathāgata is about to perish, a counterfeit semblance of the Dharma arises;
once this counterfeit semblance of the Dharma has appeared in the world, the True Dharma then perishes.
For example, if a ship laden with many precious treasures in the great ocean should suddenly sink;
the True Dharma of the Tathāgata does not perish in such a manner, but rather fades away gradually.

The True Dharma of the Tathāgata cannot be destroyed by the element of earth, nor can it be destroyed by the elements of water, fire, or wind; yet, when evil beings appear in the world—those who delight in committing evils, who desire to commit evils, and who accomplish all manner of evils—who declare what is not the Dharma to be the Dharma, and what is the Dharma to be not the Dharma; who declare what is not the Vinaya to be the Vinaya, and what is the Vinaya to be not the Vinaya; and who, with words and phrases resembling the Dharma, cause it to blaze like a wildfire—it is at such times that the True Dharma of the Tathāgata vanishes from this world.
“Kāśyapa! There are five causes and conditions that cause the True Dharma of the Tathāgata to sink and disappear.
What are these five?
If a bhikṣu does not show respect, honor, or humble devotion toward the Great Teacher;
and having failed to show respect, honor, or humble devotion toward the Great Teacher, yet continues to rely upon him for his dwelling.

Whether it be the Dharma, the training, the teachings that accord with the truth, or the various holy lives praised by the Great Teacher—if one dwells in dependence upon these without respect, without reverence, and without honoring them with a humble mind; [this is a fault].
"Kāśyapa, it is for these five reasons that the True Dharma of the Tathāgata shall sink away here. Kāśyapa!"
There are five causes and conditions that prevent the Tathāgata’s Dharma and Vinaya from vanishing, being forgotten, or declining. What are these five?

If a bhikkhu, toward the Great Teacher, dwells in dependence upon him, showing reverence, respect, humility, and making offerings; and likewise, toward the Dharma, the training, the instructions for conformity, and the various holy lives praised by the Great Teacher, he dwells in dependence upon them, showing reverence, respect, humility, and making offerings.
Kāśyapa! These are called the five causes and conditions by which the Tathāgata’s Dharma and Vinaya do not perish, are not forgotten, and do not decline.
Therefore, Kāśyapa!
One should train thus:
"Toward the Great Teacher, one should cultivate reverence, respect, humility, and offerings, relying upon him for one's dwelling;

likewise, toward the Dharma, the training, the instructions that accord with it, and all those who lead the holy life whom the Great Teacher has praised—one should cultivate reverence, respect, humility, and offerings, relying upon them for one's dwelling."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa rejoiced and was filled with joy;
he paid homage and departed. 907 (907). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.

At that time, the village headman Cāla-Cūḷa-Nāla came to where the Buddha was, exchanged greetings and expressions of courtesy with him face-to-face, and having finished his greetings and courtesy, withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Gautama!..."
I have heard that in ancient times, elderly and experienced performers spoke thus regarding song, dance, and laughter:

"If a performer, amidst a great assembly, engages in song, dance, and laughter, performing various arts to cause that assembly to rejoice and laugh, by reason of this karmic cause, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, they will be reborn in the Heaven of Joy."
"In this regard, what is taught in the Dharma of the Gautama?
The Buddha told the village headman:
"Stop for a moment!"
"Do not inquire about this matter.
Thus he spoke a second and a third time, yet the village headman did not cease his request.
The Buddha said to the village headman:
"I now ask you; answer as you see fit.

In ancient times, the beings of this village were not free from sensual desire and were bound by the fetters of sensual desire; they were not free from ill will and were bound by the fetters of ill will; they were not free from delusion and were bound by the fetters of delusion."
Those performers, amidst the assembly seated there, engaged in various songs, dances, music, and amusements, causing the multitude to rejoice and laugh.
Village headman!
"When that person rejoices and laughs, does he not thereby increase the bonds of greed, hatred, and delusion?
The village headman said to the Buddha,
"It is so, Gautama!"
“Village Headman! Suppose there is a person who has been bound with a rope.

Another person, for a long time, harbors an evil intent toward this person, wishing to bring them harm, disadvantage, lack of peace, and lack of happiness. This person repeatedly sprinkles water upon the rope that binds him. Would not the binding of this person become increasingly tight?”
The village headman said, “So it is, Gautama!
The Buddha said:
"Headman! In ancient times, sentient beings were also like this; not free from the bonds of greed, hatred, and delusion, they increased those very bonds by indulging in play, pleasure, and laughter."
The village headman said:
"It is indeed so, Gautama!
Those performers cause sentient beings to rejoice and laugh, which only serves to further increase their bonds of greed, hatred, and delusion."
"For this reason and cause, it is impossible that one should, upon the breakup of the body after death, be reborn in a happy destination!
The Buddha told the village headman:
"If one were to say that an ancient actor, by causing a great assembly to rejoice and laugh, would—on account of such karmic conditions—be reborn in the Heaven of Joy, that would be a false view!"
"One who holds wrong views should be reborn in one of two destinies: either the realm of hell or the realm of animals.
When these words were spoken, Cāra-cūḍa, the headman of the Nala village, wept and shed tears.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the village headman:
"For this reason, I previously asked you three times and you did not answer.
I said to you, village headman: 'Stop!'"
"Do not inquire about this matter.
The village headman said to the Buddha,
"Gautama!..."
It is not because of what the Gautama has said that I weep.

Rather, I reflect upon how, from the past until now, I have been deceived by those foolish, undiscerning, and unwholesome performers who claimed that by performing various musical entertainments before a great assembly, one could even be reborn in the Heaven of Joyful Birth.
"I now reflect with certainty:
'How is it that actors, through singing, dancing, and playful entertainment, are reborn in the Heaven of Delight? O Gautama!"
"From this day forward, I renounce those evil and unwholesome deeds of the actor and take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent!"
“Headman, this is the essential truth. At that time,
having heard what the Buddha had said, the headman Cālā-Cūlā-Nārada rejoiced and approved, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and departed with joy.
908. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.

At that time, the village head Kuṭumbika, who lived by the profession of arms, approached the place where the Buddha was. Having paid his respects and exchanged greetings, he withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Gautama! I have heard that in the past, veteran warriors of long standing spoke thus:

'If a warrior, clad in heavy armor and grasping sharp weapons, leads the vanguard of the army and is capable of skillfully crushing and subduing the enemy, by the karmic retribution of this deed, he is reborn in the Heaven of the Arrow-Subduers (Śara-abhāva). "
"In the Dharma of Gautama, what is the meaning of this?
The Buddha told Yodhājīva:
"Cease [your questioning] for now!"
"Do not inquire about this matter.
Thus he was stopped three times, yet he continued to question him without ceasing.
The Buddha said to the village headman:
"I now ask you; answer as you see fit.
Village headman, what do you think?

If one who lives by warfare dons armor and serves as the vanguard of the soldiers, capable through skillful means of crushing and subduing the enemy—would this person not first give rise to a mind of injury, desiring to capture, bind, fetter, chain, hack, pierce, and slaughter them?
The village headman replied to the Buddha,
“So it is, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to the village headman:
"For those who live by combat, there are three kinds of evil and deviant conduct—whether of body, speech, or mind.

It is impossible that, due to these three kinds of evil and deviant causes and conditions, upon the breakup of the body after death, they could be reborn in a happy destination as a member of the Heaven of the Subduers of Arrows."
The Buddha told the village headman:

“If those elders among the ancient warriors held such a view and spoke thus: ‘If any warriors, clad in armor and grasping sharp weapons in hand, lead the charge against the enemy and are able through skillful means to crush and subdue their foes, by this cause and condition they are reborn in the Heaven of the Arrow-Subduers (Śara-abhyudgata)’—this is a false view.”
"A person of wrong view should be reborn in one of two places: either in the realm of hell or in the realm of animals.
When these words were spoken, the village head wept and shed tears.
The Buddha told the village headman:
"For this reason, I have previously spoken to you twice and thrice: 'Stop!'"
"I did not speak for your sake.
The village headman said to the Buddha, "It is not because of the words of Gautama that I weep.
I am thinking of those elders and veterans of old who lived by warfare—foolish, unskilled, and undiscerning—who for a long night deceived others by speaking thus:"
"If one who lives by combat wears armor upon his body, grasps sharp weapons in his hands, and leads the way against the enemy, he may even attain rebirth in the Heaven of the Subduers with Arrows."
For this reason, I weep with compassion.
I now reflect with certainty:

"That those who live by combat, due to the causes and conditions of their evil karma, should, upon the dissolution of the body after death, be reborn in the Heaven of the Subduers of Arrows—that is impossible."
“Gautama! From this day forward, I renounce all evil deeds and take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus.
The Buddha said to the village headman:
"This is the essential truth.
Then, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the village headman Yodhājīva rejoiced and approved, rose from his seat, paid his respects, and departed.
909. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, a village headman who tended horses came to where the Buddha was, paid his respects with greetings, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked the village head of the Horse-Taming Village,
"How many methods are there for taming horses?
The village head replied:
"Gautama! There are three kinds of phenomena.
What are these three?"
That is to say: first, pliant; second, stubborn; and third, both pliant and stubborn.
The Buddha told the village headman:
“If, by means of these three methods, the horse is still not tamed, what should be done?”
The village headman asked,
"Should I then kill him?
The village headman addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Gautama! By how many kinds of dharmas does the Unsurpassed Tamer of Men tame men?
The Buddha told the village headman:
“I also discipline men by means of three methods. What are these three?
First, gentleness; second, firmness; and third, both gentleness and firmness.”
The village headman said to the Buddha,
“Gautama! If these three kinds of persons to be tamed by a Great Man remain untamed, what should be done with them?”
The Buddha said,
"Village headman!
If one is not tamed even after being disciplined by these three methods, then one should simply kill him."
"Why is this? So that my Dharma may not suffer any humiliation.
The village headman Aśvaka addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the Dharma of Gautama, those who take life are impure; in the Dharma of Gautama, one should not kill. Yet now you say:
'Those who are unsubdued should also be killed.'"
The Buddha told the village headman:
"It is as you have said."
“In the Dharma of the Tathāgata, taking life is impure; the Tathāgata should not take life.
Village headman!
Nevertheless, I discipline men by means of three methods; those who are not disciplined, I no longer speak with, nor do I instruct, nor do I admonish them.
"Headman! If the Tathāgata, the tamer of men, no longer speaks with one, no longer instructs, and no longer admonishes, would that not be killing?"
The village headman of Assaka addressed the Buddha, saying: “Gautama!
If a tamer of men no longer speaks with one, no longer instructs one, and no longer admonishes one, that is truly to kill him.”
"Therefore, from this day forth, I renounce all evil deeds and take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus.
The Buddha told the village headman:
"This is a true and essential commitment."

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the village headman of Aśvattha, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and approved with gladness; he then rose from his seat, paid homage, and departed.
910. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, a fierce village headman came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By not cultivating what kind of dharmas does one give rise to anger toward others?
Because of giving rise to anger, one utters evil words with the mouth, and others consequently give one the name of an evil-natured person?”
The Buddha told the village headman:
"Because one does not cultivate right view, one gives rise to anger toward others;
having given rise to anger, one utters evil words with the mouth, and others consequently give one a name of an evil nature."
Because they do not cultivate right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration, they give rise to anger toward others;
because they give rise to malice, they utter evil words with their mouths, and others consequently give them names of an evil nature.
He asked again:
"World-Honored One!
By cultivating what dharma does one not become angry with others? Because of this absence of anger, one speaks virtuous words, and others bestow upon one the name of 'noble and good'?"
The Buddha told the village headman:
"Because one cultivates right view, one does not feel anger toward others;
because one is free from anger, one speaks wholesome words, and others bestow upon one the name of 'virtuous and good'."
By cultivating right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration, one does not feel anger toward others;
because one is free from ill will, one utters kind words, and others bestow upon one the name of "virtuous and noble."
The fierce village headman addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How marvelous!
World-Honored One!”
Well said these words.
Because I did not cultivate right view, I gave rise to anger toward others;
having given rise to anger, I spoke evil words with my mouth, and thus others gave me the name of one who is of an evil nature.
Because I do not cultivate right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration, I give rise to anger toward others;
because I give rise to malice, I utter evil words with my mouth, whereby others give me the name of one who is of an evil nature.
"Therefore, I shall now abandon anger, stubbornness, and harshness.
The Buddha told the village headman:
"This is the essential truth."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the fierce village headman rejoiced and delighted in it;
he paid homage and departed. 911 (911). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the village headman Maṇicūḍa came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Recently, the King assembled his various ministers and discussed with them, saying:
"How can it be considered pure for Śramaṇa Śākyaputrīya bhikṣus to personally accept and store gold, silver, and precious objects?"
"Is it because they are impure?
Among them, some said:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, ought to accept and possess gold, silver, and precious objects."
Furthermore, there were others who said:
"One should not, for one's own sake, accept or store gold, silver, or precious objects.
World-Honored One!
When he says that the śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas should personally accept and store gold, silver, and precious objects, does he say this having heard it from the Buddha,
or does he speak from his own invention?
One who speaks thus— does he accord with the Dharma?
Is it non-conformable?
Is it a true statement?
Or is it a false statement?
"If one speaks in this manner, would one not fall into a state of reproach?
The Buddha told the village headman:
"This is a false statement; it is not a true statement, not a statement of the Dharma, and not a statement in accordance with the Dharma—it falls into a state of reproach."
Why is this so? Because it is impure for a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākya, to accept and store gold, silver, or precious objects for his own sake;
if one accepts and stores gold, silver, or precious objects for oneself, it is not the dharma of a śramaṇa, nor is it the dharma of a son of the Śākya.
The village headman addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How marvelous,
World-Honored One!”

"World-Honored One, for a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākya, to accept and store gold, silver, and precious objects is not the dharma of a śramaṇa, nor is it the dharma of a son of the Śākya; this is the true teaching!"
One who speaks thus increases what is excellent and sublime; I also speak thus:
"A śramaṇa, a son of the Śākya, should not, for his own sake, accept or store gold, silver, or precious objects."
The Buddha told the village headman:
"If the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, were pure in their acceptance and possession of gold, silver, and precious treasures for themselves, then the merits of the five desires would all be pure!"
Having heard what the Buddha had said, Maṇicūḍa, the village headman, rejoiced, paid homage, and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that Maṇicūḍa, the village headman, had left, addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Summon all those bhikṣus who reside in dependence upon the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove and assemble them in the dining hall."

Then, the Venerable Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, issued a proclamation throughout, summoning all the bhikṣus residing at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove to assemble in the dining hall.
When the bhikṣus had assembled, they went to inform the World-Honored One:
"The bhikṣus have gathered in the dining hall; may the World-Honored One know the time!
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded to the dining hall, sat before the great assembly, and having sat down, addressed the bhikṣus:
"Today, the village headman Maṇibhūta-keśa came to visit me and spoke as follows:
'A few days ago, the King assembled his various ministers and held this discussion:
"Do the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, act with purity when they accept and possess gold, silver, and precious objects for themselves?"'"
Among them, some said it was pure and some said it was impure.
Now I ask the World-Honored One: as for those who say it is pure, did they hear this from the Buddha?
“Is this spoken out of your own delusion?
… [as explained at length above] … “When the village headman Maṇicūḍa heard what I had said, he rejoiced and approved, paid homage, and departed.”
“Monks! The king and his ministers gathered together for discussion, and that village headman Maṇicūḍa, before the great assembly, uttered a lion’s roar, saying:
‘A śramaṇa who is a son of the Śākyas ought not to accept or store gold, silver, or precious objects for himself.’”

"O bhikṣus! From this day forward, if you require wood, seek wood; if you require grass, seek grass; if you require a cart, seek a cart; if you require laborers, seek laborers. Be careful never to accept gold, silver, or various precious objects for your own sake!"
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 912 (912) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the side of the Kakutthā Pond in the kingdom of Campā.
At that time, the village head Wángdǐng came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Then, the World-Honored One addressed the village head Wángdǐng:
“At present, sentient beings rely upon two extremes.”
What are these two?
First, attachment to the five desires of lowly, rustic, ordinary, and common people.
Second, the practice of self-mortification, which is improper and not conducive to righteous benefit.
"Head of the village!
There are three kinds of enjoyment of sensual pleasures that are base, vulgar, and characteristic of ordinary worldlings;
there are three kinds of self-mortifying practices that are improper and not conducive to the goal."
“Headman! What are the three kinds of base, vulgar, and ordinary pleasures that common worldlings enjoy? There are those who indulge in sensual pleasures by taking what is unlawful and improper;

they do not provide for their own comfort, nor do they support their parents, brothers, wives, children, servants, dependents, friends, or associates. Furthermore, they do not, from time to time, make offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, nor do they aspire for the superior state, the fruit of happiness, or rebirth in heaven in a future life. This is called the first way of indulging in sensual pleasures in the world.”
"Furthermore, village headman!

One who indulges in sensual pleasures acquires wealth through both righteous and unrighteous means to provide for himself, to support his parents, and to sufficiently provide for his brothers, wife, children, slaves, servants, retinue, friends, and acquaintances; yet he does not, from time to time, make offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, nor does he aspire for the superior state, the fruit of peace and happiness, or rebirth in heaven in the future. This is called the second type of one who indulges in sensual pleasures."

"Furthermore, village headman, there is one who enjoys sensual pleasures who seeks wealth through the Dharma and does not take it by improper means; he provides for himself with pleasure, supports his parents, and sufficiently provides for his brothers, wife, children, servants, dependents, and friends; he makes timely offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, aspiring for the fruit of excellence, peace, and happiness, and rebirth in heaven in the future. This is called the third type of one who enjoys sensual pleasures."

“Headman! I do not categorically state that those who enjoy sensual pleasures are equal. I say that some who enjoy sensual pleasures are base, I say that some who enjoy sensual pleasures are mediocre, and I say that some who enjoy sensual pleasures are superior.”
"What is meant by those who experience desire in a base manner?

It refers to taking what is not rightfully one's due through unlawful means, and furthermore, not aspiring for the superior state of blissful retribution or rebirth in heaven in the future; this, I call experiencing desire in a base manner."
"What is the enjoyment of desires by the middling person?

It refers to one who enjoys desires and seeks wealth through both lawful and unlawful means, even to the extent of not seeking rebirth in heaven in a future life; this is what I call the second type of middling person enjoying desires."
“What is the third type of superior person who experiences sensual pleasures whom I describe?
It is one who seeks wealth through the Dharma, even unto rebirth in heaven in the future; this is what I call the third superior person who experiences sensual pleasures.”
“What are the three kinds of self-mortifying practices that are painful, contrary to the Dharma, improper, and not conducive to the goal?

There is one who lives a life of self-mortification and emaciation; from the outset he violates and defiles the precepts, yet he practices various asceticisms, dwelling with diligent application. He is unable, in this very life, to attain the state free from burning fever, the superhuman states, the sublime knowledge and vision, and the blissful abiding.”
"Headman! This is called the first way of living in emaciation through self-mortification. Furthermore, there is another way of living in emaciation through self-mortification:

one does not violate or defile the precepts, yet practices various forms of asceticism; however, by means of this, one does not attain in this very life a state of freedom from fever, superhuman states, or the excellent, sublime knowledge and vision that lead to dwelling in happiness. This is called the second way of living in emaciation through self-mortification."

"Furthermore, there is the third way of living in emaciation through self-mortifying practices: one does not initially transgress or defile the precepts, yet by practicing various methods of asceticism, one is still unable to dwell in the bliss of superior knowledge and vision, free from the burning fever in this very life, nor attain the states that transcend the human condition. This is called the third way of living in emaciation through self-mortifying practices."

“Headman! I do not say that all those who practice self-mortification through emaciating asceticism are equal. I say that among those who practice self-mortification, some are base persons, some are mediocre persons, and some are superior persons.”
“What is the person of inferior means who practices self-mortification?

If one’s practice of self-mortification begins with the violation and defilement of the precepts, and does not even lead to the attainment of superior and sublime knowledge, vision, and dwelling in peace, this is what I call a person of inferior means who practices self-mortification.”
"What is the person of intermediate capacity regarding the practice of self-mortification?

If, in that practice of self-mortification, one does not initially transgress or defile the precepts, yet fails to attain the superior and sublime knowledge, vision, and dwelling in peace, this is what I call the person of intermediate capacity regarding the practice of self-mortification."
"What is the person who excels in the practice of self-mortification?

If one lives by the emaciated practice of self-mortification, yet from the beginning does not transgress or defile the precepts, and even fails to attain superior and sublime knowledge, vision, and dwelling in peace—this is what I call a person who excels in the practice of self-mortification."
“Headman, these are called the three kinds of self-mortification; they are painful, unrighteous, improper, and not conducive to one’s welfare.
“Headman, [these are the first].”

There is the Way and there are its traces; one does not turn toward the three types of expedient means for indulging in sensual desires—those that are base, rustic, and characteristic of ordinary worldlings—nor does one turn toward the three types of expedient means for self-mortification, which are painful, contrary to the Dharma, improper, and not conducive to benefit.
"Village chief!
What is the path and what is the track that does not lead toward the three kinds of pursuit of sensual pleasure or the three kinds of self-mortifying practices?
Village chief!"

Because they are obstructed by sensual desire, they may wish to harm themselves, harm others, or harm both; consequently, they receive such retributive results in this life and future lives, experiencing mental and physical sorrow and suffering.

Obstructed by hatred and delusion, one may wish to harm oneself, harm others, or harm both; thus, in this life and in future lives, one incurs the retribution of such offenses and experiences mental anguish and suffering.
If one is free from the obstruction of greed, one does not desire to harm oneself, harm others, or harm both oneself and others through expedient means;

nor does one undergo the retribution for such offenses in the present life or in future lives. That mind and its mental factors constantly experience joy and bliss. Likewise, being free from the obstructions of hatred and delusion, one does not desire to harm oneself, harm others, or harm both oneself and others; nor does one undergo the retribution for such offenses in the present life or in future lives.

That mind and its mental factors constantly experience peace and happiness. In this present life, one remains far removed from the burning fires of affliction; without waiting for a specific time, one draws near to Nirvana, realizing it through direct personal awakening within this very body.

"Headman! Thus, in this very life, one is eternally free from burning, independent of time, and draws near to Nirvana; that which is personally realized by means of this very body is the Eightfold Noble Path—right view through to right concentration."
When the Blessed One had spoken this Dharma, the village headman Rājagṛha was distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.

At that time, the village headman Rājagṛha saw the Dharma, attained the Dharma, knew the Dharma, and entered deeply into the Dharma; having crossed beyond doubt and no longer depending on others, he attained fearlessness regarding the True Dharma and Discipline.
He immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, I have now crossed over."
"I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus; from this day forth, for as long as life shall last, I am an upāsaka.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, he rejoiced and approved with gladness, prostrated himself, and departed.
913 (Nin-ichi-san). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the Mallas and arrived at the place of Uruvilvā, in the Śuka-jambūvana forest.

At that time, Ghaṭa, the headman of the village, heard that the ascetic Gautama was wandering among the Mallas and had arrived at the village of Uruvelā at the Sāla Grove of the Monkeys, where he was teaching the arising of suffering and the cessation of suffering in this very life.
"I shall go to that ascetic Gautama; for if I approach the ascetic Gautama, he will surely explain to me the arising of suffering and the cessation of suffering in this very life."
He immediately went to that village of Uruvelā, approached the World-Honored One, prostrated himself at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"I have heard, World-Honored One, that you constantly teach people regarding the arising of suffering and the cessation of suffering in this very life.
Excellent,
World-Honored One!"
“Explain to me the arising of suffering and the cessation of suffering pertaining to the present life.
The Buddha told the village headman:

“If I were to speak of the arising of suffering and the cessation of suffering pertaining to the past, I would know whether you would believe it or not, whether you would desire it or not, whether you would attend to it or not, and whether you would find pleasure in it or not; yet, are you currently suffering?”

If I were to speak of the future arising of suffering and the cessation of suffering, I would know whether you would believe it or not, whether you would desire it or not, whether you would attend to it or not, and whether you would find it pleasant or not; would you be suffering now?
In this regard, I shall now speak of the arising and the subsiding of suffering in the present life, village headman!

Whatever suffering arises for sentient beings, all of it has desire as its root; it arises from desire, accumulates from desire, originates from desire, has desire as its cause, and has desire as its condition that suffering arises.
The village headman said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One, you have taught the Dharma in extreme brevity without extensive analysis; I do not understand it. Excellent! [Please explain further.]”
“World-Honored One!
We only pray that you will explain this extensively so that we may understand.
The Buddha told the village headman:
"I now ask you; answer as you see fit, village headman!
What do you think?
If any sentient beings dwelling here in the village of Uruvelā were to be bound, beaten, fined, or killed, would sorrow, lamentation, distress, and pain arise in your mind?"
The village headman said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One,
it is not one-sided either.”

If there are sentient beings dwelling here in the village of Uruvelā who have desire for me, craving for me, affection for me, or thoughts of me, and with whom I am intimately acquainted—if they should encounter bondage, beating, reprimand, or execution, I would then give rise to sorrow, lamentation, vexation, and suffering.

If those sentient beings have no desire, greed, craving, attachment, or habitual intimacy with me, and they encounter binding, beating, rebuking, or killing, why should I pointlessly give rise to anxiety, sorrow, affliction, and suffering?
The Buddha told the village headman:

"Therefore, you should know that the various kinds of suffering that arise for sentient beings all have desire as their root; it is through the arising of desire, the habitual practice of desire, the emergence of desire, the cause of desire, and the condition of desire that various sufferings come into being."
"Headman, what do you think?
If you were separated from your parents and did not see them, would desire, greed, affection, or longing arise in you?"
The village headman said, “No, World-Honored One.
“Village headman! [the Buddha continued.]
"What do you think?
If one sees or hears of that [being] depending upon its parents, would desire, affection, or longing arise?
The village headman replied:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
He asked again:
"Village Headman!
"What do you think?
If those whom one relies upon—namely one's parents—are impermanent and subject to change, would sorrow, lamentation, distress, and suffering arise?
The village headman replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
If my parents were subject to impermanence and change, I would almost have died; how could there be anything other than sorrow, lamentation, vexation, and suffering?"
The Buddha told the village headman:

"Therefore, you should know that whatever suffering arises for sentient beings, all of it has craving as its root; suffering arises with desire as its origin, desire as its accumulation, desire as its emergence, desire as its cause, and desire as its condition."
The village headman said:
"How marvelous!
World-Honored One!"
Well said! Based on this analogy of the parents, I have my own parents living in a different place;
I send messengers every day to inquire after their well-being, and if those messengers do not return at the appointed time, I am filled with sorrow and distress.
How much more so, then, would I feel sorrow and distress when they are gone forever through impermanence?
The Buddha told the village headman:

"For this reason, I say that whatever sorrow and suffering sentient beings possess all have desire as their root; sorrow and suffering arise from desire, accumulate through desire, originate from desire, are caused by desire, and are conditioned by desire."
The Buddha told the village headman:
"If there are four objects of affection that are impermanent and subject to change, then four kinds of sorrow and suffering arise;
if three, two, or one object of affection is impermanent and subject to change, then one kind of sorrow and suffering arises."
"Headman! If there were no affection at all, then there would be no sorrow, suffering, or worldly defilement.
He then spoke this verse:
"If there were no worldly attachment or affection, Then there would be no affliction of grief or the troubles of defilement;
All sorrows and sufferings would be extinguished and exhausted, Just as a lotus flower is unsullied by water."

While the Blessed One was speaking this Dharma, the village headman Keṭaka became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; he saw the Dharma, realized the Dharma, and deeply entered into the Dharma. Having crossed beyond all doubt, he no longer relied on others for his deliverance, and having attained fearlessness regarding the True Dharma and Discipline, he was not led by others.
Rising from his seat, adjusting his robes, and joining his palms, he addressed the Buddha:
"I have crossed over,
World-Honored One!"
I have transcended.
From this day forth, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus; for as long as life lasts, I am an upāsaka. Pray, remember me!
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the village headman Keṭaka, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and delighted in it;
he paid homage and departed. 914 (914) Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of Magadha together with twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, one thousand upāsakas, and five hundred persons who subsisted on leftover food. Traveling from city to city and from village to village, he wandered through the human realm until he reached the village of Nāla, arriving at the Āmra Grove of Fine Garments.
At that time, there was a village head named Kṣurapāṇi, a disciple of the Nirgranthas, who went to where the Nirgrantha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the Nirgrantha said to the village head Kṣemaka:
"Are you able to engage in a 'thorn-like' debate with the śramaṇa Gautama, such that the śramaṇa Gautama is neither able to speak nor unable to speak?"
The village headman said:
"Venerable sir!
What kind of proposition must I establish as a 'thorn' so that the śramaṇa Gautama can neither speak nor remain silent?"
The Nirgrantha said to the village headman:
"Go to where the śramaṇa Gautama is and ask him this:
'Gautama, do you always wish for the welfare and prosperity of all households to be fully increased; do you make such a vow and speak thus?'"
If he answers you by saying "no," you should ask him:
"What difference is there between the śramaṇa Gautama and an ordinary fool?
If he says that he has aspirations and teachings, you should further ask:

"If the śramaṇa Gautama holds such a wish and speaks thus, how is it that he now wanders among people during a time of famine, leading a great multitude of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, one thousand upāsakas, and five hundred who beg for leftover food? From city to city and from village to village, he causes waste and depletion for the world, like a great rain of hail; this is a diminution, not an increase."
"What the Gautama says is utterly inconsistent; it is neither analogous nor similar, and its preceding and succeeding parts contradict one another.
It is thus, village headman!
"This is called the 'thorn-bush' argument; it prevents that śramaṇa Gautama from speaking, yet prevents him from remaining silent.

At that time, the village head Kṣemaka, having received the exhortation and instruction of the Nirgranthas, went to where the Buddha was staying. Having paid his respects and exchanged greetings, he withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha:
"Gautama, do you always wish for the welfare and merit of all households to increase?"
The Buddha told the village headman:
"The Tathāgata, throughout the long night, has desired to cause the merit and benefit of all households to increase, and he has always spoken thus.
The village headman said:

“If this is so, why does Gautama go on alms-round among people during a time of famine, leading a great multitude of followers... [and so forth] ...is it not inconsistent and contradictory from beginning to end?”
The Buddha told the village headman:
"I recall that for ninety-one eons since, I have not seen a single person who, having given to even one bhikṣu, has experienced exhaustion or diminution [of their merit]."

"Headman! Observe that today there are people whose households are great in wealth, possessing much money and property, many kinsmen, and many servants; you should know that these householders were fond of giving and truly tranquil for a long night, and thus they have attained such blessings and merit."
"Headman! There are eight causes and conditions that cause a person's welfare and benefit to diminish rather than increase.
What are these eight?"

There are eight such circumstances through which wealth is difficult to accumulate: being oppressed by a king, being plundered by bandits, being consumed by fire, being swept away by water, one’s own hoard diminishing, failing to repay debts, being ruined by enemies or those one hates, and being squandered by wicked sons.
"Village headman!
I declare impermanence to be the ninth statement.
Thus it is, village headman!"

You have abandoned the nine causes and nine conditions, yet you still claim that the śramaṇa Gautama destroys the families of others; since you do not abandon such evil speech and evil views, like an iron spear cast into water, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, you will be reborn in hell.
At that time, the village headman Kṣemaka felt such terror that the hair on his body stood on end, and he said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
I now repent my transgression!"
"Like one who is foolish and deluded, unskilled and lacking discernment, you have falsely deceived and spoken lies and falsehoods before Gautama.
Having heard what the Buddha said, he rejoiced and expressed his approval, rose from his seat, and departed.
915 (Nin-ichi-go). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the village of Nāla, in the Ambāṭaka Grove of Fine Garments.

At that time, there was a village head named Kṣurapāṇi who had formerly been a disciple of the Nirgranthas. He went to where the Nirgranthas were, prostrated at their feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the Nirgrantha said to the village headman:
"Are you able to engage in a 'thorn-like' debate with the śramaṇa Gautama, such that the śramaṇa Gautama is neither able to speak nor unable to speak?"
The village headman said to the Nirgrantha:
"Venerable sir!
What is this 'thorny discourse' that prevents the śramaṇa Gautama from speaking and yet does not allow him not to speak?"
The Nirgrantha said to the village headman:
"Go to where the śramaṇa Gautama is and speak these words:
'Gautama, do you not constantly desire to comfort all sentient beings and praise the comforting of all sentient beings?'"
If he says "no," one should say to him:
"What difference is there between Gautama and an ordinary fool?
If he says that he always desires to comfort all sentient beings and praises the comforting of all sentient beings, one should further ask:
"If one wishes to comfort all sentient beings, for what reason does one preach the Dharma to some individuals while not preaching it to others?"
"One who asks such a question is engaging in a 'thorn-like' debate (kaṇṭaka-vāda), which prevents that śramaṇa Gautama from speaking and yet compels him not to remain silent.

At that time, having received the encouragement of the Nirgranthas, the village headman went to where the Buddha was. After paying his respects and exchanging greetings, he withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Gautama, do you not desire to constantly comfort all sentient beings, and do you not praise the comforting of all sentient beings?"
The Buddha told the village headman:
"The Tathāgata has, throughout the long night, compassionately pitied and comforted all sentient beings, and he also constantly praises and speaks of comforting all sentient beings."
The village headman addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If that is so, for what reason does the Tathāgata teach the Dharma to some people,
yet does not teach the Dharma to others?"
The Buddha said to the village headman:
“I shall now question you; answer me as you see fit.
Village headman!”
It is like there being three kinds of fields: one field is rich, fertile, and well-watered; the second field is middling; and the third field is poor and thin. What do you think?
"Village headman!
In which field did that landowner first plow and sow?
The village headman replied:
“Gautama! One first plows and sows in the most fertile and well-watered soil.
“Village Headman! [The Buddha replied.]
"Furthermore, in what field does one next plow and sow seeds?
The village headman said, "Gautama!"
"One should plow and sow next in the middle field.
The Buddha asked the village headman:
"Furthermore, in what kind of field should one plow and sow next?"
The village headman said,
“One should first plow and sow in the very lowest and most barren field.
The Buddha told the village headman:
"Why is this so? The village headman replied,
"I do not wish to destroy the field, but merely to preserve the seeds."
The Buddha told the village headman:
"I am also like this. Just as that field is rich, fertile, and well-watered, so too are my bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs."

I constantly expound the True Dharma for them—good in the beginning, middle, and end; excellent in meaning and phrasing; pure, unified, complete, and immaculate—a holy life that is revealed and made manifest.
Having heard the Dharma, he relies upon me as his shelter, his island, his protection, his refuge, and his destination; he dwells constantly observing me with pure eyes, thinking thus:
"The Dharma taught by the Buddha, I have received and upheld it all, so that for a long night it may benefit me with its meaning, and I may dwell in peace and happiness."
"Headman! Those who are like the medium-quality fields among them are likewise my disciples, the male and female lay followers (*upāsaka* and *upāsikā*).

For their sake, I also expound the True Dharma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing; pure, single-minded, complete, and stainless—a holy life (*brahmacarya*) that is revealed and made manifest."
Having heard the Dharma, he relies upon me as his shelter, his island, his protection, his refuge, and his destination; with pure eyes, he constantly observes my dwelling and reflects thus:

"The World-Honored One has taught the Dharma, which I have received and upheld in its entirety, so that for a long night it may benefit me with its meaning and allow me to dwell in peace and happiness."
"Village Headman!

Just as that lowest field of a farmer, so for the various heterodox followers of other teachings, the Nirgranthas, I also preach the Dharma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing; purely unified, complete, pure, and holy. I reveal and manifest it to them, preaching it both to those who have heard little of the Dharma and to those who have heard much."

Nevertheless, if any among that assembly should obtain even a single phrase of my well-expounded Dharma and understand its meaning, they too will, for a long night, be enriched by its meaning, dwelling in peace, security, and happiness.
Then, the village headman addressed the Buddha:
“How extraordinary!
World-Honored One!”
"You have well explained these three similes for fields.
The Buddha said to the village headman:
"Listen, and I shall speak further similes for you."
For example, suppose a man has three water vessels: one is neither pierced nor broken, and it does not leak;
the second vessel is neither pierced nor broken, yet it leaks.
The third vessel is one that is pierced, broken, and leaking.
Why is this so? Village Headman!
"Among those three types of vessels, in which one would that man always keep pure water?
The village headman said, "Gautama!"
"One should first use a vessel that is not pierced, not broken, and not leaking to hold the water.
The Buddha said to the village headman:
"Next, what kind of vessel should be used to hold the water?"
The village headman said,
“Gautama! One should take that vessel which is neither pierced nor broken, yet leaks, and next fill it with water.”
The Buddha said to the village headman:
"Once that vessel is full, what other vessel will you use for the subsequent pouring of water?
The village headman replied:
"It is like using a vessel that is pierced, broken, and leaking to hold water for the very last time. Why is this?
Because it serves a minor purpose for only a brief moment."
The Buddha told the village headman:
"Just as that man has a vessel that is neither pierced nor broken and does not leak, so too are my disciples—the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs."
I constantly expound the True Dharma for them, even throughout the long night, benefiting them with its meaning so that they may dwell in peace, security, and happiness.
Just as the second vessel is neither pierced nor broken, yet leaks moisture, so too it is with my disciples, the upāsakas and upāsikās.

I constantly expound the True Dharma for them, even providing them with benefit through its meaning for a long night, so that they may dwell in peace and happiness; yet those who follow external paths and other heterodox teachings, such as the various Nirgranthas, are just like the third vessel—pierced, broken, and leaking.

I, too, shall expound the True Dharma for them—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing; pure, unified, and complete; a holy life that is stainless, revealing and manifesting it clearly.
I teach extensively, and I also teach briefly.
If they understand the meaning of even a single verse of Dharma spoken by me, they too shall dwell in peace and happiness for a long night.

At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the village headman Kṣemaka was seized with great terror; his hair stood on end, and he went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and repent, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"Like one who is foolish and deluded, unskilled and undiscerning, you have not perceived the truth in the presence of the Blessed One, but have spoken falsely and deceptively!
Having heard what the Buddha said, he rejoiced and approved, prostrated at his feet, and departed.
916. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the village of Nāla, in the Ambaṭṭha Mango Grove.
At that time, there was a village headman named Kāḷīśī, a disciple of the Nirgranthas, who came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the village headman:
"What is it you wish to discuss?
What has Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said?"
The village headman said:
"That Nirgrantha Jñātiputra says:
'All who kill living beings fall into hell; because they have practiced it extensively, they will be led there.'"
"In this way, those who commit theft, sexual misconduct, and false speech all fall into hell; because they have practiced these frequently, they are led there.
The Buddha said to the village headman:

"If it were as the Nirgrantha Jñātiputra says—that those who kill living beings fall into hell and are reborn there because they have practiced such acts frequently—then no sentient being would ever fall into hell."
"Headman, what do you think?
What kind of sentient beings have the intention to kill at all times?"

"Furthermore, at what time is there a mind that does not kill, and so on, up to: at what time is there a mind that engages in false speech, and at what time is there a mind that does not engage in false speech?
The village headman addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"

A person may, during the day and night, for a short time have the intention to kill living beings, or even for a short time have the intention to speak falsehoods, yet for a long time lack the intention to kill living beings, up to and including speaking falsehoods.
The Buddha said to the village headman:
"If this were so, would it not be the case that no one at all falls into hell?
As the Nirgranthas say:"
"If there are those who kill living beings, they all fall into the hells; those who habitually practice this extensively will be reborn there. This applies likewise even to false speech."
"Village Headman!
That Great Teacher appeared in the world; having awakened through conceptualization and deliberation, he entered the stage of conceptualization and dwelt therein.

On the level of an ordinary person, he himself distinguished what was to be said, deliberated according to his own will, and for the sake of his disciples, he preached the Dharma in this way: 'All who kill living beings fall into the hells; those who habitually practice it extensively will be reborn there,' and so it is likewise even for false speech."
If those disciples believe his teaching, they will say:
"Our Great Teacher knows what is to be known and sees what is to be seen; he is able to speak thus to his disciples:
'If one kills living beings, all such persons fall into the hells; because they have practiced this habit extensively, they will be reborn there.'"
"I originally had the intention to kill living beings, steal, engage in sexual misconduct, and speak falsehoods; I shall fall into hell.

Having formed such a view, as long as he does not abandon this view, does not feel revulsion toward those karmic actions, and does not awaken to remorse for them, he will not cease killing living beings up to speaking falsehoods in future lives. His liberation through mind (cetovimukti) will not be fulfilled, nor will his liberation through wisdom (prajñāvimukti) be fulfilled.
Because they are dissatisfied with liberation of mind and dissatisfied with liberation by wisdom, they fall into the wrong view of slandering the noble ones;
due to the conditions of this wrong view, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in the miserable destinies, in the hells.
"In this way, village headman!
There is a cause and a condition for the afflictions of sentient beings; there is a cause and a condition for the karmic afflictions of sentient beings.
Village headman!"

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān has appeared in the world; he constantly rebukes sentient beings for taking life and praises abstaining from killing;
he rebukes stealing, sexual misconduct, and false speech, and praises abstaining from stealing, sexual misconduct, and false speech.
He constantly uses this Dharma to transform the śrāvakas, causing them to reflect upon, delight in, believe in, and revere it, saying:

"My Great Teacher knows what is to be known and sees what is to be seen. He rebukes the taking of life and praises non-killing, and so on, up to rebuking false speech and praising non-false speech. From the past until now, out of ignorance and lack of wisdom, I have intentionally taken life; for this reason, I now repent and reproach myself."

"Although one cannot cause that karma not to be committed, because of this remorse and self-reproach, in future lives one will attain freedom from killing, and even freedom from stealing, sexual misconduct, and false speech. One will also attain fulfillment of liberation through right intention and fulfillment of liberation through wisdom. Once liberation through intention and liberation through wisdom are fulfilled, one will not slander the noble ones and will achieve right view.
By reason of right view, one will be reborn in the happy realms of the heavens."
"In this way, village headman,
there is a cause and a condition for the purification of the karma and afflictions of sentient beings.
Village headman!"
That learned noble disciple trains himself thus:
"At all times, day and night, I shall observe whether there arises in me a small amount of intention to kill living beings or a large amount of intention not to kill."
If one kills a living being intentionally, one should feel self-reproach; this is not unlike [the case of intentional action].
If one kills a living being unintentionally, without resentment or hatred, and the mind gives rise to sympathetic joy;
having given rise to sympathetic joy, gladness arises.
Having rejoiced, the mind becomes tranquil;
with the mind tranquil, one experiences happiness;
experiencing happiness, the mind becomes concentrated.

Once his mind is thus concentrated, the noble disciple dwells having attained right absorption, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), free from enmity and rivalry, without ill will—vast, immeasurable, and filling one direction;

likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, as well as the four intermediate points, above and below, throughout the entire world. With a mind imbued with loving-kindness, free from enmity and rivalry, without ill will—vast, immeasurable, and well-cultivated—he dwells having attained right absorption, fully pervading all quarters.
At that time, the Blessed One took a small amount of soil with his fingernail and said to the village headman Kṣemaka:
"What do you think,
village headman?"
"Which is more: the soil on my fingernails, or the great earth?
The village headman replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
The soil on my fingernails is but a tiny amount; the soil of the great earth is immeasurable and incalculable.
The Buddha told the village headman:
"Just as the soil upon a fingernail is very little, while the soil of the great earth is immeasurable in number, so too,

when one cultivates and repeatedly practices a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, all finite karmic actions— like the soil on a fingernail— cannot carry one away, nor can they cause one to remain [in saṃsāra]."
"In this way, taking stealing as the object for the mind of compassion, sexual misconduct for the mind of sympathetic joy, and false speech for the mind of equanimity—these cannot be compared.

When these words were spoken, the village headman Kṣemaka became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye. Having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, awakened to the Dharma, known the Dharma, and deeply penetrated the Dharma, he was freed from all doubt; no longer dependent on others and not following others, he attained fearlessness regarding the True Dharma and Discipline.
Rising from his seat, he adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
“I have crossed over, World-Honored One!”
"I have transcended them, World-Honored One!
I now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus; for as long as my life lasts, I am an upāsaka."
World-Honored One!

It is like a man who, desiring to seek the light of a lamp, takes a horse's tail and uses it as a wick, wishing to blow it into a flame; he will never obtain light, but only exhaust himself in vain, for the lamp will ultimately not burn.

I am likewise; desiring to seek clear wisdom, I associated with, conjoined with, and served the foolish Nirgranthas, only to exhaust myself in vain without attaining clear wisdom. Therefore, I now once again take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

From this day forward, you shall have little faith, little reverence, little affection, and little mindfulness toward those Nigaṇṭhas who are foolish, unwholesome, and lacking in discernment; you should now distance yourselves from them.
Therefore, for a third time, I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; until the end of my life, I shall be a lay follower (*upāsaka*), purifying my own mind.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the village head Kṣemaka was filled with joy and delight;
he paid homage and departed. 917 (917) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the world, there are three kinds of tamed horses.
What are these three kinds?
There are horses that are fully endowed with swiftness but not fully endowed with color, nor fully endowed with physical form.
There are horses that are fully endowed with color and fully endowed with swiftness, but not fully endowed with physical form.
There is a horse that is fully endowed with speed, fully endowed with color, and fully endowed with physical form.
In this way, there are three marks of a well-trained man.
What are these three?
There is a person who possesses agility but lacks beauty and lacks physical form.
There is a person who possesses agility and possesses beauty but lacks physical form.
There is a man who is swift and agile, endowed with beauty, and endowed with a well-proportioned physique. "Monks!

What is the case of the man who is undisciplined, not swift and agile, not endowed with beauty, and not endowed with a well-proportioned physique? There is a man who knows this suffering as it really is, knows the origin of this suffering, knows the cessation of this suffering, and knows the path leading to the cessation of this suffering as it really is. For one who contemplates in this way, the three fetters—personality view, attachment to precepts and rituals, and doubt—are abandoned."

By abandoning these three fetters, one attains the stage of Srotāpanna; being no longer subject to rebirth in the evil destinies, one is destined for perfect enlightenment, will be reborn among gods and humans for seven more existences, and will reach the ultimate end of suffering—this is called being endowed with swiftness.
What is the non-perfection of form?

If someone asks about the Abhidharma or the Vinaya, and one is unable to provide a complete explanation with full words and phrases, following them in proper sequence, this is called the non-perfection of form.
What is meant by "incompleteness of physical form"?

It refers to one who lacks great virtue and renown such that he cannot attract robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites, and various necessities; this is called being endowed with swiftness as a man, yet incomplete in complexion and incomplete in physical form.
“What is meant by being endowed with swiftness, endowed with beauty of form, yet not endowed with physical perfection?

It refers to a person who knows this suffering as it truly is, knows the origin of this suffering, knows the cessation of this suffering, and knows the path leading to the cessation of this suffering as it truly is, up until the ultimate end of suffering—this is being endowed with swiftness.
What is meant by being endowed with physical form?
If, when questioned regarding the Abhidharma or the Vinaya, one is even able to provide an explanation, this is called being endowed with physical form.
What is meant by not being endowed with physical form?

Without great virtue and renown, one cannot attract robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites; this is called being endowed with swiftness as a man, endowed with beauty of complexion, yet lacking in physical form.
“What is meant by a person being endowed with swiftness, endowed with beauty, and endowed with physical form?

It means that a person knows this suffering as it really is, knows the origin of this suffering, the cessation of this suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of this suffering as they really are, until reaching the ultimate end of suffering; this is called being endowed with swiftness.”
What is the perfection of appearance? If, when questioned regarding the Abhidharma or the Vinaya, one is even able to explain them, this is called the perfection of appearance.

What is the perfection of physical form? Possessing great virtue and renown, as well as bedding, seats, and medicinal requisites—this is called the perfection of physical form. These are called the perfections of a man’s agility, appearance, and physical form.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 918 (918) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the world there are three kinds of excellent horses. What are the three?
There are horses that are fully endowed with swiftness, but not fully endowed with color, nor fully endowed with physical form.

There are horses that are fully endowed with swiftness and fully endowed with color, but not fully endowed with physical form. There are horses that are fully endowed with swiftness, fully endowed with color, and fully endowed with physical form.
In this True Dharma and Discipline, there are three kinds of sons of good family.
What are the three?

There is the son of good family who is endowed with quickness, but not endowed with beauty of complexion, nor endowed with physical form; there is the son of good family who is endowed with quickness and endowed with beauty of complexion, but not endowed with physical form; and there is the son of good family who is endowed with quickness, endowed with beauty of complexion, and endowed with physical form.
“What is meant by a son of good family who is endowed with swiftness, but not endowed with physical beauty, nor endowed with bodily form?

It means that a son of good family knows the noble truth of suffering as it really is; he knows the noble truth of the origin of suffering as it really is; he knows the noble truth of the cessation of suffering as it really is; and he knows the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is.”
Having thus known and thus seen, one severs the five lower fetters—namely, the view of a self-identity, attachment to precepts and rituals, doubt, sensual desire, and ill will.

Having severed these five lower fetters, one attains the state of an Anāgāmin who attains Parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, never again to return to this world; this is called a son of good family who is endowed with swiftness.
What is meant by "deficiency in form"?

If, when questioned regarding the Abhidharma or the Vinaya, one is unable to explain the words and their meanings, following them in proper sequence, and providing a definitive exposition, this is called deficiency in form.
What is meant by "incompleteness of physical form"?

It refers to one who is not a man of great renown and virtue, yet is able to attract material gain and offerings—namely, clothing, bedding, food and drink, and medicinal decoctions for the sick. This is called a son of good family who is complete in swiftness, but not complete in color, nor complete in physical form.
“What is meant by being endowed with swiftness, endowed with form, yet not endowed with a physical body?

It refers to a son of good family who knows this Noble Truth of Suffering as it truly is, and so on, until attaining parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyī) or becoming a non-returner (anāgāmin) who is no longer reborn in this world; this is called being endowed with swiftness.”
What is the perfection of form?

If one is questioned regarding the Abhidharma or the Vinaya, and is able to provide an explanation by means of sequential phrases and meanings, in accordance with and determinedly, this is called the perfection of form.
What is meant by not being endowed with physical form?

It refers to one who is not renowned as a person of great virtue and thus cannot attract material gains and offerings—such as clothing, bedding, food, drink, and medicinal decoctions for the sick. This is called a son of good family who is endowed with agility, endowed with beauty, but not endowed with physical form.
“What is meant by a son of good family being endowed with swiftness, endowed with beauty, and endowed with physical form?

It means that a son of good family knows this Noble Truth of Suffering as it truly is, and so on, until he attains the state of an Anāgāmin and attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state of existence, never again to return to this world; this is called being endowed with swiftness.”
What is the perfection of form? If someone asks about the Abhidharma or the Vinaya, and one provides an explanation for them, this is called the perfection of form.
What is the perfection of physical form?

It refers to the renown and great virtue that can attract wealth and profit, even down to medicinal decoctions and various requisites; this is called the perfection of physical form. This is what is meant by a son of good family being endowed with swiftness, endowed with beauty, and endowed with physical form.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*Saṃyukta Āgama*, Scroll 32; *Saṃyukta Āgama*, Scroll 33.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
33.919 (919). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the world there are three kinds of excellent horses. What are the three?
That is to say: there is a horse that is fully endowed with swiftness, but not fully endowed with color, nor fully endowed with physical form;
and there is a horse that is fully endowed with swiftness and fully endowed with color, but not fully endowed with physical form.
Just as there is a horse that is fully endowed with swiftness, fully endowed with color, and fully endowed with physical form,
so too, within this Dharma and Vinaya, there are three kinds of sons of good family.
What are these three?

There is a son of good family who is endowed with agility, but not endowed with beauty of complexion, nor endowed with physical form; there is a son of good family who is endowed with agility and endowed with beauty of complexion, but not endowed with physical form; and there is a son of good family who is endowed with agility, endowed with beauty of complexion, and endowed with physical form.
"What is meant by a son of good family being endowed with swiftness, but not endowed with physical beauty, nor endowed with bodily form?
