It means that a son of good family knows this noble truth of suffering as it really is; he knows this noble truth of the origin of suffering as it really is; he knows this noble truth of the cessation of suffering as it really is; and he knows this noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is."

Having known thus and seen thus, the mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the outflow of existence, and the mind is liberated from the outflow of ignorance:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence."
This is called being endowed with quickness.
What is meant by not being endowed with physical form?
If, when asked about the Abhidharma or the Vinaya, one is unable to provide a definitive explanation, this is called not being endowed with physical form.
What is meant by "not being complete in physical form"?

It refers to one who lacks renown and great virtue, and even fails to obtain medicinal decoctions and various requisites; this is called being incomplete in physical form. This is what is meant by a son of good family being complete in swiftness, but not complete in color, and not complete in physical form.
"What is meant by a son of good family who is endowed with swiftness, endowed with beauty, yet not endowed with physical form?
It means that a son of good family knows this Noble Truth of Suffering as it truly is, up to and including the state of no further existence; this is called being endowed with swiftness."
What is the perfection of form?
It refers to being able to provide definitive explanations when questioned regarding the Abhidharma or the Vinaya; this is called the perfection of form.
What is the lack of physical perfection?

It refers to one who lacks renown and great virtue, and so forth, such that they cannot even obtain medicinal decoctions or various requisites; this is called a son of good family who possesses swiftness and physical beauty, yet lacks physical perfection.
"What is meant by a son of good family being endowed with swiftness, endowed with beauty, and endowed with physical form?
It means that a son of good family knows this Noble Truth of Suffering as it truly is, up to and including the state of not undergoing further existence; this is called being endowed with swiftness."
What is the perfection of form?
It means that if a son of good family, when questioned regarding the Abhidharma or the Vinaya, is even able to provide a definitive explanation, this is called the perfection of form.
What is the perfection of physical form?

It refers to a son of good family who possesses great renown and virtue, and even has the power to procure medicinal decoctions and various requisites; this is called the perfection of physical form. This is what is meant by a son of good family being endowed with swiftness, endowed with beauty of color, and endowed with physical form.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 920 (920). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the world there are three kinds of excellent horses upon which kings ride.
What are these three?
Just as a noble horse is endowed with excellence of color, excellence of strength, and excellence of speed, so too,
within this True Dharma and Discipline, there are three kinds of sons of good family who are honored, supported, and revered by the world, serving as unsurpassed fields of merit.
What are the three? They are:
a son of good family who is endowed with physical excellence, endowed with strength, and endowed with agility.
What is meant by being "endowed with physical excellence"?

It means that a son of good family abides in the pure restraint of the Prātimokṣa, is complete in his deportment and conduct, perceives even subtle transgressions as fearsome, and undertakes and trains in the precepts; this is called being endowed with form.
"What is the perfection of power?
It is the arising of desire, the application of diligence, and the undertaking of skillful means to abandon evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen, and to cause them to increase;
it is the arising of desire, the application of diligence, and the undertaking of skillful means so that evil and unwholesome states not yet arisen do not arise, and to cause them to increase."
To cause unarisen wholesome dharmas to arise, one generates desire, exerts effort, applies skillful means, and embraces them for their growth;

to maintain already arisen wholesome dharmas so they are not forgotten or lost, one generates desire, exerts effort, applies skillful means, and embraces them for their growth—this is called the perfection of power.
"What is the possession of swiftness?
It means knowing this Noble Truth of Suffering as it truly is, and so on, until one attains arhatship and no longer undergoes future existence; this is called the possession of swiftness."
"This is what is called a son of good family who is endowed with physical perfection, endowed with strength, and endowed with swiftness.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
921 (Sūtra 921). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the world there is a fine horse endowed with four capabilities; one should know that such a fine horse is fit for a king to ride.
What are these four? They are:
being excellent and well-behaved, being swift, being capable and enduring, and being well-trained and gentle."
In this way, a son of good family who has accomplished these four virtues is honored and revered by the world; they are served and made offerings to as the unsurpassed field of merit.
What are these four?

"It means, noble son, that one has accomplished the aggregate of precepts of one beyond training, the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training, the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training, and the aggregate of liberation of one beyond training.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
922. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“In the world there are four kinds of excellent horses: there is the excellent horse that, when harnessed to a carriage, gallops swiftly at the mere sight of the whip’s shadow; it is well able to observe the driver’s posture, whether moving slowly or quickly, or turning left or right, following the driver’s mind.”
This, monks, is called the first quality of a world-class thoroughbred horse.
Furthermore, monks:

A fine horse of the world cannot perceive its own reflection and become startled by it; however, when touched by a whip or stick on its coat or tail, it can startle and move swiftly, perceiving the mind of the driver regarding speed, slowness, left, or right. This is called the second kind of fine horse in the world.
Furthermore, bhikṣus!

If a fine horse of the world cannot even look at its own reflection, yet can follow the rider's mind upon being touched by the hair and skin, and can become alert and observant when the whip or staff slightly touches its flesh and skin, it will follow the rider’s intent regarding speed, slowness, and direction.
This, monks, is called the third kind of noble horse.
Furthermore, monks:

A fine horse of the world cannot be turned by the mere shadow of the whip; it only responds when the whip touches its hair and skin, slightly piercing the flesh, or when an iron awl pierces its body, penetrating the skin and wounding the bone. Only then does it startle, drawing the carriage onto the road and following the will of the driver—whether slow or fast, to the left or right. This is called the fourth type of fine horse in the world.
“In this way, there are four kinds of sons of good family in the True Dharma and Discipline.
What are the four? They are as follows:

when a son of good family hears that in another village there is a man or woman suffering from illness and affliction, even unto death, and having heard this, he is able to give rise to a sense of urgency and relies upon right reflection—just as a fine horse is tamed by looking at its own reflection—he is called the first son of good family who is able to discipline himself within the True Dharma and Discipline.”

Furthermore, son of good family, there is one who cannot hear of the suffering of old age, sickness, and death among men or women in another village and yet give rise to fear and rely upon right reflection;

whereas, upon seeing the suffering of old age, sickness, and death among men or women in another village, he gives rise to fear and relies upon right reflection. Just as a fine horse, when touched by its hair or tail, can be swiftly tamed and follows the will of the rider, this is called the second kind of son of good family who is able to discipline himself within the True Dharma and Vinaya.

Furthermore, noble son, there are those who cannot hear of or see the suffering of old age, sickness, and death among the men and women in other villages, and thus do not give rise to a mind of fear or rely upon right reflection; yet, when they see the suffering of old age, sickness, and death among the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and those they associate with in their own villages and towns, they then give rise to fear and rely upon right reflection. Just as a fine horse is tamed only after its skin and flesh are touched, so that it follows the will of the rider, this is called a noble son being self-tamed within the Noble Dharma and Vinaya.

Furthermore, noble son, there are those who cannot hear or see the suffering of old age, sickness, and death experienced by men and women in other villages, nor can they give rise to a mind of fear toward them or rely upon right reflection;

yet, regarding the suffering of old age, sickness, and death within their own bodies, they are able to give rise to revulsion and fear and rely upon right reflection. Just as a fine horse is only tamed after it has been lanced until the flesh is pierced to the bone, so that it thereafter follows the will of its rider—this is called the fourth type of noble son who is able to discipline himself within the Noble Dharma and Vinaya.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 923 (922) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa, the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, there was a horse trainer named Kiṃśuka who came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I observe that the world is extremely contemptible, like a flock of sheep.
World-Honored One!
Only I am capable of taming horses."

"For a wild and unruly horse, I employ skillful means to cause its various vices and ailments to manifest in an instant; then, according to those vices and ailments, I employ skillful means to tame it.
The Buddha asked the village head, the horse trainer:
"By how many kinds of skillful means do you tame horses?"
The horse trainer said to the Buddha,
"There are three methods for taming a wicked horse.
What are these three?"
"First, pliant; second, coarse and harsh; third, both pliant and coarse and harsh.
The Buddha said to the village headman, "If you employ these three methods to train a horse and it is still not tamed, what will you do then?"
The horse trainer said to the Buddha, “If it cannot be tamed at all, I shall put it to death. Why is this? Because—”
"Do not cause me to be disgraced.
The horse trainer said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, you are the Unsurpassed Tamer of Men; by how many kinds of skillful means do you tame men?"
The Buddha told the village headman:
"I also discipline men through three kinds of skillful means.
What are these three?"
"First, those that are exclusively soft; second, those that are exclusively coarse and rough; third, those that are both soft and coarse.
The Buddha told the village headman:
"That which is called 'exclusively soft' is as it has been said:"

"This is wholesome conduct of body; this is the retribution for wholesome conduct of body. This is wholesome conduct of speech and mind; this is the retribution for wholesome conduct of speech and mind. These are called devas, these are called humans, these are called rebirth by transformation in the happy realms, and these are called nirvāṇa. This is what is meant by 'gentleness'."
"Regarding 'rough and harsh,' it is as has been said:

'These are bodily misdeeds and the retribution for bodily misdeeds; these are verbal and mental misdeeds and the retribution for verbal and mental misdeeds. These are called the hells, these are called animals, these are called hungry ghosts, these are called evil destinies, these are called falling into evil destinies—this is the rough and harsh teaching of the Tathāgata.'"

"Regarding that which is both soft and coarse: this refers to when the Tathāgata at times speaks of wholesome bodily conduct, and at times speaks of the retribution for wholesome bodily conduct; at times he speaks of wholesome verbal and mental conduct, and at times speaks of the retribution for wholesome verbal and mental conduct;

at times he speaks of unwholesome bodily conduct, and at times speaks of the retribution for unwholesome bodily conduct; at times he speaks of unwholesome verbal and mental conduct, and at times speaks of the retribution for unwholesome verbal and mental conduct."
"Such is called a deva; such is called a human; such is called a happy rebirth; such is called nirvāṇa. Such is called hell;
such is called an animal; such is called a hungry ghost; such is called an evil rebirth; such is falling into an evil rebirth—this is called the Tathāgata’s teaching that is both gentle and harsh."
The horse trainer addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
If one employs three kinds of skillful means to subdue sentient beings, and there are those who remain unsubdued, what should be done with them?”
The Buddha told the village headman:
"You should also kill him. Why is that? Because—"
"Do not cause me to be disgraced.

The horse trainer said to the Buddha, "If one were to kill a living being, it would be impure according to the Dharma of the World-Honored One; yet within the Dharma of the World-Honored One, there is no killing of living beings. Now, you speak of 'killing'—what is the meaning of this?"
The Buddha told the village headman: "So it is! So it is!"
In the Dharma of the Tathāgata, taking life is impure, and in the Dharma of the Tathāgata, one likewise does not take life;
yet, within the Dharma of the Tathāgata, those who are unsubdued by the three kinds of instruction are no longer spoken to, nor taught, nor admonished.
"Headman, what do you think? In the Dharma of the Tathāgata,
if one no longer converses with others, nor receives instruction, nor receives admonition— is that not death?"
The horse trainer said to the Buddha,
“It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
I shall no longer converse with them, nor ever again instruct or admonish them; they are truly as if dead.
World-Honored One!
For this reason, from this day forward, I shall distance myself from all evil and unwholesome karma.
The Buddha said to the village headman, "Excellent is what you have said!
Then, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the village headman Kesi, the horse trainer, rejoiced and delighted in it; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and departed.
924 (924). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa, the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are eight dispositions of horses in the world. What are these eight?

When a wicked horse is about to be yoked to a carriage, it stamps with its hind legs, kneels with its forelegs on the ground, tosses its head, and bites people; this is called the first disposition of a worldly horse.
Furthermore, when a wicked horse is yoked to a chariot, it lowers its head and shakes the yoke; this is called the second manner of a wicked horse in the world.

Furthermore, when a wicked horse in the world is yoked to a chariot, it leaves the path and goes astray, or it pulls unevenly against the vehicle, causing it to overturn; this is called the third manner.
Furthermore, when a wicked horse of the world is yoked to a carriage, it lifts its head and walks backward; this is called the fourth behavior of a wicked horse of the world.

Furthermore, when a wicked horse of the world is yoked to a carriage, upon receiving even a slight lash of the whip or the snapping of the reins and breaking of the bit, it gallops off wildly in all directions; this is called the fifth behavior.
Furthermore, when a wicked horse of the world is yoked to a chariot, it lifts its two front feet and stands upright like a human; this is called the sixth behavior.
Furthermore, when a wicked horse of the world is being yoked and is struck with a whip or staff, it remains standing still and does not move; this is called the seventh behavior.

Furthermore, when a wicked horse of the world is being yoked to a carriage, it bunches its four legs together and lies prostrate on the ground, refusing to rise; this is called the eighth disposition.
"In this same way, there are eight kinds of faults in a wicked man of the world regarding the True Dharma and Discipline."
What are the eight? If,
when fellow practitioners of the holy life raise a charge against a bhikkhu on account of what they have seen, heard, or suspected, he becomes angry and instead reviles them, saying:
"You are foolish and lack discernment regarding what is unwholesome; since others have censured you, how can you in turn censure me?

This is like a wicked horse that stamps with its hind legs, kneels on its forelegs, snaps its halter, and breaks its yoke—this is called the foremost transgression of a man within the True Dharma and Vinaya.
"Furthermore, bhikkhus!

When fellow practitioners of the holy life charge one with what they have seen, heard, or suspected, he instead brings forth their faults in return—just as a wicked horse, when its neck is enraged, breaks the yoke. This is called the second fault of a man regarding the True Dharma and Discipline."
"Furthermore, bhikṣus!

When fellow practitioners of the holy life charge him with what they have seen, heard, or suspected, he does not answer correctly, but instead speaks crosswise on other matters; he acts out of anger, pride, concealment, resentment, and intolerance, acting without justification. Like that evil horse which does not follow the proper path and causes the carriage to overturn, this is called the third fault of a man within the True Dharma and Discipline."
"Furthermore, monks!
Fellow practitioners of the holy life may charge one with what has been seen, heard, or suspected, causing one to reflect, and say:
'I do not recall it!'"
"Obstinate and refusing to submit, like a wicked horse that shrinks back and retreats—this is called the fourth fault of a man regarding the True Dharma and Discipline.
Furthermore, bhikṣu!"

When fellow practitioners of the holy life raise charges against him based on what they have seen, heard, or suspected, he treats them with contempt and disregards both those individuals and the Saṃgha; he takes up his robes and bowl and departs as he pleases, like a vicious horse that, when whipped and prodded, runs off recklessly in all directions. This is called the fifth fault of a man regarding the True Dharma and Vinaya.
"Furthermore, bhikkhus!

When fellow practitioners of the holy life censure one for what they have seen, heard, or suspected, that person sits upon a high seat and contends with the senior elders over right and wrong, like a wicked horse standing on two legs. This is called the sixth fault of a man in this True Dharma and Discipline."
"Furthermore, bhikkhus!

When fellow practitioners of the holy life charge him with what they have seen, heard, or suspected, he remains silent and does not respond, thereby vexing the assembly. Like that wicked horse which, when whipped and struck with a stick, stands motionless and unresponsive, this is called the seventh fault of a man in regard to the True Dharma and Discipline."
"Furthermore, monks!

When fellow practitioners of the holy life charge one with what they have seen, heard, or suspected, one may then abandon the precepts and experience a sense of despondency and retreat. Arriving at the gate of the monastery, one says:
'You remain silent, happy, and at ease; as for me, I am abandoning the precepts and retreating.'"
"Just as that evil horse, with its four legs tucked together, lies prostrate on the ground and does not move—this is called the eighth fault of a man regarding the True Dharma and Vinaya.
These are the eight kinds of faults of a man found in a bhikṣu regarding the True Dharma and Vinaya."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 925 (925). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"A fine horse of the world that has achieved the eight kinds of virtues follows whatever the rider desires, traversing as much or as little of the path as required."
What are the eight?
To be born in the land of noble horses is called the first virtue of a noble horse.
Furthermore, to have a nature that is gentle and kind, and not to startle or frighten people, is called the second virtue of a noble horse.
Furthermore, a fine horse does not discriminate regarding its food and drink; this is called the third virtue of a fine horse.
Furthermore, a fine horse loathes impurity and chooses the ground upon which to lie down; this is called the fourth virtue of a fine horse.

Furthermore, when a noble horse quickly displays its various temperaments to the trainer, and the horse-master, through training, causes it to swiftly abandon those temperaments, this is called the fifth virtue of a noble horse.

Furthermore, a fine horse is content with its harness and carriage, pays no heed to other horses, and according to the weight of the load, can exert its full strength; this is called the sixth virtue of a fine horse.
Furthermore, a noble horse always follows the correct path and does not follow improper ways; this is called the seventh virtue of a noble horse.
Furthermore, whether the noble horse is ill or old, it exerts its strength in being harnessed for riding, neither wearying nor growing tired; this is called the eighth virtue of a noble horse.
"In this way, a man who is accomplished in eight qualities within the True Dharma and Discipline should be known as a noble person.
What are these eight?

Namely, a noble person abides in the restraint of the Pātimokkha through right morality; he is complete in deportment and conduct; seeing even the slightest fault, he is able to feel dread; and he undertakes and trains in the precepts. This is called the first quality of a man within the True Dharma and Discipline.

Furthermore, a man is by nature virtuous and good, well-disciplined and well-established, and does not afflict or frighten his fellow practitioners of the holy life; this is called the second quality of a man.

Furthermore, when a man goes on his alms round, he maintains an even mind regarding whatever he obtains, whether coarse or refined; he neither disparages nor clings to it. This is called the third virtue of a man.

Furthermore, when a man develops a sense of weary detachment toward the evil karma of body, speech, and mind, as well as unwholesome dharmas and all afflictions, and toward the blazing retribution of suffering experienced in various states of existence, and toward birth, aging, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, despair, and pain in future lives—thereby increasing his weary detachment—this is called the fourth virtue of a man.

Furthermore, if a man has the fault of being a śramaṇa who is deceitful and insincere, he should quickly inform the Great Master and his spiritual friends; when the Great Master preaches the Dharma, [the fault] will be eliminated at that time. This is called the fifth virtue of a man.
Furthermore, a man whose mind is perfected through training forms this thought:
"Whether others train or do not train, I shall train in all things."
This is called the sixth virtue of a great man.
Furthermore, when a great man practices the Eightfold Noble Path and does not practice what is not the Path, this is called the seventh virtue of a great man.
Furthermore, when a man applies himself with diligence and skillful means throughout his entire life, without weariness or fatigue, this is called the eighth virtue of a man.
When a man has thus accomplished these eight virtues, he is able to advance rapidly according to the stage of practice he occupies.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
926 (926) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Gaṅgāvatī Hermitage in the deep valley of the Naḷakalāpa village.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Cunda Kātyāyana:
"One should practice authentic meditation; do not practice forced meditation. It is like a strong horse tied to a manger:
that horse does not think, 'This is what I ought to do, and this is what I ought not to do.'"
"He merely thinks of grain and grass.

In this way, because a man has extensively practiced the fetter of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), he contemplates with a mind of sensual desire and does not know the path of renunciation as it truly is; his mind constantly runs wild, and following the fetter of sensual desire, he seeks meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).

Because he has extensively practiced ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-regret, and doubt, he does not know the path of renunciation as it truly is; with a mind characterized by the hindrance of doubt, he contemplates in order to seek meditative attainment.
"Śreṇya! If a truly noble horse is tied to a manger, it does not think of water or grass, but thinks only this:
'The time has come for me to be harnessed and ridden.'"

"In this way, a man does not dwell upon the obsession of sensual desire, but abides in renunciation and knows it as it truly is; he does not seek meditative attainment through the obsession of sensual desire. Likewise, he does not dwell upon the obsessions of ill will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-regret, or doubt, but abides much in renunciation;
he knows these obsessions of ill will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-regret, and doubt as they truly are, and does not seek meditative attainment through the obsession of doubt."
“In this way, Śreṇika!

A bhikṣu who practices meditation in such a manner does not practice meditation by relying on earth; he does not practice meditation by relying on water, fire, wind, space, consciousness, nothingness, or neither-perception-nor-non-perception.”

One practices meditation without relying on this world or another world; it is not the sun or the moon; it is not what is seen, heard, sensed, or cognized; it is neither attainment nor seeking; it is not following after mental application, nor following after contemplation.
"Śreṇya! When a bhikṣu practices dhyāna in this manner, the lords of the devas, Īśvara, and Prajāpati pay homage with palms joined, bow their heads in prostration, and speak these verses:
‘Homage to the Great Being! Homage to the Supreme among Men!’"
"Since I do not know this, upon what basis can I enter meditative concentration?
At that time, the Venerable Bakula was standing behind the Buddha, fanning him with a fan.
At that time, Bakula addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How does a bhikṣu enter meditative absorption so as not to rely on earth, water, fire, or wind, nor even upon applied and sustained thought, while practicing dhyāna-samādhi?"
How is it that the bhikṣu’s meditation is such that the lords of the gods, Īśvara, and Pārvatī join their palms in reverence, prostrate themselves, and speak this verse:
“Homage to the Great Man! Homage to the Supreme among Men!
Since we cannot know by what means you enter meditative concentration, [we pay homage].”
The Buddha told Bakula:

"A bhikṣu is able to subdue the perception of earth with regard to the perception of earth; he likewise subdues the perceptions of water, fire, and wind, the perception of the sphere of infinite space, the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the perception of the sphere of nothingness, and the perception of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."

In this world and the next, regarding what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized by the sun and the moon—whether attained or sought, whether perceived or contemplated—one completely subdues all such perceptions.
Bakkula! A bhikkhu who meditates in this way does not rely on earth, water, fire, or wind, nor does he rely on applied thought or sustained thought while practicing meditation.
Bakkula! When a bhikkhu practices meditation in this way, the lords of the devas—Īśvara and Pajāpati—pay homage with palms joined, bow their heads in prostration, and speak these verses:
“Homage to the Great Hero! Homage to the Supreme among Men!”
"Since I do not know this, upon what basis could I practice dhyāna?
When the Buddha spoke this sutra, the bhikṣu Śreṇika Kātyāyana was distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
The bhikṣu Bakula did not give rise to any outflows, and his mind attained liberation.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣu Bakula, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
927 (Ninety-two-seven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Park.
At that time, there was a member of the Śākya clan named Mahānāman, who went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by the term ‘upāsaka’?
The Buddha told Mahānāman:
“A layperson, pure and practicing the pure dwelling, endowed with the male characteristics, makes this declaration:
‘I now, for as long as life lasts, take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus; may you bear witness that I am an upāsaka!’”
"This is what is called an upāsaka.
Mahānāma addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is meant by an upāsaka being endowed with faith?
The Buddha told Mahānāman:
"An upāsaka takes right faith in the Tathāgata as his foundation; it is firm and unshakable, such that no śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Māras, Brahmās, or anyone else in the world can destroy it."
"Mahānāma! This is called an upāsaka who is endowed with faith.
Mahānāma addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘the complete observance of the upāsaka precepts’?
The Buddha told Mahānāman:
“Mahānāma, an upāsaka abstains from killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants; he does not take pleasure in committing them.
Mahānāma, this is called the complete fulfillment of the precepts of an upāsaka.”
Mahānāma addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by a lay follower being ‘complete in hearing’?”
The Buddha told Mahānāman:

“A lay follower who is endowed with hearing hears and is able to retain it; he hears and accumulates it. Whatever the Buddha has spoken—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing, entirely complete and pure, the holy life that is stainless—he is fully able to receive and uphold it.”
“Mahānāma! This is called the upāsaka’s fulfillment of learning.
Mahānāma addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘the upāsaka’s fulfillment of relinquishment’?
The Buddha told Mahānāman:

“Regarding the lay follower who has abandoned what is complete: for one who was entangled by the defilement of stinginess, the mind becomes free from the defilement of stinginess; dwelling in the homeless life, they practice the gift of liberation, diligent giving, and constant giving; they delight in relinquishing material wealth and practice impartial generosity.”
“Mahānāma! This is called the upāsaka’s fulfillment of renunciation.
Mahānāma addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by an upāsaka being fully endowed with wisdom?
The Buddha told Mahānāman:

“A lay follower endowed with wisdom is one who knows this suffering as it truly is, knows the origin of this suffering as it truly is, knows the cessation of this suffering as it truly is, and knows the path leading to the cessation of this suffering as it truly is.”
“Mahānāma! This is called an upāsaka who is endowed with wisdom.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Mahānāma of the Śākya clan rejoiced and approved, rose from his seat, paid homage, and departed.
928 (Nin-ni-hachi). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Park.
At that time, Mahānāma the Śākya, together with five hundred upāsakas, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘upāsaka’?
The Buddha told Mahānāman:
"An upāsaka is one who, dwelling in purity as a householder, takes refuge in the Triple Gem for as long as life lasts and becomes an upāsaka; may you bear witness to me!"
Mahānāma addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by a lay follower who is a srotāpanna?”
The Buddha told Mahānāma:
“Regarding the upāsaka who is a srotāpanna, he has already abandoned and fully understood the three fetters, namely: the view of a self-identity, attachment to precepts and rituals, and doubt.”
“Mahānāma! This is called an upāsaka who is a srotāpanna.
Mahānāma addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by an upāsaka who is a sakṛdāgāmin?
The Buddha told Mahānāman:
"Mahānāma, it refers to an upāsaka who has abandoned and fully understood the three fetters, and whose greed, hatred, and delusion have become thin.
This, Mahānāma,
is called an upāsaka who is a sakṛdāgāmin."
Mahānāma addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by an upāsaka who is an anāgāmin?”
The Buddha told Mahānāman:

"An upāsaka who is an Anāgāmin has already abandoned and fully understood the five lower fetters, namely: the view of a self-identity, attachment to precepts and rituals, doubt, sensual desire, and ill will."
“Mahānāma! This is called an upāsaka who is an anāgāmin.
At that time, Mahānāma of the Śākya clan looked back at the five hundred upāsakas and spoke these words:
"How marvelous!
These lay followers (*upāsaka*), though living as householders, possess such pure integrity that they have attained these profound and sublime merits.
At that time, the lay follower Mahānāma, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and expressed his approval; he rose from his seat, paid homage, and departed.
929 (929). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Park.
At that time, Mahānāma the Śākya came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is called an upāsaka?
The Buddha told Mahānāman:
“An upāsaka is one who, while living at home in purity, takes refuge in the Triple Gem for as long as life lasts and becomes an upāsaka; may you bear witness to me!”
Mahānāma addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One,
what constitutes the fulfillment of all the duties of a lay follower (upāsaka)?”
The Buddha told Mahānāman:
"If an upāsaka has faith but lacks precepts, he is incomplete; he should diligently apply skillful means to fulfill the pure precepts."
One who possesses faith and precepts but does not practice giving is incomplete;
because they are incomplete, they should diligently apply skillful means to cultivate the practice of giving so that it becomes complete and fulfilled.
If one is complete in faith, precepts, and generosity, yet cannot go at the proper time to visit śramaṇas to hear and receive the true Dharma, this is incomplete.

Because it is incomplete, although one diligently employs skillful means to go at the proper time to stūpas and monasteries to see various śramaṇas, if one does not listen to and receive the true Dharma with a single-minded focus, this is also incomplete.
Faith, precepts, generosity, and learning must be cultivated to fulfillment. If one hears the teaching but does not retain it, these are incomplete;

because they are incomplete, one should apply diligent skillful means to visit śramaṇas from time to time and listen to the Dharma with single-minded focus, so that upon hearing it, one is able to retain it.
To be unable to contemplate the profound meaning of all phenomena is to be incomplete;

because one is incomplete, despite diligent application of skillful means—such as faith, ethical discipline, generosity, and learning—one may indeed learn and retain what is heard. Yet, having retained it, if one contemplates the most profound and subtle meanings but does not accord with the knowledge of the sequence of the Dharma (dharmānudharmapratipatti), this is likewise incomplete. Because of this incompleteness, through diligent application of skillful means—faith, ethical discipline, generosity, and learning—one must receive, maintain, and contemplate them until one thoroughly penetrates the profound meaning and accords with the practice of the sequence of the Dharma.
"Mahānāma! This is called fulfilling all aspects of the duties of a lay follower (upāsaka).
Mahānāma addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by an upāsaka who can bring comfort to himself but cannot bring comfort to others?
The Buddha told Mahānāman:
"If an upāsaka is able to establish himself in the precepts, yet cannot cause others to be established in the right precepts;
if he maintains pure precepts himself, yet cannot cause others to maintain the precepts fully;
if he practices giving himself, yet cannot establish others in giving;..."
One visits stupas and monasteries oneself and sees various śramaṇas, yet cannot encourage others to go to stupas and monasteries to see the śramaṇas;
one listens to the Dharma oneself with single-minded devotion, yet cannot encourage others to delight in listening to the true Dharma;
one personally retains the teachings one hears, yet cannot cause others to receive and uphold the true Dharma.
One is able to personally contemplate the profound and subtle meaning, yet cannot exhort others to contemplate that profound meaning;

one knows the profound Dharma and is able to practice in accordance with the Dharma and the sequence of the Dharma, yet cannot exhort others to practice in accordance with the Dharma and the sequence of the Dharma.
“Mahānāma! One who is accomplished in these eight qualities is called an upāsaka who can bring comfort to himself, but not to others.
Mahānāma said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
How many dharmas must a lay follower (upāsaka) accomplish to bring peace to himself and peace to others?
The Buddha told Mahānāman:
“Mahānāma, if a lay follower (upāsaka) accomplishes sixteen qualities, he is called a lay follower who brings peace to himself and peace to others.
What are these sixteen? Mahānāma!”
If an upāsaka is endowed with perfect faith and establishes others in it;
if he maintains pure precepts himself and also establishes others in pure precepts;
and if he practices giving himself and teaches others to practice giving;
One visits stupas and monasteries oneself and sees the various śramaṇas, and likewise teaches others to go and see them;
one listens to the Dharma oneself and likewise teaches others to listen;
one receives and upholds the Dharma oneself and teaches others to receive and uphold it.
Having personally observed the meaning, they teach others to observe it;

having personally realized the profound meaning, they practice in accordance with the sequence of the Dharma and its direction, and likewise teach others to understand the profound meaning and practice in accordance with the sequence of the Dharma and its direction.
Mahānāma! One who accomplishes these sixteen qualities is called a lay follower (upāsaka) who can comfort himself and also comfort others. Mahānāma!

If an upāsaka accomplishes these sixteen dharmas, all the great assemblies—namely the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of kṣatriyas, the assembly of householders, and the assembly of śramaṇas—will go to his place; among all these assemblies, his majestic virtue will shine forth brilliantly.
Just as the orb of the sun shines with its radiance in the beginning, middle, and end,
so too does a lay follower who has accomplished the sixteen dharmas shine with majestic power in the beginning, middle, and end.
"In this way, Mahānāma!
A lay follower who accomplishes these sixteen dharmas is rare to find in the world.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Śākya Mahānāma, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and approved with gladness; he then rose from his seat, paid homage, and departed.
930. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Park at Kapilavastu.
At that time, Mahānāma the Śākya came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This city of Kapilavastu is peaceful, prosperous, and joyful, with a flourishing population. Whenever I enter or exit, I am always accompanied by a large retinue, as well as mad elephants, madmen, and mad vehicles.”
I fear that by living and dying together with these madmen, I shall forget mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Saṃgha.
I reflect upon myself: at the time of my death, where shall I be reborn?
The Buddha said to Mahānāman:
"Do not fear, do not be terrified. After the end of this life, you shall not be born in an evil realm, nor shall there ever be any evil for you.
It is like a great tree that inclines downward, flows downward, and leans downward; if its root were cut, where would it fall?"
Mahānāma said to the Buddha,
“It follows that downward flow, downward pouring, and downward discharge.
The Buddha told Mahānāma:
"You are also like this: when your life comes to an end, you will not be reborn in the evil realms, and in the end there will be no suffering. Why is this?

Because for a long night you have practiced mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Sangha. When your life ends, whether this body is consumed by fire, cast away in a cemetery, blown by the wind, or scorched by the sun until it eventually turns to dust, your consciousness—having been perfumed for a long night by right faith and perfumed by precepts, generosity, learning, and wisdom—will ascend and head toward a place of peace and happiness, to be born in heaven in the future."
At that time, Mahānāma, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and approved with gladness;
he paid homage and departed. 931 (931) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Park at Kapilavastu.
At that time, Mahānāma the Śākya came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"If a bhikṣu is on the stage of training (śaikṣa), seeking what has not yet been attained, ascending and progressing upon the path toward the peace of nirvāṇa—World-Honored One!

How should he practice, how should he dwell in frequent cultivation, so that within this Dharma and Vinaya he may attain the destruction of all outflows (āsrava-kṣaya), and with the outflow-free liberation of mind (ceto-vimukti) and liberation by wisdom (prajñā-vimukti), realize for himself in the present life and witness: [‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being’]?"
"My births have been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence.
The Buddha said to Mahānāma:

"If a bhikṣu is on the stage of training (śaikṣa), seeking what he has not yet attained, ascending and progressing toward the path for the sake of peaceful nirvāṇa, at that time he should cultivate the six recollections (ṣaḍ-anusmṛti) until he advances to attain nirvāṇa."

Just as a hungry person, emaciated and weak of body, becomes plump and radiant upon obtaining delicious food, so too, a bhikkhu dwelling on the stage of training, seeking what has not yet been attained, ascending the path toward progress, peace, and nibbāna, cultivates the six recollections; thus, he quickly attains peace and nibbāna.
“What are the six recollections? They are as follows:
the noble disciple recollects the qualities of the Tathāgata:
‘The Tathāgata is an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, a Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, a Sugata, a Lokavid, an Anuttara, a Puruṣadamyasārathi, a Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, a Buddha, a Bhagavān.’”
"When a noble disciple reflects in this way, the fetter of sensual desire does not arise, nor do thoughts of ill will or delusion; his mind becomes upright.

He attains the meaning of the Tathāgata and attains the true Dharma of the Tathāgata. Toward the true Dharma of the Tathāgata and toward what has been attained by the Tathāgata, he gives rise to a heart of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).
Having given rise to sympathetic joy, he becomes gladdened."
Being joyful, the body becomes tranquil;
with the body tranquil, one experiences happiness;
experiencing happiness, the mind becomes concentrated.
Once the mind is concentrated, that noble disciple is free from all obstructions among fierce and dangerous beings; they enter the stream of the Dharma and proceed even unto Nirvana.

"Furthermore, the noble disciple recollects the Dharma: the Dharma and Vinaya of the Blessed One are conducive to the extinction of the burning of birth and death in this very life; they do not depend on time, they are directly accessible in this life, and are to be personally realized by the wise."

When a noble disciple contemplates the Dharma in this way, they do not give rise to desire, hatred, or delusion; being permeated by such contemplation of the Dharma, they advance toward and ascend to Nirvana.

"Furthermore, the noble disciple recollects the Sangha: 'The disciples of the Blessed One are well-directed, rightly directed, straightforwardly directed, and sincerely directed; they practice in accordance with the Dharma. There are those who are stream-enterers and those who have attained stream-entry; those who are once-returners and those who have attained once-returning; those who are non-returners and those who have attained non-returning; those who are arahants and those who have attained arahantship. These are the four pairs and eight classes of noble ones. This is called the Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples, complete in virtue, complete in concentration, complete in wisdom, complete in liberation, and complete in the knowledge and vision of liberation. They are worthy of being welcomed, served, and honored, and constitute a fertile field of merit.'"
When a noble disciple thus recollects the qualities of the Saṅgha, no lust, hatred, or delusion arises; indeed, being suffused with the recollection of the Saṅgha, they advance toward Nirvāṇa.

"Furthermore, the noble disciple reflects upon his own pure precepts: precepts that are unbroken, unimpaired, untarnished, unmixed, unmisappropriated by others, well-guarded, praised by the wise, and not despised by the wise."
When a noble disciple thus recollects the precepts, covetousness, ill will, and delusion do not arise; furthermore, being permeated by the recollection of the precepts, they advance toward Nirvana.

"Furthermore, the noble disciple reflects upon the act of giving, thinking: 'I have gained a true benefit; amidst beings defiled by stinginess, I have attained a state free from the stain of stinginess. I practice the gift of liberation in the homeless life, constantly giving with my own hands, delighting in the practice of relinquishment, and fulfilling impartial generosity.'"
When a noble disciple thus recollects generosity, they give rise to no greed, hatred, or delusion; even unto being permeated by the recollection of generosity, they advance toward Nirvana.

"Furthermore, the noble disciple recollects the matters of the devas: there are the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven."
"If there are those with right faith who, at the end of this life, are reborn among those devas, I too shall practice this right faith;

if they have obtained pure morality, generosity, learning, relinquishment, and wisdom, and at the end of this life are reborn among those devas, I too shall now practice this morality, generosity, learning, and wisdom."
When a noble disciple thus contemplates the matters of the devas, they do not give rise to sensual desire, ill will, or delusion; their mind becomes upright as it takes those devas as its object.
When that noble disciple possesses such a straightforward mind, he attains the benefit of the profound Dharma, the benefit of the profound meaning, and the favor and sympathetic joy of those devas;
having rejoiced, he gives rise to gladness;
having become glad, his body becomes tranquil.
When the body is at ease, one experiences pleasure;
having experienced pleasure, one attains concentration of mind;
with the mind concentrated, that noble disciple dwells among fierce and dangerous beings without any hindrance, entering the flow of the Dharma.
Because they are permeated by mindfulness of the devas, they ascend toward and progress toward nirvāṇa. "Mahānāma!
If a bhikṣu abides on the stage of training and desires to seek the upward ascent to the bliss of nirvāṇa..."

One who thus practices extensively will swiftly attain nirvana; in this true Dharma and Vinaya, they will quickly exhaust all taints and achieve the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. In this very life, they will know for themselves and realize:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I myself know that there will be no further existence."
At that time, the Śākyan Mahānāma, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and approved with gladness.
He rose from his seat, paid homage, and departed. 932 (932) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Park.
At that time, a large number of bhikṣus had gathered in the dining hall to sew robes for the World-Honored One.

Then, the Śākya Mahānāma heard that a large number of bhikṣus had gathered in the dining hall to sew robes for the World-Honored One, and that before long, after the three-month summer retreat was concluded and the robes were finished, the World-Honored One would take his robes and bowl and travel through the human realm.
Having heard this, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
My four limbs were no longer under my control; I was disoriented regarding the four directions and have completely forgotten the Dharma I heard.”

I heard that many bhikṣus have gathered in the dining hall to sew robes for the World-Honored One, so that before long the World-Honored One will have completed his summer retreat, finished making his robes, and—carrying his bowl and robe—will travel through the human world. Therefore, I now reflect:
"When shall I again behold the World-Honored One and my venerable kinsmen among the bhikṣus?"
The Buddha told Mahānāma:

"Whether you see the World-Honored One or do not see the World-Honored One, whether you see the bhikṣus who are your spiritual friends or do not see them, you should simply keep the five dharmas in mind and practice them with diligent effort."
Mahānāma! You should take right faith as primary, not wrong faith;
you should take the fulfillment of ethical discipline, the fulfillment of learning, the fulfillment of generosity, and the fulfillment of wisdom as fundamental, not a lack of wisdom.
Thus it is, Mahānāma!
Relying on these five dharmas, one cultivates the six foundations of mindfulness. What are the six?
Mahānāma! When you recollect the Tathāgata, you should recollect him thus:
"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, up to the Buddha, the World-Honored One."
"One should maintain mindfulness of the Dharma, the Saṅgha, the precepts, generosity, and the devas, until one personally attains wisdom.

In this way, Mahānāma, a noble disciple who accomplishes these eleven qualities is one who follows the path of training; he will never decay, is capable of knowledge and vision, is capable of certainty, dwells at the gate of the Deathless, and is close to the Deathless, though he may not yet swiftly attain the Deathless Nirvāṇa."

"It is, for example, like a hen brooding over her eggs—whether five or ten—attending to them at the proper times, protecting and nourishing them; even if she should become negligent in the interim, she can still hatch her chicks by pecking at the eggs with her claws and her beak."
Why is this? It is because that hen, from the very beginning, was well-attuned to the seasons and protected her with care.
In the same way, a noble disciple who accomplishes these eleven qualities dwells upon the path of training; he will never rot away, even if he cannot yet swiftly attain the ambrosia of *nirvāṇa*.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, Mahānāma the Śākya, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and approved with gladness;
he paid homage and departed. 933 (933) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Park.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus were gathered in the dining hall sewing robes for the World-Honored One.

Then, the Śākyan Mahānāma heard that the bhikṣus had gathered in the dining hall to sew robes for the World-Honored One, and that before long, after the World-Honored One had completed his summer retreat and finished making his robes, he would take up his bowl and robe and travel through the human world.
Having heard this, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

My four limbs are now unsteady and I am disoriented regarding the four directions; the Dharma I previously heard has now been entirely forgotten. This is because I heard that many bhikṣus had gathered in the dining hall to sew robes for the World-Honored One, and so forth, until they were traveling through the human world, whereupon I thought to myself:"
"When shall we ever again behold the World-Honored One and our venerable bhikṣus?
The Buddha told Mahānāman:
"Whether you see the Tathāgata or do not see the Tathāgata, whether you see the bhikṣus or do not see the bhikṣus, you should always diligently cultivate six dharmas."
What are these six?
Right faith is the foundation; precepts, generosity, learning, emptiness, and wisdom constitute the roots. It is not that they lack wisdom; therefore, this is so.
Mahānāma! Having relied upon these six dharmas, one further cultivates the six recollections above: recollecting the qualities of the Tathāgata, up to recollecting the devas.

When these twelve kinds of recollection are accomplished, that noble disciple’s evils diminish and do not increase; they are extinguished and do not arise; he is free from dust and defilement, does not increase dust and defilement, and having relinquished them, does not grasp at them.
Because they do not grasp, they do not cling; because they do not grasp or cling, they realize their own nirvana:
"Birth has been exhausted for me, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and I know for myself that there will be no further existence."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Śākya Mahānāma, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and approved with gladness; he rose from his seat, paid homage, and departed.
934 (Nin-san-yon). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Park.
Then the Śākyan Mahānāma approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As I understand what the Buddha has taught, it is through right attainment that one is liberated, not through non-right attainment. How so?”
World-Honored One!
Is it that one first attains right concentration and subsequently liberation,
or is it that one first attains liberation and subsequently right concentration?
"Are right reception, liberation, non-retrogression, and non-regression born simultaneously, neither before nor after?
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent.
Thus Mahānāma asked a second and a third time, and the Buddha likewise remained silent three times.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the Buddha, fanning him with a fan.
The Venerable Ānanda thought to himself:

“The Śākyan Mahānāma has asked the World-Honored One about this profound matter. Since the World-Honored One’s illness has only recently been cured, I should now speak of other matters to divert his speech.”
“Mahānāma! Those in training also possess ethical discipline, and those beyond training also possess ethical discipline;
those in training also possess meditative concentration, and those beyond training also possess meditative concentration.”
“Those in training possess wisdom, and those beyond training also possess wisdom;
those in training possess liberation, and those beyond training also possess liberation.
Mahānāma asked the Venerable Ānanda:
"What is the precept of one in training?
What is the precept of one beyond training?
What is the samādhi of one in training?"
What is the samādhi of one beyond training?
What is the wisdom of one in training?
What is the wisdom of one beyond training?
"What is the liberation of one in training?
What is the liberation of one beyond training?
Venerable Ānanda said to Mahānāma:
"This noble disciple dwells in the restraint of the Pātimokkha and the code of discipline, observing the rules of conduct and training in the precepts;
having fully undertaken and trained in these precepts, he becomes detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, and dwells having attained the fourth dhyāna.

Having thus perfected this samādhi, he knows as it really is: 'This is the Noble Truth of Suffering,' 'This is the Origin of Suffering,' 'This is the Cessation of Suffering,' and 'This is the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.'"

Having known thus and seen thus, one has realized that the five lower fetters have been severed—namely, the view of a self-identity, attachment to precepts and rituals, doubt, sensual desire, and ill will. With these five lower fetters severed, one is reborn there and attains parinirvāṇa as a non-returner (anāgāmin), never again to return to this world.

At that time, he accomplished the training in the precepts, the training in concentration, the training in wisdom, and the training in liberation; furthermore, at another time, having exhausted all taints, he attained the taintless liberation of mind and the liberation by wisdom, realizing for himself and attesting:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I myself know that there will be no further existence."
"At that time, he will have accomplished the precepts of one beyond training, the concentration of one beyond training, the wisdom of one beyond training, and the liberation of one beyond training.
Thus it is, Mahānāma!"

These are what the World-Honored One has called training in the precepts, training in concentration, training in wisdom, and training in liberation; as well as the precepts beyond training, concentration beyond training, wisdom beyond training, and liberation beyond training.
At that time, the Śākyan Mahānāma, having heard what the Venerable Ānanda had said, rejoiced and approved; he rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that Mahānāma had been gone but a short while, said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"How is it that the Śākyans of Kapilavastu are able to discuss profound meanings with the bhikṣus?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
The Śākyas of Kapilavastu are able to discuss profound meanings with the bhikṣus.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The Śākyas of Kapilavastu have gained a most excellent benefit, for they are able to penetrate deeply into the profound Buddha-dharma through the noble eye of wisdom."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 935 (935) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Park at Kapilavastu.
At that time, a Śākyan named Sthavira said to the Śākyan Mahānāman:
"How many qualities does the Blessed One say a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) has accomplished?"
Mahānāma replied:
“The World-Honored One has said that a srotāpanna accomplishes four dharmas.
What are these four?”

"That is to say: unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dharma, unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha, and the accomplishment of the noble precepts—these are called the four qualities by which one is accomplished as a stream-enterer.
Śāṭha of the Śākya clan said to Mahānāma of the Śākya clan:
"Do not speak in this way!"
Do not speak thus: "The World-Honored One said that one accomplishes the stream-enterer through four factors;
however, one accomplishes the stream-enterer through three factors.
What are these three?"
That is to say: unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dharma, and unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha.
One who has accomplished these three qualities is a stream-enterer.
Thus it was said for the third time.

The Śākya Mahānāma was unable to cause Sthavira to accept the four dharmas, and the Śākya Sthavira was unable to cause Mahānāma to accept the three dharmas; they went together to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Śākya Mahānāma addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Śākya Sthavira came to my place and asked me:”
"How many dharmas does the World-Honored One say bring about the attainment of a srotāpanna? I replied:
"The World-Honored One says that four dharmas bring about the attainment of a srotāpanna."
What are these four? They are:

Why is this so? Puṇṇiya!

Formerly, all sentient beings were possessed of *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am") and false pride (*mithyāmāna*). Driven by false pride, accumulated through false pride, and lacking clear comprehension of false pride, they were as disordered as a dog’s entrails, like iron hooks and chains, or like tangled grass. They ran to and fro between this world and the next, and from the next world back to this one; thus they rushed back and forth, unable to escape.
"Puṇṇā! For all sentient beings who have eternally extinguished all forms of wrong pride without exception, those beings shall dwell in peace and happiness throughout the long night."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣu Pūrṇa, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 967 (966) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.

At that time, during the latter part of the night, the Venerable Ānanda went to the banks of the Tapodā River; he took off his robes, placed them on the bank, and entered the water to wash his hands and feet.
Returning to the shore, he put on a single robe and rubbed his body.
At that time, the renunciant of the Kūṭadanta sect also arrived at the water’s edge.
Hearing the sound of his footsteps, the Venerable Ānanda, upon hearing the sound, immediately cleared his throat to make a noise.
When the renunciant heretic Kokanada heard the sound of a human voice, he asked,
"Who is that person? Venerable Ānanda replied:
"Śramaṇa," said the non-Buddhist Kokālika.
"What kind of śramaṇa?"
The Venerable Ānanda replied,
“A son of the Śākyas.
The non-Buddhist Kokāna said:
“I wish to ask a question; would you have the leisure to grant me an answer?
Venerable Ānanda replied, “Ask whatever you wish; I shall answer what I know.”
Kukana asked: "How so?
Does the Tathāgata exist after death?"
Ānanda replied,
“What the World-Honored One has spoken of this is an indeterminate matter (avyākṛta).
He asked again:
“Does the Tathāgata not exist after death?
Does he both exist and not exist after death?
Or does he neither exist nor not exist after death?”
Ānanda said, “What the World-Honored One has spoken regarding this is an undeclared matter (avyākṛta).
The non-Buddhist Kokanada then spoke:
“How is it? Does the Tathāgata exist after death?
“He replied that this is undeclared (avyākṛta). “Does he not exist after death?”
"Does existence continue after death?
Does it not continue after death? Is it both? Or is it neither?
To these questions, he replied that they are "undeclared" (avyākṛta).
"How is this? Is it because you do not know and do not see? Ānanda replied:
"It is not that he does not know, nor that he does not see; he knows all and sees all.
He then asked Ānanda:
"In what way does he know?"
"What is seeing? Ānanda replied:
"To see the place where there is what can be seen, the place where seeing arises, and the place where the entanglements of seeing are severed—this is knowing; this is seeing."
"I know thus and see thus; why then do you say that I do not know and do not see?
The non-Buddhist Kūṭadanta asked again:
"What is the Venerable One's name?"
Ānanda replied, "My name is Ānanda.
The non-Buddhist Kūṭadanta said:
"How marvelous!
That the disciples of the Great Teacher should engage in such discussion together!
Had I known this were the Venerable Ānanda, I would not have dared to pose my question."
Having spoken these words, he immediately departed. 968 (968).
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went out every day to see the World-Honored One, paying him homage and making offerings. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada thought to himself:
"I have come out too early; the World-Honored One and the bhikṣus have not yet arisen from their meditative reflections. I should instead go to the dwellings of the various non-Buddhist teachers."
He then entered the hermitage of the non-Buddhists, exchanged greetings and expressions of courtesy with them, and withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, those non-Buddhists asked him:
“Householder!...”
“When you see the śramaṇa Gautama, how do you see him?
What is it that you see?
The householder replied:
"I do not know how one sees the World-Honored One, nor what the World-Honored One sees.
The non-Buddhists said:
"You say you see the Saṃgha; how do you see the Saṃgha?"
"What do the assembly of monks see?
The householder replied,
"I myself do not know how the Sangha sees, nor what the Sangha sees."
The non-Buddhist again asked:
"Householder!
How do you now perceive yourself?"
"From what perspective do you see it?
The elder replied, "Each of you first state what you yourselves have seen; then it will not be difficult for me to speak of what I have seen."
At that time, a certain non-Buddhist practitioner spoke thus:
"Householder!
I see that all the world is eternal; this alone is reality, and all else is false."
Again, another said:
"Householder!
I see that all the world is impermanent; this alone is true, and all else is false."
Furthermore, some say:
"Householder!
The world is both eternal and non-eternal; this alone is the truth, and all else is false."
Again, some say:
"The world is neither eternal nor non-eternal; this alone is true, and all else is false.
Still others say:
"The world has an end; this alone is true, and all else is false.
Furthermore, others say:
"The world is infinite; this alone is true, and all else is false."
Again, some say: "The world is both finite and infinite. Others say: [the world is neither finite nor infinite].
"The world is neither finite nor infinite.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"The life-principle is identical to the body."
Again, some say: "The life-principle is different from the body. Others say: [the life-principle and the body are the same].
"The Tathāgata exists after death.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"The Tathāgata does not exist after death."

Again, some say: "The Tathāgata exists after death. Others say: "[The Tathāgata] does not exist after death. Still others say: [The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death]. And yet others say: [The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death].
"The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, and all else is false.
The non-Buddhists said to the householder, "We have each spoken of our own views; you, in turn, should speak of what you have seen."
The householder replied:

"That which I perceive as real, conditioned, deliberated, and dependently arisen—if it is real, conditioned, deliberated, and dependently arisen, then it is impermanent; and that which is impermanent is suffering."
Having understood this, one finds nothing at all in any view whatsoever.
As you have seen:
"The world is eternal; this alone is true, and all else is false."

"Those who see this as real, conditioned, conceptualized, and dependently originated—whatever is real, conditioned, conceptualized, and dependently originated is impermanent; and whatever is impermanent is suffering."
Therefore, you associate with suffering, obtain only suffering, dwell firmly in suffering, and plunge deeply into suffering.
Thus, when you say that the world is impermanent, this is the truth, and all else is false.
"There would be such faults as these:

that the world is eternal, or non-eternal, or neither eternal nor non-eternal; that the world is finite, or infinite, or both finite and infinite, or neither finite nor infinite; that the life-principle is identical to the body, or the life-principle is distinct from the body; that the Tathāgata exists after death, or does not exist after death, or both exists and does not exist after death, or neither exists nor does not exist after death—claiming that this alone is the truth and all else is false," as has been explained above.
A certain non-Buddhist practitioner said to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:

"According to what you have said, if there is anything seen that is real, conditioned, conceptualized, or dependently originated, it is an impermanent phenomenon; and if it is impermanent, it is suffering."
"Therefore, Elder, is that which you perceive also associated with suffering, attained as suffering, abiding in suffering, and deeply immersed in suffering?
The Elder replied:

"Did I not say before that what is perceived is real, conditioned, conceptualized, and dependently arisen; that all such things are impermanent, and that what is impermanent is suffering? Having understood this suffering, have I not found nothing to be grasped within what is perceived?"
The non-Buddhists said, “So be it, householder!

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having suppressed the heterodox arguments in the non-Buddhist monastery and established the correct doctrine, let out a lion’s roar amidst the assembly of those of other teachings. He then went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and related to the Buddha in detail the matter concerning his previous debate with the various non-Buddhists.
The Buddha said to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"You ought from time to time to subdue the ignorant non-Buddhists and establish the correct doctrine.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada rejoiced and followed along with joy; he paid homage and departed.
969 (969). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.

At that time, a renunciant of the long-nailed heretics came to where the Buddha was. After exchanging greetings and polite inquiries with the World-Honored One, he withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Gautama! I do not tolerate any view whatsoever.
The Buddha told Agniveśyāyanaputra:
"If you say that you do not tolerate all views, do you also not tolerate this view?
The heterodox teacher Dīrghanakha replied,
"As for what I said previously— that I do not tolerate all views— I do not tolerate even this view."
The Buddha told Aggivessana:
“When one knows thus and sees thus, this view is already severed, already relinquished, and already departed; other views will no longer be continued, will not arise, and will not be produced.”
"Aggivessana!
Many people hold the same view as you; many people hold such a view and speak thus, and you are similar to them, Aggivessana!"
If those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas abandon such views and do not give rise to other views, such śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are indeed very few in this world.
"Fire-worshipper!
There are three kinds of views. What are the three?
There is one who holds such a view and speaks thus:
"I accept everything.
Furthermore, there is another who holds such a view and speaks thus:
"I do not tolerate anything at all.
Furthermore, there is another who holds such a view and speaks thus:
"I tolerate one thing, and I do not tolerate one thing."
"Aggivessana!
If one says 'I am all-enduring,' this view arises together with greed and is not free from greed;
it arises together with hatred and is not free from hatred; it arises together with delusion and is not free from delusion."
It is bound, not free from bondage; it is affliction, not purification; it is a source of grasping and the arising of defiled attachment.
If one holds such a view as:
"I do not tolerate anything at all."

This view is not associated with greed, not associated with hatred, and not associated with delusion; it is pure and not a defilement, dissociated from fetters and not bound by them; one does not delight in it, does not grasp it, and does not give rise to attachment toward it.
"Aggivessana!
If you hold such a view as:
'I accept this, but I do not accept that.'"
If one endures it, then greed arises, and so on, up to the arising of attachment; if one views it thus and does not endure it, then greed is abandoned, and so on, up to the non-arising of attachment.
That learned noble disciple trains himself thus:
"If I were to hold such a view and speak thus:
'I tolerate everything.'"
Thus, one will be reproached and interrogated by two kinds of people. What are these two?
They are those who are entirely intolerant, and those who are tolerant in one instance but intolerant in another; one will be reproached by such as these.

Because of being reproached, one is interrogated; because of being interrogated, one is harmed. Seeing himself reproached, interrogated, and harmed, he then abandons his view, and other views no longer arise.
"In this way, having severed views, abandoned views, and detached from views, other views no longer continue; they do not arise and are not produced.
Thus does that learned noble disciple train:
"If I were to hold such a view and speak thus: [text continues]"
Regarding the statement,
"I do not tolerate anything," there are two kinds of double interrogations. What are these two?
That is to say: "I endure all things," and "I endure one thing but do not endure another.
When these two reproaches and two interrogations reach the point where they no longer continue, they neither arise nor are produced.
"Thus, that learned noble disciple trains himself in this way:
'If I were to hold such a view and speak thus:
"I tolerate one thing, but I do not tolerate another."'"
"There are then two charges and two reproaches.
What are the two?
They are as follows: such a view and such a doctrine:"
“I endure all things, as well as all things I do not endure.
When these two reproaches have thus reached the point where they no longer continue and neither arise nor are produced—
furthermore, O Aggivessana!

In this way, a noble disciple should contemplate this coarse body of the four great elements as impermanent, contemplate its arising and ceasing, contemplate detachment from desire, contemplate its cessation, and contemplate relinquishment.

If a noble disciple contemplates impermanence, contemplates cessation, contemplates dispassion, contemplates extinction, and dwells in equanimity, then regarding that body, the desire for the body, mindfulness of the body, affection for the body, defilement of the body, and attachment to the body will be forever extinguished and no longer persist.
"Aggivessana!
There are three kinds of feeling: namely, painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
What is the cause of these three kinds of feeling?"
By what is it accumulated?
By what is it produced?
By what does it evolve?
That is to say, these three feelings have contact as their cause, contact as their origin, contact as their birth, and contact as their transformation.
With the arising of this or that contact, there is the arising of feeling;
with the cessation of this or that contact, there is the cessation of feeling—its pacification, its cooling, and its total extinction.
Regarding these three feelings— feeling pain, feeling pleasure, and feeling neither-pain-nor-pleasure—
he understands, as they truly are, their arising, their cessation, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them.

Having understood them as they truly are, he then contemplates those feelings as impermanent, observes their arising and passing away, observes dispassion toward them, observes their cessation, and observes relinquishment.

He knows as it truly is the feeling limited by the body; he knows as it truly is the feeling limited by life. When his body breaks up and his life ends, at that very moment all feelings are extinguished without remainder, utterly extinguished.
He thinks to himself:
"When a pleasant feeling is experienced, the body also perishes;
when a painful feeling is experienced, the body also perishes."
When one experiences a sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant, the body likewise dissolves, and this constitutes the complete end of suffering.
Regarding that pleasant sensation, one is neither bound nor unbound;
