regarding that painful sensation, one is neither bound nor unbound.
Regarding the sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant, one is detached and unbound.
From what is one detached?

One is detached from greed, hatred, and delusion; one is detached from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering. I declare that these are called the "abandonment of suffering."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra had been ordained for only half a month.
He was standing behind the Buddha, holding a fan and fanning him.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra had this thought:
"The World-Honored One has praised various teachings for the purpose of severing desire, departing from desire, the total extinction of desire, and the relinquishing of desire."

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra observed those various phenomena as impermanent; he observed their arising and ceasing, observed dispassion, observed cessation, and observed relinquishment. Thus, the outflows did not arise, and his mind attained liberation.
At that time, the renunciant of the non-Buddhist sect Dīrghanakha became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.

Having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, realized the Dharma, entered the Dharma, and crossed beyond all doubts, he was no longer dependent on others for his liberation; having entered the True Dharma and Vinaya, he attained fearlessness. He then rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, paid homage to the Buddha, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha:
"I wish to go forth in the True Dharma and Vinaya, receive full ordination, and practice the holy life within the Buddha’s teachings."
The Buddha said to the renunciant of the Long-nailed Heretical School:
"You have attained ordination and full admission into this True Dharma and Discipline, and have become a member of the community of bhikṣus."
He was immediately granted the going forth as a *svāgata-bhikṣu*. He then reflected:
"For what reason do sons of good family shave off their hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and with right faith leave the home life for homelessness to study the Path?"...
...until his mind was well-liberated and he attained arhatship.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Śāriputra and the Venerable Dīrghanakha, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Saṃyukta Āgama, Scroll 34 and Scroll 35,
translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Song Dynasty.
35.970 (970) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa of the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, there was a renunciant of a non-Buddhist sect named Śarabha living by the side of the Sumāgadhā Pond. Among his own assembly, he made this proclamation:
“I know all the teachings of the Śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya; I have already known those teachings and the Vinaya, and have completely abandoned them.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus dressed in the morning, took up their bowls, and entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms.
I heard that there was a non-Buddhist named Śarabha who lived by the side of the Sumāgadhā Pond in Rājagṛha, and who made this proclamation among his own followers:
"I have fully understood all the teachings and the discipline of the śramaṇa sons of the Śākya; having first understood their teachings and discipline, I have subsequently abandoned them."

Having heard these words, he finished his almsround, returned to the vihāra, put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This morning, having dressed and taken up our bowls, we entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms and heard that there is a renunciant of a non-Buddhist sect named Śarabha, who dwells by the side of the Sūmāgadhā Pond in Rājagṛha and proclaims among his own assembly:
"I have fully understood the Dharma of the Śramaṇa Śākyaputrīyas; having understood their Dharma and Vinaya, I have subsequently abandoned them."
"Excellent!
World-Honored One!
You should go yourself to the side of that Sumāgadhā Pond out of compassion for them!"

At that time, the World-Honored One silently gave his consent; then, in the late afternoon, he arose from meditation and went to the side of Lake Sumāgadhā, to where the non-Buddhist Śarabha was staying.
At that time, the renunciant outsider Śarabha saw the Blessed One approaching from afar; he immediately prepared a seat and invited the Buddha to sit.
The Buddha sat down and addressed Śarabha, saying:
"Is it true that you spoke these words:..."
"Have you said: 'I have fully understood all the teachings and discipline of the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas;
having understood their teachings and discipline, I have then abandoned them'?"
At that time, Śāradvatīputra remained silent and did not answer.
The Buddha said to Śāradvatīputra:
“You should speak now; why do you remain silent?”
"If that which you know is complete, I shall rejoice in it;
if it is not complete, I shall cause you to fulfill it.
At that time, Śāradvatīputra remained silent as before.
Thus he spoke a second and a third time, yet Śāradvatīputra remained silent each time.
Then, a fellow practitioner of the holy life said to Śāradvatīputra:
"Master, you ought to go to the śramaṇa Gautama and speak of what you know and see; now that the śramaṇa Gautama has come here himself, why do you not speak?"
The śramaṇa Gautama further addressed the teacher, saying:
"If it is already fulfilled, I shall rejoice in it;
if it is not yet fulfilled, I shall cause it to be fulfilled."
"Why do you remain silent and not provide an explanation?
When Śāradvatīputra’s fellow practitioner disciples urged him thus, he remained silent once more.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāradvatīputra:
"Furthermore, if someone were to say,
'The ascetic Gautama is not a Tathāgata, an Arhat,
a Samyaksaṃbuddha,' and I were to admonish him well and question him well, at the time of such good admonition and questioning, he would instead speak at length about various external matters."
Some, being obscured by anger, resentment, pride, or concealment, are blocked and unable to endure it, having no way to manifest [the truth];
others remain silent with shame, bowing their heads and reflecting privately within themselves, as Śarabha does now.

If, furthermore, someone were to say that the Śramaṇa Gautama has neither the True Dharma nor the Discipline, and I were to admonish him well and question him well, he too would remain silent just as you do today.

Furthermore, if there were anyone who said that the disciples of the Śramaṇa Gautama are not well-directed, and I were to admonish and question them skillfully, they too would remain silent, just as you do today.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had let out a lion’s roar beside the Sumāgadhā Pond, he rose from his seat and departed.
Then, a fellow practitioner of the holy life named Śarabha said to Śarabha:
"It is like a bull whose two horns have been cut off; it enters an empty cow-pen, kneels upon the ground, and bellows loudly."
The teacher is also like this: he utters a lion’s roar among those who are not disciples of the Śramaṇa Gautama.
It is just as when a woman wishes to produce the voice of a man, yet the sound she emits is still a woman’s voice;
so too is the teacher, for he utters a lion’s roar among those who are not disciples of the Śramaṇa Gautama.
For example, it is like a jackal that wishes to make the sound of a fox, yet when it utters a sound, it still makes the sound of a jackal;
so too is this teacher, who wishes to let out a lion’s roar amidst a group that is not the assembly of disciples of the Śramaṇa Gautama.
Then, having rebuked and censured Śāradvatīputra’s fellow practitioner in his presence, he rose from his seat and departed.
(971) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove of Kalanda.
At that time, there was a renunciant of the non-Buddhist sect named Upatiṣya living by the side of the Śīrṣavatī Pond in Rājagṛha. Standing by that pond, he spoke these words among his own followers:
"I shall recite a verse; if anyone can provide a response to it, I will practice the holy life under them."

At that time, a great number of bhikṣus, having dressed in the morning and taken up their bowls, entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms. They heard that there was a renunciant of the non-Buddhist path named Sthavira who resided by the side of Lake Sumāgadhā, and who spoke thus among his own assembly:
"I shall recite a verse; whoever is able to respond to it, I shall practice the holy life under him."

Having finished his almsround, he returned to the vihāra, put away his robes and bowl, and after washing his feet, went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This morning, as I entered the city with a large company of bhikṣus to beg for alms, I heard that there is an ascetic of a non-Buddhist sect named Upatiṣya who dwells by the side of Lake Sumāgadhā. Among his own followers, he has made this proclamation:
"I shall recite a verse; whoever is able to respond to it, I will practice the holy life under him."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will go there in person out of compassion!
At that time, the World-Honored One gave his consent by remaining silent; later that day, during the hour of the monkey, he arose from meditation and went to the side of the Sumāgadhā Pond.
At that time, the senior renunciant of the non-Buddhist sect saw the World-Honored One from afar; he immediately prepared a seat and invited the Buddha to sit.
Once the World-Honored One was seated, he addressed the senior renunciant of the non-Buddhist sect, saying:
"Is it true that you spoke these words:..."
"Did I say, 'If you can respond to a verse I recite, I shall practice the holy life under you'?
"You may now speak the verse; I am able to provide the reply."
Then that non-Buddhist practitioner immediately stacked rope beds to form a high seat and ascended it himself.
He then spoke this verse:
“The bhikṣu lives by the Dharma, And does not terrify sentient beings.”
"With a mind tranquil, practice equanimity and renunciation; uphold the precepts and accord with cessation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts of that senior non-Buddhist practitioner, spoke this verse:
"If you are able to act in accordance with the verses you have spoken,
I shall regard you as a true gentleman;
yet observing what you have said now, your words and actions do not correspond."
Tranquil and self-subdued, do not terrify living beings;
with a mind that practices tranquility and detachment, one who upholds the pure precepts follows the discipline of serenity,
remaining free from evil in body, speech, and mind.
“Those who properly restrain themselves in their dwelling and do not allow themselves to become heedless are said to be ‘conforming,’ ‘tamed,’ and ‘at peace.
At that time, the elder renunciant of the non-Buddhist sect had this thought:
“The śramaṇa Gautama already knows my mind.
He immediately descended from his bed, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“May I now go forth in this True Dharma and Vinaya, receive full ordination, and become a bhikṣu?”
The Buddha said to the senior non-Buddhist renunciant:
"Now you may go forth in this True Dharma and Discipline, receive full ordination, and become a bhikṣu."
Thus, having been granted the going-forth as a renunciant by the elder, and having become a bhikṣu, he reflected:
"For what reason do sons of good family shave off their hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and with right faith go forth from the home life to train in the path..."
...until his mind was well-liberated, and he attained arhatship.
972 (972) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, a great number of brahmins who had gone forth from the household life were staying by the side of Lake Sumāgadhā; having gathered together in one place, they engaged in this discussion:
"Such is the truth of the brahmins; such is the truth of the brahmins."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those many brahmin renunciants, went to the side of Lake Sumāgadhā.
When the many brahmin renunciants saw the Buddha approaching from afar, they immediately prepared a seat for him and invited the Buddha to take his place.
The Buddha took his seat and addressed the brahmin renunciants:
"Gathered together here by the side of this Lake Sumāgadhā, what have you been discussing?"
The brahmin renunciant addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Gautama! A great number of us brahmin renunciants have gathered here for this assembly and engaged in such a discussion:”
"Such is the true reality of the brahmins;
such is the true reality of the brahmins.
The Buddha addressed the brahmin renunciant:
“There are three kinds of Brahmins who are true, whom I have personally realized and awakened to as perfectly enlightened ones, and whom I then proclaim to others.
You, O Brahmin renunciant, have spoken thus:
‘Not harming any living being is the truth of the Brahmins; it is not false.’”

If one does not become attached to those [views]—whether claiming "I am superior," "I am equal," or "I am inferior"—but instead maintains a mental image of loving-kindness toward all the world, this is called the first Brahmin truth. This I have personally realized, attained perfect enlightenment, and proclaimed for the sake of others.
"Furthermore, Brahmin, you have spoken thus:
'Whatever is subject to arising is also subject to cessation; this is the true reality, not a falsehood.'"
"Furthermore, not being attached even to that ultimate truth, one observes the arising and ceasing of all worlds; this is called the second Brahmin’s ultimate truth."
"Furthermore, the Brahmin speaks thus:
'There is no locus for a self, nor is there any entity whatsoever; there is no locus for a self, nor is there any entity whatsoever—this is the ultimate truth, not a falsehood.'"

As previously explained, up to: "In that regard, there is no attachment whatsoever; in all the world, there is nothing resembling a self. This is called the third true reality of a brahmin, which I have personally realized, attained perfect enlightenment regarding, and proclaimed for the sake of others.
At that time, the many brahmin renunciants remained silent.
Then the World-Honored One thought to himself:

"Now, having eclipsed those fools and slain those wicked ones, not a single person among this assembly is able to reflect for themselves and desire to create the causes and conditions to practice the holy life within the Dharma of the śramaṇa Gautama."
Having understood this, he rose from his seat and departed. 973 (973) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kuśinagara in the Gośīrṣa Garden, and the Venerable Ānanda was also staying there.

At that time, there was a renunciant of a non-Buddhist sect named Caṇḍa who approached the Venerable Ānanda. After exchanging greetings and pleasantries with the Venerable Ānanda, he sat down to one side and asked the Venerable Ānanda:
"For what reason have you gone forth under the Śramaṇa Gautama to practice the holy life?"
Ānanda replied,
“It is for the sake of severing greed, hatred, and delusion that he has gone forth from home to practice the holy life.
Cāṇḍa asked again:
“Is he able to teach the abandonment of greed, hatred, and delusion?
Ānanda replied, “I, too,
am able to teach the abandonment of greed, hatred, and delusion.”
Cāṇḍa asked again:
"What faults and perils do you see in greed, hatred, and delusion that you speak of abandoning greed, hatred, and delusion?"
Ānanda replied:

"Because the mind is obscured and hindered by the defilement of lustful attachment, one may harm oneself, or harm others, or harm both; one incurs fault in the present life, incurs fault in future lives, or incurs fault in both the present and future lives. Such a mind constantly harbors sorrow and experiences feelings of suffering."
If one is obscured by hatred or obscured by delusion, one harms oneself, harms others, and harms both oneself and others, even constantly harboring sorrow and experiencing painful sensations.

Furthermore, sensual desire is blinding, it is being sightless, it is a lack of wisdom, it is the weakening of the power of insight, and it is an obstruction; it is not clarity, it is not equal enlightenment, and it does not lead toward Nirvana.
It is the same for hatred and delusion.
Because I perceive that greed, hatred, and delusion possess such faults and calamities, I teach the severing of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Canda asked again:
"What benefit do you see in abandoning greed, hatred, and delusion that you speak of abandoning greed, hatred, and delusion?"
Ānanda replied:
"Having severed craving and desire, one does not harm oneself, nor does one harm others, nor does one harm both;

furthermore, one incurs no fault in the present life, no fault in future lives, and no fault in both the present and future lives; rather, the mind and mental factors constantly maintain joy and experience pleasant sensations."
Hatred and delusion are likewise.

In this very life, one is constantly free from burning affliction; without waiting for a future time, there are those who attain realization through other conditions in this present life and know it for themselves.
"Because one sees such merits and benefits as these, it is said that one should abandon greed, hatred, and delusion.
Cāṇḍa asked again:
"Venerable Ānanda!"
“Is there a path and a practice, through the cultivation and repeated cultivation of which one can sever greed, hatred,
and delusion? Ānanda replied, “There is.”
"That is to say, the Eightfold Noble Path—right view, up to and including right concentration.
The ascetic Caṇḍa said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"This is indeed the noble path, the noble track; by practicing and cultivating it repeatedly, one can sever greed, hatred, and delusion."
At that time, the non-Buddhist ascetic Caṇḍa, having heard what the Venerable Ānanda had said, rejoiced and expressed his approval;
he rose from his seat and departed. 974 (974). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Then, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to the Venerable Śāriputra in various ways, instructing, exhorting, illuminating, and gladdening him;
having instructed, exhorted, illuminated, and gladdened him, he remained silent.
Then, having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Śāriputra rejoiced and, with his head bowed in homage at the Buddha’s feet,
departed. At that time, a renunciant of another sect named Pūlūtika was coming along the same road and asked the Venerable Śāriputra,
“From where have you come?”
Śāriputra replied: "Aggivessana!
I have come from my World-Honored One, having heard the Master’s teaching on the Dharma of instruction."
Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra asked the Venerable Śāriputra:
"Are you still not free from 'milk,' having heard the instructions and teachings from your teacher?
Śāriputra replied:
"Fire-kindler!
I have not been separated from the milk; I heard the teaching of the instructions from the Great Master.
Pūlūtika said to the Venerable Śāriputra:
"I have long since abandoned milk and discarded the teachings and instructions spoken by my teacher.

Śāriputra said: "Your Dharma is a poorly taught Dharma and Vinaya; it is a false awakening, not leading to liberation, nor is it the path of true enlightenment. It is a destructive teaching, a non-praiseworthy teaching, and a teaching that cannot be relied upon. Furthermore, your teacher is not a Truly Enlightened One (Samyaksaṃbuddha); therefore, you have quickly abandoned the milk and departed from your teacher’s instruction."
It is, for example, like a cow that is coarse, fierce, and restless, and yields little milk; when her calf drinks her milk, it quickly leaves.

In the same way, this is a poorly taught Dharma and Vinaya, characterized by unwholesome thoughts, not leading to liberation, not being the path to perfect awakening, a corrupting teaching, one unworthy of praise, and not a dharma upon which one can rely.
Furthermore, that teacher is not one who has attained perfect enlightenment; therefore, quickly abandon the teacher’s instructions.
My Dharma is the True Dharma and the Discipline; it is the Good Enlightenment, the path to the Perfect Enlightenment of deliverance—indestructible, praiseworthy, and worthy of reliance.
Furthermore, that Great Teacher is the Truly and Fully Enlightened One; therefore, one drinks his milk for a long time, listening to and receiving the instructions he teaches.
Just as when a calf drinks from a cow that is neither coarse nor wild and possesses abundant milk, it does not grow weary even after drinking for a long time.
“Such is my Dharma; it is the True Dharma and Discipline, wherein one may even hear the instructions on the Dharma for a long time.
Then, Pūrṇa Kāśyapa said to Śāriputra, “You have gained a great and excellent benefit, that within the True Dharma and Discipline you may even hear the instructions on the Dharma for a long time.”
At that time, the non-Buddhist renunciant Pūlūtika, having heard what Śāriputra had said, rejoiced and approved, and departed from the path. 975 (975). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the ascetic Pūraṇa Kāśyapa came to where the Buddha was staying; after exchanging greetings and polite inquiries with the World-Honored One, he withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Gautama!..."
Recently, a great multitude of various heterodox renunciants, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas gathered in the Hall of the Unprecedented and held this discussion:

"The wisdom of the śramaṇa Gautama is like an empty house; he cannot establish a formal discourse amidst the great assembly regarding what is appropriate and what is inappropriate, or what is fitting and what is unfitting."
It is like a blind ox that wanders only along the edges and does not enter the middle of the field;
so too is the śramaṇa Gautama: there is for him neither what is appropriate nor inappropriate, neither what is fitting nor unfitting.
The Buddha said to Pūraṇa Kāśyapa:
"These various debates of the non-Buddhists, concerning what is appropriate and inappropriate, or consistent and inconsistent, are like the play of children within the Noble Dharma and Vinaya."
Suppose there were a man, eighty or ninety years old, with white hair and fallen teeth, who played childish games, kneading clay to fashion elephants, horses, and various other forms;
everyone would say of him, "This is an old child."
"So it is, Aggivessana!

Various doctrines—whether they be right or wrong, consistent or inconsistent—are, within the Noble Dharma and Discipline, like the play of children; yet therein, there is no skillful means appropriate for a bhikkhu."
Pūrvāśvatika said to the Buddha:
“Gautama! In what respect is there that which a bhikṣu should apply as a skillful means?”
The Buddha told the non-Buddhists:
"To cause that which is impure to become pure—this is what is appropriate for a bhikṣu’s skillful means.
To cause that which is undisciplined to become disciplined—this is what is appropriate for a bhikṣu’s skillful means."
To cause those who are not yet settled to attain right concentration is what is appropriate for a bhikṣu’s skillful means.
To cause those who are not yet liberated to attain liberation is what is appropriate for a bhikṣu’s skillful means.

To cause what is unsevered to be severed, what is unknown to be known, what is uncultivated to be cultivated, and what is unattained to be attained—this is called the appropriate application of skillful means for a bhikṣu.
How does one cause that which is impure to become pure?
This means that for those whose precepts are impure, one causes them to become pure.
How does one cause those who are undisciplined to become disciplined?
It refers to the faculty of the eye.
To cause the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—which have not been subdued—to become subdued; this is called "subduing those who are unsubdued."
How does one cause those who are not in meditative absorption to attain it? That is to say, by causing the mind that is not correctly concentrated to attain meditative absorption.
How does one cause those who are not liberated to attain liberation?
That is to say, it brings about the liberation of the mind from greed, hatred, and delusion, which it had not previously attained.
What is meant by "not abandoning that which should be abandoned"?
It refers to ignorance and craving for existence, which are not abandoned but must be abandoned.
What is meant by "making known that which was not known"?
It refers to name-and-form (nāmarūpa), making known that which was not known.
What is meant by "cultivating that which was not cultivated"?
That is to say, regarding serenity (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), one causes those not yet cultivated to be cultivated.
How does one cause what has not been attained to be attained?
It refers to parinirvāṇa, which one causes to be attained; this is called what should be practiced by a bhikṣu through skillful means (*upāya*).
Pūrvailūka addressed the Buddha, saying: “Gautama!
This principle is appropriate for the skillful means of a bhikṣu; it is appropriate for the skillful means of a steadfast bhikṣu—namely, the exhaustion of all outflows (āsravas).”
At that time, the renunciant of the Pūraṇa-Kāśyapa school, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and approved, rose from his seat, and departed.
976 (976) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.

At that time, there was a renunciant of a non-Buddhist sect named Śiva, who came to where the Buddha was staying. After exchanging greetings and expressions of courtesy with the World-Honored One, he withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Gautama!..."
"What is meant by 'training'?
By what is one said to be a trainee? And how does one train?
The Buddha told Śiva:
"One trains in what is to be trained; therefore, it is called 'training.
Śiva addressed the Buddha:
"In what does one train?"
The Buddha told Śiva:
"At the appropriate time, train in the higher training of virtue (adhiśīla), the higher training of mind (adhicitta), and the higher training of wisdom (adhiprajñā).
Śiva addressed the Buddha:

"If an Arhat bhikṣu has exhausted all outflows, accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, attained his own benefit, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is well-liberated through right knowledge—at that time, what further training would he have?"
The Buddha told Śiva:
"When an Arhat bhikṣu has exhausted all outflows, up to being well-liberated through right knowledge—at that time, he realizes that sensual desire is forever exhausted without remainder;
he realizes that ill will and delusion are forever exhausted without remainder. Therefore, he no longer creates further evils and constantly practices all forms of goodness."
"Śiva! This is called training in that which is to be trained.
When the renunciant Śiva, a follower of non-Buddhist paths, heard what the Buddha had said, he rejoiced and approved, rose from his seat, and departed.
977 (Ninana-nanana). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.

At that time, the renunciant Śiva, a follower of non-Buddhist paths, approached the place where the Buddha was. After exchanging greetings and polite inquiries with the World-Honored One, he withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Gautama! There are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:

‘Whatever a person knows and perceives, all that is caused by what was done in the past. By practicing various austerities, one causes past karma to be exhausted; by no longer creating new karma, one severs the causal conditions, so that in future lives there will be no further outflows.’”
"Because all taints (āsrava) are exhausted, karma is exhausted; because karma is exhausted, suffering is exhausted; one who has exhausted suffering reaches the ultimate end of suffering.
Now, what is it that you, Gautama, teach?
The Buddha told Śiva:
"Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas speak thus only in a vague and superficial manner; they are neither discerning nor systematic, being foolish, unskilled, and lacking in discrimination."

Why is this? Some sufferings arise from wind, which sentient beings perceive; some arise from phlegm, some from saliva, or some from a combination of these humors (*sannipāta*); some arise from self-inflicted harm, some from harm inflicted by others, or some due to seasonal changes.

Those who harm themselves do so by either plucking out their hair, or plucking out their beard; or by constantly standing with hands raised; or by squatting on the ground; or by lying in ashes or dust; or by lying upon thorns; or by lying upon pestles or wooden boards; or by lying upon the ground smeared with cow dung; or by lying in water; or by bathing three times a day; or by standing on one foot while the body revolves with the sun.
Śivaka, such diligent practice amidst these manifold sufferings is called self-harm.
As for harm by others, it refers to having one's body harmed in various ways by the hands, stones, knives, staves, and so forth of others; this is called harm by others.

Śiva! Furthermore, if one is harmed by the seasons—such as the great cold of winter, the great heat of spring, or the simultaneous presence of both cold and heat in summer—this is called being harmed by the seasonal elements.
The world is real and not false, Śiva!
There is this reality in the world that it is afflicted by wind and even afflicted by the seasonal shifts; those sentient beings perceive it as it truly is.
"You yourself also have this affliction: the sensations caused by wind, phlegm, spittle, and even the injuries of the seasonal humors; you should perceive them as they truly are, Śivaka!"

If those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas claim that everything known and perceived by people is caused solely by past karma, they abandon the reality of the world and follow their own views, making false assertions.
"Śiva! There are five causes and five conditions that give rise to mental states of sorrow and suffering.
What are these five?
Śivaka, it means that due to the obsession of sensual desire, and conditioned by the obsession of sensual desire, mental states of sorrow and suffering arise;

and due to the obsessions of ill will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-regret, and doubt, and conditioned by the obsessions of ill will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-regret, and doubt, those mental states of sorrow and suffering arise. Śivaka!
These are called the five causes and five conditions that give rise to mental states of sorrow and suffering. Śiva!
There are five causes and five conditions by which mental states of sorrow and suffering do not arise.
What are the five? They are as follows:

when mental factors of sorrow and suffering arise due to the entanglement of sensual desire and conditioned by the entanglement of sensual desire, if one is free from that entanglement of sensual desire, those mental factors of sorrow and suffering do not arise. These are called the five causes and five conditions for the non-arising of mental factors of sorrow and suffering.
Śiva, there is another way to attain freedom from the fever of existence in this very life, independent of time, directly realized,
and personally experienced through self-awareness; that is the Noble Eightfold Path— right view, up to and including right concentration.
When this Dharma was being taught, the renunciant Śīva of the non-Buddhist sect became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.

At that time, the renunciant Śīva of the non-Buddhist sect saw the Dharma, attained the Dharma, knew the Dharma, and entered the Dharma; he was freed from all doubt, no longer dependent on others, having entered the True Dharma and Discipline, and attained fearlessness.
He immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
May I now go forth in this true Dharma and Vinaya, receive full ordination, and attain the status of a bhikṣu?”
The Buddha told Śiva:
"You may now go forth into homelessness... as described above, up until: "...with a mind well-liberated, you have attained arhatship."
978 (978). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Village of Nāla, in the Amba Grove of Fine Garments.

At that time, there was in the village of Nāla a merchant leader who had left the household life as a non-Buddhist renunciant; he was one hundred and twenty years old, advanced in age and mature in faculties, and was honored and supported by the śramaṇas, brahmins, elders, and householders of the village of Nāla as if he were an arhat.

That renunciant of the non-Buddhist sect, the merchant leader, previously had a kinsman who, having passed away, was reborn in heaven. Having seen the renunciant, the merchant leader, from that celestial realm, he thought:

"I wish to go and instruct that renunciant, the merchant leader, to approach the World-Honored One and practice the holy life; yet I fear he will not follow my words. I shall now go there and cause him to pose questions through mental discourse."
He immediately descended to the village of Nāla and went to where the renunciant of the non-Buddhist sect, the merchant leader, was staying; there he spoke a verse, asking:
"How is it that one who is a bad friend manifests the appearance of a good friend?"
"How is it that a spiritual friend is like one's own body?
Why seek cessation? How does one leave behind the blazing fire?

"If you, O Seer, should pose these questions to him using this discourse on the meaning, and if there is one who can clearly explain its significance in response to you, you may then go forth under him and practice the holy life."
Then the renunciant of the non-Buddhist sect, the merchant leader, having received the question from the deva, went to Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and asked him this doctrinal inquiry in verse.
Since even Pūraṇa Kāśyapa himself did not understand it, how could he possibly answer?

At that time, the renunciant Māṭhara the merchant leader went in turn to the places of Maskari Gośālīputra, Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra, Ajita Keśakambalin, Kakuda Kātyāyana, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra; in each case, he questioned them with this same verse of inquiry, but none were able to answer.
At that time, the merchant leader, who had gone forth as an ascetic of a non-Buddhist sect, thought to himself:
"I have questioned these teachers who have gone forth with this very doctrine, yet none of them were able to answer. Now I wish to go forth once more;
however, since I currently possess wealth and treasures, it would be better for me to return home and indulge in the five sensual pleasures."
He further thought to himself:
"I should now go to visit the śramaṇa Gautama.

However, those elders, teachers, śramaṇas, and brahmins such as Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and others were all unable to answer me; yet the śramaṇa Gautama has only recently left home at a young age—how could he possibly understand?"

However, I have heard what the elders have said: "Do not look down upon those who have newly begun their studies or young novices. There may be some young śramaṇas who, though young in their renunciation, possess great power of virtue. I shall now go to the śramaṇa Gautama.
Having approached him, he questioned him with the intent and thoughts of that philosophical system, as described in the verse.
At that time, the World-Honored One knew the thoughts in the mind of that merchant leader.
He then spoke in verse:
"What is a bad friend?
One who feels true shame and revulsion in their heart, yet says with their mouth, 'My mind is one with yours.'"
One who does not delight in shared undertakings should be known as no true friend;
though their mouth speaks words of affection, their heart does not correspond with reality.
Since their actions do not accord with one's own, the wise should recognize this.
This is called a false friend, who manifests the appearance of a true friend and regards himself as being of one essence with you.
What, then, is a true friend?
Those who are of one essence with oneself are not those who are merely "good friends" (kalyāṇamitra);
for they do not restrain one from negligence, but rather obstruct and ruin one while harboring doubts, seeking out one's vulnerabilities.
One should instead find rest in the true good friend.
Like a child lying in his father’s lap, unheard by those standing by;
one should know that the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is thus. For what reason do they seek cessation?
It is the place where joy arises, cool and praised with acclaim.
Cultivating the fruit of benefit brings about coolness and eternal cessation;
therefore, one seeks its eradication.
How does one become free from the burning heat?
The taste of tranquil stillness, knowing the taste of seclusion,
and being free from the fever of evil; drinking the taste of the joy of Dharma,
extinguishing the fire of desire— this is called being free from the fever.
At that time, the renunciant of the non-Buddhist sect, the merchant leader, thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama knows my thoughts.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"May I now enter the true Dharma and Vinaya of the śramaṇa Gautama to practice the holy life, go forth, receive full ordination, and become a member of the bhikṣu-saṃgha?"
The Buddha said to the renunciant of the non-Buddhist sect, the Merchant Leader:
“You may now practice the holy life within this True Dharma and Discipline; you may go forth, receive full ordination, and attain the status of a bhikṣu.”
Having thus gone forth, he reflected until his mind was well-liberated, and he attained arhatship. 979 (979). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Kuśinagara, in the grove of the twin śāla trees at the place where the Mallas were born.
At that time, when the time for the World-Honored One’s parinirvāṇa had arrived, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Prepare a corded couch for the World-Honored One between the twin trees with its head to the north; today at midnight, the Tathāgata will enter parinirvāṇa in the nirvana without remainder.”

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having received these instructions, prepared a rope couch with its head toward the north between the twin trees. Having finished, he approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Having already prepared a rope bed between the twin trees with the head toward the north.

Then, the World-Honored One went to the space between the twin trees and lay down upon the rope bed with his head to the north, reclining on his right side, with one foot resting upon the other, fixing his mind on the perception of light, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.

At that time, there was a non-Buddhist renunciant named Subhadra in the kingdom of Kuśinagara, who was one hundred and twenty years old; being advanced in years and mature in his faculties, he was honored and supported by the people of Kuśinagara as if he were an Arhat.

That Subhadra, having gone forth as a monk, heard that the World-Honored One was to attain parinirvāṇa in the nirvana without remainder this very day at midnight. However, he remained there with hope, thinking, "I have a doubt; the Śramaṇa Gautama has the power to awaken me. I shall now go to the Śramaṇa Gautama and ask about my doubt."
He immediately departed from Kuśinagara and went to where the World-Honored One was.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was walking up and down outside the gate of the garden.
Then, Subhadra spoke to Ānanda, saying:

"I have heard that today at midnight the śramaṇa Gautama has entered parinirvāṇa in the nirvana without remainder. I have certain doubts and remain here in hope, for the śramaṇa Gautama possesses the power to awaken me."
"If Ānanda does not mind the trouble, please go on my behalf and say to the Gautama: 'If you have a little leisure, might you answer the questions I ask?
Ānanda replied, "Do not press the World-Honored One!"
"The World-Honored One is utterly exhausted.
Thus did Subhadda repeatedly entreat the Venerable Ānanda, but the Venerable Ānanda likewise refused him three times.
Subhadra said:

"I have heard that in ancient times, the elder masters who had gone forth from home used to say that a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world only once in a very long time, like the udumbara flower."

"Now, the Tathāgata shall attain parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder at midnight tonight. I currently dwell with doubt regarding the Dharma, yet I abide in faith. The Śramaṇa Gautama possesses the power to awaken me; if Ānanda does not mind the trouble, please speak on my behalf to the Śramaṇa Gautama."
Ānanda replied again,
"Subhadra! Do not press the World-Honored One!"
“The World-Honored One is utterly exhausted today.
At that time, the World-Honored One, hearing with his divine ear the conversation between Ānanda and Subhadra as they came and went, addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Do not prevent the non-Buddhist ascetic Subhadra!”
He was then invited to enter and inquire about his doubts. Why was this?
Because this was the final debate with an outsider ascetic, and he was the last to attain the realization of a "Come, Bhikṣu" disciple, namely Subhadra.

At that time, Subhadra, his roots of goodness having been opened by the World-Honored One, was filled with supreme joy. He approached the World-Honored One, exchanged greetings and words of comfort with him face-to-face, and then withdrew to sit at one side. Having done so, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Gautama!..."
Regarding all the worldly teachers, such as Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and the other five masters, each established a doctrine, saying:
"This is a śramaṇa; this is a śramaṇa."
"How so? Gautama! Is it true that each of these doctrines exists individually?"
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for him:
"At the age of twenty-nine, I left home to cultivate the path of goodness;
from the time I attained enlightenment until now, more than fifty years have passed."
"Endowed with samādhi, clear knowledge, and conduct, constantly practicing pure precepts—apart from this, there is no path; beyond this, there is no śramaṇa.
The Buddha told Subhadra:
"One who does not attain the Eightfold Noble Path within this True Dharma and Discipline shall not attain the first stage of a śramaṇa, nor the second, third, or fourth stages of a śramaṇa."

Subhadra! In this Dharma and Vinaya, those who attain the Eightfold Noble Path attain the first stage of a śramaṇa, and they attain the second, third, and fourth stages of a śramaṇa. Apart from these, there are no śramaṇas among the outsiders; they are merely teachers of heterodox paths, empty śramaṇas and brahmins.
"Therefore, I now let out a lion's roar amidst this assembly.
When he spoke these words of Dharma, the non-Buddhist renunciant Subhadra was distanced from and freed of dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.

At that time, Subhadra saw the Dharma, attained the Dharma, knew the Dharma, and entered the Dharma; he crossed over all doubts, no longer relying on the faith of others nor being led by others, and attained fearlessness within the True Dharma and Discipline.
Rising from his seat, adjusting his robes, and placing his right knee on the ground, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda:

“You have gained a great benefit; you have obtained the Great Teacher as your master. As a disciple of the Great Teacher, you have been rained upon by the Great Teacher, who has poured the rain over your head.”
"If I were now to obtain ordination and full admission into the True Dharma and Vinaya, and attain the status of a bhikṣu, I too would surely obtain such a wholesome benefit!
Then, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"This renunciant of the non-Buddhist sect, Subhadra, now seeks to go forth in the True Dharma and Vinaya and receive full ordination; he shall attain the status of a bhikṣu.
Then the World-Honored One addressed Subhadra:
"Let this bhikṣu come and practice the holy life (brahmacarya)."
At that very moment, the Venerable Subhadra went forth; he received full ordination and attained the status of a bhikṣu.
Reflecting in this manner, his mind became thoroughly liberated, and he attained arhatship.
At that time, the Venerable Subhadra, having attained arhatship and realized the bliss of liberation, thought to himself:
"I cannot bear to witness the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha; I shall enter Parinirvāṇa first."
At that time, after the Venerable Subhadda had first entered parinirvāṇa, the World-Honored One then entered parinirvāṇa.
980 (980). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering through the human realm among the Vajjis and arrived at the kingdom of Vaiśālī, where he stayed in the Multi-storied Lecture Hall beside the Monkey Pond.
At that time, there were many merchants in the kingdom of Vaiśālī who wished to travel toward the kingdom of Takṣaśilā and were making preparations for the journey.
These many merchants heard that the World-Honored One was wandering among the Vṛjis and had arrived at the kingdom of Vaiśālī, staying at the Multi-storied Lecture Hall beside the Monkey Pond.
Having heard this, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha taught the merchants the Dharma in various ways— showing, instructing, illuminating, and gladdening them—
and having shown, instructed, illuminated, and gladdened them, he remained silent.
Then, the merchants rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, paid homage to the Buddha, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

We merchants have made various preparations and wish to travel to the kingdom of Takṣaśilā. We only pray that the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly, will accept our offerings tomorrow morning."
At that time, the World-Honored One granted his consent by remaining silent.

Knowing that the World-Honored One had accepted their invitation, the merchants rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and each returned to their own home. There they prepared various kinds of pure and delicious food and drink, spread out mats and seats, and set out pure water.
At dawn, he dispatched a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The time has come.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly, donned his robes and took up his bowl.
He went to where the merchants were, took a seat, and sat down.
Then, the merchants personally served him pure and delicious food with their own hands.
When the meal was finished and the bowl had been washed, he took a low stool and sat before the great assembly to listen to the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the merchants:
"As you travel through the wilderness, there will be various terrors that cause the heart to tremble and the hair to stand on end."
At that time, one should bring to mind the qualities of the Tathāgata—namely, that he is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and so forth, up to the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
For one who recollects him in this way, fear and dread are eliminated.

Furthermore, regarding the recollection of the Dharma: the Buddha’s True Dharma and Discipline can, in this very life, bring about freedom from the burning fires of affliction; it does not depend on time, it is accessible and immediate, and it is to be personally realized through one's own direct knowledge.
Furthermore, by recollecting the qualities of the Saṃgha— the disciples of the World-Honored One who are well-directed and rightly directed, even unto being the field of merit for the world—
one who recollects in this manner will immediately have their fear removed.
"In a past age, the devas and asuras were engaged in battle.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the host of devas:
'When you are fighting in battle with the asuras, if any among you feel fear, you should call to mind my banner named the Banner of Subjugation (Dhvaja-vinardana).'"
When one contemplates that banner, fear shall be dispelled.
If you do not contemplate my banner, you should contemplate the banner of the devaputra Īśāna;
if you do not contemplate the banner of the devaputra Īśāna, you should contemplate the banner of the devaputra Varuṇa.
"When one brings that banner to mind, fear and terror are immediately dispelled.
Thus it is, O merchants!
Should you experience fear while in the wilderness, you should bring to mind the qualities of the Tathāgata, the qualities of the Dharma, and the qualities of the Saṅgha.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses on rejoicing in offerings for the sake of the merchants of Vaiśālī:
"Make offerings to the community of bhikṣus, Providing food and drink as needed;
With focused mindfulness and careful reflection, Act with equanimity through right awareness."
Pure objects are an excellent field of merit; you all possess them in full.
By virtue of this beneficial merit, may you obtain peace and happiness throughout the long night.
Whatever you seek by generating the aspiration for it, all such manifold benefits shall be fulfilled.
May bipeds and quadrupeds be at peace; may those traveling on the roads be safe.
May they be secure by night and secure by day, free from all evils.
Like a fertile field of rich soil sown with pure and excellent seeds.
Irrigated at the proper time, the moisture brings forth a harvest beyond measure;
pure precepts are a fertile field of merit, and refined delicacies are the seeds sown therein.
Guided by right practice, one shall ultimately bring the wondrous fruit to fruition.
Therefore, one who practices giving and desires to fulfill all virtues should follow the conduct of wisdom;
then all fruits will naturally be complete.
Toward the Honored One, perfected in knowledge and conduct, one should direct a right mind and offer full reverence.
Planting the roots of manifold virtues, one ultimately attains great benefit and merit;
knowing the world as it truly is, one comes to possess right view.
Endowed with the vision of the true path, one is fully equipped and advances upward.
"Far removed from all defilements, Having attained the path to Nirvāṇa,
Reaching the ultimate end of suffering— This is called being endowed with all virtues.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having taught, instructed, illuminated, and gladdened the merchants of Vaiśālī with various dharmas, rose from his seat and departed.
981 (981). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If a bhikṣu dwells in a secluded place, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty house, and at times experiences fear such that his heart is startled and his hair stands on end, he should bring to mind the matters concerning the Tathāgata, the matters concerning the Dharma, and the matters concerning the Saṃgha... as extensively explained before.
"When one recollects the matters of the Tathāgata, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha, fear is immediately dispelled. Monks!
In the past, Śakra Devānām-indra was engaged in battle with the asuras."
At that time, Śakra addressed the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, saying:

"O worthy ones, when the gods and asuras are engaged in battle, if you should feel terror, your hearts should be struck with alarm and your hair stand on end, you must then call to mind my banner for subduing the enemy."
"When one brings that banner to mind, fear and terror are immediately dispelled.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!
If, while in a secluded place, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty house, you experience fear such that your heart is startled and your hair stands on end, you should bring the Tathāgata to mind:
"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, even unto the Buddha, the World-Honored One."
At the moment he brings this to mind, his fear and terror are immediately dispelled. Why is this?

Even Śakra, Lord of the Devas, who harbors greed, hatred, and delusion, and who has not attained liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering, still possesses fear, dread, flight, and the seeking of refuge; yet he still commands the Trāyastriṃśa gods to bring to mind my crushing of the enemy’s banner. How much more so for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, even the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who is free from greed, hatred, and delusion, liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering, and devoid of all fear, dread, or flight—how could he not cause those who bring him to mind to be rid of all fears and terrors?
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 982 (982) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Sāketa, in the Añjana Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra:
“I am able to explain the Dharma both briefly and extensively, yet those who understand it are rare.
The Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“May the World-Honored One please teach the Dharma—whether in brief or in detail—for there are those who truly understand it.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“If there are sentient beings who, regarding their own conscious bodies and all external objects, are free from the notions of ‘self,’ ‘mine,’ and the underlying tendencies of the conceit of ‘I am’; and who, having attained liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, realize for themselves in this very life and dwell in its fulfillment;”

Regarding this aggregate of consciousness and all external objects and signs, there is no "I," "mine," or underlying tendency toward the conceit of "I am" with which to be bound; therefore, my mind is liberated and my wisdom is liberated, and I dwell having personally realized and attained full realization in this very life.

“Śāriputra! Regarding this consciousness-body and all external objects, that bhikṣu is free from the views of ‘I’ and ‘mine,’ as well as the latent tendencies of pride and attachment; he dwells having personally realized and fully attained liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life.

Regarding this consciousness-body and all external objects, being free from the views of ‘I’ and ‘mine,’ as well as the latent tendencies of pride and attachment, his mind is liberated and he dwells having personally realized and fully attained liberation by wisdom in this very life.”

“Śāriputra! If, moreover, a bhikṣu, regarding this consciousness-body and all signs in external objects, is free from the views of ‘I’ and ‘mine,’ and free from the underlying tendencies of the conceit ‘I am,’ then his mind is liberated and his wisdom is liberated; he personally realizes, attests to, and fully dwells in this very life.”
“Śāriputra! If, moreover, a bhikṣu, regarding this conscious body and all external objects, is free from the views of ‘I’ and ‘mine,’ and from the underlying tendencies of pride and attachment;

his mind is liberated and his wisdom is liberated, and he dwells having personally realized and fully attained this in the present life—regarding this conscious body and all external objects, being free from the views of ‘I’ and ‘mine,’ and from the underlying tendencies of pride and attachment, his mind is liberated and his wisdom is liberated, and he dwells having personally realized and fully attained this in the present life.”
“Śāriputra! This is called a bhikṣu who has severed the bonds and fetters of craving, attained the direct realization of pridelessness, and reached the ultimate end of suffering. Śāriputra!”
I have another teaching here regarding the answer I gave to Pāṭikāputra of the Pārāyaṇa:
“The various distinctions of worldly numbers, Wherein one dwells unshakably upon encounter;
Tranquil, free from all dust, With roots uprooted and no longing.”
"Having already crossed the ocean of the three realms of existence, there is no longer any affliction of old age and death.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Śāriputra, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and expressed his approval; he then rose from his seat, paid homage, and departed.
983 (Ninuhachisan). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was also staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Dwelling alone in a quiet place, he reflects thus: "There may be a person who thinks:

'Regarding this consciousness-body and all external objects, I have no view of "I" or "mine," nor the underlying tendencies of the conceit "I am"; and with the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, I personally know, realize, and dwell in full possession of them in this very life.'"

Regarding this body of consciousness and all external objects and signs, there is no view of "I" or "mine," nor the underlying tendency of the conceit "I am. I shall, in that regard, attain liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, realizing it for myself in the present life and dwelling in its fulfillment.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda arose from meditation in the late afternoon, approached the Blessed One, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Blessed One!"
While dwelling alone in seclusion, I had this reflection: "If someone were to say:
'This consciousness-body of mine, along with all external objects and signs... and so on, up to "he personally realizes, attains, and dwells in full possession [of that state]."
The Buddha told Ānanda: “So it is! So it is!”
There is a person who reflects thus:

"In this consciousness-body and all external objects, there are no notions of 'I' or 'mine,' nor the underlying tendencies of pride and attachment; and with the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, I have realized for myself in this very life, attained full realization, and dwell therein."

"Ānanda! That bhikṣu, regarding this consciousness-body and all signs of external objects, is free from the views of 'I' and 'mine,' and from the underlying tendencies of the conceit 'I am. He dwells having personally realized and fully attained liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life;

regarding this consciousness-body and all signs of external objects, he is free from the views of 'I' and 'mine,' and from the underlying tendencies of the conceit 'I am,' and he dwells having personally realized and fully attained that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life."

“Ānanda! If, moreover, a bhikṣu, regarding this conscious body and all external objects and signs, even up to knowing for himself that he has realized and fully dwells [in liberation], this is called a bhikṣu who has severed the fetters of craving and bondage, attained the immediate realization of pride, and reached the ultimate end of suffering.”
"Ānanda! I have this further teaching regarding my response to the questions posed by Pārāyaṇa Udaya:
'Having severed the perception of sensual desire, one is likewise freed from sorrow and suffering.'"
Awakened from sleep, having eliminated the hindrance of restlessness and remorse,
and being purified by abandoning greed and hatred, one contemplates the Dharma before one’s eyes;
I call this wisdom-liberation, which eliminates the darkness of ignorance.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and delighted in it, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
984 (984) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now declare that craving is a net, a glue, a spring, and a lotus root.

These things act as obstructions for sentient beings, as veils, as adhesives, as guardians, as covers, as closures, as blockages, as darkness, as dog entrails, as tangled weeds, and as cotton wool; from this world to another world, and from another world to this world, they cause them to come and go in transmigration, never ceasing to revolve."
“Monks! What kind of craving acts as a net and as glue, even to the point that one wanders and rushes about, such that there is nothing it does not cause to revolve?
That is to say:”

"Because there is a self, there arises: 'I am,' 'I desire,' 'I am thus,' 'I possess,' 'I lack,' 'I am otherwise'; 'I shall be,' 'I shall not be,' 'I shall desire to be,' 'I shall be thus,' 'I shall be otherwise'; or 'it is I,' or 'it is my desire,' or 'it is my being thus,' or 'it is my being otherwise'; or 'it is so,' or 'it is my desire that it be so,' or 'it is my being thus,' or 'it is my being otherwise.'"
"In this way, eighteen modes of craving arise from within. "Monks!

To say 'I am,' and regarding all that exists to say 'I desire' or 'I am such,' up to eighteen modes of craving arising from without—in this manner, the eighteen modes of craving are collectively explained."
"These thirty-six modes of craving arise either in the past, or in the future, or in the present; thus, in total, they are said to be one hundred and eight modes of craving."

"This is called craving; it is a net, it is glue, it is a spring, it is a lotus root. It acts as an obstacle for sentient beings, as a covering, as glue, as a guard, as a lid, as a closure, as a blockage, as darkness, as dog entrails, as tangled grass, and as cotton wool. From this world to another world, and from another world to this world, it flows and rushes back and forth, never ceasing to revolve."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 985 (985). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There is love arising from love, and hatred arising from love;
there is love arising from hatred, and hatred arising from hatred."
"What is meant by 'love arising from love'?

It is when one person has joy, affection, mindfulness, and fondness for a certain being, and another person likewise has joy, affection, mindfulness, and fondness for that same being and follows after them; thinking thus:

'I have joy, affection, mindfulness, and fondness for that being, and since another also has joy, affection, mindfulness, and fondness for them and follows after them, I too shall give rise to affection for that other person.'"
This is called "love arising from love.
How does hatred arise from love?

It is when someone feels joy, affection, mindfulness, and attraction toward certain beings, yet another person feels no joy, affection, mindfulness, or attraction toward them; following this [latter] disposition, they form this thought:

"I have joy, affection, mindfulness, and approval toward sentient beings, yet because another acts with lack of joy, lack of affection, lack of mindfulness, and lack of approval toward them, I give rise to hatred toward that other."
This is called the arising of hatred from craving.
What is the arising of craving from hatred?

It is when one does not delight in, love, mind, or find pleasing toward a sentient being, and another person likewise follows that same course of not delighting in, loving, minding, or finding pleasing toward him; because of this, I develop a sense of affection for that other person. This is called the arising of craving from hatred.
“What is it that gives rise to hatred from hatred?

It is when someone is displeased with, does not love, does not mind, and finds disagreeable toward a certain being, while another person is pleased with, loves, minds, and finds agreeable toward that same being and follows after them;

then this person thinks: ‘I am displeased with, do not love, do not mind, and find disagreeable toward this being, whereas he is pleased with, loves, minds, and finds agreeable toward him and follows after him; I have given rise to anger toward him.’”
This is called "hatred arising from hatred.

If a bhikṣu, having detached from desires and unwholesome states, dwells fully established in the first, second, third, or fourth dhyāna—with directed thought and sustained thought, and so forth—then he has abandoned and fully understood the love that arises from love, the hatred that arises from hatred, the love that arises from hatred, and the hatred that arises from love; he has severed their root, like cutting off the head of a tāla tree, so that they can no longer sprout and will never arise again in future lives.
"If that bhikṣu has exhausted all taints and attained the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, he realizes for himself in this very life, attaining realization:
'Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I myself know that there will be no further existence.'"
At that time, one should not exalt oneself, nor cause others to exalt oneself; one should not raise up dust, nor kindle a flame, nor find fault with others.
"What is meant by exalting oneself? [The following passage explains this...]"
That is to say, one views form as the self, form as distinct from the self, form within the self, or a self within form.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; this is called self-exaltation.
What is meant by "not exalting oneself"?
It means not viewing form as the self, nor form as distinct from the self, nor the self as being within form, nor form as being within the self.
The same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. This is called "not exalting oneself."
What is counter-reproach?

It refers to reviling in return those who revile, being angry in return at those who are angry, striking in return those who strike, and touching in return those who touch; this is called counter-reproach.
What is meant by "not returning an accusation"?

It means that when one is reviled, one does not revile in return; when one is provoked to anger, one does not respond with anger; when one is struck, one does not strike back; when one is touched [offensively], one does not touch back. This is called "not returning an accusation."
"What is the arising of dust?
It refers to the notion of 'self' and 'my desire,' up to and including the eighteen kinds of craving; this is called the arising of dust.
What is the non-arising of dust?"
That is to say, the absence of self and the absence of desire for a self, up to the non-arising of the eighteen modes of craving—this is called "the non-arising of dust.
What is "blazing"?
It refers to the existence of what belongs to a self and desire for what belongs to a self, up to the eighteen external modes of craving—this is called "blazing."
What is meant by "not burning"?
It refers to the absence of "mine," the absence of what is desired as "mine," and so on, up to the absence of the eighteen external modes of craving; this is called "not burning."
"What is meant by 'disliking that'?
It refers to seeing the arising of my true self, yet not severing and not knowing the conceit of 'I', the desire for 'I', and the latent tendencies of 'I'; this is called disliking that."
What is meant by "not disliking them"?

It means not perceiving a self as real; having already abandoned and fully understood the conceit of "I," the desire for "I," and the underlying tendencies toward "I"—this is called not disliking them.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 986 (986) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are two things that are difficult to abandon and difficult to maintain. What are these two?”
If a layperson, while dwelling in a place frequented by non-humans, maintains the renunciation of clothing, food, bedding, and various necessities of life, this is indeed difficult to practice.
"Furthermore, monks, for one who has gone forth from the home life into homelessness and has severed craving, to maintain that state of severance is also extremely difficult to practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"There are two things in the world That are difficult to maintain once severed; [The first is] the severance [of craving], And the second is the maintenance thereof."
This is what the Speaker of Truth has taught, what the Perfectly Awakened One has known:
that for those living at home, the inflow and outflow of wealth, clothing, food, and all such requisites,
as well as worldly greed, craving, and pleasure— those who maintain the vow of renunciation find these things exceedingly difficult to abandon.
"The bhikṣu has already left the secular world; having faith, he has gone forth from home.
To extinguish craving and attachment, and to maintain that renunciation—this too is difficult to practice.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
987 (Ninety-eight-seven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I dwell frequently in reliance upon two dharmas. What are these two? They are:

never being content with one's cultivation of wholesome dharmas, and never withdrawing from the abandonment [of unwholesome states]. Because I am not content with wholesome dharmas and do not withdraw from the abandonment of those states to be abandoned, even until my skin wastes away, my flesh is exhausted, and only sinews and bones remain, I shall never relinquish my diligent application. I will not abandon wholesome dharmas; until I have attained what was not yet attained, I shall never rest. I shall never take pleasure in an inferior mind, but shall always delight in progress, ascending to the highest and most sublime path."
By dwelling in such diligence, one will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and other [qualities].
Bhikṣus! You should rely upon and frequently abide in two dharmas: never conceiving a sense of sufficiency regarding any wholesome dharmas; and [the second is]... [text fragment ends].

Relying upon those abandonments, he never desists, even until his skin wastes away and his flesh is exhausted, leaving only sinews and bones; through diligent application and skillful means, he remains capable of practicing wholesome dharmas without ceasing.
Therefore, bhikṣus, regarding all that is inferior, you should conceive thoughts of joy; you should cultivate the higher and higher stages, advancing and dwelling therein frequently.

By practicing in this way, before long you shall swiftly bring an end to all outflows (āsravas), attaining the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, realizing and personally witnessing for yourselves in this very life: [that birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, and there is no further state of existence].
“Birth has been exhausted for me; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
988 (Ninuhachi). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, Śakra Devendra, whose physical form was most exquisite, approached the Buddha during the latter part of the night, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The majestic power of his celestial body caused its radiance to shine everywhere throughout the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
The Blessed One once spoke thus at the cave on Mount Gijjhakūṭa:

"If there be any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who have attained liberation through the exhaustion of the highest craving, whose minds are well-liberated, they have reached the limit, the ultimate limit, the stainless limit, and the perfection of the holy life."
“What is the limit for a bhikṣu, the ultimate limit, the stainless limit, and the culmination of the holy life?
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of the Devas:

“It is when a bhikṣu, regarding whatever feelings he experiences—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—knows as they truly are the arising of those feelings, the cessation of those feelings, the gratification of those feelings, the danger in those feelings, and the escape from those feelings.”

Having known it as it truly is, one contemplates that feeling as impermanent; one contemplates its arising and passing away, contemplates dispassion, contemplates cessation, and contemplates relinquishment.
Having contemplated in this way, one reaches the limit—the ultimate limit, the stainless limit, the final consummation of the holy life.
Kauśika! This is called a bhikṣu who has reached the limit of the True Dharma and its Vinaya, the ultimate limit, the limit free from defilement, and the perfection of the holy life (brahmacarya).
Thus, when Śakra, Lord of the Devas, heard what the Buddha had spoken, he rejoiced and expressed his approval;
having paid homage, he departed. 989 (989) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain. During the latter part of the night, he rose to practice walking meditation and saw a radiance shining everywhere throughout the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
Having seen this, he thought:
"Tonight, some powerful spirit or deity must have approached the World-Honored One, which is why there is this radiance.

The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If there is a bhikṣu who, before falling ill and while the five lower fetters have not yet been severed, perceives that illness has arisen, his body is afflicted with suffering, his mind is not at ease, and his vital strength is weakened; yet, having heard the Great Master’s various teachings and instructions on the Dharma, after hearing that Dharma, he severs the five lower fetters."
Ānanda! This is the benefit of the Master’s instruction and the establishment of the Dharma.
Furthermore, Ānanda!

Suppose there is a bhikṣu who, prior to falling ill, had not yet severed the five lower fetters; subsequently, illness arises and his body is afflicted with suffering, his life-force becomes feeble, and he does not receive the instruction, admonition, or teaching of the Great Master. However, he encounters other learned and virtuous practitioners of the holy life who provide him with instruction, admonition, and teaching. Having heard the Dharma from them, he severs the five lower fetters.
Ānanda! This is called the benefit of hearing the Dharma through instruction and admonition.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!"

If a bhikkhu, when he was not yet ill, had not severed the five lower fetters, and his life-force had become weak, such that he did not hear the Great Teacher’s instruction, exhortation, or teaching of the Dharma, nor did he hear the instruction, exhortation, or teaching of the Dharma from other learned and virtuous fellow-practitioners; nevertheless, by reflecting alone in solitude upon the Dharma previously received, weighing and examining it, he may attain the severance of the five lower fetters.
Ānanda! This is called the benefit obtained through reflecting upon and examining the teachings previously heard.
Furthermore, Ānanda!

If there is a bhikṣu who, prior to falling ill, has severed the five lower fetters but has not yet attained the unsurpassed liberation through the exhaustion of craving, nor has he given rise to the non-arising of the outflows (*āsrava*) with a well-liberated mind; yet, after subsequently falling ill and encountering physical suffering and affliction such that his vital faculties become weak, he hears the Great Teacher’s instruction, admonition, and discourse on the Dharma, whereby he attains the unsurpassed liberation through the exhaustion of craving, gives rise to the non-arising of the outflows, and achieves liberation from desire.
Ānanda! This is called the benefit of the Great Teacher’s teaching of the Dharma.
Furthermore, Ānanda!

Suppose there is a bhikṣu who, before falling ill, has severed the five lower fetters but has not yet attained the unsurpassed liberation through the exhaustion of craving, nor the liberation through the fading away of desire by not giving rise to the outflows. When his bodily illness arises and he encounters extreme suffering and affliction, he does not receive the instruction, admonition, or Dharma teaching of the Great Master; however, he does receive the instruction, admonition, or Dharma teaching from other learned and virtuous fellow practitioners of the holy life, and thereby attains the unsurpassed liberation through the exhaustion of craving and the liberation through the fading away of desire by not giving rise to the outflows.
"Ānanda! This is called the benefit of hearing the Dharma through instruction and admonition.
Furthermore, Ānanda!"

If there is a bhikṣu who, prior to falling ill, has severed the five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni), yet has not attained the unsurpassed liberation through the exhaustion of craving (anuttara-taṇhā-kkhaya-vimutti) nor the liberation from desire (vītarāga-vimutti) by not giving rise to the outflows (āsrava).

When his physical illness arose and he experienced extreme suffering and distress, he was unable to receive the instruction, admonition, or Dharma teaching of the Great Teacher, nor could he receive the instruction, admonition, or Dharma teaching of other learned and virtuous elders. Nevertheless, by reflecting upon, weighing, and examining the Dharma he had previously heard while dwelling alone in a quiet place, he attained the unsurpassed liberation through the exhaustion of craving; he did not give rise to the outflows, and was liberated from desire.
Ānanda! This is called "contemplating the benefits obtained from the Dharma previously heard.
For what reason did the bhikṣu Upasena fail to attain the joy of his faculties, the purity of his complexion, and the radiance of his skin?

Before the bhikṣu Pārāyaṇa fell ill, he had not yet severed the five lower fetters. The Buddha told Aśvajit:
