"Furthermore, if a noble disciple does not view form as self, as distinct from self, or as existing within self; and does not view feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as self, as distinct from self, or as existing within self, he should instead cultivate this realization:

When greed, hatred, and delusion have been forever exhausted without remainder, all taints are extinguished; with the mind liberated from taints and liberated through wisdom, one realizes and witnesses for oneself in this very life:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and I know for myself that there will be no further existence."
When the Buddha spoke this Dharma, the Venerable Aśvajit was freed from all outflows (*āsrava*), his mind attained liberation, and he was filled with joy and exultation.

“World-Honored One!
It is not because I maintain pure precepts that I practice the holy life under the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
“By means of what dharma do you practice the holy life under me?
The bhikṣu replied to the Buddha:
“It is for the sake of abandoning sensual desire that I practice the holy life under the World-Honored One.”
"It is for the sake of abandoning hatred and delusion that one cultivates the holy life under the Blessed One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu: "So it is, so it is."
You should practice the holy life under me precisely for the sake of being free from sensual desire;
you should practice the holy life under me for the sake of being free from ill will and delusion.
"Monks! Because they are bound by the fetter of sensual desire, they cannot become free from desire;
because they are bound by the fetter of ignorance, their wisdom is not purified."
Therefore, bhikṣus!
Through detachment from sensual desires, the mind is liberated; through the departure from ignorance, there is liberation by wisdom.

If a bhikṣu, through detachment from sensual desires, realizes the liberation of the mind with his own body, and through the departure from ignorance, attains liberation by wisdom—this is called a bhikṣu who has severed all craving and desire, turned away from fetters and bonds, brought an end to conceit, attained the unconditioned, and reached the ultimate limit of suffering.
"Therefore, bhikṣus!
Reflect well upon this Dharma... as extensively explained before, up until "he received the foremost prediction.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and delighted, paid their respects, and departed.
1028 (1028). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a great multitude of bhikṣus had gathered in the Kāḷakārāma lecture hall.
At that time, many bhikṣus were afflicted with illness.
Then, in the late afternoon, the Blessed One arose from meditation and went to the Kāḷakārāma lecture hall, where he prepared a seat and sat before the great assembly.
Having sat down, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should wait for the time with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension; this is my instruction for following [the path].
Bhikṣus!"
What is right mindfulness?

It refers to a bhikṣu’s application of the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating the body as body internally, with diligent effort, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension, subduing worldly greed and sorrow;

the application of the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating the body as body externally, and the application of the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating the body as body both internally and externally; [likewise] contemplating feelings internally, externally, and both internally and externally; contemplating the mind internally, externally, and both internally and externally; and contemplating phenomena internally, externally, and both internally and externally—with diligent effort, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension, subduing worldly greed and sorrow. This is called a bhikṣu’s right recollection.
"What is right mindfulness?

It means that a bhikṣu, whether coming or going, dwells with clear comprehension; whether looking ahead or looking aside, bending or stretching, wearing his robes and carrying his bowl, walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, or waking—even when fifty or sixty years old—he acts with clear comprehension regarding speech and silence."
"Monks! This is called right knowledge.
Thus it is, monks!"
For one who dwells with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, the arising of pleasant feeling has its causes and conditions; it does not arise without causes and conditions.
What are these causes and conditions?
They are: taking the body as an object and engaging in such reflection:
"This body of mine is impermanent, conditioned, and born of mental causes and conditions;
pleasant feeling is also impermanent, conditioned, and born of mental causes and conditions.

Thus, one contemplates the body and pleasant feeling as impermanent, contemplates their arising and passing away, contemplates detachment from them, contemplates their cessation, and contemplates the relinquishing of them. Having contemplated the body and pleasant feeling as impermanent, and so on until having relinquished them, if there were any latent tendency toward craving for the body and pleasant feeling, it will never again arise.
"In this way, right mindfulness and right clear comprehension give rise to the conditions for painful feeling; it does not arise without conditions.
What are the conditions?
It is by attending to the body that one reflects in this manner:"
"This body of mine is impermanent, conditioned, and born of mental causes and conditions;
painful feeling is also impermanent, conditioned, and born of mental causes and conditions.

By contemplating the body and painful feeling as impermanent, up to their relinquishment, one will never again be driven by the underlying tendency toward aversion regarding these and painful feelings.
"In this way, the arising of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling has right mindfulness and right clear comprehension as its condition; it does not arise without a condition.
What is the condition?
It is the body as a condition, by which one reflects thus:"
"This body of mine is impermanent, conditioned, and born of mental causes and conditions;
that feeling which is neither painful nor pleasant is likewise impermanent, conditioned, and born of mental causes and conditions."

He contemplates that body and that neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as impermanent, up to their relinquishment; whatever latent tendencies of ignorance there may be toward that body and that neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, those tendencies shall never again arise.

When a learned noble disciple contemplates in this way, they become weary of form, and weary of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Being weary of them, they become dispassionate; being dispassionate, they are liberated. Having attained liberation, they possess the knowledge and vision:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I myself know that there will be no further existence."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"When experiencing a pleasant feeling, one is unable to know that pleasant feeling;
driven by the underlying tendency of sensual desire, one does not see the way out."
When a painful feeling is experienced, one is unable to know that it is a painful feeling;
driven by the underlying tendency of aversion, one does not see the path to deliverance.
The feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant is what the Perfectly Awakened One has taught.
They too cannot know it, and in the end they shall not cross to the further shore.
But if a bhikkhu is diligent, with right wisdom unshakable, he can,
through his keen intelligence, fully understand all those sensations.
"Having understood all sensations, one exhausts all outflows in this very life;
relying on wisdom at the end of life, one attains nirvāṇa beyond reckoning.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1029 (One thousand and twenty-nine). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park... as described above.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus were assembled in the Kālīla Lecture Hall; many were afflicted with illness... [as described above].
The difference is as follows:

"When a noble disciple contemplates in this way, they are liberated from form, and liberated from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. I declare that such persons are liberated from birth, old age, sickness, and death."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The wise one who has heard much is not unaware of the various feelings;
if, regarding painful or pleasant feelings, he discerns them with clear and thorough understanding."
One should know that this is a firm matter:
ordinary people experience rising and falling, yet they are neither stained by pleasure nor shaken by suffering.
Knowing the arising of feeling and its non-arising, one relies upon the awakening from greed and hatred.
Having severed these [defilements], his mind is well-liberated.
Fixing his mindfulness upon the sublime object, he proceeds rightly toward the time of his end.
If a bhikṣu is diligent, with right knowledge he remains unshakable.
Regarding all these feelings, the wise one is able to perceive them;
having fully understood all feelings, he exhausts all taints in this very life.
Passing away with wisdom as his support, he attains nirvana beyond reckoning.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus rejoiced, paid their respects, and departed.
1030 (1030) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada fell ill, and his body was in extreme pain.

Having heard this, the World-Honored One dressed in the morning, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms. Proceeding through the city in order, he arrived at the house of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
The householder saw the World-Honored One from afar and, leaning on his couch, was about to rise.
Having seen this, the World-Honored One immediately said to him:
"Householder, do not rise!
"It will increase their suffering and affliction.
The World-Honored One then sat down and addressed the householder, saying:
"What do you think?"
"Elder, can your illness be endured?
Is the suffering of your body increasing or diminishing?
The elder addressed the Buddha:
“It is extremely painful, World-Honored One!
It is difficult to endure…” and so on, as extensively explained in the Kṣemaka-sūtra regarding the three feelings, up until: “The painful feeling only increases and does not diminish.”
The Buddha told the householder:
"You should train yourself thus:
'To possess unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and to be accomplished in the noble precepts.'"
The householder addressed the Buddha:
"As the World-Honored One has spoken of the four kinds of indestructible purity, I possess these dharmas; within these dharmas, there is 'I.
World-Honored One!"
"I now possess unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and have achieved the noble precepts.
The Buddha said to the householder:
"Excellent!"
"Excellent!
[The Buddha] then declared that the elder had attained the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
The elder addressed the Buddha:
“May the World-Honored One please partake of this meal now.
At that time, the World-Honored One silently gave his consent.
The elder immediately ordered the preparation of various kinds of pure and delicious food to offer to the World-Honored One.
When the World-Honored One had finished eating, he preached various teachings to the elder, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him. Having done so, he rose from his seat and departed.
(1031) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard that the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was afflicted by illness, went to his residence.

From afar, the householder saw Ānanda and, leaning on his couch, wished to rise... [the passage continues] up to the exposition of the three types of sensation, as detailed previously in the *Camma-sutta*, up to: "The illness only increases and does not diminish."
Then, the Venerable Ānanda said to the householder:
“Do not be afraid!

It is the foolish, unlearned worldling who lacks faith in the Buddha, lacks faith in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and is incomplete in the noble precepts, who therefore experiences fear and dread of death and the suffering of future lives.”
Now that you have abandoned and understood what was previously unbelief, you possess pure faith in the Buddha, pure faith in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and are perfected in the noble precepts.
The householder said to the Venerable Ānanda:
“What is there for me to fear now?

When I first saw the World-Honored One among the mounds and burial grounds in the Cool Grove at Rājagṛha, I immediately attained unshakable confidence in the Buddha, unshakable confidence in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and achieved the noble precepts.”
From that time forth, whatever wealth the family possessed was entirely shared with the Buddha and his disciples—the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
The Venerable Ānanda said:
"Excellent, householder!"
"You yourself have declared that this is the fruit of stream-entry.
The householder said to the Venerable Ānanda,
"Please accept this meal here."
The Venerable Ānanda accepted the invitation in silence.

He then prepared various kinds of pure and delicious food and drink to offer to the Venerable Ānanda. After the meal was finished, he further preached the Dharma to the householder in various ways—showing, instructing, illuminating, and gladdening him—and then rose from his seat and departed.
1032 (1032). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra heard that the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was afflicted with a painful illness.
Having heard this, he said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Do you know?"
"The householder Anāthapiṇḍika is afflicted with a painful illness; we should go together to see him.
Venerable Ānanda consented by remaining silent.
Then, Venerable Śāriputra and Venerable Ānanda went together to the house of the householder Anāthapiṇḍika.

The householder saw Venerable Śāriputra from afar and, supporting himself on his bed, attempted to rise... [the passage continues] up until the exposition of the three kinds of sensation, as explained at length in the *Carmavastu Sūtra*: "The various pains and afflictions of his body increased further and did not diminish."
The Venerable Śāriputra said to the householder:
"You should train yourself thus:
'Do not cling to the eye; do not give rise to craving, desire, or consciousness based upon the eye-sphere.'"
He does not cling to the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; nor does he cling to the mind-element, nor does he give rise to consciousness accompanied by lustful desire based upon the mind-element.
He does not cling to forms, nor does he give rise to consciousness accompanied by lustful desire based upon the form-element;
he does not cling to sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects, nor does he give rise to consciousness accompanied by lustful desire based upon the mental-object-element.
They do not cling to the earth element, nor do they give rise to a consciousness of craving dependent upon the earth element;
they do not cling to the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements, nor do they give rise to a consciousness of craving dependent upon the consciousness element.
One does not cling to the aggregate of form, nor does one give rise to a consciousness of craving based upon the aggregate of form;
one does not cling to the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does one give rise to a consciousness of craving based upon the aggregate of consciousness.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada sighed with grief and shed tears.
Venerable Ānanda said to the householder:
"Are you now timid and weak?"
The householder said to Ānanda,
"I am not timid or inferior.
Reflecting upon myself, I have served the Buddha for more than twenty years, yet I have never heard the Venerable Śāriputra preach such profound and wondrous Dharma as I have heard this day."
The Venerable Śāriputra said to the householder,
"I too have not for a long time spoken such a Dharma to householders.
The householder addressed the Venerable Śāriputra:
“There are laypeople living at home who possess superior faith, superior mindfulness, and superior joy, yet because they have not heard the profound Dharma, they give rise to despondency and retreat.
How excellent! [May they hear it.]”
Venerable Śāriputra!
Out of compassion, you should preach the profound and wondrous Dharma for the white-robed laypeople who dwell at home!
Venerable Śāriputra!
"Please take your meal here now.
The Venerable Śāriputra and the others accepted the invitation in silence.
He then prepared various kinds of pure and delicious food and offered it with reverent hospitality.
After he had finished eating, the Buddha further preached various teachings to the elder, instructing, exhorting, illuminating, and gladdening him;
having thus instructed, exhorted, illuminated, and gladdened him, he rose from his seat and departed.
1033 (1033) The Sūtra on the Householder Dharmadinna: Just as the Blessed One spoke at length in the first sūtra concerning the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, so too was it spoken in the second sūtra.
As for the distinction:
"Furthermore, if a householder, having relied upon these four kinds of indestructible purity, cultivates the six recollections thereinabove—
namely, the recollection of the Tathāgata’s deeds, up to the recollection of the devas."
The householder addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Based on the four kinds of indestructible purity, I have now fully accomplished the cultivation of the six recollections that follow upon them; I constantly practice the recollection of the Tathāgata’s deeds, up to and including the recollection of the devas.”
The Buddha said to the householder:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"You have now personally testified to the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
The householder addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept my invitation for a meal."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted, the elder prepared various kinds of pure and delicious food and drink, making offerings with great reverence. After the World-Honored One had finished eating, he further preached the Dharma to the elder in various ways—showing, instructing, illuminating, and gladdening him—and then rose from his seat and departed.
1034. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a youth named Jīvaka, the grandson of the householder Jīvaka-śreṣṭhin, who was afflicted with a grave illness.

At that time, having heard that the youth Jīvaka was afflicted with a grave illness, the World-Honored One dressed in the morning, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms, proceeding in due order until he arrived at the house of the youth Jīvaka.

The youth Āyuṣmān saw the World-Honored One from afar and, supporting himself on his bed, attempted to rise... [the passage continues] up to the exposition of the three types of sensation, as set forth in detail in the *Śikṣamāṇā-sūtra*, up to: "The suffering of illness only increases and does not diminish."
Therefore, young man,
you should train yourself thus:
"To possess unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dharma and the Sangha, and to be accomplished in the noble precepts."
"One should train in this way.
The youth addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

As the Blessed One has spoken of the four kinds of unshakable confidence, I now possess them all: I have constant unshakable confidence in the Buddha, unshakable confidence in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and I am endowed with the noble precepts.
The Buddha told the youth:
"You should rely upon the four kinds of indestructible purity and, based upon them, cultivate the six perceptions conducive to clear knowledge.
What are these six?"

That is to say: the perception of the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena, the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, the perception of non-self in what is suffering, the perception of the repulsiveness of food, the perception of the lack of delight in the entire world, and the perception of death.
The youth addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As the World-Honored One has taught, regarding the cultivation of the six perceptions conducive to clear knowledge based upon the four kinds of indestructible confidence—I now possess them all.”
However, I had this thought:
‘After my life comes to an end, I do not know what will become of my grandfather, the householder Jyotiṣka.
At that time, the householder Jyotiṣka spoke to the youth Dīrghāyu:
“Cease for now your deliberate thoughts regarding me.
Listen now to the World-Honored One’s teaching of the Dharma; by reflecting upon and recollecting it, you shall obtain benefit, peace, and well-being for a long night.”
Then, the youth Āyuṣmān said:

“I shall constantly bring to mind the perception of impermanence regarding all conditioned phenomena, the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, the perception of non-self in what is suffering, the perception of the repulsiveness of food, the perception of the lack of delight in the entire world, and the perception of death.”
The Buddha told the youth,
"You shall now personally attest to the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin.
The youth Dīrghāyu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We only pray that the World-Honored One will stay at my residence for a meal.
At that time, the World-Honored One silently gave his consent.
The youth Dīrghāyu then prepared various kinds of pure and delicious food and drink, making offerings with great reverence.

After the World-Honored One had finished eating, he further preached the Dharma to the youth in various ways—showing, instructing, illuminating, and gladdening him—and then rose from his seat and departed.
1035 (1035). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
At that time, the householder Vasu was afflicted by a painful illness.

Then, the World-Honored One heard that the householder Vasu was afflicted by a painful illness... [as extensively described in the previous Sūtra on the householder Dharmadinna], he received the prediction of the fruit of Anāgāmin, and finally rose from his seat and departed.
1036. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Park at Kapilavastu.
At that time, there was a Śākyan named Śāla who was gravely ill.

When the World-Honored One heard that the Śākyan Śāla was gravely ill, he dressed in the morning, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Kapilavastu to beg for food, eventually arriving at the residence of the Śākyan Śāla.

The Śākya Sāla saw the World-Honored One from afar and, supporting himself on his bed, wished to rise... [the passage] continues as extensively explained in the Kṣemaka-sūtra regarding the three types of sensation, up until: "My painful affliction only increases and does not diminish."
Therefore, Śāriputra, you should train yourself thus:
"Possessing unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dharma and the Sangha, and being accomplished in the noble precepts."
The Śākyan Śāradvatīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As the World-Honored One has said:
‘One possesses unshakable clarity regarding the Buddha, unshakable clarity regarding the Dharma and the Saṃgha, and is accomplished in the noble precepts.’”
“I possess them all; I am constantly possessed of unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and I am accomplished in the noble precepts.
The Buddha told Śāradvatīputra:

“Therefore, you should rely upon unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and accomplishment in the noble precepts, and further cultivate the five bases of joy.”
"What are these five? They are:
recollecting the deeds of the Tathāgata, up to the Dharma that one has personally practiced.
Śāradvatīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"As the Blessed One has taught, relying upon the four bases of unshakable confidence, one cultivates the five grounds for joy; I too possess these. I constantly recollect the deeds of the Tathāgata, and so on, up to the Dharma that I myself have practiced."
The Buddha said,
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"You should now personally declare that you have realized the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin.
Śāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept a meal at my home today."
At that time, the World-Honored One granted his consent by remaining silent.

The householder Sāla then prepared various kinds of pure and delicious food and drink, making offerings with reverence. After the World-Honored One had finished eating, he further preached the Dharma to the householder Sāla in various ways—showing, instructing, illuminating, and gladdening him—and then rose from his seat and departed.
1037 (1037). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kuṭāgāra Śālā in the village of Naḷī.

At that time, the householder Yaśas was afflicted with a grave illness... [the account continues] until he received the prediction of the fruit of Anāgāmin, as explained in detail in the Dharmadinna Sūtra.
1038 (One thousand and thirty-eight). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the side of the Gaggarā Pond in the kingdom of Campā.
At that time, there was a householder named Maṇḍikāputta who had recently recovered from an illness.
At that time, the householder Maṇadatta said to a man: "Good son!
Go to the Venerable Aniruddha and, on my behalf, bow your head at his feet, inquire after his health, and ask whether he is living in comfort, ease, and well-being."
"Tomorrow, I wish for you and your four disciples to accept my invitation.
If you accept, please say this on my behalf:

'I am a layman with many affairs of state and cannot come in person to welcome you; I only pray that the Venerable One, out of compassion, will come at the appointed time with your four disciples to attend my invitation.'"
Then, having received the elder’s instruction, that man went to the Venerable Aniruddha, prostrated at his feet,
and said to him:
“The elder Maṇḍikāputra pays his respects and inquires after your welfare.”
"I hope you have little illness and little affliction, that your daily activities are light and easy, and that you dwell in peace and happiness.
I pray only that the Venerable Ones, together with the four members of the group, will compassionately accept my invitation for tomorrow at noon."
Then, the Venerable Anuruddha accepted the invitation in silence.
Thereupon, that man again reported the words of the householder Maṇḍikāputta to the Venerable Anuruddha:

“I am a layman with many affairs of state; I am unable to go out myself to welcome you. I only pray that the Venerable One, together with the four members of your household, will out of compassion accept my invitation for tomorrow at noon.”
The Venerable Anuruddha said:
"Rest easy for now!
I myself know the proper time; tomorrow, four of us together shall go to his house."
Then, having received the instruction of the Venerable Anuruddha, that man returned and informed the householder:
"Venerable sir,
you should know that I have already visited the Venerable Anuruddha and fully conveyed your words."
The Venerable Anuruddha said, "You need only rest at ease; I myself know the proper time.
That householder, Maṇḍikāputra, then prepared pure and delicious food and drink during the night.
At dawn, he again addressed that man, saying:
"Go to where the Venerable Aniruddha is, and say to him:
'The time has come.'"
Then, that man, having received these instructions, went to the Venerable Aniruddha, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"The provisions are prepared; please know that it is time!"
Then, the Venerable Anuruddha put on his robes, took up his bowl, and went with three others to the house of the householder.

At that time, the householder Maṇadatta was surrounded by his female attendants and stood at the left of the inner gate. Seeing the Venerable Anuruddha, he prostrated himself with his whole body, grasping the elder’s feet in reverence. He led them inside and invited them to sit; each of them bowed their heads in greeting, inquired after his well-being, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Venerable Anuruddha inquired after the householder’s health, saying:
“Are you enduring and dwelling in comfort?
The householder replied:
"It is so, Venerable One!
I am able to endure and dwell in comfort.
Previously, I was afflicted by a serious illness; at that time it was grave, but now I have been granted recovery."
The Venerable Anuruddha asked the householder,
“In what dwelling do you abide that you are able to recover from the suffering and affliction of this illness?
The householder replied:
"Venerable Anuruddha!
Because I dwell in the four foundations of mindfulness and cultivate them with focused attention, the various sufferings and ailments of my body find rest from time to time.
What are these four? "
That is to say: he dwells contemplating the body as body internally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued worldly greed and sorrow;

he dwells contemplating the body as body externally, and both internally and externally; he dwells contemplating feelings as feelings internally, externally, and both internally and externally; he dwells contemplating the mind as mind internally, externally, and both internally and externally; he dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena internally, externally, and both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued worldly greed and sorrow.
In this way, Venerable Anuruddha!

Because I bind my mind to and dwell upon the four foundations of mindfulness, all physical ailments and sufferings find rest; Venerable Anuruddha, because I so dwell, all physical ailments and sufferings find rest.
The Venerable Anuruddha said to the householder,
“You have now personally testified to the fruit of an Anāgāmin.
Then, the householder Maṇatīna personally served various kinds of pure and delicious food and drink, until they were satisfied and full.
When he had finished eating and completed his rinsing and washing, the householder Maṇatīna sat again on a low seat to listen to the teaching of the Dharma.
After the Venerable Anuruddha had taught the Dharma in various ways—showing, instructing, illuminating, and gladdening him—he rose from his seat and departed.
1039 (1039). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Goldsmith’s Monastery in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the householder Cunda came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked the householder Cunda:
"Among which śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas do you now find delight in their pure conduct?
Cunda addressed the Buddha:
“There are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who serve water, worship the god Viśvabhū, carry staffs and water-pots, and constantly keep their hands clean.”
Thus, this true person is able to skillfully speak these words of Dharma: "Good son!

On the fifteenth day of the month, cleanse your hair with sesame powder and *āmra* fruit powder; practice the fast (*upavāsa*), put on new, clean, long-haired white cotton cloth, smear cow dung upon the ground, and lie down upon it."
"Good son!
Rise early in the morning and touch the earth with your hand, saying these words:
'This earth is pure; I am likewise pure.'"
Holding a lump of cow dung and some raw grass in his hands, he spoke these words:
"This is pure; I am thus purified.
If it were as he says, then purity would be seen in this manner; if it were not so, one would never be pure.
"World-Honored One!
If śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of such a kind are pure, they are those whom I revere and look up to.
The Buddha told Cunda:
“There are dark dharmas with dark retribution—impure and yielding impure fruits—that weigh one down.
One who has accomplished such evil dharmas, even if they rise early at dawn, touch the ground with their hands, and proclaim themselves pure, they remain impure;
even if they do not touch it, they are still not pure.”
Holding a lump of cow dung and fresh grass, one may declare them pure, yet they are nonetheless impure;
even if one does not touch them, they are still not pure.
"Cunda! What is that which is black with a black retribution, impure with an impure fruit, heavy and tending downward, such that whether touched or untouched, it is entirely impure?"
Cunda! As for the evil karma of killing:

one’s hands are constantly stained with blood, the mind constantly dwells upon beating and slaughter, and being devoid of shame or remorse, one is stingy, greedy, and parsimonious, never ceasing from killing even toward all sentient beings down to the smallest insects.
Regarding the property of others, whether in villages or open lands, they never refrain from theft.

They practice various forms of sexual misconduct: toward parents, brothers, sisters, husbands, relatives, or even those who have offered them flower garlands; toward such protected persons, they use forceful aggression and do not refrain from sexual misconduct.

False speech is when, in the royal court, among those who speak the truth, or in a great assembly where one is expected to speak, one utters what is untrue: claiming to have seen what was not seen, claiming not to have seen what was seen, claiming to have heard what was not heard, claiming not to have heard what was heard, claiming to know what was not known, or claiming to know what was known. Whether for one's own sake, for the sake of another, or for the sake of material gain, to knowingly speak falsehood and not abandon it—this is called false speech.

Divisive speech consists of alienating others by conveying what is said here to those there, and what is said there to those here, thereby causing widespread destruction; it brings about the separation of those who are united and delights in the separation of those already divided—this is called divisive speech.

One who does not abandon harsh speech and abusive insults, but speaks with gentle words that are pleasing to the ear and gladden the heart—words that are upright, easy to understand, delightful to hear, independent, and beloved by many—finds contentment and accords with samādhi.
To abandon such [virtues] and instead act with harshness, becoming loathed by many, being unloved, disagreeable, and speaking in a manner that does not accord with samādhi—
such words as these, which do not depart from coarseness and abrasiveness, are called an evil mind.
Frivolous speech refers to untimely speech, untrue speech, meaningless speech, unrighteous speech, and thoughtless speech; such as these are termed frivolous speech.
"Without abandoning greed, one gives rise to covetousness for the wealth and property of others, saying:
'It would be better if this object were mine.
Without abandoning the corruption of anger, one thinks to oneself:"
"Those sentient beings should be bound, should be whipped, should be subdued, and should be killed"—
this constitutes creating difficulties for living beings.
Not abandoning wrong views and perversions, one holds such a view and speaks thus:

"There is no giving, no offering, no charity; there is no wholesome or unwholesome conduct, nor is there fruit or result of wholesome or unwholesome deeds. There is no this world, no other world; there are no parents, and no beings reborn into the world. There are no arhats in the world who have attained and realized for themselves through direct knowledge regarding this world and the next, declaring:
'Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and I myself know that there will be no further existence.'"
"Cunda! This is called the black with black retribution, the impure with impure fruit; even down to contact and non-contact, all are entirely impure."

“Cunda! There is that which is white and its white retribution, pure existence and its pure fruit. Having achieved the lightness of an ascetic who ascends, one touches the earth at dawn; for one who thinks ‘I am pure because this is pure,’ they attain purity even if they do not touch it.
Holding a lump of cow dung and grasping fresh grass—whether one holds them or does not hold them—one who possesses the cause of purity and the fruit of purity attains purity.”
"Cunda! What is that which is white and has a white retribution, up to being grasped or not grasped, yet attaining purity?
It refers to a person who does not kill, who abstains from killing, who lays aside the sword and staff, and who possesses a sense of shame and remorse, feeling compassion for all sentient beings."
He does not steal; he stays far removed from theft, taking only what is given and not taking what is not given, with a pure mind free from greed. He abstains from sexual misconduct:

whether [a woman] is protected by her parents, or even one to whom a single flower garland has been offered, he never forcibly violates her or engages in sexual misconduct. He abstains from false speech, speaking only with precision and truth. He stays far removed from divisive speech; he does not repeat here what was said there, nor repeat there what was said here, so as to break apart those who are united, but rather reconciles those who are divided and rejoices in harmony. He stays far removed from harsh speech; he is not abrasive, and many find pleasure in what he says.

He abstains from harsh speech; he speaks truthfully, speaks at the proper time, speaks what is factual, speaks meaningfully, speaks in accordance with the Dharma, and speaks according to his realization.

He abstains from covetousness; he does not conceive the thought that the wealth or possessions of others belong to himself, nor does he give rise to greedy attachment. He abstains from ill will; he does not entertain thoughts such as:
"I shall beat, bind, or kill them, or cause them various hardships."

"Having achieved right view and being free from inverted views, [one understands that] there is giving, there is the ripening of what is spoken, and there is merit; there are the fruits and retributions of wholesome and unwholesome deeds; there is this world, there are parents, and there are beings born; and there are in this world Arhats who, in this very life and in future lives, have realized for themselves through direct knowledge:
'Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and I know for myself that there will be no further existence.'"
"Cunda! This is called the white [action] and its white retribution; even regarding contact and non-contact, all are entirely pure.
At that time, the elder Cunda, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and approved with gladness, paid homage, and departed.
1040. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Goldsmith’s Hermitage in Rājagṛha.

At that time, a certain brāhmaṇa, having washed his head on the fifteenth day and observed the fast-day precepts, dressed in a new long-haired white cotton garment and holding fresh grass in his hand, approached the place where the Buddha was. After exchanging greetings and polite inquiries with the World-Honored One, he withdrew and sat to one side.
At that time, the Buddha said to the brahmin:
"Whose tradition is it for you to wash your head and wear newly grown long hair and white cotton cloth?
The brahmin replied to the Buddha:
"Gautama! This is the practice of the dharma of equanimity.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
“What is the Dharma of renunciation for a brahmin?
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying,
“Gautama!...”

Thus, on the fifteenth day, having washed one's head and observed the Dharma-fast (upavāsa), wearing new, clean long hair and white cotton garments, and holding fresh grass in hand, one should perform acts of merit through giving according to one’s capacity.
"Gautama!
This is called the practice of renunciation cultivated by a brāhmaṇa.
The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa:
“The practice of equanimity followed by the noble ones and their discipline is different from this.
The brahmin said to the Buddha: “Gautama!
“What is the practice of equanimity as practiced within the Dharma and Vinaya of the noble ones?
The Buddha told the brahmin:
“It means abstaining from taking life, not delighting in taking life... as explained at length in the preceding section on purity.
“Based on non-killing, he abandons the taking of life... and so forth, as extensively explained in the preceding section on purity.
“He abstains from stealing; he does not delight in theft; based on non-stealing, he abandons taking what is not given.”
He abstains from sexual misconduct; he does not delight in sexual misconduct, relies upon celibacy, and abandons unchaste conduct.
He abstains from false speech; he does not delight in false speech, relies upon truthful speech, and abandons untruthful words.
He abstains from all forms of divisive speech; he does not delight in divisive speech, but relies on non-divisive speech and abandons the practice of causing separation.
He abstains from harsh speech; he does not delight in harsh speech, but relies on non-harsh speech and abandons coarse words.
He abstains from frivolous speech and takes no pleasure in it; relying on the avoidance of frivolous speech, he abandons meaningless talk.
He cuts off covetousness and stays far removed from harmful greed; relying on a mind free from greed, he abandons attachment.
He eliminates ill will and does not give rise to anger or resentment; relying on non-ill will, he abandons that anger and resentment.
He cultivates right view and does not give rise to perversity; relying on right view, he abandons that wrong view.
“Brahmin! This is called the practice of equanimity as practiced within the Dharma and Vinaya of the noble ones.
The brahmin addressed the Buddha:
"Excellent! Gautama, this practice of equanimity within the Dharma and Vinaya of the noble ones is truly practiced.
Then, having heard what the Buddha had said, the brahmin rejoiced and delighted in it, rose from his seat, and departed.
1041 (1041). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.

At that time, the brahmin Jātiśroṇa came to where the Buddha was, exchanged greetings and polite inquiries with the World-Honored One, and after withdrawing to sit to one side, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Gautama! I have a kinsman whom I cherished most dearly, who suddenly passed away. For his sake, I have given gifts with faith.
What do you think?"
“World-Honored One!
Would he be permitted to receive it?
The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa:
"It is not necessarily so.
If your kinsmen have been reborn in hell, they may obtain the food of those hell-beings to sustain their lives, but they will not obtain the food and drink you have offered in faith;
if they have been reborn among animals, hungry ghosts, or humans, they will obtain the food and drink found among those beings, but they will not obtain what you have given."

"Brahmin! Within the realm of hungry ghosts there is a place called the 'Entrance' hungry ghosts; if your kinsmen are born among those hungry ghosts of the Entrance, they will receive the food you offer."
The brahmin said to the Buddha:
"If my kinsmen are not reborn among the hungry ghosts in the realm of entry, who then should consume my offerings of faith?"
The Buddha told the brahmin:

"If those for whom you have performed acts of faithful giving do not take birth in the realm of hungry ghosts (preta), then if there are other kinsmen or acquaintances who have taken birth in the realm of hungry ghosts, they shall obtain food from it."
The brahmin said to the Buddha,
“Gautama! If,
because of my gift of faith, neither my own kinsmen nor any other relatives or acquaintances are reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts, then who shall eat this food given in faith?”
The Buddha told the brahmin:

"Even if those for whom one gives—whether kinsmen or acquaintances—are not reborn among the hungry ghosts who lack a physical abode, and even if there are no other acquaintances reborn as hungry ghosts, one still obtains merit for oneself through the gift of faith; the act of giving that faithful gift is not lost, and the donor does not fail to receive the reward."
The brahmin said to the Buddha,
“How does a donor practice giving so that the donor receives that *dakṣiṇā*?
The Buddha told the brahmin:

"There is a person who kills living beings and commits evil deeds, whose hands are constantly stained with blood, and who follows the ten unwholesome paths of action... as explained at length in the Cunda Sūtra, "...yet they further give to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and even to the poor and beggars, bestowing upon them all manner of wealth, clothing, food and drink, lamps, and various ornaments."

"O Brahmin! If that donor, having violated the precepts, is reborn among elephants, because he previously gave wealth, clothing, food and drink, and even various articles of adornment to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, even while existing as an elephant, he still receives the karmic reward for those gifts: clothing, food and drink, and even various articles of adornment."

"Furthermore, if they are born among various kinds of animals such as oxen, horses, donkeys, or mules, by virtue of their original merit from practicing generosity, they will fully receive its retribution; whatever they ought to enjoy according to their place of birth, they shall obtain it all."

"Brahmin! Furthermore, if a donor maintains the precepts—refraining from killing, refraining from stealing, up to and including right view—and gives wealth, clothing, food and drink, even down to lamps and illumination, to various śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and even mendicants; by virtue of this merit, he is born among human beings and receives its retribution while seated, provided with clothing, food and drink, and even lamps and all manner of requisites."
"Furthermore, Brahmin!

If those who maintain the precepts are reborn in the heavens, they will receive the rewards for their various acts of giving there: wealth and treasures, clothing, food and drink, and even all manner of ornaments and requisites."
“Brahmin! This is called the giver practicing giving, and the recipient receiving the *dakṣiṇā*; the fruit of retribution is never lost.
At that time, the Brahmin Jātiśroṇa, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and approved, rose from his seat, and departed.
1042 (1042). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of Kosala and was staying in the Śiṃśapā Forest north of the village of Veḷudvāra.

When the brahmin householders of the village of Verañjā heard that the Blessed One was staying in the Śiṃśapā Grove to the north of the village, they gathered together and went to where the Buddha was. Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, they withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Blessed One!”
"For what cause, for what condition, do sentient beings, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, take birth in the hells?
The Buddha told the brahmins and householders:
"By reason of practicing unrighteous conduct and practicing perilous conduct, they take birth in the hells upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life."
The brahmins and householders said to the Buddha:
"What kind of unrighteous conduct or perilous conduct must one practice so that, at the breaking up of the body after death, one is reborn in hell?"
The Buddha told the brahmin householder:
"It is because of the complete fulfillment of the ten unwholesome karmic causes and conditions, from killing up to wrong view, O Brahmin."
"This is unrighteous conduct, a perilous course; when the body breaks up at the end of life, one is reborn in hell.
The brahmin said to the Buddha:
"By what causes and conditions do sentient beings, upon the breakup of the body at the end of life, attain rebirth in the heavens?"
The Buddha told the brahmin householder:
"By practicing the Dharma-conduct and practicing the right conduct, through these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, one will attain rebirth in the heavens."
He asked again:
“World-Honored One!
By practicing what kind of dharma-conduct and what kind of right conduct does one, upon the dissolution of the body and the end of life, attain rebirth in the heavens?”
The Buddha told the brahmin householder:

"By means of the causes and conditions of the ten paths of wholesome action—ranging from abstaining from taking life up to right view—one will, upon the breakup of the body after death, attain rebirth in the heavens."
"Brahmin householder!

If there are those who practice this Dharma-conduct and practice this right conduct, and who desire to be born into a great kṣatriya family, a great brāhmaṇa family, or a great householder family, they shall all attain rebirth therein."
Why is this? It is because of the causes and conditions of practicing the Dharma and practicing correctly.
Furthermore, if one wishes to seek rebirth among the Four Heavenly Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and so on up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, one will attain birth in all of them.
Why is this? Because through practicing the Dharma and right conduct, those who practice pure precepts will naturally attain all that their hearts desire.
Furthermore, if such practitioners of the Dharma and right conduct wish to seek birth in the Brahma Heaven, they shall likewise attain rebirth there.

Why is this? Because by practicing right conduct and the practice of the Dharma, one maintains pure precepts and a mind free from craving and desire; thus, whatever one aspires to will surely be attained.
"If one further desires to seek rebirth in the Ābhāsvara, Śubhakṛtsna, or even up to the Akaniṣṭha heavens, it is likewise so."
Why is this? Because their observance of the precepts is pure and their minds are free from desire.

Furthermore, if they wish to attain freedom from desire and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, up to and including the full attainment and abiding in the fourth dhyāna, they shall achieve all these entirely.

Why is this? Because by practicing those dharmas and walking in the right path, their observance of the precepts is pure, their minds are free from craving and desire, and whatever they wish for is surely attained.

"If one seeks loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, as well as the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, all shall be fully obtained."

Why is this? Because by practicing the Dharma and walking the right path, one maintains pure precepts and the mind is free from craving and desire; thus, whatever one aspires to will certainly be attained.

"If you seek to sever the three fetters and attain the fruits of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, or Anāgāmin, you shall fully obtain immeasurable supernormal powers: the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, knowledge of past lives, knowledge of the death and rebirth of beings, and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows."
"Why is this? Because through the practice of the Dharma and right conduct, by maintaining the precepts and renouncing desire, whatever one aspires to will surely be attained.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the brahmin elder rejoiced and delighted in it, paid his respects, and departed.
1043 (1043). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of Kosala and stayed in the Śiṃśapā Forest north of the village of Veḷudvāra.

At that time, the brahmin householders in the village of Vairaṃsī heard that the Blessed One was staying in the Kuru Forest near the village of Vairaṃsī. Having heard this, they mounted white horse-drawn carriages and, taking many attendants with them, carrying golden ladles, parasols, and golden water-pots, departed from the village of Vairaṃsī and proceeded to the Kuru Forest.

Arriving at the entrance of the road, he alighted from his carriage and proceeded on foot. Entering through the garden gate, he approached the World-Honored One; after exchanging greetings and inquiries of courtesy with him face-to-face, he withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying: “Gautama!
"For what cause and for what condition do some people, at the end of their lives, take birth in the hells, and so on, up to taking birth in the heavens?
... As explained at length in the aforementioned Sūtra.
At that time, the brahmin Velaṃva, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and approved, rose from his seat, and departed.

(1044) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying among the people of Kosala, traveling through the countryside, and arrived at the village of Veṇudāra, where he stayed in the Śiṃśapā Forest to the north.

When the brahmin householders of the village of Veṇudāra heard that the Blessed One was staying in the Śiṃśapā Grove to the north of the village, they gathered together and went to the Śiṃśapā Grove. Upon reaching the place where the Blessed One was, they exchanged greetings with him and sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the brahmin householder:
"I shall explain for you the Dharma of self-realization.
Listen attentively and reflect well upon it."
What is the method of personal realization?
It refers to when a noble disciple trains himself in this way:
"I form this thought:"
"If there were someone who wished to kill me, I would not rejoice;
as I do not rejoice in this, others are likewise the same.
Why, then, should I kill them?"
"Having formed this realization, one undertakes the abstention from taking life and takes no pleasure in taking life... as described above.
"If I do not delight in others stealing from me, others likewise do not delight in it; how then could I steal from others?"
"Therefore, one who upholds the precept against stealing does not delight in theft... as explained above.
"Since I do not rejoice when others violate my wife, others likewise do not rejoice in it; how then could I now violate the wives of others?"
"Therefore, one should uphold the precept against sexual misconduct... as explained above.
"I myself do not even delight in being deceived by others; since it is the same for others, how could I deceive them?"
"Therefore, one should uphold the precept against false speech... as stated above.
"I do not even take pleasure in others alienating my own friends; since it is the same for them, how could I now alienate the friends of others?"
Therefore, one does not engage in divisive speech.
Since I do not even delight in others using harsh words toward me, how much less so for others; why then would I give rise to insults and abuse toward them?
"Therefore, one does not engage in harsh speech toward others... as stated above.
"I myself do not take pleasure in others engaging in frivolous speech; since it is the same for others, how could I engage in frivolous speech toward them?"
"Therefore, one does not engage in frivolous speech toward others... as stated above.
"These seven kinds are called the noble precepts (*ārya-śīla*).

Furthermore, being endowed with unshakable confidence in the Buddha, and being endowed with unshakable confidence in the Dharma and the Saṅgha—this is called the noble disciple’s accomplishment of the fourfold unshakable confidence (*catuḥ-avetyaprasāda*)."
Observing for himself through direct realization, he was able to declare: "My existence in hell is exhausted;

my existence as an animal, a hungry ghost, and in all evil destinies is exhausted. I have attained the stage of *srotāpanna*; I am no longer subject to falling into evil destinies; I am fixed and headed toward perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); after seven more births among gods and humans, I shall reach the ultimate end of suffering."
At that time, the brahmin householders of the village of Veṇugrāma, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and approved with gladness;
they rose from their seats and departed. (1045) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There is a dharma of mutual association.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you."
What are the dharmas of habitual association?

They are as follows: those who kill associate with those who kill; likewise, those who steal, commit sexual misconduct, speak falsehoods, engage in double-tongued speech, harsh speech, or frivolous chatter, and those who harbor greed, malice, or wrong views, each associate respectively with their own kind.
Just as impure things and impure things naturally associate with one another,
so too does killing associate with killing, and so on, up to wrong view associating with wrong view.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!
Refraining from taking life associates with refraining from taking life, and so on, up to right view associating with right view.
It is just as when pure things associate with pure things: from milk comes curd, from curd comes butter, from butter comes ghee, and ghee associates with itself.

In this way, those who refrain from killing associate with one another who refrains from killing, and so on, up to those with right view associating with one another who possesses right view; this is called the dharma of mutual association for bhikṣus.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1046 (1046) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There is a practice of crawling like a snake.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall explain it to you."
"What are the practices of a serpent?

They are the evil conduct of killing, hands perpetually stained with blood, and so forth, up to the tracks of the ten unwholesome courses of action... as explained at length in the previous Cunda Sūtra.
"At that time, his body will crawl like a serpent, his speech will crawl like a serpent, and his mind will crawl like a serpent;
having thus crawled with body, speech, and mind, he will head toward one of two destinies: either the hells or the animal realm."
What are beings that move by crawling on their bellies?
These refer to beings that move by slithering on their bellies, such as snakes, rats, cats, and wildcats; these are called the dharma of crawling on the belly.
What is the dharma that is not crawling on the belly?

That is to say, abstaining from taking life, up to and including right view... as explained at length in the previous Cunda Sūtra regarding the ten paths of karmic action, "this is called the practice that is not like the crawling of a snake."

To have no serpent-like crawling in body, no serpent-like crawling in speech, and no serpent-like crawling in mind, and to be born in one of the two destinies—either among the devas or among humans—is called the dharma of non-serpent-crawling.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1047 (1047) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"There are causes of evil karma, causes of an evil mind, and causes of evil views; through these, when such beings' bodies disintegrate and their lives end, they will inevitably fall into the miserable realms of hell."
For example, like a round ball thrown into the air, it rolls upon landing and does not remain in one place.
In the same way, due to the causes of evil karma, an evil mind, and evil views, when the body perishes and life ends, one will inevitably fall into hell, with no place of rest in between.
"What is unwholesome karma?
It refers to killing, up to and including frivolous speech... as explained at length above, "...this is called unwholesome karma.
What is an unwholesome mind?"
That is to say, a mind of greed and anger... [as explained extensively above] ...this is called an evil mind.
What is an evil view?
That is to say, false and inverted views... [as explained extensively above] ...this is called an evil view.

These are called the causes of evil karma, the causes of an evil mind, and the causes of evil views; when the body breaks up and life ends, one will inevitably be reborn in the miserable realms within the hells.

By contrast, through the causes of wholesome karma, the causes of a wholesome mind, and the causes of wholesome views, when the body breaks up and life ends, one will inevitably be reborn in the happy realms among the heavens.
“Brahmin! What constitutes wholesome action?
It refers to abstaining from taking life and not delighting in taking life, up to and including abstaining from frivolous speech; this is called wholesome action.”
What is a wholesome mind?
It refers to being without greed and without ill will; this is called the wholesomeness of the mind.
What is the wholesomeness of view?
That is to say, right view is non-perverted, up to and including the vision that one will not undergo further existence; this is called "excellence of view.

This is called the cause of excellence in action, the cause of excellence in mind, and the cause of excellence in view; upon the dissolution of the body after death, one attains rebirth in the heavens.
For example, if a mani jewel from the four directions is cast into the air, it remains stable wherever it falls;
likewise, those three roots of goodness remain stable in whatever place one is born.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1048 (1048). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a person frequently practices and frequently performs the taking of life, they will be born in hell;
if they are born among humans, they will certainly have a short lifespan."
If one frequently practices and habitually engages in taking what is not given, one will be reborn in hell;
if one is reborn among humans, one will face many difficulties regarding wealth and property.
If one frequently practices and habitually engages in sexual misconduct, one will be reborn in hell.
If one is born among humans, one's spouse will be coveted by others.
By frequently practicing and habitually performing false speech, one is reborn in hell;
if born among humans, one will be frequently subjected to ridicule and censure.
If one frequently practices and frequently performs divisive speech, one will be born in hell; if born among humans, one's relatives and friends will be estranged.
If one frequently practices and frequently performs harsh speech, one will be born in hell;
if born among humans, one will constantly hear foul sounds.
If one frequently practices and frequently performs frivolous speech, one will be born in the hells;
if born among humans, one's words will lack credibility.
If one frequently practices and frequently performs covetousness, one will be born in the hells.
If one is born among humans, it increases their greed and desire.
If one frequently practices and frequently acts with hatred, they will be born in the hells;
if they are born among humans, it increases their hatred.
If one frequently practices and frequently performs wrong views, one will be born in the hells; if one is born among humans, it will increase one's ignorance.
"If one abstains from killing and cultivates this practice extensively, one will be born in the heavens;
if one is born among humans, one will certainly attain a long life."
By practicing and frequently cultivating non-stealing, one attains rebirth in the heavens;
if born among humans, one’s wealth shall not be lost.
By practicing and frequently cultivating non-sexual misconduct, one attains rebirth in the heavens.
If one is born among humans, one's spouse will be virtuous and excellent.
By practicing and cultivating the avoidance of false speech, one attains birth in the heavens;
if born among humans, one will not be subjected to censure or criticism.
By practicing and frequently cultivating the avoidance of divisive speech, one attains birth in the heavens;
if born among humans, one's friends and kin will be steadfast.
By practicing and frequently cultivating the avoidance of harsh speech, one attains birth in the heavens.
If born among humans, one will always hear sublime sounds.
By practicing and frequently cultivating the avoidance of frivolous speech, one attains birth in the heavens;
if born among humans, one’s words will be seen and trusted.
By practicing and frequently cultivating non-greed, one attains rebirth in the heavens;
if born among humans, one’s craving and desire do not increase.
By practicing and frequently cultivating non-ill will, one attains rebirth in the heavens.
If one is born among humans, one will not increase in hatred;
by correctly viewing and cultivating this through repeated practice, one attains birth in the heavens;
if one is born among humans, one will not increase in delusion.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1049 (1049) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are three kinds of killing: namely, those arising from greed, those arising from hatred, and those arising from delusion."
Even wrong view has three types: that arising from greed, that arising from hatred, and that arising from delusion.
Abstaining from killing also has three types: that arising from non-greed, that arising from non-hatred, and that arising from non-delusion.
"Furthermore, even the abandonment of wrong views is of three kinds: arising from non-greed, arising from non-hatred, and arising from non-delusion.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1050. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are what are called dharmas that lead to emergence, and dharmas that do not lead to emergence.
What are the dharmas that lead to emergence, and the dharmas that do not lead to emergence?"
"This means that non-killing arises from killing, and so on, up to right view arising from wrong view.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1051 (1051). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, a certain Brahmin named Jātiśroṇa approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Gautama! Regarding what you have spoken of as ‘this shore’ and ‘the other shore,’ what is this shore?”
"What is the 'other shore'?
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"The taking of life is called this shore."
Non-killing refers to the other shore;
wrong view refers to this shore;
right view refers to the other shore.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Few are the people who cultivate goodness And are able to cross to the other shore;
Of all classes of sentient beings, All but run hither and thither upon this shore."
"In this true Dharma and Vinaya, observing the characteristics of phenomena as phenomena,
these cross over to the further shore and subdue the army of the Lord of Death.
At that time, the brahmin Jātiśroṇa, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and approved, rose from his seat, and departed.

In this same manner, the three sūtras concerning the questions asked by another bhikṣu, the questions asked by the Venerable Ānanda, and the Buddha’s questions to the bhikṣus, are also as explained above.
1052 (1052). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are unwholesome dharmas, and there are dharmas of reality.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you."
What are unwholesome phenomena?

They are killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view; these are called unwholesome phenomena.
"What is the true Dharma?
It refers to abstaining from taking life, up to and including right view; this is called the true Dharma.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1053 (1053). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are unwholesome dharmas and unwholesome-unwholesome dharmas; there are true dharmas and true-true dharmas."
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you.
What are unwholesome phenomena?
They are killing, up to and including wrong view; these are called unwholesome phenomena.
What are the evil and unwholesome dharmas? They are:
killing oneself, inciting others to kill, and so forth, up to personally giving rise to false views and further teaching others to practice them. These are called the evil and unwholesome dharmas.
What is the true Dharma?
It refers to abstaining from taking life, up to and including right view;
this is called the true Dharma. What is the truly true Dharma?

That is to say, one does not kill living beings oneself and teaches others not to kill, and so on, up to practicing right view oneself and further teaching others with right view to practice it as well; this is called the true and real Dharma.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1054 (1054) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are unwholesome sons of good family and wholesome sons of good family.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall now speak for your sake."
What is an unwholesome man?
One who takes life, up to and including one who holds wrong views—this is called an unwholesome man.
What is a wholesome man?
"It is said that abstaining from taking life, up to and including right view—this is what is meant by a 'noble son'.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1055 (1055). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are unworthy sons of good family, unworthy sons of good family; there are worthy sons of good family, worthy sons of good family."
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you.
"What is meant by an unwholesome man?
One who commits killing, up to and including holding wrong views—this is called an unwholesome man."
What is meant by an "unvirtuous man, an unvirtuous man"?

It refers to one who personally takes life, or instructs others to take life, and so on, up to personally holding wrong views, or instructing others to hold wrong views; this is called an unvirtuous man, an unvirtuous man.
"What is meant by a 'good man' (kulaputra)?
One who refrains from taking life, up to and including right view—this is called a good man.
What is meant by a 'good man of good men'?"

That is to say, one does not kill living beings oneself and teaches others not to kill, and so on, up to practicing right view oneself and further teaching others with right view to practice it as well; this is called a "good son, good son."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1056 (1056) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one is possessed of ten qualities, like an iron spear piercing water, at the dissolution of the body after death, they will fall into the evil destinies, into the niraya hells."
What are these ten? They are:
killing living beings, up to and including wrong view.
If one accomplishes these ten dharmas—just as an iron drill bit drills upward into the void—at the dissolution of the body after death, one will be reborn in the heavens above.
"What are the ten? They are:
abstaining from taking life, up to and including right view.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1057 (1057). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one is possessed of twenty qualities, like an iron spear piercing water, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they will fall into an evil destination, reborn in the hells."
What are these twenty? They are:

killing with one's own hand, inciting others to kill, and so on, up to practicing wrong views oneself and further teaching others to practice them. These are called the accomplishment of the twenty dharmas.
Like an iron spear piercing water, when the body perishes and life ends, one is reborn in the lower realms within the hells.
This is due to the accomplishment of twenty factors.
Like an iron spear thrust upward into the void, when the body perishes and life ends, one is reborn in the heavens above.
What are these twenty dharmas? They are:

refraining from killing oneself and teaching others not to kill, and so on, up to practicing right view oneself and further teaching others to practice right view; this is called the accomplishment of the twenty dharmas.
"Like an iron spear piercing upward into empty space, when his body perishes and his life ends, he will be reborn in the heavens.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1058 (1058). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"One who is endowed with thirty qualities will, like an iron spear piercing water, at the dissolution of the body after death, be reborn in a lower realm, in the hells."
What are the thirty dharmas? They are:

killing with one’s own hand, inciting others to kill, and praising the act of killing; and so on, up to practicing wrong view oneself, further teaching others to practice wrong view, and constantly praising those who practice wrong view. These are called the thirty dharmas.
Just as an iron spear piercing water, one who possesses thirty such qualities, upon the dissolution of the body after death, is reborn in a lower realm, in the hells.
One who possesses [the opposite] thirty qualities, like an iron spear piercing empty space, upon the dissolution of the body after death, is reborn in the heavens above.
What are the thirty dharmas? They are:
personally refraining from killing, teaching others not to kill, and constantly praising the merit of non-killing;
and so on, up to personally practicing right view, teaching others to practice right view, and constantly praising the merit of right view. These are called the accomplishment of the thirty dharmas.
"Like an iron spear piercing through empty space, when his body perishes and his life ends, he will be reborn in the heavens.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1059 (One thousand and fifty-nine). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one accomplishes forty qualities, like an iron spear cast into water, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they will descend to be born in the evil destinies within the hells."
What are the forty dharmas? They are:

killing with one's own hand, inciting others to kill, praising the taking of life, and feeling joy in one's heart upon seeing others kill; and so on, up to: practicing wrong views oneself, inciting others to practice them, praising wrong views, and feeling joy in one's heart upon seeing others practice wrong views. These are called the accomplishment of the forty dharmas.
Just as an iron spear cast into water [sinks], when the body breaks up and life ends, one is reborn below in the miserable destinies, within the *niraya* hells.
If forty qualities are accomplished, like an iron spear piercing through the air, when the body breaks up and life ends, one is reborn above in the heavenly realms.
What are these forty? They are:
abstaining from killing oneself, teaching others not to kill, constantly praising the merit of non-killing with one's speech, and feeling joy in one's heart upon seeing those who do not kill;

and so on, up to practicing right view oneself, teaching others to practice it, constantly praising the merit of right view, and feeling joy in one's heart upon seeing those who practice it—these are called the accomplishment of the forty dharmas.
"Like an iron spear piercing through the air, when his body perishes and his life ends, he will be reborn in the heavens.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1060 (1060). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There is what is not the True Dharma, and there is the True Dharma.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you."
What is unrighteousness?
It refers to killing, up to and including wrong view; this is called unrighteousness.
What is the true Dharma?
