"That is to say: abstaining from taking life, up to and including right view—this is called the True Dharma.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
1061 (1061). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There is what is not the discipline, and there is the true discipline.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you.”
What is non-discipline?
It refers to killing, up to and including wrong views;
this is called non-discipline. What is right discipline?
"That is to say: abstaining from killing, up to and including right view; this is called the Right Discipline.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Just as with what is non-discipline and right discipline, so it is with the non-noble and the noble, the unwholesome and the wholesome, the non-approachable and the approachable, the not-good and the good, dark phenomena and bright phenomena, the meaningless and the meaningful, inferior phenomena and superior phenomena, blameworthy phenomena and blameless phenomena, and phenomena to be abandoned and phenomena not to be abandoned; each sutra is to be explained as stated above.
Saṃyukta Āgama, Scroll 37 and Scroll 38,
translated by the Song Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra.
38.1062 (1062) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was the Venerable Sujāta, who had recently shaved his hair and beard, donned the saṃghāṭī robe, and out of right faith had gone forth from home to lead the homeless life of study under the Way. He approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus!
You should know that this son of good family, Sujāta, possesses two forms of exquisite beauty."
First, one shaves off hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and with right faith leaves the home life for homelessness to train in the path.
Second, one exhausts all taints and attains the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, realizing and witnessing for oneself in this very life:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; I know for myself that there will be no further existence."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Tranquil and having exhausted all outflows, The bhikṣu is beautifully adorned;
Free from desire and severed from all fetters, He has attained nirvāṇa and shall not be born again.”
"Maintaining this final body, he shall crush and subdue the enemies that are the Māras.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1063 (1063). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu whose physical appearance was so hideous and repulsive that it was difficult to look upon him; he was held in contempt by the other bhikṣus as he approached the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly; seeing that bhikṣu approaching, they all conceived thoughts of contempt and said to one another:
"What kind of bhikṣu is this?"
"He came along the road with an ugly appearance, difficult to behold, and was treated with contempt by others.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bhikṣus, addressed them:
"Bhikṣus, when you saw that bhikṣu coming, with such an extremely ugly form, difficult to look upon, did it cause you to give rise to contempt?"
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha,
“Indeed, we have seen it.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Do not conceive a thought of contempt for that bhikṣu. Why is this?

That bhikṣu has exhausted all outflows (āsrava), accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, severed the fetters of existence (bhavasaṃyojana), and, through right knowledge, his mind is well-liberated."
"O bhikṣus!
Do not judge others recklessly; only the Tathāgata can truly judge others.
Those bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus:
“Do you see this bhikṣu who, having bowed his head in prostration, withdrew to sit at one side?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha: [“Yes, World-Honored One.”]
“Yes, indeed, we have seen him.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Do not conceive a notion of contempt toward this bhikṣu;”
"Furthermore, you must not judge others; only the Tathāgata can truly know a person.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The flying birds and the running beasts, None do not fear the lion."
Only the lion, king of beasts, has no equal;
so it is with one of wisdom—who, though small, is great.
Do not judge them by their physical appearance and give rise to a mind of contempt.
Of what use is a massive body, fleshy yet devoid of wisdom?
This noble one, possessed of superior wisdom, is a true superior man.
Having abandoned desire and severed all fetters, he has attained nirvāṇa and shall never be born again.
"Maintaining this final body, he shall crush and subdue the armies of Māra.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1064 (1064). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.

At that time, Devadatta had acquired great gain and offerings. Ajātaśatru, the King of Magadha and son of Vaidehī, came daily with five hundred chariots of attendants to visit Devadatta’s dwelling. Day by day, he brought five hundred cauldrons of food to provide for Devadatta, and Devadatta accepted these offerings as a separate faction together with five hundred followers.

At that time, a great number of bhikṣus, having dressed in the morning and taken up their bowls, entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms. They heard that Devadatta had arisen with such gains and offerings, even to the extent that a separate assembly of five hundred people was receiving his sustenance.

Having finished his almsround, he returned to the vihāra, put away his robe and bowl, and after washing his feet, went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

This morning, having dressed and taken up our bowls, we entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms and heard that Devadatta had given rise to such gains and offerings, even to the extent that five hundred people formed a separate assembly to receive his offerings.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You must not speak of the gains and offerings obtained by this Devadatta. Why is that?
That Devadatta, by separately accepting offerings and gain, now ruins himself and will ruin himself in future lives as well.
Just as the plantain, the bamboo, and the reed perish upon bearing fruit and are destroyed in the following year, so too is Devadatta:
by receiving those offerings and gains, he is ruined in this life and will be ruined in future lives as well.
Just as a mule that conceives will inevitably die, so it is with Devadatta;
by receiving various offerings and gains, he is ruined in this life and ruined in future lives as well.
For as long as that foolish Devadatta continues to receive such offerings and gains, he shall experience suffering and disadvantage for a long night.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"Should gain and offerings arise for us, we shall not give rise to attachment."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The plantain dies when it bears fruit; The same is true for bamboo and reeds.
The mule dies from pregnancy; So does the man through greed."
"Constantly practicing unrighteous conduct, though possessing much knowledge, one cannot escape folly;
wholesome dharmas diminish day by day, as the stalk withers and the roots are injured.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1065 (1065). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Hasta in Śrāvastī who was a son of the Śākyas; he passed away in Śrāvastī.

Then, a great number of bhikṣus, having dressed in their robes and taken up their bowls at dawn, entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms, and heard that the bhikṣu Hasta, a son of the Śākyas, had passed away in Śrāvastī.

Having heard this, he entered the city of Śrāvastī, returned from his almsround, set aside his robe and bowl, and after washing his feet, went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This very morning, a great number of bhikṣus, having dressed themselves and taken their bowls, entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms, and heard that the bhikṣu Hastaka Śākyaputra had passed away in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
"How is it,
World-Honored One?
Where will the bhikṣu Hasta be reborn after his life comes to an end?"
"How is one reborn?
What becomes of one in future lives?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Monk Isipatana, you have accomplished three unwholesome dharmas; at the end of your life, you shall be reborn in the miserable destinies, in the hells.
What are these three unwholesome dharmas?
These are greed, hatred, and delusion.
Bound by these three unwholesome fetters of the mind, the bhikṣu Śreṇika was reborn in an evil destination, in the hells.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Greed, hatred, and delusion bind the mind of a man;
arising from within, they wound him himself, just like the seeds of the bamboo or the reed.”
A mind free from greed, hatred, and delusion is called wise;
arising from within without harming oneself, this is called supreme excellence.
Therefore, one should abandon greed, as well as the darkness of hatred and delusion.
“The bhikṣu whose wisdom is luminous attains parinirvāṇa through the exhaustion of suffering.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1066 (1066) As in the case of the Bhikṣu Hasta, it is likewise stated in the Nanda Sūtra. 1067 (1067) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Nanda was the son of the Buddha’s maternal aunt; he was fond of wearing fine robes that were dyed and pressed to a high gloss, carried a fine alms-bowl, and moved about engaging in playful jesting and laughter.
At that time, a great multitude of bhikṣus came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

The Venerable Nanda was the son of the Buddha’s maternal aunt; he was fond of wearing fine robes that were beaten and polished to a lustrous sheen, carried an excellent alms-bowl, and moved about engaging in playful dalliance and jesting.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed a certain bhikṣu:
"Go to the bhikṣu Nanda and say to him: 'Nanda!'"
“The Great Teacher speaks to you.
Then, having received the instruction of the World-Honored One, that bhikṣu went and said to Nanda:
“The World-Honored One speaks to you.”
Having heard this, Nanda immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha said to Nanda:
“Is it true that you take great pleasure in wearing fine clothes, having them pounded and polished until they shine, and that you go about fondly engaging in play, frolicking, and joking?”
Nanda said to the Buddha,
“It is truly so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Nanda:

"You, son of my aunt, have left the household life as one of noble lineage; you should not wear fine clothes that have been pounded to a glossy sheen, nor carry a fine alms bowl, nor walk about engaging in playful frolics and jesting."
You should form this thought:

"I am the son of the Buddha’s maternal aunt; having left the home life from a noble lineage, I ought to dwell in the forest, practice alms-gathering, wear rag-robes, always praise the wearing of rag-robes, and constantly reside in mountains and marshes, disregarding the five desires."

At that time, having received the Buddha’s instruction, Nanda practiced the conduct of an araṇyaka; he went for alms, wore rag-robes, and also constantly praised those who wear rag-robes. He delighted in dwelling among mountains and marshes, disregarding sensual desires.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Nanda, what have you seen that you practice in the aranya,
begging for alms from house to house, and wearing robes made of discarded rags?"
"Delighting in dwelling among mountains and marshes, he disregards the five desires.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Nanda, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1068 (1068). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Tiṣya thought to himself: "Because I am the brother of the Blessed One’s paternal aunt’s son, I have failed to cultivate reverence, have been heedless and indifferent, feel no fear, and am incapable of being restrained by admonition."
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

The Venerable Tiṣya, reflecting that he was the son of the Blessed One’s paternal aunt and his own brother, failed to cultivate reverence; he was indifferent and unconcerned, felt no fear, and could not be restrained by admonition.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed a certain bhikṣu:
"Go to the place where the bhikṣu Tiṣya is and say to him: 'Tiṣya!'"
"The Great Teacher speaks to you!
Then, having received the instruction of the World-Honored One, that bhikṣu went and said to the bhikṣu Tiṣya:
"The World-Honored One speaks to you!"
The bhikṣu Tiṣya immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha said to Tiṣya:
“Did you truly have this thought?”
"I am the nephew and brother of the World-Honored One; I have failed to cultivate reverence, I have been heedless and indifferent, I have felt no fear, and I was unable to endure admonition."
"Is this not so?
Tiṣya replied to the Buddha,
"It is indeed so."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Tiṣya,
“You ought not to do so!”
"You should reflect thus:
'Because I am the son of the World-Honored One’s paternal aunt and his brother, I ought to practice reverence and awe, and be capable of enduring admonitions and rebukes.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Excellent, you, Tiṣya! It is good to be free from hatred;
do not give rise to a hateful mind, for one who hates is not virtuous.
If you can abandon hatred and pride, practice with a humble and gentle heart.”
"And thereafter, within my presence, you shall practice the holy life.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣu Tiṣya, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and delighted in it, prostrated, and departed.
1069 (1069). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Vaiśākha Pārāyaṇīputra had gathered in the Hall of Offerings to teach the Dharma to a great assembly of bhikṣus. His speech was complete and his voice was wondrously clear; the phrasing and meaning were precise and correct. He spoke in accordance with wisdom, and those who heard him delighted in listening. Teaching without reliance on external supports, he revealed the profound meaning, causing all the bhikṣus to listen with single-minded concentration.

At that time, the World-Honored One entered the meditative absorption of the day; with his pure divine ear, which surpasses that of humans, he heard the sound of the Dharma being preached. Rising from samādhi, he went to the lecture hall, sat before the great assembly, and addressed Vaiśākha Pāṭaliputra: "Excellent!

Excellent, Viśākhā! That you are able to teach the Dharma to the many bhikṣus here in this hall of offerings, with speech that is complete and even reveals the profound meaning, causing the bhikṣus to be diligent and respectful, listening with single-minded joy— you should repeatedly teach the Dharma to the bhikṣus in this way, so that they may be diligent and respectful, listening with single-minded joy, thereby gaining long-term benefit through the Dharma and dwelling in peace and happiness.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If the Dharma were not taught, The foolish and the wise would be difficult to distinguish;
This one is foolish and this one is wise— There would be no way for them to manifest themselves."
He well expounds the Dharma of coolness; through this exposition, wisdom is revealed.
His preaching of the Dharma serves as illumination, glorifying the banner of the Great Sage.
Skillful exposition is the banner of the Sage, and the Dharma is the banner of the Arhat.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Vaiśākha Pāṭaliputrīya, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and approved, paid his respects, and departed.
1070. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus had gathered in the hall of offerings and were all working together to make robes.

At that moment, there was a young bhikṣu who had not long since left the household life and had only recently entered the Dharma and Vinaya; he did not wish to assist the other bhikṣus in making the robes.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus approached the World-Honored One, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
At this time, a great number of bhikṣus have gathered in the Hall of Offerings for the purpose of making robes.”
There was a young bhikṣu who had not long been ordained; having only recently entered the Dharma and Vinaya, he did not wish to assist the other bhikṣus in making robes.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked that bhikṣu:
"Is it true that you do not wish to assist the other bhikṣus in making robes?"
That bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
According to my ability, I shall exert my strength to provide assistance.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those bhikṣus, addressed them:
"None of you should speak with this young bhikṣu."
Why is this? Because that bhikṣu has attained the four bases of psychic power (catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ), dwelling in the attainment of happiness in the present life, having acquired it without exertion.

Whatever his original purpose for shaving off hair and beard, donning the saffron robes, leaving the household life to study the Path, and progressing in his training, he now knows and realizes for himself in the present life:
“Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and I myself know that there will be no further existence.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Not by inferior means, nor by those of meager virtue and little wisdom,”
Directly heading toward Nirvāṇa, he has escaped the shackles of affliction.
This virtuous youth has attained the station of the Noble Ones;
with his mind liberated from desire, he has reached Nirvāṇa and shall not be born again.
"Maintaining this final body, he shall crush and subdue the armies of Māra.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1071 (One Thousand and Seventy-one). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Sthavira who lived alone in a certain place; he also constantly praised those who dwell in solitude. He went out alone to beg for food, and having eaten, he returned alone and sat in solitary meditation and reflection.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

There is a venerable elder named Sthavira who delights in dwelling alone and solitary; he also constantly praises those who dwell in solitude. He enters the village alone to beg for food, leaves the village alone, returns to his dwelling alone, and sits in solitary meditation and contemplation."
At that time, the World-Honored One said to a certain bhikṣu:
"Go to where that senior bhikṣu is and say to him:
'The Great Teacher addresses you!'"
The bhikṣu received the instruction, went to where the senior bhikṣu was, and said to him:
"Venerable One!
The Great Teacher addresses you!"
Then, the senior bhikṣu immediately obeyed the command, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the senior bhikṣu:
"Is it true that you alone, in a quiet place, praise those who dwell alone; that you go out alone to beg for food, leave the village alone, and sit alone in meditative reflection?"
The senior bhikṣu replied to the Buddha,
“It is indeed so, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to the senior bhikṣu:
“How is it that you, dwelling alone in a solitary place, praise those who dwell alone, who wander alone for alms, who return alone to their lodgings, and who sit alone in meditation?
The senior bhikṣu replied to the Buddha:
“I alone, in a quiet place, praise those who dwell alone, who wander alone for alms, who go out from the village alone, and who sit alone in meditation.”
The Buddha told the senior bhikṣu:
“You are one who dwells in a single state; I do not say that you do not dwell in a single state. However, there is yet another, more excellent and sublime single dwelling.”
What is the supreme and sublime single dwelling?

It is when a bhikṣu has dried up what was before and extinguished what was after, with no craving or delight in between; this is the brahmin whose mind is free from hesitation, who has abandoned sorrow and regret, who is detached from the love of existence, and for whom the fetters of the multitude have been severed—this is called the single dwelling, and there is no superior dwelling that surpasses it!
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Illuminating all things, Fully knowing all worlds,
Unattached to any phenomena, Completely free from all craving.”
"One who dwells thus in happiness, I call one who dwells alone.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Sthavira, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and delighted in it, paid homage, and departed.
1072 (1072). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Saṅgharakkhita was wandering among the people of Kosala and arrived at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, in Śrāvastī.

That bhikṣu Saṅgharakkhita had a former wife living in Śrāvastī, who heard that the bhikṣu Saṅgharakkhita was wandering among the people of Kosala and had arrived at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, in Śrāvastī.
Having heard this, she dressed in fine garments, adorned herself with flowers and necklaces, and carrying her child, came to the Jetavana and arrived before the cell of the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita.
At that time, the Venerable Saṅgharakkhita was walking in the open air for exercise outside his cell.
Then, his former wife came before him and said, "This child is still so young;
since you have abandoned him to go forth as a monk, who will provide for his nourishment?"
At that time, the bhikṣu Saṅgharakṣita did not speak with him.
This was repeated a second and a third time, yet he still did not speak with him.
Then, his former wife spoke these words:
"Though I have entreated him repeatedly, he does not speak with me nor even look at me; I shall now leave this child here.
Having placed the child at the head of the walking path, she departed, saying:
"O Śramaṇa!"
"This is your son; you yourself must support him. I am now leaving.
Yet the Venerable Saṅgharakkhita still did not look back at his son.
The former wife spoke again:
"This śramaṇa now pays no heed whatsoever to this child; he must have attained that state which is difficult even for sages to reach.
Excellent, śramaṇa!"
"You shall certainly attain liberation.
His wish not being fulfilled, he took his son and departed.

At that time, the World-Honored One entered the meditative absorption of the day; with his divine ear, which surpasses that of humans, he heard what the Venerable Saṃgharakṣita and his former wife had said, and immediately spoke this verse:
“He who does not rejoice at coming, nor grieve at departing;
who is detached from worldly associations and liberated without attachment—
him I call a bhikkhu, a true brāhmaṇa.”
One who does not rejoice at coming, nor grieves at departing;
who is unstained and free from sorrow, with both minds stilled—
him I call a bhikṣu, a true brāhmaṇa.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Saṅgārava, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and delighted in it, paid homage, and departed.
1073 (1073) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was alone in a quiet place and had this thought:
"There are three kinds of fragrances that can be wafted with the wind, but not against the wind."
What are these three?
They are the fragrance of roots, the fragrance of stems, and the fragrance of flowers.
Furthermore, is there a fragrance that perfumes with the wind, perfumes against the wind, and perfumes both with and against the wind?

Having formed this thought, he arose from meditation in the late afternoon, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
While dwelling alone in seclusion, I had this thought:
"There are three kinds of fragrance that can waft with the wind but cannot go against it.
What are these three?"
These are the scents of roots, stems, and flowers.
Furthermore, are there scents that waft with the wind, against the wind, and both with and against the wind?
The Buddha told Ānanda: “So it is! So it is!”
There are three kinds of fragrance that perfume with the wind but cannot perfume against the wind: namely, the fragrance of roots, the fragrance of stems, and the fragrance of flowers.
Ānanda, there is also a fragrance that perfumes with the wind, perfumes against the wind, and perfumes both with and against the wind.
Ānanda! It perfumes with the wind, it perfumes against the wind, and it perfumes both with and against the wind. Ānanda!

There may be sons or daughters of good family who, in whatever city or village they dwell, accomplish the true Dharma by refraining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants for as long as they live.
Thus, noble sons and noble daughters in the eight directions and above and below, honoring these virtuous persons, will all praise them, saying:

"In such-and-such a region and such-and-such a village, there are noble sons and noble daughters who maintain pure precepts, have accomplished the true Dharma, and throughout their lives refrain from killing, up to and including refraining from drinking alcohol."
"Ānanda! This is called fragrance that perfumes with the wind, against the wind, and both with and against the wind.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
Neither roots, stalks, flowers, nor incense Can perfume against the wind;
Only the fragrance of the pure precepts held by Virtuous men and women Pervades all directions,
both with and against the wind, Known everywhere without exception.
Tagara and sandalwood, utpala and mallika— among all such fragrances,
the fragrance of morality is supreme. While the scents of tagara and the like have but a limited reach,
[the fragrance of morality pervades everywhere].
Only the fragrance of virtuous precepts Rises upward as it wafts through the air;
This fragrance of pure precepts, Accompanied by heedfulness and meditative absorption,
And the liberation of right wisdom, Cannot be entered by the path of Māra.
"This is called the path of peace; this path is pure.
It leads directly toward sublime meditative concentration and severs all the fetters of Māra.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and delighted in it, paid his respects, and departed.
1074 (1074). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of Magadha together with a thousand bhikṣus.

All of them had formerly been hair-tufted ascetics who had gone forth; they were all arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who had done what was to be done, laid down their heavy burdens, attained their own benefit, completely destroyed the fetters of existence, and through right knowledge were well-liberated. They were staying at the Well-Established Caitya in the Daṇḍakāraṇya forest.

King Bimbisāra of Magadha heard that the World-Honored One was wandering through the human realm in the land of Magadha and had arrived to reside in the Daṇḍakīvana Arāma at the well-established Caitya. Accompanied by various minor kings, his ministers, and his retinue—consisting of twelve thousand chariots, eighteen thousand horses, and an innumerable multitude of infantrymen—the Brahmins and householders of Magadha all followed him.
The king departed from the city of Rājagṛha and proceeded to where the World-Honored One was, paying him respectful homage.

Upon reaching the gateway, he descended from his carriage and advanced on foot; when he arrived at the inner gate, he removed his five ornaments, took off his crown, set aside his parasol, discarded his fan, laid aside his sword, and removed his leather sandals. Arriving before the Buddha, he adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, prostrated himself before the Buddha, circumambulated him three times to the right, announced his own name, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I am King Bimbisāra of Magadha.
The Buddha said to Bimbisāra,
"So it is, Great King!"
"You are King Bimbisāra; please take this seat and sit as you find comfortable.
Then, King Bimbisāra again prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit on one side.
The various kings, ministers, brahmins, and householders all prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat down in order.
At that time, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa was also among those seated.
At that time, the brahmin householders of Magadha thought to themselves:
"Is it that the Great Śramaṇa has practiced the holy life under Uruvelā-Kāśyapa?"
"Is it for the sake of practicing the holy life under the Great Śramaṇa that you have come, O Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa?
Then, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the mind of the Māgadhaka brāhmaṇa householder, spoke this verse in response:
"What benefit do you see here, O Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, that you have come to the Great Śramaṇa?"
"Abandon those things you previously venerated—the service of fire and all such matters.
Now you may explain their meaning; tell us the reason for abandoning the worship of fire.
Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa spoke this verse to the Buddha:
"The flavors of wealth and the like, the fruits of female beauty and the five desires—
observing that what is received in the future, these are all great defilements; therefore,
I have completely renounced them, as well as my former service to the sacrificial fires."
At that time, the World-Honored One again spoke in verse, asking:
"You are not attached to the world, Nor to wealth, the five colors, or flavors;
Why then do you renounce gods and humans? Kāśyapa, speak according to the meaning."
Kāśyapa again replied to the World-Honored One in verse:
“Having seen the Path and being free from remainder, In tranquil extinction there is no further trace;
Possessing nothing and clinging to naught, There are no divergent destinies or divergent paths.”
Therefore, completely renounce all former practices of fire-worship,
the observance of great assemblies, and the service of water and fire.
Those who are submerged in such folly yet aspire to seek the path of liberation— [should abandon these].
Blind and lacking the eye of wisdom, I was headed toward birth, old age, sickness, and death;
not seeing the true path, I was forever separated from the way beyond birth and death.
Now, for the first time, because of the World-Honored One, I have attained the vision of the unconditioned path.
By the power spoken by the Great Nāga, one attains the further shore;
the Muni brings vast deliverance and comforts immeasurable multitudes.
Only now do I truly know that Gautama is the one who has transcended to the ultimate truth.
The Buddha further spoke in verse, praising Kāśyapa:
“Excellent, you, Kāśyapa! Previously, your reflections were not unwholesome;
By seeking through successive stages of discernment, You have thus reached this supreme state.”
“Now, Kāśyapa, you must comfort the hearts of your followers.

Then, Uruvilvākāśyapa immediately entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and, by means of his supernormal power (*ṛddhibala*), rose into the air toward the east. There he performed the four kinds of miraculous transformations (*ṛddhiprātihārya*): walking, standing, sitting, and reclining; he entered the fire-samādhi (*tejodhātu-samādhi*), and his entire body became ablaze with blue, yellow, red, white, crystal, and crimson hues.

Water issued from the upper part of his body and fire issued from the lower part, burning his body; then water issued from the upper part of his body to drench his body. Or, fire issued from the upper part of his body to burn his body, while water issued from the lower part of his body to drench his body.
Having thus ceased these various manifested supernatural transformations, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha is my teacher, and I am his disciple.”
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa, “I am your teacher and you are my disciple; sit back down on your seat as you see fit.
Thereupon, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa returned to his original seat.
At that time, the brahmin householders of Magadha thought to themselves:
"Uruvelā Kāśyapa must certainly be practicing the holy life under the Great Śramaṇa."

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, King Bimbisāra of Magadha, along with the brahmins and elders, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and approved, paid their respects, and departed.
1075 (1075). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.

At that time, there was a monk named Dabba Mallaputta who had long resided in Rājagṛha; he was in charge of the food and drink for the Saṅgha and assigned beds and seats in their proper order, ensuring that no one was bypassed.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Maitrībala who, having been assigned three times in succession to a place where coarse food was obtained, experienced great hardship at mealtimes and thought to himself:
"How strange! How wondrous!"
"What great suffering!
Because the bhikṣu Dharmaruci has feelings, he has troubled me with coarse food, causing me extreme distress at mealtime. How could I possibly do anything harmful to him?"
At that time, the bhikṣu Maitrībala had a sister, a bhikṣuṇī named Maitrāyaṇī, who was staying among the community of bhikṣuṇīs in the royal park at Rājagṛha.
The bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyānī approached the bhikṣu Maitrībala, prostrated at his feet, and stood to one side.
The bhikṣu Maitrībala did not look at her nor speak with her.
The bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyānī said to the bhikṣu Maitreya:
"Venerable sir!
Why do you not look upon me or speak with me?"
The bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra said:
"The bhikṣu Dharmaruci has repeatedly distressed me with coarse food, making my meals extremely painful; now you, too, have abandoned me."
The bhikṣuṇī asked, "What should be done?
The bhikṣu Maitrībala replied:
"You should go to the Blessed One and say:
'Blessed One!
The bhikṣu Dharmadinnā’s son has acted improperly and inconsistently with the Dharma; he has committed a pārājika offense against me by engaging in unchaste conduct.'"
I shall bear witness, saying: "So it is,
World-Honored One!"
"It is as you, sister, have said. The bhikṣuṇī said, "Āryā!"
"How could I possibly slander a bhikṣu of pure conduct with a *pārājika* offense?
The bhikṣu Maitrībala said, "If you do not act thus, I shall sever ties with you; I will no longer come and go with you, speak with you, or even look upon one another."
Then, the bhikṣuṇī remained silent for a moment and said:
"Āryā! If you wish to have me act thus, I shall follow your instruction."
The bhikṣu Maitrībala said, "Wait a moment;
let me go first to where the World-Honored One is, and you may follow after me.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu Maitrībala went at once to pay his respects, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyanī followed closely behind him, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How truly unwholesome and improper is Dabba Mallaputta!”
"I have committed the *pārājika* offense of unchaste conduct with me.
The bhikṣu Maitrībala again addressed the Buddha, saying,
"As this sister has said, I also knew it beforehand."
At that time, the bhikṣu Dharmadinnāputra was present among that great assembly.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣu Dharmadinnāputra:
"Did you hear these words?"
The bhikṣu Dharmapāla replied,
“I have heard it, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu Dharmapāla:
"What do you think now?
Dabba Mallaputta replied to the Buddha:
"As the World-Honored One knows; as the Sugata knows."
The Buddha said to Dhānañjāni:
"What you have said regarding what the World-Honored One knows is not the time for it now. If you remember something, you should say that you remember;
if you do not remember, you should say that you do not remember."
Dabba Mallaputta replied,
“I do not recall it. At that time,
the Venerable Rāhula was standing behind the Buddha, fanning him with a fan, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is improper and unseemly that this bhikṣuṇī says:
‘The Venerable Dharmadinnā and I have engaged in unchaste conduct.’”
The bhikṣu Maitrībala said:
“So it is, World-Honored One!
I already knew this beforehand, just as my sister has described.”
The Buddha said to Rāhula:
"I now ask you; answer me as you see fit.
Suppose the bhikṣuṇī Mṛdvīkā were to come and say to me:"
"World-Honored One!
The ignoble and unworthy Rāhula has committed the pārājika offense of unchaste conduct with me.
The bhikṣu Maitrībala then addressed me again, saying:
“If it is so, World-Honored One!
As my sister has said, ‘I also knew this beforehand,’ what would you say?
Rāhula addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
If I remember something, I shall say that I remember it;
if I do not remember it, I shall say that I do not remember it.”
The Buddha said,
"Rāhula! If even you,
a foolish person, can speak such words, why should the pure bhikṣu Dharmadinnāputra not be able to speak likewise?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"You should keep the bhikṣu Dharmadinnā’s son in mind; the bhikṣuṇī Mithilā should be dealt with according to her own confession; and the Saṅgha should strictly admonish and instruct the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra, saying:
'How do you see this?'"
“Where did you see him?
For what reason did you go to see him?
Having thus instructed them, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and entered his room to sit in meditation.

At that time, the bhikṣus called to mind the case of the bhikṣu Dharmadinnā; they granted the *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation) to the bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyanī, and they severely rebuked and exhorted the bhikṣu Maitra, saying:
"How do you see this?"
"Where did you see him?
For what reason did you go to see him?
When he was thus admonished, he spoke as follows:

"That Dabba Mallaputta has not engaged in unchaste conduct, nor has he committed a *pārājika* offense; nevertheless, the bhikṣu Dabba Mallaputta has terrified me three times with coarse food, causing me distress at mealtime."
