The bhikṣu replied,
"I shall treat it so that it may be healed!"
The deva said to the bhikṣu, “The ulcer is like an iron cauldron; how can it be healed?
The bhikṣu replied:
“Right mindfulness and right clear comprehension are sufficient to restore it.
The deva said, “Excellent!”
"Excellent!
This is the treatment for a wound administered by a true physician; treated in this manner, the wound will be completely healed and shall never recur.
At that time, in the late afternoon, the World-Honored One arose from meditation and returned to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Entering among the monks, he arranged his seat before the great assembly and sat down, addressing the bhikṣus:
"This morning, having dressed and taken my bowl, I entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food."
Having returned from alms-round, he went to the Andhavana forest to practice meditation and entered the meditative absorption of the day.

There was another bhikṣu who also returned from alms-round and went to the Andhavana forest; sitting beneath a tree, he entered the meditative absorption of the day, yet that bhikṣu gave rise to unwholesome thoughts, and his mind became dependent on evil craving.
A deva dwelling in the Andhavana grove spoke to the bhikṣu, saying:
"Bhikṣu! Bhikṣu!"
"Did you create a tumor or a growth?
... [as explained at length above] ... "In this way, bhikṣus!
Excellent!"
"Excellent! This is the governance of the assembly of the worthy.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“A person creates a festering sore, bringing suffering and affliction upon themselves;
seeking worldly desires, their mind relies on evil greed.
Because this sore has arisen, maggots and flies swarm together to gather there.”
Sensual desire is a festering sore; the filth of flies and various unwholesome thoughts, as well as all covetous and greedy minds, are born entirely from the will.
They bore into the heart of the person, seeking only flowery fame and profit.
The fire of desire blazes ever more fiercely; with unwholesome perceptions born of false imagination, body and mind grow emaciated day and night, far removed from the path of tranquility.
If the inner mind is tranquil, decisive wisdom will be clearly manifest.
Free from such sores and blemishes, one beholds the path of the Buddha’s peace.
This is the track traversed by the noble ones, well-expounded by the sages and saints;
it is the way known by those of clear wisdom, through which one no longer undergoes further existence.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1083 (1083). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, by the side of the Monkey Pond, in the Multi-storied Lecture Hall.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus dressed in the morning, took up their bowls, and entered Vaiśālī to beg for food.
Among them was a young bhikṣu who had not long been ordained; being unacquainted with the Dharma and the Vinaya, he did not know the proper order of precedence when begging for alms.
Other bhikṣus, having seen this, said to him:
"You are young and have not long been ordained; you do not yet know the Dharma and the Vinaya, so do not transgress!"
"Do not be negligent!
If you go on almsrounds with your sequence disordered, you shall experience disadvantageous suffering for a long night.
The young bhikṣu said:
"The other elders have likewise bypassed their turn, not following the proper order; it is not I alone.
Thus he spoke a second and a third time, yet they could not be made to desist.

After many bhikṣus had finished their almsround, they returned to the vihāra, put away their robes and bowls, and having washed their feet, they went to where the Buddha was. They prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This morning, having dressed and taken up our bowls, we entered Vaiśālī for alms.

There was a young bhikṣu who had not long been ordained in this Dharma and Vinaya; while going for alms, he did not follow the proper sequence, taking both before and after [the others], and even repeatedly.
The bhikṣus admonished them two or three times, but they would not accept it, saying:
"Even the elders do not follow the proper order; why then do you rebuke us?
Since we bhikṣus admonished them three times and they would not accept it, we have come to inform the World-Honored One.
“We only pray that the World-Honored One will remove this unrighteousness out of compassion!
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“It is like a great lake in a desolate wilderness where a large dragon-elephant dwells; it extracts the lotus roots, washes away the mud, and then eats them.”
Having eaten, his body became plump and healthy, and he possessed great strength and much joy; by reason of this, he dwelt constantly in happiness.

There was another elephant of a different species, whose physical form was emaciated and small; imitating that dragon-elephant, he pulled up lotus roots, but being unable to wash them clean, he ate them together with the mud.

If he eats it and cannot digest it, his body will not become plump or joyful; instead, he will grow increasingly emaciated and weak, leading to death by this cause, or suffering the same as those who have already died.

"In this way, a bhikṣu of long-standing virtue who has studied the Path for a long time, who does not delight in play and amusement, and who has long practiced the holy life (brahmacarya), is praised by the Great Master, and is likewise further praised by all other wise practitioners of the holy life."

These bhikṣus, depending upon towns and villages, put on their robes and take up their bowls at dawn to enter the city for alms. They well protect body and speech, well restrain the sense faculties, and focus their minds with mindfulness. They are able to inspire faith in those who lack it, and ensure that those who already have faith do not waver. Should they obtain wealth, gain, clothing, bedding, food and drink, or medicinal requisites, they do not become stained by them, do not cling to them, do not crave them, do not relish them, do not become deluded by them, and do not pursue them. Seeing their faults and perils, and seeing the way of escape from them, they nevertheless consume them.
Having eaten, his body and mind become radiant and supple; he gains physical beauty and strength. By these causes and conditions, he constantly attains peace and happiness.

"That young bhikṣu has not long been ordained and is not yet familiar with the Dharma and Vinaya. Relying on the elders and dwelling in a village, he puts on his robes, takes up his bowl, and enters the village for alms. He does not skillfully guard his person, does not maintain the gates of the senses, and is not single-mindedly focused in mindfulness; thus he cannot cause those without faith to believe, nor can he prevent those who already believe from changing their minds."

If one obtains wealth, clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites, yet becomes stained by attachment and pursues them greedily—failing to see their faults and failings, and failing to see the way of escape—one eats with a mind of sensual craving; this cannot bring the body refreshment, luster, peace, or happiness.
On account of this food, one turns toward death, or experiences suffering equal to death.
What is called "death" here refers to abandoning the precepts and returning to lay life, thereby losing the True Dharma and the True Vinaya.
"Those who suffer death together are those who violate the True Dharma and the Vinaya, who do not recognize the characteristics of offenses, and who do not know how to remove them.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The dragon-elephant pulls up the lotus root, Washes it with water, and eats it."
"The elephant of a different species imitated them, Mixing it with mud to take as food.
Because of eating this mixed mud, It became emaciated and ill, eventually leading to its death.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1084. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Śītavana cemetery at Rājagṛha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Life is exceedingly brief and swiftly passes into the next world; you should diligently practice the wholesome dharmas and cultivate the various pure conducts."
"There is no birth that is not followed by death, yet the people of the world do not diligently apply skillful means to cultivate wholesome dharmas, nor do they cultivate virtue or righteousness.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama is staying in the Cool Grove (Śītavana) among the charnel grounds near Rājagṛha, preaching the Dharma to his disciples in this manner:"
"The human lifespan is exceedingly brief; one does not even have time to cultivate virtue or righteousness.
"I shall now go there to cause him disturbance.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas transformed himself into a youth, went before the Buddha, and spoke this verse:
"Constantly oppressing sentient beings, though they obtain long life in the human realm,
their minds remain intoxicated and negligent, and they do not turn toward the place of death.
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:
"This is an evil Māra who has come to cause disturbance and confusion.
He then spoke in verse:
"Constantly oppressing sentient beings, They undergo births of extremely short lifespans."
One should diligently cultivate vigor, as if one's head were on fire.
Do not be idle for even a moment, lest the Mara of Death suddenly arrive.
"Know that you are an evil Mara; depart quickly from here!"
The Māra Pāpīyān thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama already knows my mind.
Ashamed, sorrowful, and distressed, he immediately vanished and disappeared.
1085 (1085). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Śītavana cemetery at Rājagṛha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all conditioned phenomena are unstable, insecure, and lack respite; they are subject to the law of change. One should therefore bring all conditioned formations to rest, becoming weary of them, disenchanted with them, and liberated from them."
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān thought to himself:
"Now the śramaṇa Gautama is staying in the Śītavana forest near Rājagṛha, teaching this Dharma to his śrāvakas:

'All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, unstable, not a source of rest, and subject to change; one should even bring all conditioned things to a halt through weariness, detachment, lack of delight, and liberation.'"
"I shall go there and cause him disturbance.
He then transformed himself into a youth, went to where the Buddha was, stood before the Buddha, and spoke this verse:
"Life flows day and night, Without any time of exhaustion."
"Life comes and goes, just like the turning of a wheel.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"This is Māra, the Evil One, who wishes to cause disturbance."
Then he spoke in verse:
"Days and nights constantly flow on, And life is likewise diminished accordingly;
The human lifespan gradually wastes away, Just like the waters of a small river."
"I know you, evil Māra; you shall vanish away of your own accord.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama already knows my mind."
Filled with shame and remorse, he immediately vanished and was no longer seen. 1086 (1086). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.

At that time, the World-Honored One rose in the night and practiced walking meditation; when the latter part of the night arrived, he washed his feet, entered the room, sat with body composed and upright, and concentrated his mind in focused mindfulness.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:

“Now the śramaṇa Gautama, in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove at Rājagṛha, has risen in the night to walk in meditation; during the latter part of the night, he has washed his feet, entered his room, sat with body erect and upright, and focused his mindfulness in meditative contemplation.”
"I shall now go there to cause him disturbance.
He immediately transformed himself into a youth and stood before the Buddha, speaking in verse:
"My mind is in the sky; I hold a long rope-noose and cast it down."
"I wish to bind this śramaṇa so that you do not attain liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought:
"The evil Māra Pāpīyān wishes to cause disturbance."
He then spoke in verse:
"I declare that in this world, there are five desires with the mind as the sixth;
having forever departed from them, all suffering has been severed."
"I have already left those desires behind; mind, intellect, and consciousness are also extinguished.
Pāpīyān, I know you now; depart quickly from here!
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān had this thought:
“The ascetic already knows my mind.
Feeling shame and sorrow, he immediately vanished and disappeared.
1087 (1087) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.

At that time, the World-Honored One rose in the night to practice walking meditation. When the latter part of the night arrived, he washed his feet, entered his room, and lay down on his right side to rest, fixing his mindfulness on the perception of light, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, maintaining the intention to arise.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:
"Now the śramaṇa Gautama resides in Rājagṛha at the Kalandakanivāpa in the Bamboo Grove, even as he gives rise to thoughts of awakening."
"I shall now go there to create an obstacle for him.
He then transformed himself into a young man, went before the Buddha, and spoke this verse:
"Why do you sleep? For what reason do you sleep?"
"Having already extinguished [defilements], why sleep again?
Why sleep in an empty house? Having attained liberation, why sleep again?
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:
"The Māra Pāpīyān wishes to cause disturbance," he said, and then spoke this verse:
"Because of the net of craving, one is stained and attached; Without craving, who could carry one away?"
"When all that remains has been exhausted, only the Buddha attains peaceful sleep.
You, evil Māra Pāpīyas, what do you have to say about this?
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:
“The śramaṇa Gautama already knows my mind.
Feeling ashamed, sorrowful, and dejected, he immediately vanished and was no longer seen. 1088 (1088) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, during the darkness of night, when the sky was slightly drizzling with rain and flashes of lightning were momentarily appearing, the World-Honored One emerged from his chamber and began walking in meditation.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:

"Now the śramaṇa Gautama is staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha; it is dark night with a fine drizzle, and flashes of lightning appear from time to time, as he has come out of his cell to walk in meditation."
"I shall now go there to create obstacles for him.
Grasping a large boulder, he toyed with it in both hands and, arriving before the Buddha, crushed it into fine dust.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"The evil Māra Pāpīyān wishes to cause disturbance.
He then spoke these verses:
"Even if Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa were to crumble before me,
it could not move a single hair of the Buddha’s liberation.
Even if all the mountains and lands within the four oceans [were to collapse],"
"Even the kinsmen of negligence could not cause even a single hair of the Tathāgata to be shattered into dust or moved.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān thought to himself:
“The śramaṇa Gautama already knows my mind.
Feeling sorrow and distress within, he immediately vanished and disappeared.
1089 (1089). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, the World-Honored One rose in the night to practice walking meditation; when the latter part of the night arrived, he washed his feet, entered his room, sat upright with his body straight, and focused his mindfulness before him.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:

"Now the śramaṇa Gautama is staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha; having risen at night, he has been walking in meditation, and during the latter part of the night he has entered his chamber, sitting upright with his body straight and his mindfulness fixed before him."
"I shall now go there to create obstacles for him.

He immediately transformed himself into a great dragon, coiled seven times around the Buddha’s body. He raised his head over the Buddha’s crown; his body was like a great ship, his head like a vast sail, his eyes like bronze furnaces, his tongue like a trailing flash of lightning, and his inhalations and exhalations sounded like the roar of thunder and hail.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"The evil Māra Pāpīyān wishes to cause disturbance.
He then spoke these verses:
"Just as in an empty house, the mind of the Muni is void and tranquil;
within it he moves about, and the Buddha-body is likewise.
Therein dwell immeasurable fierce dragons, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, fleas, and the like."
They gather everywhere to devour his body, yet they cannot move even a single hair.
They shatter the void and overturn the great earth;
all classes of sentient beings come together to strike terror.
"Swords, spears, lances, and sharp arrows—may they all come to harm the Buddha’s body;
yet such violent harms as these cannot injure even a single hair.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān thought to himself:
“The śramaṇa Gautama already knows my mind.
Feeling inward grief and dejection, he immediately vanished and disappeared.
1090 (1090) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in a stone cave within the Saptaparṇa Forest on Mount Vaibhāra near Rājagṛha.
At that time, during the night, the World-Honored One rose and stayed in the open air, either sitting or walking in meditation.

When the latter part of the night arrived, he washed his feet, entered the room, and lay down to rest. He placed his right side upon the ground with one foot resting upon the other, fixing his mindfulness on the sign of light, maintaining right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, and forming the intention to arise.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:

"The śramaṇa Gautama is staying in a stone cave within the Saptaparṇa forest on Mount Vaibhāra near Rājagṛha. During the night, he rises in the open air, either sitting or walking; then, toward the end of the night, he washes his feet, enters his room, and sits down. He lies down on his right side to rest, placing one foot upon the other, fixing his mindfulness on the sign of light, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, maintaining the perception of rising."
"I shall now go there to create an obstacle.
He transformed himself into a youth, went before the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
"Is it because of me that you sleep? Or is it for the sake of this being your final birth?"
"You possess abundant wealth and treasures; why do you dwell in solitude?
Being alone without a peer, you are addicted to sleep.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought thus:
“The evil Māra Pāpīyān wishes to cause disturbance,” he said, and then spoke this verse:
“It is not because of you that I sleep; This is not my final end.”
He possesses no great wealth, but gathers only the treasure of sorrowlessness.
Out of compassion for the world, he lies down to rest on his right side;
whether awake, he has no doubt, and even when sleeping, he is not afraid.
Whether by day or by night, there is neither increase nor decrease;
because he sleeps out of compassion for sentient beings, there is no loss or diminution.
Even if one were to pierce his body with a hundred spears, constantly prodding and shaking him, [he would remain unmoved].
"One can still sleep in peace, for one has already abandoned the internal spear.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought:
"The śramaṇa Gautama already knows my mind."
With deep sorrow in his heart, he immediately vanished from sight.
(1091) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, in a stone cave within the Saptaparṇī forest on Mount Vaibhāra.

At that time, the Venerable Gotiputa was dwelling in a black stone cave on the side of the Isigili Mountain near Rājagaha. He lived alone in solitary reflection, practicing with diligence for his own benefit. He attained temporary liberation of mind through bodily realization, yet he repeatedly fell back from it;

after falling away once, twice, thrice, four times, five times, and six times, he regained it each time, attaining temporary liberation of mind through bodily realization only to fall away again immediately.
That venerable Godhika thought to himself:

"While I was dwelling alone in seclusion, practicing with diligence and heedfulness for my own benefit, I attained and personally realized the liberation of mind through direct experience; yet I repeatedly fell back from it.
This has happened up to six times, and even now I have fallen back again."
"I shall now take my own life with a blade, lest I undergo a seventh regression.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:

"The śramaṇa Gautama resides in the Seven-Leaf Forest at the side of Mount Vaibhāra near Rājagṛha. His disciple Gautika resides in a black stone cave on the side of the Ṛṣigiri near Rājagṛha; dwelling alone in a quiet place, he has applied himself with focused diligence and attained liberation through realization of the mind in the present moment, having personally realized it with his body. Although he has regressed six times, he has regained it once more."
He thought to himself:
"I have already regressed six times and yet recovered each time; let me not regress for a seventh time. I would rather kill myself with a blade than regress for a seventh time."
"If that bhikṣu should take his own life with a blade, do not let him kill himself; let him depart from my realm, for I shall now go to inform the Great Teacher."
At that time, Pāpīyas took up a lute with a lapis lazuli handle and approached the World-Honored One; plucking the strings, he spoke this verse:
"Great wisdom and great skillful means, Mastery and great supernormal power— Having obtained disciples who blaze with radiance, You now wish to meet your death."
The Great Sage should establish a rule so that they do not take their own lives;
for how could one hear of the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
or his disciples of the True Dharma and Vinaya learning what cannot be attained and yet bringing about the end of their lives?
When Māra had spoken this verse, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
“Pāpīyān, you who are of a heedless nature, have come for your own sake;
but the steadfast man, fully endowed [with virtue], dwells ever in sublime meditative concentration.”
Diligent in effort day and night, disregarding even life itself,
seeing the three realms of existence as terrifying, he severed those cravings.
Having already vanquished the armies of Māra, Gotama entered parinirvāṇa.
Pāpīyān’s heart was filled with grief and distress, and his lute fell to the ground.
Having harbored this inner sorrow, he immediately vanished and disappeared.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You all should come together and go to the Black Rock Cave on the side of the Ṛṣigiri Mountain to see the bhikṣu Gotiputa who has taken his own life with a knife.

At that time, the World-Honored One, accompanied by many bhikṣus, went to the Black Rock Cave on the side of the Ṛṣigiri Mountain. Seeing the bhikṣu Gotiputa lying on the ground having killed himself, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you see this bhikṣu Gotiputa lying on the ground, having killed himself?"
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha:
“Indeed, we have seen them, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Do you see, monks, how black smoke rises all around the body of the bhikṣu Gotiputa, filling the four quarters?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha,
"We have seen it, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"This was the evil Māra Pāpīyān, who sought the consciousness-principle (vijñāna) all around the body of the noble son Gautika; however, the bhikṣu Gautika, with a mind that did not dwell [on anything], took up a knife and committed suicide."
At that time, the World-Honored One bestowed the first prediction of enlightenment upon the bhikṣu Gautika.
Then, Pāpīyas spoke in verse:
“Up and down, and in all directions, I have searched everywhere for that consciousness-spirit.”
"Not seeing his whereabouts at all, where has Gautami gone?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Such a steadfast man, who seeks nothing at all,"
Having uprooted the foundation of affection and love, Gautamī has entered parinirvāṇa.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1092 (1092). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the village of Uruvilvā on the banks of the Nairañjanā River, not long after he had attained enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān thought to himself:
"Now the śramaṇa Gautama resides by the Nairañjanā River in the village of Uruvilvā; it has not been long since he attained buddhahood beneath the Bodhi tree."
"I shall go there and create obstacles for him.
He then transformed himself into a young man, went before the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
"Entering alone into a solitary place, You meditate and contemplate in stillness."
Having already renounced the wealth and treasures of the kingdom, what more is there to seek here?
If you seek the benefits of a village, why do you not associate with people?
Since you do not associate with people, what will you ultimately gain?
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"The evil Māra Pāpīyān wishes to cause disturbance.
He then spoke these verses:
"Having already attained great wealth and profit, his will is contented and he dwells in tranquil extinction;
having subdued all the armies of Māra, he is not attached to sensual desires.
Solitary, he engages in meditative reflection, partaking of the sublime bliss of dhyāna."
"Therefore, I shall not associate with people nor dwell in their company.
Māra spoke again in verse:
"Gautama, if you yourself know the path to peace and nirvāṇa,"
"To find joy in solitary non-action—why do you strive to strengthen others?
The Buddha again spoke in verse, answering:
"In a place not governed by Māra, you have come to ask how to cross to the other shore."
I shall answer with the correct response, enabling him to attain nirvāṇa;
may he then achieve heedfulness and no longer fall under the power of Māra.
Māra spoke again in verse:
“There was a stone resembling congealed fat; a flying bird, wishing to come and eat it, ultimately could not find its flavor and returned to the sky with its beak damaged.
I now am just like that; my toil has been in vain as I return to the celestial palace.”
When Māra had spoken thus, he harbored inner grief and remorse arose in his heart; he lowered his head, prostrated himself on the ground, and traced figures in the earth with his fingers.
Māra had three daughters—first named Rati (Desire), second named Arati (Affection), and third named Tṛṣṇā (Thirst)—who came to where Pāpīyān was and spoke these verses:
"Father, why do you now grieve so sorrowfully? What is there for a man to worry about?"
"By the rope of desire, I have bound him like a tamed elephant;
I have brought him before his father and shall make him subject to his father's will.
Māra replied to the women:
“He has already transcended affection and love; he cannot be summoned by desire.
He has emerged from the realm of Māra; for this reason, I am sorrowful.

At that time, the three daughters of Māra emitted flames from their bodies, blazing like lightning amidst the clouds. They approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now take refuge at the feet of the World-Honored One and offer myself as a servant to attend to his every command.
At that time, the World-Honored One did not look back at him at all,
knowing that the Tathāgata was free from all craving and desire, and that his mind was well-liberated.
Thus they spoke a second and a third time.
Then the three māra-maidens said to one another:

"Men have various desires according to their forms; we shall now each transform ourselves, manifesting a hundred kinds of young maidens, a hundred kinds of newlywed brides, a hundred kinds of those who have not yet borne children, a hundred kinds of those who have already borne children, a hundred kinds of women in their prime, and a hundred kinds of elderly women. Having assumed these various forms and appearances, let us go to where the śramaṇa Gautama is and say this:"
"We now all take refuge at your venerable feet and offer ourselves as servants to attend to your every command.

Having made this proposal, they immediately performed various transformations as described above and approached the World-Honored One. They bowed their heads to his feet in prostration, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"We today take refuge at your venerable feet and offer ourselves as your servants.
At that time, the World-Honored One paid them no heed whatsoever.
"The Dharma of the Tathāgata is free from all craving and desire."
After she had spoken thus three times, the three demonesses said to one another:

"If a man who has not yet abandoned desire sees our various exquisite forms, his mind will become deluded and distracted; the force of his lust will strike him so violently that his chest will burst and hot blood will steam from his face."

Yet now, the śramaṇa Gautama does not deign to look upon us at all; as such, he must be a Tathāgata who has abandoned desire and attained liberation, having achieved the perception of perfect liberation.
"Today we shall each again speak verses as questions.
They once more approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The celestial maidens of the Realm of Desire then spoke these verses:
"Alone in solitary meditation and silence, having renounced worldly wealth and treasures;
since you have already abandoned worldly gain, what do you now seek?
If you seek the benefits of the village, why do you not associate with people?"
Having never associated with people, what will you ultimately gain?
The Buddha answered in verse:
“I have already attained great wealth and profit; my mind is content and I dwell in peaceful extinction.”
"Having subdued all the hosts of Māras, he does not cling to form or desire.
For this reason, he does not associate with or draw near to others.
The beloved celestial maiden spoke again in verse:
“By cultivating what sublime meditation Do you cross the stream of the five desires?
Furthermore, by what skillful means Do you cross the sixth ocean?
How do you cultivate sublime meditation Regarding all these deep and vast desires?”
Having reached the further shore, how can one not be held by craving?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
“The body attains the bliss of rest, and the mind attains sublime liberation.”
Unconditioned and without action, with right mindfulness unshakable,
he thoroughly understands all phenomena and gives rise to no distracted thoughts;
craving, aversion, and the veil of sleep— all these have been abandoned.
By practicing thus extensively, one attains crossing over the five desires,
and likewise at the sixth sea, one completely reaches the further shore.
By practicing dhyāna in this way, regarding all deep and vast desires,
"Having all crossed to the other shore, they are not held by those [afflictions].
Then, the goddess Priyā spoke again in verse:
"Having severed the bonds of affection, though having accumulated a deep store of desire,"
"Generating pure faith in many beings, they shall cross over the flood of desire.
Developing clear wisdom, they shall transcend the realm of the Lord of Death.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse in reply:
"By means of great skillful expedients and vast deliverance, they have entered the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata;
since these beings have all already been delivered, what more need the wise worry about?
At that time, the three goddesses, their aspirations unfulfilled, returned to their father, Māra Pāpīyān.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān saw the women approaching from afar and addressed them with these verses to mock them:
"You three women, Boast of your own capabilities;
All of you emit bodily radiance, Like lightning flashing from within the clouds."
They went before the One of Great Exertion, each manifesting their own form and appearance,
yet they were defeated by him as easily as wind blowing through cotton.
They sought to shatter mountains with their claws and bite through iron balls with their teeth.
One might wish to use a lotus fiber from one's hair to spin a great mountain;
though all things are in union and liberated, one might hope to disturb the mind.
If one could bind the feet of the wind and cause the moon to fall from the sky, [only then could one move him].
One might drain the great ocean with one's hands, Or cause the Snowy Mountains to tremble with a sigh;
Even those who are harmoniously united in liberation May be made to waver and fall.
Yet, within that deep and vast ocean, One seeks a place of firm footing.
"The Tathāgata is completely liberated from all attachments;
even if one sought to stir the great ocean of his perfect enlightenment, it would likewise remain unmoved.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān, having toyed with his three daughters, immediately vanished and was no longer seen.
1093 (1093) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Uruvilvā on the bank of the Nairañjanā River beneath the Great Bodhi Tree, having newly attained the Way of the Buddha.
The Māra Pāpīyān thought to himself:
“This śramaṇa Gautama is staying at Uruvilvā by the side of the Nairañjanā River beneath the Bodhi tree, having just attained the path of Buddhahood.”
"I shall now go there to create obstacles for him.
He immediately transformed his body, manifesting a hundred kinds of pure and impure forms, and approached the Buddha's dwelling.
From afar, the Buddha saw Pāpīyān with his hundred kinds of pure and impure forms, and he thought:
"The Māra Pāpīyān manifests a hundred kinds of pure and impure forms, desiring to cause disturbance.
He then spoke in verse:
"Throughout the long night of birth and death, He manifests pure and impure forms."
Why do you act in this way, not crossing over to the further shore of suffering?
If one does not create obstacles through body, speech,
or mind, one cannot be taught by Māra and will not follow Māra’s will.
"Thus he knows the evil Māra, and thereupon he vanishes of his own accord.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought:
"The śramaṇa Gautama already knows my mind."
With deep sorrow in his heart, he immediately vanished and was no longer seen. (1094) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Uruvelā on the bank of the Nairañjanā River beneath the Bodhi tree, having newly attained perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One was alone in a quiet place, contemplating with focused concentration, and had this thought:
"I have now been liberated from asceticism.
How excellent!"
"I have now successfully liberated myself from ascetic practices; having previously cultivated right aspirations, I have now attained the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān thought to himself:
"Now the śramaṇa Gautama dwells at Uruvilvā, beneath the Bodhi tree on the banks of the Nairañjanā River, having just attained perfect enlightenment."
"I shall now go there to create obstacles for him.
He then transformed himself into a youth and stood before the Buddha, speaking in verse:
"In this place of great ascetic practice, which can bring about complete purification,"
"Now, on the contrary, you have abandoned it; what do you seek here?
If you wish to seek purity here, purity cannot be attained.
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:
"This Māra Pāpīyān wishes to cause disturbance.
He then spoke in verse:
"Know that all those who practice asceticism Are accompanied by what is meaningless."
In the end, one gains no benefit at all, like the sound of a bow being drawn.
The path of precepts, concentration, learning, and wisdom—I have fully cultivated them all.
I have attained the foremost purity; that purity is unsurpassed.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama already knows my mind.
Feeling inner grief and distress, he immediately vanished and disappeared.
1095 (1095). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the brahmin village of Sālā.
Then, in the morning, the World-Honored One dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the brahmin village for alms.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:

"Now the śramaṇa Gautama, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl, has entered the village of Bārāṇasī to beg for food. I shall go now and enter his house first, speaking to the faithful brahmins and householders so that the śramaṇa Gautama leaves with an empty bowl."
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas followed behind the Buddha and proclaimed these words:
"Śramaṇa! Śramaṇa!"
"Is it that one may not eat at all?
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"The evil Māra Pāpīyān wishes to cause disturbance."
Then he spoke in verse:
"You have newly incurred immeasurable sin against the Tathāgata;
do you think that the Tathāgata experiences various sufferings and afflictions?"
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas spoke these words: “Gautama!
Enter the village once more, and you shall obtain food.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Even if one possesses nothing at all, One may live in peace and happiness,
Just like those gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, Who always feed upon joy."
"Even if there is nothing at all, one may live in peace and happiness,
always nourished by joy and not dependent on this physical body.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama already knows my mind.
Feeling sorrow and distress within, he immediately vanished and disappeared.
1096 (1096) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Deer Park, the Abode of Seers, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I have already been liberated from the snares of gods and humans; you, too, have been liberated from the snares of gods and humans."

"You all should go among the people; you will bring about much deliverance and much benefit, bringing peace and happiness to humans and devas. You need not travel in company; go each one by yourself."
"I shall now also go to the human realm at Uruvelā to wander about.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama is staying at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Sages near Vārāṇasī, and he is teaching the Dharma to his disciples in this way:"
"I have already liberated myself from the snares of gods and humans; you too are capable of doing so.
You should each go separately to the human world to teach and transform others, and I, too, shall travel through the human world to the dwelling place of Uruvilvā."
"I shall now go there to create obstacles for him.
He then transformed himself into a youth, stood before the Buddha, and spoke this verse:
"Those who have not attained liberation yet imagine they have attained it, Claiming to themselves that they are already liberated."
"Bound by great fetters, I shall never release you now.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought:
"The evil Māra Pāpīyas wishes to cause disturbance."
He then spoke in verse:
"I have already been liberated from all the snares of humans and devas;
knowing you to be Pāpīyān, you shall now vanish of your own accord."
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself,
"The śramaṇa Gautama already knows my mind.
Feeling sorrow and distress within, he immediately vanished and disappeared.
1097 (1097). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying among the Śākyas at the Śākya village of Śilavaṃta.
At that time, many people in the Śākya village of Śilavaṃta were dying from an epidemic.

People everywhere, whether men or women, came from the four directions to receive and uphold the Three Refuges. Among those who were ill, whether men or women, great or small, they all called out their own names as they arrived, saying:
"I, so-and-so, take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus."
"From the entire village to the entire town, it was all exactly like this.
At that time, the World-Honored One diligently preached the Dharma for the sake of the śrāvakas.
Then, those with faith who had taken refuge in the Triple Gem were all reborn among humans and devas."
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān thought to himself:
"Now the śramaṇa Gautama is staying at the Śākya village of Śilavaṃta among the Śākyas, diligently preaching the Dharma to the fourfold assembly."
"I shall now go there to create obstacles.
He transformed himself into a young man, went before the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
"Why do you labor so diligently to preach the Dharma, Teaching and transforming all the people?"
"Whether in conflict or not in conflict, one cannot avoid being driven about;
because there are fetters, for what purpose do you preach the Dharma to them?
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:
“The evil Māra Pāpīyān wishes to cause disturbance.
He then spoke this verse:
“O Yakṣa, you should know: when the multitudes of sentient beings are born, ...”
Who among those possessed of wisdom could fail to feel compassion?
Because of this compassion, one cannot but teach and transform others;
out of pity for all sentient beings, such is the natural course of the Dharma.
The evil Māra Pāpīyān thought to himself,
"The śramaṇa Gautama already knows my mind.
Filled with inner grief and sorrow, he immediately vanished and disappeared.
1098 (One thousand and ninety-eight). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying among the Śākyas at the Śākya village of Silākanda.
At that time, the World-Honored One, dwelling alone in a quiet place, engaged in meditative reflection and contemplation, and this thought arose in him:
"Is there perhaps a king who can achieve non-killing, refrain from inciting others to kill, practice exclusively according to the Dharma, and not practice what is contrary to the Dharma?
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:
"Now the ascetic Gautama is staying in the Śākya village of Silākanda, dwelling alone in meditative reflection, and has formed this thought:"
"Is there perhaps a king who does not kill living beings, nor incites others to kill, who practices solely the Dharma and never the non-Dharma?
I shall now go there and preach the Dharma for him."
He transformed himself into a youth, went before the Buddha, and stood there, saying:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
So it is, Sugata!"
"You may become king, provided you do not kill living beings, do not incite others to kill, practice the Dharma exclusively, and do not practice what is contrary to the Dharma.
World-Honored One!
You may now become king; Sugata!"
"You may now become king and will surely obtain your heart's desire.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought:
"The evil Māra Pāpīyān wishes to cause disturbance."
Then he addressed Māra, saying:
"You, Māra Pāpīyān!
Why do you speak these words?"
"Be a king! World-Honored One! Be a king!"
“Sugata! It may be obtained as one wishes.”
Māra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I have heard this teaching directly from the Buddha’s own lips:

‘If one has cultivated and practiced the four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) extensively, then if one wishes to transform the king of mountains, Himavat, into pure gold, it will become so without fail.’”

"The World-Honored One now possesses the four bases of psychic power; through their cultivation and repeated practice, he could transform the King of Snow Mountains into pure gold, just as he wishes, without any difference."
Therefore, I said to the World-Honored One: "Be a king,
World-Honored One!"
"O King! O Sugata!
It may be obtained as you wish."
The Buddha told Pāpīyas:
"I have no mind at all to become a king; how then could I do so?
I also have no mind to cause the King of Snow Mountains to transform into pure gold; by what means could it be transformed?"
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Even if there were pure gold, as vast as the king of snow mountains,
and a single person were to obtain all this gold, they would still not know contentment."
"Therefore, for one of wisdom, / Gold and stone are viewed as one.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama already knows my mind."
With deep sorrow in his heart, he immediately vanished and was no longer seen. 1099 (1099) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying among the Śākyas at the Śākya village of Śilavaṃta.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus were gathered in the assembly hall to perform work for the sake of making robes.
Then, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:

"Now the śramaṇa Gautama is staying at the Śākyas' settlement of Silākara; a great number of bhikṣus are gathered in the assembly hall to perform work for the sake of making robes. I shall now go there to create obstacles."

He transformed himself into the likeness of a young brahmin with long, matted hair, wearing a garment of animal skin and holding a curved staff; he went to the hall of offerings and stood in silence before the assembly of bhikṣus.
After a short while, he said to the bhikṣus:

"You are all young men who have left the household life; your skin is fair and your hair is black, and you are in the prime of your years. You ought to enjoy the adornments of the five desires for your own amusement. Why have you gone against your parents and turned your backs on your clansmen, departing from them with tears of grief, to place your faith in the homeless life, leaving home to study the Way?"
"Why do you abandon the happiness of the present life to seek the untimely happiness of another world?
The bhikṣus said to the brāhmaṇa:
"We do not abandon the happiness of the present life to seek the untimely happiness of another world; rather, we abandon that untimely happiness to pursue the happiness of the present life."
Māra asked again:
"How does one abandon the pleasures of the untimely and pursue the pleasures of the present life?
The bhikṣu replied:
“As the Blessed One has said, the happiness of future lives has little flavor and much suffering, little benefit and many afflictions;

whereas the Blessed One speaks of the happiness of the present life as being free from all burning fevers, not dependent on time, capable of being personally realized through investigation, and to be known by one’s own direct experience.”
“Brahmin! This is called happiness in the present life.
At that time, the brahmin thrice turned his head away, remained mute, and struck the ground with his staff; he then vanished, disappearing from sight.
At that time, the bhikṣus were immediately seized with terror; the hair on their bodies stood on end. "What kind of brahmin is this, appearing in such a guise to perform such a transformation here?
They then went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"A large number of us bhikṣus had gathered in the hall of offerings for the purpose of making robes.
A certain vigorous brahmin with matted hair and a large topknot came to where I was and spoke these words:

'You young men who have left the household life... [As described above in detail], up until three times he shook his head, remained mute, struck the ground with his staff, and then vanished without a trace."
"We were immediately struck with terror and our hair stood on end; what kind of Brahmin is this who comes to perform such a transformation?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This is not a Brahmin; it is Māra Pāpīyān who has come to your place, wishing to cause you disturbance."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"All sufferings and afflictions that arise, Are entirely due to craving and desire.
Knowing that the world is like a sword or a thorn, Who would take pleasure in desire?"
Perceiving that there remains something further in this world, which is entirely like a sword-thorn,
the wise person should therefore diligently discipline themselves.
Even a vast heap of pure gold, like the king of mountains, the Snowy Range, [is not equal to self-mastery].
"One person who indulges in enjoyments still finds no satisfaction in their mind.
Therefore, the wise person should cultivate the contemplation of equanimity.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1100. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Śākya village of Śilavaṃta among the Śākyans.
At that time, the Venerable Sujāta, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl, entered the Śākya village of Śilavaṃta to beg for alms.

Having finished eating, he returned to the vihāra, put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, took his sitting mat (niṣīdana), placed it on his right shoulder, entered the forest, sat beneath a tree, and practiced meditative absorption during the day, reflecting thus:
"I have gained a great benefit!"
I have gone forth to study the path in the True Dharma and Vinaya;
I have attained a great benefit!
I have encountered the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
I have gained a great benefit!
I have come to dwell among those who practice the holy life, who maintain the precepts, who are endowed with virtue, and who are noble, excellent, and true.
Now I shall meet my end in a noble manner, and in future lives as well, I shall likewise be noble.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:

"Now the śramaṇa Gautama has gone to the Śākya village of Śilavaṃta, where there is a disciple named Sujāta, who puts on his robes and takes up his bowl... [as described at length above], up until: "...being virtuous and good, he has passed away, and in the next world he will likewise be virtuous."
"I shall now go there to create obstacles for him.

He transformed himself into a massive body, robust and of great strength, such that all who saw him were struck with fear; they thought his power could overturn and shake the very earth. He then went to where the bhikṣu Sujāta was.
The bhikṣu Sujāta saw from afar a large-bodied, powerful, and robust warrior, and immediately felt terror.
He rose from his seat, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"This morning, having dressed and taken up my bowl... [as described at length above], up until: "...a person of noble character dies, they will likewise be noble in the next world.
I saw a great-bodied man, courageous and magnificent, whose power could shake the earth; seeing him, I was struck with terror, my heart leaped, and my hair stood on end."
The Buddha told Sujāta:
"This is not a man of great stature; it is Māra Pāpīyān wishing to cause you disturbance.
Return for now and, beneath that tree, practice the three samādhis as before. This will provoke Māra, and through this, you shall be liberated from suffering."
Then, the Venerable Sujāta returned to his own dwelling; when morning came, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the Śākya village of Silavaṃta to beg for food.
Having finished his meal, he returned to the vihāra... [as described at length above], up until: "He has lived virtuously and passed away;
in the next world, too, he shall be virtuous. At that time, Māra Pāpīyas again thought:

"This śramaṇa Gautama resides among the Śākyas and has a disciple named Sujāta... [as described at length above], up until: "He has lived virtuously and passed away; in the next world, too, he shall be virtuous."
"I shall now go there to create obstacles for him.
He then transformed himself into a massive body, heroic, powerful, and formidable, with the strength to shake the earth; he went and stood before him.
The bhikṣu Sujāta saw him from afar once more and spoke this verse:
"I have left home with right faith, And have gone forth to study the Way."
Regarding the Buddha, that priceless jewel, I abide with my mind fixed through right mindfulness.
No matter how you transform your form and color, my heart shall not waver;
perceiving you as a magical illusion, you may then vanish from here.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:
"This śramaṇa already knows my mind.
Feeling inner grief and distress, he immediately vanished and disappeared.
1101 (1101). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Deer Park, the Abode of Seers, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"The śrāvakas of the Tathāgata utter the lion’s roar, saying:
'It is known!'"
"I have known!"—
but regarding what dharma has the Tathāgata’s disciple "known" such that, having known it, he utters the lion’s roar? It is the noble truth of suffering,
the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
At that time, the Māra Pāpīyān thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama is staying in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana near the city of Vārāṇasī, preaching the Dharma to his śrāvakas, and has even caused them to know the Four Noble Truths."
"I shall now go there to create obstacles for him.
He transformed himself into a youth and stood before the Buddha, speaking in verse:
"Why, in the midst of the great assembly, Do you roar the fearless lion’s roar?
"How can he claim to have no rival and yet hope to subdue all?
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"The evil Māra Pāpīyān wishes to cause disturbance."
He then spoke these verses:
“The Tathāgata, regarding all things, In the most profound and true Dharma and Vinaya,
Roars the lion’s roar through skillful means, Possessing no fear concerning the Dharma.”
"If one possesses wisdom, why should one worry or be afraid?
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama already knows my mind."
Bearing grief and sorrow within his heart, he immediately vanished and was no longer seen. 1102 (1102) Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Wilds Trampled by Many in Rājagṛha, together with a community of five hundred bhikṣus, preaching the Dharma to them, while he placed five hundred alms-bowls in the middle of the courtyard.
At that time, the World-Honored One was teaching the Dharma of the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates of clinging to five hundred bhikṣus.
Then, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:

"The śramaṇa Gautama is staying in the open wilderness near Rājagṛha, where many people tread upon the ground, together with five hundred bhikṣus, teaching that the five aggregates of clinging are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing."
"I shall now go there to create an obstacle.
He transformed himself into a great ox and went to where the Buddha was; he entered among those five hundred bowls, and the bhikṣus immediately drove him away so that he would not break the bowls.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This is not an ox; it is Māra Pāpīyān, wishing to cause disturbance.
He then spoke in verse:
"Form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—these are neither self nor belonging to self.
If one knows this true meaning, one will have no attachment to them.
When the mind has no attachment to phenomena, it transcends the bonds of form."
"Thoroughly understanding all places, one does not abide within the realm of Māra.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1103 (1103). Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Wilds of Many-Footed Treading near Rājagṛha, together with a community of six hundred bhikṣus. He taught the bhikṣus the arising of the six bases of contact, the arising of contact, and the cessation of contact.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:

"Now the śramaṇa Gautama is staying in the wilderness near Rājagṛha, where many people tread upon the ground, teaching six hundred bhikṣus that the six bases of contact are phenomena subject to arising and phenomena subject to cessation. I shall now go there to create obstacles for him."
He transformed himself into a mighty warrior with a vast body, fierce and powerful, capable of shaking the earth, and approached the place where the Buddha was.
When those bhikṣus saw the warrior from afar—his body so large and his appearance so fierce—they were struck with fear;
their hair stood on end, and they said to one another, "What is this being? His form is terrifying!"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This is Māra, the Evil One, who wishes to cause disturbance.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and the sixth, mental phenomena—
when these are cherished, beloved, and pleasing to the mind, they are all that exists in the world.
This is the most evil greed, which binds and fetters the ordinary person.”
"Those who transcend these things are the noble disciples of the Buddha;
they have crossed beyond the realm of Māra, like the sun free from clouds.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama already knows my mind.
Feeling inward grief and sorrow, he immediately vanished and disappeared.
*Saṃyukta Āgama*, Scroll 39.
Saṃyukta Āgama, Volume 40, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Song Dynasty. 40.1104 (1104).
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka [Nivāpa].
At the Bamboo Grove, at that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one can receive and uphold the seven kinds of acceptance, by this cause and condition, one shall be born in the abode of Śakra, Lord of the Devas."

It is said that when Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was formerly a human being, he made offerings to his parents and all the elders of his household; he maintained a gentle countenance and spoke softly, refraining from harsh speech and double-tongued talk, always speaking words of truth.

Toward a world characterized by stinginess, although he lived as a householder, he was not miserly; he practiced liberating generosity, gave diligently, and constantly delighted in the practice of giving. He hosted assemblies for offerings and bestowed gifts equally upon all.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Honor your parents, as well as the elders of the family;
use words that are gentle and respectful, and avoid harsh speech and double-tongued talk."
Subduing the mind of stinginess and always practicing truthful speech—
those who practice these seven dharmas are seen by the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three,
who all say: "He shall be reborn in this heaven in the future."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1105 (1105). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, by the side of the Monkey Pond, in the Multi-storied Lecture Hall.

The Licchavi asked again:

“Licchavi!

The gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, seeing those who practice these seven dharmas, each spoke these words: "He shall be reborn in this heaven in the future.

1106 (1106). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, by the side of the Monkey Pond, in the Multi-storied Lecture Hall.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what cause and for what reason is Śakra Devānām Indra named Śakra Devānām Indra?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“When Śakra Devānām Indra was formerly a human being, he practiced sudden giving (tun-shi).

To śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, the distressed, and those seeking a livelihood who begged on the road, he gave food and drink, money and wealth, grain, silk, flowers and incense, ornaments, beds and bedding, and lamps. Because of his capability [in this practice], he is named Śakra Devānām Indra.”
The bhikṣu again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what cause and for what reason is Śakra Devānām Indra also named Purandara?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"When that Śakra Devānām Indra was formerly a human being, he repeatedly practiced giving—clothing, food and drink, and even lamps."
"For this cause and condition, he is named Pūraṇa.
The bhikṣu again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what cause and by what condition is he also named Māghava?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"When that Śakra Devānām-indra was formerly a human being, his name was Maghavan; therefore, Śakra Devānām-indra is called by his original name, Maghavan."
The bhikṣu again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what cause and by what condition is it further named Sāpāśa?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"When that Śakra Devānām-indra was formerly a human being, he frequently gave and made offerings of *pauṣkariya* robes.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, Śakra Devānām-indra is named Pauṣpaka."
The bhikṣu again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
For what cause and for what reason is Śakra Devānām Indra also named Kauśika?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"When that Śakra Devānām Indra was formerly a human being, he belonged to the Kauśika clan.
For this reason, Śakra Devānām Indra is also named Kauśika."
A bhikṣu asked the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
For what cause and for what reason is that Śakra Devānām Indra named Śacīpati?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"That asura woman is named Śacī; she is the foremost queen of Śakra, Lord of the Devas. For this reason, Śakra is called Śacīpati."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
For what cause and for what reason is Śakra Devānām Indra also named 'Thousand-Eyed'?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"When that Śakra Devānām Indra was formerly a human being, he was intelligent and wise; in a single sitting, he could contemplate a thousand kinds of meanings, observing and weighing them."
"For this reason and by these causes, that Śakra, Lord of the Devas, is further named 'The Thousand-Eyed.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"By what cause and by what conditions is that Śakra Devānām-Indra further named Indriya?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"That Śakra, Lord of Devas, is the king and sovereign among the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
For this reason, that Śakra, Lord of Devas, is named Indrāli."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Indeed, when that Śakra Devānām Indra was formerly a human being, he undertook and maintained seven kinds of observances.
By reason of these causes and conditions, he became Śakra, Lord of Devas."
What are the seven?
When Śakra Devānām Indra was formerly a human being, he made offerings to his parents;
up to and including practicing impartial generosity—these are the seven kinds of reception.
"For these reasons and conditions, he became Śakra, the Lord of Devas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse... as extensively explained above.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1107 (1107). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, by the side of the Monkey Pond, in the Multi-storied Lecture Hall.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, there was a yakṣa spirit who was ugly and of hideous appearance; he sat upon the empty throne of Śakra."
When the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven saw this ghost, so hideous and foul of appearance, sitting upon the empty throne of Śakra,
they were all filled with indignation.
As the gods became thus exceedingly enraged, that ghost gradually became more and more handsome in accordance with their anger.
At that time, the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three went to Śakra, the Lord of Devas, and said to him:

"Kauśika, you should know that there is a certain strange ghost, ugly and of hideous appearance, who is sitting upon the empty throne of the Heavenly King. When we gods saw that ghost—ugly and of hideous appearance—sitting upon the throne of the Heavenly King, we were filled with extreme anger. Yet, as those gods became angry, that ghost gradually became more handsome."
Śakra Devānām-indra told the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven:
"That is a spirit who is the antidote to anger.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, went in person to where the spirit was; he adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, and three times uttered the spirit’s name, saying:
"O Benevolent One!
I am Śakra Devānām Indra.
As Śakra Devānām Indra thus showed him respect and humbled himself, that ghost became increasingly hideous until he finally vanished.
Then Śakra Devānām Indra, having sat down, spoke these verses:
“People should not give way to anger; Seeing anger, do not repay it with anger.
Do not produce evil toward the wicked; One should destroy arrogance.”
Neither angry nor harmful, one is said to dwell among the noble assembly;
when evil offenses provoke anger, remain as firm as a mountain of stone.
Able to restrain intense anger, like one who controls a runaway horse-drawn chariot.
"I speak of a skilled charioteer, not of one who merely holds the reins.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Śakra Devānām Indra, as the sovereign king among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, praised the absence of anger."
"You who have thus developed right faith and left the household life to train in the path should likewise praise the absence of anger; you should train yourselves in this way.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1108. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having dressed in the morning and taken up his bowl, entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.

Having finished begging, he returned to the monastery, put away his robe and bowl, and after washing his feet, took his sitting mat (niṣīdana) and placed it over his right shoulder. He went to the Andhavana forest, spread out his sitting mat, sat beneath a tree, and entered the meditative absorption of the day.
At that time, two bhikṣus engaged in a dispute within the Jeta Grove; one reviled the other, while the other remained silent.
The one who had reviled him immediately felt remorse and apologized to him, but that bhikṣu would not accept his apology. Because he did not accept the apology, [the situation persisted].
At that time, many bhikṣus within the vihāra exhorted one another with loud voices, creating a great clamor.
Then, the World-Honored One, with his pure divine ear surpassing that of humans, heard this loud clamor within the Jetavana.
Having heard this, he arose from his meditation, returned to the vihāra, and sat down after arranging his seat before the great assembly. He addressed the bhikṣus:

"This morning, having gone for alms, I returned to the Andhavana forest and sat in meditation, entering into the meditative absorption of the day. There, I heard loud and high-pitched voices within the vihāra, a tumultuous and chaotic clamor. Who on earth could this be?"
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"In this monastery, two bhikṣus have fallen into a dispute; one bhikṣu reviled the other, while the other remained silent.
At that time, the reviling bhikṣu immediately repented and apologized, but the other would not accept it."
"Because they did not accept [the teaching], many people urged and admonished them, which led to loud voices and a great clamor.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "How was this?"

"Monks! A foolish person, when another comes to apologize and seek reconciliation, does not accept their confession. One who refuses to accept the confession of another is a foolish person; for a long night they shall experience disadvantageous suffering."
"O Bhikṣus!
In a past age, when Śakra Devānām Indra was contending with the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he spoke this verse as an instruction:
'Have no intent to harm others, And let not anger bind you in knots.'"
Resentment does not endure for long, as one does not dwell upon anger.
Even when fury is intense, one does not utter harsh words;
one seeks not to find fault with others, nor does one broadcast another's shortcomings.
One should always protect oneself, examining within with righteousness;
neither angry nor harmful, one should always dwell with the noble and holy.
Even if one dwells with evil people who are as stubborn and hard as mountain rock, [one must remain steadfast].
"One who can restrain intense anger within themselves, like one who controls a runaway chariot, I call a skilled driver;
it is not the one who merely holds the reins.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Śakra Devānām Indra is the sovereign king among the Trāyastriṃśa gods; he constantly practices patience and likewise praises those who practice patience.
You bhikṣus, having left the home life out of right faith to study the Path, you should practice patience and praise those who practice patience; this is how you should train!”
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1109 (1109). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, when the devas and asuras were arrayed for battle, Śakra Devānām-indra said to the asura king Vemacitrin:
'Do not kill one another; let us instead engage in debate, and whoever is defeated in argument shall submit.'"
The Asura King Vemacitrin said:
"Even if we were to engage in debate together, who would be able to testify as to whether the principles are sound or obstructed?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:
"Among the hosts of devas there are those who possess innate wisdom and clear recollection; likewise, among the hosts of asuras there are also those who possess clear recollection.
Vimalacitra Asura said, "So be it."
Śakra Devānām-indra said:
"You may first establish your thesis; afterwards, I shall establish my own in response, which will not be difficult.
Then, the Asura King Vemacitrin spoke in verse to establish his thesis:
"If I were to practice patience, there would be a deficiency in my duty;
the foolish would say that I practice patience out of fear."
Śakra Devānām-indra replied with a verse:
"Even if a foolish person speaks out of fear and endures it,
what harm does that do to the truth when they remain silent?"
"Only contemplate its meaning for yourself, and likewise contemplate its meaning for others;
when both self and others attain peace, this patience is supreme.
Thus spoke Vemacitrin, the asura, in verse:
"If one does not restrain delusion, delusion will wound the person,
just as a fierce bull, having broken loose, charges after people."
"By wielding the staff one compels; by fear, one is subdued.
Therefore, firmly grasping the staff, one should break and subdue that fool.
Śakra then spoke again in verse:
"I have constantly observed him who restrains that foolish man;
though the fool is full of intense anger, the wise one subdues him through silence."
Neither angry nor harmful, always dwelling with the noble ones,
one remains as firm as a mountain of stone when evil offenses provoke anger;
able to restrain intense wrath, like one who controls a runaway horse-drawn chariot.
"I speak of a skilled charioteer, not of one who merely holds the reins.
At that time, among the host of devas there were those with wisdom, and among the host of asuras there were asuras with wisdom; they reflected upon, weighed, and examined these verses, and thought:

"The verse spoken by the asura Vepacitti will ultimately give rise to strife, contention, and war throughout the long night. One should know that the asura king Vepacitti teaches people to engage in strife, contention, and war throughout the long night."

The verses spoken by Śakra Devānām Indra bring an end to strife, litigation, and conflict throughout the long night; one should know that Śakra, Lord of the Devas, teaches people throughout the long night to cease strife, litigation, and conflict, and one should know that Śakra is skilled in discourse and attains victory.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Śakra Devānām Indra subdued the asuras through skillful debate. Bhikṣus!”
Śakra Devānām Indra is the sovereign king among the Trāyastriṃśa gods; he establishes himself in skillful discourse and praises skillful discourse.

You bhikṣus should likewise do so: having developed right faith, you have left the home life to study the Path; you too should engage in skillful discourse and praise skillful discourse—this is how you should train!
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1110 (1110) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, there was Śakra, Lord of the Devas, when the devas and asuras were arrayed in battle against one another."
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, saying:

"Today, as the gods and the army of the asuras battle, if the gods are victorious and the asuras are defeated, we shall capture the asura king Vemacitrin alive, bind him with the fivefold bonds, and lead him back to the celestial palace."
Vemacitrin, the Asura King, addressed the host of asuras:

"Today, the devas and asuras shall battle together. If the asuras are victorious and the devas are defeated, we shall capture Śakra Devānām Indra alive, bind him with the fivefold bonds, and lead him back to the asura palace."
During that battle, the devas were victorious and the asuras were defeated.

At that time, the devas captured Vepacitti, the king of the asuras, bound him with the fivefold bonds, and led him back to the celestial palace, where he was tied up before the gate of Śakra’s Hall of Dharma Destruction.
Whenever Śakra entered or exited through this gate, Vemacitrin the asura was bound at its side, reviling him in anger.
At that time, Śakra’s charioteer saw the asura king, his body bound by five fetters, standing by the gate and repeatedly reviling him with anger whenever Śakra passed in or out.
Having seen this, he immediately spoke a verse, addressing Śakra: "O Śakra,
do you now fear him, Or is your strength insufficient,
That you can endure the Asura Who insults you right before your face?"
Śakra replied: "It is not out of fear that I endure, nor is it because my strength is insufficient;
for what wise person would ever confront a fool?"
The charioteer spoke again:
"If one practices patience alone, there will be a deficiency in one's affairs;
the foolish would say that one practices patience out of fear."
"Therefore, one should treat them with severity, subduing folly with wisdom.
Śakra replied: "I constantly observe him; I shall restrain that foolish man."
Seeing the fool’s anger raging, the wise subdue it through silence.
To exert force where there is no strength is the power of delusion;
such delusion opposes and distances one from the Dharma, and thus there is no path for them.
If one possessed great power and were able to endure those who are inferior,
that would indeed be the highest patience;
but if one lacks power, how can there be patience?
When others revile and insult one excessively, the powerful person who is able to endure it possesses the highest patience;
as for the powerless, what is there to endure?
Regarding oneself and others, one should well guard against great terrors;
knowing that another's anger is intense, one should instead maintain silence for oneself.
Thus, both purposes are fulfilled: benefiting oneself as well as others.
Those called "fools" are so because they do not see the Dharma;
these fools consider their own superior endurance to be a cause for increasing their harsh speech even further.
Not knowing that by enduring such abuse one always gains the victory over them, they remain ignorant.
To practice patience toward those superior to oneself is called "patience out of fear.
To practice patience toward equals is called "patience that endures strife.
To practice patience toward those inferior to oneself is what constitutes "supreme patience."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Śakra Devānām Indra is the sovereign king of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; he constantly practices patience and praises patience.”
"You, bhikṣus, who out of right faith have gone forth from the home life to train in the path, should likewise practice patience, praise patience, and you should train yourselves in this!"
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1111 (1111) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"The carriage is prepared; it is up to the King to know the proper time.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately descended from the Vaijayanta Palace, joined his palms toward the east, and paid homage to the Buddha.

The charioteer spoke in verse to Śakra, saying:

I constantly see Śakra, Lord of the Devas, all the great earths,
the human and celestial kings, both great and small, and the four world-protectors;
the hosts of the Heaven of the Thirty-three all pay him respectful homage.
"Where else could there be one more venerable, one more venerable than Śakra?
Yet now you face directly toward the east, joining your palms in reverent salutation.
