"I am indeed the most honored king among all those in the world, both great and small kings,
as well as the four world-protecting kings and the hosts of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
therefore, they have all come to pay me homage."
"Furthermore, there is one in the world who follows the Perfectly Enlightened One, whose name is Pūraṇa Kāśyapa; therefore, I prostrate in homage.
The charioteer spoke again:
"This one must surely be the most excellent in the world, for that reason Śakra, the Heavenly King,
respectfully joins his palms and bows his head toward the east in salutation."
"I too shall now pay homage to the one whom the Heavenly King pays homage to.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, the husband of Śacī, having spoken these verses and paid homage to the Buddha, mounted a chariot drawn by a thousand horses and departed for the pleasure grove.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Even Śakra, the Lord of the Thirty-three Heavens, who reigns as sovereign king over the Trāyastriṃśa devas, pays homage to the Buddha and likewise praises those who pay homage to the Buddha.”

"You, bhikṣus, who out of right faith have gone forth from the home life to train in the path, should likewise revere the Buddha and should also praise those who revere the Buddha; you should train yourselves thus!"
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1112 (1112) Thus have I heard:

1113 (1113) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In a past age, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, desired to enter a pleasure grove. He commanded his charioteer to prepare a carriage yoked with a thousand horses."
Having received these instructions, the charioteer immediately prepared the carriage and returned to inform Śakra:

At that moment, Śakra descended from the Palace of Constant Victory and, facing all directions, joined his palms in reverent salutation.
At that time, the charioteer saw Śakra, Lord of the Devas, descend from the palace and stand in the central courtyard, facing all directions with palms joined in reverent salutation.
Having seen this, he was struck with terror; his horsewhip fell to the ground, and he spoke these verses:
“In every direction there are only humans, born from foul and putrid wombs.

"For what reason, Kauśika, do you hold the homeless life so dear?
Explain its meaning to me; hungering and thirsty, I wish to hear it.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied in verse:
"I pay homage to him who has gone forth from the household life;
he wanders freely through all directions, unconcerned with his own coming and going."
The colors of cities and kingdoms cannot burden his mind;
he does not store up the necessities of life, remaining in a state of desireless concentration as soon as he departs.
Going forth, he seeks nothing at all, finding joy only in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
When speaking, one speaks words of certain goodness; when not speaking, one remains in tranquil stillness.
The devas and asuras each oppose one another, and humans likewise quarrel among themselves; their mutual opposition is just like this.
Only those who have gone forth from the household life are without contention amidst all disputes;
toward all sentient beings, they lay aside the sword and the staff.
Detached from wealth and free from sensual desire, they are neither intoxicated nor dissolute.
"He has distanced himself from all evils; therefore, I pay homage to him.
At that time, the charioteer spoke again in verse:
"He who is revered by the heavenly king must surely be the most excellent in the world."
"Therefore, from this day forward, I shall pay homage to those who have gone forth.

1114 (1114). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In a past age, the Asura King raised four kinds of armies—elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry."
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven were about to engage in battle.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, heard that the Asura King had mobilized fourfold armies—elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry—and was coming to fight them.
Having heard this, he immediately addressed the devaputra Subāhu, saying:
"Do you know, sir?
The asuras have raised four kinds of armies—elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry—and wish to wage war against the gods of the Thirty-three."
"Grandfather, you may issue a command to the Heaven of the Thirty-three to mobilize the fourfold army—elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry—to wage war against those asuras."

At that time, the devaputra Śubhavyūha, having received the instructions of Śakra, returned to his own celestial palace; he became negligent and lax, failing to apply himself diligently to skillful means.
When Śakra heard that the hosts of asuras had already emerged onto the road, he again addressed the devaputra Śubhavyūha: "O sir!..."
"The army of the asuras is already upon the road; Your Majesty should quickly issue orders to mobilize the fourfold army to do battle with the asuras.
Having received this instruction from Śakra, the devaputra Subāhu immediately returned to his palace, becoming indolent and lax.
At that time, as the army of the Asura King was already drawing near, Śakra-devānām-indra, hearing that the Asura host was already on the nearby road, again addressed the devaputra Subāhu:
"Do you know this?"
"The army of the asuras is already near!
O Grandfather, quickly command the gods to mobilize the fourfold forces.
At that time, the devaputra Śubhavyūha spoke these verses:
"If there is a place where nothing arises, A state of unconditioned peace and bliss—
One who attains such a place Is without action and without sorrow."
"Grant me this place, so that I may attain peace and security.
At that time, Śakra replied with a verse:
"If there were a place where nothing arises, the unconditioned peace and bliss,"
"If one attains such a state, there is neither action nor sorrow.
If you have attained such a state, you should take me with you as well.
Thus spoke the devaputra Subāhu, further reciting these verses:
“If one dwells where there is no skillful means, one does not give rise to peace or happiness;
yet if one attains such a state, there is neither activity nor sorrow.”
"Grant me this place, so that I may attain peace and security.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied with a verse:
"In a place where there is no skillful means, peace and happiness do not arise."
"If a person attains this state, there is neither action nor sorrow.
You who have attained this state—please take me with you as well.
Thus spoke the devaputra Subāhu, and he further recited these verses:
“If one dwells in heedfulness, One will not fail to give rise to peace and happiness;
If a person attains such a state, There is neither action nor sorrow.”
"Grant me this place, so that I may attain peace and happiness.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, spoke again in verse:
"If in a place one is not heedless, yet does not give rise to peace and happiness..."
"If a person attains this state, there is neither action nor sorrow.
You who have attained this state—please take me with you as well.
Thus spoke Subhūti, further reciting these verses:
"Indolent and arising from nothing, unaware of what has been done or yet to be done,
may you grant me this place where all desires are fully gathered."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, spoke again in verse:
"If one is indolent and does not exert oneself, one attains ultimate peace and happiness.
Since you have attained that state, you should take me there as well."
The Devaputra Śubhavyūha further spoke in verse:
"Without affairs one finds joy; without action there is no sorrow.
If you grant me this place, let me attain peace and happiness."
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, spoke again in verse:
“If one sees or hears that sentient beings have no agency,
and you have attained such a state, you should likewise take me with you.”
"If you fear what must be done, do not dwell upon conditioned things;
rather, you should swiftly purify the path to Nirvāṇa.

At that time, the devaputra Śubhavyūha arrayed the fourfold army—elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry—and fought against the asuras. He crushed the asura hosts, and the devas were victorious, returning to their celestial palaces.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Śakra Devānām Indra mobilized his fourfold army and fought the asuras; through diligent effort, he achieved victory. Bhikṣus!”
Śakra Devānām Indra is the sovereign king among the Trāyastriṃśa gods; he constantly employs the skillful means of diligent application and always praises the virtue of diligence.
“You bhikṣus, having developed right faith and gone forth from the home life to train in the path, you should be diligent and energetic, and you should praise diligence.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1115. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, there was a village where various sages dwelt in a secluded place on the outskirts of the village."
"At that time, various devas and asuras were engaged in battle, arrayed against one another not far from a village.

Then, the asura king Vimalacitra removed his five ornaments, took off his celestial crown, set aside his parasol, laid down his sword, withdrew his jeweled fly-whisk, and removed his leather sandals. He proceeded to the dwelling place of those rishis, entered within the gate, and looked about; yet he did not cast a glance at the rishis, nor did he offer them any greeting."
Having watched him, he departed.
At that time, there was a seer who saw from afar King Vemacitra of the Asuras removing his five ornaments and entering the garden; having watched him, he also departed.
Having seen him, he said to the rishis: "Who is this man?

He has an unrefined appearance and does not resemble the form of a human; his conduct is contrary to the rules of decorum. He looks like a rustic country boy and not the son of a noble householder. Having removed his five ornaments, he enters the garden gate, looking about with a haughty gaze, neither glancing back nor greeting the rishis."
A certain seer replied:
"This is the asura king Vemacitrin; having removed his five ornaments, he has come to look at you and is now departing."
The seer said: "This is no worthy man;

he is neither good nor virtuous, neither noble nor righteous. Having removed his five ornaments and entered the garden gate, he looked around and departed, showing no regard for or greeting the other seers."
"For this reason, you should know that the hosts of devas increase while the asuras diminish.

At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra removed his five ornaments and entered the abode of the rishis; there he exchanged greetings and offered words of comfort to the rishis face-to-face, after which he departed.
Furthermore, there was a seer who saw Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having removed his five ornaments and entering the garden gate; he went up to him and inquired after his well-being.
Having seen him, he asked the other seers, "Who is this person?"

Entering the grove, he possessed a subdued appearance, a pleasing appearance, and an appearance of dignified deportment; he was no common country boy, but resembled a son of noble family. Having removed his five ornaments, he entered the garden gate, inquired after everyone's well-being, and then departed.
A seer replied: "This was Śakra, Lord of the Devas;
having removed his five ornaments, he entered the garden gate, inquired after everyone's welfare, and then departed."

The seer said: "This is a noble person, one whose conduct is excellent, true, and in accordance with the Dharma; having removed the five ornaments, he entered the garden gate, inquired after everyone's welfare, and then departed. By this you should know that the host of devas is increasing and the host of asuras is diminishing."
At that time, when the Asura King Vemacitrin heard the seer praising the devas, his anger flared up intensely.
Then, the seer dwelling in the sky, hearing that the Asura King’s anger was burning fiercely, went to where the Asura King Vemacitrin was and spoke these verses:
“The seer has come here for this purpose, Seeking to beg for the gift of fearlessness.”
"You are able to bestow fearlessness, Granting the compassionate teachings of the Muni.
Vemacitrin replied in verse:
"In the presence of you, O seer, There is no granting of fearlessness."
"Because he has turned his back on the asuras and drawn near to Śakra,
he shall instill terror in these fearless ones.
The seer spoke again in verse:
“As one sows seeds according to their kind, so do fruits and rewards arise accordingly;
yet you, who come seeking fearlessness, instead leave them with terror.”
"One shall obtain inexhaustible fearlessness, for one has sown the seeds of fearlessness through giving.
At that time, after the seers had recited the incantation in the presence of the asura king Vemacitra, they ascended into the air and departed.
"On that very night, Vemacitrin, the King of the Asuras, was startled three times as he rose from sleep; while dreaming, he heard a sinister voice say:
'Śakra Devānām Indra has mobilized the fourfold army to wage war against the Asuras!'"
Startled and terrified, fearing certain defeat in battle, he retreated and returned to the palace of the asuras.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having secured victory by repelling the enemy, went to the secluded dwelling of those rishis; after prostrating at the feet of the rishis, he withdrew to sit facing east before them to the west.
At that time, an easterly wind arose, and a certain extraordinary seer spoke this verse:
"These sages here have been away from home for many days;
sweat flows from their armpits with a foul odor. Do not sit downwind of them."
"The Thousand-Eyed One may move his seat; this stench is difficult to endure.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied in verse:
"Various kinds of fragrant flowers were bound together to form this floral garland."
"The fragrance now perceived is such that its scent surpasses even this;
how could one ever grow weary of smelling this fragrance?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"That Śakra, Lord of the Devas, is the sovereign king among the Trāyastriṃśa gods; he reveres those who have gone forth, constantly praises those who have gone forth, and also constantly extols the virtue of reverence."

"O bhikṣus, you who have left the home life out of right faith to study the Path, should always revere those who practice the holy life (brahmacarya), and you should also praise and honor their virtues."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1116 (1116). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, came to the Buddha’s dwelling at dawn; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and by the supernatural power of Śakra, the radiance from his body illuminated the entire Jeta Grove Monastery.
Then Śakra Devānām Indra spoke a verse, asking the Buddha:
"By killing what does one obtain peaceful sleep?
By killing what does one become free from sorrow and fear?"
"What dharma must one destroy for it to be praised by Gautama?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"By destroying ferocity and ill-will, one obtains peaceful sleep."
By eliminating harm, wickedness, and anger, the mind attains freedom from sorrow and fear.
Anger is the root of poison; by extinguishing that seed of suffering, one attains freedom from sorrow and fear.
By extinguishing that seed of suffering, one attains freedom from sorrow and fear.
"Because those seeds of suffering have been extinguished, they are praised by the noble ones.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and approved with gladness; he paid homage and departed.
1117. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"On the eighth day of the month, the Four Great Kings dispatch their ministers to inspect the world, [asking]:

'Which persons provide for their parents, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas; honor their kinsmen; perform various meritorious deeds; seeing the evils of the present life, they fear the retribution of future lives; they practice giving to create merit, observe the upavāsa precepts, and on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month, as well as during the month of miracles, receive the precepts and perform the poṣadha? "
On the fourteenth day, he sent the prince down to observe the world:
"Among what kind of people do parents receive offerings, and even how do they receive the precepts and perform the *poṣadha*?"
On the fifteenth day, the Four Great Heavenly Kings descend to the world to observe sentient beings:
"Which individuals provide for their parents, and so forth, up to receiving the precepts and observing the *poṣadha*?"
"O bhikṣus! At that time, there were not many people in the world who made offerings to their parents, nor even those who received the precepts and observed the uposatha.
Then, the Four Great Kings went to the Hall of Dharma Discourse in the Heaven of the Thirty-three and said to Śakra, the Lord of Devas:"
"Your Majesty, you should know that in these present worlds, there are not many people who make offerings to their parents, nor even those who receive the precepts and observe the *poṣadha*.
When the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa gods heard this, they were displeased and said to one another:

"The people of the world today are neither virtuous nor good; they are neither noble nor upright. They lack true practice, do not make offerings to their parents, and do not even receive the precepts or observe the *poṣadha*."
"Because of these transgressions, the hosts of devas will diminish, and the hosts of asuras will gradually increase. "O bhikṣus!

At that time, if many people in the world again make offerings to their parents, and even receive the precepts and observe the uposatha, the Four Great Kings up to the Trāyastriṃśa gods will assemble in the Hall of Dharma and say to Śakra, the Lord of Devas:"
"Your Majesty, you should know that in the world today there are many people who make offerings to their parents, even going so far as to receive the precepts and observe the *poṣadha*.
At that time, the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three were all filled with joy and said to one another:

"In the world today, the noble ones are truly in accordance with the Dharma; there are many people who make offerings to their parents, even going so far as to receive the precepts and observe the *poṣadha*."
"By virtue of this merit, the hosts of asuras shall diminish, and the hosts of devas shall increase.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knew that the assembly of devas was filled with joy.
Then he spoke in verse:
“If a person, on the eighth day of the month, On the fourteenth and fifteenth days,
And during the month of miraculous transformations, Observes the eightfold fast.”
“As I practice, so shall they also practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“This verse was spoken by Śakra, the Lord of Devas:”
"If a person, on the eighth day of the month, on the fourteenth and fifteenth days,
and during the month of miraculous transformations, observes the eightfold fast."
"Just as I practice, so shall they also practice.
This is not well-spoken. Why is that?

That Śakra, Lord of the Devas, himself possesses the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion; he is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, vexation, and suffering.
"If an Arhat bhikṣu— whose taints are exhausted,
who has accomplished what was to be done, who has laid down the heavy burden, who has severed the fetters of existence, and whose mind is well-liberated—
utters this verse: 'If a person, on the eighth day of the month, Or on the fourteenth or fifteenth day, ...'"
"And during the month of miracles, one should observe the eightfold precepts;
as I have practiced, so shall they practice. To speak thus is to speak well.

Why is this? Because an Arhat bhikṣu is free from greed, hatred, and delusion; he has already been liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering. Therefore, this verse is well-spoken.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1118 (1118). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, when the asura king Vemacitrin was gravely ill and suffering, he went to where Śakra Devānām Indra was and said to him: 'Kauśika!'"
"You should know that I am now afflicted by a grave illness; please treat me so that I may attain peace and well-being!
Śakra Devānām Indra said to Vemacitrin the Asura, "You should grant me the art of illusion, and I shall treat your illness so that you may attain peace and well-being."
Vemacitrin, the asura, said to Śakra:
"I shall go back and consult the assembly of asuras; if they grant me their consent, I will bestow upon Śakra the asura’s illusory arts."
At that time, Vemacitra the asura went forth to the assembly of the asuras and said to them:
"O people, you should know that I am now afflicted by a grave illness; I have gone to the abode of Śakra Devānām Indra to seek his medical treatment."
He spoke to me, saying:
"If you can bestow upon me the illusory arts of the asuras, I shall cure your illness and restore you to well-being.
I shall now go and explain those asura illusory arts to him.
At that time, a deceitful asura said to Vemacitra Asura:
"That Śakra, Lord of the Devas, is upright, faithful, and free from hypocrisy; he merely says to him:
'O Heavenly King!'"
"This illusory art of the asuras, if practiced by a learner, causes one to fall into hell and undergo immeasurable suffering for hundreds of thousands of years.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, will surely desist from his intention and no longer seek to learn it; he will say:
"Go! You may depart!"
"I shall cause your illness to be cured, so that you may attain peace and security!
At that time, Vemacitra Asura went again to the place of Śakra and spoke in verse, saying:
"O Thousand-Eyed Honored Heavenly King, The illusory arts of the Asuras..."
"All these are deceptive phenomena, which cause people to fall into hell for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years, suffering without respite.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, spoke to the asura Vemacitrin:
"Stop! Stop!
Such sorcery as this is not what I require; you should return at once, so that your bodily ailment may be stilled and you may find rest, strength, and peace!"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Śakra Devānām Indra is the sovereign king of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; throughout the long night, he has been true, without illusion or deceit, virtuous, and upright.”

"O bhikṣus, you who have with right faith left the home life to go forth and study the Path should likewise be without guile and without deceit, being virtuous, gentle, and straightforward; you should train yourselves in this way."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1119 (1119) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and Vemacitrin, son of Virūḍhaka, King of the Asuras—both possessed of most exquisite countenances—approached the Buddha's dwelling together at dawn. They bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side."
At that time, the radiance from the bodies of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and Vemacitrin, son of Vairocana, the Asura King, shone everywhere throughout the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Asura King Vairocana spoke a verse to the Buddha:
"A person should diligently apply skillful means To ensure that their benefit is fully realized.
Once this benefit is fully realized, What further need is there for skillful means?"
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, spoke again in verse:
"If a person applies themselves with diligent skillful means, They will surely bring their benefit to fulfillment.
Once that benefit is fulfilled, There is no practice of patience superior to this."
Having spoken these verses, they addressed the Buddha together, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Which of these is well-spoken?"
The World-Honored One said:
"What you have both said is excellent.
Nevertheless, listen now further to what I shall say."
"All classes of sentient beings, without exception, seek their own benefit;
each and every being seeks what is appropriate for themselves.
All worldly unions, as well as the ultimate truth (paramārtha), [are likewise sought]."
One should know that worldly conjunctions are impermanent phenomena.
If a person applies themselves with diligent skillful means, they will surely bring their benefit to fulfillment.
Once this benefit is fulfilled, there is no practice of patience superior to this.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the Asura King Bāli, son of Vairocana, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and approved with gladness; they paid homage and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Śakra Devānām Indra is the sovereign king among the Trāyastriṃśa gods; he practices patience and praises patience."
“You monks, having developed right faith and gone forth from the home life to train in the path, you too should likewise practice patience and praise patience!
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the monks, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1120. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In a past age, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to the Buddha:
'World-Honored One!'"
I now undertake these precepts:
"As long as the Buddha-dharma remains in the world, for the rest of my life, should anyone cause me harm, I shall by no means retaliate or inflict harm upon them."
At that time, the Asura King Vemacitrin heard Śakra, Lord of the Devas, receive such a precept:
"As long as the Buddha-dharma remains in the world, for the rest of my life, should anyone cause me harm, I shall not retaliate by inflicting harm upon them."
Having heard this, he took up a sharp sword and came toward him along the path.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saw from afar King Vemacitrin of the Asuras approaching along the path with a sharp sword in hand, and immediately called out to him from a distance: "Asura!
"Stay! Be bound and do not move!
At that, the Asura King Vemacitrin was unable to move and said to Śakra:
"Have you not now received such a precept as this:
'If the Buddha-dharma abides in the world for the remainder of my life, should anyone cause me harm, I shall never retaliate'?"
"Is this so? Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:
"I have indeed undertaken such precepts; however, you remain bound while dwelling in cessation."
The asura said,
"Please release me for now!
Śakra replied:
"If you swear an oath that you will not cause further disorder,
then I shall release you. The asura replied,
"Release me, and I shall act according to the Dharma."
Śakra replied:
"First act in accordance with the Dharma, and then I shall release you!
At that time, the Asura King Vemacitrin spoke this verse:
“Wherever sensual desire leads, wherever hatred leads, wherever false speech leads,
and wherever slandering the noble ones leads— ”
"If I were to cause you distress, I would surely go to the same destination as you.
Śakra Devānām-indra then spoke again, saying:
"I release you; go wherever you find comfort."

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having caused the Asura King to make his solemn vow, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In the presence of the Buddha, I received these precepts:
"As long as the Buddha-dharma remains in the world, for the remainder of my life, should anyone cause me harm, I shall not retaliate."
When the asura king Vemacitrin heard that I had received the precepts, he took up a sharp sword and followed the road toward me.
Seeing him from afar, I said to him: "Asura!..."
Stop! Stop! Be bound and do not move!
That asura asked,
"Do you not receive the precepts?
I immediately replied:
"I have indeed received the precepts; moreover, you must now stay still, for I shall bind you so that you cannot move.
He then sought release, and I said to him:
"If you make a solemn vow not to cause further disturbance, I shall allow you to be released."
The asura said, "Please release me for a moment;
I shall speak a covenant. I then replied:
"First state a solemn oath, and then I shall release you.
He then spoke a verse, making this vow:
"To where greed leads, And to where hatred leads,"
"The destination of those who speak falsehoods is the destination of those who slander the noble ones;
if I were to cause such disturbance, my destination would be the same as theirs. "So it is."
"Blessed One!
Is it for the sake of this Dharma that I wish to cause that asura king to speak his covenant?
Will that asura continue to cause such disturbances?"
The Buddha said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"You must require him to take a solemn oath that he will not violate the Dharma; then he will no longer dare to cause further disturbances.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and expressed his approval, paid homage, and departed.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Śakra, Lord of the Devas, is the sovereign king of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; he does not cause disturbance, and he also constantly praises the dharma of non-disturbance."

"O bhikṣus, you who have left the home life out of right faith to study the Path, you too should practice in this way—without causing disturbance—and you should also praise the Dharma of non-disturbance."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*Saṃyukta Āgama*, Scroll 40; *Saṃyukta Āgama*, Scroll 41.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
41.1121 (1121). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Park in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
At that time, a great multitude of Śākyas came to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the Śākyas: "O you Gautamas!
"Do you observe the fast and precepts on the days of the Dharma-fast and during the month of the supernatural powers, and cultivate meritorious deeds?
The Śākyas replied to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One!"
Among us, on various fast days, we sometimes manage to observe the precepts and sometimes do not;
during the month of the gods (Āṣāḍha), we sometimes observe the fast and cultivate various meritorious virtues, and sometimes we do not.
The Buddha addressed the Śākyas: "Gautamas!
You have not attained any wholesome benefit; you are people of pride, people of affliction, people of sorrow and lamentation, and people of distress and suffering."
For what reason is it that on various fast days one may or may not obtain the precepts of fasting?
Or why is it that during the month of the gods (*mārgaśīrṣa*) one may or may not obtain the precepts of fasting and perform various meritorious deeds?

"O Gautamas! It is like a person seeking profit who increases it day by day: on the first day there is one coin; on the second day, two coins; on the third day, four coins; on the fourth day, eight coins; on the fifth day, sixteen coins; and on the sixth day, thirty-two coins."
"In this way, as days pass— on the eighth day, the ninth day, and so on up to a month— would the wealth and property of that man increase further and become more extensive?
The householder replied to the Buddha,
"It would, World-Honored One."
The Buddha addressed the Śākyan:
"How is it so, Gautama?"

"In this way, as that man's wealth increases, he will naturally obtain even greater abundance; furthermore, could you allow me to dwell for ten years in constant joy and mental happiness, remaining frequently in meditative concentration?"
The Śākyan replied,
“No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to the Śākyan:

"If one were to obtain joy and mental happiness for nine years, eight years, seven years, six years, five years, four years, three years, two years, or even one year, would one dwell frequently in meditative concentration thereby?"
The Śākyan replied,
“No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to the Śākyan:

"Setting aside the matter of years, could you dwell for ten months, nine months, eight months, or even for a single month with a joyful and happy mind, frequently abiding in meditative concentration?"
Setting aside one month, could you instead dwell for ten days, nine days, eight days, or even for a single day and night with a joyful and happy mind, abiding frequently in meditative concentration?
The Śākyan replied,
“No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said to the Śākyan:

"I now tell you: among my śrāvakas, there are those with upright minds who are neither sycophantic nor deceitful. If I were to teach and transform such a person for ten years, by reason of these causes and conditions, it is possible that for hundreds of thousands of millions of years they would dwell single-mindedly in joy and mental bliss, frequently abiding in meditative concentration; this is indeed possible!

Setting aside ten years, whether it be nine years, eight years, or even down to one year; ten months, nine months, or even down to one month; ten days, nine days, or even down to a single day and night—if I were to teach them, by the following morning I would be able to cause them to advance further.

Teaching from early morning until evening, he is able to cause others to progress; by these causes and conditions, he attains a state of uniform joy and mental bliss for hundreds of thousands of millions of years, abides frequently in meditative concentration, and achieves two fruits—either the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* or the fruit of *anāgāmin*—because that man had previously attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
The Śākyan addressed the Buddha: “Excellent,
World-Honored One!”

From this day forward, on all fast days, I shall observe the precepts of fasting, up to the eightfold precepts; during the month of the gods, I shall maintain these fasts and, according to my ability, practice generosity and cultivate all manner of meritorious virtues.
The Buddha said to the Śākyan:
"Excellent, Gautama!"
"This is the essential truth.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Śākyas who heard what the Buddha taught rejoiced and expressed their approval; they paid homage and departed.
1122. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Park.
At that time, a great multitude of Śākyas had gathered in the Hall of Discourse and were engaged in such discussion.
Then, one Śākya said to the Śākya Nandi:
"There are times when I am able to go to the Tathāgata to pay him respect and make offerings, and there are times when I am not."

Sometimes we are able to approach and make offerings to our preceptors and bhikṣus, and sometimes we are not; furthermore, we do not know of the existence of wise upāsakas, nor of other wise upāsakas and upāsikās who are suffering from illness and distress. How then can we instruct, admonish, and preach the Dharma to them? We should now go together to the place of the World-Honored One and inquire about this matter; according to what the World-Honored One teaches, we shall receive and practice it.
At that time, Nandi together with the Śākyas went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
“We Śākyas have gathered in the Hall of Discussion and held this deliberation, during which some Śākyas said to me:

‘Nanda! At times we see the Tathāgata and pay him respectful homage and offerings; at other times we do not see him. At times we go to visit learned bhikṣus, drawing near to them and making offerings; at other times we cannot…’” Thus it was explained in detail, up until: “‘As the Buddha has instructed and admonished us, so shall we receive and carry out his teachings.’”
"Today we ask the World-Honored One: if a wise upāsaka has another wise upāsaka or upāsikā who is suffering from illness and affliction."
"How should one instruct, admonish, and preach the Dharma?
The Buddha told Nandi:
"If there is a wise upāsaka, he should go to another wise upāsaka or upāsikā who is suffering from illness and affliction, and instruct them with these three places of consolation, saying:..."
"O virtuous one!
You should achieve unwavering clarity regarding the Buddha, and unwavering clarity regarding the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
Having instructed them with these three bases of consolation, he should further ask:
"Are you attached to your parents?
If he is attached to his parents, one should instruct him to abandon that attachment and say to him:
"If it were possible to live by being attached to your parents, then you might indeed be attached; but since you do not live by means of such attachment, what is the use of being attached?"
If he says that he has no lingering attachment to his parents, one should praise him and rejoice in his virtue, and then further ask:
"Do you have any lingering thoughts for your wife, children, servants, wealth, or various possessions?"
If he says he still has lingering attachments, you should instruct him to renounce them, according to the method for relinquishing attachment to one's parents;
if he says he no longer has such attachments, you should praise him and rejoice in his virtue, and then ask him again:
"Do you still have any lingering attachment to the five desires of the human world?"
If they say they have him in mind, one should explain to them:
"The five desires of the human realm are foul, impure, decaying, and stinking; they are not equal to the superior and wondrous five desires of the heavens."
He instructs them to renounce the five desires of the human realm and instructs them to aspire to the five desires of the celestial realms.

If they further say that their minds have already distanced themselves from the five desires of the human realm and have previously looked toward the superior and wondrous desires of the heavens, he praises them, rejoices with them, and speaks to them again, saying:
"The wondrous desires of the heavens are impermanent, suffering, empty, and subject to change and decay; yet among the various heavens, there are bodies and superior celestial five-desires."

If he says, "I have already abandoned concern for celestial desires and now concern myself with the superior desire for the existence of a body," you should praise him and rejoice, and then further instruct him, saying:

"The desire for bodily existence is likewise impermanent and subject to decay; there is the bliss of the cessation of formations, of Nirvana, and of transcendence. You should abandon concern for bodily existence and take delight in the bliss of the tranquility of Nirvana as supreme and preeminent."
"Thus, Nandiya! That noble disciple who has already been able to relinquish concern for the body and craved for nirvāṇa, may he praise and rejoice in this as excellent."
That noble disciple is instructed and exhorted in successive stages so as to attain non-arising and nirvana, just as a bhikṣu with a lifespan of a hundred years attains liberation and nirvana.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Śākyan Nandi and the others, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and were filled with gladness;
they paid their respects and departed. 1123 (1123) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Park.
At that time, there was a member of the Śākya clan named Bodhi who came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent!
“World-Honored One!
We have gained great benefit and profit, having become the kinsmen of the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told Bodhi:
"Do not speak these words:
'I have gained a great benefit because I am a kinsman of the World-Honored One. Bodhi!"
What is called "beneficial excellence" consists of unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dharma and the Sangha, and the accomplishment of noble ethical discipline.
Therefore, O Bodhi!
"One should train in this way:
'I shall possess unshakable confidence in the Buddha, unshakable confidence in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and I shall be accomplished in the noble precepts.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Śākya Bodhi, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and approved with gladness; he paid homage and departed.
1124. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Park at Kapilavastu.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a noble disciple attains and accomplishes unshakable confidence in the Buddha,
then those devas who were previously born there by virtue of having accomplished the causal conditions for unshakable confidence in the Buddha and its precepts will all rejoice greatly and exclaim:”
"Because I have attained the cause and condition for accomplishing unshakable confidence in the Buddha, I have been reborn here in this auspicious realm among the devas.
Since these noble disciples have now attained unshakable confidence in the Buddha, by this same cause and condition, they too shall likewise be reborn here in this auspicious realm among the devas."
"The same is said regarding the unshakable confidence in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and the accomplishment of noble ethical discipline.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1125 (1125). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"There are four factors of the path of the stream-enterer: associating with virtuous persons, listening to the true Dharma, correct internal reflection, and practicing the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1126 (1126). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are four factors of stream-entry. What are the four?

"It refers to unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and the accomplishment of noble ethical discipline; these are called the factors of stream-entry.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1127 (1127). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If there are those who have accomplished four dharmas, you should know them to be srotāpannas. What are these four?"

That is to say: possessing unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dharma and the Sangha, and the accomplishment of noble ethical discipline—these are called the four dharmas of accomplishment; one who possesses them should be known as a stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Just as it was explained without differentiation, so too for those who differentiate: a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, śrāmaṇerī, upāsaka, or upāsikā who accomplishes these four dharmas should be known as a srotāpanna. Each sutra is to be recited as stated above.
1128 (1128). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four fruits of śrāmaṇya. What are the four?
"Namely, the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1129 (1129). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four fruits of the śramaṇa. What are the four?
These are the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala), the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmi-phala), the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmi-phala), and the fruit of arhatship (arhat-phala).
What is the fruit of stream-entry?
It is the abandonment of the three fetters; this is called the fruit of stream-entry.
What is the fruit of the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmiphala)?
It refers to the abandonment of the three fetters and the attenuation of greed, hatred, and delusion; this is called the fruit of the once-returner.
What is the fruit of the non-returner (anāgāmiphala)?
The abandonment of the five lower fetters is called the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
What is the fruit of arhatship?
When one’s greed is forever exhausted, hatred is forever exhausted, delusion is forever exhausted, and all afflictions are forever exhausted, this is called the fruit of arhatship.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1130 (1130) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If there is a bhikṣu who practices walking meditation in a certain place and attains one of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya therein, that bhikṣu will, for as long as his life lasts, constantly keep that place in mind."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
As it was said regarding the place for walking meditation, so it was also said regarding the places for standing, sitting, and lying down.
In this same manner, for each of the bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, there are four sūtras as explained above.
1131 (1131). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Just as the four kinds of nutriment sustain, benefit, and support sentient beings within the four great elements, what are these four?
These are the food of morsels, the food of contact, the food of volition, and the food of consciousness.
These four kinds are the nourishment of merit, the nourishment of wholesome dharmas, and the food of peace and happiness.
What are the four? They are:
the accomplishment of unshakable confidence in the Buddha, which is the nourishment of merit, the nourishment of wholesome qualities, and the food of peace and happiness;

unshakable confidence in the Dharma and the Sangha, and the accomplishment of noble ethical discipline, which is the nourishment of merit, the nourishment of wholesome qualities, and the food of peace and happiness.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1132 (1132). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus... [as stated above].
The difference is as follows:
"Having achieved unshakable confidence in the Buddha, one possesses the moisture of merit, the moisture of wholesome dharmas, and the food of peace and happiness."

He possesses unwavering confidence in the Dharma; he finds delight in and cherishes all the teachings he has heard; he is accomplished in noble ethical discipline; and he is moistened by merit, moistened by wholesome qualities, and nourished by peace and happiness.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1133 (1133) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus... as described above.
The difference is this:
"One who has accomplished unshakable clarity regarding the Buddha partakes in the moisture of merit, the moisture of wholesome dharmas, and the food of peace and happiness."

Whether regarding phenomena or toward those sentient beings who are bound by the defilement of stinginess, he dwells with a mind frequently free from the defilement of stinginess; he practices liberality as liberation, gives constantly, delights in renunciation, practices giving with an impartial mind, and is perfected in noble morality—the nourishment of merit, the nourishment of wholesome qualities, and the food of peace and happiness.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1134 (1134) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus... as described above.
The difference is this:

"These four kinds of nourishment of merit, nourishment of wholesome dharmas, and food of peace and happiness—the fruit and retribution of the noble disciple’s virtues are immeasurable; one obtains such blessings and such retribution."
"However, those with much merit fall into the category of the great accumulation of merit, as described in the *Pañcanadī-upama-sūtra*, up until the verses are spoken.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1135. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, forty sons of gods, possessed of most exquisite beauty, having passed the night, came to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet in salutation, and withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the devaputras:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
“O sons of the gods!
Have you all accomplished unshakable confidence in the Buddha, unshakable confidence in the Dharma and the Sangha, and have you accomplished the noble precepts?
At that time, the sons of the gods rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, prostrated at the feet of the Buddha, joined their palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have attained indestructible confidence in the Buddha; by virtue of this merit, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, I have now been born in the heavens.
Thus spoke a son of heaven to the Buddha.
“World-Honored One!
I have attained unwavering confidence in the Dharma; by virtue of this merit, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, I have now been reborn in the heavens.
Thus spoke a son of heaven to the Buddha.
“World-Honored One!
I have achieved unwavering confidence in the Saṃgha; by virtue of this merit, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, I have now been reborn in the heavens.
Thus spoke a certain son of the gods to the Buddha.
“World-Honored One!
I have been accomplished in the noble precepts; by virtue of this merit, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, I am now born in the heavens.
At that time, forty devaputras each declared before the Buddha their attainment of the fruit of *srotāpanna*, and immediately vanished from sight.

Just as with the forty devaputras, so too did four hundred devaputras, eight hundred devaputras, ten thousand devaputras, twenty thousand devaputras, thirty thousand devaputras, forty thousand devaputras, fifty thousand devaputras, sixty thousand devaputras, seventy thousand devaputras, and eighty thousand devaputras each, before the Buddha, personally declare their attainment of the fruit of *srotāpanna*, and then immediately vanished from sight.
1136. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should dwell like the analogy of the moon; like a novice, modest, humble, and gentle, one enters another's home with a restrained mind and composed body.
Just as a man with clear vision, when facing a deep abyss or ascending a mountain peak, restrains his mind and composes his form, finding it difficult to advance quickly."

In this way, bhikṣus, you should dwell like the moon, and like those newly trained, with shame, modesty, gentleness, and humility, governing the mind and restraining the body as you enter the homes of others.

Bhikṣu Kāśyapa dwells like the moon, and like those newly trained, with shame, modesty, gentleness, and the subduing of all arrogance, governing the mind and controlling the body as he enters the homes of others.
"It is like a man with clear vision who, standing on the edge of a deep abyss or atop a mountain peak, controls his mind and restrains his body, proceeding with right observation.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus,
"What do you think?"
"What kind of person should a bhikṣu be to enter another's home?
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, you are the root of the Dharma, the eye of the Dharma, and the refuge of the Dharma; we pray that you will explain this in detail."
"Having heard this, all you bhikṣus should receive it and practice accordingly.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for your sake."

If there is a bhikṣu who is not mentally bound by or attached to the households of others, and who does not harbor thoughts of envy when others obtain profit or perform meritorious deeds—rejoicing as if it were his own—he neither exalts himself nor disparages others.
“Monks of such a character as these should enter the homes of others.
At that time, the World-Honored One stroked the empty space with his hand and addressed the monks:
“Does this hand of mine now cling to the void, bind the void, or become defiled by the void?”
The bhikṣu replied to the Buddha,
“No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
“The dharma of a bhikṣu is always thus:
one enters the homes of others with a mind that is unattached, unbound, and unstained.

Only the bhikṣu Kāśyapa enters the homes of others with a mind that is unattached, unbound, and unstained; when he gains benefits from others or sees them perform meritorious deeds, he rejoices as if it were his own, giving rise to no thoughts of envy, neither exalting himself nor disparaging others—it is only the bhikṣu Kāśyapa who should enter the homes of others.”
At that time, the World-Honored One again stroked the empty space with his hand and addressed the bhikṣus:
“What do you think?
Does this hand of mine now cling to space, bind space, or defile space?”
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha,
“No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Only Kāśyapa the bhikṣu always possesses such a mind; with a mind that is unattached, unbound, and unstained, he enters the homes of others.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“What kind of bhikṣu should preach the Dharma with purity?”
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha:
“The World-Honored One is the root of the Dharma, the eye of the Dharma, and the refuge of the Dharma; we pray that you will explain it in detail!
Having heard it, the bhikṣus shall receive and practice it accordingly.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you.
If there is a bhikṣu who, with such a mind, preaches the Dharma to others:”
"Whoever gives rise to pure faith in me, taking this as their foundation, shall obtain offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites."
"One who speaks in such a manner is said to preach the Dharma that is not pure.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma to others, he should form this thought:

'The World-Honored One has manifested the True Dharma and the Vinaya, which is free from all burning afflictions, independent of time and season, realizable in this very body through one's own self-awakening, and leading directly toward Nirvāṇa. Yet sentient beings are submerged in old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, despair, and suffering. If these sentient beings hear the True Dharma, they will benefit from its meaning and find peace and happiness for a long night.'"

By means of these causes and conditions of the true Dharma, one preaches it for others with a mind of loving-kindness, compassion, pity, and the desire to cause the true Dharma to abide for a long time; this is called preaching the Dharma purely.

Only the bhikṣu Kāśyapa possesses such a pure mind as he preaches the Dharma for others; by means of the Tathāgata’s true Dharma and Vinaya, he preaches it for others with the intention that the Dharma may endure for a long time.

Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus and teach the Dharma thus: for the sake of the Tathāgata’s true Dharma and Discipline, and even so that the Dharma may long endure, you should teach the Dharma to others with a focused mind.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1137 (1137) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

“If a bhikṣu wishes to enter another’s home, he should form this thought: ‘May they give to me; may they not fail to give. May they give all at once rather than gradually; may they give much rather than little; may they give excellent things rather than inferior things; may they give promptly rather than slowly.’”
If one approaches another's house with such a mind, and that person does not give, or gives only grudgingly, the bhikṣu’s mind will feel humiliated.
Due to these causes and conditions, his mind becomes despondent and he creates obstacles for himself.
"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu wishes to enter another's home, he should form this thought:

'When one who has left the household life suddenly arrives at another's home, on what basis can one expect that there will be giving rather than no giving, immediate giving rather than gradual giving, abundant giving rather than meager giving, excellent giving rather than inferior giving, and prompt giving rather than delayed giving?'"
Having formed such a thought, he enters the homes of others.

If they do not give, or even if they give only slowly, that bhikṣu’s mind is neither humiliated nor discouraged; he does not give rise to obstacles. It is only with such a thought, Kāśyapa, that a bhikṣu enters the homes of others.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:

with such a reflection, enter the homes of others. When a renunciant suddenly arrives at another's home, by what means can one obtain alms rather than not obtaining them, and even receive them promptly rather than slowly?
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1138 (1138) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was staying at the Eastern Park, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground, in Śrāvastī.
Then, in the late afternoon, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa arose from meditation and went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, paid his respects, and withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Mahākāśyapa:
"You should preach the Dharma, provide instruction, and offer guidance to the bhikṣus. Why is this so?"
"I constantly preach the Dharma, instruct, and exhort the bhikṣus; you too should do likewise.
Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"The bhikṣus of the present age are difficult to instruct; there may even be bhikṣus who cannot bear to hear this teaching.
The Buddha said to Mahākāśyapa, "For what reason do you speak thus?"
Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I saw two bhikṣus; one was named Pāñcika, who was a disciple of Ānanda."
The second was named Ābhūṣin; he was a disciple of Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
Those two men vied with one another regarding their extensive learning, each saying:
"Come, let us debate together as to who possesses greater knowledge."
"Who is it that possesses superior knowledge?
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the Buddha, fanning him with a fan, and said to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa:
"Wait! Please stop!"
Venerable Mahākāśyapa!
Be patient for a moment!
Venerable Kāśyapa!
"This young bhikṣu has little wisdom and possesses evil wisdom.
Venerable Mahākāśyapa said to Venerable Ānanda,
"Be silent for now!"
"Do not let me question you about this matter before the Saṃgha.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda remained silent.
Then, the Blessed One addressed a certain bhikṣu:
"Go to the bhikṣus Pāṭali and Ābhūṣin and say to them:
'The Great Teacher speaks to you.
At that time, those bhikṣus received the instruction, went to where the bhikṣus Pāṭali and Ābhūṣin were, and spoke as follows:
"The Great Teacher speaks to you.
Then, the bhikṣus Pāñcika and Ābhūṣi replied, "We accept your instruction," and immediately went together to the Buddha's dwelling. They prostrated at his feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the two bhikṣus:
"Did you two truly engage in a dispute together, each saying:
'Come, let us debate to see who is more learned and who is superior'?"
The two bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha addressed the two bhikṣus:

"Do you take the dharmas I have taught—the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, avadānas, itivṛttakas, jātaka-s, vaipulyas, adbhuta-dharmas, and upadeśas—and engage in mutual dispute and debate, each saying:
'Come, let us test one another in discussion; who is more learned and who is superior?'"
The two bhikṣus replied to the Buddha,
“No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to the two bhikṣus:
"Do you not use the sūtras, up to and including the upadeśas, that I have taught to discipline yourselves, to bring yourselves to rest, and to seek nirvāṇa for yourselves?"
The two bhikṣus replied to the Buddha,
“So it is, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to the two bhikṣus:
"Do you know the sūtras I have taught, up to and including the upadeśas? You foolish man, you should engage in debate with me to determine who speaks more or who is superior!"
Then the two bhikṣus came forward, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed him again,
saying: “We repent,
World-Honored One!”
I repent! O Sugata!
I was foolish and deluded; being unskilled and lacking discernment, I engaged in contentious debate.
The Buddha told the two bhikṣus:
"You truly recognize your transgression and repent of it; you were foolish, unskilled, and lacking in discernment that you engaged in mutual dispute.

Now that you have recognized your transgression for yourselves and seen your transgression for yourselves, and having known and seen it, you repent; thus, in future lives, the restraint of the precepts will arise."
I now accept you out of compassion, so that your wholesome dharmas may increase and never decline.

Why is this? If one knows one's own transgressions, sees one's own transgressions, and recognizes and confesses them, then in future lives the restraint of the precepts will arise, and it shall never decline.
At that time, the two bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and approved with gladness;
they paid homage and departed. 1139 (1139). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was staying at the Eastern Park, the Squirrel’s Feeding Ground Lecture Hall, in Śrāvastī. In the late afternoon, he arose from meditation and went to where the Blessed One was; having prostrated at his feet, he withdrew to sit at one side.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"You should instruct and admonish the bhikṣus!
Preach the Dharma, provide instruction, and offer admonition to the bhikṣus."
"Why is that? I have always been expounding the Dharma, instructing, and training the bhikṣus; you, too, should do likewise.
Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is now difficult to preach the Dharma to these bhikṣus; if one were to preach the Dharma, there would be bhikṣus who could not endure it or take pleasure in it.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“What causes and conditions do you perceive that lead you to speak thus?
Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One!”
If there is a bhikṣu who lacks faith and reverence for wholesome dharmas, he will fall away when he hears the Dharma being taught.

If an ignorant person lacks diligence, shame, remorse, and wisdom regarding wholesome dharmas, he will fall away when he hears the Dharma being taught. If a person is possessed by sensual desire, ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-regret, or doubt; if they are physically arrogant and violent, harboring resentment and losing mindfulness, lacking concentration and wisdom, they will fall away when they hear the Dharma being taught.
World-Honored One!
Such evil persons as these cannot even cause their minds to abide in wholesome dharmas, let alone progress further.
You should know that for such people, with each passing day and night, wholesome dharmas decline and diminish, unable to increase.
“World-Honored One!
If there is a person whose faith in all wholesome dharmas is pure, they will not regress;

if they possess diligence, a sense of shame, remorse, and wisdom regarding all wholesome dharmas, they will not regress; and if they are free from greed, ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-regret, and doubt, they will not regress.”
When the body is not coarse or violent, the mind is unstained, and one is without anger or resentment, possessing a concentrated mind, right mindfulness, and wisdom—this is non-retrogression.

For such a person, wholesome qualities increase day and night; how much more so when the mind abides [in them]? Such a person constantly seeks superior progress day and night, never falling back or diminishing.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: “It is so, it is so.
Those who have no faith in the various wholesome dharmas will surely decline and regress... He then spoke at length in succession, just as he had done for Kāśyapa.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and approved with gladness. He rose from his seat, paid homage, and departed.
1140 (1140). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was staying at the Eastern Garden, the Squirrel’s Feeding Place Lecture Hall, in Śrāvastī. In the late afternoon, he arose from meditation and went to where the Buddha was; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa:
"You should preach the Dharma, provide exhortation, and give instruction to the bhikṣus. Why is this so?
"I constantly teach the Dharma, instruct, and exhort the bhikṣus; you, too, should do likewise.
Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"

Now, it is difficult for me to provide these bhikṣus with Dharma teachings, exhortations, and instructions; there are bhikṣus who, upon hearing the Dharma taught, cannot endure it and do not rejoice in it.
The Buddha asked Mahākāśyapa,
"For what reason do you speak thus?
Mahākāśyapa replied to the Buddha:

“The Blessed One is the root of the Dharma, the eye of the Dharma, and the refuge of the Dharma. We pray that the Blessed One will teach the Dharma to the bhikṣus; having heard it, the bhikṣus shall receive and practice it.”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"In the past, forest-dwelling bhikṣus praised the qualities of forest dwelling in the presence of other forest-dwelling bhikṣus; they praised the merits of alms-gathering in the presence of alms-collecting bhikṣus;
and they praised the merits of wearing rag-robes in the presence of rag-robe-wearing bhikṣus."

If there is a bhikkhu who has few desires and is content, who practices seclusion, exerts himself with skillful means, possesses right mindfulness and right concentration, and has attained the destruction of the taints through wisdom and realized it for himself with his body, one should follow his conduct, praising and extolling it.
Kāśyapa!

If one, in the presence of those dwelling in forest hermitages (araṇya), praises and speaks of the qualities of forest hermitage life; and even in the presence of bhikṣus who have exhausted the outflows (āsravakṣaya), praises and speaks of the realization of the exhaustion of outflows through bodily witness.
If they see anyone, they all converse with them, greeting those who arrive with appropriate words of comfort and welcome:
"What is your name? Whose disciple are you?"

He offers his seat and invites him to sit, praising his worthiness and goodness, saying: "In accordance with the likeness of the Dharma, he possesses the qualities of a śramaṇa and the aspirations of a śramaṇa.
When he praises him in this way, those who dwell and travel with him will certainly follow his conduct; before long, they too shall come to share his views and his aspirations.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"If a young bhikṣu sees that forest-dwelling bhikṣu coming and hears him praise the dharma of forest dwelling, up to the point of attaining the exhaustion of outflows through bodily realization, that young bhikṣu should rise to meet him, pay respectful homage, and inquire after his well-being; even those who dwell with him shall, before long, attain their own benefit and welfare."
"One who shows such reverence shall obtain peace, happiness, and benefit for a long night.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"Today, when a bhikṣu sees one approaching and recognizes that he is a person of great virtue capable of attracting wealth, profit, robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites, he should converse with him, pay respectful greetings, and exclaim, 'Welcome!'"
"What is your name? Whose disciple are you?
He then praised his merit and virtue, noting that he was able to attract great benefits: robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites.
If one associates closely with such a venerable one, one shall likewise be provided in abundance with robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites.

Furthermore, if a young bhikṣu sees such a person approaching—one of great wisdom and great virtue who is capable of attracting wealth, profit, robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites—he should quickly rise to meet him, pay respectful greetings, and exclaim: "Welcome, O one of great wisdom and great virtue, you who are capable of attracting great benefits, robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites!"
“Kāśyapa!
In this way, such young bhikṣus will for a long night experience suffering that is meaningless and unbeneficial.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!”

These bhikṣus are a plague to the śramaṇas, a drowning place for the holy life (brahmacarya), a great obscuration, and a source of affliction consisting of evil and unwholesome dharmas. They undergo the heavy burden of various states of existence, burning within the cycle of birth and death, facing future bitter retributions: birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and despair.
Therefore, Kāśyapa, you should train yourselves in this way:

"We shall be forest-dwellers; in the forest, we shall praise and extol the wearing of rag-robes, alms-gathering, fewness of desires, contentment, the practice of seclusion, diligent application of effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, right wisdom, the exhaustion of the outflows, and the realization through bodily witness. You should praise and extol those who possess these qualities.
"You should train yourselves in this way.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and delighted in it; he paid homage and departed.
1141 (1141). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was staying at the Eastern Garden, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground, in Śrāvastī. In the late afternoon, he arose from meditation and went to where the Blessed One was; having prostrated at his feet, he withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa, saying:

"You are now old; your years are advanced and your faculties have matured. Your rag-robes are heavy, whereas my robes are light and fine. You should now remain among the Saṃgha and wear the light, dyed robes of a layperson."
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For a long night, I have practiced in the forest hermitage (āraṇya), and I have praised the forest hermitage, rag-robes (pāṃśukūla), and alms-gathering (piṇḍapāta).”
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:

"In view of how many kinds of meanings do you practice *āraṇyaka* (forest dwelling), praise *āraṇyaka*, [practice] rag-robes (*pāṃsukūla*) and alms-gathering (*piṇḍapāta*), and praise the dharmas of rag-robes and alms-gathering?"
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I contemplate two kinds of meanings: the meaning of attaining peaceful dwelling in the present life, and furthermore, acting as a great illumination for future sentient beings.”
Sentient beings in future ages should think thus:

"In the past, there was an Elder endowed with the six supernormal powers; having long been ordained, his pure conduct was mature, and he was praised by the World-Honored One and served by those practitioners of wisdom and purity."
For a long night, he has practiced in the forest retreats (āraṇyaka), praising the forest retreats, rag-robes (pāṃśukūla), and alms-gathering; he praises the practice of rag-robes and alms-gathering.
“May all who hear this rejoice with a pure mind; throughout the long night, they shall all obtain peace, happiness, and benefit.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Excellent!”
Excellent, Kāśyapa!

You have brought great benefit to many throughout the long night, bringing peace and happiness to sentient beings, showing compassion for the world, and providing peace and happiness to devas and humans.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"If there are those who disparage the dhūta practices, they disparage me;
if there are those who praise the dhūta practices, they praise me."
Why is this? Because the dhuta practices are those which I have long praised and extolled.
Therefore, Kāśyapa!
One who dwells in the forest should praise dwelling in the forest;
one who wears rag-robes and subsists on alms should praise the practice of wearing rag-robes and seeking alms.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, Mahākāśyapa, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and approved with gladness;
he paid homage and departed. 1142 (1142). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, having resided for a long time in the forest hermitage at Śrāvastī, with his beard and hair grown long and wearing tattered robes of patched rags, approached the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by an immeasurable great assembly as he preached the Dharma.
When the bhikṣus saw Mahākāśyapa approaching from afar, they gave rise to a sense of contempt toward the Venerable Mahākāśyapa and said:
"What kind of bhikṣu is this?"
“They have come with coarse and shabby clothing, lacking any dignified appearance; they have come with their robes hanging loosely.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing what the bhikṣus were thinking in their minds, addressed Mahākāśyapa: “Welcome!”
Kāśyapa! Regarding this half-seat, I now truly do not know who was ordained first: you or I?
Those bhikṣus felt terror arise in their hearts; the hair on their bodies stood on end, and they said to one another, "How extraordinary!
O Venerable One!"
"That venerable Mahākāśyapa is of great virtue and great power, a disciple of the Great Teacher; please accept half of my seat.
Then, the venerable Mahākāśyapa joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"The Buddha is my teacher; I am his disciple.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "So it is!"
"So it is! I am the Great Teacher and you are my disciple; sit now for a while, as you see fit.
Venerable Mahākāśyapa bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing again to awaken the bhikṣus and to manifest before the assembly the superior and vast merit he himself had attained—just as that of the Venerable Mahākāśyapa—addressed the bhikṣus:

"I have departed from sensual desires and unwholesome states; with directed thought and sustained evaluation, I dwell fully established in the first dhyāna, whether by day, by night, or throughout the day and night.

Mahākāśyapa is likewise like me: having departed from sensual desires and unwholesome states, he too dwells fully established in the first dhyāna, whether by day, by night, or throughout the day and night."
When I wish to dwell fully endowed with the second, third, or fourth dhyāna for a day, a night, or a day and night, Mahākāśyapa does exactly the same.
...up to and including dwelling fully in the fourth dhyāna, whether by day, by night, or by day and night.
