Whatever I desired—to dwell fully in loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; in the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; in the domain of supernormal powers; and in the knowledge of the divine ear, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of past lives, the knowledge of death and rebirth, and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows—whether by day, by night, or by day and night—the bhikṣu Kāśyapa was likewise so.
"...up to dwelling in the full possession of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows, whether by day, or by night, or by day and night.

At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst a great assembly of immeasurable size, praised Mahākāśyapa for his vast, supreme, and wondrous merits equal to his own. Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1143. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa and the Venerable Ānanda were staying on Vulture Peak Mountain.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda went to where the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was and said to him:
"We should now go together out of Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain and enter the city of Rājagṛha to beg for alms."
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa consented by remaining silent.
Then, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa and the Venerable Ānanda put on their robes, took up their bowls, and entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms.
The Venerable Ānanda said to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, "It is still too early;
let us go together for a while to the bhikṣuṇī monastery.
They then went there at once.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs saw from afar the Venerable Mahākāśyapa and the Venerable Ānanda approaching; they quickly prepared seats and invited them to be seated.
Then, having prostrated at the feet of the Venerable Mahākāśyapa and Ānanda, the bhikṣuṇīs withdrew to sit at one side.
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa preached the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs in various ways, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them.
Having thus instructed, exhorted, illuminated, and gladdened them, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā was displeased and spoke these evil words:
"How can this be?..."
"Venerable Mahākāśyapa, why did you preach the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs in the presence of the Vṛji Muni, the venerable Ānanda?

It is just as if a needle-seller were to sell his needles at the house of a master needle-maker; so it is with the venerable Mahākāśyapa, preaching the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs in the presence of the venerable Ānanda, the Vṛji Muni."
When the Venerable Mahākāśyapa heard that the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā was displeased in her heart and spoke evil words,
having heard this, he said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Look!
The bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā was displeased in her heart and spoke evil words.
How so, Ānanda?
"I am a needle-seller and you are a master of needles; shall I sell them before you?
Venerable Ānanda said to Venerable Mahākāśyapa, "Stop!
Please desist!"
"You should be patient!
This foolish old woman has little wisdom and has never practiced cultivation.
"Ānanda! [the Buddha said.]

Have you not heard how the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—possessing knowledge and vision—preached the Candra-upama Sūtra in the midst of the great assembly, providing exhortation and instruction?
"Monks! You should dwell like the moon, always as if you were newly ordained.
Thus it was said in detail for the sake of instruction, Ānanda!"
“Is it as if the moon remains always like when it was first learned?
Ānanda replied, “No, Venerable Mahākāśyapa!”
“Ānanda! Have you heard what the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—knowing and seeing—has said: ‘Monks!’”
"One should dwell like the analogy of the moon, always as if newly initiated; such is the case only for the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa!
Ānanda replied:
"So it is, Venerable Mahākāśyapa! Ānanda, has the Blessed One,
the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha— being aware and seeing you— ever invited you to sit among a great assembly of immeasurable size?"
Furthermore, the World-Honored One has praised you with words of commendation equal to his own vast virtues, saying:
"Ānanda, having abandoned sensual desires and unwholesome states, you have attained even the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows."
"Why do you praise him?
He replied, "No, Venerable Mahākāśyapa!"
"Thus it is, Ānanda!
In the midst of an immeasurable great assembly, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, spoke with his own mouth:
'Welcome, Mahākāśyapa!'"
"I invite you to share half my seat.

Furthermore, did he, amidst the great assembly, praise Mahākāśyapa by extolling his vast merits as equal to his own—ranging from the abandonment of desire and unwholesome states up to the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows?
Ānanda replied, “So it is,
Venerable Mahākāśyapa! At that time,
Mahākāśyapa had finished his lion’s roar amidst the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs.
1144. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa and the Venerable Ānanda were staying on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa near the city of Rājagṛha, not long after the Parinirvāṇa of the Blessed One.
At that time, there was a famine in the world, and it was difficult to obtain almsfood.

Then, the Venerable Ānanda was together with many young bhikṣus who were unable to properly restrain their sense faculties, did not know moderation in eating, failed to apply themselves diligently to meditative reflection during the first and last watches of the night, delighted in sleep, and constantly sought worldly gain.
While traveling among humans in South India, there were thirty young disciples who abandoned the precepts and returned to lay life; the remainder were mostly children.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was traveling through the kingdom of Dakṣiṇāpatha and returned to Rājagṛha with a small retinue of followers.
Then, the Venerable Ānanda took up his robe and bowl, washed his feet, went to where the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was, prostrated at his feet in salutation, and withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa asked the Venerable Ānanda:
"From where have you come?
Why is your retinue so small?"
Ānanda replied:

"While wandering among the people in the lands south of the mountains, thirty young bhikṣus have abandoned the precepts and returned to lay life; thus the assembly has diminished, and those who remain now are mostly children."
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa said to Ānanda:
"How many benefits did the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha know and perceive when he authorized the precept against group meals for groups of three or more?"
Ānanda replied:
"It is for two reasons.
What are these two?"
First, they will become impoverished households; second, they will have many evil people as their associates and factions, leading to mutual destruction.

Do not allow evil people to dwell within the Sangha and receive the title of "member of the assembly," for they will obscure the great multitude, splitting it into two separate divisions that harbor mutual resentment and contention.
The Venerable Kāśyapa said to Ānanda:

"Do you understand this matter? Why, during a time of famine, did you travel through the Southern Mountains with so many young disciples, causing thirty people to abandon the precepts and return to lay life, thereby diminishing the assembly, most of whom were but children?"
"Ānanda! Your followers are being destroyed; you are but a youth, lacking the capacity for prudent judgment.
Ānanda replied:
"How is this, Venerable Mahākāśyapa?
My hair is already two colors; how can you still call me a youth?"
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa said:
"During a time of famine, you traveled among the people with many young disciples, causing thirty of them to abandon the precepts and return to lay life; those who remain are likewise but children."
"The assembly has been destroyed; you did not exercise due deliberation, yet you spoke of the ruin of the community of elder monks.
Ānanda! The assembly is utterly ruined, Ānanda!
For you are but a youth, lacking in discernment."

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Tiṣyā heard the Venerable Mahākāśyapa reproaching the Venerable Ānanda as a mere boy, O Videhamuni; having heard this, she was displeased and uttered these harsh words: "How can this be?"
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa was originally a non-Buddhist ascetic; having heard that the youth reproached the Venerable Ānanda, the Videha-muni, he caused the youth’s name to become widely known.
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa, having heard with his divine ear that the bhikṣuṇī Tiṣyā was displeased in her heart and had uttered evil words,
said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Look!
The bhikṣuṇī Tiṣyā was displeased in her heart and spoke these harsh words:
"Mahākāśyapa originally heard this from non-Buddhists, yet he rebukes the Venerable Ānanda, the Videhamuni, causing the boy's name to circulate."
The Venerable Ānanda replied:
"Stop, Venerable Mahākāśyapa!"
Be patient!
Venerable Mahākāśyapa,
this foolish old woman lacks the wisdom of self-nature.
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa said to Ānanda:
"Since my own renunciation, I have never known of any other teacher except for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."

Before I went forth from the home life, I constantly contemplated birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering. I knew that living at home is a state of busy toil with many defilements, whereas going forth is a state of seclusion and leisure. It is difficult for a layperson to dwell in the homeless state, remaining consistently pure, exhausting the span of their life, wholly fulfilled and clean, with a holy life (brahmacarya) that is stainless.

When one shaves off hair and beard, dons the saṃghāṭī robe, and with right faith leaves the home life to study the Path, one takes the most precious garments worth hundreds of thousands of gold pieces, cuts them into patches, and makes them into a saṃghāṭī; yet if one is a worldly arhat, they leave the home life in darkness.

After I had gone forth, at the Cāpāla Shrine between the city of Rājagṛha and the village of Nāla, I encountered the World-Honored One sitting upright with his body straight; his marks were extraordinary, his faculties were serene, and he was supremely tranquil, like a mountain of gold.
"At that time, having seen him, I thought:
'This is my teacher!
This is the World-Honored One!'"
"This is an Arhat! This is a Samyaksaṃbuddha!
At that time, with single-minded devotion, I joined my palms in reverent salutation and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"He is my Great Teacher!
I am his disciple.
The Buddha said to me:
"In this way, Kāśyapa, I am your teacher;
you are my disciple."
Kāśyapa! You have now accomplished such a truly pure mind of reverence.

If one who does not know claims to know, one who has not seen claims to see, one who is not actually an arhat claims to be an arhat, or one who is not a perfectly awakened one claims to be a perfectly awakened one, their body shall naturally shatter into seven pieces.

Kāśyapa! Now, because I know, I say that I know; because I see, I say that I see. Being a true arhat, I call myself an arhat; being a true, perfectly awakened one, I call myself a perfectly awakened one.
Kāśyapa! It is because there is a specific cause and condition that I now teach the Dharma for the sake of the śrāvakas; it is not without cause and condition.
It is based upon something; it is not without a basis.
There is spiritual power; it is not that there is no spiritual power.
Therefore, Kāśyapa, if you wish to hear the Dharma, you should train yourself in this way:
"If you wish to hear the Dharma for the sake of benefit through its meaning, you should unify your mind, show reverence and respect, listen attentively with a focused mind, and form this thought:

'I shall correctly contemplate the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates; the gathering, arising, and passing away of the six bases of contact; dwell in the joy of right mindfulness regarding the four foundations of mindfulness; cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment; realize the eight liberations through bodily witness; constantly maintain mindfulness of the body without ever letting it cease; remain free from shamelessness and lack of conscience; and always abide in a state of shame and conscience before the Great Teacher and those of great virtue and holy life.'"
"In this way, you should train yourself!
At that time, the World-Honored One taught me the Dharma, instructing, exhorting, illuminating, and gladdening me;
having instructed, exhorted, illuminated, and gladdened me, he rose from his seat and departed.
I also followed him toward his dwelling place.
I had a saṃghāṭī robe, worth hundreds of thousands [in price], cut into pieces and arranged as a seat.
At that time, knowing my sincere heart, the World-Honored One stepped off the path at various points; I immediately spread out the robe to serve as a sitting mat and invited the Buddha to sit.
The World-Honored One sat down immediately, rubbed his robe with his hand, and sighed, saying:
"Kāśyapa! This robe is light and fine; this robe is soft and supple."
I then replied: "So it is,
World-Honored One!"
"This robe is light and fine; this robe is soft and supple. I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept this robe from me!
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"You should receive my refuse-rag robe (pāṃsukūla), and I shall receive your saṃghāṭī."
The Buddha then personally handed me his own rag-robe (*pāṃsukūla*), and I immediately offered my *saṃghāṭī* robe to the Buddha.
Thus, through gradual instruction, within eight days I received the training in the Dharma regarding alms-gathering; on the ninth day, I attained the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
“Ānanda! Suppose someone were to ask correctly:

‘Who is the son of the Blessed One’s Dharma, born from the mouth of the Buddha, born of the transformation of the Dharma, entrusted with the wealth of the Dharma—the various dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and right attainments?’”
One should answer, "I am that," for this is the correct statement.

For example, the eldest son of a Wheel-Turning Sage King is destined to be consecrated, to occupy the royal throne, and to enjoy the five desires of a king; he obtains these without effort, as they come naturally. I am likewise a son of the Buddha’s Dharma, born from the mouth of the Buddha and transformed by the Dharma; I have obtained the remaining wealth of the Dharma—meditation, liberation, samādhi, and right reception—and I obtain these without effort, as they come naturally.

For example, if a precious elephant of a wheel-turning monarch, seven or eight cubits high, could be shaded and concealed by a single *tāla* leaf, so too could my accomplishment of the wisdom of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) be shaded and concealed.

If there are those who have doubts regarding the realization of wisdom within the sphere of the supernormal powers, I am able to analyze and explain them all for them. Whether they have doubts regarding the divine ear, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of past lives, the knowledge of birth and death, or the realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), I am able to analyze and explain them all for them, causing them to attain certainty.
The Venerable Ānanda said to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa: "So it is! So it is!"
Mahākāśyapa! It is as if a precious elephant of a wheel-turning monarch, seven or eight cubits high, were to be shielded by a single *tāla* leaf.

In this same way, Venerable Mahākāśyapa, your knowledge of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) could indeed be shielded; yet, for anyone who has doubts regarding the realization-knowledge within the sphere of supernormal powers, or even regarding the realization-knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), the Venerable Mahākāśyapa is able to provide an explanation for them, causing them to reach certainty.
"For a long night, I have revered and honored the Venerable Mahākāśyapa because he possesses such great virtue and supernormal powers.
When the Venerable Mahākāśyapa had spoken these words, the Venerable Ānanda, hearing what was said, received and upheld it with joy.
Saṃyukta Āgama, Scroll 41 and Scroll 42,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
42.1145 (1145) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One,
to what kind of person should one give?”
The Buddha said,
“Great King,
wherever your heart desires.”
King Prasenajit again addressed the Buddha, saying,
“To whom should one give so as to obtain a great karmic fruit?
The Buddha said:
“Great King!
This is a different question.
As for what you asked: ‘To whom should one give?’”
This question is different.
Furthermore, the question, "To whom should one give so as to obtain a great fruit? is yet another.
I now ask you; answer me as you see fit. Great King!

Suppose in this kingdom, when an army is drawn up for battle, all the warriors have assembled, and there comes from the east a son of a brahmin who is young and immature, weak and delicate though handsome, with fair skin and black hair. He has not practiced martial arts nor studied strategic counsel; he is fearful and timid, unable to compose himself, and cannot bear to look upon the enemy. Whether it be spearing or archery, he lacks the skillful means and cannot wound the opponent.
"What do you think, Great King? Would Your Majesty reward such a man?
The King said to the Buddha:
"No, World-Honored One!
"It is so, Great King!"

Suppose a kṣatriya youth comes from the south, a vaiśya youth comes from the west, and a śūdra youth comes from the north; though they possess no skills or arts, they are all just like the brahmin son from the east—would the King reward them?
The king said to the Buddha,
“I have not rewarded him,
World-Honored One.”

The Buddha told the Great King: "When the armies of this kingdom have assembled and are on the verge of battle, there will come from the east a young Brahmin boy, youthful and handsome, with fair skin and black hair. He is well-trained in martial arts, knowledgeable in the methods of combat, brave and fearless, never retreating in bitter struggle. Remaining steadfast and observing with clarity, he can wound with his spear and destroy even the greatest enemies."
"How so? Great King!
Would you grant a heavy reward to such a warrior?"
The King addressed the Buddha, saying, “A great reward, World-Honored One! Thus it is:

a kṣatriya youth comes from the south, a vaiśya youth comes from the west, and a śūdra youth comes from the north; they are young and handsome, skilled in all arts and crafts, brave, capable, and able to withstand bitter battle and repel the enemy, just like the brahmin son from the east.”
"Would the King reward such a warrior?
The King said to the Buddha,
"He would reward him generously, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said:
"Great King!
Thus, when śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas distance themselves from five factors and accomplish five factors, they establish themselves as fields of merit."
One who gives to this field obtains great benefit and merit, and attains a great karmic fruit.
What are the five factors that must be abandoned?

They are the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt. Having severed and fully understood these, they are called the abandonment of the five factors.
What are the five factors of accomplishment?

They are the accomplishment of the untrained aggregate of ethical discipline, the untrained aggregate of concentration, the untrained aggregate of wisdom, the untrained aggregate of liberation, and the untrained aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; these are called the five factors of accomplishment.
"Great King!
Thus, having abandoned five factors and accomplished five factors, one establishes a field of merit; those who give to this field obtain a great reward."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Brave warriors who are capable of wielding spears and engaging in fierce combat,
because of their fighting, are granted rewards according to their merit."
One does not honor those of noble lineage who are timid, inferior, and lacking in courage;
rather, one honors those who practice patience, cultivate virtue, realize the Truth, and establish the field of merit.
Those who possess the full precepts of the noble ones and have perfected profound and wondrous wisdom—[it is they whom one honors].
Though one’s lineage may be lowly, they are worthy to serve as a field of merit for offerings.
Clothing, food, money, treasures, beds, seats,
and all such requisites should all be given with reverence, for the sake of upholding the pure precepts.
At the edge of forests and fields on the outskirts of towns, they dug wells to provide for travelers;
they constructed bridges over streams and ravines and built shelters along remote roads.
Thus, those endowed with the virtue of precepts and great learning could find rest while traveling on their journeys.
Just as when heavy clouds arise, Thunder and lightning flash and roar;
As rain falls everywhere upon the soil, The hundred species of plants all flourish luxuriantly;
Birds and beasts are all filled with joy, And the farmers alike rejoice.
With such pure faith, having heard the wisdom that abandons the stain of stinginess,
one constantly gives abundant wealth and food and drink to the excellent field of merit.
One’s joyful cries increase like rain and thunder falling upon a fertile field.
The flow of merit’s moisture drenches the heart of the donor;
wealth and fame spread abroad, leading to the great fruit of Nirvāṇa.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced with gladness, paid homage, and departed.
1146. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha,
saying: “How is this, World-Honored One?”
“Is it that one who dies as a brahmin is reborn in his own brahmin family, or in the families of kṣatriyas, vaiśyas,
or śūdras? The Buddha said,
“Great King!”
How can this be so? Great King, you should know that there are four kinds of persons.
What are these four?
There is a type of person who goes from darkness into darkness;
there is a type of person who goes from darkness into light;
and there is a type of person who goes from light into darkness.
There is a kind of person who enters from light into light.
"Great King!
What is the kind of person who enters from darkness into darkness?"

This refers to those who are born into low-caste families—such as the families of *caṇḍālas*, fishermen, hunters, bamboo-workers, or cartwrights—or into other various families of lowly artisans; who are impoverished, short-lived, and physically haggard, and who further cultivate the practices of these lowly households while serving as subordinates and laborers for others. This is called "darkness."

Abiding in this darkness, one further engages in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind; by reason of these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, one shall be reborn in an evil destination, falling into hell.
It is just as if someone were to go from darkness into darkness, from a latrine into a latrine, washing blood with blood, abandoning evil only to take up more evil;
so too it is for one who goes from obscurity into further obscurity.
Therefore, this is called "entering from darkness into darkness.
What is meant by "entering from darkness into light"?
It refers to those born into families of low status, even performing various menial tasks for others; this is called darkness.

Nevertheless, that person, while in this darkness, practices wholesome conduct of body, wholesome conduct of speech, and wholesome conduct of mind; by reason of these causes and conditions, when the body breaks up at the end of life, they are reborn in a happy destination, receiving birth by transformation among the devas.
It is like a person who mounts a bed, then crosses onto a horse, and from the horse ascends an elephant;
entering from darkness into light is just like this.
This is called a person who enters from darkness into light.
"What is it for a person to pass from light into darkness?

It refers to those born into families of wealth and happiness—whether among the great clans of Kṣatriyas, the great clans of Brāhmaṇas, the great clans of householders, or other various families of wealth and happiness—who possess abundant wealth, servants, laborers, and a wide circle of acquaintances; who have received a handsome body and are intelligent, clever, and wise. This is called 'light. "

Within this light, one may engage in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind; by reason of these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, one is born in an evil destination and falls into hell.

It is just as if a person were to descend from a high tower riding an elephant, dismount from the elephant to ride a horse, dismount from the horse to ride a carriage, dismount from the carriage to sit on a bench, dismount from the bench to fall to the ground, and from the ground fall into a pit—entering from light into darkness is likewise so.
"What is it for a person to enter from light into light?
It refers to those born into a wealthy and prosperous family, even possessing a handsome and dignified appearance; this is called 'light. "

Within this light, one practices wholesome conduct of body, wholesome conduct of speech, and wholesome conduct of mind; by reason of these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one is reborn in a happy destination, receiving birth by transformation among the devas.
It is, for example, like a person going from one multi-storied pavilion to another;
likewise, even from one bed to another;
and so it is for one who enters from light into light.
"This is called a person who proceeds from light into light.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
"The poor and those in distress, Lacking faith, increase their resentment."
Stingy, greedy, and harboring evil and perverse thoughts, Deluded and lacking in reverence,
Upon seeing śramaṇas or practitioners Who uphold the precepts and possess great learning,
They disparage them rather than praising them, And obstruct others from giving and receiving.
Such a person as this, passing from this world to the next,
shall fall into the hells, going from darkness into further darkness.
But if there is a poor person who possesses faith and has little anger, [they shall not suffer such a fate].
Always give rise to a sense of shame and remorse, and practice giving while remaining free from the stain of stinginess.
Upon seeing śramaṇas and brahmins who uphold the precepts and possess great learning,
inquire after them with humility and provide for their needs as is appropriate.
Exhorting others to give, praising both the giver and the recipient—
such a person who cultivates virtue proceeds from this world to the next.
Reborn in a higher realm in the happy destinies, they pass from darkness into light.
There is a wealthy and prosperous man who lacks faith and harbors much resentment;
he is stingy, greedy, quick to harbor thoughts of malice, deluded by error, and disrespectful.
Upon seeing śramaṇas and brahmins, he reviles them rather than praising them.
Obstructing the charity of others and cutting off those who receive it—
such an evil person, from this life to the next,
shall be born in the miserable hells, passing from light into darkness.
If there is a noble man who possesses faith and is free from resentment,
who constantly gives rise to a sense of shame and remorse, who practices generosity and is devoid of anger and envy,
and who, upon seeing śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, honors those who uphold the precepts and are widely learned.
First, one should go out to welcome and inquire after their well-being; provide whatever they require as appropriate;
encourage others to make offerings; and praise both the donor and the recipient.
Such a person, from this life to the next world, [will attain great merit].
"Born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, one enters from light into light.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and delighted in it; he paid homage and departed.
1147 (1147). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit came to the Buddha’s dwelling every day with his body covered in dust; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha said, “Great King!”
"From where have you come?
King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
According to the dharma of those consecrated kings, who possess sovereign power among men and employ diligent skillful means,
this king has traveled across the great earth, governing royal affairs and surveying all regions, until he has arrived here.
The Buddha said to the Great King:
"I now ask you, Great King; answer me as you see fit.
Suppose there were a person coming from the east, who was trustworthy and had a valid reason, and who, being never false, addressed the King, saying:"

"I have come from the east and saw a mountain of stone that was exceedingly vast and wide, neither pierced nor broken, and without any flaws or damage. It came rolling along, grinding the earth, and crushing all living beings, grasses, and trees into fragments."
"From the south, west, and north as well, there come people who have faith and a karmic connection; they too are not speaking falsely, and they say to the King:
'We see a stone mountain, vast, wide, high, and great, neither severed nor broken, and without any flaws, which comes grinding along the earth, crushing all sentient beings, grasses, and trees.'"
"Great King!
What do you think?
Faced with such a terrifying spectacle, with perilous slaughter and the exhaustion of the life-span of sentient beings, where the human realm is so difficult to attain—what plan should be made?"
The King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If this is so, I have no other recourse; I shall only cultivate goodness, applying myself with single-minded diligence to the Buddha’s Dharma and Vinaya."
The Buddha said to the Great King:
"For what reason do you say:

'Dangers, evils, and terrors arise suddenly in the world; the fortunes of sentient beings are exhausted; a human body is difficult to obtain; one must therefore practice the Dharma, practice righteousness, and practice merit, applying oneself with diligent skillful means to the teachings of the Buddha'?"
Why does it not say:
"The consecrated king is the head of all people; he is capable of exercising sovereign power"?
Does the king, over the great earth, have to personally manage the affairs of the multitude?
The King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Is this spoken during a period of leisure?"

"An anointed king, as the foremost among the multitude, exercises great authority over the earth; he fights words with words, wealth with wealth, elephants with elephants, chariots with chariots, and infantry with infantry."
"At that time, there will be no autonomy, whether in victory or defeat. Therefore, I say:

"When perilous and terrifying calamities suddenly arise, when the life-force of sentient beings is exhausted, and a human body is difficult to obtain, there is no other recourse; one must practice righteousness, practice the Dharma, and practice merit, single-mindedly taking refuge in the teachings of the Buddha."
The Buddha told the Great King: "So it is! So it is!"
One is constantly oppressed—by what are called evil kalpas, old age, sickness, and suffering—which oppress sentient beings.
What plan should one make?

One should rightly cultivate the meaning, cultivate the Dharma, cultivate merit, cultivate goodness, and cultivate loving-kindness, applying oneself with diligent skillful means within the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"As if there were a great mountain of rock, High, vast, and without flaw or breach,
Coming from all four directions, Grinding and crushing this great earth."
Neither armies nor spells, nor physical strength, can provide defense against the evil kalpas of old age,
sickness, and death, which constantly grind and crush sentient beings.
Even those of the four great noble lineages, as well as the caṇḍālas and hunters—
Whether layperson or monastic, whether one who upholds the precepts or one who violates them—
all are crushed by this [suffering], and none can provide rescue or protection.
Therefore, a wise person observes their own true benefit.
Establish pure faith, believing in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha;
with body, speech, and mind purified, follow in accordance with the True Dharma.
In this present life, your renown shall spread, and at the end, you will be reborn in the heavens.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and delighted in it;
he paid homage and departed. 1148 (1148). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that moment, seven Nirgranthas, seven Śākyas, and seven Ekṣvākas—each with a coarse and large physique—were wandering about, walking and standing outside the gate of the Jetavana.

At that time, King Prasenajit saw them from afar wandering outside the gate; he immediately rose from his seat, went before them, joined his palms in greeting, and three times addressed them by name, saying:
"I am King Prasenajit, the King of Kosala."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Prasenajit:
"For what reason do you now show such reverence to these individuals, reciting their names three times and greeting them with palms joined?"
The King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I had this thought:
'If there are any Arhats in the world, these must be they.'"
The Buddha told King Prasenajit:
"Cease for now!
You likewise do not know whether he is an arhat or not an arhat, because you have not attained the knowledge of others' minds."
Furthermore, you should personally attend to them and observe their conduct regarding the precepts; after a long time it will become known, so do not reach a hasty conclusion!
Examine with thorough discernment; do not merely be superficial!
You should employ wisdom, rather than ignorance.
Having undergone various hardships and difficulties, one becomes capable of self-discrimination;
through mutual engagement and critical examination, the true and the false are distinguished.
One gains insight by observing what is taught and understands it over time; this cannot be recognized instantaneously, but must be attained through reflection and the observation of wisdom.
The king said to the Buddha,
“How marvelous!
World-Honored One!”
He spoke these words well, saying:
"Having been accustomed to one another for a long time, I observed their precepts and conduct, even to the point of seeing their insights and understanding.

I have family members who likewise left the household life, assuming such outward appearances and wandering through other lands; yet they have now returned, cast off their robes, and resumed the five desires."

"Therefore, you should know that the World-Honored One has spoken well; one should dwell together with him, observe his conduct regarding the precepts, and even through his speech, know that he possesses wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"One does not know a person’s goodness or evil By observing their physical appearance."
One should not meet briefly and yet share the same mind and will;
though manifesting the secrets of body and speech, their worldly mind remains unrestrained.
They are like brass or copper coated with the color of pure gold.
"Internally harboring base and defiled thoughts, yet externally manifesting the majestic deportment of a sage, they travel through various lands to deceive and mislead the people of the world.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and approved with gladness; he paid homage and departed.
1149 (1149). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit was at the head of an assembly of seven kings and various ministers who gathered together and held this discussion:
"Among the five desires, which is the foremost?"
One person said,
"Form is the foremost.
Others likewise proclaimed that sound, fragrance, flavor, or touch is the foremost.
Among them, some said:
"Each of us has declared our own view to be the foremost, yet no definitive judgment has been reached. We should go to the World-Honored One and inquire about this matter."
“As the World-Honored One has spoken, we shall all remember and uphold it.

At that time, King Prasenajit, leading seven other kings, along with their ministers and retinues, came to where the Buddha was. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
We seven kings, together with our various ministers, deliberated in this manner:
"Among the merits of the five desires, which is the most excellent?

Among them, some said that form was supreme, some said sound was supreme, some said fragrance was supreme, some said taste was supreme, and some said touch was supreme; yet in the end, no certainty was reached.
They came to question the World-Honored One, asking, "In the end, which is superior?
The Buddha told the kings:
"As you each wish, I have further explanations for all of you; by these causes and conditions, I speak of the merits of the five desires."

However, there are some who find pleasure in form and, being attached to only one form, have their aspirations fulfilled; even if there were superior forms beyond that which they possess, because these are not what they love, they do not touch or look upon them, declaring that what they themselves love is the most supreme and that nothing surpasses it.
Just as it is with those who love forms, so it is with sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.

Regarding that which they love, they immediately declare it to be supreme; they take delight in it and become attached to it. Even if there were something superior to it, because it is not what they desire, they do not touch it nor look upon it, saying only: "That which I love is the most excellent and most wonderful; it is peerless and unsurpassed."
At that time, there was a lay follower (upāsaka) in the assembly named Candana. He rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
"Well spoken!
Well said, Blessed One!
Well said, Sugata!
The Buddha told the upāsaka:
"Well said, Cāndana!"
"Speak quickly,
Canda! At that time, the upāsaka Canda immediately spoke in verse:
"The King of the Aṅga clan, adorned with robes, pearls, and jeweled armor,
gathered amidst the celebratory assembly of Magadha, when the Tathāgata appeared in that land.
His fame spread everywhere, like the sovereign king of the Snowy Mountains."
Like a lotus flower in pure water, Pure and free from all defilement, It blooms upon the touch of the sun’s rays; Its fragrant scent perfumes the land.
The kingdom of Aṅga is made radiant, Just like the sun in the sky.
"Behold the power of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, like a torch burning in the night;
it serves as eyes and a great illumination for those who come to resolve their doubts.
At that time, the various kings exclaimed:
“Excellent speech!
Upāsaka Candana!
At that time, the seven kings removed their upper garments of the seven precious jewels and offered them to the upāsaka.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, those seven kings rejoiced and followed with approval; they rose from their seats and departed.
Then, the lay follower Candana, knowing that the kings had left, rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
“Now these seven kings have presented me with seven upper garments. I pray only that the World-Honored One will accept these seven garments out of compassion!”
At that time, out of compassion, the World-Honored One accepted his seven robes; the lay follower Candana rejoiced and followed along with joy, paid homage, and departed.
1150. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, King Prasenajit, whose body was stout and who was perspiring all over, approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side, breathing heavily.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to King Prasenajit,
"Great King, your body is exceedingly stout and robust.
The Great King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
My body is afflicted by being excessively fat; because this body is so extremely obese, I am filled with shame and weary of its suffering.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"One should maintain self-restraint and mindfulness; at every meal, know the proper measure.
Thus, all sensations will be slight, food will be easily digested, and one’s life-span preserved.
At that time, there was a young man named Uttara sitting among the assembly.
At that time, King Prasenajit said to Uttara,
"Could you receive from the World-Honored One the verse just spoken and recite it for me every time mealtime arrives?"
"If you can do so, I shall grant you one hundred thousand gold coins and provide you with food as well.
Uttara replied to the king,
"I shall recite it in accordance with your instructions."
At that time, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and approved with gladness; he paid homage and departed.

Then, once the king had left, Uttara went before the World-Honored One, received the verses he had been taught, and recited them for the king while he was eating his meal. He addressed the Great King, saying:
"As it is known and seen by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, so did he speak these verses:"
"One should maintain self-restraint and mindfulness, knowing moderation in every meal;
thus all sensations will be slight, and one shall digest in peace while preserving longevity."

Thus, after some time had passed, King Prasenajit’s body became slender and his appearance upright and handsome. Standing upon a multi-storied pavilion and facing the place where the Buddha was staying, he joined his palms in reverence, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and three times spoke these words:

“Homage and prostrations to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha! Homage and prostrations to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha! Grant me benefit in this present life, benefit in future lives, and benefit in both this present and future lives, because of my moderation in the consumption of food.”
1151 (1151). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, a young asura came to where the Buddha was and, in the presence of the Buddha, spoke harsh, evil, and unwholesome words, reviling and rebuking him with anger.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Non-anger conquers hatred; The good subdues the unwholesome;
Generosity subdues stinginess and greed; Truthful speech destroys falsehood."
Neither reviling nor inflicting cruelty, one should always abide in the mind of the noble ones;
though evil people dwell in hatred, one remains unmoved like a mountain rock.
Able to maintain composure when anger arises, one surpasses and controls a chariot drawn by wild horses.
"I speak of the skilled charioteer; it is not that one who merely holds the reins.
Then, the young asura addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Gautama! [Who is the skilled charioteer?]"
"I now repent my transgression; like one who is foolish and deluded, I failed to discern what was unwholesome, and I reviled and insulted you, Gautama, in your very presence.
Having thus repented, at that time the asura, hearing what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and followed with approval, paid homage, and departed.
1152. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a young Brahmin named Bhṛgu came to where the Buddha was and, in the presence of the World-Honored One, spoke harsh, evil, and unwholesome words, reviling and rebuking him with anger.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the young Bhṛgu:
"Is it the case that at a certain time, on an auspicious day, you gather all your kinsmen and relatives?"
"Thus it is, Gautama," Bimbisāra replied to the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Bimbisāra:
“If the members of your family do not accept the food, what will you do?
Piṅgiya said to the Buddha,
“If they do not accept the food, it shall remain my own.”
The Buddha told Bimbisāra:

"You were just like this; when you spoke harsh, evil, and unwholesome words in the presence of the Tathāgata, insulting and rebuking me, I ultimately did not accept them. To whom, then, should such insults belong?"
Bhṛgu addressed the Buddha:
"It is so, Gautama!
Although he does not accept it, if one offers it as a gift, that constitutes giving."
The Buddha told Bimbisāra:
“In this way, it cannot be called a mutual gift; how then can it be considered an exchange?
Bimbisāra addressed the Buddha:
“What is meant by ‘giving gifts to one another’ and ‘mutual bestowal’?
And what is meant by ‘not receiving gifts from one another’ and ‘not being mutual bestowals’?
The Buddha told Bimbisāra:

"If one were to respond to abuse with abuse, anger with anger, a blow with a blow, and strife with strife, this would be called 'giving gifts to one another' and 'bestowing upon one another. Furthermore, Bhṛgu!"
If one does not respond to abuse with abuse, anger with anger, striking with striking, or fighting with fighting—if it is thus, it is not a mutual gift, nor is it called a mutual bestowal.
Bhārgava said to the Buddha: “Gautama!
I have heard what was spoken in the past by the elder brahmins of old, those long-established masters who were devoted to the practice of the path:”
"If the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, when reviled, insulted, and rebuked with anger in his presence,
remains without anger or resentment— does the Gautama now possess anger?"
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"When there is no anger, how can there be anger? Subdued by right livelihood, with right wisdom and a liberated mind, the wise person has no anger."
To repay anger with anger is the mark of an evil person;
not to repay anger with anger is to lie low before the enemy when it is difficult to lie low.
Non-anger conquers anger—these three verses are as previously explained.
At that time, the young man Pingi addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I repent! Gautama!”
"Like a fool and like one deluded, you failed to distinguish what is unwholesome, yet you uttered harsh, evil, and unwholesome words in the presence of the śramaṇa Gautama, reviling and rebuking him.
Having heard what the Buddha said, they rejoiced and approved with gladness, paid their respects, and departed.
1153. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Hall of Migāramātā.
At that time, in the late afternoon, the Blessed One arose from meditation and went to the eastern shade of the lecture hall, where he walked back and forth on the open ground.

Then, the brahmin Pañcaka-Bāvarī, who was skilled in harsh speech, approached the place where the Buddha was and, in the presence of the Blessed One, spoke coarse, evil, and unwholesome words, reviling and rebuking him.
The Blessed One was walking in meditation, and he followed behind the Blessed One.
When the Blessed One had finished his walk and stood in one place, that brahmin said:
"Has Gautama been overcome?"
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The victor increases enmity; The defeated lies in unease.
Abandoning both victory and defeat— This is how one attains peaceful sleep."
The brahmin said: "Gautama!

I now repent my transgression. Like one who is foolish and deluded, lacking discernment and goodness, why did I utter such coarse, evil, and unwholesome words before Gautama, reviling and rebuking you?"
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the brahmin rejoiced and approved, then departed by way of the road. 1154 (1154). Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Eastern Park, in the Mṛgāramātṛpūrvārāma Lecture Hall. In the early morning, the World-Honored One dressed, took his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms.

At that time, the brahmin Kalmāṣapāda saw the World-Honored One from afar; uttering coarse, evil, and unwholesome words, he reviled and rebuked him with anger, seizing a clod of earth and throwing it at the Buddha.
At that time, there was a headwind which blew back the dust, so that it fell upon his own body.
Then the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"If a person is free from anger and resentment, and others should treat them with abuse and insult,"
"Pure and free from the stains of fetters, that evil returns to oneself,
just as when one throws dust against the wind, it only soils oneself. Then,
that brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I repent! Gautama!
I was foolish and deluded, unskilled and undiscerning; why did I utter such harsh, evil, and unwholesome words before you, Gautama, reviling and reproaching you with anger?"
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the brahmin rejoiced and approved, then departed by way of the road. (1155) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of Kosala and arrived at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a brahmin named Viyatta who heard that the śramaṇa Gautama had been traveling through the human realms of the kingdom of Kosala and had arrived at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Having heard this, he thought to himself:
"I shall go to where the śramaṇa Gautama is, and having heard the Dharma he preaches, I shall refute its meaning.
Having formed this thought, he went to the monastery and approached the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by an immeasurable retinue as he preached the Dharma.
Seeing from afar the Brahmin Viśārada approaching, the World-Honored One immediately remained silent.
The Brahmin Viyatta addressed the Buddha, saying,
“Gautama, I wish to hear the Dharma you teach!
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“The Brahmin who opposes the meaning has not yet understood the profound significance;
harboring within a heart of envy and malice, he seeks to create obstacles for the Dharma.
To subdue his rebellious mind and all his unfaithful inclinations—”
"When all obstacles and defilements are stilled, one then understands the profound and subtle teaching.
At that time, the Brahmin Viśvāmitra thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama already knows my mind."
Having heard what the Buddha taught, they rejoiced and approved with gladness;
rising from their seats, they departed. 1156 (1156) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
In the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms.
At that time, the Brahmin Ahimsaka approached the Blessed One and said to him:
“Blessed One!
"My name is 'Non-Harming' (Ahimsa); is this a designation that accords with reality?
The Buddha told the brahmin:

"If it is so designated according to reality, then if one does not harm through body, does not harm through speech, and does not harm through mind, then it is indeed a designation that accords with reality."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If one does not kill with the mind, And likewise with speech and thought,
This constitutes being free from harm, And not terrifying sentient beings."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the brahmin Ahimsaka, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and delighted in it, and then departed by way of the road.
(1157) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.

In the early morning, the World-Honored One dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food. Proceeding from house to house, he came to the residence of the brahmin Agnidatta.
Seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, the brahmin Agnidatta immediately prepared various exquisite foods and drinks, filling the Buddha’s bowl and offering them to him.
In this manner, on the second and third days, he went to that house again for alms.
When Agnidatta the brahmin saw the Buddha approaching from afar, he thought to himself:
"Why does this shaven-headed śramaṇa come so frequently? Is it because he craves fine food?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of Agnidatta and the brahmin, spoke these verses:
"The king and the gods rain down day after day; the farmers plow their fields by day and night.
They repeatedly sow seeds, and from those fields, grain is harvested again and again."
As a woman repeatedly conceives, as a milch cow repeatedly bears a calf,
so when there are frequent seekers, one is able to give gifts repeatedly.
Because of giving gifts repeatedly, one always attains great renown.
Again and again one discards corpses; again and again one weeps in sorrowful longing.
Again and again one is born and dies; again and again one suffers grief and pain.
Again and again one is consumed by fire; again and again one is devoured by various worms.
If one attains the path of the noble ones, one will not repeatedly undergo various states of existence,
nor will one repeatedly experience birth and death, nor repeatedly encounter sorrow, lamentation, and suffering.
One will not be repeatedly scorched by the fires [of affliction], nor repeatedly devoured by the worms [of craving].

At that time, when the brahmin Agnidatta heard the Buddha recite these verses, his faith was restored. He again filled his alms-bowl with various kinds of food and drink and offered them to him. The World-Honored One did not accept them, for they were being given because of the verses he had spoken. Thereupon, he spoke another verse:
"Because one has preached the Dharma through verses, One should not accept food and drink;
One should observe one's own Dharma, For one who preaches the Dharma does not receive food."
O Brahmin, you should know that this is how one lives by a pure livelihood;
one should offer other forms of sustenance to the Great Seer, who is utterly pure,
whose outflows are all exhausted, and whose defiled dharmas have been entirely severed.
"One who desires merit should make offerings of food and drink to this excellent field of merit;
for such a person, my field is indeed excellent.
Then the Brahmin Agnidatta said to the Buddha:
"Now, where should this food be placed?
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"I do not see among the devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, celestial beings, or worldly people anyone who can consume this gift of faith and thereby bring peace and happiness to their body."
"Take this food and discard it in water free of insects, or upon a patch of grass where little has grown.
Then the brahmin immediately took that food and placed it in water free of insects; instantly, smoke rose from the water with a hissing sound.
It was just as when a glowing iron ball, heated until it is the color of fire, is thrown into water: smoke rises from the water with a hissing sound, and it was exactly like that.
When the brahmin placed this food and drink into the water, smoke immediately issued forth and the water bubbled with a hissing sound. At that time, the Fire addressed the brahmin, saying:
"How extraordinary!
"Gautama!
You possess great virtue and great power, able to cause this food to perform such a miraculous transformation.

At that time, because of this miraculous transformation of the meal, the brahmin Agnidatta conceived a heart of faith and reverence; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
May I now go forth in the True Dharma, receive full ordination, and practice the holy life?
The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa:
"You may now go forth in the True Dharma and receive full ordination.
Having gone forth, he reflected:
"For this reason, sons of noble family shave off their hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and with right faith leave the home life to study the Path..."
...until he attained arhatship, with his mind well-liberated.
1158 (1158) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was a Brāhmaṇa woman named Vāsiṣṭhī who had faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; she took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of Bhikṣus.
Having already abandoned doubt regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, they have also abandoned uncertainty regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
having seen the truths and attained the fruit, they have acquired uninterrupted wisdom.
Her husband was a Brahmin of the Bharadvāja lineage.

Whenever he performed any task on her behalf, even if there were minor gains or losses, he would immediately cry out, "Namo Buddhāya," and facing the direction where the Tathāgata dwelt, he would join his palms toward that quarter and three times utter these words:

"Namo Tathāgatāya, Arhate, Samyaksaṃbuddhāya! Your body is of pure golden color, with a halo extending one fathom; your square body is perfectly full like a nyagrodha tree. You who skillfully preach the sublime Dharma, the Honored Muni, the foremost among sages—you are my Great Teacher!"
At that time, when the husband, the brahmin, heard this, he was filled with anger and displeasure, and said to his wife:
"Are you possessed by a ghost? Such a thing is impossible!
How can you abandon these great and virtuous brahmins, masters of the three Vedas, and instead praise those shaven-headed śramaṇas?"
"The dark side is not praised by the world.
I shall now go with you to debate with your great teacher; we shall surely know who is superior.
The wife said to her husband:

"I do not see any devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gods, or worldlings who are able to engage in debate with the Blessed One—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—whose body is golden in color, whose halo extends one fathom, whose form is as perfectly full as a nyagrodha tree, whose speech is subtle and exquisite, the foremost of sages, my great teacher."
"However, let the brahmin go for now; he shall know it for himself!
At that time, the brahmin immediately went to the Buddha, exchanged greetings and expressions of courtesy with him face-to-face, and then withdrew to sit at one side.
And he spoke in verse:
"By killing what does one sleep in peace?
By killing what does the mind attain freedom from sorrow?"
"By killing what, O Gautama, do you praise?
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the brahmin's mind, spoke in verse:
"By killing anger and hatred, one attains peaceful sleep."
One who slays anger finds that the mind is free from sorrow.
Anger is the root of poison; it can destroy even the sweetest seeds.
One who is able to overcome it is praised by the noble and the wise.
"If one were able to harm him, would his mind not be free from sorrow?

At that time, the brahmin Brahmadatta, having heard what the Buddha had said—which was instructive, edifying, illuminating, and inspiring—was taught the Dharma in its proper sequence: namely, discourse on giving, discourse on morality, and discourse on the way to rebirth in heaven; discourse on how attachment to sensual pleasures is a calamity and an affliction, and the subsequent detailed exposition of purity, the means of escape, renunciation, and the purification of merit and benefit.
It was like a pure white cloth, which is easily dyed.
In this way, the brahmin Brahmadatta, while still upon his seat, attained unimpeded realization of the Four Noble Truths—namely, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

This brahmin has seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, known the Dharma, and entered the Dharma; he has crossed beyond all doubt and uncertainty, not relying on others for his deliverance, and has attained fearlessness regarding the True Dharma and Discipline.
He immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
"I have crossed over, World-Honored One!
I have crossed over, Sugata!"
"I have now taken refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus; for as long as my life lasts, may you bear witness that I am an upāsaka!
Then, having heard what the Buddha had said, the brahmin Brahmadatta rejoiced and delighted in it; he paid homage and departed, returning to his own home.
His wife, an upāsikā, saw her husband coming from afar; having seen him, she said to him:

"Have you engaged in debate with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—one whose body is of pure golden hue, whose halo extends one fathom, whose body is as perfectly full as a nyagrodha tree, the supreme among those who speak wondrously, the foremost of sages, the Great Muni, my own Teacher?"
Her husband replied:

"I have never seen anyone among the devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gods, or worldly men who is able to engage in debate with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—whose body is of true golden color, whose halo extends one fathom, whose body is as perfectly full as a nyagrodha tree, the supreme among those of wondrous speech, the foremost of all sages, the Honored One of the Munis, your Great Teacher."
"Now, prepare a fine Dharma robe for me; I shall take it to the World-Honored One to leave the household life and study the Path.
At that time, the wife provided her with all kinds of fresh, clean white cotton cloth to have made into a Dharma robe.
At that time, the brahmin took the robe and went to where the World-Honored One was; he prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and said:
"World-Honored One!..."
"May I now go forth in the Dharma of the World-Honored One to study the Path and practice the holy life?
The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa:
"You may now go forth in this Dharma and Vinaya to study the Path and practice all the holy lives."
Having thus gone forth, he reflected in solitary stillness:
"For what reason do sons of good family shave off their hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and leave the household life to study the Path..."
...until he attained arhatship, with his mind well-liberated.
1159 (1159). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Māra-brāhmaṇa approached the place where the Buddha was; having exchanged greetings and expressions of courtesy with the World-Honored One, he withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying: “Gautama!
Within my home, I constantly practice giving: if one person comes, I give to that one;
if two, three, or even up to a hundred thousand come, I give to them all.
"By giving such a gift as this, shall I obtain great merit?
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"By giving such a gift as this, you will indeed obtain great merit."

Why is this? Because while at home they constantly practice giving—whenever one person comes to beg, they give to that one; when two, three, or even hundreds of thousands come, they give to them all—and thus they obtain great merit.
Then the Brahmin Māra spoke these verses:
"Whatever one does while living at home, such as giving and holding great assemblies—
by means of such acts of charity, one seeks to attain great merit."
Now I ask the Muni that which I ought to know:
that which is seen by the Brahmās—explain it to me in detail.
What is liberation? What is the supreme and wondrous happy destination?
"What kind of skillful means must be practiced to be born in the Brahma world?
How does one give according to one's inclination to be born in the luminous and supreme Brahma heaven?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"The donor prepares a great assembly and bestows gifts according to what others delight in;
with joyful and pure faith, they take hold of wholesome merit.
By means of what they have established, they seek liberation from all faults and evils."
Far removed from desire, their minds are well-liberated.
By cultivating a heart of loving-kindness, their merit is immeasurable;
how much more so when they further apply themselves with sincerity and extensively establish great assemblies.
If, during that interval, one attains various wholesome states of mind directed toward right liberation or other purely wholesome realms,
through such superior causes and conditions, one will be born in the Brahma world.
"Because such generosity is given with an impartial mind, one will be reborn in the Brahma world and enjoy an extended lifespan.
At that time, the Brahmin Māgandiya, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and expressed his approval; he rose from his seat and departed.
1160. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a certain brahmin, carrying a golden parasol and wearing a *śāṭaka* robe, approached the Buddha with his retinue. After exchanging greetings and polite inquiries with the World-Honored One, he withdrew to sit at one side.
And he spoke in verse:
"There is no one who is not a brāhmaṇa, for whose conduct is pure.
A kṣatriya practicing austerities is likewise at variance with tranquility."
"The three Vedas and the Brahmins—these alone are pure;
those who are thus pure do not exist among other beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse, answering:
"One who does not know the path of purity, nor the unsurpassed purities,
yet seeks tranquility elsewhere— such a person will never reach the state of purity.
The brahmin addressed the Buddha:
“Does Gautama teach the path of purification and the unsurpassed purification?
What is the path of purification?
And what is the unsurpassed purification?”
The Buddha told the brahmin:
“Right view is the path to purification; by cultivating and frequently practicing right view, one abandons greed, abandons hatred, and abandons delusion.”
If a brahmin has eternally severed greed, eternally severed hatred and delusion, and eternally severed all afflictions, this is called unsurpassed purity.
Right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—this is called the path of purification.
Having cultivated and frequently practiced right concentration, one abandons greed, abandons hatred, and abandons delusion.
If a brahmin has eternally severed greed, eternally severed hatred and delusion, and eternally severed all afflictions, this is called unsurpassed purity.
The brāhmaṇa said to the Buddha:
“Does Gautama teach the path of purity, the unsurpassed purity? Gautama!”
"The affairs of the world are many; for now, I shall take my leave and return.
The Buddha told the brahmin, "You should know that this is the time."

Holding a flower parasol and wearing a *śāṭaka* robe, he led the procession of Brahmins. Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, they rejoiced and delighted in it, rose from their seats, and departed.
1161 (1161) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a certain brahmin approached the place where the Buddha was staying. After exchanging greetings and polite inquiries with the World-Honored One, he withdrew to sit at one side and spoke in verse:
"What constitutes śīla?"
What is right deportment?
What constitutes merit?
And what is called karma?
"What dharmas must be accomplished to become an Arhat Brahmin?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"The wisdom of recollecting past lives, and seeing rebirth in the heavens and the evil realms..."
Having attained the exhaustion of all rebirths, the Sage is clear and decisive;
knowing the mind is well-liberated, he is freed from all craving.
Possessing the three knowledges, he is a Brahmin of the three knowledges.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the other brahmin, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and approved with gladness;
he rose from his seat and departed. 1162 (1162). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
In the early morning, the Blessed One dressed himself, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms, with the Venerable Ānanda following behind him.

At that time, there were an old man and an old woman, a married couple, advanced in years and with matured faculties; their backs were bent like hooks as they both crouched together by a fire at a place where refuse was being burned at the head of a street.
The World-Honored One saw that elderly couple, aged and foolish, their backs bent like hooks, both crouching toward the fire like two old cranes, gazing at each other with lustful desire.
Having seen them, he said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Do you see that couple, aged and foolish, with backs bent like hooks, both crouching toward the fire like old cranes, gazing at each other with lustful intent?"
Ānanda replied to the Buddha,
“So it is, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"This elderly couple, when they were young and in the prime of their vigor, could have become the foremost wealthy householder in the city of Śrāvastī had they diligently sought wealth;

yet, if instead they had shaved off their hair and beards, donned the saṃghāṭī robes, and with right faith gone forth from home into homelessness to study the Path, practicing with diligence, they could have attained the supreme fruit of arhatship."
In the second stage of life, while in the prime of youth, if one diligently seeks wealth, one may become the second wealthiest person in the city of Śrāvastī;

yet, if instead one shaves off hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and with right faith leaves the household life to go forth and study the Path, one may likewise realize the fruit of an Anāgāmin.
If, during the middle third of your life, you diligently seek wealth, you may become the third wealthiest person in the city of Śrāvastī;
if, however, you shave off your hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and with right faith leave the home life to study the Path, you may also attain the realization of the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin.

Today he is advanced in years and his faculties are matured; he possesses no wealth, no skillful means, and lacks the capacity—indeed, he no longer has the capacity—to acquire wealth, nor can he attain any state superior to that of ordinary men.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Because they did not practice the holy life, They did not obtain youth or wealth;
Reflecting on matters of antiquity, They sleep upon the ground like a bent bow."
"Having failed to cultivate the holy life, one does not obtain wealth in youth;
like an old crane, one dies guarding an empty pond.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1163 (1163). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park... as described above.
As for the distinction, it is expressed by a different verse:
"By that which destroys old age and death— The body and its experiences having ceased—
Only the merit of giving remains, Serving as one's own provision."
Relying on virtuous protection and the merit of practicing meditation, one should give according to one's ability—wealth and food and drink.
One should remain awake within the flock; do not live in vain for oneself.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, that brahmin, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and approved with gladness;
he paid homage and departed. *Saṃyukta Āgama*, Scroll 42. *Saṃyukta Āgama*, Scroll 43.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
43.1164 (1164). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus gathered in the lecture hall and engaged in this discussion:
"Venerable sirs!
As the Blessed One has spoken regarding what was asked by the Licchavi Vatsagotra:..."
“‘One who knows the two extremes, / And is forever unattached to that which lies between,
/ Is called a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa); / Disregarding the five desires,
/ Free from the shackles of affliction, / He has transcended the seamstress of sorrow.’”
"Venerable ones!
What is the meaning of this?
What constitutes the 'extreme'?"
What are the two extremes?
What is the middle way?
And what is the seam?
What is volition?
It is knowing with wisdom and understanding with discernment;
that which is known by wisdom and understood by discernment brings an end to suffering and liberation from suffering.
One replied: "The six internal sense bases are one extreme; the six external sense bases are the second extreme; feeling is the middle, and craving is the seam."

One who is practiced in feeling attains its various causes; the body gradually transforms, grows, and is born. Regarding this very phenomenon, one knows it with wisdom and understands it with clarity; through what is known by wisdom and what is understood by clarity, one makes an end to suffering and is liberated from suffering.
Furthermore, another says:
"The past world is one extreme; the future world is the second extreme; the present world is called the middle; and craving is the stitching."
"By associating with and cultivating this craving, one gradually experiences contact through various causes, leading to growth and birth, even unto the point of liberation from suffering.
Furthermore, another says: "Pleasurable feeling is one extreme;

painful feeling is the second extreme; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is the middle. Craving is the seamstress; by associating with and cultivating this craving, one gradually experiences contact through various acquisitions, leading to growth and birth, even unto the point of creating suffering."
Again, it is said: "Existence (*bhava*) is one extreme;
arising (*samudaya*) is the second extreme; feeling (*vedanā*) is the middle; and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) serves as the seam. Thus it is explained at length, up until: "one is liberated from suffering."
Again, it is said: "The body is one extreme;
the accumulation of the body is the second extreme; craving is the seam... Thus it is explained in detail, up to: "...liberation from suffering."
Again, some said: "All that we have said differs;
namely, the various divergent explanations we have offered just now—we do not hope for them to be understood."
"How is it that the Blessed One has delivered an incomplete teaching in the *Pārāyanavagga*, the *Sutta on the Questions of the Licchavi Vāseṭṭha*?
We should go and inquire of the Blessed One in full, so that we may receive and uphold it exactly as the Blessed One has spoken."
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus approached the World-Honored One, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
He approached the assembly of bhikṣus gathered in the lecture hall and spoke these words:
"Regarding the *Pārāyaṇa-sutta* asked by the Licchavi Vatsagotra as taught by the World-Honored One—concerning the two extremes, up to the liberation from suffering."
Some people say: "The six internal sense bases are one extreme;

the six external sense bases are the second extreme; feeling is the middle; and craving is the seam. As previously explained at length, none of these [views] are definitive. Therefore, we have come today to question the World-Honored One and inquire fully about this meaning: among all that we have said, who has grasped the true meaning?
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"What you have said is all well-spoken. I shall now speak to you of a sūtra with a remainder.

For the sake of the Malla Puṣkarasādi, I spoke a sūtra with a remainder, which is: 'Contact is one extreme; the arising of contact is the second extreme; feeling is the middle; and craving is the seam.'"

Having become habituated to and drawn near to craving, whatever is obtained, the body’s contact with objects increases and arises; regarding these phenomena, one knows them with wisdom and understands them thoroughly;
through what is known by wisdom and understood thoroughly, one makes an end of suffering and is liberated from suffering.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1165 (1165). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Venerable Piṇḍola was staying at the Gośīrṣa Garden in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, there was a king of the Vatsa kingdom named Udayana, who went to the place where the Venerable Piṇḍola was and exchanged greetings with him;
having finished his greetings, he withdrew to sit at one side.
King Udayana Vatsa addressed the Venerable Piṇḍola, saying:
"I wish to ask a question; would you have the leisure to grant me an answer?"
The Venerable Piṇḍola replied:
"Great King! Let the Great King ask first; when I know the answer, I shall respond."
King Prasenajit Udāyana asked the Venerable Piṇḍola:

"By what cause and by what condition do newly ordained young bhikṣus, who have not long since gone forth into this Dharma and Vinaya, dwell in extreme peace and happiness, with their faculties joyful, their countenances pure, their complexions bright and clear, delighting in stillness and having little agitation, living at ease like wild beasts, and being capable of maintaining the holy life purely and exclusively until the end of their lives?"
The Venerable Piṇḍola replied:
"As the Buddha has said, that which is known and seen by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, he has taught to the bhikṣus: 'O you bhikṣus!'"
If one sees an elder, one should regard them as a mother;
if one sees those of middle age, one should regard them as sisters;
