if one sees the young, one should regard them as daughters.

By this cause and condition, young bhikṣus who have not long since gone forth in this Dharma and Vinaya will dwell in peace and happiness; their faculties will be serene and joyful, their countenances pure, and their complexions bright and clear. Delighting in stillness and having few distractions, they will live depending on others, with minds like wild beasts, capable of maintaining the holy life (brahmacarya) purely and exclusively until the end of their lives.
King Udayana Vatsa said to the Venerable Piṇḍola:
“In this world today, those with greedy and seeking minds regard an elderly person as their mother when they see them;
they regard one of middle age as their sister.”
Upon seeing a young person, one forms the perception of a woman.
At that time, the mind likewise arises accordingly, burning with lust, burning with hatred, and burning with delusion; must there not be some further superior cause and condition for this?
The Venerable Piṇḍola addressed King Udayana of the Vacchas:
"There is another causal basis, as spoken by the Blessed One, which the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—knowing and seeing it—has taught to the bhikṣus:
'This body, from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, is a framework of bones smeared with flesh and covered with thin skin; within it are filled with various kinds of impurities.'"

He observed them thoroughly: hair, body hair, nails, teeth, dirt and grime, saliva, skin, flesh, white bones, tendons, veins, heart, liver, lungs, spleen, kidneys, intestines, stomach, the raw receptacle, the cooked receptacle, the bladder, tears, sweat, mucus, froth, fat, grease, marrow, phlegm, rheum, pus, blood, brain matter, lymph, feces, and urine.
"Great King!

For this cause and by this condition, a young bhikkhu who has not long since gone forth into homelessness in this Dhamma and Vinaya dwells in peace and happiness, even unto a state that is entirely pure and perfect."
King Udayana of Vatsa said to the Venerable Piṇḍola:
"The human mind is fickle and swift; if one contemplates impurity, the perception of purity nevertheless arises."

Is there perhaps another cause and condition by which a young bhikṣu, having not long since gone forth into this Dharma and Vinaya, may dwell in peace and happiness, even unto a state that is purely and entirely fulfilled and pure?
The Venerable Piṇḍola said:
"Great King!
There is a cause and there is a condition, as the Blessed One has declared; that which is known and seen by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, he announced to the bhikṣus:"
"You all should guard the doors of the sense faculties and skillfully restrain the mind.
When the eye sees forms, do not grasp at their general appearance, nor grasp at their secondary details, nor hold onto them with excessive attachment."
If one dwells without restraining the faculty of the eye, then worldly greed, craving, and unwholesome evil states will leak into the mind; therefore, one should maintain the restraint of the eye.
"It is the same for the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and flavors, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena.
This continues until one undertakes the restraint of the mind.
At that time, King Udayana of Vatsa said to the Venerable Piṇḍola:
“Excellent! Well-spoken is the Dharma, even unto the restraint of the sense faculties.
Venerable Piṇḍola!”

I am also like this: at times I do not guard my body, do not maintain restraint over my sense faculties, and do not unify my mindfulness as I enter the palace; my mind then gives rise to an extreme greed that blazes up and is consumed by delusion.
Even when staying alone in a quiet room, my mind is still scorched by the three poisons, let alone within the palace!

Furthermore, there were times when I well protected my body, well restrained my sense faculties, and concentrated my mindfulness as I entered the inner palace; yet lust, hatred, and delusion did not arise to burn my mind. Since even within the inner palace my body was not burned and my mind was not burned, how much less so when I was alone in seclusion!

For this reason, by this cause and by this condition, it enables young bhikṣus who have not long since gone forth in this Dharma and Vinaya to dwell in peace and happiness, even unto the state of being entirely pure and complete.
At that time, King Prasenajit of Vatsa, having heard what the Venerable Piṇḍola had said, rejoiced and approved, rose from his seat, and departed.
1166 (1166). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kauśāmbī in the Ghosira Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Because there are hands, one knows there is grasping and letting go; because there are feet, one knows there is coming and going; because there are joints, one knows there is bending and extending; because there is a belly, one knows there is hunger and thirst."
In this way, bhikṣus!
Because the eye exists, feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether internally experienced as painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

“Monks! If there were no hands, one would not know how to take up or discard; if there were no feet, one would not know how to go or come; if there were no joints, one would not know how to bend or extend; if there were no belly, one would not know hunger or thirst.”
Thus it is, monks!
If there were no eye, then there would be no feeling—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arising with eye-contact as its condition through internal sensation.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1167 (1167) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Gośīrṣa Park in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, there was grass in a river where a tortoise lived.
At that time, a jackal, wandering in search of food while hungry, saw the tortoise from afar and came quickly to seize it."
When the tortoise saw the jackal approaching, he immediately withdrew his six limbs; the jackal waited and watched, baring its head and paws, intending to seize and eat him.
After waiting for a long time, the tortoise never again extended his head nor his feet;
the jackal, exhausted by hunger, departed in a fit of rage.
“O bhikṣus! You are likewise today.

Know that Māra Pāpīyān constantly watches for your opportunity, seeking to bind your eyes to forms, your ears to sounds, your nose to fragrances, your tongue to tastes, your body to tangibles, and your mind to mental objects, desiring to cause you to give rise to defiled attachment toward these six sense-fields.”
Therefore, monks!

You should now constantly maintain the restraint of the eye and abide in the restraint of the faculty of the eye; thus, Māra the Evil One will find no opportunity to follow you or to take advantage of you.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
"Regarding these six sense faculties, whether they emerge or encounter objects, one finds no opportunity for them [to cause harm], just as a wild jackal finds no opportunity against a tortoise.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The tortoise fears the wild jackal, And hides its six limbs within its shell."
“A bhikṣu who skillfully restrains the mind, Secretly conceals all perceptions and thoughts.
Neither relying on nor fearing them, He covers his mind and does not speak of them.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1168. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kosambī in the Ghosita Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"It is like a grain of barley placed at a crossroads, which six strong men strike together with clubs until it is reduced to dust in an instant; then a seventh man strikes it again with a club."
"Monks, what do you think?
If a heap of barley were pounded by six people and pounded again by seven people, would it not become utterly crushed?"
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha,
“So it is, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In this way, the foolish person is beaten by the six bases of contact.
What are these six?
They are the base of eye-contact, which constantly beats him."

The spheres of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental contact are constantly being struck; yet that foolish person, though struck by these six spheres of contact, still conceives thoughts of seeking existence in a future life, like the seventh man who continues to strike until he is crushed.
“Monks! If one says ‘this is mine,’ that is wavering;
if one says ‘this is my self,’ that is wavering.”
If one thinks that in the future there will be [existence], this is wavering;
if one thinks that in the future there will be no [existence], this is wavering.
If one thinks that there will again be form, this is wavering.
If one were to have formlessness, that would be wavering;
if one were to have perception, that would be wavering;
if one were to have non-perception, that would be wavering.
Furthermore, to have neither perception nor non-perception is itself agitation.
Because of agitation there is sickness; because of agitation there is an ulcer; because of agitation there is a thorn; because of agitation there is attachment.

Regarding the statement that "suffering arises from observing movement": one attains an unshakable mind, dwells extensively through repeated cultivation, and maintains mindfulness and clear comprehension.
"As with movement..."
Thus one reflects upon this as false and deceptive:
conditioned activity arises from craving.
To say "I" is craving; to say "mine" is craving.
To say that there will be existence in the future is craving;
to say that there will be no existence in the future is craving.
To say that there will be form in the future is craving.
To dwell in formlessness is craving;
to dwell in perception is craving;
to dwell in non-perception is craving.
The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is itself craving.
Because of craving there is sickness; because of craving there is an abscess; because of craving there is a thorn.
If one skillfully contemplates that craving gives rise to suffering, one should dwell frequently in a mind free from craving, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.
“Monks! In a past age, the asuras raised an army and fought with Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the gods of the Thirty-three:”

"Today the devas and asuras are engaged in a bitter battle; if the devas are victorious and the asuras are defeated, we shall seize the asuras, bind them with the five fetters, and send them back to the celestial palace."
The asura spoke to his host, saying:
"Now the asura army is at war with the devas. If the asuras are victorious and the devas are defeated, you shall seize Śakra by force, bind him with the five fetters, and return to the asura palace."
During that battle, the devas were victorious and the asuras were defeated.
At that time, the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three seized the asura king Vepacitti, bound him with five fetters, and returned to their celestial palace.
"At that time, the Asura King Vemacitrin was bound in fivefold fetters and placed within the Hall of True Dharma, where he was entertained with the various celestial pleasures of the five desires."
The Asura King Vemacitrin thought to himself:
"Only the Asuras are noble, virtuous, and wise; although the devas are also good, I shall now return to the Asura palace."
As he was thinking this, he immediately saw his own body bound by the five fetters, and the five desires of the devas spontaneously vanished.
Vemacitrin, the Asura King, again thought:
"The devas are noble and virtuous, their wisdom clear and penetrating; although the Asuras are also good, for now I shall remain in this celestial palace."
When he had this thought, he immediately saw his own body released from its five bonds, and the five desires of the devas naturally emerged once more.
"Vemacitrin, the Asura King, possessed such subtle bonds as these; the bonds of Māra Pāpīyan are even subtler still."
Thus, when the mind wavers, Māra immediately binds it;
when the mind does not waver, Māra immediately releases it.
Therefore, O bhikṣus!
"One should train oneself to dwell frequently with an unshakable mind, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1169 (1169). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kosambī in the Ghosira Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If there is a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī who, through the causal condition of eye and form, gives rise to desire, greed, attachment, longing, or fixed clinging toward those mental states, they should skillfully guard and protect their minds against them."

Why is this so? Because these are all paths of fear, characterized by obstructions and difficulties; they are the resort of evil persons, not the resort of virtuous persons. Therefore, one should guard oneself against them.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
It is like a farmer who has excellent crops in his field, yet the guardian of the field is lazy and negligent, allowing penned oxen to enter and devour them;
so too it is with foolish worldlings.
The six bases of contact, and even heedlessness, are likewise thus.

"Just as when there is a fine crop in a field, if the guardian of the field is not heedless and does not allow the tethered oxen to run wild, and even if they should enter the field, he drives them all out;

so too, regarding what is called mind, mentation, or consciousness, the learned noble disciple well guards and protects himself against the qualities of the five sensual pleasures, exerting his whole heart to extinguish them."

If there is a fine crop in a field, and the guardian of that field does not become negligent, he will take the ox by the nose with his left hand and hold a staff in his right hand; he will strike it all over its body and drive it out of the field.
"Monks! What do you think?
After that ox has experienced such suffering, would it still go from the village to the house, and from the house to the village, as before, to graze upon the crops in the fields?"
He replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this so? Because..."
"Because he recalled the suffering of being beaten with sticks when he previously entered the fields.

"In this way, bhikkhus, whether it be the mind, the intellect, or consciousness, a well-heard noble disciple develops extreme disenchantment and dread toward the six bases of contact; his inner mind dwells in peace, and he restrains it to become one-pointed."
"O Bhikṣus!

In the past, there was a king who heard the sound of a lute playing such as he had never heard before. He conceived an intense love and delight for it, becoming deeply immersed and attached to it, and asked his ministers:
'What kind of sound is this?'"
"How very delightful!
The minister replied,
"This is the sound of a lute."
He said to the minister,
"Bring that sound here.
Following these instructions, the minister went immediately to fetch the lute and reported back, saying:
"Great King!
This is the lute that produces beautiful sounds.
The king said to the minister:
"I do not need the lute; I wish to have that previously heard, lovely, and delightful sound brought here. The minister replied:

"Such a lute possesses many constituent parts—namely, a handle, a hollow body, a neck, strings, and skin. When a skillful person plays it, sound is produced through the causal conditions of these various components. It is not possible for there to be sound without these components. The sound previously heard has long since passed away; having shifted, it has also completely ceased and cannot be brought here."
At that time, the great king thought to himself:
"Alas! Of what use are these deceptive things?"
This worldly lute is a deceptive object that causes people of the world to become addicted to and attached to it;
you should now take it away, break it into pieces, and cast them in the ten directions.
The minister, having received these instructions, divided [the body] into a hundred pieces and discarded them in various places.
"In this same way, bhikṣu!
If one knows that form, feeling, perception, volition, and desire—these dharmas—are impermanent, conditioned, and arisen through mental causes and conditions, yet one nevertheless says:..."
"This is me; this is mine. At another time, all of that will be utterly non-existent. O Bhikṣus!
"One should cultivate such impartial and correct wisdom, observing things as they truly are.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1170. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kosambī in the Ghosira Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Just as a leper whose four limbs are covered in festering sores enters a thicket of reeds and rushes, only to be further wounded by thorns, leaves, and needles, thereby doubling his agony;
so too it is with the foolish worldling who experiences various sufferings through the six bases of contact."
Just as that leper, when wounded by the prick of a blade of grass or a thorn, has pus and blood flow out;
so too do these foolish worldlings, whose nature is base and violent, give rise to anger whenever they are touched by the six bases of contact, emitting harsh words just like that leper.
Why is this so? The mind of a foolish, unlearned worldling is like a leprous sore.
"I shall now explain restraint and non-restraint."
What is restraint? What is non-restraint?

When an ignorant, unlearned worldling sees a form with the eye, they give rise to attachment toward a pleasing form and anger toward a displeasing form; subsequently, many discursive thoughts arise in succession, and they fail to perceive their underlying dangers.
Furthermore, one perceives their faults yet is unable to eliminate them.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind,
O bhikṣu!
This is called non-restraint.
What is restraint?

When a well-learned noble disciple sees a form with the eye, he does not give rise to thoughts of desire toward a form that is agreeable, nor does he give rise to thoughts of aversion toward a form that is disagreeable; rather, he does not successively give rise to a multitude of discursive thoughts that continue to dwell [in the mind], but perceives the peril inherent in forms.
Having seen the danger and affliction, one is able to relinquish them.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
This is called restraint (*saṃvara*).
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1171 (1171) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Gośīrṣa Park in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Suppose, for example, a man wandering through an empty house finds six kinds of beings.
First, he finds a dog; he then seizes the dog and ties it up in one place."
Next he caught a bird, then a venomous snake, then a jackal, then a śiśumāra, and finally a monkey.
Having caught these creatures, he bound them all together in one place.
As for that dog, it desired to enter the village;
as for that bird, it always desired to fly through the air;
as for that snake, it always desired to enter its hole.
The jackal delights in heading toward burial mounds;
the śiṃśapā tree wishes to enter the ocean;
and the monkey desires to enter the mountain forests.

These six beings were all bound together in one place; though their preferences differed and each desired to reach its own comfortable abode according to its own inclinations, none took pleasure in the other's location.
Because they were bound, each exerted its strength toward its preferred direction, yet they could not escape.
"In this way, the various objects of the six sense faculties each seek their own preferred objects and do not delight in other objects.
The eye faculty constantly seeks pleasant forms; when confronted with disagreeable forms, it gives rise to aversion."
The faculty of the ear constantly seeks sounds that are agreeable; toward sounds that are disagreeable, it gives rise to aversion.
The faculty of the nose constantly seeks fragrances that are agreeable; toward fragrances that are disagreeable, it gives rise to aversion.
The tongue-faculty constantly seeks flavors that are agreeable; toward flavors that are disagreeable, it gives rise to aversion.
The body-faculty constantly seeks tangibles that are agreeable; toward tangibles that are disagreeable, it gives rise to aversion.
The mind-faculty constantly seeks after agreeable phenomena, while disagreeable phenomena give rise to aversion.
These six faculties, with their various spheres of activity and various objects, do not each seek the objects of other faculties.
These six faculties, when they possess power, are capable of acting with mastery as they perceive their respective objects.

It is like a man who ties six living beings to a sturdy pillar; though he exerts himself to pull them away at will, they go back and forth until they are utterly exhausted, yet because they are bound by ropes, they ultimately remain dependent upon the pillar.
“O bhikṣus! I have told this parable in order to reveal its meaning to you.
The six classes of beings are like the six sense faculties;”
The firm pillar is a metaphor for the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

If one skillfully cultivates the foundation of mindfulness of the body, whether one is mindful or not mindful of forms, upon seeing a pleasing form one does not give rise to attachment, and upon seeing an unpleasing form one does not give rise to aversion.

Regarding sounds heard by the ear, odors smelled by the nose, flavors tasted by the tongue, tangibles felt by the body, and mental objects cognized by the mind: toward agreeable mental objects one does not seek desire, and toward disagreeable mental objects one does not give rise to aversion.
"Therefore, bhikṣus!
You should diligently practice and frequently abide in the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1172. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kosambī in the Ghosita Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Suppose there were four venomous snakes, fierce, cruel, and poisonous, placed together within a single basket.
At that time, there was a man who was intelligent and not foolish, possessed of wisdom; he sought pleasure and loathed suffering, sought life and loathed death.”
At that time, another man said to the first man:
"Now you must take this casket containing a venomous snake, rub and bathe it, nourish and feed it with kindness, and open and close it at the proper times."
"If these four venomous snakes should cause you distress, they might kill you or bring you close to death;
you must guard against them. At that time, the man fled in terror.
"Suddenly there are five enemies who draw their swords and pursue you, seeking to kill you; you must guard yourself.
At that time, the man, fearing the four venomous snakes and the five enemies with drawn swords, fled in haste.
Another person further said to him: "O man!
Within you there are six thieves who follow and watch for you; as soon as they find an opportunity, they will kill you, so you must guard yourself against them."

At that time, the man, terrified of the four venomous snakes, the five enemies with drawn swords, and the six internal thieves, fled in haste and returned to the deserted village. There he saw an empty house, dilapidated, decayed, and ruined, filled with various foul things; whatever he grasped was fragile and brittle, possessing no solidity.
Another person spoke again, saying: "O man!
This empty village will soon be overrun by a band of thieves; they will surely come and suddenly harm you."
At that time, the man, fearing the four poisonous snakes, the five bandits with drawn swords, the six internal enemies, and the bandits in the deserted village, fled in haste.

Suddenly, on the road, he came upon a great river with deep and swift currents. He saw that this shore was filled with various terrors, while the opposite shore appeared peaceful, blissful, cool, and free from fear; yet there was no bridge or boat by which he could cross to reach the other side. He thought to himself:
"I shall gather grass and wood, bind them together to form a raft, and using my hands and feet as oars, I will cross over to the other shore."

Having formed this thought, he immediately gathered grass and wood, tied them together by the riverbank to form a raft, and with skillful use of his hands and feet, crossed the current by swimming across.

“In this way, that man has escaped the four venomous snakes, the five enemies with drawn swords, and the six internal malevolent thieves; he has further freed himself from the bandits in the empty village, crossed the deep torrent, left behind the various terrors of this shore, and reached the other shore in safety and happiness.”
I have spoken this parable; you should understand its meaning. Bhikṣus!

The casket is a metaphor for this physical body, composed of the four coarse great elements, a substance formed from the essence of blood produced by those four elements, nourished by impure food, maintained by bathing and clothing, and subject to the laws of impermanence, transformation, decay, and fragility.
The "venomous snake" is a metaphor for the four great elements—the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.
If the earth element becomes disturbed, it can cause death or bring one close to death;
the same applies to disturbances of the water, fire, and wind elements.
The five enemies with drawn swords are a metaphor for the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
The six internal thieves are a metaphor for the six cravings and delights (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇā-nandī*).
The empty village is a metaphor for the six internal sense bases (*ṣaḍ-ādhyātmika-āyatana*).
"Good son!
Observe the sense-base of the eye: it is impermanent and subject to decay; that which grasps the eye is likewise an impermanent and deceptive phenomenon.
The sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are also like this."
The "bandits in the empty village" are a metaphor for the six external sense bases (*āyatana*).
The eye is harmed by agreeable and disagreeable forms;
the ear by sounds, the nose by odors, the tongue by tastes, the body by tangibles, and the mind by agreeable and disagreeable mental objects (*dharma*).

The deep-flowing currents are a metaphor for the four floods (*ogha*): the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*), the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*), the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*), and the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*).
The river is a metaphor for the three cravings (*tṛṣṇā*): craving for sensual pleasure (*kāmatṛṣṇā*), craving for form (*rūpatṛṣṇā*), and craving for the formless (*ārūpyatṛṣṇā*).
"This shore, full of terrors," is a metaphor for the body.
"The other shore, cool and peaceful," is a metaphor for *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
"The raft" is a metaphor for the Eightfold Noble Path.
Those who cross the stream by means of skillful hands and feet are like those who, through diligent effort and valor, reach the further shore.
The dwelling place of the brahmins is like the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"In this way, bhikṣus, the Great Teacher, out of compassion, has performed for his disciples what was to be done;

I have now completed it, and you too must now perform what is to be done. Under solitary trees, in clean dwellings, spreading grass for a seat, or in open spaces and among graves—sit apart in seclusion, apply yourselves diligently to meditative reflection, and be careful not to be negligent, lest you later feel regret!
"This, then, is my method of instruction.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly! 1173 (1173) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kosambī in the Ghosita Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"The learned noble disciple understands, as they truly are, the origin, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding all phenomena of suffering; he views the five desires as being like a pit of fire."

Having thus observed the five sensual desires, his mind is not permanently shrouded by greed for the five desires, craving for desire, thoughts of desire, or attachment to desire. Knowing the spheres of activity and the abodes of the desiring mind, he guards himself against them;
having preemptively guarded against those spheres of activity and abodes, no worldly greed, sorrow, or unwholesome, evil states leak into his mind according to those spheres of activity and abodes.
"What is meant by a learned noble disciple knowing and seeing, as they truly are, the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding all phenomena of suffering?

A learned noble disciple knows, as it truly is, this noble truth of suffering; he knows, as they truly are, this noble truth of the origin of suffering, this noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and this noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. This is called a learned noble disciple knowing and seeing, as they truly are, the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding all phenomena of suffering."
"How does a well-taught noble disciple see the five sensual pleasures as a pit of fire, such that worldly greed, sorrow, and unwholesome, evil states do not permanently shroud his mind?"
Suppose there is a village nearby, and at its edge there is a deep pit filled with blazing fire, yet without smoke or flames.
At that time, there is a man who is neither foolish nor deluded, but is clever, discerning, and wise; he delights in happiness and loathes suffering, and he desires life and abhors death.
He thinks to himself:
"This is a fire pit, filled to the brim with blazing flames; if I were to fall into it, my death would be certain beyond doubt.
Thus, he conceives a sense of distance toward it, a thought of distance, and a desire for distance.
In this way, the well-learned noble disciple views the five sensual pleasures as a pit of fire; thus, worldly greed, sorrow, and evil unwholesome states do not permanently shroud his mind.
Whether in movement or at rest, he guards against and recognizes them in advance, so that worldly greed, sorrow, and evil unwholesome states do not leak into his mind.
"It is like a mango grove on the outskirts of a village that is thick with thorns; suppose a man enters this grove to perform some work."
Having entered the forest, there were thorns all around—in front, behind, to the left, to the right, above, and below.

At that time, the man proceeded with right mindfulness; he came and went with right mindfulness, looked clearly with right mindfulness, gazed steadily with right mindfulness, and bent his body with right mindfulness.
Why is this? It is so that no sharp thorns may wound or destroy the body.

In the same way, the learned noble disciple, when dwelling in dependence upon a village or town, puts on his robes and takes up his bowl in the early morning to enter the village for alms; he well guards his body, well maintains his mind, abides in right mindfulness, acts with right mindfulness, has right mindfulness as his clear vision, and observes with right mindfulness.
Why is this? So that the thorn of gain shall not wound the Noble Dharma and Discipline.
"What is it for the thorn of gain to wound the Noble Dharma and Discipline?"
This refers to forms that are pleasing and beloved; these are called "thorns" that wound the noble Dharma and Vinaya.
What are these pleasing and beloved forms that wound the noble Dharma and Vinaya?
This refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure: when the eye-consciousness perceives forms, it gives rise to affectionate thoughts that nourish sensual desire;

when the ear-consciousness perceives sounds, the nose-consciousness perceives odors, the tongue-consciousness perceives tastes, and the body-consciousness perceives tangibles, they give rise to affectionate thoughts that nourish sensual desire. These are called "lovely forms that harm the noble Dharma and Vinaya.
This is what the learned noble disciple practices and dwells in, guarding against and knowing them in advance, so as not to allow worldly greed, sorrow, or unwholesome states to leak into his mind.

"Sometimes a learned noble disciple gives rise to right mindfulness, yet evil and unwholesome thoughts arise, nourishing desire, nourishing ill will, and nourishing delusion; such a person is of dull faculties.
Although this learned noble disciple has given rise to [the knowledge of] the arising and cessation [of phenomena], his mind is still shrouded by desire."

For example, just as an iron ball, heated until it is extremely hot, dries up and vanishes immediately when sprinkled with a little water, so too do the thoughts that arise in a learned noble disciple of dull faculties vanish immediately.
A well-learned noble disciple practices and dwells in this manner.
Should a king or a high minister go to him in person and offer him a stipend, saying:
"O man!..."
"What is the use of shaving your hair, carrying an earthen bowl, wearing the saṃghāṭī robe, and begging for food from house to house?
It would be better to comfort yourself by indulging in the pleasures of the five desires, practicing generosity, and performing meritorious deeds."
"How so? Bhikkhus! If a well-taught noble disciple is invited by kings, ministers, relatives, or donors to accept a stipend, would he then return to the precepts or fall away from them?"
He replied: "No. Why is that? Because..."

Because the learned noble disciple knows and sees, as they truly are, the arising, cessation, gratification, danger, and escape regarding all phenomena of suffering, he views the five sensual pleasures as being like a pit of fire. Thus, even when worldly greed, sorrow, and evil unwholesome states do not permanently overwhelm his mind, he anticipates and recognizes them while moving about and staying still, until no such worldly greed, sorrow, or evil unwholesome states leak into his mind.
"Furthermore, it is impossible that one who has been invited by a king, a high minister, or kinsmen to accept a stipend of emoluments would, upon returning to the precepts, fall away from them;
such a thing cannot occur! The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Excellent!"
Excellent!

That learned noble disciple has, for a long night, directed his mind toward seclusion, toward dispassion, and toward Nirvana; he is inclined toward tranquility, relinquishment, and delighting in Nirvana;
and regarding the realms of the outflows, he finds them to be cessation and coolness.
If one who has been invited by a king, a householder, or kinsmen should turn back from the precepts and regress, such a thing is impossible!
They will instead suffer great misery.

It is like the Ganges River, which for a long night flows toward, pours out, and rushes eastward; even if many people were to cut it off, attempting to make it flow toward, pour out, and rush westward—could this ever be achieved?
He replied, “I cannot,
World-Honored One.”
Why is this? The Ganges River has flowed toward the east for a long night; to wish for it to flow westward is impossible, and those great multitudes would only labor in vain!

For such a well-learned noble disciple who has for a long night been inclining toward, flowing toward, and rushing toward seclusion, it is impossible that they should ever fall back or diminish; it would be in vain and merely a source of hardship!
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1174 (1174) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying by the banks of the Abhaya River.
At that time, a bhikṣu came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha,
saying: “Excellent, World-Honored One!
"Teach me the Dharma; having heard the Dharma, I shall dwell alone in a quiet place, reflecting with focused diligence and remaining heedful:

'For what reason have sons of noble family shaved off their hair and beard, out of right faith left the home life for homelessness to study the Path, and further cultivated the holy life therein, so as to see the Dharma for themselves and realize it, knowing:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and I myself know that there will be no further existence. "
At that time, the World-Honored One observed the water and saw a large tree in the Ganges River drifting downstream. He said to those bhikṣus:
"Do you see this large tree in the Ganges River flowing along?"
He replied,
“I have seen them,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Suppose this great tree does not cling to this shore, nor to the opposite shore; it does not sink to the bottom of the water, nor is it obstructed by islands or sandbanks; it does not enter eddies, nor is it taken up by humans, nor by non-humans; furthermore, it does not rot. Would it not follow the current, flowing and surging along, until it is carried into the great ocean?"
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“So it is, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said: "A bhikṣu is also like this.

He does not cling to this shore, nor does he cling to the other shore; he does not sink to the bottom of the water, nor is he obstructed by islands or sandbanks; he does not enter eddies; neither humans nor non-humans take hold of him; furthermore, he does not rot or decay, but flows toward, pours into, and rushes toward nirvāṇa."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“What is this shore? What is the other shore?”
What is meant by "sinking"?
What is meant by "islands"?
What is meant by "eddies"?
What is human appropriation?
What is non-human appropriation?
What is putrefaction?
Excellent, World-Honored One!

Please explain this to me in detail. Having heard the Dharma, I shall dwell alone in a quiet place, applying myself with diligence and reflection, abiding without negligence, until I know for myself that there will be no further existence.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“This shore refers to the six internal sense bases (āyatana).
The other shore refers to the six external sense bases.”

“Grasping by persons” (puggalaggāha) is as follows: there is one who associates with householders and renunciants, whether they are joyful or sorrowful, suffering or happy; whatever they do, he does together with them, following them from beginning to end—this is called grasping by persons.

Regarding being "taken by non-humans": it is like a person who makes a vow to practice the holy life, thinking, "By now maintaining the precepts, practicing austerities, and cultivating all forms of the holy life, I shall be reborn in such-and-such a place, in such-and-such a heavenly realm"—this is being taken by non-humans.
"Whirling and eddying" refers to one who returns to the precepts and regresses.

"Rotting and decaying" refers to one who violates the precepts and practices evil, unwholesome dharmas; they are rotting and of little learning, like weeds among grain or the sound of a blown conch shell—neither a śramaṇa nor bearing the likeness of a śramaṇa, neither practicing brahmacarya nor bearing the likeness of one who practices brahmacarya.
"In this way, bhikṣus, this is called not clinging to this shore or the other shore, and so forth, until reaching the exhaustion of nirvāṇa.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, those bhikṣus rejoiced and were filled with gladness; they paid homage and departed.

Then, that bhikṣu, dwelling alone in a quiet place, reflected upon the teaching of the *Dārukkhandhopamasutta* (The Discourse on the Log) as spoken by the Buddha, until he personally realized that he would not undergo further existence and attained arhatship.
At that time, there was a cowherd named Nandaka who was not far from the Buddha, tending cattle with a staff in hand.
After the bhikṣu had departed, he went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Am I now capable of not clinging to this shore, not clinging to the far shore, not sinking, not being obstructed by islands or shoals, not being seized by humans, not being seized by non-humans, not entering a whirlpool, and not becoming rotten; may I go forth to practice the holy life within the True Dharma and Vinaya of the Blessed One?
The Buddha asked the cowherd,
"Will you return the cows to their owner?
The cowherd replied:
"Among all these cows there are calves who can return home on their own; there is no need to send them back. You should simply permit me to leave the household life to study the Way.
The Buddha told the cowherd:
"Although the cows can return home by themselves, you have now received the food and clothing provided by a person; you must therefore repay your debt to your master."
Then, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, the cowherd rejoiced and approved with gladness; he paid homage and departed.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was present in this assembly. Not long after the cowherd had left, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“Nandika the cowherd seeks to go forth from home; for what reason, World-Honored One, do you send him back to his house?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“It is impossible that Nandika the cowherd would return to live at home and enjoy the five desires!”

Having returned the ox to its owner, he immediately went forth into homelessness to study the Path under this Dharma and Vinaya; he purified his holy life until, knowing for himself that there would be no further existence, he attained arhatship.
Then, having returned the oxen to their owner, the cowherd Dandapāṇi went back to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"The ox has already been returned to its owner; please allow me to go forth and train in the path within this True Dharma and Vinaya.
The Buddha told the cowherd Nandika:
"You may go forth in this Dharma and Vinaya, receive full ordination, and attain the status of a bhikṣu."
Having gone forth, he reflected:

"This is why sons of noble family shave off their hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and out of right faith leave the home life for homelessness to study the Path, further cultivating the holy life, until they know for themselves that there will be no further existence."
He became an arhat. 1175 (1175).
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu who, dwelling alone in seclusion, sat in meditation and reflected thus:
"How does a bhikṣu know, how does he see, so as to attain pure vision?"
Having had this thought, he went to the bhikṣus and said to them:
"Venerable bhikṣus!
How should one know, and how should one see, so that vision becomes pure?"
The bhikkhu replied:
"Venerable sir,
one possesses right knowledge as it really is regarding the arising, passing away, gratification, danger, and escape in relation to the six bases of contact."
“Monks! One who knows thus and sees thus attains the vision of purity.
When that monk heard this declaration from the other monk, his mind was not pleased; he went again to another monk and asked him, saying:
"Venerable bhikkhus!
By what knowledge and by what vision does one attain the purity of vision?
Those bhikkhus replied:
"One who understands, as they truly are, the origin, the cessation, the gratification, the peril, and the escape regarding the six elements—
in this way, bhikkhu,
one who knows thus and sees thus attains the purity of vision."
At that time, having heard his prediction, the bhikṣu was not pleased in his heart; he went again to other bhikṣus and asked them this question:
"Bhikṣus!..."
"How does one know, how does one see, so as to attain pure vision?
That bhikṣu replied:
"One observes the five aggregates of clinging as being like a disease, like an abscess, like a thorn, like a murderer; as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self."
“By knowing thus and seeing thus, one attains pure vision.

When that bhikṣu heard the other bhikṣus making this declaration, his mind was neither pleased nor displeased. He went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
I reflected alone and in silence:
"How does a bhikkhu know, how does he see, so as to attain purity of vision?

Having formed this thought, I approached the bhikkhus and reported in detail to the Blessed One what was spoken at those three locations. Upon hearing their account, my mind was not satisfied, and so I have come to the Blessed One.
"Therefore, for this reason, I asked the World-Honored One:
'How does a bhikṣu know, how does he see, so as to attain pure vision?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"In a past age, there was a man who had never seen a *kimpuruṣa*. He went to one who had seen a *kimpuruṣa* and asked that man who had seen the *kimpuruṣa*:
'Do you know the *kimpuruṣa*? "
He replied, "I know.
He asked again:
"What is its appearance like? He replied,
"Its color is black, like a pillar scorched by fire."
When he saw it, the *kinnara* was black, like a pillar scorched by fire.
At that time, having heard that the *kinnara* was black like a pillar scorched by fire, the man was not at all pleased; he went again to another man who had previously seen a *kinnara* and asked him:
"Do you know the *kinnara*?"
He replied, "I know.
He was asked again:
"What is its appearance?
The man who had previously seen the *kimpuruṣa* replied:
"It is red and fully blossomed, resembling a piece of flesh."
When that man saw it, the *kimpuruṣa* was in full bloom, appearing exactly like a piece of raw meat.
Having heard what that man said, the gentleman was still not satisfied; he went again to another man who had previously seen a *kimpuruṣa* and asked, "Do you know the *kimpuruṣa*?"
He replied, "I know.
He asked again:
"What is its appearance like? He replied,
"It hangs down in dense clusters, like the fruit of the śirīṣa tree."
Having heard this, the man’s heart was again displeased; he went to ask another who knew of the kinnara, asking:
"Do you know the kinnara?"
He replied, "I know.
He asked again:
"What is its appearance like?
He replied again:
"Its leaves are green, smooth, and long and broad, like those of the nyagrodha tree."

"Just as that man questioned the *kimpuruṣa*, and upon hearing [the answers], was not pleased and sought elsewhere; yet those people who had seen the *kimpuruṣa* gave their accounts according to what they had seen at that time, and for this reason, their descriptions did not agree."
"In this way, monks!

If one dwells alone, applying oneself with diligence and remaining heedful, such that by means of reflecting on the Dharma no taints arise and the mind attains liberation, then one may explain things according to what has been seen.
Listen now again as I speak a parable, for the wise gain understanding through parables.

"Suppose there were a king of a bordering realm who skillfully maintained his city walls and gates, making them firm and secure; the crossroads were level and straight, and at the four city gates he stationed four guardians, all of whom were intelligent and wise, knowing who came and who went."
In the center of the city, there was a crossroads where a couch was placed for the lord of the city to sit upon.
When an envoy from the east arrived, he asked the gatekeeper:
"Where is the lord of the city?"
He replied: "The lord is at the crossroads within the city, sitting upon a couch.
Having heard this, the messenger went to the city lord, received his instructions, and returned by the same way.
When messengers arrived from the south, west, and north, they asked the gatekeepers:
"Where is the lord of the city?
And they answered them in the same way.
"At the crossroads within that city.
Having heard this, the messengers all went to the lord of the city, received his instructions, and each returned to their respective places.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I have spoken this parable; I shall now explain its meaning.
What is called the 'city' is a metaphor for the coarse physical form of the human body, as explained in the *Sūtra on the Snake in a Chest*."
Skillfully repairing the city walls refers to right view.
The level and straight crossroads refer to the six internal sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
The four gates refer to the four stations of consciousness (*catasraḥ vijñāna-sthitayaḥ*).
The four gatekeepers refer to the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).
The lord of the city refers to the aggregate of consciousness-feeling (*vijñāna-vedanā-skandha*).
The messengers refer to tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
"Speaking according to reality" refers to the Four Noble Truths.
"Returning by way of the path" refers to the Eightfold Noble Path.
Thus the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"What a Great Teacher does for his disciples, I have now done out of compassion, as explained in the Sūtra on the Simile of the Snake in a Chest.

At that time, having heard the Buddha’s words, the bhikṣu applied himself with focused contemplation, dwelt without negligence, further cultivated the holy life, and attained arhatship such that there would be no further existence.
1176. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Blessed One was wandering among the people of the Śākya clan and arrived at the kingdom of Kapilavastu, where he stayed in the Nyagrodha Park.

At that time, the Śākyas of Kapilavastu had constructed a new lecture hall, but no śramaṇas, brahmins, young Śākyas, or common people had yet resided within it. They heard that the World-Honored One had arrived at Kapilavastu among the Śākyas during his travels through the human realm and was staying in the Nyagrodha Garden, where he was discoursing on the meaning of suffering and pleasure.

This hall has been newly completed, yet no one has yet resided within it. You may invite the World-Honored One and the great assembly to make offerings therein; by doing so, you will obtain meritorious rewards and enjoy peace and security throughout the long night, while we, in turn, shall subsequently make use of it.
Having deliberated thus, they all went out of the city together to the place where the World-Honored One was. They prostrated themselves at his feet in salutation and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the essential Dharma for the Śākyas; having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them, he remained silent.
At that time, the Śākyas rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, paid homage to the Buddha, knelt with their right knees on the ground, joined their palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

"We Śākyas have newly constructed a lecture hall, but no one has yet resided there. We now invite the World-Honored One and the great assembly to receive offerings therein, so that we may obtain merit and blessings, and enjoy peace and security for a long night; thereafter, we shall follow by making use of it ourselves."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

When the Śākyas knew that the World-Honored One had accepted, they prostrated at his feet and each returned to their respective places. On that very day, they used carriages and carts to transport all the necessary implements, decorating the new hall, arranging beds and seats, spreading soft grass upon the floor, and preparing fragrant oil lamps.
When all affairs were completed, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself, and said:
"All affairs are completed; may the Holy One know the proper time.

At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by the great assembly in front and behind, went outside the new hall, washed his feet, and then ascended the hall to sit facing east beneath the central pillar.
Then, the bhikṣus, having likewise washed their feet, followed him into the lecture hall and sat down in order behind the World-Honored One, facing east with their backs to the west.
Then the Śākyas sat down facing west on the eastern side.
At that time, the World-Honored One extensively expounded the essential Dharma for the Śākyas, instructing, exhorting, illuminating, and gladdening them; having done so, he addressed the Śākyas:
“O Gautamas!”
"The first watch of the night has already passed; it is now time to return to Kapilavastu.
At that time, the Śākyas, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and approved, paid their respects, and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the Śākyas had departed, addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"You should preach the Dharma to the bhikṣus; I now suffer from back pain and must attend to myself."
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana silently accepted the instruction.

Then the World-Honored One arranged his four-fold inner robe (antaravāsaka) beneath his side, folded his outer robe (saṃghāṭī), and placed it under his head; lying on his right side with his knees bent and feet叠置 (placed one upon the other), he fixed his mindfulness on the light sign (ālokasaññā) and maintained the thought of rising.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the bhikṣus:

"The Dharma taught by the Buddha is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; it is excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing, pure, complete, and pristine—a holy life of total purity."
I shall now speak of the phenomena with outflows (*āsava*) and the phenomena without outflows; listen attentively!
What are the phenomena with outflows?

When an ignorant, unlearned worldling sees a form with the eye, they give rise to attachment toward a pleasing form and aversion toward an unpleasing form. Not abiding in the foundation of mindfulness of the body, they possess no wisdom regarding even a small portion of liberation of mind or liberation by wisdom, and thus give rise to various evil and unwholesome states that are neither extinguished without remainder nor forever exhausted without remainder.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. Bhikṣus!
When it is thus, Māra, the Evil One, goes to that person's place, watching for a vulnerability; regarding the forms perceived by the eye, he immediately finds a lapse.
It is the same for the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and flavors, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena; they likewise find their deficiency.
"It is like a heap of withered, dry grass: if fire breaks out from the four directions, it is immediately consumed."
In this way, bhikṣus!
regarding the eye and forms, the Māra Pāpīyān immediately finds an opening.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!

He does not overcome forms; with respect to sounds of the ear, odors of the nose, tastes of the tongue, tangibles of the body, and mental objects of the mind, he is constrained by phenomena and cannot overcome them. He does not overcome forms, nor does he overcome sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects; furthermore, he does not overcome unwholesome mental states, the blazing afflictions and their bitter retributions, nor the future states of birth, aging, sickness, and death.
"Venerable sirs!
I have personally received from the Blessed One these teachings on the phenomena with outflows; this is called the Discourse on Phenomena with Outflows.
What is the Discourse on Phenomena without Outflows?"

The learned noble disciple, when seeing forms with the eye, does not give rise to attachment toward agreeable forms, nor does he give rise to aversion toward disagreeable forms; he dwells with mindfulness established, knowing as it truly is the liberation of mind through the immeasurable and the liberation through wisdom, whereby evil and unwholesome states that have arisen are extinguished without remainder.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
"When such a bhikṣu as this exists, Māra Pāpīyān approaches him and seeks for a flaw in his visual forms, but finds no flaw;
he seeks for a flaw in his auditory sounds, olfactory odors, gustatory flavors, tactile tangibles, and mental phenomena, yet finds no flaw."
It is like a multi-storied pavilion with solid walls, windows and doors firmly shut, and plastered thickly and densely; even if fires break out on all four sides, they cannot burn it down.
These bhikṣus are also like this: when the wicked Māra Pāpīyān goes to their abode seeking to find a flaw, he finds no flaw.
Such bhikṣus are able to overcome those forms and are not overcome by them;
they overcome sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena, and are not overcome by those phenomena.

If one has triumphed over forms, and has triumphed over sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena, one has likewise triumphed over evil and unwholesome states, the blazing afflictions and their painful retributions, as well as birth, aging, sickness, and death in future lives.
"I have personally received this Dharma from the World-Honored One’s own lips; it is called the Sūtra on the Outflow-free Dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that Mahāmaudgalyāyana had finished preaching the Dharma, sat up with his body erect, focused his mindfulness before him, and addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Excellent!"
Excellent, Maudgalyāyana!
To preach this Dharma-sūtra for the sake of others brings great benefit and great deliverance, bringing peace and happiness to gods and humans throughout the long night.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should receive and uphold this Sūtra on Defiled and Undefiled Dharmas, and explain it extensively for others. Why is this so?"
Because it is complete in meaning, complete in Dharma, and complete in the holy life (brahmacarya), it develops supernormal powers and leads directly toward Nirvana;
even a son of good family with faith, whether lay or ordained, should receive, uphold, read, recite, and widely explain it to others.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1177 (1177) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“Suppose there were a river of ashes, its two banks extremely hot and covered with many sharp thorns, situated in a place of darkness, where numerous sinners were being swept away and submerged by the current.”
Among them was one person who was neither foolish nor deluded, but was clever, wise, fond of pleasure and weary of suffering, fond of life and weary of death. He thought to himself:
"For what reason am I now here in this River of Ashes, with its two banks so intensely hot and filled with many sharp thorns, sinking and drifting along the current in this place of darkness?"
"I shall use the means of my hands and feet to go against the current.
Gradually, he saw a faint light.
The man thought silently to himself:
"Even though I am currently ill and weak, I shall strive to see this small light.

He then moved his hands and feet, applying diligent effort and skillful means, until he finally saw level ground. He stopped there and surveyed the four directions, seeing a great rocky mountain that was neither broken nor destroyed, nor pierced by holes; he then climbed it.
Furthermore, they see the eightfold water of coolness, namely: cold, delicious, light, soft, fragrant, pure, not choking when drunk, and not obstructing the throat.
Having drunk [the water], his body was refreshed; he then entered within it, bathing or drinking as he pleased, thereby freeing himself from all afflictions and fevers.

Thereafter, he proceeded further up the great mountain, where he saw seven kinds of flowers: namely, the utpala, the padma, the kumuda, the puṇḍarīka, the sugandhika, the mṛdugandhika, and the atimuktaka.
Having smelled the fragrance of the flowers, he ascended the rocky mountain and saw a four-tiered hall; he immediately sat upon it.

Seeing a five-pillared pavilion, he entered within and sat upright with his body composed. Various pillows and bedding were spread about, covered everywhere with scattered flowers, magnificent and exquisite.
Therein he sat and reclined at will; cool breezes converged from all sides, bringing peace and stability to his body. Sitting beneath the tall trees, he raised his voice and proclaimed:
"O worthy sages and noble beings!
Just as that River of Ash has both banks intensely heated and many sharp thorns, and its depths are dark and gloomy, one must seek an escape from it."
"In the river, those who heard the sound followed its direction and asked:
'By which way can one emerge?
From what place does one emerge?'"
Among them, some said:
"Why must you ask where one can escape?

That voice which called out did not itself know or see from where it emerged; it too shall remain here in this Ash River, with its two banks intensely hot and covered in many sharp thorns, descending with the current in total darkness. What is the use of asking it?"
“In this way, bhikṣus!
I have spoken this parable; now I shall explain its meaning.
‘Ash’ refers to the three evil and unwholesome thoughts.”
What are the three?
They are the thought of sensual desire, the thought of ill will, and the thought of harmfulness.
The "river" refers to the three cravings—craving for sensual pleasure, craving for form, and craving for the formless.
The two shores that are extremely hot refer to the six internal and external sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
The many sharp thorns refer to the objects of the five desires (*pañcakāmaguṇa*).
The place of darkness refers to the obstruction of ignorance (*avidyā*) which blocks the eye of wisdom (*prajñācakṣus*).
"The many people" refers to foolish ordinary beings (*bālapṛthagjana*).
"The stream" refers to the river of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
"Among them, there is one person who is neither foolish nor deluded" refers to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
"Using the hands and feet as skillful means to flow upstream" refers to diligent cultivation and study.
"Faintly perceiving a small light" refers to attaining the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
"Attaining level ground" refers to upholding the precepts (*śīla*)."
"Beholding the four directions" refers to seeing the Four Noble Truths.
"The great rocky mountain" refers to right view.
"The eightfold division of water" refers to the Eightfold Noble Path.
The seven kinds of flowers refer to the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
The four-tiered hall refers to the four bases of psychic power (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*).
The canopy with five pillars refers to the five faculties, beginning with faith (*pañcendriyāṇi*).
"Sitting with the body upright" refers to *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
"Scattering flowers everywhere" refers to the various *dhyānas*, liberations (*vimokṣas*), samādhis, and meditative attainments (*samāpattis*).
"One who sits and lies down at will" refers to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"The winds blowing from the four directions" refers to the four bases of psychic power (*catvāri ṛddhipādāḥ*) through which one dwells in happiness having seen the Dharma.
"Raising one's voice to call out" refers to turning the wheel of Dharma.
When someone asks, "Where have the worthy and noble ones gone?
Where have they emerged? this refers to the worthy bhikṣus such as Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others who were seated there.
Among them, there are those who say: "What is it that you ask?

He neither knows nor sees any point of emergence; he too shall likewise descend along this Ashes River, which has extremely hot banks on both sides, many sharp thorns, and flows through a place of total darkness. This refers to the six masters and other followers of false views, namely Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Maskarin Gośālīputra, Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra, Ajita Keśakambalin, Kakuda Kātyāyana, Nirgrantha Jñātiputra, and others of such wrong views.
"In this way, bhikṣus!
That which was to be done for the śrāvakas by the Great Teacher has now been done by me; you must now do what is to be done, as previously explained in the parable of the casket of poisonous snakes."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*Saṃyukta Āgama*, Scroll 43; *Saṃyukta Āgama*, Scroll 44.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
44.1178 (1178). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Mithilā, in the Āmra Park.

At that time, there was a brahmin woman named Vāseṭṭhī whose six sons had died one after another. Consumed by grief for her children, she went mad; naked and with disheveled hair, she ran along the road until she reached the Āmra Garden in Mithilā.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by an immeasurable great assembly as he preached the Dharma. From afar, the brahmin woman Vāseṭṭhī saw the World-Honored One; having seen him, she immediately regained her original composure and, filled with shame and remorse, crouched down with her body drawn in.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Take your upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) and give it to that brahmin woman, Vāsuladattā, so that she may put it on and listen to the Dharma."
Venerable Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, took the robe and had her put it on.
Then, the brahmin woman, having received and put on the robe, went before the Buddha, prostrated herself at his feet in salutation, and withdrew to sit at one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for him, instructing, exhorting, illuminating, and gladdening him. Following the Buddha’s customary method of teaching the Dharma in sequence, until his faith was purified and he received the three refuges, he heard what the Buddha had said and, with joy and approval, paid homage and departed.
Later, when that laywoman Vāsīṭhī’s seventh son suddenly passed away, she did not weep at all, nor was she afflicted by grief, sorrow, or distress.
At that time, the husband of the laywoman Vāsīṭhā spoke a verse to address her, saying:
"When my sons previously passed away, I grieved for them with sorrow and pain;
Day and night I took no food or drink, Until I was driven to madness."
"Now that you have lost seven sons, why do you feel no grief or suffering?
The laywoman Vāsuladattā then replied to her husband with these verses:
"My children and grandchildren number in the thousands; they were born through the convergence of causes and conditions."
The long night has passed away; so it is with me and you.
Our children, grandchildren, and kinsmen have been beyond measure;
in each and every place of rebirth, we have devoured one another.
If one knows the essential nature of birth, why should one give rise to sorrow and suffering?
I have already known the way of transcendence and the characteristics of birth-and-death and existence-extinction;
no longer do I give rise to sorrow and suffering, for I have entered the Buddha’s True Teaching.
Then the laywoman Vāseṭṭhī’s husband spoke this verse in praise:
“A teaching never heard before, I now hear you proclaim.
Where could one hear such a teaching that does not bring thoughts of grief for a son?”
The upāsikā Vāsabhakhattiyā replied with a verse, saying:
"Today the Samyaksaṃbuddha Is in the kingdom of Mithilā, Within the Āmra grove; Forever free from all suffering."
He who proclaims all suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering,
and the Noble Eightfold Path— the secure path leading to Nirvana—
is my Great Teacher; I take profound delight in his sublime teaching.
"I have already realized the True Dharma, which can dispel your son's sorrow and suffering.
The Brahmin husband spoke again in verse:
"I too shall now go to the Mṛgadāva (Deer Park) in Āmrapālīvana."
"That Blessed One shall likewise open the way for my son’s sorrow and suffering.
The upāsikā spoke again in verse:
"One should contemplate the Samyaksaṃbuddha, With his supple, golden-colored body."
"Those who are undisciplined, he can discipline; he widely ferries across those swept by the ocean current.
At that time, the brahmin immediately prepared his carriage and mounted his horse-drawn chariot, proceeding to the Āmra Garden in Mithilā.
Seeing the World-Honored One from afar, his faith and joy increased even further, and he approached the Great Master.
At that time, the Great Master spoke a verse for him, opening his Dharma-eye regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path leading directly to Nirvana.
He immediately perceived the Dharma and attained direct realization (*abhisamaya*).
Having understood the Dharma, he requested and obtained ordination.
At that time, the brahmin was ordained; through solitary and quiet reflection, he eventually attained the state of an Arhat.
The World-Honored One declared:
"In the third night, he attained the three knowledges.
Having attained the three knowledges, the Buddha then addressed him:
He sent his charioteer to return home and inform the laywoman Vāseṭṭhī, asking her to rejoice and saying:

"The brāhmaṇa went to see the World-Honored One and attained pure faith; he serves the Great Teacher, who has preached the Dharma for him and opened his Dharma-eye. He has seen the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Origin of Suffering, the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Eightfold Path; he has securely entered toward Nirvāṇa and realized the state of analytical knowledge."
Having understood the Dharma, he immediately sought ordination.
The World-Honored One prophesied:
"In the third night, he will become fully endowed with the three knowledges."
"Then, the charioteer, having received these instructions, returned quickly.
At that time, the laywoman Vāsabhā saw from afar that the charioteer was returning with an empty carriage."
He then asked from afar:
"Brahmin, did you see the Buddha?
Did the Buddha preach the Dharma for you, opening up the eye of Dharma so that you might perceive the Noble Truths?"
The charioteer replied:

"The brahmin has already seen the World-Honored One and attained pure faith; he serves the Great Teacher, for whom the Dharma-eye was opened, as [the Buddha] preached the Four Noble Truths, whereby he achieved immediate realization."
Having understood the Dharma, he immediately sought ordination and applied himself with focused contemplation.
The World-Honored One prophesied:
"In the third night, he will become fully endowed with the three types of clear knowledge."
At that time, the upāsikā immediately rejoiced in her heart and said to the charioteer:
"The carriage and horses belong to you; furthermore, I grant you one thousand gold coins. You must convey this message:
'The brāhmaṇa Sujāti has already attained the three types of supernormal knowledge.'"
"Please do so for my sake, that you may bring me joy.
The charioteer replied,
"What use have I now for these carriages, horses, gold, and money?"
"Return the carriage, horses, gold, and money to the upāsikā; I shall now return to the place of the brāhmaṇa and go forth under him.
The upāsikā said, "If this is your intention, you may return at once."
"Before long, I too shall attain what she has attained, become fully endowed with the three types of knowledge, and subsequently go forth into homelessness.
The charioteer replied,
"So it shall be, O Upāsikā!"
"Just as he has gone forth, so shall I likewise.
The upāsikā said, "Your father has gone forth and you have followed him; before long, I too shall follow them."

Just as a great dragon in the wilderness travels through the void, followed by all its other dragons, dragon sons, and dragon daughters, so too am I: carrying my robes and bowl, I am easy to support and easy to satisfy.
The charioteer replied: “Upāsikā!

If it is so, your wish will surely be fulfilled; before long you shall see the Upāsikā with few desires and contentment, holding her robes and bowl, accepting and eating what others have discarded, having shaved her head and donned the dyed garments, severing craving for the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, becoming free from the bonds of greed, and exhausting all outflows.”

That brahmin and his charioteer, the female lay disciple Vāsīṭṭhā, and the female lay disciple’s daughter Sundarīnandā all went forth from the household life and reached the ultimate end of suffering.
1179. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Great Forest Monastery (Mahāvana) in the kingdom of Vaiśālī.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Vīrya-bharadvāja who, early in the morning, purchased a cow; before he had paid its price, he lost the cow on that very day and did not see it for six days.

At that time, the brahmin, while searching for his oxen, arrived at the Great Forest Monastery. From afar he saw the World-Honored One sitting beneath a tree; his appearance was exceptionally distinguished, his faculties were pure, and his mind was tranquil and silent. He had perfected *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and his body was golden, radiating brilliant light.
Having seen him, he immediately went before him and spoke this verse:
"How is it that you have no desires, And dwell here in empty stillness?
Alone in a secluded, vacant place, How do you find such heart's delight?"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"Whether I lose or whether I gain, my mind remains undisturbed.
O Brahmin, you should know this: do not say that he is like me."
When the mind calculates gain and loss, that mind is not at ease.
Then, the brahmin spoke again in verse:
“The state of the most excellent Brahmin is as the Bhikṣu has described;”
I shall now speak for myself; listen attentively to these words of truth.
This śramaṇa is certainly not the one who lost his ox at dawn and failed to find it after searching for six days; therefore, he dwells in peace and happiness.
A śramaṇa today is certainly not such a person;
Like one who plants a field of sesame, fearing it will be choked by weeds, Therefore he dwells in peace and happiness.
A śramaṇa today is certainly not such a person; Like one who plants a rice paddy but lacks water.
Fearing that the leaves might wither and he die, he therefore dwells in peace and happiness.
Among the śramaṇas there is now certainly no one like this:
there are seven widows who all support orphaned children; thus they dwell in peace and happiness.
A śramaṇa today certainly lacks these seven things that cause one not to cherish their children:
negligence, and being heavily burdened by debt; for this reason, he dwells in peace and happiness.
A śramaṇa today certainly lacks these: creditors standing guard at his door.
Seeking long-lasting wealth, one dwells in peace and happiness; A śramaṇa today certainly has none of it, yet dwells in peace and happiness.
With seven layers of heavy bedding, one dwells in peace and happiness; A śramaṇa today has none of these, yet dwells in peace and happiness.
Anxious and diligent in picking out insects, one dwells in peace and happiness; A śramaṇa today has none of this, yet dwells in peace and happiness.
Now there is certainly no śramaṇa here; the red-eyed, yellow-haired woman hears evil sounds day and night, and for this reason dwells in peace and happiness.
Now there is certainly no śramaṇa here; in the empty granary, a swarm of rats plays.
"Constantly worried about its weakness and exhaustion, / For this reason, it dwells in peace and happiness.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse, answering:
"Today I certainly did not / Lose my ox in the early morning."
Seeking for six days without success, I therefore dwell in peace and happiness.
Today I certainly have no sesame fields to plant;
fearing constantly that they might be ruined by weeds, I therefore dwell in peace and happiness.
Today I am truly free from this: the paddy fields lack water, and fearing the leaves will wither and die, I dwell in peace and happiness.
Today I am truly free from this: there are seven widowed daughters.
I have fully supported all orphaned children; therefore, I dwell in peace and happiness.
Today, I certainly lack those seven kinds of children who are not loved;
being free from negligence and heavy debt, I dwell in peace and happiness.
Today I am certainly free from creditors guarding my door and demanding interest on long-term debts;
for this reason, I dwell in peace and happiness.
Today I am certainly free from seven heavy sets of bedding.
Through diligent care in selecting my companions, I therefore dwell in peace and happiness.
Today I certainly have no wife with yellow hair and red eyes, whose harsh voices I hear day and night; therefore, I dwell in peace and happiness.
Today I am certainly free from [fear]; while mice play in an empty granary, they constantly worry about their own weakness and exhaustion; therefore, I dwell in peace and happiness.
Without abandoning mindfulness or non-mindfulness, sentient beings dwell in peace and happiness.
"Having severed desire and departed from affection, one attains dwelling in peace and happiness.

At that time, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma in various ways to the brahmin Puṇṇa Mantāniputta, instructing, exhorting, illuminating, and gladdening him. According to the Buddha’s customary method, he preached the Dharma in sequence: on generosity and ethical discipline, up until [the point where] his mind attained fearlessness within the True Dharma.
Immediately rising from his seat, he joined his palms and addressed the Buddha:
"May I now go forth into homelessness to study the Path within this True Dharma and Discipline, attain the status of a bhikṣu, and practice the holy life?"
The Buddha told the brahmin:
“You may now go forth in this true Dharma and Vinaya, receive full ordination, and practice the various holy life until you attain arhatship and the mind is well-liberated.”
At that time, the brahmin Vīrapāla, having attained arhatship, realized it through his own direct knowledge and, experiencing the bliss of liberation, spoke this verse:
"I am now filled with great joy, Within the supreme Dharma of the Great Sage.
Having attained the bliss of freedom from desire, I no longer harbor views regarding the Buddha."
1180. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the brahmin village of Sālā in the Śāla Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having dressed in the morning and taken up his bowl, entered a brahmin village to beg for food, when unseasonable clouds arose.
