Thereupon, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"I shall now go to the great assembly hall of the brahmin householder Brahmayu in this brahmin village."
Having formed this thought, he immediately went toward that great assembly hall.
At that time, the brahmins and householders were all gathered in the hall; seeing the World-Honored One from afar, they said to one another:
"What dharma does that shaven-headed śramaṇa actually know?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the brahmin householders of the village of Bālakalpa, saying:
"Among the brahmins, there are those who know the Dharma and those who do not;
among the kṣatriya householders as well, there are those who know the Dharma and those who do not."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"One does not wish to surpass one's friends; A king does not subdue those who are difficult to subdue;
A wife does not seek to surpass her husband; One without children does not show reverence to their father."
"One who has no assembly and no [false] wisdom, who does not speak words contrary to wisdom,
and who has completely severed greed, hatred, and delusion— such a person is called a wise one. At that time,
the brahmin householder addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Gautama! Welcome, noble sir;
please enter this hall and take a seat.
After the Blessed One had sat down, the text continues.
They immediately said, "Gautama, we wish to hear the Dharma you teach.

At that time, the World-Honored One, for the sake of that great assembly of brahmins and householders, taught the Dharma in various ways, instructing, exhorting, illuminating, and gladdening them; having done so, he further spoke these verses:
When the ignorant and the wise gather together, who but the eloquent can discern the truth?
Those capable of expounding the path of tranquility possess wisdom through their speech.
The speaker reveals the True Dharma and raises the banner of the Great Sage.
“Skillful speech is the banner of the sages; the Dharma is the banner of the arhats.
At that time, the World-Honored One established the True Dharma for the brahmin elders of the village of Bālakalpa, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them, he rose from his seat and departed.
1181 (1181). Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of Kosala and arrived at the village of Bhūri. He stayed in the Āmra grove of the brahmin Devadatta, with the Venerable Upavāna serving as his attendant.
At that time, the World-Honored One suffered from back pain and addressed the Venerable Upama:
"Having taken up your robe and bowl, go to the house of the brahmin Devadatta."

At that time, the brahmin Devadatta was in the central hall, having his barber attend to his hair and beard. Seeing the Venerable Upama standing at the outer gate, he spoke this verse upon seeing him:
"What kind of one is it who has shaved his hair and beard, yet wears the saṃghāṭī robe?"
Standing outside that gate, what do you seek to obtain?
The Venerable Upama replied in verse:
“The Arhat, the Well-Gone One of the world, suffers from a wind ailment in his back.”
"Is there perhaps a soothing water that might cure the illness of the Muni?

Then, the brahmin Devadatta, carrying a bowl filled with ghee, a jar of oil, and a jar of honey, and having someone carry warm water, followed Venerable Upavāna to the Blessed One’s dwelling. He applied the substances to the Blessed One’s body, washed him with the warm water, and provided the ghee and honey as a drink; thus, the Blessed One’s back ailment was immediately relieved.
At that time, the brahmin Devadatta rose early in the morning, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and spoke these verses:
"What is meant by 'brahmin'?"
By giving what does one obtain great fruit?
What constitutes timely giving?
And how is the field of merit purified?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"If one attains the knowledge of past lives, Sees the fixed destiny of rebirth among the devas,
And achieves the exhaustion of all outflows— The Muni has awakened to the three types of clear knowledge."
One who well understands the liberation of the mind and is liberated from all greed is called a *brāhmaṇa*.
Giving to such a person yields great fruit;
giving to them is a timely gift, for they are a field of merit according to one's wishes.
At that time, the brahmin Devadaha, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and approved with gladness;
he paid homage and departed. 1182 (1182). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the human realm of Kosala and stayed for one night in the Śāla Grove.
At that time, there was a brahmin who, not far from the Śāla grove, was engaged in agricultural work.

Rising early in the morning to labor, he went into the Śāla grove and saw from afar the World-Honored One sitting beneath a tree. His appearance was upright and dignified; his faculties were pure; his mind was tranquil and settled; he was fully accomplished in the supreme *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; his body was golden in color, and its radiance shone forth everywhere.
Having seen him, he went to where he was and said: "Gautama!
I have recently been conducting business here, and for that reason I take pleasure in this grove."
"Gautama, what business do you have here that you take pleasure in this forest?
He further spoke in verse:
"For what purpose, O bhikṣu, Do you have business in this forest?"
"Alone, guarding a secluded place, you take delight in this forest.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"There is nothing to be done in this forest; the roots of the forest have long since been severed."
"Detached from the forest and free from the forest, he does not delight in the cessation of meditative reflection.
Then, having heard what the Buddha had said, that brahmin rejoiced and approved, paid homage, and departed.
1183. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was wandering through the human realm of Kosala and stayed overnight in a śāla grove.
At that time, there was a brahmin living near the edge of that forest together with five hundred young brahmins.
That brahmin constantly praised and longed for [the Buddha], thinking:

"I wish to see the World-Honored One; when will he wander through this forest so that I may have the opportunity to meet him, ask about my doubts, and perhaps find the leisure for him to explain them to me?"

At that time, a young disciple of that brahmin, having gone into the forest to gather firewood, saw from afar the World-Honored One sitting beneath a tree. His deportment was upright and handsome; his faculties were tranquil and his mind was settled in meditative concentration. His form was like a mountain of gold, and his radiance shone forth brilliantly.
Having seen him, he thought to himself:

"My preceptor, the brahmin, always praises and admires him, desiring to see Gautama to ask about his doubts. Now that this śramaṇa Gautama has arrived in this forest, I shall go quickly to inform my preceptor."
He immediately took up a bundle of firewood and returned quickly to the study hall.
Having set down the bundle of wood, he went to the Upādhyāya and said:

"Upādhyāya, you should know that you have always praised, admired, and longed to see the śramaṇa Gautama. If he should happen to come to this grove, you should ask him about your doubts; today Gautama has already arrived at this grove—Upādhyāya, know that the time has come!"
Then the brahmin went to where the World-Honored One was, and after exchanging greetings and expressions of courtesy face-to-face, he withdrew to sit at one side.
He then spoke in verse:
"Entering alone this terrifying, Profound and dense forest,"
Firmly established and unshakable, he skillfully cultivates the dharma of right effort.
Without song, dance, or music, he dwells in silent seclusion;
such a person who delights alone in the deep forest, I have never before seen.
Do you seek to be a sovereign lord of power in this world?
Or do you desire the sovereign pleasures of the Heaven of the Thirty-three?
For what reason, in this deep forest, do you emaciate yourself through ascetic practices?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with these verses:
"If one seeks various things, One becomes attached to the many kinds of realms;
All of those are, in fact, The very root of ignorance."
All such seeking, I have long since completely cast off;
Seeking nothing and free from flattery or hypocrisy, I am untouched by anything.
Regarding all phenomena, I maintain only this single pure contemplation.
"Having attained unsurpassed enlightenment, you take no pleasure in the cultivation of meditative contemplation.
The Brahmin spoke again in verse:
"I now pay homage to you, the Greatly Tranquil Honored Muni."
The Sovereign of the Subtlety of Dhyāna-contemplation, Awakened to the boundless Great Awakening;
The Tathāgata, savior of devas and humans, Majestic as a mountain of gold.
Liberated from the thicket of existence, He is forever unattached to that forest.
Having extracted the deep and sharp thorns, he is pure without a trace remaining.
Foremost among the masters of treatises, his eloquence is most supreme;
a lion among men, he roars within the deep forest.
He reveals the Noble Truth of Suffering, Its Origin, its Cessation, and the Eightfold Path;
Able to exhaust the entire mass of suffering, One mounts [the vehicle] and emerges, pure and stainless.
Having liberated oneself from all suffering, one rescues those sentient beings who suffer;
for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to sentient beings, one expounds the True Dharma.
Having severed all affectionate attachment, one remains far removed from the net of desire.
Having severed all fetters of craving for existence,
Like a lotus born from water, unsullied by dust or water;
Like the sun suspended in the sky, pure and free from clouds.
How wonderful that today, having come to the forest of Kosala,
I have been able to see the Great Teacher, the Supreme among bipeds,
the one of great diligence in the Great Forest, who has attained the foremost and vast deliverance.
"The foremost of trainers, I pay homage to the Fearless One.
At that time, the brahmin, having recited this verse in praise of the Buddha, heard what the Buddha had said; filled with joy and sympathetic delight, he prostrated and departed.
1184. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was wandering through the human realm of Kosala and stayed by the bank of the Sundarī River.

At that time, not long after the World-Honored One had shaved his hair, during the latter part of the night, he sat cross-legged, straightening his body and applying himself to contemplation, with mindfulness fixed before him, covering his head with his robe.

At that time, there lived a brahmin on the banks of the Sundaṛī River. Rising at night to perform a sacrificial offering, he had leftover food that was not yet consumed; he then went to the riverbank, wishing to seek out a virtuous brahmin to whom he might offer it.
At that time, the World-Honored One heard the voice of the brahmin by the riverbank.
Having heard it, he cleared his throat and pulled back his robe to reveal his head.
Then, having seen the Buddha, the brahmin by the side of the Sunda River thought to himself:
"This is a shaven-headed śramaṇa, not a brāhmaṇa," he thought,
intending to take the food and return.
That brāhmaṇa then had this further thought:
"It is not only among the śramaṇas that there are those who shave their heads; there are also those among the brāhmaṇas who shave their heads. You should go to them and ask about his birth.
Then, a brāhmaṇa from the banks of the Sundaḷī River approached the World-Honored One and asked him:
"By what clan was he born?"
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Do not ask about one's birth; You should ask only about one's conduct.
Even wood carved for a fire-drill Is able to produce fire."
Within a lowly caste, there arose a steadfast Muni;
possessing wisdom and a sense of shame, diligent and well-disciplined,
he reached the ultimate limit of great illumination and purely cultivated the holy life.
"Now is precisely the time; you should offer me the remaining food.
Then, the Brahmin by the side of the Sunda River spoke again in verse:
"Today is an auspicious day; seeking merit, I practice this offering."
"If I should encounter a Great Being, the Most Victorious Honored One of the three times, and yet fail to see the Buddha, I shall instead give it to another.

At that time, the brahmin by the side of the Sunda river gained faith; he immediately took the remaining food to offer to the World-Honored One, but the World-Honored One did not accept it because it had been obtained through the recitation of verses. The detailed account of how the food was obtained due to the aforementioned recitation of verses is as previously explained.
On the banks of the Sunda river, a brahmin said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Where should this offered food now be placed?”
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"I do not see any among the devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, celestial deities, or worldly beings who are able to eat this food and cause their bodies to be at peace."
"Take this food and place it in water free of insects, or upon a patch of grass with few living beings.

At that time, the brahmin immediately took the food and placed it in water free of insects; instantly, smoke rose from the water as it boiled and surged, making a sizzling sound, just like when a red-hot iron ball is cast into cold water, causing smoke to rise and the water to boil and surge with a sizzling sound.
Thus, as that food was cast into the insect-free water, smoke arose and it boiled up, making a sizzling sound.

On the banks of the Sunda river, a brahmin, his heart seized with terror and the hair on his body standing on end, thought it to be a calamitous portent; he rushed to the shore, gathered dry wood, and made offerings to the sacrificial fire, seeking to appease the ominous disaster.
The World-Honored One saw them gathering dry wood to offer as oblations to the sacrificial fire, hoping thereby to appease calamities and portents.
Having seen this,
he immediately spoke these verses:
“The Brahmins’ fire-sacrifice burns dry grass and wood;
do not call this the pure path that can dispel all calamities.
This is merely a wicked offering, yet they claim it is wisdom.”
Through such causes and conditions, the non-Buddhists take up the cultivation of purity.
You now cast away the firewood of external fire and kindle the blazing internal fire;
constantly practice heedfulness and remain ever rich in offerings.
Everywhere they give rise to pure faith and extensively arrange great assemblies;
with the mind as the bundle of firewood, the smoke of anger arises,
the taste of false speech is the dust, and the mouth and tongue are the wooden ladle.
Where the fire of passion blazes within the breast, the fire of desire is ever kindled.
One should skillfully tame oneself and extinguish the fire of the person;
with right faith as a great river and pure precepts as a means of crossing, one may pass over.
The clear and pure flowing water is praised by the wise!
With the pure celestial virtues of a human being, one should bathe therein;
Though wading through the waters, they do not cling to the body, And one crosses to the further shore in peace and bliss.
The True Dharma is a deep abyss, Filled with the pure water of merit; It is praised by the wise!
O Pure Virtue among Men and Gods, You should bathe therein.
Crossing through the waters without being drenched, one reaches the further shore in peace and joy.
Truly well-tamed and self-controlled, one guards and cultivates the holy life;
taking compassion as one’s ascetic practice, the heart is pure in its reality.
"Bathing with the True Dharma is what the wise praise.
At that time, the brahmin by the side of the Sunda river, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and approved, and departed by way back.
1185. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of Kosala and was staying in a grove by the side of the Sundarī River.

At that time, a brahmin living on the banks of the Sundaṛī River came to where the Buddha was staying. After exchanging greetings and polite inquiries with him, he withdrew to sit at one side and asked the Buddha:
"Gautama!..."
"Have you gone to bathe in the river Sunda?
The Buddha said to the brahmin,
"What need is there to bathe in the river Sunda?"
The brahmin said to the Buddha, “Gautama!
The river Sundarī is a number of deliverance, a number of auspiciousness, and a number of purity; if anyone bathes therein, it can completely eliminate all evils from that person.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Neither the Sundaṛī River, nor the Vāhuda, nor the Gayā or Sarayu—
none of such rivers as these [can wash away defilement].”
Though one may commit various evils and unwholesome deeds, [the Dharma] can cause them to become pure.
The Ganges, the Bahudā, and the Sundarī River—
though fools dwell constantly therein, they cannot eliminate their manifold evils.
For one who is pure, what need is there for bathing?
For one who is pure, what need is there for the uposatha?
One purifies oneself through pure deeds; this arises from upholding [the precepts].
Not killing and not stealing, No sexual misconduct and no lying;
With faith in giving to remove the stain of stinginess— In this one bathes.
Toward all sentient beings, One should always give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion.
If one uses well water for bathing, why employ Gaya and the like?
When the inner mind is naturally pure, there is no need to wash the exterior.
A lowly son of a peasant has much filth upon his body; [how can external washing remove it?]
"Water may wash away external dust and filth, but it cannot purify the interior.
At that time, the brahmin by the side of the Sundaṛī River, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and approved with gladness; he rose from his seat and departed.
1186. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Park.

At that time, there was a brahmin named Jaṭila Raivata who, when he was formerly a layman, had been a spiritual friend to the Buddha. He approached the place where the Buddha was, and after exchanging greetings and words of consolation face-to-face, withdrew to sit at one side.
And he spoke in verse:
“The one who binds his hair on the outside Is merely called ‘one with bound hair’;
The one who binds his mind within Is one who fetters sentient beings.”
"I now ask Gautama: how does one untie the entangled hair?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"By upholding the pure precepts and cultivating right awakening within the mind,"
"By applying oneself with diligence and skillful means, one thus unties the entangled hair-tuft.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the brahmin Entangled Hair-tuft rejoiced and approved, rose from his seat, and departed.
1187. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Park.
At that time, a brahmin named Jaṭī-Bharadvāja approached the Buddha; having come forward to inquire after his well-being and exchange greetings, he withdrew to sit at one side.
And he spoke in verse:
“The one who binds his topknot on the outside of the body Is merely binding a topknot in name;
The one who binds his topknot within the mind Is a fetter for sentient beings.”
I now ask the Gautama: regarding one whose hair is thus matted, what means should be employed?
Where is this matted hair severed?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered with these verses:
"The eye, ear, and nose, The tongue, body, and the sense-base of mind—
Regarding those names and forms, He causes them to be extinguished without remainder."
"When all consciousnesses are eternally extinguished, / Therein one cuts off the matted locks.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the brahmin Jaṭila Bharadvāja, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and delighted in it; he rose from his seat and departed.

1188. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the foot of the Bodhi tree on the bank of the Nairañjanā River near the village of Uruvilvā, not long after his attainment of Buddhahood.
At that time, the World-Honored One was reflecting in solitude and had this thought:
"Lack of respect is a great suffering; it brings no order."
If there is no other sovereign power to be feared, then one’s progress toward the great purpose will decline;
whereas if there is reverence, order, and the presence of another sovereign power, one dwells in peace and happiness;
and with reverence, order, and the presence of another sovereign power, the great purpose is fulfilled.

Is there anyone among the devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, celestial deities, or human beings who possesses a precept-attainment superior to mine, a concentration-attainment superior to mine, a wisdom-attainment superior to mine, a liberation-attainment superior to mine, or a knowledge-and-vision-of-liberation superior to mine—such that I might revere and honor them, serve and make offerings to them, and dwell in dependence upon them?
Again, he thought:

"There is no god, Māra, Brahmā, ascetic, brahmin, deity, or human being who possesses a preeminence in the perfection of ethical discipline, a preeminence in meditative concentration, a preeminence in wisdom, a preeminence in liberation, or a preeminence in the knowledge and vision of liberation, such that I should revere, honor, serve, and make offerings to them, and dwell in dependence upon them."
"Only the True Dharma has enabled me to awaken for myself and become a Samyaksaṃbuddha; I shall revere and honor it, serve and make offerings to it, and abide in reliance upon it."
Why is this? The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past also revered, honored, served, and made offerings to the True Dharma, dwelling in reliance upon it;
the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of all future ages shall likewise revere, honor, serve, and make offerings to the True Dharma, dwelling in reliance upon it.

At that time, Brahmā Sahāmpati, the lord of the Sahā world, having understood the World-Honored One’s thought, vanished from the Brahma heaven and appeared before the Buddha in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, and he exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"So it is, Blessed One! So it is, Sugata!

For one who is indolent and lacks reverence, it is a truly great suffering... [The passage continues] until: "...the fulfillment of the great purpose. Indeed, there are no devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, celestial beings, or worldly people who possess a superiority in the perfection of ethical discipline, a superiority in meditative concentration, a superiority in wisdom, a superiority in liberation, or a superiority in the knowledge and vision of liberation over the Blessed One, such that they would cause the Blessed One to be revered, honored, served, and venerated, or upon whom the Blessed One would depend for his dwelling."

Only the True Dharma, which the Tathāgata himself realized and attained as perfect enlightenment, is that which the Tathāgata should revere and honor, serve and make offerings to, and upon which one should rely and abide.
Why is this? The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past also revered, honored, served, and made offerings to the True Dharma, and dwelt in reliance upon it;
the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the future shall likewise revere, honor, serve, and make offerings to the True Dharma, and dwell in reliance upon it.
"The World-Honored One, too, should revere and honor that True Dharma, serve and make offerings to it, and dwell in reliance upon it.
At that time, the Brahma King spoke again in verse:
"The Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past, And all the Buddhas of the future,"
The present Buddha, the World-Honored One, is able to remove the sorrows of sentient beings.
All who revere the Dharma abide by relying on the True Dharma;
such reverence is the very nature of all Buddhas' teachings.

At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the Brahmā Śikhin rejoiced and expressed his approval. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight. (1189) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the foot of the Bodhi tree on the banks of the Nairañjanā River near the village of Uruvilvā, not long after he had attained enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One, reflecting in solitary stillness, had this thought:

"There is a single vehicle path that can purify sentient beings, deliver them from all sorrow and lamentation, eliminate suffering and affliction, and lead to the attainment of the Dharma of True Suchness; it is called the four foundations of mindfulness."
What are the four?
They are the foundation of mindfulness that contemplates the body as body, and the foundations of mindfulness that contemplate feelings, the mind, and phenomena as phenomena.
If there is anyone who does not delight in these four foundations of mindfulness, they do not delight in the noble Dharma.
One who does not delight in the noble Dharma does not delight in the noble Path;
one who does not delight in the noble Path does not delight in the Dharma of the Deathless (amṛta);
and one who does not delight in the Dharma of the Deathless is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering.
If one delights in cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness, then one delights in cultivating the Dharma of the noble ones;
if one delights in cultivating the Dharma of the noble ones, then one delights in the noble path;
if one delights in the noble path, then one delights in the Dharma of the Deathless.
"Those who delight in the Dharma of the Deathless (amṛta) shall attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering.

At that time, Brahmā Sahāmpati, the lord of the Sahā world, knowing the Buddha’s thoughts, vanished from the Brahma heaven and appeared before the Buddha in the time it takes a strong man to bend or extend his arm, and uttered this praise:
"So it is, World-Honored One!"
"So it is, Sugata!

There is a single vehicle path that can purify sentient beings; namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, which lead even unto liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering."
Then, Brahmā Śikhin spoke again in verse:
“There is that which is called the One Vehicle Path, Which perceives the limit of all existences;
It proclaims the True Dharma To bring comfort to suffering sentient beings.”
The World-Honored Ones of the past, Having traversed by means of this path, have crossed over;
The World-Honored Ones of the future, Shall likewise cross over by means of this path.
The Honored One of Perfect Enlightenment in the present, Rides upon this to cross the flow of the ocean.
Having reached the ultimate limit of birth and death, his mind is tamed and pure;
regarding the cycle of saṃsāra, he has forever extinguished it entirely.
Knowing the various realms, his eye of wisdom reveals the true path.
Just as the flowing waters of the Ganges all return to the great ocean,
surging and rushing far away, so too is the Noble Path.
The One of Vast Wisdom has skillfully revealed it, leading one to attain the Dharma of the Deathless.
This supreme Wheel of the True Dharma, never heard before,
has been turned for the sake of sentient beings out of compassion for them;
it protects the multitudes of devas and humans, enabling them to cross to the further shore of existence.
"Therefore, all sentient beings / Shall together bow their heads in prostration.
At that time, Brahmā, King of Devas, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced with gladness, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, and immediately vanished from sight.

1190. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the foot of the Bodhi tree on the banks of the Nairañjanā River in the village of Uruvilvā, not long after his attainment of Buddhahood.

At that time, Brahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, with his most exquisite physical form, approached the Buddha during the late hours of the night. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and spoke in verse:
“Among all lineages, the Kṣatriya is the most honored among bipeds;
One who is perfected in knowledge and conduct is the most supreme among gods and humans!”
The Buddha told the Brahmā King:
"So it is, Brahmā! So it is, Brahmā!"
"Among all castes, the Kṣatriya is the most honored among two-legged beings;
those who are perfected in knowledge and conduct are the most excellent among gods and humans.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Brahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and expressed his approval. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.

1191. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of Kosala and stayed in a secluded place where there were no villages, lodging there for the night with a community of bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One was teaching the dharmas conducive to forest dwelling (*āraṇyaka*) to the bhikṣus.
Then, Brahmā Sahāmpati, the Lord of the Sahā World, had this thought:
"Now the World-Honored One is traveling among the people of Kośala and is staying in a secluded place devoid of villages, lodging for the great assembly in the wilderness."
At that time, the World-Honored One was teaching the Dharma of conformity to emptiness to the great assembly. "I shall now go there to accord with and praise it!

Just as a strong man might bend or extend his arm, he vanished from the Brahma Heaven and appeared before the Buddha. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and spoke these verses:
"Practicing in the seclusion of forest retreats, One cuts off all afflictions; The Tathāgata has taught this Dharma For the sake of attaining liberation."
If one does not delight in solitude, one should enter the assembly and guard oneself;
taming one's own mind, one goes from house to house for alms,
restraining the sense faculties and applying oneself with focused mindfulness.
Thereafter, one practices in seclusion, upon the seats of an araṇya;
far removed from all terrors, one dwells fearlessly and in peace.
Even if there be those who are fierce and perilous, or the manifold venomous harms of evil serpents—
Amidst black clouds and great darkness,
with thunder shaking and lightning flashing, because they are free from all afflictions, they dwell in peace day and night.
According to the Dharma as I have heard it, until the ultimate goal is reached...
Practicing the holy life alone, one does not fear the death-demon of a thousand;
if one cultivates the path of awakening, one does not fear even ten thousand.
Whether they be *srotāpannas* or those who have attained the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*, [they likewise do not fear].
"And as for those who have attained the stage of Anāgāmin, their number is likewise immeasurable;
one cannot determine their exact count, lest one fall into the terror of false speech.
At that time, Brahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced with gladness, paid homage to the Buddha, and immediately vanished from sight.

1192. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Kapilavastu forest at Kapilavastu together with five hundred bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who had done what was to be done, who had laid down their heavy burdens, who had attained their own benefit, who had destroyed the fetters of existence, and whose minds were well-liberated through right knowledge.
At that time, the World-Honored One was teaching the Dharma associated with Nirvana to the great assembly.
Then, the powerful devas from the great assemblies of the worlds of the ten directions all came to the gathering, making offerings to the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus.
Furthermore, various Brahmā kings dwelling in the Brahma-world had this thought:

"Today the Buddha is staying in the kingdom of Kapilavastu... as described at length above, up until "...having made offerings to the World-Honored One and the great assembly, we shall now go forth to praise him individually!"
Having formed this thought, in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he vanished from the Brahma Heaven and stood before the Buddha.
The First Brahmā then spoke these verses:
"In this great forest, The great assembly has gathered like clouds."
The celestial hosts of the ten directions have all come to pay their respects;
therefore, I have traveled from afar to prostrate before this most excellent and invincible Saṃgha.
A second Brahmā then spoke in verse:
"These bhikṣus of the Saṃgha, with hearts of true diligence,
within this great forest, restrain their faculties and seek deliverance.
Then the third Brahmā spoke a verse:
Through skillful means, he dissolves the deep and sharp thorns of affection;
firm and unshakable, like the banner of Indra.
Having crossed the flow of the deep moat, he is pure and seeks no sensual desires.
The skillful guide who delivers others, the great dragon among those who have been tamed.
The fourth Brahmā then spoke this verse:
“Those who take refuge in the Buddha shall never fall into the evil realms.”
"One can sever the body of a human being, And obtain a celestial body to experience bliss.
Having each spoken this verse, the bodies of the four Brahmā deities immediately vanished and were no longer seen. 1193 (1193) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was Brahmā Sahāmpati, the lord of the Sahā world, who daily applied himself with diligence to go to the Buddha’s dwelling to pay him respect and make offerings.
At that time, the Lord of the Sahā World thought to himself:

"It is too early this morning for us to come and see the Buddha, as he is currently entering the Great Samādhi. We shall instead go to the room of the bhikṣu Kokālika, who is a partisan of Devadatta."
Having formed this thought, he immediately entered that room; reaching the door, he tapped on it with his finger and spoke these words: "Kokālika!
"Kokālika!
Do not give rise to impure thoughts toward Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana; lest you suffer for a long night without benefit!
Kokālika replied:
"Who are you? Brahmā replied, "I am Brahmā,
the King of Gods, Lord of the Sahā World."
Kokālika said,
"Has the World-Honored One not declared that you have attained the stage of Anāgāmin?
The Brahmā King replied:
"So be it, bhikkhu! Kokālika said,
"For what reason have you come?"
The Brahmā King, Lord of the Sahā World, replied:
"This cannot be cured.
He then spoke in verse:
"To attempt to measure that which is immeasurable by giving rise to a mind of calculation—
what wise person would conceive such a notion?
To desire to measure the immeasurable is the characteristic of an ordinary person shrouded by the hindrances."
At that time, Brahmā Sahāmpati, the lord of the Sahā world, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"I have always come diligently to the Buddha's presence every day to pay my respects and make offerings. I thought to myself:
'It is too early this morning to see the World-Honored One, as he is currently entering a great samādhi; I shall instead go to the room of the bhikṣu Kokālika, who is an associate of Devadatta.'"
He then stood at the door, knocked gently, and spoke these words:
"Kokālika! Kokālika!"
"You should give rise to pure faith toward Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, who are virtuous and wise; do not suffer harm and pain for a long night!
Kokālika said, "Who are you?"
I then replied,
"He is Brahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World.
Kokālika said:
"Did the World-Honored One not declare that you have attained the stage of Anāgāmin? I replied: "It is so."
Kokālika spoke again,
“Why have you come?
I thought to myself:
"This cannot be cured.
He then spoke in verse:
"To attempt to measure that which is immeasurable By giving rise to the thought of calculation—”
"To attempt to measure that which is immeasurable—this is the obscuration of the foolish worldling.
The Buddha said to the Brahma King: "So it is, so it is."
Brahmā King!
"To attempt to measure that which is immeasurable—
how could a person of wisdom give rise to such a deluded thought?"
"To attempt to measure the immeasurable—this is the veil of the aggregates belonging to the foolish worldling.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Brahmā Sahampati, the Lord of the Sahā World, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and approved with gladness. He rose from his seat, prostrated before the Buddha, and immediately vanished from sight.
1194. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, Mahābrahmā and other distinct Brahmās—such as Subāhu Brahmā—daily employed skillful means to go and visit, see, and make offerings to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Brahmā Baku saw another Brahmā—Brahmā Subāhu—who was diligently applying skillful means, and asked him:
"Where do you wish to go?"
He replied, "I wish to see the World-Honored One and pay him respectful homage.
Then, the Brahmā Baku spoke this verse:
"He has four white swans and three palaces of golden hue;
five hundred and seventy-two practitioners of dhyāna,
their bodies of blazing golden color, universally illuminating the Brahma palace."
“Behold my body for a moment; what need is there to go there?
Then the Brahmā King Subrahmā and the Brahmā King Vibrahmā—Subrahmā Vibrahmā—spoke again in verse:
“Though you possess a golden body That shines everywhere throughout the Brahma palace,”
"Those who possess wisdom know that form is accompanied by afflictions;
the wise do not delight in form, for their minds are liberated.
At that time, the Brahmā Subrahmā—Subrahmā with the Excellent Arm—approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have now employed skillful means, desiring to come and see the World-Honored One to pay respectful homage and make offerings.
The Brahmā Baka, seeing my skillful means, questioned me, saying:”
"What do you intend to do with these skillful means? I replied,
"I wish to go and see the World-Honored One, to pay him homage, serve him, and make offerings."
The Brahmā deity Bhaṅgu then spoke in verse:
“There are four kinds of cranes, And three palaces of golden hue;
Within these five hundred and seventy-two, One practices meditative concentration.”
"Behold my body, golden in color, Shining everywhere throughout the Brahma palaces;
You need only observe my body— What need is there to go there?
I then spoke this verse in reply to him:
"Though one possesses a golden body that universally illuminates the Brahma palaces,
know that this 'true gold color' is itself a matter of affliction."
"The wise one is liberated from form; they no longer take delight in form.
The Buddha said to Brahmā: "So it is, Brahmā!"
Thus it is, Brahmā!
"Though there be a true golden color, universally illuminating the Brahmā palace,
you should know that this true golden color is itself a matter of affliction."
"The wise one is liberated from form; he finds no further delight in form.
Then, for the sake of the bhikṣu Kaṭamorakatissa, that Brahmā spoke this verse:
"When a man is born into the world, an axe is held within his mouth."
He even cut his own body apart; this was caused by evil speech.
To praise those who deserve censure, and to disparage those who deserve praise—such malicious speech increases one's faults, and wherever one is born, there will be no peace or happiness.
Gambling, chess, and wine squander wealth, yet their transgressions are very few;
to harbor an evil heart toward the Sugata is a truly great transgression!
There are hundreds of thousands of hells, known as the Nirarbuda hell.
"Six hundred and thirty, plus five Ābhāsvara [deities];
all these were cast into the hells for slandering the noble ones, due to the evil vows of their speech and mind.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, those Brahmā devas, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and approved with gladness; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.
1195. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, there was a Brahmā named Baka residing in the Brahma Heaven, who gave rise to this evil and false view, saying:
"This is the eternal, constant, and unchanging state; it is the singular place of definitive liberation.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the mind of the Brahmā Baka, entered into samādhi; according to his meditative attainment, he vanished from Rājagṛha and appeared in the Brahma Heaven.
The Brahmā deity Bhaṃgu saw the World-Honored One from afar and spoke this verse:
"Seventy-two Brahmās, Creating all manner of merit and happiness;
Sovereign and eternally abiding, They have transcended birth, old age, and death."
"I have reached the ultimate mastery in the study of all the vidyā-śāstras;
those hosts of devas believe that I alone am eternal.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"This is but an extremely short lifespan, not one that endures long;
yet the Brahmā deity Baka considers himself long-lived.
In the Nirarbuda hell, their lifespan numbers in the hundreds of thousands."
"I remember and know them all; you yourself claim to endure forever!
Brahmā Baka spoke again in verse:
"That which the Buddha, the World-Honored One, perceives—those kalpas are boundless."
Birth, old age, death, sorrow, and lamentation—these have all already passed away.
I pray only that you will tell me: what past deeds did I perform, what precepts did I uphold, and by what karma was it obtained that I am born here?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered with a verse, saying:
"In the distant past, eons ago, there was a great multitude traveling through a vast wilderness;
many were sages practicing the holy life."
Those who are famished and lack provisions—you have rescued them and enabled them to cross over;
with a compassionate heart of salvation that continues in succession, it remains undiminished throughout kalpas.
This is the merit you have received and maintained in the past.
I remember and know them all, as clearly as one awakens from sleep.
Long ago, there was a village that was plundered by bandits;
you rescued everyone at that time, causing them to attain liberation.
This, then, is the meritorious karma I have upheld throughout past lives;
remembering these causal conditions, it is as if awakening from sleep after a long or short time.
In the past, there was a multitude of people traveling by boat upon the Ganges River.
An evil dragon seized that boat, wishing to take your life entirely;
at that time, by means of your supernormal power, you rescued him and granted him liberation.
This was the meritorious karma you had cultivated and maintained in the past.
"I recall these causes and conditions, as one who has long been asleep awakens.
The Brahmā deity Baku then spoke in verse:
"You certainly know all things regarding me, the matters of life and death throughout the past and present."
Knowing all else as well, he is indeed the Perfectly Awakened One;
therefore, the body he has received radiates golden light everywhere,
and while his body abides here, its brilliance pervades the entire world.

At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma in various ways to the Brahmā Baka, instructing, exhorting, illuminating, and gladdening him. Having done so, he vanished from the Brahma world by means of his meditative attainment and returned to the city of Rājagṛha.
1196 (1196). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a Brahmā deity dwelling in the Brahma-heaven who gave rise to such a false view, saying:
"This place is eternal, constant, and unchanging; it is the sole, pure liberation. I have never seen anyone come to this place, much less anyone who has surpassed it."

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the mind of that Brahmā, immediately entered into samādhi; according to his meditative attainment, he vanished from Śrāvastī and appeared in the Brahmā palace, sitting cross-legged in mid-air directly above the crown of that Brahmā’s head, with body erect and mindfulness established.
At that time, the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya had this thought:
"Where is the World-Honored One staying today?
He then used his purified divine eye, which surpasses the human eye, and beheld the World-Honored One in the Brahma Heaven.

Having seen this, he immediately entered into samādhi; according to his meditative attainment, he vanished from Śrāvastī and appeared in that Brahma-world. Standing to the east and facing west toward the Buddha, he sat cross-legged, with body upright and mindfulness focused, beneath the Buddha’s seat and upon the Brahma-throne.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa had this thought:
"Where is the World-Honored One staying today?
He then used his divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, and saw that the World-Honored One was in the Brahma Heaven.

Having seen this, he immediately entered into samādhi; according to his meditative attainment, he vanished from Śrāvastī and appeared in the Brahma Heaven. To the south, facing north toward the Buddha, he sat cross-legged, with body upright and mindfulness focused, beneath the Buddha’s seat and upon a Brahma throne.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra had this thought:
"Where is the World-Honored One now?
He then used his divine eye, which is purer than the human eye, and saw that the World-Honored One was in the Brahma Heaven.

Having seen him, he immediately entered samādhi; according to his meditative attainment, he vanished from Śrāvastī and dwelt in the Brahma Heaven. To the west, facing east toward the Buddha, he sat cross-legged, with body upright and mindfulness focused, beneath the Buddha’s seat and upon the seat of the Brahma Heaven.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had this thought:
"Where is the Blessed One staying today?
With his divine eye, which is purer than the human eye, he saw from afar that the Blessed One was in the Brahma Heaven.

Having seen this, he immediately entered into samādhi; according to his meditative attainment, he vanished from Śrāvastī and dwelt in the Brahma Heaven. Located to the north, he faced south toward the Buddha, sat cross-legged with body upright and mindfulness focused, beneath the Buddha’s seat and upon a Brahma throne.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Brahmā, saying:
"Do you not now give rise to this view:
'From the very beginning, I have never seen anyone who surpasses me'?"
Brahmā addressed the Buddha:
“I now dare not again say:
‘I have never seen anyone who surpasses me.’”
"Only the radiance of the Brahmā Heaven was seen to be obscured.

At that time, the World-Honored One preached various teachings to that Brahmā, instructing, exhorting, illuminating, and gladdening him; he then entered samādhi and, according to his meditative attainment, vanished from the Brahmā Heaven and returned to Śrāvastī.

The Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Mahākāśyapa, and Śāriputra taught the Dharma to that Brahmā in various ways, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him. Having done so, they entered into samādhi and, according to their meditative attainment, vanished from the Brahma world and returned to Śrāvastī; only the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana remained there.
Then, that Brahmā asked the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Do all the other disciples of the World-Honored One possess such great virtue and great power as this?"
Then, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana spoke these verses:
“Virtuous ones endowed with the three knowledges, Who have attained mastery in discerning the minds of others,
The Arhats whose outflows are exhausted— Their number is beyond measure.”

Then, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having taught, instructed, illuminated, and gladdened that Brahmā with various discourses on the Dharma, entered into samādhi; according to his meditative attainment, he vanished from the Brahma realm and returned to Śrāvastī.
1197. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kuśinagara, in the Land of the Mallas, within the grove of twin śāla trees at the site of the Śākya warriors' birth.
At that time, as the World-Honored One was approaching parinirvāṇa, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Spread a rope bed between the twin śāla trees with the head toward the north; today, at midnight, the Tathāgata will enter parinirvāṇa in the nirvana without remainder."

Then, the Venerable Ānanda, having received the instruction of the Blessed One, prepared a rope couch for the Blessed One between the twin śāla trees with its head pointing north. Having done so, he returned to where the Blessed One was, prostrated at his feet, and said to the Blessed One:
“I have prepared a rope couch for the Tathāgata between the twin śāla trees, with its head pointing north.”
Thereupon, the World-Honored One went to the rope-couch, lay down on his right side with his head toward the north, resting one foot upon the other, and fixed his mindfulness on the sign of light.
At that time, during the middle watch of the night, the World-Honored One entered parinirvāṇa in the nirvana without remainder.
Having entered parinirvāṇa, twin *śāla* trees immediately blossomed with flowers, which hung down all around to make offerings to the World-Honored One.
At that time, another bhikṣu spoke this verse:
“The excellent and sturdy tree, With its branches bowing in homage to the Buddha,
Offers exquisite flowers as an offering To the Great Teacher who has entered parinirvāṇa.”
Immediately, Śakra Devānām-Indra spoke this verse:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; They are all subject to the law of arising and ceasing.
Though they arise, they soon perish; This very stillness and extinction is bliss."
Immediately thereafter, Brahmā Sahāmpati, the Lord of the Sahā World, spoke this verse:
"All beings born in the world, Whether standing or otherwise, must eventually pass away;
Yet such a Great Holy Teacher as this Has no equal in the world."
Having attained the powers of a Tathāgata, acting as the universal eye for the world,
he will ultimately pass into extinction and enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Then the Venerable Anuruddha spoke further in verse:
Abiding in the out-breath and in-breath, establishing the mind with skillful restraint,
one comes from that which is relied upon to the parinirvāṇa of the world.
Great terrors arise, causing the hair on one's body to stand on end.
The Great Teacher, endowed with all the powers of practice, has entered parinirvāṇa.
His mind was never indolent, nor did he dwell in any attachments;
his mind and its phenomena were gradually liberated, like a fire extinguished when the fuel is exhausted.
Seven days after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the Venerable Ānanda went to the site of the funeral pyre (citā) and spoke this verse:
“The Teacher’s precious body has ascended to the Brahma heavens;
Possessing such great supernormal power, The internal fire now consumes his body.”
Five hundred cotton cloths wrapped around his body were all consumed by fire and reduced to ashes;
a thousand fine cotton garments were likewise used to wrap the Tathāgata’s body.
Only two garments did not burn: the most excellent outer robe and the inner undergarment.
When the Venerable Ānanda had spoken this verse, the bhikṣus were silent,
moved by both grief and joy. *Saṃyukta Āgama*, Scroll 44 and Scroll 45.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.

Having finished his meal, he returned to the vihāra, put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, took his sitting mat (niṣīdana), placed it over his right shoulder, and entered the Andhavana forest to practice dhyāna.

"Now the śramaṇa Gautama resides at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. Having finished eating, he returned to the vihāra, put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, took his sitting mat (niṣīdana), placed it over his right shoulder, and entered the Andhavana forest to practice meditation.
"I shall now go there to create an obstacle for her.
He then transformed himself into a youth of handsome appearance and went to where that bhikṣuṇī was, saying to her: "Auntie!"
"Where do you wish to go?
The bhikṣuṇī replied,
"Venerable sir!"
"Go to a secluded place.
Then, Māra Pāpīyas spoke this verse:
"There is no escape in this world; what is the use of seeking seclusion?"
"Return to the enjoyment of the five desires; do not let yourself later feel regret.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Āḷavikā thought to herself: "Who is this?"
"This one wishes to terrify me.
Is he a human being,
or is he a non-human being?"
"Is this a deceitful person?
He then thought to himself:
"This must surely be an evil Māra wishing to disturb me."
Having realized this, he spoke in verse:
"There is an escape from the world; I myself know what has been attained.
You, base and evil Māra, do not know that path."
Just as a sharp blade causes harm, so too are the five desires;
just as it cuts through the form of flesh, so too is the aggregate of suffering.
As you have just said, those who indulge in the pleasure of the five desires—
This is not to be delighted in; it is a place of great terror.
Departing from all joy and pleasure, and casting off all great darkness, one realizes cessation through direct experience and dwells securely, free from all outflows.
"O evil Māra, you have been perceived; you shall immediately perish on your own.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought:
"That bhikṣuṇī Āḷavikā already knows my mind."
Filled with sorrow and finding no joy, he immediately vanished and was no longer seen. 1199 (1199). Thus have I heard:
