These bhikṣus are free from all wandering and shifting; they have no skin [of worldly attachment], being truly firm and solid.
At that time, the Venerable Vakkula was in the assembly and had this thought:
"I shall now, in the presence of the World-Honored One and the great assembly, recite verses of appreciation and acceptance.
Having formed this thought, he immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, paid homage to the Buddha, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
I wish to say something, Sugata!
I wish to say something.
The Buddha said to Vakkali,
"Speak as you please! Then Vakkali spoke these verses:
"On the fifteenth day of purification, his assembly of five hundred people severed all fetters;
there were Great Sages who had reached the end [of suffering].
Through association with those of pure character, they attained pure and vast liberation."
No further existence shall be undergone; birth and death are forever severed.
What was to be done has been done; all taints have been exhausted.
The five hindrances have been cleared away like clouds, and the root of craving—the thorn—has been uprooted.
The lion is fearless, having departed from all residual existence;
he has destroyed the hostile fetters of existence and transcended the realm of the remaining traces.
All enemies of the outflows have been completely laid low.
Just as a Wheel-Turning King embraces his retinue, he spreads his teachings widely with a heart of compassion; all within the seas receive and follow them.
Able to subdue demons and hostile enemies, he is the unsurpassed Teacher.
Serving with a heart of faith and reverence, the three knowledges have extinguished old age and death;
as a true son of the Dharma, he is free from the affliction of wandering in saṃsāra.
Having uprooted the thorns of all defilements, I pay homage to the descendant of the Solar Lineage.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1213 (1213) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Nyagrodhakappa was staying in the wilderness at a dwelling for wild beasts.

Not long after his ordination, the Venerable Vakkali lived in dependence upon villages and towns with such deportment: in the morning, having dressed and taken his bowl, he entered those villages and towns for alms, well-guarding his body, guarding the doors of his sense faculties, and maintaining mindfulness by concentrating his mind.
Having finished eating, he returned to his dwelling, put away his robes and bowl, and after washing his feet, entered his room to sit in meditation.

He soon emerged from meditation, yet remained unattached to the alms-food he had received; however, as there was no one to provide him with timely instruction or admonition, his mind found no peace and became completely obscured.
While he was thus dwelling in deep absorption, the Venerable Vakkali thought to himself:
"I have not attained what is beneficial; it is difficult to attain and not easily gained."
Since I do not receive timely instruction and admonition, I am unable to dwell with a mind that is joyful, complete, and well-guarded.
I shall now recite verses on self-reproach.
He then spoke these verses:
“One should abandon both pleasure and displeasure, as well as all thoughts of craving;
doing nothing toward one’s neighbor, one who is free from defilement is called a bhikṣu.”
One who dwells on thoughts of the six sense-objects, racing through the world,
whose evil and unwholesome states are concealed and cannot be stripped from the skin—
whose defilements delight the mind— is not called a bhikkhu.
There are others bound by fetters, who are bound by both seeing and hearing, by sensation and cognition.
But for one who has awakened to desire, there is no further defilement in that place;
one who is thus undefiled is a Muni.
The great earth and empty space, as well as all the various forms and images in the world—all these are subject to decay and extinction;
they are inherently tranquil and determined by their own nature.
When those who are vessels for the Dharma have long practiced cultivation, they attain samādhi.
"Untouched by touch and free from deceit, his mind is utterly focused and dedicated.
That Noble One has long been in Nirvāṇa; with mindfulness fixed, he awaits the time of cessation.

Then, the Venerable Vakkali spoke these verses of self-reproach; his mind was awakened within himself, and having awakened to the state beyond worldly delight, his mind came to rest in joyful gladness.
1214 (1214). Thus have I heard.
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, in the early morning, the Venerable Ānanda dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms, accompanied by the Venerable Vakkula.
At that time, the Venerable Vakkali saw a woman of exquisite beauty; having seen her, a mind of sensual desire arose within him.
Then, the Venerable Vakkali thought to himself:
"I have now met with misfortune; I have obtained suffering, not happiness. For I have seen this young woman of peerless beauty, and a mind of sensual desire has arisen."
Now, in order to inspire a sense of weary detachment, he spoke these verses:
"Because I am shrouded by craving, It burns my heart with intense heat.
Now, Venerable Ānanda, Extinguish this fire of greed for me."
Out of compassion and pity, please explain this to me through skillful means.
Venerable Ānanda replied in verse:
“Because of those inverted perceptions, his mind is burning with intense fire.”
One who distances themselves from the perception of purity nourishes the growth of craving.
Therefore, one should cultivate the contemplation of impurity and always maintain single-minded meditative absorption;
thus, quickly extinguish the fire of craving so that it does not burn the mind.
Contemplate all conditioned phenomena with discernment: they are suffering, empty, and devoid of self.
Fixing your mindfulness, observe the body correctly, and cultivate a deep sense of weary detachment.
Practice the signless state to eradicate the underlying tendencies of conceit.
"Having attained the direct realization of pride, one reaches the ultimate end of suffering.
When the Venerable Ānanda had spoken these words, the Venerable Vakkula heard what he said and, filled with joy, practiced accordingly.
1215. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain householder invited the Buddha and the Sangha to his home for a meal.
Having entered the house, the Venerable Vakkali remained there on duty as the day’s keeper and requested his portion of the food.
At that time, many women of the elders' families emerged from the village and proceeded toward the vihāra.
Then, the Venerable Vakkali saw a young woman of beautiful appearance, and a mind of sensual desire arose within him.
At that time, the Venerable Bakula thought to himself: "I am now ill-fated;
I have not gained what is beneficial, but have met with suffering instead of joy. Seeing the upright and beautiful countenance of another's wife, a mind of lustful desire has arisen within me."
"I shall now speak a verse on wearying detachment.
Having thus reflected, he spoke these verses:
"I have attained renunciation; Having left the home, I have gone forth into homelessness."
Lust pursues me like an ox longing for another's crops;
I shall be like the son of a great general, who, wielding a powerful and mighty bow,
is able to break through that heavy array, subduing a thousand alone.
Now, in the presence of the descendant of the Solar Lineage, having heard what was taught—
the path leading directly to Nirvana— my mind dwells with certainty and joy.
Thus, through non-negligence, I abide in the meditative absorption of cessation.
No one can deceive or delude my mind;
having observed with certainty and dwelling securely in the True Dharma,
even if countless beings were to come seeking to mislead or confuse me.
"Such evil Māras as these shall not be able to see me.
When the Venerable Vakkali had spoken these verses, his mind attained abiding peace.
1216. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Vakkali, who was capable of eloquent exposition through his own wisdom, felt a sense of pride arising from his cleverness regarding the Dharma and the holy life. He thought to himself:

"It is not for my benefit, it is not for my gain; I have met with suffering and not with happiness, for I have treated those who are clever in the holy life with contempt because of my own wisdom. I shall now speak verses that can give rise to disenchantment."
Then he spoke in verse:
“O Gautama, do not give rise to pride; Sever pride so that nothing remains.
Do not give rise to thoughts of pride, And do not fall back into regret.”
Do not conceal faults from others; abandon negligence, lethargy, and pride.
Right reception can eliminate sorrow, and seeing the Path, one abides in the right path.
One’s mind attains joy and bliss; seeing the Path, one maintains self-restraint.
Therefore, with unimpeded eloquence, pure and free from all hindrances;
having severed all forms of pride and arisen in all fields of knowledge;
maintaining right mindfulness regarding the three types of higher knowledge, as well as the bases of psychic power and the knowledge of others' minds.
When the Venerable Vakkali had spoken these verses of disenchantment, his mind became purified. 1217 (1217).
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Vakkali was staying at the Eastern Park, in the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground Lecture Hall at Śrāvastī. He dwelt alone in contemplation, living with diligence and devoting himself exclusively to his own practice, until he attained the three knowledges and realized them through direct personal experience.
At that time, the Venerable Vaṅgīśa thought to himself:

"While dwelling alone in a quiet place, practicing with diligence and cultivating my own task, I have realized the three knowledges through bodily witness. Now I shall speak verses in praise of these three knowledges."
He then spoke in verse:
"Originally my mind was deluded and frantic; While wandering through villages and from house to house, I encountered the Buddha, Who bestowed upon me the supreme Dharma."
Out of compassion, Gautama, please teach me the True Dharma;
having heard the Dharma, I shall attain pure faith and leave the home life for homelessness.
Having heard his teaching of the Dharma, I shall abide correctly within the instruction of the Dharma.
Through diligent application of skillful means and focused mindfulness, remaining steadfast and ever-capable,
one attains the three types of clear knowledge (*trividyā*). Having accomplished what was to be done within the Buddha’s teaching,
the World-Honored One has excellently revealed this— the lineage of the Solar Clan has thus spoken.
For the sake of sentient beings born blind, you have opened the gateway to liberation;
the suffering of suffering and its cause, the cessation of suffering, and the realization thereof—
the Noble Eightfold Path that leaves suffering behind— lead to the secure joy of Nirvana.
Excellent in meaning, excellent in phrasing, The holy life unsurpassed—
The World-Honored One has excellently revealed it, Nirvana,
for the salvation of sentient beings. (1218) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now speak of four dharma-phrases.”
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you.
What are these four?
"The noble ones who skillfully preach the Dharma—this is the most supreme."
To speak what is agreeable and not what is disagreeable—this is the second [kind of speech].
To speak the truth and not what is false—this is the third kind of speech.
To speak according to the Dharma and not with contradictory words—this is the fourth [kind of speech].
“Monks! This is called the teaching on the four dharma-phrases.
At that time, the Venerable Vakkali, amidst the assembly, had this thought:
“The World-Honored One has spoken four Dharma-phrases among the fourfold assembly; I shall praise, extol, and rejoice in them in four ways.
Thereupon, he rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, paid homage to the Buddha, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I wish to say something, Sugata!
I wish to say something.
The Buddha said to Vakkali,
"Speak as you please! Then,
the Venerable Vakkali spoke these verses:
"If one who speaks well does not distress oneself,
nor terrify others, that is truly speaking well.
One who speaks with affection speaks so as to bring joy to others."
To prevent others from doing evil is what is called speaking with affection.
Speaking the truth is known as the nectar; speaking the truth is known as the unsurpassed.
To speak according to the meaning of truth is the domain established by the noble ones.
"As the Dharma taught by the Buddha, the path to the peace of *nirvāṇa*, which extinguishes all suffering— this is called the well-expounded teaching.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

1219. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying on the side of Mount Nāga near Rājagṛha, together with a thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats—those who had exhausted all outflows, accomplished what was to be done, laid down their heavy burdens, attained their own benefit, completely destroyed the fetters of existence, and whose minds were well-liberated through right knowledge.
At that time, the Venerable Vakkali was staying in the Śītavana cemetery on the outskirts of Rājagṛha. He thought to himself:

"Now the Blessed One is staying at Rājagṛha by the side of Mount Nāga, together with a thousand bhikṣus, all of whom are arhats whose taints have been exhausted, who have done what was to be done, laid down their heavy burdens, attained their own benefit, destroyed the fetters of existence, and whose minds are well-liberated through right knowledge."
"I shall now go and individually praise the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus.
Having formed this thought, he immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
And he spoke in verse:
"The Unsurpassed Guide, dwelling on the side of Mount Nāga,
with a retinue of a thousand bhikṣus, serves the Tathāgata."
The Great Master extensively expounds the Dharma, the path to the coolness of Nirvana;
listen single-mindedly to the pure and white teachings spoken by the Perfectly Awakened One.
Honored by the World-Honored One, the Perfectly Awakened One dwells amidst the great assembly.
A great dragon among the masses of virtue, the foremost of sages,
he raises the dense clouds of merit and universally rains down upon the assembly of śrāvakas;
arising from his midday meditative absorption, he comes to pay homage to the Great Teacher.
The disciple Vakkali, having prostrated with his head at [the Buddha's] feet,
said: "World-Honored One,
I wish to say something."
"So be it, Sugata!
I wish to say something.
The Buddha said to Vakkali:
"Speak as you wish, but do not reflect beforehand.
Then, Vakkali spoke these verses:
"Māra, when even a slight evil arises, Subdue it secretly and cause it to be quickly extinguished."
Able to obscure and obstruct all Māras, causing them to realize their own transgressions;
observing and unraveling bonds and fetters, discerning the pure and white dharmas;
shining with clarity like the sun and moon, he is the king of all heterodox paths.
Having transcended through wisdom and realized it for oneself, you proclaim the supreme Dharma;
having emerged from the various floods of affliction, you teach the path in its infinite varieties.
You establish [beings] in the deathless and perceive the true Dharma of the Truths.
Such is the path that accords with truth; such a teacher is difficult to find.
He establishes the path to the Deathless, perceives the Truths, and honors seclusion.
The World-Honored One has well expounded the Dharma, able to remove the veils of the human aggregates.
"Clearly seeing all phenomena, one trains in accordance with discipline.
When the Venerable Vakkali had spoken this verse, the bhikṣus who heard what he said were all greatly delighted.
1220. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park, the Abode of Seers.

At that time, the Blessed One taught the Dharma associated with the Four Noble Truths to the assembly of bhikṣus, namely: "This is the noble truth of suffering; this is the noble truth of the origin of suffering; this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering; this is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering."
At that time, the Venerable Vakula was present in the assembly and thought to himself:
"I shall now, in the presence of the World-Honored One, praise the parable of the extraction of the arrow."
Having reflected thus, he rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
I wish to say something."
"So be it, Sugata;
I wish to say something.
The Buddha said to Vakkali:
"Speak as you wish!
Then, the Venerable Vakkali spoke these verses:
"I now pay homage to the Buddha, Who has compassion for all sentient beings."
First, he extracted the sharp arrow; he was skilled in treating all manner of ailments.
The physician Kāru administered medicine, as did Bāhula and Jīvaka;
likewise, Caṇḍa and Jīvaka treated the sick.
Some may have a slight recovery from illness, which is called having successfully treated the disease;
yet later the illness flares up again, and they die while still gripped by it.
The Perfectly Awakened One, the Great King of Physicians, skillfully administers medicine to sentient beings.
Ultimately eliminating all suffering, he shall no longer undergo further existence.
Even the hundreds of thousands of kinds of diseases, numbering in the nayutas,
the Buddha treats and heals them all, reaching the ultimate end of suffering.
To all you physicians gathered here, I now declare to you all:
having obtained the nectar-like medicine of the Dharma, take it as you please.
It is the foremost for extracting the arrow and is skilled at diagnosing all ailments.
"The most supreme among those who treat the illness, therefore I bow my head to Gautama.
When the Venerable Vakkali had spoken these words, all the bhikṣus, hearing what he said, were filled with great joy.
1221. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.

At that time, the Venerable Nyagrodhakalpa was dwelling in a wilderness inhabited by birds and beasts; he was gravely ill, and the Venerable Vakkula served as his attendant, nursing him and providing for his needs.
That venerable one, Nigrodhakappa, having fallen ill, subsequently entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the venerable Vakkali thought to himself:
"Has my preceptor attained *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*?"
"What is *nirvāṇa without remainder*?
I shall now seek its defining characteristics.
At that time, the Venerable Vakkali, having made offerings to the relics of the Venerable Nyagrodha, took his robes and bowl and set out for Rājagṛha.

Proceeding by stages, he arrived at the city of Rājagṛha. Having set down his robe and bowl and washed his feet, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and spoke these verses:
“I now pay homage to the Great Teacher, The Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Unextinguished.”
In this present life, all nets of doubt have been severed.
The bhikṣu dwelling in the wilderness has attained parinirvāṇa at the end of his life;
with his deportment governing his faculties, his great virtue is renowned throughout the world.
The World-Honored One has established a name, calling it the "perception of the nyagrodha tree.
I now ask the World-Honored One about that immovable liberation.
Please explain to me the merits of diligent effort and skillful means.
I am of the Śākya clan, a disciple of the World-Honored One’s Dharma;
and all others likewise desire to know what has been taught by the one with the perfect eye of the Way. Abiding here, we all wish to hear it.
The World-Honored One is the Great Teacher, The unsurpassed savior of the world;
The Great Muni who has severed all doubt, Whose wisdom is fully perfected.
With the divine eye that illuminates all, His radiance shines upon the fourfold assembly.
Just as Śakra, Lord of the Devas, illuminates the Heaven of the Thirty-three,
so too all greed, desire, and doubt arise from ignorance;
yet upon encountering the Tathāgata, they are utterly extinguished without remainder.
The World-Honored One’s divine eye is supreme in the world;
he eradicates the ignorance of sentient beings like the wind blowing away drifting dust.
All throughout the worlds, they are shrouded and obscured by afflictions.
If there were no others at all, With eyes as clear as the Buddha’s,
Whose light of wisdom illuminates all, Causing them to be equal to Great Diligence—
I only pray that the Honored One of Great Wisdom Will grant an explanation for the sake of the assembly.
As you utter these subtle and wondrous sounds, we listen with single-minded devotion;
as you preach with a gentle voice, it is heard throughout all worlds.
It is like those oppressed by heat and thirst, seeking out cool, refreshing water.
"Just as the Buddha possesses knowledge that never diminishes, may we too seek to attain such knowledge.
Venerable Vakkali spoke again in verse:
"Now I have heard the Unsurpassed One describe his own meritorious qualities."
Vainly have you practiced the holy life; hearing this, I am greatly gladdened.
As it was said, so shall it be attained; following the Muni’s disciples, sever the long fetters of birth and death, and the bonds of falsehood and illusion.
"Because one has seen the World-Honored One, one is able to sever all cravings, cross to the further shore of birth and death, and no longer undergo further existence.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Vakkali, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and approved with gladness; he paid homage and departed.
Saṃyukta Āgama, Scroll 45 and Scroll 46,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
46.1222 (1222) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“In a past age, the devas and asuras arrayed their forces for battle; the asuras were victorious, and the devas were defeated.”
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, seeing his army defeated and scattering, was seized with extreme terror; he mounted his chariot and fled northward, returning to his celestial palace.
Beneath Mount Sumeru, along a path through a dense forest, there was a nest of garuḍas at the foot of the trees, containing many young garuḍas.
At that time, Śakra, fearing that the chariot and horses might pass by and trample the fledglings to death, said to the charioteer:
"Turn the chariot back; do not kill the fledglings."
The charioteer said to the king:
"The army of the asuras is pursuing us from behind; if we turn back, we shall be beset by them.
Śakra replied:
"It would be better to turn back and be killed by the asuras than to trample and kill sentient beings with this army.
On the road, the charioteer turned the carriage southward.

Seeing from afar that Śakra had turned his chariot and retreated, the asura army took it for a tactical maneuver and immediately began to withdraw. Great terror seized them; their ranks broke and they scattered, returning to the asura palace.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"That Śakra, Lord of the Gods, is the sovereign king of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; by virtue of his compassionate mind, he has subdued the armies of the asuras through his majestic power, and he also constantly praises the merit of a compassionate mind."
“O bhikṣus, you who have left the home life out of right faith to train in the path, you should cultivate a mind of loving-kindness and should also praise the merits of a mind of loving-kindness.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1223. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.

At that time, there was a man in the city of Rājagṛha who, though poor and living in hardship, took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; he upheld the prohibitive precepts, was learned and widely educated, practiced generosity with diligence, and was endowed with right view.
When his body perished and his life ended, he was reborn in the heavens, born among the Trāyastriṃśa gods; there were three matters in which he excelled the other Trāyastriṃśa gods.
What are these three?
First is celestial longevity, second is celestial appearance, and third is celestial renown.

When the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three see these three qualities of this son of heaven—his celestial longevity, celestial appearance, and celestial renown—they perceive them as particularly superior.
When the other devas saw this, they went to where Śakra, the Lord of Devas, was and spoke these words:

“Kauśika, you should know that there is a son of heaven who has just been born in this deva realm; he surpasses the previous devas in three matters: celestial lifespan, celestial beauty, and celestial renown.”
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to those sons of the gods: "O worthy ones!

I see this man who, as a laborer in Rājagṛha, lived in poverty and hardship, yet has attained a mind of faith and inclination toward the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata, even achieving right view."

When his body perished and his life ended, he was reborn in this heaven; among all the gods of the Thirty-three, he excels them in three respects: celestial lifespan, celestial appearance, and celestial renown.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, spoke these verses:
“With right faith in the Tathāgata, Resolute and unshakable,
One upholds the true precepts, Never wearying of the noble discipline.”
With a mind purified toward the Buddha, and having accomplished right view,
you should know that you are not in poverty or suffering, and that your life is not lived in vain.
Therefore, toward the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, you should give rise to pure faith.
"The power of wisdom increases in clarity; contemplate the Buddha’s true teaching.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1224. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, the people of Rājagṛha were holding a great assembly and had invited various followers of different paths.
There was a follower of the Cāraṇa heretics who thought:
"I shall now invite the celestial deity of the Cāraṇa path to serve as my first field of merit.

Others had followers among those who have left home for non-Buddhist paths; some had followers of the Nirgrantha path; some had followers of the Vṛddhaśrāvaka (Elder Disciple) school; some had followers of the Agnīśrāvaka (Fire Disciple) school; and some had followers of the Buddha’s disciples, the Saṃgha—all of whom thought in this way:
"Now we must cause the community before the Buddha's face to first become a field of merit.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had this thought:
"Let not the people of Rājagṛha abandon the community before the Buddha's face to serve other paths in their search for a field of merit."
"I shall go quickly to establish a field of merit for the people of Rājagṛha.

He then transformed himself into a great brahmin of dignified and majestic appearance, riding in a white horse-drawn chariot, preceded and followed by a retinue of young brahmins, carrying golden ladles and parasols, and arrived at Rājagṛha to visit the various assemblies of the great multitude in every place.
All the men and women of Rājagṛha thought to themselves:
"We shall observe where this great brāhmaṇa goes to offer his service; we shall follow him there first to make offerings, so that he may serve as a field of merit for us."

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing the thoughts in the minds of all the men and women of Rājagṛha, mounted his carriage with his retinue and proceeded directly to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain. Arriving outside the gate, he removed his five ornaments and went to where the Buddha was; prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he withdrew to sit to one side.
And he spoke these verses:
“Skillfully distinguishing and revealing the further shore of all phenomena,
Having completely crossed over all terrors, I therefore bow my head to Gautama.”
All these people have prepared this assembly, desiring to seek great merit;
each has established a great gift, always wishing for the fruit of abundance.
We pray that you will explain the field of merit, so that the fruit of this giving may be realized.
“Śakra and Maheśvara, the celestial kings, asked a question;
on Vulture Peak Mountain, the Great Teacher gave the prophetic explanation.
All people have universally established this assembly, desiring to seek great merit.”
Each has established great offerings, always aspiring for the fruit of abundance.
Now I shall explain the field of merit, the place where giving yields great fruit.
There are four who are rightly directed; the four noble ones abide in the fruits [of the path].
This is called the Sangha-field of merit, complete in wisdom, conduct, and concentration.
The Sangha-field of merit expands and widens, immeasurable like the great ocean;
the Teacher of those who are disciplined and his disciples illuminate and manifest the True Dharma.
Those who provide such excellent offerings, giving to the Saṅgha— the field of merit par excellence— will,
according to the Buddha’s teaching, obtain great fruit from that field of merit which is the Saṅgha.
Because the Saṅgha is free from the five hindrances, it is pure and worthy of praise.
Giving to that supreme field of merit, one reaps great benefit from even a small gift.
Therefore, all people should give to the Sangha, the field of merit;
they shall increase their attainment of the sublime Dharma, which is conjoined with clear conduct and meditative concentration.
By making offerings to this Sangha of rare jewels, the donor’s heart rejoices;
giving rise to three kinds of thoughts, they bestow clothing and food.
Free from the dust and thorns of affliction, they transcend all evil realms.
Personally undertaking the request, giving with one's own hands in an impartial manner—
benefiting both oneself and others— such is the great benefit obtained from this generosity.
When the wise give in this way, they attain liberation through pure faith and understanding.
"By bestowing the gift of blameless peace and happiness, one shall ride upon wisdom and be reborn there.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and expressed his approval; he prostrated before the Buddha and immediately vanished from sight.

“I only pray that the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly, will accept my offerings.

When the people of Rājagṛha knew that the World-Honored One had accepted their invitation through his silence, they paid homage and returned. "The time has come; we pray that you know it is time.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly, put on his robes and took up his bowl, proceeding to the site of the great gathering where he spread out a seat before the multitude and sat down.
When the people of Rājagṛha knew that the Buddha was seated and settled, they personally served him various kinds of abundant and delicious food.
When he had finished eating, and the washing of his bowl and rinsing were completed, they returned to their original seats to listen to the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having taught, instructed, illuminated, and gladdened the people of Rājagṛha with various discourses on the Dharma, rose from his seat and departed.
1225 (1225). Thus have I heard:

at that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, spoke a different verse and asked the Buddha, saying:

"The embodiment of the World-Honored One possesses unobstructed knowledge and vision.

1226 (1226). Thus have I heard:

"Why is this? Great King, it is because I have now truly attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Here there are various eminent and venerable śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas—namely Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Maskarin Gośālīputra, Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra, Ajita Keśakambalin, Kakuda Kātyāyana, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra—who do not claim for themselves that they have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. The Buddha told the Great King:

What are these four?"

A Kṣatriya prince, though young and tender, must not be disregarded; a nāga prince, though young and tender, must not be disregarded; a small fire, though minute, must not be disregarded; and a bhikṣu, though young and tender, must not be disregarded.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Though a Kṣatriya endowed with the marks of excellence, A nobleman who has brought forth a great reputation—
Even if his years are few and he is young, He is not held in contempt by the wise.”
This person will surely occupy the royal throne;
considering that they may harbor thoughts of enmity or harm, one must not treat them with negligence, but should instead cultivate great reverence.
Those who seek to protect themselves well should guard themselves as they would their own life.
Protect yourself with equanimity, and protect your life with equanimity.
Whether in a village or in a secluded place, if you see that young nāga,
do not give rise to thoughts of contempt because he is but a small snake.
Even small dragons of variegated colors should be made to dwell in peace;
even tiny snakes, lacking male or female, are all harmed by their own venom.
Therefore, one who protects themselves should do so as they would protect their own life.
By means of this, protect yourself well, and protect others equally.
That which is consumed by a fierce fire, though small at first, knows no limit;
even a small torch can burn, and with sufficient fuel, it spreads ever wider.
Starting from a tiny spark, it gradually burns until the entire village and city are consumed;
therefore, one who protects themselves should do so as they would protect their own life.
By protecting oneself well in this way, one likewise protects others.
Where a raging fire burns, all the hundred species of plants are swept away and consumed.
Once extinguished, it neither increases nor diminishes; yet the fire of the precepts arises once more.
If one treats with contempt a bhikṣu who maintains the fire of pure precepts, [the consequences are grave].
Burning one’s own body and one’s descendants, a multitude of calamities flow for a hundred generations;
like burning a *tāla* tree, there is no prospect of rebirth.
Therefore, one should protect oneself as one would protect one’s own life.
Protecting oneself well by this means, one likewise protects others.
A Kṣatriya endowed with the proper marks, a young dragon, a small fire,
and a bhikṣu who possesses pure precepts— one should not harbor thoughts of contempt toward them.
"Therefore, one should protect oneself, as one would protect one's own life;
by protecting oneself well in this manner, one protects others equally.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and approved, paid homage, and departed.
1227. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

"Great King!
From where have you come, with such tattered robes and disheveled hair?"
King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha:

My late grandmother was one whom I held in the highest reverence. After she passed away, leaving me behind, I cremated her outside the city; having completed the offerings, I have come to visit the World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said to the Great King,
"Do you hold your ancestors and relatives in extreme love, respect,
and mindfulness? King Prasenajit replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
I hold you in the utmost reverence and love.
World-Honored One!”

"If there be elephants, horses, the seven treasures, or even the sovereignty of the kingdom within this land, I shall give them all away to another person; whoever can save my grandmother's life shall receive them all."
Since there is no way to save you, we must bid you a long farewell in this life and death; our grief, longing, and sorrow are such that we cannot bear them!
We have heard what the World-Honored One has said:
"All sentient beings, all insects, and all spirits—those who are born must all die; none escape this end. There is not a single being born who does not die."
"Today I have finally come to know that the World-Honored One has spoken well.
The Buddha said,
"Great King!"
"So it is! So it is! All sentient beings, all insects, and all spirits—whoever is born must die; they ultimately end in exhaustion, for there is not a single being who is born and does not die."
The Buddha told the Great King:
"Even those born into great Brahmin clans, great Kṣatriya clans, or great householder clans—all who are born must die; there is no one who does not die."

Even if a Kṣatriya great king has been consecrated and occupies the throne, ruling over the four quarters of the world with power and sovereignty, and has subdued all hostile nations without exception, he must ultimately reach his end; there is no one who does not die.
Furthermore, Great King!
Even those born in the Heaven of Long Life, who rule over celestial palaces with sovereign joy and happiness, must ultimately come to an end; there are none who do not die.
Furthermore, Great King, when an Arhat bhikṣu has exhausted all taints,

laid down the heavy burden, accomplished what was to be done, attained his own goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is well-liberated in mind through right knowledge, he too will reach extinction, attaining parinirvāṇa upon casting off the body.

Furthermore, even Pratyekabuddhas who are well-disciplined and well-peaceful, having exhausted this life and body, ultimately return to Nirvana; and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the supreme lion’s roar, likewise ultimately relinquish the body and attain Parinirvāṇa.
By such analogies, Great King, you should know that all sentient beings, all insects, and all spirits—whoever is born must die; they ultimately end in extinction, for there is none who does not die!
At that time, the World-Honored One again spoke in verse:
"All classes of sentient beings, Having life, must ultimately return to death;
Each follows where their karma leads, Receiving the fruits of good and evil for themselves."
Through evil karma one falls into hell; through goodness one ascends to heaven.
By cultivating the supreme and wondrous path, one attains parinirvāṇa with the exhaustion of outflows.
This applies to Tathāgatas, Pratyekabuddhas, and the Buddha’s śrāvaka disciples.
"One would even sacrifice one's own body and life; how much more so for an ordinary worldly person.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and delighted in it, paid his respects, and departed.
1228 (1228). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

"What is mindfulness of self?
What is lack of mindfulness of self?"
He further thought:
"If there are those who engage in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind, it should be known that such persons do not attend to their own welfare."
"If, moreover, one practices wholesome conduct of body, wholesome conduct of speech, and wholesome conduct of mind, you should know that such persons are mindful of themselves.
Having arisen from meditation, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
While dwelling alone in seclusion, I reflected and thought:
"What is mindfulness of self?
What is lack of mindfulness of self?"
He further reflects:
"If there are those who engage in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind, one should know that such persons do not attend to their own welfare."
"Furthermore, if one practices wholesome conduct of body, wholesome conduct of speech, and wholesome conduct of mind, you should know that such persons are mindful of themselves.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"It is so, Great King!"
In this way, Great King!
If there are those who engage in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind, you should know that such persons do not attend to their own welfare.
Although they say of themselves,
"I act out of self-love," in reality,
it is not out of self-regard.

Why is this? There is no evil deed committed by an evil associate that one does not reflect upon, nor is there anything one does not reflect upon that one does not love, nor is there anything one does not love that one does not act upon as if it were done for oneself; therefore, these [evil associates] are considered those who do not care for themselves.
"Furthermore, Great King!
Those who practice wholesome conduct of body, wholesome conduct of speech, and wholesome conduct of mind, you should know that they are mindful of themselves; they say of themselves:
'We do not cherish our own bodies.'"

However, these indeed constitute mindfulness directed toward oneself. Why is this? Because there is no true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who, regarding what a spiritual friend should do, would direct their mindfulness toward it;

nor is there one who, regarding what a spiritual friend should love, would love it; nor one who, regarding what a spiritual friend should do for themselves, would act accordingly. Therefore, these [instances] are indeed mindfulness directed toward oneself.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"One who is mindful of self Should not commit evil deeds;
For by means of evil deeds, One can never attain peace and happiness."
Those who are mindful of themselves will never commit unwholesome deeds;
by performing various wholesome actions, they bring peace and happiness to themselves.
If one cherishes oneself, one should protect oneself well.
Just as a well-protecting king guards the frontier cities from without,
so should one who cherishes themselves guard their own treasure most excellently;
like a well-guarding king, they protect the frontier cities from within.
"Thus, one's own treasure-store is without interruption for even a moment;
a momentary lapse brings sorrow, and one suffers long in the evil realms.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and delighted in it, paid his respects, and departed.
1229 (1229). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit, while reflecting in solitude, had this thought:

How does one fail to protect oneself?"
He further thought:
"If there are those who engage in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind, it should be known that such persons do not protect themselves."
"Furthermore, those who practice wholesome conduct of body, wholesome conduct of speech, and wholesome conduct of mind—know that such persons are protecting themselves.
Having arisen from meditation, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

As I was reflecting alone in quietude, this thought arose:

What is lack of self-protection?"
Again, he formed this thought:
"If there are those who engage in evil conduct of body, evil conduct of speech, and evil conduct of mind, you should know that such persons do not protect themselves."

The Buddha told the Great King:
"It is so, Great King!"
In this way, Great King!

If there are those who engage in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind, you should know that such persons do not protect themselves, even though they claim to be able to protect themselves.
One may protect oneself by means of elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry; yet though this is called self-protection, it is not truly self-protection. Why is that?
Although one protects the exterior, one does not protect the interior.
Therefore, Great King,
this is called "not protecting oneself."
"Great King!
If there are those who practice wholesome conduct of body, practice wholesome conduct of speech, and practice wholesome conduct of mind, you should know that such persons are protecting themselves."
Although he does not protect himself with the fourfold army of elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry, he is in fact well-protected.
Why is this? To protect one's inner self is called "protecting oneself well"; it does not mean guarding against external threats.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Guard well your body and speech, And all actions of the mind;
Restrain yourself with shame and remorse— This is called ‘well-guarded.’”
At that time, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and approved with gladness;
he paid homage and departed. 1230 (1230). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit, reflecting in solitude, thought to himself:

"In this world, there are few people who, having obtained superior and wonderful wealth and profit, are able to remain heedful, able to avoid greedy attachment, and able to refrain from committing evil deeds toward sentient beings."
"In the world, there are many who, upon obtaining superior and wonderful wealth and profit, give rise to negligence, increase their greedy attachments, and engage in various unwholesome actions.

As I was reflecting in solitude, this thought arose:

"In the world, there are many who, having obtained excellent and wonderful wealth, give rise to negligence, develop craving and attachment, and frequently engage in unwholesome conduct.
The Buddha said to King Prasenajit:

Few are those in the world who, having obtained superior and wonderful wealth and profit, are able to remain free from greedy attachment, refrain from negligence, and abstain from wrongful conduct.
In this world, there are many who, having obtained excellent wealth and profit, become heedless regarding that wealth, giving rise to greedy attachment and engaging in various unwholesome actions.

Great King, you should know that those people of the world who, having obtained excellent wealth and profit, become heedless regarding that wealth, give rise to greedy attachment, and engage in unwholesome actions, are foolish persons who shall experience disadvantageous suffering for a long night.
"Great King!

It is like hunters or their apprentices who, in the empty wilderness and forests, spread nets and set snares, killing many birds and beasts, afflicting sentient beings, and thereby increasing their evil karma."

In this same way, when people of the world obtain superior and wonderful wealth and profit, they become heedless regarding that wealth, give rise to greedy attachment, and likewise engage in various wrongful actions.
"This foolish person shall experience disadvantageous suffering for a long night.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
"Craving for superior wealth, One is deluded and intoxicated by greed."
"Madly agitated and lacking self-awareness, like a hunter, because of such negligence, one shall receive the retribution of great suffering.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and praised it with gladness; he prostrated himself and departed.
1231 (1231). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, King Prasenajit was presiding over state affairs from his main hall. He saw eminent Kṣatriya families, eminent Brāhmaṇa families, and eminent Gṛhapati families who, out of greed, were practicing deception and speaking falsehoods. Thereupon, he thought to himself:
"Stop these legal proceedings!"
Cease these judicial proceedings!
I shall no longer personally preside over them;
I have a worthy son, whom I shall appoint to adjudicate them.
How can one see for oneself that these eminent kṣatriya clans, eminent brahmin clans, and eminent householder clans, for the sake of greed, practice deception and utter falsehoods?
At that time, King Prasenajit, having formed this thought, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

While I was personally attending to the affairs of state from within the palace, I observed that members of the eminent Kṣatriya clans, the eminent Brahmin clans, and the eminent householder clans were practicing deception and speaking falsehoods for the sake of greed and profit.
"Bhagavān!
Having seen this matter, I had this thought:
'From this day forward, I shall cease this practice of litigation; I shall bring this practice of litigation to rest.'"
"I have a worthy son whom I must cause to sever [this practice].
I have not personally seen this superior kṣatriya great clan, brahmin great clan, or householder great clan engage in deceitful false speech for the sake of coveting profit."
The Buddha told King Prasenajit:
“So it is, Great King! So it is, Great King!”

Those eminent kṣatriya clans, brahmin clans, and householder clans, because of their greed for profit, practice deception and false speech; those foolish people shall experience disadvantageous suffering for a long night!

Great King, you should know that it is like a fisherman or a fisherman’s apprentice who, at rivers, streams, or valleys, sets nets across the current to slaughter living beings, causing them to undergo great suffering.
In this way, Great King!

Those eminent clans of Kṣatriyas, eminent clans of Brahmins, and eminent clans of householders, because of their greed for profit, practice deception and false speech; consequently, throughout the long night, they shall experience harm and suffering.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Conceiving greedy desire for wealth, Intoxicated and deluded by that greed,
One is frantic and lacks self-awareness, Just like a fisherman casting his net."
"Due to these evil karmic actions, one shall receive the retribution of intense suffering.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and approved with gladness; he prostrated himself and departed.
1232 (1232). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

“World-Honored One!
The householder Mahānāma, despite such immense wealth, consumes only coarse broken rice, bean soup, and rotten ginger;

he wears coarse cloth garments and simple leather sandals; he rides a dilapidated carriage and carries a parasol made of leaves. "He keeps his doors shut while eating, ensuring that no śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, travelers, or beggars see him.

Having acquired superior wealth and possessions, one does not know how to employ them extensively to reap their great benefits.
Great King!
It is like a lake or pond in a wilderness where water collects, yet no one uses it for bathing or drinking; thus, within that marsh, it evaporates and is exhausted.
"In this way, a man of unwholesome character who acquires superior wealth does not enjoy it extensively, but rather secures its great benefit, just like that pool water.
Great King!"

There is a son of good family who, having obtained superior wealth and profit, enjoys it with happiness; he makes offerings to his parents, provides for his wife, children, kinsmen, and retinue, supports his servants and laborers, bestows gifts upon his spiritual teachers and friends, and from time to time makes offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, planting excellent fields of merit, inclining toward the sublime state, and being reborn in heaven in the future.
One obtains superior wealth and is able to enjoy it extensively, thereby reaping manifold great benefits. It is just as if, Great King,

there were a pool of water at the edge of a village or a city— tranquil, pure, and cool, shaded by groves of trees— which brings joy to people and is enjoyed by many multitudes, even down to the birds and beasts.

In this way, noble son, one obtains supreme and wondrous wealth; one enjoys happiness for oneself, makes offerings to one's parents, and even plants seeds in the most excellent fields of merit, thereby gathering vast and great benefits.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"In a lake or pond in the wilderness, The water is cool, refreshing, and exceedingly pure;
Yet if there is no one to use it, It will simply vanish away right there."
Such excellent and wondrous wealth, when acquired by a wicked person,
cannot be enjoyed by themselves, nor is it used to provide for others.
They toil in vain to amass it, and having amassed it, they lose it themselves.
The wise person attains supreme wealth and is able to enjoy it with happiness.
Having performed extensive meritorious deeds through giving,
they bestow gifts upon their kinsmen and retinue as is appropriate, like a bull-king leading its herd.
"Those who practice giving and enjoy [the fruits] without failing in what is appropriate, die according to the natural order and are reborn in heaven to receive blessings and joy.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and followed along with joy; he paid homage and departed.
1233 (1233). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

"Great King! From where have you come?"
"My body is covered in dust, and I seem somewhat weary.
King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!..."

"When that Mahānāma was in the world, he wore coarse clothing and ate poor food... [as described at length above]. The Buddha told King Prasenajit:

Because when he gave to a pratyekabuddha, his faith was impure; because he did not give with his own hands, nor with reverence, and because he later regretted the gift, in whatever place he is born, although he obtains wealth, he still uses coarse clothing, coarse food, coarse and inferior bedding, dwellings, and vehicles. From the beginning, he never experiences superior forms, sounds, smells, tastes, or tangibles to bring peace to his body.
"Furthermore, Great King!

At that time, the householder Mahānāma killed his half-brother, seized his wealth, and because of this transgression, he fell into hell for a hundred thousand years. Due to the remaining retribution of that karma, he was born in the kingdom of Śrāvastī seven times; in each life he remained childless, and his wealth was confiscated by the royal house."
"Great King!

The householder Mahānāma has now reached the end of his life; having exhausted the rewards of his past giving, because of that former stinginess and greed, and because he was negligent regarding wealth and committed transgressions, upon the conclusion of this life, he has fallen into hell to undergo extreme suffering!"
King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since the householder Mahānāman has passed away, has he entered hell to undergo suffering?”
The Buddha said, “It is so, Great King!
He has already entered hell!”
At that time, King Prasenajit, mindful of those weeping piteously, wiped away his tears with his robe and spoke this verse:
"Material wealth and true gold treasures, Elephants, horses, and ornaments,
Servants and all manner of attendants, As well as fields, houses, and the like."
Having abandoned everything, the naked spirit departs alone;
when the span of one's fortune is exhausted, one forever forsakes the human body.
What does he now possess? What does he carry with him as he goes?
"In what matter is there no relinquishing, just as a shadow follows the form?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"Only the karma of sin and merit, if a person has already performed it,"
This belongs to oneself, yet that is always carried away.
Birth and death are never abandoned, like a shadow following a form;
it is like a person with meager provisions who encounters hardship while traveling a long distance.
Those who do not cultivate merit will inevitably undergo the suffering of the evil realms,
just as a person with abundant provisions travels afar in peace and happiness.
Those whose cultivation of virtue is pure and profound will long enjoy bliss in the happy destinies.
Just as a person who has traveled far abroad returns safely after many years,
and his kinsmen and virtuous friends gather together in joyful celebration,
so too does one who has skillfully cultivated merit pass away from this life and take birth in another world.
When those kinsmen and relatives see him, their hearts rejoice;
therefore, one should cultivate merit, accumulating it for the sake of eternity.
Merit is able to bring about happiness in future lives for a person.
"Meritorious virtue is praised by the devas, for one practices right conduct with equanimity.
In this present life one is not reviled by others, and at the end, one is reborn in the heavens.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and delighted in it; he paid homage and departed.
1234 (One, two, three, four). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, King Prasenajit prepared a great assembly. For the sake of this great assembly, he tethered a thousand bulls in rows and gathered all kinds of offerings. He summoned all the various heterodox teachers from afar, and they all came together to the site of King Prasenajit’s great assembly.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus also dressed in their robes and took up their bowls in the early morning, entering the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
They heard that King Prasenajit had established a universal great assembly... as described in detail above, until it was said that various non-Buddhist practitioners had all gathered there.

Having heard this, after finishing his almsround, he returned to the vihāra, put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

"Today, we many bhikṣus, having dressed in the morning and taken up our bowls, entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms and heard that King Prasenajit had prepared a great assembly... [as described at length above] ...until various followers of heterodox paths gathered at the site of the assembly."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Holding great assemblies month after month, even numbering in the hundreds of thousands,
is not worth a sixteenth part of having right faith in the Buddha.”
If one has such faith in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and regards all sentient beings with loving-kindness,
the merit of that great assembly would not equal even a sixteenth part [of it].
If a person were to perform meritorious deeds in this world for a hundred million years, [it would still not equal the merit of a single thought of loving-kindness].
"Compared to prostrating with a straightforward mind, [the former] does not equal even one-quarter of it.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1235 (1235). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, King Prasenajit was incensed with the people of the land and imprisoned many: whether they were kṣatriyas, brahmins, vaiśyas, śūdras, or caṇḍālas; whether they observed the precepts or violated them; whether they were laypeople or monastics—all were seized, some being bound with chains, some with cangues and fetters, and others with ropes.

At that time, a great number of bhikṣus, having dressed in the morning and taken their bowls, entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms. Hearing that King Prasenajit had imprisoned many people—some even locked up or bound—they finished their almsround, returned to the vihāra, put away their robes and bowls, and after washing their feet, went to where the Buddha was. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One! [We have heard that King Prasenajit has imprisoned many people,] even locking or binding some of them.”
"Today, we many bhikṣus entered the city to beg for alms and heard that King Prasenajit has imprisoned many people, even to the point of binding them with chains.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Not ropes, chains, or cangues Are called the firm bondage; [It is the bond of craving,] Which is difficult to untie."
A defiled mind that dwells upon wealth, treasures, and wife—this bondage is long and firm;
though loose, it is difficult to escape.
The wise do not dwell upon the pleasures of the five worldly desires.
"This is the severing of all bonds, / Attaining peace and forever transcending the world.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1236. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit and King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha were at odds with one another.
King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha raised a fourfold army—consisting of elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry—and marched toward the kingdom of Kośala.

When King Prasenajit heard that King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, had arrived with his fourfold army, he likewise assembled his own fourfold army—elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry—and went out to engage them in battle.

King Ajātaśatru’s fourfold army was victorious, while King Prasenajit’s fourfold army was defeated; they retreated in disarray and scattered, and [Prasenajit] fled alone on a single chariot back to the city of Śrāvastī.

At that time, a great number of bhikṣus, having dressed in the morning and taken up their bowls, entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms. They heard that Ajātaśatru, the King of Magadha and son of Vaidehī, had mobilized the fourfold army and come to the kingdom of Kośala;

that King Prasenajit had also mobilized his fourfold army and gone out to meet him in battle, but that Prasenajit’s four armies were no match for them, and having been defeated and scattered, King Prasenajit fled in terror and distress on a single chariot back to Śrāvastī.

Having heard this, after completing his almsround, he returned to the vihāra, put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

"Today, we many bhikṣus entered the city for alms and heard that Ajātaśatru, the King of Magadha and son of Vaidehī, had mobilized a fourfold army... [The text continues] at length, until: "...racing back on a single chariot to the city of Śrāvastī."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Victory increases one’s enemies; Defeat lies in misery and unrest.
Abandoning both victory and defeat, One sleeps and wakes in the bliss of tranquility.”
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1237 (1237) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit was at odds with King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha.
King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha mobilized his fourfold army and marched upon the kingdom of Kośala; King Prasenajit likewise raised his fourfold army and went out to engage them in battle.
King Prasenajit’s fourfold army was victorious, while King Ajātaśatru’s fourfold army was defeated, crushed, scattered, and dispersed.

King Prasenajit plundered all of King Ajātaśatru’s elephants, horses, chariots, money, and precious treasures; he captured King Ajātaśatru alive and placed him in the same carriage, then proceeded together to the Buddha’s dwelling. There they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This is King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī; throughout the long night he has harbored resentment toward me, though I have never wronged him, and he treats those who are good with ill intent."
"However, since he is the son of my good friend, you should release him and allow him to return to his kingdom.
The Buddha said to King Prasenajit,
"Excellent!"
"Great King!
Release him and let him go; this will bring you long-lasting peace, happiness, and benefit.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Up to the mastery of power, one is able to plunder extensively from others;
when allies assist through increased strength, one’s own and others' benefits are doubled.
After the Buddha had spoken this sutra, King Prasenajit and Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, heard what the Buddha taught.
Rejoicing and expressing sympathetic joy, they paid homage and departed.
(1238) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit, reflecting in solitude, had this thought:

"The True Dharma of the World-Honored One is a dharma for the present life, free from all burning fevers; it does not depend on time, it is directly accessible and visible, and it is to be personally realized and known. This Dharma is a good friend and a good companion, not a bad friend or a bad companion."
Having had this thought, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
While reflecting alone in quietude, I had this thought:”

"The True Dharma of the Blessed One is to be realized in this very life, free from all burning fevers, not dependent on time, directly accessible, to be personally experienced and realized; it is thus a good friend and a good companion, and not an evil friend or an evil companion."
The Buddha said to King Prasenajit:
“So it is, Great King! So it is, Great King!”

The Blessed One’s True Dharma and Discipline is a state free from all burning afflictions in this very life; it does not depend on time, it is directly accessible and visible, and it is to be personally realized through one's own awakening. This, indeed, is a true friend and a virtuous companion, not an evil friend or an evil companion.
Why is this? I am a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*);

for those sentient beings subject to birth, I bring liberation from birth; for those sentient beings subject to old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering, I cause them all to be liberated.
"Great King!
On one occasion, while I was staying at the Kūṭāgāraśālā in the Valley near Rājagṛha,
the bhikṣu Ānanda, reflecting in solitude, had this thought:
"Half of those who practice the holy life are virtuous friends and virtuous companions, not evil friends or evil companions.
Having formed this thought, he came to where I was, prostrated at my feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and said to me:
"World-Honored One!
As I was reflecting alone in stillness, this thought arose:
"Half of the holy life consists of virtuous friends and virtuous companions, not unvirtuous friends or unvirtuous companions."
I then said to him: "Ānanda! Do not speak such words.
Half of the holy life consists of virtuous friends and virtuous companions; it does not consist of evil friends or evil companions."
Why is this? Because it is purely singular, full, and pure; the holy life is stainless, consisting of virtuous friends and virtuous companions, rather than evil friends or evil companions.
Why is this? It is because I have always acted as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) for all sentient beings.
Since those sentient beings are subject to birth, you should know that the World-Honored One’s True Dharma manifests the teaching to liberate them from birth.

For those who possess old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, vexation, and suffering, he causes them to be free from all burning afflictions; without waiting for a specific time, he enables them to be liberated from distress and suffering, seeing through to realization, and attaining personal awakening and verification.
"These, then, are good friends and good companions, not evil friends or evil companions.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Praising heedfulness is the true teaching of the Buddha;
"By practicing meditation with heedfulness, one attains the realization that all outflows have been exhausted.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and praised it with gladness; he prostrated and departed.
1239. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit was reflecting in solitude and had this thought:

"Is there perhaps a single dharma which, through cultivation and repeated cultivation, results in the fulfillment of wishes for the present life, the fulfillment of wishes for future lives, and the fulfillment of wishes for both the present and future lives?"
Having had this thought, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
While reflecting alone in quietude, I had this thought:”

"Is there perhaps a single dharma which, through cultivation and repeated cultivation, leads to the fulfillment of wishes for the present life, the fulfillment of wishes for future lives, and the fulfillment of wishes for both the present and future lives?"
The Buddha said to King Prasenajit:
“So it is, Great King! So it is, Great King!”

There is one dharma which, when cultivated and practiced extensively, leads to the fulfillment of aspirations for the present life, the fulfillment of aspirations for future lives, and the fulfillment of aspirations for both the present and future lives; that is to say, the dharma of heedfulness.

By practicing and frequently cultivating the wholesome dharma of heedfulness, one attains the fulfillment of aspirations for the present life, the fulfillment of aspirations for future lives, and the fulfillment of aspirations for both the present and future lives.
“Great King!
Just as all coarse activities performed in the world are established by depending upon the earth,
so too is the wholesome dharma of heedfulness.”

Through cultivation and repeated cultivation, one attains the fulfillment of wishes for the present life, the fulfillment of wishes for future lives, and the fulfillment of wishes for both the present and future lives.
It is as with the powers.
In the same way, it is also said regarding seeds, roots, firmness, land, water, feet, walking, lions, and dwellings.
Therefore, Great King!
One should dwell in heedfulness and rely upon heedfulness.
Having dwelt in heedfulness and relied upon heedfulness, a wife should think:
"The Great King dwells in heedfulness and relies upon heedfulness; I too shall now likewise dwell in heedfulness and rely upon heedfulness."
"In this same way, it is with the queen, and likewise with the great ministers, the crown prince, and the fierce generals.
The people of the realm should reflect:

'The Great King abides in heedfulness and relies upon heedfulness; the queen, the crown prince, the great ministers, and the fierce generals abide in heedfulness and rely upon heedfulness. We, too, should likewise abide in heedfulness and rely upon heedfulness.'"
"O Great King!
If one dwells in heedfulness and relies upon heedfulness, then one can protect oneself;
one's wives and court ladies will likewise be able to preserve themselves, and the storehouses of grain and treasures will increase and become abundant."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Praise is bestowed upon the heedful, while the heedless are censured.
Because Śakra was heedful, he became the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
One praises heedfulness and censures the heedless;
by being fully endowed with heedfulness, one secures two benefits:
first, benefit in this present life, and second, likewise in future lives.
"This is called immediate realization (*abhisamaya*); it is for those of profound wisdom.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and approved, paid homage, and departed.
1240. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit, reflecting in solitude, had this thought:
"There are these three things that are not loved or cherished by anyone in the world."
What are these three?
They are old age, sickness, and death.
These three phenomena are not beloved or cherished by anyone in the entire world.

If these three things, which are not beloved by the world, did not exist, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, would not appear in the world, nor would the world know that there are dharmas realized by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, for the sake of others to be extensively taught.

Because these three phenomena—namely, old age, sickness, and death—are not loved or cherished by the world, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, appear in the world; it is known throughout the world that there are Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, who have awakened to the Dharma and extensively proclaim it.
Having formed this thought, King Prasenajit went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
He then related in detail to the World-Honored One what he had been thinking.
The Buddha told King Prasenajit:
"So it is, Great King! So it is, Great King!"

There are three things that are not beloved by the world: namely, old age, sickness, and death; even unto the point where the world knows that there are dharmas realized by the Tathāgata which he has proclaimed extensively for the sake of others.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The precious chariot upon which the king rides will ultimately return to decay;
this body is likewise so: it shifts and changes until it returns to old age."
Only the True Dharma of the Tathāgata is free from the signs of aging and decay;
those who receive this True Dharma shall forever reach the place of peace and security.
But as for ordinary, base aging and decay—those ugly, wretched, and evil forms—
Decay and old age come to trample upon the hearts of deluded and foolish men.
Even if a person lives for a hundred years, they must constantly fear that death will follow;
old age and sickness pursue one another, waiting for an opportunity to inflict their harm.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and delighted in it;
he paid homage and departed. *Saṃyukta Āgama*, Scroll 46. *Saṃyukta Āgama*, Scroll 47.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
(1241) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Whoever stays in my house shall all attain pure faith;
and whoever passes away while staying in my house shall all be reborn in the heavens," the Buddha said.
"Excellent! Excellent,
householder!"
"This is a profound and subtle teaching, to be accepted unreservedly," he said, letting out a lion's roar amidst the great assembly:
"All those who dwell in my house shall attain pure faith;
and when their lives end, they shall all be reborn in the heavens."
"Is there some bhikṣu of great virtue and supernormal power who has said to you:
'All those who die in your house shall be reborn in the heavens'?"
The householder replied to the Buddha,
“No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha asked again:
“How is it? Was it for the bhikṣuṇīs, or for the devas, or did you hear this teaching from my presence?
The householder replied to the Buddha:
"No, World-Honored One. "How so,
householder?"
"Do you know for yourself, through your own knowledge and vision, that 'all those who pass away in my house are reborn in the heavens'?
The householder replied to the Buddha,
"No, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha told the householder:

"Since you have not heard this from a bhikṣu of great virtue and supernatural power, nor from a bhikṣuṇī, nor from the devas; since you have not heard it spoken in my presence, nor have you known it through your own direct perception:
'If there are people who pass away in my house, they are all reborn in the heavens. "
"How is it that you are now able to deliver such a profound and wondrous teaching, accepting it as definitive, and uttering this lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, saying:
'Any person who passes away from my house shall all be reborn in the heavens'?"
The householder said to the Buddha:
"There was no bhikṣu of great virtue and supernatural power who came to inform me... as explained at length above, up until: "...and they all were reborn in heaven."
World-Honored One!

When there are sentient beings who are pregnant, I immediately instruct them so that for the sake of their children they may take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus;
and once the child has been born, I further instruct them in the Three Refuges.
When they have given birth and possess knowledge and vision, I further instruct them in the observance of the precepts.
Even if female slaves or lowly guests conceive and give birth, I likewise instruct them.
If there are those who sell male or female slaves, I immediately go to them and say:
"Venerable one!
I wish to purchase a person.
You should take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus, and you should receive and uphold the prohibitive precepts."
