"To those who follow my instructions, I shall immediately bestow the five precepts, and only then purchase them at their price;
those who do not follow my instructions, I will not accept.
Furthermore, if there are guests or hired laborers, I likewise require that they first receive the three refuges and the five precepts before I employ them."

Furthermore, if there are those who come seeking to become my disciples, or those who beg for loans at interest, I invariably require them to take the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts before I accept them.

Furthermore, when I made offerings in my home to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, I invoked the names of my parents, brothers, wife, children, kinsmen, friends, kings, ministers, devas, nāgas, and spirits—whether living or deceased—as well as śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, my internal and external relatives, and even down to my servants, invoking all their names and offering prayers for their blessing.

Furthermore, I have heard from the World-Honored One that by virtue of the causes and conditions of reciting names and making aspirations, all may be reborn in the heavens; whether it be through the giving of gardens and fields, or dwellings, or bedding and furniture, or through regular almsgiving, or providing for travelers—even down to giving a single morsel of food to sentient beings—all such causes and conditions lead to rebirth in the heavens.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Elder! It is because of your faith that you are able to speak thus.
The Tathāgata possesses unsurpassed knowledge and vision regarding them; he knows with certainty that those in your household who have passed away have all been reborn in the heavens."
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and approved with gladness;
he paid homage and departed. 1242 (1242). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"You should dwell with reverence, constantly bind your minds, and always maintain cautious fear toward those who practice the holy life—whether they be seniors, middling, or junior—relying upon them for guidance."

Why is this? If there is a bhikṣu who dwells without reverence, does not fix his mind, lacks fear and caution, and does not follow the senior, middle, or junior seats of those practicing the holy life with self-mastery, yet wishes to be complete in his dignified deportment—this is impossible!
It is impossible for one who does not maintain dignified deportment to fulfill the training in the Dharma!

It is impossible for one whose training in the Dharma is incomplete to become fully endowed with the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation!
"It is impossible for one whose knowledge and vision of liberation are not yet fulfilled to attain *nirvāṇa* without remainder;
such a thing cannot occur!

"In this way, bhikṣus, it is possible that you may diligently cultivate reverence, fix the mind, and maintain cautious heedfulness, following those of superior, middling, or inferior standing who practice the holy life according to their respective virtues and powers, and who are fully endowed with dignified deportment."

It is possible that one who is fully endowed with dignified conduct will become fully endowed with the training in the Dharma; and it is possible that one who is fully endowed with the training in the Dharma will become fully endowed with the aggregate of morality, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation!
"It is possible that one who has fulfilled the body of liberation through knowledge and vision will attain *nirvāṇa* without remainder.

Therefore, monks, you should diligently practice with reverence, focused attention, and careful heedfulness; following the power of others' virtues, toward those practicing the holy life—whether senior, middle, or junior in rank—and with full observance of dignified conduct, you should train yourselves thus until reaching *nirvāṇa* without remainder."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1243 (1243) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are two pure dharmas that can protect the world.
What are these two?"
These are what are called shame (*hrī*) and remorse (*apatrāpya*).

If these two pure dharmas did not exist in the world, the world would likewise not know the order of parents, brothers, sisters, wives, children, kinsmen, teachers, elders, and those of high or low station; it would be inverted and chaotic, like the realm of animals.

Because there are two kinds of purifying dharmas, namely shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), the world knows the existence of parents, and even the order of teachers and elders, so that there is no confusion, as is the case among the animal realm.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If there were none in this world who possess the two dharmas of shame and remorse,
they would transgress the path of purity and head toward birth, old age, sickness, and death."
"In this world, those who have accomplished the two dharmas of shame and remorse increase the path of purity and forever close the gates of birth and death.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1244 (1244). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There is the nature of burning and the nature of not burning.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you.”
"What is the dharma of burning?

If a man or a woman violates the precepts and practices evil and unwholesome dharmas, accomplishing misconduct of body, speech, and mind, and later falls ill with suffering and distress, lying prostrate upon a bed and enduring various agonies;
at that time, they will fully recall all the evils previously committed."
It is like a great mountain where, as the sun sets, its shadow falls across it.

In the same way, the evil deeds previously committed by sentient beings—the unwholesome dharmas of body, speech, and mind—all manifest at the moment of death, and the mind then feels remorse, thinking: "Alas!"
"Alas! Having failed to cultivate goodness in the past and having done nothing but commit various evils, I shall surely fall into the evil realms and undergo all manner of bitter suffering.
Having reflected thus, his heart was set ablaze with remorse and he felt deep regret.

Having given rise to remorse, one does not attain a wholesome mind; after the end of life, in a future existence, an unwholesome mind continues to arise in succession. This is called the "burning dharma.
What is the "non-burning"?

If a man or woman upholds the pure precepts, cultivates the true Dharma, and achieves wholesome karma of body, speech, and mind, then at the time of death, when their body is afflicted by suffering and they lie prostrate upon a bed, with various pains assailing them, their mind will recollect the wholesome dharmas previously cultivated—the wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind they have achieved.
At that moment, they will take hold of these wholesome dharmas as their object of focus, thinking:
"I have performed such wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, and committed no evil; I shall be born in a happy realm and not fall into an evil destiny."
"His mind does not waver or regret; because he does not waver or regret, he passes away with a virtuous mind and continues his virtue in future lives—this is called the 'unburning' dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Having planted the karma of burning, Living by means of what is not Dharma,"
Driven by such evil karmic conduct, one will surely be born within the hells:
Sañjīva and Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta and the two Rauravas,
Tapana and Pratāpana, as well as the Avīci Great Hell.
These eight great hells, where suffering is extreme and difficult to transcend,
consist of sixteen distinct locations each due to the various kinds of evil karma.
They have four gates opening on all four sides, and their dimensions are entirely equal throughout.
The surrounding walls are made of iron, and the four door-panels are likewise iron.
The iron ground is ablaze with fire, its flames spreading everywhere across a vast expanse of one hundred yojanas, with each flame incessantly flickering without respite.
Subduing those who are not disciplined, punishing the violent and arrogant—inflicting such bitter torment throughout the long night, its suffering is difficult to behold.
Those who see it give rise to terror; they tremble with fear until the hairs on their bodies stand on end.
When falling into that hell, one’s feet are upward and head downward.
Toward those who dwell in this state of noble ones— those whose minds are stilled, gentle, and holy, and who practice the pure life—
one might give rise to a disrespectful mind and cause harm.
Those who kill and harm sentient beings fall into this Heat Hell,
wallowing amidst the flames like fish being grilled over a fire.
Their cries of agony and lamentation resound like the trumpeting of a herd of battling elephants.
"The great fire has spontaneously arisen; this is due to one's own karma.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1245. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"One who abandons bodily misconduct is able to achieve the cessation of bodily misconduct;
as for one who does not achieve the cessation of bodily misconduct, I do not say that they have abandoned bodily misconduct."
Because they are able to attain the abandonment of bodily misconduct, I say that they have relinquished bodily misconduct.
Bodily misconduct does not bring about benefit, welfare, or happiness.
Because sentient beings, by abandoning unwholesome conduct of body, are benefited by its meaning and attain peace and happiness, I therefore speak of abandoning unwholesome conduct of body;
the same is said for unwholesome conduct of speech and mind.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1246 (1246). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the residence of a goldsmith in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"It is like a goldsmith who gathers sand and soil, places it in a trough, and then pours water over it; the coarse surface impurities, hard stones, and solid clods are carried away by the water, yet there still remains coarse sand entangled within."
Again, water was poured over it, and the coarse sand flowed out with the water; thereafter, gold appeared, yet it was still entangled with fine sand and black earth.

Again, water was poured over it, and the fine sand and black earth flowed out with the water; thereafter, the true gold was pure and free from admixture, yet there remained slight impurities resembling gold.

Thereafter, the goldsmith places it in a furnace, increases the fire, and beats it with a bellows to cause it to melt; all impurities are thereby removed. However, the raw gold remains as it was: it is neither light nor soft, its luster does not shine forth, and it breaks when bent or stretched.

That goldsmith or his apprentice places it back into the furnace, increases the fire, and blows the bellows; by turning and refining it, the produced gold becomes light, soft, and lustrous, capable of being bent and extended without breaking, so that he may fashion from it various ornaments as he desires—hairpins, bowls, rings, bracelets, and other such finery.

"In this way, as the bhikṣu advances with a purified mind, his coarse afflictions, evil and unwholesome karmas, and all wicked false views are gradually severed and extinguished, just as that native gold is cleansed by removing its grit and hard lumps."

"Furthermore, when a bhikkhu of purified mind progresses further, he removes the next level of coarse impurities—the thought of sensual desire, the thought of ill will, and the thought of cruelty—just as that native gold is cleansed of coarse sand and gravel."

"Furthermore, as the bhikṣu of pure mind progresses, he next eliminates subtle defilements, namely: thoughts of kinsmen, thoughts of social circles, and thoughts of rebirth in heaven; he contemplates them and eliminates them, just as one removes dust, fine sand, and black earth from refined gold."

"Furthermore, when a monk with a purified mind advances, he possesses wholesome states of awakening; through reflection, he eliminates [unwholesome states] and purifies his mind, just as one removes impurities resembling gold from raw gold to make it pure."

"Furthermore, a bhikkhu dwells with his meditative concentrations sustained by mental formations, just as water in a pond is held by its surrounding banks. Being thus sustained by phenomena, he does not attain tranquility or sublime excellence; he does not obtain the bliss of cessation, nor does he exhaust all taints."

It is like a goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice who smelts raw gold; though they remove all impurities, if it is not made light, supple, and radiant, and if it breaks when bent or stretched, it cannot be fashioned at will into ornamental objects.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu attains various samādhis and is no longer constrained by conditioned activities; he attains tranquil excellence and the path of the bliss of cessation; with a single mind and single intent, he exhausts all outflows."
It is like a goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice who smelts raw gold, making it light, pliant, unbreakable, and lustrous, so that it may be bent or extended according to their will.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu, having departed from applied and sustained thought, attains the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
Such meditative attainments are purely and entirely clear, free from all afflictions, supple, genuine, and immovable.
In each and every sphere of entry, whatever he seeks to realize, he is able to fully realize it.
It is like a goldsmith who refines raw gold until it is extremely pliant, soft, lustrous, and unbreakable, so that it may be fashioned into any vessel according to his will.
"In this way, bhikṣus, through the correct reception of samādhi, one is able to realize and attain [mastery] even regarding all the sense bases.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sūtra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1247 (1247). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should apply oneself with focused skillful means and, at the appropriate times, contemplate three characteristics.
What are these three?

One should contemplate the characteristic of tranquility (śamatha) at the appropriate time, contemplate the characteristic of exertion (pragraha) at the appropriate time, and contemplate the characteristic of equanimity (upekṣā) at the appropriate time."
If a bhikṣu contemplates exclusively the sign of tranquility (śamatha-nimitta), his mind will become inferior in that state.

If he again contemplates exclusively the sign of exertion (pragraha-nimitta), a distracted mind will arise in that state. If he again contemplates exclusively the sign of equanimity (upekṣā-nimitta), he will not attain right concentration and exhaust all outflows (āsrava) in that state.

"Because that bhikṣu contemplates the sign of tranquility at the appropriate time, contemplates the sign of exertion at the appropriate time, and contemplates the sign of equanimity at the appropriate time, his mind becomes rightly concentrated and he exhausts all taints."

It is like a skilled goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice who places raw gold in a furnace, increasing the fire, fanning the bellows at the appropriate time, sprinkling water at the appropriate time, and withdrawing both at the appropriate time.
If one blows the bellows exclusively, the gold produced in that place will be scorched away;
if one sprinkles water exclusively, the gold produced in that place will be hard and strong.
If one were to abandon both [fanning and sprinkling] exclusively, then the gold produced in that place would not be refined and would thus be of no use.

Therefore, a skilled smith or a smith’s apprentice, regarding that raw gold, fans it with bellows at the appropriate time, sprinkles water at the appropriate time, and abandons both at the appropriate time.
Just as this native gold, having attained perfect refinement, is used according to its purpose; so too, bhikṣu,
through single-minded skillful means, by contemplating and recollecting the three marks from time to time, one reaches even unto the exhaustion of the outflows.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1248 (1248). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"In times past, in the kingdom of Magadha, there was a cowherd who was foolish and lacked wisdom. At the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, he did not carefully observe this bank of the Ganges River, nor did he carefully observe the opposite bank of the Ganges. He drove his herd of cattle down the steep bank and up the steep bank; in the midst of the swirling eddies, many calamities arose."

"Monks! In times past, in the kingdom of Magadha, there was a cowherd who was neither foolish nor deluded, but possessed skillful wisdom. At the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, he would skillfully observe this bank of the Ganges and skillfully observe the opposite bank of the Ganges, and he would skillfully lead his cattle to places of level, broad valleys with excellent water and grass."
When he first began to ferry them across, he first ferried the great bull capable of leading the herd, thereby cutting off the swift current.

Next, he drove the second group of strong young bulls across, following behind him. Then, he drove the third group of weak and small ones, following down the stream; in this manner, they all crossed safely and in due order.
"A newborn calf, out of affection for its mother, follows after her and succeeds in crossing to the other shore.
In this way, bhikṣus, I have spoken this parable; you should understand its meaning."
Those cowherds of Magadha were foolish and lacked wisdom;
those six teachers, such as Pūraṇa and the others, were likewise so—they practiced various false views and headed toward the wrong path.

It is like that foolish cowherd who lacks wisdom; at the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, failing to carefully observe this shore and the other shore, the high precipices, and the steep cliffs, he descends from the steep bank and ascends the steep bank, where the swirling eddies in between cause many hardships and dangers.
Thus, these six teachers, Pūraṇa and the others, were foolish and devoid of wisdom; they did not observe this shore, which refers to the present world;
nor did they observe the other shore, which refers to the future world;
and they were caught in the swirling eddies in between, which refers to the various maras of sensory objects, thereby meeting with suffering and calamity themselves.
Those who hold such views, though they practice what they have learned, will likewise encounter suffering and calamity.
"That skilled cowherd of Magadha—neither foolish nor deluded, but possessing skillful wisdom—is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."

It is like a cowherd who carefully observes this shore, carefully observes the other shore, and skillfully ferries his cattle across; in a level and broad valley, he first ferries across the large bull that leads the herd, crossing the swift current at a diagonal angle and safely reaching the other shore.
In this way, my disciples are able to exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*), even knowing for themselves that they will not undergo further existence.
They have cut across the worldly torrent of craving belonging to Māra, and have safely reached the further shore of birth and death.

"Just as a skilled cowherd in the kingdom of Magadha next leads a second herd of strong, young cattle across by cutting through the current, so too my disciples, having severed the five lower fetters and attained the stage of non-returner (*anāgāmin*), are reborn there and do not return to this world; they likewise sever the flow of Māra’s craving and safely cross to the further shore of birth and death."
"Just as a skilled cowherd in the kingdom of Magadha drives his third group of weak, small, and young oxen downstream, enabling them to cross safely."

In this way, my disciples have severed the three fetters; with greed, hatred, and delusion attenuated, they have attained the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*. Returning once more to this world, they shall reach the ultimate end of suffering. They have cut across the torrent of the Evil Māra’s craving and have safely crossed to the further shore of birth and death.
"Just as in the kingdom of Magadha, a skilled cowherd has a newborn calf that is so attached to its mother that it follows her wherever she goes;

even so, my disciples who have severed the three fetters and attained the stage of *srotāpanna* do not fall into the evil realms. They are destined for full awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), will be reborn seven times at most among gods and humans, and will ultimately reach the end of suffering. Having cut off the torrent of Māra’s craving, they attain peace and cross to the further shore of birth and death."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"In this world and in the world beyond, The wise one manifests clearly;
Whether Māras have been conquered or not, Even unto the Māra of Death."
The All-Knowing One, with the wisdom of Samyaksaṃbuddha,
cuts off the flows of all Māras and destroys them so that they perish.
He opens the gate of the nectar of immortality and reveals the path of true correctness.
"The mind is constantly full of joy, having attained a state of peace and security.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1249 (1249). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If a cowherd is not endowed with eleven qualities, he will be unable to cause his cattle to increase, nor will he be able to protect a large herd of cattle, ensuring their equal peace and happiness."
What are these eleven? They are:

not knowing the form, not knowing the characteristics, failing to remove the maggots, being unable to protect the wound, being unable to produce smoke, not knowing how to choose the path, not knowing how to choose the location, not knowing how to cross the ford, not knowing where to graze, milking the cow until it is dry, and being unskilled in managing the leader of the herd. These are called the eleven qualities by which one fails to be able to protect and lead a large herd of cattle.
“In this way, monks, one who is endowed with these eleven qualities cannot establish themselves in peace, nor can they establish others in peace.
What are the eleven? They are: not knowing form; not knowing its characteristics;

being unable to eliminate its harmful insects; failing to cover its wounds; being unable to produce smoke; not knowing the right path; not knowing the place of rest; not knowing the place of crossing; not knowing the place of nourishment; milking the cow until its milk is exhausted; and, if there are elder bhikṣus who are learned, of long standing, who have long practiced the holy life, and are praised by the Great Teacher—not praising their virtues before those wise ones who practice the holy life, so as to cause them all to revere, serve, and make offerings to them.”
"What is meant by not knowing form as it truly is?
All forms whatsoever are entirely the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements; this is what is called not knowing form as it truly is."
"What is the characteristic of non-knowing?
To regard activity as a characteristic of fault and activity as a characteristic of wisdom—failing to know this as it truly is—is called the characteristic of non-knowing."
"What is meant by 'not knowing how to remove the worm'?

When sensual thoughts arise, one remains complacent with them, neither abandoning nor awakening from them nor extinguishing them; when thoughts of ill will or harm arise, one remains complacent with them, neither abandoning nor awakening from them nor extinguishing them—this is called 'not removing the worm.'"
"What is meant by 'not bandaging a wound'?

It means that when the eye sees forms, one grasps at their characteristics and fails to guard the faculty of the eye; thus, worldly greed and sorrow, as well as evil and unwholesome states, arise as outflows within the mind, which it is unable to restrain.
The same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind."
This is called not covering one's wounds.
What is meant by "not emitting smoke"?
To be unable to analyze and explain for others the Dharma as it was heard and received—this is called not emitting smoke.
“What is not knowing the right path?
The Eightfold Path and the Noble Dharma and Discipline are called the path; to not know them as they truly are is called not knowing the path.”
"What is meant by not knowing the place of rest?
It refers to failing to attain joy, delight, excellence, renunciation, and benefit regarding the dharmas known by the Tathāgata; this is called not knowing the place of rest."
"What is meant by not knowing the means of crossing over?
It refers to one who does not know the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma; who does not go at the appropriate time to those [teachers] to inquire, request instruction, and receive it, asking:
'What constitutes what is wholesome?'"
What is unwholesome?
What is blameworthy?
What is blameless?
"What kind of practice is superior and not evil?

Being unable to elucidate the hidden teachings, being unable to inquire extensively about the manifest teachings, and being unable to widely proclaim and demonstrate the profound meanings of the words that one knows for oneself—this is called "not knowing the point of transition."
"What is meant by 'not knowing the place of pasture'?
The four foundations of mindfulness and the noble Dharma and Vinaya are called the place of pasture; not knowing these as they truly are is what is meant by 'not knowing the place of pasture.'"
"What is meant by 'milking it dry'?

When kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, or those in positions of power give away robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and various necessities of life, and the bhikṣu who receives them does not know moderation—this is called milking it dry."

"What is it that causes the elders, the venerable ones, those of great learning and long-standing seniority—even up to those who are not praised for their virtues by other wise fellow practitioners of the holy life—to be held in high esteem, served, and provided with offerings, so that they may attain joy?"

This refers to a bhikṣu who does not honor that elder, nor even cause wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacārin*) to go to his presence to serve him with compliant actions of body, speech, and mind; this is called failing to honor and serve an elder who is learned and of long standing, nor causing wise fellow-practitioners to go to his presence to serve him, so as to bring him joy and satisfaction.
"When that cowherd accomplishes eleven qualities, he is capable of causing his herd of cattle to increase, protecting the herd, and making them joyful."
What are these eleven? They are:

knowing the cattle, knowing their characteristics—as explained above in the section on purification—and so on, up to being able to lead the herd and manage them according to the season, enabling them to attain peace and happiness. This is called the cowherd’s accomplishment of the eleven matters, which enables him to cause the herd of cattle to increase and be protected, and to attain peace and happiness.
"In this way, bhikṣus, one who accomplishes these eleven qualities can bring peace and happiness to themselves and can also bring peace and happiness to others.
What are the eleven? They are:

knowing form, knowing characteristics, and so on up to the eleventh... as explained at length in the *Vimalavarga*, "this is called a bhikṣu who, having accomplished these eleven matters, brings peace and happiness to himself and to others."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1250 (1250). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of Kośala and arrived at the village of Ekanālā, where he stayed in the Ekanālā forest.
At that time, the Venerable Nādikā was residing in the village of Ekasālā.

The śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the village of Ekasālā heard that the śramaṇa Gautama, while wandering through the human settlements of the Kosalans, had arrived at the village of Ekasālā and was staying in the forest of Ekasālā.
Having heard this, each of them prepared a pot of food and placed it by the door, thinking:
"I shall be the first to make an offering to the World-Honored One!
I shall be the first to make an offering to the Sugata!"
Each raised their voices loudly, chanting in this manner.
At that time, the World-Honored One, hearing the many people within the grove making loud and high-pitched sounds, addressed the Venerable Nādiya:
"For what cause and for what reason are there so many people within the grove making such loud and high-pitched sounds of chanting?"
The Venerable Nāṭika addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

When the kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and elders of this village of Sekanagara heard that the World-Honored One was dwelling in this forest grove, each of them prepared a pot of food and placed it within the park, each proclaiming:”
"I have first made offerings to the World-Honored One!
I have first made offerings to the Sugata!
For this reason, many people in this grove raise their voices and utter such loud cries.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept that food.
The Buddha told Nādikā:
"Do not seek to benefit me; I do not seek benefit."
Do not seek praise for me; I do not seek praise. Nādikas!

If one can find the bliss of renunciation, seclusion, peace, and perfect enlightenment in the Tathāgata in this way, would one then still relish or seek after the various benefits and pleasures that arise?

"Nadīga! Only I have attained, without seeking and without hardship, the bliss of definitive emergence, seclusion, cessation, and perfect awakening regarding this class of phenomena. Why then would I seek or savor any benefit or pleasure arising from this or that?"

Nādikas! Because you have not attained the essential departure, the seclusion, the cessation, and the bliss of perfect enlightenment regarding such forms as these, you have not attained the bliss of seeking nothing, nor the bliss that is free from suffering.

Nādikā! Even the devas do not obtain such a kind of bliss that is the essential departure, seclusion, and cessation; the bliss of perfect enlightenment, the bliss of no seeking, and the bliss of no suffering.
Only I have attained such a state of bliss that is the essential escape, seclusion, and cessation, the perfectly awakened bliss, the bliss of no-seeking, and the bliss of no-suffering.
"In what regard does one experience the pleasure and benefit arising from this or that, whether in its savor or in its pursuit?
Nādikā addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I now wish to speak a parable.
The Buddha told Nādikā:
"You should know that this is the time."
Nādikā addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

It is as when the heavens rain and the waters flow downward; wherever the World-Honored One dwells, there the kṣatriyas, brahmins, and householders offer them faithful service. This is because the World-Honored One’s precepts and virtue are pure, and his right view is true and direct.”
"Therefore, I now speak thus: I only pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately accept his invitation.
The Buddha told Nādikā:
"Do not seek to benefit me; I do not seek benefit."
"...up to: how can there be any relish or seeking for the benefit and happiness arising from this or that? Nādikā!
I have seen a bhikṣu who, having eaten fine food, lies down with his belly upturned, gasping and breathing heavily."
Having seen this, I reflected:
"This elder has not attained the bliss of transcendence, seclusion, and cessation; the bliss of perfect enlightenment; the bliss of seeking nothing; nor the bliss that is free from suffering."
"Furthermore, Nādikā!
I have seen two bhikṣus who, having eaten fine food until their bellies were full, walked along panting and with their bodies sprawled out."
I thought to myself:

"That elder is not capable of attaining the bliss of transcendence, seclusion, and tranquility; the bliss of perfect enlightenment; the bliss of seeking nothing; and the bliss that is free from suffering."
"Nadika! I see many bhikṣus who, having eaten fine food, go from garden to garden, from room to room, from person to person, and from group to group."
Having seen this, I had this thought:
"It is not by means of such [practices] that that elder is able to attain the bliss of renunciation, seclusion, tranquility, and perfect enlightenment;
the bliss of non-seeking, the bliss of non-suffering—such as these, I have attained."
"Furthermore, Nādikā!
On one occasion, as I was walking along a path, I saw a bhikṣu who had gone far ahead, and another bhikṣu who was also far behind."
At that time, I was in a state of quietude and non-action, and there was no toil of excrement or urine. Why is this?
Because it is by depending on food and drink and being attached to their flavors that excrement and urine arise; these, then, are the basis [of such toil].
To dwell in disenchantment through observing the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates of clinging—this is the reliance.
To dwell in disenchantment through observing the origination and cessation of the six bases of sensory contact—this is the reliance.
To diligently practice socializing while finding joy in such gatherings, and to feel aversion toward seclusion—this is reliance.
To delight in cultivating seclusion, to be diligent in solitude, and to feel weary of and detached from socializing—this is reliance.
Therefore, Nādikā, you should train yourself thus:

"Observe the arising and passing away of the five aggregates of clinging; observe the origination and cessation of the six bases of sensory contact; delight in seclusion and be diligent in seclusion."
"One should train thus.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Nādikā, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and delighted in it, paid homage, and departed.
1251 (1251). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of Kosala and arrived at the village of Naḷakalāpa... as described in detail above, including the various ways in which they sought profit.
The Buddha told Nādikā:
"I saw a monastery on the outskirts of a village where a bhikṣu was sitting in meditation.
Having seen this, I had this thought:"

"Now these venerable ones from the village, or perhaps these śrāmaṇeras, by their coming and going and their clamor, disturb his meditation, obstruct his contemplation, and hinder his realization; they create obstacles for one who seeks to reach what has not been reached, to attain what has not been attained, and to realize what has not been realized."
"Nadika! I do not approve of that bhikṣu dwelling in a village monastery. Nadika!"
I saw a bhikṣu dwelling in a secluded place, lying on his back and sighing.
Having seen this, I thought to myself:
"May that bhikṣu awaken from his sleep and contemplate the perception of seclusion."
"Nadika! I also do not delight in such bhikṣus dwelling in secluded places. Nadika!"
Furthermore, I saw a bhikṣu dwelling in a secluded place who was sitting dozing with his body swaying.
Having seen this, I thought:
"Now this bhikṣu, having awakened from sleep, has not yet attained concentration where there was no concentration; one whose mind is concentrated attains liberation."
"Therefore, Nādikā!
I do not delight in such bhikṣus dwelling in secluded places. Nādikā!"
Furthermore, I saw a bhikṣu dwelling in a secluded place, sitting upright in meditative absorption.
Having seen him, I thought:
"May this bhikṣu, who has not yet attained liberation, quickly attain liberation."
"Those who have already attained liberation, I cause them to guard themselves so that they do not fall away from it.
Nādikā! I delight in such bhikṣus dwelling in secluded places.

"Nadika! Furthermore, I see a bhikkhu who dwells in a secluded place, yet at a later time, having abandoned his secluded dwelling and his bedding and seats, he returns to the village to accept bedding and seats."
"Nadika! I do not approve of such a bhikṣu returning to the village.
Furthermore, Nadika!"

I have seen bhikṣus residing in monasteries within villages who, being renowned and of great virtue, were able to attract wealth, robes, food and drink, medicinal requisites, and various articles of utility.
At a later time, he gathered his bedding from the village where he had received offerings and went to a secluded place to lie down and rest in peace. Nādikā!
I delight in such a bhikṣu who, having abandoned the bedding of the village where he received offerings, dwells in a secluded place.
"Nadika! A bhikṣu should train himself in this way.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣu Nadika rejoiced and delighted in it, paid his respects, and departed.
1252 (1252). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, by the side of the Monkey Pond, in the Multi-storied Lecture Hall.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“The Licchavis always sleep with wooden pillows; their hands and feet are cracked and split, for they are apprehensive and fearful lest Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra, the King of Magadha, find an opportunity against them.”
Therefore, one should always admonish oneself and abide in non-negligence;
because of abiding in that non-negligence, Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra, the King of Magadha, will be unable to find an opportunity to exploit any weakness.

In the future, before long, the Licchavis will dwell in heedlessness, indulging in pleasures and remaining free from affairs; their hands and feet will be soft, they will sleep peacefully on pillows of silk and cotton, and they will not rise when the sun comes up, remaining in a state of negligence.
Because they remain in such negligence, Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra, the King of Magadha, will find an opportunity against them.

"In this way, bhikṣus, through diligent application, firmness, and capability, they do not abandon the wholesome dharmas; their skin and flesh waste away until they are reduced to a mere framework of sinews and bones."

Through diligent application of skillful means, he does not abandon wholesome dharmas; until that which is to be attained has been attained, he does not relinquish his vigor. He constantly gathers his mind and dwells in heedfulness;
because he dwells in heedfulness, Māra Pāpīyān finds no opportunity.

"In a future age, there will be certain bhikṣus who indulge in ease and have no concerns; their hands and feet will be soft and supple, they will use silk and cotton for pillows, lie down with their four limbs at rest, and fail to rise when the sun comes up, remaining in a state of negligence.
Because they dwell in negligence, the evil Māra Pāpīyān will watch for and find his opportunity."
Therefore, bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves thus:
"With diligent application of skillful means, until that which has not yet been attained is attained, we shall not abandon our skillful means."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1253 (1253) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Suppose a man were to bestow three hundred cauldrons of food upon sentient beings in the morning, and likewise at noon and in the evening."

As for the second person, who for even a brief moment cultivates a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings—even for as long as it takes to milk a cow—this merit surpasses that of the former person’s gift of alms; it exceeds it by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, or even hundreds of millions of billions of times, such that no calculation or analogy can compare them.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should train yourselves thus:
"For even a brief moment, one should cultivate a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, down to the duration of time it takes to milk a cow."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1254 (1254). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Suppose there is a household with many women and few men; you should know that such a household is easily plundered by thieves."

If such good men or good women cannot repeatedly cultivate a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings for even as long as it takes to milk a cow, you should know that such persons are easily deceived by various evil ghosts and spirits.
"Just as a household with many men and few women is not repeatedly plundered by thieves,

so too, noble son, if you repeatedly cultivate a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings— even for as brief a moment as it takes to milk a cow— you will not be deceived by malevolent spirits."
"Therefore, monks, you should always, at all times, repeatedly cultivate a mind of loving-kindness, even for as brief a moment as it takes to milk a cow.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the monks, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1255 (1255). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Suppose there were a man who possessed a sword one cubit long, with a blade both broad and sharp.
A valiant warrior then said:"
"I am able to strike your sword with my hand or my fist so that it is shattered to pieces. "O monks!
Would that strong man be able to strike that sword with his hand or his fist so that it is shattered to pieces?"
The bhikṣu said to the Buddha:
“I cannot, World-Honored One!”
"That sword with its broad and sharp blade cannot be crushed, struck, or broken by that man using his hands or fists; it would only serve to exhaust him himself.
In the same way, bhikṣus!"

If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, for even as long as it takes to milk a cow, cultivates a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, then if there are malevolent ghosts or spirits who wish to go and seek out his faults, they will be unable to find any vulnerability; instead, they will only bring harm upon themselves.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "Repeatedly,
down to the duration of a single milking of a cow, we shall cultivate a mind of loving-kindness."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1256 (1256) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One took up some soil with his fingernail and addressed the bhikṣus:
"What do you think?
Is the soil on my fingernail more, or is the soil of the great earth more?"
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
The soil upon my fingernail is extremely small; the soil of the great earth is immeasurable and incalculable, beyond comparison.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“In this way, those beings who are able to repeatedly cultivate a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, even for as little as the snap of a finger, are like the soil upon a fingernail;
whereas those beings who are unable to repeatedly cultivate a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, even for as little as the snap of a finger, are like the soil of the great earth.”
"Therefore, O bhikṣus!
You should constantly and repeatedly cultivate a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1257 (1257). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, by the side of the Monkey Pond, in the Multi-storied Lecture Hall.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are not constant, they are not secure, and they are subject to change.
O bhikṣus!"
"One should constantly observe all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), cultivating weariness, detachment, and liberation.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, prostrated before the Buddha, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
"Regarding the transition and cessation of life, how swift or slow is it?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
“I am indeed able to explain it, but it is difficult for you to wish to know.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“May an analogy be given?
The Buddha said,
“It may be given.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Suppose there were four men, each holding a powerful bow, who simultaneously released their arrows, shooting them toward the four directions.
There was one man who, before the arrows had even fallen to the ground, caught all four of them."
"What do you think, bhikṣu?
Would such a man be considered swift?"
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“It is swift,
World-Honored One!”

The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Although this man who catches the arrow is swift, there is a terrestrial deva-son who is twice as fast as he; a celestial deva-son is twice as fast as the terrestrial deva; a Cāturmahārājika deva-son comes and goes twice as fast as the celestial deva; a Sūryacandramas deva-son is again twice as swift as the Cāturmahārājika deva; and the deva who guides the sun and moon is twice as swift as the Sūryacandramas deva."
"Monks! The transition and change of life proceed even more swiftly than that deity who guides the sun and moon. Therefore, monks!"
"One should diligently apply skillful means to observe that the formations of life are impermanent and swift in this way.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1258 (1258). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In a past age, there was a man named Daśaratha. That Daśaratha had a drum named Aṇaka, which produced a fine sound, a beautiful sound, and a deep sound that reached forty li."
After that drum had been used for a long time, it became cracked and broken in various places.
At that time, the drummer cut a piece of oxhide and wrapped it all around the drum;
yet, despite being wrapped, the drum still no longer produced a loud sound, a beautiful sound, or a deep sound.
At a later time, it further decays and rots; its bark peels away entirely until only a heap of wood remains.

"In this same way, bhikṣu, one cultivates the body, cultivates morality, cultivates the mind, and cultivates wisdom. Because of that cultivation of body, morality, mind, and wisdom, regarding the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata—which are profound and illuminating, difficult to see and difficult to realize, inconceivable, subtle, secret, and definitive, and known only by the wise—one then receives them all at once and receives them completely. Hearing what is taught, one rejoices in practicing it with reverence, thereby attaining liberation and benefit."

In the future, there will be bhikṣus who do not cultivate the body, do not cultivate ethical discipline, do not cultivate the mind, and do not cultivate wisdom. When they hear the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata—profound, luminous, corresponding to emptiness, and in accord with dependent origination—they will not immediately accept and uphold them, nor will they reach the point of full realization.

When one hears such teachings, one does not rejoice in them nor practice them with devotion; instead, one single-mindedly accepts and venerates the various worldly discourses, the flowery embellishments of rhetoric, and the miscellaneous phrases of the mundane world. When one hears such things and rejoices in practicing them, one fails to attain liberation or any true benefit.

Regarding those essential teachings on the profound, luminous, and empty nature as explained by that Tathāgata—which accord with dependent origination—these shall cease here, just like that drum which has become old, decayed, and split apart, leaving nothing but a heap of wood.

Therefore, monks, you should diligently apply skillful means to cultivate the body, cultivate ethical discipline, cultivate the mind, and cultivate wisdom; and regarding the essential Dharma of the profound, illuminating, and empty characteristics spoken by the Tathāgata, which accords with dependent origination, you should receive it all at once and receive it completely.
"Those who hear this teaching will joyfully honor and practice it, thereby attaining liberation and great benefit.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1259 (1259). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Suppose an iron ball were cast into a fire until it became the same color as the fire, and then placed inside cotton or silk floss.
"What do you think, bhikṣu?
Would it not burn up quickly?"
The bhikṣu replied to the Buddha,
“So it is, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu:

“Foolish people dwell in dependence upon villages; in the morning they put on their robes and take up their bowls to enter the village for alms. Failing to properly guard their bodies and failing to maintain the sense-faculties, their minds are not focused with mindfulness. If they see young women, they engage in improper reflection, grasping at their physical forms and giving rise to a mind of lustful desire.
This desire burns their minds and burns their bodies;
once both body and mind are consumed by fire, they abandon the precepts and fall away.”
This foolish person shall for a long night obtain what is neither meaningful nor beneficial. Therefore, monks,
you should train yourselves thus:
"Guarding the body well, protecting the doors of the sense faculties, and maintaining mindfulness, enter the village for alms.
"You should train yourselves thus.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1260. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, there was a wildcat who, emaciated by hunger and thirst, lay in wait within a burrow seeking young mice."
"If a mouse comes out, I shall seize and eat it.
Once, when a mouse came out of its hole to play, the cat quickly seized and swallowed it.
Because the mouse's body was small, it entered the cat's belly alive.

Once it has entered his belly, it devours his internal organs; while its internal organs are being devoured, the cat or wildcat becomes bewildered and distressed, running frantically east and west through empty houses and among graves, not knowing where to stop, until finally it reaches death.

“In this way, bhikṣus! There is a foolish person who dwells in dependence upon a village. In the morning, he puts on his robes and takes up his bowl to enter the village for alms. He does not guard his body well, nor does he maintain the sense-doors; his mind is not focused in mindfulness. Seeing women, he gives rise to improper thoughts and grasps at their physical forms, giving rise to a mind of lustful desire. Once lustful desire has arisen, the fire of passion blazes intensely, burning his body and mind.

Having burned his body and mind, his mind runs wild and unruly; he finds no joy in the monastery, no joy in solitude, and no joy beneath the trees. Because his evil and unwholesome mind devours his inner Dharma, he abandons the precepts and regresses. This foolish person will constantly experience disadvantage and suffering throughout the long night.”
Therefore, bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves thus:
"Guarding our bodies well, maintaining the doors of the sense faculties, and binding the mind with right mindfulness, we shall enter the village for alms."
"You should train yourselves thus.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1261 (1261) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Suppose there were a wooden pestle used constantly without ceasing; it would wear away day and night.”
In this way, bhikṣus!

If śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas have from the very beginning failed to guard the doors of their sense faculties, have been immoderate in eating, and have not diligently practiced the cultivation of wholesome dharmas during the first and last watches of the night, you should know that such persons suffer constant decline throughout the day and do not increase in wholesome dharmas, just like that wooden pestle.
“Monks! It is just as, for example, the blue lotus, the red lotus, the white water lily, and the white lotus are born in the water, grow in the water, and increase in accordance with the water.”

In this way, when śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas well-guard the doors of their sense faculties, know the proper measure in eating and drinking, and apply themselves with diligence to wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night, you should know that the roots of goodness and merit of such persons increase day and night, never declining or diminishing.
One should train in this way:

"Guarding well the doors of the sense faculties, knowing moderation in eating, and being diligent in wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night, may my meritorious wholesome qualities increase day and night."
"You should train yourselves thus.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1262 (1262) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa bamboo grove.
At that time, during the final watch of the night, the World-Honored One heard the cry of a wild fox.
When the night had passed and dawn broke, the World-Honored One arranged his seat before the great assembly and sat down, addressing the bhikṣus:
“Did you hear the wild foxes howling during the last watch of the night?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha,
“Yes, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There is a foolish person who thinks thus:
'May I receive a body and obtain such a form and appearance, and produce such a voice.'"
"How could such a foolish person fail to obtain rebirth in a realm of existence such as this that they seek?
Therefore, bhikṣus!

You should simply apply yourselves with diligent skillful means to seek the severance of all forms of existence (*bhava*); do not employ skillful means to increase all forms of existence. You should train yourselves in this way."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1263 (1263) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I do not praise the acceptance of even a small amount of bodily existence, much less a great amount. Why is this?"
Existence is suffering.
It is like excrement and filth, which is foul and offensive even in small amounts, let alone in large quantities.
So too, these various states of existence are not to be praised even for a moment, let alone for many.
Why is this? Because that which exists is suffering.
Therefore, bhikṣus!
One should train thus:
"Sever all forms of existence; do not increase existence.
One should train thus.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 1264 (1264) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, during the latter part of the night, the World-Honored One heard the cry of a wild fox.
When the night had passed, he arranged his seat before the great assembly and sat down, addressing the bhikṣus:
"Did you hear the cry of the wild fox during the latter part of the night?"
The bhikṣu replied to the Buddha,
“So it is, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"That wild fox is afflicted by scabies; for this reason, it cries out.
If there were someone who could treat that wild fox's scabies, the fox would surely recognize and repay its kindness."
Now there is a certain foolish person who knows neither gratitude nor how to repay kindness.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"Know gratitude and repay kindness.
If one repays even a small kindness and never forgets it, how much more so for a great kindness?
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1265. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.

At that time, the Venerable Bakula was residing in the Goldsmith’s Monastery in Rājagṛha; he was suffering from a severe illness, and the Venerable Pūrṇa was attending to him with care and providing for his needs.
Then, Vakkali said to Pūrṇā:

"You should go to where the World-Honored One is, prostrate yourself at his feet on my behalf, and inquire after the World-Honored One’s health, asking whether he has little illness and little affliction, whether he is light and agile in his movements, and whether he dwells in peace and happiness."
He said:
"Bakkula is staying at the Goldsmith’s Monastery; he is gravely ill and confined to his bed.
He wishes to see the World-Honored One, yet because he is so afflicted by illness and his strength is utterly exhausted, he has no means to come and pay his respects."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will descend upon this goldsmith’s vihāra out of compassion!
Then, having received the words of Bakula, Pūrṇikā went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

The Venerable Bakula prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and inquired after his health, asking whether he was free from illness and affliction, whether his daily life was light and easy, and whether he dwelt in peace and happiness.
The World-Honored One replied,
"May they be at peace and happy.
Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Venerable Bakula is staying at the Goldsmith’s Monastery; he is gravely ill and confined to his bed. He wishes to see the World-Honored One, yet he lacks the physical strength to come before you.”
Excellent,
World-Honored One!
Please go to the Goldsmith’s Monastery out of compassion for us!
At that time, the World-Honored One silently gave his consent.
Knowing that the World-Honored One had granted permission, Pūraṇa prostrated at his feet and departed.
Then, in the late afternoon, the World-Honored One arose from meditation and went to the goldsmith’s vihāra, arriving at the dwelling of Bakula.
When the bhikṣu Bakula saw the World-Honored One from afar, he wished to rise from his bed.
The Buddha said to Bakula:
"Stop! Do not rise."
"Do not arise!
The World-Honored One then sat upon a separate couch and said to Bakkula,
"Is your mind able to endure this suffering of illness?"
“Is the ailment of your body increasing or decreasing?
Vakkali addressed the Buddha... as was explained at length previously in the *Sūtra* concerning the *śikṣamāṇā* bhikṣuṇī.
“World-Honored One!
My body is in agony, utterly unbearable; I wish to seek a blade to take my own life, for I find no joy in this painful existence.
The Buddha addressed Bakula:
"I now ask you; answer me as you see fit.
What do you think, Bakkula?"
"Is form permanent,
or is it impermanent? Bakula replied:
“Impermanent,
Blessed One.
He asked again:
"If it is impermanent, is it suffering?
He replied, "It is suffering."
"World-Honored One!
He asked again: "Bakkula!"
“If something is impermanent and suffering, and is subject to change, could there be anything within it that is worth craving or desiring?
Vakkali replied to the Buddha,
“No, World-Honored One.”
The same is said for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
The Buddha told Bakula:
"If one has nothing in that body to crave or desire, then there is a good death, and the next world will also be good."
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to Bakkula in various ways, instructing, exhorting, illuminating, and gladdening him; having done so, he rose from his seat and departed.
That very night, the Venerable Bakkula contemplated liberation and, finding no joy in living much longer, intended to take his own life with a knife.

At that time, there were two devas of exceedingly handsome appearance who, during the latter part of the night, approached the World-Honored One, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The Venerable Bakula, afflicted by illness and suffering, contemplated liberation; desiring to take up a blade and commit suicide, he took no pleasure in living on for long.
On the second day, it was said:
"That Venerable Bakula has attained liberation through well-liberated liberation."
Having spoken these words, they both prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.
Then, when the night had passed and it was morning, the World-Honored One arranged his seat before the great assembly and sat down. He addressed the bhikṣus:
"Last night, two devaputras of upright and handsome form came to where I was; they bowed their heads in salutation and withdrew to stand to one side."
And he spoke these words:

"The Venerable Bakula, residing at the Goldsmith’s Monastery, is afflicted by illness and suffering; contemplating liberation, he wishes to take up a blade to commit suicide, finding no joy in living on for long."
The second deva said,
"Venerable Bakula has already attained liberation through well-understood liberation.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated in salutation and immediately vanished from sight.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed a certain bhikṣu:
“You should go to where the venerable bhikṣu Bakkula is and say to him:
‘Last night, two devas came to my place, prostrated themselves in greeting, withdrew to stand to one side, and said to me:’”
“Venerable Vakkali is gravely ill and suffering; he contemplates liberation and wishes to take his own life with a blade, finding no joy in living on for long.
On the following day, it was said:
“The venerable Vakkali has attained liberation through well-liberated [wisdom].”
Having spoken these words, he immediately vanished and was no longer seen.
This was the speech of a deva, and the Buddha further predicted of you:
"If you do not give rise to sensual desire within this body, this will be a good end, and your future lives will also be good."
Then, having received the instruction of the Blessed One, that bhikṣu went to the room of Bakula at the goldsmith’s monastery.
At that time, Bakula said to his attendants who were nursing him:
“You should take a rope-bed and lift my body together to place it outside the monastery; I wish to take up a knife and commit suicide, for I do not delight in living much longer.”
At that time, many bhikṣus had come out from their lodgings and were walking up and down on the open ground.
The bhikṣu who had been sent went to where those many bhikṣus were and asked them:
"Venerable sirs!"
"Where does the bhikṣu Bakula reside?

The bhikṣus replied, "The bhikṣu Bakula has told his attendants to lift his rope bed and carry him outside the vihāra; he wishes to take up a blade and commit suicide, finding no joy in living on for long."
The monk sent as a messenger went immediately to where Bakula was.
Seeing the messenger approaching from afar, Bakula said to his attendant who was nursing him:
"Lower the cord bed to the ground; that monk is coming quickly, appearing to be a messenger sent by the World-Honored One."
The attendant who was nursing him immediately lowered the rope bed to the ground.
Then, that messenger-monk said to Bakkula:
"The Blessed One has given an instruction, and there is something the devas have said."
Then, Vakkali said to his attendant: "Support me to the ground;
I cannot receive the instruction of the World-Honored One and what is spoken by the devas while remaining on my bed."
Then, the attendants supporting the sick man helped Bakkula down and set him upon the ground.
At that time, Bakkula said:
"You may now proclaim the instructions given by the World-Honored One and what was spoken by the devas."
The messenger said to the bhikṣu:
"Bakkula! The Great Teacher has addressed you:"
"Last night, two devas came and said to me:
'The bhikṣu Bakula is gravely ill and suffering; he is contemplating liberation and intends to take up a blade to commit suicide, for he finds no joy in living on for long.'"
On the second day, he said:
"The bhikṣu Bakula has attained liberation through well-liberated liberation.
Having spoken these words, he immediately vanished and was no longer seen.
The World-Honored One further declared, "You have been well in your passing;
you will also be well in the future life. Bakula said, "Venerable Sir!"
The Great Teacher well knows what is to be known and well sees what is to be seen;
those two devas likewise well know what is to be known and well see what is to be seen.
Yet today, regarding whether form is permanent or impermanent, I am certain and free from doubt.
That which is impermanent is suffering; this is certain and beyond doubt.
If something is impermanent and suffering, it is a phenomenon subject to change; therein, there is nothing to be craved or desired; this is certain and beyond doubt.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise thus.
Yet today my illness and painful afflictions still persist within me; I wish to take my own life with a knife and do not desire to live much longer.
He immediately took up a blade and committed suicide.
Then, the bhikṣu who had been sent returned after making offerings to the corpse of Bakula; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Following the instructions of the World-Honored One, I have informed the Venerable Bakula.
He spoke thus:
'The Great Teacher well knows what is to be known and well sees what is to be seen;'"
“Those two devas also well knew what was to be known and well saw what was to be seen... [The text continues] at length until: “he took up a knife and committed suicide.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Let us go together to the Goldsmith’s Monastery to the place where Bakula’s body lies.”
Seeing the dead body of Bakkali, which bore the appearance of detachment,
he said to the bhikṣus:
"Do you see this dead body of the bhikṣu Bakkali lying on the ground, bearing the appearance of detachment?"
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“We have seen them,
World-Honored One!”
Again, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Surrounding the body of Bakkula on all four sides, was there a dark, gloomy appearance encircling his body?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha:
“I have seen it,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This is an apparition of Māra, searching all around for where the consciousness (*vijñāna*) of the noble son Bakkula has been reborn.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The noble son Bakkula did not abide in his consciousness; he took his own life with a blade."
At that time, the World-Honored One gave this first prediction concerning Bakula.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1266. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Channa was dwelling in the Āmra Grove of Fine Garments in the village of Nāla, suffering from a grave and critical illness.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra heard that the Venerable Channa was gravely ill in the Ambāṭaka Grove of Fine Robes near the village of Nāla.
Having heard this, he said to the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila:
"Does the Venerable know?"
"The bhikṣu Cchanda is gravely ill in the Āmra Grove of Fine Garments at the village of Nāla; we should go together to visit him.
Mahākauṣṭhila consented in silence.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra and the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila went together to the village of Nāla, to the Āmra Grove of Fine Garments, and arrived at the dwelling of the Venerable Channa.
When Venerable Channa saw from afar Venerable Śāriputra and Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila, he leaned on his bed and attempted to rise.
Venerable Śāriputra said to Venerable Channa,
"Do not rise for now!"
Venerable Śāriputra and Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila sat on separate seats and asked Venerable Channa,
"How is it, Venerable Channa?"
"Is your ailment bearable?
Is it increasing or decreasing?
...as explained at length in the preceding *Cakama-sūtra*.
The Venerable Chanda said:
"I am currently afflicted by a physical illness, suffering from extreme pain that is difficult to endure.
This illness that has arisen only increases and does not diminish; I wish only to take up a blade and kill myself, for I find no joy in living in such suffering."
The Venerable Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Chanda!
You should exert yourself; do not bring harm upon yourself!"
If you remain in this world, I shall come and go with you and attend to you;
if you lack anything, I shall provide you with medicinal decoctions according to the Dharma;
and if you have no one to care for you, I shall look after you, ensuring that you are always comfortable and never otherwise.
Chanda replied, “I have means of support;
all the brahmins and householders of the village of Nāla look after me, so that I lack nothing in terms of clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites.
Furthermore, my own disciples who practice the holy life attend to my illness according to my wishes, so it is not disagreeable.”
"However, I am oppressed by the pain of illness, which is difficult to endure; I wish only to take my own life and do not delight in this suffering existence.
Śāriputra said, "I shall now question you; answer me as you please."
"Chanda! As for the eye, eye-consciousness, and the forms cognized by the eye—could these possibly be the self, or be distinct from the self, or exist as the self within them?
Chanda replied:
"No, Venerable Sir.
The Venerable Śāriputra asked again:
"Cchanda!..."

Are the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as the mental consciousness and the phenomena cognized by the mental consciousness, truly the self, or different from the self, or do they exist within one another?
Chanda replied, “No.
The Venerable Śāriputra asked again:

“Cunda! Regarding the eye, visual consciousness, and forms—what do you see, what do you cognize, and what do you know such that you say that the eye, visual consciousness, and forms are not the self, are not distinct from the self, and do not exist within one another?”
Chanda replied:

"Because I have seen the cessation and known the cessation of the eye, eye-consciousness, and forms, I see that the eye, eye-consciousness, and forms are not the self, are not distinct from the self, and do not exist within one another."
He asked again:

"Cunda! Regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, mental consciousness, and mental objects—what have you seen and what have you known such that, with respect to the mind, mental consciousness, and mental objects, you see them as not-self, not distinct from the self, and not existing within one another?"
Cchanda replied: “Venerable Śāriputra!

Because I have seen and known the cessation of the mind, mental consciousness, and mental objects, I see that the mind, mental consciousness, and mental objects are not-self, are not distinct from the self, and do not exist within one another.”
Venerable Śāriputra!
However, today my body is afflicted by painful illness that I cannot endure; I wish to take my own life with a blade, for I find no joy in this suffering existence.
Then, the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila said to the Venerable Channa:
"You should now cultivate right mindfulness toward the Great Teacher according to these words:
'That which has a basis is subject to agitation;'"
That which is agitated has a direction toward which it moves;
that which moves does so without ceasing;
and that which does not cease follows its course in coming and going.
For one who wanders through the realms of rebirth, there is future birth and death;
because there is future birth and death, there is future emergence and disappearance;
and because there is future emergence and disappearance, there are birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.
"In this way, there is the arising of this entire mass of suffering.
As it is said in the verse:
"That which has no basis does not waver;"
One who is immovable attains non-orientation;
one who is without orientation attains cessation;
because there is cessation, one does not follow the coming and going of the realms of existence.
When one does not follow the cycle of coming and going through the realms of existence, there is no future arising or passing away;
for one who has no future arising or passing away, there is no birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, or suffering.
"In this way, this entire great mass of suffering ceases.
Chandaka said, "Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila!"
The service of making offerings to the World-Honored One is now complete!
Following the Sugata is now finished!
It is to my satisfaction, not unsatisfactory.
What was to be done by my disciples has now been accomplished.
If there are other disciples who wish to make offerings to their teacher, they too should likewise make offerings to the Great Teacher in a manner that is pleasing and not displeasing.
"However, today my body is afflicted by painful illness that is difficult to endure; I wish only to take my own life with a blade and do not delight in this miserable existence.
At that time, the Venerable Channa took his own life with a blade within the Āmra Grove of Fine Garments in the village of Nāla.

Then, after the Venerable Śāriputra had made offerings to the Venerable Cundaśaila, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Venerable Sir, the Venerable Cunda committed suicide with a knife in the Āmra Grove of Fine Garments at the village of Nāla.
How is this so,
World-Honored One?"
To what destination will that venerable Cchanda go?
How will he be reborn?
What will his future state be?
The Buddha told the Venerable Śāriputra:
“He did not himself declare, saying:
‘Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila!...’”
My service to the World-Honored One is now complete;
my compliance with the Sugata is now complete—this is pleasing and not displeasing.
Should there be others who wish to make offerings to the Great Teacher, they should act in this same way; it is pleasing and not displeasing.
"Is it so? At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked again:
"World-Honored One!"

Previously, in the brahmin village of Caṇḍa, that venerable Cunda had families who made offerings to him, families with whom he was extremely close, and families who were eloquent in speech toward him.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "It is so, Śāriputra!

A son of good family who possesses right knowledge and right, wholesome liberation has families that provide offerings, families with whom he is intimately acquainted, and families with whom he shares pleasant conversation."
Śāriputra! I do not say that they have a great fault.
However, if there were one who abandons this body and continues into another body, I would say that such persons indeed have a great fault.
If there were one who, having abandoned this body, did not continue into another body, I would not say that such a person has committed a great transgression.
Because they have committed no great transgression, they took their own life with a blade in the Āmra Grove of Fine Garments at Nālandā Village.
Thus, the Blessed One gave this first prediction for the Venerable Channa.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Śāriputra rejoiced, paid homage, and departed.
