48.1267 (1267). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain devaputra of exquisite beauty came to the Buddha’s dwelling during the late hours of the night; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
The various radiances from his body illuminated the Jeta Grove and Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park everywhere.
At that time, the devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Monks! Have the monks crossed the swift current?
The Buddha said:
"So it is, O devaputra!
The devaputra asked again:
"By not having anything to grasp upon and by not dwelling anywhere, does one cross over the swift current?"
The Buddha said, “It is so, O Devaputra!
The Devaputra asked again:
"What is the meaning of 'crossing the swift current without any object of focus and without abiding anywhere'?
The Buddha said,
"O Son of Heaven!..."
If I embrace [the current] in such and such a way and advance straight ahead in such and such a way, I shall not be swept away by the water.
If I do not embrace it in such and such a way,
and do not advance straight ahead in such and such a way, then I shall be swept away by the water.
"In this way, O Devaputra,
it is called 'having no object of dependence' and 'dwelling nowhere while crossing the swift current.
Then, that Devaputra spoke again in verse:
“I have long beheld this brahmin, who has attained parinirvāṇa;
he has transcended all fears and forever surpassed worldly affection.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that devaputra rejoiced and approved with gladness; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.
1268 (1268). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

The Buddha told the devaputra:

The devaputra addressed the Buddha:

At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that devaputra rejoiced and expressed his approval; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight. 1269 (1269). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

"Taking no delight in thoughts of desire, transcending the fetters of form,

1270. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kūṭāgāraśālā in the valley of Rājagṛha.

At that time, there was a celestial maiden named Kokanin, daughter of the Light-Maker (Ābhāsvara), whose beauty was unsurpassed. During the late hours of the night, she approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated herself at his feet, and the radiance from her body illuminated the entire valley.
Then, the celestial maiden Kokanin spoke these verses:
"His mind does no evil, Nor do his body or speech in this world.
The five desires are all empty; With right wisdom and right mindfulness, he is bound."
"One does not associate with manifold sufferings; these are not things that accord with the Dharma.
The Buddha told the goddess: "So it is, so it is."
"Let his mind do no evil, nor his body or speech in this world;
may the five desires be seen as entirely empty. With right wisdom and right mindfulness, he does not associate with various sufferings, which are incompatible with the true meaning."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the goddess Kokanadā rejoiced and expressed her approval. She prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.
Then, when the night had passed and morning dawned, the World-Honored One entered the assembly of monks, spread out his sitting mat, sat before the great multitude, and addressed the bhikṣus:

“Yesterday, after the first watch of the night, a goddess named Kokanadā, whose beauty was exquisite beyond compare, came to where I was. She prostrated at my feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and spoke these verses:”
"Let his mind do no evil, nor his body or speech in this world;
may the five desires be seen as entirely empty. With right wisdom and right mindfulness, he does not associate with various sufferings, for they are not in accord with the Dharma."
I then replied: "So it is, O goddess! So it is, O goddess!"
“Let his mind not engage in evil, nor his body or speech, in this world;
may the five desires be seen as entirely empty. With right wisdom and right mindfulness, he does not associate with the various sufferings that are not in accord with the Dharma.”
When these words were spoken, the celestial maiden Kokanin, having heard what I said, rejoiced and expressed her approval; she prostrated at my feet and immediately vanished from sight.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1271 (1271) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kūṭāgāraśālā in the Valley near Rājagṛha.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now speak the Sūtra of the Fourfold Dharma.
Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall explain to you what this Sūtra of the Fourfold Dharma is."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda spoke these verses:
"Let the mind commit no evil, Nor the body or speech in this world.
The five desires are entirely empty; With right wisdom, maintain right mindfulness."
"One does not associate with various sufferings; this is not in accord with the Dharma. "O Bhikṣus!
This is called the Sūtra on the Four Lines of Dharma."
At that time, there was a certain brahmin not far from the Venerable Ānanda, who was teaching and reciting the scriptures to a group of young brahmins.
At that time, the brahmin thought to himself:

Then that brahmin went to where the Buddha was staying; having exchanged greetings and pleasantries with the World-Honored One, he withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Gautama!
The verse spoken by the śramaṇa Ānanda:
"Let the mind do no evil, Nor the body or speech in this world;
May the five desires be seen as entirely empty; With right wisdom and right mindfulness, [One should dwell with a mind well-restrained]."
"Not associating with various sufferings, nor that which is joined with what is not meaningful—
such statements as these are the speech of non-humans, not the speech of humans."
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"So it is, so it is, brahmin! These are not the words of a human being; they are not spoken by a person."
At that time, the goddess Kokanadā came to where I was, prostrated at my feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and spoke these verses:
"May his mind not do evil, Nor his body or speech in this world.
The five desires are entirely empty; With right wisdom and right mindfulness, He remains ever composed."
"One does not associate with manifold sufferings;
these are not things that accord with the Dharma. I then replied: "So it is, so it is! It is just as the goddess has said:"
“Let his mind do no evil, nor his body or speech in this world;
may the five desires be seen as entirely empty. With right wisdom and right mindfulness, he shall not associate with manifold sufferings that are inconsistent with the Dharma.”
"Therefore, brāhmaṇa, you should know that these verses which have been spoken were not spoken by a human being; they were not spoken by a human being."
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, that brahmin, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and approved with gladness;
he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and departed. 1272 (1272) Thus have I heard:

"The celestial maiden Kokanadā, like a flash of lightning, blazes with radiant flames."
"Homage to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; I shall speak verses for the benefit of others.

1273. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kūṭāgāraśālā in the valley of Rājagṛha.

Kukacāndhulu, I bow my head in reverent salutation.
Never before have I heard the true Dharma and Vinaya of the Muni;
now, for the first time, I behold it directly as he proclaims the True Dharma in my presence.
If, within the Noble Dharma and Discipline, one of evil wisdom gives rise to aversion,
they will surely fall into the evil realms and suffer various miseries for a long night.
If, within the Noble Dharma and Discipline, one is fully endowed with right mindfulness and restraint, [they shall not fall].
"He shall be born in the heavens, enjoying peace and happiness throughout the long night.

1275 (1275). Thus have I heard:

To be addicted to gambling and wine, to be frivolous in one's travels, and to be attached to female beauty.
To waste and lose one's wealth and property is called the gateway of defeat;
when a woman does not maintain her own integrity, she abandons her husband to follow another;
when a man’s mind is dissolute, he abandons his wife to pursue external objects of desire.
Those who manage a household in such a manner all fall into the door of defeat.
When an old woman marries a young husband, her heart is constantly filled with jealousy;
harboring jealousy, she sleeps in unrest—this is the door of defeat.
An old man obtaining a young wife, falling into debt, likewise;
constantly delighting in sleep, consorting with companions for idle play,
being indolent and prone to anger— these are all gateways to defeat.

With meager wealth yet harboring great greed and attachment, one gives rise to the mind of a kṣatriya.

This worldly defeat, I have declared because I know and see it.

Ānanda said to the Buddha:
“So it is, World-Honored One!
What person, who is not foolish, not deluded, and possesses wisdom, would not take delight in the well-spoken Dharma of the Venerable Śāriputra?”
Why is this? That Venerable Śāriputra is one who upholds the precepts and is learned;

he has few desires and is content; he is diligent and secluded; he dwells firmly in right mindfulness; he possesses wisdom and meditative absorption—namely, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, wisdom of renunciation, decisive wisdom, great wisdom, vast wisdom, profound wisdom, and incomparable wisdom. Having accomplished the treasure of wisdom, he is well able to teach and transform others, showing, instructing, illuminating, and gladdening them; he also constantly praises showing, instructing, illuminating, and gladdening, and he tirelessly teaches the Dharma to the fourfold assembly.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“So it is, so it is, just as you have said. Ānanda!”
Who would not rejoice upon hearing the Venerable Śāriputra’s excellent exposition of the Dharma, being neither dull-witted nor deluded, but possessed of wisdom?
For what reason?

The bhikṣu Śāriputra maintains the precepts and is widely learned; he has few desires and is content, being diligent, rightly mindful, and possessed of wisdom and right concentration. He possesses transcendent wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, emergent wisdom, decisive wisdom, great wisdom, vast wisdom, profound wisdom, and incomparable wisdom. Having achieved this treasure of wisdom, he is well able to transform others, instructing, teaching, illuminating, and gladdening them, while also constantly praising such instruction, teaching, illumination, and gladdening. He tirelessly preaches the Dharma for the fourfold assembly.

The Blessed One praised what the Venerable Ānanda had said to him in this very way and in this very manner; likewise, the hearts of the assembly of the devaputra Susīma and his retinue rejoiced, and the radiance of their bodies increased, shining with pure brilliance.
At that time, the Devaputra Susīma, inwardly filled with joy, emitted a pure bodily light that shone forth, and spoke these verses:
“Śāriputra is of great learning, possessing clear wisdom and impartial insight;
He maintains the precepts and is well-disciplined, having attained the nirvāṇa of non-arising.”
"Carrying this final body, I shall subdue the armies of Māra.

At that time, the devaputra Susīma and his retinue of five hundred, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and followed with approval; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and then vanished from sight.
1307 (1307). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a devaputra named Crimson Horse, whose appearance was of exquisite beauty. During the late hours of the night, he came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The radiance of his body shone everywhere throughout the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
At that time, the devaputra Rāśtrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Is there anyone capable of traveling to the far limit of the world and reaching the place that is neither born, nor aged, nor dies?
The Buddha told Aśvajit:
"There is no one capable of passing beyond the far limit of the world and reaching the place that is neither born, nor aged, nor dies."
The devaputra Raktāśva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How marvelous!
World-Honored One!”
You have well explained this meaning.
As the World-Honored One has said:
"There is no passing beyond the limits of the world to reach a place that is without birth, without aging, and without death."
"Why is this? World-Honored One! I recall my past lives:
I was named Crimson Horse, an ascetic of the non-Buddhist path who had attained supernormal powers and was free from all craving and desire."
At that time, I had this thought:

"I possess such swift supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) that, like a strong man shooting a sharp arrow across the shadow of a *tāla* tree, I can ascend one Mount Sumeru and reach another Mount Sumeru, treading upon the Eastern Sea and leaping over to the Western Sea."
At that time, I thought to myself:
"I have now accomplished such swift supernatural power; today I should surely seek the edge of the world.

Having formed this thought, I immediately set out on my journey. With the exception of eating, resting, and attending to the calls of nature, I reduced my sleep and traveled constantly for a hundred years. When my life there came to an end, I was still unable to reach the edge of the world or arrive at the place where there is no birth, no aging, and no death.
The Buddha told Citta the Red-horse:
"With this body of mine, only one fathom in height, I shall now teach the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the path leading to the cessation of the world."
Devaputra Red Horse!
What is the world?
It refers to the five aggregates of clinging.
What are the five?
They are the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness; these are called the world.
What is the origin of form?
It is craving for future existence, accompanied by lust and delight, finding attachment here and there; this is called the origin of the world.
What is the cessation of the world?

If that craving for the future, accompanied by lust and delight, which leads to attachment here and there, is abandoned without remainder, relinquished, detached from, exhausted, free from desire, ceased, stilled, and vanished—this is called the cessation of the world.
What is the path leading to the cessation of the world?

It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This is called the path leading to the cessation of the world.
"Red-horse! One who understands the world abandons the world;
one who understands the origin of the world abandons the origin of the world."
One fully understands the cessation of the world and realizes the cessation of the world;
one fully understands the path leading to the cessation of the world and cultivates that path to cessation.
O Carmavatī!

If a bhikṣu, regarding the suffering of the world, either knows it or abandons it; regarding the origin of the world, either knows it or abandons it; regarding the cessation of the world, either knows it or realizes it; and regarding the path leading to the cessation of the world, either knows it or cultivates it.
"Red Horse!
This is called reaching the limit of the world and crossing over worldly craving.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Without ever traveling far, one reaches the limit of the world;
since the limit of the world cannot be reached, one will never exhaust the limit of suffering.
For this reason, the Muni is able to know the limit of the world."
Having well understood the limits of the world, and having established the holy life (*brahmacarya*),
those who have attained equal awakening regarding the limits of that world—
this is called the conduct of the noble ones (*ārya*), which crosses over to the further shore of the world.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the devaputra Rāstrapāla rejoiced and approved with gladness; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.
1308 (1308). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying on Mount Vaibhīra near the city of Rājagṛha.

There were six sons of gods who had originally left the household life as non-Buddhist ascetics: first, Abhibhū; second, Abhyudgata-abhibhū; third, Viśārada; fourth, Vairambha; fifth, Aṅgada; and sixth, Kāla. They came to the place where the Buddha was.
The Devaputra Abhibhū then spoke in verse:
“The bhikṣu with a concentrated mind, Constantly practicing renunciation,
During the first and last watches of the night, Reflects and maintains himself well.”
"By seeing and hearing what has been taught, one shall not fall into hell.
The devaputra Uttara-abhibhū spoke again in verse:
"One who is weary of and detached from darkness, whose mind is always self-restrained and protected,"
Forever detached from the world and its ways of speech and dispute,
Having received the dharma of the śramaṇa from the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata,
He skillfully protects and sustains the world, Causing no one to commit manifold evils.
The Devaputra Nengqiu (Aśoka) further spoke in verse:
"To sever, to strike, and to kill, And to offer as a gift to Kāśyapa—
One sees no evil therein, Nor does one see any merit."
The Devaputra Virūḍhaka spoke again in verse:
"I speak of that Nirgrantha, the outsider Jñātiputra,
who left the household life to practice the path and cultivated difficult austerities for a long night."
"Regarding the Teacher’s assembly, one who stays far removed from false speech—
I say that such a person is not far from Arhatship.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse in reply:
"A gaunt and emaciated wild fox, constantly roaming with lions,
though small and weak all day long, can never become a lion.
So too the great assembly of the Nirgranthas, falsely praising themselves."
"This evil mind of false speech is very far from the state of an Arhat.
At that time, the celestial Māra Pāpīyān, possessing the son of a deva named Aṅgula, spoke this verse:
"Diligently abandon darkness; constantly guard against and remain far removed from it."
"Deeply attached to subtle forms, they crave and delight in the Brahma world.
I shall teach and transform these beings, causing them to be born in the Brahma heavens.
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:
"If these verses spoken by the devaputra Agha were uttered through the empowerment of the Māra Pāpīyān, and not from the mind of the devaputra Agha himself, he would speak thus:
'Exerting diligence, one abandons darkness; One guards oneself in seclusion.
Deeply attached to exquisite forms, One craves and delights in the Brahma world.'"
"One should teach and transform such as these, causing them to be born in the Brahma Heaven.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Whatever forms there may be, whether here or there,"
Or again, within the void, various lights shine forth individually.
One should know that all these do not escape the bonds of Māra;
they are like bait hanging from a hook, used to catch swimming fish.
At that time, those devaputras each thought to themselves:
"Regarding the verse spoken today by the devaputra Aghaṭa, the śramaṇa Gautama says it was spoken by Māra."
"Why does the śramaṇa Gautama say that these were spoken by Māra?
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing what was in the minds of the sons of the gods, addressed them, saying:
"The verses now spoken by the son of the gods Aghaṭa were not spoken from his own mind; it is because Māra Pāpīyas has exerted his power upon him."
He spoke these words:
"Diligently casting off darkness, guarding seclusion,
deeply attached to sublime forms, and delighting in the realm of Brahmā."
When teaching and transforming these beings, I shall cause them to be born in the Brahma-heaven.
Therefore, I spoke this verse:
"Whatever forms there may be, whether here or there,"
Or again, throughout the void, various lights shine forth.
You should know that all of these do not escape the bonds of Māra;
they are like bait suspended on a hook, used to catch swimming fish.
Then, the sons of the gods again had this thought:
"How marvelous!
The śramaṇa Gautama!"
"O one of great virtue and supernormal power, you are able to see the celestial Māra Pāpīyān, whereas we cannot; let us each further speak verses in praise of the śramaṇa Gautama."
Then he spoke these verses:
“Having severed all craving for existence and the notion of self-identity,
may this well-guarded one eliminate all false speech.”
If you wish to sever the craving for sensual desire, you should make offerings to the Great Teacher.
Severing the craving for existence within the three realms and destroying all false speech,
having already severed attachment to views— you should make offerings to the Great Teacher.
Rājagṛha is foremost; it is named Mount Vipula.
Among all mountains, Himavat is supreme; among the garuḍas, he is renowned.
Throughout the eight directions and above and below, across the entire realm of sentient beings—
"Among all devas and humans, the Perfectly Awakened One is supreme.

Then, having praised the Buddha with these verses, the sons of the gods, hearing what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and expressed their approval; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.
1309 (1309). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a son of the gods named Māgha, whose complexion was most exquisite; during the latter part of the night, he came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The radiance of his body illuminated the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a Māgandiya devaputra who addressed the Buddha in verse, asking:
"By killing what does one sleep in peace?"
"By killing what does one obtain wholesome joy?
By killing what kind of person is one praised by Gautama?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"If one slays anger, one shall sleep in peace;
he who slays anger brings joy to others.
Anger is the root of poison; I praise him who slays it."
"Having slain that anger, one shall be free from sorrow and affliction for a long night.
At that time, the devaputra Māgha, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and approved with gladness; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.
1310 (1310). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a devaputra named Mṛgāra, whose appearance was most exquisite; during the late night, he came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The radiance of his body shone everywhere throughout the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the devaputra Makhādeva addressed the Buddha in verse:
“How many kinds of luminosity Are able to illuminate the world?”
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain: what is the supreme illumination?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
“There are three kinds of light that are able to illuminate the world.”
By day the sun provides illumination; by night the moon provides its light.
Lamps and fires illuminate both day and night, shedding light upon various forms and images—above, below, and in all directions—so that all sentient beings receive this illumination.
"Among the radiances of humans and devas, the radiance of the Buddha is supreme.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the devaputra Mṛgika, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and expressed his approval; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.
1311 (1311). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a Devaputra named Dāmaṇi, whose countenance was exquisitely beautiful; during the late hours of the night, he came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The various radiances from his body shone everywhere throughout the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
At that time, the devaputra Dharmajñāna spoke these verses:
"For the sake of the Brahmin’s task, Study cessation without weariness."
"Having severed all cravings, he seeks no further rebirth.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"The Brahmin has no further tasks; what was to be done has already been accomplished."
Until reaching the shore, one kneels constantly, day and night, with diligence.
Having reached the other shore and dwelling there, why would one kneel again on that shore?
This is the brāhmaṇa, who is single-mindedly devoted to dhyāna that has exhausted the outflows.
"All afflictions and distresses, blazing and fierce, have been forever severed;
this is the arrival at the other shore, where in nirvāṇa there is nothing further to seek.
At that time, the devaputra Dharmajñi, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and followed with joy. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and then vanished from sight.
1312 (1312). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the devaputra Tālakaṇṭha, whose complexion was exquisite and peerless, came to the place where the Buddha was during the late night. He bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, and the radiance from his body illuminated the entire Jeta Grove and Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the devaputra spoke a verse to question the Buddha:
"How many things must be severed? How many things must be relinquished?
How many things should one cultivate further?"
"By transcending how many accumulations is one called a bhikṣu who has crossed the flood?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"Having severed five and relinquished five, one further cultivates the five supreme dharmas."
"Having transcended the fivefold accumulation, he is called a bhikṣu who has crossed the flood.
At that time, the devaputra Tāla-kaṇḍa, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and approved, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and immediately vanished from sight.
1313 (1313). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a devaputra named Kāma, whose countenance was most exquisite. During the late hours of the night, he came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and the radiance from his body illuminated the entire Jeta Grove and Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the devaputra Kāma addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is most difficult,
World-Honored One!”
"Extremely difficult!
Well-gone One!
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"What is studied is extremely difficult: to be fully endowed with the precepts and samādhi, to leave the non-home life behind, and to delight in the tranquility of dwelling in seclusion.
Thus spoke the devaputra Kāma to the Buddha.
“World-Honored One!
It is extremely difficult to attain stillness and silence!
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"Having attained the training that is difficult to attain, Complete in both precepts and samādhi,
One should always be single-mindedly diligent day and night, Cultivating what the mind delights in.
The Devaputra Kāma addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
A mind in right meditative absorption is difficult to obtain!
At that time, the World-Honored One answered with a verse, saying:
“Abiding in the difficult-to-dwell meditative attainments, with the faculties and mind firmly resolved, one can sever the bonds of the Lord of Death;
such noble ones advance according to their will.
The devaputra Kāma addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This perilous path is extremely difficult to traverse!
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
On a perilous path difficult to traverse, one should proceed with ease and joy;
the non-sage falls therein, feet upward and head downward.
When the noble sage rides upon the straight path, the treacherous road becomes naturally level.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the devaputra Kāma, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and approved with gladness; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.
1314 (1314). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a son of the gods named Kāma, whose appearance was of exquisite beauty. During the late hours of the night, he came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The radiance of his body shone everywhere throughout the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
At that time, the devaputra Kāma addressed the Buddha in verse, asking:
“What is the cause of greed and anger? Why does one feel no joy and the hair on the body stands on end?”
"From what does fear arise? From what do perceptions and thoughts originate?
They are like a young child who depends upon a wet nurse.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
“Craving grows within oneself like a nyagrodha tree;
wherever it finds attachment, it spreads like a thicket of brambles.
If one knows its cause, one should give rise to awakening and bring about enlightenment.”
"Having crossed the current of the ocean of birth and death, one shall no longer undergo further existence.
At that time, the devaputra Kāma, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and expressed his approval; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.
1315 (1315). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a Candana Devaputra of exquisite countenance who, during the late night, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The radiance of his body illuminated the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Devaputra Candana addressed the Buddha in verse:
"I have heard that Gautama possesses great wisdom, With unobstructed knowledge and vision."
"In what does one abide and what does one train in, so as not to encounter evil in future lives?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"Restraining body, speech, and mind, one does not commit the three unwholesome actions."
Dwelling within the household, one gathers a great assembly of guests;
through the giving of faith, kindness, wealth, and the Dharma, one establishes all by means of the Dharma.
Abiding in that and training in that Dharma, one shall have no fear of the next world.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Devaputra Candana, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and approved with gladness; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.
1316. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a Candana Devaputra, whose countenance was exquisitely beautiful, who came to the Buddha’s dwelling during the late night, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The radiance of his body shone everywhere throughout the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
At that time, the devaputra addressed the Buddha in verse:
“Who has crossed over all the floods, Diligent day and night without slackening?”
"Not grasping at anything and dwelling nowhere, how could one sink into ruin?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"Fully endowed with all precepts, possessing wisdom and rightly entering meditative absorption,"
Internally contemplating with right mindfulness, one can cross the stream that is so difficult to cross;
unstained by these perceptions of desire, one transcends that craving for form.
With greed and delight entirely exhausted, one does not enter into the unfathomable.
At that time, the devaputra Candana, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and expressed his approval. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.
1317 (1317). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a devaputra named Kāśyapa, whose countenance was most exquisite. During the final watch of the night, he came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The radiance of his body shone everywhere throughout the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the devaputra Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I shall now speak of the bhikṣu and the qualities of a bhikṣu.
The Buddha told the devaputra:
"Speak as you wish."
Then, the devaputra Kāśyapa spoke in verse:
“The bhikṣu who cultivates right mindfulness, Whose mind is well-liberated,
Who constantly strives with diligence day and night, And harbors all manner of meritorious virtues.”
"Having fully understood the world and extinguished all existence, the bhikṣu attains freedom from sorrow, his mind unstained by attachment.
"World-Honored One! [he said.]
"This is what is called a bhikṣu; this is what is called the merit of a bhikṣu.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Excellent!"
"Excellent!
It is just as you have said.
Having heard what the Buddha spoke, the devaputra Kāśyapa rejoiced and praised his words; he prostrated at the Buddha's feet and immediately vanished from sight.
1318 (1318). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a celestial son named Kāśyapa, whose complexion was exquisitely beautiful; during the late night, he came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The radiance of his body shone everywhere throughout the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the celestial son Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I shall now speak of the bhikṣu and that which is spoken by the bhikṣu.
The Buddha addressed the devaputra Kāśyapa:
"Speak as you please!"
Then, that celestial son Kāśyapa spoke this verse:
“The bhikṣu who maintains right mindfulness, Whose mind is well-liberated,
Who constantly strives with diligence day and night, Attains freedom from dust and defilement.”
"Clearly understanding the world, detached from the dust and free from defilement,
the bhikṣu is without sorrow or affliction, his mind unstained by attachment.
World-Honored One!"
"This is what is called a bhikṣu; this is what is called the teaching of a bhikṣu.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said."
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the devaputra Kāśyapa rejoiced and approved with delight. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from sight.
1319 (1319) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of Magadha.
When evening fell, he stayed together with five hundred bhikṣus at the dwelling place of the yakṣa Kūṭa.
At that time, the yakṣa Kūṭa came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Then, the yakṣa Kūṭa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"I now request that the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly, stay here for the night.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

Then, the yakṣa-ghost Kūṭadanta, knowing that the World-Honored One had accepted the invitation through his silence, manifested five hundred multi-storied pavilions, complete with five hundred sets of beds for lying down, seats for sitting, and stools for squatting, each equipped with folded mattresses and pillows, all of which were miraculously transformed into existence.
He manifested five hundred lamps, free from smoke or flame.

Having completed these transformations, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and entreated the World-Honored One to enter his house, requesting that the bhikṣus in turn receive the rooms and various bedding.
Having received [the teachings] in their entirety, he returned to the presence of the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and spoke these verses:
"The virtuous possess right mindfulness; The virtuous always maintain right mindfulness."
With right mindfulness one sleeps in peace, both in this world and in the next.
The virtuous possess right mindfulness; the virtuous are always mindful.
With right mindfulness one sleeps in peace, for their mind is ever stilled.
The virtuous possess right mindfulness; the virtuous always maintain right mindfulness.
With right mindfulness they sleep in peace, having laid down their arms and conquered the enemy host.
The virtuous possess right mindfulness; the virtuous always maintain right mindfulness.
"I do not kill, nor do I incite others to kill; I do not subjugate, nor do I incite others to subjugate.
I maintain a heart of compassion toward all beings, and my mind harbors no resentment or enmity.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the yakṣa-ghost Kūṭa:
"So it is, so it is, just as you have said.
Then, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the yakṣa Kūṭa rejoiced and approved, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, and returned to his own abode.
1320. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, with the Venerable Nāgapāla serving as his personal attendant.

At that time, during the darkness of night, when a light drizzle was falling and flashes of lightning were momentarily visible, the World-Honored One went outside his chamber and walked back and forth upon the open ground.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, thought to himself:

"Today the World-Honored One is staying on Mount Makula, personally attended and served by the Venerable Nāgapāla.
