The deva Satagiri sent a messenger to Khemaka to say: "Headman,
what is the use of these hundreds of thousands of paduma lotuses?"

"Now, within my palace there is an unprecedented treasure—the emergence of a Mahāpuruṣa—namely, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. You should come at once to serve and make offerings to him."
Then, the deva Kheṇḍaka Pāṭika, together with his retinue of five hundred, went to the place where the deva Satagiri was and asked him in verse:
"On this auspicious fifteenth day, When the gods meet in joyful assembly at night,
Please tell me what fast (upoṣadha) should be observed, As received from an Arhat."
Then, Satyaka replied with a verse:
"Today the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is in the excellent kingdom of Magadha,
dwelling in the city of Rājagṛha at the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove."
He expounds the subtle and wondrous Dharma, extinguishing the suffering of sentient beings:
the suffering of suffering and the accumulation of suffering;
he realizes the cessation of suffering and the Noble Eightfold Path that leads out of suffering, proceeding securely toward Nirvana.
"I shall go to provide offerings; I am an Arhat, a World-Honored One.
Khe-ma-pa-ti spoke in verse, asking:
"Does he have a heart that delights in it? Does he compassionately seek to save sentient beings?"
"Regarding those who accept and those who do not, is his mind and thought equal toward them?
Sātāgiri replied in verse:
"With sublime vows and a compassionate heart, he delivers all sentient beings."
"Regarding all sensations, whether accepted or not, the mind and thought are always equal.
Then, Śakra Devendra spoke in verse, asking:
"Are you fully possessed of clear understanding? Have you already practiced and achieved success?"
"Have all outflows been eternally extinguished, so that you will not undergo further existence?
Sāḷha replied with a verse:
"With clear understanding fully perfected and right conduct already accomplished,"
"All outflows are forever exhausted; you shall no longer undergo future existence.
Haimavati spoke this verse in question:
"Has the Sage’s mental conduct been fulfilled, as well as his physical and verbal actions?"
"Are you one who is fully endowed with clear knowledge and conduct, and who praises through the Dharma?
Sāḍhagiri replied in verse:
"The Muni is fully endowed with a pure mind, and his actions of body and speech are perfected."
"Endowed with perfect knowledge and conduct, you praise [the path] through the Dharma.
Haimavati spoke this verse in inquiry:
"Avoiding the harming of living beings, not taking what is not given,"
"Is it for the sake of distancing oneself from dissipation, so as not to depart from meditative reflection?
Satyakaṛḍi replied with these verses:
"Always refrain from harming living beings; do not take what is not given."
"Stay far removed from dissipation, and constantly contemplate meditation day and night.
Māra Pāpīyas spoke again in verse, asking:
"Is it that you do not delight in the five desires, and that your mind is not turbid or distracted?"
"Do you possess the pure Dharma-eye, which extinguishes all ignorance?
Sājīva replied in verse:
"My mind never delights in desire, nor is it ever turbid or disturbed."
"The Buddha’s Dharma-eye is pure; ignorance is exhausted without remainder.
Kṣemaka again spoke in verse, asking:
"He is sincere and does not speak falsely; he has no harsh or abrasive speech."
"Have you attained the teaching on non-separation, and have you not spoken anything that is insincere?
Sāḍhagiri replied in verse:
"I speak with utmost sincerity and do not utter falsehoods; nor do I speak words that are harsh or abrasive."
"Do not distance yourself from those who are close and dear, and always speak words that accord with the Dharma.
Haimavati then spoke a verse in question:
"Do you maintain the pure precepts? Are you established in right mindfulness and tranquility?"
"Are you endowed with equal liberation and the great wisdom of a Tathāgata?
Sājīva replied in verse:
"I am fully endowed with pure precepts; my right mindfulness is ever tranquil."
“Having accomplished equal liberation, one attains the great wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Haimavati spoke again in verse, asking:
“With clear understanding fully complete and right conduct already purified,”
"All outflows are exhausted; I shall no longer undergo future existence.
Satyaka replied with a verse:
"Perfectly endowed with clear understanding, Your right conduct is already purified."
"All outflows are exhausted; there shall be no further existence in future births.
Khemā replied with this verse:
"The Muni is endowed with a virtuous mind, as well as the traces of his bodily and verbal actions."
"Since his knowledge and conduct are both perfected, I praise his Dharma.
Sājīva replied in verse:
"The Muni is endowed with a virtuous mind, as well as the traces of his bodily and verbal actions."
"Having fully perfected knowledge and conduct, he praises that Dharma.
Khema-pati spoke again in verse:
"The antelope-hair tuft between his brows is the supreme mark of a seer."
"Eating little and renouncing bodily greed, the Muni dwells in the forest in meditation;
you should now practice together with him—pay homage to that Gautama.

At that time, surrounded by a retinue of hundreds of thousands of spirits, Sātāgiri and Haimavata approached the Buddha, prostrated, and made offerings. Adjusting their robes and baring their right shoulders, they joined their palms in reverence and spoke these verses:
“The antelope hide of the Eṇeya deer is the supreme mark of the seer;
eating little and free from craving, the Muni delights in forest meditation.
We have now come for this purpose to inquire of Gautama:”
The lion wanders alone; the great dragon is without fear.
Now I have come to inquire: O Muni, may you resolve my doubts—how can one emerge from suffering?
"How is one liberated from suffering?
We only pray that you will explain this liberation: where is suffering extinguished?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"The five worldly objects of desire, and the sixth, the mind—having no craving for those desires, one is liberated from all suffering.
Thus one emerges from suffering; thus one is liberated from suffering."
"Now I answer the question you have asked: suffering is extinguished from this.
Sājīva and Khemaka again spoke in verse to ask the Buddha:
"From what does the spring turn back? Why do the evil realms not turn back?"
"In what way do all the sufferings and pleasures of the world come to be extinguished?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"The sense bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—"
There, name-and-form are forever extinguished without remainder;
there, at the source of rebirth, one turns back; on that path, one does not turn again;
there, suffering and pleasure attain extinction without remainder.
Sājīva and Khemaka again addressed the Buddha in verse, asking:
"How many dharmas arise in the world?
How many dharmas are harmonized in the world?"
"How many dharmas grasp and receive the world?
How many dharmas cause the world to cease?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"Six dharmas give rise to the world; six dharmas bring harmony to the world;
six dharmas grasp and receive the world; six dharmas cause the world to decay and perish.
Sājīri and Khemā then spoke again in verse, asking:
"How does one cross over the various floods, diligently applying skillful means day and night,
without grasping and without a place of dwelling, so as not to sink into the deep abyss?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered with a verse:
"Fully endowed with all precepts, possessing wisdom and right meditative absorption,
and maintaining mindfulness as one contemplates— such a person can cross the deep abyss.
Taking no delight in thoughts of sensual desires, they also transcend the fetters of form."
"Without grasping and without a place of abiding, one does not sink into the deep abyss.
Sātāgiri and Khemaka again spoke a verse, asking the Buddha:
"By what dharma does one cross over the floods?"
By what means does one cross the great ocean?
How does one abandon suffering?
How does one attain purity?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
“With right faith one crosses the river; Through heedfulness one crosses the ocean.
Vigor can sever suffering; Wisdom attains purity.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“You may further inquire about other dharmas of the śramaṇas and brahmins;
True giving and self-mastery—apart from these, there is no other dharma.”
Mārapāpīyas spoke again in verse:
"What more remains to be asked? Regarding the dharmas of the śramaṇas and brahmins, today you who possess great diligence have fully provided excellent guidance."
I shall now repay the kindness of Satagira, who,
as our guide and teacher, has instructed us.
I shall go from village to village and from house to house, following the Buddha.
They attend upon, revere, and make offerings to him, hearing the True Dharma from the Buddha.
These hundreds of thousands of spirits and deities all join their palms in reverence;
they all take refuge in the Buddha, the Great Teacher, the Muni.
Having attained the name of "Unsurpassed," one will surely perceive the true meaning;
having accomplished great wisdom, one is unstained by desire.
The wise should observe that such a person is a savior and protector of the world.
"One who has attained the tracks of the noble path—this one is a Great Sage.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, Sātāgira, Hemavata, and their retinue of five hundred spirits heard what the Buddha had said; they were all greatly delighted, and having expressed their sympathetic joy, they paid homage to the Buddha and departed.
1330. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana were staying on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra had recently shaved his hair and beard.
There were two spirits, Kāṭhaka and Upakāṭhaka;
when the spirit Upakāṭhaka saw that the Venerable Śāriputra had recently shaved his hair and beard, he said to the spirit Kāṭhaka:
"I shall now go and strike that śramaṇa on the head.
The Kāṭha ghost said, "You, Upakāṭha!"
"Do not speak such words!
This śramaṇa is a man of great virtue and great power; do not bring about long-lasting harm and suffering for yourself!
Thus he spoke a second and a third time.
At that time, the spirit Upagata repeatedly disregarded the words of the spirit Ghaṭa and struck the head of the Venerable Śāriputra with his hand.
Having struck him, he immediately cried out to himself: "Burn me, Ghaṭa!"
"Boil me, Kāṭhaka!
Having called out this three times, he sank into the earth and fell into the Avīci Hell.
When the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna heard the sound of the Venerable Sāriputta being struck by the spirit, he immediately went to where the Venerable Sāriputta was and asked him:
"How is it, Venerable One?
Can the painful sensations be endured?"
The Venerable Śāriputra replied:
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
Although there is pain, my mind is able to endure it; it does not reach the level of great suffering."
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said to the Venerable Śāriputra:
"How marvelous,
Venerable Śāriputra!"

Truly, you possess great virtue and great power; if this ghost were to strike Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa with its hand, it could shatter it like chaff and dregs—how much more so would it cause pain when striking a human being?
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra said to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"I am indeed not greatly pained.
Then, the Venerable Śāriputra and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana comforted one another.
At that time, the World-Honored One heard the sound of their voices with his divine ear; having heard it, he immediately spoke in verse:
"Whose mind is like a hard stone, Firmly established and unshakable, Who has already abandoned a mind of attachment, And does not retaliate against those who are angry."
"If one cultivates the mind in this way, how could there be suffering, pain, or sorrow?
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
1331 (1331). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus were traveling through the human settlements of the Kosalans and were staying in a certain forest for the summer retreat.
A deva resided in that forest who, knowing that on the fifteenth day the bhikṣus would observe the *varṣā* (the end of the rains retreat), was overcome with profound sorrow and distress.
Another deva said to that deva:
"Why do you suddenly give rise to sorrow, grief, and distress?
You should rejoice that these bhikṣus, pure in their observance of the precepts, are observing the *poṣadha* today."
The deva in the forest replied:

"I know that today the bhikṣu observes the *pravāraṇā* ceremony; it is not like the shameless non-Buddhists who observe their *pravāraṇā*. However, when this diligent bhikṣu has observed his *pravāraṇā*, taken up his robes and bowl, and departs for another place tomorrow, this forest will become empty."
After the bhikṣu had departed, a devatā in the forest spoke this verse:
"Now my heart finds no joy, seeing only the empty trees of the forest.
The bhikṣus of great learning, who preached the Dharma with pure hearts—"
"Where have all the disciples of Gautama gone now?
At that time, a certain son of heaven spoke in verse:
"Some have gone to Magadha, Some have gone to Kosala."
Having reached the stage of the Vajra,
one practices seclusion everywhere, like wild birds and beasts,
wandering wherever one pleases. (1332) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu living among the people of Kosala in a certain forest grove; he entered into meditative absorption during the day, and his body became utterly exhausted, so that he fell asleep at night.
At that time, a deva dwelling in that forest thought to himself:
"This is not the way of a bhikṣu; having entered meditative absorption during the day in this empty forest, he falls asleep at night. I shall now go and awaken him."
At that time, a deva approached the bhikṣu and spoke this verse:
“Bhikṣu, arise, arise! Why do you cling to sleep?”
What benefit is there in sleep?
Why do you not sleep when ill?
When sharp thorns pierce the body, how can one find sleep?
You have originally renounced the non-home, which was the desire of one who has gone forth.
You should act according to that original desire, seeking progress day and night;
do not fall into sleep, allowing the mind to become unmastered.
Impermanence and instability are desired by the deluded fool;
while others are all bound, you are now liberated.
Having left the home life with right faith, why do you cling to sleep?
Having already subdued craving, his mind has attained liberation.
Possessing supreme and wondrous wisdom, why does he who has left the home life sleep?
Diligently apply yourself with right concentration, and constantly cultivate steadfast power.
Dedicated solely to seeking parinirvāṇa, how can you sleep?
Arising in wisdom to sever ignorance, extinguish all outflows,
and bring this final body to its end— how can you be attached to sleep?
At that time, when the celestial deity had spoken this verse, the bhikṣu, having heard what was said, contemplated it with focused diligence and attained arhatship.
1333 (1333) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu staying in a grove in Kosala who, having entered a meditative attainment during the day, gave rise to unwholesome thoughts based on evil greed.
At that time, a deva dwelling in that forest thought to himself:
"It is not the way of a bhikṣu to dwell in the forest and enter into meditative absorption during the day while giving rise to unwholesome thoughts based on evil greed; I shall now go to awaken him."
Then, that celestial deity spoke in verse:
"With a mind wishing for seclusion, Yet dwelling right here in this empty forest,
The heart follows outward conditions, And turbulent thoughts race away."
Subdue the mind that delights in the world; always delight in the liberation of the mind.
One should abandon the unwholesome mind and maintain a state of abiding in peace and happiness.
Contemplate with right mindfulness and do not cling to "I" or "mine."
Just as when one is stained by dust on the head, this attachment is extremely difficult to dispel;
do not allow yourself to be stained by the attachment to pleasure, for the mind will be turbid and disturbed by desire.
Like King Śibi riding an elephant, exert yourself to cast off all defilement and impurity.
A bhikkhu, through right mindfulness, removes the dust and grime from within himself;
for "dust" refers to sensual desire, not the dust and soil of the world.
The wise one of keen intelligence should realize the nature of those various defilements.
Within the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata, hold your mind and do not be negligent.
What is called "dust" is anger and hatred; it is not the dust of the world.
The wise and intelligent person should awaken to these various defilements.
Within the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata, maintain your mind and do not be negligent.
What is called "dust" is delusion; it is not the dust of the world.
One who is wise and discerning should abandon all such dust.
"Within the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata, hold your mind and do not be negligent.
When that deva had spoken this verse, the bhikṣu, having heard what was said, applied himself with focused contemplation; he severed all afflictions and attained arhatship.
1334 (1334). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu living among the people of Kosala who dwelt in a certain forest grove. Having entered into meditative absorption during the day, he gave rise to improper mental attention.
Then, a devatā dwelling in that forest thought to herself:

"This is not the way of a bhikṣu; though dwelling in the forest and having entered into meditative absorption during the day, he has given rise to improper mental attention. I shall now go and skillfully awaken him."
Then, that deva spoke in verse:
"Why do you not practice right reflection, But instead sleep and eat upon the foundation of vitarka and vicāra?
You should abandon improper mindfulness And single-mindedly cultivate right meditative absorption."
Revering and honoring the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, And personally maintaining pure precepts, one should constantly give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy;
Delighting in this, one advances toward ever-greater excellence.
Because the mind is filled with joy, one swiftly reaches the ultimate end of suffering.
At that time, after the celestial deity had exhorted him with these verses, that bhikṣu applied himself with focused diligence and contemplation, exhausted all afflictions, and attained arhatship.
1335 (1335). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu dwelling in a forest grove among the people of Kosala who had entered into meditative absorption during the day.
Then, at midday, a sense of dissatisfaction arose in that bhikṣu, and he spoke this verse:
"At this time of midday, All the birds are utterly silent."
“In the empty wilderness, a sudden sound arose, / Causing my heart to tremble with fear.
At that time, the deva dwelling in that forest spoke this verse:
“At this hour of midday, / All the birds are utterly silent;”
"In the empty wilderness, a voice suddenly arose: 'It accords with your heart's lack of joy;
you should abandon this lack of joy and single-mindedly delight in practicing right reception.

Then, having awakened that bhikṣu with these verses, the devaputra departed. At that time, the bhikṣu applied himself with focused diligence and contemplation, abandoned all afflictions, and attained arhatship."
1336 (1336). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha was staying in a forest grove among the people of Kosala.
Then, a deva named Sālāvatī, who had been a former spiritual friend of the Venerable Anuruddha, approached the place where the Venerable Anuruddha was staying.
Having approached the venerable Aniruddha, he spoke this verse:
"May you now make a vow: May you be reborn in your original place, In the Heaven of the Thirty-three, Where all the pleasures of the five desires are fully provided."
With a hundred kinds of musical instruments, he constantly enjoys himself;
whenever it is time for sleep, these instruments awaken him.
Multitudes of celestial jade maidens attend upon his left and right day and night.
The Venerable Anuruddha replied with these verses:
“The hosts of celestial jade maidens— These are all a great mass of suffering.
Because of their perverted perceptions, They are bound by the view of a self-existent body.”
For those who seek to be born there, this too is a great suffering;
Śāḷini, you should know that I do not wish to be born there,
for birth and death are forever ended, and I shall not undergo further existence.
When the Venerable Anuruddha had spoken these words, the devaputra Śālinī, having heard what the Venerable Anuruddha said, rejoiced and expressed his approval, and then vanished from sight.
1337 (1337). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu dwelling among the people of Kosala, residing in a forest. He was diligent in reciting the sūtras and diligent in preaching them;
he applied himself with diligence to reflection until he attained the realization of the fruit of arhatship, after which he no longer applied himself diligently to recitation or exposition.
At that time, a deva dwelling in that forest spoke these verses:
“O Bhikṣu, in former times, you diligently recited and practiced day and night;
you constantly engaged with the bhikṣus in discussing the definitive meaning.”
"You now, regarding these verses on the Dharma, remain silent and say nothing;
you do not engage with the bhikṣus in discussing the definitive meaning.
At that time, that bhikṣu replied in verse:
"Originally one should have been free from desire, with a mind always delighting in the Dharma;
now that one is conjoined with the state of being free from desire, the task of reciting and explaining is finished.
Having previously known that the path was complete, what use is there for hearing or seeing the path?"
"All worldly things heard and seen, being devoid of knowledge, are entirely relinquished.
At that time, having heard what the bhikṣu had said, that deva rejoiced and expressed his approval, then vanished and was no longer seen.
1338 (1338). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu living among the people of Kosala, staying in a certain forest.
At that time, that bhikṣu suffered from an eye ailment; following the instruction of his teacher, he was told that he should smell a padma flower.

Then, having received his teacher’s instruction, that bhikṣu went to the side of the Puṇḍarīka Lotus Pond; sitting on the bank of the pond with his back to the wind, he smelled the fragrance carried by the breeze.
At that time, a deva who presided over this pond spoke to the bhikṣu, saying:
"Why do you steal these flowers?
You are now nothing but a thief of fragrance!"
At that time, the bhikṣu replied in verse:
“Neither destroyed nor taken away, I dwell afar yet follow the scent.
For what reason do you now say that I am a thief who steals fragrance?”
At that time, a celestial deity spoke again in verse:
"To seek nothing yet not renounce—such a person is called a thief in the world.
You now take for yourself exclusively what others have not given."
"This one is truly called a thief of fragrance in the world.
At that time, a certain man took those lotus roots and departed, carrying them on his back.
At that time, the bhikṣu spoke these verses to the deva:
"Just as that man now, Who cuts and severs the *pundarīka* lotus,
Uprooting it to carry it away as a heavy burden— He is indeed a deceitful and cunning person."
"Why did you not stop him, yet say, 'I am stealing the incense'?
At that time, the celestial deity answered in verse:
"A person who is crazed, disorderly, and deceitful is like the garment of a wet-nurse."
What need is there to add further words? It is fitting that you may speak with me.
A soiled *kāṣāya* does not show its stain; black garments are not defiled by ink.
Toward those who are treacherous, cunning, and wicked, the world does not converse.
As fly-spots defile pure white silk, so even a slight transgression appears to the wise;
like a speck of ink on a conch shell, though small, it is clearly visible.
One should always seek purity from that [transgression], becoming free from fetters and liberated from afflictions.
"An evil as small as a hair, when seen by others, appears like Mount Tai.
At that time, the bhikṣu spoke another verse, saying:
"Excellent, excellent is this teaching; with its meaning you have comforted me."
"You should always recite this verse for me again and again.
Then, that deva spoke another verse:
"I am not a slave bought by you, nor was I given to you by anyone else."
"Why do you always follow me and repeatedly speak to me?
You yourself should now know what various beneficial matters there are.

When that deva had spoken this verse, the bhikṣu, having heard what was said, rejoiced and expressed his approval. He rose from his seat and departed; then, dwelling alone in a quiet place, he applied himself with focused diligence and contemplation, severed all afflictions, and attained arhatship.
1339 (1339). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Daśabala-Kāśyapa was staying in the Rṣipatana Cave at Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a hunter named Cīcī who, not far from Daśabala Kāśyapa, had spread a net to capture deer.
Then, Daśabala Kāśyapa, out of compassion for that hunter, preached the Dharma to him.
At that time, the hunter did not understand what was being said.
Then, Daśabala Kāśyapa immediately manifested supernatural power, causing fire to blaze from the tips of his fingers, yet the hunter still did not awaken.
At that time, the deity dwelling within the seer’s cave spoke these verses:
“The hunter in the deep mountains, Of little wisdom, blind and sightless— Why do you speak at an improper time?
Lacking merit, devoid of eloquence and insight.”
Even what they have heard they do not understand; even in the light, they have no vision.
Regarding all the excellent and sublime dharmas, their folly prevents them from comprehending them.
Even if they were to burn off ten fingers, they would ultimately never see the Truth.
When that deva had spoken this verse, the Venerable Daśabala-Kāśyapa remained silent. 1340 (1340) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Vajjiputta was dwelling in a certain grove near the city of Pāṭaliputra.
When the four months of the summer retreat had passed, the people of Pāṭaliputra held the Great Assembly for the Koliyans.
At that time, the Venerable Vajraputra, hearing of the great assembly of the world, felt a sense of detachment and spoke these verses:
"Alone in a solitary, empty forest, like a discarded withered tree;
when the four months of summer have passed, the world’s festive adornments [bring no joy]."
"Beholding all the worlds universally, none suffer more than I.
At that time, the deity dwelling in the forest spoke this verse:
"Alone in the empty forest, you are like a discarded withered tree."
"May I be born among the Thirty-three Gods, which my heart always aspires to;
yet, as if from within hell, I long for birth in the human realm.
At that time, having been exhorted by those devas, Vajraputra applied himself with focused diligence, severed all afflictions, and attained arhatship.
1341 (1341). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu living among the people of Kosala, dwelling in a forest grove; he took pleasure solely in observing the precepts, yet was unable to increase or advance in superior merit.
At that time, a deva dwelling in that forest thought to himself:

"This is not the way of a bhikṣu; though he dwells in the forest, he delights only in maintaining his precepts and is unable to cultivate further superior merit. Now I shall employ a skillful means to awaken him."
Then he spoke these verses:
"Merely observing the precepts, cultivating extensive learning, practicing solitary meditative concentration,
or dwelling in seclusion and practicing renunciation— these alone do not suffice."
"The bhikṣu who leans on his breath shall never attain the exhaustion of outflows;
the bliss of equanimous perfect awakening is far removed from the ranks of ordinary worldlings.
At that time, having been thus exhorted by the deva, that bhikṣu applied himself with focused contemplation, severed all afflictions, and attained arhatship.
1342 (1342). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Venerable Nāgadatta was staying in a certain forest among the people of Kosala, where he was constantly associated with both householders and renunciants.
At that time, a deva dwelling in that forest thought to himself:

"This is not the way of a bhikṣu; while residing in the forest, he socializes and associates closely with both householders and those who have left the home life. I shall now go there and skillfully awaken him."
And he spoke in verse:
“The bhikṣu sets out early at dawn, Returning to the forest at the close of day;
As the monastic and the lay dwell in proximity, Their suffering and joy shall surely be shared in common peace.”
"I fear that you will arise in negligence and fall under the power of Māra.
Then, the bhikṣu Nāgadatta, having thus awakened that deva in such a manner, [ceased].
In this way, through such focused and diligent reflection, he severed all afflictions and attained arhatship.
(1343) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there were many bhikṣus dwelling in a forest in the land of Kosala. They engaged in idle chatter and play, remaining distracted throughout the entire day; their minds failed to attain concentration, and they left the gates of their sense faculties unrestrained as they rushed about among the six objects of perception.
At that time, a deva dwelling in that forest saw this bhikṣu who did not maintain his dignified deportment; her heart was not pleased, and she spoke in verse:
"These former disciples of Gautama, Who lived by right livelihood, Begged for food with a mind of impermanence, And accepted beds and seats with a mind of impermanence."
Observing that the world is impermanent, one attains the ultimate end of suffering;
yet now there are those who are difficult to support, dwelling as śramaṇas,
seeking food and drink everywhere and wandering through the homes of others.
"Seeking wealth, he has left the household life;
lacking the true aspiration of a śramaṇa, he wears the saṃghāṭī robe like an old ox dragging its tail.
At that time, the bhikṣu spoke to the devaputra:
"Do you wish to revile me?
Then, that deva spoke again in verse:
"Without mentioning his name or clan, Without disparaging his character,"
Turning toward that assembly as a whole, he spoke of those who were unwholesome and those whose conduct was lax;
he skillfully explained their faults,
while to those who practiced with diligent vigor, he offered refuge, respect, and prostrations.
Once those bhikṣus had been exhorted by the deva, they applied themselves with focused diligence and contemplation, severed all afflictions, and attained arhatship.
1344 (One thousand three hundred forty-four). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu living in a forest grove among the people of Kosala.
At that time, that bhikṣu engaged in amorous play with the wife of a householder, which gave rise to an evil reputation.
At that time, the bhikṣu thought to himself:
"I am now in an unseemly state, having incurred an evil reputation for being with another's wife; I now wish to take my own life here in this forest."
At that time, the deva dwelling in that forest had this thought: "This is improper and unseemly;
this bhikṣu is blameless and without fault, yet he desires to take his own life in the forest. I shall now employ a skillful means to awaken him."
Then, that deva transformed herself into the body of a merchant’s daughter and said to the bhikṣu:
“In the streets and at the crossroads, people of the world have brought ill repute upon both me and you, saying that we are intimate with one another and engaging in improper conduct.”
"Since you already have an ill reputation, you may now return to secular life so that we may enjoy ourselves together.
The bhikṣu replied, "Because of me and you, an evil reputation has arisen in the lanes and crossroads of that village; we have associated with one another and engaged in improper conduct."
"I shall now take my own life!
At that moment, the celestial deity restored himself to his divine form and spoke these verses:
"Though he hears many evil reports, the ascetic endures them."
One should not inflict suffering upon oneself, nor should one give rise to vexation.
Those who are terrified by sounds are like wild beasts in the forest;
such fickle beings do not fulfill the way of renunciation.
O benevolent one, you should endure it; do not dwell upon evil words.
One who holds the mind firm and steadfast—this is the Dharma of the renunciant.
Do not let the words of others cause you to become a thief.
"Nor by the words of another shall you attain arhatship;
as you know for yourself, so too shall the devas know.
At that time, having been awakened by that celestial deity, the bhikṣu applied himself with focused contemplation, severed his afflictions, and attained arhatship.
1345 (One thousand three hundred and forty-five). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Bhadrika was dwelling in a forest grove among the people of Kosala, wearing rag-robes.
Then, the Brahmā King Śikhin, accompanied by seven hundred Brahmās, mounted his celestial palace and came to where the Venerable Bhadrika was, paying him respectful homage and service.
At that time, a deva dwelling in that forest spoke these verses:
"Behold him whose faculties are stilled; he is worthy of receiving excellent offerings.
Having perfected the three types of higher knowledge and attained mastery, he has obtained the Dharma that cannot be shaken."
Having mastered all skillful means, with few concerns and wearing rag-robes,
seven hundred Brahma-sons mounted their palaces to come and pay their respects;
seeing that birth and death have an end, they now bow to the One who has crossed to the further shore.
At that time, having praised the bhikṣu Jeta with these verses, the deva vanished on the spot and was no longer seen. 1346 (1346).
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu living among the people of Kosala, dwelling in a certain forest.
At that time, the bhikṣu’s body was utterly exhausted, and he fell asleep at night.
At that time, a deva dwelling in that forest awakened him and spoke this verse:
"Arise, arise, O bhikṣu! Why do you remain in sleep?"
"What is the purpose of sleep?
Do not sleep while practicing dhyāna.
At that time, the bhikṣu replied with a verse:
"If you are unwilling to take responsibility, what will become of you?
Being indolent and lacking skillful means, when your life-span is exhausted, your four limbs will grow weak, and at night you shall be consumed by sleep.
Then, that celestial deity spoke again in verse:
"Furthermore, you should maintain firm resolve; do not cry out in loud lamentation.
You have already attained the state of cultivation and seclusion; do not let it fall away.
Then, that bhikṣu replied with a verse:
"I shall follow your words and diligently practice skillful means;
I will not allow that sleep to repeatedly shroud my mind.
Then, that deva awakened that bhikṣu in this manner and with these words.
At that time, that bhikṣu, through focused application of skillful means, severed all afflictions and attained arhatship.
Then, that deva spoke again in verse:
"Could you not have risen by yourself, Through focused application and diligent skillful means?"
"The hosts of Māra shall not cause you weariness or induce sleep.
Then, that bhikṣu replied with a verse:
"From this day forth, for seven nights, I shall sit constantly in right mindfulness."
His body was filled with joy and bliss, leaving no part unsatisfied;
in the first watch of the night he contemplated his past lives, in the middle watch his divine eye became purified,
and in the final watch he eliminated ignorance, beholding the suffering and happiness of sentient beings.
Whether of superior, middling, or inferior form, whether of beautiful or ugly appearance—
knowing the causes and conditions of what karma, one receives such retribution.
Whatever a person has done, they shall see the results of those deeds returned to themselves.
"The virtuous see their own virtue; the wicked see their own wickedness.
Then, that deva spoke again in verse:
"I know all those who came before, the fourteen bhikṣus."
All are stream-enterers, having fully attained meditative absorption;
they have come to this grove intending to attain arhatship.
Yet seeing you so indolent, lying prostrate and fast asleep—
"Do not let them dwell as ordinary worldlings; therefore, awaken them through skillful means.
At that time, the bhikṣu spoke again in verse:
"Excellent, you divine being, you have comforted me with this meaningful truth."
"Through sincere devotion, I have attained awakening, Causing me to exhaust all outflows.
Then, that deva spoke again in verse:
"A bhikṣu should be thus: With faith, he has gone forth from the home life."
Leaving home while harboring folly, I have now attained the vision of purity.
I shall now embrace the Dharma and contemplate it for as long as my life lasts;
should you fall ill, I shall provide you with excellent medicine.
When that deva had spoken this verse, he immediately vanished and was no longer seen. 1347 (1347).
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was staying among the people of Kosala, dwelling by the side of a field near a certain village.
Then, in the early morning, the Venerable Śāriputra put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the village for alms.
At that time, there was a Nirgrantha who was drunk and intoxicated from drinking liquor; carrying a jar of liquor, he emerged from the village and, seeing the Venerable Śāriputra, spoke this verse:
"The fragrance of rice-essence permeates my body; Carrying a jar of this rice-essence, The mountains, earth, grasses, and trees— To my eyes, they all appear as a single golden color."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra thought to himself:
"This wicked and heterodox being utters such evil sounds yet recites this verse; how could I not respond to him with a verse of my own?"
Then, the Venerable Śāriputra spoke these verses:
"Perfumed by the savor of the signless, Carrying the vessel of the samādhi of emptiness,
He regards the earth, mountains, grasses, and trees As if they were tears or spittle."
1348. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu living in a forest in the human realm of Kosala who had attained the knowledge of others' minds but still possessed residual defilements.
Not far from the forest was a well; a jackal was drinking from it, its neck caught in a jar.
At that time, the jackal employed various means to seek escape, thinking to himself:
"The dawn is approaching; if the farmers emerge, they will surely terrify me."
"You have terrified me with your water-jar for a long time; may you now allow me to escape.
At that moment, the bhikṣu, knowing what the jackal was thinking in his mind, spoke this verse:
"The sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom has risen; Leaving the forest, he proclaims the Dharma of emptiness."
"My mind has long been terrified by you; you may now release me and let me go.
At that time, having instructed himself, that bhikṣu was freed from all fetters and attained arhatship.
1349 (1349). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of Kosala and stayed in a certain forest.
At that time, a deva who dwelt in that forest saw the Buddha’s footprints; bowing his head, he gazed at them intently and cultivated mindfulness of the Buddha.
At that moment, there was an owl perched on the path, intending to step upon the Buddha’s footprints.
At that time, the deva spoke in verse:
"You are now a *ulūka* bird, With round eyes perched among the trees;
Do not disturb the tracks of the Tathāgata, And ruin my realm of mindfulness of the Buddha."
When that deva had spoken this verse, he remained silent and called the Buddha to mind. 1350 (1350) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying among the people of Kosala, dwelling in a certain forest, residing beneath a pāṭali tree.
At that time, there was a deva dwelling in that forest who spoke this verse:
"Today a sudden wind arose, blowing upon the pāṭali trees;
the pāṭali flowers fell, as an offering to the Tathāgata."
When that deva had spoken this verse, he remained silent. 1351 (1351).
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, there were many bhikṣus dwelling on the side of Mount Cetiya; they were all āraṇyaka bhikṣus who wore rag-robes and constantly practiced alms-gathering.
At that time, a mountain deity dwelling upon that mountain spoke these verses:
“With a body adorned with peacock patterns, Dwelling on Mount Vaidehaka,
He utters wondrous sounds at the proper time, Awakening the bhikṣu seeking alms.”
With a body adorned with peacock-patterned embroidery, dwelling on Mount Vaidehī,
he utters wondrous sounds according to the season, awakening those who wear robes of discarded rags.
With a body adorned with peacock-patterned embroidery, dwelling on Mount Vaidehī...
"At this moment, he utters a wondrous sound, awakening those who sit beneath the tree.
Having spoken this verse, that celestial deity remained silent.
1352. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.

At that time, there were many bhikṣus dwelling on Mount Cetiya; they all practiced the conduct of forest-dwellers (āraṇyaka), wore rag-robes made from refuse heaps, and constantly went on alms-rounds.
At that time, the bank of the Nāsikya River collapsed, killing three bhikṣus who were engaged in construction work.
Then, a deva dwelling on Mount Caitya spoke this verse:
“O alms-seekers of the araṇya, take care not to engage in building or construction.”
He did not see that the Khadā River had suddenly collapsed along its bank,
crushing the three bhikṣus who were engaged in construction— the one who provided the materials, the one who oversaw the work,
and the one who wore rag-robes. Therefore, be careful not to engage in such construction.
Not seeing the Khadā River, its bank suddenly collapsed,
crushing the three bhikṣus who were engaged in construction work.
A bhikṣu dwelling under a tree should carefully refrain from building or constructing.
"He did not see the Khadā River, And its bank suddenly collapsed.
It crushed the three bhikṣus Who were engaged in construction work.
When that deva had spoken this verse, he remained silent.
1353 (1353). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu dwelling on Mount Piṇḍa.
At that time, a great forest fire suddenly broke out, and the entire mountain blazed forth.
Then, a layperson spoke this verse:
"Now upon this Vindhya Mountain, A great fire blazes fiercely."
"He burns that bamboo grove, and he also burns the fruit of the bamboo garden.
At that time, the bhikṣu thought to himself:
"If these laypeople can speak such verses, why should I not now respond with a verse?"
He then spoke this verse:
"All that exists is ablaze; Without wisdom, there is no one who can extinguish it.
It burns all sensations and desires, And it also burns those who do not create suffering."
Then, having spoken this verse, that bhikṣu remained silent. 1354 (1354).
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu staying in a forest grove on the banks of the Ganges.
Then, a woman of noble family who was constantly rebuked by her parents-in-law went to the riverbank of the Ganges and spoke this verse:
"I now desire the waters of the Ganges, To flow gently with the current into the sea."
"May I no longer cause my parents-in-law to be repeatedly vexed and rebuked by them.
At that time, seeing the noble woman and hearing her speak this verse, the bhikṣu thought:
"If even this noble woman can speak a verse, why should I not now respond with a verse?"
He then spoke in verse:
"With pure faith, I now desire to follow those eight holy waters and flow gently into nirvāṇa, where Māra has no power."
When that bhikṣu had spoken this verse, he remained silent.
1355 (One thousand three hundred and fifty-five). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu staying in a forest in the human realm of Kosala. Not far from the forest, there was a melon field.
Then, a thief came at night to steal the melons; seeing the moon about to rise, he spoke this verse:
“O bright moon, do not rise! Wait until I have finished cutting these melons.”
"Once I have taken the melons and departed, it is up to you whether you appear or not.
At that time, the bhikṣu thought to himself:
"If even that thief who stole the melons can speak a verse, how could I not be able to answer with a verse?"
He then spoke in verse:
“Evil Māra, do not emerge; wait until I have severed my afflictions.
Once those afflictions are severed, it is up to you whether you emerge or not.”
When that bhikṣu had spoken this verse, he remained silent. 1356 (1356) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu dwelling in a forest grove among the people of Kosala.
At that moment, a śrāmaṇera spoke this verse:
"What is called 'permanent'?"
Alms-seeking is the constant practice.
What is the impermanent? Eating the food provided by the Sangha is the impermanent practice.
What is called "straight"?
Only the Indra-dhvaja banner.
What is called "crooked"?
"The crooked one sees only the hook.
At that time, the bhikṣu thought to himself:
"This śrāmaṇera is able to speak such a verse; why should I not now respond with a verse?"
He then spoke in verse:
"What is called 'permanence'?
Permanence is only nirvāṇa."
What is impermanence? It refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
What is called "straight"?
It refers to the Noble Eightfold Path.
What is meant by "crookedness"?
Crookedness is exclusively the evil path.
When that bhikṣu had spoken this verse, he remained silent. 1357 (1357) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a disciple of Śāriputra who, having taken medicine, immediately ate some gruel.
Then, the Venerable Śāriputra went to the potter’s house and begged for a clay bowl.
Then, that potter spoke in verse:
"How can one be called 'victorious' when not giving away even a single coin?"
"What is the supreme, true virtue?
It is that one's wealth does not diminish.
At that time, Śāriputra replied with a verse:
If one does not eat meat, yet gives meat to them;
if one practices the holy life (*brahmacarya*), yet gives women to them;
if one does not sit on high beds, yet gives them high and wide beds—
To those who are about to depart, one gives a place of rest;
by giving such gifts as these, one's wealth is not diminished.
Thus one gains renown, yet does not part with even a single coin.
"True virtue and fame shall flow forth, and there will be no decrease in wealth.
At that time, the potter spoke again in verse:
"What you have now said, Śāriputra, is truly excellent."
"I now give you one hundred bowls; no others shall be obtained.
Venerable Śāriputra replied in verse:
"In those Trāyastriṃśa heavens, Yāma, and Tuṣita..."
"The gods of the Nirmāṇarati heaven, And those of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven,
Have gained faith through this earthen bowl, Yet you have not given rise to faith.
Having spoken these verses, the Venerable Śāriputra departed silently from the potter’s house.
1358 (1358). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu dwelling in a forest grove among the people of Kosala.
Nearby, in the vicinity of the forest, there was a poor man who, harboring such a hope and reflection, spoke this verse:
“If I could obtain one pig, And a jar full of fine wine, ... [he would be content].”
“Carrying a single bowl, with people repeatedly offering me alms—
if I can obtain such as this, what should I have to worry about?
At that time, that bhikṣu thought to himself:
"This poor man is still able to speak verses; why should I not speak them now?
He then spoke this verse:
"If one attains the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, And a bhikṣu who skillfully expounds the Dharma,"
"I am not ill and constantly hear [the Dharma]; I do not fear the many māras and enemies.
Having spoken this verse, that bhikṣu remained silent.
1359 (1359). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu living among the people of Kosala, dwelling in a certain forest grove.
Then, that bhikṣu reflected thus:
"If I could obtain fine cotton cloth, seven cubits long and two cubits wide, and having made a robe from it, I would delight in cultivating wholesome dharmas."
At that time, a deva dwelling in that forest had this thought:
"This is not the way of a bhikṣu; while residing in the forest, he dwells on such thoughts and longs for fine robes."
At that time, a deva manifested as a skeleton and danced before the bhikṣu, speaking this verse:
“The bhikṣu thinks of a cotton cloth, Seven cubits long and six feet wide;
If he dwells on such thoughts by day, What do you think he will contemplate at night?”
At that time, the bhikṣu was immediately seized with terror; his body trembled and he spoke in verse:
"Stop, stop! There is no need for cotton cloth; I shall now wear robes of discarded rags.
By day I see a dancing skeleton; what shall I see when night falls?"
At that time, having become terrified in mind, that bhikṣu immediately engaged in correct reflection and practiced with focused diligence; he severed all afflictions and attained arhatship.
1360 (1360). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu living among the people of Kosala, dwelling in a certain forest grove. He had attained arhatship; his taints were exhausted, what was to be done had been done, the heavy burden was laid down, the fetters of existence were severed, and his mind was well-liberated through right knowledge.

At that time, there was a woman who, during the darkness of night when the heavens were drizzling with rain and flashes of lightning momentarily illuminated the scene, passed through a forest on her way to meet another man; she fell into deep mud, her bracelets and bangles broke, and her flower garlands were scattered.
Then, that woman spoke in verse:
“With hair all disheveled and loose, Flower garlands fallen into the deep mud,
And bracelets and bangles all shattered— In what can a man find delight?”
Then, that bhikṣu thought to himself:
"If even this woman can speak verses, how could I not be able to answer her with a verse?
'All afflictions are completely severed and destroyed; one has crossed over the mire of birth and death.'"
"All attachments and entanglements have fallen away; the Honored Ones of the ten directions behold me.
Having spoken this verse, that bhikṣu remained silent.
1361. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu dwelling among the people of Kosala, staying amidst the trees of a grove on the bank of a river.
At that moment, a man accompanied by his wife crossed the river and stood upon the shore; playing the lute and sporting together, he spoke this verse:
"Out of love and heedlessness, We roam leisurely among the green trees."
"The flowing water flows with such clarity, the sound of the lute is most harmonious and beautiful, and the spring air is temperate for wandering; what joy could ever surpass this?
At that time, that bhikṣu had this thought:
“If that man can even speak verses, how could I not be able to respond with verses?
‘One who upholds the pure precepts, Loves and honors the Samyaksaṃbuddha,
And bathes in the three liberations, Is well-cooled to the utmost.’”
"Adorned with human implements, how could happiness ever surpass this?
At that time, having spoken this verse, the bhikṣu remained silent.
1362 (1362). Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu living in a forest grove among the people of Kosala.
At that time, a deva saw the pigeons and birds and spoke this verse:
"Pigeons and birds, you should gather together Sesame, rice, millet, and the like;
Upon the tree at the mountain peak, Build a lofty and prominent nest."
"If it rains on that day, settle there for food and lodging.
At that time, the bhikṣu thought to himself:
"He has also enlightened me!"
Then he spoke in verse:
"When ordinary people accumulate wholesome dharmas And show reverence to the Triple Gem,
At the time their bodies perish and their lives end, Their spirit and mind find peace and happiness."
Then, having spoken this verse, that bhikṣu attained immediate awakening; through focused and diligent contemplation, he eliminated all afflictions and realized arhatship.
The Path of Practice Leading to the Aggregates (duḥkha) [3]. *Body-suffering* [CB] [Song] [Yuan] [Ming]; *Body* [Da]. Body-suffering. Wén Zōngkūn and Sū Jǐnkūn:
"Many evils; Vāḍiśa Monastery; Rauruka; Nālandā; Saṃghārāma; Fallen view;
body; Tāla tree; Ārāma; constant perception; gate; vehicle; fruit; discipline; tree-grove; study; Tīrthika; heavenly path; level; protection; severance."

For the sake of the Śākyas, he established the Real Dhyāna at the Jīvaṃdhara Monastery; do not practice the "Strong and Good" [meditation]. At Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Place, he was born as a Śākya.

On Mount Vulture Peak, he was Anāthapiṇḍada. He was the son of King Māndhātṛ. He contemplated dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and established the liberation of the *Vajra* (or *Vajrapāṇi*). *Note:

The Laṅkā garden of the Asura King Rāvaṇa; the Nyagrodha grove, the dwelling place of the fruit-eaters;
